10571-the-old-man-of-the-sea-ship-s-comp:
W. W. Jacobs published this comic tale as the eleventh part of Ship's Company, opening with George Wright asking old sailor Kemp to be his uncle. Wright wants a rich uncle from New Zealand, who will leave him all his money, to impress a young lady pursued by another man. Kemp, mystified over beer, agrees to play the part.

Wright must lend Kemp a little money, since a rich uncle needs brass to show, though Kemp admits he never yet paid back a loan. A letter calling Kemp home to New Zealand will end the game. Readers get a short, funny Jacobs tale of love, pretense, and a sailor's ready wit.
10791-double-dealing-sailor-s-knots-part:
W. W. Jacobs's "Double Dealing," the eleventh tale in Sailors' Knots from 1909, opens on a seaside common where Fred Carter, a holiday Londoner, meets two hostile strangers. A strongly built man of fifty and his younger son eye Carter closely, declare "That's him," and demand what he has to say for himself. Carter, puzzled, waits for the charge.

The story unwinds a case of mistaken identity and double dealing, with Jacobs's trademark twists and dry humor. Seaside talk and suspicion carry the plot. Readers get a short comic mystery, complete on its own, from the author's popular riverside collection.
11481-dirty-work-deep-waters-part-11:
Near high water on a summer evening, the night-watchman sits aboard a lighter by the wharf, smoking and praising a job done alone from six at night to six in the morning. No foreman calls, no mates run into him with a loaded truck, and he is, as he puts it, his own master.

The story turns on a visitor who rings for a tanner, a sixpence, while the watchman has a purse of twelve pounds waiting in the dock. He pays to be rid of the man, and tells the tale with the same slow relish. Jacobs keeps the humour in the watchman's grumbling voice.
12131-a-golden-venture-the-lady-of-the-b:
Part 11 of Jacobs's Lady of the Barge stories, A Golden Venture, opens on the Tidger family at breakfast: Mrs. Tidger seated with knees wide apart, the youngest child nestled against her print dress, and Mr. Tidger holding a small child in a red flannel frock and a slipper on one moleskin knee.

The larger Tidger children take the solids of their breakfast up and down the room. This domestic scene sets up a venture in gold, speculation, or treasure, as Jacobs's sailors and villagers chase sudden wealth. The comedy lies in the gap between the Tidgers' crowded, ordinary morning and the golden dreams that will shortly unsettle it.
12211-a-spirit-of-avarice-odd-craft-part:
Mr. John Blows, a free-born Englishman, has been paid off at eleven in the morning for sleeping in a shed when he should have laid bricks. That dismissal opens A Spirit of Avarice, a comic tale from W. W. Jacobs Odd Craft.

Blows, proud and lazy in equal measure, drifts home to a wife who thought him drowned, after a tale of falling in water and a rescue. He coughs, holds up his glass, and spins his absence into heroism, while his wife weighs belief against habit. Jacobs comedy rests on a man who turns every failure into a grievance and every return into a triumph. The story is short, sharp, and fond of its rogue.
15533-the-present-picture-of-new-south-w:
D. D. Mann, many years resident in official situations in New South Wales, published this picture of the colony in London in 1811, sold by John Booth. Four large colored views, drawn on the spot, show Sydney, the seat of government. A plan of the colony, taken from actual survey by public authority, heads the volume.

The first chapter runs from discovery and the arrival of a colony from England. It follows governors Phillip, Hunter, and King, with a printing press, a playhouse, numbered houses, a town clock, and a newspaper. Convicts, natives, lost cattle found wild, earthquakes, floods, and executions fill the chronicle. Mann writes as an insider, proud of progress yet plain about disorder, giving an early and detailed portrait of Australia's first colony.
15717-books-and-persons-being-comments-o:
Arnold Bennett gathered this book of comments on a past epoch, 1908 to 1911, in London in 1917, from Chatto and Windus. The contents were chosen from weekly articles that enlivened the New Age in those four years, under the pseudonym Jacob Tonson. A dedicatee read the whole series in four hours one Sunday afternoon, then demanded a volume.

Frank Swinnerton approved the selection and added slightly, Bennett suggested a few more, and the total amounts to one third of the original matter. Bennett's own works list fills pages. Novels run from A Man from the North and Anna of the Five Towns to Clayhanger and The Card. Fantasias like The Grand Babylon Hotel and belles-lettres like How to Live on Twenty-Four Hours a Day follow. The book is Bennett as critic: sharp, gossipy, and sure of his taste.
16394-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Charivaria leads the February 11, 1920 Punch, joking about burglars, Lady Beecham's telephone plan, and Miss Iris Hoey's plan to recite Shakespeare at an intruder. A libel case over a German cartoon of the ex-Crown Prince, food officials in Petrograd, and the Dempsey boxing row all get short, sharp jabs.

Cartoons, poems, and short funny pieces fill the rest of the number, all aimed at postwar London life. Each joke assumes a reader who follows the news, and the humor stays light even when the topics are grand. Set beside its February neighbors, this number is distinct in its own news jokes and its own cartoons.
17331-history-of-egypt-from-330-b-c-to-t:
S. Rappoport, a doctor of philosophy from Basel, wrote this eleventh volume of the Grolier history of Egypt. He was a scholar of Russian, German, and French oriental studies. It runs from 330 before the common era to the present time. It carries over twelve hundred coloured plates and pictures. The volume covers the Roman, Christian, and Arabic periods of Egyptian history.

Augustus remakes the government of Egypt, Christianity rises, the Arian controversy divides the church, monastic life grows, Alexandria declines, and Arab armies bring a new faith and new dynasties. Readers get a long sweep from Roman province to Arab land, told with the confidence of early twentieth-century scholarship. Its plates make the later history of Egypt unusually vivid.
18661-the-empire-annual-for-girls-1911:
A. R. Buckland edited this 1911 Empire Annual for Girls at London, with color plates and sixteen black-and-white pictures. Contributors include Lady Catherine Milnes-Gaskell, Mrs. Creighton, Mrs. Macquoid, Agnes Giberne, and Edith C. Kenyon, beside many more. The volume runs 384 pages in cloth gilt, uniform with a companion annual for boys.

Stories range from a Christmas child and a girl's adventure for her father's sake to a trooper of the North-West Mounted Police. A race for life on the frontier and a Christmas with Australian Blacks follow. Advice pieces cover golf for girls and girl life in Canada. The annual gives a warm picture of Edwardian girls' reading.
19081-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
The March 17, 1898 number of The Great Round World was a weekly paper for boys and girls. It mixed world news, travel notes, and book talk in short pieces. Young readers and their elders both could enjoy it. The paper came out each Thursday from New York.

One item touches on Mexico, where a house linked to Cortes and Maximilian still stands. Another notes new books from Germany, including doll-clothes patterns for girls. Short items keep the tone bright and instructive. Young readers get a window on the world of 1898, as a children's paper chose to show it.
2111-history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-:
Carlyle reaches Frederick's accession in Book Eleven, from June to December 1740, when the old king died on 31 May and Berlin closed its gates and stopped the post for days. On Thursday the regiments swore, and messengers shot forth. The accession closed the gates of Berlin for days, a mark of how seriously Prussia took a new king.

A young king talked of for talent and aspiration took the reins, and Europe watched with hope. Carlyle captures the buzz of a capital at a turning point, before the new king's first wars tested every promise. Frederick, at twenty-eight, had already read widely and dreamed of a philosopher's reign.
23548-the-raid-of-the-guerilla-1911:
Charles Egbert Craddock set this Civil War tale in Tanglefoot Cove, a secluded nook among the Great Smoky Mountains, where judgment day seems to come early. A noted guerrilla, commanding a reckless troop, has declared his intent to raid the cove, and its few, feeble folk can only tremble.

Volunteering and conscription have already thinned the men, from the very young to the verge of the venerable, robbing cradle and grave alike. Only ancient weaklings, frail youths, women, and girls remain. Craddock writes the dread with mountain detail and a keen ear for cove talk, as a community of non combatants faces a warlike menace it did nothing to earn. Readers will find a tense, atmospheric tale of a small place under a great war's shadow.
23549-wolf-s-head-1911:
Charles Egbert Craddock set this outlaw tale in a vast tract of dense mountain forest, craggy ravines, and swirling torrents, a country of panther, bear, catamount, and wolf. Like the beasts, ferocious and fugitive, fearsome and afraid, lives the man with a wolf's head. A price is set on him as the state sets a bounty on brute scalps.

One gloomy October afternoon, sportsmen camped in the wild learn the region's repute and the chance of serving on a sheriff's posse for the grimmest of duties. Seymour, prig and purist, bookish yet a good shot, argues the phrase wolf's head survives while the fact is obsolete. Craddock writes the wild with force and dialect, making a tense tale of law, legend, and men who hunt men in mountain country.
23550-una-of-the-hill-country-1911:
Charles Egbert Craddock set this hill country tale at a silent sawmill on Headlong Creek, in the water gap of Chilhowee Mountain. Sawdust spread thick over a level open space marks the footing for a long heralded bran dance, destined to end strangely, while a barbecue roasts shoats underground to a turn.

Elder men and sun bonneted matrons discuss the feast on a shady slope by a crystal spring, as youths and maidens of nearby coves dance on, insensible to fatigue, hunger, or heat. Una, of the title, moves through this mountain gathering, where dance, custom, and faith tangle. Craddock writes the scene with rich dialect and mountain colour, making a vivid, if period bound, portrait of hill folk at play and at prayer.
23551-who-crosses-storm-mountain-1911:
Charles Egbert Craddock set this winter tale on Storm Mountain, where wind stirs weighted pines and snow lies smooth and white. Footprints mark the woodland gentry abroad: pronged turkey claws, swift mink paces, padded wolf paws, and great hoof marks leading to a little log cabin crouched in winter, loneliness, and poverty.

Icy ranges ring the slope, rock ledges jut, crags beetle overhead, and a dark, starred sky arches above. Smoke steals from a stick and clay chimney, and a clapboard roof shelters a group within. Who crosses the mountain, and why, drives the tale, as law, sorrow, and the world seem far from so slight a thing. Craddock writes the winter with stark beauty, making a tense, atmospheric story of a cabin, a storm, and a crossing that matters.
23552-the-phantom-of-bogue-holauba-1911:
Charles Egbert Craddock set this ghost tale on the Mississippi at midnight. Gordon stands beside the Mississippi at midnight and watches its flow pour sideways into Bogue Holauba, a bayou, as if the great river served as a tributary to the lesser waterway. Moonlight lies large and low, forests tower dark on either hand, and the river runs unshadowed, solitary, and silent.

Then Gordon's eye catches a singular sight on the bank of the bogue, and he gasps, seeking to explain it as illusion or trick of sense. Craddock builds the phantom from river lore, delta geography, and moonlit dread, letting the strange waterway do half the haunting. Readers who like a Southern ghost tale, slow and atmospheric, will enjoy the phantom's first appearance and the mystery it leaves on the bank.
23553-the-christmas-miracle-1911:
Charles Egbert Craddock wrote this Christmas tale of Jubal Kennedy, a man of line and rule who yearns for a sign from heaven to confirm his faltering faith. Impervious to spiritual subtleties, he looks through a mountain gap at autumn splendour: amethyst haze, red and russet woods, a hunter's moon high in the east while a vermilion sun sinks west.

He knows sap sinks, growth fails, and snow will shroud all. Spring will quicken it again to bloom and fruit, and still he stays deaf to the lesson. The Christmas miracle of the title must speak in terms even Jubal can measure. Craddock writes the mountains with rich, slow colour, making a gentle tale of doubt, seasons, and a sign that comes, at last, in a form a practical man can trust.
23554-a-chilhowee-lily-1911:
Charles Egbert Craddock wrote this short mountain tale around a single flower. It is a tall, delicate, stately Chilhowee lily, with the finished symmetry of a cultivated plant yet the fragility of an unheeded weed. Long familiar, the bloom now bears a special meaning, and its sight brings the hero to a sudden pause.

The cluster grows in a niche on a rocky verge above a rugged road on the ridge slope. Its great pure white bloom, trumpet shaped and crowned with a flaring, many cleft crown, stands bright against a deep blue sky. Moss, ochre water stains, ferns, and pendant vines heighten the whiteness by contrast. Craddock writes the flower as a sign of grace in rough country, and readers who love nature writing will enjoy the tale's slow, luminous focus.
23555-the-lost-guidon-1911:
Charles Egbert Craddock set this Civil War tale on a stricken field at nightfall, where clouds shaken asunder by artillery give way to direful rain, the steady sequel of battle shock. Wounded men who might have lived face exposure through the night, awaiting tardy succour that must take its turn.

A surgeon at a hasty field hospital, sheltered under cliffs on a slope, pauses amid his grim scalpel work. His face is set and haggard, less from fresh horror than from its weary return. The lost guidon of the title, a small flag of a troop, becomes a sign of honour, loss, and rallying in the rain. Craddock writes war as weather, wounds, and waiting, making a sombre, powerful tale of a field after the guns fall silent.
23556-his-unquiet-ghost-1911:
Charles Egbert Craddock set this ghost tale on a still mountain night, moon high and wind laid, where dew glints over a vast wilderness. Three men lurk in the shadow of a crag in a narrow pass, hearing for an hour only a rill tinkling far below in a black abyss. That sound is so slight it proves the quiet rather than breaks it.

At last a slow wheel and the clank of a tire on stone reach them from three miles down the winding valley road. The sound grows by slow degrees as horses' heads appear in moonlight between pines and sky. The driver of the vehicle, and the ghost that rides with him, give the tale its dread. Craddock writes the approach with patience and mountain detail, making the unquiet ghost a figure of guilt and night rather than of mere fright.
23557-the-crucial-moment-1911:
Charles Egbert Craddock wrote this tale of Walter Hoxer, a man whose years of labour, skill, and integrity seem nullified in a mere moment, as sudden and potent as lightning. Hoxer himself likens it not to angry skies but to a river trick. A mattress spur of woven willow wands, set at a crafty angle, turns the Mississippi's swirling current.

Waves like herds of wild horses hesitate at the spur, scour a new channel, and leave the old bank bereft, no longer the margin of the stream. That image stays in Hoxer's mind all afternoon, as he weighs how a trifle can divert a life. Craddock writes the crucial moment with river force and moral weight, showing how one small choice, or chance, can remake years of steady work.
25405-honey-bee-1911:
Anatole France's Honey-Bee, translated by Mrs. John Lane and illustrated by Florence Lundborg in 1911, is a fairy-tale romance. The Countess of Blanchelande was widowed when her husband fell in single combat with an Irish giant. A white rose left on her prie-Dieu warns her of a coming death in her house's line of countesses.

She weeps over her three-year-old son George, whose eyelashes shadow cheeks like flowers. Honey-Bee, the heroine, later rides beside a duchess in silver flowers and pearls, her gold circlet bearing three gold flowers. A tailor's grandson wonders whether she is alive or a wax image, so lovely is she.
25821-the-great-events-by-famous-histori:
Rossiter Johnson edits volume eleven of The Great Events by Famous Historians, a readable account of world history in eminent historians' own words, with associate editors Charles F. Horne and John Rudd. Imperial Austrian councillors thrown from a Prague castle window by Bohemian deputies front the book, precipitating the Thirty Years' War.

That defenestration scene, painted by Vacslav Brozik, marks the volume's early modern scope, from religious wars to revolutions and empires. Brief introductions by specialists connect celebrated narratives in chronological order, with indices, bibliographies, chronologies, and courses of reading guiding students through world history.
27796-buchanan-s-journal-of-man-december:
Joseph R. Buchanan's December 1887 Journal of Man, volume one, number eleven, leads with an essay on the world's neglected or forgotten leaders and pioneers. It celebrates the unveiling in Boston of a statue of Leif Ericson, the Norse discoverer of North America.

Other contents cover social conditions, expenses at Harvard, Edison's phonograph, autotelegraphy, Antarctic exploration, and capital punishment, with a continued chapter on the law of location in organology. The issue shows Buchanan's journal linking history, invention, and mind science in one monthly miscellany. Professor E. N. Horsford related the Norse history at the unveiling, drawing on an address quoted at length.
29558-boy-scouts-handbook-the-first-edit:
Printed as the first edition of 1911, the Boy Scouts Handbook served as the official guide of the Boy Scouts of America. Its pages teach camping, knots, first aid, woodcraft, and the Scout oath and law, with pictures of Scouts at camp. Notes in the text flag tips with serious consequences, such as using lead acetate to waterproof a tent, so readers learn care with every skill.

The handbook aims to build character through outdoor life: strength for work or play, readiness, and service. Its tone is earnest, practical, and boyish, in the manner of its age. Scouts, historians, and lovers of scouting lore will find the founding manual that shaped a movement.
3087-original-short-stories-volume-11:
The Umbrella opens volume eleven, where thrift turns comic and then cruel. Madame Oreille, a very economical woman, knows the value of a centime. She keeps a storehouse of strict principles about multiplying money, so her cook struggles for market pennies and her husband gets hardly any pocket money. The volume adds Belhomme's Beast, Discovery, The Accursed Bread, The Dowry, and The Diary of a Madman. Later tales include The Mask, The Penguins Rock, A Family, Suicides, An Artifice, Dreams, and Simon's Papa.

A railway scene has a woman left by her husband crying out in bewilderment while an inspector dismisses her trouble. The volume shows Maupassant's late manner, where thrift, madness, and family cruelty meet.
30870-the-works-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Held here is volume eleven of the Swanston Edition of Robert Louis Stevenson's works, printed in London in 1912. The edition ran to twenty-five volumes, with two thousand and sixty copies printed and two thousand for sale. This volume holds one novel, Catriona, in two parts: The Lord Advocate, and Father and Daughter. A monument to Stevenson in St. Giles's, Edinburgh, fronts the volume.

Part one follows its hero from a beggar on horseback and a Highland writer to Pilrig and the house of Lord Advocate Prestongrange. Then he marches again with Alan, to Gillane Sands, the Bass, and Black Andie's tale of Tod Lapraik. Part two crosses to Holland in a voyage. Readers get a Jacobite adventure of law, loyalty, and young love, told in Stevenson's vivid Scots voice.
31761-wilson-s-tales-of-the-borders-and-:
Volume eleven of Wilson's Tales of the Borders and of Scotland, revised by Alexander Leighton and published in London and Newcastle-upon-Tyne in 1884, gathers historical, traditionary, and imaginative stories with a glossary. Contributors include John Mackay Wilson, Leighton himself, Professor Thomas Gillespie, Alexander Campbell, and Alexander Bethune.

Its contents run from The Dominie's Class and The Contrast of Wives to The Ghost of Howdycraigs, The Ghost of Gairyburn, and The Smuggler. They also include The Schoolfellows and The Red Hall, or Berwick in 1296. Readers get a rich Border miscellany of school, church, ghosts, smuggling, and medieval war, told in Scots-flavored prose.
3349-the-wandering-jew-volume-11:
Eugene Sue's serial reaches Book Eleven in this volume, near its end. The ruins of the abbey of St John the Baptist open it, with the calvary, the council, and happiness. Duty, the improvised hospital, and hydrophobia follow, with the guardian angel, ruin, and memories. The ordeal, ambition, and a letter to a socius, a socius and a half, lead to Faringhea's affection.

An evening at St Colombe's, the nuptial bed, and a duel to the death close the movement. Sue brings his wanderers, lovers, and conspirators toward a final accounting, in abbey ruins and sickrooms alike. Readers who have followed eleven volumes will find the long story gathering itself: happiness claimed, duty paid, and old debts settled at last.
3561-memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volum:
This eleventh volume of Bourrienne's memoirs covers Napoleon in 1812, the year of the invasion of Russia. Bourrienne, the emperor's former private secretary, writes from his knowledge of the government that planned and supplied the campaign, even though he no longer served at Napoleon's side. Supply, distance, and winter do more damage in these pages than any single battle.

The year moves from grand plans and a vast army marching east to retreat, cold, and ruin. Bourrienne records the confidence of the spring and the shock of the autumn, as the empire's strength broke on distance and winter. Readers following the series will find 1812 as the turning point, told with the detail of a man who knew the system from inside.
3578-recollections-of-the-private-life-o:
Constant's eleventh volume covers the last full years of the empire, when invasion reached France itself and the household faced its hardest choices. He describes a court preparing for siege and flight, servants packing and unpacking, and an emperor who refused to believe the end had come. Loyalty, in these pages, is tested by fear and by offers from the other side.

The volume shows the private side of a public collapse: families divided, papers hidden, and farewells said in haste. Constant writes as a man who stayed to the end of this phase of the story. Readers following the series toward its close will find a tense, personal account of an empire falling apart at home.
3591-essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volum:
This eleventh volume of Montaigne's Essays gathers chapters thirteen through seventeen of Book Two. They treat judging the death of another, the ways the mind hinders itself, the growth of desire when difficulty increases, glory, and presumption. Montaigne opens the volume by warning that death is the most remarkable action of a life, yet we judge it badly, since men hardly believe in their own end.

The essays ask why we chase fame, why we value what resists us, and why we think too well of ourselves. Montaigne answers with stories from history and from his own conduct. The volume suits readers interested in pride, ambition, and the mind's tricks, written in Montaigne's plain, self searching style.
37643-the-esperantist-vol-1-no-11:
The Esperantist, Volume One, Number Eleven, is a magazine number dated September 1904. Its subtitle, in Esperanto, names it the Esperanto gazette for the propaganda of the international language. Bolingbroke Mudie edited it at Kensington Gardens Square, London. Single copies cost fourpence; the year cost three shillings, or four francs.

The contents mix movement news with reading matter. A Deal in Ostriches, translated by Westcott, leads the fiction. Reports come from Havre and from Brussels, and a club committee meeting is minuted. A simple permanent calendar and a paper on the vowels in Esperanto serve the student. Esperanto in Belgium, and the Spectator on Esperanto, track the cause in the press. A note hopes that gentlemen willing to form local groups will write to the editor, who will do all in his power to assist them. The number is the young language's English beachhead in print.
3911-the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rou:
Jean Jacques Rousseau's eleventh book opens with the triumph of Eloisa, his novel long in the press at the end of 1760. Madame de Luxembourg spoke of it at court, Madame de Houdetot spoke of it at Paris, and Saint Lambert read the manuscript to the King of Poland, who was delighted. Booksellers in the Rue Saint Jacques and the Palais Royal were beset by buyers asking when it would appear, and its success answered the impatience.

The dauphiness called it a ravishing performance, men of letters differed, and women of high life became intoxicated with book and author alike. Rousseau then turns to solitude, fearing the great machine of monarchy may fall in pieces. Readers who like Rousseau at his peak will find fame, flattery, and foreboding together.
41930-a-select-collection-of-old-english:
A Select Collection of Old English Plays, Volume Eleven, is one part of Dodsley's famous anthology of early drama. Robert Dodsley first published the collection in 1744. The fourth edition, revised and enlarged by Carew Hazlitt with the notes of all the commentators and new notes of his own, is the text here. Benjamin Blom of New York reprinted it.

The volume opens with A Woman is a Weathercock, a comedy by Nathaniel Field. The old title page of 1612 says it was acted before the King at Whitehall, and privately at the White Friars by the Children of Her Majesty's Revels. Collier's preface notes Field's fame from The Fatal Dowry, written with Massinger. A joint letter of Field, Daborne, and Massinger to Henslowe, begging a small loan, shows the players' world from below. The volume is a cornerstone of old-play scholarship.
5285-tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontain:
La Fontaine's eleventh volume opens with the author's preface to his second book of tales. He vindicates there the boldness and privilege he has assumed. He notes that he will write no more tales in this manner. He defends his rhymes, his run-on lines, and his licence, before offering Friar Philips Geese and Richard Minutolo.

The volume thus marks a turning point in the collection, as La Fontaine bids farewell to the manner of his tales. Readers get both the author's apology and two new stories, in which friars and lovers provide the usual comedy of desire and deception.
5527-the-bride-of-the-nile-volume-11:
Paula passes a fearful night in a small, frightfully hot prison cell in the eleventh volume of Georg Ebers's The Bride of the Nile, shut up with Betta. She cannot sleep. Whenever she closes her eyes, yells and clanking chains from the common prison wake her, along with the heavy step of another sufferer pacing overhead, even more restless than herself.

The volume centers on imprisonment, with Paula wondering about her fellow victim above. Ebers writes the cell's heat and noise as a form of torment. Readers get a harrowing stretch of the romance, where a young woman endures a night that will not end.
5540-a-thorny-path-volume-11:
Scarcely has Macrinus closed the door when Caracalla throws himself exhausted on the throne in the eleventh volume of Georg Ebers's A Thorny Path. He orders wine, and his gloomy gaze stays fixed on the ground. His physician notes with anxiety how his master's breast heaves and eyelids quiver, but when a soothing potion is offered, Caesar waves it away and commands the man to stop troubling him.

The volume shows the emperor at his most weary and unapproachable, with court attendants watching helplessly. Ebers portrays power as exhaustion and refusal. Readers get a dark, courtly stretch of the romance, centered on a ruler who will accept no comfort.
55686-the-review-vol-1-no-3-march-1911:
The Review for March 1911 is volume one, number three of a monthly paper put out by the National Prisoners Aid Association in New York. One copy cost ten cents, and a year cost seventy five cents. O F Lewis served as secretary of the group and as editor of the paper.

The lead piece, A Valley of Life, asks what would happen if New York freed hundreds of men from Sing Sing to a farm colony with no armed guard. It notes that the Philippine Islands did just that with good results, at Bilibid prison in Manila under warden George N Wolfe. Other work in the issue serves the cause of men in prison and men just out. Readers see early reform thought in plain, bold form.
55753-the-review-vol-1-no-10-october-191:
The Review for a month in the fall of the early nineteen teens is one sheet of a jail aid guild of New York. It came out each month from a street in that city, at a dime a copy or a set sum a year. Its mast names the guilds chiefs in a row.

Its lead piece takes some jail woes as its theme. It draws on the talks of a late meet of the jail guild of the land. A quote there is from the head of a great reform school of a north west state. The sheet stands as a voice of the jail reform cause of its day: aid for the man just out, and a push for laws more kind and more wise.
56099-the-review-vol-1-no-2-february-191:
The Review was a monthly paper put out by the National Prisoners' Aid Association at 135 East 15th Street in New York City. This number, volume one number two, came out in February 1911 at ten cents a copy or seventy-five cents a year. O F Lewis served as secretary of the association and editor of the paper, with E F Waite as president.

The issue leads with legislation, since these are the months that count for lawmaking. It reports bills brought in across many states to better prison conditions and to help the prisoner. The editor urges prisoners' aid societies to work for these bills together. Getting results, he says, matters more than getting out annual reports, and no one should lose heart when a bill looks hopeless this year.
56213-nazi-conspiracy-and-aggression-vol:
Nazi Conspiracy and Aggression, volume two, is a documentary record of the Nuremberg case. The United States Government Printing Office issued it at Washington in 1946. American and British prosecuting staffs prepared the evidence for the tribunal. The case names the United States, France, Britain, and the Soviet Union as accusers. Hermann Goering heads the list of accused Nazi leaders in the dock.

Rudolf Hess, Joachim von Ribbentrop, and Wilhelm Keitel stand among the accused. Ernst Kaltenbrunner, Alfred Rosenberg, and Hans Frank join that grim roll. The set was sold complete by the Superintendent of Documents in Washington. Documents in the volume were laid before the International Military Tribunal. Students of war crimes law still mine these volumes for proof.
56812-a-history-of-the-peninsular-war-vo:
Charles Oman wrote the great modern history of the Peninsular War, and this fourth volume covers one grim year. December 1810 to December 1811 fills its span. Wellington holds Portugal while Massena starves before the lines, and Spain bleeds on.

The head matter here is a scholar's map key: old spellings matched to new. Algesiras is now Algeciras, Bussaco now Buçaco, and Çaragoça now Zaragoza. Cordova takes its accent as Córdoba in the modern lists. Such care marks Oman's whole set: archives in three tongues, ground walked mile by mile. This volume holds the siege year of Ciudad Rodrigo's front, the fight at Fuentes, and Albuera's red field.
5913-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1:
One chapter fills this Don Quixote installment: chapter twenty-nine, on the droll device adopted to free a love-stricken knight from his self-imposed penance. The chapter opens mid-tale, as a sad adventurer asks listeners to judge whether sighs, lamentations, and tears had sufficient cause, and whether consolation is idle where no remedy exists. All he asks is a place to live unharassed by fear of discovery.

Cervantes offers his plotting at its most theatrical, as friends stage a rescue for a knight who will not be rescued plainly. The single chapter favors speech, disguise, and comic persuasion over swordplay. It suits readers following Quixote in order, since the device here finally moves the penitent knight toward home, with Dorothea's part still to play.
618-codex-junius-11:
Translations from the Anglo-Saxon Junius manuscript fill this volume, covering Genesis A and B, Exodus, Daniel, and Christ and Satan. Written between the seventh and tenth centuries, these poems tell creation, the fall, the flood, and the harrowing of hell in stern, alliterative verse. Genesis B, set inside Genesis A, gives Satan's revolt its fullest early form.

An editor's note warns the poems are not one man's work, though once ascribed to Caedmon. The translations keep the old poems' gravity and music in modern English. The book serves as a key source for early English faith and poetry, where Bible tales wear a warrior's dress.
65948-the-little-review-february-1915-vo:
The Little Review for February 1915 is the eleventh number of a Chicago modernist magazine. Margaret Anderson edited and published it. The magazine covered literature, drama, music, and art. It sold for fifteen cents a copy. This issue closes its first year.

The editor's own piece, Our First Year, leads. She weighs the qualities that make a genius. Energy and imagination dispute first place. Poems by Amy Lowell open the contributions. Aldington writes on French poetry. Powys discourses on the vice of simplicity. Knopf treats muck and music. Soule sends a New York letter. Book discussion and a reader-critic column close the number. No policy had yet been set forth, Anderson cheerfully confesses.
66239-the-collected-works-of-henrik-ibse:
Volume four of the collected works of Henrik Ibsen holds Peer Gynt, his verse drama of 1867. William Archer revised and edited the copyright edition. The series list shows eleven volumes in the set, with a twelfth in the fuller issue.

Neighbouring volumes hold Brand, A Doll's House, Ghosts, The Wild Duck, and Hedda Gabler. An introduction notes that the publication of Brand in March 1866 brought Ibsen fame in Scandinavia. Peer Gynt followed a year later, sending its bragging hero through trolls, deserts, and asylums. Archer's translations carried Ibsen to the English stage and page. The set sold at four shillings a volume in crown octavo. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
69086-the-review-vol-1-no-6-june-1911:
The Review for June 1911, volume one, number six, is a number of the monthly periodical of the National Prisoners' Aid Association. The association published it at 135 East 15th Street, New York, at ten cents a copy or seventy five cents a year. O F Lewis was secretary of the association and editor of the Review. Prison reform is its whole subject.

This number prints papers from the committee on lawbreakers at the National Conference of Charities and Correction, held at Boston in June 1911. The keynotes were bold for their day. Local and county jails should be abolished as prisons for the convicted, and state workhouses set in their place. The mentally defective delinquent needed a new treatment. Misdemeanants, vagrants, drunkards, and offenders under twenty one needed another. Probation work wanted a standard method.
69732-the-review-vol-1-no-7-july-1911:
The Review, volume one, number seven, for July 1911, is one issue of a monthly paper put out by the National Prisoners Aid Association at 135 East 15th Street, New York City. One copy cost ten cents, or seventy five cents a year. O F Lewis served as secretary and editor.

The lead piece treats the farm treatment of misdemeanants, by James F Jackson, chief of charities and correction at Cleveland, Ohio. Jackson says the old type jail for small offenders failed in mind, body, and soul results. It could not build habits of work, and it lacked fresh air and sorting of men. A piece on what Kansas City is doing follows. A piece on systems of probation and parole, and events in brief, close the number. Reform fans get early prison aid thought in print.
69740-the-review-vol-1-no-8-august-1911:
The Review for August 1911 is the eighth number of a monthly journal on prison aid. The National Prisoners' Aid Association published it in New York City. A copy cost ten cents, and a year cost seventy-five cents.

The lead piece treats the New York State Board of Parole, by a member of that board. It reports that of each one hundred men paroled from Sing Sing, Auburn, and Clinton since 1901, eighty-three have made good. Some two thousand men, it says, have met all terms and won discharge in ten years. A second piece links the probation and parole systems and asks how they should work as one. Short items of events in brief close the number. The tone is hopeful and reforming throughout.
70750-the-review-vol-1-no-12-december-19:
The hosted text is the December 1911 number of The Review, a monthly paper of the National Prisoners' Aid Association of New York. It is volume one, number twelve, priced at ten cents a copy or a dollar a year. The association worked from East Fifteenth Street.

The lead piece is an address on labour's attitude toward prisoners' labour. The speaker is Sonsteby, who speaks for the United Garment Workers of America. That union, made up largely of women and girls, feels the contest with convict labour more than most. The editor prints the speech in large part. He offers to print statements of other views on the prison labour question as well. The number thus opens a debate rather than closing one.
72941-the-review-volume-i-no-9-september:
The Review, volume one, number nine, for September nineteen eleven, is a monthly periodical published by the National Prisoners Aid Association in New York City. The price was ten cents a copy or seventy five cents a year. O F Lewis served as secretary and editor. A lead article treats prison labor legislation of nineteen eleven, by E Stagg Whitin.

The state property right in the prisoner labor rests on the Thirteenth Amendment, Whitin argues. Slavery or involuntary servitude may be a punishment for crime after due process of law, it provides. The state may lease that labor or keep it for its own use, he notes. To be of value the labor must be productive, he adds. Distribution of the product raises the problem of competition with free labour. Reform readers get prison policy in plain terms.
7596-the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume:
Part eleven of The Caxtons mixes travel humor with family conscience. At home, graver matters wait: the mother blames herself for what was, the narrator insists, his uncle's misfortune rather than his fault. He lays the blame on their horrible progenitor, William Caxton, whose defunct shoulders must carry it. The Caxtons reckon here with an inheritance that is moral as well as material.

The journey that frames that reckoning is bookish comedy from start to finish. On the Cambridge Telegraph, one outside passenger impresses his fellows with lore in dead languages, yet utters not a syllable in a live one from mounting to alighting. A joke about sleep as a better cover than a cloak, credited to Sancho, had already been said in substance by Tibullus. Learning travels badly, and Lytton enjoys the joke.
7669-what-will-he-do-with-it-volume-11:
Waife returns to his cottage in Book Eleven of Edward Bulwer Lytton's What Will He Do With It? He will not move into Lady Montfort's house, though she spends hours each day in his small parlor and garden plot. Sophy stays close by, and George promises to return soon to plan their future.

Later scenes show Sophy watching by Waife's sickbed as he gains strength, while Guy Darrell visits in private. Fairthorn's flute drifts from the woods where Sophy walks for air. Love, gratitude, and a good name long clouded shape this gentle, late volume.
7712-my-novel-volume-11:
Hate as a force in civilized life opens Book Eleven of Lytton's My Novel. Randal Leslie, clever and well taught, holds that roguery pays best. He shows the marks of a mind at war with the world: over-cunning, restless suspicion, and a belief that all conspire against him.

The volume follows his money schemes. A baron advises buying up a kinsman's bills while the young heir's father still lives in health. Post-obits on sound security cost dear, Randal notes. Through finance and family talk, the book shows ambition dressing itself as cleverness.
7725-the-last-of-the-barons-volume-11:
Warwick and Clarence escort King Henry in blue velvet to St. Paul's in Book Eleven of Edward Bulwer Lytton's The Last of the Barons, subtitled The New Position of the Kingmaker. On October 6 the restored king gives thanks in public, then lodges at the Bishop's Palace while a proclamation wins seeming assent across the realm.

No private revenge stains Henry's second reign, save Worcester's head on the scaffold. Master Adam Warner earns praise and advancement, as greatness tells wisdom their fates are joined. Yet Hilyard finds London traders call his plans for steady reform mere fanatic dreams. Triumph already sours.
7747-the-parisians-volume-11:
A meeting long planned in private goes wrong in Book Eleven of Lytton's The Parisians, when Graham sits beside Isaura in common company. Words rehearsed in the heart cannot be said, looks imagined in a magic glass give way to groups and chatter, and a chill tells him she has changed.

Her touch at greeting and the tone of her few words confirm it. Through the irony of chance, the volume shows how love can cool in silence and absence. It is a study of two people who meet again only to find the old closeness gone.
8481-life-on-the-mississippi-part-11:
As a backward glance closing the book, Part 11 of Life on the Mississippi opens with chapter 51, Reminiscences. Twain travels toward St. Louis aboard the City of Baton Rouge on a hot day. Town social life drew him in. So instead of the hundred steamboatmen he had hoped to interview, he managed only brief talks with a couple dozen of them.

This closing section gathers the book's backward glances, with old pilots, old boats, and a river changed by railroads. Readers get Twain taking leave of his subject, affectionate and a little rueful. It is a fitting end to a book that began with geography and became a memoir of a vanished working world.
9773-alice-or-the-mysteries-book-11:
Book eleven of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Alice, or The Mysteries, returns to Lord Vargrave at the height of his hopes. Evelyn Cameron's hand is pledged, the wedding day fixed, and in less than a week she will give a ruined peer a splendid dowry. Deeds to transfer the Maltravers baronial estates near completion, and Lisle Court awaits the pair. Politics, too, seems to favor him.

The final book tests whether Vargrave's triumph can hold, as old deeds and loves press their claims. Lytton's prose favors high, moral drama. A reader gets the closing book of a Victorian mystery romance, where ambition meets its reckoning.
a-general-history-and-collection-of-voya: Volume fifteen of Robert Kerr's voyages continues James Cook's voyage toward the South Pole and round the world. Its chapters follow Cook from leaving New Zealand toward his return home. The Resolution and Adventure carry the story through southern seas. Kerr's volume completes the Cook account begun in the fourteenth volume.
a-golden-venture-the-lady-of-the-barge-a: William Wymark Jacobs tells a golden venture in this part of The Lady of the Barge and others. Its scenes follow the Tidger family at breakfast in a stone flagged court, with weak tea and small pieces of bloater. Mr. Tidger urges his wife Ann to peg away at her work. Jacobs writes comic domestic life with his usual Thames side humor.
a-spirit-of-avarice-odd-craft-part-11: William Wymark Jacobs tells a comic story of avarice in which Mr John Blows, a free-born Englishman, is summarily paid off at eleven in the morning. The foreman, who caught him dozing in a shed instead of laying bricks, tells him to take his ugly face home and bury it in the backyard. Blows answers with fluent reflections on the foreman's ancestors, and the tale follows greed meeting its match in plain speaking.
a-thorny-path-volume-11:
Georg Ebers brings A Thorny Path near its climax in Volume 11, with Emperor Caracalla alone on his throne. Ebers shows the ruler worn out, calling for wine and waving away the soothing draught his anxious physician offers. Macrinus, his prefect, has just left the room, and reports arrive that the city's youths are gathering on the race course in a loud, unruly mood.

Chapter XXX listens to the songs the young men keep demanding, each one aimed at Caesar himself. Caracalla lets them sing, comparing their sport to a last meal granted before a final journey. His talk turns to a prison, and his smile tells the high priest of Serapis that the threats are meant in earnest. A ruler nursing insult and pain is the most dangerous figure in the book here.
alchemy-ancient-and-modern-being-a-brief:
Alchemy: Ancient and Modern, published in 1911 by H Stanley Redgrove, is a brief account of the alchemistic doctrines. Redgrove sets out to explain what the alchemists taught and how their doctrines connect in two directions. On one side they relate to mysticism, and on the other to recent discoveries in physical science, which in his day were reviving old questions about the elements.

Alongside the doctrines, the book gives particulars of the lives and teachings of the most noted alchemists. That mix of history and comparison made it a standard short introduction of its time. Readers get both the old art's ideas and its famous practitioners, surveyed by a chemist writing when radioactivity had made transmutation thinkable again.
alice-or-the-mysteries-book-11: Edward Bulwer Lytton finds Vargrave's hopes realised in the eleventh book of Alice, or the Mysteries, with Evelyn Cameron's hand pledged and the wedding day fixed. A splendid dowry promises to smooth the ruined peer's climb, while deeds transferring the Maltravers estates near completion. Triumph seems within reach, yet the very completeness of his success sets up the novel's reckoning.
andreyev-king-hunger-1911:
King Hunger, Leonid Andreyev's allegorical play, appeared in English in Poet Lore in the winter of 1911. Eugene M. Kayden made the translation. King Hunger, a gaunt personified power, rouses the starving poor of a great city to rise against the rich who feast above them.

Bells, judges, and workers people the stark, symbolic stages of the play. The rising swells toward a climax that Andreyev shapes as vision rather than report. He called such works dramas of ideas, meant to stage the forces that move crowds. Of all his plays, this one presses revolution most directly. The Poet Lore printing gave American readers an early taste of his radical theater.
arxiv-2412-00311:
Dafne Zorzetto and four co-authors build a statistical method for asking how air pollution shapes social mobility, in this 2024 paper. Education is the tricky middle step: pollution may cut schooling, and schooling drives later mobility, so a simple comparison mixes the two paths. Their approach sorts people into hidden groups defined by how their schooling would respond to exposure.

The new Bayesian method models outcomes with flexible mixtures, which sharpens guesses for the unseen alternative world that causal work depends on. Simulations show it beats existing options. Applied to data from more than three thousand United States counties, the method finds mobility falls about five percent where pollution also cuts schooling. A smaller drop appears even where schooling is untouched, hinting at other paths from dirty air to stalled lives.
arxiv-2412-00411:
Mohammad Hasan Rahmani, Rafael Berkvens, and Maarten Weyn test emotion reading from chest vibrations in this 2024 paper. A small accelerometer on the chest picks up vibrations from the heart and breathing. That signal is called seismocardiography. Such sensors are cheap, common, and easy to wear all day.

Past work mixed these signals with many others for emotion recognition. Their solo value was untested. The team first rebuilt a known pipeline from the DEAP emotion dataset and matched its results. They then applied it to the EmoWear dataset using only the chest signals. Performance showed the signals carry real emotion information on their own. Fewer sensors would make emotion aware devices simpler to build and wear.
arxiv-2412-00711:
Carson Kohlbrenner and co-authors built in 2024 a design pipeline that grows touch-sensitive skins to fit a specific robot and its job. Off-the-shelf skins are modular but ignore the machine's shape and setting. Their toolbox generates the skin's mesh from the robot's own geometry, then uses task simulation to place sensors where they earn their keep.

Multi-material 3D printing then fabricates the skin for almost any form. The team made six capacitive skins and fitted them to a research robot arm for a human-robot interaction test. The skins worked in place. The authors frame the shift plainly: from one-size-fits-all sensors to context-driven designs. They argue whole-body touch should be tailored like clothing, not bolted on like armor.
arxiv-2412-00811:
Bao and co-authors cut the labeling cost for finding moments in video in a 2024 paper. The task takes a sentence and locates the matching span in a raw video. Hand labels are slow to make, so the team first trains on unlabeled wild videos with machine-made draft labels. Their data set holds over fifty thousand videos and two hundred thousand draft spans.

Draft labels carry flaws: mismatched pairs and loose time edges. Their fix runs in two phases. A meaning-guided pass cleans bad pairs and rough edges. A memory pass then nudges edges toward the model's settled calls. With no hand labels, the method reached most of the fully trained score on two test sets.
arxiv-2412-00911:
Suresh Kumar Amalapuram and co-authors present SOUL, a continual learning guard for network intrusion in 2024. Attack traffic shifts over time, and labeled data are scarce in security work. A classifier trained on two days of traffic saw attack scores halve within three fresh days in their tests.

SOUL learns from partly labeled streams in an open world, where new attack types appear. A gradient projection memory built from buffer samples guards old knowledge. Confidence scores plus the buffer let the system label new tasks that resemble known ones. Replay of buffer samples fights forgetting. With at most a fifth of labels, scores neared fully supervised rivals.
arxiv-2412-01011:
Moritz Baumgart, Lukas Wegmeth, Tobias Vente, and Joeran Beel present a 2024 paper on saving energy when testing recommender systems. The standard test method, k-fold cross-validation, reruns training many times and uses much power. Their variant, e-fold cross-validation, cuts the number of folds to save energy while keeping results trustworthy.

They tested the method on five recommender algorithms across six data sets, against the usual ten-fold method. On average, the new method used only 41.5 percent of the energy. Its results differed from the standard method by only 1.81 percent. The authors conclude the trade is worth it. Their work offers labs a greener way to check recommender quality without giving up sound results.
arxiv-2412-01211:
Xiaoyang Shen and co-authors study neutral excitations in a twisted material in a 2024 paper. Fractional Chern insulators are flat-band states with exotic order, recently found in twisted molybdenum telluride. Their inner excitations, called magnetorotons, carry no charge. The team models them with a classic ansatz plus a geometric response method.

Magnetorotons at finite momentum turn out to be universal in these states, with clear size scales, they find. At long wavelengths they are gapped and chiral, with angular momentum two. The trait stems from how the state resists compression in momentum space. Tuning the twist may expose phase changes, and lab detection routes are proposed.
arxiv-2412-01511:
Xiaoqi Liu, Pablo Pascual Cobo, and Ramji Venkataramanan studied crowded wireless channels in a 2024 paper. In their setup, very many users share a Gaussian channel, but only some are active at any moment, and the receiver knows neither how many nor which ones. The number of users scales with the code length, a regime that matches modern massive-access networks. The team derived two limits on the errors that any scheme must accept.

One bound covers finite block lengths with random codebooks and best-possible decoding. The other is asymptotic, using coupled codebooks and an approximate message passing decoder. Against these yardsticks they test a practical CDMA-style scheme with the same decoder, backed by the first state evolution proof for coupled message passing with matrix iterates. Tests showed promising error rates.
arxiv-2412-01711:
Large language models can repeat the biases in their training data. Such bias may harm groups already pushed to the margins. Schrasing Tong and co-authors offer a cheap fix in a 2024 paper: two small expert models, one biased and one anti-biased, produce a correction signal. That signal is added to the big model's output as it writes, and only the small models need training, not the large one.

Because the shift is a visible change in word odds, users can inspect exactly how debiasing acts. Tests on gender, race, and religion bias showed clear reductions on several measures while writing quality held steady. The method can be retargeted by swapping training data.
arxiv-2412-01811:
Joaquín Moraga and Wern Yeong state and test a conjecture about hyperbolic varieties built from adjoint bundles, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. On a smooth projective variety with an ample divisor, a very general member of one stated linear system should be hyperbolic. The claim already holds for surfaces, products of projective spaces, and Grassmannians.

Toric varieties are the test bed here. For smooth projective toric varieties the conjecture is confirmed outright. For Gorenstein toric varieties the system is shown pseudo hyperbolic. A sharper bound settles the Gorenstein threefold case as fully hyperbolic.
arxiv-2412-02311:
Jed Homer, Oliver Friedrich, and Daniel Gruen test a hidden bias in simulation-based inference for cosmology. Their twenty twenty-four paper asks if learning-based methods dodge a known trap. In classic work, a noisy covariance matrix warps the width and place of result ranges.

Simulation-based methods skip covariance matrices, so many assumed they were safe. The authors probe neural posterior and likelihood tools for like effects. They find the trap has a twin in this world, but the method can flag it from inside. Knowing the bias exists, and that it can be self-checked, helps sky survey teams trust their numbers on the universe makeup.
arxiv-2412-02911:
Xinchen Yu and three co-authors build measures of how nasty online conversations get after someone answers hate speech, in a 2024 paper. Replies to hate can cool a thread or pour fuel on it. Knowing which replies steer talk back to civility would help moderators and users alike.

The authors score follow-up conversation incivility along several dimensions of antisocial and prosocial behavior, not a single toxicity number. Their best metric matches human judgment better than earlier ones. Analyses then cover how hostile and kind posts differ in language, how each kind draws engagement, and which reply styles tend to draw civil continuations. The work turns a vague hope, that good replies help, into something measurable and forecastable.
arxiv-2412-03111:
Ruiqi He and Falk Lieder ask how people invent new planning strategies rather than merely choosing among old ones. Efficient planning with a limited mind suggests we carry a toolbox of strategies and know when each fits. Where the tools themselves come from was the open question. The authors propose that we discover them by a kind of inner reinforcement learning, where the mind rewards its own better plans.

They built a new experiment to catch strategy discovery in the act. Their learning models, fitted with this metacognitive mechanism, did discover fresh strategies in the task. The models also explained the human data better than rival learning accounts. One gap remained: the models learned more slowly than the people did. The authors leave that speed difference as a target for the next round of theory.
arxiv-2412-03211:
Aditi Bhatnagar and co-authors trace the magnetic wiring behind small solar flares in a 2024 paper. The events, called quiet-Sun Ellerman bombs, are tiny reconnection bursts in the Sun's lower air. Some coincide with brightenings higher up, in the transition region, and the link between them was unclear.

Using sharp telescope images of the Sun, the team located the bursts by clustering methods. They rebuilt the magnetic field above the surface from polarization data. Four wiring patterns tied bursts to upper brightenings, including fan-spine shapes with a special null point where field lines meet. Brightenings sat near the null, while bursts clustered at the feet of the loops. Some near pairs, though, shared no wiring at all.
arxiv-2412-03411:
Rafael Luque and co-authors observe a hot rocky planet with a space telescope in 2024. The planet orbits a small red star and is larger than Earth. They watched it for a full orbit to read its air and heat pattern.

The air readings rule out a light hydrogen cover, but cannot tell thin secondary air from none at all. Heat readings look like a plain dark rock with no heat spread to the night side. The team reads the planet as a dark, bare rock with low reflectivity. The result adds to a growing count of airless rocky worlds around red stars.
arxiv-2412-03511:
Spin glasses are magnets with frozen, disordered spins, and their energy landscape breaks into many far-apart clusters at low temperature, a phenomenon called shattering. Ahmed El Alaoui studies shattering in the Ising pure p-spin model. He shows it occurs at all inverse temperatures in a stated range once p is large enough as a function of temperature. The lower edge of that range matches the asymptotic mark of the dynamical transition predicted by physicists.

The proof runs through a soft version of the overlap gap property, which places a distance gap between points of typical energy and a typical sample from the Gibbs measure. He then shows this property confines stable algorithms to an exponentially rare slice of the high-energy set, provided their success chance is not vanishingly small. The work tightens what theory can say about where algorithms can and cannot reach in spin glass landscapes.
arxiv-2412-03711:
Krzysztof Gołębiowski proves that the distance rule on a space can be reset to steer how points spread over time, in a paper from 2024. The setting is a space with a distance rule and a map that sends each point to a new point, applied again and again. The question is how far apart points drift after many steps.

He shows a fitting distance rule exists for any such map, and even for whole families of maps under one extra condition. Under the new rule, the drift after each step count follows a preset list of stretch factors. Those factors can grow without bound. In short, any system of this kind can be re-gauged so that spread over time is controlled by design rather than left to chance.
arxiv-2412-04011:
Tuğçe Gökdemir and Jakub Rydzewski (2024) explain a machine learning trick for finding the few variables that matter in a molecular movie. Molecular dynamics simulations track every atom, thousands of dimensions, yet the interesting events, a protein folding, a bond rearranging, are rare, because energy barriers dwarf thermal energy. To understand such events, scientists compress the motion into one simple coordinate that captures the change. Choosing it usually relies on intuition.

The note describes spectral map, an unsupervised method that builds the variable automatically. It arranges the compression to widen the gap between slow motions, the rare transitions, and fast jitter. The slowest coordinate then becomes the collective variable worth watching. The authors summarize how the method works and why the timescale criterion picks out physically meaningful coordinates. For simulators drowning in atoms, a sound shortcut to the one dial that matters is the prize.
arxiv-2412-04411:
Lyubashevsky and co-authors build a theoretical model of spin in fission fragments in work from 2024. When a heavy nucleus splits, the fragments carry spin, and their angular patterns reveal how that spin arises.

The model covers spin formation mechanisms, including the role of transverse vibrations of the splitting nucleus. It reveals a link between the anisotropy of the angular distribution and a correlation coefficient between fragment spins. Predictions are compared with experimental data and with models from other groups. The work aims to tighten the theory of fragment spin in fission.
arxiv-2412-04711:
Diluka Galappaththige and co-authors wrote this 2024 survey of a wireless design that merges two ideas for next-generation networks. The first idea drops fixed cell borders and lets many access points serve users as one team, which cuts clashes and boosts coverage. The second lets a radio send and receive at once on the same channel, which can double the use of the airwaves.

No survey of the merged design existed, so the authors start from the basics of both parts, including how a radio silences its own echo. They then work through the joint design: how channels are measured, how well the system performs, and how power and links are shared. Case studies and a wide sweep of past work round out the picture for massive antenna networks of this merged kind.
arxiv-2412-04811: Evgeny Korotyaev counts, in a short 2024 math note, the special energy values of a system whose rules repeat in time. The system is a discrete Hamiltonian living on a graph that also repeats in space. Such time-periodic systems do not keep a fixed energy; instead they carry quasi-energy values. The paper estimates how many of those values can fall inside a finite interval.
arxiv-2412-05311:
Chen-Chia Chang and co-authors automate a dull but skilled job in chip design: writing the code that checks a layout against the maker's rules. Each new chip process brings new rules, and experts must pore over long specs, test layouts, and fix code by hand, again and again.

Their system, DRC-Coder, uses a team of language model agents with vision. Two agents split the work of reading rules and writing code, and a self check step helps debug. On a leading edge process, the system scored a perfect mark next to a trade tool, far above plain prompting. Each rule took about four minutes of work.
arxiv-2412-05411:
Roame Hildebrand and four co-authors shift laser light cleanly with a radio trick in a 2024 paper. Light shoved through a modulator gains a comb of side tones, handy for many tasks. Some jobs want one clean shift with no side tones at all, such as locking a laser to a cavity or nudging single photons. Past ways trade shift range against side tone junk.

Their serrodyne setup drives a fiber modulator with tones from a radio chip. It shifted a near infrared laser by forty to eight hundred megahertz, holding stray tones more than fifteen decibels down and losing under one and a half decibels of light. As a proof of use, a cavity locked laser's offset slid smoothly across a wide span.
arxiv-2412-05811:
Regular black holes dodge the crushing singularity at their centers, and recent work builds them from pure gravity alone, using an endless tower of small corrections to Einstein's theory. Sheng-Wei Wang, Shan-Ping Wu, and Shao-Wen Wei ask whether these objects, valid in five dimensions and up, share one thermodynamic family. They treat each black hole as a defect in a topological map of its free energy.

One fact anchors the study: the temperature always hits zero at the smallest horizon size. From there, all the purely gravitational examples show the same thermal behavior and land in a single topological class. The sameness hints at a deep unity among the constructions.
arxiv-2412-05911:
Alexandre Andorra and Maximilian Göbel build a statistical model that separates a soccer player's true skill from the strength of the team around him. Raw counts of goals or assists flatter players on strong teams and shortchange those on weak ones, which makes costly recruitment calls risky.

Their Soccer Factor Model adjusts for that team effect, giving each player a cleaner skill estimate. They built a fresh dataset from public sources covering well over a hundred players and tens of thousands of matches across more than twenty seasons. The model beat simpler benchmarks at forecasting, and the authors add two fair-comparison measures based on how far a player sits above a typical replacement. They even apply it to the debate over the best player of the century so far.
arxiv-2412-06111:
Alberto Bucci and Gianfranco Verzella give a fast way to shrink huge multi-way data sets in a 2024 paper. Such data, called tensors, can be held in a tree form that groups their parts by links. Shrinking them well in one pass, while data stream by, saves both time and memory. Their method grows a known matrix trick, the Nystrom method, to the tree tensor case with random sampling at its core.

The method keeps the traits that made the matrix trick prized: one pass, low cost, and ease of parallel runs. The team proves a firm error bound, plus a chance-based bound for one common random map. A stepwise variant does better on dense data sets. Bench tests show the pair shrink and re-pack tree tensors with speed and care. The work unifies past tricks for two simpler tensor forms.
arxiv-2412-06411: Steven Krantz and Kaushal Verma revisit a classic result in complex analysis in a short 2024 paper. The Wong-Rosay theorem picks out the unit ball from all strongly pseudoconvex domains by the way its symmetry maps act. The authors ask what happens when those maps are loosened to quasiconformal ones, a wider class that allows bounded stretching, and they develop variants of the theorem in that looser setting.
arxiv-2412-06611:
Hoang Anh Nguyen and Ali Tura use quantum annealing to solve a seismic imaging problem, in work from 2024. Seismic traveltime inversion builds a map of how fast waves move underground. Such maps must be precise for tasks like storing carbon deep below the surface.

The team first turned the inversion into a binary optimization problem of the kind quantum annealers are built to solve. They then ran the annealer on a synthetic model of a carbon storage site at depth. The method also faced a test with noisy, complex data. The work shows early promise for quantum tools in geophysics and sets a base for sharper seismic imaging.
arxiv-2412-06711:
Bar Genossar and co-authors tackle feature choice in a 2024 paper on data sets split into subgroups with missing values. In such data, a whole subgroup may lack some measures for all its members, due to privacy rules or faulty data merges. Standard ways to rank features by shared information break down when those values are gone.

The team models features, subgroups, and the target as a linked graph and lets a neural network pass information along the links. That flow helps them guess the missing links between features and the target. Tests show the method picks good feature sets and runs at scale. It suits health and social data, where missing blocks are common.
arxiv-2412-07111:
Bo-Wen Zhang, Yan Yan, Boxiang Yang, Yifei Xue, and Guang Liu forecast sudden new skills in large language models with stand-in tasks, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Scale rules tune training well but cannot foresee skills that small models never show. Stand-in tasks that track the target skill offer a detour.

Candidate tasks are first scored by how their results track the target across many models. Small model groups then vet the best stand-ins for trust. Scores from the chosen stand-ins combine into a forecast for the target. A tool-use case study showed forecasts that tracked real results closely. Readers who plan model training get a way to see jumps coming.
arxiv-2412-07211:
Teng Ee Yap, Konstantin Batygin, and François Tissot study the early solar system in a paper from twenty twenty-four. The first small bodies, called planetesimals, are the parent bodies of most meteorites studied today. Isotope patterns split meteorites into two groups, non-carbonaceous and carbonaceous. The first group was long thought to come from the dry inner disk, the second from the wet outer disk.

That neat split is now in doubt. The oldest non-carbonaceous bodies show much higher oxidation states than expected. That hints they held a fair amount of liquid water before their cores formed. The authors use a model of outgassing to test what this means. Readers see how water in dry-zone bodies can bound how turbulent the young disk was.
arxiv-2412-07411: Gayathri Dandugula, Santhosh Boddana, and Sudesh Mirashi build radar object detection for small edge devices such as a Raspberry Pi. Their model, DSFEC, uses lean convolutions to cut the computing load. A new module sharpens and compresses features inside the encoder. On the nuScenes data set, the mid-size version beats the base model by about fifteen percent. It also cuts compute by sixty percent. The small version runs about three quarters faster on the Pi itself.
arxiv-2412-07711:
Yu-Feng Li and Zhao Xin present a 2024 calculation of the energy spectrum of geo-neutrinos, faint particles sent out by radioactive decay deep inside Earth. Detectors catch these particles to learn about the planet's inner heat and makeup. Reading the signals well depends on knowing the exact shape of the spectrum.

Their calculation uses the newest nuclear data, adds decay paths that earlier work had skipped, and applies refined corrections to the decay maths. Compared with the standard older estimate, the new spectrum has a clearly different shape. Predicted detection counts shift by several percent for the two main decay chains. The authors note that past results from two large detectors could shift by up to a fifth when the new model is used, which sets a fresh benchmark for the field.
arxiv-2412-07811:
Dustin Enyeart and Guang Lin study what happens when a rival training step is added to two popular neural operator designs. Their paper appeared in 2024. Neural operators learn how one function maps to another, and two common designs are DeepONets and Koopman autoencoders. Both designs compress and rebuild their input. Adding a rival, or adversarial, step has improved such compress-and-rebuild models in other areas.

The authors add that rival step to both designs and test how each one performs. The paper is brief and reports the comparison in plain terms. Readers get a first look at whether the trick that helps image models also helps models that learn operators. The work points to a cheap change that other groups can test on their own problems.
arxiv-2412-07911:
Chin-Hung Chen and co-authors design a better receiver in 2024 for wireless links hit by bursts of impulsive noise. Such noise comes from power devices and can wreck signals. Their setting uses differential phase-shift keying, a common sending scheme, plus error-correcting codes. First they compute the best rates any receiver could reach on this channel.

Then they build a receiver that folds the differential decoder into the noise detector. It gained about four and a half decibels over the standard design and came within about one decibel of the theory limit. A simpler version kept near-best results at half the complexity. Simulations backed both designs under real-world limits.
arxiv-2412-08111:
Sri Harsha Dumpala and co-authors probe how well vision-language models grasp sentence structure. These models pair a text encoder with image tools and power tasks like caption writing. Past work found weak spots in meaning, but the cause was unclear. The team tests how much syntax, the rules that order words, each encoder holds. They compare joint models with text-only models of varied size and training.

Text-only encoders picked up syntax better than the joint models did. What shaped syntax most was the training goal, not model size or data volume. One model, CLIP, lost syntax in deeper layers, while others held it best in middle layers. The results help explain why joint models can stumble on word order.
arxiv-2412-08411:
Riccardo Borsato and Sibylle Driezen study particle creation in a deformed version of a famous string theory spacetime, in work from twenty twenty-four. The Jordanian deformation warps the anti de Sitter and sphere product space while keeping the model classically integrable. A Lax connection certifies that tidy structure.

Fixing light cone gauge around a pointlike solution, they expand the energy in small fields. Cubic terms appear in the gauge fixed Hamiltonian. Those terms open three particle processes among the physical excitations, an unexpected outcome. The authors weigh the surprise against the model's Lax integrability, which might have suggested cleaner scattering. The result probes how deformation bends string dynamics.
arxiv-2412-08711: Francisco Duque gives lecture notes on extreme mass ratio inspirals moving through fundamental fields, from a two hour lecture at a 2024 school and workshop in Lisbon. The notes model binaries with very unequal masses that evolve inside a cloud of an ultralight scalar field. Black hole perturbation theory supplies the tools, with a simpler case of a spherical cloud around a non rotating black hole. A companion notebook derives and solves the equations of motion for the system.
arxiv-2412-08811:
Carolyn Volpert and co-authors measure loss in thin aluminum circuits that will guide space detector design. The circuits, called resonators, ring at set tones, and any loss dims the detectors built on them. The team at a NASA center built test resonators in two lengths and varied how they couple. Their 2024 study reads the films and sorts the loss sources in dark, cold runs.

Loss came out very low, near the best marks for such films. At mid to high read powers, one loss kind, tied to tiny two-state flaws, was suppressed more than the standard model says. At the coldest heats and low powers, the standard model broke down. A tweaked model fit the odd behavior. The results feed design of sensitive sky detectors.
arxiv-2412-08911:
Shijun Li, Hilaf Hasson, Jing Hu, and Joydeep Ghosh propose a learning method for recommendation systems in this 2024 paper. Online shops must balance several goals at once, such as clicks, sales, and user satisfaction. Training one model for conflicting goals is often complex and costly.

Their method extends goal-conditioned learning, where goals become lists of target values rather than single numbers. The design drops the need for complex model shapes and extra constraints. It also filters out noisy training cases that never reach good long-term rewards. A new goal-picking step chooses targets that are both wanted and reachable. Tests on recommendation tasks showed strong, scalable performance.
arxiv-2412-09211:
Wilfried Buchmuller, Arthur Hebecker, and Alexander Westphal test an old conjecture about the wave function of the universe, in a 2024 paper. Their arena is a stripped-down gravity model: two-dimensional de Sitter space, the setting called JT gravity. Even this small model carries the full physics of how a universe's size can vary.

In the model, two numbers describe the cosmos: a scale factor for slice size and a dilaton read as the size of an extra slice. Where both shrink to zero, space turns singular. DeWitt guessed that true wave functions must vanish at such edges. The team solve the governing equation across the whole field range and check where solutions fade as the conjecture demands.
arxiv-2412-09411:
Antoine Amarilli and four co-authors study how hard it is to break a path query on a graph database. Their twenty twenty-four paper defines resilience: the fewest facts one must delete to make a query false. They focus on regular path queries, which ask whether a path exists whose labels spell a word from a set language.

The goal is to sort languages by whether resilience is easy or hard to compute. For local languages, it is tractable, even in strict combined terms. For finite languages with a repeated letter, and for a broad class of non-local ones, they prove hardness. Some non-local classes stay easy, and the full sorting is not yet done.
arxiv-2412-09511:
Dongyue Lu, Lingdong Kong, Tianxin Huang, and Gim Hee Lee teach 3D objects their use zones from words, in a way that holds on new kinds and dirty data. Past methods lean on scarce hand labels and on shape-first backbones that wilt in noise. Their 2024 framework, GEAL, pairs a 3D branch with large 2D models. A splatting step draws realistic 2D views from sparse point sets.

A fusion block tuned to grain size and a block that aligns the 2D and 3D views pass 2D knowledge to the 3D branch. Two new corruption benchmarks grade toughness, one for object images and one for hand zones. On clean, new-kind, and corrupted sets the framework beats past methods. Code and the corruption sets are free for all to use.
arxiv-2412-09611:
Yusuf Dalva, Kavana Venkatesh, and Pinar Yanardag present FluxSpace, a domain free image editing method for rectified flow transformers such as Flux. These models make fine images but struggle to edit one trait without touching the rest. Their work came out in twenty twenty-four.

The method works in a space built from what the transformer's own blocks learn. From those hidden states, the authors draw meanings a reader can steer. That control spans tasks from fine grained fixes to artistic creation. The team frames the result as a scalable editing route whose chief gain is clean separation of traits, so a change stays where it belongs.
arxiv-2412-09811:
Ivan Grytsenko and co-authors characterize a tiny oscillator for reading out qubits in a 2024 paper. Reading electron spin qubits needs microwave tones deep inside a fridge, and racks of room temperature gear scale badly. A tunnel diode oscillator sips only about one microwatt, letting it live on the coldest stage.

The device centers near one hundred forty megahertz, the band used for semiconductor electron readout, and tunes across ten megahertz with a varactor. Its amplitude held steadier than commercial sources. Swapping the bench power supply for a lead acid battery cut phase noise sharply, reaching a clean figure at one megahertz offset. The authors pitch the design for large scale qubit arrays.
arxiv-2412-10111:
