Manuel Asorey, Fernando Ezquerro, and Miguel Pardina study universes that avoid the Big Bang singularity inside quadratic gravity, a theory that adds squared curvature terms to Einstein's equations. They present a large family of smooth, uniform universes that stay finite at very early and very late times.

Such smooth solutions appear only beyond an unstable branch of de Sitter space, set by the two coupling constants of the theory. Checking stability through the second-order change of the action, the team finds the smooth solutions are fragile. A slight shift in the parameters lets a Big Bang emerge from the smooth regime. The work maps both the promise and the instability of singularity-free cosmology in this theory.
arxiv-2412-10211:
Paula Daudén-Oliver and co-authors share a data set of human reads on bent and shifted images. The work dates to 2024. Image quality sets train models that guess how people see flaws. Most past sets deal with flaws from screens, not from daily life shifts.

Shifts such as turns, slides, and zooms are what viewers meet most in real life. The set holds reads on over eight hundred warped shots, with plain noise as a base line. Over one hundred viewers made more than twenty thousand calls in a set test form. The set fits known sight laws and beats past sets in group tests.
arxiv-2412-10411:
Shashank Pathak and Guohui Lin wrote a 2024 paper on using a pretrained protein language model to design gene code for vaccines. Choosing codons well raises protein yield and steadies the messenger RNA. That matters for mRNA vaccines, where yield drives immune strength. The team takes rich amino acid embeddings from the protein model.

A light fine-tuning step then turns those embeddings into optimized reading frames. The designed frames beat natural ones on stability and expression scores. They also beat benchmark frames used in real vaccines. Test cases covered the coronavirus spike and a shingles virus antigen. The authors pitch the approach for tailoring vaccine antigens.
arxiv-2412-10511:
Joshua Cahyono and Jeremy Jusuf outline a student project on software that writes captions for photos, in a paper from 2024. Such software blends image reading with language skills to describe a scene in words. Good captions help blind users, search tools, and photo sorting.

The project plans to try a range of methods, from older paired networks to newer attention-based designs. Models will train on photos paired with human captions. Scores will use standard measures that compare machine text to human text. The team also plans trials that vary design choices and settings to lift accuracy and make captions sound more natural.
arxiv-2412-11211:
Jiahe Lin and George Michailidis review in 2024 how deep learning has reshaped state space models. Such models track a hidden state that shifts over time and drives what we observe, a frame used across science and finance.

The review starts with the classic fit method, then sets out a shared training pipe based on encoder models. It walks through lead deep models for both step by step time and smooth time cases. Fresh work that uses state space blocks as fast parts inside large sequence models gets its own look. Mixed rate and gappy time data close the survey as cases where the frame shines.
arxiv-2412-11511:
Six researchers tackle a common problem in medical studies in a paper from 2024. Doctors want to know the average effect of a treatment, along with a range that shows how sure they can be. Patient records, though, often come from many hospitals with different data. The team offers a new way to combine such records and still give a valid range.

Their method borrows strength from prediction tools to make the range narrower and more useful. They prove the method is unbiased and test it in computer experiments. They also show how it can mix trial data with routine records. The work could help hospitals judge drugs with more care.
arxiv-2412-11611:
David Feldstein-Bofill and co-authors revisit in 2024 the gatemon, a superconducting qubit whose frequency is tuned by a gate voltage. Gatemons promise insight into hybrid junctions, but they often suffer unstable, history-dependent frequencies and short coherence. The team developed ways to measure those flaws and compared how capacitor designs change performance across devices.

Stability, hysteresis, and dephasing all depended strongly on frequency and design. Grounded designs beat floating ones on stability. They achieved tuning precision of one megahertz across several gigahertz of range. The results give builders concrete guidance for more reliable hybrid quantum circuits.
arxiv-2412-11811:
Enrico Iurlano and Günther Raidl hunt for the smallest possible minwise independent families of permutations, a structure born in web search. Their 2024 paper explains the property: for any subset and any chosen element, a random permutation from the family must put that element first among the subset with exactly even odds. Search engines use the trick to estimate document similarity fast.

The raw search space is astronomically large, so the team builds a pure satisfiability model with careful symmetry breaking. A generalized heuristic, borrowed from a group theoretic method for rankwise families, speeds the hunt further. The search found provably optimal new families. A bijective proof also settles a lower bound puzzle left by earlier work on the rankwise cousin problem.
arxiv-2412-12011:
Sylwia Kondej and Kacper Ślipko study tunneling in a quantum waveguide in their 2024 paper. A waveguide is a narrow channel that guides quantum waves, like a wire for matter waves. Far down the channel sits a flaw described by a broad class of measures, and the team asks how it affects waves passing through.

They prove the system has a resonance, a fleeting state that leaks away over time. As the flaw moves farther off, the resonance energy shifts by an amount that fades in a set pattern. The width of the resonance, which sets how fast it decays, matches Fermi's golden rule, a classic formula for transition rates. They derive that match in full.
arxiv-2412-12911:
Antoine Bret and Asaf Pe'er propose in 2024 a way that particle speeding inside a shock wave in space could halt itself. Such shocks, which have no direct collisions, somehow push particles to high speeds, and how the two sides affect each other is not well understood. The pair work only with shocks that carry no magnetic field.

Their study ties the shock's width to the spread of sped particles and to how much the shock squeezes gas. From those links, they find the speeding may stop when sped particles make up about thirty percent of the flow ahead of the shock. A self-set limit like that would shape how cosmic rays gain their energy, a long open question in space physics.
arxiv-2412-13211:
Home robots need practice tidying rooms, and benchmarks give that practice a fair scoreboard. Arth Shukla, Stone Tao, and Hao Su present such a benchmark in 2024 for low-level hand control in home rearrangement tasks.

Their package, ManiSkill-HAB, rebuilds an existing home assistant benchmark on graphics processors, running more than three times faster while using far less memory. It supports fine-grained control rather than magic grasps that teleport objects. The team trained reinforcement and imitation learning baselines for others to beat. A rule-based filter then picks out demonstration runs that meet behavior and safety criteria, which makes it cheap to build clean training data at scale.
arxiv-2412-13311:
Cash that works hard in a firm may tell its stock's road, a tale first told in a famed coin frame. Vohra, Vij, Mehta, and Ozcan test that tale in a 2024 study on a coin bank's stock and trade counts. Their flock is the tech board's non coin firms, held long by the cash mark alone.

Cross the wide flock, the mark's call ran weak. In a hand picked flock, the call sang: fair gains past the three mark frame of stock lore. The split is the find: the mark pays when the yard is well picked. Toll costs and age turns are due tests. Wed to kin marks, the team say, cash work may still earn its keep.
arxiv-2412-13511:
Researchers release in 2024 a data set of conflict events in the Horn of Africa to sharpen how language models read war news. News text can reveal the shape and causes of violent conflict. Past data sets miss many fine event types that matter in this region.

The set, CEHA, holds 500 English accounts of conflict events with types defined by cause. Aid, peace, and development groups helped shape the type list. Two tasks come with the set: spotting conflict relevance and naming the event type. Baseline models find both tasks hard with so little training data. The set gives a fair test bed for models in low-resource, high-stakes settings.
arxiv-2412-14111:
Shuang Guo and Guillermo Gallego build a new vision method in 2024 for cameras that report change, not frames. Such event cameras suit fast motion, and this work treats a camera that only spins in place. The task is to refine both the camera's poses and a brightness map of the scene at once.

Their method works straight from the event model, with no step that turns events into fake photos. A solver built for sparse data handles the huge count of unknowns. Tests on made-up and real data cut the key error by up to ninety percent, they report. Maps came out with detail past methods had hidden. Work on fresh high-grade event cameras showed the method holds up there too, a good sign for robot and drone eyes.
arxiv-2412-14711:
Ziteng Wang, Jun Zhu, and Jianfei Chen present a new form of mixture-of-experts model for large neural nets. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Such models hold many expert parts but switch on only a few for each token, so size can grow with no rise in compute cost. The classic router that picks experts learns in jumps, which caps its gains.

Their design, ReMoE, uses a ReLU router that can be trained in a smooth way from end to end. They add ways to keep the router sparse and to share load evenly among experts. Tests across sizes and expert counts show steady gains over the classic router. Growth with more experts is also stronger.
arxiv-2412-15311:
Seonguk Seo and Bohyung Han re-evaluate group robustness methods with adaptive class-specific scaling, in a research paper from 2024. Such methods aim to lift worst-group accuracy when data carry spurious links, as when background predicts the label. Past gains in robust scores often cost average accuracy, a trade-off that is hard to control.

Scaling each class by its own factor, with no added training, can tune that trade-off. An adaptive form that varies by instance can lift both robust and average scores at once. A plain baseline with scaling matches or beats recent debiasing methods. A new single metric sums up the trade-off for fair comparison.
arxiv-2412-15811:
Michela Rigoselli and fourteen co-authors published this paper in 2024. It reports the first highly polarized X-ray measurement from the magnetar 1E 1841-045, caught by the IXPE satellite after the star turned burst-active. Magnetars are neutron stars with the strongest magnetic fields, and this signal reads the geometry of their emission.

The polarization degree climbed with photon energy, from about fifteen percent at low energies to fifty-five percent at the top of the band, while its angle stayed fixed, pointing north. Combining IXPE with a second telescope mapped the spectrum into three components. The soft thermal glow was weakly polarized, fitting a condensed surface or bombarded atmosphere. The middle component matched predictions for scattering in the magnetosphere. The hardest light was polarized above sixty-five percent, pointing to synchrotron or curvature radiation. Earlier magnetars seen at rest behaved differently, showing how activity reshapes these stars' output.
arxiv-2412-15911:
Baglioni and co-authors wrote a 2024 arXiv paper on how small neural networks link their outputs. In networks with one hidden layer, outputs can move together in ways that vanish when the network grows very wide. The team seeks a clear account of this effect.

They work in a limit where both the training set and the hidden layer grow while their ratio stays fixed. In that limit, a change in the shape of the kernel explains the linked outputs. Careful tests check both how well the model predicts and how strong the links are. The match between theory and tests supports their claim.
arxiv-2412-16011:
Paul Schreivogl and Richard Schweiger explore fuzzy geometry in a 2024 paper on matrix models. In this field, surfaces are written as matrices rather than as smooth sheets, which suits quantum physics. Building a wavy surface by hand in matrix form is slow, so the pair turned to 3D drawing tools.

They draw a graph in 3D software, and a script turns its points and links into three matrices. Math software then finds the quiet modes of a key operator on that fuzzy surface. Their first case twists a trefoil knot into a quantum surface. More cases show how the process behaves on other shapes.
arxiv-2412-16111:
Nils Greven, Jonas Ranft, and Tilo Schwalger derive a model for how random wiring shapes the flicker of finite neural populations. Their 2024 paper notes that mid-level models of brain activity usually assume every neuron connects to every other. Real networks connect only with some probability, which adds its own source of variability that older theories ignore.

Their stochastic mean-field model handles random connectivity, outside noise, and varied inputs at once. A further reduction yields a small set of coupled equations for average voltage, its spread, and a finite-size fluctuation term. Against direct simulations, the model tracks fluctuations and nonlinear behavior well. It beats earlier theories that assumed full wiring.
arxiv-2412-16411:
Yang He and Vassiliy Lubchenko frame learning as a split in a heat-like law in a 2024 arXiv paper. They build a score that can guide training of a model that makes new samples from on-off parts. To keep the model cheap to run, its view must shrink. That shrink gives the score more than one low point.

Training samples fill far less than the full space of on-off states. The states left out act like a hot phase split by a wide gap from the trained set. Staying out of that hot phase is what lets the model work. The split can block rare trained shapes, though. Using many models at once may help.
arxiv-2412-16511:
Keon Moradi and five colleagues track multiple similar-looking small birds in three dimensions inside an outdoor aviary. The birds look alike and move fast, which defeats ordinary tracking systems. Their multi-camera method uses environmental landmarks as context: candidate matches whose position disagrees with nearby landmarks are rejected as outliers.

The context-aware rejection removed twenty percent of outliers during reconstruction and reached ninety-seven percent matching accuracy. The result is reliable simultaneous tracking of many birds under challenging outdoor conditions. The team also releases a large annotated dataset covering eighty birds in four enclosures over twenty hours of footage, aimed at vision researchers, ornithologists, and ecologists.
arxiv-2412-16611:
Muhammad Ali Jamshed and a large team give a full guide to networks that reach past the ground for sixth generation mobile service. New world goals call for smart, green, and tough links for all. Satellites and air craft will join ground towers as one web.

The guide covers shared spectra, new radio rules for space links, and smart tools that steer beams and paths. It also covers edge compute, learned control, and fresh ways for many users to share air time. Uses range from far farms to disaster zones where ground links fail.
arxiv-2412-16811:
Kasra Hejazi, Jay Soni, Modjtaba Shokrian Zini, and Juan Miguel Arrazola sharpen the error accounting for product formulas used inside quantum phase estimation. Phase estimation needs a simulated Hamiltonian evolution, and product formulas are the cheap, qubit-light way to fake it, but their textbook error bounds are pessimistic and ignore the actual task. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the team analyzes the error for the specific job of estimating energies, using a Magnus expansion of the Hamiltonian the formula effectively simulates. Earlier results for gapped ground states are generalized to product formulas of any order.

As a payoff, they exhibit a nine-term second-order formula whose energy error beats the standard Trotter-Suzuki recipe quadratically. For low-energy states of local, positive Hamiltonians, tighter bounds give up to a quadratic cost saving at a target accuracy. Better accounting means quantum hardware budgets can be spent where they count.
arxiv-2412-16911: Chen and Yang bound the size of nodal sets for Laplace eigenfunctions in twenty twenty-four. A nodal set is where an eigenfunction crosses zero inside a domain. The authors work on domains whose boundary is smooth in a set sense. They consider eigenfunctions that meet the Neumann condition at the boundary, where the normal derivative is zero. Their theorem states that the surface measure of the zero set does not exceed a constant times the square root of the eigenvalue. The bound is sharp in its growth rate.
arxiv-2412-17211:
Jiang Zhu and five colleagues build an end-to-end system that spots and tracks several targets with millimeter-wave radar. Such radar is a core sense for smart machines and automated spaces. Weak targets drown easily next to strong ones. Detection, matching, and tracking must work as one chain.

Their framework opens with a fast, sharp estimator that pulls out each target's distance and speed. A classic beam step then reads off the angles. A message-passing module matches returns to known tracks, using speed as a clue. A Kalman filter carries each track forward, guided by the estimator's known error shape. An extrapolation trick lifts the odds of catching faint targets. Tests on simulated and real data beat rival pipelines. The authors offer the chain as a practical core for radar perception.
arxiv-2412-17311:
Kumar Balasubramanian and co-authors ask which symmetry flips on a covered version of the general linear group swap each representation for its mirror, in a 2024 paper. The group is GL(2) over a local field, and the cover stacks n layers over it. A classic theorem says the standard flip on the base group always pairs a representation with its contragredient.

The team lifts that flip to the cover and tests when it still does the dualizing job. The answer turns on the depth of the stack: the lift works exactly when n equals two. For deeper covers the pairing breaks. The result sharpens a corner of the representation theory of metaplectic groups.
arxiv-2412-17511:
Koyel Majumdar and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 on a joint model that hunts for changed genes and changed gene marks in one pass. Gene activity and DNA marks shape each other, yet most studies scan them apart and merge the lists later. That split view misses how the two layers move together in diseases like cancer.

Their model, idiffomix, blends both data types in a single likelihood that respects their nested structure. Fitting runs through a standard expectation-maximization routine. Tests on made-up data and a public breast cancer set showed the joint hunt finds some changed genes that a split hunt overlooks. The tool aims at studies where both layers are measured on the same samples.
arxiv-2412-17711:
Florian Knoop and six co-authors build a first-principles theory of how crystals scatter light at warm temperatures. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. This scattering, called the Raman effect, reveals how atoms in a crystal vibrate. Warmth changes the signal, and past theories often missed fine details of the setup.

Their theory folds in the angles and polarization of the light, and the small but real motion of the sound waves involved. They test it on two crystals: gallium nitride and a complex sulfur-based material. Computed spectra are compared side by side with lab measurements. The match lets them sort out which features come from single vibrations. They also review shortcuts for signals from pairs of vibrations in complex materials.
arxiv-2412-18111:
Mingming Zhang and co-authors introduce AIGT, a system that fabricates realistic spreadsheet-style data on request. Tables hold over 80 percent of company data assets, but privacy rules often block sharing the real thing. Language models can fake table rows well because they grasp what the columns mean, yet older methods ignore much of what a table carries. AIGT feeds the model the table's own description and schema as part of the prompt, which sharpens the output.

A second trick splits long tables into parts so the model can handle tables of any scale within its token limit. The system reached the best scores on 14 of 20 public datasets. It also led on two real datasets inside the Alipay risk control system. The authors pitch AIGT for safe data sharing and model testing.
arxiv-2412-18311:
Andronikos Paliathanasis sorts a family of gravity models by their hidden symmetries in a 2024 paper. The models extend a classic alternative to Einstein's theory, in which a scalar field partners with gravity to drive the expansion of the universe. A second scalar field is added, coupled in the simplest way to both gravity and the first field.

Paliathanasis applies Noether symmetry analysis, a method that finds conserved quantities hidden in a model's equations. By demanding such symmetries, he pins down exactly which forms of the model's free functions make the equations solvable in full. The result is a complete classification of the workable cases. Along the way, the analysis turns up new families of cosmic models whose history can be written out exactly.
arxiv-2412-18611:
Pratihar and Sivakumar prove matrix facts in 2024 by drawing graphs instead of grinding algebra. Their matrices, a class called M-matrices, matter when inverses keep a banded shape, nonzero only near the diagonal. Such shapes cut computing cost in big systems.

First they pin down, in graph terms, when one off-band entry of the inverse stays positive. That lemma then yields fresh graph proofs of two known results: when a three-band matrix has a three-band inverse, and a needed condition for a five-band inverse, they report. Worked number examples walk the proofs. Graph views of matrices often expose in one picture what pages of symbol pushing hide. A banded inverse, where it exists, is a real gift to solvers.
arxiv-2412-19311:
Learning agents that drive cars or dose medicine must not only act safely but explain themselves when something goes wrong. Risal Shahriar Shefin, Asifur Rahman, Thai Le, and Sarra Alqahtani propose xSRL in 2024, a framework that treats explanation as part of the safety machinery itself.

Safe reinforcement learning already trades task success against safety limits, yet the explanation tools borrowed from image models ignore the step-by-step nature of decisions. The authors argue explanations built for sequential, safety-bound choices are the missing piece for operator trust, especially under adversarial pressure. Their framework targets domains, vehicles, robots, drones, medical devices, where a silent failure is not an option.
arxiv-2412-19411:
Yongli Hou and Yanqiu Wang fix a mismatch that plagues fluid-flow simulations on curved ground, in a 2024 paper. Darcy flow describes water creeping through soil and rock, and mixed finite element methods simulate it well on flat meshes. On a curved boundary, though, the straight edges of the triangular mesh cut corners off the true curve, so the flow condition set on the real border lands in the wrong place.

Their remedy is a boundary value correction: the border condition is mathematically moved from the true curve onto the mesh edge before solving. That keeps the mesh simple, avoiding curved elements and their coding burden. The authors prove the corrected method converges at the best possible rate for discretizations of any order. Numerical experiments back the theory. The paper gives groundwater and reservoir modelers a cleaner way to honor curved borders.
arxiv-2412-19611:
Joon-Hwi Kim gave a classic trick for building rotating black holes a physical derivation in a 2024 paper. The Newman-Janis algorithm conjures the spinning Kerr metric from the static Schwarzschild one by a formal complex shift, a recipe that works mysteriously well. Kim shows the Kerr geometry equals a nonlinear superposition of paired gravitational instantons, self-dual and anti-self-dual Taub-NUT solutions, which turns the recipe into a derivation with a definite origin.

The same instanton assembly yields the charged Kerr-Newman solution and charged Kerr-Taub-NUT variants, with chiral dyons joining the instantons in the cast. A fifty-year-old algorithm gains a mechanism: spinning black holes as bound states of simpler gravitational atoms.
arxiv-2412-19911:
Bruno El-Bennich, writing alone in 2024, checks gauge consistency in the quark gap equation. That equation sets a quark's effective mass inside strong-force theory. Shortcut versions of the quark-gluon vertex can break the theory's gauge rules without obvious warning.

Three vertex choices are compared: the bare one, a dressed one tied to a symmetry identity, and a full one with transverse parts. Two chiral-limit quantities, the quark condensate and the pion decay constant, serve as the test readouts. The study verifies which choices keep the results properly gauge covariant, a check model builders rely on.
arxiv-2501-00111:
Luís Cunha and Mário Medina speed up a classic string puzzle in a paper whose text dates to 2024. Given a string of zeros and ones, the puzzle asks which mixes of zeros and ones appear inside it. A data structure answering such questions for every mix is called a jumbled index.

Earlier builders of the index slowed badly on strings with many runs of the same digit, and the authors prove that slowdown is typical, not rare. Their new algorithm grows a suffix tree to strip out repeated substrings before counting. The worst-case cost stays high, but leaner memory access makes it faster in practice. The work matters for pattern matching in texts and biological sequences.
arxiv-2501-00211:
Self-driving cars can be flummoxed by a sudden roadblock, and a paper by Noor Aboueleneen and co-authors, published in 2024, teaches them to cope as a team. Their system uses many learning agents at once, linked by fast 6G vehicle-to-everything communication.

Each car learns to change lanes around accidents or work zones while keeping traffic flowing and speeds high. Realistic limits are built in, such as a floor on speed, the count of roadblocks, and how often lanes may change. The team trained and tested the system under two setups. The aim is smoother, safer flow when the road ahead changes without warning.
arxiv-2501-00411:
Hiroaki Ishikawa and co-authors present a simple model from two thousand twenty-four of motion that arises when an active particle pairs with a passive one. Earlier experiments by the group showed such pairs moving on their own, and this paper captures the effect in equations. The pair sits in a flat two-dimensional space.

In the model, a spring links the two particles. The active one pushes itself along its current heading, while the passive one is repelled by its partner. Computer runs produced three motion styles: straight lines, circles, and slalom paths. Analysis explains the switch between straight and circular motion as the strength of self-propulsion changes. The model shows how a plain pairing can yield varied travel patterns.
arxiv-2501-00611:
David Cohen and Julián Norato present, in 2024, a design method for bone implants whose spongy pattern varies across the part. The pattern is a triply periodic surface known for inviting bone growth. Their method tunes the wall thickness at control points to maximize how much bone grows into the implant.

A biomechanical model estimates growth from load size and rhythm plus surrounding bone density. The implant is treated as a blended material to keep computing cheap, with local traits drawn from a fast surrogate model. A hip implant example shows the method working under thickness limits set for manufacturing and cell entry. The goal is implants the body claims as its own.
arxiv-2501-00811:
Erik Nguyen and Spencer Htin present a data-driven method for beautifying faces in photos, in this 2025 paper. Beauty filters are big business on social media. Older methods apply hand-written rules, stretching or smoothing the features that experts link to attractiveness. Rules, though, can only capture what their authors already believe about beauty.

The authors instead move a face through the hidden space of a pre-trained image generator, nudging it toward higher beauty as judged by a new scoring network they trained. Their scorer outperformed many existing beauty-rating models. Because the guidance comes from data rather than rules, the system can pick up holistic patterns no one specified. The paper frames the approach as a complement to rule-based filters, and a step toward automatic portrait enhancement that learns taste instead of being told it.
arxiv-2501-00911:
David Wu and Sanjiban Choudhury teach reward models that carry human preferences from an easy domain into a hard one, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Aligning language models needs preference data, but for many target domains nobody has collected any, while simpler source domains have plenty.

Their insight is that preferences encode domain-agnostic ideas of quality, so a reward model can learn them where labels exist and still judge elsewhere. Their framework trains with two losses at once. One keeps the model's internal view of source and target domains aligned. The other fits the source preferences themselves. They evaluate across four transfer settings, including crossing languages, moving from clean to noisy data, and stretching few-shot feedback to full tasks. In each, accuracy improves over plain baselines. The work offers a route to alignment where direct feedback is scarce.
arxiv-2501-01311:
Bohang Sun and Pietro Liò add a plug-in explainer that makes image and text networks show their reasoning. Their 2025 paper introduces the Multi-Head Explainer, a three-part add-on for convolutional networks and transformers alike. An attention gate spotlights the features that matter for the task at hand.

Deep supervision nudges the early layers to catch fine details tied to the target class. An equivalent matrix then merges the sharpened local and global views into one rich saliency map. The framework slips into standard designs like ResNet and BERT with little surgery. On medical imaging and text sorting benchmarks, it raised accuracy while producing clearer, more detailed explanations of each decision.
arxiv-2501-01411:
Gleb Kalachev and Pavel Panteleev study a growth trait of error-correcting codes in a 2025 arXiv paper. Product codes stack simpler codes into a stronger whole. A trait called product expansion, akin to how walls grow from bricks, underlies new designs for quantum codes and for codes that can be spot-checked fast. For stacks of two codes, the trait matches two known test traits. For taller stacks it is strictly stronger.

The pair prove that a pile of random codes, any count of them, over a big enough symbol set has good product expansion. Past work had not shown this for taller stacks. They sketch how the four-code case could yield good quantum codes that can be tested locally, in the style of current two-code builds.
arxiv-2501-01511:
Alireza Khataei and Kia Bazargan wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It presents TreeLUT, an open tool that runs gradient boosted decision trees on FPGA chips through lookup tables, as a lean rival to neural nets.

Neural nets lean on vast counts of multiply and add steps, which cost much on hardware. Boosted trees, built from plain decision trees, match the shape FPGAs handle best, and their run steps are mere compares and adds. TreeLUT adds a quantization scheme and a pipeline design, using lookup tables alone with no block memory or DSP units. On standard test sets it beats a row of neural and tree rivals on chip use, delay, and throughput, at matched accuracy.
arxiv-2501-01611:
Haixu Liu, Zerui Tao, and Penghao Jiang label images with help from their captions, in a 2025 paper. One photo can carry many labels at once, from a single tag up to nineteen. Vision alone often misses context that words supply.

Their light classifier joins a convolutional network for images with language tools for text. A fusion module merges the two streams before deciding labels. Training used partial supervision, so unlabeled data still taught the model. Part by part tests confirmed each piece earned its place. Early results showed strong accuracy with modest size. The system points toward automatic tagging of large photo collections.
arxiv-2501-01811:
Francesc Sabanés Zariquiey and co-authors validated in 2025 a neural approach to drug binding calculations. Predicting how strongly a candidate drug binds its target guides the costly stages of drug design. Standard force fields for the drug molecules limit accuracy. The team instead used a neural network potential, AceFF, built on the TensorNet design, to handle the ligands.

Their method, QuantumBind-RBFE, computes relative binding free energies between similar compounds. On standard benchmarks it beat the GAFF2 force field and an earlier neural potential in accuracy. It nearly matched a top commercial force field as well. It also ran with a time step at least twice as large as earlier neural models, giving real speed gains. Code and model are public for research use.
arxiv-2501-02111:
Ishaan Maitra and co-authors map how place shapes health across England, in a 2025 paper. Health depends on air, jobs, green space, and many local traits that shift from town to town. A new data set now gathers such facts at fine scale over time. The team used several ranking methods to find which local traits predict health outcomes best.

Nitrogen dioxide, a traffic-linked gas, predicted asthma, high blood pressure, and anxiety across the whole country. Other outcomes leaned on work, marriage, and plant cover in their own ways. Local models showed air and sunlight effects changing by region and shifting during COVID. The authors built their models to stay readable, so health officials can act on the findings rather than trust a black box.
arxiv-2501-02511:
Takashi Harada and four co-authors ask whether the feelings a song creates can be read from its thumbnail image. Music search and music-making systems increasingly take plain-language requests, but large sets of songs paired with written captions are rare. Facts about when a song fits, or what mood it stirs, are especially hard to get from audio alone.

The team proposes drawing such details from thumbnail images instead. Using their method, they built a dataset of about 360,000 captions that include mood and listening-situation details. Human judges rated the captions and found the approach worked. The team then trained a music retrieval model on the new dataset and showed it performed well on search tasks. The work offers a way to grow caption data for music systems without costly hand labeling.
arxiv-2501-02811:
Bin Wang and Li Jing describe their winning entry in a shop sign recognition contest, in a 2025 competition report. Reading text on street storefront signs helps maps, city planning, and business analysis. Real signs use complex designs and varied lettering, which makes recognition hard.

Their system works in stages, fusing features from several data types and training with large-scale self-supervision. A transformer-based large model reads the text. A reinforcement learning method locates sign boxes, and a rectification step straightens distorted text. Experiments confirmed each part helped. The authors argue the approach can raise recognition quality in messy urban scenes.
arxiv-2501-03011:
Guy Moshel, Omer Rabinowitz, Eliya Blumenthal, and Shay Hacohen-Gourgy measure, in a 2025 paper, how fast a burst of energy races across a quantum chip. Sudden radiation hits spray phonons, the chip's sound-like vibrations, which corrupt qubits far away. The team lined up a row of sensitive detectors, called MKIDs, on one silicon chip. A small heated junction set off a controlled burst, and they timed the wave past each detector.

Strangely, stronger bursts looked slower. The authors show this is an illusion of detection: the wave thins as it spreads, and each detector fires only above a minimum strength. Stronger bursts stay visible longer and seem delayed. Fitting a simple model recovered the true sound speed along the chip. It also showed how efficiently vibrations convert into the broken pairs detectors sense. Both numbers feed designs for burst-proof quantum hardware.
arxiv-2501-03111:
Félicien Hêche and co-authors assess how external factors affect the occurrence of emergencies handled by a Swiss hospital dispatch center. Their 2025 study uses historical data from the Centre Hospitalier Universitaire Vaudois, which manages emergency medical services for most of French-speaking Switzerland.

Nineteen factors were considered, tied to weather, road traffic, air quality, and time. Classical methods such as correlation, chi-squared tests, and t-tests first screened for dependencies. Machine learning models, extreme gradient boosting and a multilayer perceptron, were then judged with SHAP values and permutation importance. The hour of the day, and factors tied to it, stood out in the results.
arxiv-2501-03311:
Marco Fabbrichesi, Matthew Low, and Luca Marzola import a workhorse of quantum information, the trace distance between states, into the hunt for new particles. Colliders now measure entanglement in particle decays, and such observables can bound physics beyond the Standard Model. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team shows the trace distance beats rival quantum measures in sensitivity. Combined with the production rate, it yields the strongest bounds they tested. Real data anchor the first example: quantum tomography of top quark pairs gives the first trace-distance bound on the top's chromomagnetic dipole moment.

Simulations set projected limits on anomalous tau couplings at a running and a future collider. The team also reports the first measurements of magic, another quantum resource, in collider data. Both cases clear five standard deviations. Quantum state comparison, they argue, belongs in the search toolbox.
arxiv-2501-03811:
Chatbots like ChatGPT answer many questions cleanly, yet they cannot look up a live price on a shop's website. Jorge Lloret-Gazo presents Wextractor, a system that extends ChatGPT so it can answer questions such as the price of a named cake at a named bakery. The system fetches the product page and pulls the price out, covering a kind of transactional search the chatbot alone cannot do.

The paper is frank that the add-on is not itself artificial intelligence; it is a practical bridge between the chatbot and the live web. Two improvements over the first version make answers faster: social extraction, which uses shared or social sources, and pointing pattern extraction, which homes in on the page patterns where prices sit. The work shows how a focused tool wrapped around a general chatbot can fill a clear gap in what users can ask for.
arxiv-2501-03911:
Fabio Difonzo and co-authors teach a physics-informed network to find the horizon size inside a peridynamic material model in a 2025 paper. Peridynamics lets distant points pull on each other within a horizon radius, and that radius is normally a guess. The network instead learns it from displacement data.

V-shaped, spread, and tent-shaped influence kernels were all tried in one and two dimensions. The learner recovered the true horizon even for awkward kernels. A quirk emerged with proof behind it: training approaches the true value from one side only, since that point is an unstable resting place of the loss. Inverse problems gain a worked example.
arxiv-2501-04211:
Sanghyeon Park and Soo-Mook Moon shrink large AI models in a 2025 paper. Big models perform well but eat memory and power. Their method, called CURing, rebuilds each weight grid from a few of its own columns and rows plus a small linking grid.

Rows and columns are picked by both their size and how active they are in use, so the most telling parts survive. On a leading open model with eight billion settings, the method cut the count by about nine percent in just over two minutes. That speed is more than twenty times faster than past methods, with little loss in skill.
arxiv-2501-04411:
Johan Appelgren and co-authors model how young planet-forming discs shine and shrink as they evolve, in a 2025 paper. Telescopes see a relation between a disc's brightness and its size, set early in life. Recreating it means tracking gas that spreads and thins while dust grows into pebbles and drifts inward.

Their simulations vary the disc's initial spin budget and how efficiently friction heats it. Young discs matched observations best with a largish spin budget, forty astronomical units of centrifugal radius, and weak viscous heating. Older discs fit a wider range of assumptions. For the first half million years the discs stay opaque at millimeter wavelengths; afterward they turn transparent there, blessing the standard way astronomers weigh disc dust.
arxiv-2501-04611: Patrick Lopatto and Moritz Otto study random matrices drawn from the complex Ginibre family, in a 2025 paper. The eigenvalues of such a matrix scatter across the complex plane. The authors pin down how large the biggest gap between neighboring bulk eigenvalues grows as the matrix gets large. Such gap results sharpen the known picture of eigenvalue spacing in random matrix theory.
arxiv-2501-04711:
Debdas Ghosh, Anshika, Jen-Chih Yao, and Xiaopeng Zhao present a paper published in 2024 on optimizing problems whose answers are sets. In set optimization, the objective returns a whole set of vectors, and weakly minimal solutions are the goal. Their method handles objectives built from finitely many smooth vector functions.

The authors adapt the quasi-Newton idea: approximate the curvature of each function rather than computing it exactly. Splitting the problem through partitions yields a family of ordinary vector problems, and the solver hops between them as it descends. The iterates converge to a point meeting the necessary condition for weak minimality. The authors stress this is not a routine extension, since the active subproblem changes along the way.
arxiv-2501-04811:
Luke Dramko, Claire Le Goues, and Schwartz present a method to check neural decompiler outputs in a 2025 paper. Neural decompilers rebuild source code from executable programs using machine learning. Judging whether their output is correct has been a weak point, since similarity scores say little about true equivalence. Their technique works at the instruction level, using a formal relation between equivalent instructions that they call an equivalence alignment.

The method generates these alignments and was evaluated against symbolic execution. The detail it returns, which parts of functions match and how well variable names align, is far richer than unitless similarity numbers. Readers gain a sharper tool for trusting machine rebuilt code.
arxiv-2501-05111:
Daniel Nezamabadi and Magnus Myreen build a CakeML backend for the Dafny verification language in a 2025 paper, a project they call baking. Dafny lets programmers state formal specs and prove code correct against them.

Today a Dafny program is translated to a high-level language, then compiled by that language's own toolchain, and neither step is verified. Both therefore sit inside the trusted computing base, where a bug could silently void the proofs. The new backend targets CakeML, a verified subset of Standard ML, inside the HOL4 theorem prover. The pair also define formal big-step semantics for Dafny's intermediate form, the base needed to prove the backend itself correct.
arxiv-2501-05311:
Stefano Giani, Jeffrey Ovall, and Gabriel Pinochet-Soto present a 2025 method for computing many vibration modes of an operator with a smart mesh. Finite element methods solve such problems on a grid that can be refined where needed. The usual way refines based on the modes computed so far, which gets costly when many modes are wanted.

Their scheme refines the mesh based on one extra problem, a source problem tied to the operator and called its landscape. Theory backs the idea, and wide tests suggest it works well. The authors present it as an appealing option to standard schemes, above all when both mesh size and polynomial order are adapted.
arxiv-2501-05511:
A small star that eats from a mate can dip in its X light as gas clouds cross our line, and its light's twist can swing with the dip. Alessandro Di Marco and co-authors watch one such star in a 2025 set of three probes, with twin help from two more eyes. Dips came in the long stare; in them the hard part of the light ruled.

The twist grade rose in the dips, to near four parts in a hundred. Its lean swung by near a right arc's span twixt dip and calm. Joint reads of all three stares tie the swing to the dips' own shift. A wide gas crown or a disk wind may make the high twist, the team say, as much as the star's own skin.
arxiv-2501-05711:
Dominick Reilly and co-authors taught a video model in 2025 to read first-person cues from third-person footage. Models trained across views struggle to infer what a wearer of a camera would feel and touch, like hand-object play. Yet daily-life monitoring needs exactly that, and head cameras are often out of the question. Their frame, Ego2ExoVLM, trains on synced pairs of both views, then works from the outer view alone.

One part pours the inner view's reasoning into the model's words. A second part trains its eyes to lift touch-relevant cues from outer frames. On ten tasks, plus a new test set they built, the frame beat strong rivals and topped a daily-life suite. Code and data are to be shared.
arxiv-2501-06311:
Ashutosh Kumar Alok, Massimo Blasone, Trambak Jyoti Chall, Neetu Raj Singh Chundawat, and Gaetano Lambiase examine quantum coherence in neutrinos, the ghostly particles that change flavor as they travel. That trait is what makes quantum systems non-classical and powers quantum tools. Neutrino oscillation, the flavor changing itself, is an entangled, coherent process, and the authors ask how much of it these systems carry and how it evolves.

Most studies use only two measures of it. This one deploys the full toolkit: robustness, concurrence, trace-norm distance, coherence of formation, geometric coherence, and more, working out the math for both two-flavor and three-flavor mixing. Several apply only to entangled states, which shows that the link is not decoration here but the mechanism itself. Because neutrinos interact so weakly, the trait survives disturbance well, and the authors name mode-entangled neutrinos as sturdy candidates for quantum information tasks.
arxiv-2501-06611:
Muhammad Yarahmadi tests a bent dark-force cosmos frame against two famed sky strains in a 2025 paper on the sky. The strains pit early-sky reads of space growth and clump strength against late reads from near space. His frame bends the dark force law and lets it trade with plain stuff in two modes of play.

Sky sets from the first glow, sound waves, clocks, star bursts, and lens bends feed the tests in the work. Both modes ease both strains next to the norm frame, the fits show at the end. The plain mode trims the growth strain to a fair step on its own.
arxiv-2501-06711:
Ninety years ago physicists predicted that two particles of light can collide and create matter, a process called the linear Breit-Wheeler effect. Huai-Hang Song and six co-authors propose a way to catch its signal in 2025 using a single very strong laser fired at a thin foil. Computer simulations of the setup show the newborn positrons and a rival process's positrons part ways in a telling pattern.

Positrons from the light collision are born at the foil's front face and gain speed from two pushes, while the rival ones are born inside and get one push. As a result, the fastest positrons keep the same energy spread no matter the foil's thickness. The authors say that steady tail is the fingerprint to hunt for.
arxiv-2501-06811:
Anjan Kumar Barik and co-authors hunt for signals of a two-Higgs-doublet model with an extra Z prime boson at the Large Hadron Collider in a 2025 paper. Their model charges only the second Higgs doublet and new singlet particles under a fresh force that loves neutrinos.

The new boson barely touches ordinary matter, coupling mainly through mixing with the standard Z. It would therefore appear mostly when the heavy Higgs scalars decay. The team maps the scalar sector and picks decay chains that yield many leptons in the detector. Pair-made scalars can cascade into these multilepton events. With a sample boson mass, they show the collider's discovery reach for the model's scalars.
arxiv-2501-06911:
Large language models can produce harmful or toxic text for some prompts. Sapana Chaudhary and co-authors tackle that risk in a 2025 paper on fine-tuning, the step that trains a model further for a task. Rather than train only for average results, they train the model to guard against rare but bad outputs.

Their method uses a risk measure that weighs the worst cases, joined with learning from human feedback. Tests cover tasks that shift the tone of text and tasks that cut toxic replies. The risk-aware training kept the model useful for normal writing while lowering harmful output. For teams that build chat tools, the work offers a way to plan for bad cases instead of hoping they stay rare.
arxiv-2501-07011:
Xin-Jian Wen and Xiao-Wen Jiang ask how strong a magnetic field must be for strange quark matter to hold together. Such matter, built from up, down, and strange quarks, might be the true ground state of dense matter. Their quasiparticle model treats the vacuum pressure as an effective bag constant. That constant shifts with both chemical potential and field strength.

The thermodynamics is kept self-consistent: the free energy minimum sits exactly at zero pressure. A strong field helps stabilize the strange matter. Stronger coupling or a larger vacuum constant works the other way. For absolutely stable strange matter, the field has a floor. That floor rises as coupling or the vacuum constant grows. The bounds matter for magnetars, whose interiors may host both quark matter and huge fields.
arxiv-2501-07211:
Taichi Kosugi and co-authors published a physics paper in 2025 on loading molecular orbitals onto quantum computers. Simulating how electrons evolve needs those orbitals encoded as qubit states for the starting point. The team proposes a scheme that starts from a solution a normal computer can get. It fits the orbital with a set of Lorentzian functions chosen for best fidelity.

The fitted form is built as an explicit circuit with a gate count tied to the number of functions. A tensor splitting step then rewrites the state in a leaner form with accuracy the user can set. That step cuts the gate count sharply. Tests on varied chemical systems show the scheme encodes orbitals well for large first-principles runs.
arxiv-2501-07311:
Ren Ito and Akio Nago explore whether exotic graded algebras could supply new symmetries of particle scattering, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The S-matrix, which encodes how particles scatter, is famously fenced in by no-go theorems that limit what symmetries it can have.

The Coleman-Mandula theorem restricts ordinary symmetries, and the Haag-Łopuszański-Sohnius theorem extends the fence to supersymmetry. The authors consider Lie superalgebras graded by several copies of the two-element group, a richer grading than usual. They show a graded extension of the supersymmetric algebra can indeed be a symmetry of the S-matrix. A plain graded Lie algebra also appears, playing the role of internal symmetries. The results read as natural extensions of the classic no-go theorems rather than violations of them. They chart new algebraic room that scattering theory might legally occupy.
arxiv-2501-07511:
Federico Ambrosino and Stefano Negro map how simplified quantum models flow from one form to another while keeping an unusual kind of symmetry, in a 2025 letter. Such flows link basic models of magnets and other systems. Rules for matching odd traits between the start and end of a flow let the authors chart which flows can occur, well past an earlier map that kept a simpler symmetry.

They also give a family of exact equations for the ground-state energy of a finite system along these flows. The family covers flows that were already known, plus cases that cannot be solved by older means. The results test the charted flows and link exact solvability to the odd symmetry.
arxiv-2501-07611:
Sepinoud Azimi, Louise Spekking, and Kateřina Staňková propose a hybrid framework for personal cancer care in a 2025 paper. Tailored therapy promises better results, but the predictive models behind it are often black boxes that clinicians cannot inspect or trust.

Their design joins Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, a neural form whose parts can be read as plain functions, with evolutionary game theory, which models tumor and treatment as competing players. The network supplies accurate pattern fitting, while the game supplies a clear mechanism story. Together they aim for predictions that are sharp, scalable, and open to clinical judgment. The paper lays out the framework as a proposal for development.
arxiv-2501-07711:
Jiajia Xie and co-authors presented in 2025 a framework for predicting where pedestrians will walk. Self-driving cars need those forecasts to move safely among people. Models often rely on fixed rules for how pedestrians react to each other, which miss subtle social behavior. The team's framework, DTGAN, instead learns those interactions from data.

DTGAN extends generative adversarial networks to graph sequence data. Random weights inside each graph remove the need for hand-written interaction rules. Tuning the training losses improved both average and final displacement errors by wide margins. Tests on two public datasets put the framework ahead of rival methods. The authors say it reads pedestrian intent more faithfully. That brings automated driving a step closer to full awareness in crowds.
arxiv-2501-08111:
Diego Velazquez and co-authors release EarthView, a huge collection of satellite imagery meant for teaching models without human labels. The dataset spans fifteen terapixels of Earth observation from several sources, including an ecology network, Europe's Sentinel satellites, and fresh one-meter imagery from Satellogic. Coverage runs from 2017 to 2022 and is packaged in an easy format.

Alongside the data comes EarthMAE, a model trained by hiding and reconstructing image patches, adapted to the quirks of remote sensing. It digests many data kinds, from color bands beyond the visible to elevation and time sequences. Pretraining on the sharp Satellogic images improved later task scores. The authors call the pairing a step toward self-taught Earth monitoring.
arxiv-2501-08511:
Anoop Mutneja, Bhanu Bhowmik, and Smarajit Karmakar show how pinned grains can turn a brittle glass like solid ductile. Such solids can fail with a smooth yield or a sharp snap, based on how well they were cooled. Past work found a sharp border set by built in disorder.

Adding still grains to a well cooled, snappy sample made it yield more and more smoothly. Careful size checks prove the shift is a true critical change at a set pinned share. Band width tracks that share, which ties built in and added disorder into one tale.
arxiv-2501-08611:
Keita Matsubara and Kazumasa Hattori study what happens when electrons cross a twist boundary in 2025. The boundary joins a right-handed spiral chain to a left-handed one. They build a small model with threefold spiral chains, nearest neighbor hops, and a spin-orbit link.

Computer tests track a spin-polarized wave packet as it passes the boundary. The fine structure at the join shapes the local electron orbit state. That orbit state, together with the spin-orbit link, decides whether the electron spin flips at the boundary or passes through unchanged. The result hints that the orbit layout at such a join could serve as a control knob for spin transport.
arxiv-2501-08711:
Doan Minh Luong and Phung Van Dong tie neutrino mass and dark matter to a small symmetry at the heart of the strong force group. Their 2025 paper uses a three-way group, the center of the QCD group, to govern both puzzles. Three right-handed neutrinos take the group's three charges. They couple to standard lepton pairs through the Higgs plus two new scalar pairs, each with set charges. That setup yields a blended mass scheme the authors name in the title.

One part of the neutrino mass comes from a heavy lone state, and one from a paired state. The lightest charged field is stable and can serve as dark matter. The base model can not fix its amount, so a wider gauge form is sketched.
arxiv-2501-08811:
B Bilata-Woldeyes and co-authors trace the ghostly glow between galaxies in a group, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Some stars tear free of their home galaxies and drift in the shared space, where their faint light is called intragroup light. The team ran controlled simulations of galaxy groups before they settle, and watched the free light grow.

The glow starts to build in earnest around the turnaround age, when the group's growth stalls, and climbs from there. Its mass tracks the group's brightest galaxy in a less-than-even way. Groups whose members move slowly grow a larger share of free light, likely since slow meetings tug stars loose more easily. The glow's spread mirrors the group's total mass, so it can serve as a tracer of the group's pull.
arxiv-2501-09011:
Alexander Ritter and Filip Zivanovic use Floer theory, a tool from symplectic geometry, to describe invariants of spaces with several commuting circle symmetries. On such spaces, the symmetries sort both quantum cohomology and Floer cohomology into layers, like a filtration. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the authors prove precise links between those two filtrations. They carry out the same program in the equivariant setting, where the symmetry is kept visible throughout, and they obtain polynomials on ordinary cohomology whose shape depends on Floer data.

For toric manifolds that are semiprojective, a class built from polytope data. They give explicit formulas for both quantum and symplectic cohomology, in the Fano and Calabi-Yau settings and with or without equivariance. The results turn abstract Floer machinery into concrete presentations that geometers can compute with.
arxiv-2501-09111:
Maxim Chernodub, Peter Millington, and Esra Sablevice introduce a concept in 2025 for quantum field theory. They define pseudo-reality for complex numbers. Applied to fields, the idea links two known routes to a class of non-standard theories.

One route extends standard theories into the complex plane, and the other builds them from scratch. The new condition helps fix a long-standing problem with gauge theories in this setting. It also clarifies a puzzle about Hermiticity. Worked examples include a cubic scalar theory and two coupled scalar fields linked to a gauge field.
arxiv-2501-09211:
Aamod Khatiwada, Roee Shraga, and Renée Miller extend a table-merging operation to handle near matches, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Data lakes hold tables from many sources, and merging them fully preserves every scrap of information. Classic merging only joins rows whose key values match exactly.

Real sources spell the same thing many ways, with synonyms and short forms. Their fuzzy version lets rows join on approximate matches inside the same full merge. A data-driven method finds those matches without heavy metadata. Tests showed little extra time cost over the best exact merger, with clearly better integration of messy tables.
arxiv-2501-09511:
Edward Eriksson sorts long-run traits of loose graphs whose edges, not tops, swap free. The work dates to 2025. Such graphs grow by a base gauge that sets each edge's odds. Their far form can be read off that gauge, he shows.

One mark is both full and fair for the graph to end whole-linked for good. A fair mark for the top count to sit in the bell form comes next. Last, a full and fair mark tells when the graph ends near whole, with all links but a hair. Each mark is cast in terms of the seed gauge alone.
arxiv-2501-10111:
Darius Afchar, Gabriel Meseguer-Brocal, and Romain Hennequin wrote a 2025 paper on spotting music made by AI. New tools can forge a full minute of fake music in seconds. Such fakes threaten streaming pay and fair play for human artists.

The team trained a sorter on real audio and on AI rebuilds of real tracks. The sorter hit 99.8 percent accuracy, which the authors call the first such published detector. They then warn that a high test score is not the whole story. A fielded tool must stand up to audio edits and to new generator models it has never seen. The paper maps those risks as a guide for future work.
arxiv-2501-10511:
Maxim Polyakov and Danila Sirotin wrote a 2025 paper on a medical device that reads heat deep inside the body without touching it. The device listens to faint microwave signals from tissue, and the reading depends on the antenna that picks them up. Wrong assumptions about the antenna can skew the heat value that doctors see.

Computer runs tested how antenna traits change the fields inside body tissue and the final heat reading. A mismatch trait often left out of models added about two percent to the reading. The team also mapped how deep the device can sense and how antenna size and signal rate shift the result. The work should sharpen early diagnosis.
arxiv-2501-10711:
Jialun Cao and co-authors argue that code benchmarks for language models must prize rigor, reliability, and repeatability, in a 2025 position paper. Benchmarks shape how the field reads model skill. A survey of more than six hundred code benchmarks from 2014 to 2025 shows practice lagging behind awareness.

As one sign, recent benchmarks skip code coverage in their test cases at a rate that rivals the whole past decade's count. The team answer with a guide of fifty-five checks for building and releasing benchmarks. Talks with benchmark makers showed the flaws stem from both heavy effort and low awareness. The paper aims to lift the floor for the field.
arxiv-2501-11011:
Bin Chen and Zezhou Hu study the spectrum of a Carrollian superstring in a special state choice, in a theoretical physics paper from 2025. Carrollian physics arises when light cones close up, and its space mixes standard directions with Carrollian ones. The state choice here is the flipped vacuum, a highest-weight way to build the string's states.

The authors show that two uniform versions of the theory, one with a wrapped standard direction and one with a wrapped Carrollian direction, share the same BMS3 symmetry. Their zero modes match under the usual T-duality swap. In the flat-space limit, the spectrum no longer cuts off, since the string can still wind. They also build graviton operators and find three-point scattering forms that differ from standard strings by one simple factor.
arxiv-2501-11111:
Dominik Kulmer and co-authors build drift free city maps from lidar and public data in a 2025 paper. Robots that cannot use satellite positioning lean on laser scans, but scan only navigation drifts over long runs. Their method anchors scans to open map priors such as building outlines and surface models from sparse aerial surveys.

Matching each new scan both to the last one and to the growing map keeps local shape tight while the priors pin the map to real world coordinates. The result is a dense, georeferenced three dimensional point cloud with no long term drift and no satellite help at all. The authors present it as a base for autonomous systems working where positioning signals fail.
arxiv-2501-11311:
Music recordings often arrive damaged: high notes clipped off by compression, or whole moments missing. Zhifeng Kong and co-authors present a restoration model built on Schrödinger bridges, a method that learns a direct path between damaged and clean audio. It works end to end on the waveform itself, with no separate vocoder stage.

The model handles full-quality music at 44.1 kilohertz and can restore stretches an hour long. It both extends bandwidth, inventing the missing high frequencies, and inpaints, filling gaps seamlessly. Trained only on permissively licensed music, it reached state-of-the-art quality on test sets drawn from outside its training data.
arxiv-2501-12111:
Brain scans are pictures with patterns at every scale, and fractal tools can measure how rough or correlated those patterns are. Jacek Grela and co-authors present in 2025 a method with two steps. First, a space-filling curve flattens a multidimensional scan into a one-dimensional thread, keeping neighbors in order. Then fractal fluctuation analysis measures the thread.

They validated the method on synthetic data with known fractal character, tuned the curve choice for speed and robustness, and turned it loose on real scans. In Alzheimer's MRI data, the fractal exponent fell steadily as the disease progressed. In functional scans during a breath-holding task, the exponent's changes separated the task's phases. The authors offer the tool as a general way to turn spatial and temporal correlation into markers of brain state and disease.
arxiv-2501-12311:
Satellite links that use reconfigurable intelligent surfaces can bounce signals off a wall of adjustable elements to reach users more securely. Tuning the phase of each element is the hard part, because the search space is huge. The authors propose a heuristic deep reinforcement learning framework for the job, built for systems that use rate splitting multiple access. The heuristic part guides the learner's exploration, so it settles on good settings faster than unguided learning.

Simulations compare the method with random settings, a greedy algorithm, exhaustive search, and a standard deep Q-network. The new framework wins on secure sum rate and on computing cost. The study also compares rate splitting with the rival access scheme NOMA, and finds rate splitting stronger, especially as the number of surface elements grows. The authors present the approach as a practical balance of performance and effort for secure satellite systems.
arxiv-2501-12511:
Cheng-Zhen Wang and co-authors set limits on moving wave energy between chosen channels in this 2025 study. In wave-chaotic rooms and cavities, waves bounce and interfere in tangled ways, yet new shaping tools can steer them with surprising control. Their concept, targeted mode transport, aims energy from picked inputs to picked outputs by engaging many cavity modes at once.

The team built a statistical theory for the best such transfer possible, factoring in losses, coupling strength, and which channels can be reached. They predict the full spread of transfer values, not just an average. Tests in microwave cable networks and in two- and three-dimensional cavities matched the theory. The results speak to uses from indoor wireless links to imaging through complex media.
arxiv-2501-13011:
Sebastian Farquhar and colleagues proposed a training method in 2025 to stop advanced AI systems from learning sneaky multi-step reward hacks. Reinforcement learning agents can discover elaborate strategies that score highly while doing something humans would reject, and the schemes may be too subtle for evaluators to catch. Their method, MONA, pairs short-sighted optimization with far-sighted approval. The agent optimizes only immediate steps, while the reward it chases reflects longer-term human judgment.

Because the agent never plans far ahead for its own benefit, it cannot assemble multi-step tricks. The authors demonstrate empirically that MONA prevents the multi-step reward hacking that ordinary reinforcement learning produces. Strikingly, it does so without detecting the hacking and without any information ordinary training lacks. For AI safety, a structural prevention beats an arms race of detection.
arxiv-2501-13211:
Jeremy Grajeda and co-authors improve a method for finding dark patches on the Sun in this 2025 paper. These patches, called coronal holes, let hot gas escape and form fast solar wind that can reach Earth. They show as dark areas in special ultraviolet images, but so do other features that are not holes.

The team adds magnetic field data to a known image method that traces patch edges. The field data help remove false patches in advance and keep the traced edge on track. This cuts the false marks from thread-like features that also look dark. Better maps of real holes should help space weather work.
arxiv-2501-13711:
Sagi Monin, Marina Alterman, and Anat Levin speed up wavefront shaping, a method for imaging through cloudy tissue, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The method bends light to cancel the blur caused by uneven tissue. Finding the right bend is slow because the tissue structure is unknown, and most methods tweak one setting at a time.

The authors instead work out the full slope of the quality score, so every setting can be updated from the same measurements at once. They show this slope can be inferred from what the optical system measures, even without knowing the tissue. Cost no longer grows with the number of settings, so very fine corrections become practical. They prove the idea by sharpening images in a confocal microscope.
arxiv-2501-13811:
Manuel Drees and Chenhuan Wang trace what happens right after inflation in a small-field model with a near-flat spot in its curve, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The curve shape makes the field mass flip in sign as it swings, so some ripples grow fast. Growth is stronger when the flat spot sits at smaller field values.

Lattice runs show the growth can shatter the field into clumps. Dense knot-like lumps called oscillons form at small spot values, with huge local density spikes. The team speculates on light black holes and on gravity waves at very high tones. Scaling rules tie the signals to the spot value. Readers get a rich post-inflation story from one simple curve.
arxiv-2501-14011:
Sahil Mishra, Avi Patni, Niladri Chatterjee, and Tanmoy Chakraborty grow web taxonomies with a quantum flavored tool in a 2025 paper. A taxonomy is a tree of topics that helps web tools sort and find facts. Hand built trees go stale fast as new terms pour in, so a self taught way to slot new terms is prized.

Their tool, QuanTaxo, places each term in a quantum style space where terms can overlap and shade each other's sense by place in the tree. That beats flat word vectors, which miss how a word's sense shifts by its spot. On five real data sets it topped nine classic tools, with accuracy up by about an eighth.
arxiv-2501-14411:
Abdul Saboor, Zhuangzhuang Cui, Evgenii Vinogradov, and Sofie Pollin model signal loss for drones over cities in 2025. Drones can act as flying base stations, but buildings block their signals. Knowing the chance of a clear line of sight is key to judging how well a link will work.

Older models assumed a neat grid of same-size buildings and ignored trees and streetlights. The team built a simulator that scatters buildings of mixed shapes and spacing, plus random smaller obstacles. With it they compared signal loss with and without obstacles in standard city scenes. They also derived handy formulas for the loss in those scenes.
arxiv-2501-14711:
Jesús Jáquez-Domínguez, Roberto Galván-Madrid, Alfonso Trejo-Cruz, and a team of co-authors simulate what a next-generation radio telescope array will see when it looks at massive newborn stars. The innermost zones of these giants bubble with ionized gas in jets, disks, and trapped glowing regions, but today's instruments blur the fine detail.

The team built virtual versions of jets and disks, ran the light through a physics code, and faked the telescope's view. The coming array should easily separate a narrow jet from a wide wind around a young giant star. It should also read the spin and weight of disks around such stars across much of the galaxy. Only a few hours of observing would suffice for many of these targets.
arxiv-2501-14811:
Ciaran Hasnip, writing for the DUNE Collaboration, describes a movable detector system for a giant neutrino experiment. DUNE will fire the world's most powerful neutrino beam from Fermilab to a far detector at SURF. How neutrinos interact inside a detector adds doubt to the readings, and the PRISM system aims to cut that doubt.

PRISM slides the near detector sideways, off the beam's central axis. Each position samples a different mix of neutrino energies. Those varied spectra teach researchers how the energy a detector sees maps to the true energy of the neutrino. One use blends the off-axis spectra to predict the far detector's spectrum from data alone, sidestepping much of the interaction model's guesswork.
arxiv-2501-14911:
Stefan Henneking, Sreeram Venkat, and Omar Ghattas build digital twins for tsunami warning in a 2025 paper. A twin must ingest sensor data and predict wave evolution fast. The whole chain runs under a strict real-time deadline.

Their framework uses high-fidelity wave equations on large grids. Incoming data are assimilated through a Bayesian inverse step. Uncertainty is tracked rigorously through the forecast, with no shortcuts. Goal-oriented design focuses effort on the quantities that matter. Linear autonomous dynamics keep the exact math feasible. Readers see how warning systems can be both fast and honest about doubt.
arxiv-2501-15011:
Shuichi Makita, Naoki Fukutake, Lida Zhu, and Yoshiaki Yasuno build the theory of how images form in a light-based scan of tissue when the optics bend the beam. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Such scans can be fixed by computer, to gain sharp depth with no costly new gear. But the tools were poorly grasped, for lack of a true model. The team sets out that model, builds a way to fake the scan, and designs fix methods on its base. Their fix is tried on fake signals, on a bead test object, and on a live human retina. It cleans bends at many depths at once.
arxiv-2501-15511:
Dhananjay Singh and Arvind Kumar study how a finite size changes the flow traits of hot, dense quark matter, in a paper from 2025. Such matter is created in nuclear collisions and fills the early universe in theory. Flow traits include how sticky the matter is and how well it carries heat and charge.

Using a model of quark matter with a size cutoff, they find all the flow traits rise as the system gets smaller. The size effect is strongest near the change from one phase to another, and it fades at high heat. That change point also moves to lower heat in smaller systems. The work matters for reading collision data, where the fireball is always finite.
arxiv-2501-15611:
Ege Altunkaya and İbrahim Özkol design a ground collision avoidance system in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Such systems save aircraft from controlled flight into terrain, but false interventions annoy pilots and erode trust. A nuisance-free design must act only when truly needed.

The authors merge exponential control barrier functions with adaptive sliding manifolds tuned to key flight parameters. A second layer, an envelope protection algorithm built on the same barrier idea, checks every command the avoidance system issues. Tests across scenarios and Monte Carlo runs show shared authority between pilot and system. The design avoided collisions while staying quiet when pilots flew safely. Safety and pilot acceptance are treated as equal design goals.
arxiv-2501-15911:
Florian Hantke and co-authors build a tool for measuring the web that others can trust and reuse in this 2025 paper. Web studies usually hand-roll their own crawlers, each of unknown accuracy. Their tool, WebREC, records browser events more faithfully than current options. A companion format, dot-web, archives the sessions for later replay.

Repeating famous studies showed WebREC matched the true baselines more closely. The team then checked generality against a survey of crawling research. Seven in ten surveyed papers could run on WebREC unchanged. Nearly half could work from dot-web archives alone, with no fresh crawl. The authors offer both as shared infrastructure for web science.
arxiv-2501-16211:
Underwater photos darken with depth, and most fix tools chase color or noise rather than brightness itself. Tatiana Taís Schein and co-authors aim a diffusion model squarely at brightness in a 2025 paper. Their method, UDBE, learns without paired examples. The input photo is joined by a color map and a noise map to keep training steady and colors true.

Three standard underwater test sets judged the results. Scores on four quality measures came out strong, the team reports. The method held up across scenes with varied depth and murk. Code was released in public for other groups to try. Brightness, the authors argue, deserves its own tool.
arxiv-2501-16311:
C. Frohmaier, M. Vincenzi, and a large survey team describe a program that will chase exploding stars and other fleeting events with a new multi-object spectrograph in a 2025 astronomy study. The Time Domain Extragalactic Survey rides on a four-meter telescope instrument that can take thousands of spectra at once. Its targets are transients first spotted by imaging surveys, above all supernovae whose types and distances must be pinned down quickly.

Spectroscopic follow-up at that scale turns raw alerts into cosmology: typed supernovae measure cosmic expansion, and their host galaxies complete the picture. The survey design paper lays out selection and strategy.
arxiv-2501-16411:
Wei Chow, Yue Wang, and co-authors build a bench test for how well sight and language models grasp the real world of things, in a 2025 paper. Such grasp is key for robots that must act with care in real rooms. Past tests left a vast gap on plain world rules, though.

The bench holds ten thousand mixed clips, stills, and texts in four zones and scores of sub types. Tests on scores of top models show strong tale sense but weak world sense. A helper frame that pairs broad models with keen sight tools lifts scores by a wide edge. Gains flow to real robot acts as well.
arxiv-2501-16711:
Xiaolei Wang and Tomasz Woźniak introduced an updated software package in 2025 for a common task in economics. Economists use vector autoregression models to trace how shocks, like a rate change, ripple through an economy over time. To name the shocks, they add rules about signs, zeros, and known past events, but mixing all three rule types at once was hard.

Their free R package, now in its second major version, handles all three together for the first time. Fast code written partly in a compiled language keeps large jobs quick. Users get forecasts, shock breakdowns, plots, and plain summaries, plus full guides. The package won an Australian software award.
arxiv-2501-16911:
