TeTRA squeezes the transformer step by step down to two bit precision and binarizes its final embedding layer. A staged distillation plan keeps the small model's power close to its full size teacher. On standard benchmarks TeTRA cut memory use by up to 69 percent and latency by 35 percent against efficient baselines, with recall equal or slightly better. The authors aim it at real field robots.
arxiv-2503-02611:
Parker Knight, Ndey Isatou Jobe, and Rui Duan published a 2025 statistics paper on finding effects that stay the same across different datasets. Prediction models often fail when moved between hospitals or populations, because most patterns shift. A few influences, though, may act identically everywhere. Models built on those invariant features could travel safely. Finding them has been slow or fragile in earlier methods.

The authors present a framework that estimates invariant effects quickly and under flexible assumptions. A robust extension guards against a corrupted or misspecified data source, so one bad dataset cannot poison the rest. Simulations confirm the protection works. They then build a transferable prediction model for a health endpoint as a demonstration. The work targets precision health, where a model trained in one clinic must serve another. Invariant structure, they argue, is the part of the data worth trusting abroad.
arxiv-2503-02811:
Wang and Anlage build a microwave microscope to watch single trapped vortices move in superconductors, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Trapped vortices add resistance in radio cavities and upset quantum circuits. Their detailed motion under oscillating fields was hard to observe. The new probe applies a local radio field and listens for a faint echo.

The echo at twice the drive frequency comes only from trapped vortices. It excludes signals from surface flaws and shielding currents. Simulations of niobium with pinning sites match the measured patterns well. Tests on a film with an antidot array resolve pinning traits micron by micron. The tool can catch single depinning events as they happen.
arxiv-2503-02911:
Xuan Cai and co-authors turn plain text into self-driving test scenes in a 2025 paper. Hand-built scenes eat hours and slow car stack checks. Their frame, Text2Scenario, lets a language model read a test wish in plain words. A tuned prompt scheme guides the parse. Parts come from a tiered scene bank, picked to fit the wish. A domain tongue then links the parts in run order into a workable test.

Most built scenes matched the wish with care, the team report. Fine scene marks hid in loose text forms yet still came out. Stack checks can now run sans hand scene craft. The authors pitch text as the new scene desk for car tests.
arxiv-2503-03311:
He-bin Zhang, Yuanjiang Tang, and Yong-Chun Liu show how to make light pass through an opaque medium in an extraordinarily narrow color band, in this 2025 paper. The classic effect, electromagnetically induced transparency, uses laser fields to open a see-through window in an atomic gas. Its window is normally wide, limited by how long the atoms' quiet state stays coherent.

Their version swaps in nuclear spins, the slow-turning compasses inside atomic nuclei, which keep their coherence far longer. They couple light and magnetic fields to a gas where alkali atoms exchange spin with noble-gas nuclei. The window they open is orders of magnitude narrower than the standard one, possibly below a thousandth of a hertz. So fine a filter could slow light to a crawl for storage, or sense magnetic fields with exquisite precision.
arxiv-2503-03711:
Elizabeth Paul and co-authors study wave patterns in stellarators, a type of fusion device, in a 2025 paper. Stellarators hold hot plasma in twisted magnetic fields. Waves in that plasma can drain energy from fast particles, so designers need to know where wave tones can and cannot live.

The team built theory for fields with a near-symmetry that stellarator designers favour. Using a near-axis model, they solved for the wave bands and gaps and checked the math with number-based examples. Field shape changed the gap pattern in clear ways. The work ends with a design tuned to dodge high-tone gaps, a step toward steadier fusion machines.
arxiv-2503-03811:
Yael Alush and Nicholas Stone follow torn-apart stars in twenty twenty-five. When a star passes too close to a black hole, it is shredded into an accretion disk. Classic disk models predict the inner region should be viscously unstable. Late-time observations of these tidal disruption disks show no such instability.

Rather than patching the viscosity recipe, the authors change the physics. Their time-dependent disk model is dominated by magnetic pressure instead of radiation pressure. Such disks are thermally stable. Their ultraviolet light fades with a characteristic power law for decades to centuries. A simpler linear viscosity model can mimic that fade for chosen parameters. The disks also stay ultraviolet bright for a long time. Readers get a physically motivated fix for a standing mismatch between theory and observation.
arxiv-2503-04111:
Lijia Yu and co-authors bound how well risk trim nets can do on new data by how much they can say, in a paper from 2025. Old bounds lean on size counts that fail for fat nets, which oft read new data well in the field. Their bound rests on the net own say span.

With data and net size both rich, such nets can reach a set floor of new data truth, fat or lean. A must term flips the tale: for some data kinds, the data bulk a net needs to read true past its own size. Fruit reads shed light on firm truth, fat gain, and loss pick in deep learn, they say.
arxiv-2503-04311:
Jesse Laeuchli and Rolando Trujillo Rasua examine a proposal to use quantum devices to prove that a remote gadget memory has not been tampered with. Remote attestation matters for small internet-connected devices, where a checker asks a possibly compromised device to prove its memory state. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the authors pick apart a published quantum-based attestation procedure and find flaws and traps in its reasoning. They also argue that attesting quantum memory itself is a fundamentally different problem from attesting ordinary memory, because of limits on copying and reading quantum states.

Lessons from the failure feed a redesign. Their replacement protocol attests classical memory with quantum tools while using less communication and offering stronger security. The paper is written for designers of quantum security protocols who must assume the proving device may be corrupt.
arxiv-2503-04511:
Broadcasting means spreading a message from any starting node to every node in a network as fast as possible, and the leanest networks that still allow it are called minimum broadcast graphs. Pierre Fraigniaud and Hovhannes Harutyunyan study these networks under a space constraint: each node may store only an ordered list of neighbors, saying in what order to pass a message on.

The constraint turns out to cost nothing. For every network size, the authors find graphs where such simple list-based protocols still finish in the fewest possible rounds, matching what unrestricted protocols achieve. The same graphs stay nearly as sparse as the sparsest known broadcast graphs, within a constant factor. The result says compact local instructions are enough for optimal spreading.
arxiv-2503-04711:
Gonzalo Álvarez-Pérez and co-authors show that free electrons in semiconductor waveguides can bend light with unusual strength, in a 2025 physics paper. The Kerr effect answers almost instantly but is normally too weak to use. In heavily doped semiconductors, waves of free electrons called bulk plasmons add a huge response of this kind, which the team computed with a fluid-style model of the electron gas.

The predicted strength surpasses ten million per watt-kilometer, and the guided light modes travel over a hundred micrometers. The effect survived checks with damping included. Built into an interferometer, the waveguide shifted its transmitted spectrum on command, showing light-only control of mid-infrared light. The authors pitch the design for compact photonic circuits.
arxiv-2503-04811:
Amos Brocco extends a software library that keeps shared data in sync across copies, in a paper from 2025. The library, Melda, handles data in a common web format and lets many users edit at once without clashes. Reordering items in a list already worked, but moving items between lists went wrong.

Moves used to yield doubled entries, which broke the shared record. Brocco revisits the core method and adds the smallest changes that make moves work. The fix adds near no run cost and no storage cost over the prior version. The paper walks through the changes in detail and gives worked cases that show moves landing as they should.
arxiv-2503-05011:
Renjie Li and co-authors probe warm-hot gas around galaxy clusters in sim work dated 2025. Much of the normal matter in space hides in that gas, too dim to catch head-on. The team used The Three Hundred sim set, run with two physics codes. They tracked gas heat and share with distance from cluster cores.

Gas heat fell to the warm-hot cap at a set span out. The warm-hot share rose with span, then leveled near seventy percent. Fake X-ray views show the gas adds more glow at wide spans. Stacked real sky data should catch that glow at a fair signal level.
arxiv-2503-05311:
Anirban Basak and Shaibal Karmakar count how often random graphs hold suspiciously many copies of a lopsided pattern. In the Erdős–Rényi graph, each possible edge appears with some small probability p. For regular patterns the odds of an excess are well understood; for irregular ones, where vertices carry uneven degrees, the team works out the upper tail of the count.

Across a wide band of p, they pin down the large deviation rate for any irregular pattern graph. In a sparser band, for balanced patterns, the excess behaves like a Poisson count with a growing mean. Star graphs fill the middle ground: there the excess comes from one crowded hub, a localized cause. Knowing which structure the rare event builds tells probabilists where to look.
arxiv-2503-05611:
Oxley and Kerswell show two push ways join to drive short growth in streak shear flow. Short growth in such flows is thought to keep wall rough flow alive. Three ways sit in play: Orr, lift-up, and push-over in the set. Past work found Orr and push-over must both sit to keep sway. Lift-up lone failed that role in the past streak runs. Their form is Kelvin's free shear with side streaks laid on.

In that form, push-over can pair with a streak Orr way. That pair makes much more short growth than each lone way. The pair clears the first growth tale from Schoppa and Hussain. It proves one half of a straight shake way at streak bends. Those bends were first seen by Swearingen and Blackwelder in print. Rolls from that shake can re-feed streaks by lift-up.
arxiv-2503-06011:
Panatchakorn Anantaprayoon, Masahiro Kaneko, and Naoaki Okazaki show that stating intentions clearly helps large language models correct their own biased outputs. Self-correction, where a model revises its answer from feedback, resembles slow, deliberate thinking and may cut social bias. But models react strongly to vague context, so the intent behind each step must be explicit. The authors split self-correction into three parts: instruction, response, and feedback.

In the instruction, a plain debiasing prompt states the goal. In the response, chain-of-thought text lays out the reasoning. In the feedback, defined aspects guide a scored, multi-angle critique. Experiments show this intent-aware setup reduces biased replies more steadily than standard baselines. Results also vary with the bias level of the model and with whether separate models write and judge the replies.
arxiv-2503-06111:
Nikola Sandrić gives a clean test for uniform ergodicity of diffusions in a 2025 note, writing solo. A diffusion driven by an Itô stochastic differential equation settles toward its steady law, and uniform ergodicity is the strong form of that settling. Sandrić states one integral condition, built from the drift and diffusion coefficients, that secures it.

The condition speaks to the transition kernel in total variation terms, a strict yardstick. Results then extend to a class of subordinate diffusion processes, where a base diffusion runs on a warped clock. The note adds a handy check to the ergodicity tool kit.
arxiv-2503-06211:
Cuervo and colleagues present in 2025 LF2AR, an architecture for adapting text-trained language models to audio and images. They start from a pattern seen inside transformers: layers first build abstract meaning, then refine fine detail. Perceptual inputs are finer-grained than text, so adaptation should add fine-to-coarse processing at the input and the reverse at the output. Their design combines late fusion, an output-side split they call late fission, and attention residuals.

Tested on text-as-images and speech tasks across model sizes, the design improved cross-modal alignment and benchmark scores. Alignment emerged with less compute, and sparse layer use allowed faster decoding.
arxiv-2503-06311:
Sizhen Bian, Vitor Fortes Rey, Siyu Yuan, and Paul Lukowicz test if the body's own electrostatic field can sense motion, as a partner to the standard inertial sensor. Human body capacitance sensing is a newer wearable mode with scant hard data to set it next to rivals. A gym workout tracker makes a tough real-world test case.

Ten volunteers logged fifty sessions. That gave fifty hours of marked-up data from both inertial and capacitance sensors. A hybrid network that mixes convolutions, dilated self-attention, and attention read both streams at once. The capacitance stream made workout recognition a bit better than inertial sensing on its own. For counting repetitions, it held substantial advantages. The team open-source their work to spur more work on this way of sensing.
arxiv-2503-06411:
Krti Tallam, a solo author, argues that AI governance needs moral imagination alongside technical controls, in a 2025 paper. Black-box systems in defense, finance, health, and education hide risks that pure engineering checks miss. The framework blends systems engineering, risk measurement, and ethical evaluation.

Case studies of a chatbot that turned abusive and a school grading algorithm that sparked public anger show how bias, weak security, and missing accountability cascade into lost trust. Tallam draws on two influential books about algorithms and systems thinking. The paper closes with strategies: adaptive rules, stronger security practice, and oversight that crosses disciplines.
arxiv-2503-07011:
Fauzi and three co-authors model what a spinning black hole would look like in a 2025 paper. They study a regular black hole, a type without a crushed center point. Pushed past its spin limit, such an object would turn into a naked superspinar. The team surrounds it with a thin disk of glowing matter.

Their images show the black hole looking much like the standard spinning kind, with small differences. The superspinar form shows an extra inner ring of light. They also model the change after a falling shell destroys the hole. Apart from a possible burst of light, the inner ring shifts slowly, over times that matter for giant black holes.
arxiv-2503-07511:
Chengmeng Li and colleagues give robot control models eyes for depth by adding point clouds to vision-language-action systems. Such models learn from flat images and vast image-text training, yet flat views limit their sense of space. Retraining them on 3D data costs too much, and dropping the 2D training wastes it. PointVLA instead freezes the trained action part and slips 3D features into its least useful blocks.

In tests the system beat leading 2D methods on both simulated and real robot tasks. It learned four tasks from twenty demos each, told real objects from photos of them, and coped with table heights never seen in training. It also handled long jobs like packing goods off a moving belt.
arxiv-2503-07711:
Fazeel Mahmood Khan and co-authors simulate how the odd compact galaxies nicknamed little red dots could become today's ellipticals in this 2025 paper. Webb telescope images found these early galaxies with dense centers and oversized black holes. Their descendants should be far less dense, which needs explaining.

The team ran direct simulations of such galaxies merging, following their black hole pairs into the gravitational-wave phase. During mergers, the paired holes fling stars out of the core, cutting central density by about tenfold. Kicks from gravitational waves can thin centers further. The change takes only a few hundred million years, so the dots could become normal ellipticals early. Merger times ranged widely with orbit and mass ratio. The authors call black hole pairs efficient remodelers of dense cores.
arxiv-2503-07811:
Florian Gunsilius gives a primer on optimal transport for causal work in a 2025 review. Optimal transport is a frame for comparing chance spreads by their base states. Causal work also turns on states that could have been, so the two fields fit well.

Yet clear work at their crossing is only now taking shape. Many classic causal models, Gunsilius shows, used transport ideas for years without naming them. The review ties the terms and symbols of math, statistics, and economics into one tongue. It also points to new problems both fields can take up. Readers new to either field get a shared starting map.
arxiv-2503-08311:
Recasens and co-authors argue in 2025 that the true brake on serving large language models in big batches is memory, not raw compute. Beyond a point, adding more requests stops helping, which most blame on compute limits. Their chip level study shows graphics memory bandwidth saturating while most computing units idle.

An advisor tool then trims memory per request with little speed loss. Freed memory and idle compute host copies of the model running side by side, lifting total throughput. The findings recast how serving fleets should be sized and shared. Smaller models hit the wall earliest, they note.
arxiv-2503-08611:
Linnea Heitmeier and Thomas Voigtmann study the surface of glass-forming fluids, in a 2025 preprint, when the fluid is being sheared. Surface tension normally gets read off from the pressure drop across a surface. That habit works for simple fluids at rest. Glass-forming fluids flow in a more complex way, and the surface itself can be put under shear. The authors ask what surface tension even means in that state.

They show that the usual pressure-drop recipe gives an effective value that mixes bulk and surface traits. That mix can mislead anyone measuring the surface of such a fluid. Using the unevenness of pressure in different directions, they mark off where the bulk ends and the surface begins. On that basis they pull out a true surface tension that does depend on shear rate. The results matter for lab methods that probe the surfaces of complex fluids.
arxiv-2503-08811:
Somnath Jana and co-authors use, in twenty twenty-five, element-specific light spectroscopy to settle a debate on ultrafast magnetism. In an iron-nickel alloy, a laser pulse strips magnetism from nickel a bit later than from iron. Two theories compete to explain the delay. One blames spin waves born at iron sites that then spread to nickel. The other claims spin moves directly from nickel to iron by light. The team varied the laser strength, called fluence, and watched the delay change.

The delay shrank markedly as fluence rose. That clashes with the direct transfer theory's predictions. Iron's loss of magnetism also saturated right when nickel's began. Both facts favor the spin-wave account, the authors argue, via an instability in the spin-wave picture.
arxiv-2503-08911:
Sara Billey and Stark Ryan study three new partial orders on ordered set partitions, named with a coffee lover's humor, in a math paper from 2025. The classic Bruhat order on permutations grew out of Schubert geometry and has ruled the topic for a century. The new orders, decaf, medium roast, and espresso, live on configurations of lines indexed by Fubini words.

The decaf order generalizes the weak order, built from simple swaps. The medium roast order generalizes the strong Bruhat order, defined by how the subvarieties close up. The espresso order comes from how the subvarieties intersect. The authors show that many classic properties of Schubert varieties and Bruhat order carry over to one or more of the three, and they map out which ones.
arxiv-2503-09011:
Amirmohammad Azadi, Sina Zamani, Mohammadmostafa Rostamkhani, and Sauleh Eetemadi describe their system for a shared task on finding fact-checks. Their 2025 paper covers SemEval-2025 Task 7, where a system gets a claim and must retrieve the fact-checks already written about it. The source collection, MultiClaim, mixes social media posts and fact-checks in several languages, which makes the search cross-lingual as well as multilingual.

The team first tested strong retrieval models off the shelf, in English and multilingual forms, with no task training. They then fine-tuned the most promising systems, using machine translation to strengthen retrieval across languages. The best model reached eighty-five percent accuracy on the cross-lingual part and ninety-two percent on the single-language part. The paper reports a simple recipe: start from a strong general retriever, then teach it the task.
arxiv-2503-09111:
Four physicists work out an exact formula in a 2025 paper for how a quantum system spreads when the rules include a smallest possible length. The system they study, the Arthurs-Kelly setup, is a classic model of measuring a particle with pointers. The added rule comes from a generalized uncertainty idea tied to physics at the Planck scale.

They derive the Feynman propagator, the core function that carries a state from one time to the next, keeping terms to first order in the new small parameter. A smallest length shows up in many approaches to quantum gravity, from strings to loops. The authors also touch briefly on what the result could mean for the very early universe. The exact form gives other theorists a firm base to build on.
arxiv-2503-09211:
Marius Jahrens and Thomas Martinetz argue that language models cannot think in a 2025 paper. They first define thought in a way that fits such models. The thought must take place inside the model's feature space. Classic views of thought inform their definition.

They then show current designs block that kind of thought. The block comes from both the architecture and the training method. Language modeling trains models to predict text, not to decide. The paper is a theory piece, not an experiment report. Fixes are proposed to let feature-space thought take place. The authors weigh what those changes would mean more broadly.
arxiv-2503-09611:
Louis-Vincent Bouthier, Romain Castellani, and Rudy Valette extended a setup linking stress and strain in deformed stuff in a 2025 paper. Continuum mechanics describes rubber-like and flowing solids through the second Piola–Kirchhoff stress and the Green–Lagrange strain. The Sequence of Real Processes setup organizes how one is built from the other. The standard version, however, drops some geometrical nonlinearities that matter once warps grow large.

The extension adds those geometrical fixes, opening the door to studying rheological nonlinearities inside the same setup. Applied to two old-style viscoelastic models, the linear Maxwell and Kelvin–Voigt models. The fixes show how certain complex actions can be rationalized once shapes is accounted for. The work targets engineers who model polymers and soft stuff under serious warp.
arxiv-2503-09811:
Maciej Mrowinski, Aleksandra Buczek, and Agata Fronczak study how citations to a researcher's work build up, with a focus on self-citations, in a paper from 2025. A classic rule, preferential attachment, says papers gain citations in step with those they already have. Whether self-cites follow that rule was less known.

The team traced single citation events in the DBLP set and two Scopus-based sets. Overall, about 70 percent of citations fit the rich-get-richer rule. Self-citations broke the pattern: only 20 percent fit it. The rule also grew stronger as an author's average citations per paper rose. The authors note that self-cites can sway indices such as the h-index, and urge care in how impact is scored.
arxiv-2503-09911:
Kohei Hayashi, Masanori Koyama, and Julian Jorge Andrade Guerreiro present a world model that can work across settings in work from 2025. World models let a system predict what will happen next so it can plan actions.

Their method, called WLA, learns smooth control signals that work in many settings at once. It uses ideas from Lie group theory and a part-based image encoder. Trained on video frames alone, with few or no action labels, the model adapted fast to new settings with new action sets. Tests used both made-up tasks and real-world data.
arxiv-2503-10111:
Zecheng Zhao, Zhi Chen, Zi Huang, Shazia Sadiq, and Tong Chen study video search that must keep learning in a 2025 study. Text to video retrieval finds clips matching a written query. As new video keeps arriving, a search system must absorb new tasks without forgetting old ones or misaligning past queries with stored features.

The authors introduce the first benchmark for this continual version of the task. Their framework pairs a frame fusion adapter, which captures how frames relate over time, with task aware routing. Together the parts aim to keep the model flexible for new data while protecting what earlier tasks taught it.
arxiv-2503-10311:
Yoshihito Kuno and co-authors explore mixed-state topological order in a doubled space in a 2025 paper. Open quantum systems blur the pure-state order catalog. Decoherence acting on a cluster model is their test bed. New construction tricks work in the doubled Hilbert space.

Pure gapless order plus duality builds two mixed states: a strong protected one and a double average one. The double state hosts two orders at once, a strong-to-weak symmetry breaking and a remaining average protection. Tuning decoherence strength flips the system between the mixed phases. Numbers confirm both states and the transition. Rich average orders may bloom from many decoherence channels.
arxiv-2503-10411:
Pierpaolo Della Monica and co-authors study fair exchange of digital assets when sellers first advertise what they hold, in work from 2025. In a fair exchange, neither side should gain an edge over the other. Sellers usually show off an asset to raise interest while keeping it partly hidden, yet past definitions left that advert phase out.

The team gives the first clear definition of fair exchange with an advert phase, in a setting where parties use broadcast messages only. They then build a protocol that meets the definition, using proofs that reveal nothing extra and public platforms for contracts and storage. Tests confirm the approach works in practice. The method could support open marketplaces where users trade digital assets without direct contact.
arxiv-2503-10711:
Nirmal Baishnab and five co-authors use an image-generating model to design the inner structure of advanced materials, in a research paper from 2025. Making fine 3D structures with chosen traits by simulation is slow. Their model creates such structures on demand, in seconds.

Users can dial in traits such as how much of each phase is present and how winding the paths through it are. The model was shown on two-phase and three-phase structures at high resolution. It also predicts the factory settings that would produce each design. Tests used the active layer of organic solar cells, but the team says the approach can adapt to other materials.
arxiv-2503-10811:
Meriem Behiri and co-authors survey the radio traits of blazars, the bright cores of galaxies whose jets point toward Earth. Their 2025 paper studies one hundred sixty-five blazars from a Fermi gamma-ray catalogue. They look for matches in a large radio survey made with the Australian SKA Pathfinder telescope.

The team combined high-resolution radio data with archival millimeter observations to build energy profiles across wavelengths. Most blazars showed peaked spectra that suggest one main emitting zone, as if the jet had been re-triggered. Radio and gamma-ray brightness tracked each other closely. A tight radio and X-ray link held for one blazar class but scattered for another, hinting at unlike engines.
arxiv-2503-10911:
Peter Weichman studies how a many body light effect could boost atom based radio sensors in a 2025 paper. Sensors built on highly excited Rydberg atoms could in principle beat wire antennas, above all at low frequencies where wires must be very long. Their response grows steeply with the excitation level, yet beyond classical sensitivity has not been shown after decades of work.

A vapor effect called optical bistability, a sudden phase shift at higher density, has raised sensitivity when tuned near its critical point. But advanced standard setups do still better by using a resonant pair of atom levels. Weichman extends the bistable analysis to that resonant pair, with an exact treatment of thermal atom motion.
arxiv-2503-11011:
Abrar Hossain, Abubeker Abdurahman, Mohammad A. Islam, and Kishwar Ahmed present a job scheduler for large computing centers in this 2025 paper. Big centers that run heavy research jobs spend a large share of their budget on power. The team's system, called TARDIS, tries to cut that power bill without slowing the work down.

TARDIS first uses a neural network to predict how much power each job will draw. It then shifts jobs in two ways: in time, toward hours when power costs less, and in space, toward sites where prices are lower. Tests on traces of real workloads cut costs by up to 18 percent for time shifts, and by 10 to 20 percent across sites. Speed and job flow stayed close to normal, so the savings did not come at the cost of output.
arxiv-2503-11211: Trishan Mondal, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, walks through a classic proof of the first few stable stems, a set of counts in the math of spheres. The paper is a work of clear telling, not new proof. He sets out the base tools, then links framed shapes to the stable counts by a known build. With it, he works out the counts in dims zero, one, and two. A last part shows why a past claim on the second count was wrong.
arxiv-2503-11311:
A large team takes the sharpest portrait yet of the odd electrons inside a strained crystal of strontium ruthenate. In a normal metal, electrons behave as tidy quasiparticles; near a quantum critical point they should fall apart. Squeezing the crystal with uniaxial pressure tunes it to that edge. By milling the sample with an ion beam and reading it with laser photoemission, the team mapped the excitations right at the critical strain.

The electrons' scattering rate did turn non-Fermi liquid, the signature of the strange metal. Yet the quasiparticles themselves stayed surprisingly robust across the transition instead of dissolving. The authors offer the maps as a benchmark for theories of anomalous metals. The result settles a long-standing question: quantum-critical systems do host quasiparticle excitations, however strained their behavior.
arxiv-2503-11411:
Xu Liu and co-authors survey fake data for time series work in a 2025 paper. Time series are runs of values over time, from heartbeats to stock prices. New giant models can learn such data in a broad way, much like chat models learn text. But they need huge, varied, clean data sets to train on. Real data is often locked by rules, thin, or patchy.

Made-up data, built by other models, offers a way out. This survey sorts the ways such data is made and used. It covers training from scratch, fine-tuning, and testing of both time series giants and chat-based models. The authors weigh the gains in scale and fairness. They close with open problems and paths for later work in the field.
arxiv-2503-11611:
Fergus Donnan and co-authors plan a census in 2025 of the most hidden galaxy cores. The growth of supermassive black holes drives galaxy evolution, but most of that growth is veiled by dust, so visible-light tracers miss it. A proposed far-infrared space telescope could change that.

Its camera spans wavelengths where a deep dust dip betrays buried active cores out to early cosmic times. Its spectrograph can read spectra of such cores nearly as far, spotting organic molecules, ices, and glowing gases. The authors argue the mission would finally count and characterize the obscured majority, settling how black holes grew.
arxiv-2503-11911:
Naome Etori, Kevin Lu, Randu Karisa, and Arturs Kanepajs benchmark frontier language models in Latvian and in Giriama, a Kenyan language tested this way for the first time, in a 2025 paper. Model skill is usually graded in English, which hides weakness elsewhere. Their test set adapts a standard multitask exam with native speakers, keeping the questions linguistically and culturally apt.

Eight leading models sat the exam with no worked examples. OpenAI's o1 led everywhere: about ninety-three percent in English, eighty-nine in Latvian, seventy-one in Giriama. Two big open models trailed badly on both target languages, under forty-five percent. The gap between Latvian and Giriama grades the resource ladder itself. The authors argue for localized benchmarks and human evaluation as the price of honest multilingual claims.
arxiv-2503-12111:
Rajiv Kumar and Rajib Sarkar bound a key invariant of path ideals for trees and one-cycle graphs in 2025. A 3-path ideal collects the length-three paths of a graph as algebra generators. Regularity measures how complex the ideal resolution is, a central cost gauge in algebra.

For any graph, they prove regularity sits at or above twice the 3-path induced matching number. Trees hit that lower bound exactly, which settles their case. For graphs with exactly one cycle, regularity stays within two above twice the matching number. An example shows the upper bound cannot be tightened in general.
arxiv-2503-12211:
Nir Ailon and co-authors swap the core math act of taught nets in a 2025 paper. Nets live on vast grid-times-grid acts, whose cost caps how big and fast they run. The team seeks an act the card can run at home speed with less work.

Their act shifts the base on small tiles of the net weights and the live grid, then times the tiles part by part. The trade is three-way: fewer steps, more stored weights, some loss of aim. The hard ask is how to tune the shift well. Net teams gain a new dial twixt speed, size, and aim.
arxiv-2503-12511:
Tianyang Zhou and six co-authors present a tool that translates C code into Rust in a 2025 paper. Rust offers stronger memory safety than C, but hand translation is slow and error prone. Language models write fluent Rust yet give no guarantee the code behaves the same as the original.

Their tool works in two steps: first a plain translation that preserves meaning, then a polish pass to make the code idiomatic Rust. Mixed C and Rust code is tested end to end through a cross language interface as translation proceeds function by function. On two hundred test programs and real projects, the tool achieved high correctness with far fewer style warnings than baselines.
arxiv-2503-12711:
Spencer Kraisler and co-authors present a 2025 method for planning trajectories on smooth curved spaces. Spacecraft attitude paths live on manifolds, not flat grids. Standard optimizers bolt the manifold rules on as side constraints. That adds redundant work and ties results to the chosen coordinates.

Their intrinsic convexification builds the geometry into the method itself. Steps stay on the manifold by construction. A spacecraft attitude case with non-convex limits shows the approach. Cleaner math promises faster, sturdier planning. The idea extends to robots and other curved-state machines in air and space.
arxiv-2503-12811:
Kairong Luo and co-authors present a law that forecasts how a large language model's training loss falls under varied learning rate plans, in a 2025 paper. Training such models eats time and compute, so knowing how settings shape results matters. Their law blends several power curves. One tracks the sum of learning rates over time. Others capture the extra drop in loss that comes when the rate decays.

The team fit the law on a few rate plans across model sizes and shapes. It then forecast loss curves for unseen plans with fresh shapes and lengths, and did so with care. By picking the plan with the lowest forecast end loss, they found one that beat the widely used cosine plan. Their found plan echoes a recently proposed three-stage plan, yet ends a touch lower. The authors offer the law as a cheap guide for training design.
arxiv-2503-13311:
Simone Cacace, Roberto Ferretti, and Giulia Tatafiore present a 2025 numerical method for Hamilton-Jacobi equations on loose triangle grids. A classic scheme family lags on such grids, since finding each step's start point costs much and the hunt repeats. Their scheme works from node values and grid links alone.

A base form keeps the answer well-behaved and monotone, while a quad polish lifts accuracy at some extra cost. Both time-run and steady cases fit, and a fast rule-based solver speeds the steady case. Proofs and a wide test set back the claims.
arxiv-2503-13611:
Li-Ren Liu and co-authors report, in a 2025 physics paper, a precision measurement of the electric dipole moment of aluminum monochloride. This small molecule matters for models of stars and planets. Until now, those models borrowed a stand-in value for its dipole.

The team used a cryogenic beam of the molecules and watched how their energy levels shifted in an electric field. They derived dipole values for two vibrational states in each of two electronic states. The numbers differed between ground and excited states in a clear pattern. Computer calculations of the property proved sensitive to fine physical effects. Measured values now replace the borrowed one in astrophysical models.
arxiv-2503-13811:
Zehao Su and Xing Wei map how a young planet-forming disc can clump under its own gravity. Their 2025 paper studies a thin, flat disc that is cooling as it orbits its star. Such clumping is one path to making planets, and cooling sets its pace.

Solving the ripple equations across the whole disc, they find every growth mode. Faster cooling speeds growth and favours broad patterns. Three mode families appear, set by where they sit in the disc and how fast it cools. A middle family takes over when the cooling time matches the orbit time. That family stirs the disc the most. The authors link it to rings seen in outer discs.
arxiv-2503-14111:
Egor Kuznetsov, Kirill Aistov, and Maxim Koroteev study attacks on an image quality score in a 2025 paper. The score, called VMAF, is meant to match how people judge picture quality. The team asks whether tiny image changes can fool it into giving high marks.

Using gradient methods, they built small, targeted changes to images. A modest brightness shift in one region raised the score by about 60 percent, while people saw almost no change. The size of the changes tracked image brightness in a near-linear way. Restoring noisy images by chasing the score also split metric and human views. The work shows quality scores can mislead.
arxiv-2503-14411:
Siwei Zhang and colleagues present CROSS, a frame that lets temporal graph neural networks handle graphs whose nodes carry text that changes. Temporal graph networks model dynamic graphs well. But real temporal graphs often hold rich text. That creates temporal text-attributed graphs. Past methods embed texts in a static way and stress structure. They miss how text sense evolves and how sense and structure should aid each other.

CROSS splits the work into two phases. The first pulls out temporal semantics, and the second joins semantic and structural facts. Its Temporal Semantics Extractor uses large language models to grasp the changing text around each node. It catches semantic dynamics that static embeddings miss. The frame then makes joined forms that unify sense and structure. CROSS is built as a flexible add-on.
arxiv-2503-14511: Ramón Ruiz-Medina and Victor Lara-Gómez study an algebraic structure in twenty twenty-five. A group G acts on a set X, and some functions on X commute with that action. All such functions form a monoid under composition, meaning they can be combined and include an identity. The authors take the case where X is finite. They compute the Green relations for this monoid, a classic set of tools for grasping semigroup structure. Their account is built around special elements they call elementary collapsings.
arxiv-2503-14811:
Filippo Calderoni and Dima Sinapova sort when two forced worlds count as the same kind of same, in a study from 2025. Forcing grows new sets by fair picks, filters that meet each dense ask. Two such growths can be set side by side; the ask is when that side-by-side is smooth, tame in the scale of same-kinds.

A pure shape trait, condensation, gives the full call: the growths whose same-kind is smooth are just those with it. That call then shows wild growths whose same-kind is not smooth. For Prikry growths, the same-kind proves fine in a strong sense, hyperfinite. Cohen growths get part calls in that dir. Shape, the pair shows, rules same.
arxiv-2503-15311: The Euclid Collaboration takes a first look at how common barred structures are among massive galaxies at redshifts below one, using the mission's Quick Data Release Q1, in a 2025 paper. Bars are elongated stellar structures across many spiral galaxies, and their frequency over time tests models of galaxy change. Euclid's early data open a fresh window on that count.
arxiv-2503-16011:
Besjon Cifliku and Hendrik Heuer ask investigative journalists where AI could actually save them work in a 2025 study. Newsroom AI research usually stays general, missing the peculiar needs of investigations: huge document dumps, source protection, and verification under legal risk. The authors ran a study with a small group of working investigative journalists, using speculative design prompts in interviews to surface concrete use cases.

Participants described automation help that could, in one journalist's words, save months of work. The cases center on sifting and structuring evidence rather than writing stories. Grounding design in newsroom practice keeps tools honest about where they help.
arxiv-2503-16311:
Aritra Bhowmik and co-authors improve self-supervised learning for video and audio by masking with colored noise in a 2025 paper. Masked modeling hides parts of the input and trains the model to fill them in. Standard practice hides random patches, ignoring that video moves through time and audio spreads across frequencies.

Their method filters white noise into colored patterns, so the masks themselves carry structure matched to each medium. No hand-designed rules and no peek at the data are needed, and the cost of training does not rise. Across masked video and audio frameworks, structured masks consistently beat random ones. The authors argue masking should respect the shape of the data it hides.
arxiv-2503-16411:
Shamisa Shoja, Daniel Arnstrom, and Daniel Axehill speed up complexity checks for control algorithms in a 2025 paper. Model predictive control for hybrid systems solves a mixed-integer optimization problem at every sampling instant. Recent work made it possible to certify how hard those branch-and-bound solves can get, which matters for safety timing.

Certification itself can be expensive on large problems. The authors design parallel algorithms that split the domain and certify pieces at once, for both linear and quadratic versions. Faster certificates widen where guaranteed real-time control can be deployed.
arxiv-2503-16611:
Katja Schwarz and four co-authors give a recipe in twenty twenty-five for building 3D worlds from one image. Their trick is to treat the job as in-context learning for a 2D inpainting model. That means little new training is needed, since existing generative models do most of the work. The result should suit display in virtual reality.

The process has two main steps. First, a diffusion model makes a coherent panorama from the image. A depth estimator then lifts that panorama into three dimensions. Next, the inpainting model fills unseen regions, guided by rendered point clouds, with only light fine-tuning. Tests on synthetic and real images beat video-based methods on several quality metrics. Readers get a simple path from a photo to a world.
arxiv-2503-16711:
Mihaela-Larisa Clement and co-authors show, in a 2025 study, that adding depth sensing makes small self-driving agents steer far better. Their agents decide in real time from sight alone. A normal camera gives color but no sense of distance. The team fuse color images with depth maps and feed both to light recurrent controllers that issue steering commands.

Training data came from a small real car driven by an expert with a physical wheel, over routes of rising difficulty. On real hardware, the depth-aware agents dodged still and moving obstacles, even on routes unlike their training. Early fusion of depth proved best. The controller stayed robust when frames dropped or noise rose, without losing focus on the driving task.
arxiv-2503-16911:
Hongjian Zhou and co-authors review, in a 2025 article, the state of research on an exotic particle at China's BESIII experiment. The particle, chi_c1(3872), sits at the center of a long debate over what exotic matter is made of. Rival pictures cast it as a loose molecule of known particles, a compact four-quark state, a hybrid, or a plain charmonium state with odd traits.

Two decades of work have sharpened measures of how the particle decays and the exact shape of its signal. BESIII, with its clean conditions and huge data samples, has driven much of that progress. The review sums up what the experiment has established and looks ahead to the runs that could settle the particle's true nature.
arxiv-2503-17211:
Zilin Dai and co-authors harden image models against both domain shift and label noise in a 2025 paper. Models love to lean on spare, flashy traits that fail in new places, and wrong labels deepen the trap.

Their method anchors each training image to a word based sketch of its class from a language model. Such sketches hold steady across domains. A weighted loss then trims the say of images that sit far from their anchor. Bench tests across sets and noise rates beat lead domain methods on accuracy and toughness. The language anchor acts as a fixed star for noisy training.
arxiv-2503-17311:
Atma Anand and co-authors predict what magnetic fingerprint the asteroid Psyche should carry, depending on how it got magnetised, in a 2025 paper. Psyche is a metal-rich world, possibly a stripped planetary core, and a spacecraft is on its way. If it kept an ancient magnetisation, the field's shape would betray its source. The team simulated three pathways: magnetisation by the young solar wind after a giant impact, a core dynamo in an intact or reassembled body, and fields in the solar nebula itself.

Each pathway leaves a different topology. Wind-induced fields come out dipolar and spin-aligned; dynamo fields are dipolar but tilted, or messy and multipolar; nebula fields are multipolar too. Strength limits accompany the first two. Merely detecting a field will not settle Psyche's history, the authors warn; its shape must be mapped.
arxiv-2503-17611:
Jhixon Macías studies which polynomials behave in a smooth, unbroken way on a number space built from coprime sets, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The space takes the counting numbers as its points. Its basic open sets hold all numbers that share no common factor with a given number.

Over that space, most polynomials break the smoothness rule. Macías characterizes exactly which ones keep it. The answer is stark: only monomials, the single-term polynomials, pass the test. The proof gives a full sorting of the smooth cases, with no mixed or multi-term cases left open.
arxiv-2503-17811:
Wenqi Pei and co-authors present a light framework in 2025 that lets small language models turn plain questions into database queries. Big models do this task well, but they are often closed, costly, and a risk for private data. Small models that a team can run itself tend to fail at the task and do not fit frames built for big ones.

Their framework first prunes the database layout to the parts a question needs, and links words in the question to those parts. It then drafts several query paths and several candidate queries. A pairing scheme joins a small model with a second one, so the two cover each other's weak spots. The aim is queries that run and give the right answer, from models cheap enough to keep in house.
arxiv-2503-17911:
Xiaoyao Zhong and co-authors present VSAG, a framework that speeds graph-based search for near matches among vectors. Such search powers vector databases and much of modern AI tooling. Graph methods are accurate, yet in live service they suffer from scattered memory access and heavy distance math.

VSAG attacks those costs on three fronts. It reshapes vector layout and prefetches data to cut cache misses. It tunes its own settings without costly index rebuilds. It also uses smart hardware tricks and low-precision forms to slash distance costs. The system already runs at scale inside Ant Group services. Tests on real datasets show strong gains over prior graph search tools. For teams running vector search in production, VSAG offers a tested path to faster, cheaper queries.
arxiv-2503-18211:
Zhengyuan Li and co-authors edit 3D human motion from text orders in a 2025 computer vision paper. A user might ask to make a walking figure raise an arm higher, and the system must change just that. A new data set of source, text, and motion triplets made training possible, but past models often drifted from the words.

The team adds a side task: judging how similar two motions are. Training on editing and similarity together forces the model to learn meaning-rich motion features. Their diffusion transformer handles the two tasks in separate streams. Tests show the best scores yet on both faithfulness to the text and closeness to natural motion. The authors credit the side task for the tighter control.
arxiv-2503-18311:
Mohammed Alqedra and co-authors demonstrate a leaner way to fully characterize light-based quantum bits, in a 2025 paper. Standard tomography, the full readout of a quantum state, grows impractical as qubits multiply, since the measurement count explodes. Their Fourier method instead turns a single rotating waveplate per qubit and reads the state from the pattern that results.

They tested it on faint laser states and on entangled photon pairs from two sources, a quantum dot and a crystal converter, at telecom wavelengths. The rebuilt states matched standard tomography closely, with quality scores agreeing within error bars. Because settings grow only in step with qubit count, the authors offer the method as a practical route for larger photonic systems.
arxiv-2503-19711:
Sian Gooding and co-authors use writing as a test case for open-ended AI agents. In such tasks the space of good answers is huge. Success has no single right measure. They study whether large language models can act as co-writers. A co-writer suggests and applies text improvements on its own.

Three leading models are compared. They are Gemini 1.5 Pro, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o. The team scores the range of actions each model tries. They check how well its choices match human judgment. They also track how much drafts improve over repeated passes. The work sets out a frame for scoring such agents. Its lessons carry over to other open-ended work where the goal is taste.
arxiv-2503-19811:
Adriano Di Pietro and co-authors study how the curve of a magnetic domain wall affects its slow creep motion, in this 2025 paper. In some layered materials, a special interaction twists the magnetism, and round magnetic bubbles grow or shrink under a field. Standard creep theory treats the wall as straight, which misses real bubble shapes.

The team extended the creep model to walls with finite curvature. The effect is easy to measure in platinum-cobalt stacks: below a sample-dependent bubble size, speed falls sharply. They also show, in theory and in tests, that bubble size can skew measurements of the twist interaction itself.
arxiv-2503-19911:
Ruben Van Assche and six co-authors clean up distorted light signals with a chip that computes with light itself. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Signals in optical fibres blur and warp from dispersion and nonlinear effects. Digital cleanup works, but it burns power and adds delay. The team pursues an all-optical fix instead.

Their silicon photonic chip joins a recurrent reservoir with a tunable readout layer. It is, to their knowledge, the first live online demo of its kind. The chip restored a fast on-off keying signal across varied power levels and fibre lengths. It coped even where the fibre behaved in a strongly nonlinear way. The result points to lower-power, lower-delay links for future networks.
arxiv-2503-20111:
Quantum memories must swap information between electron spins and light without losing it. Siavash Mirzaei-Ghormish, Jeddy Bennet, and Ryan Camacho design an interface that beams the light straight up, free-space style. Their device patterns a diamond microdisk with two etched layers. The first bends the trapped light toward the axis; the second trims side lobes and piles the beam into a clean central spot.

The design gathers ninety-six percent of the light within a standard lens opening, with a ninety-five percent match to an ideal beam shape. A shortcut model does the math millions of times faster than full simulations. The team says the looser alignment demands suit the design to scaled-up quantum hardware.
arxiv-2503-20311:
Hamid Arian Zad and co-authors study quantum entanglement in molecular magnets built from four nickel and four gadolinium ions. The complexes form two matching cube-like units joined by acetate and hydroxide links, and are modelled as Heisenberg spin systems. Exact diagonalization under a magnetic field gives the states, and negativity serves as the entanglement measure.

Two families are compared, one with single-ion anisotropy and one without. Without anisotropy, strong entanglement sits mainly between nickel ions and fades by set temperature and field levels. With anisotropy, all forms studied, across two, three and four parties, take sizable values. One measure also flags ground state changes sharply in both families.
arxiv-2503-20411:
Zakaria Said and co-workers coupled single perovskite quantum dots to a tunable optical cavity in a 2025 paper. Perovskite dots emit single photons of high purity even at room heat level, making them attractive for quantum light sources. Placing one dot deterministically inside a cavity, where light-matter coupling can speed and purify emission, had remained the missing step. Their fiber-based Fabry-Pérot microcavity offers high quality and tiny mode volume, tunable in place at low heat level.

By sliding the cavity in space and rate onto one cesium lead bromide dot, they doubled its emission rate through the Purcell effect. The dot's split emission lines also let them estimate the vacuum coupling strength. Reversible, controlled coupling is the milestone quantum photonics needed.
arxiv-2503-20511:
Ramón Nartallo-Kaluarachchi, Renaud Lambiotte, and Alain Goriely argue that mathematical biology must stop taking living systems apart on paper. Their 2025 paper contrasts physics-style reductionism with the mess of real biology, where parts vary, serve many roles, and interact across scales. Broad complex-systems theory, they add, often fails to yield testable predictions.

Using neuroscience as the test case, they propose a holistic modeling style. Rich network structures, agent-based models, and simulation-led inference from data take center stage. High-resolution data and modern computing now make that approach feasible. The authors stress it still seeks basic biophysical principles, just by fitting whole systems rather than fragments.
arxiv-2503-20811:
Steven Louis, Hannah Bradley, and Vasyl Tyberkevych recast the motion of a ferromagnetic macrospin as an electric circuit, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. A macrospin, such as the free layer of a magnetic tunnel junction, is their test case. Its motion is set out through capacitor charge and inductor flux. The picture mirrors a standard LC circuit.

Unlike a simple circuit, the capacitance and inductance here are strongly nonlinear and coupled. The account still takes in Gilbert damping and spin transfer torques. The payoff is a fairly simple circuit that stands in for a magnetic device. Engineers can model it in LTspice or like software for electric circuits. That makes it easy to simulate advanced circuits. Such circuits mix tunnel junctions with standard electronic parts. In effect, the paper lets circuit designers treat a spintronic element like ordinary electronics.
arxiv-2503-20911:
Xiaoyong Chu and Josef Pradler sum up their work on how light dark matter, with mass in a low band, could have frozen out of the hot young cosmos. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

They treat two paths. In one, dark matter wipes out into normal particles, such as light, electrons, and ghost particles. A full count of heat flow sets the least mass that can work and the true rates. Some tuned zones let ghost end states save paths that were ruled out. In the next path, strong forces in the dark side bind states, which open fresh two-body paths. The two paths give twin routes to a workable early loss.
arxiv-2503-21011:
Ana Ma and Derek Powell asked in 2025 whether large language models can predict links among human attitudes. Past work showed models can guess one attitude from close, related ones. Human attitudes, though, often link strongly across unlike topics too.

Using a new data set of responses to diverse statements, the team tested a frontier model. It recreated pairwise links among attitudes and predicted one person's attitudes from others. Even without surface likeness between topics, the model still made meaningful social inferences, though likeness helped accuracy. The findings suggest models capture deep, hidden structure in human belief systems, beyond surface wording.
arxiv-2503-21311:
Jun Gao and co-authors carry out a global analysis of fragmentation functions for light neutral hadrons, in their 2025 arXiv paper. Fragmentation functions describe how quarks and gluons turn into hadrons, and they are essential inputs for predictions in quantum chromodynamics. Their targets are neutral kaons, eta and pi-zero mesons, and Lambda baryons.

The fit draws on electron-positron annihilation, deep-inelastic scattering and proton-proton collision data, with careful cuts to keep the theory valid. New data types, including hadrons inside jets, help pin down the gluon distribution and separate quark flavors. Fits were generally good, and the extracted kaon functions let the team probe isospin symmetry in kaon fragmentation.
arxiv-2503-21811:
Dan Ryczanowski and eight co-authors lay out a chase plan to find the light twin of a gravity wave bent by a lens in space. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

A firm claim of a lensed wave is hard with today's tools, since the sky place and other facts are loose. For crashes of two neutron stars, the light twin can save the day. If its bent copies are found, the lens is proved and the place is pinned at once. That opens rich joint science. The plan must solve two tasks: how to pick likely lensed cases from the wave data, and how to hunt their light in time. The paper sets out both.
arxiv-2503-22311:
Ilia Grishmanovskii, Taesoo Song, Carsten Greiner, and Elena Bratkovskaya compute how heavy quarks move through the hot soup of particles created in nuclear collisions. That soup, called quark-gluon plasma, existed just after the Big Bang and is now made for instants in colliders. Heavy quarks serve as probes, since their drag and spread reveal the soup's properties.

Earlier work counted only simple two-body collisions. The new study adds rarer events where a heavy quark also emits a gluon, a three-body process. Both kinds of events are computed inside a model tuned to match lattice calculations. From them the authors derive drag and spread measures for a charm quark at several temperatures. The results sharpen readings of collider data.
arxiv-2503-22411:
Petter Törnberg and Juliana Chueri show that harsh talk by political elites has spread across Western democracies. Their paper from twenty twenty-five mines millions of tweets by parliament members in dozens of countries. A validated language model grades the severity of abuse in each post. The share of severe incivility near doubled across the late twenty teens into the early twenty twenties.

Populism is the strongest party-level predictor of toxic posts. Its link grows stronger when a party sits in opposition. Sturdier liberal democracy pulls the rate down. The rise is mostly behavioral: parties of all stripes grew rougher, not just bigger radical blocs. Nationalist and radical-right parties stay the roughest, though their lead shrinks. The authors warn of a mainstreaming of abuse, with trust and democratic health at stake.
arxiv-2503-22711:
Emotion in speech is graded by humans who disagree, and Vikramjit Mitra and three co-authors argue the disagreement is data, not noise, in a 2025 paper. Standard practice takes a vote and crowns one emotion as truth, discarding the ambiguity real listeners heard.

Training instead on the full distribution of grader opinions beat the literature's consensus-trained results on benchmark sets. A saliency-driven method picks which foundation model representation to trust, yielding a state-of-the-art emotion recognizer for both dimensional and categorical judgments. The authors then warn against leaderboard thinking: overall scores hide how a model fares across speakers and genders, and across recording conditions it never trained on. Their evaluation spreads those cuts wide open, arguing an emotion model is only as good as its worst demographic slice.
arxiv-2503-23211:
Sepideh Mosaferi, Abolfazl Safikhani, and Peiliang Bai detect change points in the spectral density of time series in two thousand twenty-five. Their drive comes from EEG reads of seizure patients. Seizures break coherence and links across brain zones. Sharp timing of that break is a clinical need.

Their method rests on the Wold form, which writes a series as an endless lag process. That process is cut and fit near each candidate change point. A first scan hunts across time in a set order. A refined step hits the best rate and gives trust bands. Tests on EEG and video beat past methods.
arxiv-2503-23311:
Daniele Corradetti and Alessio Marrani present a 2025 paper at the seam of language theory and geometry. They define three notions: a language change step, a loop of such steps that returns to its start, and a semantic deficit that a loop can carry. With Lie group tools and higher geometry, they build invariants that capture the whole loop's structure in a few numbers.

The move opens a new research line that brings hard geometry into language studies. The authors also hint at a bolder prize: a math sketch of thought before words. If loops that change words leave a fixed trace, that trace may mirror the pre-verbal frame beneath speech. The paper is a theory sketch, offered as a seed for a field.
arxiv-2503-24011:
Bürkner, Schmitt, and Radev chart the roles of mock runs in stats work in this twenty twenty-five paper. Mock runs help set, check, and grade models, and can even drive the fit step itself. Fresh tools and fast chips have stretched what such runs can do a lot.

Inside, the trio looks back at how mock runs grew into each part of stats work. They map where the runs now sit in day-to-day work with real data. Next they weigh what new run-based tools could change in years to come. The piece ends with a take on how stats craft may shift as runs grow cheap and broad.
arxiv-2503-24211:
Efstratios Koukoutsis and co-authors present a quantum-style algorithm for waves in plasma in a 2025 paper. Their method models how electromagnetic waves travel and scatter inside magnetized plasma, the hot charged gas found in fusion devices and space. It builds on a quantum walk, a step-by-step process run on a lattice of qubits that store the wave values.

Rotation gates inside the walk reproduce the basic wave motion, and added operators handle the effects of plasma density and circling charged particles. The scheme stays fully unitary and matches the target equations to second-order accuracy. In the worst case it still beats a standard classical method on resources and error growth. A later extension adds energy loss from particle collisions.
arxiv-2504-00011:
Mohammad Parsa and Lukasz Golab mine Reddit discussions to learn what the public misunderstands about migraines, and sum it up as four things everyone should know. Low understanding of the condition is known to wear on the people who live with it.

Their four lessons are plain. Migraine is a serious disease, not a bad headache. It strikes people of all ages. It can be set off by many different triggers, which vary from person to person. It affects women more than men. And it can grow worse alongside COVID-19. The authors used text mining on social media posts to surface these themes from patients' own words, hoping the short list helps close the awareness gap.
arxiv-2504-00111:
Gennaro Zanfardino and a team including Stefano Paesani and Marco Leonetti link light-based quantum devices to a classic model of memory, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The Hopfield model treats memory as a network of simple units that settle into stored patterns. It is a basic model for both memory and machine learning.

Their setup sends several photons through an optical circuit with set phase shifts. The output counts match the behavior of a Hopfield network with four-way links between units. As more patterns are stored, the system shifts from recalling memories to a blacked-out, glassy state. The link may let light devices simulate messy, complex systems with ease.
arxiv-2504-00411:
Mingqian Feng and co-authors build a privacy-preserving training method for deep networks that learns forward only, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Standard private training clips gradients and adds noise during backward learning passes. Forward methods instead add noise up front and guess gradients from randomness, hinting at built-in privacy.

Their method adds a rejection-based batch sampling step with its own privacy proof. A controller adjusts noise each step to spend the privacy budget wisely. Tests matched the accuracy of standard private training at nearly the same privacy cost. The result opens a backward-free route to private learning.
arxiv-2504-00611:
Michael Balzer (2025) designs better group testing schemes for factory quality control. Testing every item alone is slow and costly, so factories test pooled groups and follow up only on suspect pools. Balzer studies multi-stage schemes built on regular designs, in which each item joins a fixed number of pools and each pool holds a fixed size. He derives unified formulas for the expected number of tests and the expected time the process takes.

Simulations backed the math. The new schemes beat established ones when defects are rare, which is the normal case in good factories. Their test counts came close to the theoretical lower bound while staying simple to run. The author frames the work for real production lines, where both test count and total duration matter. The results suggest regular multi-stage designs can cut quality-control cost without adding hard-to-manage complexity.
arxiv-2504-00711:
Du and five co-authors breed graph data with a crew of tongue-model agents in this twenty twenty-five paper. Big graph models starve for lack of vast, rich graph sets to drill on. Past breed tricks shift shape yet leave node words thin and dull.

Inside, four agent roles run the breed loop as a team with set jobs. One leads, one reads, one lifts, and one grades each new graph in turn. The loop hones each graph till its words and shape both hold true. Thin-cut forms of six known sets test the crew in data-poor terms. The crew beat past breed tools by wide gaps on those sets.
arxiv-2504-00811:
Cory Hargus and co-authors derived the rules of motion in 2025 for a solid object sitting in a swirling bath of self propelled particles. Such baths are not still water: their swirl breaks time symmetry and pushes objects in odd ways.

Starting from the bath's own dynamics, the team built the random walk equations for a heavy rigid body. The swirl gives the object sideways drift, sideways mobility, and ratchet like turning that depends on its shape. For round objects, a hidden symmetry lets its sliding and spinning each settle into their own calm descriptions. The authors also predict how the object stirs the bath far away, out to the second order of detail. The results guide designs for micro machines.
arxiv-2504-00911:
Xiongfei Wu and ten co-authors chart a path for foundation models in self-driving cars in a 2025 paper. Foundation models include large language and vision-language systems. They open new routes for sensing, reasoning, and driver interaction. But cars are safety-critical systems with strict demands.

The roadmap rests on a structured review of the field. It spans three layers, from model infrastructure to road deployment. Each layer gets a state-of-the-art summary and a gap list. Data curation, system design, and assurance stand out as hard parts. The authors sketch research lines for safe, trusted systems. Their aim is a shared map for a fast-moving area.
arxiv-2504-01011:
Elena Caviglia, Zurab Janelidze, and Luca Mesiti lift a notion of exactness from category theory into the two-dimensional world of 2-categories, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. In an abelian category, the family of subobjects and the family of quotients mirror each other exactly, and that mirror encodes the category's exactness structure.

Grandis exact categories are precisely those where this mirror appears relative to a chosen factorization system. The authors ask what happens one dimension up, where objects, arrows, and arrows between arrows all live. They characterize the factorization systems on a 2-category for which relative 2-subobjects and relative 2-quotients match, in the weak sense suitable there. That match defines a new notion of two-dimensional exactness. They then compare it with rival notions built from enrichment in pointed groupoids. The paper is foundational, sorting out what exactness should mean for higher categories.
arxiv-2504-01311:
Trevor Karpinski and co-authors present a 2025 paper on saving flight energy in electric aircraft. Battery limits still block wide use of electric planes for cargo and passengers. Energy must be spent with care on each flight. Models of energy use keep getting sharper. Real-time control that follows those models is scarce. Take-off and landing energy are often left out of the math.

The team states core energy equations for the full flight. A model-predictive planner sets the plan along a fixed path. A classic PID controller then regulates airspeed in flight. Tests run in simulation. Operators get a control scheme that chases low energy use minute by minute. Even small savings per flight compound across a fleet, and they stretch range where batteries cannot grow.
arxiv-2504-01511:
Ivana Ban, Jacopo Bonari, and Marco Paggi build a computing frame to evaluate friction between tires and asphalt, including road roughness, in a 2025 paper. Road surface texture is captured by a photogrammetry method that builds three-dimensional surface models. The question is whether simple roughness measures match detailed simulated friction.

Texture parameters are computed from the surface profiles. Contact simulations use a finite element scheme where roughness is built into special interface elements. Across scenarios, the roughness measures showed a notable trend with simulated friction. The authors see promise for predicting friction performance from surface scans, which could aid road safety work.
arxiv-2504-02011:
Shrinking a giant image generator into a nimble student model usually needs piles of training images. Dohyun Kim and co-authors propose Random Conditioning in 2025, a distillation trick that pairs noised images with randomly chosen text prompts instead of matched ones. Freed from condition-specific pictures, the student explores the whole prompt space while copying its teacher.

The student even learns to render concepts absent from its training images, borrowed through the teacher's responses to random prompts. Applied to conditional diffusion models, the method improved both quality and efficiency. The authors release code and models, aiming at cheaper, wider deployment of generative tools.
arxiv-2504-02111:
Giannis Chatziveroglou, Richard Yun, and Maura Kelleher test how well language models keep their logic when prompts get messy in a 2025 paper. Real prompts carry stray facts, odd orders, and side notes. A model that can not sort the wheat from the chaff will slip on such input, no matter how strong its base skills are.

The team bent grade-school math prompts in four set ways and ran 13 top models on them. Stray facts inside the prompt hurt scores the most by a wide gap. The harm did not grow with task steps and did not track model size. Some bends even sparked step-by-step logic on their own. The team urges tougher guards for noisy input.
arxiv-2504-02311:
Hemani Acharya and co-authors model an ultra-dense dead star, the pulsar PSR J0952-0607, with a flexible spacetime recipe, in a 2025 paper. The framework, a generalized Tolman-Kuchowicz metric, is paired with a quadratic rule linking pressure and density. Such models let theorists test whether a real star's mass and size can sit inside Einstein's theory without breaking physics.

A bound on the model's free parameter is read off from graphs. The resulting star then holds together under every standard check: the balance equation, energy conditions, sound speed limits, and cracking tests. The model stays free of central singularities. The authors present it as a viable portrait of the pulsar.
arxiv-2504-02611:
Survey data often locates points only roughly, inside a region rather than at a spot. Five authors tackle a classic task under that handicap: find the convex hull, the rubber-band outline, of the true points, while paying for each precise measurement you choose to make. Earlier work optimized either the number of measurements or the computing time, never both.

Their algorithm is optimal on both counts at once for an input of polygon regions. It makes only the minimum number of measurements any method could need for that particular input. It also decides each next measurement in polylogarithmic time, an exponential speedup per step over rivals that match its frugality. Extensions cover many-sided polygons and disjoint disks of bounded size range. The result matters wherever precision is expensive, from sensors to geographic data.
arxiv-2504-02711:
Meguya Ryu and co-authors read the grain of bamboo and teeth with polarized light. Their 2025 paper uses four-angle polarization micro-spectroscopy in the mid-infrared to map how chemical bonds are oriented inside two very different biomaterials: plant cellulose and tooth enamel.

In bamboo slices thinner than a micrometer, the method revealed where a key cellulose bond keeps a steady alignment and where it switches off. The detail reached a few micrometers across cell walls and vascular bundles. In tooth slices, enamel showed clear directional order while dentin did not. Modeling showed the trick can sense the orientation of features ten times smaller than the light spot. The authors offer the technique for reading hidden order in biological materials.
arxiv-2504-02911:
Explanations of why a language model answered as it did should reflect what the model truly used. Mohammad Reza Ghasemi Madani and co-authors present a method in 2025, called Noiser, that explains by controlled damage. Each input word's signal is blurred by a bounded amount. The words whose blurring shakes the answer most are credited with driving it.

They also propose a scoring idea, answerability. It asks whether the top-credited words alone can rebuild the model's output. Across six models and three tasks, Noiser beat gradient, attention, and rival damage-based methods. It won on both faithfulness and answerability. The authors offer it as a sturdier lens on model behavior for builders who must defend their systems' decisions.
arxiv-2504-03211:
Yiding Feng and Wei Tang study honest forecasts from a self-interested sender in a 2025 paper. A principal issues predictions that an agent takes at face value to make calls. Standards demand the forecasts stay calibrated, yet the sender's aims may clash with the agent's.

Given a small allowed calibration error, the team ask which predictor serves the sender best and how to compute it. Viewing predictors as edits of perfectly calibrated ones reveals the shape of the answer. For the common error measure, the best predictor overstates high odds and understates low ones, staying true in the middle. Fast algorithms compute near-best predictors in general, and exact ones for two key measures.
arxiv-2504-03411:
G Koutentakis and co-authors study a dressed impurity in a quantum gas in 2025. A single spinning atom sits inside a one dimensional gas of bosons. Light couples its two spin states, while only one state feels the gas. That setup dresses the atom in both light and sound waves of the gas.

Exact many body simulations test a simpler effective model of the system. The model reads off energy, weight, mass, and stiffness of the dressed atom well. Strong light coupling strips away the sound dressing and frees the atom. The tug of war between two dressings may guide future cold atom work.
arxiv-2504-03511:
Pikovsky studied how energy spreads in a chain of particles in this physics paper from twenty twenty-five. The particles sit in a row and interact through an endless-well rule, like hard balls that bounce. At the start, only a small group moves while the rest sit still. The question is how the active zone grows over time.

Pikovsky tracks the growth with averages and entropy measures of the energy spread. In two special cases the spreading follows a single clean scale. One is the plain hard-particle gas. The other fixes the spacing at half the well width. In all other cases the spread mixes several scales at once, a pattern called multiscale anomalous diffusion. The result sorts when simple laws of spreading apply.
arxiv-2504-03611:
George Elliott and Zhuang Niu link two traits in the theory of operator algebras, in this 2025 paper, the second in a series. One is the small boundary property: a system whose sets can be picked with borders thin enough to barely count.
