The other is Z-absorption, a self-similarity in the algebras built from such systems, which helps sort them into classes.

The authors set out Property (C), a new trait for a commutative subalgebra inside a larger C*-algebra. It is a comparison test stated through almost normalizers, which all but keep the smaller algebra as it is. For algebras from a free, minimal system with a uniform Rokhlin property, they prove a clean result. Then Property (C) for the natural subalgebra is exactly the system's small boundary property. That gives both fields a shared test. It also feeds the program that sorts these algebras by computable invariants.
arxiv-2504-03911:
Harrison Gimenez studied squares and cubes built inside Coxeter groups, in a solo mathematics paper published in 2025. Such groups act by mirror reflections and govern much of symmetry mathematics. A key set for each member lists the roots it flips. His core question asks when one member maps one such set onto another member's set. Four member charts that square with each other form the base tile.

Tiles glue edge to edge into cube charts of any dimension. In a finite group whose rank matches the dimension, such cubes must exist. For the type A family, he pairs the cubes, up to rotation, with binary trees of a set leaf count. He also pins down which members can edge a cube: just one named class of permutations.
arxiv-2504-04011:
Siva Rama Krishna Kottapalli and co-authors present a 2025 survey of foundation models for time series data. Such models, borrowed from language AI, now tackle forecasting, anomaly spotting, and trend work on data that unfolds over time. The field grew fast and lacks a shared map. The survey sorts the models with a new scheme that cuts across several lines.

Models split by design: some read data in patches, others take the raw stream. They split again by whether they give one forecast or a range of chances, and by whether they take one stream or many. The scheme also weighs model size and the training goal each model used. That last line is new for such surveys. The map helps builders pick a model and shows where fresh work is needed.
arxiv-2504-04111:
A mathematics paper from 2025 studies completely inert subgroups of Abelian groups, a delicate refinement of subgroup largeness. A subgroup is inert if every outer symmetry of the ambient group moves it only slightly. The sharper notions of complete and uniform inertness tighten that condition further. The paper defines those two notions carefully and then examines how they relate to each other.

The main results show that a subgroup is completely inert exactly when it is characteristically inert, a neighboring notion. The same equivalence holds for the uniformly completely inert versions. Those equivalences strengthen and extend earlier results by other mathematicians on totally inert subgroups, published the same year. The paper adds further related results on inertness in Abelian groups.
arxiv-2504-04211:
Junrong Lai and Changhong Li speed up the hunt for the source of a cosmic hum, in a 2025 paper. Pulsar timing arrays have detected a faint background of gravitational waves at very low frequencies. Telling which source made the hum means comparing many models, and the standard sampling method takes about ten days per dataset.

The pair train a type of neural network called a normalizing flow on the fifteen-year NANOGrav dataset. The trained network estimates how well each of ten source models fits, from merging giant black holes to cosmic strings and early-universe events. Total time drops to about twenty hours. Accuracy in picking between models stays close to the slow method. Faster checks let scientists test new ideas about the hum as fresh data arrives.
arxiv-2504-04711:
Alhajir and six co-authors present a paper from twenty twenty-five on AI models that learn from data they produce themselves. Today's large models are bounded by human-made training data. Their framework lets agents generate and check new knowledge by acting in an environment. A hard-to-game numeric reward, like disk space gained, steers learning. Agents write strategies and code to raise that score. Winning outcomes feed back into retraining the model. Checks favor real-world success over text similarity to dodge collapse.

Modular agents split analysis, strategy, and coding tasks. Fine-tuning uses a group-based reinforcement method. The authors sketch a path toward self-improving systems. Human-set limits are the barrier they aim to pass.
arxiv-2504-04911:
Ziyun Liang, Xiaoqing Guo, and their co-authors present IterMask3D, a 2025 method that finds and outlines anomalies in three dimensional brain MRI scans without labeled examples. Such methods learn what normal scans look like, then flag anything that departs from normal. The usual trick damages the input image and rebuilds it, but the damage also erases healthy detail, which causes false alarms.

Their method masks only part of the image at a time, rebuilds that part, and then shrinks the mask where the rebuild error is low. Round by round, healthy regions are unmasked and only odd regions stay covered. The final mask marks the anomalies. This test time loop aims at cleaner outlines of tumors and lesions with fewer false positives.
arxiv-2504-05011:
Pirogov and Zenin collect extra results on dark holes, odd objects that pair a central black hole with an outer halo made of scalar gravitons. The objects arise in a changed theory of gravity built on a quartet of metrics, where the usual symmetry of relativity breaks on its own. One exact solution anchors the study and could, in principle, explain why galaxy rotation curves stay flat far from the center.

To make the picture more realistic, the pair vary the base solution into a family of modified ones and study them on the computer across a spread of settings. The note gathers talk material that had to be left out of the printed proceedings for space.
arxiv-2504-05211:
Communication faces a chicken-and-egg trap: feedback about meaning seems to need meaning already shared. Richard Blythe and Casimir Fisch break the trap in a 2025 model where sheer individual differences do the bootstrapping.

In their large simulated population, agents differ slightly in how they behave in each situation. Two ordinary capacities do the rest: acting predictably in context, and lining up mental states before signaling, a shared-intentionality skill that need not involve language. From those ingredients, a system able to express unbounded meanings grows without anyone ever grading success. The result supports views of language as a flower of general social cognition rather than a dedicated module that had to come first.
arxiv-2504-05311: Ylli Prifti, Alessandro Provetti, and Pasquale de Meo present a web data tool in this 2025 paper. Their engine pulls structured facts out of web pages through a simple query tongue. It is built in modules, so parts can be swapped as needs change. The paper walks through hard build points, such as pages that load content late and messy page layouts. It also covers the steps taken to release the engine in public as open source work.
arxiv-2504-05411:
Reading personality from a person's posts is useful, but fine-tuning huge language models for the job costs a fortune. Lingzhi Shen and co-authors design a leaner route. Their framework, PersLLM, lets the big model read the raw text once and store rich features in a dynamic memory layer. A small, replaceable output network then learns the personality task from those stored features.

Because the features are cached, the expensive model never needs retraining for each scenario. The light output network doubles as a probe: its scores predict how the whole system will do. Experiments on benchmark datasets show sharply lower computing costs with competitive accuracy. The design also adapts easily across detection tasks. The paper argues personality detection can be less, but better.
arxiv-2504-05511:
Michael Rutkowski and co-authors studied quiet galaxies in a 2025 letter using Hubble Space Telescope data. Massive quiescent galaxies formed stars fast in the early universe, then shut down. The team picked such galaxies at redshifts between 0.5 and 1.5 in deep survey fields. They modeled each galaxy's light across wavelengths, adding new ultraviolet images from the UVCANDELS program.

About fifteen percent of these quiet galaxies showed minor recent star formation, under a tenth of their mass within the last billion years. That recent activity linked only weakly to how rich the local environment was. If the link is real, mergers and encounters with neighbors play only a small part in shaping these galaxies. Most of their growth story must come from inside, or from earlier times.
arxiv-2504-05911:
Jie Liu examines the stability of explosive wave solutions in a 2025 note. Semilinear wave equations can blow up in finite time, forming self-similar profiles that repeat their shape as they grow. Whether nearby solutions settle onto those profiles decides if the blow-up is a curiosity or a real fate.

The note works in the superconformal regime and in every dimension. Its engine is an equivalence: the linearized operators around the blow-up look the same under Lorentz transformations once written in self-similar variables. That mirror lets Liu prove mode stability with unusual economy. The ordinary blow-up family then falls out as asymptotically stable, stretching classic results by Merle and Zaag and a newer one by Ostermann. The author hopes the mirror trick will serve kindred blow-up problems.
arxiv-2504-06211:
Alhad Daftardar and six colleagues build hardware to speed up zero-knowledge proofs, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Such proofs let one side convince another that a claim is true while revealing nothing else.

They matter for blockchains, private machine learning, and electronic voting, but making a proof is slow. Past accelerators sped up schemes that either need a fresh trusted setup for each use or yield large proofs that cost more to check. The team's design, zkSpeed, targets HyperPlonk, a scheme that avoids those trade-offs. The paper lays out the hardware and what it gains. Faster proving could widen the real-world use of private, checkable computing. The work appeared at a computer architecture conference in Tokyo.
arxiv-2504-06611:
Chrisantha Fernando, Dylan Banarse, and Simon Osindero explore why agents might seek to be understood, in a 2025 paper. People seem to want both to grasp others and to be grasped by them, even when no reward is at stake. The authors test this idea with learning agents in a classic setup where two agents sense each other by crossing paths.

They try rewards for curiosity alone, and rewards for copying, swaying, and quickly guessing the other agent. Curiosity alone did not make agents seek contact. Rewards tied to mutual grasp did, and they also helped agents work together when only one side gained from the other's act. The study offers a model for how social drive may arise.
arxiv-2504-06811:
Abhinav Roy and co-authors graft polynomial mathematics onto convolutional networks to sharpen lung nodule diagnosis. Their 2025 paper addresses a hard imaging problem: telling benign from malignant nodules in CT scans, where nodules vary wildly in size, shape, and texture. Standard networks can miss the fine spatial and spectral detail the distinction hides in.

Their hybrid inserts Chebyshev polynomial expansions into the network layers. The polynomials' orthogonality and recursion let the model represent complex patterns with greater fidelity and capture high-frequency features ordinary filters blur. Trained on two benchmark lung datasets, the model beat conventional networks on accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. Medical imaging has many such borderline tasks, where the signal is real but faint. The paper's wager is that classical approximation theory, centuries old, still has gifts for deep learning's hardest corners.
arxiv-2504-06911: Christopher Cashen classifies a family of symmetry groups defined by right-angled building rules. He asks which two-dimensional right-angled Coxeter groups look, at large scale, like right-angled Artin groups built from trees; the large-scale sameness here is quasi-isometry. He shows that whenever such a Coxeter group matches a tree-based Artin group in that sense, the match is concrete. It contains a finite-index copy of such an Artin group. The result turns a geometric resemblance into an exact algebraic containment.
arxiv-2504-07111:
Shaping soft materials by computer, so a part bends just right under load, needs a score for how each tweak shifts the goal. Anurag Bhattacharyya speeds that score up in a solo 2025 paper. The slow way, for one such material on one processor, took about forty-five minutes a pass.

The new method walks the model's mesh in depth-first order and works the score out with a time-aware mirror method. It is built in a parallel frame that splits the work across many processors at once. That scale is what makes the design loop fit in a workday. The paper lays out the frame and its use for large design tasks where soft stuff must bear complex loads. Such tools feed fields from medical gels to soft robots.
arxiv-2504-07311:
Alain Brizard solves a set of paths by which a magnetic X-point can collapse in a refined plasma model, in a 2025 paper. The model, extended magnetohydrodynamics, keeps effects that simpler versions drop, including the inertia of electrons. In two dimensions it binds the flow field and the magnetic field into one system. That system can blow up in finite time at an X-point, where field lines cross and snap.

Brizard shrinks the four fields onto a self-similar frame, so the whole problem falls to five coupled rate equations. Those he solves in closed form with elliptic functions, sorting the paths by how a particle would move in a four-power well. The closed forms match direct computer runs closely, down to the very time the X-point gives way. The author offers the paths as exact benchmarks for collapse physics.
arxiv-2504-07611:
A medical image model can be right on average yet dangerously wrong on some patients, missing disease in a subset of scans. Rui Luo and Zhixin Zhou tackle that unevenness in a 2025 paper on uncertainty for image segmentation. Their method, conformal risk adaptation, builds a new score so that prediction sets adjust per image, aiming to keep the miss rate steady across cases.

They prove a fresh link between risk control and classic prediction theory, and add a calibration step for the poorly scaled probabilities segmentation models produce. On polyp segmentation tests, their variants held valid overall risk while spreading errors far more evenly across images.
arxiv-2504-07711:
Federica Granese, Benjamin Navet, Serena Villata, and Charles Bouveyron wrote a 2025 paper on topic modeling for text that arrives as a stream. Social media pours out text daily, so models must update as new batches land, not retrain from scratch. Topics also drift over time, and real shifts should be flagged.

Their method, StreamETM, extends a neural topic model that embeds topics and words in one space. Models trained on successive batches are merged with an unbalanced optimal transport method, which matches topics across time at low cost. A change point detector watches the stream and marks when topics truly shift. Tests on simulated and real data showed the method beating rivals. The code is public for other researchers.
arxiv-2504-08311:
Georg Junker shows that a spinning electron in a perfectly round electric or magnetic field hides a supersymmetric structure, in this 2025 paper. The Pauli equation governs a non-relativistic electron with spin under outside potentials. When those potentials depend only on distance from a center, the mathematics splits in an elegant way. Supersymmetry here means partner Hamiltonians whose energy levels interlock.

Both scalar and vector round potentials get the full treatment. Old friends like the radial oscillator and the Coulomb problem gain new insight, and a few new exactly solvable models appear, one mixing translation and scaling in its shape rules. The spin-orbit coupling turns out to play the role of Witten parity, the grading at supersymmetry's heart. Exact solutions anchor the approximations everyone else must use.
arxiv-2504-08511:
Mazhari and Rituraj work out the limits of a compact way to make photon pairs: a single emitter inside a doubly resonant cavity. Photon pairs are basic currency for quantum information, but the standard down-conversion route is inefficient and bulky. A cavity device could be smaller and far more effective.

Modeling the system with the Lindblad master equation, the authors derive an approximate analytical solution for achievable efficiency and brightness. The best operating point matches the cavity's two-photon outcoupling rate to the atom-field coupling strength, while suppressing one-photon leakage. Peak efficiency near thirty-five percent far exceeds down-conversion devices. Correlation measurements confirm the output is strongly bunched two-photon light with super-Poissonian statistics.
arxiv-2504-09311:
Jiaxin Jiang and five co-authors present a parallel framework for spotting fraud in huge transaction networks, in a technical report from twenty twenty-five. One proven trick is to find the densest cluster of accounts, where fraud rings hide. Existing methods crawl through such networks one step at a time, which is far too slow for billions of links.

Their system peels the graph in parallel, exploiting quirks of that peeling process, with guarantees on quality and speed. Simple interfaces let users reshape the goal for differing fraud patterns. In tests it ran up to a hundred times faster than rivals. Prevention of bad transactions leapt in their trials, while density error shrank to a few percent.
arxiv-2504-09611:
Steering a system whose memory lingers calls for math that can handle rates of change with memory built in. Dev Prakash Jha and Raju George build such a frame in work from twenty twenty-five, for a class of wavy, memory-based systems. Start values can also depend on the whole past path, not just one instant.

The team rewrites the task as a single operator puzzle, which opens the door to known tools. Rules are given that prove good steering plans exist, in both smooth and rough cases. For square-shaped cost scores, they work out the best-plan rules and tie them to a classic low-point law. Worked cases close the work and show the frame in action.
arxiv-2504-09811:
Mean curvature flow moves a surface inward at a speed set by its bending, and the flow breaks down at singular points. Hanbing Fang and Yu Li study those bad points in a 2025 paper, for flows that start from a smooth, closed, mean-convex surface.

The pair establish volume estimates for the singular set, and for the finer layers inside it that sort points by how the breakdown looks up close. Their bounds are uniform, holding across the whole flow, and sharp, meaning the rates cannot be improved in general. Such estimates help geometers measure how large the singular part of a flow can be, a key step in using flows to prove facts about shapes.
arxiv-2504-09911: Ken Sato builds special cycles on K3 surfaces in a 2025 paper. The cycles are higher Chow cycles of a set type, placed on families of K3 surfaces that carry a twist of order three. He proves the cycles cannot be split into simpler parts for very general members of those families. The proof joins degeneration arguments with direct computations of a regulator map that tests the cycles.
arxiv-2504-10611:
Netan Dogra explains a p-adic route to unlikely intersections in a 2025 number theory survey. Some conjectures ask when a curve can meet a special algebraic set more often than dimension counting allows, and the Manin-Mumford conjecture, now a theorem, is the classic case.

The Buium-Coleman approach attacks such problems with p-adic analysis, studying solutions through prime-tinted glasses rather than complex ones. Dogra lays out the method and its generalizations for a broad audience. As a worked illustration, he gives a p-adic proof of a theorem by Bombieri, Masser, and Zannier about curves inside tori.
arxiv-2504-11011:
Francesca Pezzuti and co-authors study how to score web page quality so crawlers waste less time in this 2025 paper. The web holds huge amounts of low-quality content. Search engines must still return good, relevant results. Crawling and indexing junk burns resources that better pages deserve. Quality scores can steer where crawlers go first. They also feed pruning and tiering of the index itself.

Earlier work used neural scores of meaning to prune indexes. The team extends that idea to live crawling decisions. A learned scorer rates pages cheaply enough for web scale. The study tests whether quality-guided crawling keeps results strong. Search quality and cost both ride on such choices. The paper is information retrieval research.
arxiv-2504-11211:
Jing Li and co-authors prove a still pulse must wobble in skew-tilt flow sets, by a path count craft. Still pulses are lone waves that hold shape; their stand or fall rules what a yard will show. Old firm tools lean on self-pair build, which skew sets lack. Their 2025 craft swaps in a cross count and a flow mark to bridge that gap. A fail mark for still pulses falls out.

The FitzHugh-Nagumo set, a nerve-tale stock form, is the show case. Both its goad and its brake bear in-born bends there. Path craft can thus call pulse fate where pair tools are blind. Such calls guide nerve and wave lore.
arxiv-2504-11311:
Supersymmetry, the idea that every known particle has a heavier partner, reshaped physics in the 1970s. Castellani traces how it grew out of symmetry ideas and then became local, giving supergravity, a theory that folds gravity into the scheme. The developments took about six years, from 1970 to 1976, and drew on several lines of work that were partly independent.

The essay follows the interplay of insights, methods, and motives across those lines. It shows how results in one area unlocked steps in another, and how the community converged on a shared framework. Castellani closes with a reflection on the style of science this episode displays. The piece was invited for a volume marking fifty years of supergravity, and it reads as history and philosophy of physics rather than a new research result.
arxiv-2504-11711:
Haonan Li, Hang Zhang, Kexin Pei, and Zhiyun Qian present BugLens, a system that uses large language models to clean up the output of static code analysis. Static tools scan software for bugs, but on huge code bases such as the Linux kernel they raise many false alarms. Language models read code well, yet alone they reason too loosely for this job.

BugLens places the model after the static tool, as a filter. It walks the model through set steps: judge the security impact of a flagged spot, then check path and data limits in the code. On Linux kernel taint-style bugs flagged by static tools, the filter raised precision about seven-fold. False alarms fell sharply. The process also surfaced four bugs that had not been reported before. The authors present the work as a way to pair classic tools with language models.
arxiv-2504-12111:
Hubert Lam and co-authors hone how well a lone photon meshes with a laser pulse, in a 2025 paper. The clash of the two is a workhorse for shaping odd light states in quantum tech. A dot-based photon source could join that work, if the mesh can be read and raised with care.

Two read tricks, both built on photon pair counts at a beam splitter's exits, gauge the mesh. One watches the classic dip in joint counts; the other watches bunching at a single exit. Tuning the laser across its traits lifted the mesh to about three quarters. Mismatched tone and timing shapes, plus slow charge noise in the source, capped the gain. The authors map the caps for future builds.
arxiv-2504-12211:
Elise Paradis and co-authors describe how to benchmark AI coding tools in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Model benchmarks are common, but products built on models also need tests of the user experience. Without them, teams chase model quality and neglect how the tool feels to use.

The case study shares the team's process for building sturdy, modular test parts. These include surveys on who users are and how they view AI, a standard task that can be scored, and surveys on tasks and features. The parts are built for enterprise use and can be reused across products. The authors hope the work lowers the bar for testing developer experience in AI code products.
arxiv-2504-12411:
Antiferromagnets on a triangular lattice settle into a spiral order that textbooks describe with plain spin rotations. Bastián Pradenas and co-authors show in this 2025 paper that the true symmetry is larger than that. The order parameter answers to an extended group, combining rotations in two spaces at once, and the ground state breaks only part of it.

What survives leaves conserved charges behind, and those charges give the spin waves, called magnons, a brand-new label: isospin. Magnons thus carry more than energy and momentum. The framework ties these magnets to chiral symmetry breaking in particle physics, where the same pattern appears. The result reshapes how degeneracies in non-collinear magnets should be counted and read.
arxiv-2504-12511:
Shravan Chaudhari and co-workers used multimodal models as assistants for studying human visual perception in a 2025 paper. Rather than training yet another network to predict complexity scores. They hand the models set up rules from psychology and cognitive science and ask them to match and interpret visual content through those lenses. The aim is a tagging-free setup for judging how useful such models are as cognitive assistants in human-computer contact research.

Benchmarking runs across explainability rules relevant to perception test where model thinking aligns with human accounts and where it slips. The authors frame the exercise as groundwork for principled review of model interpretability. Meant to improve human thinking and expose biases in current perceptual metrics.
arxiv-2504-12611:
Quantum computers may one day crack hard scheduling and packing problems, but real problems come with constraints, and forcing constraints into the math usually costs extra qubits. Lee and Lau test a slack-free penalty scheme for gate-based quantum machines.

The standard trick turns inequality constraints into penalties with slack variables, which bloats the problem and warps the search. Instead, the authors encode the constraints directly with step-like penalties, an exponential function and a Heaviside step, which suppress invalid answers without new qubits or delicate tuning. On the multiple knapsack problem, the step formulation beat unbalanced penalization on both feasibility and quality of solutions, while using fewer qubits overall. The work borrows ideas from quantum annealing and threshold methods and ports them to gate-based algorithms.
arxiv-2504-12811:
Michael Steiner and co-authors fix flaws in a fast way to draw three dimensional scenes, built from many soft blobs called Gaussians. The method is quick, but it can show jagged edges, warping, and pops as the view moves, since each blob is treated as a flat shape.

Their method judges each blob in full three dims at each step. A smart smoothing filter cuts the jagged edges, and a steady way to bound blobs stops the pops. A new culling step speeds the draw and cuts sorting costs. Tests show top quality on known views and far better results on new views than rival methods.
arxiv-2504-12911:
Weijie Shi and ten co-authors built a benchmark to test whether large language models match the values of a user's country. Their twenty twenty-five paper notes that a model can take stands that clash with local policy, law, or morals. Past checks leaned on ethics reviews or hand-made quizzes, which miss that breadth and do not scale.

Their benchmark, NaVAB, covers five nations: China, the United States, the United Kingdom, France, and Germany. A pipeline pulls value topics from raw sources, tags them, and drops cases where values do not clash. Tests across many models show where clashes arise. The bench can also pair with alignment methods to cut those clashes.
arxiv-2504-13011:
Six physicists wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on hard math needed for collider experiments. When protons collide, they can make a pair of top quarks plus a W boson. To predict that event with high precision, physicists must compute a full set of two-loop Feynman integrals, which are large sums that describe particle paths.

The team computed the full set in a simplified color scheme. They used a method based on differential equations, meaning equations that track how the sums change. Tricks from finite field arithmetic helped them handle the algebra. They solved the equations with numbers in the range where real collisions happen.
arxiv-2504-13111:
Kumar Manas and co-authors presented this 2025 method for forecasting where road users will move next. Self-driving systems need those forecasts, plus honest doubt when the scene is unclear. Deep models often fail on rare scenes and report confidence poorly. Their framework, SHIFT, rebuilds the task as sorting paths into classes rather than drawing one line.

The model separates doubt from lack of data and doubt from plain chance, using a guarded Gaussian process design. It also learns from driving rules written in plain words, such as stop rules, pulled from labels by a language model pipeline. On the nuScenes data set, SHIFT beat prior methods on doubt quality and path error. It did best at crossings, where doubt runs highest.
arxiv-2504-13811:
Feijiang Han and a team of co-authors test whether large language models can spot webshell attacks, in two thousand twenty-five. A webshell is a malicious script planted on a web server. Older detectors need task-specific training and can break when data are scarce or attacks shift quickly.

The team graded seven language models against standard detectors on a large set of PHP scripts. Off-the-shelf prompting lagged behind the established tools, with big models precise but missing attacks. Their behavior-aware framework focuses the model on risky functions and well-chosen examples. It lifted every model's score, and three models beat the prior best marks. A small model also became competitive.
arxiv-2504-14111:
Zhijun Zhou, Xin Luo, Yinjian Zhao, and Daren Yu studied how a lumpy magnetic field sways a Hall thruster's fast waves. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with SPT type thrusters for spacecraft. Their magnet build, with conductive posts, makes the field uneven round the ring by design. That lump can bend how electrons drift in a closed loop and cross the field. The team ran two dimensional particle in cell sims in the radial and ring plane.

The lumps shaped the drift speed spread and fed a high tone ring instability. That wave in turn drives odd electron cross flow, a long stand puzzle in these engines. Readers in electric propulsion get a link from magnet build to loss paths.
arxiv-2504-14811:
Bowen Yang classified a family of quantum cellular automata in a 2025 paper using symbol-based L-theory. Clifford quantum cellular automata are locality-preserving transformations built from Clifford operations, acting on tiny bits of any dimension placed on any metric space. Sorting them up to circuits and separated motions tells physicists which exotic transformations are truly distinct.

Yang recasts the automata as even formations in a category built from the space's shapes, using a delooping method from symbol-based topology. The stabilized classes then match a Witt group from that category, which depends only on the space's large-scale shape. For plain lattices the sorting recovers and extends known lists, while cones and other spaces link automata to broad homology theories.
arxiv-2504-14911:
Yixin Lan uses, in a 2025 solo-authored paper, Lusztig's perverse sheaves to build canonical bases for certain algebra modules. The modules arise as layered pieces of tensor products and of restricted modules for symmetric Kac-Moody algebras, objects at the heart of modern representation theory.

Realizing the modules geometrically, through sheaves on multi-framed quivers, supplies the bases directly. As an application, Lan proves that the decomposition and restriction numbers of these algebras equal the dimensions of top Borel-Moore homology groups of certain regions inside Nakajima's quiver varieties. Algebra counts become geometry measurements.
arxiv-2504-15511:
Isaac Dobes and Naihuan Jing prove that a classic algebra object measures quantum entanglement in a 2025 paper. Cayley first hyperdeterminant already encodes two known entanglement scores for even qubit counts. The pair ask whether a power of it counts as a true measure under physics rules. A true measure must vanish on separable states and never grow under local work.

Their proof covers both pure and mixed states in full. The quantity stays fixed under local unitary moves. It also fails to rise on average under local operations with messages. Worked examples show it detects genuine many party GHZ type links. The result widens entanglement scoring to higher level systems.
arxiv-2504-15711:
The MEG II collaboration reports a sharper limit on a forbidden particle decay in a 2025 paper. The decay, a muon turning into a positron and a photon, would break a rule of the standard model of physics, and seeing it would signal new laws.

The search ran at a Swiss institute using data from 2021 and 2022. The new detector reached more than twice the sensitivity of its predecessor in a quarter of the running time. No sign of the decay rose above background noise. The team sets the chance of the decay below a strict ceiling, the tightest yet. More data already gathered should push the ceiling lower still.
arxiv-2504-16011: Fabien Le Floc'h derived pencil-and-paper formulas for pricing a class of Asian basket spread options under the standard Black-Scholes model, in a 2025 paper. Such options blend an average price over time with a spread between assets, and exact prices are hard to get. His formulas come from a stochastic Taylor expansion around a simpler log-normal stand-in model. Tests show the formulas stay highly accurate for Asian and spread options in practice. Unlike rival approaches, they need no numerical integration and no root solving.
arxiv-2504-16311: Bruno Bauwens and Bruno Loff give a short proof of a deep link in computer science. On one side stands secret key agreement, the base of secure codes. On the other stands a hard problem about Kolmogorov complexity, which measures how short a description of data can be. Ball, Liu, Mazor, and Pass had shown the two ideas stand or fall together. Bauwens and Loff widen that result and supply a brief proof of its hard direction.
arxiv-2504-16511:
Fengze Liu and co-authors present a 2025 paper on picking training data for large language models with quality and diversity held in balance. Builders often filter for quality first and fix the mix later, which hides the trade-off between the two. With a fixed training budget, each added text must be judged both on its own merit and on what it adds to the whole.

Their framework, QuaDMix, tunes the data mix automatically against both goals at once. It weighs each source's quality against how much fresh ground it covers. The authors present the joint approach as a more efficient route to strong pretraining than one-metric filtering.
arxiv-2504-16811:
Jessica Eck and co-authors present a new method to measure attenuation length and group velocity in clear liquids, serving particle physics detector builders. How clear a liquid is decides how well big instruments perform, and the method uses a cavity that stacks many bounced light passes. A pulsed source feeds the Fabry-Pérot-like setup.

Very long attenuation lengths can be measured with small error. Standard light tools struggle beyond ten meters of clarity, and the cavity spacing also yields light's group velocity. No standard method supplies that second value. Careful tests and a real run confirm the setup. Teams can certify scintillators and water with more trust. Neutrino experiments gain the most.
arxiv-2504-17111:
Tekin Gunasar and Virginia de Sa work on moving brain-computer interfaces from one person to another without starting training from scratch, in a 2025 paper. Their focus is imagined movement: a user pictures moving a hand, and the system must detect that intent from brain waves. Each person's signals differ, so filters tuned on one user often fail on the next.

Their method first aligns the signal patterns of different users on a curved math surface built for such data. A fresh spatial filter is then computed from the aligned patterns. Across three data sets, the method beat the standard filter by a small margin overall. The edge grew clearly larger when only a little training data was available. That matters for real use, where long setup sessions tire users.
arxiv-2504-17211:
Abdallah Alalem Albustami and Ahmad Taha wrote this 2025 paper on hidden cyberattacks against water networks. Cities pipe water through systems run by sensors and software. That digital layer opens a door: an attacker who fakes sensor data can bend operations while looking normal.

Such stealthy false data attacks are the paper's focus. Past work studied either how to spot them or single attack recipes, leaving a gap: how much system knowledge an attack needs, and how much damage each level buys. The authors run a systematic study across mixes of physical limits, monitoring demands, and detection evasion. Their attack designs range from finely tuned strikes that obey every rule to crude data tweaks. The results map the real threat for utilities planning defenses.
arxiv-2504-17311:
Yulia Otmakhova, Hung Thinh Truong, and their co-authors present FLUKE, a 2025 framework for testing how robust language models are to changes in wording. The name is short for a linguistically driven, task free evaluation approach. It varies test texts in small, controlled ways, from spelling and punctuation up to dialect and style.

Large language models help create the changed texts, and human checks confirm the changes are sound. The team tested tuned models and large models on six tasks, four of sorting type and two of writing type. Effects of the changes depended strongly on the task. Even large models broke under some changes, above all natural ones in syntax, style, and negation. Bigger models helped mainly with surface level changes.
arxiv-2504-17811:
Anirudhan Badrinath and co-authors from Pinterest describe a single system that learns compact codes for the many kinds of items on the platform, in a 2025 paper. Such codes power search and recommendations. Older methods each handled one angle: links between items, the order of user actions, or the content of posts themselves.

Their system, OmniSage, blends all three through several paired learning tasks. Custom infrastructure trains it on graphs with billions of nodes. Once learned, the same codes serve many products at once. The company reports about a two and a half percent rise in saves across five applications after rollout. The model code was released in public, an unusual step for work at this scale.
arxiv-2504-17911:
Ali Akil and co-authors revisit Hawking's black hole radiation argument in a 2025 paper. Hawking's derivation treated the matter forming the black hole as a vacuum state. The authors ask how the radiation changes when the initial matter sits in a non-vacuum quantum state instead.

They classify which excitations of the initial state can be told apart by measuring the outgoing radiation at future infinity. Using algebraic quantum field theory, they give the results a clear local meaning. The work speaks to the black hole information problem, which asks whether information falling in is truly lost.
arxiv-2504-18111:
Yohei Nishino, James Gardner, Yanbei Chen, and Kentaro Somiya propose a new sensor design in two thousand twenty-five. Their speed meter uses quantum teleportation to measure displacement with an interferometer. The aim is to cut quantum noise that comes from radiation pressure on the mirrors.

They give two versions of the scheme, one that acts in real time and one that works through post-processing. Both beat the standard quantum limit for displacement sensing. The team points to gravitational-wave detectors as a key use. Their design boosts low-frequency sensitivity without changing the core optics of a standard interferometer. They frame it as a new route to dodging measurement back-action, using entanglement.
arxiv-2504-18211:
Russell Standish, writing alone, ports a dynamic memory management library for graphics processors from CUDA to SYCL in this 2025 arXiv paper. Code running on a graphics card normally cannot allocate memory on the fly, which limits some programs. The original library, Ouroboros, added that ability for NVIDIA's CUDA platform.

SYCL is a cross-platform standard for accelerator chips, so the port could free the library from one vendor's hardware. Because SYCL can also compile to a CUDA back end, Standish can compare the port's speed head-to-head with the original code. The port can also be tested on other hardware, such as Intel's Xe graphics. The paper reports on that porting work and what the comparisons show.
arxiv-2504-18311:
Four physicists prove a universal pattern in quantum operator growth in a paper from 2025. Complex quantum systems are hard to track exactly, so methods split motion into fast and slow parts. The recursion method studies that split in a special operator space. The team asks what the fast part looks like when the chain of steps grows very long.

They prove the fast dynamics settle into universal forms from random matrix theory. The pattern appears in both chaotic and calm systems, as long as spectra are smooth. At some settings the shape matches a classic semicircle law, and at others a Bessel form. As a bonus, they give a numeric method to estimate spectra. The proof ties into a known growth hypothesis.
arxiv-2504-18411:
Christopher Zawacki and Eyad Abed propose, in 2025, a privacy method that adds heavy-tailed noise to data answers. Privacy worries grow as platforms collect more personal data, and differential privacy gives a formal way to measure protection. The common Gaussian noise method only reaches an approximate form of that guarantee.

Their stable-distribution method reaches the pure form of the guarantee while keeping a prized property: noise sums stay in the same family, which suits adding up many answers. They map how the privacy level depends on the noise settings. Error comparisons with the Gaussian method follow. The authors present it as an appealing choice for privacy-first uses.
arxiv-2504-18511:
Ethari Hrishikesh and co-authors introduce co-change graph entropy, a new process metric for predicting software defects, published in 2025. Process metrics are prized because they ignore programming language and are easy to collect, and they often beat product metrics. Change entropy, which measures how scattered edits are, is a well-known file-level example.

The new metric models files that change together as a graph and measures that scattering. Across eight Apache projects, it correlated significantly with defect counts, with correlation up to a moderate level. Swapping it in for change entropy improved defect classification in most settings, though not significantly on its own. Combined with change entropy, it improved results in most settings with statistically confirmed gains. The authors conclude the two metrics complement each other in practice.
arxiv-2504-18611:
Two authors explore whether today's cosmic acceleration could be the afterglow of a decayed false vacuum. Their model starts with a quintessence field stuck in a metastable state that carries real vacuum energy. When that state decays, the field is freed and rolls on. The team imposes the string swampland criteria, which demand a steep enough slope in the field's effective potential, with a pressure condition tied to the slope.

Under those rules, the coupling must stay below 0.6. In a narrow band of couplings, the dark energy equation of state lands between -0.8 and -0.4 and the field settles into slow roll at a stable point. The authors suggest the present dark energy may be a slowly shifting scalar rather than a fixed constant. Push the values slightly off, though, and the swampland rules break.
arxiv-2504-19111:
Brianna Zawadzki and co-authors image planet-forming disks with a sharper method in a 2025 paper. The exoALMA program observed fifteen young disks at fine spatial and speed resolution. Gas in those disks should circle in smooth Keplerian flow, so kinks in that flow betray hidden planets or physics.

Regularized maximum likelihood imaging rebuilds the disk picture from raw radio data. The method hunts small non-Keplerian features that standard imaging smears away. Such features are faint and easy to fake with noise, so care is vital. Cleaner maps of gas motion tighten the case for unseen worlds. The pipeline serves the whole exoALMA disk sample.
arxiv-2504-19211:
Yuhang Li and co-authors apply a film equation to image sharpening in a 2025 paper. Thin-film equations track how a surface layer flows and levels. With a slope term that shifts over space and time, they gain new uses beyond physics.

The team sort when solutions last for all time and when they blow up in finite time. A reshaped well method handles the moving sets that variable terms create. Decay rates for lasting solutions and lifespan bounds for blow-ups are also set. Image tests then show the equations sharpen pictures well. The work joins hard analysis to a plain, useful task.
arxiv-2504-19311:
Chaoming Song recasts a deep fix-up scheme for field maths as a split of a linked system in a 2025 paper. The scheme tames wild poles in sums over a field's own rules. Song views the set of those rules as a link on a plane that pairs space with a dial disc.

A known match splits the link into a bare form part that holds all poles and a smooth part that stays finite. Fix terms then match the bare part's jump data, he shows. The known graph scheme falls out as a pale shade of the split.
arxiv-2504-19611:
Arata Jingu and co-authors present Scene2Hap, a system that generates vibration signals for full virtual reality scenes, in a research paper from 2025. Touch feedback deepens immersion, but designing it object by object for a whole scene takes long. A system that reads the scene and writes plausible touch signals could scale the work.

A multimodal language model estimates each object's meaning, material, and vibration traits from scene data. Those traits drive audio signals that convert into touch signals, or guide retrieval of ready ones. Spread and fading of vibration to neighbor objects are also modeled. Three user studies confirm the estimates and the realism of the signals produced.
arxiv-2504-19711:
Anil Raghav and co-authors argue for a new universal route to energizing charged particles in a 2025 paper. Magnetic reconnection heats cosmic plasmas, yet how its energy reaches particles stayed unclear, and wave or flare models fall short for the million degree solar corona and the fast solar wind. Their candidate, called the Raghav effect, has particle magnetic moments trading energy with shifting magnetic fields in sudden jumps.

Data from the Wind spacecraft show proton heating that matches the effect predictions. The authors present it as one mechanism behind energy flow across many magnetized space settings, from the solar wind to distant astrophysical plasmas.
arxiv-2504-19811:
Takuya Tamura, Taro Yano, Masafumi Enomoto, and Masafumi Oyamada ask whether a language model's family tree can predict how well it will score, in this 2025 paper. Builders often fine-tune or merge existing models, so new models descend from known parents. Guessing a child's score before costly training would save time and computing power.

Their method adds family ties to a standard prediction model, rewarding scores that stay smooth along parent-child links, even across several steps. They tested it on 2,934 public models and more than 21,000 scores across six benchmarks. Family-aware forecasts beat plain methods by a clear margin, and they worked even for brand-new models with almost no data. The authors offer the approach as a cheap guide for tuning, data choice, and model merging.
arxiv-2504-19911:
Four mathematicians, Aidan Sudbury, Arthur Sun, David Treeby, and Edward Wang, study a chance puzzle about broken sticks. They imagine stick lengths drawn at random, then ask how likely it is that no three of them can form a triangle.

Their answer links the puzzle to the famous Fibonacci numbers. The chance of avoiding a triangle equals one divided by the product of the first Fibonacci numbers, one for each stick. The paper proves this neat result and then extends the same idea to four-sided shapes and to shapes with more sides. It is a short, clean piece of probability work with a surprising pattern at its core.
arxiv-2504-20011:
Aditya Vatsavai and co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, a lightweight tool that lets microscopes hunt structure-property links with less waste. In materials work, a map of tiny structure must be paired with slow probe readings of how each spot behaves. Full grids waste time on dull spots. Past active learning tools learn the link as they go, but they bog down when outputs are many and correlated.

Their tool is driven by curiosity. It steers the microscope to spots whose structure-property relation the model has not yet learned, flagged by the model's own predicted error. Tests show it beats random sampling at predicting properties from structures. The authors offer it as a convenient aid for fast mapping in materials laboratories. It runs with far less computing cost than the heavy active learning tools.
arxiv-2504-20111:
Anubhav Jain and co-authors forge and erase image watermarks with a single example in a 2025 paper. Diffusion model watermarks hide a key in the starting noise and were thought hard to copy or strip. The attack needs no access to the model's weights, only one watermarked picture.

The key insight is geometric: many clean images map back to the same starting noise, so each watermark owns a region of image space. Nudging a plain image into that region forges the mark; nudging a marked image out erases it. The team broke four watermark schemes across two generator versions. They close by urging stronger designs, since provenance tools fail if one sample suffices.
arxiv-2504-20211:
Mattia Perrone and co-authors present a 2025 study on how defects are born inside metals. A new structure forming inside a uniform one is called nucleation. In metals, the key defects are dislocations, line flaws that rule how the metal bends and carries heat. Simulations can watch atoms move, yet pinning the birth path and its rate stays hard. The tracking gauge a study picks turns out to matter a lot.

A poor gauge bends the rate that the same data seem to give. The team turn that flaw into a tool: a data-driven scheme hunts the best gauge by a variational rule. The best gauge yields a faithful picture of the birth path. Their test case is dislocation birth in a crystal. Sound gauges could sharpen many rate studies in materials science.
arxiv-2504-20411:
Amartya Mukherjee and co-authors apply diffusion models to streams of timed events in a 2025 paper. Temporal point processes model sequences like trades, clicks, or quakes: what happens, and when. Forecasting them well means capturing how timing and type entangle. Diffusion models generate data by reversing a noise process, and the authors give them an uneven clock.

Their noise schedule corrupts later events more slowly than early ones. Early events therefore crystallize first during generation and anchor the forecast of the far future. Training rests on a flow matching objective that fits a broad family of such schedules. On benchmark data the method topped rivals at predicting both the next gap and the next event type, and it shone on long horizons and flexible forecast windows.
arxiv-2504-20811:
Alessandro Giovagnoli, Sigurd Huber, and Gerhard Krieger translate a radar imaging algorithm into quantum circuits. Their 2025 paper concerns synthetic aperture radar, the Earth-observing technique that builds sharp images from a moving antenna. Image resolution keeps climbing, and with it the computing cost of focusing raw radar echoes into pictures. The range-Doppler algorithm is a standard focusing method.

Quantum computing's proven edge in Fourier transforms, a core ingredient of focusing, motivated the translation. The authors show how reference functions, the algorithm's steering templates, become quantum gates, and they lay out the full focusing circuit. Gate counting gives the core routine a cost that grows only linearly with problem size. The paper weighs honestly where a quantum advantage might one day appear in radar processing.
arxiv-2504-20911:
Bug reports are often long and tangled, and a 2025 study by Zhiyuan Chen and co-authors tests whether language models can split them into clean, small units. Splitting a report well helps developers grasp and fix each issue faster, which protects software quality.

The team gathered 127 resolved privacy-related bug reports from Apache Jira and tested ChatGPT and DeepSeek under several prompting styles. With plain one-shot prompts, both models did poorly at the split task. After the prompts were improved with worked examples, ChatGPT's rate of correct splits rose by 140 percent and DeepSeek's by about 164 percent. The authors close that the models can help, but their skill hinges on prompt quality.
arxiv-2504-21111:
Drones and ground robots make a natural team, if their routes are planned well, and a 2025 paper by Md Safwan Mondal and co-authors builds a learning system for that planning. Drones cover ground fast but run out of battery, while ground vehicles move slowly yet can carry charge and act as mobile recharging stations.

The team's deep reinforcement learning system plans routes for the mixed team so all task points are visited in the least time. Drones drop back to the ground vehicles to recharge along the way. A transformer-based design assigns task points and meeting spots, and a switching scheme hands work between agents sortie by sortie. The aim is a planner that scales to larger teams.
arxiv-2504-21311:
Zhang and a large team (2025) study how to send prompts to language model services over wireless links without being detected. A covert channel protects both privacy and the fact of communication itself. The team frames the task as cutting delay while keeping answers faithful and the transmission hidden. They tune transmit power and prompt compression together.

Their framework first compresses the prompt with help from a small local model. That model scores how surprising each token is and keeps only the ones that carry meaning. A light permutation cipher then scrambles the result. For the wireless side, they train a policy method that samples groups of candidate actions and penalizes drift. In simulations, compression cut preprocessing delay hugely with answer quality intact. The transmission method cut covert delay by up to about 39 percent against rival learning strategies.
arxiv-2504-21711:
Jingbo Sun and a large team of co-authors report the first mid infrared lags for two prototype intermediate mass black holes, in the galaxies NGC 4395 and POX 52. Solid proof of such mid weight holes bears on how giant black holes were seeded. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Using archive light data and a sky survey telescope, the team caught dust glow lagging light swings by days in one galaxy and weeks in the other. For POX 52 this is the first echo based proof of a low mass active hole. Both lags fit the known size versus brightness trend from heavier systems, the authors report.
arxiv-2505-00011:
Tahoori, Ozer, Zervakis, Balaskas, and Pal survey computing with printed and flexible electronics in twenty twenty-five. Such devices are built on bendable materials, not stiff silicon chips. They suit uses at the extreme edge where low cost matters most. Examples include wearable health products and fast moving consumer goods.

Recent work focuses on machine learning circuits that process sensor data on or near the sensor. These circuits can work in digital or analog form. The survey reviews progress in fabrication, such as ultra thin substrates and new printing methods. It also covers open problems in reliability, device integration, and memory design. Cross layer optimization and co-design are presented as paths forward. The authors see the field reaching new application areas.
arxiv-2505-00111:
Five authors report lessons from securing a telecom edge platform with open source tools in this 2025 paper. The platform, GENIO, runs edge computing over passive optical network infrastructure, and the team applied security by design inside an industrial research project.

They mapped threats and matched them with defenses: system hardening, vulnerability management, digital signatures, and static and dynamic code analysis, all using open source software. The paper's value is practical. It records where these free tools proved mature enough for industry and where they fell short, so other teams building on open source at the network edge can plan around the gaps.
arxiv-2505-00511:
Esteban Rivera, Loic Stratil, and Markus Lienkamp teach in 2025 self-driving perception systems to ask for the labels they actually need. Object detectors for LiDAR point clouds are hungry for hand-labeled examples, and labeling three-dimensional scans is slow, expert work.

Active learning lets the model choose which scans are worth a human's time. The team built several selection rules based on inconsistency, moments where the model's own readings disagree, as a sign of a valuable example. Their tests across settings show such rules can match full-data training with far fewer labels, trimming one of autonomy's hidden costs.
arxiv-2505-00811:
Vikas Bhat and three co-authors tune a high-dimensional quantum key system that uses photon position and momentum, in a 2025 paper. Quantum keys let two sides share secret codes with proof against spying. Higher dimensions per photon can raise the key rate. The setup here is fully passive, with one lens for reads and no slow or lossy parts.

The team picks the best dimension by packing more clean zones into the beam while cutting overlap errors. Tossing events from fuzzy border zones lifts the rate. Their trick overlaps the tossed zones of neighbors to cut total loss. Math gives the best dimension for set beam traits, and a lab demo shows the plan can run.
arxiv-2505-00911:
Jia-Jie Li and Armen Sedrakian ask how the choice of likelihood shape affects what astronomers infer about neutron stars, in a 2025 study. They work within relativistic density functional models of dense matter. Bayesian inference combines such models with telescope data, and low-density matter constraints enter through that chosen shape.

The authors compare Gaussian and uniform likelihoods, designing the uniform one to match the Gaussian's normalization and marginalization. Across three test scenarios, both choices gave nearly identical mass-radius and density-pressure relations. Their confidence regions overlapped closely. Yet the inferred character of nuclear matter split by channel: compression coefficients varied widely across scenarios, while the symmetry energy slope barely moved. The study tells modelers that likelihood shape matters less than which sky data they feed in.
arxiv-2505-01111:
Yukun Li and Li-Ping Liu add built-in bias to energy-based generative models. Their 2025 paper joins a fresh wave of interest in such models, trained by score matching and sampled by Langevin steps. Neural energy functions are flexible but start from zero knowledge. Their hybrid bolts on a fixed statistic function, borrowed from exponential family models.

Training then pushes the model's statistics toward the data's, even without exact likelihood heights. That match lets users place direct constraints on what the model must respect. Tests show the hybrid fits and generates better when the added statistics truly inform the data. The authors offer a way to teach generative models what matters before they learn.
arxiv-2505-01511:
Iñigo Robredo and colleagues introduced a new family of crystals in 2025 where two exotic kinds of physics meet. The compounds pair a rare-earth or similar element with arsenic and sulfur. They are topological insulators, materials with protected surface states, and at the same time their electrons behave as if enormously heavy. Systems built on f-electrons, with strong correlations, are prized hunting grounds for such combined behavior.

Examining the crystal structure, the team found a variant different from earlier reports. Calculations showed that the yttrium and samarium members host hourglass fermions, unusual quasiparticles protected by a glide symmetry of the crystal. The samarium compound showed especially strong heavy-fermion character. Materials hosting both topology and heavy electrons let physicists study how the two phenomena influence each other, with possible payoffs for quantum devices.
arxiv-2505-01611:
Alexander Plakhov and Vladimir Protasov present a 2025 math paper on how the slope gauges of a concave sheet can compare. The sheet sits on a convex region and dies to zero at its rim. The question is whether one direction's slope size can dwarf the other's without bound. For the mean-size gauge, the answer is no: the ratio stays capped, and the authors find the sharp caps.

For stronger gauges, the cap's fate turns on the region's shape. A roundish region and a knife-thin one answer unlike. Slope ratios matter in shape design and in bounds for spread equations. The work sorts a clean question into shape cases, with exact lines where they exist.
arxiv-2505-01811:
Jona te Lintelo and co-authors show a new way to plant a hidden flaw in image models, in a computer science paper from 2025. The models split work among expert parts, using only a few parts for each image. That split breaks older attacks, which spread a trigger mark across the whole image.

Their attack, called BadPatches, hides the trigger inside single image patches. That way the mark is sent whole to the active expert parts, as the model routes each patch. In tests, the attack worked at very low rates of poisoned training images and kept normal accuracy high. It also worked when the attacker knew only part of the routing plan. A common defense, pruning unused parts, was not enough to stop it.
arxiv-2505-02011:
Minhyuk Lee, HyeKyung Yoon, and MyungJoo Kang present, in a 2025 paper, an add-on that makes Transformer forecasts of long time series cheaper and sharper. Long-range forecasts feed tasks like weather and traffic calls. Past add-ons still cost much compute and miss links across the parts of a series. Their part, CASA, runs the series through a small CNN autoencoder first. A score-based attention then weights what that squeeze kept. The part drops into many Transformer forms with no change to their core.

On eight real data sets, CASA cut compute use by up to 77.7 percent. It sped runs by 44 percent as well. Scores came first in 87.5 percent of the gauges used, a state-of-the-art mark for this task class.
arxiv-2505-02811:
Retrieval augmented generation lets a language model look facts up before answering, and hard questions need several rounds of searching. Diji Yang and co-authors note that such systems judge their own progress poorly: they keep searching when they know enough, or answer boldly when they do not. Their framework, SIM-RAG, teaches a system to know when it does not know. First the system practices alone, trying many search paths for known questions and noting which paths reach the right answer.

From that practice data they train a small critic model that judges, at each round, whether gathered information suffices. During real use the critic tells the system to stop or to search again. Tests on several benchmarks show better answers with this self check in place. The method adds a light component and needs no costly human labels for the middle steps of searching.
arxiv-2505-03011:
Mauricio Bellini and co-authors asked what dimension spacetime appears to have near a black hole that is slowly evaporating. They used a quantum gravity formalism in which radiation from a Schwarzschild black hole deforms the surrounding geometry. A single parameter measures how strong the quantum deformation is compared with the classical field.

At one special value of that parameter, an observer falling toward the horizon measures a spectral dimension of about 2.88 rather than four. Every black hole they studied, from Planck-scale to enormous, lands in the same stability state. The value differs from the dimension found at cosmic scales, so dimension seems to depend on scale. Hawking radiation also reshapes the gravitational pull near the horizon, stopping it from plunging without limit.
arxiv-2505-03611:
Fangling Jiang and co-authors teach face guards to spot unknown fakes from real faces alone in a 2025 paper. Face checks guard ID systems, yet guards fail on new fake kinds and new sites. Two shifts drive the flaw: shifts in how data is caught, and shifts in fake kind.

Text prompts for real faces and for unseen fake kinds are learned from a vision-word model's store. A prompt tune frame keeps fake prompts wide, split, and far from real face prompts. Tests on nine sets show top cross-site skill with no fake face used at all.
arxiv-2505-03711:
Baharul Islam, Nasim Ahmad, Ferdous Ahmed Barbhuiya, and Kuntal Dey describe the system their team entered in a shared contest on tagging academic texts with subjects across languages, in a 2025 paper. The contest, SemEval-2025 Task 5, asked systems to recommend subject labels for work in English and German. Their entry trained on both languages at once, using negative sampling, where the model learns by contrasting right and wrong labels, and a margin-based goal that pushes matches and mismatches apart.

The core is an attention design called dimension-as-token, which reads a sentence's embedding dimensions as if they were words, while keeping its inner size small. The system reached an average recall of about 32 percent in the broad test, with higher scores on one quality check. It ran on minimal graphics hardware, which the authors stress: strong subject tagging need not demand heavy machines.
arxiv-2505-03811:
Chakrabarty, Talwadker, and Mukherjee tackle rare-event hunting in long data streams in a 2025 paper. Their tool, ScarceGAN, seeks scarce samples in telemetry data where labels are few and weak. The bulk of data is unlabeled, and the normal class splits into many uneven groups. Some unseen behavior may hide in the unlabeled mass.

ScarceGAN reshapes a semi-supervised GAN to learn from the many normal groups and the few known rare cases. A leeway term softens noisy labels so they do not distort training. On a gaming risk task, recall passed 85 percent, far above the plain method. On a classic intrusion set, it set a new mark for one rare attack type.
arxiv-2505-03911:
Hans Hohenfeld, Marius Beuerle, and Elie Mounzer (2025) extend a quantum-inspired method that not only flags odd data but explains the flags. The method uses tensor networks, compact structures borrowed from quantum physics for describing complex states. An earlier team had shown the idea on discrete cyber-security data with one network shape. This work moves to real-valued data and adds a second shape, the tree tensor network. Both shapes learn what normal data look like.

The authors tested the approach on three benchmark problems. Detection quality held up well against several standard baseline models. More importantly, the networks could point to what made each flagged sample unusual. That explanatory power is the point of the work: a bare alarm is less useful than an alarm with reasons. The authors present the results as a path toward richer tensor designs for explainable detection in messier, real-world data.
arxiv-2505-04211:
Gaur and co-authors define a new class of stellarators with a sharp, winding edge, in a research paper from 2025. Stellarators confine fusion plasma in a twisted magnetic cage. The shape of the plasma edge guides how the field behaves there, which matters for divertor designs that handle exhaust heat.

The new class, called umbilic stellarators, has one unbroken high-curvature edge that loops around several times before closing. The team built a method that shapes the plasma boundary and the edge curve together. It also enforces omnigenity, a field trait that keeps trapped particles confined. The designs tended to favor a piecewise form of that trait. Coil sets were drawn for some cases, and one plan would convert an existing tokamak into a stellarator.
arxiv-2505-04311:
Jens Krinke and Chaiyong Ragkhitwetsagul warn that a famous data set for code clone detection has been widely misused. The set, BigCloneBench, was built to test tools that find copied code by its text. Lately many teams used it to train and judge tools that judge code by meaning, a job it was never made for.

A hand check of a fair sample of its weakest clone pairs found that ninety-three in a hundred pairs did not in fact do the same job, so their labels were wrong. A sweep of 179 papers found most of the meaning-based studies built on those labels, with scores that likely reflect quirks of the set, not true skill. Text-based use stays valid, they stress.
arxiv-2505-04511:
Aparna and co-authors present a solar physics paper from 2025 on how magnetic fields move on the sun's surface. One theory of heating the sun's outer air blames churning gas that tangles field lines. Tangling feeds tiny current sheets that snap and release heat. How fast the gas can drag the field depends on field strength, but that link had never been measured.

The team tracked a full day of field maps for six sunspot regions. They measured sideways drift speed at each point where the field stood well above noise. Speed fell steadily as field strength rose, from about 110 meters per second in mild zones to about 10 in dark spot cores. A smooth curve fits the trend well. The numbers can now feed models of outer-air heating.
arxiv-2505-04611:
Adrien Corenflos strips the swap step out of a famed sampling method for hidden-state models. Such models hide a path that data only hints at, and both path and dials must be read off. The old method swaps twixt path draws and dial draws, which can crawl when the two cling tight. His form folds the path odds into the dial step, in the style of a kin method.

The Gibbs bit of the title is that swap, now gone from the loop. A toy case known to choke the rival method shows the gain in the work. State-space teams in weather, speech, and funds use kin tools each day. A leaner loop can cut their compute bills.
arxiv-2505-04711:
Mateusz Zelent, Maciej Krawczyk, and Konstantin Y. Guslienko study tiny magnetic swirls in this 2025 paper. These swirls, called skyrmions, can store data bits in future memory devices. Their size is usually fixed by the material, which limits design. The team places a magnetic ring next to a thin magnetic dot. They test the idea with math models and computer simulations.

The ring's stray field steadies the swirl inside the dot. It can hold the swirl at two or more set sizes, picked by the ring's magnetic direction. The states sit behind energy walls far above room-temperature jitter. Tuning the ring's shape gives fine control of size. That opens a path to memory cells that hold more than one bit.
arxiv-2505-05611:
Kohler and Schubert test a sound-wave score pitched as a fine gauge of early harm. The score, called SPC-I, counts side peaks in a wave test. Wave tests that bend are said to beat straight tests for faint harm. The pair ran SPC-I on carbon plates hit with more and more force. Their data point to a less rosy read of the score. Small, oft unlogged shifts in how the score is worked sway its value.

That sway fails the bar for a sound gauge, they hold. More, shifts in wave size did not track harm as the pitch claims. Harm bend thus looks like a weak, not chief, source of the score. The pair asks peers to re-check their data and past tests alike.
arxiv-2505-05711:
Ho-Joong Kim and co-authors present a 2025 model for finding when actions start and end in video. Query-based detectors were borrowed from still-image work and fit video poorly: stacked features repeat themselves, and time context stays thin. Their model, DiGIT, swaps in a gated encoder that reads time at several spacings, cutting repeats while keeping fine and long-range detail.

A new decoder samples the center and near regions of each candidate action, which gathers richer cues for the boundaries. On three public video sets, the model set new state-of-the-art scores. The team posts the code online, aiming at uses from sports clips to surveillance review.
arxiv-2505-05911:
Luca Colagrande and Luca Benini dissect the hidden tax that heterogeneous chips charge every time work is handed to their accelerator cores. Their testbed is an open-source many-core RISC-V system-on-chip with a few big host cores and hundreds of small ones. Writing in twenty twenty-five, they measure offload overheads cycle by cycle and track how they grow with core count. Fine-grained tasks suffer most, because synchronization and communication eat the speedup. The fix is co-design: smarter offload routines plus multicast support in the on-chip network.

With multicast, offloaded applications ran up to more than twice as fast. Most of the ideally attainable speedup was restored. A quantitative model then predicts runtimes with offload costs included, erring by under fifteen percent. The study guides designers of massively parallel open hardware.
arxiv-2505-06511:
Vipul Rohit, Vikram Dharodi, and Sharad Yadav simulate a swirling dipole drifting through dusty plasma of uneven density, in this 2025 paper. Dusty plasma can act like a stretchy fluid, and a dipole here is two counter-spinning vortices paired together. The team asked how the pair's fate depends on its spin strength against the medium's elastic strength.

Stronger spin, or a softer medium, let the dipole live longer and bend toward the denser side. Edge style mattered for shape: smooth density ramps grew mushroom-like rims around the vortices, while sharp ramps wrapped them in spirals.
arxiv-2505-06811:
Tan-Hanh Pham, Ovidiu Andronesi, Xianqi Li, and Kim-Doang Nguyen fill gaps in brain chemistry maps with deep learning, in a 2025 paper. The imaging method, MRSI, charts brain metabolites without surgery. Motion, field flaws, and failed fits often leave holes in the maps, above all in detailed three-dimensional scans.

Most repair tools need a mask that marks the missing spots. The new method needs none: U-shaped networks in two and three dimensions sense the gaps from context and estimate the lost values. A staged training plan hardened the models against heavier damage. On simulated and real patient data the method beat standard interpolation. Scores stayed high even with a fifth of the map missing. The models also worked on fresh real data without retraining, a plus for clinics.
arxiv-2505-06911:
Lishan Yang and five co-authors patch missing data kinds in shared learning in a 2025 paper. In shared learning, many sites train one model without pooling raw data, which guards privacy. When sites hold mixed data kinds, like text with scans, some kinds often go missing at some sites, which warps the joint model.

Their frame, called MMiC, works inside clusters of like sites. It swaps in shared parts for the parts a site lacks, drawn from its cluster kin. Tests show the swaps blunt the harm of gaps. The frame keeps mixed learning sound when data is patchy.
arxiv-2505-07111:
Alexandre Goy's notes introduce infinite trees in descriptive set theory, in a 2025 text. The work opens at the ground floor: words and languages. Finite words string letters from an alphabet; infinite words run on forever, indexed by the natural numbers. The notes fix notation for length, the empty word, and joining words end to end.

From that base, the text builds toward trees whose branches never end, a basic object in this corner of logic. The tone is that of lecture notes: terms first, machinery second. Readers meet left-concatenation rules, and how an infinite word swallows anything placed after it. The notes suit logicians wanting the toolkit in one place.
arxiv-2505-07511:
Mauricio Orbes-Arteaga and co-authors present MAIS in 2025, a way to make interactive medical image outlining remember past help. In interactive segmentation, a model drafts an outline of an organ or tumor, and a user clicks to fix its errors. Top models treat each round of clicks as if it were the first, which wastes effort.

MAIS adds a memory that stores past clicks and past outlines. With that context, each new round builds on the last instead of starting over. The authors say the change lifts both speed and accuracy of corrections across many scan types. The work aims to cut the time experts spend tracing medical images by hand.
arxiv-2505-07711:
Pranav Sinha, Sumit Kumar Jha, and Sunny Raj ask large language models to cut quantum circuits into pieces small enough to optimize. Their 2025 paper works in today's noisy quantum era, where compilers can only polish circuits of a handful of qubits. Anything bigger must be partitioned first, and existing partitioners are heuristics blind to the optimization that follows.

The authors test whether language models, Llama and Mistral among them, partition with the downstream step in mind. A smarter cut means fewer noisy gates survive compilation. The study is an early probe of language models as engineering tools inside the quantum software stack, judged on real circuit quality.
arxiv-2505-07811:
Rachid Benbrik and five co-authors ask whether two odd signals at particle colliders could share one cause, in a research paper from 2025. One signal hints at a heavy new particle near six hundred fifty giga-electronvolts. The other hints at a light Higgs-like particle near ninety-five.

The team tests a model with two Higgs doublets instead of one. In their setup, a heavy particle decays into a normal Higgs and a Z boson, which matches the heavy signal. A light Higgs in the same model matches the low signal. Their fit explains both signals at once at a modest level of confidence. More data will be needed to confirm the idea.
arxiv-2505-08111:
Papillon and co-authors classify sleep positions from a pressure mat under a mattress, using transfer learning. The mat tracks patients without wires or wearables. Sleep posture affects sleep quality and disorders like apnea. Data came from a clinic's low-resolution mat in a sleep lab. Patients had suspected sleep disorders. Labels for training such models are scarce in clinics.
