The team adapted vision models pre-trained on images with a masked learning method. Transfer let the models learn from the small clinic set. Four sleep positions were the target classes. Borrowed features beat training from scratch in this low-data setting. The approach suits hospitals that cannot gather huge labeled datasets.
arxiv-2505-08211:
Eugene Gorsky and co-authors study shapes built from braids, a topic in pure math, in this 2025 paper. For each positive braid they look at a space called a braid variety. They carve that space into open pieces, one for each whole-number step along the braid and each way of reordering its strands.

Each piece, they show, splits neatly into a product of two smaller braid varieties. They also guess that the pieces carry a cluster structure, a bookkeeping system of linked variables, and that freezing some variables gives each piece its own such structure. The guesses are proved in some key special cases, which anchors the wider claim.
arxiv-2505-08511:
Shaoshuai Chu, Michael Herty, and Alexander Kurganov extend a stability framework for flow systems to cases where the inputs are random, in a 2025 paper. The systems are hyperbolic conservation laws, the math behind waves and traffic-like flows. Here the boundary controls and starting data carry uncertainty, which the older deterministic frame did not cover.

Building on a finite volume scheme, they define a random version of the energy-like Lyapunov function. With it, they prove that numerical solutions decay at an exponential rate. For linear systems they give explicit rates tied to control settings, grid fineness, and the spread of the random inputs. Tests on wave and shallow-water flows confirm the rates.
arxiv-2505-08711:
Sakai and a large team measure electron density structure where an intense laser beam hits plasma, using scattered laser light. Intense short pulse lasers can recreate extreme astrophysical conditions in the lab. Diagnostics for the velocity distribution at the interaction region are limited, which motivates a scattering based approach.

Imaging records the spatial pattern of scattered light and the ratio of its polarization parts. That ratio matches the drive beam, which confirms the light truly comes from the laser interaction. Images reveal the density structure, the lowest moment of the electron velocity distribution. A pre-pulse that damages the target before the main pulse arrives visibly changes that structure. The method adds a direct window on laser plasma interaction physics.
arxiv-2505-09211:
Giuseppe Cuono and co-workers asked when two kinds of face tiny charged bits can coexist purely in a 2025 stuff paper. Shape-based insulators host Dirac tiny charged bits on their face, assured by the bulk. Rashba tiny charged bits appear where inversion balance breaks, as faces naturally do. On a uniform face of a even shape-based insulator the two hybridize into a giant Rashba effect. Neither stays pure, an apparent dead end.

Inspired by tests, the team studies the polar face of lead selenide turned shape-based by strain, decorated with transition metals. Pure Dirac and Rashba bands can sit jointly near the Fermi level only if the stuff is non-homogeneous. The two bands born in effectively separate regions. Spatial separation rescues purity.
arxiv-2505-09511:
Tianfu Wu and co-authors help one human pilot fly a whole swarm of indoor blimps, in a 2025 paper. Formation flying is hard for blimps: they drift, wallow, and turn wide. Their system lets the operator steer only a leader; followers hold formation by watching with onboard cameras and a laser altimeter. The twist is dynamic leader switching: any blimp can take the point, spreading the maneuvering strain.

When a sharp turn looms, the switch hands leadership to the blimp best placed, steadying the formation. Experiments confirm the scheme keeps the swarm coherent in changing indoor spaces. The design treats the operator as a partner, not a bottleneck.
arxiv-2505-09611:
Carolina Marques and a team reported a giant coupling in twenty twenty-five. It links magnetism and lattice shape in Sr4Ru3O10, a layered ferromagnet. Magnetoelastic coupling is in most cases feeble. It shows up only in bulk samples. The team held sway over just the surface layer's magnetism. That let them single out how exchange forces shape the lattice.

With scanning tunneling microscopy they saw subtle electronic changes. The changes hang on how the surface and the layer below line up. The two can align ferro- or antiferromagnetically. The surface layer loosened in a way that showed giant magnetostriction. Exchange alignment drove that strain. The tests quantify how electronic correlations make electron-lattice coupling strong in a quantum material. Such direct reads of exchange-driven strain are rare. They are prized for the design of magnetic materials.
arxiv-2505-09711:
Jiawang Li, writing solo, speeds up beam focusing for large smart surfaces in a 2025 paper. These surfaces, arrays of many small elements, are planned for 6G networks and must aim radio beams at near users. Exact convex math can find the focus, but on large arrays it crawls.

Li's method first uses a greedy search to pick likely element spots, working in one quarter of the array and mirroring the rest by symmetry. Convex math then runs only on those spots until the focus is sharp enough. On a mid size array the mix ran about 15 times faster than standard methods, and near 97 times faster on a larger one.
arxiv-2505-09811:
Avinash Khare, Fred Cooper, and Avadh Saxena find a hidden bridge between two wave equations and a classic field theory, then walk a crowd of new solutions across it. Their 2025 paper studies the negative-order Korteweg-de Vries equation and its modified sibling, each in two formulations. Written in a shared Lou form, both reduce, for traveling waves, to one equation in the moving frame.

That reduced equation matches the static solution equation of phi-four field theory in one space dimension. The mapping imports a large stock of solutions, most of them new for the wave equations. The pair also derive the negative KdV equation from an action principle in both forms. A separation ansatz further splits space and time dependence, yielding novel solutions in focusing and defocusing cases, plus new rational solutions.
arxiv-2505-09911:
Xiaoyu Wang, Long Yuan, and Yao Yu published a paper in 2025 on neural networks that can handle jumps when solving physics equations. Many equations of motion have solutions with sharp breaks, and ordinary smooth networks smear them. Allowing the network itself to be discontinuous promises accuracy at lower cost, since smooth networks approximate well in standard senses but waste effort at a break.

The authors build a hybrid method with a new loss that adds three ingredients: a variational form of the equation, penalties for jumps across internal interfaces, and boundary conditions. Two optimizers split the work, one tuning the network's nonlinear parameters and a Galerkin scheme handling the linear ones. The design aims to guarantee the loss settles while keeping the solution sharp where the physics demands it.
arxiv-2505-10011:
Taygun Recep Gungor, Ayse Gul Gungor, and Yvan Maciel sort out how pressure shapes the thin layer of turbulent flow that hugs a surface. Their 2025 study splits the pressure force into three effects. One is its direct local push, one its local unbalancing effect as the push changes along the flow, and one the stored effect of upstream events.

Drawing on several flow data sets, the team tracks two pressure measures through the layer's inner and outer zones. In the outer zone, both local unbalancing and upstream history reshape speed and stress profiles even at matched pressure values. The inner zone reacts faster, yet the local effect still alters its slowest sublayer. The results clarify how flows remember pressure changes.
arxiv-2505-10111:
Jeonghyun Woo, Joyce Qu, Gururaj Saileshwar, and Prashant Nair show that a shield against memory attacks can itself leak secrets. The shield counts how often each row of memory chips is hammered and pauses traffic when a row looks abused, but those pauses take measurable time.

Their attack, PRACLeak, reads the timing of the pauses like a signal. By watching delays, it can steal information such as secret keys from encryption running nearby. The team then redesigns the shield so its pauses run on a fixed schedule, blind to what programs are doing. The fix needs only a tiny extra queue inside the chip. It closed the leak while slowing the system by only a few percent.
arxiv-2505-10211:
Alexander Benedix Robles and co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, a software tool for one of the hardest steps in quantum simulation. Simulations of quantum matter run in imaginary time. Turning their output into real dynamic behavior requires an inversion that is notoriously unstable.

Their tool, PyLIT, expresses the target spectrum as a sum of kernel functions whose transforms are known. Those kernels are tailored to obey the physics the answer must respect. A least-squares fit, steadied by a Bayesian prior, picks the mixing weights. A stabler inversion would unlock dynamic measures like the structure factor from standard simulations. The reformulation attacks the ill-posedness at its root rather than patching results afterward.
arxiv-2505-10311:
Jeffrey Alido, Tongyu Li, Yu Sun, and Lei Tian wrote a 2025 paper on computer models that restore flawed images. The catalog creator field lists their university addresses instead of names, but the head gives the authors. Their models work by learning how images degrade into noise, then reversing that path. Standard versions assume the noise is even in all directions, which real sensors often violate.

Their whitened version learns a adjusted score that sidesteps a costly matrix step in training. That lets the noise stretch unevenly, matching structured noise in real devices. Tests on photo sets showed the new models restored images better than standard ones across several tasks. The work is aimed at science and medical imaging, where noise rarely behaves evenly.
arxiv-2505-10411:
Geza Kovacs hunts for the faintest flickers in a class of pulsating stars. RR Lyrae stars throb steadily, but many also swell and fade over weeks, the Blazhko effect. How many do so at tiny amplitudes was unknown. Kovacs scanned four years of Kepler data on three dozen stars with a purpose built code.

Seven new modulated stars emerged, six with the weakest signals ever seen, and one old claim was struck. Two thirds of the field's stars now count as modulated. A wider sweep of the backup mission pushed the true share to about three quarters. Modulation may be the rule, not the exception.
arxiv-2505-10511:
Victor Zheleznov and co-authors learn nonlinear dynamics for making sound from physical models, using neural differential equations and targeting vibrating musical systems. Modal methods have long modeled how strings and bodies sing. Loud string motion bends pitch and brightens tone in nonlinear ways, and a modal split turns that motion into coupled equations.

Such equations can learn motion straight from data. The new model keeps the exact solution for linear modes, and a neural network handles only the leftover part. The physical settings stay readable after training ends. Data made from a model string proved the concept, and the model reproduced the string's bent motion well. Sounds go with the results for listening checks.
arxiv-2505-10611:
Philippe Yao and Eliot Quataert model stars torn by giant black holes in a 2025 paper. A star that orbits close to a supermassive black hole gets heated by tides. That heat can puff the star up far beyond its normal size. The authors pair simple models with a star simulator called MESA. They track heating, swelling, orbit decay, and loss of gas in one frame.

For such stars, the rate of steady gas loss is set by how fast tides heat the star, not by orbit decay. That rate may run from a hundred-thousandth to a thousandth of a sun's mass per year. Gas at that pace could power faint active galactic cores in many galaxies. Where the heat lands inside the star decides if the loss stays stable.
arxiv-2505-10711:
Sebestyén Kamp, Giovanni Stracquadanio, and Ian Simpson release a benchmarking suite for graph neural networks in biomedicine in a paper from 2025. The head title styles it GNN-Suite, slightly different from the catalog title, and the description follows the head. Comparing graph models fairly is hard when every lab codes its own pipeline. Their framework standardizes setup through a workflow engine. A demonstration hunts cancer-driver genes on protein interaction networks.

Nine graph architectures faced a logistic baseline under identical settings. Every graph model beat the baseline. One variant topped balanced accuracy on the main network. Ten seeded runs made the numbers trustworthy. The authors aim to raise benchmarking standards in computational biology.
arxiv-2505-10811:
Scruggs tackles a control design problem where the controller itself must not inject energy in this 2025 paper. The setting pairs a passive plant with bounded gain and demands feedback that stays output-strictly passive, all while chasing the best average performance. Such constraints suit vibration control, where rogue energy spells trouble.

He shows the problem reshapes into a convex, infinite-sized optimization over a standard closed-loop parameter. Two finite stand-ins then bracket the answer: one yields workable controllers, the other yields lower bounds on the best possible score. Both tighten toward the true optimum as their size grows. A simple vibration damping example demonstrates the machinery end to end.
arxiv-2505-10911:
Jiahui Zhang and seven co-authors introduced ReWiND in twenty twenty-five, a framework that teaches robots new tasks from language alone. Robot learning usually needs a hand-built reward or fresh demonstrations for every task. ReWiND instead starts from one small demonstration set and learns two things from it: a reward function guided by language, and a starter policy trained offline with those rewards.

For a new task variation, the learned reward labels fresh experience and the policy fine-tunes with little live interaction. The reward model generalized to unseen tasks up to two point four times better than baselines on reward quality measures. Adaptation beat baselines twofold in simulation and improved a real two-armed robot's pre-trained policies fivefold. The work targets scalable robot learning in the real world.
arxiv-2505-11011:
Darija Barak and Miguel Costa-Gomes ran a lab experiment on how people play a guessing game against language models versus against humans, in this 2025 arXiv paper. In the p-beauty contest, players pick a number hoping to land near a fraction of the group average, and the Nash play is zero. Paid volunteers played both kinds of opponent, so each person served as their own control.

Against language models, players chose far lower numbers, and outright zero picks surged. Skilled reasoners drove most of the shift. When asked why, they credited the models with sharp reasoning and, surprisingly, a cooperative streak. The authors say mixed human-AI systems must reckon with these expectations when their rules are designed.
arxiv-2505-11111:
Lin Zhu and co-authors present FairSHAP, a data cleaning method that makes training sets fairer, in a 2025 paper. Biased training data can lead models to treat groups unfairly, with grave effects in high stakes fields. Past fixes often hide why data were changed.

FairSHAP uses a value method that credits each feature for its role in a call. Cases that drive unfairness are flagged, then matched and adjusted across sensitive groups. Tests on varied table data showed gains in two fairness gauges with tiny data changes. Scores sometimes rose as well. The method is open about its changes and fits into standard training pipelines.
arxiv-2505-11211:
Francisco Madaleno and three co-authors propose a new method in a 2025 arXiv paper on finding causes that stay stable across settings. Their method, called Bayesian Hierarchical Invariant Prediction, reworks an older approach known as Invariant Causal Prediction. It uses layered models to test whether a causal link holds when data differ.

Because the method is Bayesian, it can also use prior knowledge. The layered setup makes it faster to run when there are many possible predictors. The team tests it on both made-up and real data sets. They present it as a useful option beside the older method and related tools.
arxiv-2505-11511:
Sidney T da Silva and co-authors use machine learning to forecast monthly average temperatures in the capitals of Brazilian states. Their 2025 paper covers 27 cities plus the whole country, with records from 1961 to 2022. A random forest algorithm does the forecasting. Inputs tested were greenhouse gas emissions, the past three months of temperature, and the two combined.

Breakpoints in the records fell mostly in the 1980s and 1990s, after which temperatures and emissions rose. Forecasts for 2010 to 2022 were very precise under all three input plans. The Northeast region forecast best, above all with the combined inputs. A second test on data with the yearly cycle removed also favored gas inputs for that region.
arxiv-2505-11611:
Bofan Gong, Shiyang Lai, James Evans, and Dawn Song probe polysemantic interference in language models in two thousand twenty-five. Single neurons and features often carry many meanings at once. That tangle blocks interpretation and control of model acts. Sparse autoencoders let the team map the tangle in two small models.

They find feature pairs that clash though their meanings seem apart. Tweaks at prompt, token, feature, and neuron points shift outputs in set ways. Patterns from the small models transfer to far larger tuned models. Shifts stay predictable with no access to the big models' insides. Structure, not chance, seems to rule the tangle.
arxiv-2505-11711:
Sagnik Mukherjee and co-authors report a 2025 finding about how reinforcement learning changes large language models. The method boosts task scores and fit with human values, yet the team noticed something odd: only a small slice of the model's weights actually move during training. The rest stay near their start values, with no rule forcing that pattern.

Across seven training methods and ten models, the moving slice ran from five to thirty percent of weights. Training that slice alone matched full training almost exactly. Slices from unlike runs overlapped far more than chance allows, and the updates spread across nearly all layers. The authors link the pattern to training data that sits close to what the model already does.
arxiv-2505-11811:
Answering a question that needs several hops of evidence is a team sport. Taolin Zhang and co-authors first sort multi-hop questions into four types. They test five reasoning styles against them, from chain-of-thought to adaptive stepping. Each question type favors different styles. Their framework, BELLE, turns each style into an operator. A first level of agents debates and drafts a plan mixing those operators.

A second level watches the debate itself. Fast and slow debaters check whether shifts in position make sense. Across datasets BELLE beat strong baselines. Its cost profile also looked better than single models on the hardest questions, the authors report.
arxiv-2505-12011:
Artificial spin ices are grids of tiny magnets that can settle into ordered states, and one new family shows a rare property called toroidization. The authors study these magneto-toroidal spin ices with computer simulations, with and without breaking the grid's spatial symmetry. They compute the energies and resonance spectra of the four lowest states, which include states with matching toroidicity, opposing toroidicity, and none. Breaking the symmetry splits the resonant modes, as theory expects.

The team then checks whether the system hosts protected edge modes, using semi-analytical calculations of the band structure. The bands turn out topologically trivial in every case, which means the dynamic coupling between the magnets is weak. On the positive side, field protocols can reconfigure the states, and the spectra depend on which state the grid is in. The authors argue that stronger coupling must be engineered before these grids can serve magnonics.
arxiv-2505-12111:
Akın and four co-authors ran sims in twenty twenty-five on how air flows round hot giant planets that sit close to their stars. Star light drives those flows and the waves that feed fast jets. They test eight known hot giants with a world flow code.

As star heat rises, heat spread round the globe falls and small waves fade. Large waves then rule, and flow shifts from jets to a plain day-to-night rush. For the hottest case, a light gas mix brought back some spread and fine flow. The frame may aid reads of real hot giant skies.
arxiv-2505-12811:
Wei-Chen Liao, Ti-Rong Wu, and I-Chen Wu tackle how far game agents should see in a 2025 paper. In team learning tasks, a short view starves agents of facts, while a wide view floods them with noise. Their method, called Dynamic Sight Range Selection, shifts each agent's view range as training runs.

A bandit rule that favors bold picks steers the shifts. Tests ran in three known team tasks: food hunts by levels, a robot warehouse, and a space battle game. The method lifted scores in all three, and it boosted two base learning methods as well. It grew faster and steadier than fixed views.
arxiv-2505-13211:
A large team introduced MAGI-1 in 2025, a world model that generates video chunk by chunk. Each chunk is a fixed run of frames, and the model predicts the next one in turn. Training teaches it to clean noise that grows steadily over time, which supports streaming output.

The model scores strongly on turning images into video guided by text, with high consistency over time. Prompting chunk by chunk gives users control as the video forms. Peak computing cost stays constant no matter how long the video runs, aiding real-time use. The largest version holds twenty-four billion parameters and handles very long contexts, showing the approach scales.
arxiv-2505-13311:
Saleh Soudijani and Rayna Dimitrova compute communication plans for robot teams that keep working when bandwidth shrinks in this 2025 paper. Teams of agents must cooperate toward a shared goal. Their goal here mixes reaching a target and avoiding hazards. Each agent sees only its local state. Sharing those states takes bandwidth, which may be cut mid-task. Their method synthesizes two policies at once: what to do and what to say.

The plans aim to honor the communication limits as far as possible. When bandwidth is free, they keep the best success odds. Robustness here means grace under restriction, not perfection. Swarms and rescue robots face exactly such limits. The paper is formal methods for stochastic systems. It offers a synthesis algorithm with guarantees.
arxiv-2505-13411:
Matthias Beck and Emily Clader develop in 2025 a numeric measure for how consonant a musical chord sounds. Ears favor intervals with simple frequency ratios, like the octave and the perfect fifth. Chord studies rarely use that simple-fractions lens, which the authors adopt for their model of chord consonance.

Their measure has key symmetry features: it is unchanged by shifting, inverting, or reordering a chord's intervals. They apply it to chords in various scales. Results are compared with existing models and empirical studies of listener judgment. The work extends the old math of intervals to full chords.
arxiv-2505-13611:
Tortora and co-authors present sharp images of a distant relic galaxy in a 2025 astronomy paper. Relic galaxies built most of their stars early and then sat untouched, missing the later growth by mergers. They offer a close look at the first phase of galaxy growth. A project called INSPIRE has confirmed dozens of them at moderate distance.

Ground images can blur their tiny shapes, so the team used adaptive optics in the near infrared on a large telescope. The galaxy proved disky and very compact, with a half light radius near one kiloparsec. The result confirms it as the first fully verified relic beyond the nearby universe.
arxiv-2505-13711:
Maxime Van de Moortel extends a key method for wave equations in a 2025 note. The method, known by a short symbol-based name, proves that waves fade over time near black holes and in other settings. Hard cases add a strong time-changing potential or extra first-order terms.

The new version absorbs error terms into the weighted energy with a fresh argument. That move allows a wider range of weights than the standard proof. The approach grew from earlier work on a weakly charged field around a black hole. The note gives analysts a stronger tool for decay problems where older energy methods fall short. It may apply well beyond black hole settings.
arxiv-2505-13811:
Parikshit Bansal and Sujay Sanghavi tackle, in a 2025 paper, a known problem of fine-tuning language models: gains on a new task often come with losses on earlier skills. This loss is called catastrophic forgetting. The pair work in a hard setting, where only the model weights are available and the original training data is gone.

A natural guard is to penalize the new model when it drifts from the original one, measured by KL divergence. The hard part is estimating that drift without the old data. Their solution is context-free generation: the model writes text with no prompt context, and that text gives a fair estimate of the drift. Adding such text to the fine-tuning data reduced forgetting in two settings, for a pretrained model and for a reasoning model. Context-rich synthetic data, and even real pretraining data, did worse.
arxiv-2505-14311:
Shamsuddeen Hassan Muhammad and co-authors survey the state of natural language processing for Hausa, in a 2025 paper. Hausa counts over one hundred twenty million first-language speakers and eighty million more second-language speakers, yet computers handle it poorly. Data is scarce, open resources are few, and models barely represent the language.

The paper reviews work across text classification, translation, name recognition, speech recognition, and question answering, naming the gaps in each. The authors launch a public catalog gathering Hausa datasets, tools, and studies in one place. They also flag dialect variation and poor tokenization inside large language models, and they close with a research agenda for this low-resource language.
arxiv-2505-14411:
Götz, Kollovieh, Günnemann, and Schwinn chop time series into recurring motifs instead of fixed-length chunks, borrowing the byte-pair trick from language models. Standard tokenizers slice every stretch of a series into equal pieces, wasting effort on long flat runs. Their 2025 scheme learns a vocabulary of frequent patterns and merges matching samples into single tokens, compressing adaptively.

A light decoding step then refines forecasts with no gradient math and no added cost. Plugged into recent forecasting foundation models, the tokenizer lifted accuracy by forty percent and efficiency more than twenty fold on average. The extra decoding cut error by up to half again. Tests also show the tokens capture real traits like trend and spread.
arxiv-2505-14711:
Yohei Ogawa, Rikuhei Umemoto, and Keisuke Fujii build a way to grade open space anywhere on a soccer pitch. Space matters most at transitions, when the ball changes hands and a quick counterattack can start far from goal. Older scores rate space by the chance of scoring, which makes them weak far from goal. The head title frames the work as space evaluation at the starting point of soccer transitions.

Their score, called OBPV, rates every spot on the field and leans on real pass patterns to reflect what each position usually does next. Tests on tracking and event data from Spain's La Liga 2023/24 season showed the score lighting up well-used space in counterattacks. It also revealed habits that differ by team after they win or lose the ball, work published in 2025.
arxiv-2505-14811:
Huster Zapke and Holdsworth study monopoles, Dirac strings, and magnetic noise in model spin ice. Their 2025 arXiv paper draws a deep parallel with vacuum monopoles. In the dumbbell model of spin ice, monopole paths trace Dirac strings. Those paths are simulated through graphs of spin flips. A classic monopole hunt experiment is rebuilt inside spin ice.

Fragmentation steps recreate the Stanford detection setup in the model. Stochastic dynamics then mimic magnetic noise experiments. Noise from monopoles can be separated from noise of their strings. The long-time correlated signal came mostly from the strings. That flips the usual focus on monopoles themselves. The result matters for reading real spin ice noise data.
arxiv-2505-15011:
Kryspin Varys and co-authors teach learning agents to respect written and unwritten rules in this 2025 paper. Laws and safety rules can be stated in logic, but social norms hide inside trained networks. No single method had joined both kinds. Their approach, HAVA, watches how well an agent follows each norm.

Compliance feeds a single reputation score. That score then scales the rewards the agent receives, nudging it toward valued behavior. Tests include a continuous traffic problem where both norm types matter. Removing either norm group weakened the results. The combined method found policies that did the task while honoring safety and social expectations.
arxiv-2505-15111:
Guo and four co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on self-driving that plans around draft routes. Most end-to-end systems plan straight from a dense top-down grid of the road. That route wastes effort and can blur the plan. Their system instead puts a set of draft future routes at the center. A core part refines those drafts step by step as it reads camera views. Two light side tasks, mapping and forecasting, support the main plan.

Tests on two public driving benchmarks gave top scores for their system. It also ran much faster than prior leading methods. The side tasks lifted plan quality with little extra cost. The authors say draft-first planning is a leaner path for self-driving.
arxiv-2505-15411:
Valentina Mantovani Sarti, writing alone in 2025, studies how pairs of matter and antimatter particles pull or push on each other. Data on proton pairs is rich, but data on pairs with lambda particles is thin. New high-precision data from proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider now makes a closer look possible.

Sarti uses collision data from the ALICE experiment to draw out the strength of the force for two pair types. A new method handles pairs where much of the force is lost to other outcomes. Results show the two pair types differ in how they vanish into other particles. The finding tests a common shortcut that treats both pairs the same way.
arxiv-2505-15511:
Duderstadt, Nussbaum, and van der Maaten introduce NOMAD Projection in a 2025 paper. The method visualizes large unstructured data sets by nonlinear dimensionality reduction. Older tools such as t-SNE and UMAP have not kept pace with the growth of AI data sets.

NOMAD runs on multiple GPUs during training, a first for this kind of method. The authors give theory that places it as an approximate upper bound on a known t-SNE loss. Tests show better performance and speed than leading methods. As a proof of scale, they built the first complete data map of multilingual Wikipedia. The work targets exploratory analysis for AI explainability.
arxiv-2505-15611:
Emilio Barucci and Yuheng Lan study how a broker's bonus target can warp trading behavior. Their 2025 paper models optimal execution, the task of working a large order into the market. The broker is paid to reach a performance barrier while steering clear of a downside one.

Wealth in the model blends trading gains with the value of shares still held, minus a quadratic cost for carrying stock. Over short horizons the target pushes the broker to trade more boldly yet hold a safer book than the classic plan. Over long horizons the payoff turns poorer and more spread out. The authors frame short-term targets as a quiet engine of both aggression and excess risk.
arxiv-2505-15811:
Eric Michaud, Asher Parker-Sartori, and Max Tegmark study how to build strong yet narrow AI in a 2025 paper. Big base models rule the day, but small tight tools may win on cost and safe use. Two bars face that build. First: some narrow skills need wide data to learn at all, since skills stack in tiers. Broad sets then act as a school path that speeds the learn.

Next: skills in a big model smear past neat part sets. Prune craft can still beat pour-over teaching, they find. A push term can line skills up with prunable parts while stray skills fade. Both bars stem from how nets hold what they learn.
arxiv-2505-16011:
Bradley Coles, Yahya Hmaiti, and Joseph J LaViola survey ways to let a person walk far in virtual reality while in a small room. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. The trick, called redirected walking, bends the user's path in small ways they do not notice. That lets a large virtual world fit in a tight real space.

They review a large set of past papers and keep those that fit their rules. They sort methods by gain, how gain is applied, how the target heading is set, and extra boosts. Patterns in the field show where work is dense and where gaps stay. Their scheme can guide new designs and point to open lines of study.
arxiv-2505-16311:
Marc Brooks, Gabriel Durham, Kihyuk Hong, and Ambuj Tewari build a bandit algorithm for health interventions, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. The interventions' content is written on the fly by generative AI. In mobile health, an app must keep choosing which message to send, learning from each response, a classic bandit problem.

Generated content breaks the classic setup. The system chooses a query, but the user actually experiences a message sampled stochastically from the generative model. The action and the treatment are no longer the same thing. The team's method, GAMBITTS, is a Thompson sampling variant that models both layers: which query was picked and which treatment actually landed. That explicit split lets it credit outcomes correctly. The motivating case is text-based support generated by a language model. Adaptive interventions in health need exactly this care, because the delivered dose is what changes behavior.
arxiv-2505-16511:
Hao Yin and co-authors design neural network controllers for systems whose rules are not known in advance, in a paper from 2025. Many machines and processes bend in ways that defy neat formulas. A network can learn the motion from data, but a learned model alone gives no safety promise. The team uses contraction theory, which checks whether all paths of a system pull together over time.

They build a network-based model of the unknown motion and find conditions that make it contractive. Hard conditions are recast into a form that solvers can handle with ease. When the model contracts, the true system settles near its resting point, with the gap set by the learning error. If the model fails the test, a mixed controller forces the trait. Two worked cases show the method in action.
arxiv-2505-16611:
Cabra and Rossini reviewed a mechanical model of how magnetism and electric order couple in multiferroic materials in twenty twenty-five. Multiferroics hold magnetic and electric order side by side. That pairing could serve new data storage, sensors, and actuators. How the two orders sway each other is still not fully grasped.

The work they review uses a pantograph, a lattice of linked parts. Bends in the lattice carry the pull between quantum spins and electric dipoles. Studies in math and on computers show the model matches key traits of improper multiferroics. This holds most when spin links break spin symmetry in an XXZ pattern. Added work covers ions with higher spin and lattices in more dimensions, closer to real materials. The authors cast the pantograph view as a single small-scale account of this coupling.
arxiv-2505-16711:
Matveev, Sitnikov, and Sarantsev build the math for reading resonances that decay into four mesons. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Partial wave analysis untangles overlapping states in collision data. Four-meson final states strain older formalisms. Their method is fully covariant and ready for high-statistics samples. Two decay topologies are covered.

In one, two intermediate resonances each split into two mesons. In the other, a cascade passes through three-meson states. Production settings include central collisions of hadrons. Radiative decays of the J/psi particle are also treated. The formalism hands experimenters a ready tool. Hadron spectroscopy gains reach into richer final states. Future datasets can be mined for states that decay in fours.
arxiv-2505-16811:
Shangquan Sun and co-authors present a semi-supervised system for removing rain from real world video. Deep learning has advanced rain removal, but methods trained on paired fake rain data often fail on real footage. Rain in the wild differs from synthetic streaks, leaving a stubborn gap.

Their design splits into two branches that read space and time patterns across frames. A dynamic filter fuses features from several frames at the pixel level. A loss based on stacking frames lets the system learn from unlabeled real video, using the rarity of rain as a prior. The team also built a real world test set for object detection and tracking in rain. Results beat prior methods on quality and speed.
arxiv-2505-16911:
Ofir Yaish, Yehuda Mishaly, and Eliya Nachmani set out, in 2025, a way to lift speech that goes past noise cancellation. The old way just cuts noise that comes from outside the speech. Their way works on the speech itself. It cuts the noise in the mix and lifts the tones that help speech stay clear, so speech is both cleaner and easier to hear.

The system joins a Transformer-Mamba architecture with a loss made for this task. The loss is set to cut noise and lift speech at the same time. The system beat past baselines at three tasks. The tasks were taking noise out, taking echo out, and fixing clipped speech. The team holds that steering the signal in this active way, not just cleaning it, works best when it is hard to hear. They name this new paradigm Active Speech Enhancement.
arxiv-2505-17111:
Can Rong and co-authors generate the world's commute flows where no census has counted them. Origin destination data map how people travel from home to work, the backbone of city planning. Surveys to gather them are slow and dear. The team instead fed a generative model with demographics, satellite views, and place data for over sixteen hundred cities.

The synthetic flows hug the real distributions where checks are possible. Coverage spans six continents and nearly one hundred eighty countries. The authors offer the set as open infrastructure for transport and sustainability research. Cities too poor for travel surveys gain a planning lens overnight.
arxiv-2505-17211:
Nandini Das and co-authors build a dark matter model with a heavy light-like particle, in this 2025 paper. The setup extends the two-Higgs-doublet model with a new hidden force. A lone charged scalar gains a vacuum value, giving the hidden force carrier its mass.

That scalar also bridges the hidden sector to ordinary matter through the Higgs. An exact mirror symmetry keeps the carrier from mixing with the photon, so the dark particle stays stable. The extended Higgs sector allows a lighter extra Higgs. That freedom places dark matter in the 40 to 60 GeV band, where direct searches press hardest. The team check all known limits.
arxiv-2505-17411:
Yuan-Yao He, writing alone in 2025, develops a sharper way to pin down a special kind of phase change in flat materials. In flat systems, some materials become superconductors through this change. Usual tools to locate it suffer size effects in models. He proposes tracking the share of particles that sit in the condensed state. That share follows one pattern below the change point and another above it. The test case is a standard model of attracting particles on a grid.

Exact computer methods let him reach grid sizes far larger than past work. The new measure showed much smaller size effects than the standard one. That makes the change point easier to find with modest grids. He also pulled out the change temperature and a known size correction. A heat peak sat just above the change point, a detail his method helped confirm.
arxiv-2505-17511:
Aditya Gautam wrote a 2025 paper on a team of AI agents that handle false content across its whole life cycle. Single model checkers work in isolation and give thin reasons. His design splits the work among five specialist agents that pass results along a chain.

One agent keeps trusted sources up to date. Others sort the claim type, pull and rank evidence, draft a fact based correction, and verify the output while tracking source trust. Each agent can be tested and tuned on its own. That makes the system easier to scale and audit. Gautam stresses clear evidence and source history in every output, so users can see why a claim was flagged.
arxiv-2505-17811:
Vinayak M Kulkarni studies, in a 2025 paper, how steady driving can make a single impurity in a Dirac material behave like a system with parity-time symmetry. Such symmetry is a mark of non-Hermitian physics, where gain and loss balance. Here no real gain is present; the effect emerges from the drive and the surrounding bath.

Kulkarni derives the mechanism for a spin-orbit coupled impurity that lacks inversion symmetry. The drive and bath together create a spin-dependent decay, and once shared damping is removed, a parity-time core appears in the math. A steady rotating drive then supports special points where two poles merge, certified by winding and pole-exchange tests on small chain models. The author is careful to bound the claim: the results are controlled finite-chain findings, not a full limit theorem.
arxiv-2505-18311:
Sushant Sharma Chaudhary, Gianmarco Puleo, and Marco Cavaglià speed up gravitational wave analysis with a neural network, in work from 2025. When two compact objects merge, detectors must size up the event fast. Standard fitting is slow and can err, above all for heavy systems.

Their quantile regression network outputs bounds on chirp mass, mass ratio, and total mass. Tests used synthetic data plus real events from a published catalog. Accuracy stayed above ninety percent across all test sets. Feeding the bounds as priors cut later fitting work by about nine percent. Sky positions were unaffected by the shortcut. Faster early estimates help telescopes chase the light of a merger.
arxiv-2505-19011:
Yu-Te Hsu and co-authors probe the normal state of a new high-temperature superconductor in thin film form. The material, a layered nickel oxide, superconducts above eighty degrees in bulk under pressure. To see past the superconducting state, the team drove films with pulsed magnetic fields up to sixty-four tesla. They tracked resistance and Hall signals from near zero to room warmth, in a 2025 study.

With the superconducting state suppressed, the films behaved like a classic Fermi liquid. Resistance grew with the square of heat, and magnetic response followed known scaling laws. A standard ratio gave quasiparticles about ten times the mass of a free electron. The team says the films match scaling seen across many strong superconductors.
arxiv-2505-19211:
Abdelaziz Salama and four co-authors allocate resources for federated learning in twenty twenty-five. Federated learning over wireless networks must move model updates through a shifting radio environment. Open radio access networks offer modular control through intelligent controller apps. Their system, FedORA, uses that flexibility in two stages.

A reinforcement learning app first picks each user's best radio access technology. It balances energy efficiency against network performance. A model-based app then optimizes resource allocation in near real time. Predefined policies guide that second stage toward optimal performance. Dynamic selection adapts as conditions change across heterogeneous networks. Readers in wireless systems get federated learning tuned by the network itself, not just running on top of it.
arxiv-2505-19511:
Aggrey Muhebwa and Khalid Osman teach small language models to reason causally by copying the explanations of a large one. Their 2025 paper names the method causal distillation. Big proprietary models explain cause and effect well; compact open models lag. Rather than copying answers, the student trains to produce structured cause and effect explanations that match the teacher's.

Judging such training needs a yardstick, so the authors add a metric, Causal Explanation Coherence. It aligns each sentence of a student explanation with the teacher's reference and scores faithfulness and coverage of the causal chain. Together, method and metric aim to make small model reasoning both stronger and measurable, instead of trusting fluent text at face value.
arxiv-2505-20011:
Maciej Świechowski and Dominik Ślęzak survey what makes it hard to build game agents that act like humans. Such agents can lift a game as rivals, teachers, or partners, and tools that can tell bot from human are in demand where bots are banned.

The survey works through thirteen challenges, both in ideas and in craft. The authors then test the flip side in a tactical video game: can a machine tell human players from bots by their play data alone? Their deep network, built for the task, takes on that test. They argue the two tasks mirror each other in a neat way.
arxiv-2505-20311:
Anton Hummel and co-authors link explainable AI to European law in a 2025 paper on clinical decision support. The EU AI Act makes explainability urgent for high-risk systems, yet most explainable AI work uses technical scores alone. Legal duties fall on providers and deployers, groups that research often overlooks.

The authors argue the link runs both ways between methods and rules. Rules pull research toward real deployment needs in clinics and other high-risk sites. Skilled practitioners can also shape how explanations prove that a system follows the law. Their analysis maps stakeholder needs to Act duties. End users, whose needs matter most, gain a clearer place in design.
arxiv-2505-20411:
Ibragim Badertdinov and co-authors build an automated pipeline that harvests coding tasks for training and testing software agents. Their 2025 paper names two bottlenecks: good interactive tasks are scarce, and fixed benchmarks go stale as models train on them. Real tasks should force an agent to run code, read results, and adapt.

Their pipeline continuously mines tasks from many public code repositories. The resulting public data set holds tens of thousands of interactive Python tasks suited to reinforcement learning. Fresh tasks drawn the same way supply evaluations that models cannot have memorized. Scale plus freshness could let software agents improve on realistic work instead of rehearsed puzzles.
arxiv-2505-20711:
Ding Xia and five co-authors test whether language models can design signals for self-driving cars in a 2025 paper. Driverless cars cannot wave or shout, so they use outer screens and lights to speak to people on the road. Hand-made signal moves do not adapt well to messy real scenes.

Their pipeline pairs a language model with a 3D renderer: the model drafts the move, and the renderer plays it as a clip. They built a scored set of 320 action clips for eight messages and four signal types. Raters judged the model-made moves close to human level, most of all for text-based signals.
arxiv-2505-21011:
Liang Cheng, Zhaowei Wang, and Mark Steedman wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It shows that large language models, when fine-tuned on reasoning tasks about whether one sentence follows from another, mostly learn a shortcut: word frequency patterns.

In standard datasets, the words in a correct follow-on sentence tend to be more common than those in the starting sentence. The team tested models on cases that follow this bias and cases rigged against it. Models leaned hard on the frequency cue and stumbled on the rigged cases. Fine-tuning made the leaning stronger, not weaker. A check against a large word database showed the bias echoes how specific and general words relate in real language. The findings explain part of why fine-tuning lifts scores, and warn that the gain may rest on a crutch.
arxiv-2505-21211:
Walz and five co-authors present a 2025 physics paper on disentangling strain from magnetism in a laser-struck magnetic alloy. Terfenol, a terbium-iron alloy, swells strongly in magnetic fields, so light-driven signals mix true magnetization change with mechanical strain. The team measured the magneto-optical response of films with and without a glass cap, watching reflectivity to time the arrival of strain pulses.

The magnetic signal lagged several picoseconds behind, marking it as a genuine magnetization response rather than an instant optical artifact. Modeling sound-speed strain pulses through the film, with a large damping term, reproduced the delay. It also revealed that slow thermal expansion strain near the surface, not just the passing pulse, dominates the dynamics. The authors show that even purely lengthwise strain couples efficiently through the crystal's tilted frame. The work sharpens ultrafast magnetism measurements.
arxiv-2505-21311:
Wang and Hsiao predict how a charmed baryon decays into light scalar mesons, using flavor symmetry bookkeeping, in a 2025 paper. The light scalars are oddballs whose inner makeup is disputed: ordinary quark pairs or four-quark states. The team drew the decay's topological diagrams under SU(3) symmetry and fit both readings to the data on hand.

The four-quark reading fit notably better. It naturally explains one branching share that long-range effects alone undershoot tenfold. Two headline predictions follow, one near five percent and one near half a percent. Mixing between two of the scalars suppresses their channels sharply. Those suppressed modes, the authors say, are the sharpest probes for the coming experiments at three colliders.
arxiv-2505-21811:
Clark Mingxuan Ju and a team of co-authors went back to the core of self attention for cross domain advice. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with sequential recommendation: to guess what a user does next from their past acts, across many fields at once. Past frames pile domain blocks on a transformer base. The team says that path skips the strength that sits in self attention it self, a born tool to learn links between acts.

Their work hones that core part in place of new blocks. The test is if a lean model with a tuned core can beat fat frames. Readers who build advice systems get a less is more read on a hot task.
arxiv-2505-22611:
Piotr Kaminski, Artur Tyliszczak, Witold Elsner, and Pawel Niegodajew test in a 2025 paper a tilted wavy wall for holding airflow to a surface. Flow that peels off a wing or blade wastes energy and lift. A plain wavy wall had already delayed that peel at high speeds in past work.

Tilting each wave in the new design clears the stall pockets that form in wave troughs. Large eddy simulations map both instant and average flow over the surface. Against the best plain wave shape, drag drops 14% with the tilt. Peel control improves 70% at the same time in the tests. Pushing peel control even further is possible, though at a drag cost the authors note.
arxiv-2505-22711:
Yasaman Farzan and Matheus Hostert propose a dark-particle explanation for a puzzling telescope event in this 2025 paper. One detector, KM3NeT, caught an extremely energetic muon that a larger detector, IceCube, did not see. The mismatch has raised questions about where the particle came from.

Their scenario has short-lived cosmic sources spraying dark particles toward Earth. Inside the Earth, those particles convert into unstable partners that decay into muons after traveling about a hundred kilometers. The muons then leave long tracks in the detectors. Because the signal depends strongly on direction and geometry, the event could appear in one detector and miss the other. The authors argue this dark flux story fits the lone event without clashing with the missing signal elsewhere.
arxiv-2505-22911:
Matthew Beveridge and Shree Nayar present a layered system for recognising materials from a small patch of appearance, in a 2025 paper. Knowing what a surface is made of helps vision systems in robotics and imaging. Their taxonomy of materials is arranged by physical traits and is motivated by real vision uses, rather than by abstract classes.

Alongside the taxonomy, they release a varied in-the-wild data set with photos and depth maps for each class. Their recognition method uses a graph attention network that exploits how close classes sit in the taxonomy. It reached state-of-the-art results in their tests. The model also held up under poor, real-world imaging, and new views rendered from the depth maps helped further. In few-shot tests, it learned new materials from just a handful of examples.
arxiv-2505-23111:
Alexander Elias and John Wen published this study in 2025. It pins down a missing definition for the ABB YuMi, a two-armed collaborative robot. Each arm has seven joints, one more than a pose demands. That spare freedom is captured by a single arm angle, which planners need to steer the elbow. ABB uses the angle inside its own simulator, but the exact definition was not public. Planners working outside that tool were stuck guessing.

The authors give the first complete, tested definition, built on the standard shoulder-elbow-wrist angle frame. They also fix the shoulder reference point and derive the angle's rate formula. All singular poses, where planning breaks, are cataloged. With the definition in hand, their inverse solver finds every valid arm pose by a two-dimensional search. Code examples are public.
arxiv-2505-23211:
Atte Pennanen characterizes when maps between Bergman-Zygmund spaces of analytic functions are bounded or compact, for weights that double in a set way. These spaces blend classic Bergman spaces with a growth factor in the size gauge. The work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The setting is the unit disc, with a radial weight that has two sided doubling traits. The author pins down which measures make the plain inclusion map into a lower power space bounded, and which make it compact. Growth factors on both sides are near monotone with doubling traits. The same frame then sorts when a derivative map between the spaces is bounded or compact.
arxiv-2505-23811:
Hadi Askari and co-authors grade the layers inside large language models in a 2025 paper. A trained model is a stack of layers, and their quality varies by task. Most tools for judging layers look only at the model's own numbers, ignoring the training data that shaped them. The authors' method, LayerIF, uses influence functions, a statistics tool that asks how much each training example moved the model's errors.

By isolating each layer's gradients, the method scores how much that layer's training helped or hurt on a given task. The same model earns distinct scores for distinct tasks, showing how layers specialize. The scores then guide two practical jobs: assigning expert modules in a mixture model, and choosing where to prune. Across several model families, the data-guided choices beat standard heuristics. The authors stress the method needs no change to the model itself.
arxiv-2505-24011:
Bastien Anézo, Denis Arčon, and Chris Ewels compute how a fullerene guest trades charge with a diamond defect near two surface skins, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The defect is a prized quantum sensor, and the guest carries a free spin. First-principles math covers both hydrogen and fluorine skins.

On the hydrogen skin, the guest steals the charge and the spins die. On the fluorine skin, the defect keeps its charge and both spins live. Surface bending from unlike electron pull drives the split. The math matches seen light dimming on the first skin. Fluorine coats may shield sensors from guest theft. Readers get a surface fix for fragile quantum bits.
arxiv-2505-24211:
Jiwan Chung and co-authors test whether all-in-one AI models stay coherent across media in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Any-to-any models read and write text, images, and more in one system. Fans assume unity brings consistency, but that was unproven. The team built a test set of one thousand images with captions, edit instructions, and question-answer pairs. Half the images were newly contributed.

They scored models on three checks: going in a circle and returning unchanged, and two kinds of order-swapping consistency. Unified models did not clearly beat specialist models on the pointwise checks. Finer tests showed weak but real coherence. The study tempers hype with measurement. Multimodal AI researchers are the audience.
arxiv-2505-24311:
Yi Gu and Antonio Auffinger study the equilibrium distribution for t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding with generalized kernels, in a mathematics paper from 2025. The method, known as t-SNE, maps high-dimensional data into a low-dimensional picture that keeps neighbor structure. Its large-sample behavior was known for one kernel pair, but not for the broader family used in practice.

The authors extend the limit results to wide classes of input and output kernels. Under natural conditions, and when the perplexity setting grows in line with data size, the point clouds and their minimizers settle to an equilibrium distribution. Numerical cases compare kernels. The theory grounds choices that users make by habit.
arxiv-2505-24411:
Feng Chen and six co-authors report a contest winning system for reading body pose from mixed camera views in a 2025 paper. The EgoExo4D contests ask a model to track twenty one hand joints from head worn video, where hands move fast and often hide. The same event also tests full body pose and how skilled the person in the video is.

Their hand system blends a vision transformer with a standard image network and mixes the two scores. It won both the hand and body pose contests at a 2025 vision meeting. The team then reused the same core tricks to judge skill level, taking the top score there as well.
arxiv-2505-24511:
Mingyue Cheng and co-authors ask if slow thinking language models can forecast time series by reasoning, in a 2025 paper. Most forecast tools follow a fast path: they pull patterns and map them straight to values. Slow thinking models, by contrast, work through steps and have shown strong reasoning in many fields.

Their study, TimeReasoner, frames forecasting as a reasoning task with set conditions. Prompt plans draw out step by step thought from ready trained models, with no new training. The models showed real zero shot skill, most of all at catching broad trends and shifts in context. Limits also showed, which the team maps for future work.
arxiv-2505-24611:
Gonzalo Martínez-Lema and co-authors coax a microstrip plate into glowing and multiplying charge inside liquid xenon. Noble-liquid detectors for dark matter and neutrinos crave single-phase designs that both sense charge and flash light. Their plate, modeled on a virtual cathode chamber, carries two-micrometre anode strips on semiconductive glass with a cathode film behind.

Immersed in liquid xenon, the plate produced electroluminescence in the fierce field near its strips, the first such observation for this design. The light yield began near four hundred sixty photons per drifting electron, then faded within tens of minutes to a lower plateau. A modest charge gain accompanied the light. The authors say understanding and stopping the fade is the next job, with other substrates waiting.
arxiv-2505-24711:
Orsolya Fehér and co-authors map thick gas marks in and past our star home's arms to find where stars form. The work dates to 2025. Huge gas threads give clean labs for that hunt at scales now seen in far star homes. Two threads were mapped, one in an arm and one past it.

Three thick-gas marks were read next to thin gas and dust maps. One mark filled the least sky yet traced the true thick gas best. Its glow sat near flat in arm and gap, while thin marks swung a lot. Swings in mark pairs thus come from thin gas, not star-form gas. Zone shifts in one thread topped arm-gap shifts.
arxiv-2506-00311:
Ankit Kumar and Hajime Sotani studied neutron stars mixed with dark matter in 2025. Dark matter is modeled as a second fluid bound by gravity, linked to normal matter through a Higgs-portal coupling. Three standard equations of state for dense nuclear matter anchor the models.

A dark matter profile that scales with baryon density is set by two knobs, a mass factor and a steepness index. Adding dark matter squeezed the stars and lowered their maximum mass. Radial vibration modes shifted in ways that depend on the steepness. Broader vibration patterns, tied to known universal relations, stayed mostly intact, bending only in extreme setups. The authors offer the frame as a way to probe dark matter through star vibrations.
arxiv-2506-00611:
Adam Vernon and Mitch Peaks scheme fast entanglement for barium ion qubits in a 2025 paper. Trapped ions entangle through shared motion, which caps gate speed. Rydberg states of barium offer strong, tunable pulls instead, if each ion can be lit alone.

The pair computed jump strengths and polarizabilities with a semiclassical method. A two photon path from the ground state to a high Rydberg state stood out as the best ladder. Near a telecom wavelength the ground state bends strongly in light, so a plain laser can address ions by brightness and tune pair gates below a microsecond.
arxiv-2506-00711:
Wei Dai and co-authors build QoQ-Med in 2025, a clinical foundation model that reasons across images, signals, and text. Hospital decisions blend all three, yet most multimodal models lean on images alone and generalize poorly across specialties. The team wanted one open model for many clinical domains.

Training used millions of instruction pairs across nine domains. A new reinforcement method scales rewards by domain rarity and modality difficulty, fighting imbalance in the data. Diagnostic scores rose sharply against rival training methods in the report. A version tuned on segmentation data could also highlight regions, aiding review.
arxiv-2506-00911:
Deploying a language model means juggling rivals: helpful against harmless, cheap against accurate, rewarding against safe. William Overman and Mohsen Bayati introduce Conformal Arbitrage in a 2025 paper. It is a referee that routes each request between a bold primary model and a cautious guardian, which may be another model or a human expert.

A learned threshold decides who answers, tuned by conformal risk control so the long-run rate of bad events, errors or safety breaches, stays under a quota the user sets. The method works at the API level, never touching model weights or internals. In tests it traced a clean frontier between the competing goals and beat cost-matched random routing on accuracy. The authors pitch it as a practical, guarantee-backed layer for trustworthy, economical model deployment.
arxiv-2506-01111:
Shunian Chen and co-authors build a data set of over a million detailed audio captions using models that fuse many cues. Their 2025 paper notes a gap: automated captions for sound are often thin and context poor. Human hearing, by contrast, weaves speech, music, and scene cues together. Their two stage pipeline imitates that. Specialist models first extract cues such as speech, music, general sounds, and video frames.

A large language model then merges those cues into fine grained, context aware captions. The result is a data set of 1.2 million captions plus six million question answer pairs. Models trained on it improved, notably an audio encoder with stronger sound text alignment. The authors present the set, called FusionAudio-1.2M, as a base for richer automated listening. Code and data are public, they note.
arxiv-2506-01311:
Leo Mei and Mark Stamp measure the electricity cost of training large pretrained networks, and whether shrinking them saves power, in a 2025 paper. Big models perform well but eat compute and current. Past shrink work chased keeping accuracy, rarely the power bill itself. Nine models, from eight million to one hundred thirty eight million weights, were trained plain first for a baseline.

Three shrink methods were then applied: pruning, low rank splitting, and a steganographic capacity cut. Power, time, and accuracy were logged each way. Pruning and low rank gave no real power gain. The capacity cut, oddly, saved much in nearly every case. The authors weigh what that means for greener model training.
arxiv-2506-01611:
Wangyou Zhang and co-authors draw in 2025 lessons from the URGENT 2024 speech enhancement challenge. The contest pushed for tools that work across many voices, noises, and rooms. Two understudied fronts get the deep look here: data cleaning and grading metrics.

Declared and true audio bandwidth often clash, and even prized corpora carry label noise. The hardest scenes, like speech overlap and strong echo, still defeat top systems. No single metric tracks human judgment well, so mixed metric sets are urged. The authors hope the lessons reshape how speech cleaning pipelines get built.
arxiv-2506-01711:
Sierra Miranda, Studer, and Zenger give a uniform way to translate proofs between systems that allow infinite proofs, in a 2025 logic paper. Non-wellfounded proofs can run forever, so rules must force every infinite path to pass a certain rule again and again, blocking empty loops. Such systems serve modal logics whose frames run backward in a well-founded way. Earlier translations were built case by case.

Their method rests only on coalgebras, the categorical machinery for corecursion. It guarantees the path condition survives translation. As a showcase, they prove cut-elimination for a non-wellfounded system of the logic Grz, matching an earlier result that needed metric space fixed point theory. The authors pitch the coalgebraic route as the cleaner general tool.
arxiv-2506-01911:
Ravi Kuchimanchi defends a classic solution to a particle physics puzzle in a 2025 paper. The strong CP problem asks why a certain term in the theory of the strong force seems to vanish when it could be large. One family of answers uses mirror symmetry, called parity, and its partner CP symmetry, with no need for new particles.

A recent paper argued those answers fail if the early universe began in a mixed state of the theory's vacuum parameter. Kuchimanchi examines that claim closely, focusing on what the vacuum state really is. He concludes the conventional framing stands on firm ground. In his account, symmetry-based solutions remain valid, and the objection rests on a misreading of the vacuum's nature.
arxiv-2506-02211:
Maxime Robeyns and Laurence Aitchison showed in twenty twenty-five that reinforcement learning can train language models to write not just correct code, but good code. Execution-based training rewards passing unit tests and ignores maintainability, quality, and safety — dimensions that decide whether generated code helps or haunts a project. The authors built a library that quantifies those aspects of code quality.

Using that quality score as the reward in a group-relative policy optimization procedure, they found measurable quality gains in the generated code. Blinded expert human annotators confirmed the improvement independently of the automatic metric. The study opens a route to aligning code generators with the standards human reviewers actually apply, beyond whether the program merely runs.
arxiv-2506-02311:
Qiufeng Li, Yiwen Liang, and Weidong Cao study the safety of a new kind of chip in a 2025 paper. Compute-in-memory chips do math inside memory itself, which speeds up neural networks. Their reliability under faults was little studied, above all for the high-precision form needed for careful work.

Their framework injects faults and tracks how errors spread through several networks. High-precision models proved very sensitive to errors in the part of a number that sets its scale. Guided by that finding, they tuned models and added a light error-correcting code. The protection kept accuracy while adding only a small amount of extra logic.
arxiv-2506-03011:
Aditya Bharat Soni and co-authors ask in a 2025 paper what least set of tools lets one smart agent solve many kinds of tasks. Most agents are built for one trade, such as code or web work, and fail outside it. Each new trade tends to spawn its own custom tool kit.

Their agent pairs code skill with the power to browse with eyes as well as text. With that spare kit, it takes on a wide span of tasks at a high level. The result hints that broad tools beat narrow ones for general work. Agent builders gain proof that less kit, well chosen, can do more.
arxiv-2506-03111:
Victor Armegioiu, Yannick Ramic, and Siddhartha Mishra present a 2025 paper on fast computer models of fluid flow. Flows are hard to mimic because they change across many scales and react sharply to starting conditions. Diffusion-based surrogates are accurate but need hundreds of sampling steps. The team proposes a rectified-flow surrogate that learns a velocity field carrying inputs to outputs along nearly straight paths.

Prediction then becomes a short deterministic solve, needing about eight steps where diffusion needs well over a hundred. The authors back the method with theory that splits error into coverage of fine detail and fit to the target. A smart sampler adjusts its steps using a running measure of path straightness. On two-dimensional flows, both calm and compressible, the method matched diffusion quality at far lower cost. Fine structures survived that simpler models blur.
arxiv-2506-03411:
Melissa Dutz, Han Shao, Avrim Blum, and Aloni Cohen model strategic court cases through machine learning theory in a 2025 paper. In common law, one case can set precedent that binds later courts. A strategic litigator picks cases not just to win, but to shape the rule that lower courts will apply next.

Their model treats the lower court as a learner that infers its rule from higher court rulings. The team asks how much sway such a litigator holds, which cases to bring, and whether filing a sure loser can pay off. Even simple settings show odd effects. For two classic learning rules, they describe which future rules can be induced and give methods to pick the best case set.
arxiv-2506-03511:
Fangyi Cao and seven co-authors published this paper in 2025. It releases a large data set of telescope images for training AI to find planets and dust disks around other stars. Direct images of such systems are rare prizes, and sorting them takes heavy hand labeling.

The data set, called POLARIS, draws on more than a million images from over ten thousand exposures taken by top planet-hunting cameras. It sorts images of plain reference stars from those holding disks, using a public archive of polarized light gathered since 2014. Less than a tenth of the set needed hand labels. The authors test many model types and share baseline scores. Their own unsupervised method learned the strongest features. They hope the set draws data scientists into the planet hunt.
arxiv-2506-04311:
Stefano Antonini and co-authors present a theoretical physics paper, published in 2025, defending entanglement islands in black hole physics. Islands are regions inside a black hole whose information turns out to be encoded in radiation far outside. They arose in work that traced how information escapes a black hole, matching a curve first described by Page.

Some writers argued islands need gravitons with mass and a reservoir outside gravity, features of the first setups used. The authors show islands also appear without those features, giving examples in flat space and in gravitating settings. With careful experiments on many copies of a black hole, they argue, the Page curve remains something that can in principle be observed.
arxiv-2506-04411:
Achleshwar Luthra, Tianbao Yang, and Tomer Galanti closed a theory gap for contrastive learning in a 2025 paper. In self-supervised contrastive learning, a model learns by pulling two views of one item together and pushing the rest apart, with no labels at all. Why that works so well lacked a firm proof.

The trio show the standard loss quietly mimics a supervised loss that skips same-class pairs. The gap between the two fades as class count grows, under a bound that needs no labels and no model shape. They also map the shape of the best codes under that loss. The proof grounds a daily tool of AI.
arxiv-2506-04611:
Ho-Lam Chung and six co-workers wrote a 2025 survey on giving language models more time to think at test time. Extra compute while answering can lift reasoning scores. The survey sorts methods into sampling, search and path-tuning groups. The team notes a snag: models tuned for reasoning tend to give like answers, which caps the gain.

Their fix is a light tuning method that prizes varied outputs. It uses a small set of trainable prefix parts plus a data plan built for diversity. On math tasks, it hit a strong score with far less compute than top rivals. Diversity, they argue, is key to test-time gains.
arxiv-2506-05011:
Drone video of crowds is hard to turn into fresh views, because one camera looks down on many small, moving people. Jaehoon Choi and six co-authors present UAV4D in 2025, a system that rebuilds such scenes so they can be rendered from new angles. It joins a general 3D model with a human body model to rebuild both the ground scene and each person.

A key step finds where feet meet the ground, which fixes the true scale of the scene. Body shaped starting points then guide the rendering method the team use. On three drone data sets with ten to fifty people, the system beat earlier methods on image quality scores. The authors aim it at real world footage rather than staged scenes.
arxiv-2506-05111:
Bruno De Filippo and co-authors design an AI receiver for sparse code links in future satellite networks in two thousand twenty-five. Sixth-generation networks will merge ground and space systems for everywhere coverage. Sparse code multiple access packs many senders onto one channel, but the overlap garbles classic receivers, and heavy error codes eat the gain.

Their receiver learns several tasks at once to unmix the stacked signals. Link-level simulations track error rates and total throughput against signal strength. The AI design hit a ten percent block error target with three and a half decibels less signal energy than the standard method. The authors close by weighing deployment in real space-edge systems.
arxiv-2506-05511:
Ming-Wei Li and co-authors revisit, in a 2025 particle physics paper, a model built to explain a long-standing mismatch in the measured magnetism of the muon. New final results from a major lab, paired with fresh theory work, now agree much more closely. That shift loosens the bounds on the model but does not close it off.

The model adds a new force carrier tied to muon and tau particle numbers. Past data from neutrino scattering had forced that carrier to be very light if it was to explain the old gap. With the gap now small, heavier values are allowed again. The authors also check effects on other particles and argue a future muon collider could test the model well.
arxiv-2506-05611:
Abhishek Kumar Mishra, Mathieu Cunche, and Héber Arcolezi present a 2025 paper stress-testing the anonymity of a large public data set of movement traces from Japan. One hundred thousand users' trajectories were released after protective transformations. The team shows the protection leaks: density patterns and daily rhythms let them rebuild the true map frame and the real calendar behind the data. On that rebuilt base they measured how easily individuals can be singled out.

A handful of observations, home and work anchors, or visits to sensitive places often sufficed to identify a person or their social circle. They then tried standard sanitizing methods, from noise addition to heavy spatial scrambling. Strong settings wrecked the data's usefulness, while gentle ones left the leakage largely intact. The authors conclude current techniques cannot safely publish large-scale mobility data and demand trajectory-aware privacy methods and stronger standards.
arxiv-2506-05911:
Simon Dupourqué and Didier Barret test a fast fitting method for X-ray spectra in a 2025 paper. The method trains a neural network on simulated spectra, then reads real ones in a fraction of the usual time. Their target is a planned space instrument that will record spectra at very fine detail.

Fine detail means many channels, so the team compressed each spectrum into a few telling summary numbers. Ratios and counts in set bands worked far better than raw full spectra. The network's answers matched slow exact methods on smooth and complex test models alike. Repeated rounds converged fast, while a single-round version needed more training up front. Line features need their own summaries, the authors note.
arxiv-2506-06311:
Meiyan Kang and co-authors teach a neural network to spot buried pipes in radar scans by first sharpening the shapes in the data, in this 2025 paper. Ground penetrating radar is a standard non-destructive way to map what lies underground, and pipes show up as hyperbola curves. Noise and clutter make those curves easy to miss.

The team derives shape-aware features from the scans with topological data analysis, a method that reads the structure of data at many scales. Those features are fed to a YOLOv5 detector, making it more alert to the geometry of buried objects. Because labeled real scans are scarce, they trained with a simulation-to-real plan that builds varied synthetic scans. Detection scores improved clearly over the base approach. The authors point to city planning, safety checks, and upkeep of buried networks as natural uses for fast, reliable pipe finding.
arxiv-2506-06411:
Paul Fogel, Christophe Geissler, and George Luta set out CoxNTF, a joint way to group and predict in survival work. Hidden trait maps of base traits can aid how results are read. But the standard tool for such maps, nonnegative matrix factorization, skips survival data. That skip caps how well it can predict. A tool that learns traits tied to results would serve both aims at once.

CoxNTF runs nonnegative tensor factorization on a weighted trait tensor. Odds of survival from a Coxnet model guide how the tensor is built. Its calls on who lives match Coxnet run on the raw traits. At the same time, the traits give a clear, neat grouping of patients that is easy to read. The tool also copes well with traits that repeat each other. That fit suits messy trait sets from clinic work.
arxiv-2506-06511:
Ivan Burbano and co-authors prove a general result for computing particle scattering on simulators in a 2025 paper. Quantum computers and tensor networks can now probe real-time behavior of field theories directly. Turning those probes into scattering data, the bread and butter of particle physics, needs care in finite boxes.
