The team shows that real-time estimators work for all scattering observables in gapped theories. Errors from the finite box shrink exponentially fast, at a rate set by a chosen regulator that shifts the spectrum into the complex plane. Averaging over boosts restores part of the lost symmetry and shrinks errors further. The same logic covers wavepacket scattering. The result is a needed step toward hadron data that classical machines cannot reach.
arxiv-2506-06611:
Xing Wei derives how energy splits in magnetohydrodynamic turbulence in this 2025 paper. Turbulent conducting fluids, like plasmas, carry both motion energy and magnetic energy. How the total divides between them was first studied decades ago. Wei revisits the question with a simple, direct method.

Starting from the energy equation, the two dissipation channels come out comparable. Viscous loss and ohmic loss are of similar size in this regime. When turbulent viscosity and magnetic diffusivity are also comparable, a clean rule follows. The energy ratio then depends on the size ratio of the largest magnetic and velocity eddies. Equal largest scales give equipartition between motion and field. The short derivation clarifies an old result.
arxiv-2506-06911:
Malman proves a sharper version of a classic result on when boundary data force a function to vanish. A set on the unit circle has the Khinchin-Ostrowski property if test sequences that fade on it must fade everywhere. Earlier theorems by Kegejan and Khrushchev set terms for when this holds.

One step in Khrushchev's proof needed the growth bound to be log-integrable. That need blocked some generalized Beurling-Carleson settings from the result. Malman drops that assumption with a new domain shape. The domain cuts out areas bounded by hyperbolic arcs between gaps of the set. Harmonic measure estimates then go through without the extra condition.
arxiv-2506-07111:
Vabishchevich presents a paper from twenty twenty-five on computing averaged models for diffusion in patterned materials. Fine-scale models are too costly to solve across whole parts. Averaging builds macro models from one repeating cell's solution. With weakly conducting inclusions, the macro model gains memory terms. The memory kernel comes from a time-varying cell problem. An effective spread tensor follows from standard finite element work. The kernel is then matched by a sum of decaying exponentials.

That match turns the nonlocal model back into local form. Extra helper problems carry the memory effects cheaply. Stability of the time stepping is proved. A two-dimensional test case illustrates the whole method.
arxiv-2506-07311:
Thomas Joshi and co-authors fuse two memory tricks to speed long-text work in big word models in a 2025 paper. Long inputs swell the store of past word keys, and block-wise stores waste room. The new build pages that store like an operating system and runs it through a bendy attention tool in a shared IBM stack.

On a mid graphics card, lag grew in a straight line as text grew from short to two thousand words, where the no-cache way spiked hard. Peak memory stayed near flat in one-step tests. The paged store adds a touch of waste past that length. The full build is open source.
arxiv-2506-07511:
Stijn Cambie and Ajay Tiwari settle a distance puzzle for hypergraphs and weighted graphs. Their paper from twenty twenty-five studies Šoltés objects, where removing any one vertex leaves total distance unchanged. The classic problem asked whether such graphs exist beyond one known case. Hypergraphs widen the stage: edges can hold many vertices at once.

The team proves each uniform Šoltés hypergraph needs at least a set count of vertices. Such hypergraphs exist for near all orders and uniformities. One example is not even regular, which widens the family. Infinitely many weighted Šoltés graphs are built as well. Together these say the puzzle answers yes for the most natural widenings of graphs. Total distance can indeed survive any single vertex loss.
arxiv-2506-07811:
Tieyuan Chen and co-authors teach video question answering to read between the lines in a 2025 paper. Many video questions target hidden intent or symbolism, where no single segment holds the answer. The team defines this implicit task and builds a dataset for it, then proposes a reasoning model with two clue streams.

One module gathers action and intent clues, checking their relations. Another sharpens the visual features with the best clues. The model edges out top commercial systems and a tuned rival on the new benchmark. It also leads on ad understanding and traffic prediction tasks. Readers get a framework for unspoken video meaning.
arxiv-2506-07911:
Yann-Situ Gazull extends two flavors of persistent homology, steady and ranging, from graphs to general objects, and checks when the summaries stay stable. Persistent homology tracks how features of data appear and vanish across scales. The steady and ranging variants were built to follow a chosen feature along graph filtrations. Writing in twenty twenty-five, Gazull rebuilds them with category theory so they apply far beyond graphs. The study then investigates stability: small changes in the input should move the summary only slightly. A characterization identifies exactly which features induce balanced behavior in both persistence types.

A working implementation for hypergraphs illustrates the machinery. Hypergraphs, where edges join many vertices, are a natural test case beyond ordinary graphs. The results widen topological data analysis while keeping its reliability guarantees in view.
arxiv-2506-08311:
Ira Ceka and co-authors trace in 2025 how automated repair agents, driven by large language models, go about fixing real software bugs. Such agents plan, reason, and use tools on their own, and they score well on leaderboards. Yet little was known about where their choices go wrong.

The team followed five leading agents through five hundred repair tasks, from the bug report to the final patch check. Agents handled simple fixes well but faltered on logic-heavy bugs, often writing long patches that passed tests without fixing the root cause. Weak test writing and plain tooling were common limits. The authors urge earlier testing, richer tools, and mixed agent designs.
arxiv-2506-08611:
Shiji Zhao, Chi Chen, Ranjie Duan, Xizhe Wang, and Xingxing Wei fight class bias in adversarial training with an anti-bias label trick. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes a fairness flaw. Models hardened against attacks stay strong on easy classes but fold on hard ones. Distillation variants share the flaw. The team traces much of it to how smooth each class's soft labels are.

Their ABSLD method sits inside knowledge distillation. It tweaks the teacher's label smoothness class by class, through set heat values per class. The tweak shrinks the gap in student error risk across classes. Being label-based, it stacks with sample-based fixes. Wide tests show it beats prior methods on the joint score of robustness and fairness. The work treats even defense, not just high average defense, as the goal.
arxiv-2506-08811: Alice Dell'Arciprete and Lorenzo Putignano grow a known algebra shortcut to a wider family of algebras. For a base family, a famed result links key counts across two forms of a counting board: add blank lanes to the board, and the counts shift in a set way. Their 2025 study asks if the same link holds for the wider Ariki-Koike family. Short cuts of this kind save hard sums in the field of symbol algebra.
arxiv-2506-08911:
Petar Jakus and Hrvoje Dzapo implement, in a 2025 paper, a keyword spotting system on a microcontroller with a built in neural accelerator, aiming at voice control that never leaves the device. Always listening wake word detection usually leans on phones or the cloud. A tiny chip that hears the keyword itself enables cheap, private, low power interfaces.

Their pipeline extracts standard sound features from speech and classifies them with a small convolutional network. Training was quantization aware, so the model shrank to fit the chip with minimal accuracy loss. Running on the neural unit instead of the main processor cut inference time by a factor of fifty nine. The final model reached about 97 percent accuracy in just 30 kilobytes. Numbers like those move voice control into toys, appliances, and sensors that could never host a big model, without sending audio anywhere.
arxiv-2506-09611:
Hao Du and Yuan-Yao He speed up auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations in a 2025 paper on ground states of interacting fermions. These methods are key tools for quantum phases, but local updates of the field slow them down.

Two new update schemes attack that bottleneck. A delayed update swaps many small vector steps for one matrix step. A block force-bias update keeps the speed of a dilute-system trick while letting users tune acceptance by block size. Tests on plain and spin-orbit Hubbard models show clear speedups. Gains reach about eightfold on large lattices. The schemes apply broadly across fillings and settings, aiding studies of phase changes in fermion systems.
arxiv-2506-09811:
Pieter Belmans wrote this mathematics paper, published in 2025, in algebraic geometry. It proves that a family of elegant spaces, the coadjoint and adjoint partial flag varieties, fail a strong vanishing property that a long-standing conjecture said they should fail.

Bott vanishing, named for Raoul Bott, demands that certain cohomology groups vanish when the cotangent bundle is twisted by ample line bundles. A conjecture by Buch, Thomsen, Lauritzen, and Mehta predicted that partial flag varieties, beyond simple products of projective spaces, would not satisfy it, despite their many nice properties. The easiest case was settled with classical theorems. Belmans now handles the (co)adjoint varieties of every classical and exceptional symmetry type. The proof confirms the conjecture for this whole class, sharpening the map of which spaces enjoy the strongest vanishing behavior.
arxiv-2506-10611:
Mokhtar Kirane, Ahmad Fino, Berikbol Torebek, and Zineb Sabbagh extended a classic blow-up problem to Heisenberg groups in 2025. Fujita's problem asks when a heat equation with a power source has solutions that live for all time. Here the equation also carries a memory term that weighs the whole past.

A critical exponent splits the fates. Below or at it, no global solution exists for any starting data. Above it, small starting data give a global positive solution. The exponent blends the memory's strength with the group's dimension. Lifespan bounds for short-lived solutions are also given by case. Proofs use test functions and a fixed point argument, echoing a known Euclidean study.
arxiv-2506-10711:
Li Luo improves a diffusion-based refiner that keeps long simulations of partial differential equations on track. The work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Rolling a simulation forward for many steps is notoriously unstable, and errors in fine detail grow first.

An earlier refiner polished each step with a denoising model, treating all frequencies alike. For harder equations like Navier-Stokes flow, that flat treatment over-smooths the fine scales. Luo's version adjusts in spectral space, weighting each frequency band separately. A new prediction trick restores the simple training target on the first pass. Across backbones, from U-Net to neural operators, rollouts grew more accurate in both one-step and long-run error.
arxiv-2506-10811:
Rutger van Haasteren examines how pulsar timing arrays compute p-values for their gravitational wave detection statistics. These projects hunt for a background hum of gravitational waves through correlations between pulsars. A p-value states how unlikely the observed signal would be if nothing were there, but the teams cannot sample from that empty case directly. A popular workaround scrambles the data to cancel pulsar correlations, and it has been praised as model-independent.

Working from first principles, van Haasteren analyzes every scrambling method in the literature and derives the needed formulas. The verdict is that scrambling is not model-independent after all, so it is not fully empirical either. The paper instead backs rigorous Bayesian and frequentist routes built on the generalized chi-square distribution, and shows the common claim that no correct frequentist p-value exists so far in this setting.
arxiv-2506-10911:
Jari Kolehmainen and co-authors present NoLoCo, a training method for large models that needs no collective communication between machines. Their 2025 paper starts from a cost: training big language models takes clusters of thousands of accelerators linked by fast networks, and scaling those clusters is pricey. Recent low communication methods still pause to sync all weights at once.

NoLoCo skips that global step. It syncs weights only in part, by averaging them inside small random subgroups through a variant of the Nesterov momentum optimizer. The authors give a convergence proof and training results on language models. Communication needs fell well below fully sharded training and below a widely used low communication baseline.
arxiv-2506-11111:
Kun Zhang and co-authors survey what it takes for a large language model to stay right when the world stops being polite. Robustness, as they define it, means consistent, correct output under toxic prompts, noisy data, and out-of-distribution surprises. The survey organizes the young field under three roofs.

Adversarial robustness covers deliberate attacks: manipulated prompts, long contexts, poisoned data. Out-of-distribution robustness covers honest strangeness: detection, zero-shot transfer, and hallucination. A third section collects the benchmarks, metrics, and tools used to verify robustness claims. The authors close with open problems and maintain a public paper collection so practitioners can search the fast-growing literature without drowning in it.
arxiv-2506-11211:
Anyons are odd particles that live only in flat, two-dimensional worlds, and giving them a spread of energies takes a broken symmetry. Mina-Lou Schleith, Tomohiro Soejima, and Eslam Khalaf place anyons on a sphere lit by a magnetic field that is stronger at one pole than the other. That uneven field breaks the sphere's full rotation symmetry while keeping each particle's own energy perfectly flat.

A neat mapping lets them reuse known results from the even-field case to work out how the anyons push on each other. The push alone creates a spread of energies, which they compute exactly up to one overall scale factor. The anyons end up circling the sphere at fixed height, much like a spinning top's slow turn.
arxiv-2506-11311:
Yue Liu, Philip Maini, and Ruth Baker wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about designing experiments for models of living systems. Such models contain unknown values that must be inferred from data. If an experiment is poorly designed, the data may not pin those values down, and rival models may stay hard to tell apart.

The authors explore how to shape an external stimulus, used as a control input, so the data reveal the most. They judge value identifiability with a profile likelihood approach. They then recast design for choosing between models as an optimal control problem that can be solved with known tools. Common equation models of biology serve as worked examples throughout the paper.
arxiv-2506-11611:
Web tools that learn on link maps can be fooled by a few fake links, and most shields train for the known tricks. Yaning Jia and co-authors shield with no train at all in a 2025 study. Their scale is a grid mark, drawn from the map's own core grid, that bounds how far the tool can stray.

Each link earns a score: how much the grid mark falls when that link is cut. Fake links score high, since they bend the map's true grain. High score links are pruned ere the tool reads the map. The shield fits any web tool as a plug, and lifts old shields it rides with. Sums and wide tests back the claim.
arxiv-2506-11711:
Two classic puzzles, packing a knapsack and finding the shortest path, grow harder once their rules gain extra twists. Five researchers solve them in 2025 with algorithms borrowed from quantum computing but run as tensor networks on ordinary hardware. Their equations return the exact best answer, not an estimate. The method grows from imaginary time evolution, with the problem's restrictions built straight into the network.

Two tricks cut the cost: reusing partial results, and leaning on symmetries in the problem. Tests compare the new solvers with standard classical algorithms on varied versions of both puzzles. The authors present the approach as a practical path to exact answers for wider families of hard planning problems.
arxiv-2506-11811:
Some sounds evoke nothing you can name, and blending two sounds into a genuinely new one is an art. Jing Liu and co-authors automate that fusion in this 2025 paper using diffusion model inversion. Inversion runs the generation process backward, recovering the hidden seed of a real sound so it can be steered.

Their new inversion schemes, built on a fast solver family, fix the seed terms as constants to avoid circular logic in the noise estimates. No text prompt is needed to steer, yet guidance stays flexible during synthesis. The aim is abstract sound design: fused audio whose features go beyond simply layering the two sources. The authors position the method for sound artists and media production.
arxiv-2506-12111:
Óscar Boullosa Dapena, writing alone under the name Oscar Boullosa Dapena in the head, presents a 2025 paper on a neural network design for learning from streaming data. Models that learn step by step from endless streams face cost and stability limits with classic backpropagation through time. His design reframes updates as integrals over past data.

The trick borrows Feynman's method of differentiating under the integral sign. The result is smoother, steadier learning that stays readable in physical terms and cheap to run. The design also fits quantum gradient tools, which opens a path to hybrid classical-quantum networks. Tests on made-up and real streaming tasks showed the model works. The author sets out next steps for quantum versions and scale-up.
arxiv-2506-12511:
Rommel Tchinda Djeudjo and co-authors study in 2025 chimera states on directed webs where groups, not just pairs, interact. A chimera mixes synced and unsynced zones in a crowd of identical oscillators. Most past work used fair, two-way pair links, yet real systems often pull unevenly and in groups.

Their structure, called an m-directed hypergraph, lets group links point one way. Some chimera forms appeared only thanks to that direction, never in its absence. Chimeras also spanned a wider range of settings on group webs than on pair webs. A phase reduction check confirmed the nature of the phase chimeras.
arxiv-2506-12611:
Piotr Kica and co-authors speed a cloud pipe that reads the gene script of cells at scale. The pipe, from a transcript atlas, lines up gene reads with a fast aligner called STAR before counts are made. Such runs chew tens to huge spans of data and rack up cloud cost. Their 2025 study moves the pipe to a cloud-native shape and tunes it part by part.

Each tune is timed in mid runs, then all are stacked in one big run. An early-stop tune cuts align time by near a fourth. Cloud type picks and cheap spot slots get checked for fit. The end shape runs the same reads for less time and cash. Labs with heap-sized read sets can lift the recipe whole.
arxiv-2506-12711:
Yuefeng Liu and Boyang Yu extended work in two thousand twenty-five on a special line defect in a holographic duality between gravity and field theory. The defect, a thin shell operator, had earlier helped reveal chaos in the high-energy sector of the theory. Past work covered a single scalar defect in simple settings.

Here they compute correlators for spinning defects, which match bulk walls made of dust with angular momentum. The wall's junction rule departs from the classic one, leaving a jump in the metric. They also work out correlators with many scalar defects, where insertion order matters. Both extensions match across field theory, statistical, and gravity calculations.
arxiv-2506-12911:
Pantelis Dogoulis and co-authors present a 2025 method to fix machine learning outputs so they obey hard rules. Such rules can be laws of physics, links in a graph, or ties between columns in a table.

Older fixes tend to be built for one domain or work only for simple, straight rules. The new method starts from a rough guess and refines it step by step along a fixed diffusion path, guided by a learned prior and by rule based corrections. It handles curved and non convex rules and can be added to any base model. Tests on table data attacks and on power flow under Kirchhoff's laws improved both rule keeping and accuracy.
arxiv-2506-13011:
Safety walls for control systems are often trained on sample states, which can leave holes off the samples. Erfan Shakhesi and co-authors close those holes with a check-and-fix loop, in work from twenty twenty-five. Their walls must hold under input caps and bounded shakes. Past training forced all samples to obey the wall, which made the wall too strict.

A checker hunts for states where the wall fails, and those states feed the next training round. Step by step, the wall grows valid across the whole zone, not just the samples. The trained wall then slots into a live solver that steers the system safely. Tests on number cases back the flow.
arxiv-2506-13111:
Amornyos Horprasert and co-authors tackle a known weakness of reinforcement learning in a 2025 paper. Agents trained for a long time in one fixed setting often overfit to it. When test conditions shift, their performance can drop sharply, a problem that hits deep network policies in particular.

The team proposes a method that pairs a diffusion model with a Gaussian process model to choose actions. The second model steers action choices toward moves that score well on learned value. Its kernel-based form also helps the agent explore when conditions change. On a standard walking robot test, the method beat leading rivals by a wide margin under shifted conditions. It held up about as well as rivals when conditions stayed normal.
arxiv-2506-13311: Christos Papadimitriou studies a basic equation from maths in a solo 2025 paper. The equation links a curved graph to a given source spread over a short interval, with the graph set to zero at both ends. He defines reshaped forms of that source, made by a kind of balancing. He then compares mean values of the first solution with those of the reshaped ones. His main result shows that one solution gives the largest such mean, and that it is the only one to do so.
arxiv-2506-13411:
Subba and co-authors present a 2025 brief review of MXene sheets as light-driven hydrogen makers. Splitting water with sunlight is a clean route to hydrogen fuel. MXenes, flat crystals of metal carbides and nitrides, offer tuned electron traits, strong charge flow, and rich surface chemistry. As helpers or main catalysts, they can catch light and pass charges to the split site.

The review covers how the sheets are made, how their electron bands shape the work, and how the split proceeds. Core snags get a hard look: the sheets rust easily, charges recombine too fast, and the light gap is off pitch. Closing paths point to mixes and coats that shore up the weak spots. Green hydrogen needs catalysts this cheap and tunable.
arxiv-2506-13511:
Wojciech De Roeck and Amirali Hannani prove many-body localization and Poisson spectral statistics in the Quantum Sun model, published in 2025. The model places interacting spins on a half-line. Spins farther from the origin couple to the rest ever more weakly, with a strength that shrinks by a fixed factor at each step.

Theory and numerics suggested a localization transition at a critical coupling value. The authors prove that well below that value the model is localized, and the statistics of its energy levels follow the Poisson pattern typical of localized systems. The novelty stressed in the abstract is that the model is a genuine many-body system: interactions strongly shape the behavior, unlike simpler settings where earlier proofs applied.
arxiv-2506-14011: George Kontogeorgiou and co-authors prove a graph theory claim in a 2025 paper. Take any two graphs, one to be marked and one to serve as the stamp. The edges of the first graph can be told apart, in the strong sense used by graph theorists, by laying down copies of the second graph with edges split by added points. Single edges fill the gaps where needed. The count of copies grows only in a straight-line way with task size. The result settles a conjecture by Botler and Naia.
arxiv-2506-14111:
Essential AI presents Essential-Web in 2025, a vast organized dataset for training language models. Good training data is the fuel of model skill, yet clean web corpora are costly to build. Their set holds twenty-four trillion tokens of web text. Every document is tagged, not just dumped.

A twelve-part taxonomy labels topic, format, complexity, and quality for each page. A small in-house model does the tagging and nearly matches a far larger model in agreement. Simple database filters then carve out strong sets for math, code, science, and medicine. Some filtered sets beat prior best results by wide margins. The dataset is public on HuggingFace.
arxiv-2506-14211:
Sina Abdidizaji and co-authors build a tool to spot hidden influence moves inside conversations. Bad actors now plant subtle verbal tricks across a chat rather than in one blunt post, aiming to draw out facts from a target. Their 2025 system also marks where in the chat each trick sits.

To train it, the team grew the data set with the help of strong language models that can reason through examples. The new setup lifted detection of hidden influence by six percent. It also raised scores for naming the tricks used by 33 percent, and for naming the weak points of targets by 43 percent. The authors frame the work as a guard for online talk.
arxiv-2506-14411:
John Wikman, Alexandre Proutiere, and David Broman teach reinforcement learning agents to cope with delays they cannot measure. Real systems, from robots to networked controllers, act late: commands arrive after random, hidden lags. Standard methods play safe by assuming the worst-case delay at every step, wasting performance when delays are usually small.

Their interaction layer has the agent emit a matrix of possible future actions, covering a horizon of plausible delays and even lost packets. On top sits a model-based actor-critic algorithm that adapts to the delay pattern it experiences. Across locomotion benchmarks the method significantly beat leading approaches. The framework is general, not tied to one robot or network.
arxiv-2506-14611:
Jacob Miller and co-authors test whether large multimodal models can judge network drawings the way people do, in a paper from 2025. Network layouts are judged by traits such as stress, a measure of how faithfully distances in the drawing match the true links. Human studies have charted how well people read such traits by eye.

The team reran a human experiment with three leading models in place of people. Given the same briefing as trained participants, the models matched expert humans and beat untrained ones. Tweaks to the prompt that broke from the human setup pushed scores even higher in some cases. Like people, the models seemed to lean on visual shortcuts rather than compute the true value. Their written reasons also echoed those given by human judges.
arxiv-2506-15111:
Bryce Thomson counts exactly how many ways a simple knot-like shape can be filled, in a 2025 paper. The shape is the standard Legendrian Hopf link, two linked loops in contact geometry. A filling is a smooth surface, a Lagrangian surface, that caps the link in a controlled exact way. Two fillings were known, and the question was whether exotic others hide nearby. Thomson proves the two known ones are all there are, up to smooth deformation.

The proof stretches the neck of the surrounding space until a hidden fibration appears, forcing any filling to fiber over a real curve. From that structure an explicit deformation to a standard filling can be built. Classification results like this anchor the young dictionary between geometry and algebra in contact topology.
arxiv-2506-15311:
Joao Alvares and Alex Vano-Vinuales track a charged wave field near a charged black hole in a 2025 paper. Such fields ring at set tones after a jolt, then fade in a slow tail. Past work had charted those tones and tails, yet most reads stopped at the hole edge. Their method uses a warped slice of spacetime that reaches all the way to far null infinity, where signals can be read clean.

Full non-linear runs on those slices gave the tone and tail for the charged case. The plain case matched past fits well, which checks the rig. Tone pitch links between the field real and wave parts matched past rules. Tail fall matched the known power law too. Far reads thus back the near reads in print.
arxiv-2506-15511:
Temfack and Wyse join two models of disease spread in a 2025 paper, and they run the pair as one ensemble. One model, a Hawkes process, tracks how cases cluster in time. The other sorts people into groups: susceptible, exposed, infectious, and removed. Each model misses what the other one catches, most of all when spread shifts fast.

A sequential Monte Carlo method weights the two models by how well each one fits the data as it comes in. The joint result takes in doubt about both the model and its inputs. In tests with sharp shifts, and on Irish influenza and COVID-19 data, the pair gave better paths and spread rates than either model alone.
arxiv-2506-15711:
Le Jiang, Liyan Ma, and Guang Yang propose a shield for joint learning across hospitals that keeps shared updates from leaking patient images. Their paper appeared in twenty twenty-five. In joint learning, sites train one shared model without sending raw data. Yet foes can rebuild training images from the shared slopes, a trick called gradient inversion.

The shield uses a shadow model to find which image parts are most at risk. Noise is then added just where it is most needed, in a dose set for each image. Tests on chest X-ray and eye scan sets showed strong blocks on rebuild tries. Loss in model scores stayed small, under one percent on the main score.
arxiv-2506-15811: Will Roper and co-authors present a software package that turns galaxy models into mock observations in a paper from 2025. Their package, Synthesizer, produces spectra, brightness measures, images, and data cubes from model galaxies, with modeling assumptions that users can swap easily. Heavy computing runs in fast threaded code behind a simple Python interface, so forward-modeling workflows stay quick without low-level data handling by the user.
arxiv-2506-15911:
Mohammad Amaan Sayeed and co-authors published this machine learning paper in 2025. It builds an evaluation pipeline for medical answers drawn from classical Islamic medicine, including Avicenna's Canon and the Prophetic tradition of Tibb-e-Nabawi. These texts hold centuries of guidance on prevention, nutrition, and holistic care, yet modern AI systems rarely draw on them, and benchmarks seldom test culturally grounded advice. The pipeline, called Tibbe-AG, aligns thirty curated questions with human-verified remedies.

Three language models were tested in three modes: answering directly, answering with retrieved text, and answering with a self-critique filter. A second model then graded each answer on a single quality score. Retrieval raised factual accuracy by thirteen percent, and the self-critique step added another ten percent, improving depth and safety. The authors argue the blend makes culturally sensitive medical question-answering more reliable.
arxiv-2506-16211:
Li and a team including Huang propose ControlVLA in twenty twenty-five, a way to adapt robot models with few examples. Large models for vision, language, and action can learn broad skills from many demos. Adapting them to a new task with just a few demos is still hard. Past methods often need simulation data or fixed grasp modules.

ControlVLA adds object focused signals to the base model through new layers that start at zero. Those layers learn slowly, so old skills are not erased at once. In real tests on six tasks, such as pouring cubes and folding clothes, the method hit a high success rate. It needed only ten to twenty demos per task. Past methods needed more than one hundred demos for like results.
arxiv-2506-16411:
Zhen Xu and co-authors ask in this 2025 paper when splitting a long text into chunks helps a large language model. Teams often hand each chunk to a separate agent and merge the answers, but the gains are uneven. The authors sort the ways such tasks fail into three kinds of noise: links across chunks, mix-ups that grow with length, and weak merging of part answers.

Tests on search, question answering, and summary tasks matched the theory. Chunking helps when the three noise types stay low, and hurts when cross-chunk links matter most. The work also shows why a weaker model with chunking can beat a top model reading a huge input in one pass.
arxiv-2506-16711:
Chang Xu and Dunkun Yang use a known transformation formula to generate a batch of classic-looking identities in the theory of q-series, in a 2025 paper. Q-series are infinite sums built from a base raised to growing powers, and the Rogers-Ramanujan identities are their most famous members, linking sums to products in surprising ways. New identities of this type are still prized a century after the first ones appeared.

The authors start from a transformation formula due to Liu and combine it with other known summations. That mix yields a family of identities with free parameters that can be tuned. By choosing the parameters with care, they recover 75 identities from Slater's classic list. The same tuning also turns up several identities that appear to be new. The paper shows how one strong general formula can organize a whole shelf of special cases.
arxiv-2506-17411:
Jiaming Pan and co-authors derive 2025 starting values for cosmic perturbation maths in theories that modify gravity at early times. Such maths needs exact starting values, or the whole run drifts off and the bounds drawn from sky data go wrong. A known family of modified gravity theories can be handled in a broad effective frame, but its starting values had not been set in a consistent way.

The team works out those values under the take that the frame's functions are constant at early times. They code the result into a public cosmic solver and show the expected early behaviour of perturbations comes out right. Sky spectra built with the new values split clearly from those built with standard gravity values. The gap underlines why theory-consistent starts matter for sound bounds.
arxiv-2506-17711:
Evans Owusu and co-authors test whether current models of the Galaxy's chemical growth can explain a rise in sodium seen in young thick disc stars. Survey data showed sodium climbing in stars richer in iron than the Sun. The team ran a galactic evolution code with four mixes of element yields from dying stars.

They varied the source mix and tested two views on how one class of supernova explodes. That choice barely mattered. Every model failed to match the observed sodium rise. The authors suggest that iron rich supernovae may pollute this star group less than assumed. The work marks a step toward solving the sodium puzzle.
arxiv-2506-17811:
Jacky Kwok and co-authors present RoboMonkey, a way to make robot control models more reliable at the time of use, in work from 2025. Models that join vision, language, and action can guide robots, yet they can falter in messy real settings. More tries at run time may help, if the best try can be picked.

The team first shows that action error falls in a set pattern as more samples are drawn. RoboMonkey draws a few actions, adds small noise, and votes to shape a proposal set. A vision language model then checks the set and picks the best action. The method boosts strength without retraining.
arxiv-2506-18011:
Eddie Conti, Alejandro Astruc, Alvaro Parafita, and Axel Brando poke transformer models with tiny word swaps in a 2025 paper. Interpretability asks how meaning flows through a model's layers. Their probe changes one token at a time and measures how far the internal representation shifts.

Rare tokens tended to trigger the largest shifts. As the perturbation traveled deeper, its trace blended into the whole representation, so input details intermix more with each layer. Early layers kept the change most readable, which backs the habit of using them as stand-ins when explaining a model. The authors offer the poke-and-measure method as a general interpretability tool.
arxiv-2506-18411:
A team led in the byline by its student project members reports, in 2025 work, a new limit in the hunt for axion dark matter. The axion is a guessed particle that may make up the unseen mass in space. The search, run by students in Germany, is the first of its kind in that land.

A tuned hollow chamber sat in a very strong magnet field while the team scanned a narrow band of masses. No clear signal showed up. That lets them cap how strongly such particles could link to light, at a level far below past caps across the band scanned. The team says the student-built setup beat older bounds by more than a hundredfold at its best.
arxiv-2506-18511:
Yu Han, Aaron Ceross, and Jeroen Bergmann present a 2025 framework to judge which standards apply to a medical device, across lands with distinct rules. Picking the right standard is a key step in device compliance, yet it is little studied and often needs expert reads of split and mixed texts.

Their modular system uses retrieval-augmented generation. From a plain text sketch of a device, it pulls candidate standards from a set corpus. A language model then classes each one, by land, as required, advised, or not a fit, with reasons that can be traced. A benchmark data set backs the tests.
arxiv-2506-18711:
Marianne Bossema, Somaya Ben Allouch, Aske Plaat, and Rob Saunders study older adults drawing alongside robots in a 2025 paper. Robot help for creativity in later life is barely explored. The team co-designed a Drawing with Robots course with art educators for adults over sixty-five.

Sessions mixed human partners and several robot types. Participants liked acting as curators, judging robot suggestions while the robot played teacher or coach. A language-model upgrade gave one robot spoken dialogue, which participants enjoyed, though its feedback sometimes missed their artistic intent and context. The findings point to conversational, context-aware robots as creativity companions for older adults.
arxiv-2506-18911:
Anikin studies Radon transforms, a math tool that rebuilds a shape from its slice sums, in a 2025 paper on the complexity of such transforms. Rebuilding needs the inverse transform, and its exact form turns on whether the sums carry complex values. Real starting data can leave that point in doubt.

Anikin looks at the Fourier slice theorem and its singular points as one source of the needed complexity. He also shows other ways to create it during the work. A mixed Wigner-like function, he argues, brings the complexity in on its own. The point matters for hard rebuild tasks, where the added terms change both the result and the search for a best fit.
arxiv-2506-19011:
Pietro Brighi and Alberto Biella study the dissipative quantum North-East-Center model, a two-dimensional spin lattice with chiral, kinetically constrained dissipation, in a two thousand twenty-five physics paper. Local spin flips follow an asymmetric majority-vote rule.

A cluster mean-field analysis maps the steady-state phase diagram under several Hamiltonians. Two phases appear consistently: a bistable phase and a normal phase, with instabilities at finite wavevectors near the transition. In the bistable phase the dynamics are nonergodic in a specific way: islands of minority spins are always reabsorbed by the majority background at constant velocity, whatever their size. The authors propose an equation of motion for that velocity and benchmark it numerically.
arxiv-2506-19211:
Takafumi Kita studies heat signals of a hidden phase in electron systems, in this 2025 physics paper. Earlier work predicted hidden Bose-Einstein singularities that could open a pseudogap phase, a state seen in some superconductors. This third paper in a series works out the thermodynamic side: free energy, internal energy, entropy, and heat capacity. The formulas come from a standard field theory starting point and suit computer evaluation.

Kita applies them to a weakly attractive Hubbard model in three dimensions. All three phases, normal, pseudogap, and superconducting, are computed on the same footing. Entering the pseudogap phase shows up as kinks in the heat quantities, above all a jump in heat capacity. That gives experiments a concrete signal to hunt for.
arxiv-2506-19311:
Rui Chen defines a logarithmic version of the Laplacian operator on curved spaces, in a 2025 paper. The operator is built through spectrum methods and heat flow, with care for the flat directions where the standard operator gives zero. On those directions the new operator is set to vanish.

A formula writes the operator as an integral mixing constant decay with heat flow over time. On flat space it matches the classic pointwise form. Under curvature and heat conditions, a pointwise integral form follows on open curved spaces. Chen also computes the related kernels on hyperbolic space, with their behaviour near zero and far away. Spectral and heat definitions are compared, and their gap is named in terms of lost heat mass.
arxiv-2506-19511:
Nina Haugland Andersen and co-authors study why pair programming takes hold in some software teams and fades in others. Working in pairs can share knowledge and improve code, yet many teams use it only now and then. The team explored one mature agile firm in Norway.

Through two rounds of interviews with staff in varied roles, they traced what helps or blocks the practice. Key factors were felt gains in daily work, effort to start a session, team and firm attitudes, tools, and the kind of task. Lasting use, they find, needs firsthand proof of benefit and a form fitted to each team's own way of working.
arxiv-2506-19611:
Miriam Doh, Corinna Canali, and Nuria Oliver write a 2025 position paper on beauty filters. Phone filters that reshape faces are often sold as fun, neutral tools. The authors argue the filters act as a form of governance over how bodies should look.

Naming choices, biased training, and platform rules push narrow standards tied to race, gender, and ability, the paper says. The push happens quietly, since the filters hide their own influence on taste. Drawing on debates in human-computer interaction about body politics, the authors call for open disclosure of how filters work. They also urge a fresh look at the values built into digital body tools and their design.
arxiv-2506-19811:
Sofia Samario-Nava, Alejandro Aviles, and Juan Carlos Hidalgo ask in a 2025 study how much sky lore hides in rare triple links. Light from far galaxies bends as it passes mass, and that bend is read in pairs by most teams. Triple links hold extra lore, but they are vast and hard to store.

The team had built a way to split triple links into tones on the sky. They now test how many tones must be kept to hold the full lore. Just the first few tones, they find, catch near all the extra lore. Sky surveys can thus squeeze triple data hard with small loss, a real gain for next grand maps.
arxiv-2506-20111:
Mario Guarracino and five co-authors extend a clustering test to directed graphs in a 2025 paper. Many networks, from money flows to web links, have one-way edges. Before clustering such a graph, an analyst should ask whether clusters exist at all: if local density is not higher than the graph's overall density, clusters say little about the whole.

Their version of the delta test samples a small share of neighborhoods, which suits huge networks where checking every node is out of reach. Even samples near one percent gave sound calls, and the test held up when its statistical assumptions bent. The paper also studies how large the sample should be, giving users a practical rule.
arxiv-2506-20311:
Jingwen Wei develops real-time obstacle avoidance for drones and ground robots, aimed at search and rescue in disaster zones. The 2025 report notes that drone research lavishes attention on mapping and fusion, while autonomous flight through burning, unfamiliar terrain stays underexplored. A flying early-warning scout that dodges debris on its own could speed response and spare rescuers.

The work builds in phases, starting with a two-dimensional fusion navigation strategy for ground robots in dynamic settings. That base then grows toward full three-dimensional flight. The through-line is safety at speed: navigation that stays secure when the environment is both complex and changing under the vehicle.
arxiv-2506-20511:
Arno Geimer, Karthick Panner Selvam, and Beltran Fiz Pontiveros tune a hidden dial in federated learning. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with local batch size: how many samples each participant uses per training step. In a federation, members train on shared hardware but never swap notes, so a bad setting can quietly slow all of them.

The team uses a greedy randomized search that exploits the parallel nature of the federation. It seeks batch sizes that suit each member's hardware and data at once. Against default settings, the search sped up convergence a lot. It nearly matched the case where each member's settings were tuned on their own.
arxiv-2506-20611:
Hsiu-Chung Yeh and Aditi Mitra connect operator spreading under periodic driving to orthogonal polynomials on the unit circle, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. They study how operators spread under stroboscopic change driven by a unitary. A Krylov space is built for this dynamics. It links to both orthogonal polynomials and a Floquet Ising chain's edge operator.

The Verblunsky coefficients of this representation match Krylov angles of the inhomogeneous transverse-field Ising model. The authors sum up how the polynomials relate to spectral functions. Uses include analytic forms for persistent periodic dynamics. They also build the polynomials by computer for autocorrelations in two models. In the Z3 clock model, long-lived period-tripled autocorrelations show a striking spatial pattern that repeats. That pattern leads to an analytic solvable model copying the conduct.
arxiv-2506-20911:
Advait Gupta and co-authors build FaSTA, an agent that edits images over many turns without wasting search effort, in a 2025 paper. Chained requests, such as recoloring a bench, removing a cat, and repainting a wall, force an agent to plan a path through many editing tools. Pure search is accurate but pricey, and it repeats work on look-alike subtasks.

The design pairs fast planning by a language model with slow, careful A-star search per subtask. Crucially, it mines past successful paths for reusable subroutines, storing them as new tools. Easy subtasks then ride the fast lane, and only novel ones trigger the slow search. Tests against recent editing systems show the savings hold up in practice.
arxiv-2506-21011:
Qizhi Xie and co-authors teach large video models to both score video quality and explain the score in words, in work from twenty twenty-five. A plain number says little about flaws such as blur or noise. Word based answers are more useful but need much training data.

Their pipeline scores parts of a raw video first, then turns the scores into levels and clear reasons. From that step they built a large set of more than three hundred twenty thousand question and answer pairs. A staged training plan then lifts both scoring and word skills in video models. A new test set of four hundred open questions checks the word side. Gains held across several models.
arxiv-2506-21111:
Chengchao Yuan and co-authors argue that a feeding frenzy at a distant black hole explains the most energetic neutrino ever caught, in this 2025 paper. The KM3NeT detector recorded the event, dubbed KM3-230213A, and the blazar MRC 0614-083 sits closest to its sky position, flickering across wavelengths. Blazar jets are the usual suspects for such neutrinos.

The team reads the optical, infrared, and X-ray light curves jointly and sees something else: a super-Eddington accretion flare that also accelerated protons efficiently. Light from the flare echoed later off the surrounding dust ring, and protons striking those photons would spawn neutrinos by photomeson reactions. The predicted flux matches joint fits with lower-energy IceCube data, and the flare's timing explains the X-ray brightening near detection. One gap remains: the blazar's redshift is unknown, and they urge spectroscopy to pin it down.
arxiv-2506-21411:
Aristeidis Tsaris and co-authors present a distributed method for training vision foundation models on many-channel scientific images, in a 2025 paper. Turning rich images into tokens and merging them is compute-heavy, and standard parallel training handles it poorly. Their approach aggregates channels hierarchically across machines and slots into any model-parallel layout and any vision transformer design.

Tests covered hyperspectral imaging and weather forecasting. Combined with tensor parallelism and model sharding, the method cut memory use by up to 75 percent and more than doubled sustained throughput. The runs scaled to 1,024 graphics processors on the Frontier supercomputer.
arxiv-2506-21511:
Michalis Titsias and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on sampling methods that keep a Gaussian shape fixed. Samplers walk through a space of values to sum up hard totals. The team builds Gaussian fixed forms of three known walks, from a plain random walk to a manifold form. Plain forms lack a neat trait the new ones hold.

For Gaussian targets, the team can solve a key equation in exact form. Those solutions yield tricks that cut the noise in sums for any hard target. Tests on latent Gaussian models in high dimensions beat strong rivals. They also prove how fast the walks settle and how the best take rate hangs on how Gaussian the target is.
arxiv-2506-21611:
Zhang and co-authors ask when adding text to a forecasting model actually improves its guesses about the future. Many recent tools feed news or reports into time series models, with mixed claims. Their 2025 study tests two styles of mixed forecasting across sixteen tasks in seven fields, from health to economics.

Gains proved patchy rather than universal. Text helped most when the text model was strong, the time series model was weak, and the joining method fit the task. On the data side, gains needed enough training data and text that added signal beyond the numbers alone. The authors sort these conditions into a checklist for builders. They frame the study as a firmer base for judging mixed forecasting claims.
arxiv-2506-21811:
Graph tools are judged by benchmarks that miss much of what users feel, and Lingkai Meng and co-authors built a fuller yardstick in work from twenty twenty-five. Old tests, they argue, pick too few core tasks, make weak fake data, and never grade how pleasant the tool's controls are.

Their test picks eight core tasks from wide reading of school and shop use. A flexible maker builds eight fresh data sets. A model-based grader scores control ease in layers, a first for this field. Seven known platforms were run through it. The new yardstick ranked them with more spread and sense than old tests, the team reports.
arxiv-2506-21911:
Sohan Kumar Jha studies a black hole wrapped in dark matter in a 2025 paper. A background field that breaks a core symmetry of physics fills the space. The dark matter is cast as a perfect fluid around the hole.

Jha derives the still, round solution and probes its core faults with standard curve measures. Strong lensing, where light bends hard near the hole, is then charted. Both the symmetry-break and fluid knobs drag the lensing values down. Telescope bounds on two giant black holes pin which knob values fit real data. The study maps how the two effects could show up in sky reads.
arxiv-2506-22011:
Shaoshi Chen and three co-authors proved in 2025 bounds on the equations that define slices of special power series. The catalog title ends with a stray journal placeholder, while the hosted text is clean. D-finite series, which obey finite systems of differential equations, appear across combinatorics, number theory, and physics. Taking a diagonal, the slice where all indices match, was known to stay in the class, but size bounds were loose.

The team give a single-exponential bound on the degree and order of the diagonal's equation, in terms of the input system's size. Their proof also repairs a gap in an older proof for rational series and extends it to the full class. The result helps computer algebra systems predict the cost of diagonal computations.
arxiv-2506-22111:
Ruthvik Bokkasam and co-authors introduce a dataset for predicting pedestrian behaviour in unstructured Indian traffic, in work from 2025. Self-driving systems must forecast where people will walk, yet most datasets come from orderly traffic with signals and marked crossings. Indian streets add occlusions, mixed vehicles, and unsignalised scenes.

The dataset carries rich annotations, from broad scene labels down to fine details, focused on pedestrians the vehicle must attend to. Leading intention prediction methods lost up to fifteen percent in performance on this data compared with standard datasets. Trajectory methods fared far worse, with errors rising by an order of magnitude. The team provides full quantitative and qualitative analysis of baseline methods. They offer the dataset as a harder testbed for safety research.
arxiv-2506-22211:
Jolien Kamphuis and Martina Chirilus-Bruckner study pattern growth in a classic model equation in 2025. The Swift-Hohenberg equation is a standard test case for how stripes and spots form. Here its terms vary in space in a repeating way, and the terms are large, not small.

The authors find a threshold where patterns arise as Bloch waves shaped by a second, simpler equation. They split the work into cases where the forcing rhythm matches the natural rhythm and cases where it does not. Working in Bloch space reveals richer forms. The frame should carry over to land plant models where ground shape varies.
arxiv-2506-22311:
Tarikul Islam Tamiti and co-authors show that pressure sensors inside building air systems can be turned into eavesdropping tools, in a 2025 paper whose head titles the system WaLi. These sensors sit near people, sample fast, and respond to the same small pressure range as human speech. Earlier work could only spot hot words in such data, not rebuild full speech.

Their method rebuilds clear speech from samples as slow as five hundred per second, restoring both loudness and phase of missing tones while stripping fan and duct noise. Tests in two real facilities gave speech clear enough to pose a serious privacy risk. The authors also propose defenses against the attack.
arxiv-2506-23011:
Nasreen and a team including Majumdar study a faint radio signal from the early universe in twenty twenty-five. The signal comes from hydrogen gas during cosmic dawn, when the first stars lit up. Its strength is often worked out with a simple approximation. That shortcut can fail when the gas blocks a large share of the light.

The team runs simulations that vary how strongly X-rays heat the gas and which halos can host light sources. They find that higher order terms in the optical depth change key statistics of the signal. Skewness, a measure of lopsidedness, can shift by several hundred percent when heating is weak. The power spectrum and bispectrum also shift by large amounts. They conclude that terms up to third order are needed for accurate models.
arxiv-2506-23111:
Janki Nawale and co-authors build, in 2025 work, a test set for fairness of language models in India. Most fairness tests come from the West and miss India's mix of castes, faiths, regions, and tribes. Their set covers many such groups and draws on expert advice for its topics.

The team wrote and hand-checked a large set of real-life scenes where bias may show. Models face three tasks: judge if a scene is likely, judge a choice, and write text of their own. Tests of many known models found strong ill bias against groups on the margins, with models often backing stock views. Even when told to reason it out, models failed to shed the bias. The set is released for open use.
arxiv-2506-23211:
Abdelhak Abouqateb and Othmane Dani study special connections on spaces with a symplectic form, in two thousand twenty-five. Their spaces are built from a group divided by a subgroup, with a form that the group leaves unchanged. Examples include symplectic Lie groups, symmetric spaces, and flag manifolds.

The pair introduce a two-parameter family of group-invariant connections on such a space. One member is flat exactly when the space is locally a symplectic Lie group. Within the family, exactly one connection is symplectic, a fact they say had gone unnoticed. They compute its curvature and check that a known favored connection on a flag manifold matches theirs.
arxiv-2506-23411:
Jiale Zhang and four co-authors survey datasets used to benchmark fairness in language models. Fairness benchmarks shape claims about model bias, yet the datasets beneath them are rarely examined in depth. The survey characterizes the most used datasets by provenance, demographic scope, annotation design, and intended use.

A unified evaluation framework reveals consistent patterns of demographic disparity across benchmarks and scoring metrics. Applied to sixteen popular datasets, the framework uncovers overlooked biases that can distort fairness conclusions. Guidance follows on how to select, combine, and interpret these resources more responsibly. The authors call for new benchmarks that cover broader social contexts and fairness notions, and they release all data and code for transparency.
arxiv-2506-23511:
Ahmad Abdel-Qader and co-authors taught a network to code and modulate in two thousand twenty-five. Wireless links must protect data against noise. Classic coding and modulation are designed separately. Their autoencoder learns both jobs end to end. It must work across many noise levels without retraining. Earlier AI coders tested only a few codes, risking false claims.

The design splits messages into blocks per level. Each block is encoded by its own network stage. Every possible codeword at a level can then be tested. That exhaustive check makes conclusions trustworthy. Performance held across signal-to-noise ratios. Adaptivity suits channels that change by the second. The work pushes AI-designed radios toward practice.
arxiv-2506-23911:
Matthew Antrobus describes an algebraic operator on the cohomology of a twisted product of two algebras. Hochschild cohomology reads an algebra's deformations and symmetries. Its Batalin-Vilkovisky operator is a prized extra structure, hard to compute on products.

Given two Frobenius algebras, he writes the product's operator through twisted operators on smaller summands. Those summands come from earlier work by Briggs and Witherspoon. Dropping the twist recovers the plain product case and widens a result of Le and Zhou. Several computations in the literature shrink as a result. Pure algebra advances by such shortcuts. What took pages may now take lines.
arxiv-2506-24011:
Hoang Nhan Luu, Yu-Cheng Qiu, and Henry Tye estimated the lifespan of the universe in 2025 from new dark energy data. Two large surveys report that the dark energy equation of state differs from the value a pure cosmological constant would give. The authors explain that shift with a model that joins an ultralight axion to a cosmological constant.

Within that model, the constant is very likely negative, despite a wide range of fits. A negative constant means the current expansion will halt and reverse, ending in a big crunch. Using the best-fit values as a benchmark, the team puts the total lifespan at 33 billion years. The catalog creator field is garbled and drops the first authors, so the head byline governs here. Readers get a concrete, if model-bound, end date for the cosmos.
arxiv-2506-24111:
Standard option pricing models assume prices move without memory, yet real markets show long-range patterns and sudden jumps. Nader Karimi prices derivative contracts under a richer model that mixes fractional Brownian motion with jumps. This process keeps a memory of past moves and allows sharp breaks. Under it, he derives an equation that governs how an option price evolves over time. Using semigroup theory, he shows the equation has exactly one mild solution.

For European options, Karimi obtains a closed-form price through Mellin-Laplace transform methods. He also builds a numerical scheme based on the Grünwald-Letnikov approach and checks its stability and convergence. Tests show the model fits market features like memory and heavy-tailed jumps, with barrier options as an example. The author presents fractional-jump models as a flexible tool for financial engineering.
arxiv-2507-00111:
Altmann and co-authors present a sampling method for particle physics calculations in a 2025 paper. The catalog record shortens the author names to initials, while the text byline spells them out in full. Their tool handles sharp, spiky functions defined over spaces of many particles.

Three ideas drive the method. A Sudakov step sweeps the space in order from hard to soft events. Spaces for more particles nest inside simpler ones in sequence. And near the edges, complex amplitudes split into simpler factors. The team built the method in code, named Sunshine, and ran it on decays of the Z boson. Tests checked a sector shower program's accuracy at a set order of precision. The work may sharpen event generators used across collider physics.
arxiv-2507-00311:
Crispim and co-authors compute tidal forces around black bounce objects in a 2025 paper. A black bounce blends a regular black hole with a wormhole, giving a rich causal structure that can differ fundamentally from an ordinary black hole. Tidal forces, the stretching and squeezing felt by falling objects, are a sharp way to compare such spacetimes.

Starting from the geodesic deviation equation, the team computed radial and angular tidal components for several black bounce models. Both stayed finite everywhere, including at the wormhole throat. Finite tides mean a traveler could in principle survive passage, unlike the classic black hole center.
arxiv-2507-00611:
Chenyang Cao, Miguel Rogel-Garcia, Mohamed Nabail, Xueqian Wang, and Nicholas Rhinehart speed up robot learning from human preferences. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Instead of hand-writing a reward score, trainers pick which of two robot behaviors they like better. That route works well but needs a lot of costly human feedback.

Their model splits the true reward into two parts: a prior guess and a learned fix. The prior can come from a rule of thumb, from a language model, or from watching demos. Preferences then train only the fix, as a residual on top of the prior. This avoids the instability of switching training goals midstream. Tests in simulated suites and on a real robot arm showed faster learning and higher success with fewer steps.
arxiv-2507-00711:
Jhouben Cuesta-Ramirez and two co-authors show that reasoning models often refuse to stop thinking in a 2025 paper. Large language models trained to reason step by step now top math contests, but their chains of thought keep growing longer. The team asks whether those long chains mean better reasoning, or just more of it.

In their tests, models were handed correct solutions outright, and still kept reasoning. The extra steps often talked the model out of the right answer and into a wrong one, a failure the authors call overthinking. Three leading models showed the pattern on a hard 2024 math contest set. The results warn that benchmark scores can flatter these models, and that teaching a model to accept a good answer, and stop, is an open problem for reliable reasoning.
arxiv-2507-00811:
Abbas Heydari and Sadegh Mohammadi study a curvature measure on spaces that carry both a contact form and a statistical structure, in a paper from 2025. Such spaces arise in geometry where a metric is paired with twin connections. The measure gauges how sections aligned with the contact direction bend.

The authors prove this curvature is never positive on such spaces. They also give matching statements for when the curvature vanishes outright. From those, they derive a test that is enough to class the space as cosymplectic, a calm special case. The results add to the map of how statistics-flavored geometry behaves on contact spaces.
arxiv-2507-00911:
Luise Hauser and Alexandros Stamatakis examine a data bottleneck in language family tree research in a 2025 paper. Computer tree methods could exploit rich models and machine learning, but they need far larger data sets than the hand built word lists now available. The key data are cognates, words shared by descent across languages. No known method can auto build such lists at scale, the authors argue.

They tried extracting data from a large multilingual dictionary and built character tables from it. Trees inferred from those tables clashed heavily with trusted gold standard trees. Other multilingual sources are unlikely to do better, they discuss. Readers face an open problem: powerful methods may stay unusable for this data type.
arxiv-2507-01311:
Electric catalysts could wean energy off fossil fuels, but they wear out, and Varada Purohit and Avdhoot Datar survey the field with that decay in focus, in work from twenty twenty-five. The review opens with the green reactions that matter, from fuel making to clean burning in reverse. Catalyst families are then walked through one by one.

The closing half names the wear paths that kill activity and the shields that slow them. Decay, the authors stress, is the wall between lab promise and plant duty. Readers get a map of reactions, materials, failure modes, and fixes in one pass.
arxiv-2507-02011:
Vidya Sagar G and co-authors build a machine learning stress tester for Indian markets in a 2025 paper. Banks must imagine bad days for their portfolios, but classic stress tests are rigid. The framework covers five sectors, from finance and tech to energy and pharma. It first shrinks the data with component analysis and autoencoders to find hidden market factors.

A probabilistic upgrade then treats those factors as distributions, not points. Sampling from them with Monte Carlo runs creates many plausible stressed markets. Standard risk gauges, value at risk and expected shortfall, summarize the damage. Nonlinear links between stocks survive the shrinking, unlike in linear tests. The authors present the pipeline as a more flexible, realistic way to rehearse a crash.
arxiv-2507-02111:
Markus Aschwanden reviews fifteen years of solar physics from one spacecraft that changed how the Sun is watched. His 2025 survey covers the Solar Dynamics Observatory, whose three instruments have imaged the solar atmosphere and magnetic field almost without pause since 2010. The review walks through what that flood of data taught physics, topic by topic.

The highlights run from waves rippling through the corona to the temperature structure of loops and the size statistics of flares. A fractal model of self-organized criticality ties many flare findings together. Automated maps of temperature and emission, and pattern-recognition codes, turned petabytes of images into physics. Aschwanden also covers magnetic energy release and the global energy budget of flares. The paper doubles as a field guide: which instrument answers which question, and where the open puzzles remain.
arxiv-2507-02211:
In the prisoner's dilemma, two players do best together by both helping, yet each is tempted to cheat, and the tension has made the game a lab for how teamwork starts. Gustavo Mangold, Heitor Fernandes, and Mendeli Vainstein add learning agents and open space to that lab in a 2025 paper. Their players sit on a grid, can move, and can be thinned out, leaving gaps in the crowd.

Each agent learns from its own rewards rather than copying a fixed rule. With room to drift and team up, fresh patterns emerge, including a mutual-help pact between groups that act as partners. Some games with learned rules matched the shape of games with fixed rules, a useful check. The setup gives game theorists a broad bench for testing how space and motion shape teamwork.
arxiv-2507-03311:
Himanshu Dutta and co-authors present GRAFT, a system for translating whole documents with language model agents, in a 2025 paper. Sentence-by-sentence translation loses discourse links, so names, pronouns, and tone drift across a document. Rule-based splitting into discourse units rarely matches a text's true structure.

GRAFT instead segments the document, models links between the parts as a directed graph, and translates with those links in view. The graph keeps references consistent from start to finish. Across eight translation directions and six domains, the system beat strong rivals by clear margins on standard scores. The gains show document translation improves when structure is modeled openly rather than left to chance.
arxiv-2507-03411:
Ali Nikseresht proposes, in a 2025 paper, a hybrid forecasting system for tourist arrivals that weights social media voices by their influence, computed through game theory. Tourism planners live or die by arrival forecasts. Online chatter carries early signals of travel intent, but not all voices matter equally.

The method gathers internet data for destinations and finds coalitions of opinion leaders, weighting their content more heavily. A wavelet transform, applied without peeking ahead, tames the data's nonstationarity. A stacked bidirectional memory network, tuned by Bayesian search, then makes the forecasts. The game values behind the weighting have a closed form, and the best coalition can be found exactly and quickly, the author proves. Tests covered Hong Kong arrivals from five markets and a Chinese resort city through the pandemic shock. Adding internet data cut forecast error substantially, and leader weighting cut it further.
arxiv-2507-03511:
Jonas Esser and co-authors offer, in a 2025 tutorial paper, a guide to flexible regression methods for judging whether a treatment is worth its extra cost when only observational data exist. Health choices often pit a better but pricier option against a cheaper one. In such data, hidden bias can warp simple estimates of costs and effects.

Many studies still lean on plain regression or matching, which can mislead. The tutorial focuses on a tree-based Bayesian method that bends to complex data patterns. It gives code and step-by-step advice for use in cost studies. The authors argue the method yields sturdier, more believable estimates for real policy choices.
arxiv-2507-03711:
Sang Quang Nguyen, Kiet Van Nguyen, Vinh-Tiep Nguyen, and a wider team wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It tests whether large language models can play a traditional Vietnamese board game, using the game as a probe of planning and decision making.

The game, Ô Ăn Quan, is a sowing game of token moves and captures played in a chain, where each choice reshapes the board many steps ahead. The authors gave language models different playing personas, from aggressive to defensive, and set them to play. Three models of rising size from one family were tried. The study tracks how the models plan moves, hold the game state in mind, and adapt their strategy. The authors say the results expose both the strengths and the blind spots of current models at step-by-step reasoning.
arxiv-2507-03911:
Sarga Varghese and Manab Kundu work out the core laws of a win-phase wave split that joins two older crafts. One craft cuts a wave by a slide win to read it place by place; the next bends phase by a square law. Their 2025 study proves the join's base traits: line play, shift and bend rules, pair play, and mirror laws. A core grain is drawn that can re-build the wave whole from its split, and the split's reach is marked.

Fold laws are proved for both the wave yard and the split yard, with span marks for the fold's size. A fold sum is then solved by the new law as a show case. Fresh splits earn their keep when laws, not just shots, are proved.
arxiv-2507-04611:
Xiaoqing Liang, Jie Xiong, and Ying Yang solve a competition problem in investing, where many agents chase growth while fearing loss over an uncertain time span, in a 2025 paper. Each agent's caution shifts with current wealth, and the game ends at a random time. Everyone can hold a safe asset plus their own stock, with stocks linked by a shared noise.

Using stochastic control theory, the authors set up the governing equations for both a finite group and a smoothed large-group version. For an exponentially distributed end time, they solve both cases outright, giving each agent's best feedback strategy and its value. A striking point: the right move depends on rivals' wealth, not only one's own. Special cases match two known results from earlier work.
arxiv-2507-04711:
Minsub Shin, Johan Lim, and Seongoh Park estimate network structure from data arranged as matrices in a 2025 study. Graphical models map which variables depend directly on which others, but flattening matrix data, such as repeats over time, into vectors loses structure and power. Likelihood methods with separable covariance exist, yet their guarantees can be partial.

Neighborhood selection, which learns each variable's partners by regression, is adapted here to the matrix setting. The authors aim to recover the full graph. Honest structure recovery matters for gene, brain, and climate data that arrive as matrices.
arxiv-2507-04811:
Jianlong Fu studies, in a 2025 physics paper, ladder-shaped spin systems whose ground patterns are built from multipole moments rather than plain magnetism. Such phases show rich order with zero net magnetization, a puzzle for standard probes. The models carry exact local conserved quantities made of paired spin terms, which split the state space into sealed sectors.

Inside each sector, the system acts like a single higher-order spin. Fu works out phase maps for two ladder shapes with quadratic couplings. Adding more conserved pairs yields higher multipole phases in the same way. The phases are read off from the conserved values plus the pattern of the effective spin. Rydberg atom arrays steered by electric fields could build them.
arxiv-2507-05011:
Maxence Boels and co-authors published a computing paper in 2025 comparing imitation learning and reinforcement learning for surgical action planning. The task predicts the next instrument, action, and target triplets during robotic surgery. Their imitation system, DARIL, learns from expert demonstrations in an autoregressive way. Three reinforcement variants were built against it on a gallbladder surgery dataset.

DARIL scored far higher, and its planning quality faded gently out to ten seconds. Every reinforcement approach fell well short, one collapsing almost fully at long horizons. The authors argue test sets built from expert labels reward matching experts, hiding valid policies that differ. The result challenges faith in reinforcement learning for this task.
arxiv-2507-05111:
Hao Zhang and four co-authors present a 2025 system for checking the identity of drones in a network while keeping data private. Drones move fast and face jamming, spying, and cyber attack, so a network must confirm which drones are genuine and reject fakes. Their system learns from radio spectrograms, pictures of a signal's frequency pattern, using a small neural network. Training is federated, meaning the drones share model updates rather than raw data, and access follows a zero-trust rule.

In tests, the network scored above 80 percent accuracy on drone types it knew. It also flagged unknown drone types fairly well. The model stayed small, with low storage needs, compared with older benchmarks. Tests varied the number of training clients and the share of unknown drones, and the system held up well.
arxiv-2507-05211:
Han and co-authors propose in 2025 one framework for all 3D point cloud segmentation tasks, guided by visual descriptions. Unified segmentation aids scene understanding, but sparse structure, few labels, and fine class splits make it hard. Past methods lacked rich semantic and context cues.

Their VDG-Uni3DSeg draws text descriptions from large language models and reference images from the web, through pretrained vision language models. A contrastive loss aligns point features with those queries. A spatial module models scene wide relations at low cost. The work runs in a closed set mode with knowledge made offline, and reports leading results across semantic, instance, and panoptic tasks.
arxiv-2507-05911:
Changfeng Gao, Zhihao Du, and Shiliang Zhang fine-tune text-to-speech systems without ever rendering the audio during training. Modern speech models speak through neural codec tokens. Standard feedback training scores the finished sound, a slow loop. Their method scores the tokens directly.

A trick called Gumbel-Softmax makes that token reward smooth enough to train by gradient. A multi-task reward model grades several angles at once, such as clarity and emotion. The result topped a standard benchmark for word error rate, meaning cleaner pronunciation. The extra reward heads also steered tone and quality in zero-shot use. The authors pitch it as faster, sharper speech tuning.
arxiv-2507-06011:
Daghash Alqahtani and four co-authors present ECORE, a 2025 framework that routes vision tasks across edge devices with an eye on energy. Edge computing runs detection near the camera, cutting delay for surveillance and smart city feeds. Small devices, though, drain power fast when models run at full tilt.

ECORE picks, for each image request, the device and model pair that fits the objects in view. Its routing mixes an estimation method with a greedy selection rule. Tests used three known detection models across boards ranging from a Jetson module to Raspberry Pi units and a TPU chip. Against accuracy first baselines, energy fell by about a third and delay by about half. Detection accuracy slipped by only two percent.
arxiv-2507-06111:
Mohamad Danesh and co-authors make robot learning safer by never practicing in the real target setting, in a 2025 paper. A common trick, domain randomization, trains a policy across many fake worlds so it survives the real one. But checking and fixing the policy usually means live trials, which can break hardware or worse.

Their frame scores the policy's own doubt with a team of critics. It then widens the fake worlds step by step, drilling the spots where doubt runs high, all inside simulation.
