Tests on standard control tasks and a four-legged robot showed surer flags for out-of-place states, better scores, and fewer samples than rival methods.
arxiv-2507-06811:
Samuel Brevitt and Rainer Klages punch a hole in a weakly chaotic map and watch chaos die in a 2025 paper. Weak chaos spreads trajectories slower than exponential rates. Its Lyapunov exponent reads zero by the standard scale. Open systems with holes link escape to entropy in strong chaos.

The test bed is the classic Pomeau-Manneville map. Numerics and a stochastic model tell the same story. A generalized stretching measure collapses once a hole opens. The fractal repeller's structure was rebuilt to confirm it. Entropy growth matches the collapsed stretching in the data. They conclude no escape-rate formalism fits weak chaos. The negative result closes a tempting theory path.
arxiv-2507-07311:
Alhabib Moumni and co-authors study, in 2025 work, two linked wave systems that sway through their speeds. Such systems appear in maths models of rods, strings, and other flexing forms. The question is when the pair will settle down fast, even if only one part is slowed by friction.

Two cases are treated. In the first, one part is damped while the other feels a set time delay. The team recasts the pair in a broad frame and uses energy tools to show fast decay under set terms. In the second, the second part has damping that can flip sign. Fast decay still holds there, and under a weaker term than the first case needs.
arxiv-2507-07511:
A brain-computer interface that reads imagined movement is only as good as its honesty about doubt. Joris Suurmeijer and co-authors compare how well classic and deep learning classifiers report their own uncertainty. The classic methods sort brain signals by spatial patterns or by geometric measures. The deep methods include ensembles and networks trained to state their confidence directly.

The deep networks showed the familiar flaw of overconfidence, while the classic methods mostly did not. One geometric method leaned the other way, too unsure, until a simple temperature fix corrected it. The classics with the fix gave the best uncertainty estimates overall. Deep ensembles and plain networks still classified slightly better. All methods could flag their own shaky guesses, letting the system skip them and raise accuracy.
arxiv-2507-07711:
Zhen Zhang and co-authors propose a new way to sell sponsored search ads in a 2025 paper. In the classic model, stores bid alone for ad slots. A newer joint model pairs one store with one brand in a bundle, and the platform takes pay from both. Each model suits a unlike set of users, so clicks suffer when the wrong one shows.

Their hybrid model lets each slot go to a lone store or to a bundle. They design a neural network that builds auction rules for this mix while keeping bids near honest and taking part worthwhile. On fake and real data, the rules raised platform revenue over known baselines by a clear margin.
arxiv-2507-07811:
Gauthier Rotsart de Hertaing, Dani Manjah, and Benoit Macq compare two ways to train a Vision Transformer for lung tumor motion forecasting in a 2025 paper. Good forecasts help deliver proton therapy doses with care. Their markerless method needs no implanted markers.

One model was trained for a single patient, the other on data from many patients. Tests used radiographs built from planning scans. The single-patient models were more exact on planning data. The multi-patient model held up better when anatomy changed between sessions and worked without retraining. The authors frame the choice as precision against ready use in busy clinics.
arxiv-2507-08111:
Aster Taylor and Darryl Seligman estimate the age of the third known interstellar visitor, in this 2025 paper. The object, called 3I/ATLAS, races through the solar system far faster than the two earlier visitors. Speed hints at age, since stars and their debris spread out over time.

The authors argue the visitor's glow likely comes from comet-like activity, not bare rock. Feeding its speed into age models for stars gives a likely age of three to eleven billion years. Its birth star was probably poor in heavy elements. The result suggests planets form readily even in the galaxy's lean early days.
arxiv-2507-08611:
Sina Beyraghi and co-authors evaluate a reconfigurable intelligent base station by ray tracing in a 2025 paper, based on the head byline. Massive antenna arrays boost wireless capacity but need many costly radio chains. A newer design pairs the array with a smart surface that shapes signals, reaching similar performance with far fewer chains.

Site specific prediction matters for such systems, so the team simulated one with a ray tracing tool and compared it against a standard statistical channel model. Power and surface settings were tuned to maximize total data efficiency. Ray tracing predicted better performance in the test scene, which hints at the value of site aware modeling, though field tests must confirm it.
arxiv-2507-08711:
Andreas Lolos and co-authors present a learning method from 2025 for medical image tasks where only whole-image labels exist. In digital pathology, slides are huge and only the slide-level diagnosis is known, not which small patches matter. Their method, SGPMIL, judges patch importance with a probabilistic model that also states how unsure it is.

Older attention methods give a score with no measure of doubt. Here a sparse Gaussian process learns a spread of scores, so maps of key patches come with a confidence read. Tests on known pathology data sets kept slide-level accuracy high and made patch-level picks more trustworthy and easier to read.
arxiv-2507-08911:
Is our Sun a typical star, and our planetary system a typical one? Guillermo Gonzalez, writing alone in 2025, weighed the Sun and the Solar System against survey data on nearby stars and known exoplanets. The comparison draws on sky surveys and spectroscopy, with statistics used to strip out side effects before judging what counts as unusual.

The Sun is somewhat metal-rich, unusually heavy for its neighborhood, calm in brightness, and slow to flare and spin. The system stands out for lacking super-Earths while hosting a cold Jupiter, for its planets' near-circular orbits, and for its wide span. The Sun's path through the galaxy is also unusually tame and currently passes through a crowded spot.
arxiv-2507-09411:
Md Ajwad Akil and co-authors test whether large language models can rewrite malware into fresh variants, in this 2025 paper. Their framework, LLMalMorph, works semi-automatically on malware source code. It pulls out function-level details and prompts the model with engineered transformations, no costly retraining involved.

From ten varied Windows malware samples, the team generated six hundred eighteen variants. The variants slipped past antivirus engines more often, cutting detection by ten to fifteen percent on complex samples. Against a learning-based detector not targeted at all, attack success reached up to ninety-one percent. The paper also maps where current models still fail at the task. The authors frame the work as a warning for defenders.
arxiv-2507-09911:
Marvin Auf der Landwehr, Julia Topp, and Michael Neumann wrote this 2025 review of the four-day workweek and what it does to company performance. Short weeks have taken many shapes over the decades, and their effects are debated. The team focused on agile IT firms, where staff organize themselves and work in close teams.

The review joined a classic sweep of research papers with a scan of practice writing from the web. From the pooled picture, the authors built a frame that matches each shape of short week to its likely effects on the firm and its people. The frame is meant to guide managers: pick the shape that fits your starting point and your goals. The authors argue that less time can yield more value when the fit is right.
arxiv-2507-10111:
Netan Dogra, writing alone, offers a 2025 math paper on a method for finding rational points on curves. The method builds on a height pairing that swaps a simple group for a richer one drawn from higher Chow groups. Two gaps stood in the way: where the pairing is defined, and how to compute it.

Dogra ties the question to a set of classic conjectures about cycles on surfaces. He shows that if the Albanese kernel of the curve crossed with itself is torsion, then an algorithm can compute the pairing for a pair of rational points on the Jacobian. The result points to refined versions of the cohomology spaces used in this nonabelian approach.
arxiv-2507-10211: Mao presents a short note from twenty twenty-five on telling whether two space-time metrics are secretly the same solution. Coordinate freedom lets one Einstein solution wear wildly different forms. A recent proposal uses Weyl curvature invariants to separate solutions. Mao flips the idea to prove sameness instead. Two metrics of unlike form are shown to match through their invariants. The coordinate change linking them is also supplied. The note complements the separation use of the same invariants.
arxiv-2507-10311:
Liming Wang and co-authors detect dementia from the sound of cognitive testing, in this 2025 paper. The standard pencil-and-paper tests of memory and thinking are scored by hand, slowly and unevenly. Automatic systems instead listen to recordings of the tests and infer decline from speech. Their system, Demenba, rests on state space models, a sequence architecture whose memory and compute grow gently with recording length.

Training used over a thousand hours of assessments from the long-running Framingham Heart Study, where diagnoses were settled by expert review. The system beat earlier approaches at fine-grained classification. Scalable listening could turn routine cognitive screening into something clinics can run widely and often, catching decline while help still helps.
arxiv-2507-10411:
Fangzheng Tian, Jinyuan Fang, Debasis Ganguly, Zaiqiao Meng, and Craig Macdonald ask in a 2025 paper if a search score can flag when an AI agent is on track. In agent based search, the model itself picks when to call a search tool while it thinks. Little is known about the queries it writes or how search quality shapes the final answer.

The study tests query performance prediction inside two such systems, Search-R1 and R1-Searcher. Strong search tools gave better answers with shorter chains of thought. Scores for the agent's own queries also rose and fell with the quality of the final answer. The authors see the score as a live signal that can tell the model if search results are likely to help.
arxiv-2507-10711:
A team led by Roy-Saillant asks in a 2025 paper what gravity does to a wing that rows itself in water or air. The wing needs no motor: flow shakes it into a beat that pulls power out. Laid flat, gravity pulls straight down its lift path, which may bend that beat.

Two wing kinds, driven by unlike shake births, were run in sums with gravity on. When mass forces rule or match gravity, the pull is slight. At slow flow grades, weight starts to drag scores down, in one kind far more than the other. Pond and river power teams gain a when for a force they had set aside.
arxiv-2507-11611:
Sameer Patil and co-authors read the heat state of the early universe from faint dips in quasar radio light. The 21-cm forest is a set of thin absorption lines left by neutral hydrogen on the way. Noise and weak signals make the lines hard to use. Their 2025 study races five inference pipelines on fake spectra built for a redshift of six, with real telescope noise mixed in.

Machine learning routes beat classic Bayesian fits by a wide margin. The winner skips the usual power spectrum. A U-Net squeezes each spectrum into a compact code, and a gradient boosting model reads the gas traits from that code. One 50-hour sightline then pins down the neutral share and X-ray heating. Past routes needed far longer stares.
arxiv-2507-12211:
Traffic cameras and road sensors cost money to install and keep up, so Fenollosa tests a passive alternative: listening to the mobile phone signals already in the air. Two receivers compare channel data from LTE broadcasts and read the Doppler shifts that moving objects leave behind, canceling out the hardware's own phase errors. The setup runs on a software-defined radio with open base station software.

Indoor tests caught over ninety percent of motion above a slow walking pace, and outdoor trials gave usable speed estimates for walkers and vehicles. Low speeds, direction ambiguity, and signal bouncing in cities remain problems. The author maps next steps, from arrival angles to machine learning.
arxiv-2507-12411:
Dante Kalise and two co-authors build a control method for a hard class of equations in a 2025 paper. The equations, named McKean-Vlasov, describe crowds of interacting particles, from swarms to spin systems. The goal is to steer such a system toward a chosen steady state, or to help it settle there faster, by applying a control that changes over time.

The team reshapes the problem so the math becomes easier to handle, turning the system into a form much like one from quantum physics. In that form they can check that control is possible and build a feedback rule from the linearized system. They prove the rule settles the system quickly, at a chosen rate. Tests on three known models, including one for how oscillators fall into step, showed faster settling and stable control of states that were unstable before.
arxiv-2507-12711:
Kartikeya Kansal and Arunabha Sen propose a new way to judge a network's strength before dismantling it. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Police, epidemiologists, and platforms all remove nodes to weaken harmful networks, but structure-only scores can misjudge what remains dangerous.

Their metric blends graph structure with how people actually perceive a network's power. Surveys of human subjects checked the blend against older measures. The new score tracked human judgment more closely. It also picked out authoritative nodes better, in both synthetic and real criminal-style networks. Removing nodes by its guidance weakened the leftovers more. The authors argue perception is data, not noise, when the goal is real-world disruption.
arxiv-2507-12811:
Abhra Puitandy and Shradha Mishra study, in twenty twenty-five, a round passive disc placed in a bath of tiny self-driven particles that swirl. The disc, which they call a torquer, has no motor and a perfectly symmetric shape. Yet it rotates persistently. The spin comes from uneven torques where the swirling particles collide with it at biased angles. No shape asymmetry and no external force are needed. The symmetry breaks purely through interaction.

Simulations show two spin regimes. At low swirl, density gradients near the disc drive the spin. At high swirl, more frequent impacts drive it. The authors say the result shows how non-equilibrium baths can move symmetric objects, a fresh angle on symmetry breaking in active matter.
arxiv-2507-13111:
Justin Brown and Thad Walker survey atom-based quantum sensors in a 2025 perspective piece. Clouds of atoms, steered and read by light and other fields, form flexible quantum systems for sensing. Atoms are identical, easy to isolate, and well understood, and modern lasers make their quantum traits simple to prepare and detect. Those traits make them attractive for practical devices.

The authors discuss both the promise and the path from lab systems to field-ready sensors. They stress that the same features that make atoms clean physics tools also ease engineering. The piece is a roadmap-style overview rather than a report of new experiments, aimed at readers weighing where atom sensors can win.
arxiv-2507-13311:
Chuancheng Shi and co-authors generate fashion imagery that obeys both a pose and the lighting described in words. Online fashion needs models in any posture under any scene's light, yet older pose systems borrow rigid skeletons from estimators and shoot everything under flat studio light. FashionPose runs as a cascade steered by text alone.

A contrastive alignment step grounds the description into a pose manifold, making template-free poses. An identity-anchored module then renders the person with appearance intact, and a relighting stage uses that pose as a spatial anchor to shade the scene realistically. The team built PoseCap, over forty thousand caption and keypoint pairs, to train it. Benchmarks showed wins in pose accuracy and physical realism.
arxiv-2507-13511:
Nabil Abdelaziz Ferhat Taleb and three co-authors redesign an AI traffic assistant around a graph of tasks, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Earlier assistants handled jobs one after another, which wastes tokens and slows replies on complex city questions. Real traffic work mixes many linked jobs at once.

Their system draws each query as a graph of tasks and links, so jobs can run side by side where possible. A lead agent splits the query, builds the graph, and directs helper agents for data, analysis, charts, and simulation. Smart context handling cuts waste further. In tests, token use fell by about half and replies came faster than with the older chain design.
arxiv-2507-13611:
Dry, windy days raise wild fire risk, and fire can fell power lines and black out wide zones. Juan-Alberto Estrada-Garcia, Ruiwei Jiang, and Alexandre Moreira build a plan tool for that threat in a 2025 study. Their tool flips lines on and off in stages as a fire spreads, to keep the grid whole.

One hard twist is that a line's odds of life hang on how much it is used, so choice shapes the odds. The team guards that twist with a worst case frame and a staged solve method, sped by dual maths cuts. On real California grid data, the staged plan beat two stage plans by a clear span. They also give light plans that run fast in real time.
arxiv-2507-14111:
Xiaoya Li and co-authors present a 2025 learning frame that speeds up code for graphics chips. Demand for chip time keeps surging, and hand tuning each core task is slow. Smart text models can draft code, but they rarely beat the stock forms by much on their own.

Their frame, called CUDA-L1, learns by contrast, weighing fast drafts against slow ones to sharpen its picks. Trained on one chip type, it sped tasks by more than threefold on average across 250 test tasks. Top gains ran far higher. Readers see a path to cheap, self-led tuning of chip code at scale.
arxiv-2507-14211:
Federico Mason and a team of co-authors present a simulation framework for vehicle networks in a 2025 paper. Cars that are driven from afar need a network that warns of drops in service before they bite. The framework, called PRATA, joins a full model of a fifth generation radio network with tools that make driving data and a smart unit that plans ahead.

They use the framework to build a learning unit that adjusts how driving data are split when the network is strained. That unit nearly doubled system performance over baseline methods in their tests. The team also probe how the cost of gathering network data shapes learning.
arxiv-2507-14311:
Matias Cattaneo and Filippo Palomba explain how to use covariates well in regression discontinuity designs in this 2025 article. Such designs compare cases just above and below a cutoff, such as a test score threshold, to estimate a policy effect.

Adding background variables is common in economics, but in this design it can serve three distinct aims. It can sharpen the main effect estimate, reveal how effects vary across groups, or change the very quantity being estimated. The authors discuss each aim and show them at work in real data. The piece is a guide for applied researchers who want the gains without mixing up the goals.
arxiv-2507-14511:
Marijan Markovic, a solo author, presents a 2025 math paper on harmonic functions over unbounded domains. The domain sits above a Lipschitz graph, like a wavy floor with no ceiling. Harmonic functions solve the classic Laplace equation inside. The question is when such a function is Holder continuous across the whole domain. Holder continuity bounds how fast values can change with distance.

Markovic proves an exact equivalence. Full Holder continuity holds exactly when the function is uniformly Holder along vertical straight lines. One direction of travel thus certifies the whole domain. The result cuts a hard global check down to a family of line checks. Analysts who study boundary behavior on rough, endless domains get a sharp tool. Epigraph domains model half-spaces with rough ground, a shape that shows up in physics and finance models alike.
arxiv-2507-14611:
Yijue Ding wrote a 2025 physics paper that models an experiment where light breaks apart a small molecule and the pieces fly off as ions. The aim is to match what detectors see when three ions are caught at once. The model keeps only the key motions to stay fast and clear.

Two motions describe the bond breaking and the turning of the main fragment. Three more describe the later blast apart of the charged pieces. The model gives a turning time that matches past computer work. Its energy patterns match lab signals in part. Ding notes where the match is good, which helps confirm the paths the molecule takes apart.
arxiv-2507-14911: Parazian works out an exact Green function for fermions placed in an outside non-Abelian gauge field, in a short math physics paper from 2025. The field has an SU(N) symmetry group. As the outside field, the paper uses a solution of the Yang-Mills equation given as a plane wave on the light cone. The result gives the full Green function for that setup in closed form.
arxiv-2507-15011:
Saumen Acharjee models a gas sensor built from a sheet of hexagonal boron nitride in a field-effect transistor, using quantum transport maths rather than plain density methods. The framework tracks how four gases change the band structure, charge flow, quantum capacitance and current of the device, across bias and temperature.

Carbon dioxide perturbed the device most, then nitric oxide, both by adding mid-gap states and shifting band edges. Hydrogen fluoride had a middling effect and hydrogen sulfide the weakest. A vertical electric field narrowed the band gap and sharpened response. Heat helped charge transfer at mid levels but drove gases off when high. The study maps how to tune such sensors.
arxiv-2507-15311:
Hao Wang, Hao Zhou, Yi-Zhong Fan, and Da-Ming Wei wrote this 2025 paper extending a code that models the afterglow of gamma-ray bursts. Real bursts fire structured jets, wider and lopsided rather than uniform cones, and the shape of the afterglow betrays that structure. Their code, jetsimpy, already handled arbitrary angular profiles; now it takes radial layering too.

Layering creates a reverse shock running back into the jet, and the team model it by energy conservation rather than the usual pressure balance. The change matters: in thin-shell cases, older analytic models badly overestimate the glow of the reverse shock. Off-axis viewers should still catch a thin-to-thick transition, though the light curve hides it well. The code also fits refreshed shocks, shown on a kilonova afterglow.
arxiv-2507-15511:
Salas gives a subset sum solver whose speed scales with how many distinct sums an instance holds in twenty twenty-five. Subset sum asks if some picks from a list hit a target total. The classic best method takes time tied to half the list size. His counter lists every distinct sum in time tied to their count.

A double meet in the middle plan plus a trick that forces aliased states into one form cuts deeper. The blend beats the classic bound outright for large lists, a first. He also pins down which hard cases past hardness proofs quietly assumed. The work links run time to an instance's own information size.
arxiv-2507-16311:
Zhou, Ding, and Zhang (2025) design polarforming for movable antenna systems. Polarforming lets an antenna reshape its polarization to line up with an incoming wave or to set the polarization of the wave it sends. Movable antennas add position as a second freedom. The letter studies a single-link system where both ends can adjust antenna position and polarization at once, and it writes the channel response as a function of those choices.

To maximize the data rate, the authors build an optimization routine that improves antenna positions and phase settings in turns, using successive convex approximations. In simulations, the joint design beat conventional fixed systems, coping better with polarization mismatch and with fading. The authors present the gains as evidence that spatial and polarization freedoms are worth using together in future wireless links.
arxiv-2507-16411:
Zineb Sabbagh and co-authors find the critical exponent that decides whether solutions to a heat equation on the Heisenberg group live for all time or blow up. This group, the simplest noncommutative geometry, sits under quantum theory and signal analysis. Their equation mixes a local power term with a nonlocal one, so heat and feedback act in two registers at once.

They prove local existence and uniqueness for mild solutions from smooth nonnegative data, and global existence under growth limits. By the capacity method they also prove no global solutions exist past a critical Fujita exponent. Such thresholds mark the line between models that settle and models that explode.
arxiv-2507-17211:
Jiandong Chen and co-authors built a search frame in 2025 for picking a lean set of stocks. A sparse portfolio holds few assets, which keeps costs down but makes the pick hard. Old methods use fixed goals and adapt poorly when markets shift. Their frame uses a large language model to write scoring factors for stocks. An evolution loop then breeds and refines those factors based on how the picks perform.

A clean-up step cuts overlap among factors that pile up in the search. Tests ran on four standard data sets and three real markets, in the United States, Hong Kong, and mainland China. The frame beat past math and tuning methods across those markets. Checks showed that wording, factor variety, and model choice all matter.
arxiv-2507-17311:
Zijie Guo and co-authors introduce, in a 2025 paper, an AI agent system built to help climate scientists handle data spread across many Earth systems. Data volume and fragmentation now exceed what people can sift by hand. Their system, EarthLink, takes questions in plain language and runs the full research workflow itself.

EarthLink plans tasks, writes and runs code, analyzes data, and reasons about physical causes in one loop. Expert judges rated its work on core climate tasks as close to a junior researcher. Given an open problem about a warm Atlantic pattern, it formed a plan, tested ideas against data, and proposed a sound mechanism. The authors see a new pattern where scientists judge results while AI does the heavy analysis.
arxiv-2507-17511:
Jiajun Luo and co-authors squeeze the chat twixt chips in split image mills, sans a loss of shine, in a study from 2025. Diffusion mills make rich pics and films but eat compute; split them cross chips and the chips must swap vast mid-states per step, which eats the wire.

The team's eye: steps near in time make near-twin states, so the wire hauls dups. Their frame, CompactFusion, sends just the step diff, shrunk. A light feed-back loop keeps diff drift from piling into flaws. Proof in math and bench backs the cut: near all the dup bulk gone, shine held. Split mills, they pitch, can now scale past the wire wall that capped them.
arxiv-2507-17611: Jasper Postema and co-authors study a family of quantum error-correcting codes in a 2025 paper. The codes, built from a pair of classical codes, have a prized feature: a key logical operation can be applied across the physical qubits without machinery. The authors extend the definition of these codes to alphabets built as binary extension fields, beyond the binary case treated before. Their result shows that good sequences of these codes exist with sparse checks, the low-density kind favored for practical decoding, over any field.
arxiv-2507-17911:
Dou Hoon Kwark and co-authors present a 2025 method for filling in damaged or diseased parts of brain scans with tissue that looks healthy. Such filling is a key first step before a scan can be studied. Methods that work slice by slice give sharp detail within a slice but leave breaks between slices, while full three-dimensional methods need more training data than clinics often have.

Their design stacks two stages that work in crossing views. A first diffusion model fills the volume in the axial view, giving a rough but consistent whole. A second model, working in the coronal view, then sharpens the anatomy. By blending the two views with adaptive resampling, the method keeps data needs low while holding the volume together.
arxiv-2507-18111:
Peyman Tehrani and Anas Alsoliman slice shared radio networks by worst-case delay, not averages, in a 2025 paper. In open radio systems, several virtual carriers rent blocks of airtime from one tower grid. Each must keep its users' delay under a bound with high chance, while wasting few blocks. Average-based tuning misses the tail delays users actually hate.

Their learner trains on a reward built from a large-numbers law, then shaped for real use. It grades itself by delay percentiles, the mark that tail pain sets. Against average-based learners it cut mean delay by more than a third while holding the bounds. The team also lets carriers share model weights by trust in each other's scores, a personal touch that beat plain averaging. The work targets private 5G-style sharing.
arxiv-2507-18611:
Tomohiro Soejima and co-authors derive in 2025 an exact rule for the current a sliding electron crystal carries in a magnetic field. The answer shapes how such crystals move and vibrate, yet older treatments leaned on special symmetries. The team defines a sliding crystal precisely and computes its current without perturbative shortcuts.

The current depends on electron density minus a term set by the crystal's many-body Chern number times the flux density. When the two cancel, the sliding crystal carries no current at all. That single fact fixes the force on the crystal and counts its gapless vibration modes: one when current flows, two when it does not.
arxiv-2507-18811:
Maksymilian Wojnar makes particle detector simulation dramatically faster with a generative technique called flow matching. The ALICE experiment's zero degree calorimeters sit far forward, catching stray neutrons and protons. Simulating their responses the slow way eats computing budgets. Wojnar trains small surrogate models to imitate those responses directly.

His training strategy keeps the models tiny yet faithful. For the neutron detector, fidelity matched the best existing score while each sample took under half a millisecond, against about a hundred before. A latent variant cut sampling to a few hundredths of a millisecond with slight accuracy loss. For the proton detector, fidelity clearly beat the reigning best score. Code is public. The work shows fast generative surrogates can carry real detector workloads.
arxiv-2507-18911:
Zhihao Luo, Luojun Lin, and Zheng Lin address camouflaged object detection in this two thousand twenty-five computer vision paper, presented at a major multimedia conference. Finding animals or objects that blend into their surroundings needs labeled training images, which are expensive to collect and annotate. Synthetic images could fill the gap, but models trained only on synthetic data perform worse on real scenes. The authors define a new task: learning from annotated synthetic images plus a limited set of unlabeled real images.

Their framework, built on a student-teacher design, carries class information from the labeled synthetic domain to real images through pseudo labeling and consistency regularization. A recurrent learning loop builds an evolving intermediate real domain to bridge the two. Extensive experiments showed the approach mitigates the scarcity of labeled camouflage data effectively.
arxiv-2507-19311:
Claudio Campagnari and a large team describe the detector design for SUBMET in a 2025 paper. SUBMET is the SUB-Millicharge ExperimenT. It hunts for millicharged particles. Such particles carry a tiny charge, and that part of the field has barely been probed so far.

The search targets light particles with charge far below that of an electron. The detector is tuned to catch their faint hits while cutting out background events. The paper walks through the scintillation modules in full: how they are built and how they fit in the setup. It also shows how the design keeps sensitivity high across the range in view.
arxiv-2507-19411:
Ali RajabiNekoo and co-authors present SILS in 2025, a framework for spotting key liquidity providers in concentrated-liquidity exchanges. In these markets, providers place funds in set price ranges, and standard checks judge them by size or raw activity.

SILS instead treats each provider as an active agent whose moves affect market stability. It builds time-weighted profiles from chain records and flags odd behavior. Its core score asks how much the market would degrade if a provider withdrew. The frame finds high-impact providers that size-based checks miss and supports warning tools and trader signals.
arxiv-2507-19611:
Michael Celentano and co-authors extend a powerful prediction tool for iterative algorithms into harder territory. Many modern methods, from signal recovery to machine learning, can be tracked by state evolution, a deterministic recursion that forecasts their random behavior. Earlier theory covered only simple first-order updates, applied coordinate by coordinate.

The new toolbox handles algorithms that mix first-order steps with saddle-point updates and that refuse to separate by coordinate. The authors prove the prediction is exact in the large-system limit. They also bound how far a real, finite run can stray from the forecast. Technical ingredients include a Hilbert space lifting that pins down the recursion's form and a Gaussian comparison argument adapted to sequential data.
arxiv-2507-19811:
Kia Boon Ng and co-authors reported this 2025 first calculation of a nuclear Schiff moment for fluorine-19. Schiff moments are tiny nuclear tilts that would betray broken mirror and time symmetries in nature. Hunting them tests physics beyond the Standard Model. No one had computed one from first principles in a nuclear framework before.

The team used a no-core shell model for the nucleus, then quantum chemistry to see how a molecule holding fluorine would respond. Merging their numbers with precise lab measures of that molecule's electric dipole gave the first experimental bound on the fluorine moment. The bound on related coupling constants is not yet the tightest. Still, the work founds a route for first-principle limits in this hunt.
arxiv-2507-19911:
Tatsuru Kikuchi built a frame in a 2025 paper for how AI reshapes where work piles up in Japan. Japan's cities face fast aging and shrinking towns, and AI may pull jobs and firms into new patterns. Past theory on why firms cluster did not cover what AI adds to that pull.

Kikuchi extends that theory with five AI-linked forces, from shared learning among algorithms to gains when people and AI work as a team. He tests the frame on Tokyo with five distinct checks for true cause, not just linked trends. He also runs learning models across 27 future scenes. The work aims to guide city policy in an aging land.
arxiv-2507-20311:
Zeyu Xia and co-authors present SWIFT, a 2025 framework that adapts image fusion models to new satellite sensors in about a minute. Pansharpening merges a sharp gray image with a soft color one to make sharp color maps. Models trained on one sensor fade badly on another, and retraining is slow.

SWIFT picks just three percent of the new sensor's data, chosen to span its shape well. Probing the old model with that subset flags the weights most sensitive to the shift. Only those weights get updated. On a single graphics card, adaptation falls from hours to near a minute. The plug-in frame fits many fusion models, and adapted models beat their stale versions by clear margins.
arxiv-2507-20411:
George Ibrahim and co-authors build ConCap, an image captioning system that speaks many languages without leaning on translated English. Caption models lag outside English for lack of training data. Retrieval can help by fetching example captions in the target language, but those are often translations, carrying English habits with them.

ConCap pairs retrieved captions with concepts drawn from the image itself, grounding the wording in what is actually shown. Tests on the XM3600 benchmark, built across many languages and regions, show strong results. Grounding captions in concepts rather than translations respects how each language carves up the visual world, a step toward vision tools that are native everywhere.
arxiv-2507-20611:
Dominik Leib, Till Heller, and Raphael Kühn solve a factory scheduling problem in a 2025 paper. One machine must run a queue of jobs, and switching between jobs costs setup time that depends on the order chosen. The work is motivated by calendering in rubber flooring, where changes of heat and color between jobs eat time and energy.

The authors turn the scheduling problem into a shortest-path problem on a layered graph. The graph's structure encodes the order effects directly, so classic path algorithms can find the best job sequence. For the two-color case, the method runs in polynomial time. The approach also reveals structural features of optimal schedules, making it useful both in theory and on the factory floor.
arxiv-2507-20711:
Filip Cano, Thomas Henzinger, and Konstantin Kueffner argue that fairness in AI should be watched while a system runs, not just checked once. Real systems act step by step, and their surroundings drift over time. A one-time audit can miss unfair patterns that emerge only in sequence.

To study the problem cleanly, the authors use a stripped-down model: a stream of coin tosses whose bias may slowly change. Fairness can then mean fair outcomes or a fair coin, and the two are not the same. The paper surveys ways to monitor fairness from the stream and to enforce it by steering the system. It sorts the options by how the setting drifts, the time horizon, and the certainty required. General results cover the simplest cases. The authors frame runtime fairness as a distinct field with its own tools.
arxiv-2507-20911:
Jason Hindes, George Stantchev, Klimka Szwaykowska Kasraie, and Ira Schwartz present a 2025 paper on swarms that shape themselves to a target spread. The goal is a swarm that hits a set pattern by local feel alone, with few knobs and no constant steering. Their agents walk at random on a grid and nudge by rough local counts of swarm density.

Mean-field math plus small-wobble and finite-count reads sort how close and how fast the swarm lands on target. Sensing noise, bump rates, swarm size, and target roughness all enter the forecast. The frame aims at design rules for hands-off swarms.
arxiv-2507-21411:
Kentaro Takahira and co-authors let presenters steer data charts by handling real objects on the desk. Data storytelling on stage usually runs on voice and gesture, while the props at hand sit idle. Their approach, augmented physical data storytelling, binds chart commands to pushes, turns, and lifts of everyday things tracked by the room.

The team first surveyed real presentations to list the commands speakers actually use, then workshopped with nine researchers to pair gestures of objects with those commands. The resulting system, InSituTale, watches through a depth camera and a vision language model that spots the events. Twelve users in a study found the handling natural, useful, and engaging. Slides, it suggests, can be played like instruments.
arxiv-2507-21611:
Arash Shahirpour, Jakob Gebler, Manuel Sanders, and Tim Reuscher train a network to spot wind turbines and their key parts. Their twenty twenty-five paper serves drone inspection of turbine blades. A drone must find the turbine and its features to position safely and avoid a crash.

Labeled real photos are scarce and narrow in weather, light, and turbine type. The team instead makes synthetic training images, where those factors can be varied at will. A YOLOv11 network trained only on fake images, with a tweaked loss, was tested on both fake and real photos. It scored high on real images it had never seen, a strong sign for the synthetic route.
arxiv-2507-21811:
Cynthia Zastudil and seven co-authors test in 2025 whether generative AI helps trainee speech-language pathologists build communication displays for children who cannot speak. Visual scene displays embed tappable hotspots in photos to link words to real contexts, but setting them up is slow and skill-heavy. Their prototype suggests hotspots automatically.

Trainee clinicians used the tool and a standard setup in a within-subjects study, timed and rated on quality. The guiding question sits in the title: does AI help, or does it homogenize everyone's designs toward the same template? Answers matter for clinical training, since tools that speed setup but flatten individual tailoring could underserve the very children these displays exist for.
arxiv-2507-21911:
Chen Liang sorts the closed paths in a key space used to study the classic symmetry groups of algebra. The 2025 work deals with groups such as the general linear, orthogonal, and symplectic groups. The space joins a group's Lie algebra with its most basic action space. Finding which paths in it are closed is a basic step in the wider theory.

For each closed path, Liang shows it stays fixed when the group is stretched by a set twist. He also works out, case by case, the exact set of moves that hold each path in place. Last, he spells out how the group acts on the space at right angles to the path. The results feed into descent methods used across this branch of algebra.
arxiv-2507-22211: Srinivas Arigapudi, Yuval Heller, and Amnon Schreiber study a curve in 2025 that gives the chance a count of successes passes a set threshold. Such curves are known to bend and change direction at just one point. The authors ask whether that single-bend trait survives when curves of this type are stacked inside each other.
arxiv-2507-22411:
Hyeonseok Moon and Heuiseok Lim (2025) argue that popular tests overrate how well language models understand long texts. Most long-context tests bury a few useful facts in filler, so a model can pass by finding snippets instead of reading everything. The authors show that when every sentence matters, even a strong model such as GPT-4o fails to combine facts reliably in texts as short as two hundred tokens.

They introduce a benchmark called NeedleChain. In it, all of the given text is evidence the model must use in full. It comes in three versions that differ in the order facts must be combined, plus a parallel needle-in-a-haystack version for comparison. The authors propose a training-free trick that shortens the model's position encoding to push it toward using the whole input, and discuss what the results mean for trustworthy long-text reasoning.
arxiv-2507-22811:
Debayan Banerjee and co-authors link names in text to a scholar graph in a 2025 paper. The DBLP graph logs papers, authors, and now venues as node types. A linker must match a name in plain text to the right node.

Past builds trained code vectors and rankers on tagged sets. The new build asks a chat model to rerank matches with no such training. It reads the model inner yes odds to sort the picks. Zero shot linking skips costly tag work as the graph grows. Libraries can thus keep name links fresh at low cost.
arxiv-2507-23411:
Lemar Abdi and co-authors detect, in a 2025 paper, out-of-place medical images by watching how a diffusion model bends them. Spotting rare diseases without labeled examples favors outlier detection, but older generative methods are slow, shaky, or need retraining when normal data changes.

Their method never rebuilds the image. It follows the forward diffusion path of a score-based model and measures the path's curvature through the estimated score, needing only five steps. One model pretrained on a large aligned medical set topped benchmarks for both near and far outliers. Gains reached about ten and eighteen percent while inference costs fell sharply.
arxiv-2507-23511:
Yadong Niu and co-authors introduce MECAT, a 2025 benchmark for fine-grained audio understanding by AI models. Large audio models answer open questions about sound, yet they still miss nuance that humans catch. Old test sets use thin labels and weak scores, so generic answers can look as good as rich ones.

MECAT builds its items with a pipeline that joins expert models for parts of a sound with step-by-step reasoning from a language model. The result is detailed captions and open question pairs from many angles. A new score, DATE, rewards detail and punishes stock phrases by mixing closeness to the target with contrast against other samples. The team also grades leading audio models, mapping where each stands. Data and code are public.
arxiv-2508-00011:
Driverless cars need information that is both fast and fresh; a stale warning can be worse than none. İnce, Canbilen, and Yanikomeroglu study freshness, measured as age of information, in networks where high-altitude platform stations relay vehicle messages. These airships or planes in the stratosphere give wide coverage with low delay, a useful backup where ground networks are thin.

The team applies deep reinforcement learning, using a method that learns smooth control policies, to assign network resources on the fly. Each learner acts without a central coordinator. The goal is to keep information young and the network reliable for safety-critical driving, such as platoons of vehicles moving together. The results suggest the pairing of high platforms and learning-based control can keep data fresh. The work targets sixth-generation network design.
arxiv-2508-00211:
Esen Tütüncü, Mar Gonzalez-Franco, and Eric Gonzalez blend mouse and hand tracking for virtual reality work, in a 2025 paper. Their system, HandOver, targets a common trade-off: mice aim precisely but cannot grab, while hand tracking grabs naturally but aims loosely.

With HandOver, the mouse drives a depth-aware cursor for exact targeting. Resting a hand over the mouse then switches seamlessly to direct hand control of the picked object. In a formal study, volunteers docked objects in three dimensions using HandOver and two ray-based rivals. HandOver produced fewer errors at every distance. Posture analysis and self-reports also favored it for comfort and workload. The authors argue that mixing old and new input styles beats forcing one style to do everything. Immersive tools, they suggest, should let each device do what it does best.
arxiv-2508-00611:
Thomas Bakx and co-authors speed up a core calculation in cosmology by orders of magnitude. Their 2025 paper computes the two-loop power spectrum of matter clumping under effective field theory. That value is needed to read the universe's makeup from galaxy maps, but it was long too slow to use in fitting.

A method called COBRA returns the spectrum in about a millisecond at high accuracy for any era and scale where the theory holds. Tested on a large simulation, the two-loop version gave unbiased values for the matter share, expansion rate, and clumping strength using far smaller scales than the one-loop version could reach. Precision on those values improved by up to about a third.
arxiv-2508-00811:
Matthew Casey and Edith Elkind study fair representation in elections where voters approve candidates and several winners are chosen. A fair system should give large, cohesive groups their share of seats. The standard fairness rules measure group size against the Hare quota, the total voters divided by the seats. This paper swaps in the tougher Droop quota, which demands slightly less support per seat and so strengthens the fairness promise. For each of the seven standard fairness axioms, the authors find a voting rule that meets the Droop version.

Some proofs adapt known rules; others need new modifications. Experiments with simulated voters show the Droop versions are considerably harder to satisfy in practice. The authors say the results push out the frontier of fairness guarantees that election rules can actually deliver. The work matters for any body, from parliaments to committees, that elects several members by approval ballots.
arxiv-2508-01111:
John Ormrod wrote a physics paper in 2025 giving a causal derivation of the algebraic approach to quantum systems. The algebraic approach represents a quantum system by an operator algebra, a structured set of quantities representable on a Hilbert space. That representation is usually simply assumed. Ormrod opens with an apparent quantum system that no operator algebra naturally represents, casting doubt on the assumption.

He proposes an alternative, the causal view: a quantum system is defined by the causal structure of its unitary dynamics alone. He proves that every system so defined corresponds to a unique von Neumann algebra. He extends the result to a 'classical quantum system,' inspired by quantum Darwinism, and shows it too corresponds to a unique, commutative von Neumann algebra. He contrasts the causal view with an incompatible epistemic view, which reads quantum systems as states of knowledge.
arxiv-2508-01211:
Yile Li and Shandian Zhe teach models to solve new families of physics equations from a few examples in a 2025 paper. Neural operators learn the solution map of a partial differential equation, fast surrogates for slow solvers. Standard versions need abundant data for each equation and fail on new families.

Their framework, MOFS, learns across many operators at once in a multimodal frame. Shown only a few data points from an unseen equation, it adapts to solve it. Few-shot transfer like this mirrors how engineers reuse intuition across related systems. The method could cut simulation costs across fluid, heat, and wave problems, where each new design variant currently demands a fresh mountain of solver runs.
arxiv-2508-01611:
Hui-Ling Wu and Lou present a new class of whole numbers tied to their own digit sums. A Niven number is one that its digit sum divides with no remainder. Their 2025 class asks for more: each shuffle of the digits, with leading zeros dropped, must also be a Niven number. That is a stiff bar, since a shuffle can wreck the sum match that made the first form work.

The pair prove that such numbers are not rare gems. They show that the class runs on with no end and that its members grow past any bound. A full search method for small cases closes the paper, so fans can hunt their own. The work adds a fresh branch to a classic play field of digit sums.
arxiv-2508-01911:
Muhammad Farhan Khan and four co-authors design a wireless system meant to raise data rates in crowded future 6G cities. Their model combines drone-carried reconfigurable intelligent surfaces, non-orthogonal multiple access, and coordinated transmission between cells. Each piece attacks a different limit: capacity, spectrum use, and interference.

A practical snag is feedback: receivers must send quantized phase settings back to the surface, but the channel cannot carry much. The authors use a machine learning autoencoder to compress that feedback while keeping accuracy high. They also study how the number of surface elements and power sharing between users affect each person's data rate.
arxiv-2508-02111:
Huang and Huang present a 2025 computer vision paper on reversible image conversion, where a picture must flip between forms and back without loss. The forward step is underdetermined, so many backward answers fit. Standard invertible networks paper over the gap with random variables, keeping the problem ill-posed at heart. The pair instead build an approximate left inverse from an overdetermined system with a nonzero determinant.

Their new convolution block drops random sampling entirely. Two networks follow, a plain one and a stronger one with skip connections for long-range memory. Across hiding, rescaling, and decolorizing tasks, both beat prior methods. Code is public, the authors note, for others to test.
arxiv-2508-02511:
Chenxu Yang and co-authors tackle a flaw in reasoning language models in 2025: their chains of thought often ramble, repeating checks and circling back. Training that rewards only the final answer encourages the bloat, and step-by-step reward data is hard to build at scale. Their fix steps in while the model is already thinking.

Their framework, prompt intervention, has three parts that decide when to step in, how to steer, and how to sample afterward. It folds human problem-solving habits into the model's reasoning live. Across models and data sets, the method shortened reasoning chains and cut made-up claims, giving briefer, more reliable answers. The design also aims to make reasoning easier to steer and interpret.
arxiv-2508-03111:
Francesco Leonardi, Markus Orsi, Jean-Louis Reymond, and Kaspar Riesen teach a neural network to price the edits that turn one graph into another, in a 2025 paper. Graph edit distance scores how different two graphs are, but computing it exactly is hard, so approximations rule. Most learned versions charge one flat price per edit, which rarely matches real tasks where structure and meaning diverge.

Their framework, GEDAN, learns fine-grained edit costs end to end. It pairs a self-organizing approximation of the distance with a flexible additive model for the costs. Experiments show it beats methods that learn costs in separate stages. The learned matchings stay readable, expose meaningful structure in complex graphs, and transfer to jobs like molecular analysis. The authors frame cost learning as the missing piece in graph comparison.
arxiv-2508-03211:
Pablo Diego-Simón and co-authors stress-test the probes that read grammar out of language model brains. Structural probes claim to find syntax trees in a model's inner firing. Most past checks used random sentence piles. Their 2025 study runs probes on three tightly controlled test sets. That control lets word traits be varied one at a time.

Three flaws stand out. Probes lean on a shallow cue: words near each other look linked whether grammar agrees or not. Deep sentence structures come out poorly. Clashing nouns and broken verb forms also throw the probes off. Word predictability, by contrast, left them unmoved. The team offers the sets as a fairer yardstick. Probe scores, they warn, flatter the models' true grammar grasp.
arxiv-2508-03311:
Xinqiu Chen, Ning Jiang, and Yi-Long Luo prove a math link between two ways of viewing gas made of mixed parts. Their 2025 paper starts from the Boltzmann view, which tracks fast, tiny particles. Under a slow spread-out scaling, that view should yield the Maxwell-Stefan laws for how each part drifts and shares heat. Heat flow makes this case harder than past work with fixed heat.

The authors first show the target laws have sound, lasting solutions. They then build a proof that the particle view stays close to those laws for all time. A key step deals with cross effects between parts, which break the usual rest state used in such proofs.
arxiv-2508-03411:
Diana-Nicoleta Grigore and co-authors present SlotMatch in 2025, a lean way to segment video without labels. Sorting objects in video with no supervision is hard, and leading slot-based models are large and costly. The team wanted the same object sense in a small student model.

SlotMatch teaches the student by aligning its object slots with a teacher's slots, using direction of the slot vectors only. Size of the vectors, which can encode false confidence, is ignored. No extra losses or labels are needed. The simple scheme transfers object structure at low cost. Such light models could run video sorting on modest hardware.
arxiv-2508-03511:
Yazhou Zhu and Haofeng Zhang adapt a large vision model to medical image segmentation with no extra training. Their 2025 paper tackles few-shot segmentation across domains, where labels are scarce and images come from new sources. Past models need heavy training on other medical sets, which hurts ease of use. Their method prompts the Segment Anything Model instead.

The prompting plan has three parts. Cluster-based prompts cover the image area broadly. An uncertainty step aims prompts at hard regions. A third step adjusts prompts to the target's complexity. A pre-trained feature encoder feeds the process. On three medical data sets, the training-free method matched or beat trained rivals. Code is shared in public for reuse.
arxiv-2508-03611:
Wei Da and Evangelia Kalyvianaki present a scheduler for fleets that serve large language models in a 2025 paper. When many copies of a model run side by side, fresh asks must land on the least loaded copy. Shifting asks after they land costs dearly, since their stored context must move too.

Their tool, Astrolabe, sends each ask once, guided by a guess of its reply length and a fast fake run of each fleet copy. A two-pick rule spreads load while it stops herding onto one copy. On a standard test rig it matched the best rival's rate cap and cut wait times by wide gaps. It also held its edge when rigs and traffic shifted.
arxiv-2508-03711:
Wenchuan Mu, Menglin Li, and Kwan Hui Lim built a system in 2025 that spots housing and estate events in social media posts. Platforms like Twitter and Facebook carry a fast stream of local news and personal reports. In growing cities, that stream can reveal estate problems, from outages to disputes, earlier than official channels.

Their system uses language models in two stages. A first filter keeps only posts tied to estates, and a second sort places them into topics that managers can act on. For posts with no clear location, extra steps infer where they concern. The work shows how public posts can feed a live watch system for housing managers and city services.
arxiv-2508-03811:
Snehalata Sahu, Antoine Bédard, Boris Gänsicke, Pier-Emmanuel Tremblay, Detlev Koester, Jay Farihi, Hermes, Mark Hollands, Tim Cunningham, and Seth Redfield wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It reports carbon in the ultraviolet light of a hot white dwarf, a sign the star is the merged core of two.

Six like dwarfs show carbon in plain light, but their carbon loads are huge. The new find holds far less, seen only with the Hubble scope in the far ultraviolet. Its hydrogen and helium skins are far too thin for a lone star's life tale. The team reads that as proof of a merger past. A thin top layer over a semi-convection zone explains the faint carbon. More such hidden remnants may lurk among plain dwarfs.
arxiv-2508-03911:
Marius Dubosc and co-authors present Holovibes, software for rendering digital holograms in real time, in this 2025 paper. Holography records full wave information, letting computers rebuild images after capture. Rebuilding each frame is heavy work, above all at very high speeds.

Holovibes renders ultrahigh-speed hologram streams and analyzes them over short time windows. The long author list reflects a large open software effort. Real-time display lets users steer experiments while data flow in. Short-time analysis can catch fast events in fluids, cells, or materials. Such tools serve microscopy and vibration sensing alike. The project shows how modern graphics hardware can carry optical computing loads. The code base is shared so labs can adapt it to their rigs.
arxiv-2508-04011:
Hamza El Alaoui and co-authors present StepWrite, a voice system for writing long texts hands-free, in a 2025 paper. Dictation handles short notes well but falters on structured, thoughtful writing, above all when the user is moving and cannot watch a screen. Keeping track of context and plan falls on the writer, and the load adds up.

StepWrite splits writing into small subtasks and guides the user through them with spoken prompts. The prompts adapt as the text and the user's aims evolve, while the writer keeps final say. In tests, twenty-five people wrote while mobile or with hands busy. The system cut mental load and beat both plain dictation and a chatty voice assistant on usability and satisfaction. The authors pitch it as structured help that does not take the pen away.
arxiv-2508-04311:
Estaremi, Al Ghafri, and Shamsigamchi define and study a class of operators on infinite spaces in two thousand twenty-five. Operators are rules that map a space of functions into itself, and their traits shape many results in analysis. The new class, called lambda-hyponormal, widens a known family.

The authors find a group of such operators that can never be hypercyclic, meaning their repeated action never comes near every point. They also study when the range of such an operator is closed. Weighted composition operators, which mix a function change with a weight, are checked against the new class on a square-integrable space. Worked examples show the main claims in action.
arxiv-2508-04511:
Ayoobi and three co-authors hunt tool bias by staged clash in this twenty twenty-five report. Biased tools can bar whole groups from fair shots in life. Most bias hunts hide their steps, yet fair calls need clear steps most.

Inside, a clash graph holds claims on group odds in small town zones. Signs tell which zones count and how much weight they bear. Each claim fights or backs its kin in the clash rounds. The clash end then names if bias stands in the read zone. Tests gainst a clash base tool show the build's worth in the hunt.
arxiv-2508-04811:
Lin Jiang, Yu Yang, and Guang Wang design a ride-hailing dispatcher that treats people fairly. Their 2025 paper presents HCRide for matching riders to drivers. Most dispatchers chase revenue alone, which can sour trips for riders and drivers alike. Fairness for passengers and respect for driver likes pull against each other.

A multi-agent learning method called Habic steers the balance. It mixes competition among agents, a flexible actor, and a twin critic. Real trip data from Shenzhen and New York City tested the system. Efficiency rose about two percent over top rivals. Fairness gained about five percent, and driver preference about ten. Human-centered dispatch, the results suggest, need not cost the platform.
arxiv-2508-05311:
Andrew Kiruluta wires decision trees into a team of language model agents so the system can both reason and show its rules. Prior hybrids coupled symbolic and neural parts loosely. Here trees and random forests serve as callable oracles inside one reasoning system. They deliver interpretable rule inference and causal logic on demand. The language agents handle abduction, generalization, and interactive planning.

A central orchestrator guards belief consistency and routes messages among agents and tools. Structured and unstructured inputs both fit the pipeline. On a logical entailment benchmark, tree validation lifted consistency by about seven percent. Multistep math accuracy rose about five percent with symbolic help, and abstraction accuracy about six percent on a reasoning suite. Clinical decision support and scientific discovery trials show domain rules encoded symbolically while models handle context.
arxiv-2508-05511:
Rasman Mubtasim Swargo, Engin Arslan, and Md Arifuzzaman build a fast fetcher in a 2025 paper for vast gene data sets. Gene projects now spawn data by the terabyte, kept in shared troves. Old fetch tools set a fixed count of streams, which wastes the wire when the net shifts.

Their tool treats the fetch as a live tune task. A score and slope rule nudges the stream count up or down in real time to ride the best pace. Full tests span net kinds and file sizes. Labs gain shorter waits for data that once took days to pull, with less strain on their own gear.
arxiv-2508-05611:
Yan Xi Foo and co-authors review, in 2025, a puzzling effect where twisted molecules filter electrons by spin at room temperature. The effect has been seen in many labs, yet its origin is still debated. Open questions include whether the twist itself or a broader handedness drives it, and whether one mechanism can cover films, single molecules, and soft matter.

The review maps the main theories and what each term in the effect's name really means. It also surveys uses in electron transfer, sensing, light-emitting materials, and DNA-based detectors. A special focus falls on quantum sensing, where a firm theory could turn a curiosity into a tool.
arxiv-2508-05911:
Wenqian Zhang settles which networks squeeze the most connectivity out of a forbidden pattern, in a 2025 paper. A graph's spectral radius, the largest eigenvalue of its adjacency matrix, measures how densely it is wired. A fan is formed by joining one hub vertex to every vertex of a path. The extremal question asks for the highest possible spectral radius among graphs with a given number of vertices that contain no fan of a given size.

Zhang completely characterizes those extremal graphs for every fan length of four or more, once the graph is large enough. A nesting surprise appears along the way: the extremal graphs for an even fan of one size remain extremal for the next odd size up. Such characterizations anchor spectral extremal graph theory.
arxiv-2508-06111:
Dewi Gould, Bruno Mlodozeniec, and Samuel Brown propose, in a 2025 paper, letting AI models test each other in a tournament. Grading frontier models normally takes scarce human experts, which cannot keep pace with the models. In their framework, SKATE, models take turns inventing verifiable challenges for rivals and solving the ones set for them. A challenge must have an objectively checkable answer, so no model judge is needed.

Their trial run used code-output prediction, where a model must state what a program prints. Six frontier models were ranked by a skill-rating system. Weaker models reliably told the stronger ones apart, a hopeful sign for scalable oversight. Models also showed self-preference, crafting challenges that played to their own strengths. The authors argue such games can surface fine differences between models automatically, at whatever scale the field reaches.
arxiv-2508-06211: Tudor Popescu proves a matching result on a two-sided colored graph in a 2025 note. The graph is complete and bipartite, with 2n points on each side. Edges wear red or blue. Each point holds n red and n blue edges, a fair split. The note states a clean claim about perfect matchings in that set: matchings exist with set color counts, as the title frames it. The proof is short and combinatorial, aimed at graph theory readers.
arxiv-2508-06411:
Ze Shen Chin, a solo author, presents a study from twenty twenty-five on the gravest risks from advanced AI. Talk of such risks has grown, but it lacks a shared frame and clear paths from spark to harm. Chin takes six oft cited risks, from bio and chem weapon aid to loss of control and strife between states. He scores each on seven axes.

The axes span intent, skill, who acts, and how far the harm can reach. He then maps each risk as a step chain from first hazard to last harm. The axis view yields broad guards that fit many risks. The chain view shows where a block can cut one path. Both feed a more crisp base for risk work.
arxiv-2508-06511:
He Feng and co-authors build DiTalker, a tool that makes a still face talk in a 2025 paper. The aim is a clip that moves with a voice track, keeps the lips in step, and wears the talk style of a cue clip, from mood to head pose.

Past tools tend to nail the lips or freeze the mood, and they run on a pair of nets that costs time. DiTalker's one-net frame reads style and mood through two arms: one takes the talk style of the face at hand, the next takes mood in a face-free way. A fuse step keeps voice and style apart as it steers the frames. Two checks guard lip step and fine face marks. Tests put the tool ahead on both scores.
arxiv-2508-06611:
Alastair Kay and Christino Tamon simplify, in a 2025 quantum computing paper, a landmark algorithm that solves linear systems on quantum hardware. The classic method strings together phase estimation, amplitude boosting, and simulated dynamics, a heavy chain. Their version swaps the phase estimation steps for a continuous quantum walk.

The trick uses weak couplings to reach the matrix inverse hiding inside perturbation theory. The walk runs on the graph tied to the matrix, and its motion encodes the solution state the algorithm must output. The authors argue the leaner design keeps the power of the original while easing both analysis and, someday, hardware demands.
arxiv-2508-06811:
Benjamin Laufer, Hamidah Oderinwale, and Jon Kleinberg map the open model ecosystem in this two thousand twenty-five study. They analyzed about one point eight six million models hosted on Hugging Face, the leading peer production platform for machine learning. Their focus is model family trees, the networks linking fine-tuned models back to their base or parent models. An evolutionary biology lens frames the analysis, treating metadata and model cards as genetic markers.

Fine-tuning lineages turned out sprawling and widely varied in size and structure. Models within a family resemble each other, yet sibling models are often more similar than parent and child, because mutations are fast and directed. Directional drifts surprised the authors: licenses drift from restrictive toward permissive terms, sometimes violating upstream conditions, and models drift from multilingual toward English-only support while their cards shrink and standardize.
arxiv-2508-06911:
Woohyuk Noh and Changhoon Lee present a simulation method in 2025 for supersonic flows that drops a long-standing speed limit. Lattice Boltzmann methods track fluid parcels on a grid, but shock-speed flows strain them and the time step is capped by the sound speed. Their version moves with the flow, uses entropy rules to keep results physical, and streams only key moments to save memory.

Benchmark tests cover shock tubes in one dimension and shock patterns around cylinders and airfoils in two. The method held stable through these harsh cases. Precise control of viscosity and heat flow is built in. Aerospace designers could use it to test high-speed designs more cheaply.
arxiv-2508-07311:
Verdier and nine co-authors describe how targets were chosen for a huge galaxy survey, in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The 4MOST telescope's Cosmology Redshift Survey will measure distances to galaxies and quasars across fifty-seven hundred square degrees of southern sky.

From imaging data they built two samples: bright galaxies limited by brightness, and luminous red galaxies picked by color, each tuned to a target density on the sky. Star contamination stayed below a few percent, checked against star catalogs and early spectroscopy data. Clustering tests showed the samples are clean of imaging artifacts. Forecasts say the survey alone should pin down the cosmic expansion marker to three percent, and sharpen existing constraints when combined with a sister survey.
arxiv-2508-07611:
Zifan Wang and seven co-authors teach a humanoid robot to walk safely and politely among people, in a 2025 paper. Real spaces are cluttered and shifting. Blind controllers cannot see obstacles, and camera systems miss 3D depth.

The policy reads raw LiDAR point clouds and outputs motor commands directly. Safety was written into training as hard costs, using barrier function ideas. Extra rewards favor smooth, predictable motion that does not crowd people. The trained policy moved from simulation onto a real humanoid. The robot threaded past still and moving obstacles with ease. The work joins provable safety with social grace in one controller.
arxiv-2508-07811:
Sicheng Gao, Nancy Mehta, Zongwei Wu, and Radu Timofte present a method to restore low-quality video without new training for each task, in a paper from 2025. Restoration covers sharpening, noise removal, and blur removal. Older methods often invent poor detail, while recent generative methods can flicker between frames.

Their system pairs a diffusion transformer with attention that follows motion paths across frames. A cache picks the most relevant tokens from nearby frames. The sampler enforces match with the input only in smooth image bands, which keeps fine detail and speeds convergence. It set new best scores for zero-shot restoration and stayed robust when motion was noisy.
arxiv-2508-08211:
Zhuohao Yu and co-authors watermark language model text after generation by picking outputs whose hidden features match a secret key, in work from twenty twenty-five. Watermarks support content tracing and misinformation control. Older methods degrade text or need control over the model's inner scores, which closed services deny.

Their framework never touches the model's scores and needs no retraining. It samples finished outputs and keeps those whose measured features align with key derived targets. Sparse autoencoder features drove the tests. Detection hit near perfect scores on English, with strong multi bit reading across four data sets. Theory ties success odds to the compute budget. The method works across languages and with closed models.
arxiv-2508-08611:
Nafisa Anjum and Robiul Hasan wrote, in two thousand twenty-five, on a sheet that soaks up terahertz waves, and on learned codes that tell how well it will soak. Terahertz waves sit between microwaves and infrared light. The sheet does not care how a wave is tilted.

The sheet is a metamaterial: a vanadium dioxide face, an MF2 spacer, and a gold back plane. It soaks up more than 90 per cent of waves from 5.72 terahertz to 11.11 terahertz, with a mean of 98.15 per cent. The pair made 9,018 cases by shifts in patch width, spacer depth, and wave rate. They trained six codes that guess a score from such facts, from plain line fits to groups of trees. Tree groups did best. The best, Bagging, hit a fit of 0.9985, with a mean miss of only 0.0146. Fast codes can stand in for full wave sums.
arxiv-2508-09611:
Xian-Hui Ge and Chenhao Zhang investigate the replica problem in supersymmetric versions of the SYK model, in a 2025 paper. The SYK model is a solvable model of interacting fermions used in quantum gravity studies. Replicating it raises structural questions.

First, they find the replicated non-supersymmetric model is solvable only under specific conditions. Adding supersymmetry and its symmetry lets them build a multi-ordered trick covering the replica structure. With ordered couplings between replicas, they study thermal phases under higher-order interactions and the time dynamics. In the low-energy limit, an emergent symmetry appears, and they propose a matching action with constraints for gravity duals.
arxiv-2508-10111:
Niels Mundler, Jasper Dekoninck, and Martin Vechev force diffusion language models to output only valid formal text in this 2025 paper. Many uses need exact syntax: code, JSON, structured records. A model's free output may break the rules of that format. Constrained decoding trims generation to what a grammar allows. Older methods work only for the usual step-by-step models. Diffusion models write text in a different, parallel way.

Theirs is the first such method built for diffusion models. A context-free grammar states the allowed shapes. Correct C++ or JSON output is the practical prize. Formal guarantees matter where bad syntax breaks pipelines. The work is a systems and theory paper in AI. It extends a safety technique to a new model family.
arxiv-2508-10411:
Self-driving cars detect lanes in 3D, but judging the road's height on slopes trips up many systems that assume one fixed incline. Chaesong Park and co-authors present SC-Lane, a framework that estimates a height map of the road ahead while adapting to whatever slope the road actually takes. Instead of anchoring on preset slopes, it learns from the image how to blend slope-specific height features into one map.

A second module keeps height estimates consistent from frame to frame, steadying the picture as the car moves. The authors also argue the field should grade height estimation with standard error metrics, not only lane scores, and they benchmark accordingly. On the OpenLane dataset their system reached an F-score of 64.3 percent, clearly ahead of earlier methods on both height and lane detection.
arxiv-2508-11511:
Siyamalan Manivannan trains skin lesion classifiers with little labeled data in a 2025 paper. Deep learning reads skin images well, but expert labels are slow and costly to gather. Using unlabeled images alongside the labeled few could cut that burden.

An ensemble of convolutional networks learns together through online knowledge distillation. Each network absorbs the group's combined judgment while training proceeds. After training, any single member can run alone with near-ensemble skill. That matters in clinics with modest computers. Tests show the distilled single model beats models trained on their own. The approach points toward accurate skin screening where labeled examples and hardware are both scarce.
arxiv-2508-11611:
Nathanael Arkor, a solo author, proves results about double categories in a 2025 mathematics paper. Double categories track two kinds of arrows at once, and lax functors are maps that respect that structure in a loose way. Arkor studies when one such system can act as an exponent of another.

He shows that every pseudo double category can serve as such an exponent. From that fact, the system of lax functors gains a clean universal description. The view yields short proofs of facts that once needed long calculations. It also simplifies presheaf theory for double categories, including the match between presheaves and a class of fibrations.
arxiv-2508-11711:
Irash Perera, Hiranya Abeyrathne, Sanjeewa Malalgoda, and Arshardh Ifthikar present a 2025 paper on keeping GraphQL services safe from hostile queries. GraphQL lets clients ask for data in flexible ways, but that freedom opens paths for attacks such as denial of service and data theft through injection. Older defenses, like fixed rules and rate limits, often miss attacks that adapt to context.

The authors combine fixed checks with learning models. Large language models help set up the system from the schema, while other models turn each query into a numeric form that captures its meaning. Several classifier types then judge whether a query is harmful. In tests, the system caught injection and scripting attacks with high accuracy and also blunted service and request forgery attacks under load.
arxiv-2508-11811:
A large survey team reports a 2025 cosmology study based on the first data release of the DESI sky survey. DESI maps galaxies to trace how the universe expands. The catalog record names only one author, while the text byline lists the full collaboration, so the work is best read as a team effort.

Most such studies use Bayesian methods, which can shift with prior choices. This team instead used a frequentist method that does not rest on priors. They fit galaxy clustering patterns plus other data sets, such as the early-universe glow and exploding stars. For an extended model of dark energy, their ranges shifted notably from Bayesian ones unless the star data were added. The contrast shows how method choice shapes cosmic claims.
arxiv-2508-11911:
