The same approach covers the known results for four through seven runners, and he expects minor improvements could push the method to settle the cases of nine or ten runners as well.
arxiv-2509-14311:
Pedro Guicardi and Mrunmay Jagadale build in 2025 a field theory for the Z-hat values of three dimensional shapes. Those values, brought in by Gukov, Pei, Putrov and Vafa, link maths and physics in many areas. How they fit a full field theory was not well known.

Their theory uses decorated Spin rules in the style of the Atiyah-Segal axioms, a standard way to state such laws. A new way to quantise Chern-Simons theory gives the state space for a torus, the donut shaped surface. From that space, the values for a large class of plumbed shapes follow in just one way. Glueing, surgery and cabling rules also come out, so the values form a working tool kit, not a lone list.
arxiv-2509-14511:
J. Kataoka and thirty-four co-authors revisit a data cut in 2025 for Compton gamma ray cameras, instruments that image high energy light from event geometry. Overlapping cones from many events create artefacts that blur images and cut sensitivity. Better cuts clean the picture.

The adaptive ARM cut works when the source direction is already known, discarding events whose geometry fits poorly. The authors apply it to the INSPIRE detector programme and compare with standard statistical reconstructions. The cut complements, rather than replaces, rigorous image methods. Compton cameras now serve astronomy surveys and medical imaging concepts. A simple validated cut that suppresses artefacts raises the value of both existing and planned detectors.
arxiv-2509-14811:
Marco Picerni proves that a class of hard partial differential problems has solutions, in a solo 2025 math paper. The problems are elliptic in type, but they can degenerate, and their coefficients are rough: known only to be measurable, not smooth. Solutions must also be zero on the edge of the region. The main term comes from a set of vector fields that obey a Poincaré bound and a doubling rule.

Picerni also shows the solutions gain extra regularity, of the same kind known for classic Leray-Lions type problems. That gain means the solutions are better behaved than the raw data would suggest.
arxiv-2509-14911:
Hendrik Roch and Chun Shen test normalizing flows as learned prior distributions for Bayesian calibration in a 2025 statistics paper. Bayesian inference often runs in stages, and the posterior from one analysis could inform the next as a prior. Normalizing flows are flexible models that can capture awkward, correlated posterior shapes from earlier results.

The authors compare training strategies and loss functions for fitting such flow priors. Training with Kullback-Leibler divergence and unsupervised learning reproduced reference distributions most faithfully. They then run a sequential workflow on a high-energy nuclear physics calibration problem. Flow-based priors match one-shot joint inference well when target distributions have a single peak. With multiple peaks or tension between datasets, distortions can appear, so the authors urge care in multi-stage Bayesian work. Sampler choice also matters in their comparison.
arxiv-2509-15011:
Vasiliki Ismiroglou and four co-authors improve how synthetic underwater images are generated in a 2025 computer vision paper. Underwater vision suffers because water scatters and absorbs light, and murkier water hides distant objects in a distance-dependent way. Many data generators model the color loss but skip forward scattering, a key part of that visibility loss.

Their pipeline adds the missing forward scattering term and allows the water medium to vary from place to place. To check realism, they collected the BUCKET dataset, filming scenes under controlled turbidity with clean reference images for comparison. Human survey participants preferred the new model's images over the reference model's in most comparisons, especially as turbidity rose. Better synthetic data helps train robots and cameras for genuinely murky water.
arxiv-2509-15111:
Thales Azevedo and three co-authors find a clash inside a shortcut for string scattering sums in a 2025 paper. The pure spinor superstring works out scattering with a special ghost measure. A recipe from Berkovits, based on past work by Lee and Siegel, claims to skip that measure and make the math simpler.

Direct checks with free-field products, though, fail to give a symmetry the sums must obey. The tree-level results should stay fixed under a key rotation group in complex space, and the new recipe breaks that rule. Checks by more than one route agree on the break. A sum with that flaw cannot keep the gauge symmetry physics demands. The authors also flag risks for a linked hybrid form of the theory.
arxiv-2509-15411:
Anika Tabassum Biva leads a team that studies secure links for smart devices. Their setup joins a radio link with a light beam link, helped by smart surfaces that steer signals. An eavesdropper is assumed to listen on the radio part. Such mixed links suit hard settings, but their secrecy must be measured with care.

The team derive exact formulas for three secrecy scores, using models for weak radio signals and for shaky air on the light path. They also give simple forms for the high signal case. Their numbers show the value of a certain light sensing method when aim is off. Adding more smart surfaces lifts secrecy by a large share. The work guides safe design for future networks.
arxiv-2509-15611:
Tiffany Tang, Elizaveta Levina, and Ji Zhu make forest based prediction work with networked data. Standard tools assume each data point stands alone. When points are linked in a network, that link both hurts and helps: it shrinks the useful sample, yet neighbors carry useful hints. Many network aware tools are hard to read, which limits their use for insight.

Their family of models builds on a widened form of random forests. It reaches accuracy that rivals strong rivals while staying readable. Built in tools name the traits that drive each forecast and weigh how much the network adds. Both broad and local trait scores are part of the suite. Sample sway can be traced as well.
arxiv-2509-15811:
Sara Rajaee leads a team that ranks math answers across languages, not just within one. Language models reason in many tongues, and their paths in each tongue may complement each other. The team train a reward model to rank answers to the same question across languages. That cross lingual judge is the core of their method.

Math scores rise a lot versus ranking within one language alone. Even strong languages gain from the mix. English often leads in these models, yet cross lingual sampling helps English most when few samples are allowed. The findings open a path: pool the strengths of many languages to reason better. The work tests multilingual models on math tasks.
arxiv-2509-16111:
One early galaxy seems to have built huge mass fast, then stopped forming stars less than a billion years after the Big Bang. Jack C. Turner and seven co-authors search a large simulation of the early universe for twins of this odd object. They find two massive galaxies whose stars also formed in a fast burst that soon shut off.

One twin matches the real galaxy's traits well. In the simulation, heat from a central black hole drives gas out, which stops new stars and enriches the gas with heavy elements. Count gaps may stem from survey quirks, though stronger black hole effects may also be needed.
arxiv-2509-16411:
Search engines that embed queries and documents as points work well until the document set forms a tree, where a query must match all ancestors of a leaf. Chong You and five co-authors prove such dual encoders can handle tree search, as long as the point space grows with tree depth. Yet in practice, matches far up the tree get lost during training.

Their two-stage recipe, broad pretraining then focused fine-tuning, lifts far-match recall sharply on a word hierarchy test, from under a fifth to over three quarters. Near matches held steady. Product search data showed the same gain.
arxiv-2509-16811:
Zihan Ding and co-authors build an agent that edits long videos from a text prompt in a 2025 paper. Cutting story-rich footage takes hours of searching and planning. Text search and embedding tools miss character arcs and motives. Their system instead comprehends the story on its own, then assembles an edit.

Users get a film-like cut and can refine clear mid-steps if they wish. Tests used hundreds of videos with expert ratings and user studies. The system kept story flow while scaling to long footage. It balances machine speed with creator control. Such tools could reshape how editors handle large archives.
arxiv-2509-17111:
Yuzhen Qin, Alberto Maria Nobili, Danielle S. Bassett, and Fabio Pasqualetti study groups of oscillators that must fall into step together. Their 2025 arXiv paper deals with cluster synchronization, where each group keeps its own rhythm. When these patterns break down, harm can follow, as in some brain disorders where nerve cells fire in the wrong groups.

Most fixes steer the system using live readings of its state, but such readings can be hard to get, as with brain activity. The authors instead use fast shaking inputs that need no readings at all. They give conditions under which this open-loop method locks the clusters back into place. They also give a workable design method, and computer tests back up the theory.
arxiv-2509-17211:
Alessandra Azzollini, Sara Buson, and Alexis Coleiro study a distant blazar that seems to change its class over time. Their 2025 arXiv paper focuses on the source 5BZQ J1243+4043, a candidate linked to high-energy neutrinos seen by IceCube. Blazars of this kind appear to switch between two classes as their optical lines wax and wane.

The team took a fresh optical spectrum with the Gran Telescopio Canarias and set it beside two older spectra. The new data show broad emission lines, much like the first epoch, at the known redshift. The middle spectrum looks almost blank, so the authors place limits on any lines there. Both the continuum and the lines vary across the three epochs. The feeding rate of the central black hole, though, stays much the same, which hints the change lies in what we see, not in the engine.
arxiv-2509-17411:
Siqi Li and five co-authors tackle fairness in prediction when the harmed groups are hidden. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that models tuned for average accuracy can fail vulnerable subpopulations. Standard fixes need the groups named in advance, yet real group structure may be latent, overlapping, and driven by tangled mixes of traits.

Their framework, ROME, learns the hidden group structure while optimizing worst-group performance. It joins latent-variable modeling with distributionally robust optimization in two forms. One form uses expectation-maximization with robust pooling for linear models. The other uses a neural mixture-of-experts design for nonlinear cases. On simulations and three real regression data sets, ROME lifted worst-group scores while keeping overall accuracy competitive. It suits settings where fairness traits may guide group discovery but should not drive the outcome model directly.
arxiv-2509-17811:
Thrinadh Pinjala, Aswin Ram Kumar Gannina, and Debasis Dwibedy aim to forecast road crashes in a city. Their 2025 paper builds a model named MSGAT-GRU. Crash risk rests on place, time, traffic flow, road traits, and weather, all mixed in hard ways.

The model watches both near and far road links, then tracks how risk shifts over time. On a Beijing crash data set, it beat strong base models on error and score. It also held up on a Los Angeles traffic set. Tests of parts show a sweet spot for how wide and deep the model should be.
arxiv-2509-17911:
Pierre Larue leads a large team that studies how star activity shifts starlight by colour. Their 2025 paper deals with the hunt for planets by the wobble method. A planet pulls its star in a way that looks the same at all colours, while spots on the star do not.

Data from two starlight tools, one in visible light and one in heat light, cover the active dwarf star EV Lac. Lines were grouped by how spots or magnet fields should move them. Two line groups moved in clear opposed ways, which partly cancels the total wobble. That split helps explain the strong colour trend seen.
arxiv-2509-18111:
Faizul Rakib Sayem and Shahana Ibrahim flag odd inputs for vision-language models with just a few known cases. Their 2025 paper deals with open-world use, where a model meets inputs unlike its training set. Past prompt-based tools rest on class chance scores alone, which waste the rich codes such models learn.

Their frame tunes prompts and splits the code space in two. Known-class codes are pushed into a zone spanned by the prompt codes. Off-class parts fall into the null zone at right angles to it. A single training goal holds both odd-input skill and class score high.
arxiv-2509-18311:
General robot policies can do many tasks, but people often tune them to their own tastes. That tuning can leak private facts, like the foods a person likes. Benjamin A. Christie, Sagar Parekh, and Dylan P. Losey study this privacy problem in their 2025 paper. They ask how a robot can learn personal habits while keeping them hidden from others.

Their answer is PRoP, a framework that works with many model types. Each user gets a unique key that reshapes the weights inside the robot network. With the right key, the robot acts on that user's tastes. With a wrong key, it falls back to its plain default behavior. Tests covered learning from demos, reward-based learning, and sorting tasks. PRoP beat older encoder-based methods and kept the base policy intact.
arxiv-2509-18511:
Missions near the Moon need a shared, precise way to tell time. Xu Lu, Tian-Ning Yang, and Yi Xie present LTE440, a ready-to-use lunar time package, in this 2025 paper. It computes Lunar Coordinate Time and its links to two barycentric time scales used for the solar system. The definitions follow the international resolutions on relativistic time scales.

The team integrates the time-dilation effect numerically, using a planetary ephemeris that includes the Sun, planets, and many small bodies. Output files come in the standard SPICE format used by space missions. Estimated accuracy stays better than a fifth of a nanosecond before 2050. The lunar and barycentric scales drift apart at a steady rate the paper states. Yearly and monthly wobbles ride on that drift. The package is public and built for mission use.
arxiv-2509-18611:
Models that forecast how fluids and fields evolve could serve many science tasks if trained once at scale. Zituo Chen and Sili Deng present Flow Marching, a generative method for such a foundation model, in this 2025 paper. Older models of this kind predict the next state directly and cannot express uncertainty. Their errors also pile up over long rollouts.

Flow Marching learns a velocity field that carries a noisy current state toward its clean next state. Noise level and time step are sampled together, which curbs drift and enables varied ensemble forecasts. A physics-trained compressor shrinks states into a compact space. A transformer design then makes training up to fifteen times cheaper than full video diffusion models. The team trained on about 2.5 million trajectories across twelve equation families. Tests showed stable long rollouts and strong few-shot adaptation to unseen turbulence.
arxiv-2509-19011:
Takuro Abe and two co-authors work on hyperplane arrangements, sets of flat slices through a space that show up across algebra and geometry. A Ziegler pair is two arrangements that share the same underlying matroid, a record of how the slices meet, yet differ in their modules of logarithmic derivations. Such pairs test how much the matroid alone can tell us. The question connects to Terao's freeness conjecture, a long-standing open problem in the field.

The authors give a general construction that produces Ziegler pairs in any dimension and any size. No such families were known before. Their starting point is examples that live in the complex projective plane. From those seeds, the construction lifts pairs upward step by step. The result gives researchers a rich supply of test cases for probing the limits of the freeness conjecture.
arxiv-2509-19111:
Power electronics must lock onto the phase of the grid or a motor's current to work correctly, and the standard tool is a phase-locked loop. Michael Ruderman and four co-authors give that loop a stronger design. In the common synchronous reference frame version, a feedback controller chases a three-phase signal. Distortions in the signal and changes in its strength can throw the lock off.

Their design maximizes the phase margin, a safety measure against instability, and normalizes the input so strength changes do not matter. The big gain comes from a feed-forward frequency estimator that needs no model of the signal and handles noise and drift. Tests on real three-phase currents from a standard motor drive, at varying speeds and loads, confirm firm tracking of both frequency and phase.
arxiv-2509-19211:
Chien-Hao Liu and Shing-Tung Yau lay foundations for a noncommutative version of mirror symmetry, the duality that pairs very different geometric spaces in string theory. Their notes, titled simply Proof, chase what they call a D-brane fantasy: that noncommutative mirror symmetry might be realized through the physics of stacked D-branes. Unlike a string's world-sheet, the world-volume of stacked branes already carries a noncommutative structure, making it a natural probe of noncommutative spaces.

They construct a class of noncommutative ringed spaces over manifolds with corners, by gluing local resolutions of certain singularities. Dynamical branes become maps from a special noncommutative manifold equipped with a connection. They define an adjusted kinetic energy for such maps, in parallel with the classic Polyakov action for strings. The notes set a stage for the program rather than finishing it, sampling the questions beyond.
arxiv-2509-19311:
Giorgi Tutberidze and two co-authors study how well chopped-off Fourier sums approximate a function when the building blocks go beyond the usual sine and cosine waves. General orthonormal systems include families tuned to weighted spaces or built from orthogonal polynomials. The question is how a function's smoothness controls the speed and style of convergence. Classical theory answers this mainly for trigonometric systems, leaving the general case thinner.

The authors derive error estimates in several norms and give conditions that guarantee uniform or pointwise convergence. Differentiability, they show, buys sharper results than plain square-integrable functions enjoy. Properties of the system itself, like how localized its members are, also shape the sums' behavior. Examples with commonly used systems illustrate the theory. The work speaks to spectral approximation in numerical analysis and signal processing.
arxiv-2509-19411:
The Internet Yellow Pages gathers routing information from many sources into one graph-shaped knowledge base, but querying it demands fluency in the Cypher query language and its exact schema. Vasilis Andritsoudis and three co-authors present ChatIYP, a poster paper describing a system that opens that base to plain questions. Their design is a retrieval-augmented generation system tuned to this domain: it fetches relevant schema and data context, then lets a language model compose the query and answer.

Evaluation shows solid performance on simple questions, with clear directions for improvement on harder ones. The authors also discuss which evaluation metrics actually fit this kind of querying agent. The audience is the network operations and measurement community, for whom the Yellow Pages are a working tool. Removing the query-language barrier could widen that tool's user base considerably.
arxiv-2509-19511:
Bridges, buildings, and machines are watched by sensors that sample at mixed speeds. Dhiraj Ghosh, Adrita Kundu, and Suparno Mukhopadhyay present a direct way to fuse that mixed data. Their method feeds each reading into an unscented Kalman filter as it arrives. The filter tracks motion states such as shift and speed, plus unknown traits of the structure itself.

Older routes first rebuild missing motion data, then identify the system in a second pass. This route skips that split and uses all readings at each moment. The team shows the method on computer trials and on lab-scale tests. It handles sensors placed at spots that do not match each other. Sound state tracking from messy sensor mixes helps spot damage early in real structures.
arxiv-2509-19611:
Translation quality is now so high that judging it well has become the bottleneck. Syeda Jannatus Saba and Steven Skiena propose a telephone-game test: translate a text back and forth many times and watch it drift. Texts that drift in telling ways reveal where translators stumble. The pairs produced this way become training data for scoring systems, with no human labels needed.

Their scorers beat a popular evaluation system on two tasks. One task grades a translation against a human reference. The other asks which of two translations sits closer in the chain to the source. Because the data builds itself, the method scales to long and literary texts. Better automatic judges could unlock training gains that current scores cannot see.
arxiv-2509-19911:
Economic data often arrive as matrices that evolve over time, such as state-by-industry employment each quarter. Alain Hecq, Ivan Ricardo, and Ines Wilms build a framework that keeps that matrix shape instead of flattening it. Their reduced-rank autoregressive model splits shared movements into three readable parts: row-driven, column-driven, and joint interactions. Standard statistical inference applies to the estimates.

A BIC-style criterion picks the ranks and lag length together. Simulations, including cases where the rank guess is wrong, check the method's manners. Applied to labor data from nine Midwestern states, it exposes distinct movement patterns. Preserving structure that vector models discard yields interpretations economists can actually use. The method bridges time series theory and regional labor analysis.
arxiv-2509-20211:
Explaining a model's output is easier when the explanation respects cause and effect. Alvaro Parafita and three co-authors improve a causal form of the popular SHAP explanation method in a 2025 arXiv paper. The causal variant, do-SHAP, asks interventional questions about the data. Its dependence on chosen estimands had blocked practical use on complex causal graphs.

The team replaces that dependence with estimand-agnostic inference, which answers any identifiable query from a single fitted model. A new algorithm then speeds up the computation greatly at negligible cost. They also add a way to explain data-generating processes that cannot be observed directly. Tests covered estimation accuracy, runtime, and two real-world datasets. The results support do-SHAP as a practical tool for reliable, causally grounded explanations.
arxiv-2509-20311:
Signals that evolve over time across many channels rarely come with a ready-made network. Om Roy, Yashar Moshfeghi, and Keith Smith build the network from the signal itself in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their starting point is graph variate signal analysis, which pairs a stable support graph with instantaneous connectivity profiles. On that base they define a new neural layer.

Graph Variate Neural Networks convolve signals with a connectivity tensor that mixes the long-term support with live, data-driven links. The design captures changing dependencies at each time step without sliding windows. It also runs with cost that grows only linearly in sequence length. On forecasting benchmarks, the networks beat strong graph-based baselines and matched popular sequence models. Brain signal classification for motor imagery also scored strongly, hinting at brain-computer interface uses.
arxiv-2509-20411:
Generative adversarial networks can forge attacks or block them, and Tharcisse Ndayipfukamiye and four co-authors review the defensive side in a 2025 arXiv survey. Their scope covers work from 2021 through August 2025 on threat detection and mitigation. A PRISMA-compliant search across five major libraries started from more than eight hundred records. One hundred eighty-five peer-reviewed studies survived screening.

The authors organize the field with a four-dimensional taxonomy: defensive function, network architecture, security domain, and threat model. Gains appear across intrusion detection, malware analysis, and internet-of-things security. Stable training variants and conditional generators count among the notable advances. Persistent problems include training instability, missing shared benchmarks, heavy compute costs, and weak explainability. The survey ends with a roadmap stressing hybrid models, unified evaluation, real-world trials, and defenses against language-model-driven attacks.
arxiv-2509-20511:
Pulling a clean signal out of flawed measures is the classic inverse problem. Oscar Leong and Yann Traonmilin build the theory for diffusion-based solvers in a 2025 arXiv paper. Diffusion models give strong learned priors and striking results in practice. Proofs of when they must work have lagged behind. The team studies a fixed, deterministic form of a known solver.

When data piles up near a low-dimensional set, the model's smoothed scores act like projections onto that set, with the target moving over time. The solver then reads as gradient descent with moving projections. If the sensing grid meets a standard isometry trait on the set, clear rates for convergence follow from the noise plan. Two test cases ground the theory: flat spreads on convex sets, and low-rank Gaussian mixtures. The mixture case still converges from any start, though the set is not convex.
arxiv-2509-20711:
Two unusual particle states seen by the BESIII experiment may be made of six quarks. Xuan-Heng Zhang, Sheng-Qi Zhang, and Cong-Feng Qiao test that idea in a 2025 particle physics paper. The states, called X(2075) and X(2085), appeared in a proton-antiproton-lambda system.

The authors model the states as compact hexaquarks built from a triquark joined to an antitriquark. Using QCD sum rules, they compute masses and decay constants for states with four spin-parity options. They find six separate candidate states. Two of them match the mass of X(2075) well, while others differ clearly from both observed states. The remaining candidates serve as predictions for future experiments to check.
arxiv-2509-20811:
Small language models fix grammar carefully but often miss errors, while large models fix too much and change correct text. Taehee Park, Heejin Do, and Gary Geunbae Lee combine the two behaviors in a 2025 paper for EMNLP 2025. Their method is called PoCO, short for post-correction via overcorrection.

PoCO first lets a large model overcorrect on purpose, revising widely to catch every possible error. That step favors recall, catching many true mistakes along with some false changes. A smaller fine-tuned model then reviews the output and repairs the wrong edits. The authors aim to keep the large model's thoroughness while restoring the small model's precision. The approach targets practical grammar correction tools.
arxiv-2509-21111:
Purifying a noisy quantum state sounds like a basic right, but quantum theory itself forbids a universal version of it. Zhenhuan Liu and four co-authors prove that restriction in a 2025 quantum information paper. The result follows from the linearity and positivity of quantum mechanics.

No quantum operation, they show, can take finitely many copies of an unknown state or channel and output an exactly pure state that genuinely depends on the input. The ban covers both static states and dynamical channels. Relaxing exact purity, the authors then derive quantitative bounds on how much purification is possible and at what sample cost. A revised version tightened those bounds considerably. The work sets a fundamental limit for error handling across quantum technology.
arxiv-2509-21211:
Hiding a person group membership inside a social graph, without wrecking the graph, is the privacy task here. The paper is the work of Dario Loi and 3 co-authors. A graph maps people as nodes and links as edges. Tools can guess which group a person belongs to, which can expose private facts. The task is to change a few edges so a target node leaves its group. Past work dealt with groups that do not overlap.

Real groups do overlap, and simple tricks fail there. The authors are the first to formalize this hiding task for overlapping groups. They propose a deep reinforcement learning method that learns how to edit the graph. It can also add proxy nodes as decoys. Tests on real data beat past baselines in effect and speed, while keeping the graph shape largely intact.
arxiv-2509-21311:
Orestis Kaparounakis and Phillip Stanley-Marbell wrote a 2025 paper on sensor uncertainty in real time. Many apps make live decisions from advanced sensors. Those sensors rely on stored calibration data. Users need to know how uncertain each output is. Quantized calibration values add error that must be tracked.

The authors present a method for dynamic uncertainty tracking on the device itself. They show how calibration equations carry uncertainty from stored parameters to the output. A low cost thermal sensor serves as the test case. Prototypes ran on two hardware platforms that track uncertainty. One used low power and ran far faster than Monte Carlo sampling at equal accuracy. The work shows live uncertainty tracking is practical.
arxiv-2509-22011:
Echo state networks are simple recurrent models whose inner weights stay fixed while only the output is trained. Yessin Moakher, Malik Tiomoko, Cosme Louart, and Zhenyu Liao analyze how well they learn in this 2025 paper. They use random matrix theory, the study of large random matrices, in a clean setup where a student network learns from a linear teacher with known weights.

The analysis gives closed-form formulas for the network's bias, variance, and total error in the large-size limit. Two findings depart from classic regression. These networks show no double descent, the odd second improvement seen in some models. They also err less when training data and teacher memory are both limited. The authors also give a formula for the best regularization strength in a simple case, and a numerical method for the general case, as practical tuning guidance.
arxiv-2509-22111:
Maria Iannario, Dae-Jin Lee, and Manuele Leonelli map how mental traits hang together in volleyball players. Their 2025 paper analyzes a new dataset of one hundred sixty-four female players from Italy's C and D leagues, combining standard profiling with background information. The variables are of mixed types: ordered questionnaire scores, categorical demographics, and continuous measures.

To learn directed links among such mixed variables, the authors introduce a hybrid learning method built on a latent Gaussian copula, with a constraint-based skeleton and a score-based refinement. In simulations it recovered network structure more accurately than recent rivals. Applied to the players, the network organized mental skills around goal setting and self-confidence. Emotional arousal linked motivation and anxiety, and personality traits sat upstream of the skill clusters. Scenario analyses show how improving one skill would ripple through preparation, confidence, and self-esteem.
arxiv-2509-22511:
Davide G. F. Lombardo and 5 co-authors test phase-change memory devices at near-freezing temperatures. In-memory computing does math inside the memory array itself, and phase-change memory is a lead candidate for it. Such chips could serve quantum computers and deep-space electronics, both cold settings. The team characterized devices down to five kelvin, across the range those uses need.

They studied the physics that governs programming at low temperature, including phase transitions and threshold switching. They also measured charge transport, structural relaxation, and read noise. Those traits set how precise computations can be when read out. The work maps what to expect from this memory in the cold.
arxiv-2509-22711:
Divyanshu Kumar and 5 co-authors probe partisan associations in language models beyond Western politics. Most bias tests use broad Western lenses. This team looks at harmful, adversarial associations around leaders and parties in the United States and India. They built two data sets of 440 prompts each, one neutral and one adversarial. The prompts ask models to judge comparative plausibility between political figures.

Models proved highly susceptible to biased partisan associations. The patterns were asymmetric: United States Democrats drew far more favorable associations than Republicans. Around India's BJP, associations clustered with mixed polarity. The authors read these results as systemic risks. They argue for standardized, cross-cultural evaluation of partisan bias in deployed models.
arxiv-2509-22811:
John D. Dixon and 5 co-authors compute neodymium abundances in old stars without assuming local equilibrium. Neodymium is a hallmark of the rapid neutron-capture process that forges heavy elements. Its sites are still debated, and metal-poor stars are the main probe. In their thin atmospheres, the usual equilibrium shortcut fails badly. The team built a model atom for neutral and ionized neodymium to get non-equilibrium abundances right.

Calibrated on the Sun, the model matched the meteoritic value. For metal-poor, r-process-rich stars, corrections ran both positive and negative by line type. They also publish a large grid of corrections for over a hundred lines, spanning typical dwarf and giant parameters.
arxiv-2509-22911:
Simon Guldager Andersen and 6 co-authors find a critical state in active nematics, a class of driven soft matter. Topological defects, flaws in the local order, shape the flows and patterns of such systems. Near the critical point, defect counts settle more slowly and swings grow much larger. Defect links also stretch across the whole system size.

At large scales the system turns anti-hyperuniform, meaning number swings beat even random spread. Tests on wide views of endothelial cell layers back the claim. The state held up under changed settings, added friction, and new boundary rules. The authors trace the effect to defects bunching into clusters, not to defects splitting apart.
arxiv-2509-23111:
Factory robots face glare, clutter, and shifting light that lab data sets rarely capture. Chen Yizhe and 12 co-authors release an industrial data set built for that mess. It records a cobot doing pick-and-place work under graded interference. Size, color, and lighting all vary in planned ways. Sensors capture vision, torque, and joint states in sync.

Some scenes share over eighty-five percent geometric similarity, a hard test of discrimination. Microsecond-level sync and vibration-resistant rigs keep the data clean. The team report better model validation robustness from the data. Robot operation stayed more stable in dynamic settings. The data set is public.
arxiv-2509-23411:
Finding communities in a network usually needs either labels or a known count of groups. Dalila Khettaf and 3 co-authors remove both needs by upgrading the Louvain algorithm with graph neural networks. Node embeddings from the network capture richer structure and feature data. Those embeddings steer a sharper Louvain pass. A merging step then trims excess communities.

The authors claim the first Louvain upgrade of this kind. On real-world data sets, the method adjusted community counts on its own. Detection accuracy beat benchmark solutions in their tests. The design keeps Louvain's speed while adding learned feature sense.
arxiv-2509-23511:
Swapping tokens on a graph, like sliding puzzle tiles, generalizes into friends-and-strangers graphs. Amogh Akella and Rupert Li study how many swaps a solution can need. In their setup, one graph encodes friendships and another encodes which positions touch. Two arrangements count as neighbors when a swap trades two friends standing on adjacent spots. Earlier work asked mostly whether such graphs connect at all.

Akella and Li bound the diameter of the connected parts, the longest shortest path between arrangements. When both graphs have high minimum degree, that diameter stays polynomial in size. For random Erdős-Rényi graphs, distances between almost all pairs are likewise polynomial under stated conditions on edge chances.
arxiv-2509-23611:
Neural networks made of light could compute very fast on little power, yet stacking their layers in a row degrades the signal. Jianwei Qin and 5 co-authors propose a parallel layout for all-optical neural networks. Instead of passing light through layers one after another, the input splits into identical copies that enter separate layers at the same time. Interference among the parallel branches creates the needed nonlinearity, with no active nonlinear parts.

A modular 4F optical system put the design to work on image classification tests. Adding more parallel branches steadily raised accuracy, noise tolerance, and expressive range. The authors present spatial parallelism as a practical, scalable path for optical computing.
arxiv-2509-23711:
Most continuous-time reinforcement learning uses random policies, which demand frequent action sampling and costly averages. Ziheng Cheng and 2 co-authors develop deterministic policy gradient methods for that setting instead. They derive a gradient formula built on an advantage rate function, a running score of how much better an action is than average. Martingale characterizations of the value function and the advantage rate make the gradients estimable in practice.

On that base they build CT-DDPG, a model-free deep algorithm for problems with continuous time and state. In experiments it learned more stably and converged faster than stochastic-policy rivals, across varied time steps and noise levels.
arxiv-2509-24011:
When a neutrino hits a nucleon, the pair can pass through a short-lived excited state. Oleksandr Tomalak, the sole author, counts what that path adds to the cross section for charged-current elastic scattering. This is the first such count for virtual resonance states in this process. The main state is the Delta(1232). Its jump from the nucleon is treated with the lead magnetic dipole term for the vector part.

The added share is tiny, at the permille level, for both the elastic and the radiative cross sections at set neutrino energy. The math shows the right infrared trend in the cross sections. The work clarifies how inelastic paths feed an elastic channel.
arxiv-2509-24211:
The brightest line from star-forming galaxies may be hiding in old survey maps, swamped by brighter glow. Shubh Agrawal and 2 co-authors search archival far-infrared maps for the redshifted carbon line at the peak era of star formation. They stack a deep galaxy catalogue on survey maps of the COSMOS field and subtract each galaxy's smooth continuum.

The leftover signal in each redshift bin was weak, at about the one-sigma level. Their upper limits clash with an earlier claim from cross-matching quasar data with Planck maps. The limits imply far gentler growth of the line's strength across the star-formation peak than some models predict. The stacking method itself is offered for future surveys and fainter lines.
arxiv-2509-24411:
Spiking networks promise cheap, brain-like computing, while standard networks train smoothly and score high. Nhan T Luu and 3 co-authors merge the two in a hybrid design where spiking blocks sit layer by layer inside a normal network. Past hybrids kept the parts separate or used spiking only at the input, since spike coding is not differentiable and blocks joint training.

Their fix uses surrogate gradients for a bit-plane spike coding function, making the whole pipeline trainable end to end. The design scores on par with leading pure models of either kind. It keeps the efficiency and timing benefits of spikes, and the authors call it a first of its kind.
arxiv-2509-24611:
The fireball of a heavy-ion collision passes through a quark-gluon phase whose diagram shifts under magnetic fields and chiral imbalance. Xiang-Qiong Liu and Sheng-Qin Feng explore that structure in a two-flavor NJL model with non-extensive statistics, a framework meant to capture non-equilibrium effects in collisions. A single parameter dials how far the statistics depart from the standard case.

Raising that parameter lowers the critical temperature, so chiral symmetry returns sooner. The chiral chemical potential can flip the magnetic response from catalysis to inverse catalysis. Pressure turns anisotropic in strong fields, and the speed of sound dips near the transition. The results offer a lens for reading collision data.
arxiv-2509-25011:
Nader Khonji and three co-authors propose in 2025 a new way to build nuclear star clusters in giant elliptical galaxies: black hole dragging. Dense central star clusters were thought impossible beside the largest black holes, since black hole mergers should scatter their stars away. Yet central light clumps appear in up to a third of massive ellipticals.

After two black holes merge, gravitational waves can kick the product backward through the galaxy. At middling kick speeds, stars bound to the hole ride with it while friction scatters others inward, and the bound swarm can outshine the galaxy's own core. The dragged cluster matches observed sizes and densities. A merger's recoil, long seen as destructive, may instead plant the cluster.
arxiv-2509-25111:
Yazdan Babazadeh Maghsoodlo and co-authors ask in 2025 when a crude yes or no model of public opinion can stand in for a rich sliding scale one. Models that couple people to their environment face a trade. Sliding opinions read true but cost heavy math and many knobs. Binary opinion models are lean but might miss the feedback that matters.

The team ran both kinds side by side across four set ups. Two opinion rules were paired in turn with a climate carbon system and a forest grassland system. Across wide sweeps of learning speed, stubbornness, conformity, and ecological turnover, the binary version tracked its detailed twin closely, usually within a modest error band. It broke away mainly when people were extremely swayed by others or when the ecology barely turned over. The authors offer the simple model as a practical stand in, not a universal swap.
arxiv-2509-25211:
Rémi Genet and Hugo Inzirillo introduce Large Execution Models, neural networks built to schedule trade orders. Their paper appeared in 2025. Executing a big order well means slicing it over time to limit market impact. Older neural methods assumed a fixed time window. The new models allow the window to stretch between set bounds, as in share buyback deals.

One shared pipeline reads market data and builds context. Separate small networks then decide allocations for each case: fixed amount or fixed value, buy or sell. Tests on crypto markets within a day and on big United States stocks over days showed the models beat standard benchmarks. The authors argue one unified model can serve many execution desks at once.
arxiv-2509-25511:
Marco Bussoletti, Mirko Gallo, Amir Jafari, and Gregory Eyink study how a dissolved substance spreads in a still liquid in this 2025 physics paper. Standard theory treats the small random swings in concentration as smooth and bell shaped.

The authors show that those swings are in fact skewed, even when the mean gradient is close to zero. They reach this result both with math and with a large computer simulation that tracks many particles. The skew comes from a link between the swings and heat driven motion in the fluid. Their finding breaks a common rule for such systems and will matter for models of mixing at small scales.
arxiv-2509-25711:
Yuan Gao, Sangwook Kim, Jianzhong You, and Chris McIntosh built a medical AI in 2025 that ties together four kinds of patient data without forcing them into one rigid map. Chest X-rays, heart traces, heart ultrasounds, and written notes often come in many-to-many links: one note may match several scans. Older models ignore that looseness.

Their system, ProbMED, places each item as a spread of likely spots rather than a single point. Training pulls matching spreads together across data types and keeps each type's own spread honest. Across thirteen datasets, it beat current rivals at cross-type search and at sorting new cases with few or no examples. Mixing several data types also sharpened forecasts of patient outcomes. The authors call the spread-based map a better fit for real wards.
arxiv-2509-25811:
Zichen Liang and eight co-authors reframe in 2025 logo recognition as visual comparison rather than memorization, in a system called Logo-VGR. Product moderation teams must spot brand logos in the wild, including brands never seen in training. Memorizing tens of thousands of logos does not scale, and models that memorize fail on new brands.

The model instead matches a product image against candidate logos, judging sameness directly. A grounding stage injects logo-specific knowledge, and guided visual reasoning sharpens the comparisons. Training used only a small slice of brands, yet the system generalized to the open world of unseen marks. Comparison-based recognition mirrors how human moderators actually verify a suspicious product.
arxiv-2509-25911:
Yu Wang and co-authors present a 2025 paper on how software agents that use language models can remember things over time. Such agents can only hold a limited amount of text at once, so they store facts in an outside memory. Set rules for what to store often lose key facts or store them in a poor form.

Their method trains the agent by reward, based on how well it later answers questions. The agent learns what to keep, how to shape it, and when to update it. Training uses long chats paired with test questions. The goal is memory that keeps what matters for long tasks.
arxiv-2509-26211:
Zhongyi Jiang and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on a better coupler for superconducting quantum processors. Couplers switch the link between qubits on and off. Even when off, stray wave spread leaves weak crosstalk, and single mode couplers cannot tune one and two excitation links apart, which leaks errors into gates.

Their multi-mode coupler pins excitations in place at the off point, giving near perfect isolation. Its extra modes let each link type be tuned on its own, with large on-off ratios. The design aims at bigger machines with cleaner gates. The authors present it as a route to the next class of couplers for high fidelity work.
arxiv-2509-26311:
Hassaan Hashmi, Spyridon Pougkakiotis, and Dionysis Kalogerias tackle reliable wireless transmission in a 2025 paper. In a downlink network with several antennas at the base station, total data rate is usually maximized on average, which can leave some users with deep fades. The authors instead build reliability into the goal using a risk measure that focuses on the worst outcomes.

They prove a link between their risk aware beam design problem and a weighted error problem, which makes it solvable. A graph neural network policy is then trained to produce the designs. In tests, the trained network removed deep rate fades per user entirely and cut rate variability sharply, while keeping average performance adequate.
arxiv-2510-00111:
Kevin Hainline and a large team of co-authors published this 2025 astronomy paper on the coldest brown dwarfs. T and Y dwarfs are failed stars cooler than about 1200 degrees, once found only near the Sun. The team mined deep James Webb Space Telescope images from the JADES survey instead. Those images stare at distant galaxies, yet nearby cold dwarfs can photobomb them.

The search turned up 41 brown dwarf candidates across two famous deep fields. A new open tool called NIFTY fit each one's temperature, composition, and distance. Many candidates sit several thousand light-years away, far beyond earlier samples. Most look poor in heavy elements, matching old stars in the galaxy's thick disk and halo. The authors also warn that such dwarfs can masquerade as ultra-distant galaxies in other searches.
arxiv-2510-00311:
Bowen Wei and six colleagues published this 2025 paper on CORTEX, a team of AI agents for security alert triage. Security operations centers drown in tens of thousands of alerts each day. Only a small share mark real attacks, and the flood breeds fatigue and missed threats. Single language models asked to judge alerts end to end struggle with noisy company data.

CORTEX splits the work among specialized agents that share real evidence. One agent studies behavior sequences, others query outside systems for proof, and a reasoning agent writes the verdict. Every step leaves an auditable trail of artifacts. The team also releases a dataset of real investigations, with analyst actions and tool outputs recorded. In their tests CORTEX cut false alarms from about a quarter of alerts to about a seventh. Its reports cite explicit evidence, easing review and compliance work.
arxiv-2510-00411:
Ran Tong and five colleagues published this 2025 paper asking whether bigger AI models beat small ones at reading chest X-rays. They pitted a lightweight supervised convolutional network against BiomedCLIP, a large zero-shot vision-language model. Two tasks framed the contest: pneumonia detection on a standard benchmark and tuberculosis detection on a Shenzhen dataset. The small network proved a strong baseline in both tasks.

Out of the box, the big model's zero-shot scores lagged behind the small network. A simple fix changed the picture: tuning the decision threshold on validation data. Calibration lifted the big model past the small one on pneumonia detection. On tuberculosis, its score leapt dramatically and nearly matched the supervised baseline. The authors argue that reporting uncalibrated zero-shot scores badly undersells such models. Careful calibration belongs in any fair comparison of diagnostic AI systems.
arxiv-2510-00711:
Telkamp and nine co-authors at ETH Zurich report a new semiconductor-superconductor hybrid material in this 2025 arXiv paper on quantum devices. Hybrid platforms pair a tunable semiconductor with a superconductor to build gate-controlled devices and hunt for topological superconductivity. The standard aluminium-on-InAs stack works, but indium arsenide antimonide offers lower effective mass and stronger spin-orbit interaction. Niobium, meanwhile, superconducts at higher temperatures and fields than aluminium.

The team grew an InAsSb surface quantum well by molecular beam epitaxy and deposited the niobium in place, which keeps the interface clean and strongly coupled. Transport measurements on Josephson junctions showed an induced superconducting gap of about 1.3 millielectronvolts in the well. They also built a planar asymmetric SQUID whose oscillations were gate-tunable and combined junction and loop signals. The large gap plus strong spin-orbit coupling makes the platform attractive for topological device experiments.
arxiv-2510-01111:
Parker, Chan, Zhang, and Ghobadi teach a language model to reason about time series in this 2025 arXiv paper. Time series drive decisions in healthcare, finance, and environmental science, but analysing them often needs surrounding text, domain questions, and explanations. Classical forecasters accept only numbers and return only numbers, while language models reason yet handle numerical sequences badly. The team bridges that split with a patch-based encoder-decoder that gives the language model a time series sense.

Their model, TsLLM, trains on over two million interleaved examples of series paired with text. The tasks span context-aware forecasting, question answering, pattern explanation, classification with outputs, and report generation. The authors stress that TsLLM is not meant to beat specialized forecasters on benchmarks. Its strength is the mixed work no approach offers: one system that reads a signal, uses its context, and explains what it sees.
arxiv-2510-01211:
Agazzotti and Aguilar price European options under jumpy price models with formulas simple enough to write down. Stock returns carry fat tails and asymmetry that the classic normal model misses entirely. Tempered stable processes capture those features, but their option prices usually need heavy numerical machinery.

Series expansions for the densities and contract prices replace that machinery here. Several famous pricing models fall out as special cases of the general result. The formulas need no tunable hyperparameters, unlike the standard Fourier approach. Benchmarks showed the method competitive with the best current pricing techniques. Mellin-Barnes representations are the engine behind the expansions. Digital options receive the same closed treatment as vanilla contracts. Bilateral gamma and one-sided cases collapse to remarkably simple forms. Hyperparameter-free design removes a whole category of user error. Traders gain speed without surrendering the fat tails.
arxiv-2510-01611:
Zeng asks whether language models know enough psychology to sit the exam that licenses human counselors. The United States National Counselor Examination demands roughly seventy percent accuracy from human candidates. A new benchmark rebuilds that standard from about twenty-two hundred carefully curated exam questions.

Models faced the questions under the same pass bar that people must clear. Top proprietary systems led the field, with a clear hierarchy below them. Book knowledge alone does not make a counselor, but it is the gate every counselor passes. The benchmark gives deployment debates a concrete, exam-based yardstick. Single-choice format mirrors the real licensing test's style. Questions were curated to require genuine reasoning, not recall of trivia. Counseling is high-stakes, so a knowledge floor is a reasonable first demand. Weaker models trailed far behind the leaders. Passing an exam and helping a person differ.
arxiv-2510-01711:
Kim and seven co-authors improve robot manipulation models in this 2025 robotics paper. Vision-Language-Action models steer robots using representations borrowed from vision-language models. Those borrowed representations describe pictures and words well. They respond weakly, though, to control actions and to the robot's own body state.

The team adds a training objective called Robot State-aware Contrastive Loss, or RS-CL. It pulls representations of similar body states closer together during training. Distances between the robot's proprioceptive states serve as soft supervision for that pull. The extra loss is light and fits standard training pipelines without new stages. On RoboCasa-Kitchen pick-and-place tasks, success rose from about thirty-one percent to about forty-two percent. On real robot hardware, success on hard tasks rose from forty-five percent to over fifty-eight percent.
arxiv-2510-01811:
Brazitikos, Garefalakis, and Tzanaki extend a powerful decoding method to a broad family of error-correcting codes in this 2025 paper. Evaluation codes encode messages as values of polynomials at chosen points. Toric codes generalize them using a convex polytope that shapes the point set. List decoding returns every plausible message within some error radius, not just one guess.

The authors generalize the Guruswami-Sudan algorithm to this toric setting. Their version exploits both the geometry and the combinatorics of the underlying polytope. From that structure they compute bounds on the decoding radius the method can reach. Famous code families appear as special cases of the framework. Reed-Solomon and Reed-Muller codes both fit inside it. The work gives coding theorists a single decoding story for many polytope-based codes at once.
arxiv-2510-01911:
Ren and Gao analyze trapped elastic waves in sharply contrasting materials in this 2025 paper. They study two-dimensional media whose stiffness and density differ hugely between regions. Such high contrast can trap waves at frequencies far below what the inclusion size suggests. These subwavelength resonances matter for phononic crystals and vibration control.

Layer methods turn the wave problem into boundary equations on the inclusion edges. They build an invertible operator from the kernels of those operators. Resonant frequencies then follow from an orthogonality condition, with asymptotic formulas for their leading terms. They also describe the interior scattered field across wave regimes. Far-field patterns split into lengthwise and crosswise parts outside the resonators. Finally, they examine the bandgap of a dilute sound crystal built from such inclusions. The machinery gives designers formulas for tuning elastic resonators instead of blind numerics.
arxiv-2510-02211:
Allie, du Preez, Reagon, and Roux bound how fast a monitoring process sweeps a graph in this 2025 combinatorics paper. Power domination models placing monitors so their influence propagates: a vertex with all but one neighbor monitored becomes monitored itself. A minimum power dominating set is the cheapest full placement. Its propagation radius is the number of steps the sweep needs.

The authors derive bounds on that radius across graph families. Speed matters because each propagation step is time a network sits partly unobserved. Their results separate graphs where optimal placements finish quickly from those with slow forced cascades. The interplay between set size and sweep time is the paper's focus. A minimum set is not automatically a fast one, and the radius quantifies the gap. Sharp radius bounds tell planners when patience is unavoidable.
arxiv-2510-02511:
Brozena tracks four years of his sleep and mood in a single person study. His 2025 health data paper uses a wearable ring and a phone diary. The Oura Ring recorded nightly sleep quality scores. An app called eMood Tracker logged depressed and anxious moods. Self-tracking supports long term care for chronic illness. Bipolar care is one setting where such awareness matters. Brozena fit a vector autoregression model to the series. Granger causality tests then probed which series leads the other. Lag choices and stationarity checks came before the modeling.

Sleep scores helped predict later mood states. The model showed sleep Granger-causing depressed and anxious mood presence. A two day lag structure carried the effect. The reverse pathway was not the headline result. One person limits how far the finding travels. Sensor based warnings of coming episodes remain the goal. Cheap wearables make such long records possible.
arxiv-2510-02811:
Gjurković presents a doctoral thesis from the University of Zagreb. It was finished in 2025 at the Faculty of Electrical Engineering and Computing. The supervisor was Jan Šnajder, a natural language processing researcher. The thesis runs to 145 pages. Its topic is personality assessment from text. It asks how to judge traits from social media writing. It also asks how to keep those judgments open to inspection.

The core of the thesis is a framework called SIMPA. SIMPA builds its scores from layered cues in the text. Each cue carries a clear weight, so a reader can trace any score back to its sources. That openness sets it apart from black-box predictors. The framework suits tasks with few labels and rich label systems. The author notes that it can serve other constructs beyond personality. The thesis closes with limits of the approach and paths for wider use.
arxiv-2510-03511:
Islam and a large team, largely at the University of Amsterdam, present a 2025 arXiv paper giving transformers a built in sense of geometric symmetry. Standard transformers ignore the rotations and flips that science data obey. Older symmetry aware designs pay for their awareness with heavy, awkward computation. Their Platonic Transformer measures attention against reference frames drawn from the symmetry groups of the Platonic solids. Weight sharing then enforces the symmetry at no extra cost.

The method keeps the exact shape and speed of a normal transformer. The authors also prove the attention equals a dynamic group convolution, which yields a fast linear time variant for huge jobs. Benchmarks covered image sorting, 3D point cloud tasks, and molecule property prediction. Scores stayed competitive across all of them while the geometric bias came free. Symmetry respecting models could spread through chemistry, physics, and vision without the usual efficiency tax.
arxiv-2510-03611:
Yousuf and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper benchmarking whether language models can rebuild a graph from long text. Context tests ask models to find a needle sentence in a haystack, which is simpler than reasoning. Here the text encodes a relational graph whose links are scattered across irrelevant filler. The model must induce the structure, not just retrieve one fact. The authors measure failure with a memory drift metric that tracks how structure degrades as inputs grow.

Models began drifting and forgetting at shorter lengths than needle tests suggest. Structural complexity and cues made the degradation worse. Even OpenAI's o1, a reasoning model, showed early memory drift in this setting. The benchmark exposes tradeoffs across model families that retrieval scores hide. The authors add guidance on using models for structure heavy tasks. Teams building document analysis tools should distrust advertised context windows and test on tasks that resemble their workloads.
arxiv-2510-03811:
Laajil and co-authors present this 2025 arXiv paper on designing messenger RNA sequences with a type of generative model called a GFlowNet. An mRNA sequence tells cells which protein to build, and good designs must balance stability, output, and other traits. The search space is huge, and rewards are rare and delayed. The team aims to make these models learn faster and produce more plausible candidates.

Their method, called CAGFN, adds a length curriculum that starts training on short, easy sequences, then moves to longer ones. They also built a new design setting that scores sequences against a target protein and biological goals. In tests, CAGFN reached high-quality designs faster than the same model trained without a curriculum. It also kept a diverse set of candidates and handled unfamiliar sequence lengths well. Better design tools could speed the search for RNA-based medicines.
arxiv-2510-04011:
Liu and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper using quantum information tools to probe the early universe. Many quantum gravity theories give cosmic sound a nonstandard speed, which changes how primordial ripples evolve. The universe also behaves as an open system, leaking information to its surroundings. The authors track a chaos measure called Krylov complexity across the inflation, radiation, and matter eras.

They derive new evolution equations for the squeezed-state parameters that describe primordial fluctuations. With those, they compute Krylov complexity numerically under both standard and nonstandard sound speeds. The complexity itself followed similar trends in both cases, so it could not separate them. A companion measure, Krylov entropy, did show a clear difference between the two scenarios. The Lanczos coefficients further suggested the nonstandard case behaves as a maximally chaotic system. The study offers a fresh diagnostic for distinguishing early-universe theories that look alike by other measures.
arxiv-2510-04111:
Luo and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on estimating motion from event cameras quickly and lightly. Event cameras report pixel changes instead of frames, suiting fast motion and low light. Meshflow, a smooth sparse motion field used for video stabilization and alignment, had no event-based dataset or method. The authors also flag event data density, which varies wildly between cameras, as an ignored problem.

They built HREM, a high-resolution event meshflow dataset with optical flow labels, dynamic objects, and complex motion. Their network, EEMFlow, uses a crafted encoder-decoder to predict meshflow far faster than recent flow methods, about thirty times quicker. A confidence-based completion module extends it to dense optical flow while preserving sharp motion boundaries. An adaptive density module rescales input density toward an optimal range, improving results on both tasks. Event vision needs exactly this kind of efficiency to run on real devices.
arxiv-2510-04511:
Samantha Tseng, Abhyudaya Chouhan, and Dominic Cupidon wrote this 2025 paper comparing quantum algorithms for a classic equation. The heat equation describes how warmth spreads, and it stands in for many partial differential equations in science. Quantum methods promise speed, but no single best method has emerged. The team surveyed quantum solvers built since 2020 and ran two of them on the one dimensional heat equation.

Their analysis counted the full cost of each method, including the price of reading the answer back out in classical form. That reading step often hides and can erase a claimed speedup. One method offered a principled route with clean scaling in its error terms. Once output costs were counted fairly, its precision matched the other pipelines. In one dimension, it did not beat a classical Fourier baseline. The authors close by naming the constants and build details that will decide real usefulness.
arxiv-2510-04611:
Pawel Weichbroth, Maciej Lotysz, and Michal Wrobel wrote this 2025 survey paper on feelings and output among software developers. Coding under pressure wears people down, and teams feel the cost in mood and health. Whether mood changes how productive developers feel was an open question. The team asked nine experts to check their measurement model. They then surveyed eighty eight developers about emotional state and perceived productivity.

A path analysis of the survey data gave an answer. Emotional state showed a strong positive link with how productive developers felt. The effect was statistically firm in their sample. In plain terms, developers who felt better rated their output higher. The authors argue that well being work is not a perk but a lever. Cutting burnout and stress should pay back in output that teams can see. The study is about perceived productivity, not lines of code, and the authors keep that scope.
arxiv-2510-05111:
Ian McDougall and four co-authors argue that cloud GPU pricing charges for the wrong thing in this 2025 arXiv paper. Computing power per dollar keeps improving across GPU generations. Memory bandwidth per dollar does not, and it now lags badly. Renting GPUs by the hour ignores that growing scarcity.

The authors propose feature-based pricing, where bills track actual resource use, bandwidth included. Their system, Agora, samples usage fast enough to price almost perfectly in tests. Sampling every 50 microseconds lost only about 5 percent of ideal revenue. Finer sampling lost even less. The design points toward a fairer, more transparent market for scarce GPU capacity.
arxiv-2510-05311:
J. G. F. Campos, A. Mohammadi, and T. Romanczukiewicz collide exotic waves called kinks in this 2025 arXiv paper. Kinks are stable lumps in a scalar field, and their reach can be tuned from short to long range. When a kink meets an antikink at middling speed, the outcome can alternate wildly. Physicists call those sensitive speed bands resonance windows.

The authors show resonance windows survive even when both kinks have long-range tails. The energy exchange runs through quasinormal modes, which leak energy slowly like a struck bell. A spectral analysis extracted those modes for a rational model and a phi-ten model. The team also built a new convection-diffusion algorithm to start such collisions cleanly. In the rational model the windows vanish once the tails grow too fat.
arxiv-2510-05811:
Boisson and colleagues turn an extremal graph problem into a two-player game. Generalized Turán problems ask how many copies of a structure a constrained graph can hold. In the Constructor-Blocker game, Constructor claims edges while avoiding forbidden patterns. Their 2025 paper focuses on maximizing triangles under such bans.

Constructor must never create short paths or short cycles in her graph. Blocker claims edges freely, trying to keep her triangle count low. The authors derive precise asymptotics or bounds for every game studied. A variant replaces the forbidden-subgraph rules with planarity constraints instead. Optimal play from both sides determines the game's score. Mantel's classical theorem anchors the triangle case historically. The trivial ceiling from classical Turán theory always applies above. Game versions reveal how an adversary changes extremal outcomes. The framework extends naturally to other target structures beyond triangles.
arxiv-2510-05911:
Schestag studies how weighted food webs complicate conservation planning. Phylogenetic diversity measures the evolutionary history a saved species set represents. Greedy algorithms maximize it easily when species are independent. His 2025 paper adds a food web whose edges weight predator-prey importance.

A saved species must find enough food among the other preserved species. With weighted webs, the problem is NP-hard even when both structures are stars. Unweighted food-web versions were already known to be NP-hard. Special cases require only a given fraction of prey to survive. Parameterized analysis then maps where tractability returns. With a star tree, the problem is fixed-parameter tractable in the food web's vertex cover number. Several XP algorithms cover other structural parameters. Whether some XP results improve to FPT remains open. Limited budgets make such prioritization unavoidable in the sixth mass extinction.
arxiv-2510-06011:
Calvert, Richa, and Randall ask when a group's behavior changes simply because the group grows, in a 2025 paper on collective behavior. Pharaoh ant colonies of 700 or more forage along pheromone trails, while smaller colonies do not. A water cluster needs roughly 90 molecules before ice can persist.

The authors define critical numerosities, the head counts where behavior flips abruptly rather than gradually. They show that a small change to standard bifurcation analysis can locate these thresholds, even for transitions blamed on noise or discreteness. The thresholds arise when competing feedbacks grow at different rates with group size. The team also finds overlooked thresholds in earlier studies and shows that smooth deterministic models can fail near them. Their framework helps scientists predict when adding or losing members changes what a whole group does.
arxiv-2510-06411:
Knipper and five co-authors build a framework for generating virtual-lab questions aligned with teachers' goals in a 2025 education technology paper. Virtual labs support inquiry-based science learning, but third-party materials rarely match teachers' goals. Writing custom questions is slow and hard to scale.

Their framework combines four components. Teacher dialogue extracts instructional goals in natural language. Knowledge-unit analysis captures what the simulation teaches. A question taxonomy structures cognitive and pedagogical intent. The TELeR taxonomy controls prompt detail. The evaluation analyzed over eleven hundred questions from nineteen open-source models. Grounding in goals and lab content improved alignment measurably. The taxonomy raised quality by roughly a third of a point, especially for open-ended questions. Optimized prompts reached eighty percent parsability and over ninety percent adherence. Larger models gained most, adding nearly a full Likert point of quality.
arxiv-2510-06511:
Moston-Duggan, Howls, and Lustri show discretizing the Airy equation creates asymptotic behavior the continuous one never has in a 2025 mathematical physics paper. The continuous Airy function has a simple classical Stokes structure. Higher-order Stokes phenomena normally require third-order or nonlinear equations. A mere discretization should change nothing so deep.

The discrete Airy equation is an advance-delay equation. Steepest descent and series methods reveal its asymptotic solutions and Stokes structure. That structure is far more intricate than the continuous case. Higher-order Stokes phenomena appear throughout. Infinitely accumulating Stokes and anti-Stokes curves arise. In continuous theory, such accumulations are strictly nonlinear effects. Here they emerge from a linear discretization. Numerical simulations confirm the predictions. Comparison with the continuous equation pinpoints how discretization rewrites the structure. The cautionary tale: discretize first, and the asymptotics may solve a different problem.
arxiv-2510-06711:
Batu El, Mert Yuksekgonul, and James Zou examine machines that design other AI agents. Their 2025 paper studies meta-agents, which propose and refine new agent architectures automatically. Such automation could cut the human effort of building agentic systems. The authors find three deep problems in a common meta-agent design.

First, they test how the meta-agent learns across design rounds. Feeding it every past design performed worse than ignoring history entirely. An evolutionary approach, breeding new designs from the best parents, worked better. Second, the designed agents behaved too much alike. That low diversity wastes the chance to combine complementary agents. Third, they check the economics of automated design. Only on two datasets did the savings beat human design costs, and only past fifteen thousand uses. For other datasets, the design cost never paid for itself.
arxiv-2510-06811:
Philipp Mondorf, Mingyang Wang, Sebastian Gerstner, and Ahmad Hakimi compete in a shared task on finding circuits inside language models. Their 2025 paper reports a system built for the Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark. A circuit is the subnetwork responsible for one specific behavior. Several methods can score which connections matter, and each has blind spots.

The team tests whether combining methods beats using any one of them. In a parallel ensemble, scores from different methods are merged by averaging or taking extremes. In a sequential ensemble, a fast method's scores warm-start a slower, more precise pruning method. Both styles improved the benchmark scores. A hybrid that ensembles everything, including the sequential method, did best of all. It earned the lowest error scores and highest precision scores on both leaderboards. The result is practical guidance for interpretability researchers. Complementary methods combined find truer circuits than any method alone.
arxiv-2510-06911:
Hacane Hechehouche, André Antakli, and Matthias Klusch make it easier to build software agents on Semantic Web standards. Their 2025 paper presents an editor for the AJAN agent framework. Agents store knowledge in RDF and OWL, and their behaviors are behavior trees driven by SPARQL queries. Writing those queries by hand is error-prone, and small identifier typos break agents silently.

Their development environment wraps the whole modeling process in one tool. Users manage agent templates, draw behavior trees, and watch agents run. A language model interface generates working behaviors and queries from plain instructions. People can even speak their requests, since voice input is transcribed automatically. Generated pieces stay modular and editable, unlike fully automatic generators. The SPARQL generation also avoids a weakness of earlier language model tools. It does not depend on one specific knowledge graph. A 3D simulation scenario demonstrates the full workflow for new users.
arxiv-2510-07311:
Ackermann, Malyshev, and Malyshev review the faint glow that fills the sky at megaelectronvolt energies and the huge structures inside it. Their 2025 article looks ahead to new gamma-ray survey telescopes with far sharper vision. Diffuse continuum light dominates the sky at these energies. It arises when fast particles strike gas and radiation across the Milky Way. Two giant features stand out: the Fermi bubbles and Loop I, both vast outflows or shells in our galaxy. An extragalactic background glow completes the picture.

Better measurements in this band can reveal how cosmic rays are born and how they wander the galaxy. They can also settle what the bubbles and Loop I really are. The authors argue the MeV range has been underused compared with its neighbors. New instruments could make this quiet band a prime window on high-energy astrophysics.
arxiv-2510-07411:
Liptrott and co-authors test whether a strange stellar system near the Milky Way's center helped build the galactic bulge. Their paper studies Liller 1, an object inside the innermost kiloparsec with stars of widely spread ages and chemistries. That spread suggests great mass, and some astronomers proposed it as a major bulge building block. The team used infrared spectroscopy from the APOGEE survey. A random sampling method compared Liller 1's chemical fingerprint against the bulge, both disks, and the solar neighborhood, element family by element family.

Liller 1's chemistry departed from the bulge pattern at a statistically firm level for key elements like magnesium, silicon, and calcium. Its progenitor therefore was not a major contributor to bulge mass. The pattern also differed from inner disk stars, killing a rival story in which an old cluster was rejuvenated there.
arxiv-2510-07511:
Boone and co-authors build a correction method that keeps survey flaws from faking dark matter signals in stellar streams. Their 2025 paper concerns the thin ribbons of stars torn from dead galaxies around the Milky Way. Bumps in a stream's density can betray invisible dark matter clumps that nudged it. But changing sky brightness and image sharpness also fabricate bumps by hiding stars unevenly. The team used Balrog, a system that injects fake sources into real Dark Energy Survey images, to measure detection and classification rates as functions of survey conditions across the footprint.

Detection and misclassification rates proved nearly separable by property, so each could be estimated with ample statistics. Applying the corrections cut the spread of relative detection rates fivefold. The inferred density of the faint Phoenix stream changed significantly once faint objects were corrected.
arxiv-2510-07911:
Abid wrote this 2025 paper in nonlinear analysis on a fractional Kirchhoff-type equation with a singular term. Such equations model elastic strings whose tension depends on the whole deformation. The fractional p-Laplacian adds long-range interactions, and the singular term blows up as the solution nears zero. A second term changes sign, which complicates the search for solutions. Abid looks for positive solutions that are genuinely nontrivial, on a bounded domain.

He works with the Nehari manifold, which splits candidate functions by their energy behavior. Fibre maps and Ekeland's variational principle organize the argument. For a suitable range of the positive parameter, the problem admits at least two positive solutions. The result holds in both the subcritical and the critical growth cases, which are usually handled separately.
