Reza Karimzadeh and colleagues explain vision models with contours instead of masks. The usual explanation tools shade dense pixel masks showing what a classifier used, but those masks come out fragmented and overfitted, needing cleanup before a person can read them.

Their method, Extremal Contours, needs no training. A star convex region, described compactly by a truncated Fourier series, is optimized against an extremal preserve and delete objective using the classifier's own gradients. The result is guaranteed to be one simply connected mask with orders of magnitude fewer free parameters and stable updates. On ImageNet classifiers it matched the fidelity of dense masks with better run to run consistency, and explicit area control yields importance contour maps. A multi contour extension localizes several objects at once.
arxiv-2511-01511:
Hannah Schunker and Asha Lakshmi K review Joy's law, a pattern noticed in sunspot groups: their tilt away from an east-west line grows with latitude. Explaining that tilt matters. In leading theories of the solar dynamo, the tilt is the step that converts the Sun's toroidal magnetic field back into a poloidal one. Observed tilts also help flip the sign of the Sun's global magnetic dipole.

The review gathers what observations say about when and how the tilt first appears. It places those results inside a picture where active regions emerge largely passively near the solar surface, shaped by near-surface convection rather than by forces deep below. Any successful theory of active region emergence has to match this record.
arxiv-2511-01811:
Sanaea Rose and four colleagues simulate what happens when stars collide head-on in the crowded centers of galaxies. A nuclear star cluster packs millions of stars around a supermassive black hole. The hole whips them to hundreds of kilometers per second. So direct collisions are inevitable. They shape the cluster's stellar population.

The team ran a couple hundred high-resolution smoothed-particle hydrodynamics simulations of collisions between one-solar-mass stars at galactic-nucleus speeds. From that dataset they built physically motivated fitting formulas for collision outcomes. They add a new framework for hit-and-run encounters. In it, velocity changes follow the tidal-dissipation limit for grazing blows. Deflection angles match point-particle dynamics when the closest approach is wide enough. Two machine learning predictors were tested on the data, and a neural network beat k-nearest neighbors at forecasting outcomes.
arxiv-2511-02011:
Toby Meadows, a philosopher of logic, takes up a basic question: when should two theories count as saying the same thing in different words? For theories written in first-order logic, mathematicians already have a precise tool, based on translation between languages, called relative interpretability. Many real theories in physics and mathematics, though, are not written in any such formal language.

Meadows aims to extend the translation-based account to cover those cases, a direction associated with the Hudetz program. The proposal treats definability as definability in the language of mathematics itself, rather than relative to one chosen structure. The result is a framework meant to judge theory equivalence far beyond first-order settings.
arxiv-2511-02211:
Morteza Sadeghi, Hadi Keramati, and Sajjad Bigham search globally for heat sink shapes that keep electronics cool without wasting pumping power. Their framework describes cooling fins with smooth Bézier curves, so a handful of variables can generate many topologies. Rather than simulating every candidate in full 3D, which is slow, the method couples two interacting 2D layers. One serves the fluid and one the base plate, with heat transfer coefficients calibrated from detailed simulations.

An evolution strategy optimiser then minimises pressure drop while holding the average surface temperature within a set limit. Checked against full 3D simulations, the fast model matched temperatures and pressure drops while running orders of magnitude faster. Optimised designs cut pressure loss by up to fifty percent compared with conventional straight fins, exposing a clear trade-off between cooling and hydraulic efficiency.
arxiv-2511-02711:
Daren Chao, Kaiwen Chen, Naiqing Guan, and Nick Koudas tackle questions asked over messy, unstructured files. Their 2025 framework, ReDD, turns such data into clean relational tables shaped by each query. Older retrieval tools lack a sense of schema and often misalign facts across documents, with error rates that can reach high levels.

ReDD first discovers a small joinable schema for the query, then fills the tables using light classifiers trained on hidden states of a language model. Its SCAPE method flags likely errors with statistical coverage guarantees, and a hybrid variant balances accuracy against the cost of human fixes. Across varied data sets, errors fell from up to 30 percent to below 1 percent, with full recall of the needed schema.
arxiv-2511-03111:
Justin Swain and Giordano Tierra design numerical schemes for a three-component Cahn-Hilliard system, equations that track how three mixed fluids or alloys separate and form interfaces. Their 2025 paper works on a penalized version of the system and aims for schemes that are fast, accurate, and respect the physics by never gaining energy. Three designs trade those virtues differently.

The first scheme is linear, split by component, first-order accurate, and stable at any time step. The second trims the computing cost sharply while keeping conditional stability. The third couples the unknowns but reaches second-order accuracy while staying linear. Simulations in two and three dimensions map the costs and benefits, and the ideas extend to four or more components.
arxiv-2511-03711:
J Pereira and R O Ruiz extend a fast stand-in for how metamaterials shake when their shape shifts a lot. The base method blends reduced matrices on a shared modal base. That trick skips fresh mesh and matrix builds for each new shape. But the shared base caps how far the shape can shift.

Three moves loosen that cap for aperiodic parts with big shifts. The method splits the shape space into zones. Each zone keeps a base that fits it well. Clear dynamics insight shows where the old cap bit hardest. Fast response curves let designers sweep odd cell shapes cheaply. They need no full run per shape tried. The search for tuned shake traits speeds up a lot.
arxiv-2511-03811:
Jacob F Steiner, Larissa Melischek, and Felix von Oppen extend the standard model of a Josephson junction, the resistively and capacitively shunted junction model, beyond the tunneling limit. They work past the regime where that model is usually derived. That limit misses effects now of interest, including the Josephson diode effect.

Their generalized model allows dissipative currents with nonlinear voltage response and supercurrents with arbitrary current-phase relations. A generalized fluctuation-dissipation result supplies the random Langevin current, deduced along lines used for mesoscopic conductors. The work gives theorists a microscopic basis for junction dynamics in regimes where the textbook model no longer applies, including modern diode studies.
arxiv-2511-04011:
Higo T P Da Silva is the lead author among five authors surveying noise-based communication, which encodes information in the statistical properties of noise instead of a clean carrier signal. Sixth-generation networks and mass Internet of Things devices need wireless links that use very little power while staying secure and hard to detect.

Methods covered include thermal noise modulation, noise modulation and its variants, and a Kirchhoff-law Johnson-noise scheme for secure key exchange. Practical hurdles such as channel estimation and hardware design get attention, as do energy transfer and non-orthogonal access applications. The survey finds strong advantages in efficiency and covertness and maps research needed for autonomous, secure networks.
arxiv-2511-04111:
Debamita Chatterjee, Himanshu Lekharu, and Riddhi Shah study how automorphisms of a connected Lie group act on a compact space built from its closed one-parameter subgroups. The action is judged by distality and expansivity. For a torus, the setting where the sharpest results land, symmetry actions turn out to be tightly constrained.

Only finite-order automorphisms act distally on that subgroup space for a torus, the team show. Distality there connects to distality on the group itself and to compactness of the subgroup generated inside the automorphism group, except for vector groups. No automorphism acts expansively when a central torus has dimension at least two, extending earlier distal and expansive results.
arxiv-2511-04311:
Ahmed Barbar, writing alone, studies an ensemble proposal in holographic duality where a 3D topological field theory summed over topologies is dual to an ensemble of 2D conformal field theories. In that proposal, topology sums come from genus reduction and boundary theories are Lagrangian condensations of the bulk theory.

Each ensemble member, Barbar shows, carries a symmetry weight: the invertible symmetry group of its categorical symmetry relative to the bulk theory acting as its symmetry theory. That weight is the natural uniform-up-to-isomorphism measure on the groupoid of Lagrangian algebras. Topology sums are rewritten through Heegaard splitting classes with their weights, framing the duality as a broad Siegel-Weil formula, with lessons for non-compact cases.
arxiv-2511-04611:
Maximilian Matthe, writing alone, presents evomap, a Python toolbox for dynamic mapping. Maps that place objects by their relationships help many fields picture structure. Most software, though, draws only a static map frozen at one time.

Evomap extends mapping across time, following the EvoMap framework from Matthe, Ringel, and Skiera in 2023. It supports multidimensional scaling variants, Sammon mapping, and t-SNE for the layouts. Extra utilities help users build and read the moving maps. Watching relationships drift over time can reveal trends that no single snapshot would show. That fills a clear gap left by static-only tools in standard statistical software.
arxiv-2511-04711:
Wenyuan Yang leads seven authors with SWAP, a way to audit copyright in soft prompts. Soft prompts are small trained modules that adapt big vision-language models like CLIP. Owners need to prove when a suspect model quietly reuses their prompt.

Standard ownership checks fail here for structural reasons, the authors show. Non-intrusive audits raise false alarms when independent models share data patterns. Backdoor-style intrusive methods also break under prompt learning's traits. SWAP instead uses sequential watermarking designed for this setting. Reliable auditing could let prompt creators share their work without losing control of it.
arxiv-2511-04911:
Piotr Kowalski, Omar León Sánchez, and Amador Martin-Pizarro give a new account of forking in the theory of fields that are closed under a set of derivations, in positive characteristic. Their work sits in model theory, where forking tracks when facts add real new information.

Using algebra with derivations, the authors show that types over closed sets in the real sort do not split. They also study one key equation and prove its non-zero solutions form a strongly minimal set with split geometry. That set turns out to be free over the prime field.
arxiv-2511-05011:
Ravshan Ashurov and Elbek Husanov tackle an inverse problem for a fractional subdiffusion equation whose rates change with time. One rate, the reaction term, is unknown, and the task is to find it from added data on the solution.

First the authors prove the forward problem has one and only one solution. Then they prove the same for the inverse task, using a fixed-point theorem based on shrinking maps. They note this is the first such study for this class with time-linked rates, a step for models where spread slows over time.
arxiv-2511-05311:
Valeriu Dimidov and co-authors test large language model agents as cleaners of maintenance logs, a key data source for predicting faults in cars. Predictive upkeep has been held back by cost, scarce shared data, and a lack of expert hands.

Messy logs, with typos, short forms, and mixed styles, poison the models that learn from them. The agents take on the cleaning pipeline steps, which the authors test for quality and speed. Their work checks if such agents can lift car upkeep from lab demos toward plant-floor use, where clean logs are rare.
arxiv-2511-05411:
Zsolt Páles and a co-author establish when Hölder, Minkowski, and Jensen style inequalities hold for generalized quasi-arithmetic means. Such means swap the usual average's fixed rule for a chosen monotone generating function, which widens the family a lot.

The authors give necessary and sufficient terms for a broad functional inequality in these means. Special cases then yield the named inequalities. Their generating functions need only be strictly monotone, not also continuous, which is a wider base than the classic one. Sharp terms of this kind anchor many proofs in analysis and probability.
arxiv-2511-05711:
Rafael Ceja Ayala, Isaac Harris, and General Ozochiawaeze extend a shape-finding method to waves bending in a thin elastic plate. The task is inverse scattering: from waves measured far away, locate a hidden object inside the plate that absorbs energy. Because the plate is thin, the wave motion follows the biharmonic equation.

The authors rigorously justify the factorization method for this setting. It gives a yes-or-no test for whether any chosen point lies inside the object, using only far-field spectral data. They also study a simpler Born approximation for weak scatterers. Numerically they measure its error against exact data, showing it is limited but still useful for faint objects.
arxiv-2511-05911:
Marcy Robertson and Chandan Singh connect a deep symmetry group of algebra to the geometry of braids and tangles. The profinite Grothendieck-Teichmüller group is a vast symmetry object first built for number theory. The authors identify it with the group of self-transformations of a completed operad of parenthesized ribbon braids.

That action carries over to an operad of framed configuration spaces. Using an associated metric prop, they also obtain an action of the group on a category of framed, unoriented tangles, and compare it with a known action by Kassel and Turaev. The rational version of their action gives a fresh proof that the cyclic framed little-disks operad is formal, a structural result in topology.
arxiv-2511-06111:
Aysin Tumay and co-authors teach an algorithm to wean heart-failure patients off mechanical blood pumps safely, using only past records. These pumps unload the left ventricle in cardiogenic shock, but weaning practice varies by care team and lacks data-driven rules. Learning from live patient interaction is not allowed, so the training must be offline.

Their framework pairs a new offline learning algorithm with a transformer-based digital twin of the circulation. The algorithm suppresses out-of-distribution actions and shapes rewards with clinical knowledge. The twin evaluates policies on rich physiological and clinical metrics. Theory backs the algorithm under mild assumptions. On real and synthetic data it beat standard offline baselines on reward and on clinical scores by wide margins.
arxiv-2511-06311:
Seiichi Yamamoto and colleagues give soft robots a sense of touch without burying sensors inside their skin. Their module clips onto the outside of a silicone skin and watches how the surface deforms, using reflected light to infer contact force. Keeping the sensor off the contact face protects it and preserves the robot's softness.

Compression tests showed a steady force response matching theory, with low hysteresis and high repeatability across cycles. Mounted on a soft gripper, the module reliably detected grasp events. Because it reads skin strain patterns, the same idea could estimate joint angles or actuator states, offering a durable and simple route to force sensing.
arxiv-2511-06511:
Jean Lévine and Jaume Franch extend the checklist for when a control system counts as flat by pure prolongation. Differential flatness lets a system's behavior be captured by a few free outputs, but general tests for flatness are famously intractable. Driftless systems, those with no motion of their own, are a friendlier special case.

The paper covers driftless systems whose state count is twice the input count, or one less. Flatness by pure prolongation is a stricter flavor with a remarkably simple output computation and mild verification demands. The new conditions differ from earlier criteria, so the family of systems certified as flat grows beyond what previous tests could recognize.
arxiv-2511-06611:
Jiajun Jiang, Xiao Hu, Wancheng Liu, and Wei Jiang measure the exact centers of circles seen by laser scanners and cameras. Aligning a LiDAR unit with a camera, a standard calibration step, rests on matching a circle's three-dimensional center with its projected center in the image. Standard pipelines bias both numbers, and the ellipse center in a photo is not the projected circle center under perspective.

A conformal geometric algebra estimator, hardened by random sample consensus, recovers center, tilt, and radius jointly from noisy or partial laser points. A chord-length test then locates the projected center, resolving its two-way ambiguity by homography checks. Synthetic and real sensor trials showed better center accuracy and smaller calibration errors.
arxiv-2511-06811:
Gines R Pérez Teruel and Antonio Peña Peña explore a modified theory of gravity that leaves Einstein's geometric side of the equations untouched. Instead, the matter side is weighted by a function of the trace of the energy-momentum tensor, changing how matter curves spacetime. The change acts like a renormalization of matter, strong at high densities and vanishing at low ones.

Within this setup the authors find a robust window of parameters where the universe bounces smoothly instead of beginning in a singularity. Density stays bounded at the bounce, and at large scales the theory recovers the standard cosmological model. The mechanism offers a route to singularity resolution that keeps the tested successes of general relativity and standard cosmology.
arxiv-2511-06911:
Yazeed Tawalbeh, Marwa Ghazi, and Mauro Fernandes Pereira present a theory for controlling nanoparticle size with a magnetic field. Their system joins first-principles thermodynamics with a sphere packing picture of how particles nucleate and grow. It is calibrated on diamagnetic silver nanoparticles, which measure about twenty nanometers across with no field and only five nanometers at 250 millitesla.

The model yields a closed-form relation between particle radius and field strength that reproduces the observed shift toward smaller particles. Within classic capillarity, the field lowers the barrier to nucleation, favoring many small particles over fewer large ones. The authors show the approach is robust for radii above three nanometers, discuss where very small or ferromagnetic particles break its assumptions, and note it extends to paramagnetic systems.
arxiv-2511-07611:
Dale Worley classifies the lattices hiding behind the Robinson-Schensted algorithm. That celebrated procedure links permutations to tableaus, and its variants arise from growth diagrams built on special lattices. Known examples share strict traits: modular structure, a weighted-differential rule, and distributivity.

Worley classifies all lattices meeting those criteria. One new family appears, though it cannot build a Schensted-type correspondence. The Young-Fibonacci family stands as the lone known exception to distributivity. A near-complete census tells combinatorists where to look, and where not to, for new tableau algorithms. Classification results like this quietly bound a whole research direction.
arxiv-2511-07711:
Felipe Arenas-Uribe, Hasan Poonawala, and Jesse Hoagg make spacecraft thruster choices solvable in real time. Thrusters fire in discrete settings, turning trajectory planning into mixed-integer problems too slow for safety-critical rendezvous. Lossless convexification rewrites such problems as convex ones without losing optimality, when conditions allow.

Geometric conditions for that trick are pinned down for linear time-varying systems. Reformulating cost form into terminal form through an epigraph step preserves system normality, a key condition. The framework targets rendezvous missions where answers must arrive fast and be provably right. Convex speed with integer fidelity is a rare combination.
arxiv-2511-08311:
Hala Alqubelat and co-authors monitor accretion bursts in DQ Tau, a young binary star system still surrounded by a protoplanetary disk. In eccentric close binaries, accretion pulses near closest approach as gas streamers feed the stars. Spectroscopy from the Very Large Telescope, taken alongside a JWST disk chemistry program, lets the team refine the orbit and track which star gains mass when.

The argument of periastron has advanced by thirty degrees. This apsidal motion may be caused by the massive disk acting like a third body. An unseen companion with a stated minimum mass is another possible cause. Calcium emission shows the primary accreting more at periastron, the secondary dominating afterward, and unusually strong accretion at apastron.
arxiv-2511-08711:
Abhipsa Basu and three co-authors fight bias in image classifiers by manufacturing fairer training data with diffusion models. Skewed datasets teach skewed rules, as when blond hair in face photos comes mostly from women, and plain text-to-image generation often drifts away from the real data distribution.

Fine-tuning tricks such as LoRA and DreamBooth teach the generator from each group's own samples, so synthetic images stay faithful to their group. Clustering within a group and training one generator per cluster keeps any single model from being swamped by internal variety. Classifiers pretrained on the balanced synthetic data, then fine-tuned on real photos, beat plain Stable Diffusion data on average. They match top debiasing methods and pull ahead as dataset bias gets more severe.
arxiv-2511-09511:
Diego Garcia Ovalle and Aurelien Manchon sort out two rival conversion routes in materials lacking inversion symmetry. Both turn spin and orbital currents into electric charge signals. The Hall effects deflect currents sideways, while the Rashba-Edelstein effect converts them at surfaces and interfaces. Studies often stress one and slight the other.

The authors build a general formalism treating both on an equal footing, using only large-scale observables. They test it on ferroelectric germanium telluride, finding an effective Rashba value smaller than reported before for that material. Feeding those values into a drift-diffusion model, they show the charge current produced is governed mainly by the Rashba-Edelstein effect. The Hall contributions, by contrast, play a secondary role there.
arxiv-2511-09911:
Sara C. Beck and nine co-authors report the emission-line results from JWST observations of the supernebula in the dwarf galaxy NGC 5253. This compact radio-infrared nebula is powered by a very young, bright super star cluster buried inside it. Using the MIRI medium-resolution spectrometer across roughly five to twenty-five micrometers, they detected more than seventy emission lines from hydrogen, molecular hydrogen, and metal ions.

Extinction derived from hydrogen recombination lines against the radio continuum turned out nearly flat with wavelength across this range. Nebular conditions fit very young, very massive stars, and every region showed high excitation. Oddly, the spatial pattern of the strongest lines suggests photons near fifty electron volts are escaping the core despite thirty-five magnitudes of visual extinction.
arxiv-2511-10411:
Benjamin Stoler, Jonathan Francis, and Jean Oh study motion prediction for self-driving cars, focusing on rare and dangerous situations. Real driving data holds too few of these cases to test systems properly. They build new test sets by splitting driving scenes into ego and social context factors, then holding out combinations never seen in training.

Performance gaps of 5.0 percent in the closed-world setting and 14.7 percent in the open-world one appear for a strong baseline. Their fix adds modular gating and a difficulty prediction head inside the predictor. The gaps shrink to 2.8 percent and 11.5 percent respectively, while everyday in-distribution accuracy improves as well.
arxiv-2511-10511:
Ana Vieira, Thais Nascimento, Juan Cruz, and Willer Costa work in PI-theory, the study of polynomial identities that algebras satisfy. Their subject is central polynomials, a special family whose values always land in an algebra's center, examined here for superalgebras graded by sign.

The paper focuses on the only supervarieties whose graded codimensions grow almost polynomially, built from five specific superalgebras including the Grassmann algebra and upper triangular matrices. For each minimal subvariety, the authors find generators of the space of central polynomials, compute the central codimensions exactly, and give the full decomposition of the central graded cocharacters. Together these results complete a full census of central behavior for this borderline class of supervarieties.
arxiv-2511-10611:
Alagappan Ramanathan, Eunju Kang, Dongsu Han, and Sangeetha Abdu Jyothi describe ArachNet, a system that uses large language model agents to build Internet measurement workflows on their own. Measurement research has an access problem: serious analyses require stitching together special tools, and network operators facing a disruption need that expertise fast.

ArachNet's core insight is that expert measurement work follows predictable patterns. Four special agents mirror the expert process, from breaking down the problem to building the solution. Tested on harder and harder Internet resilience scenarios, the system generated workflows whose reasoning and outputs matched specialist work. It handled multi-framework integrations that usually take days of manual work. The authors argue such tools can widen access to research-quality measurement.
arxiv-2511-10711:
Aqsa Mushtaq, Chaimae Banouni, Mahboob Ul Haq, and S. M. Zangi study how quantum correlations hold up in a pair of qubits driven by external pulses and battered by decoherence. They track three measures together: negativity, quantum discord, and a memory-assisted entropic uncertainty, across damping, dephasing, and pulse-induced noise.

Coupling strength and energy splitting shape the dynamics strongly, producing oscillations under weak coupling and protecting existing entanglement under strong coupling. Negativity proves the most fragile measure, discord lasts longer, and the entropic measure shows quantum signatures surviving even when both others fade. Pulse amplitude and width can steer the creation and loss of correlations, and a partially entangled starting state weathers perturbations better than a separable one. The authors frame the results as design guidance for quantum computing and secure communication.
arxiv-2511-10811:
François Charton and Ashvni Narayanan train transformers to compute long steps of the Collatz sequence and then dissect exactly what the models learned. Predicting a distant successor in the sequence is a genuinely hard arithmetic task, and accuracy swings wildly with the number base used to write the digits.

Accuracy reaches 99.7 percent in bases 24 and 32 but collapses toward 25 percent in base 3, yet every model follows the same learning pattern. Training proceeds class by class, where each class of inputs shares a residue and a loop length readable from its binary form, and models master one class at a time. Almost all errors are near misses in estimating loop length, not hallucinations, suggesting the hard part of such arithmetic is learning the control structure, not the calculation.
arxiv-2511-11111:
Xin Wang, Pietro Lodi Rizzini, and their colleagues present SMART, a stand-in model that predicts how long programs run on Dragonfly supercomputer networks. Dragonfly links are shared, so jobs slow each other down, and full event simulation of that clash is too costly for large or live use. A learned stand-in inside the simulation offers a faster path.

SMART joins a graph network, which reads the network's layout, with a language model that reads change over time, both fed by port-level router data. It beat standard stats and learning baselines on runtime forecasts. The authors argue it can power efficient hybrid simulation of large Dragonfly systems.
arxiv-2511-11311:
Petros Koutsouvelis, Matej Gazda, and their colleagues pre-train large foundation models on unlabeled brain MRI scans so the models learn anatomy that transfers across scan types. Most self-supervised frameworks were shaped for natural images, and their fit to multi-modal MRI, where one patient yields several contrast types, is underexplored. A shared representation could improve few-shot work such as lesion segmentation.

Their modality-invariant setup aligns representations across MRI types during large-scale pre-training. Tested on stroke and epilepsy lesion segmentation, results suggest a twist: despite good cross-modality alignment, segmentation gains came mostly from keeping fine-grained modality-specific features. Model checkpoints and code are released publicly.
arxiv-2511-11511:
Raúl Alonso, Kâzım Büyükboduk, Antonio Cauchi, and Antonio Lei build an Iwasawa theory for diagonal cycles. The setting is hard: all three factors are non-ordinary at the prime p. The authors call this case trito-non-ordinary. The objects are triple products of modular forms over a quaternion algebra. The third factor moves inside a Hida family.

A signed Euler system of diagonal cycles is set up. When the algebra splits and the family has complex multiplication, a signed anticyclotomic theory follows. A main conjecture in the style of Perrin-Riou is stated to match. The work extends deep links between cycles, L-values, and Selmer groups. It pushes them into ground that was largely unexplored.
arxiv-2511-11711:
Tsogt-Ochir Enkhbayar asks which features found by sparse autoencoders inside a neural network are real patterns and which are accidents. Sparse autoencoders are a leading tool for interpreting models, but their long feature lists mix genuine computation with spurious correlation.

Model-X knockoffs, a statistical device that builds fake twin features, are adapted to feature selection with false discovery rate control and finite-sample guarantees. Of five hundred twelve high-activity features for sentiment classification in a small language model, one hundred twenty-nine were selected at the target rate, showing a strong separation from the rest. About a quarter of examined features carried real task signal, a sobering ratio for interpretability work.
arxiv-2511-12011:
Sam Buss and four co-authors formalize a landmark result in computer science: Reingold's theorem that the complexity classes L and SL are equal. In plain terms, a problem solvable with very little memory in a directed graph setting can also be solved in the symmetric case with the same tight limits. They carry out the proof inside a weak formal theory for logspace reasoning.

The formal proof follows an alternative route by Rozenman and Vadhan, and avoids talk of eigenvalues, which the theory cannot easily handle. Instead it uses combinatorial facts about graph expansion. As a result, the theories for logspace and symmetric logspace reasoning turn out to be the same.
arxiv-2511-12511:
Jialiang Shen and ten co-authors present DINO-Detect, a framework for spotting AI-generated images even after motion blur degrades them. Detectors often fail in real settings because blur wipes out fine textures and the high-frequency traces that reveal a synthetic image. Handheld photos and compressed video make that failure common.

The method uses teacher-student distillation. A large teacher model trained on sharp images gives stable, rich representations, and stays frozen to keep its generalization. A student trained on blurred copies learns to match the teacher's features and outputs, so its representations stay consistent under motion damage. Experiments report state-of-the-art detection under both blurred and clean conditions.
arxiv-2511-12911:
Muhammad Nadeem, MirSaleh Bahavarnia, and Ahmad F. Taha compare two philosophies for controlling a renewables-heavy power grid. Solar and wind make grid dynamics harder to model, while sensors now stream rich real-time data to control centers. That tempts operators toward reinforcement learning controllers that learn from data with no model at all. The authors pose the wide-area feedback control problem on a detailed nonlinear model of such a grid, then solve it both ways: a model-free learning design. A model-based design built on Lyapunov stability theory with guarantees.

Earlier learning studies often used simplified grids; this study keeps the full dynamics. Case studies and analysis then lay out where each approach is stronger. The authors do not crown a winner. Their aim is a fair, detailed account of whether data-driven control should displace its model-driven counterpart in grids that can least afford instability.
arxiv-2511-13011:
Qingsen Ma and five co-authors reconstruct three-dimensional scenes from photographs taken almost in the dark. Novel view synthesis builds a scene you can look around in from a set of images, and 3D Gaussian splatting is its current fast method. In extreme low light it breaks down: brightening each view independently makes colors disagree between viewpoints and warps the geometry. DTGS instead optimizes enhancement and reconstruction together in a cycle, with a thermal branch supervising color restoration and geometry, and a Retinex decomposition inside the loop separating reflectance from illumination.

For evaluation the team built RGBT-LOW, a multi-view dataset pairing visible and thermal images under severe illumination degradation. Against low-light enhancement and reconstruction baselines, DTGS gave better radiometric consistency, geometric fidelity, and color stability. Thermal cameras see heat, not light, so they stay informative exactly where ordinary cameras fail.
arxiv-2511-13111:
Rasmus F. Orsoe and seven co-authors release NuBench, an open benchmark for reconstructing neutrino events with deep learning. Neutrino telescopes in water and ice detect faint Cherenkov light from neutrino hits, and reconstruction means working backward from that light to the neutrino's energy, direction, and interaction point. Each experiment built its own data and methods, which blocked fair comparison. NuBench supplies seven simulated datasets with nearly one hundred thirty million muon-neutrino interactions, across six detector geometries drawn from real and proposed detectors.

The team evaluates four reconstruction algorithms, including ones used by the KM3NeT and IceCube collaborations, on up to five tasks from energy to inelasticity. Pulse-level and event-level data are both included for water and ice environments. Prepared for an instrumentation journal, NuBench gives the field shared ground truth. Work can now be compared across detectors instead of within each team.
arxiv-2511-13211:
Yijia Fan and five co-authors align text with three-dimensional objects at a scale of millions. Fine-grained 3D-text alignment, matching a phrase to the right part of the right object, degrades badly as databases grow. Their framework, 3DAlign-DAER, attacks both phases: in training, a dynamic attention policy represents alignment as learnable token-to-point attentions, fused hierarchically. Calibrates those weights with Monte Carlo tree search driven by a hybrid reward; in retrieval, an efficient hierarchical search strategy keeps accuracy and speed up over large embedding spaces.

To train and test at scale, the team built Align3D-2M, a dataset of two million text-3D pairs with fine-grained annotations. The system targets cross-modal retrieval and classification across diverse tasks. Searchable 3D libraries, for games, manufacturing parts, and digital twins, need exactly this: language queries that land on geometrically specific results, fast, at catalog scale.
arxiv-2511-13911:
Vasiliki Tassopoulou, Charis Stamouli, Haochang Shou, and two co-authors add reliable uncertainty bounds to forecasts of patient biomarkers over time. Predicting how a brain marker linked to Alzheimer's disease will move is useful, but clinic visits come at random times and wrong forecasts carry real risk. Their method extends conformal prediction to this irregular-timing setting.

A new nonconformity score produces bands that are guaranteed to cover the true path with a probability the user picks. Across many standard and leading predictors, the bands hit their target coverage while staying tighter than baseline bands. Group-specific versions hold up across demographic and clinical subgroups, and the authors show the bands can flag patients for closer review.
arxiv-2511-14611:
Charles Cheng Ji and Brandon Kong present SecureSign, a mobile Web3 wallet architecture that tries to keep both security and ease of use. Mobile Web3 loses most users, raising acquisition costs sharply. Embedded wallets are easy but vulnerable to clickjacking. App wallets are safer but lose users through downloads and app switching.

SecureSign adapts desktop extension sandboxing to mobile through a provider standard. Decentralized apps run in isolated frames inside a trusted parent app. Threat analysis shows resistance to clickjacking, overlay, and skimming attacks. A drop in software kit needs no code changes for existing apps. Native mobile features like push alerts remain available.
arxiv-2511-15011:
Rishikesh Jha and four co-authors study why fundamental and harmonic emissions of solar radio type II bursts vary in relative strength. Type II bursts drift slowly and show band splitting and fine structure. Sometimes the fundamental is stronger, sometimes the harmonic is. That reversal lacked a thorough observational explanation.

The team analyze fifty-eight bursts with both emissions over fourteen years of data. Spectrometers at several sites plus a dedicated solar spectrograph supply the records. Intensity ratios are tracked against heliographic longitude of the source. Patterns in that dependence point to viewing geometry effects. The long baseline makes the statistical picture more reliable than single event studies.
arxiv-2511-15111:
Michael Fodroci and Teruyuki Kitabayashi adjust a neutrino mixing model so it reproduces all three measured mixing angles at their current best-fit values. Neutrinos swap flavors as they travel, and the three angles governing that swap are now measured quite precisely. A realistic model of the underlying mass pattern must land on those numbers, not just near them.

Their modified TM2 model hits every angle within one standard deviation of the best fits. The authors also stress that the fit is robust: if future measurements nudge the best-fit values, the model can still track them. Simple, sturdy mixing patterns like this help theorists guess the symmetry behind neutrino masses.
arxiv-2511-15211:
Xinli Tao, Xin Dong, and Xuezhong Zhou present OEMA, a team of cooperating AI agents that finds medical terms in clinical notes without any labeled training examples. Pulling diseases, drugs, and procedures out of electronic health records is vital for research and care, but hand-labeling records is expensive. Language models can do the task zero-shot, yet their example choice and self-checking are often sloppy.

OEMA splits the work among agents: one drafts candidate examples, another filters them at the token level using the SNOMED CT medical ontology, and the design adds self-improvement on top. Matching example granularity to the task is a core concern throughout. The framework aims at dependable clinical extraction with no annotation budget.
arxiv-2511-15411:
Wenlun Zhang, Yunshan Zhong, and three co-authors present D4C, a way to shrink vision-language models without ever seeing real training data. Quantization compresses a model by storing its numbers more coarsely, and data-free methods do it with synthetic stand-in data, which suits private or lost data sets. Applied naively to CLIP-style models, though, accuracy falls hard.

The authors trace the damage to synthetic images that are semantically thin and too alike within each image. D4C synthesizes richer, more varied pseudo-images instead, starting with prompt-guided semantic injection that aligns generated pictures with meaningful content. As the first data-free quantization framework built for CLIP, it aims to keep compressed multimodal models useful on phones and edge hardware.
arxiv-2511-16311:
Pacôme Van Overschelde studies exact locally conformally symplectic manifolds, geometric spaces that look symplectic up to a local change of scale set by the Lee form. The paper asks a quantitative question: which rescalings of the Lee form keep the structure exact, a property summed up as the elasticity of the pair.

From elasticity, Van Overschelde characterizes manifolds of the first kind. The main theorem shows that a rank-one exact manifold admitting an exact pair, with bounded complement of elasticity, must be a mapping torus. Mapping tori over closed contact manifolds meet the condition in return. A further link ties the elasticity limits of such a torus to the long-run average of the contact map's conformal factor. It also yields bounds on that factor.
arxiv-2511-16511:
Yuenong Ling, Imran Hayat, Konrad Goc, and Adrian Lozano-Duran present the baseline of a general-purpose data-driven wall model for large-eddy simulation of low-speed flows. Wall models predict the shear stress at a solid surface without resolving the thin near-wall layer, and classic equilibrium models fail on curved walls, strong pressure gradients, and separation.

Following a building-block principle, the model learns essential physics from simple flows and aims to generalize to complex geometry. A neural network regresses wall shear stress from local, dimensionless inputs chosen by information-theoretic criteria. Training data include a new direct simulation set for boundary layers under favorable and adverse pressure gradients. Across 140 test datasets the baseline beat the equilibrium model in ninety percent of cases.
arxiv-2511-17311:
Anjitha John William and four co-authors measure how quasars cluster on the sky in the Kilo-Degree Survey's fourth data release, and what that clustering says about their homes. Quasars were selected from images rather than spectra, so their distances come from photometric redshifts. The team improved those distances with a deep learning method combining survey imaging and magnitudes, trained on recent spectroscopic catalogs, then assembled about 157,000 quasars across a wide redshift range.

Split into four distance bins, the quasars' angular clustering was compared with dark matter predictions to extract their effective bias, which grew steadily with redshift. The bias implies the quasars live in dark matter halos of a characteristic mass that changes little across the bins. Stellar contamination proved negligible, but the assumed redshift distribution mattered greatly. The study is the first cosmological use of KiDS quasars.
arxiv-2511-17411:
Nikolay Nikolov and six co-authors argue that robot foundation models fail to generalize largely because their vision-language backbones never learned three-dimensional structure. Those backbones were trained on flat image and text tasks, while robot control happens in 3D space. Collecting enough robot demonstrations to teach the missing geometry is costly. The team's alternative: enrich ordinary, easy-to-collect images with 3D annotations and teach the backbone spatial understanding from those.

Their 3D-aware model, SPEAR-VLM, infers object coordinates in space from a single image. On top of it sits SPEAR-1, a robot foundation model joining grounded 3D perception with language-instructed control. Trained on about 45 million frames from public robot datasets, SPEAR-1 matched or beat leading models while using twenty times fewer robot demonstrations. Weights and the 3D-annotated datasets are publicly released.
arxiv-2511-17611:
Lucía Schmidt-Santiago, David Rodríguez-Temporal, Carlos Sevilla-Salcedo, and Vanessa Gómez-Verdejo explore making synthetic microbe spectra to aid clinical identification. The lab method in question reads a microbe's mass spectrum and names it quickly and well, but data-driven tools are held back by small, uneven, and unstandardised spectral collections. The team asks whether generated spectra can fill those gaps.

They adapt three kinds of generative model, based on autoencoders, adversarial training, and diffusion, to produce spectra labelled by species. The fakes are then judged for realism and variety with several measures. If synthetic spectra prove faithful, labs could train stronger diagnostic tools without waiting years to gather rare samples, a point of value for clinical microbiology.
arxiv-2511-18011:
Jun Zhang, Xin Zhang, Jie Feng, and five co-authors benchmark multimodal language models on fine grained spatial understanding in city road scenes. General spatial tests miss the small details that matter on roads, so they center the benchmark on road markings and the traffic system they form.

RoadBench contains thousands of hand checked cases from bird's eye and first person images gathered in five Chinese cities, across eight tasks that move from local recognition to global reasoning. Testing twenty mainstream models shows large shortcomings: on some tasks models fall below simple rule based or random baselines. The benchmark aims to push spatial skills forward.
arxiv-2511-18311:
S. V. Gabielkov and six co-authors test how faint a crystal signal their data method can still find. In X-ray diffraction a phase in a mix shows as small peaks over a noisy base. Peaks weaker than the noise are most often lost, so trace phases go missed.

The team find the signal to noise levels at which their method still pulls out such weak peaks. Weak peaks from quartz serve as the test case. In use, the method can name the phases in a mixed sample even when a phase makes up as little as a tenth of a percent by weight. Up to eight phases can be told apart this way. The gain aids checks of mixed raw materials.
arxiv-2511-18411:
Sultan Alrashed, Chadi Helwe, and Francesco Orabona build high grade Arabic training data by translation. Good Arabic data for the first training stage exists, but large sets with multi turn chats, reasoning, and tool use are scarce. Plain translation can scale, yet the later training stage needs far tighter quality than raw output gives.

SmolKalam translates the Smoltalk2 set with a team of models that vote and cross check, then filters for quality. The team also test, by controlled cuts, which translation tricks work best for standard decoder only models. The result is a large, clean Arabic set aimed at post training. The pipeline shows how care at scale can lift translated data to a high bar.
arxiv-2511-18511:
Ashkan Javaherian releases an open MATLAB package that turns ultrasound travel data into sound speed maps of tissue. Sound speed shifts with tissue type, so a map can flag disease. The package traces rays in pairs through the body model to link each measure to a path.

Two rebuild routes ship with the code. A travel time route gives a coarse, low contrast map with few false marks, fast. A ray Born route blends ray paths with a wave scatter model for a sharp map. Early coarse maps seed the sharp route. Four ray tracers are checked against known exact paths and lengths. Tests on fake data with known truth back both routes.
arxiv-2511-18611:
Mengdi Wang, Efe Bozkir, and Enkelejda Kasneci scale split learning, a way to train one network across clients and a server with no raw data shared. The net is cut in two: clients hold the front part, the server the rest. Step by step training scales poorly, while parallel forms pile load on the server and lose accuracy to client drift and lag.

CycleSL drops the merge step that causes much of that cost. It treats server side training as its own higher level task, in the spirit of alternating block updates, and cycles work between clients and server. The frame plugs into past methods with ease. Gains in scale and score are the aim. Private joint training on spread devices is the use case.
arxiv-2511-18811:
Yuqiu Jiang and five co-authors curb long tail bias in human object interaction detection with a cache that needs no training. The task names what a person does with an object in a scene. Vision language models lift scores, but rare pairs starve for examples, and past fixes pay with extra training or prompt tuning.

Their Adaptive Diversity Cache builds a store per class at inference time, stocked with high confidence, varied features as they stream in. Cache size per class adapts to need. The module plugs into past detectors as is. Rare pairs gain support from their own cached best cases. Field use on skewed scene sets is the aim.
arxiv-2511-19011:
Jiale Zhang and five co-authors build a vehicle following system that runs on one fisheye camera alone. Platooning, where cars follow in tight train, lifts road capacity and cuts fuel use. Past systems lean on lane marks or costly precision sensors, which narrows where they can run.

Their end to end method learns the follow task from camera input in general scenes, not just marked lanes. A semantic mask fights causal confusion when many frames are fused, a flaw where the model copies the lead car's past in place of reacting. A dynamic sampling scheme tracks the lead car's path with care. One cheap eye thus steers the follow task.
arxiv-2511-19111:
Hai Ci, Ziheng Peng, Pei Yang, Yingxin Xuan, and Mike Zheng Shou release DiffSeg30k, a data set for finding AI-edited regions inside images. Diffusion editors can alter a small region so realistically that whole-image detectors miss the point: the task is to localise the edit, not just flag the picture. Their set holds thirty thousand diffusion-edited images with pixel-level annotations marking exactly what was changed, collected from real-world image sources for diversity.

Local edits come from eight leading diffusion models, and each image goes through up to three rounds of editing in sequence, as real misuse would. A vision-language pipeline picks meaningful regions and writes context-aware prompts covering additions, removals, and attribute changes. The public data set gives detection researchers a fine-grained test that matches how edited fakes are actually made.
arxiv-2511-20211:
Yu, Zhan, Wang, and colleagues unify image tasks that need transparency. Their 2025 paper presents OmniAlpha for RGBA generation and editing. RGBA images carry an alpha channel for see-through regions. Single-task models handle alpha but lack range. Unified models, meanwhile, ignore alpha entirely.

OmniAlpha treats layered images as sequences to transform. A new position method, MSRoPE-BiL, tracks the layer axis. Its diffusion transformer processes many input and output layers. Layers can extend in both directions along that axis. A dataset called AlphaLayers powers the training. One thousand high-grade multi-layer triplets were synthesized automatically. Twenty-one diverse tasks were trained jointly. Matting, layer splitting, and completion all improved together. Mask-free matting error fell by nearly eighty-five percent. Human judges preferred its completions over ninety percent of the time. Shared training beat strong specialist baselines overall. Layer-aware generation gets its first generalist model.
arxiv-2511-20711:
José Camacho lays out in 2025 a short rulebook for validating data-driven models, checking a model's skill on data it has never seen. Bad validation is everywhere: test data leaks into training, scores get reported selectively, and headline numbers fail to match real-world use. Regulators have noticed, and the EU AI Act of 2024 makes validation a legal requirement for higher-risk systems.

Camacho's five rules push practitioners toward honest, comparable evaluation. The first demands independent data for building a model and for judging its generalisation, since reusing data inflates scores. The second requires the test data to match both the population the model will serve and its real-life application. The remaining rules extend the same discipline to planning, limitations, and reporting. No scheme is flawless, Camacho concedes, but the rules make plans sufficient for practical use, with limits stated openly and metrics others can compare.
arxiv-2511-20911:
Pratik Brahma and colleagues build in 2025 dedicated hardware that samples frustrated magnets far faster than graphics processors. Frustrated lattices, whose bonds cannot all be satisfied at once, host exotic phases but resist simulation. Restricted Boltzmann machines can represent their states, yet fully connected versions waste effort on interactions the lattice lacks. The team's convolutional version bakes in the lattice's repeating symmetry, so its filters mirror the unit cell's bonds and parameter count stops growing with system size.

On the classical Shastry-Sutherland Ising lattice, they simulated up to 324 spins and recovered every known phase, including the long-range ordered fractional plateau. The chip also probed behaviour at critical points and inside spin-liquid phases. Sampling ran 3 to 5 orders of magnitude faster than on GPUs, with step times from 33 nanoseconds to 120 milliseconds. Its time-to-solution lands within a factor of about a hundred of quantum annealer times, at room temperature.
arxiv-2511-21011:
Sid Bharthulwar, Stone Tao, and Hao Su fix in 2025 a subtle flaw in how massively parallel reinforcement learning resets its worlds. GPU simulators run thousands of environments at once, and short rollouts keep updates frequent. But when every environment resets in sync, each training batch covers the same slice of the task, skewing the learning signal and destabilising training. Their remedy is staggered resets: start and reset each environment at a varied point in the task horizon.

Batches then mix early, middle, and late task states, restoring temporal diversity. Toy environments reveal which task dimensions benefit most, such as those with strong phase structure. On challenging high-dimensional robotics tasks, staggered resets delivered much better sample efficiency, quicker convergence in wall-clock time, and stronger final policies than synchronised rollouts. The advantage also grows as more parallel environments are added, making it a cheap default for GPU-era training pipelines.
arxiv-2511-21211:
Rubén Fernández-Farelo and colleagues argue in 2025 that gene hunting works better when most genes are thrown away first. Gene prioritisation ranks genes by their likely role in a process, here dietary restriction, but omics datasets carry thousands of features and no confirmed negative examples. Their pipeline inserts Fast-mRMR, a feature selector that keeps features relevant yet minimally redundant, before classification.

They tested Gene Ontology annotations and PathDIP data, separately and combined, on dietary restriction datasets, keeping 5 percent of features for the big sets and 25 percent for the smaller PathDIP set. Classifiers were a Balanced Random Forest and CatBoost. Judgement used nested ten-by-five cross-validation. The combined feature set had been weak because of its size. With Fast-mRMR it reached an AUC-ROC of 0.872 and an F1 score of 0.560, significant at the 0.05 level. Simpler models, the authors conclude, can be the reliable ones.
arxiv-2511-21611:
Eli Gendreau-Distler and seventeen coauthors clock a giant planet circling a dead star, extending a timing record fivefold, in 2025. WD 1856 b transits its white dwarf host, a system that puzzles theorists because the planet sits too close to have survived the star's red-giant phase in place. High-eccentricity tidal migration, a slow spiral inward, is the favored explanation, and earlier timing hinted the orbit might still be growing.

Adding 18 new transit measurements stretched the baseline from 311 to 1,498 epochs, and the growth signal vanished: the period is constant, changing by only 0.04 milliseconds per year, plus or minus 0.43 in the same units. That stillness bounds the planet's tidal quality factor above 3.1 million, comparable to Jupiter's value in our own system. The team also ruled out any companion heavier than 4.1 Jupiter masses with a period under 1,500 days, and capped the planet's orbital eccentricity below one percent.
arxiv-2511-21811:
Gao reviews a puzzling result from the Belle II experiment in Japan, which saw more B meson decays into a kaon plus something invisible than the Standard Model predicts. A popular explanation adds an axion-like particle, a light, hypothetical, as-yet-undiscovered particle that escapes detectors unseen. Gao focuses on one specific theory of such particles, the DFSZ model.

Two updates stand out. First, certain two-loop diagrams, normally expected to be minor corrections, can actually dominate the simpler one-loop diagrams, so leaving them out badly misjudges the predicted rate. Second, the low-energy version of the theory misses an unusual effect called apparent non-decoupling, where heavy particles fail to fade away as expected. The decay itself fits the data well at 3.6 standard deviations of significance for a particle near 2 GeV in mass, which makes getting the theory right worthwhile.
arxiv-2511-21911:
The ATLAS Collaboration reports a search for Higgs bosons decaying into charm quark pairs. The team also measures Higgs decays into bottom quark pairs. Both use Higgs bosons produced by vector-boson fusion at the Large Hadron Collider. The data come from proton-proton collisions at 13 teraelectronvolts and at 13.6 teraelectronvolts, the higher of the two energies. The first dataset holds 37.5 inverse femtobarns and the second holds 51.5 inverse femtobarns of collisions.

No charm signal appeared, so the team sets an upper limit instead. The charm rate is at most 41 times the Standard Model prediction, where 28 was expected. Combined with an earlier search, the Higgs-charm coupling modifier is below 4.7, where a limit of 3.9 had been expected. The bottom-pair signal strength came out at 0.97, close to the predicted value of one. Combined with earlier results, the bottom signal reaches 3.2 standard deviations, the first evidence for this production mode.
arxiv-2511-22111:
Xu, Zhao, Tagsinsit, and colleagues, particle theorists, compute the spectrum of tetraquarks carrying the exotic quantum numbers 1−+. No ordinary quark-antiquark meson can have that combination, so any confirmed state is automatically an exotic four-quark object or hybrid. Working in a constituent quark model with Cornell-like potentials and spin corrections from the Breit-Fermi interaction, they calculate masses and branching patterns for light, charmonium-like, and fully-charm tetraquarks of this type.

The ground states land near 1.9, 4.2, and 6.6 GeV in the three sectors respectively. Decay ratios are worked out channel by channel, for example omega plus h1 versus eta plus f1 for the neutral light states, giving experimentalists concrete places to look. Comparing with observed exotic candidates, the authors conclude the reported eta1(1855) state is unlikely to be a compact tetraquark, a useful negative result for interpreting the growing exotic-hadron zoo.
arxiv-2511-22611:
Brito, Bernar, and Crispino compute light from a charged particle circling a black hole in a universe with a cosmological constant. The setting is a Schwarzschild-de Sitter black hole. The method is semiclassical: they calculate the probability amplitude for the orbiting charge to emit a photon, then derive emitted power and frequency spectra. Results are compared against scalar field radiation, minimal and conformal couplings, and the electromagnetic case around a Schwarzschild black hole.

For slow orbits, electromagnetic power is about twice the conformal-coupling scalar power, echoing the Schwarzschild behaviour, while for minimal coupling scalar power can exceed electromagnetic. The spectra differ too: the electromagnetic spectrum is broader, with lower multipoles contributing non-negligibly. The authors examine synchrotron-like emission from orbits near the photon sphere, where light itself circles the hole. Such calculations feed models of extreme-mass-ratio systems, targets for space-based wave detectors.
arxiv-2511-22711:
Münzenberg finds a shortcut to bubble speeds in cosmic phase transitions. During a first-order transition, bubbles of the new phase nucleate and grow, and their terminal wall velocity controls baryogenesis prospects and the gravitational wave signal for detectors like LISA. Computing it normally means solving the scalar field's equation of motion in a realistic plasma. Münzenberg instead studies a velocity-dependent modified potential, the pseudopotential.

The pseudopotential difference between two extrema equals the net outward pressure, so terminal velocities are those making the minima degenerate, zero net pressure. No simplified equation of state or guessed field profile is needed, provided the plasma stays in local equilibrium and temperature depends weakly on field gradients. In a singlet extension of the Standard Model, it reproduces the pressure dip for hybrid bubbles, implying stationary deflagrations are stable while detonations are unstable. It matches full velocities to about half a percent.
arxiv-2511-23211:
Turoczy and Lin improve online algorithms for multi-level aggregation with deadlines. Requests arrive over time at nodes of a tree, and each must be served before its deadline. Serving one request costs a root-to-node transmission. But batching several requests into one subtree transmission can be cheaper. And the algorithm must decide without seeing future arrivals, in settings from multicasting to supply chains.

Their memory-based method builds each transmission by extending subtrees used for requests. And it achieves a competitive ratio that improves the depth-based constant from six times the depth-plus-one factor to roughly e times that factor. A second algorithm is parameterized by the tree's caterpillar dimension, one for paths, two for caterpillars, three for lobsters, the first guarantee of its kind. It beats all prior ratios whenever that dimension grows more slowly than depth and tree size.
arxiv-2511-23311:
Sakajo and colleagues teach large vision-language models to act as automatic driving instructors. Watching two synchronized dashcam feeds at once, one facing the road and one facing the driver. The second view matters because some dangers, like a driver using a phone, are invisible from the road camera alone. And the team built a dataset of paired videos with step-by-step question-answer pairs about events and recommended actions.

Gold answers for the dataset were drafted by GPT-4o from human-annotated event labels, and the experiments compare off-the-shelf models against versions fine-tuned on this material. Pretrained models proved limited at the task, while the fine-tuned ones generated accurate, safety-aware instructions for the driver. Although detecting subtle or complex events in the videos remained difficult even after fine-tuning, a weakness their error analysis documents in detail in this domain.
arxiv-2511-23411:
Brivio and colleagues revisit Higgs pair production through gluon fusion inside Higgs Effective Field Theory. The more general of the two standard effective theories for physics beyond the Standard Model. Producing two Higgs bosons probes how one- and two-Higgs couplings to fermions and gauge bosons correlate. Correlations that stay linked in the rival SMEFT framework at dimension six but can fully decouple already at leading order in HEFT.

The authors show that a consistent power counting combined with next-to-leading-order diagrams forces the inclusion of higher-dimensional operators beyond the usual leading set. And they quantify what those extra operators do to observable distributions. Re-examining the kinematic benchmark scenarios used in experimental di-Higgs searches, they conclude the uncertainties on angular distributions must shrink sizably before such modifications could be distinguished. So robust operator identification will need a global fit across many observables.
arxiv-2512-00011:
Pablo Villacorta-Aylagas and co-authors present MRSeqStudio, a web platform for designing MRI sequences. Magnetic resonance imaging depends on pulse sequences, the timed patterns that produce each kind of scan. Building and testing them usually needs specialist software and hardware access.

Their free, open-source service pairs a sequence designer in the browser with the KomaMRI physics simulator behind it. The mix of accessibility, interactivity, and flexibility suits both teaching and research. Students can learn sequence design hands-on, without a scanner. Education and research are the twin audiences, since the same environment serves classroom learning and sequence development.
arxiv-2512-00311:
Intelligent tutoring systems work best when they know what a student understands right now. Jungyang Park and co-authors trace mathematical proficiency through problem-solving processes in 2025, rather than through answers alone. Traditional knowledge tracing models rely only on whether responses were correct.

Correctness hides the rich information inside a student's steps, false starts, and strategies. Using the process itself should improve predictions of future performance and make the model's judgments explainable to teachers. Better tracing supports tutoring that responds to how a student thinks, not just to a string of right and wrong marks. Problem-solving traces can be captured by tutoring software without extra testing time. That makes the approach cheap to add to systems already in classrooms.
arxiv-2512-00411:
Superconducting leads joined through a normal metal form Josephson junctions, workhorses of quantum devices. Bobkov and co-authors develop a theory of planar quasi-ballistic Josephson junctions in 2025. Multiple leads couple through a large, nearly ballistic normal metal crystal.

Their approach rests on quasiclassical Eilenberger equations. It emphasizes reflections of electrons from crystal surfaces or single impurities, a mechanism distinct from both purely ballistic and diffusive limits. The theory matches the multiterminal devices now being built, helping experimentalists predict supercurrents in cleaner, larger junctions. Quasi-ballistic means electrons cross the metal almost without scattering, yet reflections still matter. The framework is built to match the planar devices experimentalists now fabricate. For teams who build such links, the gain is a firm base for tests. They can check a new chip face to face with what the math says it should do.
arxiv-2512-00511:
Compressing speech for automatic recognition is different from compressing it for human ears. Ellison Murray, Morriel Kasher, and Predrag Spasojevic present a low-complexity speech codec using parametric dithering in 2025. Dithering, usually a perceptual trick, is justified here by proofs and by tests for recognition input.

The authors pin down what best recognition performance means under lossy input compression. Their parametric dithering technique then shapes the compression noise deliberately. A cheap codec that keeps recognition accuracy high would help voice assistants and transcription services run on low-bandwidth links and small devices. Recognition systems care about word errors, not how pleasant the audio sounds. Low complexity keeps the codec usable inside the recognition pipeline itself. For folks who build voice tools, the gain is a cheap front end. Speech can be shrunk hard, and the words still come through for the tool to read well.
arxiv-2512-00811:
Tony Puthenpurakal wrote a 2025 algebra paper on invariant rings. A finite group can act on a vector space, reshuffling its points by symmetry. The invariant ring collects the polynomial functions that the group leaves unchanged, a central object in algebra.

The paper studies fixed points and the grade of a Hilbert polynomial tied to that ring. The Hilbert polynomial counts dimensions of the ring's pieces and grows in a regular way for large sizes. Results like these link symmetry, counting, and depth in one package. They give algebraists sharper tools for rings that arise from group actions.
arxiv-2512-01411:
Fabrice Baudoin, Teije Kuijper, and Jing Wang study Brownian motion on a quaternionic flag shape. That shape is a space of nested planes over quaternions. Brownian motion there is a random walk with no jumps. The team gives a clean way to build it.

They build it from a symplectic Brownian motion as a matrix flow. They then link its radial part to motion on a quaternionic sphere. That link yields a closed form for a key joint law. Such forms help in random matrix theory and in physics models with quaternionic traits.
arxiv-2512-01511:
Sabalbal and co-authors sharpen planet hunting in the SHINE survey. High-contrast imaging seeks faint planets next to bright stars. A new method, the Regime Switching Model, mixes many image tricks at once. It aims to split true planet light from star speckles.

The team gauges how much the method lifts detection limits in the F150 data. Better limits mean smaller, dimmer planets can be found. Each new find adds to the census of young giant planets. That census tests how such planets form and move in their first ages. RSM gains grow where speckles are worst, near the star, which is just where young planets are most prized and hardest to see.
arxiv-2512-02011:
Robots with multi-fingered hands struggle to learn delicate tasks in simulation, because contact forces and touch signals are so hard to imitate faithfully. Elvis Hsieh and co-authors present DexScrew in 2025, a framework that carries skills learned in imperfect simulations onto real hardware.

They demonstrate the transfer on two demanding jobs: fastening a nut onto a bolt and driving a screw with a multi-fingered hand. Both tasks depend on rich contact and tactile feedback, exactly what simulators model worst. Showing that learning can survive those flaws widens the range of manipulation skills robots can practice safely in virtual worlds first.
arxiv-2512-02211:
A group in algebra can sometimes be covered entirely by the centralizers of its elements, the subgroups of members that commute with a given one. Mark Lewis and Ryan McCulloch prove in 2025 two clean statements about such covers of finite groups.

They show that the centralizers that are maximal under inclusion already form a cover, and so do those that are minimal. Both extremes suffice, a tidy symmetry in the structure of finite groups. Covering problems sound abstract, but they measure how a group's commuting patterns fit together, a basic fingerprint used across group theory.
arxiv-2512-02611:
Semeon A. Bogaty and Alexey A. Tuzhilin extend a classic way to compare shapes and spaces. The Gromov-Hausdorff distance measures how far two metric spaces are from matching exactly. Shape comparison tools across geometry and data science rest on this idea.

Their continuous version also accounts for topological differences, not just distances. Two spaces can sit close in distance yet differ in how they connect. A distance that sees both gaps gives a fuller test of sameness. The paper lays foundations for this refined measure, which may serve geometry, imaging, and shape analysis. A sharper yard stick for shape helps fields as far apart as drug scans and parts checks for planes.
arxiv-2512-02911:
Hsuanling Lee and four co-authors present FluxLab, a toolkit for printing objects that change shape and sense their own bending. Shape changing devices promise interfaces and tools that adapt in the hand. Sensing the deformation from inside the printed part is the hard part.

Their printable nesting structure wraps a shape memory alloy channel for sensing and actuation. Lattice padding gives support and tunable elasticity, while helix surface wires preserve form and anchor guided motion. Designers of tangible interfaces gain a route to custom, responsive objects without hand built electronics. Print, bend, and sense in one part cuts the wires and boards that make soft rigs stiff, dear, and hard to fix in the field.
arxiv-2512-03311:
Agents that know almost nothing about their network can still coordinate. Sandy Irani and Michael Luby introduce a broadcast model called the singing model in this 2025 work. Agents do not know the network's size or shape, not even their own neighbors.

Agents can sing several notes, heard by neighbors nearby. The model extends the beeping model, where agents emit only one tone. The authors use it to sing a maximal independent set, a group with no two members linked. Simple rules like these aid sensor networks. Singing uses pitch variety, which gives agents a richer signal than a single beep.
arxiv-2512-03411:
Dark energy may change over time, recent data suggest. Tonatiuh Matos presents a conformal holographic model for it in this 2025 work. Results from the DESI collaboration favor evolving dark energy over a fixed cosmological constant.

The data also show tension in the inferred matter density between DESI and Planck. Neutrino mass estimates press against their lower bounds too. A holographic model tied to conformal ideas offers another account of the expansion. Testing it against data may clarify the cosmic energy budget. Holographic ideas tie dark energy to entropy bounds, a link this model explores.
arxiv-2512-03511:
Magnetic groups change how some algebraic objects are sorted. Higinio Serrano and Bernardo Uribe work out a Brauer group for that case in this 2025 work. For a magnetic finite group, they look at classes of graded algebras over the complex numbers.

These algebras are central and simple, and they transform under the group in a set way. The classes form the magnetic graded Brauer group. The authors find its full structure as an abelian group. Such sorting tools serve topology and physics, where Brauer groups label states of matter. The result gives other scholars a firm base for later work.
arxiv-2512-03611:
Seeing the Sun's poles directly was long impossible from Earth. D. Calchetti and a large team report the first such observations in this 2025 work. Views from the ecliptic plane, where Earth orbits, hide the solar poles.

In spring 2025, Solar Orbiter observed the poles from out of the ecliptic with its remote-sensing instruments. The team presents the first out-of-ecliptic look at the polar magnetic field. Polar fields drive the Sun's activity cycle and solar wind. Direct views could improve space weather forecasts. Spring 2025 gave the first window, as Solar Orbiter's tilt grew enough to see over the Sun's equator toward its poles.
arxiv-2512-03811:
A calorimeter measures particle energy by watching how much light a material gives off when particles pass through. Sergey Barsuk, Mykhailo Yeresko, and colleagues tested a small prototype of the GRAiNITA detector concept at a CERN test beam in June 2024. Their 2025 instrumentation preprint reports the first results from two days of pion beam data.

The analysis estimates how much detector non-uniformity blurs the energy measurement, a contribution captured by a constant term in the resolution. Even with a small prototype, that term came out well below one percent. The team also confirmed that the statistical contribution from counting photo-electrons shrinks with energy in the expected way. Together the numbers match the design hopes for GRAiNITA. They now feed into plans for optimising a full-scale version of the detector.
arxiv-2512-03911:
Brain-inspired computer chips promise robot control that is fast and frugal with energy. Kenneth Stewart and colleagues demonstrate that promise in a 2025 robotics preprint, running a learned controller for the Astrobee free-flyer on Intel's Loihi 2 neuromorphic hardware. Their pipeline converts ordinary neural networks into spiking ones that such chips can execute.

The original policy was trained by reinforcement learning entirely in simulation, using simple rectified units. The team transformed it into a spiking sigma-delta network compatible with the Loihi 2 architecture, then closed the loop inside a detailed physics simulator. They compare execution on the neuromorphic chip against a graphics processor. The converted controller still flies the simulated robot, showing that simulation-trained policies can survive the move to spiking hardware. The authors frame the work as a path toward real-time, energy-efficient autonomy for space and ground robots alike.
arxiv-2512-04011:
Gravitational waves born in the early universe carry a spectrum that later cosmic conditions can bend. Giuseppe Fanizza, Eliseo Pavone, and Luigi Tedesco study one influence in a 2025 cosmology preprint: shear viscosity in the cosmic fluid after inflation.

The authors show viscosity adds a damping term to the wave equation, reshaping both the transfer function and the energy spectrum. Constant viscosity relative to the expansion rate tilts the spectrum redder, while time-varying viscosity makes the spectral index run with frequency. Their framework applies to standard and exotic histories alike. As a case study, they compute the effect of the electron-photon-baryon plasma before recombination. Wave freeze-out from that phase leaves a slight blue tilt. Future detectors could read such tilts as fossils of the cosmic fluid.
arxiv-2512-04311:
Farming house crickets for food protein is growing, yet farms still raise males and females mixed together with no way to sort them by machine. Juan Manuel Cantarero Angulo and Matthew Smith describe a cheap bench device that sorts live crickets by sex in real time, in work posted in 2025. Sorting matters because it lets farms breed on purpose, keep the best mix of males and females, and use the two sexes in distinct food products.

A small board computer with a camera runs a light vision model trained to tell male from female crickets, and a motor arm then nudges each insect to the right side. In lab tests the model scored near the top of its accuracy scale, and trials with groups of live crickets sorted close to nine in ten correctly. The result shows that low-cost gear can carry this task on real farms.
arxiv-2512-05311:
Sadat Shahriar, Navid Ayoobi, and Arjun Mukherjee ask whether machine-written scientific ideas can still be told from human ones after repeated paraphrasing. As language models increasingly act as research agents, attributing an idea's source matters for understanding what the models contribute. Text detection has been studied heavily; idea detection has not, and ideas are exactly what paraphrasing preserves while wording changes.

The authors evaluate leading detection models on human and model-generated research ideas across successive rounds of paraphrasing.
