Performance erodes steadily — after five rounds it has dropped by roughly a quarter on average. Adding the research problem as context helps detection somewhat. The steepest losses come when ideas are paraphrased into a simplified, non-expert style, which scrubs the signatures detectors rely on. The study warns that provenance for scientific ideas will get harder to police the more text is rewritten.
arxiv-2512-05711:
Ali Krayani, Seyedeh Fatemeh Sadati, Lucio Marcenaro, and Carlo Regazzoni plan drone flights that stay connected even when an enemy tries to jam the radio link. Their 2025 framework rests on Bayesian active inference, the idea that an agent acts to test and improve its own model of the world. Expert flown demonstrations seed the system, shaping both high level plans and low level motion.

In flight, the drone keeps inferring: it anticipates interference, works out where jammers likely sit, and bends its path in response, using signal feedback. In simulations the method flew nearly as well as the expert demonstrations. It cut interference and mission cost sharply compared with model free reinforcement learning rivals. It also held up as conditions changed, a key need for real missions. The work shows how a principled model of sensing and acting can beat trial and error learning when the airwaves turn hostile.
arxiv-2512-05911:
Iñigo Asiáin, Antonio Dobado, and Domènec Espriu clean up the particle spectrum of a famous modified gravity theory. Adding a squared curvature term to Einstein's action gives the Starobinsky model, a workhorse of early universe cosmology. Its scattering amplitudes must be unitarized to respect probability. The team applies an improved K-matrix algorithm to do exactly that, wrestling with infrared divergences that need careful regulation along the way.

The focus is a scalar resonance, a particle-like bump, known to exist in this theory. A previous study had reported another apparent resonance. With the regulated, unitarized amplitudes in hand, the authors show the genuine resonance behaves as expected, while the apparent one fades: it was an artifact manufactured by the infrared regulator itself. A bump in a plot is not yet a particle.
arxiv-2512-06011:
Thibaut Paumard and seven co-authors share a practitioner's guide to inclusion inside French research units, where diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility are legal and professional duties, not optional values. The paper lays out the rules, the findings, and basic principles. It follows a research life from early education to retirement, asking where bias enters.

The most concrete material comes from one institute, where the authors describe working initiatives: internal communications, exhibitions, and accessible teaching activities. A dedicated commission inside the unit council coordinates them, with institutional backing. A standing body keeps the work from evaporating. Nothing here is a grand theory. That is the point. Research units elsewhere, in France or beyond, get actionable guidance: what to set up, what to watch, and how to keep the effort alive after the first enthusiasm fades.
arxiv-2512-06111:
Arthur Mukwaya and seven co-authors ask a deceptively practical question: if you can only count traffic on a few days, which days should you pick? Agencies must report annual average daily traffic. Permanent counters are costly, so most roads get short counts extrapolated to a year. Texas data from two recent years anchor the study. Their framework picks the most informative counting days.

The optimal days win across the top five. The best day cut errors substantially. Features borrow across similar road segments without leakage. The payoff: better estimates from the same budgets. Choosing counting days wisely is leverage in a calendar.
arxiv-2512-06411:
Victor Duarte Melo and Willian Buchanan present KyFrog, a key exchange scheme built for a security margin far beyond today's needs. Such schemes let two parties agree a shared secret over an open network, safe even from quantum computers. The current standard, ML-KEM, favors small keys and messages. KyFrog takes the other trade: it accepts a very large message in exchange for a huge safety cushion.

Its design rests on the Learning with Errors problem, a lattice puzzle thought hard for both classic and quantum machines. With a larger dimension and a small modulus than the standard, plus narrow noise, the authors rate its strength far above the standard under current attack cost models. Keys stay about the same size, while the exchanged message grows to roughly half a megabyte. All code is free open source. The work maps what that margin costs in size.
arxiv-2512-06511:
Mengqi Xu, Subha Maity, and Joel Dubin test whether knowledge borrowed across diseases can sharpen death forecasts for intensive care patients. A patient with heart failure and a patient with sepsis may both be critically ill, yet the drivers of risk differ by diagnosis. Models trained on one diagnosis alone starve for data, while one pooled model can blur those differences away.

Working with a large public intensive care database, the team applies transfer learning: train broadly, then adapt to each diagnosis. Both a classic regression model and a tree based booster were tested this way. Transfer learning beat models trained only on single diagnosis data, and beat a well known severity score used alone, while its risk estimates stayed better calibrated than the pooled model's. The authors also argue for a data driven cutoff over the usual fixed one when turning scores into calls.
arxiv-2512-06811:
Xiang Lin and co-authors address a practical snag in adapting big vision-language models, such as CLIP, when only a few training examples exist. Full retraining is costly, and light tuning can make a model forget the broad skill it started with. Their answer, RMAdapter, adds a small two-branch unit to the frozen model. One branch learns the new task, while the other rebuilds the model's own features to guard its general knowledge.

Careful design keeps the extra branch cheap. The rebuilding loss is computed locally at each layer, and parts are shared between branches. A further rule balances sharp task performance against broad transfer. Tests cover three hard settings: new categories, new data sets, and new domains. In each setting RMAdapter beat the leading rival methods on every score the authors report, without extra data tricks or repeated prompts.
arxiv-2512-07011:
Daniel Ohayon and co-authors speed up the attention step inside large language models, the operation whose cost balloons as documents grow long. Their method, Block Sparse Flash Attention, is a drop-in replacement for a widely used fast attention kernel. Rival shortcuts guess which parts of a text matter before doing the math. This one instead computes exact match scores, then keeps only the blocks of text with the strongest scores for each query.

Blocks whose best score falls below a calibrated threshold are skipped entirely, saving about half the computation and memory traffic. The thresholds are learned once, per layer and per attention head, on a small sample, and no retraining of the model is needed. On a standard long-context benchmark with an eight-billion-parameter model, the full system ran faster with only a tiny accuracy loss.
arxiv-2512-07111:
Jin Lei presents a cleaner way to compute how atomic nuclei scatter off one another, a basic input for nuclear physics. The standard framework, the R-matrix method, works but needs auxiliary operators and a two-step matching procedure to connect the inner region to the outgoing waves outside. Lei's direct boundary matching method folds the outgoing-wave condition straight into the last row of the matrix equation, removing that machinery.

The calculation expands the wave function in Lagrange-Legendre functions, keeping everything in ordinary real space and in a localized, square-integrable form, a bound-state style treatment of a continuum problem. The method extends to coupled channels, where several reaction paths interact, through an effective source potential that separates the entrance channel from the rest. As a benchmark, proton scattering on carbon-12 was computed and matched the trusted Numerov integration method closely.
arxiv-2512-07211:
Frederik Hagelskjær and co-authors teach robots to admit when they cannot tell which way an object is facing. Pose estimation usually returns one answer, yet many factory parts look the same from several sides, by symmetry of turning or mirroring. A robot that trusts a single guess can grasp wrong. Their method estimates a whole distribution over poses, using only three-dimensional point cloud data, with no color, which factory cameras often lack.

The authors describe theirs as the first deep learning approach to pose distributions without color input. The test bed is real bin picking, the classic chore of plucking parts from a jumbled bin, using objects of varying ambiguity. For now the system handles the two symmetry families in its title, revolution and reflection, but the design is built to extend to the full space of poses.
arxiv-2512-07411:
Zawar Hussain and co-authors ask a deceptively simple question about a promising wireless gadget: which way should it face? A reconfigurable intelligent surface is a panel of elements that reflects radio waves in chosen directions. And mounted on a drone it can bounce a base station's signal around a blockage to users on the ground. The team studies how physically rotating the panel, in azimuth and in tilt, changes the channel and the data rate users get.

Using a standard channel simulator built for such surfaces, they sweep rotation angles and draw heatmaps of throughput. The pattern is unmistakable: alignment matters a lot, and the best orientations stand out clearly from the rest. A panel left at a careless angle wastes much of its promise, while the right pose recovers it. The authors' practical moral is that deployments must optimize orientation as a first-class variable.
arxiv-2512-07611:
Yongsheng Lian wrote this 2025 machine learning study comparing three ways to train language models with rewards. The methods, called PPO, GRPO, and DAPO, all aim to sharpen complex reasoning. Most comparisons train and test on the same kind of task, which can hide weak spots.

Lian instead uses a transfer test with a strict order. Models first learn on a narrow number game called Countdown. They then face a suite of general reasoning benchmarks they were not trained on. Every reward-trained model beats its own base version, though the gains vary by test. The study also tunes key settings to give practical guidance. Larger groups in GRPO and DAPO make training steadier and answers more accurate. The effect of the KL penalty, which keeps models near their start, is not simple or one-directional. One surprise stands out: DAPO does best with its dynamic sampling part switched off.
arxiv-2512-07811:
Sascha Hauck, Matthias Kabel, and Nicolas Gauger wrote this 2025 computing paper on materials simulation at extreme scale. Modern CT imaging produces datasets of staggering detail. Averaging such data into bulk material properties is called homogenization.

Classic Fourier methods handle moderate datasets well enough. Their memory and cost explode as resolution climbs toward factory scale. A newer algorithm leans on tensor trains, compact low-rank data structures. Those structures shrink storage and computation for well-behaved data. The original ran only on plain processors. The authors benchmark core tensor train operations on modern accelerators instead. Graphics and tensor processors join the comparison through the JAX framework. Strengths and weaknesses of each architecture come into focus. They then port the algorithm itself to accelerators. Scales once infeasible for the best graphics-card methods become reachable. Scaling still depends on the sample's geometry, they note honestly.
arxiv-2512-07911:
Ishan Swamy and Deobrat Singh wrote this 2025 astrophysics paper on a strange suspect in binary star timing. Cosmic strings, if they exist, could latch onto a spinning black hole. A string attached that way drains the hole's rotation, shedding mass and spin.

Low-mass X-ray binaries offer a place to look for that drain. Some of these systems show orbital period changes nobody has explained. The authors propose string-driven mass loss as a possible cause. Their method builds on existing literature for detecting such effects. Matching the observed period drift fixes the string tension required. That tension lands inside the range theory predicts for cosmic strings. The analysis then widens to several low-mass X-ray binary systems. A larger tension would make the period shift significant and observable.  Orbital clocks may detect exotic physics.
arxiv-2512-08011:
Francisco C Alcaraz, a statistical physicist, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025 about one dimensional quantum spin chains. A known family of multispin models with a special symmetry has free particle energy spectra, which makes them exactly tractable. In all known examples, every interaction spans the same number of spins, so the interaction range is uniform along the chain.

Alcaraz extends the algebra behind those models to chains where the interaction range varies from site to site. He derives the general conditions that site dependent ranges must satisfy for the free particle spectrum to survive. Several simple examples illustrate the new family. He then studies critical behavior in detail when even and odd sites each keep a constant range. The dynamical critical exponent is computed in several cases, guiding future work on these inhomogeneous chains.
arxiv-2512-08311:
K Vijay Kumar, Mandar M Inamdar, Pramod A Pullarkat, and Gautam I Menon, biophysicists in India, posted a wide ranging review on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is force at the scale of the living cell. That molecular forces sculpt biological form has been clear for over a century. Accounting for them demands physics, statistics, and experiments all adapted to cells.

The review first lays the groundwork: cell biophysics basics, soft matter in and out of equilibrium, and the tools that measure tiny forces. It then follows forces as they are made, carried, and sensed in real processes. Examples include the push of growing polymers, the pull of molecular motors, the contractile cell cortex, cell division, and shape change across tissues. The authors stress active matter ideas, which handle non equilibrium effects systematically. They close by arguing that cell function needs forces and information processing treated together.
arxiv-2512-08411:
Mingwei Li, Xiaoyuan Zhang, Chengwei Yang, Zilong Zheng, and Yaodong Yang, robotics researchers in China, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their model, PRISM WM, helps robots plan in physical worlds where smooth motion is interrupted by sudden events like contact and impact. Standard world models use one smooth network, blurring modes such as sticking and sliding, and planning errors then compound.

PRISM WM instead splits the dynamics into composable pieces with a mixture of experts design. A gating mechanism senses the current mode, and the matching expert predicts that mode transition. A training objective keeps the experts diverse, so they do not collapse into copies. On continuous control benchmarks, including high dimensional humanoids and multi task settings, the model cut rollout drift. Planners built on it worked from a higher fidelity picture of the future, and the authors offer it as a foundation for model based robot agents.
arxiv-2512-08511:
Wenxi Yang, Yuzhong Zhao, Fang Wan, and Qixiang Ye, computer vision researchers in China, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Some multimodal models reason by thinking with images, weaving visual material into their chain of thought. Training that interleaved style with reinforcement learning is hard, because good multimodal reasoning data are scarce.

Their approach, Self Calling Chain of Thought, recasts the process as language only reasoning with self calls. A main agent breaks a hard visual task into atomic subtasks. It then invokes copies of itself, sharing its parameters, to solve each subtask in its own clean context. No explicit weaving of image and text is needed, which makes training far more efficient. A group relative policy method reinforces the reasoning habits that work. On a high resolution visual benchmark, the method improved overall reasoning while using about three quarters fewer graphics hours than strong baselines.
arxiv-2512-08911:
Fabio Koepp and coauthors use Bayesian analysis to ask whether observations of neutron stars can reveal quark matter inside them. Hybrid stars would contain normal nuclear matter that transitions to deconfined quark matter at high density. Mass and radius measurements offer a way to constrain whether that transition occurs and at what density.

Hadronic matter is modeled with a relativistic mean field approach, using parameter sets with nucleons only and with hyperons included. Quark matter is modeled with a vector version of the bag model, and the transition is built with a standard Maxwell construction. Three quark model parameters are fitted by Bayesian inference against the observations. Results suggest a transition could occur below twice normal nuclear density for the main parameter sets. The inferred parameters imply hybrid stars with large quark cores. The study shows how current astronomical data already limit exotic matter models.
arxiv-2512-09311:
Kuldeep Singh Yadav and Lalan Kumar build tools for estimating suspiciousness in surveillance video, a task meant to flag threats early in crowded public places. Human watchers cannot monitor every camera, and judging risk from a single image cue is unreliable. The authors aim for a system that scores risk in real time and can explain its score.

They release USE50k, a dataset of tens of thousands of images from airports, stations, restaurants, parks, and other public areas. The images cover cues such as weapons, fire, crowd density, odd facial expressions, and unusual postures. Their DeepUSEvision system combines an object detector, two networks reading facial expression and body language, and a transformer that fuses those signals into one interpretable score. Experiments show the framework beating earlier approaches on accuracy and robustness, and the authors offer both dataset and model as a base for real-time risk assessment.
arxiv-2512-09611:
Hendrik Alsmeier leads a team behind a real-time predictive controller for switching systems, shown on a three-tank system, a lab setup where liquid levels are run through valves and pumps. Model predictive control plans actions over a horizon, but switching systems change behavior abruptly between discrete modes, creating jumps that break numerical methods.

Their scheme models the system with Filippov dynamics and discretizes it with finite elements plus switch detection, turning the control problem into a program with complementarity constraints, without mixed-integer formulations. The program is solved through a sequence of smoothed problems. Modeling adjustments add modes to avoid points where the dynamics are undefined or not Lipschitz continuous. Hardware experiments showed handling of switching events, mode-consistent tracking through reference changes, boundary behavior, and constraint satisfaction. Performance and computation time stayed within real-time limits under model mismatch. The controller is implemented in the NOSNOC framework.
arxiv-2512-09811:
Chandler Martin and five coauthors present a faster way to compute how quantum dots respond to light. Predicting that response matters for absorption spectra and optical behavior in nanoparticles. The polarization propagator gives a rigorous route, but building it is expensive. Costs grow with electron correlation, the size of the excitation basis, and the evaluation of two electron integrals. The team develops first and second order versions of the calculation for lead sulfide and cadmium sulfide dots.

Their method avoids fully diagonalizing the response matrix. A frequency dependent inverse Krylov subspace method is combined with a folded spectrum technique, which picks out excitation energies inside a chosen frequency window. Everything runs matrix free, using only matrix vector products, and the ground state is treated at a standard correlated level. Computed ultraviolet and visible spectra for both materials show the approach stays accurate while cutting the cost sharply for large systems.
arxiv-2512-10011:
Lennart P. L. Landsmeer and colleagues give spiking neurons a sense of place. In spiking neural networks, the delay before a signal arrives helps encode time. Existing models learn a separate delay for every synapse, which costs memory, computation, and biological realism. In real brains, delays come from physical distance between neurons. The authors' spatial spiking networks instead learn each neuron's coordinates in a low dimensional space. Delays then simply follow from the distances between neurons, as in tissue.

On two standard benchmarks, the spiking Heidelberg digits and a Yin-Yang task, the spatial networks beat networks with free delays while using far fewer parameters. Accuracy peaked in two and three dimensions, a geometric regularization effect. Even with most connections pruned away, accuracy held, matching delay trained networks with a small fraction of the parameters. Learned layouts also map naturally onto neuromorphic hardware.
arxiv-2512-10111:
Marianne Bauer and a large group of coauthors recap a workshop on unifying theories for high dimensional biology. Modern biology drowns in dimensions: datasets now span cells, species, immune systems, neurons, and behavior, with thousands of measured variables. The ICTS workshop asked whether that dimensionality is a problem for theory or an opportunity. Participants discussed methods, models, and schemes that might describe, explain, and predict such systems. This document collects the challenges and open questions that emerged, organized as separate contributions rather than a single consensus statement.

That structure is the point. High dimensional data strain classical theory built for a few variables, yet physics has repeatedly found that high dimensional systems can simplify, with a few collective variables carrying the behavior. Biology may enjoy similar luck, or may not. The summaries range across the fields represented, from ecology and evolution to neuroscience and immunology.
arxiv-2512-10411:
Yijiong Yu and co-authors look for a cheaper way to run large language models on very long inputs. Full attention, the standard method, grows costly fast as text lengthens, while the simpler sliding window method looks at only nearby words and often collapses in quality on long material. Their 2025 paper asks how to get the savings without the collapse.

Their toolkit, SWAA, adapts a fully trained model to sliding window attention without expensive retraining. It mixes four fixes, including keeping some full attention layers, saving special sink tokens, and light fine-tuning. Single fixes failed, but the right combinations recovered long-context quality and sped up long inputs by roughly a third to double. Code, data, and model weights are public.
arxiv-2512-10511:
O Kozlov and co-authors show that heat can flip the magnetic alignment inside a synthetic antiferromagnet, a stack of thin iron layers separated by spacers. In their stack, a middle spacer is paramagnetic at room temperature and above. And its pull adds a ferromagnetic push that grows as the sample cools toward the spacer's Curie point.

The result is a stack that aligns antiferromagnetically when warm and ferromagnetically when cold, even though the iron layers carry no built-in directional preference of their own. When a field drives the magnetisation to reverse, the stack shows a field-induced one-way anisotropy of antiferromagnetic character. The reversal unfolds like that of a metamagnet, with a sudden spin-flip style transition, a behaviour that could serve temperature-aware magnetic devices.
arxiv-2512-10611:
Minghao Li and co-authors automate data centre design, work that today leans on human experts driving separate simulation tools and scales badly as systems grow more complex. Generative tools can draft room layouts for people, but data centres answer to hard physics: cooling, airflow. And strict operating targets that a pretty floor plan may violate outright.

Their framework, Phythesis, pairs a large language model with physics-guided evolutionary optimisation in a two-level loop. The model proposes three-dimensional layouts, criticises its own work, and refines the arrangement. While the physics level tunes asset parameters and picks the best combination of equipment. Across three scales of generation, the designs succeeded far more often than a plain language-model approach. They also used power measurably more efficiently. The authors report that gain in the standard power usage effectiveness measure.
arxiv-2512-10811:
Charlie Lind-Thomsen and co-authors characterise a quasar seen three times over. A foreground galaxy's gravity lenses the distant quasar into three mirror images. And such systems are prized cosmic tools: they expose faint black holes, probe the gas along the sightlines, and can weigh in on the Hubble constant. They are rare, and finding them without bias is hard. This one, at redshift 2.67, was picked out from the Gaia mission's astrometry.

An eleven-month spectroscopic campaign followed all three images. Their emission lines differ between sightlines and evolve over time, with rising ionisation and shifts in velocity and strength. A lens model built from spectra and imaging gives a robust halo mass for the foreground galaxy. And the model's time delays let the team stitch an eighteen-month history of the quasar at monthly cadence. The work doubles as a selection recipe for Gaia lens hunts.
arxiv-2512-11011:
Maxim Krasnov, Maxim Khlopov, and Ufuk Aydemir investigate how the early universe could have produced more matter than antimatter through spontaneous baryogenesis. A slowly moving field linked to a pseudo Nambu Goldstone boson can drive particle production that favours matter. The team focuses on cases where the field starts at a large initial angle.

Their numerical work confirms the known pattern for small starting angles, where the matter excess grows with the cube of that angle. For larger angles the pattern breaks down. As the starting phase nears its maximum, particle production saturates instead of continuing to grow. The study clarifies the limits of the simple scaling picture in flat spacetime and refines how such scenarios should be calculated.
arxiv-2512-11111:
Miroslav Kuchta, Rami Masri, and Beatrice Riviere analyse a numeric method for diffusion problems posed on networks of intersecting pieces. The domains are either webs of line segments or webs of flat surfaces joined at junctions, like cracks, fibres, or folded sheets. Standard methods struggle where the pieces cross.

The authors apply an interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin method, which lets the answer jump between elements while penalising those jumps. They prove stability by establishing a discrete version of a standard inequality on these network domains. Convergence is shown for answers of moderate smoothness, and a weaker consistency result covers rougher cases using generalised lifting operators. Numeric tests confirm the theoretical rates. The work gives a firmer base for simulating diffusion on complex intersecting forms.
arxiv-2512-11911:
Shuo Lu and co-authors compute the gravity waves from a small body looping a big black hole in a modified gravity theory. The theory extends general relativity with higher curvature terms from effective field theory. Extreme mass ratio systems, a stellar mass object around a giant hole, are prime targets for future space detectors.

Periodic orbits are classed by three whole numbers that fix their zoom and whirl pattern. The team tracks how the new curvature terms shift those orbits. Higher zoom counts make wave shapes with richer substructure, tying orbit shape to signal shape. Those links could let future LISA style data test whether Einstein theory holds in the strongest fields known.
arxiv-2512-12011:
Denise Gonzalez-Cruz and co-authors study how funding cuts could shrink access to sexual health care in California. Court and budget moves, including the Medina ruling and a recent federal act, target Medicaid funding for Planned Parenthood centers. Federally Qualified Health Centers are offered as a backfill, but location matters as much as count.

The team maps Planned Parenthood and qualified center sites and applies topological data analysis, a shape based data method. Nearest neighbor checks estimate travel time changes if centers close. Persistent homology flags coverage gaps across scales. The goal is to name the areas where access is most fragile and to show how shape based tools expose health inequality.
arxiv-2512-12411:
Ely Hahami and four co-authors test whether language models can sense changes to their own inner states in a 2025 paper. They use activation steering on Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, injecting signals into the model's layers. Earlier binary tests looked strong, but the authors show those scores came from a global shift that biased yes answers.

On sharper tasks, real but partial introspection appears. The model picked which of 10 sentences got an injection with up to 88 percent accuracy, against 10 percent by chance. It judged relative injection strength at 83 percent, against 50 percent by chance. The skill held only for early layer injections and fell to chance later.
arxiv-2512-12511:
Zeyu Zhang and four co-authors give a formal treatment of spatial resilience for cyber-physical systems in a 2025 paper. Resilience means a system recovers from a violation fast and then avoids new ones for long. In space, both are measured in distance along a route rather than in time, yet no agreed formal method existed.

Their framework builds on STREL, a logic for space and time rules. A spatial resilience specification states that recovery must occur within distance d1 and the rule must then hold for distance beyond d2. A scoring function returns the best trade-off pairs of recovery and persistence across routes. Algorithms evaluate the scores, and two case studies show the method at work.
arxiv-2512-12811:
Saeed Abdallah and four co-authors design channel estimation for full duplex multi-tag ambient backscatter systems in a 2025 paper. Ambient backscatter lets tiny tags communicate by reflecting existing radio signals, using very little energy, a draw for Internet of Things networks. Full duplex multi-tag setups scale well but suffer self interference and hardware flaws like I/Q imbalance, so accurate channel estimation is essential.

They propose a three stage training protocol with pilot based estimation that keeps signals orthogonal and avoids error floors. Two semi-blind estimators, one decision directed and one based on expectation conditional maximization, exploit pilots and data symbols for higher accuracy at more complexity. Cramer-Rao bounds are derived for both types, and the pilot and ECM estimators approach their bounds.
arxiv-2512-13511:
Piyush Bagad and Andrew Zisserman present TARA, a method to adapt a large multimodal model for video search. Their 2025 paper deals with hard queries, such as telling apart opening a door from closing one. It also deals with queries that say what should not appear, and queries that pair a video with a text edit.

The method turns a text-making model into one that maps text and video into a shared space. Training uses text alone, with hard contrast cases chosen to teach time, negation, and mix of modes. Still, the model scores best on all tests for this kind of video search, and text-only training shrinks the gap between text and video maps.
arxiv-2512-13711:
Aadya Goel and Mayuri Sridhar present Hessian Reassignment, a fast way to unlearn a whole class from a document classifier. Machine unlearning removes the effect of chosen training data without full retraining. Most work targets large language models, leaving document classifiers understudied.

Their two-step method first subtracts the target class's training effect with one influence-style update. That step solves a Hessian-vector system with conjugate gradients, using only gradients and Hessian-vector products. Next, a Top-1 rule gives a decision-space guarantee for deleted-class samples, unlike random reclassification baselines. On standard text benchmarks, retained-class accuracy stayed close to full retraining, at far lower cost. Membership inference advantage on the removed class also fell.
arxiv-2512-14011:
Yue Wan and co-authors present a curated data set and benchmark for MHC-II epitope discovery in computational immunotherapy. MHC-II proteins present antigens to the immune system, a key step for therapies. MHC-II binding is harder to model than MHC-I, with complex specificity, ambiguous motifs, and smaller, less standardized data sets.

Their resource, built from the Immune Epitope Database and other public sources, extends and standardizes peptide-MHC-II data and adds an antigen-MHC-II set with richer biological context. They define three machine learning tasks of rising scope: peptide binding, peptide presentation, and antigen presentation. A multi-scale evaluation framework benchmarks existing models and compares modeling designs, giving future epitope discovery work a firmer base.
arxiv-2512-14411:
Mohammed Ayman Habib and Aldo Petruzzelli describe Omnia, a pipeline that builds synthetic training data for military humanoid robots. It turns first-person recordings from point-of-view cameras, smart glasses, and AR headsets into large sets of simulated scenes made for specific missions.

Automated labeling and model training are built into the same flow. Training this way avoids the cost, risk, and time of big field trials. The data sets can be tuned fast for new places and threat conditions. They support basic skills like perception and navigation, plus advanced subsystems. The aim is faster training, testing, and readiness for humanoid autonomy.
arxiv-2512-14611:
Neutral atoms offer many internal states, and the Zeeman sublevels of an atom, its magnetic sub-states, can serve as the levels of a qudit, a multi-level unit of quantum information. A general method is presented for engineering quintets, five such levels, that can be addressed one by one.

The recipe combines a large linear Zeeman shift with a state-dependent light shift, lifting the degeneracy between neighboring states. At the same time it tunes the energy gaps into the radio-frequency range, where drives are easy to generate. That makes coherent control within the Zeeman manifold practical. The approach widens the menu for atom-based quantum devices beyond simple qubits.
arxiv-2512-14711:
Online social networks spread information fast and wide, but not evenly. Users in minority groups can be less likely to receive what circulates, simply because their position in the network is disadvantaged.

Four researchers study how to promote fairness in that information access, so that spreading processes do not systematically bypass the poorly connected. The problem matters because information on these networks carries job leads, health guidance, and civic news. Their work speaks to platform design choices that decide who hears what, and how quickly, when information moves through a social network.
arxiv-2512-15011:
Damian Hodel and a coauthor ask whether spreading knowledge across many AI models protects it better than piling it into a few giants. AI systems now train partly on content that earlier AI made. That loop can shrink diversity and accuracy over time, a slide called knowledge collapse.

The authors split a fixed pool of training data at random across more and more language models, then run ten rounds of self training. Diverse ecosystems kept long term performance higher, while a monoculture of one dominant model slid into collapse faster. The best level of diversity grew with each round of self training. The pattern held across model families, sizes, and sampling settings, and bigger systems made collapse worse when uniform. The study argues for ecosystems of specialized models, much as varied species keep a habitat healthy.
arxiv-2512-15311:
Wenke E and five coauthors teach a cheap camera setup to see like a LiDAR for self driving scene parsing. Their task is bird's eye view segmentation from a single 360 degree panoramic camera. LiDAR gives rich geometry but costs much; the trick is to transfer its knowledge during training, then drop it.

The teacher network fuses LiDAR and camera data, using a new LiDAR image built from range, intensity, and ambient channels, and a voxel aligned transformer that keeps spatial fidelity. The student learns from the teacher by cross modality distillation, yet runs on the panoramic image alone. On the Dur360BEV dataset the teacher beat camera based rivals by 25.6 percent in IoU. The student gained 8.5 percent IoU and ran at 31.2 frames per second, the fastest reported. Tests on KITTI-360 confirm the method transfers to fisheye setups.
arxiv-2512-15511:
Gabriel Cunningham and co authors classify symmetric polytopes whose automorphism groups are 2-groups in a 2025 paper. A 2-group is a group whose order is a power of two. The paper covers regular, semiregular, and chiral polytopes of any rank from three upward with that symmetry restriction.

Many small examples exist, and for polytopes with toroidal rank three sections, those sections can be prescribed almost freely. The authors also prove the property is hereditary: taking a universal extension raises the rank by one while keeping an infinite 2-group as the automorphism group. The results map out how much freedom builders of such polytopes have.
arxiv-2512-15611:
Marcos Rubin-Osanz and co authors carry out the quantum Fourier transform on a molecular spin qudit in a 2025 paper. Qudits store information in more than two levels, and lanthanide molecules offer tunable versions of them. Long pulse sequences, though, make precise control of the phase links between levels hard.

Working with an ytterbium trensal qudit, the team runs the quantum Fourier transform, a core step in many quantum algorithms that stores data in coherence phases. A full refocusing protocol built into the algorithm counters broadening and recovers the state with high fidelity. Complete state tomography confirms the performance. The work shows quantum logic is feasible on molecular qudits.
arxiv-2512-15711:
Divam Gupta and co authors present Gaussian Pixel Codec Avatars, photorealistic head avatars that render efficiently on mobile devices, in a 2025 technical report. Purely Gaussian avatars look real but cost much memory and rendering time. Mesh based avatars run fast but miss hair and other non surface detail.

GPiCA mixes both forms: a triangle mesh carries surface areas like skin, while anisotropic 3D Gaussians handle hair and beard. A unified rendering pipeline treats the mesh as a semi transparent layer inside Gaussian splatting. Networks decode an expression code into a mesh, an RGBA texture, and a Gaussian set. Results match Gaussian realism at mesh like rendering speed.
arxiv-2512-15811:
Feifei Zhang and co authors present Keep the Core, a data centric method for brain MRI segmentation, in a 2025 paper. Segmentation models suffer from sparse pathological annotations, and common augmentation tricks are blind to meaning: they can corrupt the very features a diagnosis rests on. The team builds augmentation around feature importance instead.

An offline module, SAGE, finds minimal image tokens whose tiny perturbation flips segmentation boundaries, building a token importance map. The online KEEP module then augments high importance tokens while restoring their original pixels, and masks low importance tokens for reconstruction training. The method fits any backbone with no inference cost and reaches state of the art robustness on 2D medical data sets.
arxiv-2512-16111:
Hamed Ajorlou and four co-authors present a causal discovery algorithm in an arXiv paper uploaded in 2025. A directed acyclic graph, or DAG, shows which variables cause which others, with no loops. Under a linear Gaussian model with equal noise levels, the true graph can in principle be recovered from data alone.

The team's method, BUILD, works from the bottom up. It spots leaf nodes, variables with no outgoing effects, finds their parents, then prunes them away and repeats. Given the exact precision matrix, it rebuilds the graph perfectly. With real data the matrix must be estimated, so BUILD re-estimates it as nodes are pruned, trading speed for robustness. On tough synthetic benchmarks it matched or beat leading DAG learners.
arxiv-2512-16511:
Hossein Javidnia presents a face analysis network in their 2025 arXiv paper. Splitting a face photo into its intrinsic parts, the skin's true color plus separate maps for shading and shine, enables realistic relighting and digital doubles. Doing that from one portrait under unknown lighting is the hard problem.

His network, MAGINet, predicts a light-normalized albedo map at 512 by 512 pixels using multi-scale attention, then upsamples and refines it to 1024 by 1024. A translator network then predicts five more rendering passes: ambient occlusion, surface normal, specular reflectance, translucency, and raw diffuse color. Together the six passes form a complete decomposition. Trained on the FFHQ-UV-Intrinsics data set, the pipeline set state-of-the-art results for albedo and improved the full rendering stack, enabling high-quality relighting and material edits of real faces.
arxiv-2512-17111:
Anjali Sarawgi, Esteban Garces Arias, and Christof Zotter present the first end-to-end handwritten text recognition pipeline for Old Nepali manuscripts, a historically rich but low-resource script. No prior full system tackled the language written heritage in this form.

Working line by line, the team tests encoder-decoder designs and data-centric tricks to lift accuracy. Their best model reaches a character error rate of 4.9 percent. Decoding options and token-level confusion studies show where the model still slips. The test data stay confidential, but training code, model settings, and scoring scripts are released, giving other low-resource historical scripts a working template.
arxiv-2512-17311:
F Marino and eight co-authors compare ways to compute the insides of atomic nuclei from first principles. Their main tool, coupled-cluster theory, works best for nuclei whose shells are neatly closed. Many real nuclei have open shells, so theorists extend the tool with tricks such as breaking symmetry in the starting state or using an equation-of-motion method.

The team runs each variant on chains of calcium and nickel isotopes, feeding in two-body and three-body forces from chiral effective field theory. They compare ground-state energies, the cost of removing two neutrons, and shell gaps. The variants agree well on these bulk traits across medium-mass chains. That agreement gives confidence that open-shell nuclei can be computed with the same care as closed ones.
arxiv-2512-17411:
Xingyu Feng digs through the Ethereum blockchain to see what non-payment material people have hidden inside it. A blockchain can never be edited, so anything smuggled into its records stays there for good. The study builds a tool that finds and rebuilds files tucked into Ethereum data, then sorts what it finds.

The haul held 175 ordinary files, 296 images, and 91,206 texts. A language tool graded the texts with 0.9 accuracy: 70,189 neutral, 5,208 positive, and 15,810 negative. An image checker flagged seven indecent pictures, all correctly. Mixed in sat harmless content beside personal data, explicit images, and hate speech. Some sensitive items targeted Chinese officials, a finding the author offers to regulators as a warning.
arxiv-2512-17511:
Francois Dufour and Tomas Prieto-Rumeau study the geometry behind long-run decision problems that end in an absorbing state, such as a machine finally failing or a patient leaving care. Planners judge a strategy by its occupancy measure, the long-run share of time spent in each state and action. The set of all such measures forms a shape whose faces the team maps in full.

They show the faces, their flat hulls, and their inner parts can all be read off from the process's own parameters. The payoff is practical: for this class of problems, mixing a few fixed deterministic strategies at random can match any complex strategy, across several goals at once. They also give the smallest size of such a mixture. The arXiv record carries an admin note flagging substantial text overlap with arXiv:2510.04808.
arxiv-2512-17711:
Chanh Kieu and a large team use deep learning to recount how many tropical cyclones were born before satellites watched the oceans. Storm records reach back to the 1940s, but early counts leaned on rare ship reports and scout planes, so quiet storms over open water went unlogged. Any claim about storm trends since then rests on that shaky base.

The model first proves itself on the satellite era, matching the known birth patterns of storms in the western North Pacific. Turned loose on 1940 to 1960, it finds many missed storm births, clustered in the autumn months over the central basin, far from coasts. Near land, old records look sound. Climate historians gain a corrected yardstick for judging a warming world.
arxiv-2512-17811:
Adrien Hélias, Sarah C Gallagher, and Pauline Barmby test whether a black hole's flicker speed can weigh it. Feeding black holes in distant galaxies brighten and dim at random, and heavier holes tend to vary more slowly. If that link were tight, a light curve alone could give masses where spectra cannot, especially for small holes.

The team mined a Gaia catalog of 872,228 active galaxies, matching spectra from SDSS and light curves from the ZTF survey. Gaia's own sampling proved too sparse for reliable flicker measures outside a narrow band of timescales. ZTF's denser curves behaved. Their catalog of 127 galaxies, with both flicker fits and spectrum-based masses, confirms the timescale-mass link found before, no tighter. No low-mass holes turned up in the sample, leaving that end of the scale still uncalibrated.
arxiv-2512-18011:
A. Damonte leads a six author team charting the high energy light of Proxima Centauri, the nearest star to the Sun. The star is a restless red dwarf with a rocky planet in its mild zone, and its X-ray and ultraviolet flares can strip or reshape that planet's air. Past records rarely caught how the light changes hour by hour.

Using the full archive of the XMM-Newton telescope, the team built spectra from 1 to 920 angstroms across about 260,000 seconds of watching. At any moment the X-ray flow can run from 20 times the average down to one fifth of it. Modelers of the planet's air, they argue, should build in that restless range.
arxiv-2512-18511:
Siyi Wang, Zifan Wang, and Karl Henrik Johansson design an optimizer that learns from comparisons instead of scores. In many interactive systems, people can say which of two options they prefer but cannot grade either one precisely. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, builds a method that needs only noisy pairwise verdicts between two candidate actions.

At each step, the algorithm perturbs the current action evenly on a sphere, asks which of the two losses is smaller, and uses the answer to estimate a downhill direction. They prove that, under standard smoothness and bounded-noise assumptions, the method settles at a stationary point when the smoothing and step sizes are chosen well. Tests on a linear-quadratic control system show the comparison-driven optimizer working in practice. The approach suits settings where human preference is the only feedback available.
arxiv-2512-18911:
Yongteng Gu and Xiangdi Huang ask how long a magnetized, compressible fluid can flow before its mathematics breaks. They study strong solutions of the compressible MHD equations coupled with entropy transport and no magnetic diffusion, in the presence of vacuum, regions where density vanishes. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, derives an upper bound on the solutions' lifespan.

After establishing local well-posedness on bounded domains, they examine radially symmetric two-dimensional and cylindrically symmetric three-dimensional cases. If the starting density vanishes in an interior region around the origin while the magnetic field there is not zero, the solution must blow up in finite time. The results sharpen earlier work on the isentropic system and extend to the free boundary problem, where tracking the boundary's expansion yields a concrete maximum lifespan. Blow-up theorems tell modelers exactly when their simulations must fail.
arxiv-2512-19311:
Hui Li, Fu-Yun Wang, Haoyuan Xia, and Jiayue Lyu attack exposure bias in diffusion models, the gap between training and generation. In training, the model sees noisy data built from the truth. In generation, it sees its own earlier output, so small errors can compound. The mismatch quietly caps image quality.

The team noticed a slow-flow pattern: the truth-based input nearest to a generated sample sits at a higher noise level than the sampling step suggests. Their MixFlow training feeds the model mixtures from those slowed steps, teaching it to handle its own outputs. Across image and text-to-image tests, including several modern backbones, quality improved clearly.
arxiv-2512-19411:
Himadri Halder introduces an arithmetic Bohr radius for operator-valued pluriharmonic functions on Reinhardt domains. The classical Bohr radius bounds how far a power series can run before its partial sums lose control. Halder's version mixes that idea with arithmetic and with values in operator spaces, on domains in several complex variables.

Local Banach space theory supplies the tools. He pins down the radius's asymptotic growth in finite and infinite dimensions, for convex and non-convex domains alike. The framework covers mixed Minkowski, Lorentz, and Orlicz sequence spaces, far beyond the classical setting. Consequences extend known Bohr results for holomorphic and pluriharmonic maps.
arxiv-2512-19611:
Finance researcher Jherek Healy examines a calibration headache inside the Heston model, the most widely used stochastic volatility model for pricing and risk-managing exotic derivatives. Even a popular model can be hard to fit to market prices, and unstable fits make exotic option prices unreliable. Healy zeroes in on one parameter, the vol-of-vol, and asks how it connects to the VVIX, the market index of volatility-of-volatility.

Four ways of estimating the VVIX inside the Heston model are laid out side by side. Two rest on the known transition density of the variance process, one is an analytical approximation, and one solves the Heston partial differential equation using the underlying S&P 500 directly. Healy then tests whether these estimates can steady the calibration process.
arxiv-2512-20011:
Blessing Agyei Kyem and five colleagues unify a fragmented corner of road-safety vision. Automated pavement defect detection needs training data, but existing datasets disagree on annotation styles, distress definitions, and file formats, which blocks combining them. PaveSync consolidates several public sources into one standardized collection: nearly fifty-three thousand images from seven countries carrying over one hundred thirty-five thousand bounding boxes across thirteen distress types.

The images vary in quality, resolution, viewing angle, and weather, mirroring the real world the models must survive. Benchmarks with detectors from the YOLO family, Faster R-CNN, and DETR achieved competitive performance across those scenarios. The authors present PaveSync as the first globally representative benchmark for pavement distress, enabling fair model comparison and zero-shot transfer tests to new environments.
arxiv-2512-20711:
Jan Mikula and Miroslav Kulich plan a searcher's route through a continuous world. In expected-time mobile search, a robot hunts a hidden object and the goal is cutting the expected discovery time. Global optimization in smooth 2D settings is largely unexplored because evaluating the objective is too costly, tangled up with motion and sight constraints.

Their approach, Milaps, reframes the problem through minimum latency problems on graphs, unlocking strong metaheuristics for route optimization. Novel extra objectives and an anytime method adapted from the travelling deliveryman problem do the heavy lifting under tight runtime budgets. On a new large-scale dataset, the best strategy quickly drafts a route, fixes sensing weights, then optimizes globally, beating state-of-the-art benchmarks on the quality-versus-runtime trade-off. A final study shows flexibility across scenarios.
arxiv-2512-20811:
Rommel Cortez and Bala Krishnamoorthy fix a blind spot in how classifiers are graded. Standard scores treat every test case as equally important. In practice some cases matter far more than others, and a model that aces the important ones should outscore a twin that only aces the trivial ones.

They propose a weighted version of the Matthews correlation coefficient, a respected grading measure, for both two-class and many-class problems. The weighted score rewards success on heavily weighted cases. They prove small changes in the weights can only nudge the score slightly, so the measure stays stable. Computer checks confirm the new scores separate models that older scores rated as identical.
arxiv-2512-20911:
Jing Guo, Xiushan Jiang, and Weihai Zhang solve a control problem without knowing the system they control. Their setting is the stochastic linear quadratic regulator for discrete-time systems disturbed by two kinds of noise: multiplicative noise that scales with the state, and additive noise on top. Classical solutions need the system matrices; theirs learns the optimal control gain directly from data.

Reformulating the problem through its dual, which is convex, they link the dual optimum to the parameters of the Q-function. They then build a single semidefinite program that estimates the gain in one non-iterative step. No initial stabilizing controller and no noise measurements are required. Tests on a pulse-width modulated inverter confirm the method works without hyper-parameter tuning, and the analysis doubles as a new lens on Q-learning theory.
arxiv-2512-21011:
Shuyin Xia, Guoyin Wang, and five co-authors make image augmentation respect the structure of what it hides. Masking parts of an image forces a model to use complementary cues, but blind masking can erase exactly the region that carries the meaning. Their method, Granular Ball Guided Masking, borrows granular-ball computing to judge which regions are semantically rich and structurally important. It masks coarse-to-fine, so the important parts survive and redundant areas take the cuts.

The augmented images stay representative yet discriminative, and benchmarks improve across the board: image classification, masked-image reconstruction, and even image-tampering detection, where structure is the whole signal. The scheme is model-agnostic, dropping into convolutional networks and vision transformers without surgery, which makes it an easy upgrade for data-limited training.
arxiv-2512-21111:
Alexandra Carpentier and Nicolas Verzelen survey a deceptively simple question: given many experts answering many questions, can we rank the experts by ability, and can we do it both optimally and quickly? In the crowdsourcing model, each expert's chance of correctness rises with ability, and the ability matrix is monotone once the experts are placed in their true, unknown order. Ranking is then estimation of that hidden permutation.

The survey's center of interest is the computational-statistical gap, the regime where the information exists but no fast algorithm is believed to recover it. Recent results surveyed here disprove such a gap for this ranking problem. The argument is built from a simpler sub-problem, detecting a hidden submatrix, whose lower bounds come from low-degree polynomial methods. Statisticians and platform designers alike learn when crowdsourced judgment can be sorted at full efficiency, and where the genuine limits lie.
arxiv-2512-21811:
Qiaolin Qin, Heng Li, Weiyi Shang, Ettore Merlo, and Jianchen Zhao propose a way to judge log parsers without labeled data. Log parsers turn raw system log lines into structured event templates, the first step of automated log analysis. Choosing the right parser for a system normally requires ground-truth labels, which industry rarely has, and published ground truths have proven inconsistent between versions.

Their metric, PMSS, scores a parser by cohesion and separation: how tight each template's group of log lines is, and how far apart the groups sit. It uses medoid-based silhouette analysis with edit distance between lines, and runs in near-linear time. On the corrected Loghub 2.0 benchmark, the parsers ranked best by PMSS scored within a few percent of the best by label-based metrics. PMSS also correlates significantly with both standard label-based scores. The authors discuss when the label-free score can mislead.
arxiv-2512-21911:
Jikai Wang, Min Zhang, and their co-authors speed up speculative decoding, where a large model checks several drafted tokens in parallel instead of generating one at a time. In long-context and mixture-of-experts models, that verification stage becomes the cost, eating the savings speculation was meant to create.

The authors apply sparse computation methods to verification and find redundancy across several dimensions of the computation. Their method sparsifies attention, feed-forward, and expert components jointly during verification. A reuse strategy shares computation between draft tokens and between layers, cutting repeated work without additional training. Across summarization, question answering, and reasoning benchmarks, the methods improved the efficiency-accuracy trade-off while keeping the acceptance length, the number of tokens verified per round, stable. The lesson is that the verification step, long treated as a fixed cost, contains the same kinds of sparsity as ordinary decoding.
arxiv-2512-22011:
Fluctuation theorems describe the spread of quantities far from equilibrium, and their quantum versions remain unsettled. Sounak Bandyopadhyay and Arnab Ghosh review the field's arc from equilibrium through near-equilibrium response to far-off results, then connect recent quantum fluctuation theorems with linear response.

The link yields new insight into quantum fluctuations and irreversibility near equilibrium. Dissipated work in quantum systems gets emphasis as a route to non-classical effects in quantum thermodynamics. The authors frame the stakes broadly: understanding quantum fluctuations underpins both the foundations of the field and coming technologies such as quantum computers and sensors.
arxiv-2512-22211:
Shaun Khoo, Jessica Foo, and Roy Ka-Wei Lee propose the Agentic Risk and Capability Framework, a governance toolkit for organizations deploying autonomous AI agents. Agents that execute code, browse the internet, and modify files bring real benefits but also risks unlike those of usual software. Organizations struggle to spot, assess, and reduce those risks as the systems evolve. The ARC System is their answer.

Its first move is capability-centric: judge an agent by what it can do rather than by its label. The system then sorts risk into three sources, components, design, and capabilities, and links each source to concrete materialized risks and matching technical controls. A structured rollout approach helps organizations apply it in practice. The system is released openly for others to adopt.
arxiv-2512-22911:
Samin Riasat and Hessam Mahdavifar study covering problems, placing a limited set of points so every point in a space lies near one of them. They work in Hamming spaces of strings and in Grassmann spaces of subspaces. They treat covering as quantization, the compression of data into representative points. Alongside the classical worst-case covering radius, they introduce an average covering radius measuring typical rather than worst distortion.

Using one-shot rate-distortion theory, they derive explicit random-coding bounds on average covering for both spaces. On the constructive side, puncturing generalized Reed-Solomon codes yields covering algorithms in Hamming space, and a new family called character-Reed-Solomon codes does the same for subspaces under chordal distance. Numerics show these structured codes, despite weak worst-case guarantees, often beat random codebooks on average covering, and in one dimension nearly match the random-coding bound at high rates.
arxiv-2512-23211:
Kirill Borusyak, Jiafeng Chen, Peter Hull, and Lihua Lei revisit a bleak result in the econometrics of product demand. Demand models for varied products are fit to market-level data, and product characteristics may be endogenous, chosen by firms knowing demand. Earlier work suggested that without instruments built from exogenous characteristics, flexible demand models cannot be pinned down, no matter how clever the price instruments.

The authors show the discouragement was premature for the questions economists care about. Price counterfactuals, what demand would look like at different prices, are identified using recentered instruments that mix price variation from outside with the possibly endogenous characteristics themselves. The proof needs a weaker index restriction than usual plus a new condition they call faithfulness, which they argue is a technical strength test akin to completeness, not an economic assumption. The paper closes with guidance for estimating demand counterfactuals with fitted models.
arxiv-2512-23711:
Paulo Cavalin and four co-authors introduce CAT, a framework for judging language models on two virtues at once: being right and being consistent. A model can score well on a benchmark yet change its answer when the question is slightly reworded, a serious flaw in high-stakes use. Current evaluations report accuracy, and sometimes consistency, but rarely study how the two trade off.

CAT varies model inputs in controlled ways and plots consistency-accuracy relation curves, showing how accuracy changes as the required consistency threshold rises, using multiple-choice benchmarks as the test case. A summary index, CORE, compresses each curve's area and shape into one number for the overall trade-off. Demonstrations span generalist and domain-specific models. The authors also sketch how the framework can extend to open-ended, long-form answers with adaptable scoring.
arxiv-2512-23811:
Itamar Allali, Mudit Jain, and Shi Yan simulate where loops of cosmic string would end up inside a galaxy like our own. Cosmic strings are hypothetical relics of the early universe, and their loops radiate gravitational waves unevenly, which kicks them like a rocket. Whether galaxies capture loops or the rocket effect expels them has been disputed, with analytic studies disagreeing and the answer depending on loop size.

The team added tracer particles with a constant recoil force to the GADGET-4 simulation code and grew a Milky-Way-like halo from the early universe to today. Captured loop counts peaked sharply at an intermediate size parameter, where rocket ejection and the natural scarcity of large loops balance. Loops with weak recoil traced the dark matter, while the abundant near-peak loops, still captured despite stronger kicks, concentrated toward the halo's center.
arxiv-2512-24511:
Mikaila Gossman and three colleagues study the input-output burden of saving language model checkpoints. Training at scale splits across tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism. Many processes hold many tensors of varied shapes. Checkpoints must reach stable storage often. That turns saving and restoring into a big-data problem of volume, variety, and velocity.

Data climbs a ladder of storage tiers. Graphics memory, host memory, local disks, and parallel file systems differ hugely in speed. Bottlenecks form under concurrency despite asynchronous flushing. The team microbenchmarks a kernel-accelerated I/O library against the standard interface. Aggregation, alignment, and coalescing are the variables. Uncoalesced small writes halve throughput. File-system-aware aggregation restores bandwidth and trims metadata cost. Against leading checkpoint engines, their approach multiplies write throughput several times over.
arxiv-2512-24911:
Wanlou Wu proves near-match results for Lyapunov exponents of hyperbolic measures under smooth vector fields with dominated splitting. For an ergodic hyperbolic invariant measure not supported on singularities, and whose Oseledec splitting is dominated, cyclic measures can match the given measure. Their Lyapunov exponents match the exponents of the original measure as well.

Periodic orbits thus capture the average growth and shrinking rates of a much more complex invariant measure. Dynamical systems readers get a bridge from abstract motion to concrete cyclic data. Such near-match theorems justify computing exponents from cyclic orbits in chaotic systems.
arxiv-2601-00111:
J Eisert, writing alone, gives a strikingly short proof that interacting bosons on a lattice cannot carry particles faster than some finite speed of sound. His 2026 paper builds on physical intuition and on Lieb-Robinson bounds, which already guarantee a finite group velocity for locally interacting quantum systems with finite-dimensional parts. Whether bosonic systems also limit particle propagation had stayed open until recently.

Working with generalized Bose-Hubbard models on general lattices, Eisert shows in a few elementary lines that suitably perturbed stationary states carry a finite speed of sound in particle number. Elementary here does not mean obvious: the short argument closes a question that resisted the field for years. A finite propagation speed is also what keeps causality intact in these lattice models. The proof offers physicists a far simpler route to a foundational safety property of bosonic matter.
arxiv-2601-00411:
Alistair Plum, Laura Bernardy, and Tharindu Ranasinghe present a dataset for named entity recognition in Luxembourgish, a language with few digital resources. Systems that tag names of people, places, and organizations need labeled text, which is costly to make for smaller languages. Their 2026 paper describes judgeWEL, a corpus built mostly by machine, then checked by large language models.

The starting labels come from Wikipedia links, whose types are inferred from linked Wikidata entries. Because those labels are uneven, several language models judge and filter them, keeping only high-quality sentences. The finished corpus is about five times larger than the Luxembourgish dataset available before. It also covers entity types more evenly, giving low-resource language research a stronger base.
arxiv-2601-00811:
Zhuoyuan Qu presents a short note encoding Russell's paradox directly inside type theory. Russell's paradox, the famous argument about the set of all sets that do not contain themselves, is the standard illustration of how naive set theory contradicts itself. Qu asks what it takes to reproduce that contradiction in a typed framework instead.

The encoding uses a type-in-type universe, where a universe contains itself, together with sigma types, which package a value with data depending on it. It goes through under either of two treatments of identity: extensional identity, or intensional identity supplemented by the uniqueness of identity proofs. The note is a compact exercise showing exactly which assumptions make a type theory inconsistent.
arxiv-2601-01011:
Patricio Vera studies the moment a language model's inner intent collapses into one stream of words. Generation maps a rich internal state to a single token sequence, a many-to-one projection Vera calls intention collapse. He defines three cheap metrics on the state just before collapse: intention entropy, effective dimensionality, and recoverability, the last measuring how well a probe can predict eventual success from that state.

The metrics were evaluated across three models and three reasoning benchmarks, comparing plain generation, chain-of-thought prompting, and a babble control. Chain-of-thought raised average accuracy substantially, driven by large gains on grade-school math but consistent losses on a science challenge set. The metrics are model-agnostic and meant to diagnose reasoning quality before any answer appears.
arxiv-2601-01311:
Hong Chu builds a geometric tool for certifying risk when the true data pattern is uncertain. Distributionally robust methods promise a worst-case risk inside a ball of plausible patterns. Common certificates are either loose, because they assume the worst slope everywhere, or shallow, because they use only local slope information.

Chu's concave certificates instead cap the loss's growth curve with the tightest concave curve above it. That yields a tight risk bound that still works when the loss is not smooth. She extends the idea to generalization, bounding how much worse a model can do on fresh data, and to the gap between attacked and clean complexity measures. Some dependencies on network size drop out entirely. A practical version, the adversarial score, allows layer-by-layer checks of neural networks. Numerical tests on classification and regression back the theory.
arxiv-2601-02011:
Endurance athletes may face a higher risk of arrhythmia. That is an irregular heartbeat. It is usually diagnosed with an electrocardiogram. Athletes do not wear such a device while training. Andrew Nugent, Yi Ting Loo, and Jack Buckingham refine a proposed warning sign. It comes from ordinary heart-rate data. The sign is gappiness: sudden jumps in heart rate under exertion. The Crickles project first linked it to reported rhythm problems.

Several spike-detection methods were compared on simulated data; smoothing with a moving average and thresholding the residuals worked best. Real data came from one hundred sixty-eight athletes. Raw spike rates showed no significant link to survey responses. Spikes above one hundred sixty beats per minute were different. Those did correlate significantly. Jumps at high heart rates, specifically, may carry the arrhythmia signal.
arxiv-2601-02311:
Deep Pankajbhai Mehta offers a systematic way to choose how to split the training of a large language model across many accelerators. Builders currently pick a strategy, such as data, tensor, or pipeline parallelism, or the ZeRO family, mostly by trial and error. No shared framework predicted in advance how much memory each choice uses or how much data it must move.

His placement semantics describes each strategy by where four kinds of training state sit, parameters, optimizer state, gradients, and activations, using five placement modes such as copied or sharded. From placement alone he derives memory and communication costs, matching published figures for ZeRO exactly. He also proves two conditions that guarantee split training matches single device training, and gives rules for safely combining strategies.
arxiv-2601-02411:
Kaiwen Tang and six co authors present SpikySpace, a forecasting model for time series that runs on spiking neural networks. The event driven networks prized for very low power use on edge devices. Forecasting traffic or industrial signals in real time needs that efficiency, yet earlier spiking forecasters relied on heavy transformer blocks with quadratic cost.

SpikySpace replaces attention with a spiking state space design and selective scanning, cutting the cost to linear in sequence length. Two cheap approximations replace costly exponential and division steps with simple bit shifts. On four multivariate benchmarks it beats the leading spiking forecaster on accuracy by up to about three percent, while cutting energy use by more than ninety six percent. The authors present it as the first fully spiking state space model.
arxiv-2601-02511:
Bahareh Golchin, Banafsheh Rekabdar, and Danielle Justo combine large language models with reinforcement learning to find anomalies in time series, the unusual points in streams from finance, health monitors, sensors, and factories. Labels for such data are sparse, patterns over time are complex, and expert labeling is costly, so a detector must learn from very little marked data.

An LSTM based reinforcement learning agent is guided by semantic rewards derived from a language model, which shape its search. A variational autoencoder adds an unsupervised signal from reconstruction error, and its output scales the reward dynamically. Active learning picks the most uncertain samples for labeling, and label propagation spreads those labels further. On the Yahoo and SMD benchmarks the combined system reaches leading detection accuracy under tight labeling budgets.
arxiv-2601-02811:
Marios Papamichalis, Regina Ruane, Simon Lunagomez, and Swati Chandna ask how much trust to place in decisions drawn from Bayesian network models when the model is slightly wrong. Random graph models, from Erdős Rényi and stochastic block models to graphons, are workhorses in neuroscience, epidemiology, and social science. Yet real networks are sparse, uneven, and dependent in ways the models miss. A small misspecification could in principle flip a policy choice.

Their local robustness analysis lets the posterior distribution wander within a small Kullback Leibler neighborhood of the fitted one and picks actions that minimize the worst case expected loss. For exchangeable graphs, graphon limits supply low dimensional summaries that make sharp small radius expansions possible. Under squared loss the leading risk inflation is governed by the posterior variance of the loss, and near percolation thresholds the decision uncertainty blows up with a universal critical exponent.
arxiv-2601-03111:
Yiyuan Li and eight co-authors show that a single training example, chosen and engineered with care, can teach reasoning models a surprising amount. Reinforcement learning for language models usually leans on large volumes of high-quality samples. Their framework, polymath learning, instead designs one training sample meant to trigger improvement across many disciplines at once.

One strategically selected math reasoning sample produced significant gains not only in math but also in physics, chemistry, and biology benchmarks. By analyzing which mathematical skills such samples exercise, the authors identify what makes a sample effective. An engineered synthetic sample that packs in broader skill coverage did even better than natural examples. Across benchmarks, polymath learning with tiny data beat training on much larger datasets.
arxiv-2601-03311:
Marcial Sanchis-Agudo and four co-authors explain turbulent flow in terms of cause and effect, with a pipeline called X-CAL. The method compresses flow data with a variational autoencoder. It then applies a causality decomposition that separates synergistic, unique, and redundant information flows among the compressed variables. Shapley-based explanations finally map those latent causes back into physical space.

The test case is direct numerical simulation data for flow around a wall-mounted square cylinder. The team learns a compact latent space with nearly independent variables. It quantifies the directed information flows among them. Percolation analysis on the explanation fields then extracts the coherent structures that drive each variable. The result is a general methodology for causal analysis of high-dimensional flows.
arxiv-2601-04111:
Vishaal Krishnan and L. Mahadevan model how swarms move goods well without any central control. Ants and other groups use stigmergy: each agent changes a shared setting, and that changed setting then guides the next agents. Trails are the classic case, laid down and then followed.

The pair cast stigmergic transport as a stochastic optimal control problem, where agents together lay trails and singly follow them while cutting expected travel time. Simulations and analysis show two effects: paths straighten in uniform ground and bend at borders between materials, like light bending between media. Both match observations of insect trails. The picture shows how local, noisy contact between agents and field can yield shortest-path behaviour with no global knowledge.
arxiv-2601-04311:
Vera Berger and four co-authors follow a star being torn apart by a black hole across five years of X-ray data in a 2026 arXiv paper. The tidal disruption event AT2019teq flickers violently, changing brightness by tenfold within minutes to days. late in its life it grows a hard X-ray corona that outlasts any seen before in such an event.

The spectrum hardens over time, shifting from disk-dominated soft emission to a power-law state much like state changes in X-ray binaries, only brighter and faster, with a late radio brightening alongside. In one epoch they detect faint quasi-periodic oscillations, checked against red-noise simulations. Several mass estimates from the X-ray behaviour agree with each other but point to a black hole well below the mass inferred from the host galaxy.
arxiv-2601-04411:
Ali Rad and four co-authors ask whether a lying examiner merely slows a student down or changes what the student becomes, in a 2026 arXiv paper about reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. That popular recipe grades a language model's answers automatically, but real graders are noisy: unit tests miss cases, labels err, and model judges can be gamed, especially on hard problems.

The team builds a tractable bandit model of the training dynamics. Grouping answers into recurring reasoning styles and tracking how probability mass flows between them, then checks it against controlled experiments on programming tasks. Everything hinges on one quality measure of the grader, the gap between its true-positive and false-positive rates. Above zero, wrong reasoning dies out and noise only stretches the training time; at zero, learning stalls; below zero, wrong answers amplify until training collapses. Rate or fate is decided by a single sign.
arxiv-2601-04911:
Mustafa F. Abdelwahed and 3 co-authors evaluate behaviour planning, a diverse planning approach, across stories, cities, and games in a 2026 paper. Diverse planning aims to produce a set of plans that genuinely differ from one another, useful in risk management, stream analysis, and malware detection. Behaviour planning extends older methods by building a diversity model directly into planning and supporting several planning categories.

The authors test the approach qualitatively in real-world-style settings rather than only on abstract benchmarks. Showing one framework serving narrative, urban, and game domains argues for its generality. Planners that return varied options, not near-copies of one answer, give decision makers real choices when the first plan fails or circumstances shift mid-execution.
arxiv-2601-05011:
