Lei Wang builds a fuller way to read the spins of hyperon pairs produced in particle collisions. Spin correlations measured after hadronisation show how quantum information survives confinement. Experiments usually report one scalar number for a lambda and anti lambda pair. Wang's framework is process independent and uses the weak decay angles of the pair. Those angles can fix the whole two spin tensor, not just its scalar trace.

Applied to a short range correlation measured by the STAR experiment, the framework exposes a hidden freedom. Many density matrices share the published scalar value. Some completions are separable, while others violate the positive partial transpose test for entanglement. A string breaking benchmark turns the trace into a sharp, falsifiable pattern of component signs. Feed down from heavier particles must be handled as a tensor effect, Wang argues, not a blanket dilution.
arxiv-2606-24911:
François Pachet gives sequence generators a dial that can attract or repel chosen patterns. Variable order Markov models generate symbolic sequences, like melodies, while preserving local style. Over long runs they fall into tunnels of repeated suffixes and near periodic passages. Earlier work compiled regular constraints into automata and sampled exactly with belief propagation. Pachet shows the same machinery works softly, in both directions. A weighted automaton scores how active a family of target patterns is in a candidate continuation.

Belief propagation then samples from a distribution tilted by that score. With negative coupling, target patterns grow costly and get avoided. With positive coupling, the same patterns become controlled attractors. Targets can be mined from the generated history, read off a score, drawn from a style vocabulary, or designed as probes. The main experiments target whichever patterns become overactive during sampling. Monophonic symbolic music is the test material throughout.
arxiv-2606-25411:
Magnetism in a one dimensional chain of fermions can ripple in waves whose spacing tracks the electron sea itself. Jie Liu, Xiaofan Zhou, and Suotang Jia study a dynamical lattice in 2026, where moving fermions hop between sites whose bonds carry localised spins. The hop strength depends on those spins through an Ising like coupling, so motion and magnetism shape each other directly. Large scale numerical simulations map the ground state across fields and coupling strengths.

Two phases appear: a paramagnetic phase with no ordering wave, and a spin density wave phase. In the partly polarised regime the wave's spacing switches between two distinct values, each matching the nesting vector of one spin population's Fermi surface. Both wave phases survived turning on a repulsive interaction between the moving fermions, which the authors highlight as a tuning route for magnetic patterns.
arxiv-2606-25611:
Modified gravity theories try to explain flat galaxy rotation curves without invisible dark matter, and their spinning black holes should lens light slightly differently from Einstein's. G Tuleganova and colleagues compute in 2026 how a pulsar passing behind a Kerr-MOG black hole would betray the difference through arrival times. Frame dragging makes signals on one side of the lens arrive at different times than signals on the other. Their formula extends the classic zeroth order result to third order in a post Newtonian expansion, inside a thin lens treatment.

Both the black hole's spin and the theory's extra parameter shape the delay, in size and in sign. Setting that parameter to zero recovers general relativity exactly, so any measured offset constrains the theory directly. The authors note the catch: a suitable pulsar black hole binary must first be found before the test can bite.
arxiv-2606-26111:
Zuhaib Hussain Butt examines whether AI music generation infringes United States copyright law. Modern tools blend copied lyrics, machine-composed melodies, and synthetic vocals imitating real artists. His analysis walks through a hard case: a user feeds one artist's protected lyrics into a system, directs another artist's voice and style, then publishes and monetizes the song. Title 17 doctrine frames each step of that chain.

Exclusive rights in reproduction, derivatives, and distribution cover the lyrics and melody strongly. Unauthorized lyric copying carries high infringement risk. Voice imitation fares differently under federal law. Sound recording protection is narrow, so a synthetic voice usually falls outside it. State publicity rights and new voice-cloning statutes fill part of that gap. Recent lawsuits and Tennessee's ELVIS Act illustrate the split. Butt maps each step of the technical pipeline onto legal exposure points. Clearer federal rules for vocal likeness are his closing recommendation.
arxiv-2606-26311:
József Solymosi studies point sets in the plane where every pairwise distance is a whole number. Infinite such sets must lie on one line, an old theorem of Anning and Erdős says. Finite non-collinear examples exist, but their tiny distances turn out constrained. Solymosi proves that very short distances in these sets are essentially one-dimensional in nature.

Below a certain size threshold, at most one pair of points can sit that close together. The only escape is for all such short pairs to share a single line. A construction shows the escape is real: arbitrarily large non-collinear sets exist with one off-line point and smallest distances of two and four. A conjecture closes the paper. With no three points on one line, even the smallest distance should be large. Only a linear lower bound is proved so far, leaving the gap as an invitation.
arxiv-2606-26411:
Michael C. Cushing and twelve colleagues report a Spitzer Space Telescope program hunting for variability in Y dwarfs. Y dwarfs are the coldest known brown dwarfs, failed stars too small to burn hydrogen steadily. Variability means their brightness changes over time. The team watched fourteen Y dwarfs for a full day at two infrared wavelengths. They repeated the observations months later.

Adding two more Y dwarfs observed the same way completed the sample. About three fifths of the dwarfs varied in the first round at each wavelength. The second round gave fractions from about one third to three quarters. Light curves, meaning records of brightness over time, were mostly stable across months. Some dwarfs did change their swing size clearly. Combined with an earlier survey of warmer dwarfs, the results weakly support patchy condensate clouds as the cause.
arxiv-2606-27011:
Zapletal continues a study of the Solovay model, a classic setting in set theory where many choice-like principles fail in a controlled way. This second instalment offers a new axiomatic description, meaning a short list of starting rules that capture the model. The approach is geometric, built around an independence relation that resembles tools from model theory. Zapletal then develops balanced forcing within this cleaner frame during the 2026 instalment.

Forcing is the standard method for building new set-theoretic worlds with chosen features. Balanced forcing is a special kind suited to the Solovay setting and its generic extensions. Zapletal gives a new definition, proves basic results, and shows simple examples. Layers of weaker independence relations then sort balanced methods into flexible classes. Each layer comes with examples, ways to build independent tuples, and a preservation result with a matching consistency outcome.
arxiv-2606-27211:
Gasnier and Guémard design quantum error-correcting codes whose built-in gates reach beyond the Clifford set. Fault-tolerant quantum computing needs logical gates applied transversally, spread thinly so errors cannot snowball. Non-Clifford gates are the expensive missing piece for universal logic. Their quantum group codes grow from classical quasi group codes in CSS form. In their 2026 coding theory paper, multi-control Z gates act transversally on them, and those gates are both addressable and parallelisable.

A lifting procedure borrowed from algebraic geometry codes upgrades good starting codes. Square-sized alphabets result, keeping the transversal gate while adding parallel lower-level gates. Decoding runs in quasi-quadratic time with a linear error radius, beating the cubic decoders of earlier algebraic geometry codes. Magic-state distillation, the costly factory behind non-Clifford logic, gets faster by almost a linear factor.
arxiv-2606-27311:
Belrhali, Poisson, and Renaux-Petel compute the fingerprints of the early universe by pretending, locally, that space is flat, in a 2026 cosmology paper. Cosmological correlators record how primordial fluctuations correlate, but curved expanding spacetime makes them hard to evaluate. Deep inside the Hubble radius, each mode still oscillates like a flat-space plane wave; curvature bites only as modes stretch toward the horizon. A Laplace transform turns that picture into a method, resolving each curved mode into a continuous stack of plane waves. A kernel dresses the stack with the geometry.

Every time integral then collapses to a basic flat-space one, yielding simple diagram rules. The massive single-exchange correlator illustrates the machinery. Its energy singularities become transparent, and a single closed-form series converges quickly across the whole kinematic domain. Flat-space intuition becomes a working calculator for curved-space observables.
arxiv-2606-27611:
Operations research gives rigorous tools for high-stakes decisions. Building a good model still demands deep domain knowledge and solver skill. Recent language-model systems automate only parts of that work. They struggle with hard problems, opaque outputs, and narrow solver support. Chuanhao Li and five colleagues propose COOPA in 2026 to close those gaps.

COOPA is a modular agent system with three parts. One part drafts several candidate formulations and scores them. It then picks the candidate with the best worst-case confidence. A second part links each variable and constraint back to quoted source text. That link gives humans an audit trail. A third part routes each problem to a specialised solver agent. Tests spanned three benchmarks and eight language-model backbones. COOPA had the best average accuracy on six of the eight. It beat the strongest baseline by up to six point seven percentage points.
arxiv-2606-28011:
Fault detection in process plants is only half the job. Someone must still choose a safe recovery action. Javal Vyas and four colleagues propose an agentic framework in 2026 for active fault-tolerant control. A multi-agent workflow splits operator duties. Monitoring, planning, action synthesis, simulation, validation, and reprompting each get an agent. A digital plant twin supplies data, models, and pre-execution simulation. A graph retrieval layer grounds the agents in plant knowledge.

Corrective actions are generated as minimal-risk recovery paths. Each path is checked, deterministically, against interlocks and envelopes and for dynamic feasibility before any actuation. When no acceptable plan appears in time, a safety fallback takes control. Two benchmarks test the framework in simulation. One is a discrete batch mixing module. The other is a continuous stirred-tank reactor under PID control. With lightweight models, the agents derived valid recovery decisions within the process's latency budgets.
arxiv-2606-28111:
Dense, cold quark matter appears inside compact stars. Effective models, such as the Nambu–Jona-Lasinio model, describe it, but their maths produces divergent terms. Francisco Azeredo and five colleagues review two schemes for that handling in 2026. They are Magnetic-Field-Independent Regularization (MFIR) and the Medium Separation Scheme (MSS). Both keep vacuum terms apart from medium terms, regularising only the vacuum part.

Within that framework, the team analyses cold, dense quark matter, including colour-superconducting phases. The superconducting gap stays finite at large chemical potentials. It stays finite even in strong magnetic fields. No switch to a normal phase at zero temperature is found. Older schemes had suggested such a switch, and could inject fake artefacts in magnetised, dense settings. Spurious oscillations and other artefacts vanish under the cleaner separation. Compact stars and heavy-ion collisions motivate the work.
arxiv-2606-28311:
Fergus R. Donnan and seven colleagues hunt for dusty outflows from active galactic nuclei, the bright centers of galaxies powered by feeding black holes. Gas outflows are well documented, but measuring how the dust itself moves is hard because dust emits broad molecular features rather than sharp lines.

Donnan's team used the James Webb Space Telescope's mid-infrared spectrograph on five type 2 quasars and built velocity maps from features of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, the smallest carbon dust grains. For three quasars the maps were clean enough, and all three showed outflowing dust once the galaxy's rotation was subtracted. Molecular hydrogen lines agreed. Dusty outflows looked more common in quasars feeding at high rates, suggesting they matter for how these nuclei evolve.
arxiv-2606-28611:
Vishnuram Arumugam, Cheryl E. Praeger, and Daniel Rademacher explore Cayley codes, error-correcting codes built by Kaufman and Wigderson from a Cayley graph of a group together with a smaller code. Their algebraic symmetry makes them attractive, but the general theory of the construction was thin.

The authors prove a reduction: attention can be restricted to codes from connected Cayley graphs without losing rate, minimum distance, or symmetry. For any given Cayley code, they pick out a family of symmetric Cayley codes, each tied to a normal edge-transitive graph. The family's direct sum contains the original, letting symmetric pieces carry the analysis. Several families of examples are worked through, including how the construction behaves under direct and cartesian products of graphs. A list of open questions points at where the theory of these highly symmetric codes goes next.
arxiv-2606-29111:
Singh, Ghosh and Dai model a management dilemma created by workplace AI: how much work should stay with humans? A firm deploying autonomous AI chooses worker engagement. Engagement can lower today's output for weaker workers, yet it builds or erodes the skill workers will need when the AI fails, since the system works only with some probability.

Their two-period model separates AI capability, how good the system is when it works, from reliability, how often it works. In a single firm, engagement is only fallback insurance, so the least-skilled workers get engaged most: their gaps are largest and cheapest to close. Worker mobility flips the pattern. Workers prefer jobs that build valuable skills, so firms invest in higher-skill workers near the AI frontier instead. Mobility also splits the effects of AI progress: more capability raises engagement, while more reliability can raise or lower it.
arxiv-2606-29211:
Feichtinger offers an easier way into mild distributions, a kind of generalised function used in Fourier analysis. His Banach Gelfand triple links three spaces: a test-function algebra, the space of square-integrable functions, and the dual space whose members are the mild distributions. The triple is a basic tool for Gabor analysis and for the Fourier transform. But the usual build rests on Lebesgue integrals and tempered distributions, hard for newcomers.

His new route is sequential. It is inspired by Lighthill's work, and by the way real numbers can be seen as infinite decimals. The objects are classes of mild Cauchy sequences: chains of bounded, continuous functions that match the mild distributions defined by duality. The key result shows this match holds, using standard arguments plus concrete facts about the test-function algebra. He aims the note at engineers who need the tool without the heavy build-up.
arxiv-2606-29411:
Georgadze presents a compact detector that can tell which direction gamma rays, a very energetic form of light, come from. Instead of heavy collimators, meaning metal parts that block most rays, or complex Compton cameras, the design uses one sodium iodide crystal. Silicon photomultipliers, small light sensors, sit on both faces of that crystal. Light patterns from the two faces reveal where each ray struck inside.

Simulations with the GEANT4 toolkit tested rays from a caesium source. Georgadze reports an energy resolution near seven percent and sharp direction estimates. One method, called active masking, uses the crystal itself to block low energy rays. Another uses Compton scattering, where a ray bounces inside the crystal, for higher energies. Background radiation from below fell by a factor of about 320 in two minutes. The design also meets a standard for handheld radionuclide identification devices, which name radioactive materials.
arxiv-2606-29511:
Ponnock and Ho ask whether the famous first level of Super Mario Bros, World 1-1, really teaches players through its layout, as designers often claim. They rebuild the level from scratch as a discrete environment for reinforcement learning, where an agent learns by trial and error from rewards. Four algorithms then play three versions of the level with rising complexity.

Monte Carlo, which learns from complete game episodes, emerges as the strongest agent. It wins about ninety-five percent of games, well ahead of the Deep Q-Network. Its edge comes from chasing intermediate rewards along winning paths instead of rushing to the exit. The team then shuffles the level's six canonical segments across twelve orderings. The original ordering converges fastest, learns most efficiently, and is the only one that avoids catastrophic failures entirely. No random permutation matches all three marks.
arxiv-2606-30011:
Huy Truong, Alexander Lazovik, and Victoria Degeler help graph neural networks adapt after deployment. New data often drift away from the training distribution. Labeled examples are usually too costly to collect then. Test-time training adjusts weights using an unlabeled auxiliary task. Standard versions update only a shallow slice of the network. Their method, T3R, aims for much deeper adaptation.

Truong and colleagues use several Rotograd matrices to rotate gradient directions. This improves alignment between the target and auxiliary tasks. Self-supervised signals become surrogate gradients for the real task. Nearly the whole architecture can then adjust at test time. In regression tests, mean absolute error falls versus plain inference. On cross-domain Open Graph Benchmark classification, relative gains reach about nine percent. The authors frame this as practical where retraining is infeasible.
arxiv-2606-30111:
Jian Zhou, Sihao Lin, Jin Li, Shuai Fu, Gengze Zhou, and Qi Wu automate the design of embodied agent architectures. Such agents combine perception, memory, planning, and action modules. Researchers currently wire those modules together by intuition alone. The design space of storage, processing, and connections is huge. The team tests whether architecture search can explore it.

Their runtime, AgentCanvas, hosts agents as editable node-and-wire programs. A search procedure called KDLoop cycles proposal, critique, experiment, and distillation. Reflection kicks in when progress stalls. Three search variants face four embodied executors in a full matrix. The tasks cover navigation, embodied question answering, and manipulation. Search yields deployable, directional success-rate gains on embodied tasks. One high-scoring candidate was rejected as leaking test information. Rollout noise, local edit traps, and weak credit assignment limit the method.
arxiv-2606-30211:
Peng-Qi Wang and Zhi-Hui Guo compute how doubly charmed baryons scatter off light mesons, guided by real lattice data. Doubly charmed baryons carry two heavy charm quarks each. Their interactions with pions, kaons, and eta mesons probe strong-force dynamics. Chiral effective theory organizes the calculation order by order. The authors push it to next-to-leading order.

Unknown constants at that order are fixed by fitting lattice simulations. The fits use elastic scattering data from CLQCD ensembles. The scattering amplitudes are then unitarized in the S-wave channel. Extrapolating to physical quark masses yields concrete predictions. Resonance, virtual, and bound doubly charmed states emerge from the channels. Single-channel and coupled-channel scattering both contribute such states. Scattering lengths, effective ranges, and phase shifts are also calculated. Future experiments and lattice studies can test these numbers.
arxiv-2606-30511:
David Ma, Jeremy Feinstein, Shreya Pandit, Arkaprabha Ganguli, and Eugene Yan map floods from two satellite sensors whose images never quite line up. Optical images suffer clouds, shadows, and urban look-alikes. Radar images carry speckle noise and registration errors. Their framework attacks both sensors' weaknesses together. A new dataset covers the contiguous United States. It pairs Sentinel-2 optical with Sentinel-1 radar imagery.

Pixel-accurate water masks mark flooded areas at ten-meter resolution. Hard weather and urban scenes are emphasized deliberately. Labels were made carefully on optical images by hand. They transfer to radar through near-simultaneous acquisitions. A shift-invariant loss tolerates leftover misalignment between the sensors. A conditional variational autoencoder cleans radar speckle generatively. It preserves flood-relevant structure while suppressing the noise. Standard segmentation networks score strongly on optical data. Radar flood mapping improves significantly over classical filters. The gains are statistically significant across the experiments.
arxiv-2606-30611:
Seongro Yoon, Donghyeon Cho, Jinsun Park and François Brémond improve how video models read facial expressions. Vision transformers, the dominant video architecture, learn from self-supervised pretraining, meaning they train on unlabelled video first. Their attention, though, favours big global motions and coarse timing. Subtle cues such as brief wrinkles or frowns get drowned out, which limits expression recognition in uncontrolled settings.

Their plug-in, MiRA, redistributes attention using the attention maps themselves. It scores each frame's marginal importance from its own attention maps, then shifts weight toward frames and spots carrying local expression cues. MiRA adds no new trainable parameters. An exact mode reshapes attention after the softmax step, while a lighter flashLite mode copies it earlier for speed inside fast attention kernels. On hard facial expression benchmarks, MiRA improved strong transformer baselines consistently.
arxiv-2606-30711:
Rohan Naidu and twenty-two colleagues propose that the James Webb telescope's Little Red Dots are powered by intermediate-mass, super-Eddington engines wrapped in dense gas. The authors notice parallels with the nineteenth-century Great Eruption of the star Eta Carinae and with Type IIn supernovae, where outflows crash into dense surrounding gas.

In their scenario, outflows build a slow, enormous wind. The wind is so opaque that a pseudo-photosphere, a glowing surface inside the gas, hides the engine and produces the observed blackbody-like light. An escape-velocity argument caps the typical engine's mass below one hundred thousand solar masses. Low variability and low surface gravity point to engines of roughly a thousand to a million solar masses, shining well above the Eddington limit.
arxiv-2606-30911:
Yongbin Kim, Yashar Talebirad and Osmar Zaïane present HASTE, a system that lets machine learning engineering agents carry skills from one Kaggle competition to the next. Today's agents start every competition cold and waste compute rediscovering known techniques. HASTE organises accumulated knowledge into three tiers, global, domain and competition-specific, each matched to an agent level, with an orchestrator coordinating specialists and promoting lessons upward by abstraction.

In an ablation holding a 159-skill inventory fixed across 8 competitions, tiered loading won medals every time, while flat loading reached 62.5%, no better than loading nothing, and used twice the output tokens. On the full 22-competition MLE-Bench Lite, HASTE medalled at 77.3% in a single-seed campaign. Warm starts needed 52% fewer refinement iterations, and the share of proposed changes kept rose from 42% to 85% once 50 or more skills were available.
arxiv-2606-31011:
Yiming Yu and seven colleagues propose reading out a qubit's state from how fast it radiates, rather than from a frequency shift. Standard dispersive readout lets the qubit nudge a cavity's frequency and reads the phase of the outgoing microwaves, but the signal only builds after the cavity fills, a two-step delay. In their linewidth-encoded channel, the qubit state enters the radiative amplitude directly, through a state-dependent decay process. Starting from an empty cavity, the output field carries state information immediately, growing linearly in time instead of quadratically.

That head start yields faster signal-to-noise growth under a matched filter. The advantage persisted through fair comparisons with photon-number caps, linewidth budgets, cavity depletion and pulse-optimised dispersive baselines. The team also outline a route using an auxiliary mode to convert a state-dependent response into the needed state-dependent linewidth.
arxiv-2606-31411:
Dao and three colleagues tackle a hidden weakness in voice spoofing detectors: they may learn language content instead of fakeness cues. A detector trained on one dataset then fails on new data where the words differ. The team call this linguistic bias and show it drives poor cross-dataset performance.

Their framework uses teacher-student adversarial learning. A teacher trained on the linguistic content of an outside dataset guides the student through gradient reversal, pushing the student to drop linguistic information. A variational information bottleneck guards the non-linguistic cues that must stay. Across nine DF Arena datasets the method cuts the equal error rate by up to about a third against the baseline, a relative gain that matters for voice biometrics under attack.
arxiv-2606-31611:
Jia, Viti, Behrens and Zhang map the molecular gas in NGC 1068, a nearby galaxy whose center hosts an active nucleus beside a ring of intense star formation. Archival ALMA observations in three bands supply lines from molecules such as HCN, HCO+, HNC and CS. They are sampled across the circumnuclear disk and the starburst ring at 56 parsec resolution.

Combining non-LTE radiative transfer, which models how molecules emit, with time-dependent chemistry inside a hierarchical Bayesian fit, the team replaces slow chemistry runs with a neural network emulator. It reproduces them cheaply. Density, temperature, column density and cosmic-ray ionization rate all vary with radius and angle across the galaxy. Disturbed gas and skewed carbon monoxide profiles at the inner edge of the ring point to the nuclear outflow reaching into the ring itself.
arxiv-2606-31911:
Vidal Alegría, Vieira and Edfors examine how gigantic MIMO base stations for 6G can be built from decentralized hardware. Keeping today's antenna aperture in the upper mid-band means four to eight times more antennas than 5G massive MIMO. Processing complexity and interconnect bandwidth then become the binding constraints on any design.

The WAX framework offers trade-offs between complexity and performance by splitting processing across modules. It was unknown whether it survives hard-boundary constraints, where modules cannot cooperate. Their adaptation runs decentralized processing on non-cooperating modules that map onto current massive MIMO baseband units. Results show that it still exposes useful trade-offs. This backs practical gigantic MIMO implementations that stay backward compatible with existing hardware generations.
arxiv-2606-32011:
Huffman and three colleagues test whether market competition disciplines bad business decisions, using bonus contracts at United States auto dealers. A manufacturer offered two contracts, one suited to high-sales dealers and one to low-sales dealers. Dealers picked the contract that did not maximize their profit in 20 percent of observations, at an average cost of 18,453 dollars per year to those who chose wrong.

Greater competition substantially lowered the mistake rate, in both cross-market comparisons and changes within the same dealer over time. Mistakes nevertheless persisted even in the most competitive markets. Competition worked mainly by prompting existing dealers to choose better, not by driving poor choosers out. Anomalous decisions shrink under rivalry but do not vanish.
arxiv-2608-00011:
Madha and co-authors present DLLM-TTS, a diffusion language model for speech synthesis. Current speech systems face a trade-off. Autoregressive codec models sound clear but need large models and data. They also decode tokens one by one. Non-autoregressive systems run faster but lose linguistic accuracy.

DLLM-TTS frames synthesis as block discrete diffusion over X-Codec2 tokens. Blocks are handled in sequence, with masked diffusion inside each. This learns local acoustic coherence plus global text-speech alignment. Parallel prediction inside blocks gives a real-time factor of 0.15. A 0.6B model trained on 20,000 hours scored well on Seed-TTS-eval. The result shows block diffusion can be practical and data-efficient, they report.
arxiv-2608-00411:
Yuan and Lu prove robustness for propagating bound states in the continuum. Such states are localized modes with frequencies inside the radiation continuum. Their existence breaks uniqueness for scattering with set incident waves. Near-BIC systems show strong resonance effects with many uses. Whether a BIC survives small shape changes is the key question.

Past work found robustness rules for a 2D Helmholtz class not guarded by symmetry. It built the perturbed BIC by a formal series method. Here they give a rigorous theory for 2D dielectric structures with one periodic direction. Solvability and error bounds are proven order by order. Convergence of the series is also proven.
austen-sense-and-sensibility-1811:
Jane Austen published Sense and Sensibility in 1811, her first novel in print. The story tracks the Dashwood sisters after their father's death strips their income. Elinor stands for sense, and Marianne for open, strong feeling in love and grief.

Both sisters fall in love, and both face loss, gossip, and hard reversals. Marianne's romance with Willoughby ends in public shame and deep illness at Cleveland. Elinor hides her own pain while she nurses her sister back to health. Austen weighs heart and reason without mocking either side of the scale. The prose is crisp, ironic, and quietly fond of its flawed young women.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-11:
Volume eleven of Rodkinson's Babylonian Talmud holds the first part of Tract Baba Metzia, the Middle Gate. Baba Metzia is the Talmud's richest field of everyday civil law. Its cases come from markets, workshops, and shared courtyards across the rabbinic world.

The tractate opens with two men clutching one cloak, each swearing it is his: the court must split the claim. From there it runs through found goods, deposits left with a keeper, wages owed to laborers, and loans and interest. Rodkinson's notes flag the hardest turns in the debate. Business readers meet an ancient law of trade that still feels alive.
bakunin-oeuvres-vol5-1911:
Volume 5 of Guillaume's Bakunin edition appeared in 1911, gathering the writings of the revolutionary's last great campaigns. By 1870 Bakunin was old and ill, but the Franco-Prussian War and the Paris Commune drew him back into action. He even joined a failed rising at Lyon, hoping to spark a wider revolt.

The texts include his appeals for a commune in Lyon and his letters and drafts from the Commune's brief life in Paris. He argued that war and empire had to be answered by revolution from below, not by new governments. The volume shows the old rebel's energy undimmed at the end of his active life. Guillaume's edition moves toward its close with Bakunin still, in his editor's phrase, in full cry.
bancroft-history-us-vol-11:
Bancroft turns to the making of the Constitution in the first volume of his 1882 sequel on its formation. Delegates gather at Philadelphia in 1787 to rebuild a failing union. Their debates, kept half secret, invent a republic meant to last.

The old historian treats the Convention as the capstone of his life's work. State rivalries, bold plans, and wise compromises fill his account. He sees the founding as deliberate, almost sacred work. Readers meet Washington, Madison, and Hamilton in the act of design. Bancroft's fervor gives the dry work of framing laws the glow of national epic.
bergson-creative-evolution-mitchell-1911:
Henri Bergson published Creative Evolution in 1907, a French work of philosophy about life and change. The English text here is Arthur Mitchell's translation of 1911. Bergson sets the elan vital, a vital impulse driving life forward, against cold mechanism. Evolution, he argues, creates new forms in ways no machine model can capture.

He criticizes both Darwinian mechanism and fixed final goals. Intellect, he says, slices living flow into static parts, while intuition grasps it whole. The book was a sensation and won Bergson worldwide fame. It shaped process thought and much art of its era. Many call it the most influential philosophy of life of its century.
bergson-laughter-brereton-1911:
Henri Bergson published Laughter in 1900, a short French essay on why we laugh. The English text here is the 1911 translation by Cloudesley Brereton and Fred Rothwell. Bergson argues that laughter targets rigidity in people. We laugh when a living person acts like a stiff machine or a thing.

Comedy, he says, works as a social correction that shames inelastic habits. The comic figure is often vain, absent-minded, or stuck in a groove. Bergson studies farce, caricature, and wordplay for support. The theory is elegant and still widely taught. Later theories of humor often start by answering Bergson.
bergson-matter-memory-paul-1911:
Henri Bergson published Matter and Memory in 1896, a French study of mind and body. The English text here is the 1911 translation by Nancy Margaret Paul and W. Scott Palmer. Bergson asks how memory joins the material world. He argues that memory is not stored in the brain like goods in a box.

He distinguishes habit memory, held in the body, from pure memory of the past. Perception, for him, selects images for action rather than copying the world. The book attacks materialism while respecting science. It founded much modern philosophy of mind. Thinkers on time, self, and brain science still engage its claims.
blackwood-centaur-1911:
Algernon Blackwood turned from ghost tales to a tale of faith in The Centaur, his novel of 1911. A man who feels trapped by town life sails and walks in search of a truer world. In the hills he meets hints that old myths still live.

The tale claims that earth holds a deep shared soul. The last centaurs stand for a pure bond with wild life. Blackwood pours his love of woods and hills into the prose. It is the peak of his tales of awe in wild places. Some fans find its creed dense. Yet its love for green hills and clean air rings true, and its quest has real ache in it.
bleek-lloyd-specimens-of-bushman-folklor:
Wilhelm Bleek and Lucy Lloyd preserved the |Xam people's stories in Specimens of Bushman Folklore, published in 1911. In Cape Town, |Xam men dictated myths, legends, and beliefs to the two scholars over years of patient work. The original |Xam text stands beside the English translation, line for careful line.

The trickster Mantis, the moon, rain, and the early people of the world move through these tales. The speakers' own people and language have since nearly vanished, which makes the record irreplaceable. The volume stands as the founding text of Khoisan ethnography, a whole world saved in notebooks.
boas-mind-primitive-man-1911:
Franz Boas taught at Columbia and is often called the father of American anthropology. His 1911 book The Mind of Primitive Man attacks the claim that some races are born with stronger minds than others. It draws on years of field work and museum study.

Boas shows that race, language, and culture move on separate tracks and must not be confused. A people's tools, tales, and habits, he argues, grow from their history, not from their blood. The book laid the ground for cultural relativism, the view that each culture must be judged on its own terms.
bonaventure-tria-opuscula-1911:
Bonaventure, the Franciscan master who led his order and taught at Paris, wrote three short works that hold his whole thought in seed. The Quaracchi edition of 1911 prints them together in Latin: the Breviloquium, the Itinerarium Mentis in Deum, and the De Reductione Artium ad Theologiam. No complete English version in the public domain exists.

The Breviloquium sums up the whole of theology in seven tight parts. The Itinerarium leads the soul up six steps, through the world and the mind, to rest in God. The third piece shows how every art and science leads back to theology. Together they are the handbook of Franciscan thought at its height.
books-and-persons-being-comments-on-a-pa:
Arnold Bennett collected Books and Persons with Chatto and Windus of London in 1917, from weekly pieces he wrote for the New Age. Bennett had signed the pieces Jacob Tonson between 1908 and 1911. Hugh Walpole, the dedicatee, pressed him to reprint them.

Week by week the pieces judge new books, living authors, and the trade that sells them. Bennett attacks the circulating libraries for their moral purge of memoirs and novels. He praises craft, sales sense, and plain hard work in writing. French letters draw his eye as much as English ones. The tone stays brisk and worldly, with jokes at the expense of prudes. Readers get a working novelist's view of Edwardian book life from inside the shop.
boule-la-chapelle-aux-saints-1911:
Marcellin Boule, a French sage of fossil man, wrote this memoir in French on the La Chapelle-aux-Saints find in 1911. Quarry men in France had found a near whole Neanderthal frame in a cave in 1908. Boule got the bones for his full study in Paris.

His rebuild of the man stooped, bent at the knees, with a brutish, ape like gait. That image of the Neanderthal as a dull brute held sway for some forty years in books and museums. Later work showed the frame was bent by age and joint pain, not by race.
brentano-aristoteles-weltanschauung-1911:
Franz Brentano published his study of Aristotle and his worldview in German in 1911. Brentano, the Austrian philosopher who revived the close study of the mind, had lectured on Aristotle for decades. He found his own leading ideas, above all the mind's direction toward objects, foreshadowed in the Greek master's texts.

The book follows Aristotle's development through the stages Brentano saw in his career, from early promise to mature system. It treats the soul, knowledge, and the divine mind as Aristotle's texts present them. Brentano reads the ancient philosopher as a living thinker rather than a museum piece. The study carried his reading of Aristotle to a new generation, including students who would reshape twentieth-century philosophy.
brown-acquaintances-old-and-new-among-re:
Olympia Brown wrote a memoir of reform folk she had known, in a text dated 1911. Her mother stands first in the tale. On a small Michigan farm, amid wash, dairy, and spin work, Lephia O. Brown read wide and kept up with each cause of the day. Equal rights for women filled her talk at home.

Long before Stanton or Anthony reached the girl's ears, the farm table had taught the same creed. Force and fire marked the mother's words on it. Child rearing at that farm ran ahead of its time, the daughter holds, though new land and hard work pressed the home. Courage of thought and act is the trait praised most. The book's span, by its title, runs from such home roots to the wide ring of reform names of her grown years.
cannizzaro-sketch-chemical-philosophy-19:
Stanislao Cannizzaro's Sketch of a Course of Chemical Philosophy began as his 1858 Italian Sunto. The Alembic Club reprinted the English version in 1911 as Reprint number 18. Cannizzaro revived Avogadro's hypothesis, the idea that equal gas volumes hold equal numbers of molecules. Chemists had let that idea sleep for decades.

With it, he showed how to fix atomic weights on one firm scale. His paper reached the Karlsruhe congress of 1860 and spread among its members. The atomic weight chaos that had plagued chemistry soon ended. The short sketch changed how every chemist reckoned. It reads as a letter that reset a science.
chatelaine-de-vergi-mason-1911:
The Châtelaine de Vergi is an anonymous French tale from medieval Burgundy. It is short enough to read at one sitting, and it ends in grief. Eugene Mason translated it into English in 1911 with other tales of its period.

A knight loves the châtelaine in secret, and the secret itself keeps them safe. A jealous duchess drags the confidence out of the duke, her husband. One whispered word follows another until the trust is broken in public. The lovers die of the betrayal, and few medieval tales punish a loose tongue so harshly.
christopher-columbus-and-the-new-world-o:
Volume 4 of Filson Young's life of Columbus finds the Admiral back in Espanola on the second voyage, reading ruin where he left a fort. Guacanagari, the friendly cacique of the first landing, comes aboard the flagship now guarded and strange. A Carib prisoner, a handsome woman the Spaniards named Dona Catalina, holds the king's attention while trust drains away. The cacique who once loved Spanish trinkets shrinks from the cross they offer him as an emblem of their faith.

Young uses the soured friendship to mark the turn from discovery to occupation. The colony at Isabella sickens, supplies fail, and the Admiral's justice begins to make enemies of Spaniards and natives alike. What the first voyage promised, the second begins to charge for. Readers in the fourth volume watch Young's Columbus change from visionary to colonial governor, and the New World from wonder to administration, debt, and fever.
chrystal-perpetual-motion-1911:
George Chrystal, a Scots scholar of maths and physics, wrote this survey of perpetual motion for the Encyclopaedia Britannica in 1911. By then the laws of heat and work had long since closed the case. Chrystal set out the full tale for the lay reader.

He walks from the old wheel schemes to the strict proof that no such machine can work. He notes the French Academy's ban of 1775, when it shut its doors to all such claims. The piece is the learned world's last word on the long dream. It can be read in full in a short, clear sitting.
cia-0000009811:
Information on a prisoner of war camp in Ha Dong town, Ha Tay province, is set out in a November 1971 item. Ha Dong was a town on Hanoi's southwestern edge, close enough to the capital to sit under its direct control. Urban-edge camps differed from jungle sites in routine and risk.

A camp near the capital could hold men in transit between interrogation and long-term prisons. Reports from such towns came through different channels than jungle sightings. Officials weighed them alongside the known Hanoi system. This item adds a suburban point to that system, described from sources available in late 1971.
cia-0000009911:
Three American prisoners of war were used by the Viet Cong for propaganda meetings, a November 1966 report states, with an audience the title cuts off. Propaganda meetings paraded captives before villagers, cameras, or foreign guests. The men had no real choice in the performance.

Such reports told officials two things: the three were alive on a date, and their captors were exploiting them. Both facts entered the men's files. Families learned of the meetings with pain, yet the proof of life mattered too. This file captures that bitter double value in one small reported event.
cia-0000012311:
An Acting Director of Central Intelligence receives this undated Helms memo, its year estimated as 1962. Acting chiefs inherit live cases midstream, and the Penkovsky operation was the livest file in the building that year. The memo adds one more page to a record that thickened month by month as events accelerated toward the autumn crisis.

The paper trail's growth is itself evidence of the stakes. Each memo to the top marked another turn in a case moving toward October. For readers, the letter preserves the summit's attention in the climactic phase, recorded before anyone knew the ending.
cia-0000012411:
Meeting number thirty gets a bare title and a year, 1961: a milestone recorded in the plainest possible form. Thirty sittings with one Soviet colonel in a single year. The number alone conveys an intelligence haul without parallel. Each meeting meant hours of answers and hundreds of pages. Each also meant fresh risk, accepted by the source on his return to Moscow.

The record's bareness speaks as loudly as any summary could. Clerks by then were numbering history as routine paperwork. For readers, the page is the operation's scale stated in a single figure, with everything else left to imagine.
cia-0000013211:
Prison camps for allied prisoners in Cambodia, and where they answered in the chain of command, are mapped in a CIA paper from January 1971. The camps sat under the Central Office for South Vietnam, the headquarters that ran the southern war from across the border. The files diagram the structure: orders flowing down to jungle camps, reports flowing back up the same channels.

The paper shows the dungeons run like an army outfit, not a scatter of huts. Understanding who commanded the camps mattered for every rescue plan and protest. For readers, it is the prison system drawn as an organization chart.
cia-0000013611:
Could Venezuela's young democracy last? A CIA paper from January 1964 weighs the prospects for political stability there. The country had just managed a rare feat. Power had passed between elected presidents peacefully for the first time in its history. The left's gunmen still tested the state, though. They fought its troops in the hills and the cities, while oil money funded the government's promises.

The paper forecasts the vote's future with care. It asks whether ballots could survive bullets in a land new to both. For readers, it shows a working democracy graded by skeptics who had watched many others fall.
cia-0000013911: South Vietnamese soldiers and two American prisoners were seen in Laos, in a CIA note dated November 4, 1967. The prisoners belonged to the ARVN, South Vietnam's army, and to U.S. forces. Laos lay outside Vietnam, yet its trails carried much of the war. A sighting there showed prisoners could be held beyond Vietnam's borders.
cia-0000014611: A London Reuters item is preserved in a CIA file dated January 1, 1949, mis-dated against its own subject. The item quotes the wife of convicted atom spy Morton Sobell speaking in London. Sobell's spy trial came later, so the file's date sits oddly beside its text. The clip shows how press words on spy cases entered the agency's files.
cia-0000014711: Impact of the Rosenberg case is the broad subject of a CIA paper dated November 4, 1952. The paper weighed what the case had done to opinion and politics. Few spy trials have echoed so long or so far. A paper taking the case's full measure shows officials knew they were living through a landmark, not a routine trial.
cia-0000015311: A letter to Leon Davidson from J. S. Harman fills a CIA file dated April 1, 1958. Harman thanks Davidson for his letters of April 2, another small date slip. Davidson's stream of questions never quite stopped. Each reply from the agency was short, civil, and firm, and this file holds one more of them.
cia-0000015411: On April 4, 1958, CIA officers met with Mr. Chapin to plan a reply to Leon Davidson, a dogged writer on flying saucers. Notes from May add a later phone call with Major Tacker of the Air Force. Chapin agreed to draft the answer along lines used in an earlier reply. Davidson kept asking what the government knew, and the file shows how carefully each answer was weighed.
cia-0000022811: American casualties and grave sites in Kratie Province, Cambodia, are recorded in a CIA item dated in 1974. Kratie, on the Mekong, saw heavy fighting as the war spread west. Grave sites marked where men might one day be recovered and named. Mapping them was grim duty, done so that no resting place was lost to the record.
cia-0000037111: A CIA record dated February 4, 1943 lists disbursements for travel and other expenses, naming Shaw, McDonough, Sherwood, Tyler, and Wood. The page is wartime bookkeeping from the OSS years, when American secret work was still new. Each entry ties a payment to a person in the plain style of an accounts ledger. Pages like this show the office routine that supported work done far from home.
cia-0000049111: Members of the MNR issued a communique in 1985, preserved in a CIA item kept with the Truth Commission records. The MNR was a social democratic party in the opposition front, speaking for the political wing of the struggle. Communiques were how such movements put their line on record, for friends and enemies alike.
cia-0000049211: The verbatim text of a discussion on the Jesuit murders fills a CIA item from 1991, kept with the Truth Commission records. Verbatim records keep what summaries smooth away: hedges, orders of speaking, and the exact words used. In a case built on who said what, such a transcript was evidence in itself.
cia-0000049311: Declassified CIA document 0000049311, dated October 6, 1980, is titled El Salvador: Growing Rightist Ascendancy and carries a Truth Commission note. Like its companion paper of the same date, it treats the growing power of the right in El Salvador. The file offers the agency's wording on that shift, preserved as a short declassified item rather than a narrative history.
cia-0000049411: Guerrillas continuing a war of attrition in El Salvador are the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049411, dated July 1, 1985. Marked for the Truth Commission, the item describes the conflict as attrition. Readers get a short declassified record whose title carries that judgment, one of the agency's mid-war characterizations of how the fighting was being waged.
cia-0000095211: A cable from Leopoldville about the intended course of action is declassified CIA document 0000095211, dated August 3, 1960. The heading does not say whose action or toward what end. The short file is a declassified cable record from the Congo station, preserved with a title that announces a plan while revealing almost nothing about it.
cia-0000112811: Herbert Moy, Active Collaborator is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112811, dated October 5, 1944. The title gives a name and a label: Herbert Moy, called an active collaborator. Collaborator is a charge, stated flatly in the heading itself. The brief record is a name and charge file from the autumn of 1944 in the files as released.
cia-0000117911: Dated June 3, 1967, declassified CIA document 0000117911 gives Prince Sihanouk's condition for restoring ties between the United States and Cambodia. Its heading calls that idea restoration, its key word in the title itself. He is named in the heading, and his condition is the whole stated topic of the file. The brief record is a short item on one man's terms for a return.
cia-0000119211:
From about January 1985, this CIA document concerns reports that American prisoners of war were executed during the 1970s. Claims like these were the darkest the agency had to weigh in its missing-persons work. The paper preserves the allegation together with the agency's handling of it.

Judging such reports meant sorting rumor, faulty memory, and possible fact. A claim of executions, if true, changed both history and policy, and if false, it could torment families for nothing. The document shows that weighing process at work. It stands as part of the record of how the government treated the hardest questions left by the war.
cia-0000119711:
An October 1953 CIA paper forecasts probable developments in Iran through 1954. It was written two months after the coup that drove out Prime Minister Mossadegh and restored the Shah's power. Washington now had to judge what the new order would bring.

The paper looks ahead at Iran's politics and at the stability of a government America had helped install. Forecasts made just after a coup carry a special interest, since they show what the winners expected and feared. For readers, this estimate is a check on those hopes: a statement of where Iran seemed bound, made when the Shah's long second reign was only beginning.
cia-0000124311: A July 1951 CIA document reports on American prisoners held at North Korean camps. The camps along the Yalu River held large numbers of men in harsh conditions. What happened inside them became one of the war's lasting disputes, and the paper records the agency's picture. Camp reporting built slowly from escapees, repatriated sick men, and letters, and papers like this one mark stages in assembling a picture long kept deliberately dark.
cia-0000132311:
Kuwaiti oil fires and the major threat they posed fill Situation Report 621 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series. The report is dated February 6, 1991. Hundreds of wells were burning at once. Smoke from the fires choked much of the region and darkened the daytime sky.

The report assesses what the fires threatened most. Health, weather, water supplies, and shipping all stood at risk. So did the hard work of putting the wells out once fighting stopped. The burning fields became one of the war's most lasting images around the world. Readers get the agency's judgment, made while the fires still raged, of how serious the damage could become.
cia-0000132511: February 4, 1961 brought yet another CIA briefing titled simply Cuba. The pile of same-day papers shows the priority the island held for Kennedy's new team, which wanted constant updates while the Bay of Pigs operation was being planned. Cuba led the agenda that winter. Released long afterward, this declassified copy is preserved from the CIA Reading Room via the Internet Archive.
cia-0000132611: Cuba alone fills part three of a CIA item dated July 1, 1960. The section is headed the West. In that section Cuba stood as the standing headline through 1960, needing no further label. A single word carried the whole Cuba file for that day. The short item preserves the entry exactly as the series labeled it.
cia-0000135711: A document in Spanish dated 1 February 1961, from the declassified papers of Brigade 2506, the Cuban exile force assembled by the CIA. February opened the brigade's last stretch of training. The catalog record names no topic for this item. Preserved in the original Spanish, it is part of the dense February run of brigade paperwork that the agency later released, and its contents must be read in the text itself.
cia-0000135911: A CIA cable dated 5 May 1954 deals with the true story, in the cable's own words, in files since declassified. The paper sits inside the CIA drive against President Arbenz, run under the code name PBSUCCESS and crowned by the June 1954 coup. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136611: An estimated date of 4 November 1960 heads this Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade files, with the estimate flagged in the catalog title. The brigade was training that fall for the invasion of Cuba. Because the date is estimated, the agency's reviewers assigned it rather than copying it from the page. No subject is recorded for the item. It is preserved in Spanish in the declassified release, among the brigade's November paperwork.
cia-0000137011: Meet with the ambassador, SKILLET proposes in this July 1954 cable. It asks the Guatemala City station to discuss a conference with JMBLUG. The ambassador hopes the station will do this. He wants the station to press him at a 23 July conference. A fragment notes he failed to mention something in a referenced message. The sample here is too short and garbled for more. The conference's subject cannot be recovered. The cable still shows the new ambassador being drawn in fast.
cia-0000137111: An estimated-date 1961 Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade papers; the catalog gives only the year and marks it as estimated. The Brigade was the CIA-trained Cuban exile force that landed at the Bay of Pigs in April 1961. The record names no subject or month for this item. It is preserved in the original Spanish in the declassified release, a loosely dated piece of the brigade's final-year archive.
cia-0000137411: Spanish paperwork from Brigade 2506 fills document 0000137411, dated to 1961 with the date itself marked as an estimate. The brigade was the exile unit the CIA built for the Bay of Pigs, and much of its internal writing stayed in the men's own language. No subject line comes with this record, so its precise business is left to the page itself. It stands as one small piece of a failed invasion's archive, now open to any reader.
cia-03150411:
The Gulf of Aqaba opens the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 9 March 1957. A comment weighs Israel's stated intention to force passage for its shipping. Foreign Minister Meir told the UN secretary general on 5 March that Israeli vessels would sail the Straits of Tiran within the week. Ben-Gurion told parliament force would protect Israeli rights. Egypt's shore guns commanding the gulf had been destroyed.

The comment still counts Egypt's Red Sea frigate, torpedo boats, and thirty-five IL-28 bombers as a threat. Israeli air and naval strength is judged sufficient to cover the passage. Indonesia's government fears a revolt in Borneo. Tension rises in Hungary before the 15 March holiday. Gomulka warns the Polish press to end its anti-Stalinist campaign. A Ghana official suggests relations with the Soviet bloc may follow independence.
cia-03186011:
Laos opens the Central Intelligence Bulletin dated 16 March 1961. Talks between Souvanna Phouma and a Vientiane delegation on 14-15 March failed. Souvanna now insists on a fourteen-nation conference before any settlement. His new rigidity contrasts with last week's flexibility toward General Phoumi. Bloc disapproval of their joint communiqué is the likely cause. Peiping broadcasts a Pathet Lao call to prepare for protracted resistance.

In the Congo, a United Arab Republic mission in Stanleyville reports a concealed dispute between Gizenga and Lundula. Army and public went unpaid in February, raising the risk of disorder. Hammarskjold weighs his Congo representation amid questions of Indian prestige. Paris announces willingness to negotiate with the Algerian rebels. South Africa withdraws from the Commonwealth. Portuguese authorities in Angola uncover plans for an attack near Luanda. Saudi rivalry between King Saud and Crown Prince Faysal may soon come to a head.
cia-06345911:
Directorate of Intelligence paper dated 30 April 1990 assesses how German unification and East European reforms might affect EC farm policy. Its summary states that neither change was likely to move the European Community away from its protectionist Common Agricultural Policy. East German food demand in 1990 was expected to outrun any rise in farm output there.

The paper assesses that the Community would stay with a gradual path on farm trade and oppose American efforts to end subsidies. Some experts cited expected a 20 percent rise in East German farm output. If that came, the paper argues, CAP spending would rise to handle surpluses in goods such as grain. By the late 1990s, a revived East European farm sector could force basic CAP reform, the paper concludes.
codex-junius-11:
Codex Junius 11 preserves the great biblical poems of Anglo-Saxon England, here in English translation: Genesis A, Genesis B, Exodus, Daniel, and Christ and Satan. The poems were composed between the seventh and tenth centuries and once ascribed to Caedmon, though scholars now see several hands. The manuscript's first book retells scripture from creation onward.

Genesis gives the fall of the angels and of Adam, with the flood and Abraham's journeys, while Exodus turns Moses' escape into a heroic sea-battle. Daniel and Christ and Satan close the volume with prophecy and the harrowing of hell. The translation keeps the poems' strong, alliterative flavor, opening a door into the oldest English Christian poetry.
conrad-under-western-eyes-1911:
Joseph Conrad, born in Poland under Russian rule, returned to the world of revolutionaries in Under Western Eyes, published in 1911. An English teacher of languages in Geneva tells the story. It is often called Conrad's darkest political novel.

A St. Petersburg student named Razumov shelters an assassin who has just killed a minister. Fearing ruin, Razumov betrays him, then is sent to Geneva as a spy on the exile circle. There he falls in love with the dead man's sister while living his lie. The novel dissects guilt, autocracy, and the blindness of the watching West.
constitution-canada-2011:
Canada's constitution is not one act but a set of acts, gathered here in a consolidation through 2011. The core is the Constitution Act of 1867, which united the provinces in one federal state under the Crown. It splits lawmaking between a federal Parliament and the provinces. The Senate and the House of Commons form Parliament, with a Governor General for the monarch.

Layered on top is the Constitution Act of 1982. It adds the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, covering speech, faith, fair trials, and language rights. It also protects the rights of the Aboriginal peoples of Canada and sets the rules for changing the constitution itself. Those change rules are famously hard to meet.
constitution-gabon-2011:
Gabon adopted this constitution in 1991, as one-party rule ended across much of Africa, and the hosted text carries changes through 2011. Early titles cover the state and sovereignty. Gabon is a republic, and French is the official language. Rights and freedoms follow, with duties for citizens set beside them.

A president with wide powers leads the executive, naming a prime minister and government. Parliament pairs a National Assembly with a Senate, the Senate added in a later change. Other titles cover the courts, a Constitutional Court, local areas, and ties with other states. In practice, one party and one family held power for decades under this text, which critics said the rules did little to check.
constitution-morocco-2011:
Morocco gained a revised constitution in 2011, after street protests across the Arab world reached its cities, and the hosted text is that version. Early titles give general provisions. Morocco is a constitutional monarchy, Islam is the state religion, and both Arabic and Amazigh, the Berber tongue, are official languages, a first for the country. A title protects basic freedoms and rights.

The King stays head of state, commander of the faithful, and chair of the top security and religious bodies. Under the 2011 rules, the King must name the head of government from the party that wins elections. Parliament pairs a House of Representatives with a House of Councillors. Later titles cover the courts, local regions, and finance.
constitution-oman-2011:
Oman's Basic Statute of the State was issued by Sultan Qaboos in 1996, the country's first written basic law, and the hosted text includes changes through 2011. Early parts cover the state and its system of rule. Oman is a hereditary sultanate. Islam is the state religion, and Arabic is the official language. Later parts list the principles guiding the state's policies and public rights and duties.

The Sultan heads the state and the government, names ministers, and commands the armed forces. A Council of Oman joins an elected Shura Council with an appointed State Council, both advisory in weight. Other parts cover the courts and finance. Changes in 2011, after rare protests, promised the councils a somewhat larger say over laws and budgets.
constitution-paraguay-2011:
Paraguay adopted this constitution in 1992, three years after the long Stroessner dictatorship fell, and the hosted text includes changes through 2011. Early parts give the basic statements on rights, duties, and promises, then the political order of the republic. Paraguay is a single republic that calls itself bilingual: Spanish and Guarani are both official languages, and Guarani is spoken by most of the people.

A president leads the executive and is barred from re-election for good, a guard written after decades of one-man rule. Congress pairs a Senate with a Chamber of Deputies. Later parts cover the courts, a constitutional chamber, local departments and towns, elections, and public finance. The charter also protects indigenous peoples and their lands by name.
constitution-spain-2011:
Spain adopted this constitution in 1978, three years after Franco's death, and the hosted text includes changes through 2011. A preliminary title founds a social and democratic state based on law, in the form of a parliamentary monarchy. A long title protects basic rights and duties, from life and free speech to schooling and work, then lists the principles that should guide social and economic policy.

The King heads the state, while a prime minister, called the President of the Government, holds real power. The Cortes Generales pair a Congress of Deputies with a Senate. Later titles cover the courts, a Constitutional Court, and the autonomous communities that give Spain's regions wide self-rule. The text's care with both unity and self-rule is its core bargain.
conte-ponthieu-mason-1911:
The Count of Ponthieu is an anonymous French tale from the age of the Crusades. It calls itself a story of beyond the sea. Eugene Mason translated it into English in 1911, in a volume of old French tales of love and war.

Its heroine, the count's daughter, is seized while traveling and carried off overseas. A Saracen emir falls in love with her and treats her with honor. Around her gather questions of ransom, faith, and conversion. The tale shows how medieval Christians imagined the Muslim world they fought, feared, and sometimes admired.
cotgrave-french-english-1611:
Randle Cotgrave published his Dictionarie of the French and English Tongues in 1611, the first great French-English dictionary. Cotgrave served as secretary to a great lord and spent years gathering French words from books and speech. His England was learning the tongue of Montaigne and needed a bridge between the languages.

The dictionary gives French words with generous English equivalents, proverbs, and turns of phrase, often with a flash of humor. It records the spoken French of its day beside the literary language, which makes it a treasure house of early modern speech. Four hundred years on, it remains a foundation of French study in England. Scholars of Shakespeare's age use it to catch meanings that modern French has lost, and students of both tongues still delight in its riches.
cumont-oriental-religions-showerman-1911:
Franz Cumont's The Oriental Religions in Roman Paganism appears in Grant Showerman's translation of 1911. Cumont studies the cults that flowed into Rome from the East. Isis from Egypt, Mithras from Persia, Cybele from Asia Minor, and Syrian gods transformed Roman religion. Their rites promised purity and life after death.

Cumont argues these faiths prepared the way for Christianity's triumph. His synthesis was a masterwork that reshaped the study of Roman religion. Later scholars corrected details, yet his map still guides the field. The lectures read clearly for general audiences. They remain the classic short account of Rome's eastern cults. Showerman's version served English readers well.
de-lapide-philosophorvm-tractatvs-dvodec:
Twelve Latin tracts on the philosophers' stone fill this Frankfurt book of 1611. Johann Bringer printed it at the cost of Anthony Humm. The title says the tracts are drawn from nature's fount and from hand-worked experience, that is, from practice at the furnace.

The author hides his name in a Latin anagram that points to Michael Sendivogius. His preface greets all seekers of the chemical art, true sons of Hermes, and scorns the false books abroad in the art's name. Mars and Venus, sun and moon, copper and mercury pass in review. Some, he says, can make the moon from Saturn, yet miss the one thing worth more than all treasure. The book is a core text of the new chemical light.
descartes-philosophical-works-haldane-ro:
Elizabeth S Haldane and G R T Ross published Volume 1 of The Philosophical Works of Descartes in 1911. Their translation became the standard English Descartes for most of the twentieth century. René Descartes, the French founder of modern philosophy, wrote the works gathered here across his career.

Volume 1 holds the Rules for the Direction of the Mind, the Discourse on Method, and the Meditations on First Philosophy. Selections from the Principles of Philosophy, The Search after Truth, and The Passions of the Soul follow. Readers meet the cogito, the doubt of the senses, and the split of mind and body in Descartes's own order. No single volume gives a fuller start on him.
dirty-work-deep-waters-part-11:
One night-watchman tale, Dirty Work, fills this eleventh part of W. W. Jacobs's Deep Waters. The watchman sits aboard a lighter at near high water, smoking his pipe as the wharves empty. Perfumed clouds of shag tobacco drift toward the Surrey shore.

His job, he says, is done all alone, from six at night to six in the morning, with no foreman to holler at him. He gave up letting folk sit with him after one chap fell overboard while showing how he put his wife's mother in her place. Three foot of mud waited in the dock that night. A row over a tanner, a sixpence, and a bell rung without pause fills the sampled talk. Jacobs lets the watchman's voice carry all.
double-dealing-sailor-s-knots-part-11:
W. W. Jacobs tells a seaside mix-up in Double Dealing, part eleven of his Sailor's Knots tales dated 1909. Mr. Fred Carter, a Londoner on holiday, stands on the common breathing in the salt air when a burly man of fifty and his son walk up and greet him with plain spite. They claim they have him at last.

The pair take Carter for one Bert, a man who has wronged their Nancy, and they talk of hammering him and throwing him in the sea. Carter smiles and asks what reason he would have to claim a name not his. Nancy herself, when she comes, settles the point at a look: it is not Bert. Jacobs spins the joke on stubborn pride, family honor, and a face that fits the wrong story. The tale is short, dry, and built for a laugh at the end.
dreiser-jennie-gerhardt-1911:
Theodore Dreiser published Jennie Gerhardt in 1911, eleven years after his first novel was buried by its own publisher. His editors cut the manuscript heavily, fearing its treatment of an unmarried mother. Dreiser based Jennie partly on his own sisters' hard lives in Indiana poverty.

Jennie, a poor laundress in Columbus, is seduced by an aging senator who dies before he can marry her. She then devotes herself to a rich man's son, Lester Kane, living with him outside marriage and sacrificing her happiness to protect his. Dreiser refuses to judge her; his slow, heavy prose builds pity instead. Jennie Gerhardt is his most tender and morally complex novel, and the one many readers love best.
essays-idleness-sansom-1911:
G. B. Sansom Englished Yoshida Kenko's Essays in Idleness in 1911, the first English rendering of the Tsurezuregusa. Kenko, a fourteenth-century courtier turned recluse, set down short pieces as thoughts came to him. Beauty, death, manners, and the folly of ambition drift through his meditations without fixed order.

Kenko loves old things, quiet rooms, and the turning seasons, and distrusts fuss of every kind. His book became one of Japan's most loved classics, a model of the zuihitsu, the follow-the-brush essay. Sansom's translation introduced that gentle art to English readers for the first time.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-11:
Volume 11 of Michel de Montaigne's Essays, in Charles Cotton's English translation, gathers five chapters from the French writer's long self-study. Montaigne (1533-1592) wrote the Essays in retirement at his estate in southwestern France. He tests every subject against his own feelings and limits. Few topics stay abstract for long in his hands.

Readers meet essays on judging how another person faces death, and on the mind tripping over itself. One chapter argues that difficulty makes desire stronger, not weaker. Another weighs glory and the hunger for praise from strangers. A closing chapter on presumption mocks people who rate their own worth too high. Montaigne fills each piece with Roman stories, Latin lines, and frank talk about his body and moods. People open these chapters for clear sight about pride, fear, and wanting what stays out of reach.
eucken-truth-religion-1911:
What truth does religion hold, and where does that truth rest? Rudolf Eucken, the 1908 Nobel laureate from Jena, took up both questions in Der Wahrheitsgehalt der Religion in 1901. W. Tudor Jones translated the work, and the text here follows the second edition of 1913.

Eucken argues that religion speaks to the deepest layer of human life, the life of the spirit. He tests rival views of faith and sets out the ground on which belief can stand. His case ties religion to moral effort and inner renewal. The book forms a key part of his philosophy of religion.
europmc-pmc10210811:
Lt.-Colonel Joseph A. Capps of the Medical Corps reported a year of fighting streptococcus and other breathing infections at Camp Grant in 1918. Trouble began with lobar pneumonia in the fall. Then, in December 1917, some 6,500 troops arrived from Jefferson and Columbus Barracks carrying colds, and the wards filled with bronchitis, broncho-pneumonia, and empyema. A second outbreak in late January brought sore throats, swollen neck glands, and deep exhaustion.

Capps describes the defense his camp built: wards divided into cubicles, and every patient issued a clean mask each day, pinned to the cubicle sheet when not worn. Men were told the cubicle was like a dug-out in a gassed area: safe inside, risky to leave unmasked. He gives figures on cross-infection with scarlet fever before and after masking. Readers get a camp doctor's account of stopping spread in crowded wards.
europmc-pmc10767911:
Milacic and co-authors updated Reactome in 2024, a free knowledge base of biological pathways. Reactome charts cell processes as ordered chains of molecular steps. Each entry is curated by hand in one shared data model. The bank serves both as an archive and as a tool to mine gene data.

Work pushes toward notes on the full human protein set, Milacic reports. Disease-causing gene variants and small-molecule drugs gain pathway context as well. Cell- and tissue-specific paths are a further growth front. Links with kin resources, such as the Gene Ontology, need care to keep the web sound. The team weighs how to keep that shared network in good health.
europmc-pmc10776411:
Lin and Peddada present a new stats method for gut and soil microbe studies in this 2024 paper. A microbiome is the full mix of tiny living things in a sample. Labs often ask which microbes grow or shrink between groups of samples. Older tools handle two groups well, but many studies have three or more groups, such as stages of a disease.

Their method, ANCOM-BC2, compares many groups at once. It can adjust for other factors that differ between samples, and it can use repeat samples from the same source. Pair-by-pair checks waste power and raise false alarms, the authors note. They show the method on soil samples sorted by dryness and on gut samples from bowel disease patients before and after surgery.
europmc-pmc11122111:
GBD 2021 Diseases and Injuries Collaborators report health loss for 371 diseases and injuries across 204 countries in this 2024 study. Detailed counts of sickness and early death by cause are crucial for spotting shifting patterns over time. For three decades the Global Burden of Disease study has filled that need. This round adds, for the first time, health loss from the COVID-19 pandemic.

The team estimated years lived with disability, years of life lost, a combined burden measure, and healthy life expectancy. Counts are split by age, sex, and place, including 811 subnational locations, for 1990 to 2021. A global network of collaborators supplied, reviewed, and analysed the data. Methods were refined with each update, the authors note. They frame the estimates as a base for evidence-based action and for tracking health targets.
europmc-pmc11456611:
Li and colleagues review the signalling pathways behind colorectal cancer and its targeted therapies in this 2024 paper. Colorectal cancer is still among the top causes of cancer death worldwide. Networks that govern cell proliferation, survival, differentiation, and death run its development. Their dysregulation turns normal colon lining malignant.

The review dissects the foundational mechanisms and the molecular hallmarks of the disease. Genomic, epigenomic, and microbial features are covered: changes to DNA, changes to its chemical tags, and the gut microbes present. Targeted and immune therapies are then assessed for their clinical impact. Deepening knowledge of oncogenic signalling has revealed key nodes that drugs can exploit, the authors say. Remaining challenges include resistance and patient selection. The paper aims to state the general principles of neoplastic evolution in this cancer.
europmc-pmc12369211:
Izquierdo and a large expert panel set exercise guidance for older adults in 2021. Aging weakens every body function over time. How people live shapes how fast that decline runs. Staying active is the strongest known brake.

The panel writes for the ICFSR, an international research body. Regular exercise guards muscle, fitness, and daily independence. It also lowers risk of heart disease, stroke, and diabetes. Gains extend to mobility, mood, and quality of life. Izquierdo merges global evidence into shared advice. The guidance aims to keep older adults active and independent longer.
europmc-pmc1239911:
Wolfe, Kohane, and Butte tested a common shortcut in gene research in 2005. Genes that switch on together often share a job. So an unknown gene may be judged by the company it keeps. That shortcut is called guilt by association.

How far the shortcut truly holds was untested at scale. The team built scores linking each gene to known job groups. They checked five networks across three mammal species. Expression data came from a large and varied collection. Wolfe shows where the shortcut works and where prior knowledge misses it.
europmc-pmc1280411:
Brown, Lockwood, and Sonawane reviewed environmental risks for degenerative brain diseases in 2005. America is aging, and these diseases grow more common. Causes of most remain unknown. The review gathers population evidence on environmental suspects.

Diseases covered include Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, and ALS. Related parkinsonian syndromes also enter the survey.
