Suspect exposures range from metals and pesticides to solvents and fields. Evidence for each link was judged not conclusive overall. Still, indications of causal links appear across studies. Brown calls the need for more research obvious. Electromagnetic fields are among the exposures surveyed. Metals and solvents get their own checks in the text.
europmc-pmc1382011:
Kilpatrick and co-authors explained West Nile epidemics through mosquito feeding shifts in 2006. The virus arrived in North America in 1999. It is now the dominant mosquito-borne disease there. Spillover from birds to humans sets epidemic intensity.

The main urban mosquito shifted feeding from birds to humans seven times. The shift came in late summer and early fall. It coincided with dispersal of its preferred host, the American robin. Human infections rose at the same time. A western mosquito showed the same amplifying shift in Colorado and California. Feeding behavior, not just virus presence, drives epidemics. Robins leave the Northeast as fall comes on.
europmc-pmc1435411:
Spending on nature protection runs into billions, yet few ask if the money works. Ferraro and Pattanayak made that charge in 2006. They argue the field of conservation policy leans on gut feel and stories from the field. Other fields, such as poverty aid and disease control, test programs with care.

The pair call for the same rigor used to test ideas about ecosystems. A sound test asks if a program beats doing nothing at all. Ferraro notes that a major global review found data-rich biology chapters, but thin proof on policy results. Without such tests, scarce funds may flow to plans that feel right but fail.
europmc-pmc1479811:
Each blood cell type runs its own set of genes. Palmer and co-authors charted those sets in 2006 for the main white cell types in human blood. They purified B cells, two T cell kinds, and other white cells from donors. Then they compared their gene activity on chips.

Like cells from unlike donors grouped together by their patterns. Each type had a signature set of genes: 427 for B cells, 411 for granulocytes, and smaller sets for others. Surface protein genes stood out among the markers. Palmer suggests the signatures can guide work on the many genes whose jobs remain unknown.
europmc-pmc1764711:
Gene-swapping enzymes for mammals mostly meant one tool, Cre. Raymond and Soriano added two more in 2007 by synthesizing mouse-optimized versions, FLPo and PhiC31o. Site-specific recombinases cut and rejoin DNA at set addresses, letting researchers delete or flip genes.

Earlier FLP and PhiC31 versions worked poorly in mammalian cells. Recoding their genes with mouse-preferred codons lifted their efficiency to match Cre. Having three efficient enzymes opens more complex genome engineering, like sequential edits using different address systems. Raymond reports the new enzymes function in living cells at high efficiency.  Tests in cells confirmed both new enzymes recombine their target sites with high efficiency.
europmc-pmc1779511:
Bonneau and colleagues presented in 2006 a computer method named the Inferelator. The method learns gene control networks from large biology data sets. A control network shows which genes switch other genes on or off, and which outside signals matter.

The core problem is that data are scarce next to the many possible controls. The Inferelator picks a short, simple set of likely controls for each gene, favoring models that stay lean. It can also handle cases where two control proteins act together, or where light and other signals change a control. Tested on the salt-loving microbe Halobacterium, the learned network predicted gene activity under new test conditions the model had not seen. That success showed the approach could rebuild global control maps from scratch.
europmc-pmc1800311:
Boutron, Ravaud and colleagues cataloged in 2007 how trialists hide treatment assignment in studies of non-drug care. Blinding, where patients or clinicians do not know who got which treatment, guards against bias. It is hard to achieve for surgery, devices, rehab, or talk therapy, so teams invent nonstandard tricks.

The authors searched major databases for randomized trials published in 2004 in high-impact journals. They found 145 reports, with the blinding method described in 123 of them. Sham procedures that mimic surgery were a main route for participants and providers. Device trials used sham prostheses, identical but switched-off machines, or machines blocked by a barrier. Another common tactic blinded patients to the study hypothesis itself rather than to the treatment they received.
europmc-pmc1849911:
Gojova, Barakat and co-authors tested in 2007 whether tiny metal oxide particles stir inflammation in human blood vessel cells. Ultrafine particles can cross from the lung into the blood, which may explain their link to heart disease. The cells lining vessels, the endothelium, drive much of that disease process.

They exposed human aortic endothelial cells for up to eight hours to particles of iron oxide, yttrium oxide, and zinc oxide across a wide dose range. They then measured three inflammation markers, including interleukin-8 and a monocyte-attracting protein. Particle delivery to the cell surface and uptake inside the cells tracked directly with the inflammatory response. Composition mattered: the three oxides did not provoke equal reactions at equal doses. The work supports direct vessel contact as a route from inhaled particles to cardiovascular harm.
europmc-pmc1854911:
Matsuo and co-authors traced in 2007 why one fruit fly species loves a fruit its cousins avoid. Drosophila sechellia feeds on Morinda citrifolia, the Tahitian noni, whose ripe fruit gives off hexanoic and octanoic acids. Sister species are repelled by those acids, while sechellia is drawn to them.

Crossing sechellia with deletion strains of a sister species pinned part of the difference on a gene named Obp57e. It codes an odorant-binding protein, a carrier that ferries smell molecules. Knocking out Obp57e and its neighbor Obp57d in the sister species changed responses to both acids. Putting the sechellia or cousin versions of the two genes into the knockout flies shifted egg-laying site choice to match the donor species. The genes thus help set host-plant preference through taste.
europmc-pmc2125011:
Ernest M. Watson, writing from Brown University and the Johns Hopkins hygienic laboratory, argued in 1913 that the Negri bodies of rabies are living parasites. Since 1903, when Negri found them inside the nerve cells of rabid brains, opinion had split on whether they were the cause of rabies or a by-product of it.

Watson studies their forms stage by stage. He finds two repeating phases: a multiplying phase and a spore-forming, reproductive phase. On that life history he places them among the protozoa, in the Microsporidia, single-spore makers of the Glugeidae family. He expects tissue culture, then advancing fast, to settle the matter soon. Readers get a confident period answer to a famous question, argued from a parasite's supposed life cycle drawn in detail.
europmc-pmc2125511:
Oswald H. Robertson and Peyton Rous asked in 1917 how red blood cells normally end. In animals made plethoric by transfusion, the surplus cells are destroyed mainly by fragmentation: the corpuscles break apart in circulation without losing their hemoglobin. The spleens of such animals fill with the debris pieces, the microcytes and poikilocytes.

The same fragments explain an anemic puzzle. In severe anemia after hemorrhage, those small misshapen cells are not manufactured undersized by the marrow. They are shards of circulating cells, and for the most part of the new cells the marrow rushed out. The spleen's accumulations mark it as a clearing house for fragments. The normal end of a red cell, in species where eating cells are minor, is to be broken one by one into fine hemoglobin-bearing dust. Readers get blood's death certificate rewritten as shattering.
europmc-pmc2125811:
Ada Hart Arlitt and H. Gideon Wells fed alcohol to male white rats to see what steady drinking does to the reproductive tissues. Their 1917 Journal of Experimental Medicine paper reports daily doses mixed into food over months, followed by close study of the testicles. They also checked the other organs, and set human autopsy findings beside the animal results.

After two or more months, nearly every rat showed marked decay in the testicles. Damage struck the steps of sperm formation in reverse order, so males long produced faulty sperm of every degree before full sterility set in. Individual rats differed widely in how much harm the same dose caused. The fibrous and vessel parts of the testicle stayed sound, and no liver cirrhosis or fatty change appeared. The authors note the clear risk to offspring from such damaged sperm.
europmc-pmc2128211:
Wade H. Brown and Louise Pearce asked whether partly cured syphilis leaves a rabbit open to a second infection. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1921. Rabbits with well-marked testicular lesions received doses of arsphenamine or neoarsphenamine too small to cure, then were reinoculated with the same Treponema pallidum strain at the height of the first reaction.

An existing infection, the results show, is no bar in itself to planting a second one. Animals that had become resistant could again become open to new infection under the right conditions. Treatment with either drug produced exactly that state: treated but uncured rabbits were as open to a second skin inoculation as normal animals. The second infection's lesions looked like a first infection's. Underdosed treatment, the work warns, can return a patient to full susceptibility while the first infection still lives.
europmc-pmc2128411:
Louise Pearce and Wade H. Brown transplanted their rabbit malignant tumor by seven different routes and compared the results. Their paper is the fourth based on that tumor, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1923. Testicular inoculation, the series' standard, served as the contrast for brain, eye, muscle, skin, and body cavity placements.

Inoculations into the brain, the front chamber of the eye, and the muscles took almost every time, giving large, vigorously growing tumors. Skin placements did less well, and placements under the skin, in veins, or in the belly grew in only a fifth to a quarter of animals. Against the testicular route's malignant course, these tumors behaved mildly: they stayed local, sometimes invading nearby tissue, but never seeded distant organs. Brain tumors killed by pressure alone. The route, more than the tumor, decided how deadly the growth would be.
europmc-pmc2128611:
Louise Pearce, Wade H. Brown, and Chester M. Van Allen analyzed which factors drove the wandering behavior of their transplanted rabbit tumor. Their paper is the second section of the sixth study based on that tumor, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1924. The first section had recorded twenty generations of results; this one weighs passage, inoculum, animal, and season.

The material used for inoculation mattered comparatively little to the final results. The animals mattered more: the tumor showed definite growth and malignancy peculiarities tied to the host's age and to its breed or color markings. Even so, none of these factors seemed able to explain the observed swings. Two principal drivers remained: adaptation to passage, acting on the energy of cell growth, and the season and weather during each experiment, acting on the animal's economy. Growth, in short, answers to the tumor's history and the year's season together.
europmc-pmc2131311:
Richmond Moore studied the Hering-Breuer reflex in a 1927 paper in The Journal of Experimental Medicine. That reflex links lung inflation to the control of breathing through the vagus nerves. Moore recorded the breathing of each lung apart, then cut one vagus nerve, blocked one bronchus, or did both, to see which change drove the altered breathing.

Cutting one vagus slowed and deepened the breathing of both lungs alike, with no special effect on the cut side. Blocking a bronchus first slowed and deepened the other lung's breathing, then made it fast and shallow as oxygen ran short. The combined tests show the slow, deep pattern after nerve cutting does not depend on air moving in the lung whose nerve was cut.
europmc-pmc2242811:
Hansen, Chandra, Mitic, Onken, Driscoll and Kenyon tested in 2008 whether autophagy is required for dietary restriction to extend lifespan in worms. Autophagy is the cell's large-scale recycling of its own proteins and organelles. Eating less extends life in many species, partly by quieting the nutrient sensor TOR. TOR inhibition switches autophagy on. The team blocked autophagy genes in Caenorhabditis elegans under dietary restriction and TOR inhibition.

Both interventions produced an autophagic state in the worms. Blocking autophagy genes prevented both from extending lifespan. The response also needed the transcription factor PHA-4, which dietary restriction requires for longevity. Yet autophagy alone was not sufficient to extend life. Long-lived insulin-pathway mutants needed both autophagy and the factor DAF-16. The authors suggest DAF-16 directs recycled material into protective proteins.
europmc-pmc2244711:
Sandin and a large team surveyed coral reefs in 2008 across the Northern Line Islands to set a pristine baseline. Most reefs are degraded by fishing, pollution and global change, tangling local and global effects. The team studied uninhabited atolls, Kingman and Palmyra, and increasingly populated ones, Tabuaeran and Kiritimati. They compared reef community structure along that human gradient.

Top predators and reef-building organisms dominated the unpopulated atolls. Sharks and other large predators made the biomass pyramid inverted, with more predator weight than prey. Small plankton-eating fish and fleshy algae dominated the populated atolls. Those showed the typical bottom-heavy pyramid. Reefs without people had less coral disease and greater coral recruitment. The authors argue protection from fishing and pollution builds resilience against warming.
europmc-pmc2267811:
Morrison, Zielinski-Gutierrez, Scott and Rosenberg set out challenges in 2008 for controlling the mosquito Aedes aegypti. This daytime-biting mosquito spreads dengue, yellow fever and chikungunya, and lives in and around human homes. History shows control can work: eliminating breeding sites enabled Panama Canal construction, and eradication campaigns cleared both diseases from most of Central and South America in the 1950s and 1960s.

Yet those successes were usually short-lived, and dengue has reoccupied Latin America. Urbanisation expands mosquito habitat, global travel spreads vector and virus, and poverty hobbles household protection. The authors argue eradication is unrealistic. The practical goal is reducing adult mosquito numbers or human contact below the level that sustains an epidemic. Suppression done properly remains a practical method, they conclude.
europmc-pmc2291011:
Adibi and colleagues characterised phthalate exposure in pregnancy in 2008 by testing how stable urine and air measurements stay over time. Phthalates are plastics and cosmetics chemicals measured through their breakdown products in urine, but repeatability during pregnancy was unknown. The team measured metabolites in spot urine from 246 pregnant women of Dominican and African-American background. Some samples were repeated over six weeks. They also sampled personal and indoor air for five parent compounds.

Phthalates appeared in 85 to 100 percent of air and urine samples. Reproducibility of urine metabolites varied. Correlation coefficients started at 0.30 for mono-ethyl phthalate and rose to 0.66 for monobenzyl phthalate. The strongest air correlations reached 0.83 for butylbenzyl phthalate across repeated home samples. Air levels tracked matching urinary metabolites. Urine from late pregnancy was best adjusted by specific gravity. One indoor air sample suffices, but urine needs repeated sampling.
europmc-pmc2360111:
Eckel and Schmid pooled trial results for advanced biliary tract cancer in 2007. This cancer grows in the bile ducts or gallbladder, and no standard drug treatment existed. Randomised trials, the strongest kind, were missing, so doctors relied on small early studies of drugs such as 5-fluorouracil and gemcitabine.

The authors analysed 104 trials with 2,810 patients, covering work from 1985 to 2006. Across all trials, tumors shrank in 22.6% of patients, and disease was controlled in 57.3% of them, figures the analysis linked to longer survival. Gallbladder cancer shrank more often than bile duct cancer but patients died sooner. Regimens pairing gemcitabine with a platinum drug performed best. The authors called that pairing the provisional standard until stronger evidence arrives.
europmc-pmc2394311:
Adami and colleagues tracked cancer risk after organ transplants across Sweden in 2003. Transplant patients take drugs that suppress the immune system, which may let cancers grow unchecked. The study followed 5,931 people who received a kidney, liver, or other organ between 1970 and 1997.

Linking to national registers gave nearly complete follow-up. The team counted 692 first cancers against 171 expected from general population rates, a four-fold excess overall. Non-melanoma skin cancer stood out at a standardised ratio of 56.2, and lip cancer at 53.3 in the same measure, while lymphoma ran six-fold high. Patients with organs other than kidneys faced far higher lymphoma risk than kidney recipients. Twenty-fold excesses appeared for vulva and vagina cancers, and ten-fold for anal cancer. The excess persisted over time.
europmc-pmc2518111:
Dwan and a large group of collaborators reviewed the evidence in 2008 that clinical trials are published selectively. Two distortions were in view: whole studies going unpublished, and published reports quietly changing which outcomes they feature. Both can mislead the reviews that doctors rely on to judge treatments.

Sixteen cohort studies that tracked trials from approval onward met the criteria. Trials with positive, statistically significant results were more likely to reach print. Significant outcomes had 2.2 to 4.7 times the odds of being fully reported compared with non-significant ones. Between 40 and 62 percent of studies changed, added, or dropped at least one main outcome between protocol and publication. The authors call for better trial reporting to curb both biases.
europmc-pmc2527811:
Lammers, Hennink, and Storm reviewed in 2008 how tiny drug carriers could deliver cancer medicines straight to tumours. These nanomedicines are particles measured in billionths of a metre that ferry chemotherapy drugs through the bloodstream. Without them, injected drugs clear fast, only a small share reaches the tumour, and healthy tissues suffer the toxic effects.

The review covers the main carrier families, including liposomes, which are fat bubbles, and polymer particles, plus the strategies for steering them. Some designs raise drug levels inside the tumour to boost killing power. Others steer drug away from sensitive organs to cut side effects. The authors report clear evidence that such targeting improves the balance of benefit to harm for anticancer agents, and they map where the field should go next.
europmc-pmc2569211:
Paulsen, reporting for the Predict-HD Investigators and Coordinators of the Huntington Study Group, presented in 2008 evidence that Huntington's disease develops measurably decades before diagnosis. The study followed 438 people who carry the disease gene but show no functional decline. Using each person's gene repeat length and age to estimate years until diagnosis, the team modelled thinking, movement, mood, and brain imaging measures against that clock.

Nearly every marker tracked the estimated time to diagnosis. The pattern suggests detectable changes begin one to two decades before doctors could traditionally diagnose the disease. The findings held up across very different kinds of measurement. The authors propose these early markers as candidates for prevention trials, which need ways to measure disease long before symptoms declare themselves.
europmc-pmc2585011:
Petkova and Ehrsson reported in 2008 a laboratory illusion in which people feel they have swapped bodies with another person or a mannequin. Feeling located inside one's own body is central to selfhood, yet how the brain produces it was unclear. The team manipulated what volunteers saw through head-mounted displays while delivering matching touches to two bodies at once.

The combination of an outside visual perspective and synchronised touch was enough to relocate the sense of self. Volunteers felt the other body was their own, even while facing their real body. The effect grew so strong that participants could shake hands with their own body while experiencing it as someone else. The authors identify the perceptual processes, vision plus correlated multisensory signals, that create body ownership.
europmc-pmc2613511:
Zhang, Lv, Li, Xu, and Chen refined a rat model of type 2 diabetes in 2008, combining a high-fat diet with injections of streptozotocin, a chemical that damages insulin-producing cells. Existing models often miss the human pattern of insulin resistance plus failing insulin release. The team fed male Wistar rats a fatty diet for four weeks, then varied the dose and number of streptozotocin injections.

A single 45 milligram per kilogram dose produced diabetes in every rat but slashed insulin too far, unlike human disease. Two weekly injections of 30 milligrams per kilogram worked best, succeeding in 85 percent of rats. Those animals showed the classic trio of insulin resistance, high blood sugar, and disordered blood lipids. The plant compound berberine then reversed these symptoms, validating the model for drug screening.
europmc-pmc2631711:
Chambers argued in 2001 that the epidemiology of Staphylococcus aureus is changing, as methicillin-resistant strains escape the hospitals where they had been confined. MRSA had lived almost exclusively in hospitals and long-term care facilities, striking patients with prior antibiotics, surgery, or intensive care. New reports described resistant infections in children from the community with none of those risk factors.

Chambers draws a striking parallel with the emergence of penicillin resistance in the same bacterium decades earlier, which also began in hospitals and then spread outward. Whether the community strains escaped from hospitals or arose independently was unknown. Either way, their prevalence in the community seemed likely to increase substantially. A quarter to a half of people carry S. aureus harmlessly. A resistant reservoir could therefore spread quietly through ordinary contact.
europmc-pmc2657211:
Viaud and colleagues showed in 2009 that tiny parcels shed by immune cells can wake up a second line of defense against cancer. The parcels, called exosomes, come from dendritic cells, which normally show invaders to T cells. A first human trial of exosome vaccines shrank some tumors even though T cells barely responded, so something else had to be at work.

In mice, the parcels switched on natural killer cells, a fast-acting killer cell type, and made them multiply. Two signals on the parcel surface did the work: one feeding a growth receptor, the other pressing an activation switch called NKG2D. In trial patients, the vaccine restored killer cell numbers and function in seven of fourteen people. The parcels, it seems, fight tumors through this side door, not only through T cells.
europmc-pmc2679711:
Mo, Palsson, and Herrgård showed in 2009 that what yeast spills into its surroundings can reveal the hidden traffic inside its cells. Chemists can measure the chemicals a cell excretes far more easily than the flows among its internal reactions. The team asked whether a genome-scale map of yeast chemistry could turn those outer readings into inner knowledge.

They rebuilt the map, called iMM904, with 904 genes and 1,412 reactions, and checked it against nearly 2,900 gene-deletion growth tests from the literature. Then they fed in measured spill patterns from yeast whose nitrogen handling had been disturbed, in genes or in food. The model's sampled flow patterns matched published inner measurements. The changed flows also pointed back to the right neighborhoods of the network, the ones actually disturbed. Outer chemistry, handled this way, becomes a window on the cell's inner state.
europmc-pmc2717911:
Metscher showed in 2009 that simple stains let X-ray microCT, a scan that builds three-dimensional images from X-rays, reveal soft animal tissues in fine detail. Soft tissues absorb X-rays weakly, so they showed up poorly beside bone. Toxic osmium stains helped a little, but no easy, general method existed for comparing body form across species.

Stains based on iodine and phosphotungstic acid proved easy to handle, far less toxic, and strong across many tissues. Images of vertebrates, embryos, insects, and other invertebrates resolved single muscle fibers and even single blood cells in place. The method keeps specimens intact, so the same animal can be studied again with other tools.
europmc-pmc2745811:
van der Heijde and co-authors checked in 2009 whether adalimumab slows spinal damage in ankylosing spondylitis. They worked with the Canadian (M03-606) study group and ATLAS study group. The disease is a chronic rheumatic condition that stiffens the spine. The drug eases symptoms and improves quality of life. Whether it also stops structural damage was the open question.

They pooled spine X-rays from three hundred seven treated patients. Change was compared against a historic untreated cohort of one hundred sixty-nine. Mean progression scores over two years were nearly identical in both groups. No significant difference appeared even in a matched eligible subset. Symptom control thus did not translate into slower radiographic damage in the spine.
europmc-pmc2760211:
Gutenkunst, Hernandez, Williamson, and Bustamante introduced in 2009 a method to infer the joint demographic history of several populations. It works from multidimensional SNP frequency data, counts of genetic variants shared across groups. Such models illuminate prehistory. They also serve as null models when scanning genomes for selection. Their method computes the expected joint frequency spectrum under candidate histories with up to three populations.

Applied to resequenced DNA from sixty-eight people in four populations, they dated a key split. West African and Eurasian groups parted about one hundred forty thousand years ago. That is earlier than other genetic studies found, partly because migration is included. European and East Asian groups split far later. East Asian and Mexican-American groups split with no sign of later mixing.
europmc-pmc2774511:
MacConaill and co-authors implemented in 2009 OncoMap, a platform for profiling critical cancer gene mutations in clinical tumor samples. Knowing a tumor's mutations can predict outcomes and point to targeted drugs, but testing many mutations at once in routine samples was underdeveloped. Their system checks about four hundred mutations across thirty-three known cancer genes, many tied to drug response or resistance.

On fresh frozen tissue the platform reached sensitivity near ninety-four percent with perfect specificity. On DNA from preserved, paraffin-embedded samples it stayed near eighty-nine percent sensitive and over ninety-nine percent specific. It found known mutations at expected rates in common cancers, plus new ones likely to matter for therapy. In children's low-grade gliomas, profiles split tumors by BRAF mutation status, a grouping with immediate treatment implications. Routine high-throughput profiling, they conclude, is clinically feasible.
europmc-pmc2780911:
Carr and co-authors grew retinal pigment epithelium cells from human induced pluripotent stem cells and transplanted them into rats with retinal dystrophy. In many blinding diseases, including age-related macular degeneration, the failing tissue is this support layer, which keeps light-sensing cells alive. Stem cells reprogrammed from adult cells could supply replacement tissue without embryos.

The grown cells looked like natural retinal pigment epithelium and carried its markers. They ate discarded photoreceptor material in the dish, as healthy support cells do. After transplant into the dystrophic rats, they kept doing so in the eye. Photoreceptors survived better in the short term thanks to that cleanup work. Vision held up long term even though the grafted cells were eventually lost, hinting that the host mounts its own protective response. The work offers a new tissue source for retinal therapy.
europmc-pmc2846311:
Davis and Gaskell set out a theory in 2009 of how adults learn new spoken words, drawing on memory research and brain evidence. Words like blog pass from total novelty to instant familiarity, and the authors argue the journey runs in two stages. A fast recording stage in the hippocampus, the brain's memory hub, captures the new word at first hearing. A slower stage then weaves it into the cortex during rest and sleep.

Meta-analysis of brain scans plus behavioral studies supported the split. Hippocampal responses shifted during first learning, whereas cortical responses to new words only turned word-like after overnight consolidation, meaning sleep- or rest-based strengthening of memories. The account unites word learning with general memory systems.
europmc-pmc2852311:
Cowtan tested several new tricks in 2010 for sharpening the fuzzy first maps produced in X-ray crystallography, and packaged them in a program called Parrot. Solving a structure starts with rough phase estimates, the missing half of the diffraction data. This editing process then improves them by repeatedly forcing the electron-density map to look like a plausible molecule. Classical methods alternate between editing the map and re-imposing the measurements.

Cowtan tests refinements to the standard edits: flattening solvent regions, matching the expected spread of density values, and averaging over duplicate molecules in the crystal. He judged which additions truly helped phases within the classical framework. Parrot carries the winning combination forward as a working tool for structure-solving pipelines.
europmc-pmc2881011:
Frei, Stamm, and Buddeberg-Fischer reviewed in 2010 two decades of published mentoring programs for medical students, while planning one for Zurich. Mentoring is widely praised as a key to a satisfying medical career, yet most countries offer students no formal program. Their search of the medical database for 2000 to 2008 found hundreds of papers, of which twenty-five described structured programs or student surveys.

Fourteen program reports aimed at career advice, professional conduct, research interest, and personal growth. Formats ranged from one-to-one pairing to group mentoring, usually starting in the first two years and lasting to graduation. Students valued the personal faculty bond most, saying it made advice feel individual and pushed them to think harder about career choices.
europmc-pmc2891811:
Eriksson and a team at a consumer genetics company showed in 2010 that web-based, participant-driven research can find real genetic associations. Volunteers mailed in DNA, answered trait surveys online, and received their results back, letting one cohort serve studies of twenty-two traits at once. The design controls for the tangled ancestry that self-selected web samples bring.

Known links for hair color, eye color, and freckling replicated cleanly, validating the self-report approach. Fresh findings followed. Variants near three genes tied to hair shape and curl, and a new freckling locus emerged. So did a smell receptor gene behind detecting asparagus odor in urine. Two regions behind the photic sneeze reflex, sneezing in bright light, rounded out the list. Cheap, parallel trait collection worked.
europmc-pmc2928211:
Kent and co-authors set out a proposal in Trials in 2010 about how clinical trials should report uneven treatment effects across patients. Trial averages can hide wide gaps in risk, so a mean benefit may describe few real patients well.

Their plan puts multivariate risk-based analysis first, grouping patients by combined risk rather than testing one trait at a time. Other subgroup checks should be labelled clearly as primary, when backed by prior evidence and meant to guide care, or secondary and exploratory. Following the scheme would make trial reports clearer and more useful for treatment choices.
europmc-pmc2929211:
Kong and co-authors studied prostate cancer cells in 2010, asking whether a shape-shifting programme called epithelial to mesenchymal transition connects with stem-like traits. Recurrent prostate tumours that resist hormone therapy spread widely and kill many patients, so their cell biology matters.

Cells showing the transition programme carried higher levels of stem-linked genes such as Sox2, Nanog, and Oct4, formed spheres and colonies more readily, and grew tumours in mice. Restoring small RNAs of the miR-200 family reversed the state and cut sphere growth. Lowering Lin28B raised let-7 RNA and weakened self-renewal, pointing to targets for future therapy.
europmc-pmc2936111:
Webster and colleagues used deep gene sequencing in 2010 to survey bacteria living inside three Australian sponges. Sponges host dense microbial communities of ecological and drug-discovery interest, and many members were thought to live only in sponges.

Tag sequencing yielded hundreds of thousands of reads sorted into thousands of kinds across many bacterial phyla, a diversity unmatched in other invertebrate hosts. Nearly half the known sponge-linked groups appeared only in adults and larvae, hinting at passing from parent to offspring. The rest also turned up rarely in seawater, suggesting rare sea microbes can seed sponge populations.
europmc-pmc2962811:
Morris and Zeggini weighed methods for finding rare gene variants tied to complex traits in a 2010 evaluation. Genome-wide scans had found many common variants, yet rare ones remained a largely untapped source of risk.

They propose a method that looks for pile-ups of rare minor variants within the same functional unit, then test strategies by simulation. Approaches built on such pile-ups from resequencing data proved far more powerful than standard scan analysis. The gain, they argue, opens a promising route for the next round of trait gene discovery as sequencing data grows.
europmc-pmc2994911:
Lindsley and colleagues measured flu virus in the coughs of sick volunteers in a 2010 study, aiming to settle how much virus rides in tiny airborne particles. Flu spreads by several routes, and the airborne share was disputed.

Patients at a student clinic coughed into a spirometer while samplers caught the spray by size. Most confirmed flu patients shed viral genetic material in coughs. The material split across sizes, with the largest share in the finest particles under a micrometre, and live virus grew from a couple of samples. Fine particles staying aloft support a real airborne route.
europmc-pmc3016411:
Tse and Engler grew mesenchymal stem cells on gels with stiffness gradients in a 2011 study, asking whether cells migrate toward stiffer ground before choosing a fate. Real tissues vary in stiffness smoothly, and heart scars create steep local gradients.

On a gentle, body-like gradient the cells crawled uphill toward stiffer regions rather than staying put, over three weeks in culture. There they adopted a more contractile, muscle-like character. Cells still travelling kept a hint of a nerve marker, so their fate was not fully fixed en route. Gradient itself, not just stiffness, steers stem cell behaviour.
europmc-pmc3020611:
Vandenesch and colleagues compared community-acquired drug-resistant staph strains from six regions worldwide in a 2003 study. Resistant Staphylococcus aureus, long a hospital problem, had begun infecting healthy people with no hospital contact, raising the question of one spreading clone.

Over a hundred isolates shared the same compact resistance cassette and a toxin gene pair, yet their other toxin genes differed by continent. Fingerprinting showed distinct genetic backgrounds per region, separate from local hospital strains. The pattern suggests resistant community strains arose independently in several places, united by the same two genetic acquisitions.
europmc-pmc3035611:
McCambridge, McAlaney, and Rowe reviewed in 2011 what happens in adulthood to people who drank alcohol heavily as older teenagers. Many cohort studies had followed young drinkers over time, linking teen drinking to later poor health and social trouble. The reviewers set out to judge how strong that long term evidence really was.

Their verdict was cautious. Studies did suggest links between late teen drinking and worse adult physical and mental health, plus wider social costs. Yet the overall quality of the evidence was poor, with bias and confounding hard to rule out. Heavy drinking late in the teen years is common and peaks before the early twenties in rich countries. The authors argue better long term studies are needed before firm claims about lasting harm can guide policy.
europmc-pmc3164711:
Michaela Kirschner and colleagues warned that broken red blood cells distort blood tests for tiny RNA biomarkers in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Cell-free tiny RNAs in plasma are chased as disease markers, and one of them doubles as the yardstick others are measured against. The team asked whether red cell breakage during sample handling corrupts that yardstick.

In clean samples the yardstick RNA barely varied between healthy people and patients, qualifying it as a reference. Once breakage crept in, its level rose in direct proportion to the damage, as did a second red-cell-rich RNA, wrecking its reference value. Spiking plasma with lysed red cells let them set a haemoglobin cutoff below which readings stay trustworthy. Without breakage, both RNAs are steady enough to normalise results.
europmc-pmc3186011:
Mikayla Thompson and colleagues reviewed how the innate immune system first detects viruses in a 2011 paper in Viruses. Before tailored defences can be built, sentinel cells must spot infection fast. They use built-in receptors stationed on cell surfaces, in internal compartments, and free in the cell interior, each tuned to different viral traces, most often viral genetic material.

Receptor families differ in post and prey: some watch the cell's import sacs, others patrol the main compartment for RNA or DNA where it should not be. Tripping any of them launches interferons and inflammatory signals that slow the virus and summon the wider immune response. Placing sensors in several compartments lets cells catch viruses that replicate in different hideouts. The review traces each pathway and its contribution to antiviral defence.
europmc-pmc3213011:
Feng Cheng and colleagues introduced BRAD, a genome database for Brassica crop plants, in this 2011 paper in BMC Plant Biology. Brassicas include major vegetables and oilseed crops, and the newly assembled genome of Brassica rapa opened the door to deep data mining. BRAD was built to organize that genome and related resources in one web-accessible place.

The database holds the assembled sequence, predicted genes with annotations, non-coding RNAs, transposable elements, genetic markers, and linkage maps. It also maps Brassica genes to their counterparts in the model plant Arabidopsis. Search tools let users query by gene, position, or marker, run BLAST searches, and browse the genome visually. The authors present BRAD as a working resource for both researchers and plant breeders.
europmc-pmc3235811:
Elena Barbieri and Piero Sestili reviewed the double life of reactive oxygen species in skeletal muscle in this 2012 article in the Journal of Signal Transduction. These reactive molecules were long seen purely as toxic byproducts behind stress, disease, and aging. Evidence has since shown they also serve, at modest levels, as useful signals that regulate normal body processes.

Muscle is a special case because hard contraction makes its mitochondria release large flows of these molecules. Depending on where they are produced, how long the flow lasts, and how well the cell's antioxidant defenses are stocked, the result can range from healthy adaptation to cell death. The authors argue a single toxic threshold is the wrong idea; what matters is which levels fit normal physiology. They discuss the main signaling pathways involved.
europmc-pmc3271711:
J. Gregory Caporaso and colleagues filmed the human microbiome changing over time in this 2011 study in Genome Biology. Knowing how much a healthy person's microbes normally fluctuate is essential before blaming the microbiome for diseases such as obesity or inflammatory bowel disease. Earlier studies took only occasional snapshots, limited by sequencing cost and computation.

The team sampled two people at four body sites across nearly four hundred timepoints, the densest series then published. Beneath stable differences between sites and between people, each person's community varied strikingly across months, weeks, and even days. Only a small fraction of organisms at any site were present at every timepoint. So no permanent core community exists at high abundance. Many taxa instead persist for stretches, then vanish. The work defines what normal variation looks like for judging disease states and treatments.
europmc-pmc3291411:
Kilbourne surveyed the three worldwide flu pandemics of the twentieth century in a 2006 article. Each event differed in its virus, its spread, and how deadly it was, and they did not arrive on any steady schedule. For the two later pandemics, in 1957 and 1968, laboratory science could show that a key surface protein of the virus had changed sharply.

Much of the article looks back at 1918 and at reports that are often skipped. Observers at the time described a new flu like illness in American pigs that seemed to pass from people to animals, not the other way around. Kilbourne also notes that many deaths involved bacterial lung infections on top of flu, a fact that matters when judging whether a pandemic like 1918 could return.
europmc-pmc3304411:
Cuzick and colleagues tested a gene based score for predicting death from prostate cancer, reporting in 2012. Prostate cancer behaves very differently from man to man, and many patients are watched rather than treated at once. The score, built from the activity of thirty one genes that drive cell division, had already predicted outcomes in men diagnosed during prostate surgery.

Here the team applied it to nearly three hundred fifty men diagnosed by needle biopsy and managed without early radical treatment. The score was the strongest predictor of cancer death in their analysis, adding information beyond the usual grade, stage, and blood marker measures. Because it worked on stored biopsy tissue, the authors say it could help doctors choose which men need treatment and which can safely wait.
europmc-pmc3316511:
Ananworanich and colleagues studied the first days of HIV infection and an intensive early treatment plan, reporting in 2012. Screening more than twenty four thousand people in Bangkok, the team found forty people caught very soon after infection and enrolled thirty in close follow up. Gut tissue loses immune cells fast in early HIV, and hidden virus reservoirs form early, so timing matters for any hope of drug free control.

Half the group took an intensified five drug combination for twenty four weeks. By then, virus levels in blood and gut had fallen below detection in nearly everyone treated, and total hidden virus shrank, vanishing in a few. Gut immune cell shares also recovered, especially in those worst hit at the start. The authors say the earliest virus levels predicted reservoir size months later, arguing for treatment as early as possible.
europmc-pmc3408111:
Beetz, Uvnäs-Moberg, Julius, and Kotrschal reviewed in 2012 the effects of interacting with animals on human minds and bodies. Pets and animal-assisted therapy have gained wide acceptance over the past decade. The team sifted sixty-nine original studies that met firm standards for size, review, and design.

Well-documented benefits include better mood and social behavior, lower stress readings such as cortisol and blood pressure, and less self-reported fear and anxiety. Weaker evidence points to better pain control, trust, and empathy, and less aggression. The authors propose that the hormone oxytocin, switched on by friendly animal contact, drives most of these effects. That shared mechanism, they argue, ties the scattered findings into one story.
europmc-pmc3411811:
Zhang and co-workers reported in 2012 that berberine, an active ingredient of a Chinese herb long used for diarrhea, prevents obesity and insulin resistance in rats by reshaping gut bacteria. Rats on a high-fat diet gained less and ate less when given berberine. Blood markers of inflammation and hormone imbalance improved as well.

Sequencing the gut community showed berberine narrowed its diversity and shifted its structure markedly. Most of the bacterial types that responded vanished, while a few that produce helpful short-chain fatty acids grew richer, and those acids rose in the gut. A statistical model built on the responding types predicted body fat and hormone levels well. Gut remodeling, the authors conclude, carries much of berberine's benefit.
europmc-pmc3420011:
Matzuk and colleagues reported in 2012 a small molecule that blocks sperm production in mice, pointing toward a male contraceptive pill. Drug-based male contraception has been a longstanding challenge. The compound, JQ1, jams a family of proteins that read chemical marks on DNA packaging; one family member, BRDT, works only in the testis and is essential for sperm formation.

Crystal and chemical studies showed the drug fills BRDT's reading pocket, stopping it from gripping its target marks. Treated male mice grew smaller testes and made fewer, weaker sperm, while hormone levels stayed normal. They mated as usual but fathered no pups, and the effect reversed fully after treatment stopped. The result gives drug hunters a lead aimed squarely at the male germ cell.
europmc-pmc3488411:
Aptamers are short single strands of DNA or RNA that fold to grip a chosen target, and Maureen McKeague and Maria C. DeRosa survey why so few grip small molecules. Their 2012 review covers aptamers as recognition tools for biosensing, diagnostics, and therapy.

Small molecules make hard targets: they offer little surface to grip and few chemical handles. The authors walk through selection methods, the technical traps that stall them, and ways researchers work around those traps. They also map the openings, since small molecules drive much of biology, medicine, and commerce. Better probes for them, the review argues, would pay off across chemical biology and sensor design.
europmc-pmc3491411:
DNA methylation patterns can now be read genome-wide, but the data are costly and hard to handle, and Kasper D. Hansen, Benjamin Langmead, and Rafael A. Irizarry present BSmooth in 2012 to fix the analysis side. Their pipeline serves whole-genome bisulfite sequencing, the method that maps methylation base by base.

BSmooth aligns reads with bisulfite chemistry in mind, checks quality, and estimates methylation profiles accurately even when coverage is low. It handles biological replicates properly and reports differentially methylated regions, stretches where groups differ. Tests show it beats approaches based on Fisher's exact test. The software is open source, a deliberate bid to widen use of an expensive technology beyond specialist labs.
europmc-pmc3605911:
Erik Volz, Katia Koelle, and Trevor Bedford introduced viral phylodynamics in PLoS Computational Biology in 2013. The term, coined in 2004, names the study of how spread, immunity, and evolution together shape a virus's family tree. RNA viruses change fast, so their genetic variety records how transmission ran: who infected whom, how quickly, and where. Their primer maps the field's growth from those foundations to its present reach.

Tree patterns carry more than spread history. Selection presses on traits such as infectiousness, which tissues a virus favors, and the surface features that help it dodge immune memory, and each leaves marks on the tree. Studies range from single hosts, where cells pass virus along, to whole populations and cross-species jumps. Quantitative tools for reading trees back into epidemic history form the field's core craft. The article serves newcomers as a guided entry and veterans as a stocktaking.
europmc-pmc3662311:
Swelling does not just fade; it is actively cleared, Ortega-Gómez, Perretti and Soehnlein review in a 2013 EMBO Molecular Medicine article. Clearing, called resolution in the text, is a planned process that restores tissue build and function. The review draws the molecular and cellular steps into one picture, from the first halt of attack cells to the final return to balance in the tissue.

Step one cuts the chemical calls that keep drawing white attack cells in. Dying attack cells then call in eater cells, which clear them away. That meal reprograms the eaters toward a healing mode, a key turn for restoring balance. The authors close on treatment promise: drugs that copy the body's own clearing steps might end swelling without the costs of blocking defence outright. The piece gives drug hunters a map of those steps.
europmc-pmc3664011:
A womb-lining condition raises the risk of some ovarian cancers but not others, Pearce and a large consortium team report in a 2012 Lancet Oncology pooled study. The condition, endometriosis, sees womb lining tissue grow outside the womb. Whether the risk covered all cancer kinds was not clear. The team pooled 13 case-control studies from an international ovarian cancer group and split cases by tissue kind.

Self-reported endometriosis tied to about triple the odds of clear-cell ovarian cancer, and about double the odds of low-grade serous and endometrioid kinds. No tie showed for mucinous or high-grade serous kinds. The split matters for care: risk checks and watch plans can be aimed at the kinds where the link is real. The authors rest the case on thousands of cases and controls.
europmc-pmc3682911:
Lizards and snakes get their largest family tree yet from Pyron, Burbrink and Wiens in a 2013 BMC Evolutionary Biology study. Squamates, the group at issue, count over 9,400 known species, yet no past tree sampled the group at scale. The new tree holds 4,161 species, covering all recognised families and subfamilies. It rests on up to 12,896 DNA letters per species from 12 genes, seven from the nucleus and five from the power plant genome.

The tree backs recent gene-based views of higher-level relations, which differ sharply from older body-form schemes. Many branches also depart from past gene studies and from textbook groupings. A revised classification follows, with new and reshaped subfamilies. The authors offer both tree and naming scheme as a base for comparative studies of form, ecology and evolution across this vast radiation of land vertebrates.
europmc-pmc3693611:
Ghasemi and Zahediasl wrote a guide to normality testing for researchers who are not statisticians. Many common procedures, including correlation, regression, t tests, and analysis of variance, assume that data follow a normal distribution, and conclusions drawn when that assumption fails badly can be wrong.

The guide explains how the assumption matters less as samples grow, with the sampling distribution turning roughly normal in larger samples by the central limit theorem. It then walks through checking normality in SPSS, both by eye with plots and with formal significance tests. Readers can judge whether a deviation is serious enough to change the analysis, and what to do when the data fail the check.
europmc-pmc3701611:
Huys and colleagues used a model-based meta-analysis to pin down what goes wrong with reward in depression. A core symptom, anhedonia, blunts reactions to reward, but standard tasks cannot separate two possible faults: caring less about rewards themselves, or learning less from the surprises that signal them.

Pooling six behavioural datasets, the team fitted reinforcement learning models to a probabilistic reward task. Depression and anhedonia mainly reduced reward sensitivity, leaving the learning rate comparatively intact. A low dose of a dopamine drug did the reverse, and stress mixed both effects. The authors argue that reward problems in mood disorders split into separable parts with different chemistry.
europmc-pmc3782411:
Daniel Feikin and co-authors, with the Serotype Replacement Study Group, published a pooled analysis in PLoS Medicine in 2013 on invasive pneumococcal disease after vaccine introduction. The seven-valent pneumococcal vaccine, PCV7, joined national programs from 2000 onward and cut disease from the serotypes it covers. The open question was how much disease from other serotypes rose to replace it.

The team pooled surveillance data from multiple sites to compare settings directly, since vaccine schedules, coverage, and monitoring varied so much that single-site reports clashed. Understanding replacement matters most for low-income countries, where most pneumococcal deaths occur and serotypes are more diverse. The analysis was commissioned after a World Health Organization expert meeting in 2010 called for a comprehensive estimate of replacement's size and variability.
europmc-pmc3844611:
Joel J. Gagnier, Gunver Kienle, Douglas G. Altman, David Moher, Harold Sox, and David Riley report a reporting guideline in the Journal of Medical Case Reports in 2013. Case reports tell the story of one patient's illness for teaching and science. Without shared rules, many reports skip facts that readers need.

The guideline, called CARE, was built by group agreement in three phases. Experts reviewed past work, met to draft items, then tested and refined the list. The final checklist has thirteen items, from title and patient facts to timeline, treatments, outcomes, the patient's own view, and consent. The authors urge journals to adopt the list so case reports grow more complete and open, and thus more useful for care and study design.
europmc-pmc3935411:
Florian Jupe and colleagues present RenSeq in The Plant Journal in 2013. RenSeq is a targeted sequencing method for plant resistance genes. The targets are NB-LRR genes. These genes encode the immune sensors that detect plant pathogens. Their counts and places are often poorly recorded in genome sequences. That slows breeding for resistance.

The method fishes out just these genes with matching DNA baits. It then sequences them deeply. Used on the reference potato genome, it raised the known count from 438 to 755. Most of the new genes sat in poorly mapped regions. The team placed 704 of them on the twelve chromosomes. A public genome browser shows the map. The same method raised the tomato count to 394 loci. The paper also shows how to map a resistance gene fast in a breeding cross.
europmc-pmc3942711:
Joanna Fiedor and Kvetoslava Burda review carotenoids as antioxidants in Nutrients in 2014. Carotenoids are the pigments that color many plants and microbes; humans cannot make them but carry them in blood and tissue from food. They are strong quenchers of singlet oxygen and scavengers of other reactive oxygen species, though they can also be consumed in the process and sometimes act the other way.

Losing the balance between antioxidants and reactive oxygen creates oxidative stress, implicated in many chronic diseases. Trials and population studies link adequate carotenoid intake with lower risk of several such diseases. The authors focus on protection in cancer, cardiovascular disease, and light-sensitivity disorders, while noting that the chemistry behind the effects, including when carotenoids turn pro-oxidant, is still not fully mapped.
europmc-pmc3949711:
Emma L. Giles and colleagues ask whether paying people helps them adopt healthier habits, in PLoS ONE in 2014. Financial incentives are a popular policy tool, but their average effect across behaviors was not settled. The team systematically reviewed controlled studies in non-clinical adults in high-income countries, then pooled results by behavior and probed whether effects depended on follow-up length or the size of the payment.

Seventeen papers covering sixteen studies qualified: ten on quitting smoking, five on attending vaccination or screening, and one on physical activity. Incentives clearly beat control conditions, roughly doubling short-term quit rates and raising attendance, with the combined effect solid across behaviors. Hints that bigger payments or longer follow-up shrink effects were weak. The authors conclude incentives work, at least while the behavior is being rewarded.
europmc-pmc3958311:
Vadim Makarov, Benoit Lechartier, and colleagues report a new tuberculosis drug candidate. Their paper appeared in EMBO Molecular Medicine in 2014. The drug family is the benzothiazinones. These drugs kill the TB bacterium by jamming DprE1. DprE1 is an enzyme the bacterium needs for its cell wall. The team's new lead is called PBTZ169. It binds the enzyme for good. A crystal picture shows how it locks onto the active site.

PBTZ169 beat the older lead drug on three counts. It was stronger, safer, and more effective in animal tests. Zebrafish and mouse models of TB both responded. Mixed with other TB drugs, it added its strength. With bedaquiline, the pair did better than the sum. A three-drug mix with pyrazinamide beat the standard mix in mice. The mice had chronic disease. The team calls PBTZ169 a strong candidate for human trials.
europmc-pmc3965411:
Eric C. Strunz and colleagues pool the evidence on whether clean water, sanitation, and hygiene protect against soil-transmitted worms, in PLoS Medicine in 2014. More than a billion people carry these intestinal worms, caught from eggs or larvae in soil, and control has leaned on mass deworming drugs. Whether water, sanitation, and hygiene improvements add protection was scattered across many small studies, so the team ran a systematic review and meta-analyses using adjusted estimates.

Water, sanitation, and hygiene access and habits were generally, though not always, tied to lower odds of infection. Wearing shoes showed a strong link against hookworm, and soap use or availability also cut the odds significantly. Most pooled estimates suggested at least a one-third reduction. Evidence quality was low, the authors caution, but the pattern supports pairing WASH with deworming.
europmc-pmc4053811:
Eduardo Lee and nine colleagues introduce Web Apollo, a browser-based editor for genome annotation, in Genome Biology in 2013. Sequencing a new genome is now common. Describing its genes still takes expert hand work, long done with desktop tools at big centres.

Web Apollo moves that editing onto the web. Several annotators can open the same genome in ordinary browsers and refine gene structures together, seeing each other's changes at once, from the same room or across the world. Curators can correct predicted exons, merge or split genes, and record evidence as they go. The paper describes the design and early use by research communities. The aim is to spread careful annotation beyond the large centres, so the many groups now sequencing their own organisms can describe them to a shared standard.
europmc-pmc4068111:
Carla L. DeSisto, Shin Y. Kim, and Andrea J. Sharma estimated how common gestational diabetes was in the United States using two reporting systems. Their study appeared in Preventing Chronic Disease in 2014. The true rate of this pregnancy form of diabetes was unknown, and the sources did not agree.

For 2010, birth certificates gave a rate of about four to five in a hundred births, while a survey of new mothers gave close to nine in a hundred. Counting either source pushed the figure slightly higher still. The two sources agreed on most individual cases, mostly on negatives. Rates did not change significantly between the late 2000s and 2010. The authors say the gap between sources needs study.
europmc-pmc4131211:
Angela Huttner, Didier Pittet, and a team of peers gave a world view of drug-proof germs from a 2013 world forum on ward-gained ills. Their report came out in Antimicrobial Resistance and Infection Control in 2013. Proof germs are a threat in all lands. Their rise rests on too much drug use in people and in farm beasts, and the world's close links help them spread.

Some lands have held back proof germs of one class by firm acts. Proof germs of a second class, some of which shrug off all but the last drugs, still spread fast. Plans to save drugs work but reach rich lands most. Farm drug use has scant checks in most of the world. New drugs are a dire need. The forum called for joint world acts and an end to farm use that is not for cure.
europmc-pmc4177411:
Alexander V. Alekseyenko, Martin J. Blaser, and seven co-authors compared skin microbes in psoriasis in Microbiome in 2013. Psoriasis is a long-lasting skin disease where patches turn red and scaly. The team asked whether the bacteria living on sore skin differ from those on healthy skin.

They swabbed three matched sites from 51 sets of people: a psoriasis patch, the same spot on the patient's other side, and skin from a healthy control. Gene sequencing showed patch skin held a wider mix of bacteria, richer in four common skin genera. The samples also fell into two broad community types, and one type showed up far more often on psoriasis skin. The changes reached even the patient's unhurt skin, hinting at body-wide effects.
europmc-pmc4205511:
Mohsen Tavakol and Reg Dennick explained a widely used reliability statistic in the International Journal of Medical Education in 2011. Teachers and researchers build tests and questionnaires from many items, and they need to know whether the items hang together. Cronbach's alpha is the standard measure of that consistency, needing only one sitting of the test.

Their short guide unpacks what alpha actually measures and the assumptions under it. A reliable tool is not automatically a valid one, they stress, and alpha is often quoted without understanding. They cover how item count and item spread move the number, and why a very high alpha can signal redundant items rather than a good test. The aim is more careful use and reporting of alpha in medical education research.
europmc-pmc4256011:
Hua Cheng, Nick V. Grishin, and six co-authors presented a protein family classification called ECOD in PLoS Computational Biology in 2014. Proteins fold into domains, and sorting those domains into families reveals how structure evolved. Most existing schemes group domains by shape, which can split true relatives whose shapes drifted apart.

ECOD, short for Evolutionary Classification of protein Domains, groups by ancestry first. That choice keeps distant relatives together even when their topology differs, throwing light on the sequence and structure regions that matter most. At launch it held about 100,000 structures in 9,000 sequence families and close to 2,000 evolutionary groups, the most links of any such scheme. An automated pipeline classifies each week's new structures from the Protein Data Bank, keeping the catalogue current.
europmc-pmc4338111:
Martina Kutmon and seven co-authors present PathVisio 3, the third version of a free tool for drawing and analyzing biological pathways. Their paper appeared in PLoS Computational Biology in 2015. Pathway diagrams, maps of the steps in a cell process, help researchers grasp and share complex biology, and PathVisio has served that role since 2008.

Beyond drawing, the new version layers experimental data onto pathway maps and runs statistics to flag changed pathways. A plugin system lets outside developers add features, which the team expects to keep the tool growing. PathVisio also powers editing inside WikiPathways, the community pathway database. The paper catalogs what changed and how labs can extend it.
europmc-pmc4393511:
Matthias Arnold, Johannes Raffler, Arne Pfeufer, Karsten Suhre, and Gabi Kastenmüller built SNiPA, a browser for annotating genetic variants, in Bioinformatics in 2015. Genome-wide studies flag variants linked to disease, but connecting a variant to genes and function is slow, because annotation sits scattered across resources in clashing formats. SNiPA integrates many annotation data sets into one user-friendly web server, organized around the variant itself rather than around any single source.

A user can pull up a variant and see genetic, experimental, and informatics evidence in one view, across the variant, gene, and chromatin levels. That single view helps prioritize which flagged variants are most likely to act in the body, the key step between a statistical hit and a disease mechanism. The server is free online. Variant-centered design answers the question researchers actually ask: what does this change do?
europmc-pmc4430111:
Rosemary Bagot and a team of co-authors traced a brain circuit for depression risk in Nature Communications in 2015, using mice put through repeated social defeat. A reward area called the nucleus accumbens receives excess drive in depression, but the source of that drive was unclear. Three input areas were candidates: the prefrontal cortex, the ventral hippocampus, and the amygdala.

Mice that withstood defeat showed quieter ventral hippocampus input to the reward area. Using light-based control of nerve cells, the team found that weakening that one input made mice more resilient, while boosting it made them more prone to defeat's effects. Stimulating either of the other two inputs had the opposite, protective effect. The circuit, they argue, is a specific lever on stress susceptibility and a possible target for treatment research.
europmc-pmc4463411:
V V Gusel'nikova and D E Korzhevskiy reviewed NeuN, a protein used to mark nerve cells, in Acta Naturae in 2015. NeuN sits in the nucleus and nearby body of most mature neurons in mammals. Antibodies against it have been a standard lab tool for more than twenty years. Labs use them to tell neurons apart, judge their state in health and disease, and follow their development. Cancer diagnosis has begun to use them too.

What NeuN actually is stayed unknown for most of that time, and its job is still not fully clear. The mini-review sums up what is now known about its structure, its forms, where it sits in the cell, and the roles proposed for it. It also details where NeuN staining helps, in research and in clinics, and the traps in reading results, including cell types that lack the protein and cases where staining fades.
europmc-pmc4525211:
Tanmoy Mondal leads a twelve-author team explaining how a long noncoding RNA finds its target genes, in Nature Communications in 2015. Long noncoding RNAs do not build proteins; some instead latch onto chromatin, the packed DNA in the cell nucleus, and tune gene activity. How they pick their spots was poorly understood.

From breast cancer cells, the team pulled out 276 such RNAs bound to repressive chromatin and focused on one, MEG3. MEG3 shares target genes with a known silencing protein, including genes of the TGF-β pathway, which it tunes from distant control sites. Its binding spots carry GA-rich stretches. The team shows MEG3 reaches them by forming RNA–DNA triplex structures, three-stranded pairings they found widespread, and proposes triplexes as a general targeting trick.
europmc-pmc4531311:
Menelaos Pavlou and six co-authors explain how to build sound risk models from sparse data, in The BMJ in 2015. Doctors use risk models to forecast a patient's chance of an outcome and guide treatment choices. When the outcome is rare but many predictors are fed in, standard regression overfits: it memorizes the sample, then rates low-risk patients too low and high-risk ones too high.

Penalized regression, which shrinks the weight given to each predictor, counteracts that pull. The paper shows, with theory and examples, that penalized methods forecast better than standard ones when events are few. It also sets out how to judge whether a model is truly more accurate, so sparse-data models can be trusted on new patients.
europmc-pmc4542311:
Matthias Farlik and six co-authors present a method to read DNA methylation one cell at a time, in Cell Reports in 2015. Methylation marks help set a cell's identity, and tissues mix many cell states. Single-cell methods existed for genes and transcripts, but methylation could only be read from pooled cells, blurring those states.

Their assay adapts whole-genome bisulfite sequencing to tiny samples and single cells, tuned for many samples at shallow depth. Companion software reads collections of single-cell profiles to infer how states shift over time. In three lab models of cell differentiation, the team saw characteristic remodeling patterns and wide cell-to-cell variety. The method suits embryos, stem cells, and cancers.
europmc-pmc4595711:
In 2015, a study showing that formaldehyde made inside the body can damage blood stem cells was published by Lucas B. Pontel and colleagues. Formaldehyde is produced by normal body chemistry, yet it can link DNA and proteins together. What happens when it builds up was unclear. The work appeared in Molecular Cell.

Mice lacking the enzyme that removes formaldehyde stored DNA damage marks. When a DNA repair protein was also missing, blood stem cells were lost and bone marrow failed. Liver and kidney cells were harmed too, and the animals later developed fatal cancers. A bone marrow transplant restored blood making and, surprisingly, protected the kidneys. The study names formaldehyde as a real internal threat that healthy cells must constantly clear.
europmc-pmc4598811:
A 2015 world survey by Gemma Henderson and colleagues deals with microbes in the rumen, the first stomach of cattle, sheep, and similar animals. Rumen microbes break down feed and make methane, a strong greenhouse gas. The Global Rumen Census asked whether microbes differ by diet, host species, or place. The work appeared in Scientific Reports.

The team analysed 742 samples from 32 animal species across 35 countries. The same bacteria and methane-making archaea dominated almost everywhere, while protozoa varied more. Diet explained most differences, ahead of host species. Because the methane makers are few and widely shared, the authors argue that targeted ways to cut methane output could work across many farming systems.
europmc-pmc4681811:
Dora Brites and Adelaide Fernandes examined links between brain inflammation and depression in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience in 2015. People with long-term inflammation often develop depression, and depressed patients tend to carry higher levels of immune signal chemicals in their blood. Brain scans and tissue studies also show active microglia, the brain's own immune cells, in depressed patients. The authors ask how these immune changes might help cause low mood.

Tiny vesicles shed by cells, carrying proteins and small RNA pieces, form a second thread of the review. These packages move messages between brain cells and may spread harm or support repair. Changes in small RNAs found in depressed patients point to pathways for mood, learning, and memory. The authors suggest vesicles could one day serve as markers for tracking disease or as vehicles for treatment.
europmc-pmc4710611:
Joseph M. Braun, Chris Gennings, Russ Hauser, and Thomas F. Webster asked what epidemiology can say about chemical mixtures, in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2016. People carry many environmental chemicals at once, yet studies usually test one chemical at a time. That habit leaves the health effect of the real, mixed exposure largely unknown. The four authors sort the special problems mixtures pose for measuring exposure and for statistics.

They propose three questions that population studies can actually answer. What does each single agent do? How do agents interact, helping or blunting each other? And what does the total, cumulative exposure do? Framing studies around those questions, they argue, would sharpen methods and make results usable for public health action. The piece is a roadmap for a young field, written to help researchers choose designs that fit the question they truly mean to ask.
europmc-pmc4718211:
Stephen P. H. Alexander, Doriano Fabbro, Eamonn Kelly, and eight colleagues plus the CGTP Collaborators compiled the Enzymes section of the Concise Guide to PHARMACOLOGY 2015/16, in the British Journal of Pharmacology in 2015. The parent guide summarizes more than 1,750 human drug targets and links each to a free online knowledgebase. Enzymes, the protein catalysts that run body chemistry, form one of its eight target classes. A naming committee sorts them into six families by reaction type.

Entries pair naming guidance with the best pharmacological tools for each enzyme and suggested reading. Though enzymes vastly outnumber receptors in biology, relatively few serve as drug targets, a point the section notes without dismissing their importance. Like its sister sections, this one is a fixed late-2015 snapshot; the online guide keeps moving. It consolidates two older databases into one permanent, citable record of enzyme pharmacology.
europmc-pmc4746611:
Pan and 21 colleagues test whether SIRT6, a longevity-linked enzyme, directly protects human mesenchymal stem cells, the tissue-repair cells whose decline marks aging of bone, cartilage, and fat. They delete SIRT6 from human stem cells using targeted gene editing and watch the cells fail early.

The loss does not destabilise chromosomes. Instead it scrambles redox balance and leaves the cells fragile under oxidative stress. SIRT6 normally partners with the master antioxidant regulator NRF2 and the transcription machinery to switch on protective genes such as HO-1. Restoring HO-1 alone rescues much of the premature decline, identifying the SIRT6-NRF2 axis as a guardian of stem cell health.
europmc-pmc4746911:
Tricco and sixteen colleagues take stock of scoping reviews by performing one on the method itself. Scoping reviews map broad fields to find knowledge gaps and set research agendas, but their conduct varies wildly. Searching nine databases, the team includes 516 articles, of which 494 are scoping reviews published between 1999 and 2014.

Output has climbed steeply since 2012, mostly from North America and Europe. Yet only 13 percent of the reviews report using a protocol, and a minority use two reviewers for screening or data charting. No reporting guideline for scoping reviews exists at all. The authors call for standardised guidance to make the method trustworthy.
europmc-pmc4810511:
Padaphet Sayakhot and Mary Carolan-Olah review how pregnant women use the internet in BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth in 2016. Expectant mothers now rank among the most active health searchers online. The team gathered quantitative studies from the past decade to map what women look up, how often, and what they make of what they find.

Seven studies, with samples from under two hundred to over thirteen hundred women, met their bar. Most women searched at least monthly, with fetal development and nutrition the top topics. Women with more schooling searched more; most rated what they found reliable and useful. Strikingly, most never raised the findings with their midwife or doctor. The authors warn that wrong beliefs can thus go uncorrected, and call for work on guiding women to sound sources.
europmc-pmc4819611:
Mubeen Goolam leads nine authors in Cell in 2016 asking when a mammalian embryo's cells first stop being equal. In the mouse, the first fork sends some cells toward the fetus and others toward the placenta and support tissues. Textbook views held the early cells interchangeable until later; this team read every cell's gene activity across early development and tracked living cells to test that.

At the four-cell stage, the targets of two master stemness genes already varied sharply from cell to cell. One gene, Sox21, varied most. Cells low in Sox21 leaned toward the support lineages, and lowering it artificially woke a differentiation switch early. A chemical-tag enzyme sat upstream, raising or lowering Sox21. Uneven gene activity, the authors conclude, starts fate choices far earlier than assumed.
europmc-pmc4848511:
Bao-Jun Yang and co-authors reported in Nature Communications in 2016 that a protein called PROTEASOME REGULATOR1, or PTRE1, tunes the plant hormone auxin. Auxin guides plant growth. It works by sending repressor proteins to the proteasome, the cell machine that shreds unneeded proteins. How auxin steers that machine was unclear. PTRE1 is the plant kin of a known proteasome blocker, yet here it boosts the machine.

Plants lacking PTRE1 lost the normal auxin-driven pause in proteasome work. Their repressor proteins broke down more slowly, and growth traits tied to auxin shifted. Auxin also moves PTRE1 within the cell. The work adds a control dial between hormone sensing and protein shredding in plants.
europmc-pmc4854911:
Natalie E. de Picciotto and co-authors tested in 2016 whether a nutrient called NMN could undo age-linked blood vessel decline in mice. NMN feeds production of NAD+, a cell helper that falls with age. Old mice showed stiff arteries and poor vessel widening next to young mice, tied to oxidative stress and low activity of a vessel enzyme, SIRT1.

NMN in drinking water restored vessel widening and eased stiffness in old mice. Oxidative stress markers fell and the protective enzyme's activity rose. Young mice gained little, since their vessels were already sound. The results point to NAD+ support as a route to protect aging arteries, at least in animals.
europmc-pmc4872611:
May Sudhinaraset, Christina Wigglesworth, and David T. Takeuchi reviewed social and cultural forces on alcohol use in 2016, within a social-ecological frame. Alcohol misuse accounts for 3.3 million deaths a year, about 6 percent of all deaths worldwide. Harm spreads from drinkers to family, friends, and whole communities. Most research still centers on personal risk factors.

The review widens the lens: adverts and marketing, immigration and discrimination, and the pull of neighborhoods, families, and peers. Each layer can raise or lower drinking and its harm. Future work, the review argues, should test these outer forces head-on, since policy at that level can shift whole populations, not just single drinkers.
europmc-pmc4878611:
Nicholas J. Schurch and co-authors ran a 48-replicate RNA sequencing test in 2016 to answer a design question: how many repeats does such a study need? They compared two yeast conditions with many biological replicates and graded 11 analysis tools against the full-set answer. With just three replicates, nine tools found only 20 to 40 percent of truly changed genes.

For genes changing more than fourfold, three replicates caught over 85 percent. Catching most changed genes of any size took over 20 replicates. Nine tools kept false alarms at or under about five percent; two did not. The hard numbers give labs a budget guide: spend on replicates, not just on deeper reads.
