europmc-pmc4915811:
Sandy F. Sleiman and co-authors showed in 2016 how exercise raises a brain growth factor, BDNF, through a ketone body. Exercise lifts BDNF, which supports learning and eases depression and anxiety, but the trigger chain was unclear. After long exercise, the liver-made ketone beta-hydroxybutyrate rises in blood and reaches the brain.

In mice, that ketone switched on the Bdnf gene's key promoters, above all promoter I. It acts by blocking two gene-silencing enzymes, HDAC2 and HDAC3, at those promoters. A fuel molecule thus doubles as a gene signal, linking body effort to brain plasticity. The route hints at exercise-mimicking drugs for mood and memory.
europmc-pmc4921111:
Robert W. Mahley, writing alone, reviews apolipoprotein E across heart disease and brain disease. His review appeared in the Journal of Molecular Medicine in 2016. ApoE is a protein that moves lipids in the blood and docks with receptors that clear them. It comes in three forms, apoE2, apoE3, and apoE4, which differ by a single amino acid change.

Mahley explains how form shapes risk. ApoE2 binds poorly to its receptors and raises harmful lipid levels. ApoE4 raises LDL levels and also raises risk for Alzheimer's disease and related disorders, with earlier onset. He argues that apoE4 harms neurons because its folded shape lets it be cut into toxic fragments. Those fragments damage cell power plants and internal scaffolds. Small drugs that fix the shape, called structure correctors, are offered as a possible way to cut that harm.
europmc-pmc4935811:
Vincenzo Bronte leads a panel of fifteen authors setting shared standards for a disputed immune cell group. Their recommendations appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. The cells are called myeloid-derived suppressor cells. They expand in cancer and in long lasting inflammation, and they damp the immune response. Labs, though, named and measured them in clashing ways, so results were hard to compare across studies.

The panel proposes minimal reporting rules for work in mice and in people. It defines which markers and tests a claim about these cells should rest on. The goal is a common language that lets results stack up instead of talking past each other. The authors frame the guidance as a floor, not a ceiling. They hope journals and funders will ask authors to meet it when they publish or propose new work.
europmc-pmc4990711:
Andrew M. Borman, Adrien Szekely, and Elizabeth M. Johnson compare the virulence of Candida auris, an emerging hospital fungus, with other Candida species. Their study appeared in mSphere in 2016. Candida auris was first described in 2009 and has since caused outbreaks in hospitals worldwide. Invasive Candida infections already kill many patients, and Candida albicans is rated the most pathogenic species. The team infected wax moth larvae, a standard fungal infection model, with United Kingdom isolates of several species.

Virulence varied by strain within C. auris. The strongest isolates matched C. albicans in killing power. Weaker ones trailed clearly. The authors warn against treating the new species as uniformly mild or uniformly deadly. Its outbreak record plus top end virulence, they argue, justify serious infection control. They call for strain level tracking as the species spreads.
europmc-pmc5023411:
Paweł Śledź and Martin Jinek report the structure of the m6A writer complex in eLife in 2016. Cells mark RNA with a chemical tag called m6A, which steers how the RNA is processed, read, and cleared. Two proteins, METTL3 and METTL14, install the tag together and work far better as a pair than either does alone. Why the pair is stronger was the puzzle.

Using X-ray crystallography, the team mapped the joined core of the two proteins and saw how METTL3 grips the tag's source material. Tests with altered proteins showed a clear split of labor: METTL3 does the tagging, while METTL14 has a worn-out active site and instead holds the pair together and helps it grip RNA. The joined shape closely matches paired bacterial enzymes that tag DNA, hinting that the RNA writer evolved from such an ancestor.
europmc-pmc5039111:
Angelo Amabile, Alessandro Migliara, Paola Capasso, Mauro Biffi, Davide Cittaro, Luigi Naldini, and Angelo Lombardo silence genes without cutting them, in Cell in 2016. Switching a gene off for good can probe its job or treat disease, but older tools either fade or break the DNA. The team borrowed the silencing machinery stem cells use on invading retroviruses and aimed it at chosen genes.

They briefly delivered a trio of engineered repressor proteins that meet at the target gene. Together they lay down repressive marks and fresh DNA methylation, a lock passed to daughter cells after the tools are gone. Three genes were silenced in adult-type cells, with genome-wide checks showing tight aim and no spread to neighbors. Strong cell signals could not wake the genes; only removing the methylation could. The method worked across cell types, including human T cells, and on several genes at once.
europmc-pmc5100611:
Daniel I. Swerdlow and a wide team of co-authors offered guidance in the International Journal of Epidemiology in 2016. Their subject is Mendelian randomization. That method uses gene variants as stand-ins for exposures such as blood markers, to test cause and effect. Such studies grew more than tenfold between 2004 and 2015, fed by genome-wide association studies.

Those big gene hunts now supply far more candidate variants than early studies had, and picking the wrong ones can mislead. The authors lay out what to weigh. They start with the method's core assumptions and the biology of the marker. They add how its variants are spread and how strong they are. They also ask whether a variant affects only the marker of interest. Their advice aims to help planners design cleaner studies and readers judge them.
europmc-pmc5226511:
A. Marcell Szász and nine colleagues cross-checked survival markers in gastric cancer in Oncotarget in 2016. Gene expression studies had repeatedly proposed markers that predict how long stomach cancer patients live, but a marker means little until it holds up in patients it was not derived from. The group built one shared database so old and new candidates could be tested on the same footing.

The database joins tumour samples and expression data from 1,065 patients across three major centers and public sources. Of 29 established markers tested, higher expression of seven genes, including BECN1 and CASP3, tracked with longer survival. Higher expression of eleven others, including EGFR, HER2, and VEGF, tracked with shorter survival. The strongest performers included BIRC5, CASP3, CTNNB1, TIMP1, MMP2, SIRT1, and VEGF. Testing every gene in the same patients made the comparison direct.
europmc-pmc5238111:
Guthrie Rankin, physician to the Dreadnought and Royal Waterloo Hospitals, lectured on cerebral haemorrhage at the London School of Clinical Medicine, printed in The Hospital on April 13, 1912. Apoplexy, a sudden stroke-like collapse, follows damage to the brain's blood flow and can come from bleeding, clotting, or a travelling blockage. The lecture covers only the bleeding form.

Bleeding is rare before age forty and usually follows decay of artery walls, Rankin explains, while clots at young ages point mostly to syphilis and blockages usually follow valve disease. Central brain vessels suffer most because they are short, wide, and take the full shock of each heartbeat. One vessel, singled out by Charcot as the artery of cerebral haemorrhage, supplies the internal capsule region and ruptures most often. Rankin traces where the escaped blood spreads and when lost function may return as the clot shrinks.
europmc-pmc5355811:
Ken Uchibori and co-authors found a drug pair that beats lung cancer resistance, in Nature Communications in 2017. Some lung tumors run on a flawed growth switch, EGFR, and shrink under drugs that jam it. In time, a second flaw lets them grow again. A newer drug, osimertinib, beat that second flaw, but a third flaw has now shut it out as well. No care yet cracks the triple flaw.

A screen picked brigatinib, a drug from a kin cancer field, as a hit against cells with all three flaws. Computer models showed it fits the flawed switch pocket, and the team traced which part of the drug does the work. Adding an antibody that tags EGFR made the pair far stronger, since the tag strips EGFR off the cell surface and lowers its total. Mouse tests backed the cell work.
europmc-pmc5363011:
Kei Long Cheung and co-authors compared two ways of gathering teens for a health survey in BMC Public Health in 2017. Health checks on youth can skew when the teens most prone to risk are the least prone to answer. A mail survey sent home rests on free choice and draws thin replies. A survey taken in class time is near mandatory and draws near all. The team had both forms from two twin Dutch regions.

The same online survey went to more than nine thousand teens in the class region and near two thousand in the mail region. Rates of risk traits came out lower in the free choice group, even after age and sex gaps were stripped out. Links inside each teen's answers bent less, but group rates bent a lot. The study gives the first direct proof that the gathering method sets the size of the skew.
europmc-pmc5371211:
Dagny von Ahrens, Tushar D. Bhagat, Deepak Nagrath, Anirban Maitra, and Amit Verma reviewed support cells in pancreatic cancer in the Journal of Hematology & Oncology in 2017. This cancer is lethal and shrugs off most standard care. Its tumors sit in a dense scar-like web, called stroma. Much of that web is built by fibroblasts that the cancer has bent to its side.

These fibroblasts talk with tumor cells in both ways. They trade signal chemicals and tiny bubbles, and they share fuel in the low-sugar space. Their signals lift tumor growth, spread, and drug resistance through a clutch of inner paths. Marks on the cells can sort patients by outlook. Drug work now aims at the web itself: blocking its growth signals, or riding its leakiness to smuggle drugs in. The review maps that young field.
europmc-pmc5440811:
Laronda and co-authors print a working artificial ovary that restores fertility in sterilized mice. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Cancer care can destroy ovary function. Survivors may face early menopause and infertility. Children with spreading cancer have few options. A printed implant could one day replace the organ. Pore shape inside the implant turned out to matter greatly.

The team printed hydrogel scaffolds with varied pore angles. Tight corners hugged the egg follicles on several sides. Follicles there spread less and survived better. Open pores gave weak contact and poor survival. Seeded scaffolds grew rich blood vessel networks. Implanted into sterilized mice, they restored ovarian function in full. The mice mated naturally and bore pups. The pups thrived on maternal milk. The authors show pore design is a key dial in printed tissue. The work is a step toward fertility care after cancer.
europmc-pmc5445611:
Houser and Tansey ask whether gut inflammation silently drives Parkinson's disease. Their review appeared in NPJ Parkinson's Disease. The gut and brain talk constantly. Microbes, barrier function, and peripheral nerves carry the signals. Immune activity is their shared language. Chronic inflammation now looks central to brain degeneration. In Parkinson's, intestinal trouble often comes first. Constipation and gut symptoms can precede motor signs by years.

The authors assemble evidence for a gut-first model. In their model, the disorder originates in the intestine. Inflammation supplies the driving mechanism. Pathology then progresses toward the brain. The vagus nerve may act as a direct conduit. Microbes also sway brain chemistry directly. They produce hormones and neurotransmitter-like molecules. Barrier leaks can feed immune activation. Better grasp of these pre-motor pathways could pay off. New diagnostics might catch disease earlier. New therapies might slow it before motor damage.
europmc-pmc5535911:
Okonkwo and DiPietro review how diabetes harms new blood vessel growth in healing skin wounds. Their article appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Type 2 diabetes slows healing at each stage of repair. Foot ulcers are a common result, and some lead to loss of a limb.

Healthy wounds grow fresh capillaries in set steps, then reshape and mature them. In diabetes, those steps go wrong, the authors explain. Vessel walls, support cells, and growth signals all fail in part. The review tracks faults in the growth, reshaping, and maturing phases. It also weighs treatments that aim to restore blood flow and help wounds close.
europmc-pmc5553211:
Blanchet and co-authors present a conceptual paper on health system resilience. The term gained force after the 2014 Ebola outbreak in West Africa. Experts agree systems must be more resilient. They do not all mean the same thing by the word, though.

The authors define resilience as a system's capacity to absorb, adapt, and transform under shock. Shocks can be pandemics, disasters, war, or money crises. Their framework rests on systems thinking and complexity theory. It focuses on governance: the rules and actors that steer a system. A scoping review of definitions informed the model. Readers get shared language and a path toward measures that can be tested.
europmc-pmc5558711:
Ocana and co-authors present a review in Molecular Cancer on neutrophils in cancer. Neutrophils are the most common white blood cells. High levels of them inside tumors link to worse outcomes in many solid cancers. The authors ask why, and how doctors might use that fact.

Neutrophils can aid tumor growth, spread, and new blood vessel growth. Simple blood measures, such as the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, may help predict a patient's course. The review also covers drugs that aim to cut neutrophil numbers or block their move into tumors. Early models support some of these tactics. Readers get a compact guide to an immune cell now seen as a cancer target.
europmc-pmc5581411:
Moore and co-authors tackle a wording problem in Implementation Science. Health programs aim to last, yet the field lacks one shared definition of sustainability. Most studies that judge sustainability never define it at all. That gap makes research hard to compare and build on.

The team searched reviews of the topic and found 209 source articles. Only 24 of them stated a definition. Mapping those definitions gave five core parts. A program or behavior change endures past a set time. It may evolve or adapt as it goes. It keeps producing benefits for people or systems. Three coders agreed on the mapping 94 percent of the time. Readers get a shared yardstick for future work.
europmc-pmc5589211:
Jiménez-Sánchez and co-authors present a case study in Cell. One patient with advanced ovarian cancer showed a rare split pattern. Some of her metastases shrank during a break from chemotherapy. Others grew at the same time. The team compared the lesions to find out why.

Growing lesions kept immune cells out. Shrinking and stable lesions were full of T cells. Those T cells had expanded from a few clones. Blood taken almost three years later still held T cells that reacted to tumor neoepitopes. The case shows that one patient can host several distinct tumor immune settings at once. That mix may explain uneven responses after therapy. Readers get a close, single-patient view of tumor immunity.
europmc-pmc5605711:
Tian and co-authors hunt for gene variants that change the risk of common infections. Their study ran in Nature Communications. They ran 23 genome-wide scans at once. The data came from more than 200,000 people of European ancestry. Each person had answered questions on past infections and related care.

The scans covered chickenpox, shingles, cold sores, mumps, pneumonia, strep throat, and more. The team found 59 strong links in all. Many sit in genes tied to immunity and early development. Fine mapping of the HLA region pointed to exact amino acid changes. Those changes sit in the grooves where immune cells show foreign parts. Virus-linked ills tied more to one HLA class, and bacteria-linked ills to the other.
europmc-pmc5641211:
Rong and co-authors present a review in Oncotarget. It covers circular RNAs, a class of noncoding RNA. These molecules form closed loops with no free ends. That shape makes them stable and long-lived. They occur widely in plants, animals, and humans. Expression often varies by cell type and tissue.

Some circular RNAs act as microRNA sponges. By binding microRNAs, they change which genes stay active. These linked chains are called circRNA-miRNA-mRNA axes. Faults in them feed pathways of cell death and vessel growth. They also affect invasion and metastasis in cancer. The review sums up synthesis, traits, and classes of these RNAs. It highlights disease links in and beyond cancer.
europmc-pmc5735911:
Jull, Giles, and Graham compare two ways of doing health research with the people it should serve. One is community-based participatory research, or CBPR. The other is integrated knowledge translation, or IKT. Both stress partnership between researchers and knowledge users.

The authors trace the roots of each approach and where they meet. They differ in drive, social place, and ethics, yet share one aim. That aim is knowledge made jointly by researchers and users. Picking between them hinges on the goal, they argue. Social change points one way, direct use in care the other.
europmc-pmc5809511:
Wheway and co-authors review signaling through the primary cilium. Most cells carry one thin, still cilium. For decades it looked like a useless leftover. Work in 2003 tied it to hedgehog signaling in mice.

That find recast the cilium as the cell's antenna. Most vertebrate signal pathways now route through it. It guides embryo patterning and organ building. Faults in cilium genes cause the ciliopathy disorders. The review sums up each pathway's ciliary role. Readers get the story of a tiny structure with an outsized job in development and health.
europmc-pmc5842611:
Weir and co-authors catalogue fixes for a common headache in meta-analysis, trials that never report means or spread. Their systematic review appeared in BMC Medical Research Methodology. Without those numbers, studies get dropped and pooled answers lose precision.

Two searches screened over 1,600 papers between them. Fifteen methods surfaced for rebuilding a missing standard deviation. Tricks ranged from algebra on other summaries to Bayesian models. In test analyses, guessing the spread from the range lost the least precision. For missing means, a formula built on the median and quartiles held up best.
europmc-pmc5856411:
Dehaene-Lambertz and co-authors track how the brain builds a region for written words. Their article appeared in PLoS Biology. Literate adults have a small area that responds strongly to letter strings. The team asked how that area forms as children learn to read. They scanned ten six-year-olds six or seven times each. The scans spanned the months before and during the first school year.

Children saw words, numbers, faces, houses, and other pictures during scans. Reading skill rose sharply in the first school term. Word-specific responses then emerged at the expected brain site. The authors report that word responses grew on weakly tuned cortex. Responses to other categories largely stayed in place. Their model revises how new skills recycle brain tissue.
europmc-pmc5940111:
Levine and co-authors build a new epigenetic biomarker of aging from blood DNA methylation. Their study appeared in Aging. First-generation aging clocks were trained on chronological age alone. The team instead used a composite measure of phenotypic age. That measure captures differences in lifespan and healthspan. A two-step process produced the marker, called DNAm PhenoAge.

The new marker beat earlier measures at predicting aging outcomes, they report. These outcomes include all-cause mortality, cancers, and physical functioning. It also predicted Alzheimer's disease risk. Though built from whole blood, it tracks age in every tissue tested. Faster epigenetic aging came with more active inflammatory pathways. Repair and mitochondrial signatures were less active.
europmc-pmc5945811:
Gkretsi and Stylianopoulos review how cell adhesion and matrix stiffness drive cancer invasion and metastasis. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Oncology. The extracellular matrix links to the cell through integrins. Those links reach the actin cytoskeleton and many signalling pathways. Cues from adhesion proteins help set a cell's invasive potential. Many such proteins are proposed targets against metastasis.

Tumours also stiffen as matrix builds up around them. That stiffening helps the tumour displace host tissue and grow. It also shapes cell and matrix interactions, the authors note. Stiff surroundings can push cancer cells to invade nearby tissue. The review ties these mechanical and adhesive cues together.
europmc-pmc5983611:
Chan and Tay review noncoding RNA regulatory networks in cancer. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Noncoding RNAs make up most of the human transcribed genome. They include microRNAs and many kinds of long noncoding RNAs. These molecules compete in regulatory webs called ceRNA networks. Long noncoding RNAs can act as decoys for microRNAs. That decoy work shifts gene expression across the cell.

One faulty part can derail the whole circuit, the authors note. Such faults can drive cancer growth and spread. New computing platforms can now pick out key interactions. Those finds may yield biomarkers and drug targets.
europmc-pmc5983711:
Aouache and co-authors review oxidative stress in preeclampsia and other placental diseases. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Preeclampsia is a hypertensive disease of pregnancy. It brings high blood pressure and protein in the urine. It appears from the second trimester onward. The placenta's release of free radicals is closely tied to it. Some see that stress as the disease's main driver.

The authors survey recent work on free radical production. They cover normal and diseased placentas in humans and animal models. They then judge effects on the placenta and maternal vessel lining. Possible treatment avenues close the review.
europmc-pmc6015111:
Sardar Sinha and co-authors show that exosomes carrying toxic amyloid-beta oligomers spread Alzheimer's disease pathology. Their study appeared in Acta Neuropathologica. Alzheimer's decline parallels a stepwise spread of amyloid and tau. Toxic amyloid oligomers may seed that spread prion-style. The team examined small vesicles from Alzheimer patients' brains. The vesicles held raised levels of amyloid-beta oligomers. They passed the toxic species between cultured neurons.

Blocking vesicle formation, release, or uptake slowed the spread, they report. Toxicity fell along with the transfer. Exosomes thus sit centrally in the disease process. They could serve as targets for new diagnostics and therapies.
europmc-pmc6054611:
Takahashi and co-authors find a protein that closes the cell's recycling sacs. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Cells build double-membrane sacs to trap waste for breakdown. How the open sac seals shut was unclear. Telling open sacs from closed ones was technically hard.

The team built a new assay using a tagged marker protein. It separates open, fresh, and mature sacs cleanly. Screening with it flagged a protein called CHMP2A. This protein moves to the sac during autophagy. It helps split the inner and outer membranes apart. Blocking its partner enzyme also stalled completion. Proper closure keeps lysosome proteins in the right place. Readers get a tool and a mechanism for autophagy research.
europmc-pmc6102211:
Wang and co-authors build nanoflowers that make reactive oxygen inside tumors without outside triggers. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Such oxygen bursts can push cancer cells to die. Light-based systems fail in deep or oxygen-poor tumors. The flowers assemble from two nanozymes.

Platinum-cobalt particles seed the growth of manganese dioxide petals. One part mimics an oxidase enzyme. The other mimics catalase. Together they run a reaction cascade inside cells. The cascade eases oxygen shortage while raising toxic species. Tumor growth slowed sharply in their tests. Normal oxygen levels were not required. Readers get a self-powered design against stubborn hypoxic tumors.
europmc-pmc6109311:
Greathouse and co-authors present a research article in Genome Biology on lung microbes and the TP53 gene in lung cancer. Lung cancer is the top cause of cancer death worldwide. Cigarette smoke is its main risk factor. Smoke weakens the lung's barrier and raises the chance of infection.

The team sequenced bacterial genes in lung tissue from 33 controls and 143 cancer cases. Data from a large cancer atlas served as a check. Bacterial mixes shifted with tumor type and with TP53 mutation status. The authors argue that smoke and gene changes may together foster a microbial imbalance tied to how the cancer develops.
europmc-pmc6170611:
Woods and co-authors wrote a review in Frontiers in Endocrinology on how the placenta develops and how that shapes fetal growth. The placenta controls nutrient supply to the growing embryo. When it works badly, the fetus may grow too little, a problem called intrauterine growth restriction. Mouse models offer a way to find the genes involved.

New screening of mouse mutants, plus fast CRISPR gene editing, has changed the picture. Far more genes are needed for normal placenta formation than once thought. The review explains how placental defects translate into poor fetal growth. It also draws lessons for human pregnancy, where the same failure is a common complication.
europmc-pmc6211011:
Huang reviews an enzyme called MMP-9 as a cancer marker. MMP-9 cuts proteins in the matrix around cells. It also frees proteins from cell surfaces. High levels link to tumour spread and new blood vessels. The review appeared in Sensors.

The author sums up recent work on MMP-9 in cancers. Studies tested its value as a marker for specific cancer types. The review then covers new biosensors for MMP-9. These devices detect the enzyme in fresh ways. Together, the two parts show a fast-moving field. Better tests for MMP-9 could aid early cancer checks. They could also help track how a tumour changes over time.
europmc-pmc6227911:
The GBD 2017 SDG Collaborators measured progress on health goals for 2030. The United Nations set Sustainable Development Goals in 2015. Health goals need tracking beyond national averages. This study built a health goal index for 195 countries. It appeared in The Lancet. It covers 1990 to 2017.

The team measured 41 health-related indicators. New ones included health worker density and sexual violence. Indicators were projected forward to 2030. Scores varied widely between countries. Some states within countries lagged far behind national scores. The authors link scores to development levels. They warn that many countries will miss 2030 targets. Faster progress needs stronger health systems and equity focus.
europmc-pmc6267411:
Knudsen and Ochs review the fine mechanics of the lung's air sacs. Their review appeared in Histochemistry and Cell Biology. Gas exchange happens in these tiny sacs, called alveoli. Air and blood meet across a very thin wall there. Breathing stretches that wall with every breath. The sacs must not over stretch, and they must not collapse.

Two systems keep the sacs stable. A fibre network runs through the lung like a tense frame. A soapy film, called surfactant, coats the inner wall and lowers surface pull. Type II cells in the wall make that film. The review lays out each part and its job. It then shows how injury breaks the balance. Failed mechanics can end in lung scarring. The account joins structure detail with working function.
europmc-pmc6325111:
Tokarew and co-authors review next-generation CAR T cell therapy for cancer. Their review appeared in the British Journal of Cancer. CAR T cells are patient T cells fitted with synthetic receptors. The receptors guide them to attack cancer cells. Approved versions treat some leukemias and lymphomas. Most other tumors still escape this approach.

Success needs the cells to reach, enter, and last in tumors. Solid tumors have resisted far more than blood cancers. Their inner environment also suppresses immune attack. The review surveys plans to sharpen tumor recognition. It covers better entry into tumor tissue and longer cell survival. It also covers ways to resist the suppressive setting. The goal is strong cancer control without added harm. The piece maps where this therapy must improve next.
europmc-pmc6359811:
Li and co-authors present a research article in Cardiovascular Diabetology on a diabetes drug and heart damage. They tested empagliflozin, an SGLT2 inhibitor, in type 2 diabetic mice. The question was whether the drug protects heart muscle beyond its effect on blood sugar.

Thirty diabetic mice received the drug by mouth daily for eight weeks. The authors report better heart structure and function after treatment. Oxidative stress fell, and scarring in the heart muscle eased. They link the benefit to blocked TGF-beta signaling and to switched-on Nrf2 defenses. The team presents the drug as a promising option against diabetic cardiomyopathy.
europmc-pmc6382411:
Schulthess and co-authors report a research article in Immunity on butyrate and gut defense. Butyrate is a short-chain fatty acid made by gut bacteria. Macrophages grown with butyrate killed gut bacteria far better than usual.

Butyrate shifted how these cells burn fuel and lowered a key growth signal. The cells then made more bacteria-killing peptides and cleared germs more actively. It did this without raising inflammatory signals. The program is set as the cells mature from monocytes. The work shows how a gut product can train calm, strong defense.
europmc-pmc6451011:
Jones and co-authors hunt genes behind sleep behavior using wrist accelerometer records from 85,670 UK Biobank participants rather than questionnaires. Eight derived traits covered sleep quality, quantity, and timing, and findings were validated in 5,819 more people. Objective measurement avoids the distortions of self-report.

Forty-seven genetic associations passed the standard threshold, including 26 new ones for sleep quality and 10 for night-time duration. Most variants touched a single trait. A missense change in PDE11A stood out as the likely causal variant for duration, and sleep-quality loci clustered near serotonin-processing genes. Restless legs variants were a noted complication, since the condition can masquerade in movement data.
europmc-pmc6453311:
Liu and co-authors chart China's path to eliminating hepatitis B disease by 2030 and name the priorities still standing in the way. China carries the world's largest hepatitis B burden; globally the virus held 257 million people chronically infected in 2015 and kills about 887,000 a year. Three decades of vaccination cut new infections sharply.

Childhood coverage and timely birth-dose vaccination both exceed 95 percent, blocking mother-to-child transmission. Mortality is the stubborn target: a 65 percent reduction by 2030 demands better diagnosis and treatment capacity, lower patient costs, and one integrated system spanning prevention, screening, and lifelong care. The authors align their steps with the World Health Organization's global strategy.
europmc-pmc6535011:
Razgour and co-authors test a new way to forecast how climate change will shrink species' ranges, writing in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Standard forecasts treat a whole species as one unit. That misses local adaptation, since populations in warm spots may already carry genes for heat. The team built that variation into their models.

They used two cryptic Mediterranean bat species as the test case, linking gene variants to local climate. Counting adaptive variation cut the projected range losses for both bats. It also raised the odds the two species will compete as their ranges shift. Ignoring within-species differences, the authors warn, overstates future biodiversity losses. They urge protection of landscape links so helpful genes can spread.
europmc-pmc6544911:
Zhao, Li, Jiang and Li review a DNA-repair flaw that predicts who gains from cancer immunotherapy, writing in the Journal of Hematology & Oncology. When mismatch repair fails, copying errors pile up at short repeats called microsatellites. Such tumors, labeled dMMR or MSI-high, carry many mutations.

Those mutations create fresh antigens that draw immune attack, so checkpoint drugs work unusually well in these patients. Trials showed long responses in bowel and other cancers alike. Pembrolizumab won approval for any stubborn solid tumor with this flaw — the first cancer approval tied to a marker rather than an organ. The review covers the biology, the trial record, and how this test sits beside PD-L1 and tumor mutation counts.
europmc-pmc6554411:
Haythorne and co-authors trace how diabetes shuts down energy production inside insulin-making cells, writing in Nature Communications. Beta cells release insulin when glucose metabolism raises their ATP. Why that response fades as diabetes progresses has stayed unclear. The team combined gene, protein and metabolite measurements to find out.

In islets from diabetic mice, genes for sugar breakdown rose while genes for mitochondrial energy production fell. Glucose no longer lifted NADH or ATP, and both energy routes ran slower. Beta cells kept in high glucose showed the same pattern. High blood sugar itself, the authors argue, reprograms the cell to make far less energy — a failure that would steadily weaken insulin release.
europmc-pmc6660511:
Boza-Serrano and co-authors name galectin-3 as a harmful partner of TREM2 in Alzheimer's disease. Their study appears in Acta Neuropathologica. Microglia switch on in a hallmark way in this disease. Galectin-3 was sharply raised in patient brains. It sat in microglia clustered around amyloid plaques. Changes in its gene raised Alzheimer's risk. In 5xFAD mice, deleting the gene calmed microglia. Amyloid burden fell and memory improved.

Close imaging placed galectin-3 right against TREM2. Binding tests confirmed a direct link. It fired TREM2-DAP12 signals in reporter cells. Shots of galectin-3 with amyloid seeded lasting clumps. Without it, those clumps failed to form. The authors propose blocking galectin-3 as therapy.
europmc-pmc6696211:
Quek and co-authors meta-analyse the global prevalence of anxiety among medical students. Their analysis appears in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. Anxiety is common yet undertreated in this group. The team searched for cross-sectional prevalence studies. Sixty-nine studies covered 40,348 medical students. Random-effects pooling produced the global estimate. Anxiety prevalence reached 33.8 percent overall. The confidence interval spanned roughly 29 to 39 percent. Rates ran highest in the Middle East and Asia. Gender showed no significant prevalence difference. Year of study showed none either.

One in three students is affected. That far exceeds general population rates. The authors urge destigmatisation by school leaders. Help-seeking behaviour needs active promotion.
europmc-pmc6769011:
Hanlon and co-authors found that gene therapy vectors often insert themselves into CRISPR cut sites. Adeno-associated virus, or AAV, is a favored delivery truck for gene editing tools. The team tracked where AAV DNA lands in genomes. It integrated at up to 47% of Cas9-induced breaks in treated genes. Tests spanned cultured mouse neurons, brain, muscle, and inner ear.

Across the whole genome, AAV landing rates did not rise. The exception was the exact CRISPR target site. A miniature test vector let them read entire inserted copies. Both full and broken vector genomes appeared at cut sites. Anyone using AAV for editing, they warn, should expect such insertions as a common outcome.
europmc-pmc6779111:
Ahuja considers how artificial intelligence in medicine will change the physician's role. AI systems already sharpen diagnosis and treatment in several specialties. Heavy AI focus in radiology has led some experts to predict that radiologists may be replaced one day. Ahuja asks the broader question: replacement, or support? The paper examines AI at work in radiology, pathology, eye care, and cardiology.

The verdict is support, not replacement, for physicians in these fields. AI tools handle narrow pattern tasks well, and they keep improving with computing power. Medicine as a whole, though, turns on judgment and the bond between doctor and patient. Rule-based expert systems faded in the 1990s for exactly that complexity. AI will assist physicians rather than displace them.
europmc-pmc6787111:
Catoira and co-authors overview natural hydrogels for regenerative medicine. Hydrogels are water-rich gels that can cradle cells and healing tissue. Biological hydrogels come from proteins such as collagen and elastin, or from sugars such as alginate. Their properties, including stiffness, swelling, and breakdown rate, can be tuned by how they are made.

A newer route builds hydrogels from decellularized tissue. Such gels keep natural growth factors, sugars, and hidden bioactive peptides. These retained molecules can promote cell growth, blood vessel formation, and healing signals. Hydrogels can also carry cross-linkers, drugs, growth factors, or living cells. The review traces recent progress in making and using these materials across regenerative medicine.
europmc-pmc6813111:
Avan and co-authors present an ecological study in BMC Medicine on wealth, income, and stroke around the world. Stroke is a leading cause of death and disability. Its risks, such as high blood pressure and smoking, are not spread evenly. The team asked how stroke burden tracks with social and economic status.

They drew on the Global Burden of Disease Study 2017. They compared stroke rates, deaths, and years lost to ill health from 1990 to 2017 across levels of development. Rates fell in most places over that span. Still, poorer regions carried a heavy share, and risk factors such as high blood sugar explained much of the death toll.
europmc-pmc6929211:
Kany and co-authors review cytokines, the signal proteins that drive inflammation. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Cytokines shape many inflammatory diseases. Yet studies disagree on what each one does. They can serve as markers of disease, and as targets or guides for therapy.

The authors focus on a short list: interleukin-6, interleukin-1, and interleukin-33. They also cover tumour necrosis factor-alpha, interleukin-10, and interleukin-8. For each, they set out known biology in plain terms. They then link these signals to shock, trauma, immune breakdown, and bone loss. Critical illness also gets attention. Clearer roles, they argue, would make these markers far more useful in the clinic.
europmc-pmc6953111:
Ryu and co-authors review spheroid culture, a way of growing stem cells as floating balls. Their review appeared in Cells. Flat, layered cell culture poorly matches conditions inside the body. In spheroids, cells clump into spheres, touching neighbours and matrix much as they would in tissue.

Methods include hanging drops, gel embedding, magnetic levitation, and spinner flasks. Materials such as hydrogels, films, particles, and beads shape the cultures. Uses span tumour research, drug screening, transplantation, and drug delivery platforms. Co-cultures of mixed cell types also become possible. Limits remain: cores can starve of oxygen and die, and freeing single cells from spheres is tricky. The authors argue such systems will matter more as stem cell medicine grows.
europmc-pmc7008511:
Scheres describes a better starting point for solving amyloid structures in the RELION software. The paper appeared in Acta Crystallographica Section D. Amyloid fibrils, the tangled protein threads behind several brain diseases, are increasingly solved by cryo-electron microscopy. Refinements, though, can get stuck in wrong shapes, local minima that look plausible.

Helical objects have a head start: one long image holds every view needed for a three-dimensional rebuild. Older methods demanded near-perfect symmetry. Modern segment-based approaches allow deviations but lean on the starting model. Scheres presents a new way to generate that first model inside RELION-3.1. A test case on paired helical filaments reached about 3.8 ångström resolution. The map showed the expected two C-shaped protofilaments with clear repeating densities along the axis. A sound start, the paper argues, keeps the whole refinement honest.
europmc-pmc7026711:
The GBD 2017 Pancreatic Cancer Collaborators present a systematic analysis in The Lancet Gastroenterology and Hepatology. They measure the global burden of pancreatic cancer from 1990 to 2017. The study covers 195 countries and territories. It also estimates how much of the burden comes from known risk factors.

The team built estimates from death records and cancer registries. Global cases reached 448,000 in 2017, and deaths reached 441,000. Both had more than doubled since 1990. Death rates were highest in the high-income super-region, led by Greenland and Uruguay. Smoking was the largest attributed risk, at about one-fifth of deaths. High blood sugar and high body mass followed. The authors urge prevention, screening, and better treatment.
europmc-pmc7038611:
Kramer and co-authors update standard protocols for cardiovascular magnetic resonance in the Journal of Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance. The document revises the Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance's 2013 guidance on how heart MRI scans should be performed. Standard protocols keep image quality consistent between centres and make results easier to compare from one patient visit to the next.

The update expands the section on general principles and techniques, since more methods have settled into standard practice. A new section covers imaging patients who carry implanted devices, an increasingly common situation in daily practice. Companion documents handle clinical indications, reporting, and post-processing, while congenital heart disease gets its own document. The authors intend the protocols as a patient-based approach to clinical scanning, to be refreshed at regular intervals as the field advances.
europmc-pmc7040011:
Cao and co-authors write a short research letter in Cell Discovery about the ACE2 gene and the new coronavirus. ACE2 makes the protein the virus uses as its doorway into cells, the same receptor used by the earlier SARS coronavirus. How much ACE2 a tissue makes may shape susceptibility to infection, symptoms, and outcome. The team asked whether gene variants differ between populations.

They compared expression-linked variants and potentially functional coding variants of ACE2 across population datasets. A report that Asian males might express more ACE2 had raised the question of population differences. Clinical reports from non-Asian populations were still few when the letter was written. The analysis maps where variants sit and how their frequencies vary worldwide. It sets a baseline for later studies testing whether ACE2 genetics helps explain why the infection hits some groups harder than others.
europmc-pmc7054211:
The GenomeAsia 100K Consortium reports its pilot phase in Nature. Non-European people are badly missing from human genetic studies, which limits how far the results apply. Reference datasets for each population are needed to catalogue local variation and support gene studies across the world. The group set out to build such a resource for Asia.

The pilot produced whole-genome sequences for 1,739 people drawn from 219 population groups in 64 countries across Asia. The team catalogued genetic variation, mapped population structure, and flagged disease links and founder effects, where a small founding group leaves a strong genetic imprint. The dataset also improves imputation, the filling-in of unmeasured variants, for Asian groups. The work lays groundwork for genetic medicine that serves the region's diversity rather than only European ancestry groups.
europmc-pmc7058611:
Vos de Wael and co-authors present a software toolbox in Communications Biology. Understanding cognition means knowing how separate brain regions fit into the cortex as a whole. Recent work describes that large-scale organisation with cortical gradients: smooth maps that summarise how structure and function change across the brain. Studying gradients needs tools for finding, aligning, and comparing them.

BrainSpace, written for Python and Matlab, does those three jobs and adds visualisation. It also supports association studies between gradients and other brain features, using null models that account for spatial autocorrelation so nearby regions are not mistaken for independent evidence. Validation experiments show the tools behaving consistently on functional and microstructural gradients at different spatial scales. The authors offer the toolbox to researchers studying brain organisation across species, development, ageing, and disease.
europmc-pmc7068211:
Cianconi, Betrò, and Janiri review climate change and mental health in Frontiers in Psychiatry. Heat waves, floods, hurricanes, droughts, fires, and lost landscapes can harm minds as well as bodies, directly and indirectly. Yet psychiatry has been slow to study the link, a gap the authors set out to measure and fill.

They searched three databases for work up to the end of June 2019, finding 445 articles and association reports, of which 163 were selected for close review. The material links climate events with anxiety, schizophrenia, mood disorders and depression, suicide, and aggressive behaviour, plus grief at losing a familiar landscape. Sections treat temperature, water, air pollution, and drought one by one, and weigh exposed groups and mental adaptation. Native groups and the elderly appear as especially at risk. The review calls the slow pace of psychiatric attention itself a finding worth fixing.
europmc-pmc7101111:
Vaughan and co-authors report human-to-human spread of monkeypox virus in the United Kingdom in October 2018, in Emerging Infectious Diseases. A patient returning from Nigeria passed the virus to a health care worker, probably through contact with contaminated bedding. Monkeypox is related to smallpox but usually less severe.

Health officials vaccinated contacts, monitored them daily, and kept them home from work. Of 134 potential contacts, 4 became ill, and all patients survived. Before 2018, monkeypox outside Africa had appeared only in a 2003 United States outbreak tied to imported rodents, with no human-to-human spread. The report shows how infection control contained a rare event.
europmc-pmc7154011:
Rubino and co-authors issue a joint international consensus statement calling for an end to obesity stigma, in Nature Medicine. A multidisciplinary panel of experts, including scientific organisations, reviewed the evidence on weight stigma and agreed recommendations through a Delphi process. People with obesity face discrimination at work, in education, and in health care itself.

The panel finds stigma causes physical and psychological harm and leads to worse care, undermining health and human rights. Old narratives blaming laziness or weak willpower contradict modern science on body weight regulation. Universities, professional bodies, media, health authorities, and governments are urged to teach the reality of weight stigma and build a public story that matches the evidence.
europmc-pmc7206111:
Zhang and co-authors test whether a muscle-related protein can protect the heart from a common chemotherapy drug. Their study appeared in Cell Death and Differentiation. Doxorubicin fights cancer but often damages heart muscle. Oxidative stress and heart cell death drive that harm. The protein FNDC5 and its fragment irisin were known to guard mitochondria.

The team boosted FNDC5 in mouse heart cells using a virus delivery system. The mice then received doxorubicin. Hearts with extra FNDC5 showed far less cell death. Oxidative damage also fell. The protection ran through activation of the AKT signaling pathway. Without that signal, the benefit faded. The study points to a possible shield for patients on this drug. It ties exercise-linked proteins to heart protection.
europmc-pmc7242911:
Kitchen and co-authors find a new way to control the water channel behind brain and spinal cord swelling. Their study appeared in Cell. Such swelling, called CNS edema, affects millions of people yearly. Every drug tried against it has failed in trials. Care still rests on managing symptoms. The channel protein aquaporin-4 sits in astrocytes and moves water across brain barriers.

When oxygen-starved cells swell, more of this channel moves to the cell surface. A protein called calmodulin grabs the channel's tail and drives that move. Blocking calmodulin in rats kept the channel inside the cell. That reduced swelling after injury in their experiments. Instead of plugging the channel, the strategy hides it from the surface. The authors propose location control as a fresh drug angle.
europmc-pmc7243111:
Spampinato and co-authors look for new uses of old drugs to heal stubborn wounds in diabetes. Their review appeared in Pharmaceuticals. Chronic wounds are common in diabetes because healing itself is impaired. They burden patients and health systems alike, and diabetes keeps spreading. Current treatments often fail to close such wounds fully or fast.

The authors first survey standard wound care. They then focus on drug classes already sold for other purposes. One example is propranolol, a heart drug. A 1 percent cream of it sped skin regrowth in diabetic mice. Beta-blocker effects on skin cell movement explain the interest. Other repurposed candidates are weighed by evidence strength. The review argues the pharmacy shelf may already hold wound therapies.
europmc-pmc7289711:
Xia and co-authors examine a distinctive feature of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein: a furin cleavage site missing from its closest relatives. Their letter appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. The spike must be cut at two places before it can fuse with a cell membrane and release the viral genome. The inserted site, with the sequence RRAR, was suspected of making the virus more infectious.

Comparing spikes with and without the site, the team tested fusion ability with and without the enzyme trypsin present. Their results clarify when the furin site helps fusion and when other enzymes can do the cutting instead. The question matters because cleavage controls how easily the virus enters cells, which in turn shapes how fast it spreads through a population.
europmc-pmc7323511:
Okba and co-authors build and check blood tests for antibodies to SARS-CoV-2. Their study fills a gap from the first pandemic months. Gene tests could find live infection, but blood tests that show past infection were still scarce. Such tests are key for tracing contacts, hunting the source of the virus, and counting how far it has spread.

The team made tests for three things: antibodies that block the virus, and antibodies to its spike and its nucleocapsid. They checked the tests on blood from proven patients and from people with other coronaviruses or chest ills. Most proven patients turned antibody-positive by 2 weeks from the start of illness. Shop-bought spike tests varied in quality. One type was less exact, and an IgA kit caught more cases than an IgG kit.
europmc-pmc7400911:
Charoenngam and Holick review vitamin D's effects on the immune system in Nutrients. Vitamin D is best known for regulating calcium and keeping bones mineralized, but its active form also acts as an immune-modulating hormone. Experiments show it influencing both innate and adaptive immune cells, and the lining of blood vessels.

Low blood levels of the storage form are tied to higher risk of psoriasis, type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, tuberculosis, sepsis, respiratory infection, and COVID-19. Trials of supplementation for these diseases have given mixed results. People also differ widely in gene response to the same dose, which may explain the patchiness. The authors advise keeping levels adequate while the optimal target stays debated.
europmc-pmc7427911:
Moullin and co-authors give ten recommendations for using implementation frameworks in research and practice. Such frameworks help teams put proven care into real-world use. Reviews show they are often used too little or too late.

The advice runs in rough time order across a project. Teams should pick a fit framework, build community partnerships, and set clear questions. They should draw a logic model, choose study methods, and name the factors that block or aid change. Later steps cover tailored strategies, outcome checks, and clear reporting. Examples use the EPIS framework, which tracks exploration, preparation, implementation, and sustainment. Used well, frameworks help knowledge grow across projects.
europmc-pmc7523011:
Rajkumar and Kumar set out treatment algorithms for multiple myeloma. The cancer affects plasma cells in bone marrow. New drugs and trial results keep changing care choices.

Their algorithms cover newly diagnosed and relapsed disease. Choices depend on age, fitness and other illness. Transplant eligibility also shapes the plan. Risk groups rest on gene changes such as t(4;14) and del(17p). The authors base steps on randomized trials where they exist. Where trials are lacking, they use other data and expert practice. They advise that trials be considered first for all patients.
europmc-pmc7553211:
Boersma, Black and Ward estimate chronic condition prevalence among US adults in 2018. Data came from the National Health Interview Survey. Ten diagnosed conditions were counted for each adult.

More than half of adults had at least one condition. That share was 51.8% of the adult population. A total of 27.2% had multiple chronic conditions. Rates were highest among women in the survey. They were also highest in adults aged 65 or older. Non-Hispanic white adults and rural residents ranked high too. The sample held 25,417 adults in total. The results help track chronic disease burden over time.
europmc-pmc7581511:
Swanson and co-authors present an ISAPP consensus statement defining synbiotics. A panel met in May 2019 to update the term. Experts in nutrition, physiology and microbiology took part.

A synbiotic is a mix of live microbes and substrates. The substrates are used by host microbes selectively. The mix must confer a health benefit on the host. A complementary synbiotic pairs a probiotic with a prebiotic. A synergistic synbiotic uses a substrate picked for its partner microbes. The panel set out evidence levels for claims. Safety, targets and stakeholder effects are also covered. The statement aims to keep innovation open in this field.
europmc-pmc7654011:
Wu and co-authors use genetics to test whether bowel disease causes bone loss. They apply Mendelian randomization, a method that uses gene variants as natural tests. The bowel diseases are ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. The outcome is bone mineral density at several body sites.

The team drew on public genome-wide study data and used several checks for bias. They report that genes linked to ulcerative colitis cause lower total body and forearm density. Genes linked to Crohn's disease affect density at the femoral neck. The results split by disease and by site, which past survey studies had blurred.
europmc-pmc7656711:
Zhang and co-authors report a new cell therapy built from stem cells. The team made macrophages from induced pluripotent stem cells. They gave these cells a chimeric antigen receptor, or CAR. The aim is a ready supply of cancer-fighting cells.

The CAR cells acted only when they met the target antigen on cancer cells. They released signaling proteins, shifted to an attack state, and ate more tumor cells. They also fought cancer in living tests. The authors say the platform could yield an unlimited source of such cells, unlike cells taken from each patient.
europmc-pmc7665311:
Turoňová and co-authors study the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 in its natural setting. The spike lets the virus enter host cells and is a prime target for antibodies. About 20 to 40 spikes stud the surface of each virus particle. Past work used lab-made spike, not spike on real virus.

Using imaging of intact virus, the team found the spike stalk bends at three hinges. Sugar chains shield these hinges well. This flex may let many spikes grip a flat host cell surface at once. The results ground vaccine and drug design in how the spike truly sits and moves.
europmc-pmc7758411:
Jin and co-authors review how COVID-19 activates and damages the lining of blood vessels. Endothelial cells line all vessels and carry high levels of the viral entry protein ACE2. They govern inflammation and clotting at the vessel wall. Evidence ties their dysfunction to severe disease.

When these cells switch on, the vessel barrier leaks and clots form more readily. Inflammation at the wall grows, and white blood cells slip into tissue. Lung vessel damage is a hallmark of the acute respiratory failure that kills patients. The authors set out the cell and molecular steps in this process. They end with treatments that aim to protect the vessel lining.
europmc-pmc7806511:
Meredith and co-authors report fast use of virus sequencing to trace COVID-19 spread inside a hospital. The burden of hospital-linked SARS-CoV-2 infection was unclear. The team set up rapid genome sequencing during care. Genetic data were combined with clinical details.

Sequencing results came back fast enough to act on. Staff could judge whether cases on a ward were truly linked. Linked cases point to spread within the hospital. Unlinked cases suggest separate introductions from outside. That split guides infection control steps. The authors present rapid sequencing as a practical surveillance tool. It can run as a standing part of hospital safety work.
europmc-pmc7808711:
The CDC COVID-19 Response Team, with the Food and Drug Administration, reports allergic reactions after the first Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine doses. The report covers the United States from December 14 to 23, 2020. The vaccine had gained emergency use approval on December 11.

Cases include anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction. By January 3, 2021, the country had logged 20,346,372 COVID-19 cases. Deaths stood at 349,246. Against that backdrop, reaction reports were tracked closely. The document sets out what was seen in the first days of rollout. It gives clinicians guidance on spotting and treating such reactions. All 20 people with follow-up information had recovered or been discharged home.
europmc-pmc7857411:
Ng and co-authors test whether past cold coronavirus infections leave useful immunity to SARS-CoV-2. Seasonal coronaviruses infect most people in childhood. Memory from them might soften the new virus. The team checked people never infected with SARS-CoV-2.

The cohort held 350 uninfected people. A small share carried antibodies that reacted to SARS-CoV-2. Those antibodies came from seasonal virus exposure. Some could even block the new virus weakly in tests. Children and teens showed such cross-reactivity more often. The authors weigh what this means for disease spread. Old immunity may bend, but not stop, the pandemic's course.
europmc-pmc8026611:
Tang and co-authors review ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death, and its stakes for health. Ferroptosis was first described in 2012 as non-apoptotic and driven by lipid peroxidation. It starts when oxidants overwhelm antioxidant defenses. Redox-active enzymes sit on both sides of that balance. Regulation reaches from epigenetic marks down to protein modification.

The review lays out two routes into ferroptosis. One depends on transporters, the other on enzymes inside the cell. The transcription factor NFE2L2 anchors the defense against it. Selective autophagy, by contrast, can push cells toward ferroptotic death. The authors then trace what goes wrong in disease. Cancer, neurodegeneration, tissue injury, inflammation, and infection all feature. The synthesis links a young death pathway to wide clinical terrain.
europmc-pmc8027411:
Wei and co-authors identify RAB31 as the marker and driver of an ESCRT-independent exosome pathway. Exosomes form as small vesicles inside multivesicular endosomes, then leave the cell. The ESCRT machinery was long thought essential for making them. Yet vesicles still formed without it, hinting at another route. The team tracked what that route requires.

The authors report that active RAB31, switched on by EGFR phosphorylation, starts the process. It engages flotillin proteins in lipid raft patches of membrane. That drives EGFR into endosomes to form the inner vesicles, no ESCRT needed. RAB31 then recruits TBC1D2B to switch off RAB7. That move stops the endosomes from fusing with lysosomes. Cargo escapes destruction and ships out as exosomes instead.
europmc-pmc8075011:
Shmueli asks which beliefs predict the intent to take a COVID-19 vaccine. The study joined two classic models of health behavior. An online survey reached Israeli adults from May 24 to June 24, 2020. It asked about risk, benefit, social pressure, and confidence. Of 398 eligible respondents, 80% said they would take the vaccine.

A unified model drawing on both theories predicted intent well. It explained 78% of the variance in answers. Men, the more educated, and past flu shot takers showed higher intent. Perceived benefit of the vaccine was the strongest single push. Perceived severity of the infection and cues to act also raised intent. Social norms and self-efficacy mattered on the planned behavior side. Half the sample had skipped the last flu shot. Even so, two-thirds of those skippers planned to take the COVID shot.
europmc-pmc8106311:
Tremblay and Ainslie count how many people live at high altitude, country by country. Old global guesses swung wildly, and national figures did not exist. The pair layered LandScan population grids over global terrain data. They tallied residents in 500-meter elevation bands for every country. Thin air, cold, and strong sun shape life up high. Knowing who lives there shapes health research.

Their count comes to 500.3 million people living at 1,500 meters or higher worldwide today. Of those, 81.6 million live at 2,500 meters or more, and 14.4 million live at 3,500 meters or more in the final tallies. Ethiopia holds the largest high population at the lower two bands. China leads at the highest band counted. Bolivia has the greatest share of its people up high. Most altitude science still studies visiting lowlanders. Half a billion permanent residents argue for a shift.
europmc-pmc8106911:
Hockenberry and Wilke present BACPHLIP, a tool that predicts a bacteriophage's lifestyle from its genome. Phages split into two camps by habit. Temperate phages hide inside host cells in a latent phase. Virulent ones copy themselves at once and burst the cell. Knowing the camp matters for ecology and for therapy. Guessing it from sequence alone was unreliable.

The tool scans a genome for a set of conserved protein domains. A random forest classifier reads that pattern and calls the lifestyle. Training used 634 phage genomes with known habits. On a separate test set of 423 phages, the calls hit 98% accuracy in the authors' hands. Older tools managed only 79% on the same test. The code is free on GitHub for anyone to use. Users can even retrain the model themselves. Fast, open lifestyle calls help sort the phage flood.
europmc-pmc8123811:
Vogt and co-authors lay out how the body moves, stores, and rations iron. Most body iron rides in red blood cells as hemoglobin. Worn-out red cells are recycled by macrophages in spleen, liver, and marrow. Food iron enters gut cells through the transporter DMT1. Ferroportin then hands it to the blood, where transferrin carries it. The liver stores the surplus locked in ferritin.

One hormone runs the whole rationing system. When iron loads rise, liver cells release hepcidin. Hepcidin binds ferroportin and drags it inside for destruction. Less iron then escapes into the blood from any cell. The review follows each player at cell and system level. Receptors, transporters, and stores each get their mechanism. Too much iron burns tissue; too little starves blood. The hepcidin dial keeps the balance fine. Its faults explain inherited and acquired iron diseases.
europmc-pmc8271111:
Andreatta and Carmona present UCell, an R package for scoring gene signatures in single-cell data. Researchers often need to grade each cell against a gene set. Many scoring tools slow down or wobble on large, mixed datasets.

UCell scores rest on the Mann-Whitney U statistic. They stay stable as dataset size and mix change. Computation takes minutes, even on modest machines. The package plugs straight into Seurat objects. Any single-cell data matrix can be scored. Code and documents sit on GitHub for free use. The tool suits the huge atlases now common in the field.
europmc-pmc8284311:
Jones and co-authors show that the antibody LY-CoV555 protects primates from SARS-CoV-2. The antibody targets the viral spike protein. Neutralising antibodies can treat infection or guard people before vaccines reach them.

In lab tests, LY-CoV555 neutralised the virus. In nonhuman primates, it protected the airways against infection. The study spans antibody design through animal proof. Teams from drug and academic labs shared the work. Such antibodies offered a stopgap early in the pandemic. The data supported moving the antibody toward human use. Airway protection was the key sign they sought.
europmc-pmc8319411:
Qiu and co-authors show that soil erosion cuts microbial diversity and soil function. Erosion drives land degradation worldwide. Its effect on soil microbes and their many jobs stayed unclear.

The team studied two sites with unlike soil texture and climate. Eroded plots held fewer microbial taxa than intact plots. Their microbe networks were simpler, with fewer links. Dominant groups such as Proteobacteria and Bacteroidetes shrank. Other groups gained ground instead. Soil lost part of its multifunctionality with the microbes. Restoration plans must rebuild the living soil, not just the surface.
europmc-pmc8361711:
Donoso-Quezada, Ayala-Mar, and González-Valdez review lipids in exosome biology and cell talk. Exosomes are tiny vesicles cells release to signal each other. Their mix tracks with diseases such as cancer and diabetes.

Lipids form a core part of exosome makeup. They shape how vesicles form, release, and find targets. They also steer uptake by receiving cells. The review covers those functions in order. It then surveys the tools that read exosome lipids. Uses in diagnosis and therapy close the picture. Membrane chemistry turns out to carry much of the message.
europmc-pmc8370411:
Williams and co-authors test the role of CD4 T cells in a mouse model of Parkinson's disease. The protein alpha-synuclein builds up in this disease and stirs the immune system. T cells enter the brain, but their exact effect was unclear.

Mice with extra alpha-synuclein in the midbrain showed more MHCII protein on brain immune cells. Interferon-gamma producing CD4 and CD8 T cells also moved in. Mice that lacked CD4 were protected from the loss of dopamine nerve cells. Blocking T cells with genetic changes or the drug fingolimod cut the immune response. The authors suggest that aiming at these T cell responses could slow the disease.
europmc-pmc8539411:
Burgess and co-authors review the science of wound healing in diabetes. Diabetes is a growing chronic disease marked by long high blood sugar. Poor wound healing hits about a quarter of patients, per the authors. It often ends in lower limb amputation, at high human and money cost.

High sugar helps germ films grow on wounds and makes them hard to treat. The review covers weak vessel growth, nerve damage, and a stalled inflammatory response. Barrier breaks and mixed infections add to the burden. Current and future treatments are matched to each fault. The authors urge plans that strike many causes at once.
europmc-pmc8728211:
Del Toro and co-authors report on IntAct, a database of molecular interactions between proteins and other molecules. The data are curated from published work and direct deposits. Twelve global partners of an international consortium share the curation work. As of August 2021, the database held more than one million binary interactions.

IntAct aims for fine detail in each record. That detail helps users judge what an experiment really showed. Recent work focused on key curation areas and fresh progress there. A rebuilt website presents the data in a friendlier, fuller way. The authors describe the new site and the curation model behind it.
europmc-pmc9139611:
Grochans and co-authors review the epidemiology of glioblastoma multiforme, an aggressive brain tumor. It accounts for 14.5% of all central nervous system tumors and 48.6% of malignant ones. Median survival is only about 15 months. The review asks who gets this tumor and what may raise the risk.

Data show it is the highest-grade primary brain tumor and is more common in men. Risk of glioma rises with age, and survival stays low despite medical gains. Proof on possible risk factors is murky in several areas. Those areas include stimulants, some drugs, cell phone use, and heavy metals. Readers get a clear summary of spread, pattern, and open risk questions.
europmc-pmc9238111:
Salari and co-authors pool worldwide studies on how often older adults fall. Falls are among the most common and serious problems of old age. Injuries can be fatal or can cut the ability to manage daily life. The team searched major databases with no time limit up to August 2020.

They included 104 studies with a total sample of 36,740,590 people. The pooled prevalence of falls in older adults was 26.5%. Oceania had the highest rate at 34.4%, followed by the Americas at 27.9%. Rates fell as sample size and study year rose. The authors urge policymakers and care providers to plan prevention programs. Such steps could cut a common cause of harm in later life.
europmc-pmc9276711:
Caliendo and co-authors trace how highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 crossed the Atlantic in 2021. In December 2021 the virus was found in poultry and a free-living gull in St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador. It was the first such report in the Americas since June 2015. The team used family-tree analysis plus wild bird migration data.

The Canadian viruses matched most closely those in northwestern Europe in spring 2021. Likely routes ran via Iceland, Greenland and the Arctic, or open-sea pelagic paths. Wild birds, not trade, appear to have carried the virus. The finding raises concern about further spread across the Americas. The lineage already threatens poultry, wildlife, and human health on other continents.
europmc-pmc9470311:
Chagas and co-authors examine flavonols and flavones as anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and antibacterial compounds. Plant compounds have served as medicines for centuries. Flavonoids are plant chemicals with a wide range of such effects. Diet supplies many of them through fruit and vegetables.

The review profiles key flavonols such as quercetin and kaempferol. It also profiles flavones such as luteolin and apigenin. Food sources and structural traits are set out for each. The authors then trace how these compounds act. They calm inflammation and blunt oxidative damage. They also act on bacterial metabolism. Pairing them with antibiotics may help against resistant strains. Cell targets that back these effects get a full account. The work frames diet compounds as aids in infectious and inflammatory disease.
europmc-pmc9671811:
Xu, Xie, and Al-Aly chart long-term neurologic outcomes after COVID-19 in a Veterans Affairs cohort study. Brain effects of the acute illness were well mapped already. A full one-year account of later brain harms had not been done. The team built the count from national health records.

The COVID cohort held 154,068 people with the infection. Two control sets held more than five million people each for contrast. At 12 months, risks ran high across a wide harm list. Stroke, memory faults, and peripheral nerve disorders all rose. Migraine, seizures, and movement disorders also rose in the data. Mental health and sensory harms joined the pattern as well. The hazard ratio for any neurologic aftereffect was 1.42 overall. Risk stayed up even in people never sent to hospital. The authors urge care plans that expect lasting brain effects.
europmc-pmc9729111:
Aragam and co-authors hunt and sort risk variants and genes for coronary artery disease at huge scale. Their genome-wide study drew 181,522 cases among over a million people. Finding risk spots has run ahead of grasping how they act. The team set out to close that gap with deep follow-up.

The scan found 241 signals, including 30 new risk sites. A cross-ancestry blend with a Japanese study added 38 more. Fine mapping narrowed many spots to a few likely variants. Clustering hints pointed to early growth pathways. Cell cycle and vessel cell movement paths also stood out. Eight sorting methods together named 220 candidate genes. Most top picks won support from three or more methods. Lab tests backed one gene tied to vessel cell motion. The authors offer the map for experiments on disease roots.
europmc-pmc9961011:
More and co-authors review silver nanoparticles as killers of drug-resistant bacteria. The review covers how the particles are made from elemental silver. It then details how they attack multidrug-resistant and biofilm-forming pathogens. Studies show they cause oxidative stress and membrane damage in bacteria.

Protein dysfunction and DNA damage also drive bacterial death. The particles can block cell adhesion and so prevent biofilm formation. Benefits in medicine face limits from harm to humans and the environment. Ongoing clinical trials are briefly noted. Other uses include diagnostics and wound healing support. The authors discuss functionalized particles as a path to safer use. The review weighs a potent tool against its real risks.
europmc-pmc9977911:
Calabresi and co-authors revisit alpha-synuclein in Parkinson's disease and related disorders. The protein's key role in Parkinson's was found twenty-five years before this review. Abnormal forms trigger slow, selective nerve cell death. Harm runs through mitochondrial faults, lysosome failure, and calcium imbalance.

The same protein drives dementia with Lewy bodies and multiple system atrophy. Pure autonomic failure and REM sleep behavior disorder also link to it. Early synaptic changes arise before overt nerve loss. Inflammation appears early in models and in patients. That timing hints at a link between inflammation and synaptic failure. The authors stress early mechanisms as routes to biomarkers. They also frame them as targets for disease-modifying therapy.
evans-wentz-fairy-faith-1911:
W. Y. Evans-Wentz walked the Celt lands to ask folk what they held on fays. The Fairy-Faith in Celtic Countries came out in 1911. He went through Ireland, Scotland, Wales, Cornwall, Brittany, and Man. Old men and women told him what their kin had seen and feared.

First-hand tales fill the book: troops of fays, hid folk, and stolen babes. Evans-Wentz then weighs what the tales may mean for the mind and soul. He treats the faith with care, not with scorn. The book is the base work for all grave study of fay lore.
examen-des-principes-des-alchymistes-sur:
Pousse's Examen des principes des alchymistes examines alchemists' claims about the philosopher's stone. François Pousse wrote the work in French. Its Paris title page is dated M. DCCXI, or 1711. It was sold by Daniel Jollet and Barthélemy Girin, with royal approval and privilege.

A dedicatory epistle to Jean Paul Bignon, Abbé de Saint-Quentin, fronts the book. Bignon led the royal academies of sciences and medals. Pousse jokes that his book will rob alchemy's believers of promised happiness. Kings would trade sceptres for shepherd staffs under its critique, he writes. The epistle frames the work as a bold, ironic attack. The body then tests alchemical principles piece by piece.
florio-italian-1611:
John Florio published Queen Anna's New World of Words in 1611, a greatly expanded Italian-English dictionary. Florio taught languages at the court of James the First and had already issued a smaller word book in 1598. The new volume, dedicated to Queen Anne, carried some 46,000 Italian words explained in English.

Entries give rich clusters of English equivalents, along with proverbs and phrases from Italian writers. Florio also translated Montaigne's essays, and his word-hoard fed the English of his age; scholars still debate his links with Shakespeare's circle. The dictionary was the first full bridge between Renaissance Italy and Jacobean England. Students of both languages still consult it for words that later books dropped.
fouque-undine-1811:
Friedrich de la Motte Fouque, a German officer and writer, wrote this tale of a water spirit in 1811. F. E. Bunnett turned it into English, in the full text of nineteen parts. The tale grew from old lore of the undine, the maid of the waters.

Undine is raised by a fisherman, weds a knight, and by that bond wins a human soul. Joy turns to grief as the knight fails her, and the waters call her back at last. The short tale fixed the form of the water spirit in the books of Europe.
froude-history-england-vol-11:
After the Armada comes triumph in the eleventh volume of Froude's History, from 1865. Spain lies humbled at sea, and England stands exalted among the powers. Elizabeth sits at the very zenith of her glory as queen.

Froude savors the victory toward which his long narrative has built. Sea dogs raid, courtiers scheme, and the queen holds her state with cool mastery. He writes the moment when England became a great power in earnest. The volume glows with national pride, and its flowing style shows why Froude ranked as the most dramatic English historian of the Victorian age.
frus-1861-d11:
On 16 July 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Baron von Gerolt, Prussia's minister in Washington. Gerolt was Prussia's minister in Washington. The letter is document 11 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

A letter to a foreign envoy in Washington worked the home end of diplomacy. Seward used such talks to press the Union's view of the war on each court through its own man. This exchange with Prussia's envoy sits just before the first great battle at Bull Run. Prussia's weight in Germany made its envoy a man worth the Secretary's direct time.
frus-1861-d111:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Anson Burlingame on 13 April 1861. Burlingame was named the American minister to China that spring. The letter is document 111 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.
