In a later chapter of the same book he is called the son of Jarah. A second mention of the name is not explained here at all. The entry sends the reader to the article on Almon for that one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-algazi-hayyim-1: Hayyim Algazi was a rabbi in Constantinople in the seventeenth century. He studied under Joseph di Trani. He wrote notes on a civil law part of an older code. That older code was by Jeroham ben Meshullam. Hayyim's notes came out in Constantinople in 1668. They bear a Hebrew title that means the paths of justice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ararat-1711:
Ararat is a district in eastern Armenia, between lakes Van and Urmia and the river Araxes. The Bible name matches the Assyrian Urartu. Assyrian kings Asshurnazir-pal and Shalmaneser II invaded and partly conquered that land, the entry says.

Cuneiform writing reached Urartu by the ninth century B.C., and many stone inscriptions have been found there. A strong native line of kings rose about the middle of that century. Assyria revived under Tiglath-pileser III about 740 B.C. and attacked for a generation. Urartu won its freedom again, until Scythians overran it near the end of the seventh century. The Bible names Ararat four times, once as the refuge of Sennacherib's killers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aronson-rudolph:
Rudolph Aronson, composer and theatrical manager, was born in New York on April 8, 1856. After New York high school he trained at the Vienna Conservatory and then at the Paris Conservatoire, where he studied the French composers closely. His taste ran to light, lyrical music rather than the classics. Back in America he first won notice directing fashionable concerts in Madison Square Garden.

Their success let him build a concert hall at Forty-first Street and Broadway, opened on May 27, 1880, where he introduced the roof garden as a summer feature. With new capital he opened the Casino on October 22, 1882, a Moorish-style theater devoted to light opera, called here the first lasting home of light opera in America. He also wrote over 150 dances, marches, and orchestral pieces.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ash-ariya-1911:
Ashariya was a Muslim theological school founded at the start of the tenth century by Abu el-Hasan al-Ash'ari. Its aim was twofold. It fought the doctrines of the Rationalists, the Motazilites. At the same time it softened the hard, unbending line of the Orthodox party. Three questions drove the quarrel: whether the Koran existed before creation, whether human acts are fixed beforehand, and how God's attributes are to be understood.

On the Koran, the school took a middle path. The book as handed down was created, it held, but its principles existed before the world. The entry notes that rabbis held a like view of the Torah. On human acts, the Ash'ariya sided in the main with the Orthodox, who read the Koran literally, yet sought room for justice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asiel-2011: Three men share the name Asiel in this entry. The first stands only in the genealogy of Simeon, in First Chronicles chapter 4. The second was one of the five skilled writers who wrote out the law for Ezra, in Second Esdras chapter 14. The third was an ancestor of Tobit, in the first chapter of the book of Tobit, where the older version reads the name as Asael. Nothing further is stated about any of the three.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-auerbach-benjam:
Benjamin Hirsch Auerbach was a leader of modern German orthodoxy. He was born at Neuwied in 1808 and died at Halberstadt on Sept. 30, 1872. His father Abraham was a rabbi of old family stock. Benjamin studied at the schools of Krefeld and Worms, then at the University of Marburg from 1831 to 1834.

Auerbach became chief rabbi of Hesse at Darmstadt, beating out Zunz for the post. His strict orthodoxy clashed with a mostly liberal flock, and he resigned in 1857 after twenty-three years. In 1863 he took the rabbinate of Halberstadt and held it till death. He was among the first Orthodox rabbis to preach in pure German. His textbook for religious teaching won wide use. The entry lists his sermons, his defense of the oral law against Frankel, and his edition of a medieval ritual code.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-azevedo-david-s: David Salom d'Azevedo was a diplomat of the seventeenth century. He died in 1699. He served at Amsterdam as minister resident of the dey of Algeria. In that post he worked out a trade treaty between Algeria and the Netherlands. He was also an active member of the building committee for the great synagogue of the Portuguese congregation in Amsterdam. The entry calls him renowned for his wisdom and learning. His tombstone text can be found in de Castro's collection of Amsterdam gravestones.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bachrich-sigism: Sigismund Bachrich, a Hungarian violinist and composer of operas, was born at Zsambokrét on Jan. 23, 1841. He studied violin at the Vienna Conservatory from 1851 and finished in 1857. After posts in Vienna and a hard spell in Paris, he played viola in the Helmesberger Quartet for twelve years. He later taught at the Conservatory. The entry names his comic opera "Muzzedin" of 1883 and the operetta "Der Fuchsmajor" of 1889, which it calls his most successful work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ballin-joel-241:
Joel Ballin was a Danish engraver born in Vejle, Jutland, on March 22, 1822. He died in Copenhagen on March 21, 1885. At eleven he went to Copenhagen to study painting, but work for his living slowed him. A new copying method, the chemitype, drew him toward engraving as a surer trade. Danish support sent him to Paris, where he arrived Oct. 5, 1848, and finished his training.

In Paris, Ballin mastered engraving on steel plates, so well that his plates could hardly be told from copper. He took a gold medal at the Paris exhibition in 1861 and was made a knight of the Dannebrog in 1862. The war of 1870 drove him to London, where he lived until 1883. Copenhagen then called him home to teach young engravers and copy great Danish works. The entry ends with a list of his chief engravings after famous paintings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barby-meir-b-sa:
Meïr b. Saul Barby, Talmudist and rabbi, was born about 1725 at Barby near Halberstadt and died at Presburg on July 28, 1789. His father, a poor tradesman, carried the weak boy part of the way to the yeshibah at Halberstadt to save traveling costs. The boy became one of its keenest pupils. He studied two years at Frankfort under Jacob Joshua, then became dayyan and acting rabbi at Halberstadt. After a year at Halle, he held the Presburg rabbinate and its yeshibah for twenty-five years.

Barby ranked among the greatest dialecticians of his time. His "Sefer Ḥiddushe Halakot" (1786–92) earned him the surname "Ḥarif." He wrote explanations of the Talmud only, refusing to present his views as rules for practice. He also studied secular subjects, above all medicine, and pressed a rational diet on his circle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-basel-land-2611: Basel-Land is a Swiss canton whose capital is Liestal. The entry says the canton long barred Jews from settling there. Jews who had settled in Liestal were expelled in 1839, despite French protests. A law of Nov. 17, 1857 still forbade settlement, crafts, and trade to every Jew. Fines fell on anyone who housed a Jew in business or rented him a store. Jews could still visit fairs, pass through, and stay for short periods.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beck-klinos-271: Klinos Beck was a Hungarian singer born at Budapest in 1868. He went to commercial schools, then trained in music at the National Musical Academy there. At nineteen he began study as an opera singer against his father's wishes. Beck won a free scholarship and two prizes at the Paris Conservatoire. Back in Budapest in 1892, he first sang in the opera Hamlet and was engaged at once. The entry says he still held a leading place among Hungary's opera artists in 1902.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belilla-david-2:
David Belilla was one of the leading Jews of Cranganore, in southern India, near the middle of the sixteenth century. With three named partners he built a synagogue in that town in the year 1568. Cranganore lay sixteen miles north of Cochin.

A Hebrew chronicle of the Malabar Jews, kept at Cambridge, says his grandfather came from Jerusalem. The entry warns that this may not be literal, since the white Jews of Cochin are sometimes called Jerusalem Jews. The same chronicle names a cantor of his family from Safed. His partners in that building work were Samuel Castiel, Ephraim Salah, and Joseph Levi of the town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bendetsohn-mena:
Menahem Manus Bendetsohn, a Russian teacher and Hebrew writer, was born in Grodno in 1817 and died there on March 20, 1888. After Talmudic study at home, he went young to Breslau for further study. In 1853 he returned to Russia and taught for more than twenty years in the government school for Jewish children at Grodno.

He also ran a private school there, and his pupils included the poet Konstantin Shapiro. Fluent in Russian and German as well as Hebrew, he knew Scripture by heart. His books include a Hebrew grammar in question-and-answer form and tales for Jewish children.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernal-ralph-31:
Ralph Bernal, a politician and art collector, died in 1854. His family came of Spanish Jewish stock, and his father was a West Indian merchant. Ralph read at Cambridge and was called to the bar in 1810. Rich West Indian property led him to choose Parliament over law instead.

He sat in the Commons for thirty-four years, from 1818 to 1852, and chaired its committees for two decades. Raised a Christian, he still backed bills to lift the bars on Jews. His fame in his day rested chiefly on his collection of old china and plate, sold after his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernstein-aaron:
Aaron David Bernstein, a German publicist and reformer, was born on April 6, 1812, in Danzig. He died on Feb. 12, 1884, in Berlin. Meant by his parents for a rabbi, he got a deep Talmudic schooling. At twenty he reached Berlin and taught himself German tongue and letters without school or university.

Writing soon became his trade, on themes from the Song of Songs to the turning of the planets. He led in the drive for religious reform and kept the respect of its foes. In 1849 he founded a political paper that won a wide readership and fame.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bing-solomon-33: Solomon Bing was a German physician. He was born about the year 1615. His father was Abraham Bing of Bingen. His father-in-law was Joseph Solomon del Medigo. As a boy he learned Latin at Jesuit colleges. He studied medicine under Del Medigo first. Then he took degrees at Padua. In 1645 he sought to succeed Del Medigo at Frankfort. Padua's degree spared him a new examination. In 1653 a patient-death charge hit him. Jewish practice was then confined to the Jewish quarter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blood-relations:
Blood-relationship means kinship other than by marriage. Old Testament genealogies look strictly paternal. Fathers name sons down long lists. Yet some lists also name mothers. Mothers name children in many passages too. That split hints at older customs. Kinship once ran broadly as brotherhood. All Israel counted as bone and flesh together.

Closer kin still carried special duties. Restitution went first to the nearest of kin. The entry's critical view surveys Semitic evidence. Among Semites kinship first ran through mothers. Jacob's children belonged to their mother's clan. Artificial brotherhoods also used shared blood. Covenanters tasted each other's blood together.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bondi-elijah-be: Elijah ben Selig Bondi was an Austrian preacher born at Prague at the end of the eighteenth century. He died there about 1860. He studied Talmud at Presburg and at Alt-Ofen. In 1826 he became preacher in his native town and held the post till his death. His sermons, printed at Prague from 1832 to 1856, draw on Bahya, Judah ha-Levi, and Albo. They treat ethical subjects in a philosophical vein.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bright-john-371:
John Bright was an English statesman and orator born at Greenbank on Nov. 16, 1811. He died in Rochdale on March 27, 1889. A claim that his mother was a Jewess is wrong, the entry states first.

Bright stood again and again for the political emancipation of England's Jews. He called that cause justice to the Jewish population of the country. On May 14, 1849, he spoke strongly for a bill letting Jews sit in Parliament. He took the same stand in 1851, when the Salomons case raised the question. His fullest speech on religious equality for Jews came on April 15, 1853. Principle, not personal feeling, drove his stance.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-calamani-joshua: Joshua Abraham Calamani, son of Simhah, was an Italian Talmudist born at Venice in 1704. His surname may come from Kalman or Kalonymus, borne by an ancestor. The entry calls him a precocious child. His only surviving work was written when he was thirteen years old. It parodies the language and style of the Talmud, complete with Rashi and Tosafot voices. He wrote it for the festival of Hanukkah. It was printed at Venice in 1717. No later work by him is recorded here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-captives-4011:
Captives taken in war get no rules of their own in the Bible, the article states. They counted as slaves and fell under the laws for a non Jewish slave. In the first wars in Canaan, orders to destroy whole peoples left no captives at all. Later kings at times showed mercy: Ahab freed a beaten Syrian king, and a trapped Syrian army was sent home fed.

One case stands apart: the beautiful captive a soldier wished to wed. She got a full month to mourn her parents. If he then refused her, he had to free her, not sell her. The rabbis read that law as a grudging yield to passion. They stretched her stay to three months, barred all force in urging the faith, and kept the duty to free her.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cassel-david-41:
David Cassel, a German historian and theologian, was born on March 7, 1818, at Gross-Glogau, in Silesia. He died in Berlin on Jan. 22, 1893. He studied at Berlin University and took his rabbinical diploma in 1843. Though gifted as a preacher, he never took a rabbinical post.

From 1846 to 1879 Cassel headed an educational institute in Berlin. He taught religion in Jewish schools and, from 1872, at the new Lehranstalt für die Wissenschaft des Judenthums. His own years of poverty led him to help found a society aiding poor Jewish students. His books include a guide to Jewish history and literature, a Hebrew-German dictionary, and a textbook used in schools. He also edited older scholars' responsa and lexicons, with introductions and notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cherub-plural-c:
Cherub, in the plural cherubim, is the name of a winged being named often in the Bible. Ezekiel describes the cherubim as a group of four living creatures. Each had four faces: of a lion, an ox, an eagle, and a man. Each had a man's stature and hands, a calf's feet, and four wings. Two wings rose to hold up God's throne, and two covered the creatures.

In Solomon's Temple, the Ark stood between two great cherubim of olivewood plated with gold. They stood ten cubits high, with wings meeting in the middle and touching the walls. Cherubim were also woven into the Temple veil and curtains. Two cherubim of solid gold stood on the Ark cover, facing each other. In early Israel the cherubim formed God's chariot, bearing his throne. A psalm pictures God riding on a cherub, on the wings of the wind.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-child-the-13911:
Child, in Jewish thought, was the greatest blessing God could bestow, a view held since Abraham's day. To be without children counted as the greatest curse. The Rabbis called the childless man as good as dead. Medieval cabalists held that a man dying without offspring had failed his mission in this world.

Legends fill the time before birth. The soul is warned of its duties and swears to lead a holy life. Two angels teach it the Torah and show it paradise and hell. The child then forgets all, so that free will stays intact. Customs at birth include planting a tree, a cedar for a boy and a pine for a girl. Boys received their sacred names at circumcision. Girls were named about a month after birth. The firstborn was redeemed on the thirtieth day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-clement-xiv-lor:
Lorenzo Ganganelli, Clement XIV, the 256th pope, was born on Oct. 31, 1705, near Rimini, elected on May 19, 1769, and died on Sept. 22, 1774. Jews greeted his rise with joy. As a councilor of the Holy Office he had declared them innocent of the blood accusation in a memorandum of March 21, 1758.

Two months into his reign he moved Roman Jews out from under the Inquisition to the Vicariato di Roma. In 1773 he confirmed an older bull guarding their Jus Gazaka rights. The entry gives long space to that 1758 report, written after a blood charge at Yanopol in Poland. Ganganelli showed the charge groundless and reviewed its whole history, granting only two old cases any weight.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-tanugi-ju: Judah b. Abraham Cohen Tanugi, called Hadria, was a rabbi and writer who died at Tunis about 1835. He died at an advanced age, the short entry adds. Two Hebrew works stand under his name. Both hold notes on the Talmud. The first, Erez Yehudah, or Land of Judah, came out at Leghorn in 1797. The second, Admat Yehudah, or Soil of Judah, came out at the same city in 1828. Cazes's notes on Tunisian Jewish writing are the only source named.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-consanguinity-a:
Consanguinity Among Jews treats how often Jews married near kin. Scattered among peoples of other faiths, Jews married relatives more often than the rest of the world, the entry opens. First-cousin marriage, and even uncle-niece marriage, stayed legal and common among them. Limits on priestly families narrowed Cohen choices further still.

Two studies anchor the numbers. Jacobs, using the same-surname method, reckoned English Jewish first-cousin marriages well above the rate for the peerage and for London at large. Stieda counted far more kin marriages among the Jews of Alsace-Lorraine than among Catholics or Protestants there. The entry sums it up plainly: the Jewish rate ran about three times the non-Jewish one. Such unions also seemed more fertile and less often sterile. Old claims blaming deaf-mutism on kin marriage are no longer credited.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cousseri-cousse: Cousseri, or Cousser, was a Jewish family of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. It lived in Riva di Trento and nearby towns of northern Italy. The tomb of Meshullam Cousseri, who died on July 20, 1541, marks Riva as the family's first home. His son Mordecai wrote letters kept in a Halberstamm manuscript. Scholars split on the name's source. Steinschneider derived it from Jekuthiel, while a Mayence record of 1470 points to German origin. The name Cuzzeri still exists in northern Italy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-curiel-jacob-kn: Jacob Curiel, known in public life as Alexander Nuñez da Costa, was the Portuguese court's resident at Hamburg. He died there in 1665. Earlier he had lived at Amsterdam. There he helped reunite the split Portuguese community in April, 1639. John IV. of Portugal spotted his gift for finance. About 1650 the king sent him to Hamburg as his agent. He also made Curiel a Noble of the Royal House. In 1655 Curiel served as warden of the Portuguese synagogue and gave it a reading desk.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dayyan-abraham-: Isaiah's son Abraham Dayyan was a Turkish rabbi who lived at Aleppo in the first half of the nineteenth century. He wrote four books, all printed at Leghorn. "Shir Ḥadash" (A New Song), an Arabic glossary on the Psalms, came out in 1841. "Zikron ha-Nefesh," ethical talks arranged in alphabetical order, followed in 1842. His two-part work of 1850 joined a similar book of talks with a volume of responsa. At its end he added a history of Aleppo from its conquest by David onward.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-diogo-justinian:
Diogo Justiniano Alvares da Annunciação was archbishop of Cranganor, born at Lisbon in 1654. He died at Evora on Oct. 28, 1713. A doctor of theology, he served on a special mission at Rome. King Pedro II named him archbishop of Cranganor, a Portuguese town in India, in 1692.

Diogo never took up his seat and resigned in 1695 to serve at Evora. He wrote sermons and the collection Trofeo Evangelico, printed at Lisbon from 1693 to 1713. His sermon at the Lisbon auto da fé of Sept. 6, 1705, stirred sharp debate. An anonymous Jewish reply, the Ante Exordio, appeared in 1709 and was later Englished by Moses Mocatta.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dreams-5311:
Dreams, in early ages, were taken as real messages, not as tricks of the mind. Peoples thought spirits or gods spoke in them. Since hidden things were known to gods, dreams counted as foretellings. Their strange speech needed skilled interpreters. So a whole art of dream reading arose.

The Bible, the entry stresses, lets God alone speak through dreams. Its dreams serve the whole race, not private fortune. Genesis gives the best-known cases. Talmudic teachers read dream images by wordplay and folk roots. One teacher gave two men opposite readings of the same olive-wreath dream. Medieval dream books, some drawn from Muslim sources, close the survey.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ebionites-from-:
The Ebionites were a sect of Jewish Christians of the second to fourth centuries. Their name comes from a Hebrew word for the poor. They held Jesus to be the Messiah. Yet they denied his divinity and his supernatural birth.

Ebionites kept all the Jewish rites, circumcision and the seventh-day Sabbath among them. They used a Hebrew or Aramaic gospel of Matthew. Paul's writings they rejected, calling him an apostate. Some of them did grant a supernatural birth to Jesus. Later writers invented a founder named Ebion, but the entry treats that figure as legend.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elath-or-in-the: Elath was a port of Idumea at the north end of the Aelanitic Gulf. Later ages knew the place as Aila. The entry says the Old Testament also calls it Elparan. Deuteronomy names Elath next to Eziongeber. In the days of Solomon the town passed into Israelite hands. Israel later lost it, and King Uzziah won it back. Under Ahaz it was lost once more. The entry ends with the source of the name. The town took its name, it says, from the many palm trees that grew near it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliezer-liezer-:
Eliezer ben Jacob is a name borne by two tannaim. The first lived in the first century. Of his life nothing is known at all. He had seen the Temple at Jerusalem in his youth. He knew the use of each of its many rooms. Later ages took his views as law for that reason.

The second Eliezer ben Jacob lived in the second century. He sat among the younger pupils of Akiba. He outlived the fall of Bethar and the bans that came after. With his peers he argued points of law in many tractates. The entry quotes his rule on dress from Deuteronomy. A woman must not bear arms or go to war, he held. It also gives his saying on good deeds. A good deed wins a man an advocate on high. A sin makes him an accuser of his own soul.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elyas-of-london: Elyas of London led the Jews of England for years. He held the post of presbyter from 1237 to 1257. He died in London in the year 1284. He spoke for London at a Jewish meeting at Worcester in 1240. King Henry the Third squeezed huge sums from him. The king took ten thousand pounds and a yearly fee on top. In 1253 Elyas led a plea to leave the land. Two years later he was jailed as a pledge for Jewish taxes. In 1257 the king cast him from his post.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ephrath-or-ephr: Ephrath, or Ephrathah, carries two senses in the entry, and the entry gives no more than those two. First, it names the wife of Caleb, son of Hezron, and the mother of Hur. The entry cites First Chronicles for that use. Second, it is another name for Bethlehem. Genesis, Ruth, Psalms, and Micah are cited for the place name. The form Ephratah appears once joined with Caleb, as Caleb-ephratah. That is the whole content of this short entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eusebius-5911:
Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea and father of Church history, was born about 270. The entry notes his zeal to convert the Jews and his sharp dislike of them. His Demonstratio Evangelica attacks Judaism head-on. It argues that Mosaic law was local only, never meant as a world religion. It then reads the Bible's messianic prophecies as fulfilled in Jesus. Only ten of its twenty books survive.

His Praeparatio Evangelica holds more value for Jewish readers, the entry says. Its last eight books treat Judaism and rank it above paganism. Books eight and nine preserve fragments of Jewish-Hellenic writers such as Philo and Josephus. Eusebius likely learned Hebrew from a Jewish teacher and used Jewish traditions in his Bible work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fano-hebr-6011:
Fano was a small town in the Papal States near Pesaro where Jewish bankers thrived early. In 1332 they already handled a large deal with the Malatesta rulers. Farm country around Fano lacked capital, so loans were in high demand. The bankers won the rulers' trust, wide privileges, and strong protection. At one point their taxes equaled half the town's whole take.

When heretics were expelled in 1367, the Jews were expressly spared. The Malatestas shielded them from a papal Jews' tax in 1447. Bankers counted as full citizens and paid no taxes. A badge came in 1464, but bankers were excused from wearing it. The city was excommunicated three times in forty years for treating its Jews too kindly, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fig-and-fig-tre:
Fig and fig tree share one Hebrew word, te'enah, in the Bible. The entry sorts out the names for figs at each stage. Early figs ripen in June and were held a great treat. Late or green figs may stay on the tree through winter. Figs were a chief fruit of Palestine before the Hebrews entered the land.

Dried figs were pressed into round cakes. People ate them as food and used them as a remedy for boils. Fig leaves are named as the dress of Adam and Eve. With the vine, the fig tree stood as a sign of peace and plenty. A failed fig crop, by contrast, was read as a curse from God.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fodor-armin-621: Armin Fodor was a Hungarian jurist born at Nagy Mihály on Jan. 27, 1862. The entry is short and gives his career in a few lines. He studied law at Budapest and was admitted to the bar in 1886. In 1890 he was made a district judge at Budapest. In 1895 the Ministry of Justice called him in as a legal expert. His chief works both deal with Hungarian civil court procedure. One is a handbook of that procedure, printed at Budapest in 1894-97.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frankfurter-mos:
Moses ben Simon Frankfurter was a judge and printer of Amsterdam, born in 1672. He died in 1762. His epitaph shows that in old age he took the name Aaron. In 1720 he set up a printing press at Amsterdam and issued some of his own works from it. His first book is a commentary on Isaac Aboab's Menorat ha-Ma'or, with a Judæo-German translation. It was printed in 1701.

Frankfurter went on to comment on the Mekilta and to gather prayers for the sick. He drew the moral teachings of his first author into seven chapters. Later glosses of his treat parts of the Shulḥan 'Aruk, printed in 1746 and 1749. He also edited a rabbinic Bible with many commentaries not found in other editions. It includes his own glosses to the Pentateuch, printed in 1724.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fuchs-isidor-64: Isidor Fuchs, an Austrian journalist born in Leipnik, near Biala in Galicia, on September 25, 1849, spent most of his life in Viennese news work. He wrote light essays and handled drama coverage. He began on Die Bombe, where his versions from Italian drew praise. He then joined several Vienna papers in turn. With partners he also wrote stage pieces, songs, and sharp topical verses on city life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gaon-plural-geo:
Gaon was the title of the heads of the two Babylonian academies, Sura and Pumbedita. The period of the Geonim is set from 589, when Hanan of Iskiya became gaon of Pumbedita. The last gaon of Sura died in 1034. The last of Pumbedita, Hai, died in 1038. Their span thus runs near 450 years.

The Geonim led the academies and taught there. Where the Amoraim built the Talmud and the Saboraim edited it, the Geonim read and applied it. They gave legal rulings in line with its teaching. The gaon also sat as supreme judge. In the two kallah months, Adar and Elul, students gathered for shared study before him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gordon-lord-geo:
Lord George Gordon was an English agitator who converted to Judaism. He was born in London on Dec. 26, 1751, and died in 1793. He was the son of the third Duke of Gordon. He served in the navy and entered Parliament in 1774. In 1778 he led a mob against repeal of Catholic relief laws. Riots followed, and he was sent to the Tower but acquitted.

He later asked London's chief rabbi for conversion and was refused. A Birmingham rabbi received him without the authorities' sanction. Some thought he hoped Jews would back his financial plans. After a libel conviction in 1787, he lived quietly in Birmingham as a Jew. Newgate prison held him from 1788. He kept kosher and wore phylacteries there. He died of fever in prison. Dickens later drew him in "Barnaby Rudge."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-grunwald-max-69:
Max Grunwald was a German rabbi and folklorist. He was born at Zabrze, Prussian Silesia, on Oct. 10, 1871. He studied at Breslau's university and its Jewish theological seminary. In 1895 he took the rabbinate of Hamburg's Neue Dammthor Synagogue. In 1903 he became rabbi of Vienna's Fifteenth District. In 1897 he founded a society for Jewish folk-lore and presided over it. From 1898 he edited its journal. He also helped found the Hamburg Jewish Museum.

His books treat Spinoza, Hebrew names, and Portuguese graves in Germany. He wrote on Jews as shipowners and sailors. He also covered Hamburg's German Jews up to 1811. A 1903 work took up the modern women's movement and Judaism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halafta-4211:
Ḥalafta was a scholar of the first and second centuries, of the second tannaitic generation, always cited with no father's name or byname. His line is traced back to Jonadab the Rechabite. He was an older fellow of Gamaliel II and Johanan b. Nuri, and he ran a rabbinic school at Sepphoris. There he brought in some reforms of rite.

Tradition says he saw, with Hananiah b. Teradion and Eleazar b. Mattai, the stones Joshua set in the Jordan. He lived to a great age: he passed to Gamaliel II an order heard from Gamaliel I in Judea's last free years. Few laws stand in his name. Most came down through his more famous son, R. Jose.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halperine-kamin:
Ely Halperine-Kaminsky was a Russian writer born at Vassilkof on April 9, 1858. He finished his studies at the University of Odessa, then went to Paris in 1880 and stayed there. French ministers of state and of commerce drew more than once on his grasp of French and Russian affairs and gave him key missions, which he carried out with success.

Since 1883 he has edited the "Franco-Russe," a Paris paper printed in both French and Russian. His chief fame is as a translator. He turned Pushkin, Gogol, Tolstoi, Turgenef, Dostojevski, Nekrassov, and others into French, and he writes for the leading journals of both lands. His own books include "Pushkin et Sa Correspondance" of 1887 and "Chez Tolstoi" of 1898-1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hanina-hinena-b: Hanina (Hinena) b. Ika (Yake), called Bar Beroka or Beri, was a scholar of the fourth century, a contemporary of Pappa and Zebia. His Babylonian birth shows in the halakot he reports from Judah b. Ezekiel, who never visited Palestine. The Gemara tells the end of his life: R. Pappa and R. Huna b. Joshua met him on the road and, not having seen him for at least thirty days, blessed God over him and thanked God for the sight of him. Hanina returned their compliments, and thereupon died.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hazak-jacob-rap: Jacob Raphael Hezekiah Hazak, born in 1689, was an Italian rabbi of the eighteenth century. He studied at Verona and at Padua, where Moses Hayyim Luzzatto was among his teachers. He followed Menahem Modena as rabbi of Padua. He fell into a number of disputes with the rabbis of Venice. His writings include answers to legal questions and notes on the four Turim. He also wrote a work on the Gemara and the later law codes. He died at Padua in 1782.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heinemann-heinr: Heinrich Heinemann, born in East Prussia on Sept. 15, 1842, was a German actor. After school in Berlin he went on stage, debuting at Breslau in 1864. He played in Konigsberg, Wurzburg, and Vienna, among other cities. Since 1878 he has been engaged at the Court Theater at Brunswick. He plays serious and comic character parts, such as Malvolio and the Miser. He also wrote plays, more than thirty of them. Several titles are listed, from farces to a piece on daily bread.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-herschel-sir-wi:
Sir William Herschel, born at Hanover on Nov. 15, 1738, was an English astronomer who first earned his living as a musician. He came to England in 1755 with the Hanoverian Guards band. He taught music and became an organist at Bath in 1760. In spare time he studied astronomy and made telescopes.

With a large instrument Herschel found Uranus on March 18, 1781, and became astronomer to the king. He reviewed the northern heavens three times and fixed 2,500 nebulæ. He identified 209 binary stars and studied Saturn and the Milky Way. His sister Caroline helped him and found eight comets herself. He died at Slough on Aug. 22, 1822.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hillquit-morris:
Morris Hillquit, born at Riga, Russia, on Aug. 1, 1870, was an American lawyer and socialist. Educated at Riga, he emigrated to the United States in 1887. He studied law and joined the New York bar in 1893. He had entered the Socialist Labor party in 1888.

Hillquit helped frame the Rochester convention platform in 1899-1900. He then aided the fusion of his party wing with Debs' Social Democratic party at Indianapolis in 1900. By 1903 he was New York's national committeeman in the Socialist party. He served as counsel for trade unions in labor disputes. His book on socialism in the United States appeared in 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hourwich-isaac-:
Isaac Aaronovich Hourwich was an American statistician born at Wilna, Russia, on April 27, 1860. He studied at Minsk and at the University of St. Petersburg. As a student he joined nihilist propaganda. He was arrested in 1879 and later banished to Siberia without trial.

After his release he took a law degree in 1887 and practiced law. Facing a second exile, he left Russia in 1890 for the United States. He earned a doctorate at Columbia in 1893 and lectured on statistics at Chicago. From 1900 he worked as a government statistician. His essays treat the persecution of the Jews and religious sects in Russia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-ben-samso: Isaac ben Samson ha-Kohen was a Bohemian Talmudist who died at Prague on May 30, 1624. He was assistant rabbi and magistrate of the community, and a son-in-law of Prague's chief rabbi, Lewa ben Bezaleel. His sons Hayyim and Naphtali became rabbis at Frankfort, Posen, and Lublin. Isaac liked writing acrostic introductions. His works include a German commentary on the Pentateuch, notes on Midrash Tehillim, and a commentary on Rashi to Genesis. He also spent time on a cabalistic work, "Sidre Bereshit."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-ben-hanan: Jacob ben Hananeel Sekili of Sicily was a Bible commentator and cabalist of the fourteenth century. His "Minhat ha-Bikkurim" survives in part in manuscript at the Bodleian. Its first part holds homilies on Genesis, Exodus, and Leviticus, preached on Sabbath afternoons. Each section is tied to verses from the Prophets, and cabalistic readings are frequent. Jacob knew Arabic and quotes Maimonides. He refers to his own larger Pentateuch commentary, and he also wrote on Palestine, its places, and the tombs of its great men.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-janina-or-yanya: Janina, also called Yanya, is a city in Albania, in European Turkey, set on the lake of Janina. Its Jewish community had flourished in the middle of the nineteenth century but was now shrinking. The entry counts about 1,000 families in a total population of 30,000. The town had two synagogues and two private prayer rooms. It also had a Talmud Torah, a school with 400 boys and 150 girls taught in Turkish, Greek, and Hebrew, and about ten aid societies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jeshurun-8611: Jeshurun is a poetic name for Israel that occurs four times in the Bible, in Deuteronomy and Isaiah. All commentators in the entry agree the term means Israel. Old versions mostly render it simply as Israel. The Greek version gives a word meaning the beloved one, and Jerome in one place did the same. In three other places Jerome used a word for the most upright, a reading that takes the name from a root meaning to be upright. Other teachers derive it from a root for behold.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ben-abra:
Joseph ben Abraham ha-Kohen, known in Arabic as Abu Ya'kub al-Basir, was a Karaite thinker who worked in Babylonia or Persia in the first half of the eleventh century. Though blind, he was called ha-Roeh, the seer, and he traveled widely, likely as a Karaite missionary. He studied with the Motazilite schools and defended their teaching in his books. He taught Joshua ben Judah.

His chief work, the Muhtawi, sets out Karaite belief in forty chapters. It covers the unity of God, atoms and accidents, creation, divine justice, free will, and reward and punishment. He argued against Christians, Dualists, Magians, and Epicureans. Other books by him deal with the commandments, festivals, inheritance, and purity. The entry credits him with a reform of the Karaite laws on forbidden marriages and calls him one of the great Karaite authorities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joshua-jesus-be: Joshua, or Jesus, ben Damnai was a high priest about the years 62 to 63. King Agrippa II set him in office after Anan, son of Anan, had been removed. Joshua too was soon removed by the king. His place went to Jesus b. Gamaliel. A bitter fight broke out between the fallen priest and the new one. They traded insults in the public streets and even threw stones at each other. In the end Jesus b. Gamaliel kept the office.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kadelburg-gusta: Gustav Kadelburg, a German actor and playwright, was born on Jan. 26, 1851. He first acted at Leipsic in 1869 and played at the Wallnertheater in Berlin two years later. He did well in comic roles but left the stage to write. The entry names his best known comedies and farces, some written with Blumenthal and Von Schönthan, among them "Grossstadtluft," "Der Herr Senator," and "Im Weissen Rössl."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kof-9411: Ḳof is the nineteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and the entry treats its sound, its use, and its number value. Its name has an uncertain meaning. In form it matches the Greek koppa and the English q. In sound it differs from Kaf because it is made with a glottal catch at the rear of the palate. The letter appears only as a root letter, never as a prefix or suffix. In later usage it stands for the number 100.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kremser-simon-9: Simon Kremser, a German army commissary born at Breslau on Sept. 15, 1775, died in 1851. He became commissary agent to Blücher in 1806 and held the Prussian war chest. Saving that chest at risk of his life won him a high order. After the Napoleonic wars he retired, married, and lost his fortune. In 1822 he gained leave to run omnibuses in Berlin, and the vehicles took his name. In 1827 he left for Russia as a commissary and gained the honorary rank of major there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-landau-wolf-961: Wolf Landau, a German rabbi and author born at Dresden on March 1, 1811, died there on Aug. 24, 1886. Talmud training came from his father and from Dresden and Bohemian teachers. Gymnasium study began in 1830 and Berlin university study in 1836. Back home he taught at the religious school. In 1854 he was chosen by all votes to follow Zacharias Frankel as chief rabbi of Dresden. Like Frankel he leaned to historic Judaism and held a middle line. His works include a funeral rites book dated 1875.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levi-david-9811:
David Levi, a Hebraist and author, was born in London in 1742 and died in 1801. His parents meant him for the rabbinate, but that plan was dropped. He was apprenticed to a shoemaker, then set up as a hatter. Losses drove him out of that trade too. All the while he kept up his Hebrew study, above all in the Prophets.

From 1783 to 1797 Levi issued a stream of books on Jewish faith, grammar, and ritual. He turned the prayers into English for London Jews. He also defended the faith in print against Priestley and Thomas Paine. His "Lingua Sacra" of 1785-87 is a Hebrew dictionary and grammar in three volumes. Late in life he worked as a printer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-bacrat-abr: Abraham Levy Bacrat was a rabbinical author of the start of the sixteenth century. He was expelled from Spain in 1492 and settled at Tunis. There, in 1507, he wrote "Sefer ha-Zikkaron," a supercommentary on Rashi. The work stayed in manuscript until 1845. It was then found in a Jewish library in Tunis and printed. The book has several prefaces. In one of them the author tells his own sufferings at the expulsion from Spain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lippe-chaim-dav: Chaim David Lippe was an Austrian publisher and bibliographer born on Dec. 22, 1823, at Stanislawow, Galicia, and he died at Vienna on Aug. 26, 1900. For a time he was cantor and religion teacher at Eperies, Hungary. He then moved to Vienna and ran a Jewish publishing house that issued several popular works. He edited a bibliographic lexicon of modern Jewish literature, first published at Vienna in 1881. A second edition came out in 1900, the year he died.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lopez-rosa-1011:
Lopez Rosa was a Portuguese Marano family of Lisbon that owned a printing shop there in 1647. Duarte Lopez Rosa, a physician born at Beja, was condemned by the Inquisition at Lisbon on Oct. 10, 1723, as a follower of Judaism.

Moses Duarte Lopez Rosa, also a physician and poet, settled at Amsterdam and openly professed Judaism in 1680. He wrote sonnets and longer poems for royal occasions. Simon Lopez Rosa led the oldest Spanish-Portuguese congregation at Amsterdam and died on Dec. 14, 1618. His liberal views split the congregation, and a new one was founded that year. Ruy Lopez Rosa, an astrologer, explained a passage in Daniel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lyon-robert-102:
Robert Lyon, an American journalist, is the subject of an entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in London on January 15, 1810, he tried business there first. In 1844 he emigrated to the United States. A manufacturing venture failed, and he turned to publishing. He died in New York City on March 10, 1858.

The article remembers him for one paper above all. On October 26, 1849, he launched The Asmonean, the first American Jewish weekly of its kind. He ran it until his death, while also editing the New York Mercantile Journal. Writers such as Isaac M. Wise contributed to the paper regularly. The Asmonean never won more than local fame, the entry admits. Still, the piece preserves the start of the American Jewish press and the editor who began it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-makai-emil-1031:
Emil Makai, a Hungarian poet, receives a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Mako on November 17, 1871, he was the son of Rabbi A. E. Fischer. He studied at the Rabbinical Seminary in Budapest. There he stood out early for his poetical talent. He died at Budapest on August 6, 1901.

The article praises his gift for carrying Hebrew poetry into Hungarian. He rendered medieval poets such as Gabirol, Ha-Levi, Moses ibn Ezra, and Al-Harizi. Immanuel of Rome also found a voice through him. His own works include Absalom, a biblical drama, and a collection drawn from the Hebrew poets in 1891. The Song of Songs followed in 1892, beside volumes of his own lyrics. The brief entry preserves a poet who died at twenty-nine, having spent his short life as a bridge between two literatures.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marhab-ibn-al-h:
Marhab ibn al-Harith, a Jewish warrior of Arabia, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was killed during Mohammed's invasion of Khaibar about 628. Of Himyarite descent, he won fame for bravery in defending one of Khaibar's forts. The sources picture a giant of a fighter.

The article lingers on his last combat. Marhab wore two cuirasses, a double turban and helmet, with a sword at each side and a three-pointed lance. Following Arab custom, he sent out a poem challenging any of Mohammed's heroes to single combat. One account gives the answering fight to Ali, Mohammed's cousin. Ibn Hisham instead names Mohammed ibn Maslamah, avenging his brother. In that telling the two men fought around a tree until its branches were cut away. Marhab dropped his sword, and his foe struck the fatal blow. The entry weighs both versions of a famous duel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mem-10611:
Mem is the thirteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Crawford Howell Toy and M. Seligsohn describe it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its name means "water." Its early shape is said to have looked like waves. Like some Hebrew letters, it has two forms, one for the start and middle of a word and a final form for the end. In post-Biblical reckoning its value is forty.

The second half of the article is grammar. As a labial, mem swaps with the other labials. This happens across the Semitic tongues. At times it swaps with the liquids too. In word building it works as a prefix. It marks place, time, instrument, or agent. It builds the participles of most Hebrew verb stems. It builds a large class of nouns too. One short paragraph carries the whole entry, cross-referred to the article on the alphabet.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meshullam-ben-i:
Meshullam ben Isaac, called in full Salem ben Joseph, was an Italian poet of the Hebrew printing houses. Richard Gottheil and Isaac Broydé enter him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at Mantua and Venice around the turn of the seventeenth century. Like his father before him, he worked as a corrector in the Hebrew presses of those cities. He graced the trade by supplying the books he corrected with laudatory poems of his own, printed at their heads.

Three liturgical poems of his are named. One is a kinah, an elegy on the great fire at Mantua in 1610, which dates his activity. One treats the Exodus from Egypt. One is a selihah built as a fourfold alphabetical acrostic. The entry rests on Steinschneider's catalogue and Zunz's history of the liturgical poets. It preserves a working poet of the press room rather than the academy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-modona-leonello:
Leonello Modona was an Italian Orientalist born at Cento in 1841. Isidore Singer and Vittore Castiglione give him a short Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He was educated at Florence's Istituto degli Studi Superiori. His working life joined two trades. He compiled library catalogues. He also wrote studies that range across classics, folklore, and Jewish letters.

His titles show the range. L'Uomo e la Natura treats man and nature. Another study covers the historical Sappho and the myth of Sappho and Phaon. A third reads the Christian legend of the fall of the angels against two British Museum tablets. For Jewish readers he wrote on Sara Copia Sullam, the Venetian poetess. He also wrote on an edition of the prayer-book. The entry rests on De Gubernatis's biographical dictionary alone.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moreno-morenu-1:
Moreno, or Morenu, began as a proper name, by Moses ibn Ḥabib's account. Spanish-Portuguese Jews adopted it as a family name, as the Jewish Encyclopedia records in 1906. It travels in company with Paz, Shalom, and Henriquez. Families of the name appear in the seventeenth century at Bayonne, London, Amsterdam, and Hamburg. Others still live in Turkey.

The entry's notices are brief lives. David Shalom Moreno of Bayonne was celebrated for wisdom and Talmudic learning. Gabriel Moreno belonged to Amsterdam's Academia de los Floridos. Jacob Isaac Morenu was an Amsterdam physician who died in 1667. His tombstone was carved with a count's coronet for arms. A surname entry doubles as a map of the western Sephardic diaspora.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-mesharshe:
Moses Kahana ben Jacob, called Mesharsheya, was gaon of Sura from 832 to 843. Wilhelm Bacher and Max Schloessinger wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He was the son of an earlier gaon, Jacob ha-Kohen ben Mordecai. Tradition also makes him a student of the Cabala who used amulets and charms.

His fame rests on two surviving responsa. One treats questions of inheritance and was drawn on by Alfasi and other later authorities. In the other he allowed a Torah scroll to be written on untanned skin when no tanner could prepare parchment. He was the only gaon to allow it, and many Babylonian communities acted on his ruling.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-muller-gabriel-:
Gabriel Müller was a dayyan, a rabbinical judge, at Mattersdorf in Hungary, born at Nadas in 1836. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He learned much of his Torah in his father Hayyim's yeshiva. In 1860 he was appointed dayyan of the community of Mattersdorf.

His books are working tools for rabbis. Birkat ha-Mizwot sets out the laws of the benedictions, and Shi'ure Mizwot treats the weights and measures of the Talmud. His Ozar Agadot gathers haggadic passages from the Talmud in four parts, issued over twenty-five years. A late work, Ma'gele Zedek, turns to ethical reflection.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naphtali-ben-da: Naphtali ben David was a German Hebrew author who lived at Amsterdam in the early eighteenth century. Solomon Schechter and A. S. Waldstein give him a short Jewish Encyclopedia notice. He came of the family of Moses Isserles, was a distinguished Talmudic scholar, and won great fame as a cabalist. His one book, Ben Dawid, printed in 1729, criticizes Lonzano's cabalistic Omer Man.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-necromancy-1141:
Necromancy is divination by aid of the dead. Joseph Jacobs and Ludwig Blau wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Persians, Greeks, and Romans all practiced the dark art. Israel may have borrowed it from Persia. The Bible bans it again and again in strong terms.

Three kinds of workers are named in the sources. The ob spoke as if from joints and arms. The yidde'oni used a bone held in his mouth. At Endor, Samuel rose as an old man in a mantle. Only the witch saw him; Saul heard just the voice. Saul had banned such workers, yet he sought one out. The art lived on into Talmudic times regardless.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-novogrudok-1161:
Novogrudok is a Russian town in the Minsk government. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews first appear there in a deed of 1484. King Casimir leased its customs to four Troki Jews. Royal tax farming shaped its early Jewish life.

In 1529 its Jews shared a special military tax. A royal edict of 1563 fixed their quarter. They were to settle below the castle there. Building on Podlyaskaya street was barred to them. Slow removal brought a fine of 1,600 ducats. Stephen Bathori renewed their charter in 1576. The Orientalist Albert Harkavy was born in Novogrudok. Of 13,656 souls in 1897, 8,137 were Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-onias-honi-ha-m:
Onias, called Honi the Circle-Drawer, was a teacher and wonder worker. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the first century before Christ. Some tales make him kin to Moses himself. He was an Essene, a man of strict faith.

Honi was held in high regard for his pure life. When he entered the school house, all grew clear. He gave plain replies to hard points of law. Yet no rule of his has come down to us. His fame rests on his wonders, the piece says. In a dry year, men begged him to pray for rain. He drew a circle and stood in its midst. Rain came at once at his word of prayer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ottinger-joseph:
Joseph Öttinger was an Austrian doctor from Tarnow, in Galicia. Isidore Singer and A. Beck wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born on May 7, in 1818. He died at Cracow on October 2, 1895. He read at the University of Cracow in youth.

Joseph took his first degree in the year 1843. He took a surgeon's degree in the year 1850. In 1851 he took charge of talks at the school. Those talks were on the past of cures and their law. The right to teach was kept from him for years. His love of Poland stood in the way, men said. In 1867 he won that right at long last. He was chief doctor at the Jewish hospital of Cracow.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-parhon-solomon-:
Solomon ben Abraham ibn Parhon was a Spanish word scholar. Crawford Howell Toy and Wilhelm Bacher wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the twelve hundreds in Spain. He was born at Kal'ah, a town in Aragon land. Two great Spanish scholars were among his teachers.

Those teachers were Judah ha-Levi and Abraham ibn Ezra. Solomon tells of talks held with Judah ha-Levi in person. He tells of their stays in North Africa in past days. One work of his has lived to our own time. That one work is his word book, or lexicon, in full. In it he stands as a true pupil of Ibn Ezra. He spread the Hebrew word lore of Spain to new lands. At Salerno he found folk who knew none of that lore.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pentateuch-1201:
The Pentateuch is the five books of Moses. Emil G. Hirsch and Joseph Jacobs wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its name is Greek for the five scrolls of the Law. In Hebrew its name means the five fifths of the Law.

The five books run from Genesis to Deuteronomy. Tradition gave their writing to Moses himself. Only the last eight verses, on his death, were excepted. Later readers spotted clashes inside the text. Ibn Ezra hinted at doubts in the Middle Ages. Spinoza later gave the work to Ezra instead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phillips-george:
George Lyon Phillips was a leading politician in Jamaica. He was born in 1811 and died at Kingston in 1886. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He ranked among the island's most trusted men.

Phillips held the chief magistracy of the privy council. He filled other high executive posts on the island too. His hour of trial came in the Saturnalia of Blood. That was a season of panic and harsh rule. His calm and gentle manner steadied the councils. The colony owed much of its safety to him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-plotke-julius-1: Julius Plotke was a Frankfort lawyer and communal trustee. Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Borek in 1857 and died in 1903. He practiced first at Bockenheim, then in Frankfort itself. He sat on the board of the Frankfort congregation. He served as trustee for several great relief bodies. His pamphlets described the Jews of Russia and Rumania.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-psalms-of-solom:
The Psalms of Solomon are songs that stand outside the Bible. Crawford Howell Toy wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The work is not in the Greek Bible of old. So it forms no part of the Apocrypha either. It comes down to us in Greek alone. Versions made from that Greek exist as well.

The work was most likely written in Hebrew first. It is a Palestinian work, and Hebrew was its natural tongue. Its Greek is rough and at times hard to grasp. Many dark spots come from Greek misuse of Hebrew words. That fact points back to a Hebrew source. The article weighs the songs' age, place, and faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabinovitz-samu:
Samuel Jacob Rabinovitz was a Russian rabbi and author, born in 1857. Herman Rosenthal and Benzion Eisenstadt wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Chelm in the Kovno government. In 1887 he became rabbi at Jevije. That same year he was called to Alexoty instead. His pen was as busy as his pulpit in those years.

Rabinovitz wrote many pieces for the paper Ha-Meliz. They were later made into a book at Warsaw. The book came out in 1900 on faith and nation. In 1897 he sat as a delegate at Basel. That was the first Zionist Congress of Theodor Herzl. In 1900 he became rabbi of Sopotkin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-revai-mor-12711:
Mór Révai was a Hungarian publisher and deputy born at Eperies in 1860. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied at the universities of Budapest and Leipzig. In 1880 he joined his father's publishing house.

The article says that firm was Révai Brothers, founded in 1869. Révai gave great service to popular education in Hungary. He edited a fiction magazine from 1880 to 1885. He helped issue a grand work on the Austro-Hungarian monarchy. He introduced book canvassing into Hungary, they say. His lexicon drive won twenty thousand subscribers. His hundred volume Jókai edition won a Paris grand prize. In 1901 the Szék district sent him to Parliament.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-romaner-benjami:
Benjamin Zeeb Wolf Romaner was a rabbi and preacher. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He worked in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. He served as darshan, or preacher, at Semigrod.

The article says he later preached at Dessau. In his old age he lived at Metz. His book is called Ir Binyamin. It treats the haggadot of both Talmudim in two parts. Part one appeared at Frankfort on the Oder in 1698. Part two appeared at Fürth in 1722. Four bibliographies support the short entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rothschild-mena:
Menahem Mendel Rothschild was a German rabbi born in Frankfort-on-the-Main about 1650. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was a grandson of Isaac, the Rothschild family's forebear.

Menahem preached for several years at Prague, in Bohemia. In 1686 he became chief rabbi of Bamberg, serving Bayreuth and Baiersdorf as well. He stayed at Bamberg until 1718, then moved briefly to Hesse. His last post was the old community of Worms, held until his death in 1731. Like many rabbis then, he was a man of considerable wealth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-jaco: Samuel ben Jacob of Troyes was a French Talmudist of the first half of the thirteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and A. Peiginsky wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was a descendant of Rashi. In his youth he addressed a circular letter, probably cabalistic in nature, to Asher ben David in Provence. Asher later alludes to it in his own cabalistic work on the thirteen attributes of God.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sarug-saruk-isr:
Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Israel Sarug. He was a cabalist of the sixteenth century, also called Ashkenazi. Sarug was a pupil of Isaac Luria, the great mystic of Safed. When Luria died, Sarug spread his master's system. He won followers for it in many parts of Italy.

His leading Italian disciple was Menahem Azariah da Fano. Sarug persuaded him to spend large sums buying Luria's manuscripts. Aaron Berechiah of Modena also joined his circle. Sarug lectured in Germany and in Amsterdam as well. Abraham de Herrera was among his Amsterdam pupils. His writings include a cabalistic essay printed in 1629. Another work teaches an ascetic way of life. He also commented on three of Luria's Sabbath hymns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schottlander-ju:
Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on a second Julius Schottländer. He was a German gynecologist, a doctor for women's diseases. Schottländer was born at St. Petersburg on April 12, 1860. He studied medicine at Munich and Heidelberg. He took his doctorate in 1887. He then assisted Kehr at Halberstadt and Martin at Berlin.

In 1893 Schottländer settled at Heidelberg as a physician. He became a privat-docent in gynecology at the university there. In 1897 he was appointed assistant professor. He has written several essays for the medical journals. His book Eierstocktuberculose, on tuberculosis of the ovary, appeared at Jena in 1896. The entry rests on Pagel's lexicon of physicians. The shared name with the Breslau merchant is a coincidence of the catalog.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-semiatitsch-ged:
Gedaliah Semiatitsch was a Lithuanian Talmudist who lived in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. In 1700 he joined a Hasidic party that sailed for Palestine under Judah Hasid. That journey became the subject of his best known book.

His work, printed at Berlin in 1716, tells the full story of the pilgrimage. It covers the party's adventures and the death of Judah Hasid. It also describes Jerusalem, its ruins, and holy burial places across the land. The entry preserves the memory of a traveler whose book outlived him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-she-heheyanu-13:
She-heheyanu is the blessing that thanks God for keeping Jews alive to reach a season. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Its words praise God who sustained us and brought us to this time. People first said it on meeting a loved one after long parting.

The blessing also fits good news and first uses of new things. A new house, garment, utensil, or book called for it. Trivial goods did not, unless the buyer was poor and glad. In modern use it marks first fruits of each season. It is also said after Kiddush on festival first nights. The entry traces a thank-you prayer from reunions to holidays.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-showbread-13611:
Showbread, better called presence-bread, was twelve cakes set before God in the sanctuary. Joseph Jacobs and Emil G. Hirsch wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the offering. Each cake held two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour. The cakes stood in two rows on a pure table.

There they stayed exposed to view for a full week. Each Sabbath fresh cakes replaced the old ones. Priests then ate the old bread in a holy place. Cups of frankincense rested on the rows of cakes. That incense served as a memorial offered on the altar. Kohathite priests had charge of baking and arranging the bread. Their method was kept as a family secret, later writers said. The entry explains a quiet weekly rite at the Temple's heart.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-ha-pakol: Simeon ha-Pakoli was a tanna of the second generation, a contemporary of Gamaliel the Second at Jabneh. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He arranged the eighteen benedictions of the daily prayer, the Shemoneh Esreh. He set them in the sequence handed down ever since. His name Pakoli likely came from his trade. Rashi explains that he dealt in flax and wool. Nothing further is known about his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-smolensk-13811:
Smolensk was the capital of the government of Smolensk in Russia. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Julius Gottlieb wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It stands on the Dnieper, 250 miles from Moscow. Jews lived there as early as 1489. A letter of that year names Jewish customs collectors there.

The city changed hands again and again over time. Russians, Poles, and Lithuanians held it in turn. Its Jewish people suffered greatly from those changes. In 1654 Russia annexed Smolensk for good. By 1899 Jews numbered 4,567 of 56,389 people. Their numbers had fallen since 1896 under residence laws. The town then had two synagogues and five hadarim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steindorff-geor:
Georg Steindorff was a German Egyptologist born at Dessau on November 12, 1861. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. Steindorff studied Oriental languages at Leipsic and Berlin. In 1893 he succeeded his teacher Georg Ebers as professor of Egyptology at Leipsic. He later embraced Christianity.

Steindorff served as associate editor of a leading journal on Egyptian language and antiquities. His books include a Coptic grammar first printed in 1894. He also wrote on burial finds from the Middle Kingdom in Berlin museums. Other works cover Egyptian art and the glory days of the pharaohs. He edited Baedeker's guide to Egypt as well. The entry maps the output of a busy scholar of ancient Egypt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sumptuary-laws-:
Sumptuary laws limit what people may spend on food and clothing. Wilhelm Bacher and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. The Mishnah records such limits from times of war. Hard times led sages to ban costly wedding customs. The rules aimed to cut display in dark days.

During Vespasian's war, grooms lost their crowns and wedding drums. Titus's war banned the crowns of brides as well. In the last war brides could not ride in curtained litters. Teachers debated crowns of salt, myrtle, or plain reeds. One bride's crown pictured a golden city wall. Modesty later brought the litter back into use. The entry shows law trimming luxury after national disaster. It ties private spending to public mourning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tally-14211:
A tally was a wooden stick that recorded a debt. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. Notches along its edge marked the sum due. The stick was then split lengthwise in two. Each half kept part of every notch.

The debtor took one half and the creditor the other. In medieval times this was the standard receipt. Jews and others used tallies for loans. Some survive at Westminster from before the Expulsion. When a debt was claimed, the halves were joined. Any mismatch in the notches exposed fraud at once. The exchequer's stored half settled disputes as decisive. Britain's exchequer used tallies for general receipts too. The entry explains a receipt that could not be forged easily.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-templer-bernhar:
Bernhard Templer was an Austrian theologian born at Brzesko, Galicia, in 1865. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Templer studied at the University and Bet ha-Midrash of Vienna. He also studied at the Berlin Hochschule for Jewish learning.

Templer began writing for Hebrew periodicals at age fifteen. Two years later he published a book on hard Talmudic passages. Other books treated Bible passages and medieval Jewish views of the soul. His 1895 work covered immortality, messianic belief, and the world to come. It drew on Jewish philosophers of the Middle Ages. The entry is short, but it maps a young scholar's early career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-titles-of-honor:
Titles of honor marked birth, rank, learning, and piety in Jewish life. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. In the Bible, adon, or lord, named a master of property. Guests of honor and benefactors received the word too. Abraham was called lord and mighty prince.

A people's leader bore the title melek, or king. Dukes, called aluf, ruled clans under a tribal head. The king's second was the mishneh. Joseph held that rank under Pharaoh in Egypt. Moses earned the titles man of God and servant of the Lord. Other prophets shared those same honors. First-born sons held the title bekor, with its rights. Priests and Levites carried titles by descent.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trier-herman-14:
Herman Trier was a Danish educator, writer, and politician of Copenhagen. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born in 1845, he studied law briefly at the university. In 1864 he turned to pedagogics, his life's field. In that field he won international fame.

From 1876 he published studies of cultural and historical figures. His first pedagogics book argued it was a true science. With P. Voss he ran a youth periodical from 1879. He also wrote on medieval Copenhagen's history. Voters sent him to the Danish Folkething in 1884. In 1898 he joined Copenhagen's board of aldermen. The entry catches a reformer mid-career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-visontai-soma-1:
Soma Visontai was a Hungarian lawyer and member of parliament. He was born at Gyöngyös on November 9, 1854. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He studied at Budapest and became an attorney in 1882. As a student he wrote papers on political economy.

Visontai won fame as a courtroom speaker in 1890. He defended a Serbian newspaper editor in a political murder trial. The defense succeeded, and grateful voters sent him to parliament. Since 1899 he has represented his native town. He is an expert on criminal law. He also helped draft large parts of Hungary's criminal code.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wiesbaden-14911:
Wiesbaden is a German town, capital of former Nassau. Gotthard Deutsch and Moritz Silberstein wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A local history claims Jews lived there in the thirteen hundreds. No documents support that early claim. No record shows persecution in Nassau either. Neither the Armleder riots nor the Black Death struck there.

A Judengasse, or Jews' street, proves their early presence. During the Thirty Years' War, Jewish families found shelter there. Clergy pressed for their removal afterward. Many citizens and officials protected them instead. Friendly feeling toward Jews grew in the town. One citizen in 1700 even adopted Jewish rites. The entry follows the community into modern times.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-woolf-sidney-15:
Sidney Woolf (1844-1892) was an English lawyer famed for cases on failed firms. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in London, he schooled at a private school and University College. He first worked with his brother in a law firm.

He then read law and joined the bar in 1873. He pled trade and crime cases at first. In time he led the bar in cases of failed firms. In 1890 he was made queen's counsel at last. His first law book treats bad food sold in shops. Later books treat pay for loss and firm wind-ups. He gave time to Jewish schools and synagogue work too. He sat on the board of the Anglo-Jewish Association.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhaki-abraham:
Abraham Yizhaki was a Turkish Talmud scholar at Salonica in the late 1500s. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served as a judge in that town's court. He served under Rabbi Solomon ha-Levi in that role.

His name stands third on a court writ of 1597. It stands second on a writ of the next year. He wrote a work with the name Ahot Ketannah. That work is quoted in two books of later men. It was bound at the end of a book by Jacob Hagiz. Some lists give that work to the wrong man by slip. The work has four parts on the laws of one writ. That writ is the bill that frees a wife who is a minor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zedekiah-ben-be:
Zedekiah ben Benjamin was an Italian Talmud man and hymn scribe. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at Rome in the thirteenth century of this era. He died at a date past the year 1280.

He was the elder cousin of Zedekiah ben Abraham Anaw. That man quotes him oft in his great rite book. He was a pupil of Meir ben Moses at Rome. He went to Germany to sit with a top tosafist there. That man was Abigdor ben Elijah ha-Kohen of that land. He kept in touch with that teacher in late years. One peer calls him a mate in a note of that book. Some hold he was a pupil of Abraham Abulafia as well. His own hymns of pardon live on in one draft set.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zweifel-paul-15:
Paul Zweifel was a German gynecologist who taught at Erlangen and then at Leipsic. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Höngg, near Zurich, on June 30, 1848, he took his medical degree at Zurich in 1871. That same year he won the right to lecture at Strasburg.

Erlangen made Zweifel professor of gynecology in 1876, and Leipsic called him in 1887. He held the title of Geheimer Medizinal-Rat, a senior medical honor. He wrote over one hundred papers for medical journals. His books include a textbook of operative obstetrics, often reprinted, and studies of digestion in newborns and of rickets, its causes and cure.
journal-of-discourses-vol-11:
Volume Eleven, from 1865, greets the Civil War's end from Utah's pulpits. Young reads the slaughter as the nation's chastisement, long foretold. The prophet who warned of judgment now watches it fulfilled.

Vindication brings no triumph in the sermons' sober, watching tone. Speakers turn the Saints toward building, gathering, and the years ahead. The republic counts its dead while the mountain kingdom endures intact. Old prophecies get reread in light of smoking battlefields back east. The discourses close one age of warning and open one of patient work. Grief for the nation mixes oddly with pride in Zion's peace.
justice-pg2911:
Justice is John Galsworthy's play, first produced at the Duke of York's Theatre on February 21, 1910. Its people include two solicitors named How, their managing clerk Cokeson, and junior clerk William Falder. A judge, advocates, a prison governor, chaplain, doctor, and warders fill the cast. Ruth Honeywill, a woman tied to Falder's fate, stands among them.

The acts move from the solicitors' office in July to the assizes in October. Act three enters a prison in December: the governor's office, a corridor, and a cell. Two years later the last act returns to the office in March. Galsworthy's design is plain: one small crime, then the slow machinery of law and prison working on a man.
keith-ancient-types-of-man-1911:
Arthur Keith, a Scots doctor and sage of man's rise, wrote this plain survey of fossil man in 1911. It was made for the lay reader, with clear plates and a brisk pace. Keith was then one of the best known names in the field in Britain.

He walks from the Neanderthal and Piltdown finds to the frames of Gibraltar and Java. His famed rebuild of the Gibraltar skull shows his hand at the craft of the time. The book taught a whole age the tale of fossil man as its chief men then told it.
king-john-pg1511:
This edition of Shakespeare's King John prints the full cast and scene plan. King John heads the English list, with Queen Elinor and Prince Henry. Young Arthur, Duke of Bretagne, stands as the rival claimant. Philip Faulconbridge, the Bastard, and Hubert de Burgh hold key parts.

France fields King Philip the Second, his son Lewis, and the Austrian duke. The contents move from Northampton to the French camp before Angiers. St. Edmundsbury, a battlefield, and Swinstead Abbey's orchard close the plan. Peter of Pomfret, a prophet, appears in the cast, true to the chronicles. The edition's apparatus shows the play's shape plainly: two kings, one boy's claim, and a bastard who holds England together.
lagrange-mecanique-analytique-1811:
Joseph-Louis Lagrange builds mechanics without a single diagram in Mecanique analytique, Volume One, in the 1811 edition. The whole of dynamics flows from one deep principle in his hands. Lagrange boasts in his preface that no figures will be found in the work, only algebra of the purest and most general kind.

Statics and dynamics gain a unity no earlier writer had reached. His methods still anchor how physicists treat motion and force today. The prose in French is calm, spare, and quietly proud throughout. Many call it the most elegant physics book ever written, a cathedral of reason raised on the work of Newton and his heirs.
lai-graelent-mason-1911:
Graelent is an anonymous Breton lai about a knight and his fairy mistress. Tales like it were told at medieval courts across France and Britain. Eugene Mason translated this one into English in 1911, alongside other lais of the same kind.

The fairy lady gives Graelent love and wealth, but she sets one hard rule. He must never speak of her to anyone. At court he breaks his word, and she vanishes. To win her back he must chase her through fountain and forest, past a white stag, in a pursuit that tests whether love can survive a broken promise.
lai-lespine-mason-1911:
L'Espine is an anonymous Breton lai, a short medieval tale of knights and fairy folk. No author is known for it. Eugene Mason translated the French text into English in 1911, when he gathered several of these old tales into one volume.

A young knight rides out to a thorn tree at night, drawn by a challenge and a strange summons. There he crosses into the land of the fairy king. Mortal rules stop working in that place, and wonder turns quickly to danger. The tale is brief and eerie, told in the spare way of the old Breton storytellers.
lawrence-white-peacock-1911:
D. H. Lawrence was a young schoolteacher in the Midlands when he wrote The White Peacock. His first novel, it was published in 1911 after years of drafting. Lawrence set it in the countryside around his home town of Eastwood in Nottinghamshire.

Two sisters, Lettie and Meg, move through courtships that go wrong in different ways. Around them, the gamekeeper Annable preaches a rough gospel of the body against polite society. Farming life, poaching, and the pit villages fill the background with rich detail. The novel is uneven and lush, but Lawrence's eye for nature and class tension is already fully alive.
life-on-the-mississippi-part-11:
Part Eleven opens with Chapter 51, called Reminiscences. Twain leaves for St. Louis aboard the City of Baton Rouge. He regrets talking with only two dozen steamboatmen, not a hundred. Social life in town had pleasantly swallowed his research time.

From the pilot-house bench he watches the boat straighten up. A cub takes the wheel as Captain Bixby steps in. The cub allows too much water between boat and ships. Twain feels nervous, remembering his own cub days exactly. Black smoke piled from the chimneys in the old-fashioned way. The cub presently closed up on the rank of steamships ahead.
london-south-sea-tales-1911:
Jack London cruised the South Pacific on his yacht Snark in 1907 and 1908, gathering material until illness forced him home. South Sea Tales, published in 1911, holds the fiction that came out of the Solomon Islands and Hawaii. It is his Pacific work at its most brutal and most humane.

The stories confront white traders, missionaries, and planters exploiting island peoples, and islanders answering in kind. One tale visits Molokai's leper colony, where London finds courage and dignity among the outcast sick. Another follows a pearl diver and a hurricane. London neither romanticizes the islands nor excuses the whites. The sea, the heat, and sudden violence rule these pages, told in his hardest prose.
mansfield-german-pension-1911:
