Katherine Mansfield published this first book in 1911, when she was twenty-two and newly arrived in London from New Zealand. The sketches grew from her stay at a Bavarian spa, taking the waters among German guests she observed with a cold eye.

She skewers the pension's residents: their appetites, vanities, sentimentality, and casual cruelties. The pieces are short, sharp, and funny, with dialogue that pricks like pins. Mansfield later thought the book crude and tried to suppress it. Even so, the voice is already unmistakable: the outsider girl watching, and missing nothing. Her great stories were five years away.
marie-de-france-bisclavret-mason-1911:
Bisclavret, the Were-Wolf, is Marie de France's great medieval werewolf tale in Mason's 1911 translation. A Breton nobleman vanishes three days each week without explanation. His wife presses him until he confesses his secret.

He turns wolf each week and must hide his clothes to return human. The wife betrays him to a lover, who steals the clothing. Trapped as a wolf, Bisclavret lives gently at the king's court. The king's hound and the wolf's own behavior reveal the truth at last. Treachery, loyalty, and the beast within drive the lai. Marie treats her werewolf with surprising sympathy throughout the tale.
marie-de-france-chaitivel-mason-1911:
Chaitivel, the Dolorous Knight, is Marie de France's lai of love's cost in Mason's translation. Four accomplished knights all love one lady in Brittany. She cannot choose among them and keeps all four hopeful.

A tournament turns festive rivalry into real disaster for the suitors. Three knights die, and the fourth is maimed for life. The survivor proposes the lai be named for his sorrow. The lady instead argues it should bear her own grief's name. Marie leaves readers to judge whose loss runs deeper here. The debate over the title becomes the poem's true subject. Mason's 1911 translation closes Marie's set with this thoughtful, melancholy piece.
marie-de-france-chevrefoil-mason-1911:
Marie de France wrote short verse tales called lais in the twelfth century, and Chevrefoil is her smallest one. Its subject is Tristan and Iseult, the famous doomed lovers of medieval romance. Eugene Mason turned the poem into English prose in 1911.

Banished from court, Tristan cuts a message for Iseult into a hazel branch left beside her road. The sign works like the honeysuckle wound round the hazel tree. Neither plant can live once the two are pulled apart. In just a few pages the tale says all it needs about love that cannot be parted, even by exile or death.
marie-de-france-deus-amanz-mason-1911:
Deus Amanz, the Two Lovers, is Marie de France's bleakest lai in Mason's 1911 translation. A king in Normandy sets a brutal condition for his daughter's marriage. Any suitor must carry her up a steep mountain without resting.

A young lover accepts the test and obtains a strength potion beforehand. Pride makes him refuse the drink when the climb grows hard. He reaches the top carrying her, then dies of the effort. The lady dies of grief beside him on the summit. Love's cruel arithmetic governs the short, sad tale. Mason's translation preserves Marie's restraint, which makes the ending hurt more.
marie-de-france-eliduc-mason-1911:
Eliduc is one of the lais of Marie de France, the twelfth-century poet who wrote short verse tales of love and magic. Eugene Mason translated it into English in 1911. Its knight hero is torn between his wife at home and a new love across the sea.

Eliduc's second love falls into a deathlike sleep, and grief seems certain to win. Then a weasel wakes its dead mate by laying a red flower on it. Eliduc uses the same flower, and the shock of grace that follows changes every life in the tale. All three end by taking holy orders.
marie-de-france-equitan-mason-1911:
Marie de France's Equitan, translated by Eugene Mason in 1911, is a lai of adultery punished. King Equitan of the Bretons falls in love with his seneschal's wife. The seneschal is his loyal right-hand man and closest companion.

The lovers plot to kill the husband in a boiling bath. Equitan himself is forced into the scalding water instead and dies. The wife follows him into the same bath in the tale's grim justice. Marie draws the moral that evil planned for others falls on the planner. Mason's translation keeps the sting of her irony. The short lai shows Marie at her most crisp and unforgiving.
marie-de-france-fresne-mason-1911:
Fresne, the Ash Tree, is among Marie de France's tenderest lais in Mason's 1911 translation. A lady slanders a neighbor for bearing twins, then bears twins herself. Fearing the same charge, she abandons one baby at an ash tree.

A porter finds the child, and nuns raise her behind convent walls. The girl, called Fresne for the ash, grows into a lord's beloved. Her twin sister's wedding finally reveals the truth of her birth. A brocade cloth and a ring serve as the recognition tokens. Hidden birth and love recognized close Marie's delicate tale. Mason's English keeps its gentle, forgiving tone throughout.
marie-de-france-guigemar-mason-1911:
Eugene Mason translated Marie de France's Guigemar into English in 1911. Marie wrote her lais, short Breton tales in verse, in the twelfth century. Guigemar stands first among the twelve lais she composed.

A hunting accident wounds the knight Guigemar in the thigh. A magical ship with no crew carries him to a foreign shore. There a lady, locked away by her jealous husband, heals and loves him. A knotted shirt and a belt serve as tokens of their fidelity. Separation and recognition close the tale in Marie's delicate manner. Mason's translation introduces the twelfth century's great woman poet to English readers gently.
marie-de-france-lanval-mason-1911:
Lanval is Marie de France's most Arthurian lai, in Eugene Mason's 1911 translation. Sir Lanval, a poor foreign knight, receives little favor at Arthur's court. A fairy mistress chooses him in secret and enriches him.

She forbids him ever to speak of her love to anyone. Queen Guinevere then propositions Lanval and, when refused, accuses him falsely. Forced to defend himself, he breaks his vow and names his mistress. The fairy lady rides into court and vindicates him before all. Love on trial frames the tale's bright, strange climax. Mason's version keeps Marie's sparkle in this favorite among her lais.
marie-de-france-laustic-mason-1911:
Laustic, the Nightingale, shows Marie de France in miniature in Mason's 1911 translation. Two knights live as neighbors, and one loves the other's wife. The lovers can only talk through adjoining windows at night.

They claim their meetings are for listening to the nightingale sing. The jealous husband traps and kills the bird in revenge. He hurls its small body at his wife, staining her dress with blood. She sends the dead nightingale to her lover as a final message. He keeps it cased in a jeweled vessel forever afterward. Love, spite, and a dead bird fill Marie's shortest perfect tale.
marie-de-france-milun-mason-1911:
Milun is Marie de France's lai of patience rewarded, in Mason's 1911 translation. The famous knight Milun loves a lady he cannot marry openly. Their son is sent away to be raised by his aunt.

For twenty years a swan carries secret letters between the lovers. The swan flies the messages hidden under its feathers, year after year. The grown son becomes a champion and unknowingly faces his father in combat. Recognition comes through Milun's ring before either man is harmed. Father, mother, and son finally unite after the long separation. The swan post never fails in Marie's most patient love story.
marie-de-france-yonec-mason-1911:
Yonec is a lai by Marie de France, the twelfth-century writer of short verse tales about love and the strange. Eugene Mason made this English version in 1911. Its heroine is a young wife locked in a tower by an old, jealous husband.

A knight reaches her window in the shape of a hawk, and the two become lovers in secret. The husband sets a trap, and the hawk-knight dies of his wounds. Their son, Yonec, grows up hearing the hidden story. When he learns the truth, he takes up his father's sword and settles the debt in blood.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-11: Bourrienne's eleventh volume bears etext number 3561 at Gutenberg. Its head note joins the title to the year 1812. December 2002 is listed as the release date for the file. Inside the sample, though, a reader finds the license text and nothing else. The secretary's own words do not begin within the portion held here. So this note names the volume and its file facts, and claims no more than that.
my-novel-volume-11:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton's eleventh book weighs hate as a force in civil life. Kind men call all wickedness a kind of madness, he notes. Yet clever rogues share much with the insane, he argues. Randal Leslie is his case: cunning, restless, and suspicious.

Randal thinks the whole world plots against his rise. His schemes grow wire-drawn to hide their own ugliness. Pride in his own wit blinds him to his shame. Lytton defends the portrait as true to refining minds gone wrong. The volume digs into ambition's dark engine, as the long tale moves toward its reckoning of hearts.
nansen-northern-mists-vol1-1911:
In Northern Mists, from 1911, Nansen turned historian of the Arctic quest itself. Volume One runs from the Greek sailor Pytheas to the Norse voyages. The great polar explorer traces how the North was slowly found, imagined, and mapped.

Nansen sifts sagas, maps, and travelers' tales, testing each claim of early discovery. Vinland, the Irish monks, and the Greenland settlements all get his keen, skeptical eye. He writes as a sailor who knows ice and fog from his own decks. The volume remains a classic survey of early northern exploration, learned and readable at once. Old maps are reprinted so readers can test his claims for themselves.
nansen-northern-mists-vol2-1911:
Volume Two of Nansen's In Northern Mists, also 1911, carries the history of Arctic discovery from the late Middle Ages toward Cabot. Nansen the explorer reads the old records like a man checking a chart. Myths slowly give way to coasts that can be sailed.

He treats Marco Polo's northern hints, the fabled islands on portolan maps, and the search for a sea road to Asia. The volume weighs what the Norse truly found against what later ages claimed for them. Nansen's verdicts are careful and sometimes sharp. The two volumes together survey a thousand years of northern dreaming and discovery.
nasa-tm-19680021153-research-achievement:
Instrumentation research for ground testing fills volume 11 of Marshall's Research Achievements Review, a 1968 memorandum, TM X-53743. Ground tests of rocket hardware are only as good as the instruments that measure them. Albert E. Schuler introduces the volume, which gathers new measurement tools built at the center in Huntsville, Alabama.

Alvin M. Payne describes gear for measuring the density of hydrogen slush, a partly frozen fuel, using radiation based densitometers. Harlan S. Harman then presents pressure sensors built for environmental extremes. His designs include a high temperature transducer with fast response. Together the pieces show how Marshall sharpened the measurements behind its test stands.
nasa-tm-19720010301-low-gravity-venting-:
Thomas L Labus, John C Aydelott, and Raymond F Lacovic of the Lewis Research Center reported these venting tests in February 1972, as NASA TM X-2479. They vented saturated Refrigerant 11 from a small cylindrical tank in low gravity. The Lewis five second zero gravity facility gave brief weightless runs. In orbit, liquid does not settle, so venting a tank can expel liquid instead of gas. Their tank was fifteen centimeters across.

The team studied three gravity levels, from full weightlessness to stronger pulls. The liquid clung to the tank walls with a near zero contact angle. Observers watched the liquid and vapor behavior during each venting run. The results guide the design of spacecraft tank vents. Refrigerant stood in for harder to handle propellants.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-11:
Volume eleven of Schaff's Nicene Fathers, first series, holds Chrysostom's homilies on the Acts of the Apostles and on the Epistle to the Romans. The volume dates from 1886. Chrysostom preached the Acts series near the end of his time in Constantinople.

The Acts homilies follow the apostles from Jerusalem outward, with Chrysostom marveling at their boldness and shaming his own softer age. The Romans homilies then work through Paul's hardest letter, untangling faith, law, and grace for lay hearers. His praise of Paul runs through both series like a refrain. The volume pairs the church's first story with its first theology, preached by its greatest preacher.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-11:
Volume eleven of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890, joins Sulpitius Severus, Vincent of Lerins, and John Cassian. The three are the voices of early western monasticism. Schaff and Wace edited the series.

Sulpitius wrote the life of Martin of Tours, the soldier-saint whose cloak, shared with a beggar, became legend. Vincent's Commonitory gives the famous rule for telling old faith from new error: what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all. Cassian's conferences then carry the wisdom of Egypt's desert monks to the West, on prayer, purity, and grace. The volume shaped how western monks lived and prayed for centuries.
nietzsche-twilight-idols-ludovici-1911:
Friedrich Nietzsche published Twilight of the Idols in 1889, a short summary of his mature thought. The English text here is Anthony M. Ludovici's translation of 1911. Nietzsche said he wrote it as a rest between larger works. Its subtitle calls it how to philosophize with a hammer.

Short sections strike at Socrates, German culture, morality, and metaphysics in turn. Famous maxims open the book, including what does not kill me makes me stronger. Nietzsche tests old idols by tapping them for hollow sounds. The style is fast, funny, and cutting. It is one of the best short entries into his thought.
onions-widdershins-1911:
Oliver Onions filled Widdershins, his set of tales from 1911, with ghosts that gnaw at the mind. Its most famed tale lures a painter to a flat where a fair voice calls. The flat holds him. Art, love, and dread blur till he can't break free.

Onions writes with care and a slow, sure hand. Fear grows from mood and small signs, not shocks. The set is a high mark of ghost tales from its age. Its lead tale is oft called the best house tale. Onions had a deft hand for folk who drift and dream. His ghosts prey on that drift, which makes the scares feel close and sad.
openalex-w1747388711:
Daniel Furtado Ferreira described this statistics software in 2011. His review appeared in a Brazilian agricultural science journal. Sisvar is a computer system for statistical analysis. It was first released in 1996, he reports. Work on it began in 1994 in Pascal language.

Three goals drove the project from the start. It served a statistics course at Lavras university first. It aimed to be a truly Brazilian free software tool. It also aimed to give researchers fast, trusted analysis. All initial goals were achieved, Ferreira reports. Users praise its accuracy, simplicity, and interactive design.
openalex-w1975654711:
Tom Wingfield, Carlton Evans, and co-authors ran this cohort study. It appeared in PLoS Medicine in the year 2014. Tuberculosis care is free in Peru, they note. Hidden costs still hit patients and their households hard. Such extreme costs are called catastrophic, yet poorly defined.

The team studied TB-affected households in Peru prospectively. They defined catastrophic costs and measured their weight. They compared that weight with drug-resistant disease. Both can drive adverse treatment outcomes for patients. Clear cost definitions help design support for poor households. The work links TB control to poverty protection.
openalex-w2059292511:
Avi Raveh, Phillip Delekta, Craig Dobry and colleagues searched sea microbes for antiviral compounds. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2013. Microbe products have yielded many medicines. Few had been tested against viruses. Marine bacteria offered a fresh place to look.

The team screened extracts from marine actinobacteria. A cell-based test flagged active extracts. Step-by-step separation isolated the active compound. It came from a new Streptomyces species off Papua New Guinea. The compound blocked many RNA viruses in cell tests. It worked by stalling a key energy pathway in cells. That stall starves viruses of building blocks. Related compounds showed similar antiviral effects. The work opens a route to broad antiviral drugs.
openalex-w2094457711:
Daniela Silva Canella, Renata Bertazzi Levy, Ana Paula Martins and colleagues linked ultra-processed foods with obesity in Brazil. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. Factory-made food and drink sales have risen worldwide. Obesity and chronic disease rose in parallel. The team tested the link with household data.

They used a national household budget survey. It covered nearly fifty-six thousand Brazilian homes. Homes were grouped into similar strata. Ultra-processed goods supplied very different energy shares across groups. Higher availability tracked with higher average body mass. It also tracked with more overweight and obesity. Plain processed foods showed no such link. The pattern held after adjusting for other factors.
openalex-w2127901511:
Jane Bryan, Phil Shearman, Gregory Asner, and colleagues published this study in PLoS ONE in 2013. They compared forest damage in the three parts of Borneo: the Malaysian states of Sabah and Sarawak, and the small nation of Brunei. Timber cutting and oil palm planting had changed these forests faster than field surveys could track.

Using satellite images since 1990, the team mapped forest cover and logging roads across the region. They found hundreds of thousands of kilometres of roads cut through the forest. By 2009, nearly four-fifths of Sabah and Sarawak had felt high-impact logging or clearing. Brunei looked very different, with over half its land still under unlogged forest.
openalex-w2159061711:
Oliver Brady, Michael Johansson, Carlos Guerra, and colleagues published this study in Parasites and Vectors in 2013. They modeled how temperature shapes the survival of adult Aedes mosquitoes, the biters that spread dengue. A female must live long enough for the virus to mature inside her, so survival sets transmission risk.

The team fitted models to hundreds of published lab survival experiments for both major species. Field survival data then adjusted the lab curves to real-world conditions. One species survived better in both settings, while the other tolerated a wider temperature range. Full tables split survival by age and temperature. The authors stress that local, site-specific survival estimates matter for judging outbreak risk.
openalex-w2624462411:
Julien Emile-Geay, Nicholas P. McKay, and Darrell S. Kaufman lead the PAGES2k Consortium behind this 2017 database paper in Scientific Data. It gathers temperature-sensitive records from natural archives across the globe. Trees, ice, sediments, corals, and cave deposits all record past climate in their growth. Together they let scientists rebuild temperatures across the Common Era, the last two thousand years.

The database holds six hundred ninety-two records from six hundred forty-eight locations. It covers every continent and the major ocean basins. Record lengths run from fifty to two thousand years, with a median near five hundred fifty years. Nearly half the series track modern surface temperatures closely enough to help validate them. Reconstructions built on this shared, quality-checked foundation can be reproduced by others. That helps place today's warming firmly against natural climate variability.
openalex-w2788363011:
The ATLAS Collaboration evaluated missing transverse momentum reconstruction in this 2018 paper in the European Physical Journal C. Missing momentum is the imbalance hinting that unseen particles, like neutrinos or dark matter candidates, escaped. Almost every ATLAS search depends on measuring it well. The study uses the full 2015 dataset at thirteen TeV.

Rebuilding it combines calibrated electrons, muons, photons, taus, and jets. Soft activity from leftover tracks joins the sum, with careful steps to avoid counting any signal twice. The authors test scale, resolution, and sensitivity to running conditions with several metrics. They also lay out how errors on the measurement are derived. Good performance here underpins the credibility of ATLAS's new-physics searches. This paper is the reference for how the 2015 measurement behaved.
openalex-w2900756811:
Clotilde Théry, Kenneth Whitaker Witwer, and Elena Aïkawa lead the International Society for Extracellular Vesicles' 2018 position statement, MISEV2018. Cells release tiny membrane bubbles called extracellular vesicles, now studied worldwide. Early studies used inconsistent methods and names, blocking comparison. The society's 2014 guidelines set minimum reporting standards. This paper updates them.

MISEV2018 tells researchers what studies of these vesicles must report. Hundreds of experts backed the consensus. Basic standards cover how vesicles are isolated, characterized, and described. Following them makes results repeatable across labs. The statement also updates terms and best practices since 2014. Fields drowning in hype need such ground rules to separate signal from noise. This document is the reference editors and reviewers now apply to vesicle research.
openalex-w3020256411:
Nancy Chow, José Muñoz, Lalitha Gade, and colleagues posted this preprint on bioRxiv in January 2020, before peer review. It traces the history and global spread of Candida auris, a drug-resistant yeast that has emerged in hospitals worldwide. The yeast spreads within health care settings and resists many antifungal drugs.

An early study had split the yeast into four regional groups, or clades. The team compared the genomes of three hundred four isolates from nineteen countries on six continents. The same four clades still dominate, though most now mix across regions. One South American clade kept the strongest geographic pattern. Two clades with opposite mating types even turned up in a single Kenyan facility.
openalex-w3091700111:
Ana Pedrosa, Letícia Bitencourt, Ana Fróes, and colleagues wrote this review in Frontiers in Psychology in 2020. It surveys the emotional, behavioral, and psychological impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. The illness began as a cluster of pneumonia cases in Hubei, China, in December 2019.

Within nine months, confirmed cases worldwide had passed twenty-six million. The authors searched the fast-growing literature through early September 2020, favoring case series, guidelines, pooled analyses, and forward-looking cohort studies. They reviewed and selected the work with a critical eye. The review gathers what was known about fear, grief, isolation, and strained behavior during the crisis. It offers clinicians and policymakers a map of the pandemic's mental toll.
openalex-w3119960611:
Ahmed Abdelfattah, Shiri Freilich, Rotem Bartuv, and colleagues published this global study in 2021. It asks whether all apples carry the same microbes, by analyzing the fruit microbiome of one variety, Royal Gala, at harvest. Apple is among the most eaten fruits on Earth and the largest fruit crop of temperate regions.

Theirs is the first worldwide study of its kind, sampling fruit across many countries. Both fungal and bacterial communities on and in the fruit differed strongly by place of harvest. Even tissue within the fruit mattered, with skin and core hosting unlike mixes. Fungal diversity shifted enough to suggest links with the rot diseases each country later sees. A small shared core of microbes appeared in fruit from everywhere.
openalex-w4410636511:
M. Abdul Karim, J. Aguilar, Steven Ahlen, and the DESI collaboration present results from the survey's second data release. Their paper appeared in Physical Review D in 2025. The universe's expansion is speeding up. Explaining that acceleration is a central problem in cosmology.

The team measures baryon acoustic oscillations in the new data. These are frozen sound-wave patterns from the early universe. Their spacing works as a standard ruler for cosmic distances. Tracking the ruler across time reconstructs the expansion history. The measurements then constrain models of dark energy and gravity. Sharper constraints can rule out whole families of explanations for cosmic acceleration.
openalex-w4411165211:
Shigenori Ueda and Ikutaro Hamada study the valence bands of 4f rare-earth elements. Their paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2025. It is part four of a series combining spectroscopy with theory. Rare-earths matter for strong permanent magnets and other technologies.

The authors use polarisation-dependent photoemission that probes deep below the surface. They compare the spectra with density functional theory calculations. Rare-earth 4f electrons stay tightly localised and create complex multiplet patterns. Matching measured and calculated bands tests whether theory captures those patterns. Better electronic maps of rare-earths support both basic physics and the design of magnetic materials.
openalex-w4415393411:
Ricard Ferrer and Toshiaki Iba review the molecular mechanisms of heatstroke. Their review appeared in the Juntendo Medical Journal in 2025. Heatstroke strikes when core body temperature passes forty degrees. Confusion, seizures, or coma follow, with inflammation and organ failure.

The authors trace the damage inside cells. Extreme heat unfolds proteins and triggers oxidative stress. Inflammatory signals spread through the body. Several programmed cell-death pathways switch on. Together these processes injure the liver, kidneys, brain, and blood system. Mapping the molecular cascade shows where treatment might interrupt it. That knowledge grows more urgent as heatwaves intensify worldwide and heatstroke cases climb.
openalex-w7155040111:
Ippei Osugi, of Juntendo University Nerima Hospital in Tokyo, led a 2026 study of difficult emergency transport. Cases where finding a hospital to accept a patient takes many attempts under the city's Tokyo Rule. The team reviewed records for nearly four thousand such patients transferred to their hospital between 2010 and 2022, splitting the group at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Death within thirty days was the outcome tracked. Before the pandemic, weekends and holidays, high blood pressure history, and certain diagnostic groups predicted death. During the pandemic period, weekends and holidays still mattered, joined by respiratory symptoms and respiratory disease history. The authors conclude that the risk profile of hard-to-place emergency patients changed with the pandemic.
openalex-w7204221811:
Thayla Carolina Rosato da Silva Assugeni led a Portuguese-language nursing study, published in Brazil in 2026, on care for women grieving after a spontaneous abortion. Miscarriage brings intense emotional suffering to the woman and her family, and the authors ground their work in Jean Watson's Theory of Human Caring. The study combined a review from 2016 to 2025 with a survey of primary care nurses in Tambaú, São Paulo state, using a semi-structured questionnaire.

Nurses recognized that a systematized care plan promotes humanized, safe, empathic, and complete care, yet reported obstacles: work overload, lack of time, and difficulty applying standard nursing taxonomies. Managing emotional suffering and grief stood out as a major problem. The team produced a dedicated care plan and an school folder for nurses.
openalex-w7204991111:
Antonio Rogerio Custodio dos Santos wrote a Portuguese-language paper, in Brazil in 2026, proposing an integrated cognitive artificial intelligence model for the Military Police of Paraná. Growing rule complexity in public management forces police organizations to balance legal security, office efficiency, and field readiness. The propositive study reviews national and global work on public control, digital change, AI, knowledge management, and strategic administration, and tests the model against one complex office process.

The proposed design has four layers: intelligent document cognition, normative intelligence, interoperable intelligence, and cognitive control of human capital. Its real novelty, Santos argues, is not automating procedures but reorganizing human capital, shifting low-value office work to intelligent systems so professionals can focus on judgment, leadership, and choices. The conceptual model can adapt across public bodies.
openalex-w7207615311:
Vanessa Pinho Palmezoni and five colleagues tell of a class test in a Brazil nurse course. Forty-three third-term students at a state school in the Triangulo Mineiro took part in early 2026. Three themed classes on the nursing process came first. Then the class played quiz games on phones and screens, built with help from smart tools and run on the Kahoot stage.

Staff saw the class join in more. Kids worked in teams more, and bit into the theme with more zest. The games showed gaps and weak spots as they ran, so staff could go back to hard points on the spot. The pair of game play and smart-built quizzes, the team holds, is a strong tool. It backs learning by doing, sharpens thought for the ward, and pulls students into the lesson.
openalex-w7213314311:
Mariana Mota Botelho leads a team that sums up a set of drugs for those whose body guard is weak or hushed. The drugs ape a gut sign that rules blood sugar and weight. The team read cohort counts, trials, and match reads on those with weak guards: folk with the HIV germ, and those whose own guard turns on them.

The drugs, they find, held their gains in these groups too. Death from all roots fell by more than half in one big group with both sugar ill and guard-turned flesh. Big heart harms fell by a third. In those with the HIV germ, a week's shot cut deep belly fat by a third, with no fresh grave harms. The team's close: the set is safe and of use in these frail groups.
openalex-w7213436711:
Marcos Fernandes Silva and colleagues study agroecology in a rural primary school in Caetité, Bahia. Their 2026 case study is set at a municipal school in the Maniaçu district. Interviews were held with two teachers and two pedagogical coordinators involved in the work.

Agroecological practices were still at an early stage, the team finds. Even so, they raised children's engagement and linked science knowledge with community know-how. Food, farming, and local territory became shared themes across subjects. Obstacles included money, training, planning, continuity, and collective participation. The authors see strong potential to strengthen rural education and bring school and community closer together.
openalex-w7213442611:
Plinyo Paccioly Rodrigues Santos examines election flags filling streets and squares in Ceará ahead of Brazil's 2026 elections. His single-author 2026 article questions the mass use of flags on roads, roundabouts, and avenues. It works qualitatively from legal and documentary sources across electoral, environmental, and urban law.

A flag that is lawful in itself can still harm the urban scene, the author argues. Dense repetition may damage mobility, access, road safety, and shared enjoyment of public space. The study reads the problem through proportionality and the informative purpose of campaign material. It proposes clearer rules on concentration, density, and placement that protect free campaigning.
openalex-w7213942111:
Masaharu Ishida leads a surgical team explaining how to combine the Frey procedure with removal of the pancreatic tail. Their 2026 how-to article appears in Surgery Today. The Frey operation treats chronic pancreatitis by coring the pancreatic head and draining the duct, yet late relapse can occur in the tail.

Key steps include tail removal, opening the main duct lengthwise, head coring, and a lengthwise joint to the bowel. Outcomes for nine combined-operation patients were compared with thirteen Frey-only patients treated from 2016 to 2024. Combined surgery took longer and lost more blood. Stay, deaths, pain return, and new diabetes were similar. The trade-off is defended for severe tail disease.
openalex-w7214119211:
Higor Henrique Sousa Ribeiro leads an integrative review on nursing care and adolescent pregnancy. Their 2026 review runs in six stages across three databases, using combined search terms on pregnancy, nursing, and primary care. Eleven studies from 2016 to 2025 met the inclusion criteria, from dozens first found.

Nursing in primary care plays a basic part in preventing early pregnancy and following pregnant teenagers, the results show. Education actions, sexual and reproductive health guidance, contraceptive counselling, and prenatal follow-up stand out as strategies. Nursing care promotes health, prevents pregnancy risks, and strengthens the bond between teenagers and health services, they conclude. Full, joined care for adolescent health is the wider claim.
openalex-w7218584311:
Érika Jamile Demoner, Acary de Moraes Neto, and Flavio Viganor Silva wrote a 2026 tax law article on the presumption known as presunção hominis. It is inference from known facts to unproven ones, used by Brazilian tax administrations. Structured tax fraud hides taxable events behind simulated legal deals, front companies, and fictitious firms, making direct proof hard. Their qualitative, deductive study reads doctrine, legislation, and administrative and judicial precedents on admissibility.

The presumption proves to be a relevant tool with legally valid probative force that does not violate constitutional principles and guarantees, the study shows. Its use is admissible and necessary against structured tax fraud, they conclude, provided it rests on serious, precise, and concordant indications and the taxpayer keeps a full possibility of counterproof. The article speaks to auditors and tax lawyers who must prove fraud designed to leave no direct trace.
original-short-stories-volume-11:
Madame Oreille's stinginess opens volume eleven of Maupassant's Original Short Stories. In The Umbrella she guards every centime on strict principles, doles her husband barely any pocket money, and sleeps badly after any necessary expense, though the couple are comfortably off and childless. A damaged umbrella becomes the battlefield of the marriage.

Thirteen tales make up the volume, among them Belhomme's Beast, The Diary of a Madman, The Accursed Bread, Suicides, and Simon's Papa. The contents tilt darker than some earlier volumes: madness, cursed food, despair, and children at the mercy of adults. Yet the comedy of the Oreilles' umbrella feud keeps Maupassant's balance of laughter and cruelty in view from the first page.
plaw-111-347-2011:
The James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-347, signed on January 2, 2011. It amends the Public Health Service Act to aid people harmed by the September 11, 2001, attack on New York City. Title I of the act builds a health program for them.

Title I adds a World Trade Center Health Program to the health act. Its parts cover expert and steering committees, outreach, and uniform data gathering. It names Clinical Centers of Excellence and Data Centers to run the care. A second part covers the finding of responders and their health checks and treatment.
plaw-111-348-2011:
Public Law 111-348 of 2011 bears the heading Shark and Fishery Conservation Act. It amends two fishery laws to improve the conservation of sharks. The laws are the High Seas Driftnet Fishing Moratorium Protection Act and the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act.

Title I is the Shark Conservation Act of 2010, built from those two amendments. Title II covers an international fisheries agreement and how it fits with other laws. Title III holds side items, among them small fixes to the law for the Western and Central Pacific fisheries and a part on the Pacific Whiting Act of 2006.
plaw-111-349-2011:
Public Law 111-349 of 2011 sets up a pilot program in certain federal district courts. Its aim is to grow skill in patent cases among district judges. It reaches cases under any act of Congress on patents or plant variety protection.

In each pilot court, judges who ask to hear such cases are named by the chief judge to take them. Cases are still handed out at random to all judges of the court. A judge who is not named may decline a patent case, and it is then reassigned at random to a named judge. Senior judges may also serve if an active judge is named.
plaw-111-350-2011:
Public Law 111-350 of 2011 enacts a further title of the United States Code. Title 41, called Public Contracts, gathers the general laws on government contracts into one title. Like other such acts, it is a restatement rather than a change of policy.

The act says the restatement must match the understood policy and intent of Congress in the laws it replaces. Corrections are allowed only to remove vagueness, clashes, and other flaws. Its later sections make matching changes to other laws, set cross-references, and repeal the old texts. It was approved on January 4, 2011.
plaw-111-351-2011:
The Predisaster Hazard Mitigation Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-351, signed on January 4, 2011. It amends the Stafford Disaster Relief Act to reauthorize the pre-disaster mitigation program of the Federal Emergency Management Agency. That program pays to cut risks before disasters strike.

Congress found the program a success that has cut deaths, injuries, and damage to property. A 2007 budget office report found it cut losses by roughly three dollars for each dollar spent. A 2005 study of FEMA hazard programs found about four dollars of benefit per dollar spent. Congress cited these savings as its reason to keep the program funded.
plaw-111-352-2011:
The GPRA Modernization Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-352, signed on January 4, 2011. GPRA is the Government Performance and Results Act, the law on how agencies plan and report their work. The act calls for reviews of program results four times a year.

Its contents cover strategic plans, performance plans, and performance reports. They set priority goals for the government as a whole and for each agency, with quarterly checks on progress. The act names a Chief Operating Officer in each agency. It also creates Performance Improvement Officers and a Performance Improvement Council to guide the work.
plaw-111-353-2011:
The FDA Food Safety Modernization Act is Public Law 111-353, signed on January 4, 2011. It amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act as to the safety of the food supply. It is a broad reworking of how the Food and Drug Administration guards food.

Title I aims to stop food safety problems before they start. Its parts cover checks of records, listing of food plants, and hazard review with risk-based preventive controls. It sets performance standards and produce safety standards. It also covers defense against the deliberate spoiling of food and the gathering of fees.
plaw-111-354-2011: Public Law 111-354 is the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center Clarification Act, signed on January 4, 2011. It amends a 1978 law, Public Law 95-232, on trust land for Indian pueblos in New Mexico. The act strikes one sentence from that law, which had said the land must not count as Indian country under title 18 of the code. It then adds a bar on gaming, as defined by the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, on land held in trust under that law.
plaw-111-355-2011: Sharon Center, Ohio's post office is the Emil Bolas Post Office under Public Law 111-355. The act was approved on January 4, 2011. It covers the Postal Service site at 1332 Sharon Copley Road. Under the act, references to the site in federal laws, maps, regulations, and records mean the Emil Bolas Post Office. H.R. 4602 passed the House in September 2010 and the Senate on December 16.
plaw-111-356-2011:
The Northern Border Counternarcotics Strategy Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-356, signed on January 4, 2011. It amends the Office of National Drug Control Policy Reauthorization Act of 2006. The missing piece it adds is a strategy for the northern border of the United States.

Within 180 days, and every two years after, the drug policy chief must write that strategy. The chief must consult federal drug agencies and state, local, tribal, and foreign officials. The strategy goes to a long list of congressional committees, among them the judiciary, armed services, and homeland security panels of both chambers.
plaw-111-357-2011:
The National Wildlife Refuge Volunteer Improvement Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-357, signed on January 4, 2011. It amends the Fish and Wildlife Act of 1956. Its subject is volunteer programs and community partnerships for national wildlife refuges.

The act reauthorizes two million dollars a year for fiscal years 2011 through 2014 for the Interior chief to run those programs. It renames one part of the 1998 volunteer act as a National Volunteer Coordination Program. It also makes small wording fixes to the name of the refuge system law in the older act. It was signed on January 4, 2011.
plaw-111-358-2011:
The America COMPETES Reauthorization Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-358, signed on January 4, 2011. COMPETES stands for Creating Opportunities to Meaningfully Promote Excellence in Technology, Education, and Science. The act invests in new ideas through research and aims to sharpen United States competitiveness.

Title I covers the Office of Science and Technology Policy, with parts on joint federal work in STEM schooling and advanced manufacturing research. It also covers public access to research and prize contests for new ideas. Title II turns to NASA and its role in new ideas, schooling, and the space station.
plaw-111-359-2011: Public Law 111-359, approved January 4, 2011, names a post office building in Carlstadt, New Jersey. The Postal Service site at 331 1st Street is now the Staff Sergeant Frank T. Carvill and Lance Corporal Michael A. Schwarz Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name. The bill passed the House in June 2010 and the Senate on December 16.
plaw-111-360-2011: Public Law 111-360, signed on January 4, 2011, carves one product type out of an energy rule. The rule sets no-load efficiency standards for Class A external power supplies under the Energy Policy and Conservation Act. Under this act, those standards do not reach power supplies for certain security and life safety alarm and watch systems. Such a system is gear sold to watch for, record, or report intrusion or threats to life safety, or to control entry to property, working at all times.
plaw-111-361-2011: Public Law 111-361 named the Uniontown, Pennsylvania, post office for George C. Marshall. The act was approved January 4, 2011. It covers the Postal Service site at 47 East Fayette Street, now the George C. Marshall Post Office. That name governs references in federal laws, maps, regulations, and records. The bill, H.R. 5605, passed the House in September 2010 and the Senate on December 16.
plaw-111-362-2011: In Indiana, Pennsylvania, the post office building at 47 South 7th Street bears the name of James M. 'Jimmy' Stewart. Public Law 111-362 set the name, with approval on January 4, 2011. The full name is the James M. 'Jimmy' Stewart Post Office Building. Federal laws, maps, regulations, and records must use it for that building. H.R. 5606 passed the House in September 2010 and the Senate on December 16.
plaw-111-363-2011: Public Law 111-363, approved January 4, 2011, names a post office in Miami, Florida. The Little River Branch site at 140 NE 84th Street is now the Jesse J. McCrary, Jr. Post Office. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name from then on. The bill passed the House in November 2010 and the Senate on December 16.
plaw-111-364-2011:
The Diesel Emissions Reduction Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-364, signed on January 4, 2011. It amends the Energy Policy Act of 2005 to renew and reshape the diesel emissions reduction program. That program funds work to cut pollution from diesel engines.

Section 2 of the act rewrites parts of the program's definitions in section 791 of the 2005 act. One change widens who may qualify as an eligible party to include private owners of diesel vehicles or fleets. Their vehicles must run under a contract, license, or lease with a federal body, with notice to that body.
plaw-111-366-2011: Public Law 111-366, signed on January 4, 2011, amends the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to let the United States Tax Court appoint its own employees. The court may name a clerk and other needed staff outside the title 5 rules for competitive service hiring. Judges and special trial judges may also appoint their own staff in numbers the court approves. Law clerks named this way sit outside the federal leave rules, though leave already earned stays to their credit. The court sets pay for its staff outside the normal grading system.
plaw-111-367-2011: Public Law 111-367, approved January 4, 2011, names a post office building in Centreville, Virginia. The Postal Service site at 5003 Westfields Boulevard is now the Colonel George Juskalian Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name from then on. The bill passed the House in November 2010 and the Senate on December 16 of that year.
plaw-111-368-2011: Public Law 111-368, approved January 4, 2011, names a post office in St. Louis, Missouri. The Postal Service site at 111 North 6th Street is now the Earl Wilson, Jr. Post Office. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name from then on. The bill passed the House on December 7, 2010, and the Senate on December 16.
plaw-111-369-2011: The Access to Criminal History Records for State Sentencing Commissions Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-369. Its whole text is one inserted phrase in title 28 of the code. In the part on sharing criminal records with the states, it adds the words including State sentencing commissions. The Attorney General must thus share such records with those state bodies. The act was signed on January 4, 2011.
plaw-111-370-2011: Public Law 111-370, signed on January 4, 2011, orders the head of the General Services Administration to convey a parcel of land in Houston, Texas, to the Military Museum of Texas. The parcel holds 3.673 acres at 8611 Wallisville Road in Harris County, in Lot 3 of the Moers Subdivision. The museum must pay market value, set by an outside appraisal based on the land's current use, which the museum also pays for. The sale covers the buildings and fixtures on the land as well.
plaw-111-371-2011:
The Local Community Radio Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-371, signed on January 4, 2011. It carries out the advice of a Federal Communications Commission report on low-power FM radio service. Such stations are small, local broadcasters.

The act orders the Commission to rewrite its low-power FM rules to guard co-channels and the first and second channels next to a station's own. No one who has run an unlicensed station may get a low-power license. The act also ends the minimum distance rules tied to the third channel out, between low-power and full-power FM stations.
plaw-111-372-2011:
Public Law 111-372 is the Section 202 Supportive Housing for the Elderly Act of 2010. It amends section 202 of the Housing Act of 1959 to improve the program for supportive housing for older people. Section 202 is the main federal program of its kind.

Title I reforms new building under the program, with rules on how projects are picked, cost limits, owner deposits, and the definition of a private nonprofit group. Title II covers refinancing of older projects, among it the use of leftover funds. Title III turns to grants that turn elderly housing into assisted living facilities.
plaw-111-373-2011:
The Pedestrian Safety Enhancement Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-373, signed on January 4, 2011. It directs the Transportation chief to study and set a safety standard for motor vehicles. The standard must give a way to alert blind and other walkers that a vehicle is near.

The act defines an alert sound as a sound a vehicle makes so walkers can tell its presence, direction, place, and motion. It also defines cross-over speed, the speed at which tire and wind noise make a set sound needless. The concern behind the act is the quiet running of electric and hybrid cars at low speed.
plaw-111-374-2011:
The Frank Melville Supportive Housing Investment Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-374, signed on January 4, 2011. It amends section 811 of the Cranston-Gonzalez National Affordable Housing Act. That section funds supportive housing for persons with disabilities.

Section 2 of the act concerns tenant-based rental assistance under the program. Such aid is now given through section 8 of the United States Housing Act of 1937. Money is authorized to convert existing disability vouchers to that system, in an amount at least enough to cover the vouchers in force when the act passed. The act was signed on January 4, 2011.
plaw-111-375-2011:
The National Alzheimer's Project Act is Public Law 111-375, signed on January 4, 2011. It sets up the National Alzheimer's Project inside the office of the Health and Human Services chief. In the act, Alzheimer's means Alzheimer's disease and related dementias.

The Project must build and keep up one national plan to overcome Alzheimer's. It must link research and services across all federal agencies and speed work on treatments that could prevent, halt, or reverse the disease. It also aims at earlier diagnosis, better care, and care for groups at higher risk or least likely to get help.
plaw-111-376-2011:
The Anti-Border Corruption Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-376, signed on January 4, 2011. It orders Customs and Border Protection to give polygraph tests to all applicants for law enforcement posts. It also orders the agency to start all periodic background re-checks of set law staff.

Congress found that since 2003, 129 agency officials had been arrested on corruption charges, with 576 probes opened in 2009 alone. Agency policy already called for polygraphs for such applicants, yet under 15 percent got one in 2009. A backlog of about 10,000 background re-checks was set to grow to about 19,000 by the end of fiscal year 2010.
plaw-111-377-2011:
The Post-9/11 Veterans Educational Assistance Improvements Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-377, signed on January 4, 2011. It amends title 38 of the code to improve schooling aid for veterans who served after September 11, 2001. That aid is the Post-9/11 GI Bill.

Title I lists the fixes. They cover who qualifies, aid amounts for degree programs at public, private, and foreign schools, and aid for study while on active duty. They cover half-time study, non-degree programs, the monthly housing stipend, and tests for licenses. They also cover the transfer of unused benefits to family members.
plaw-111-378-2011:
Public Law 111-378, signed on January 4, 2011, amends the Federal Water Pollution Control Act. It clarifies the federal duty to pay for stormwater pollution control. The change is made to section 313 of that act, on federal facilities and water rules.

The act states that reasonable service charges include any fair fee set by a property's share of stormwater runoff or pollution. Such fees may fund the full costs of a stormwater program, from gathering runoff to cutting pollutants and flow. The name given to the fee, even if called a tax, does not change that result. One limit bars paying such fees from permanent Treasury accounts.
plaw-111-379-2011: Public Law 111-379, approved January 4, 2011, names a post office building in Tyrone, Georgia. The Postal Service site at 100 Commerce Drive is now the First Lieutenant Robert Wilson Collins Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name from then on. The bill passed the Senate on December 16, 2010, and the House days later.
plaw-111-380-2011:
The Reduction of Lead in Drinking Water Act is Public Law 111-380, signed on January 4, 2011. It amends the Safe Drinking Water Act to cut the lead in pipes and plumbing. The core change is a stricter meaning of the term lead free.

Lead free now means no more than 0.2 percent lead in solder and flux. For the wet surfaces of pipes and fittings, it means a weighted average of no more than 0.25 percent lead, worked out by a set formula. The act exempts pipes used only for non-drinking uses, such as factory work and irrigation, plus items like toilets and large gate valves.
plaw-111-381-2011: Public Law 111-381, signed on January 4, 2011, grants one more tribe long lease power over its trust land. It amends the Act of August 9, 1955, with a single inserted phrase. The phrase adds lands held in trust for Ohkay Owingeh Pueblo to the list of lands that may be leased for up to 99 years. The bill passed the Senate on December 21, 2010, and the House the next day.
plaw-111-382-2011:
Public Law 111-382, signed on January 4, 2011, clarifies the power of the National Credit Union Administration to spend from its stabilization fund without borrowing from the Treasury. The fund backs insured credit unions in hard times. The act amends section 217 of the Federal Credit Union Act.

One change adds the words and any additional advances to the fund's borrowing terms. The main change rewrites the assessment power of the agency's Board. The Board may charge each insured credit union a special premium to cover fund spending, due within 60 days. In setting the charge, it must weigh the effect on credit union earnings.
plaw-111-383-2011:
The Ike Skelton National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2011 is Public Law 111-383. It authorizes appropriations for fiscal year 2011 for military work of the Department of Defense and for defense work of the Department of Energy. It also sets the personnel strengths of the armed forces for that year.

The act is split into three divisions. Division A holds the Department of Defense authorizations, Division B military construction, and Division C energy national security and other authorizations. Title I of Division A covers procurement, starting with the Army and the Navy and Marine Corps.
plaw-112-1-2011: Public Law 112-1 is the first public law of the 112th Congress, approved on January 31, 2011. It gives small business programs another temporary extension. The act amends the 2006 law that kept certain Small Business Administration powers in force for a set time, striking January 31, 2011 and inserting May 31, 2011. The swap covers programs under the Small Business Act and the Small Business Investment Act of 1958, and it takes effect on January 30, 2011.
plaw-112-10-2011:
Public Law 112-10 is the Department of Defense and Full-Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2011, approved on April 15, 2011. It funds the Defense Department and the rest of the government for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2011, well after that year had begun.

Division A holds the Defense Department spending for 2011. Title I begins with military personnel, paying for Army pay, allowances, clothing, food, and travel. Division B carries full-year continuing appropriations for the other departments and agencies. Division C is separate subject matter: the Scholarships for Opportunity and Results Act. It stands apart from the spending titles around it.
plaw-112-11-2011: Public Law 112-11, approved on April 25, 2011, names a federal building and courthouse in Martinsburg, West Virginia. The building at 217 West King Street is to be known as the W. Craig Broadwater Federal Building and United States Courthouse. Section 2 adds the references rule: any mention of that building in a federal law, map, rule, or record counts as a mention of the Broadwater name.
plaw-112-12-2011: Public Law 112-12 is a joint resolution of the 112th Congress, approved on April 25, 2011. Acting under section 5581 of the Revised Statutes, it appoints Stephen M. Case of Virginia as a citizen regent of the Board of Regents of the Smithsonian Institution. Case fills the vacancy left by the resignation of Phillip Frost of Florida, in the class of regents who are not members of Congress. The appointment runs for a term of six years, effective on the date of enactment.
plaw-112-13-2011: Public Law 112-13, approved on May 12, 2011, gives the Ronald Reagan Centennial Commission more time to finish its work. It amends the commission's act in two places. The due date for the commission's final report moves from April 30, 2011 to November 30, 2011. The commission's termination date moves from May 30, 2011 to December 31, 2011. Both changes are plain date swaps, with no other terms altered in the text shown.
plaw-112-14-2011: Public Law 112-14 is the PATRIOT Sunsets Extension Act of 2011, approved on May 26, 2011. It extends two sunset dates in federal surveillance law. In the USA PATRIOT Improvement and Reauthorization Act of 2005, the cutoff of May 27, 2011 becomes June 1, 2015. The same swap is made in the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004. The act's stated purpose line speaks of small business programs, but the operative text shown does only this: it keeps those expiring powers alive for four more years.
plaw-112-15-2011: Public Law 112-15, approved on May 31, 2011, names a post office in Inverness, California for a specialist. The Postal Service facility at 12781 Sir Francis Drake Boulevard is to be known as the Specialist Jake Robert Velloza Post Office. The references clause adds that any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, rule, or record counts as a mention of the Specialist Jake Robert Velloza Post Office.
plaw-112-16-2011: Public Law 112-16 is the Airport and Airway Extension Act of 2011, Part II, approved on May 31, 2011. For one month only, it extends the taxes that fund the Airport and Airway Trust Fund. The fuel tax and ticket tax dates move from May 31, 2011 to June 30, 2011. The trust fund's spending authority moves from June 1, 2011 to July 1, 2011. The changes take effect on June 1, 2011, and the act's purposes also include extending the airport improvement program.
plaw-112-17-2011: The Small Business Additional Temporary Extension Act of 2011 is Public Law 112-17, approved on June 1, 2011. It extends programs under the Small Business Act and the Small Business Investment Act of 1958 once more. The end date moves from May 31, 2011 to July 31, 2011, effective May 30. Section 3 also extends the end dates of two research programs. They are the Small Business Innovation Research program and the Small Business Technology Transfer program. In the sample, the change swaps 2008 for 2011 in the termination rule.
plaw-112-18-2011:
The Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2011 is Public Law 112-18, approved on June 8, 2011. It authorizes spending for the intelligence work of the United States Government, for the Community Management Account, and for the Central Intelligence Agency Retirement and Disability System.

Title I covers budget and personnel authorizations, including a classified schedule of authorizations, so the largest sums stay off the public page. Title II funds the CIA retirement system. Title III handles general intelligence community matters, such as limits on intelligence acts, staff pay rises allowed by law, details of outside personnel, and officer training. Title IV turns to parts of the community, starting with the Director of National Intelligence's office.
plaw-112-19-2011: Public Law 112-19 is a joint resolution, approved on June 24, 2011, that keeps a Smithsonian regent in place. Acting under section 5581 of the Revised Statutes, Congress fills the vacancy on the Board of Regents of the Smithsonian Institution left by the end of Shirley Ann Jackson's term. The resolution reappoints Jackson, of New York, as a citizen regent for six more years. Her new term runs from May 6, 2011, in the class of regents who are not members of Congress.
plaw-112-2-2011: Public Law 112-2, approved on February 17, 2011, names a courthouse then under construction in Yuma, Arizona. The building at 98 West First Street is to be known as the John M. Roll United States Courthouse. The references clause says any mention of that courthouse in a federal law, map, rule, or record counts as a mention of the John M. Roll United States Courthouse.
plaw-112-20-2011: Robert P. Kogod stays on the Smithsonian's board under Public Law 112-20, a joint resolution approved on June 24, 2011. The vacancy on the Board of Regents of the Smithsonian Institution arose when Kogod's term expired. Congress, acting under section 5581 of the Revised Statutes, fills it by reappointing the incumbent, of the District of Columbia, as a citizen regent. The new term is six years, effective May 6, 2011.
plaw-112-21-2011: Public Law 112-21 is the Airport and Airway Extension Act of 2011, Part III, approved on June 29, 2011. Like Part II before it, the act buys weeks, not years. The fuel taxes and ticket taxes that fund the Airport and Airway Trust Fund now run to July 22, 2011 instead of June 30, 2011. The trust fund's authority to spend moves from July 1, 2011 to July 23, 2011, with a matching change in a related clause. The tax changes take effect on July 1, 2011.
plaw-112-22-2011: Public Law 112-22, approved on June 29, 2011, names a post office in Rootstown, Ohio for a Marine sergeant. The Postal Service facility at 4865 Tallmadge Road is to be known as the Marine Sgt. Jeremy E. Murray Post Office. Under the references clause, any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, rule, or record counts as a mention of the Marine Sgt. Jeremy E. Murray Post Office.
plaw-112-23-2011: Public Law 112-23, approved on June 29, 2011, names a post office in Cary, Mississippi. The Postal Service facility at 95 Dogwood Street is to be known as the Spencer Byrd Powers, Jr. Post Office. The references clause says any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, rule, or record counts as a mention of the Spencer Byrd Powers, Jr. Post Office.
plaw-112-24-2011:
Public Law 112-24, approved on July 26, 2011, extends the term of the sitting Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Robert S. Mueller III. Congress finds that the President asked for a two-year extension on May 12, 2011, citing the need for continuity at the Bureau amid ongoing threats and leadership changes at security agencies.

The act creates a new term of service for the office, running from on or after August 3, 2011 until September 4, 2013. The sitting director may be appointed to that term, and only that term, with the advice and consent of the Senate. Congress stresses that this is a one-time exception to the ten-year term limit, made after the killing of Osama bin Laden, and is not a precedent.
plaw-112-25-2011:
The Budget Control Act of 2011 is Public Law 112-25, approved on August 2, 2011. Congress passed it to impose budget control on the federal government, and its table of contents maps a broad bargain.

Title I sets ten-year discretionary spending caps with a sequester, meaning automatic cuts if the limits are breached, plus Senate budget enforcement rules. Title II calls for a vote on a balanced budget amendment to the Constitution. Title III sets a debt ceiling disapproval process, a way for Congress to object to raising the debt limit. Title IV creates a Joint Select Committee on Deficit Reduction, with fast-track handling for its proposals.
plaw-112-26-2011:
The Restoring GI Bill Fairness Act of 2011 is Public Law 112-26, approved on August 3, 2011. It preserves, for a time, higher tuition and fee rates at private colleges for students already enrolled in the Post-9/11 GI Bill before a 2010 improvements act changed the maximum.

For the period from August 1, 2011 to July 31, 2014, the amount paid for a covered student is the greater of two sums. The first is $17,500. The second is the charge found by using the Veterans Affairs table of 2010-2011 in-state maximums, published on October 27, 2010, as if that table still governed the student's program.
plaw-112-27-2011: Public Law 112-27 is the Airport and Airway Extension Act of 2011, Part IV, approved on August 5, 2011. It pushes the aviation tax dates out by roughly eight weeks. Fuel taxes and ticket taxes for the Airport and Airway Trust Fund now run to September 16, 2011 instead of July 22, 2011. The trust fund's spending authority moves from July 23, 2011 to September 17, 2011. The tax changes take effect on July 23, 2011.
plaw-112-28-2011:
Public Law 112-28, approved on August 12, 2011, gives the Consumer Product Safety Commission greater authority and discretion in enforcing the consumer product safety laws. Its first section deals with lead limits in children's products under the Consumer Product Safety Improvement Act of 2008.

The limits now apply only to a children's product made after the effective date of the limit in question, a change called prospective application. The act adds a functional purpose exception. The Commission may excuse a product, material, or part that needs lead. It may act on its own move or on a petition. The excuse holds where making the item without excess lead is not practicable or not technically workable, and a child is not likely to mouth or swallow it.
plaw-112-29-2011:
The Leahy-Smith America Invents Act is Public Law 112-29, approved on September 16, 2011. It amends title 35 of the United States Code to reform the patent system, the largest such rewrite in decades.

The table of contents shows the breadth. Early sections set a first inventor to file rule, remake the inventor's oath, and allow a defense based on prior commercial use. Others create post-grant review proceedings and a Patent Trial and Appeal Board, and allow third parties to file material before a patent issues. Later sections cover fee setting, office funding, satellite offices with one named for Detroit, and priority examination for important technologies.
plaw-112-3-2011: Public Law 112-3 is the FISA Sunsets Extension Act of 2011, approved on February 25, 2011. The operative text extends two sunset dates, in the USA PATRIOT Improvement and Reauthorization Act of 2005 and in the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004. In each, February 28, 2011 becomes May 27, 2011. The powers covered concern access to business records, lone terrorists as agents of foreign powers, and roving wiretaps. The act's own purpose line instead names December 8, 2011.
plaw-112-30-2011:
The Surface and Air Transportation Programs Extension Act of 2011 is Public Law 112-30, approved on September 16, 2011. It extends surface and air transportation programs while Congress worked on longer laws for each field.

Title I extends the surface programs. Subtitle A covers the federal-aid highway programs and their administrative expenses. Subtitle B extends highway safety programs run by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration and the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration, plus added programs. Subtitle C covers public transportation: planning funds, a special rule for city area formula grants, capital investment grants, and grants for areas that are not urbanized.
plaw-112-31-2011: Public Law 112-31, approved on September 23, 2011, names a courthouse in Jefferson City, Missouri. The United States courthouse at 80 Lafayette Street is to be known as the Christopher S. Bond United States Courthouse. The references clause says any mention of that courthouse in a federal law, map, rule, or record counts as a mention of the Christopher S. Bond United States Courthouse.
plaw-112-32-2011:
The Combating Autism Reauthorization Act of 2011 is Public Law 112-32, approved on September 30, 2011. It renews the Combating Autism Act of 2006, which set up federal work on developmental disabilities surveillance and research.

Three sections of Part R of the Public Health Service Act gain new end years, 2014 in place of 2011. A report deadline moves from four years after the 2006 act to two years after this act, and a study span grows from four years to six. The funding clause authorizes $22,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2012 through 2014 for the developmental disabilities surveillance and research program.
plaw-112-33-2011:
Public Law 112-33 is the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2012, approved on September 30, 2011. It makes continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2012, the stopgap funding that keeps agencies running when the year's regular bills are not yet law.

Section 101 funds projects and activities carried on in fiscal year 2011, at the rate and under the terms of the 2011 laws. The acts named are the Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 2011 and the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2011, the two halves of Public Law 112-10. The rate for operations is then cut by 1.503 percent. Section 102 bars the Defense Department from using these funds to start new production or raise production rates.
plaw-112-34-2011:
The Child and Family Services Improvement and Innovation Act is Public Law 112-34, approved on September 30, 2011. It amends part B of title IV of the Social Security Act to extend the child and family services program through fiscal year 2016.

Title I extends the Stephanie Tubbs Jones Child Welfare Services Program, swapping the years 2007 through 2011 for 2012 through 2016. State plan rules change as well. Plans must cover response to emotional trauma, including trauma tied to a child's maltreatment and removal from home. They must include protocols for the proper use and watching of psychotropic medications, and a description of work to cut the time children under 5 spend without a lasting family.
plaw-112-35-2011: The Short-Term TANF Extension Act is Public Law 112-35, approved on September 30, 2011. It extends the block grant program of aid to needy families, under part A of title IV of the Social Security Act, through December 31, 2011. Activities continue in the manner allowed for fiscal year 2011. Grants may be paid quarterly through the first quarter of fiscal year 2012, at the level of the matching quarter of fiscal year 2011. It also shifts the maintenance of effort years in section 409(a)(7).
plaw-112-36-2011:
Public Law 112-36, approved by the 112th Congress in 2011, carries the short title Continuing Appropriations Act, 2012. It is a stopgap funding law for fiscal year 2012. Congress passed it because the regular spending bills for that year were not yet done.

The act funds federal work at the rate set in the fiscal year 2011 spending acts. It covers work run under the defense act and the full-year act for 2011, named in section 101. Money comes from the Treasury and from agency receipts and funds. The text then sets a rate cut, which the sample shows only in part.
plaw-112-37-2011:
Enacted in 2011 by the 112th Congress, Public Law 112-37 is the Veterans Health Care Facilities Capital Improvement Act of 2011. The law deals with building and leasing major medical sites for the Department of Veterans Affairs. It also extends some expiring rules and changes some powers of the Secretary.

Early sections back fiscal year 2012 major medical facility projects and leases. They also change past project approvals and fund the work. Later sections limit how Congress must approve some site buys. They also curb the use of bid savings to widen a project's scope.
plaw-112-38-2011: Schertz, Texas, is home to the site renamed by Public Law 112-38 of the 112th Congress, passed in 2011. The Postal Service site at 1081 Elbel Road in Schertz must be known as the Schertz Veterans Post Office. Any mention of that site in a federal law, map, rule, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name. The act does nothing else.
plaw-112-39-2011: Naming a Texas mail site is the whole job of Public Law 112-39, approved in 2011 by the 112th Congress. The Postal Service site at 5014 Gary Avenue in Lubbock must be known as the Sergeant Chris Davis Post Office. Federal laws, maps, rules, records, and other papers must use that name when they refer to the site.
plaw-112-4-2011: Public Law 112-4 is a joint resolution of the 112th Congress from 2011, called the Further Continuing Appropriations Amendments, 2011. It amends the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2011, which had kept the government funded. The resolution moves the end date in section 106 to March 18, 2011. It also adds new sections on war funds and on earmark language, though the sample cuts off mid-way through that part.
plaw-112-40-2011:
Trade relief for poor countries sits at the center of Public Law 112-40, passed by the 112th Congress in 2011. The act extends the Generalized System of Preferences, a program in the Trade Act of 1974. That program lets some goods enter the United States with low or no duties.

Section 1 moves the program's end date from December 31, 2010, to July 31, 2013. The change takes effect for goods entered on or after the fifteenth day after the act passed. Goods entered in the gap can still get the old treatment. Their entries are settled again as if they had come in on that fifteenth day.
plaw-112-41-2011:
Public Law 112-41, enacted by the 112th Congress in 2011, puts the United States-Korea Free Trade Agreement into United States law. Title I approves the deal and covers its start date. It also covers how the deal fits with federal and state law, plus dispute steps and claim handling.

Title II turns to customs work. Its sections cover tariff changes, rules of origin, and customs user fees. Those rules decide which Korean goods get the deal's lower rates. They also set how customs staff check where a good was made. The act was approved on October 21, 2011.
plaw-112-42-2011:
Colombia trade terms are the subject of Public Law 112-42, approved by the 112th Congress in 2011. Its short title is the United States-Colombia Trade Promotion Agreement Implementation Act. Title I approves the trade deal and covers when it starts. It also covers the deal's fit with United States and state law.

Title II covers customs. The listed sections deal with tariff changes and rules of origin. They also cover how trade disputes are run and how claims are judged. In short, the act gives the Colombia deal legal force inside the United States.
plaw-112-43-2011:
Public Law 112-43 of the 112th Congress, passed in 2011, carries out the United States-Panama Trade Promotion Agreement. Title I approves the deal and sets its start rules. It also states how the deal relates to United States and state law. Other sections cover steps taken before the deal starts and how disputes are handled.

Title II sets the customs side. It covers tariff changes and extra duties on some farm goods. It also covers rules of origin, which decide if a good counts as Panamanian. Those rules control which goods earn the deal's lower rates.
plaw-112-44-2011: Keeping the United States Parole Commission at work is the aim of Public Law 112-44, passed in 2011 by the 112th Congress. The act amends the Sentencing Reform Act of 1984. Each mention of 24 years in the key section now reads as 26 years. That change adds two years to the time the Commission keeps its role. The act also orders a report to the House and Senate Judiciary Committees within 180 days. The report starts with a count of offenders, but the sample cuts off there.
plaw-112-45-2011: Public Law 112-45, enacted in 2011 by the 112th Congress, sorts out control of the C. C. Cragin Dam and Reservoir. Section 1 covers a land withdrawal and reservation for the Cragin Project. The covered land runs to about 512 acres. It takes in about 300 feet of the dam crest and spillway, a reservoir pool of about 250 acres, and a linear corridor. The act also defines the project and names the Salt River Project district in its terms.
plaw-112-46-2011:
Ski land on national forests gets wider use under Public Law 112-46, the Ski Area Recreational Opportunity Enhancement Act of 2011. The 112th Congress passed it to amend the National Forest Ski Area Permit Act of 1986. That older act governs ski area permits on National Forest System land. The Secretary of Agriculture issues those permits.

The stated purpose has two parts. First, snow sports beyond nordic and alpine skiing may be allowed on permit land. Second, the Secretary may allow fitting added recreation in any season, all year. Sample text stops while stating that second aim.
plaw-112-47-2011: In Barrigada, Guam, a post office building takes the name set by Public Law 112-47 of the 112th Congress, passed in 2011. The site at 489 Army Drive in Barrigada must be known as the John Pangelinan Gerber Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, record, or other paper counts as a mention of that full name.
plaw-112-48-2011: A Pasadena mail site gains a new name under Public Law 112-48, approved by the 112th Congress in 2011. The Postal Service site at 281 East Colorado Boulevard must be known as the First Lieutenant Oliver Goodall Post Office Building. References to the site in federal laws, maps, rules, records, and other papers count as references to that name.
plaw-112-49-2011: Public Law 112-49, passed in 2011 by the 112th Congress, names one post office in Massachusetts. The Postal Service site at 45 Meetinghouse Lane in Sagamore Beach must be known as the Matthew A. Pucino Post Office. Any mention of that site in a federal law, map, rule, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-112-5-2011:
Highway and transit programs get more time under Public Law 112-5, the Surface Transportation Extension Act of 2011. The 112th Congress passed it while a longer, multiyear law was still pending. It extends federal-aid highway, highway safety, motor carrier safety, and transit programs. The Highway Trust Fund pays for those programs.

Section 1 also tells the Transportation Secretary to reconcile funds. Amounts for fiscal year 2011 must be cut by sums already given out under the two 2010 extension acts. That cut covers the span from October 1, 2010, to March 4, 2011. Title I then extends the highway programs.
plaw-112-50-2011: Public Law 112-50, enacted by the 112th Congress in 2011, names a Postal Service site in Hawaii. The site at 4354 Pahoa Avenue in Honolulu must be known as the Cecil L. Heftel Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, record, or other paper counts as a mention of that full name.
plaw-112-51-2011:
Moving suits against federal staff to federal court is clarified by Public Law 112-51, the Removal Clarification Act of 2011. The 112th Congress amended title 28 of the United States Code. The target is section 1442, which covers removal of cases against federal officers or agencies. The act aims to clear up and improve those rules.

One change widens what counts as a civil action or criminal prosecution. Any case where a court order is sought or issued counts, at least in part. That reach covers subpoenas for testimony or papers. The sample stops in the middle of that new rule.
plaw-112-52-2011: One Utah water district may pay its federal debt early under Public Law 112-52 of the 112th Congress, passed in 2011. The Interior Secretary must allow early payment of repayment contract number 6-05-01-00143. The United States and the Uintah Water Conservancy District signed it on June 3, 1976.
