Lamivudine stunted onion root growth, and every drug damaged chromosomes in root tips. The mix hit water fleas harder than any single drug, suggesting the drugs boost each other's toxicity. It also killed one salmonella tester strain outright while sparing others. The authors warn that drug mixtures in waterways may threaten the microbes and small creatures at the food web's base.
pmc-10656511:
Neutron beams can image the inside of large, dense objects that X-rays cannot pierce. Richi Kumar, Lucas Sommer, Anton Tremsin, and Adrian Losko work at the NECTAR instrument, where a neutron beam also makes gamma rays as a by-product. Those rays travel along the same path as the neutrons and were long treated as contamination to shield against.

The team instead swaps in screens that respond to gamma rays and lets the same camera record a gamma image. Neutrons and gamma rays react differently with materials, so the two views together reveal more about what an object is made of. By changing screens and filters, one instrument can take both kinds of pictures of centimeter-sized objects. The authors present this dual view as a richer, non-destructive inspection method.
pmc-10657011:
Li Shi and co-authors probe whether gut microbes and their waste products play a role in schizophrenia. Their 2023 study uses the brain-gut axis, the two-way link between the gut and the brain that is drawing wide study. The team sampled stool from 44 healthy people, 41 patients in an acute phase, and 39 patients in remission.

Gene sequencing mapped the gut community, and a broad chemical scan profiled its products. Patients showed 20 clear shifts in their microbes, spread across orders, families, genera, and species, with some tied to symptom severity. The scans also found 145 unusual microbe products in patients, linked to pathways for metabolism and disease. Diagrams traced links between odd microbes, odd products, and symptoms. The authors offer the map as a lead for new treatment ideas.
pmc-10657611:
Morenike Oluwatoyin Folayan and a large team of co-authors published a scoping review in 2023 on ocean health and tooth decay in young children. The review links Sustainable Development Goal 14, which covers life below water, with early childhood caries. That term means tooth decay in children under six years old.

The team searched three databases in January 2023 and kept 13 studies from work published between 1960 and 2022. Some studies tested agents taken from marine products against plaque and decay. Others discussed sea salt as a source of fluoride. Readers get a first map of a sparse field and a sense of where the evidence is still thin.
pmc-10670511:
Yu-Hsun Chang and co-authors grow fallopian tube lining cells from reprogrammed stem cells in this 2023 study. Those lining cells matter because a deadly ovarian cancer appears to start in them, yet they are hard to keep for lab work.

The team turned fallopian tube cells into induced pluripotent stem cells using a four factor virus system. The stem cells proved able to form all three germ layers in dish tests and in tumors grown in mice. Guided by signals including a growth factor called WNT3A, they then matured into tube lining cells with the right markers and tube like shapes. Tube sourced stem cells matched skin sourced ones in this power, opening a clean route to model the disease.
pmc-10687911:
Julia Rey-Brandariz and five co-authors wrote this 2023 review on the level of silica dust at work above which lung cancer risk becomes clear. Breathing fine crystalline silica is tied to lung cancer, but the safe line is disputed. The team gathered studies that sorted workers by how much dust they breathed.

Twenty studies met the rules, and their exposure bands and risk calls varied widely. Most found no firm risk in their lowest bands. The pooled picture hints at low risk where average levels sit below 0.07 milligrams per cubic meter of air. Agency limits around the world run from 0.025 to 0.1 in the same units. The authors note that the cut points differ on paper yet cluster close in practice.
pmc-10691111:
Jianfeng Zhang and co-authors study a lung germ that causes hard to treat illness, in a paper from 2023. The germ often carries small rings of DNA that hold genes for drug resistance and for harm to the body. The team asks how one type of ring, which cannot move on its own, still spreads from cell to cell.

Lab tests show that these rings hitch a ride with a helper ring that can move on its own. The team also checked close to four thousand rings from many full germ genomes. They find that the hitchhiking rings hold about one fifth of the drug resistance genes and most of the harm genes. The work shows a quiet route by which drug resistance spreads.
pmc-10692111:
Shuo Diao and Yude Geng grade how well a state forest region is reinventing its industry, in a 2023 study. Heilongjiang's state-owned forests, long logged, must shift toward protection and new livelihoods as sustainability rules tighten. Whether the shift is efficient, not just underway, is the question.

The pair built an evaluation system using data envelopment analysis, which scores units against the best performers. They added a nonlinear, multi-goal optimization model to search for better industry mixes under constraints. Scores for 2015 to 2021 showed technical and overall efficiency lagging scale efficiency, averaging well below the frontier. The diagnosis says the region's transformation has size but weak technique, pointing reform at skills and process rather than expansion.
pmc-10693611:
Marlena Baranowska and co-authors studied in 2023 how nursery methods change fungi in soil and roots of silver fir seedlings. How trees are raised can shape the fungi that later support them. Samples came from a Polish forest district, with fungi named from a gene region and matched to a reference library.

Soil chemistry was also tested. Production methods split the response of root and soil fungal groups strongly. Set soil conditions shaped which fungi thrived and raised helpful root fungi in particular. In soil, three named fungi dominated the helpful group. In roots, a truffle-like fungus and two others led. Growth conditions, not just place, set the fungal mix.
pmc-10693711:
Xiaoyan Zeng and co-authors wrote a study from 2023 on a star-cell protein that may drive Alzheimer's disease, tested by removing it in mice. The protein, YKL-40, pours out of astrocytes and runs high in patients' spinal fluid as the disease advances. Whether it merely marks the disease or helps cause it was unsettled. The team used mice bred to develop amyloid plaques and memory loss.

In these mice the protein rose with age and tracked with astrocyte activation. Amyloid itself switched the protein on in cultured astrocytes, and the protein harmed neurons grown in dishes. Deleting the protein only in astrocytes, for just one week in already sick mice, cut plaque load across several brain regions. Glial activation eased, neuron loss slowed, and memory recovered. Cells without the protein ate and digested amyloid faster, with stronger acid in their recycling sacs.
pmc-10694811:
Stilbene dyes can flip between two shapes when light hits them, which makes them handy as tiny switches whose behavior depends on their surroundings. Dóra Vörös and co-authors study one such dye, known as DANS, in this 2023 paper, asking how it settles onto amorphous silica glass.

Computer calculations show the dye's nitro end forms strong hydrogen bonds with hydroxyl groups on the glass, anchoring both of its shapes flat against the surface. Weaker contacts with its rings help, while other contacts add little. Knowing exactly how the dye lies on glass helps designers of light-based sensors and coatings.
pmc-10694911:
Sneha Patil, Rajanikanth K, and Nitin Bhola test stretchy tape for relief after wisdom tooth surgery in a 2023 trial. Removing stuck lower wisdom teeth injures soft tissue and bone, causing pain, swelling, and stiff jaw opening. Kinesio tape, borrowed from sports care, may aid blood and fluid flow.

Fifteen patients had both sides treated, with tape on one side only. Pain was lower on the taped side on the first day. Swelling was lower on days two and three, and mouth opening was wider from day two onward. The authors conclude that tape can ease recovery and improve comfort after this common surgery.
pmc-10695911:
Ruirui Zhang and co-authors explained in 2023 why a conductive web at the surface of a silicon-based battery anode makes fast charging work. Such anodes store much, but they conduct poorly and swell hard. The team combined two-dimensional modeling, frozen microscopy, force probes, and light scattering to watch the interface under fast charging.

A complete conductive web calmed the electrical crowding at the surface. The protective film that forms there grew richer in conductive minerals, and the energy barrier for lithium ions fell in a straight line as the web improved. The web also shed stress, cutting leftover strain and swelling in step. The authors say interface quality, long a side note, is the main lever. Their design rules target anodes that charge fast and survive it.
pmc-10696711:
Sagarjit Aujla and co-authors published this 2023 study on reading newborn lung scans with a computer's help. Lung disease is a leading killer of newborns in poorer countries. Ultrasound scans of the lung are cheap, portable, and safe, but few trained readers work where they are needed most. The team built a tool to sort scans into the six most common newborn lung conditions.

Their method pulls line and texture patterns from images using a wavelet transform, a math lens for structure. The data held 1,550 images from 42 babies. With raw class sizes, per-image accuracy reached about 74 percent. After balancing the classes, accuracy jumped to about 93 percent. Per-baby accuracy was lower, near 65 percent, showing where work remains.
pmc-10698311:
Jason Haas, Paul Oakley, and Deed Harrison report one case of shoulder pain after a COVID-19 shot, in a 2023 case report. A man in middle age had sharp pain in his left shoulder and neck. His posture was stooped, with his head pushed far forward.

Care used a posture based method plus a shoulder rehab plan over many visits. After four months the man said the pain was gone. Neck strain scores fell, and posture measures got much better. A check two years later found the gains still held with no more care.
pmc-10698811:
Anaphylaxis, an allergic reaction, sometimes has no findable trigger and is called idiopathic. Thushali Ranasinghe and co-authors, at a specialist allergy clinic in Sri Lanka, suspected sensitivity to alpha-gal might explain some cases. Alpha-gal is a sugar found in red meat and linked to tick bites. They screened two hundred patients with anaphylaxis over one year. After skin tests and evaluation found no culprit, sixty-five were classified as idiopathic.

For those patients the team recorded events, foods, and treatment around each episode, ran an allergy chip test on blood samples. Patients whose chip test stayed negative had a blood test, which came back normal. The letter argues allergen patterns differ by region because diets, genes, and environments differ, so triggers common elsewhere may be missed locally. The authors present alpha-gal testing as a step worth adding for unexplained anaphylaxis.
pmc-10698911:
Yunhui Zhou and seven co-authors show a long mute chain curbs pancreas cancer spread in low air. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three. This cancer grows in low-air ground and oft comes back. The chain, GATA6-AS1, ran low in tumor cuts and tied to poor fate. Gain and loss runs in cells and mice traced its work.

The chain curbed cell growth, push, move, and form shift in low air, and cut growth and lung spread in mice. A low-air switch hushed the chain first. The chain then curbed a tag-scrub part, which left a spread part's chain less firm. The three-part line is pitched as a cure aim.
pmc-10699011:
Zoya Khan, Christa Lilly, Caterina DeFazio, and Elizabeth Claydon pilot a sensitivity training for clinicians in 2023. Pregnant patients with eating disorders face higher risks yet rarely disclose their history. Many clinicians also lack confidence to care for them well.

Fifty-four professionals took the training while sixty-one got a reference document instead. Surveys before and after measured knowledge, attitudes, and behavior. The trained group gained more in seeing the topic's relevance and in comfort offering resources. They also introduced care strategies more often and wanted more of them. The authors back wider training of this kind.
pmc-10699111:
A genetically modified maize called MON 810 grows across parts of the European Union, and its environmental monitoring reports are checked each year. The European Food Safety Authority assesses the 2021 report at the European Commission's request. The maize makes a bacterial protein, Cry1Ab, that kills corn borer pests. The report covers farmer compliance with refuge planting, pest susceptibility tests, farmer questionnaires, and the wider literature.

Farmers in Portugal fully meet the refuge rules, while those in Spain comply only partly. Tests on borer populations show no clear resistance, yet unexpected damage in one Girona field trial hints that resistance genes may be present locally. No unanticipated harm to health or environment appears anywhere in the evidence. EFSA keeps its earlier safety verdict but demands stronger monitoring in the Girona area and better tests overall.
pmc-10699311:
Heba Shahaed and co-authors present a 2023 paper drawing lessons for Canada from countries where nearly everyone has a regular primary care clinician. Canada spends a smaller share of its health budget on primary care than the typical rich country: 5.3 percent against 8.1 percent. Attachment to a regular doctor or clinic also lags.

The authors study four peer countries where more than 95 percent of people have a regular clinician or place of care. The United Kingdom, Norway, the Netherlands, and Finland each got there by a different route. The paper extracts what Canada could copy in funding, training, and sign up systems to close its own gap.
pmc-10702111:
Xuebin Zhang and seven co-authors read the gene activity of a mountain plant under cold stress in a 2023 study. The plant, Bergenia purpurascens, serves as food, medicine, and garden ornament in high cold places. No past work had shown how it rides out the cold at the gene level, so the team grew it under low heat and logged which genes switched.

Thousands of genes rose or fell next to warm grown controls. Many sat in paths for calcium signals, stress cascades, plant hormones, and fat handling. Four hundred gene switches from two large families answered the cold most. Five brand new genes stood out as leads for the plant's cold shield work.
pmc-10703211:
Ziyu Guo and co-authors tested how economic uncertainty bends health in China in a 2023 study. When the economy feels unsure, firms stall, jobs wobble, and stress spreads, all of which can harm health. Past theory and data on that link were still young, and a straight-line link was presumed more than proven.

The team fit both straight and curved models across the range of health outcomes. Their method reads short-run and long-run effects at each level of the outcome spread. A curved link would mean deep slumps hurt more than mild ones help. Such shape facts guide how hard policy should push back in hard times.
pmc-10703811:
Shangfeng Han and co-authors build a made-up Chinese face set with deep-learn craft to fill gaps in stock sets. Past sets lean on still shots, lack age spread, and draw on few faces, since crowd shoots cost time and cash. Their 2023 set grows faces with a style net, in a spread of feels and ages. Slide blends of the net's code yield smooth feel shifts at set force tiers.

Judges rate the faces for feel kind and for three feel marks: cheer, buzz, and rule feel. Scores hold firm and true in the team's checks. A broad, cheap face set frees mood labs from shoot bounds. Mind labs gain a tool for tests on how folks read a face.
pmc-10704711:
Qujia Gama and co-authors reviewed outcomes for young women who kept their fertility while treated for cancers of both the womb lining and the ovary at once, in a 2023 study. The dual diagnosis is uncommon, and standard care removes the uterus. Their hospital in Shanghai treated eight carefully chosen patients with hormone-based, organ-sparing care between 2016 and 2022.

Half the women had true dual cancers and half had lesser ovarian stages. Seven of eight reached a complete response in a median of under four months, and none relapsed after responding. Four of five women who tried became pregnant and delivered. The authors call the approach feasible for well-selected patients.
pmc-10704811:
Jie Wang and nine co-authors find a fresh gene fault in a large kindred with a stiff-leg disease, and trace how it harms the cell. Their study is from two thousand twenty-three.

The reigning view held the disease comes from too little of the gene's protein, which trims cell rails. Some cases do not fit that tale. The team read the full gene text of a five-span kindred of near fifty souls, with a small set ill. A shift fault in the gene was found. Lab tests on the changed protein showed it piles up, not fades, and fouls the rails' play. That gives a new path for the disease.
pmc-10706311:
Alicja Napiórkowska and co-authors sealed fragile essential oils into tiny capsules in this 2023 study. Juniper and black pepper oils fade fast in air and light. The team wrapped them by coacervation, a classic method where gelatin and gum arabic form skins around oil droplets, then freeze-dried the result into powder.

Three mixing ratios of the two wall polymers were tried, with the oils pre-dissolved in carrier oils to cut losses. The best batches trapped about sixty percent of the essential oil. One wall ratio gave powders that dissolved least in water; another gave the finest grains, under six micrometers. All powders flowed poorly, being sticky. The authors map the trade-offs for food and cosmetic uses.
pmc-10707111:
Abraham Espinoza-Culupú and colleagues test mygalin, a lab-made copy of the natural compound spermidine, as a possible anti-inflammatory and antioxidant drug lead. Earlier work showed it kills Escherichia coli and calms macrophages facing bacterial toxin. Computer screens first checked its safety and likely targets, and docking placed it on three inflammation enzymes, COX-2, iNOS and 5-LOX.

In cell tests, mygalin cut the toxin-driven rise of iNOS and COX-2 and lowered oxidative stress, all without harming cell survival. It also showed strong antioxidant action in a standard assay and blocked heat-driven red cell damage. The authors see mygalin as a sound candidate for deeper study as a new inflammation fighter.
pmc-10708111:
Ivan Reznik leads a nine-author team shrinking calcium carbonate particles toward the nanoscale inside microfluidic chips, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Vaterite is a fragile crystal form of chalk, prized for drug delivery since it dissolves gently. To make it continuously, at uniform small sizes, is hard.

A custom chip ran syntheses in one phase and in two phases. Precipitation inside emulsion droplets was the two-phase route, and it held size in check better than the rest. Electron microscopy, diffraction, and scattering gauged the products, giving size distributions, shapes, and crystal composition. The team tracked how particle size shifts from one regime to the next. Continuous production stands in place of batch beakers, pointing to pharmaceutical-grade vaterite made on demand.
pmc-10709311:
Saeedeh Mohammadi and co-authors find opinion leaders in a Twitter network with random matrix theory in a 2023 paper. The test case is the retweet web around Iran's 2021 presidential election. Standard counts can miss how influence truly pools inside camps.

Borrowing tools from physics, the team compared the network's spectrum against random baselines to expose real structure. Influence on both poles broke the simple one to many pattern: a small set of users steered talk inside their own cluster and across the whole network. The authors argue the method reveals dynamics that plain structural counts hide. They pitch it for political and everyday debate networks alike.
pmc-10709411:
Sogand Sajedi and co-authors release, in a 2023 software paper, a package that fuses two kinds of molecular data into a single gene network. Gene activity and DNA methylation are often read apart, which hides faint signals that both support. Their tool lines the two up gene by gene and builds one patient-similarity network from the blend.

On five independent data sets, the fused network forecast patient outcomes better than standard clinical markers. It also beat a similarity approach that used only one data type. The package is free through a public repository. The authors pitch joint reading as a general power boost for multi-layer biology data.
pmc-10709511:
Takahiro Tsuzuno and ten co-authors published a 2023 study of human periosteal cells, the cells in the membrane that wraps bone. That membrane supplies the starter cells that build new bone, so cell therapy with them holds promise for fixing bone defects from injury or disease. Yet the mix of cell types in a grown culture was unclear.

The team grew human periosteal cells from small tissue samples. They then profiled single cells by their gene activity to map the culture's variety. Standard gene tests backed up the profiling. They also tested how well the cells formed bone in living models. Knowing which cells in the mix drive bone growth could help labs grow better grafts and predict which batches will heal best.
pmc-10709911:
Cayo Vinnycius Pereira Lima and co-authors map what drives Brazilian teens' intention to be physically active, in a 2023 study. Intention matters because many teens fall short of healthy activity levels, yet say they would move if given the chance.

The study drew on a national school health survey with nearly fifty-four thousand students. A network analysis weighed personal, social, school, and regional factors together. Boys showed stronger intention than girls, as did teens who saw themselves as fat. Private school students showed higher intention, and such schools offer more after-school sports. The authors point to school provision as a lever policy can actually pull.
pmc-10710511:
Mario Pérez-Jiménez and co-authors aim virus machines at the math that guards public-key codes. Virus machines are a nature-inspired computing model that mixes virology with number handling. Code safety rests on problems like splitting a semiprime, the heart of RSA. No fast classic method is known. Their 2023 paper designs a virus machine that solves a broadened form of that splitting task.

The design is not just sketched but formally verified. That proof step sets the work apart in unconventional computing. The result does not break real codes today. It maps how a bio-style machine could, in principle, chew a hard number problem. Such maps help judge which computing oddballs deserve a second look.
pmc-10710711:
Wang and co-authors test how germ density weakens two antibiotic combos in this 2023 study. Both combos pair a classic antibiotic with a shield drug that blocks bacterial enzymes. The question is whether a heavier starting load of germs blunts their killing, a quirk called the inoculum effect.

Nineteen strains of two common gut germs, bred to make various shield-breaking enzymes, faced both combos at rising densities. The effect appeared in about a quarter of tests for one combo and over half for the other. At the highest density, neither drug worked at all. The weaker combo needed far higher doses to finish kills. The authors warn that dense infections may demand dose care.
pmc-10711811:
Yuxin Chen, Haoyu Yang, and Faguang Wang lead a team testing whether gentle electrical pulses to the ear sharpen attention. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-three. The pulses target the vagus nerve through the outer ear, a noninvasive route to brain modulation. Past results on attention were mixed, perhaps because attention is several systems at once.

Fifty-nine healthy volunteers received either real stimulation or a brief sham. Before and after, they performed a task probing alerting, orienting, and control. Real stimulation sped right-hand responses and steadied their timing. Brain signals tied to those responses grew larger as well. A rhythm band at one scalp site also shifted with treatment. Mediation models traced how the brain changes carried the behavior gains. The authors argue the method tunes specific attentional machinery. That precision matters for future clinical trials.
pmc-10711911:
Ann-Helen Patomella and co-authors lay out a stroke prevention trial in a 2023 protocol paper. Their program, called Make My Day, uses enjoyable daily activities as the engine of healthier living. A phone-supported team approach guides people at risk for stroke. Keeping new habits is the hard part of prevention, so meaning and fun are built in from the start.

The trial will enroll 104 adults at risk and split them by chance. Half get the phone-supported program, and half get usual primary care. The program runs ten weeks with team support. A side study will track how the program was delivered and what made it work. Results should show whether activity-led prevention beats standard advice.
pmc-10712011:
Sudeep Dhillon and co-authors review a family of glowing tracer compounds meant to image amyloid plaques in Alzheimer's disease. The compounds, called chalcones, can be tagged with radioactive labels and read by PET or SPECT scanners, which could flag the disease early. The review covers how these molecules are made, what they do in the body, and how they serve as starting points for natural product chemistry.

The authors walk through the main tracers in use, from fluorinated sugars to carbon-11 and iodine labeled agents, and weigh their worth for diagnosis. They also discuss the compounds' possible roles beyond imaging, in drug development and treatment. The review frames chalcone tracers as a meeting point of chemistry and brain imaging, with early detection as the prize.
pmc-10712111:
Muhammad Haroon Stanikzai and co-authors examined what care pregnant women in Afghanistan actually receive at clinic visits, in a study published in 2023. Good care before birth lowers deaths for mothers and newborns, yet visits can be rushed and patchy. The team used a national health survey from 2018 covering 6,627 women who had recently given birth or were pregnant. They counted how many of eight services each woman got.

Only about three in ten women received five to eight of the services, and barely one percent received all eight. Blood pressure checks were the most common service, given to about seven in ten women. Fuller care was more likely for women who could read, whose husbands could read, and who knew the danger signs of a troubled pregnancy. Women using private clinics tended to get fewer services. The authors urge stronger, more even care across clinics.
pmc-10712311:
Siti Aisyah Razali and co-authors wrote a 2023 review of immunoinformatics, the use of computing to design and judge vaccines, in fish farming. Disease outbreaks cap how much aquaculture can grow, and vaccination is the cheapest strong defence farms have. Immune data, though, now arrive in volumes no team can sort by hand.

The review explains how these tools manage and picture immune data, and how they spark fresh ideas about how fish respond to vaccines. Recent gains in biotechnology have widened what the tools can do, from picking vaccine targets to improving weak ones. The authors present the field as a wave worth riding for healthier farmed fish.
pmc-10712911:
Doroteia Höfelmann and Cynthia Braga assess Brazil's food and nutrition tracking system in a 2023 paper. The system, known as SISVAN, gathers data on what people eat and how their bodies grow, through public clinics across the country. It feeds into the national health system, which has watched nutrition since a 1990 health law set the duty.

Coverage grew when tracking was tied to welfare programs, so families in cash transfer schemes came into clinics and were measured. That link widened the data but also shapes who shows up in it. The paper weighs what the system can and cannot show about the whole population's diet profile. It is a grounded guide for officials and researchers who use these numbers to plan food and health policy in Brazil.
pmc-10715011:
Liao, Chien, Yu, and Li study if Chinese herbal medicine lowers heart disease risk in women with a hormone disorder, in a study from twenty twenty-three. The disorder affects many women of childbearing age and raises heart risk. Herbal care is widely used for its symptoms in Taiwan. Whether it also cuts heart disease was unknown.

They tracked national insurance records over nineteen years. After matching, each group held close to three thousand women. Herbal users had far lower heart disease rates than non-users. The gap held across all subgroups checked. Four herbs and formulas stood out in the prescriptions of protected users. The team calls for lab work to learn how the herbs protect the heart.
pmc-10715511:
Amy Clair, Emma Baker, and Meena Kumari link housing conditions to the speed of biological aging measured in DNA, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Housing shapes health in many ways, but the inner pathways, especially the mental and social ones, are poorly mapped. Genetic aging clocks from a large British household study offered a way to test one pathway.

Private renters aged faster biologically than outright owners. The renting effect outweighed the measured effects of unemployment and of being a former smoker. Past housing trouble mattered too: repeated rent arrears and exposure to pollution each tracked with faster aging. Because such aging can reverse, the authors argue housing policy is a genuine health lever.
pmc-10716111:
Qianyan Li and co-authors reported a 2023 study on radiation care after breast cancer surgery. Their aim was to lower harm to the lung on the treated side. The team built a trigger tool based on a chart that shows how much the target area and the left lung overlap. They then used the tool to redo treatment plans for sixteen cases after breast-saving surgery.

The cases split into two groups based on how close the target sat to the left lung. After the plans were redone, lung dose measures fell at several levels, and the mean dose to the heart fell as well. Tests showed clear gains in both groups. The authors say the tool raises plan quality and may cut lung injury.
pmc-10716411:
After ischemic stroke, both high and low blood pressure predict poor recovery, a contradiction that suggests a third factor. Sarah Gunkel, Andreas Schötzau, and Felix Fluri test cerebral small vessel disease as that factor. They prospectively analyzed 423 stroke patients, recording systolic and diastolic pressure at admission and over 72 hours, and scoring small vessel burden on MR scans. Good outcome meant a Rankin score of two or less.

Small vessel burden predicted poor outcome strongly. Admission pressures did not predict outcome, but diastolic pressure over 72 hours interacted with vessel burden at discharge, and its changes tracked outcome too. The link was U-shaped: both rises and falls hurt. At 12 months the diastolic relation persisted. The authors argue for individualized pressure care, lowering or raising diastolic pressure according to each patient's vessel burden.
pmc-10717111:
Huiwen Zheng and co-authors compare two blood tests for hidden tuberculosis infection in children and ask why results so often come back unclear, in work from 2023. The interferon gamma release assay is the main tool for finding latent infection. In children, indeterminate answers are common, and the reasons were mostly guesswork.

Records from a Beijing children's hospital covered over thirty-three thousand tested children from 2019 to 2022. Two test brands were compared head to head. Children with lung disease showed more positive and more unclear results than others. The analysis names risk factors for the unclear zone, where a family learns neither yes nor no.
pmc-10717711:
Lei and co-authors trace the role of a gene regulator, HDAC9, in the wearing out of spinal discs, in a 2023 paper. Disc degeneration drives most low-back pain, and data mining showed HDAC9 sharply reduced in worn human disc tissue.

Mice lacking the gene developed age-related disc decay on their own, while boosting it in disc cells eased damage in a surgical model. In cell tests, losing HDAC9 cut survival and raised cell death, and restoring it reversed both. The team found the protein steadies a partner, RUNX3, by stripping acetyl groups from it. They propose HDAC9 as a drug target for disc disease.
pmc-10719011:
When the Omicron variant of the coronavirus swept the world, health teams needed cheap ways to tell its subvariants apart. Sininat Petcharat and co-authors evaluated two such test platforms in 2023, using 618 positive samples from patients in Bangkok, Thailand. The platforms sorted samples among the Delta variant and two Omicron subvariants, BA.1 and BA.2.

Both Omicron subvariants spread far faster than Delta, at roughly two to three times the rate. The authors present their approach as a cost-efficient form of virus surveillance. It lets officials put numbers on how each variant behaves, which feeds better public health strategy as the virus keeps changing.
pmc-10719111:
Jonah Langlieb and co-authors charted, in a 2023 atlas study, the cell types of the whole adult mouse brain and where each one sits. Brain function rests on many specialized cells in exact places, yet their full roster was incomplete. The team paired single-nucleus gene reads with a spatial method that keeps each cell's location.

Merging the two views yielded the makeup of every brain structure. Diversity ran highest in the midbrain, hindbrain, and hypothalamus, where most cell types need at least three marker genes to tell apart. The atlas also maps signaling molecules, region-specific activity genes, and links to human disease risk. It is posted as a public resource for the field. Genetic tools for reaching each cell type can now be designed from the map.
pmc-10719611:
Theresa Erlenbach and seven co-authors trace how fruit flies that eat mushrooms came to survive poisons that kill almost everything else. The toxins, cyclopeptides found in deadly mushrooms, wipe out most eukaryotes. Within one fly radiation, many mushroom feeders shrug them off. The team rebuilt the family tree of 48 species from nearly a thousand shared genes, settling old disputes about who is related to whom. They then fed sixteen species a diet laced with the toxin alpha-amanitin.

Six species grew on the poisoned diet. Placing that result on the tree showed tolerance was present early in the mushroom-feeding line and then lost several times independently. The authors read the pattern as a warning against simple stories of gain. Tolerance in this group is an old trait with a patchy afterlife, and its chemistry is likely complex.
pmc-10725911:
Juan Garcia and co-authors scan in 2023 how easily three banned doping drugs can be bought online. The web has become a back door for anabolic agents, sold outside pharmacies with no prescription and no quality checks. The team searched from six countries for pages selling oxandrolone, DHEA, and androstenedione.

Availability split sharply by country and drug. Sports-themed shops dominated the sales pages. Some drugs were pitched as performance boosters with no detail on dose or risk. Pharmacies played little role in the trade the team found. The study maps a trade that anti-doping rules struggle to reach.
pmc-10726011:
Yiwei Zhang and co-authors study whether antioxidant rich diets link to lower death rates in Americans with osteoarthritis. Their 2023 study uses a national health survey from 2001 to 2018. It covers 3,197 adults with the joint disease. Diet quality was scored by a composite antioxidant index. Deaths were tracked through national records. The team modeled the link while adjusting for other factors.

Higher diet scores went with lower death risk. The top quarter had a hazard twenty nine percent below the bottom quarter. The middle quarters sat in between, and the trend was clear. The relation looked straight rather than curved overall. Activity level changed the picture, though. In the least active group the link was straight and negative. In other groups the curve bent. The authors suggest diet advice for joint patients should be paired with activity guidance.
pmc-10726111:
Recine and co-authors introduce a 2023 research topic on the immune cells that enter sarcomas, a broad group of rare cancers of soft tissue and bone. Their editorial frames those immune cells, and the tissue around the tumor, as a model for learning how such cancers grow and spread. Sarcomas span more than 100 subtypes with unlike behavior.

The editorial sums up papers in the topic, including work on blood vessel growth and immune entry in bone sarcoma. The shared point is that a better grasp of the tumor immune setting could lead to new immune based treatments. It also may clarify the natural course of these rare tumors and guide care.
pmc-10726311:
Katinka Kuehn, Andreas Hahn, and Lothar Seefried test a special diet in adults with a rare bone softening disease, in a 2023 paper. The disease leaves muscles and mood impaired, and a low phosphorus diet had been proposed but never tried in a formal study. Twenty six outpatients in Germany ate set daily amounts of phosphorus and calcium for eight weeks.

Walking speed and a chair rise test improved clearly by the end. A six minute walk and a timed stand and go test did not change, and pain scores stayed put. Energy, on a standard health survey, did improve. The diet looks safe and partly helpful, though bigger controlled trials would be needed to confirm the gains.
pmc-10726411:
Rhian Stavely and co-authors review stem cell therapy for gut disease in a 2023 paper. Oxidative stress, an overload of harmful oxygen products, drives many gut disorders and harms the nerve network that keeps the gut moving. When those nerves fail, patients face pain, poor motion, and at times life-threatening problems, and current drugs offer little help.

Stem cells from body tissue have shown they can regrow cells, calm swelling, and support sick tissue. Fresh proof also points to protective effects against oxidative harm and nerve damage. The review gathers that proof across gut conditions and weighs how stem cell tools might be shaped into care. The authors see a path to fill a real gap in treatment.
pmc-10727911:
Colleen Loo and co-authors report a phase 3 trial of ketamine injections for depression that has not responded to standard treatment. The trial ran at seven centres in Australia and New Zealand, and patients got twice-weekly injections under the skin of either ketamine or midazolam for four weeks. One group got a fixed dose. A second group got flexible doses that rose when response was weak.

In the flexible-dose group, ketamine clearly beat the comparison drug: about one in five patients reached remission, against one in fifty on midazolam. In the fixed-dose group the two drugs did not differ. Side effects such as odd mental states and raised blood pressure settled within two hours, and the drug was well tolerated. The authors conclude that well-dosed under-skin ketamine is a practical, effective option for hard-to-treat depression over a four-week course.
pmc-10729211:
Mylaine Breton and ten co-authors map how Quebec primary care teams practice advanced access. Their 2023 study covers university-linked team clinics across the province. Advanced access aims to give patients timely appointments. Uptake, though, varies widely among doctors and nurses.

A survey drew three hundred thirty-five replies from thirty-five clinics. Fourteen measures covered clinic size, area, and twelve access strategies. A latent class method sorted providers into six practice profiles. Two profiles each held a quarter of respondents. One barely planned supply against demand; another leaned on reactive teamwork. The taxonomy gives clinic leaders a mirror for their own habits. It also targets help where planning lags most.
pmc-10731211:
Feng Xiang and co-authors review, in a 2023 paper, an extra foot bone in kids and how to treat it. The bone, the accessory navicular, is a growth variant at the navicular's side knob. One in ten who bear it feels pain that cuts walk and life. The bone shifts where the back shin tendon ties, so flat foot and weak tendon work oft ride with it. First care is with no cut: rest, shoes, and drug care. When that fails, surgery is the path. The review reads the cause, the signs at hand, the ills that ride with it, and the care paths in turn.

Types of the bone and their fit care get their own span. The end aim is a fit pick for each child.
pmc-10731311:
A stress hormone that rises as fruit ripens can be used to steer flavor, softness, and color, surveys a 2023 review by Wei Wu and co-authors. Abscisic acid builds up during ripening in most fruits, and spraying it on speeds the traits buyers pay for.

The review covers how the hormone is made, broken down, and read by the fruit's cells, then follows its effects trait by trait. It also maps the hormone's talks with ethylene, the classic ripening gas, and with other plant signals. The authors close with open questions, aiming the summary at growers and breeders who lose money to fruit that ripens wrong.
pmc-10733211:
Carolin Fleischmann-Struzek and Kristina Rudd review why counting sepsis cases worldwide is so hard, in a 2023 paper. Sepsis, the body's runaway response to infection, ranks among the top killers on Earth. Yet solid numbers on how often it strikes and kills exist for only a few rich countries.

Models and pooled studies put global yearly cases at 276 to 678 per 100,000 people, with death rates near a quarter of cases. The catch is the data: hospital billing records capture sepsis poorly, and clinical studies rarely tie back to whole populations. The authors survey the evidence for Germany and the world, then argue that better definitions, better sources, and policy push are needed before vulnerable groups can be spotted and helped.
pmc-10733511:
Xiaokai Shi and co-authors study an enzyme as a marker in bladder cancer in a 2023 paper. The enzyme, MTHFD2, is often overproduced in cancers and may shape immune response. Using large public cancer data, the team asked whether its level in bladder tumors tracks the immune state of the tumor and predicts who gains from immune therapy.

Tumors with high levels showed the marks of an inflamed setting: active immune cycles, more immune cells inside, and higher scores for T cell activity. Such patients were more often of a subtype that responds to treatment and did better on immune therapy in a trial cohort, with higher response rates and longer survival. The authors propose the enzyme level as a guide for choosing therapy in this cancer.
pmc-10733911:
Horyomba Ouandaogo, Souleymane Diallo, Eddy Odari, and Johnson Kinyua profile a Kenyan medicinal basil in a 2023 paper. Local tradition uses the plant for measles, stomach pain, diarrhea, insect bites, and chest complaints. The team extracted leaves in methanol and in hot water and screened both extracts for plant chemicals.

Both extracts held alkaloids, phenolics, flavonoids, saponins, and tannins, but amounts split sharply by solvent. Water drew far more flavonoids and tannins, while methanol led on other classes. Gas chromatography with mass spectrometry then named the individual compounds, high and low weight alike. The chemical map gives a base for testing the plant's traditional uses in the lab.
pmc-10734011: Juan Guerrero-Pérez argues that safety training should be a core part of chemical engineering degrees, in a viewpoint piece from 2023. He notes that some degree programs around the world still leave process safety out of their courses. The piece calls for a global update to how chemical engineers are taught. It aims to start a broad debate, win support from experts, and draw in new voices, with a focus on countries that have not yet made this change.
pmc-10735411:
Yan Wang and seven co-authors presented a study in twenty twenty-three on how to measure inner health through signals between body systems. They used transfer entropy, a math tool that tracks how much one signal helps predict another. Their data came from seventy-one people in the MiSBIE project, who faced a five-minute public speaking task.

Heart rate, blood pressure, and breathing were recorded for two hours, before, during, and after the task. The group included healthy people and patients with gene faults that harm the cell's energy units. Signal flow differed between the groups at set stages. After the task, flow from blood pressure to breathing ran nineteen percent higher in healthy people than in one patient group. The authors see promise in this as a health measure.
pmc-10735511:
Opeyemi Kolade and co-authors reviewed ways to involve older adults and family carers in health policy, in this 2023 study. Their input can make care plans cheaper and more responsive. The review, part of a European program, searched both journal and grey sources.

Eleven papers described thirteen engagement methods, sorted into standard, deliberative, and other types. Older adults and carers were most often asked for views at the agenda stage. Their role in drafting, running, and judging policy was unclear. Power was rarely shared equally. The authors guide officials on picking methods and call for studies that judge how well each method works.
pmc-10735811:
Castillo-Azofeifa reported in twenty twenty-three on how long-term inflammation harms the aging gut. The gut lining renews itself fast when young, but that power fades with age. The author infected young and old mice with a gut bacterium that damages the lining. Young mice healed well. Old mice did poorly and often did not survive the infection.

Old infected guts held high levels of interferon gamma, an immune signal. Their lining broke down more, with fewer stem cells and skewed cell types. Lab-grown gut tissue told the same story under steady exposure. Old tissue died within a day, while young tissue was unharmed. A brief signal boost helps repair, the work shows. A constant signal in old age instead blocks healing.
pmc-10735911:
Gail Towsley and co-authors build an online coach that helps families speak up in nursing homes, in a 2023 paper. After the pandemic strained staffing, relatives of residents with dementia became essential advocates, yet many dread the hard conversations about what their loved one wants and needs. The tool, CONTACT, walks a care partner through preparing for such talks.

Its four parts teach how nursing homes work, guide the partner to set a clear goal, draft an action plan, and reflect afterward. Eight care partners tried it and rated its acceptability, fit, and feasibility in surveys and a focus group. Ratings came back favorable, with users asking for refinements rather than rejecting the concept. Coached families could shift nursing home care from something done to residents toward something decided with them.
pmc-10736011:
A standard dementia screening test, the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, is given again and again to the same patients, and practice itself can bend the scores. Kuan-Ching Wu, Jessica Jin, Shao-Yun Chien, and Oleg Zaslavsky tracked that bending in a 2023 study. They followed eight older adults with mild to moderate dementia for six months.

Scores were taken every two weeks, twelve times in all, inside a study of conversational speech. Total scores drifted against the clock: longer test sessions went with lower totals. Word recall trials swung both ways across sessions, rising at first, then falling. Over 60 percent of participants trended downward on naming tasks, while orientation items showed no clear drift. The authors warn that repeated testing carries a learning effect, so a rising or steady score may hide real decline.
pmc-10736311:
Jennifer Reckrey and co-authors studied who gets paid care at home among older adults with serious illness, in a 2023 study. The team followed Americans over sixty-five in a long-running health survey from 1998 to 2018, linked to Medicare records. The final group held 2,521 people who had newly come to need help with daily self-care tasks.

Paid care was most common among people facing several problems at once. Among those with self-care limits, dementia, and another serious illness, about forty-two percent had at least forty hours of paid care per week. Where paid care existed, it covered over half of all care hours. People on Medicaid were more likely to get paid help, while the richest got the most hours. Dementia brought more hours of paid care than other illnesses.
pmc-10736411:
Jared Doan and co-authors evaluate a geriatric co-management program for kidney transplant candidates in a 2023 study. Older patients fare worse after transplant, so one hospital paired surgeons with geriatricians and social workers. The program assessed fifty-five candidates over five months in 2022, testing frailty, daily functioning, and cognition with standard scales. Its reports helped the surgical team decide who to list for surgery.

About a third of those assessed were women. The study examines how the extra geriatric picture changed listing decisions, and where the assessment's role needs clarifying. Transplant teams must weigh a scarce organ against a frail body's odds; structured vulnerability data makes that call less of a guess.
pmc-10736511:
Angela Perone studies the hidden legal role of social workers in nursing homes. Rights clash often in these homes, among residents, staff, and families. Social workers sit where those claims cross. Her 2023 study joins staff interviews, a read of hundreds of home policies, and months of watching daily life in two homes.

Though few in number, social workers were the go-to solvers for rights clashes of all kinds. Aides, nurses, and bosses alike passed hard cases to them, by written rule and by habit. The cases spanned bias claims, care quality, and clashes between safety and a resident's free choice. Social workers solved most of them but felt unready for the legal edge of the role. Perone calls for training and support for this quiet duty.
pmc-10736711:
Julian Scheffer and seven co-authors follow family caregivers after the caregiving ends and find money shapes the recovery. Thirty-six caregivers of people with neurodegenerative disease rated emotional well-being and energy during care and again about ten years later, once care had ended by death or institutional placement. On average, well-being and energy both improved after the role closed.

Household income, reported after caregiving, split the story. Lower income predicted smaller gains, and the link held with starting levels controlled. The authors suggest that lean budgets block rest, travel, and other repairs that rebuild a former caregiver's life.
pmc-10736811:
Nanna Notthoff reviewed studies on whether pet owners and their pets are active together, in a 2023 paper. Social support can get people moving, and pets have come to count as close social partners, above all for older adults who may have lost human partners. Past reviews compared people with and without pets, but that does not show whether person and pet move at the same times.

Searches of two databases began with more than seventeen thousand records and, after two screening steps, kept nine studies. Only five of those directly computed the link between owner and pet activity; four found a positive link and one found none. Four studies included adults over sixty, but none tested whether the link changes with age. Notthoff suggests joint activity with pets could anchor programs to raise activity in older adults, if the link holds up in stronger work.
pmc-10737011:
Eric Cerino, Dakota Witzel, Chloe Horowitz, and David Almeida study daily stress in 2023 with data from a national diary project. A sense of control is known to aid healthy aging, but its role in ending daily stressors was less clear. The sample held 1,766 adults who logged stress across eight days in each of two waves about ten years apart.

People who felt more control over their stress were far more likely to see it resolved. On days when a person felt more control than usual, closure was also more likely. That day-level link grew stronger in the later wave, which points to control as a lasting resource.
pmc-10737111:
Jordan Lewis and co-authors listen to Alaska Native caregivers of relatives with dementia, in a 2023 study. Dementia rates are climbing among Alaska Native people, and the tribal health system is ill-equipped for the care load. Caring for kin is a deep cultural value, so many families shoulder the work themselves. Twenty-one caregivers from rural and urban communities shared their experiences in interviews.

Caregivers proved inventive and resourceful, yet flagged urgent gaps. Costs ran high, many health workers lacked dementia training, and almost no training materials felt safe for their culture. They asked for plain guides to dementia's stages and to the supports on offer. The authors urge timely resources rooted in Native culture, so families are not left to improvise alone.
pmc-10737311:
Shayna Gleason and co-authors ask, in a 2023 study, why many towns doing age-friendly work never join the national network built for it. The network now counts over seven hundred member communities, and joining brings peer contacts and resources. Yet many places helping older residents stay outside. The team interviewed leaders in twelve communities in Maine and Massachusetts that do aging work without membership.

Leaders cited confusion about what joining requires and doubts that it would pay off. Political worries, thin staff capacity, and competing budgets, from children's programs to pandemic relief, also held towns back. Many wanted to keep local control over their aging plans. The authors recommend clearer explanations of membership, stronger technical help, and support that respects local direction. Their aim is to widen age-friendly work beyond the network's current reach.
pmc-10737611:
Nicole Schindler and five colleagues ask a deceptively simple question: when older adults stop sedative sleeping drugs, do falls drop? Benzodiazepines and Z-drugs are known fall risks, but real-world proof that deprescribing helps was missing. Health records from one academic system supplied a retrospective cohort of chronic users over sixty-five.

Stopping was defined by dispensing gaps of ninety or one hundred eighty days, with matched non-stoppers as the comparison. Under the stricter definition, fall events ran lower among stoppers, though the estimate was imprecise. Under the looser one, no benefit appeared. The authors stress the small, single-site sample: the answer depends on how stopping is defined, and bigger studies must follow.
pmc-10737711:
Jose Diaz and David Almeida linked uneven sleep to brain size in two thousand twenty-three. Their focus was the hippocampus, a brain part vital for memory. Brain shrinkage begins in midlife, well before old age. Poor sleep has been tied to weaker memory in older adults. Far less was known about sleep and the midlife brain.

Adults wore motion sensors for seven days to track sleep. The team measured how much sleep length jumped from night to night. Brain scans gave the size of the hippocampus for each person. More uneven sleep lined up with a smaller hippocampus. Steady sleep may thus matter as much as total sleep. The findings support sleep care as part of healthy aging plans.
pmc-10738011:
Francesca Falzarano and Sara Czaja study give-and-take inside dementia care pairs and how it shapes caregiver outcomes, in work from two thousand twenty-three. Data came from near one hundred pairs of family caregivers and their care recipients in a support program. Traits of both partners were weighed against caregiver burden and mood.

Harder nursing tasks and more distress over the recipient's limits tied to higher burden and lower confidence. Lower mutuality between partners also tied to worse caregiver outcomes. Male caregivers and task distress linked to fewer positive views of caregiving. Female recipients, mutuality, and readiness linked to more positive views. Both partners matter, the authors stress.
pmc-10738211:
Daniel Adekunbi and six co-authors tested heart cells from baboons whose growth was restricted before birth, in a study published in 2023. Restricted growth speeds heart aging, and baboons age much like humans. Cells were grown from the hearts of restricted and normal donors, all old. Some cells then faced a two-hour low-sugar stress while breathing rates were read.

Normal cells breathed more than restricted cells in each state. Fuel demand and side breathing counts ran nearly even. Stress hurt the energy-producing parts of all cells alike, restricted or not. Restricted cells kept the marks of their donors even in the dish. The authors present the cells as a laboratory model of heart aging and injury, for work on cell strength and protective drugs.
pmc-10738411:
Abulaiti Abudurezake and co-authors present a 2023 study on jaw muscle size and weak bones in older adults. The jaw muscle drives chewing, and chewing links to nutrition and bone health. The team studied 1,534 people aged 65 to 84 in one Tokyo ward. Bone density and body makeup were scanned, and jaw muscle volume was measured from 3D images.

People were split into fifths by muscle volume, split by sex. In men, the smallest-muscle group had far higher odds of hip osteoporosis than the largest. Hip bone density also rose with muscle volume in men. In women, prevalence did not track muscle size, though mid-range groups had denser hips than the smallest. The authors say a small jaw muscle flags low hip density.
pmc-10738711:
What separates people who merely reach old age from those who pass one hundred? Brianna Barnett and Alexander Bishop mined the life stories of 1,858 deceased Oklahoma centenarians in 2023, coding their autobiographies for family, work, marriage, and habits. Years lived past a century was the outcome they tried to predict with a standard model of human development.

Three predictors stood out. Race was the strongest: the authors report people of color in the sample lived longer. Having a father who farmed for a living came second. The total years spent married came third. The authors suggest life stories, carefully coded, can reveal patterns that ordinary records miss.
pmc-10738911:
John McHugh and Gregory Alexander ask if spare cash in a nursing home feeds its tech growth. Homes run lean, so few build a spare pool of cash, staff, or good will, a pool scholars call slack. Their 2023 study links a 2018 home tech survey, with just over five hundred homes, to cost and zone facts from set banks. Tech growth is scored by how deep tech runs in care, clinic aid, and office work.

Top-stage homes clear far more cash per bed over three years than base-stage homes. Homes with more Medicare mix and a near hospital also score high on tech. The link fits the slack tale: a cash pad buys room to try new tools. Lean homes may need aid to cross that gap.
pmc-10739011:
Kimberly Oosterhouse and co-authors describe a mentoring program joining nursing students and older adults in a paper from two thousand twenty-three. Loneliness and isolation rose during the pandemic for both groups. Ageist views also block contact across generations, and nursing courses often stress frailty over wellness.

Working with five community groups of older adults, the team built the program inside a required nursing course. Partners shaped the forms, activities, schedules, and evaluation tools together. Video modules and talk prompts help students and elders start conversations. The program aims at mutual wellness through shared connection, and the authors discuss how others can access and adapt the materials.
pmc-10739211:
Betsy Kemeny and five co-authors tested in 2023 whether seated yoga plus falls lessons beat lessons alone for older adults. A quarter of older adults fall each year, and standing yoga cuts falls but demands balance many lack. Chair-based yoga eases pain and fear while building steadiness.

Fifteen residents of public housing took eight weeks of seated yoga with falls education, while a control group got education alone. Body tests such as timed standing and walking were compared. The study asks a plain question with practical stakes: is education enough, or does gentle movement add real protection?
pmc-10739411:
Daniel Lai and co-authors compare social capital between Chinese and South Asian older adults in Hong Kong. Their 2023 study surveys 1,015 people aged fifty-five and up, eight hundred Chinese and 215 South Asian, by phone and face-to-face interviews in turn. Social capital, the web of ties that brings help, trust, and standing, is a known support for well-being in old age.

A standard twenty-five-item World Bank tool measured six sides of that capital, from group membership to trust. Ethnic background can shape those ties through language, custom, and migration history. The study's aim is to show where the two communities differ, so services can meet each on its own terms.
pmc-10740711:
Francesca Spirito and co-authors test a lab assay that could guide drug choice in advanced oral cancer. Their 2023 study deals with tumors that hold a small pool of cancer stem cells. Those cells help tumors grow, persist, and resist treatment. Killing bulk cells alone may not stop recurrence. The assay grows stem cells from a patient's biopsy and tests drugs on them.

Eleven patients with advanced oral squamous cell carcinoma were included. Their enriched stem cells were exposed to standard chemotherapy drugs. Predicted responses varied from patient to patient. That spread is the point: the same drug will not suit everyone. The authors argue the assay could steer oncologists toward more precise, personal choices. They call for trials in larger groups to confirm the test's clinical value.
pmc-10741411:
Peng Xie and co-authors review, in a 2023 paper, the two way relationship between cell membrane proteins and the bending of the membrane itself. Membranes are not flat sheets; their curvature shapes how cells divide, move, and take in material. Proteins can sense bends, cause bends, and be changed by them in return.

Many diseases involve this interplay gone wrong, the authors argue. The review first introduces membrane curvature and its links to membrane proteins. It then works through how the interaction plays out in disease, and what that implies for treatment. Drug strategies might target the protein, the curvature, or their coupling. The closing part weighs prospects and hurdles for turning this knowledge into therapy. The authors aim to give drug designers a fresh angle on diseases that resist current approaches.
pmc-10742111:
Ogoegbunam Okolo and co-authors wrote a 2023 review of lab models for studying how mouth and throat microbes interact with head and neck cancer. The human microbiome helps keep tissues healthy, and shifts in it are linked to this cancer type. Flat two-dimensional cell cultures have revealed some of those links, but direct proof of mechanisms lags. The review weighs the model systems available, from animals to dishes.

Newer three-dimensional models, grown from patient tumors, keep the genetic and epigenetic traits of the source tissue. That fidelity may show how host and microbe responses drive cancer in a way flat cultures cannot. The authors survey the evidence on the microbiome's role in this cancer and the in vivo and in vitro methods used to probe it. They frame 3D models as the field's next step.
pmc-10742211:
Gantsova and co-authors read kidney gene activity in mice missing an alkali sensor. Their 2023 paper studies the receptor IRR, which wakes when fluid around kidney cells turns alkaline. Mice without its gene cannot dump bicarbonate into urine properly after an alkali load. The team compared kidney transcriptomes with and without the gene, at rest and after loading.

Ten genes checked by a second method truly differed between the groups. One channel gene rose after loading in normal mice but stayed flat in the knockouts. Enrichment maps pointed at energy and electron transport chains as the sensor's main beat. The work sketches how the kidney hears and answers alkali.
pmc-10742711:
Linda Altieri, Daniela Cocchi, and Giulia Roli present in 2023 faster tools for measuring how unevenly things spread across space, using entropy scores. Such scores are widely used, yet software and reading guides lagged behind practice. Their updated R software package aims to close that gap.

The package covers three known families of spatial entropy, from area splits to distance based forms. The authors show its use on a hard real case: nesting sites of an endangered gorilla species in Cameroon. Points lie in an odd shaped region, with habitat data at hand. The tools link nest diversity to habitat traits.
pmc-10743211:
Haoyu Zhou and co-authors review studies on social support and low mood after stroke in a 2023 paper. Support from family and friends is known to guard against low mood in general. Far less was known about that link in people who had a stroke.

The team searched medical databases for peer-reviewed work from 2016 to early 2023. Of 172 papers found, eight studies fit the topic well. Seven of them found that more support went with less low mood after stroke. One study found no clear link. Most links were strong enough to pass standard tests. The review urges care teams to build up the support that stroke patients feel they have.
pmc-10743411:
Alexandra Ivan and co-authors track how stem cells grown from shed baby teeth change as they are cultured over time, in a 2023 study. These cells, called SHEDs, can renew themselves and turn into several tissue types, so labs grow them for many passages. Long growth, though, may age the cells and dull their healing power.

The team followed the cells through ten passages, checking surface markers, growth speed, and their power to become bone, cartilage, fat, and nerve-like cells. Young cells grew fast and kept a wide range of fates. Aged cells grew more slowly, lost ground on bone and cartilage fates, and leaned more toward fat. Their self-cleaning system also weakened. The mix of free fatty acids in the cells shifted from an anti-inflammatory pattern toward a pro-inflammatory one, which the authors link to the aging shift.
pmc-10743511:
Lorenzo Bertolino and co-authors ask whether a leadless pacemaker can be safely placed in patients whose old device is infected. Their 2023 study reviews 49 patients who got the wire-free device between 2017 and 2022. One group had it placed around the removal of an infected wired system.

Most of that group had body-wide infection, and many had germs on the pulled leads. In most cases the new device went in during the same session as the removal. Over a median follow-up of about two and a half years, no infection of the new device appeared. Deaths in follow-up came to one in five patients. The authors back the approach for dependent patients.
pmc-10743611:
Ulrike Wittig and co-authors compare hand measures with software measures for knee surgery planning, in a 2023 study. Before a knee joint is replaced, surgeons measure leg angles on long X-ray images. Small errors in those angles can affect how the new joint sits and lasts.

Two observers measured fifty-five leg images by hand, twice each, and then again with a new software tool. Hand measures of some angles shifted between rounds, while the software results stayed stable. Yet hand and software values also differed from each other on several angles. The authors weigh what that gap means for clinics that plan to switch tools.
pmc-10743811:
Roberto Abundo and co-authors report, in a 2023 case study, how a new ribose cross-linked collagen sponge heals in tooth sockets. After extraction, the jaw ridge shrinks unless preserved, but common graft materials linger forever inside the new bone.

One patient had hopeless lower molars removed on both sides, and each socket was filled with the sponge and left open. Six months later, cores taken just before implant placement went under the microscope. The healing pattern looked promising: fresh bone had replaced much of the sponge, and little residue remained. A fully resorbing filler would simplify later implant work.
pmc-10744311:
Chin-Sheng Huang and colleagues studied radiation resistance in mouth cancer. Oral squamous cell carcinoma is a common oral cancer. Radiation often fails when tumors become resistant. Many possible drug targets remain poorly explored. The team screened kinase genes in resistant cell lines. One kinase, called DYRK3, stood out strongly. A partner enzyme, called PAICS, also drew attention. Both connect to building blocks for cell growth. Human tissue samples and cell models were used.

Resistant cancer cells were built in the laboratory. Gene and protein patterns were compared carefully. The two enzymes appear to work together closely. Their partnership may help tumors survive radiation. Cell structures called purinosomes organize that growth chemistry. Blocking the partnership could restore radiation sensitivity. The study maps a possible new treatment route. Further tests must confirm the mechanism first.
pmc-10744811:
Koichiro Hayashi and co-authors show that the shape of the empty space inside a bone scaffold steers how new bone and vessels grow. Surgeons use printed scaffolds to rebuild bone, and the inner channels decide how cells wander in. Their 2023 paper prints carbonate apatite scaffolds whose channels allow cell movement in one, two, or three dimensions, with the same gap size throughout.

The scaffolds sat in rabbit thigh bones for four weeks. In the one-dimensional channels, the new blood vessels grew two and a half to four times larger and far better aligned than in the freer spaces. Bone formation there was also about forty percent higher. The authors reason that single-file movement stops vessels from branching wastefully, while open spaces invite random wandering. The design lesson is simple and strong: narrow, directed channels grow the big, straight vessels that feeding new bone requires.
pmc-10745411:
Yifan Wu and co-authors compare gut microbes in rats under two harms in 2023. One harm is lack of selenium in the diet, and the other is a fungal toxin. Both are tied to a joint disease that deforms bones in children in some regions.

Knee and stool samples were taken, and gene sequencing mapped the gut mix. Two large microbe groups dominated in both harm groups, at slightly different shares. Certain genera ran higher in the low-selenium group, while others led in the toxin group. Two species stood out as markers for the toxin group, giving a base for study of the joint disease.
pmc-10746511:
Syed Asadullah and colleagues coated polyimide composites with tantalum pentoxide for orthopedic implants. Their 2023 paper targets better bone integration of implant materials. Polyimide is strong, stable, and kind to living tissue. Its stiffness sits close to that of human bone. It lacks bioactivity, though, which cells need to attach and grow.

A polydopamine layer bonded the oxide coating to the polyimide surface. More oxide in the mix left more particles on the surface. The coating raised surface roughness and water attraction. Bone marrow stromal cells grew better on coated samples. They attached more readily and shifted toward bone-forming behavior. The authors say the coating lifts both compatibility and bioactivity. Polyimide could thus serve more widely in bone repair.
pmc-10747711:
Ying Li and co-authors improve speech sound alignment for clinicians in a 2023 paper. Phonetic transcription helps diagnose speech sound disorders, but it depends on the transcriber's ear and can carry bias. Forced alignment tools mark what was said and where, yet most need a hand written transcript first. Their model works with no transcript.

A pretrained wav2vec model splits speech into tokens and labels sounds on its own. An unsupervised tool sets sound boundaries, and extra cleaning steps sharpen the result. Scores on a normal speech set and a disorder speech set are competitive, they report. The method promises more objective assessment.
pmc-10748311:
Lina Hou and co-authors strengthened desert sand concrete with two kinds of fibers in a 2023 study. Desert sand is plentiful where river sand is scarce, but the concrete it makes can be brittle. Plastic and glass fibers were mixed in at varied doses, alone and together.

Fiber mixes cut the fresh concrete's flow, glass more than plastic. Strength gains ran largest in bending, then splitting, then crushing. A small equal blend of both fibers lifted bending strength by about forty percent. Pore scans showed the blend halved the void share and shrank large pores. Microscopy showed fibers, cement, and grains locked in a dense web. The authors credit fibers with bridging cracks at different load stages.
pmc-10748411:
Ni Zhou and co-authors review how metal ions in the body shape heart harm from a cancer drug, in work from 2023. The drug is widely used against many tumors, but it can damage the heart. Finding ways to cut that harm is an urgent need.

The review sums up decades of work on ions such as iron, copper, zinc, and calcium inside cells. Shifts in these ions can feed or curb the heart harm, in part through an iron-linked cell death path. Plans that target the ions look safe and promising in early work. The authors hope the lessons will also help with heart harm from other drugs.
pmc-10750411:
Sara Biagiotti, Elena Perla, and Mauro Magnani review red blood cells as drug carriers in a 2023 article. The cells that ferry oxygen also, by their nature, soak up and hold many drugs. Their walls carry gates that let compounds in and out, and their insides offer binding sites. So a drug's fate in the blood is partly written by how it partitions into these cells.

The review first tours the cell's normal workings, then shows cases where red cells act as natural carriers, shifting how a drug travels and lasts. It then turns to engineering: loading the cells with drugs, metabolites, or proteins on purpose. One trick boosts a metabolite that makes cells release oxygen more freely, handy for transfusion. Another preloads enzymes that could treat disease from inside the circulation. The authors map a carrier the body already makes by the trillion.
pmc-10751811:
Seven authors present a study from two thousand twenty-three on screening heart patients for an under-skin defibrillator. The device watches for dangerous rhythms and shocks the heart, but the heartbeat pattern during pacing must pass an automated screen first. Pacing can come from several sites in the heart, and fit may depend on the site.

One hundred two patients with pacing devices were screened at one center. Pacing sites included the heart's natural conduction system, both ventricles, and single right-side spots. Screening passed far more often with conduction system pacing than with the other sites. The authors also hunt for tracing features that predict a pass.
pmc-10755611:
Sayaka Fukuda and four co-authors, with the Japan Environment and Children's Study Group, ask whether a mother's folic acid level affects her baby's risk of Kawasaki disease, in a 2023 study. The disease inflames blood vessels in infants and small children, and no firm risk factors were known. A previous report had hinted at a folate link.

The nationwide birth cohort followed 87,702 children for their first year; 336 developed the disease. Mothers who took supplements had higher blood folate, as expected. Babies of mothers with higher late-pregnancy folate levels developed Kawasaki disease less often: 0.27 percent versus 0.41 percent, about a third lower odds after adjustment. Supplement timing analyses accompanied the blood-level result. The authors present folate status as the first reproducible lead on preventing this puzzling illness, while stopping short of prescribing supplements for that purpose.
pmc-10756211:
Saeed Sovizi leads a team of ten authors who review how blasting atom-thin semiconductors with plasma changes their traits on purpose. Two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides promise next-generation optoelectronics. But how devices work hinges on defects, surfaces, and interfaces that are hard to control. Plasma treatment is cheap, easy to steer, and scalable, and these materials react strongly to it.

The review lists the roles of plasma: adding functional groups, engineering defects, doping, oxidizing, switching crystal phases, etching, healing damage, reshaping morphology, and changing surface energy. It covers the plasma science behind it and the synthesis of high-quality material. The team place plasma processing as the all-round workbench to tailor these materials to set devices.
pmc-10756911:
A vine fruit used in Chinese medicine sells well, and its quality depends on where the plant grows. Jingjing Shang and co-authors mapped the plant's best ground in this 2023 study. The plant is Schisandra sphenanthera, and its dried fruit is a long-used remedy. Climate and soil shape both where it thrives and how much active compound its fruit holds.

The team built a habitat model tuned for accuracy and ran it for current and future climates. Three future paths, from low to high emissions, were tested. Under today's climate, good ground covered about nineteen percent of China. The model also flagged which factors — rain, heat, soil — most drive the plant's spread and its medicine content. Growers and conservation teams can use the map to pick planting sites as the climate shifts.
pmc-10758611:
Ruben Alejandro Ortiz-Guerra and co-authors catalog what social media says about penile cancer, a rare and little-discussed disease. They gathered posts under three hashtags across Twitter, Facebook, and Instagram over one year, with two blinded reviewers sorting each post. Nearly 800 posts qualified.

Twitter held half the posts, and most came from rich countries, led by the United Kingdom. Support communities and clinicians wrote most content; urologists led among doctors. Prevention and awareness posts dominated. Counts did not track disease rates. The authors urge a shared space where doctors and the public actually meet.
pmc-10767911:
Milacic, Beavers, Conley, and co-authors describe the 2024 edition of the Reactome Pathway Knowledgebase. Reactome is a free, expert-checked store of how molecules act together inside cells. It covers normal body processes and also processes that go wrong in disease, all checked by hand.

Each process is stored as an ordered chain of molecular events, from a signal arriving to a cell response. That structure lets researchers place their own data on known pathways and spot what changed. As a core shared resource, Reactome helps labs compare results and build on the same trusted map.
pmc-10768511:
Christina Oleson and co-authors report in 2023 the case of a woman whose spinal cord was damaged by a blood clot during a COVID-19 infection.
