Cord strokes of this kind are very rare after the virus, and their long course had not been described. The patient, a woman aged seventy, lost feeling and movement below the chest at once.

Tests confirmed complete paraplegia from the clot. Her pain, spasms, and bladder troubles were worse than those of many patients with like injuries, and she needed six extra hospital stays in the first year for infections or pain. Bowel problems and skin damage stayed mild. The case shows the added burden when long COVID follows a cord injury.
pmc-10774811: Rachad Ghazal and four co-authors describe a rare heart case in a 2023 report. A patient arrived with a new irregular heartbeat known as atrial fibrillation. Scans suggested the cause was inflammation of both upper heart chambers, a rare finding called isolated atrial myocarditis. A PET scan played the central role in spotting the inflammation. The case shows how rhythm problems can present in unusual ways. It also weighs choices for long-term treatment once this rare diagnosis is made.
pmc-10777411:
Adriana Marsola leads a team that makes foam from waste streams. Their study from twenty twenty-three uses PET waste, fly ash, and glass waste. The foam is a flexible polyurethane type.

PET was broken down by a heated glycol process first. The products were mixed with other parts and fillers. Foam samples were checked by light, scope, and stress tests. Low filler samples gave the best strength in tests. High filler samples stood heat the best of all. Waste based foams could cut use of new stock.  Heat tests completed the set of checks used.
pmc-10797411:
Ershi Hua and five co-workers wrote a 2023 review on a family of enzymes called DPP4 and their links to lung disease. One member sits in cell walls across many tissues and is most active in lung and gut. It cuts a wide range of signal molecules. Drugs that block it are used for type 2 diabetes.

A sister enzyme, DPP9, may act in like ways inside cells. It plays roles in cell survival, growth, movement and death. Recent work ties it to a sensor that triggers cell death by swelling. The review searches the literature for both enzymes in lung disease and sums up the links.
pmc-10805811:
Rena Selya remembers Everett Mendelsohn, the Harvard historian of science who advised her doctoral work, in a personal tribute written after his death. She recalls arriving for a graduate interview on a snowy day in 1996 and leaving with a mentor who shaped her path to a 2002 doctorate. Mendelsohn steered her toward writing on Salvador Luria, his own friend and fellow activist, and the suggestion grew into her dissertation.

Because Mendelsohn had known Luria since their shared antiwar organising in 1960s Boston, he became a primary source as well as an advisor. He opened his own archived papers to her, helping her reconstruct Luria's role in a faculty group on public issues. Selya portrays a scholar who championed students generously, connecting personal warmth with serious historical work on science and politics.
pmc-10808611:
Storni, Vogel, Bachmann, and Engeroff review how IgG antibodies restrain allergic reactions in this article. Allergy runs through IgE antibodies, which arm mast cells via a high-affinity receptor. When allergen returns, those cells dump inflammatory chemicals.

IgG has emerged as a key negative regulator of that axis. The review gathers the proposed routes: IgG can intercept allergens, block IgE binding, and engage inhibitory receptors on the same cells. Each route quiets the activation of the IgE receptor in a different way. The authors then show how current allergy therapies already exploit these mechanisms. Understanding the routes may guide safer, disease-changing treatments beyond symptom control.
pmc-10809011:
Wang, Okada, Wloka, and Bi unravel how IQGAP proteins control cell division across species. IQGAPs play a crucial role in cytokinesis, the final split of one cell into two, in many organisms. Yet the mechanism behind that control was not fully understood before this study.

Work in budding yeast, fission yeast, and human cells found a shared two-domain module. The module steers where IQGAPs sit in the cell and how the actomyosin ring builds up and breaks down. Strikingly, their calponin homology domains grip distinct actin targets in each system. The pattern shows an old, conserved design with local twists.
pmc-10809711:
Serife Kilicarslan and co-authors studied what factors are linked to suicidal tendency among women in Turkey in a 2024 paper. Their data come from a national survey on domestic violence against women, covering thousands of women aged fifteen to forty nine who were married or in relationships. A statistical model sorted which traits and experiences tracked with suicidal tendency.

Many factors showed links: age, schooling, health, number of children, household income, and the partner's job, drinking, fighting, cheating, and controlling behavior. Exposure to violence, from a partner or from others, also mattered. The authors suggest that prevention efforts will work best when they first reach the highest risk groups they name. Those include very young women, women in poor health, women with low incomes, and women facing violence at home.
pmc-10809811:
Athanasia Vlahou and three co-authors follow in 2024 what happens to a moderately widened aorta over the years. When heart surgery is done for other reasons, doctors must decide whether a somewhat enlarged aorta should be replaced then or left and watched, and its later fate was poorly documented.

From two hundred fifty-two patients treated between 2010 and 2019, the team followed one hundred sixty with CT scans. One group kept their dilated aorta during other heart surgery; another had the ascending aorta replaced. The scans showed how the root and arch changed in each path, informing a common judgment call.
pmc-10812911:
Trpcic and coauthors check how exact lab tooth scanners are in practice. Dentists use bench scanners to build false teeth and crowns. Each scan must match the true jaw shape quite closely. The team tested seven bench scanners on two jaw models.

One model was plain, with sharp edges and posts. The next model held real-shaped teeth like a true jaw. Each scanner made ten scans of each model type. Gold scans gave the true shape for contrast. The team scored both closeness to truth and scan-to-scan match. Results show which scanners meet clinic needs.
pmc-10822911:
Mun-Su Ju leads a team that tests a mixed feed add for Korean steers. Their study deals with fungus, probiotics, and ginseng waste. Tests were run both in lab fluid and in live steers.

In lab tests, gas output rose with the add in feed. Key acids in the gut fluid also rose in most groups. In live tests, steers were split to get feed with or sans the add. Growth, gut ferment, and carcass traits were all checked. The team used stats tools to judge each result. Natural adds are sought for cattle feed.
pmc-10824911:
María Guzmán-López and co-authors test wheat lines bred to be safer for people with a severe, exercise-triggered wheat allergy. In this condition, eating wheat and then exercising can spark anaphylaxis; today the only defense is strict avoidance. Six wheat lines made with RNA interference carry far less of the prolamin proteins that drive reactions.

Chromatography compared the gluten fractions across lines. Blood serum from five patients then tested how strongly their allergy antibodies bound each line's proteins. Some lines bound far less, marking them as hypoallergic candidates. Breads from such wheat could one day give these patients a safer staple, pending fuller trials.
pmc-10826511:
Eva Paradiž Leitgeb and co-authors watch how a diabetes drug cousin stirs insulin-making cells, in a 2023 study. The compound, exendin-4, mimics a gut hormone that boosts insulin release. The team filmed calcium signals, the cells' inner trigger, across whole networks of beta cells in mouse pancreas slices.

At low sugar, the compound woke about a quarter of the cells. With strong sugar, cells switched on faster, reached half strength in half the time, and stayed active longer. Their calcium waves also grew more regular, most of all early on. The study maps how the drug shapes teamwork among beta cells, not just single cells. That network view may help refine drugs that nudge insulin release.
pmc-10833411:
Martin Möbs and Florian Kraus remake and remeasure the crystal structure of niobium pentafluoride, in work from 2023. The compound is a strong fluorinating agent with a classic structure from 1964. Modern tools can pin its atomic layout far more exactly than the first study could.

Crystals grew by reacting niobium metal with dilute fluorine gas, then purifying by sublimation. Powder scans and vibration spectra confirmed the bulk sample was pure. A single crystal was read at low temperature for sharp data. Cell sizes and atom positions came out with much finer precision than before. Individual thermal motion ellipses were refined for every atom. The update gives chemists a firmer reference structure.
pmc-10841011:
Yi Cheng and co-authors run a placebo-controlled trial of stool transplants for Parkinson's disease, in this 2023 report. Gut imbalance has been tied to how Parkinson's starts and unfolds, but whether transplanted microbes actually take hold in these patients was unknown. Fifty-six people with mild to moderate disease were randomized at a Chinese hospital, twenty-seven to transplant and the rest to placebo. Treatment ran in early 2019.

The trial tracks symptoms and whether the donor community engrafts in the gut. A positive result would open a wholly different treatment lane for a disease short on options. A null one still teaches the field about the gut-brain link's strength. Either way, the randomized design keeps hope honest.
pmc-10878311:
Issaku Kawashima and co-authors translate a rapid personality disorder screen into Japanese and test how well it works, in this 2023 paper. The eight-item scale screens in minutes, a rare virtue when other tools take far longer. No Japanese version existed.

Undergraduates first checked the scale's stability over time. Its items hang together loosely, which the authors accept, since the screen samples broad traits with very few questions. Further studies probed its structure and agreement with other measures. The work opens quick personality screening to Japanese clinics and large surveys, where the trait burden is otherwise easy to miss.
pmc-10889111:
Philip Rosenberg and Adalberto Miranda-Filho review new statistical methods for cancer tracking research. Cancer rates are sorted by age group, time period, and birth cohort. Those three factors are tied together, so plain methods can mislead and miss real trends.

The authors built a toolbox of new methods and tested them on many United States cancer data charts. The charts covered major cancers in men and women across race and ethnic groups. One filtering method cut error sharply across the panel. Another gave smooth, well tuned estimates by age, period, and cohort. The toolbox helps analysts read cancer trends with more care.
pmc-10903311:
Pelin Duru Çetinkaya and nine co-workers wrote a 2023 study on quit-smoking success in patients aged sixty and over in Turkey. Quitting late still cuts death risk from heart attack, stroke and cancer. Six stop-smoking clinics in four provinces fed the records. More than nine hundred older patients were reached after treatment.

Quit rates slid from just under half at one month to about three in ten at one year. Men quit at higher rates than women by the end. The authors note the one-year rate matches that of younger adults. They argue clinics should press harder to offer treatment to older smokers.
pmc-10909111:
Nilgun Tekkesin and co-authors screen men in Turkey for human papillomavirus and map which types they carry, in work from twenty twenty-three. Some types raise the risk of genital cancers, while others are low risk. Knowing the local mix helps shape vaccine and screening plans.

The lab tested more than thirteen hundred samples with a kit that can name and count many types at once. About thirty-six in a hundred samples held at least one type. Slightly more than half of the positive cases held low risk types only. One high risk type stood second in frequency yet held the highest average amount. The authors call for fresh checks of vaccine effect and a screening plan for men.
pmc-10911011:
Benjamin Krajacich and a large team of co-authors test a new way to track past COVID-19 infection in rural areas, in a study from 2023. In places with weak health systems, many infections cause no symptoms and go uncounted. Sending medical teams to draw blood across a whole country is costly and slow.

Their idea uses mosquitoes that have just fed on human blood. The blood inside the insect carries the person's antibodies, which can be tested in a lab. The team tried the method in the lab and at five field sites in Mali. Antibodies to several parts of the virus were found in the samples. The proof of concept work suggests insects could give a cheap, broad sample of a population.
pmc-10993811:
Tayler Truhan and Cherie Armour test whether friendships guard veteran men against anger after childhood harm in a 2023 study. Five hundred ninety male veterans in Northern Ireland gave survey data. Childhood abuse, neglect, and household strain were scored beside support from family, friends, and partners. Anger levels formed the outcome of interest.

Strong friend support erased the link between abuse and anger. The same held for household strain under high friend support. Top partner support also cut the abuse link to anger. Family support, by contrast, changed nothing in the models. Friendship programs like Men Sheds may blunt lifelong anger risk, the authors suggest.
pmc-10994611:
Alia Ali Galadari and Moteb Al Otaibi describe a skin case in a seven-year-old boy in a 2023 report. The boy developed purpura, small purple spots from blood under the skin, on his cheeks. The cause was the Valsalva maneuver, a hard breath out against a closed throat that raises pressure in the chest and head.

The boy had been doing deep breathing drills and holding his breath under water at swim sessions. That strain can burst tiny vessels in the face and leave the marks seen here. Few such cases in children have been written up, and cheek cases are rarer still. The report reviews how the maneuver links to purpura and compares similar cases, giving doctors a clear picture of a harmless but striking pattern.
pmc-11001311:
Wen-Yi Huang and co-authors describe strokes in patients with a kidney disorder in this 2023 study. Nephrotic syndrome leaks protein into urine and raises blood clotting, and its patients suffer blocked-artery strokes more often than others. Details of those strokes, though, were little known.

Using a large Taiwan research database, the team compared over two hundred such patients with more than thirteen hundred stroke patients without the syndrome. After stroke, the syndrome group was far more likely to end up dependent on others for daily life. The gap was widest for small-artery strokes. Death and repeat stroke within a month were similar between groups. The authors urge intensive treatment and rehab for this group.
pmc-11046611:
Gurvinder Sahota and co-authors defend the evidence base for situational judgement tests used in medical selection, in a 2023 article. Such tests present workplace scenarios and ask candidates to rank responses. The piece answers a recent opinion article that had promoted a new preference-based way of allocating UK foundation training posts, which replaced ranking by grades and test scores.

The authors argue the opinion piece read the evidence in a one-sided way, above all on gaps between groups. They supply findings it left out and offer what they call a fairer reading of the test's validity for medical selection. They also weigh the test's effects on under-represented groups against those of rival selection tools. The wider point, they say, is how poorly the evidence on these tests is understood in current debates.
pmc-11081111:
Denise Smith describes a university course that sends health sciences students to improve Wikipedia, in this 2023 program report. Wikipedia is where patients and the public actually read about health, and its quality is a public health issue. At McMaster University, a librarian-led course spends a full term teaching undergraduates how the encyclopedia is written, then has each student adopt a health article and upgrade it.

Across five runs of the course, students have contributed to twenty-five articles, adding more than 120,000 words and over two thousand references to solid literature. Classroom discussion turned to what it means to write for a real audience of strangers rather than for a grade. The course doubles as training in information literacy and science communication: students learn to judge sources by being forced to defend them in public, with their names attached.
pmc-11140311:
Prashanth Bajantri and colleagues compare how four dental cements affect soft tissue cells linked to dental implants. Their 2023 laboratory study uses human gingival fibroblasts exposed to cement samples over several time intervals.

Zinc phosphate, zinc oxide non-eugenol, a resin cement, and glass ionomer cement were tested following international standard methods. All four test materials proved cytotoxic, reducing cell viability after exposure. The order of harm ran from zinc oxide non-eugenol strongest, through zinc phosphate and glass ionomer, to the resin cement least. Measurements were repeated at twenty-four hours through six days. The results matter for choosing cements used near implant tissues.
pmc-11157511:
Lalita Simpson and co-authors rebuilt the family tree of one of the largest orchid genera from its chloroplast genomes, in a study published in 2023. Bulbophyllum spans the tropics with its diversity centered in Asia; one section, Adelopetalum, centers instead on Australasia. Genome skimming of eighty-nine samples yielded seventy plastid genes plus nuclear ribosomal DNA, topped up with older sequence data for eighteen more.

Ten named sections proved not to be natural groups at all. Adelopetalum emerged as a tight clade with a relative, sharpening questions about how the lineage reached Australasia and spread. The tree gives orchid taxonomy a firmer skeleton and biogeography a dated trail.
pmc-11503811:
Birk Fritsch and co-authors trim the chemistry models used to judge beam damage in liquid cell microscopy in a 2023 paper. The method lets researchers watch tiny processes in liquid, but the electron beam itself splits water and changes what is seen. Simulations of that radiation chemistry can correct the reading, yet their cost grows fast with each added reactant.

The team tuned the model for water systems in general and for a gold salt solution in detail. Leaner reaction networks still matched the steady state outcome well. The workflow can be applied to any multi path kinetic model and sets up cheaper modeling in more dimensions.
pmc-11532311:
Peter Simmonds and co-authors reported this 2024 update to the official naming system for viruses. An international committee votes on how viruses are grouped and named. Its full membership weighed 203 proposals that an executive panel had cleared in 2023. Every proposal passed the online vote.

The changes add one new phylum, nine new orders, and 51 new families. They also add 820 new genera and 3,547 new species. The update finishes a shift to two-part species names, like those used for animals and plants. In total, 14,690 virus species now stand as established. Reports of this kind keep labs, databases, and health agencies speaking the same language about viruses.
pmc-11532411:
Jessie Lynda Fields and co-authors map the outer parts of bacterial propellers in a 2024 study. Bacteria swim with spinning filaments built from a protein called flagellin. The inner core of that protein is much the same across species. About half of all species add extra outer domains, and those vary wildly.

Atomic structures of filaments from three species were solved for this work. One species, an oxygen shy kind, carries a far more negative surface charge than the others. Grouping the outer domains by shape and charge hints at what they do, from grip to defense. The catalog widens the known range of this key swimming part.
pmc-11533311:
Stig Tengesdal and four co-authors published national recommendations in twenty twenty-four for diagnosing and treating polymyalgia rheumatica in Norway. The working group wrote the guidance for doctors in both primary and specialist care. The goal was advice that is current, evidence-based, and aligned with European and American guidance.

A narrative review of the evidence fed a draft that the national rheumatology society discussed and revised under its standard procedures. Ten recommendations emerged, covering first investigations, comorbidity checks, imaging, and when to refer. Treatment advice centers on glucocorticoids and steroid-sparing drugs, plus follow-up care. The authors expect the shared standard to improve consistency and outcomes for Norwegian patients.
pmc-11533411:
Fan Liu and seven colleagues present a free database of binding pockets on human G-protein coupled receptors, in a twenty twenty-four paper. These receptors are the largest family of membrane proteins in the body and are targets for many drugs. A receptor shifts between on and off shapes, and its drug pocket shifts too. Knowing both pocket shapes helps drug design.

The database holds near 128,000 predicted pockets from more than eight hundred receptors in both states. Pockets came from known structures plus predicted ones, screened by three geometry tools. Tests on known structures showed two tools found the true drug pocket in over sixty percent of cases. Users can search, view, and compare pockets on the public website.
pmc-11535711:
Flanagan and co-authors test a gene-based assay for head and neck cancer in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Many patients see this cancer return or spread, and only some respond to immune drugs that block a protein called PD-1. Doctors need a way to tell in advance who is likely to benefit.

The study ran at seventeen health systems in the United States. The test reads RNA from a tumor sample taken before treatment and sorts patients into low, medium, or high groups. Its scores matched disease control in patients on the immune drug alone and in those also getting chemotherapy. It also beat two older markers on accuracy. The authors say the test is clinically valid for guiding treatment.
pmc-11536711:
Yuhang Li and co-authors study gut germs in golden snub-nosed monkeys as diet shifts by place in a 2024 paper. The monkeys eat a wide range of foods, and their diet differs across their range. Gut germs help hosts digest food, so the mix of germs may help the monkeys adjust when local food changes.

The team compared four groups of monkeys, with samples from 44 animals. They measured what the monkeys ate, the energy nutrients in that food, and the germs in their droppings. Diets and germ mixes differed between some groups. Germ shifts mirrored shifts in nutrient intake, with a strong role for carbohydrate intake in the pattern.
pmc-11536911:
Chunxiao Han, Changshui Chen, Yuxin Zhang, and Haibo Li present a 2024 study of two families with a rare inherited syndrome. The syndrome causes several birth defects and is passed down when one parent carries a changed gene. Only about forty cases had been reported in the world.

The team gathered health records and family history for three patients in the two families. They read the full set of protein coding genes to hunt for the cause. Suspect changes were checked with a second method and with computer tools. The gene at fault makes a zinc finger protein. The paper adds new cases and new gene changes to the small record of this syndrome.
pmc-11538211:
Qian Jiao and co-authors study, in a 2024 paper, a gene variant that seems to protect liver cells against hepatitis B. The gene belongs to an immune sensor family and normally helps the virus infect cells. Patients with hepatitis B carry this variant more often than healthy people, which raised a puzzle.

The team built liver cells carrying a surface protein the virus uses to enter. They then inserted the normal gene and the variant form, which changes one building block at position 707. The variant suppressed infection of the cells, the title reports. It also favored a partnership between two antiviral signaling proteins. Understanding the variant could reveal a natural defense worth copying in therapy.
pmc-11538411:
Yi Wang and colleagues compared foot and walking patterns in people whose knee osteoarthritis affects one knee or both knees. Their cross-sectional study, published in twenty twenty-four, measured foot posture, unevenness between the two sides, walking measures, and pressure under the feet. They also recorded symptom scores and disease severity. One group had disease in a single knee, and the other group had disease in both knees, with equal numbers in each group.

Both groups showed uneven foot posture and uneven walking. Uneven foot posture was stronger in the one-knee group than in the both-knees group. Many walking and pressure measures tracked closely with symptoms and with how advanced the disease was. The authors advise that care should address both knees together, and that foot posture and walking checks can help track this condition.
pmc-11545511:
Maajid Mohi Ud Din Malik and co-authors review molecular imaging for finding cancer early, in this 2024 paper. The method lights up cancer-linked molecules inside the body, promising diagnosis before a tumor grows large enough for plain scans. The team searched five databases for studies from twenty ten to twenty twenty-three and checked each study's risk of bias.

Fifty studies passed the screen. Tracers used with PET scans gave the best marks, with average sensitivity near ninety percent and specificity near ninety-one percent. New tracers for prostate and breast cancer stood out as promising. Light-based imaging shone during surgery, where it helps surgeons see tumor edges. The authors back wider clinical use but call for standard methods and cost studies first.
pmc-11545711:
Jiyang Li and colleagues published a bibliometric analysis in 2024. They mapped research on SSRI antidepressant drugs. SSRIs are widely used to treat depression worldwide. Thousands of studies exist, but overall trends were unclear. Little quantitative mapping of the field existed before. The team searched a major citation database thoroughly. Over one thousand publications were included in total. Papers spanned more than three decades of research. Software tools charted authors, journals, and institutions.

Yearly output rose steadily until the mid two thousands. Output then held roughly stable each year. The United States led the field by volume. One university and one author stood out strongly. A European journal published the most work there. Maps like this reveal crowded and neglected areas. New researchers can find key groups more quickly.
pmc-11548311:
Xianfeng Wang, Hui Liu, Guoxiong Liu, and Dan Xu present a two thousand twenty-four modelling study on sensing steady stress inside structures with embedded piezoelectric plates. Working stress reveals structural health. Passive piezo sensing catches changing loads, but steady loads leak their charge away.

Experiments had hinted that steady stress alters a plate's electrical impedance signature. Existing theory, built on purely dynamic models, could not explain why. The authors recast the steady load within the plate model to close that gap. A working theory would let engineers read static stress from impedance, extending piezo monitoring to bridges and frames under constant load.
pmc-11569911:
Pietro Refolo and eleven co-authors weigh moral issues in health technology assessment in a 2024 paper. Such assessment judges the value of new health tools and drugs. It has long leaned on data from strict clinical trials. New data types now pour in from many more sources.

The authors ask what this wider mix means for fair practice. Looser proof standards raise hard questions about trust. Proof from daily care and patient reports can add real value. But it can also blur what counts as strong proof. The team argues that all these issues share one core task. Assessors must keep their work worthy of public trust as the proof base changes.
pmc-11571711:
Hashimoto and colleagues ask in twenty twenty-four what a dim heart signal on cancer scans means for patients with advanced lung cancer. The scans use a tagged sugar to find tumours, but the heart also takes it up, and the meaning was unclear. The team reviewed several dozen patients who had lost weight before treatment and graded heart uptake by eye on a five-point scale.

Low heart uptake tied to higher tumour activity, more inflammation, and lower body mass. Low uptake plus wasting marked the patients with the worst survival. Wasting alone was common, but its pairing with a dim heart signal sharpened the forecast. The authors read the heart signal as a cheap window on nutrition and outlook in this cancer.
pmc-11572111:
Amélie Kechichian and co-authors trial letting physiotherapists, not doctors, be the first contact for back pain in France, in a 2024 study. A new care model lets physiotherapists working with family physicians assess and manage acute low back pain on their own, even prescribing medication. The trial ran across six multidisciplinary primary care centers. Patients aged twenty to fifty-five saw either the physiotherapist or the physician first.

Disability at six weeks was the main yardstick, with pain, satisfaction, wait times, and care use also tracked. The design tested whether the new model was no worse than usual physician care. Results inform whether France should widen advanced physiotherapy practice. First-contact models promise faster access for a very common complaint.
pmc-11572611: Gowda Parameshwara Prashanth comments in 2024 on how social media shapes mothers' choices and breastfeeding habits. Feeding choices rest on personal traits, support systems, and media sway together. The commentary weighs a recent study's frame against that wider web of forces. Method limits and narrow sampling in such studies draw a caution flag. Culture, policy, and personal factors all tug at the same decision. Future work, the author urges, should trace how those forces play together. Single-cause reads of feeding behavior miss the real picture.
pmc-11573711:
Douglas Kelley and co-authors weigh in 2024 what controls how much of the tropics is covered by trees where rainfall is in the middle range. In such zones, tree cover is hard to explain, and the role of fire is hotly debated. The team used a new Bayesian method to pin down the strength of each force from real observations.

Rainfall had the largest effect, at roughly 12 to 40 percent of the variation. Direct human pressure came next, then heat stress and the seasonal spread of rain. Fire's share was small, at well under five percent, though it grew a bit when human effects were set aside. The team also found a possible weak point in how tree cover responds. Firm shares like these help land managers and climate modelers argue from data, not hunches.
pmc-11574111:
Mengqiang Shen and co-authors test in a 2024 field study whether injecting polymer grout can firm a slope of mudstone gravel. They sheared the slope in place before and after grouting, and built a computer twin to map stress. Before grouting, shear stress rose and then leveled as the ground slid.

After grouting a clear peak appeared, a sign of much greater strength. More grout meant more strength, and the peak came later under heavier loads. The twin's stress map matched the field tests within a few percent. Engineers can use the link between grout dose and slope strength in real works.
pmc-11574211:
Dhayana Dallmeier and co-authors study, in a 2024 paper, whether changes in a heart stress marker over three years predict death in older adults. The marker, a sensitive troponin T test, rises with heart muscle injury, and high levels already track higher death rates in this age group. What a change over time means was less known.

The data come from a study of activity and function in the elderly. In all, 745 people with a typical age near 76 took part, and 98 died over the follow up. The team sorted people into six groups by their starting level and three year change. The reference group stayed below detection at both points, and had the lowest death rate. Groups ending at higher levels fared worse. Models weighed age, sex, schooling, heart and kidney disease, and other markers, to test the marker's own signal.
pmc-11574311:
Heusler alloys built from hafnium and vanadium are candidates for spintronics, electronics that use electron spin as well as charge. Sharma and Gupta run a full computational survey of three such alloys, with gallium, indium, or thallium as the third element.

Density functional calculations confirmed the alloys' stability in their expected crystal phase and pinned down their lattice sizes. Band structure analysis predicted half-metallic ferromagnetism: one spin direction conducts like a metal while the other has a gap, the property spintronics prizes. Elastic tests showed the materials are ductile rather than brittle. The authors also worked out heat, light, and thermoelectric behavior across temperatures and pressures, finding stable performance that suits these alloys to spin devices, heat-to-electricity uses, and optical applications.
pmc-11575011:
Chabot, Sun, and co-authors wrote a 2024 study on a mobile DNA element at the heart of fruit fly centromeres. Centromeres are the chromosome sites that anchor cell division. They rely on a special histone variant called CENP-A, but the role of the repetitive DNA there is unclear. A retroelement named Jockey-3 is enriched at these sites.

Working in Drosophila melanogaster, the team found Jockey-3 is a major part of the centromere transcript output. Its RNA copies stay at the centromeres during division. Using natural variation and a built-from-scratch centromere system, they showed the RNAs remain tied to their own DNA copies. Jockey-3 activity also tracks with CENP-A presence, and recent jumps of the element were detected. The work probes why centromeres transcribe at all.
pmc-11575111:
Fathers shape toddlers' emotional growth, but exactly how their involvement links to a young child's emotion control stayed fuzzy. Nilo Puglisi and co-authors systematically reviewed the evidence for children from birth to five. Searching four databases up to 2023, they found just ten studies that measured both father involvement and emotion regulation in this age band.

No study showed a straightforward direct link. Instead, connections appeared only through moderating factors: how involvement and regulation were measured, and traits of father and child. The authors urge future work to watch fathers and children directly rather than rely on reports, to add body-based measures of regulation, and to account for mothers and the wider family. The thin evidence base itself is a headline finding.
pmc-11576611:
Marissa Ramirez and a large team lay out a trial plan on how hard a lifting session should be for people with prediabetes or type two diabetes. Their protocol paper was published in twenty twenty-four. Lifting weights improves blood sugar control, but very hard effort can feel bad and may drive people to quit.

The planned trial uses a crossover design with three arms. Fifteen participants will first learn seven lifting exercises well. Each will then try sessions at different effort levels, so each person serves as their own comparison. The team will track blood sugar responses and how the sessions feel. The aim is to find whether gentler effort still gives most of the sugar benefit. That balance could help more patients stick with lifting for the long term.
pmc-11576911:
Mild but nagging gut troubles, like bloating, constipation, and loose stools, are common in older adults and often go with an off-balance gut community. Klaudyna Borewicz, Yifan Zhao, and Yaqiong Zhu test a dairy-based supplement drink on forty-six Chinese adults with such symptoms. Volunteers drank it daily for twenty-one days in their normal lives, giving stool samples and symptom reports along the way.

By the third week, self-reported gut symptoms had clearly improved. The stool community shifted gradually, with helpful bifidobacteria rising in the first week. Two less welcome groups, Bacteroides and Helicobacter, fell over the same span. Fatty acid levels in stool did not change. The authors describe this as a first real-world test of the blend in a Chinese group.
pmc-11577711:
Danielle Nunes and eight co-authors describe lethal violent crimes against women in Alagoas, in northeast Brazil, before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. Most such killings are committed by partners, and lockdown measures may have trapped women with aggressors for longer spans. State security records cover all such deaths in the period.

The study compares March 2018 to February 2020 with March 2020 to December 2021. Variables include age, crime type, means used, day of week, and time of day. In total 316 deaths were recorded. The death rate in 2020 exceeded rates in earlier years. The profile aims to guide prevention and protection policy in the state.
pmc-11577811:
Xishu Wang and co-authors report a 2024 gene-based study on sex hormones, reproductive factors, and heart rhythm disorders. Sex shapes who gets rhythm trouble and why, and hormones look like part of the cause, yet plain observation cannot prove it. A method that uses genes as a stand-in for hormone levels can test cause with less bias.

The team drew hormone data from a large UK gene bank, split by sex, and rhythm and heart trace data from a Finnish group and other big studies. In men, genes for higher levels of one female hormone linked to lower risk of a common rhythm disorder. Genes for higher total male hormone linked to lower heart rate variability. No links showed for other rhythm disorders or trace measures in men. In women, no clear links showed at all.
pmc-11577911:
Amna Malik and co-authors record the wild food plants known to four communities sharing one district in Pakistan in this 2024 study. Wild greens and fruits still feed families around Mianwali, and neighbors of different tongues have traded knowledge for generations. The team interviewed members of all four groups to map the overlap.

Fifty-nine plants were named, most eaten as cooked vegetables or snacks, and many doubled as medicines prepared the same way. About a quarter were used by every group. Three groups, Muhajir, Punjabi, and Saraiki, shared the most, while Pathans named fewer plants but kept more unique uses. Each group kept its own names for several plants even when recipes matched. The authors say the knowledge is alive but unwritten, and urge programs to record and use it before it fades.
pmc-11578511:
Ruiqi Xia and co-authors published this global health study in 2024 on heart disease and stroke. Using the Global Burden of Disease 2019 data, they tracked new cases of both ills from 1990 to 2019 and matched them against eighty-seven risk factors. World rates for both fell over the span. Yet heart disease rose in parts of Africa, Asia, and Oceania, with Uzbekistan a stark case.

Eight factors ran against the trend in an odd way, linking to rates in reverse at the country level. The list spans diet gaps, body mass, indoor smoke, and job exposures. The reverse links were strong in some regions and absent in rich lands. The authors say shifts in these exposures help explain why trends split by region. They frame wealth change as the deep driver behind both the risks and the rates.
pmc-11579011:
Tobias Suess and Gerald Kerth study slight left-right unevenness in bat wings in a 2024 paper. Such unevenness, called fluctuating asymmetry, can signal stress during early growth. The team used nearly three decades of capture records for tagged females of three forest bat species in southern Germany, close to nine hundred animals in all.

Forearm unevenness beyond measuring error appeared at the same low rate, under two percent, in all three species. In the best-sampled species, the rate did not rise over the study years, even as young bats grew larger in warmer summers. Strong unevenness did not shorten life or cut lifetime breeding success. The authors conclude that this trait is a poor guide to fitness in these bats, at least so far under a warming climate.
pmc-11579611:
How unhealthy goods firms shape United Kingdom health policy is mapped by Amber van den Akker and co-authors in work dated 2024. Tobacco, alcohol, gambling, and junk food firms are known to bend policy toward their gains. Ten experts built a loop map of that sway in a group workshop. The map shows a tight, self-feeding web across five themes.

Market rule, team-up norms, and firm ties to policy makers sat at the web's core. The group named twenty-two fix points in the web. Two deep shifts stood out: stop treating such firms as rightful policy partners, and put health ahead of profit. Fixes should back each other, they say.
pmc-11583211:
Giacomo Gardella and co-authors test how two amino acids change the growth of aragonite, the mineral of coral skeletons and mollusk shells. Shell proteins are rich in aspartic acid and glycine, and they help steer crystal growth. Their 2024 study grows aragonite in vitro at conditions matched to coral calcification fluid, adding the acids free or bound in short peptides.

Nearly all the additives slowed crystal formation, plain glycine being the exception. The molecules entered the crystals and twisted their carbonate groups, with the four-aspartate peptide strongest. That peptide also beat free aspartic acid at slowing growth at matched doses. Biomineral researchers get a ranking of how molecular form, not just chemistry, steers a shell mineral.
pmc-11583911:
Zhaoying Chen and co-authors profile blood chemistry in early pregnancy for women whose immune systems attack the thyroid. They compared 26 such women with 30 healthy peers using a mass spectrometry scan. Babies of the patient group were born lighter.

The scan found 92 differing compounds, spread across amino acids, fats, and steroids, and four shifted pathways. A slim model picked 15 marker compounds, several of which tied to anemia, uric acid, blood sugar, or birth weight. Most markers also tracked thyroid antibody levels. The authors propose the panel for early screening of risky pregnancies.
pmc-11585211:
Khalil Khashei Varnamkhasti and seven co-authors hunt for infertility risk letters in immune genes in a 2024 study. Signaling proteins called interleukins help run the immune system, and spelling variants in their genes have been suspected in female infertility. The team tested eleven variants across five interleukin genes.

Five separate case-control groups were recruited, each with two hundred infertile women and two hundred fertile controls, one group per gene family. Samples were typed with a mutation-specific amplification method. Statistical checks, corrected for multiple comparisons and population structure, found risk versions at every substitution site examined. Haplotype analysis added pattern-level evidence. The authors read the sweep as support for a shared genetic thread: immune signaling variants tilt fertility odds. Replication in other populations is the natural next step before any screening use.
pmc-11585511:
The LHP Recommendation Development Group sets out shared standards for laser hemorrhoidoplasty, a gentle laser procedure for symptomatic hemorrhoids. The technique has spread quickly among surgeons, but practice varies widely from clinic to clinic. A common baseline would protect patients and make results easier to compare.

Surgeons practiced in the procedure formed the group, searched the literature in depth, and filled gaps by expert discussion. A wider panel then voted through a Delphi process, with consensus defined in advance. The result is a set of basic principles for patient selection, procedure steps, and aftercare. Such ground rules help a promising option mature into routine care.
pmc-11585611:
Li, Xiang, and Duan built this detection method in twenty twenty-four for finding objects in near-dark images. Standard detectors miss targets or fire falsely when light is low. Their model, DimNet, reworks several parts of a baseline detector at once. The aim is sharper features and cleaner boxes under poor light.

A new neck design mixes fine spatial detail with high-level meaning. A fusion module blends channel, spatial, local, and global cues together. The detection head was rebuilt and slimmed by sharing parameters. A fresh loss function focuses on target centers and downweights poor guesses. On a public dark-image dataset, DimNet beat both its baseline and the prior best method by clear margins.
pmc-11586411:
Nine authors probe how a drug blocks drink effects on a brain switch in a 2024 cell study. The drug, naltrexone, is a known aid for drink urge, yet its full play past switch block stays dim. Live cell light reads with one-molecule sharpness track the kappa switch in its skin.

Drink at real doses shifts how the switch meets skin fats around it. The drug fights back in two ways, by switch block and by shifts in fat drift and lay. A kin drug in trials lacks that fat play.
pmc-11586511:
Cristina Bravo and colleagues reviewed movement awareness therapies for eating disorders in 2024. Care for eating disorders often needs a broad, team-based approach. Movement and body awareness therapies aim to help patients reconnect with their bodies. The team searched health databases for randomized trials of these therapies.

Eleven articles with 437 patients met the review rules. The therapies included yoga, dance, body awareness therapy, and psychomotor therapy. No high-quality trials were found among them. Results hinted at small gains in areas such as emotion control and self-compassion. Gains also appeared for anxiety, body attitude, and quality of life. The authors stress that stronger trials are still needed.
pmc-11587411:
Emilia Vassilopoulou and six co-authors translated and checked a parent questionnaire on food allergy life quality in a 2024 study. Food allergy is rising, and its weight on family life needs measuring in each culture's own terms. Parents of Greek children with food allergy, aged up to twelve, filled the thirty-item form.

Eighty-one families were kept for the checks. The Greek form held together very well and tracked life quality in younger children as hoped. Scores linked to how many foods were banned, symptom load, worry in parent and child, and limits on activities. Sex and general health did not link. The authors offer the form as a sound tool for Greek clinics and research.
pmc-11589411:
Jeremy Ng and co-authors survey biomedical researchers worldwide about preprints, the manuscripts posted openly before peer review. Preprints are spreading, but uptake lags. The survey asked corresponding authors about their knowledge, habits, and hesitations, and drew over seven hundred replies from many fields and career stages.

Most respondents knew what preprints are, yet most had never posted one. The lead author's choice and journal policy swayed decisions most; employers mattered least. Supporting open science ranked as the top incentive, and raising visibility as the top motivation. The authors say hesitation persists around the lack of peer review, and that journals, funders, and universities could do more to encourage the practice.
pmc-11589611:
Will Strawson and his eleven co-authors, publishing in 2024, compare the stream of thought in autistic and non-autistic adults. Earlier work on students had linked autistic traits to thinking more in words than in pictures. Whether diagnosed autistic adults show the same pattern was unknown. The team used experience sampling during a memory task of varying difficulty, asking participants to report their thoughts as they worked.

Both groups shifted toward word-based thought when the task got hard. But the autistic group's shift was much smaller; their thought style stayed steadier across conditions. The autistic participants also showed a weaker link between task performance and drifting into social thoughts during breaks. The authors read the results as context changing inner life less in autism, and they replicate the earlier trait finding in a clinical group.
pmc-11590011:
Mohammed K Abdel-Rahman and co-authors present a 2024 journal article on the chemistry of printing platinum with an ion beam. Two platinum-bearing gases feed the process, and the team watched single-layer films react under ion bombardment in vacuum, then checked real deposits. Spectroscopy showed the beam first knocks both carbon monoxide ligands off the molecule by sheer momentum.

That step leaves an involatile platinum halide and lowers the metal's oxidation state. More dose sputters the film, halogens leaving faster than platinum, until pure metal remains past a threshold dose. Heavy argon ions ran the sequence fastest. The authors confirm pure platinum films result.
pmc-11590311:
Jean-Jacques Rouby and co-authors test a breathing support rotation for patients at high risk of failing after the ventilator tube comes out. The French-Chinese trial enrolled ventilated adults without chronic lung disease whose lung ultrasound scores during a breathing trial marked them as high risk. After extubation, one group alternated noninvasive ventilation with high-flow nasal oxygen for forty-eight hours; the other got standard oxygen.

Of two hundred forty randomized patients, two hundred twenty-seven were analyzed. Breathing failure at forty-eight hours was roughly halved in the intervention group, and the benefit held at day seven. Reconnections to the ventilator did not fall, and oddly, when control patients who failed got rescue ventilation, they avoided reintubation more often. The authors still back ultrasound-guided prophylaxis.
pmc-11590511:
Yaru Sang and co-authors track how traits vary in backcross offspring of a triploid poplar clone in 2024, using team framing for a long author list. Uneven chromosome counts cause wide swings in plant form and function. The team crossed a diploid poplar with the triploid clone. Nearly four hundred offspring were grown and measured.

Seed leaves came in twos, threes, and fours. Chromosome counts spread from thirty eight to seventy four. Offspring with mid range counts grew taller and thicker than others. Trait links tied chromosome dose to stem size and leaf traits. Light capture traits linked weakly to the rest. The material can help breeders use chromosome dose in poplar programs.
pmc-11590611:
Bibi Leila Hoseini and co-authors grade scales that measure fear of childbirth in a 2024 review. Such fear is the most common mental health strain in pregnancy, and sound scales are key to finding who needs help. The team searched five databases for scale studies to May 2024 and scored them with the COSMIN checklist.

Of more than a thousand records, 47 studies fed the review, and half of them used one leading questionnaire. Eighteen scales were weighed in all. One, the Fear of Childbirth Questionnaire, earned the top grade, while eleven more landed in sound bands. The guide helps clinics pick a scale with proof behind it.
pmc-11590811:
Bernhard Fasching and co-authors co-create a music-supported exercise program for people with multiple sclerosis in this 2024 study. The program is video-based and built with patients, not just for them. Two Austrian MS centers ran the participatory project together.

Dozens of people with MS took part, from mild to severe disability. Patient representatives and support group members helped shape the content. Family members also joined the stakeholder group. Music sets rhythm and mood, which can lift effort and mood alike. A program people helped design is more likely to be used at home. The study reports how the shared design process worked. Videos let people join from home at their own pace.
pmc-11591011:
Raquel Garcia Romero and co-authors describe use of a strong antibiotic in a children's intensive care unit in 2024. Infections from drug-resistant gut bacteria are rising in such units and are hard to treat. The drug pair they study has been reported to work against those germs.

Ten patients had twelve treatment rounds for suspected or proven resistant infections. Most rounds were started on suspicion, since the children already carried resistant germs. Six in ten rounds paired the drug with a second one for the toughest strains. No germ proved resistant to the main drug, and courses were short when cultures came back clear.
pmc-11592711:
Célia Gotorbe and a large team of co-authors target a surface protein to boost radiation against a child's brain tumor, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. Medulloblastoma resists radiation when it carries integrin alpha-V-beta-3. Cells stripped of that part died in a distinct way after radiation.

The death mode was ferroptosis, driven by rust-like damage to cell fats. Protein levels tracked both radiation response and the cell's ferroptosis shields. Signaling through the protein raised stress defenses via a growth hub. Blocking the protein, the authors propose, could force tumors into this death path.
pmc-11592811:
Saki Kamata and co-authors report a rare emergency: a thirty-five-year-old first-time mother, twenty-five weeks pregnant, whose uterus tore open along an old surgical scar. Years earlier she had undergone removal of growths from the uterine wall. Scans for an odd fetal position found the baby alive but lying wholly outside the womb, inside the abdominal cavity, still wrapped in its membrane.

Remarkably, she felt fine and showed no bleeding. The placenta stayed inside the uterus, so cord blood kept flowing and the baby survived. Magnetic resonance imaging nailed the diagnosis and guided the timing of the rescue caesarean. The authors stress that imaging, not symptoms, saved this child, since the rupture gave almost no warning signs.
pmc-11594811:
Shengli Jing and co-authors silence a gene in a rice pest in a 2024 study. The brown planthopper drains rice plants and cuts yields across the world each year. It also keeps outwitting sprays, so fresh, green ways to curb it are in need. The gene under test runs a step that trims and caps the cell's gene messages.

The team used RNA blocking to dim the gene and watch the pest grow. Dimming it stalled growth and killed many of the pests, which shows the gene is key to its life. The find names a fresh target for RNA-based pest sprays.
pmc-11594911:
Alexander Zimmermann and colleagues search blood proteins that predict aneurysm sac shrinkage after stent repair, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Endovascular repair treats abdominal aortic aneurysms, but sacs shrink in only some patients. Plasma from thirty-two patients was profiled by mass spectrometry. Twenty had shrunk sacs; twelve had stable or growing ones.

Six hundred thirty-two proteins were identified in the samples. After clinical adjustment, several differed significantly between the groups. One protein tracked with hypertension and smoking history. Another varied with statin use. Proteins tied to aortic diameter included a protease inhibitor and a ubiquitin enzyme. The patterns suggest biology that could be targeted to improve repair outcomes. The authors urge deeper study of how sacs remodel after repair.
pmc-11595611:
Natalia Cmikova and a large team analyze the nutrition and bioactive traits of three seaweeds, in a 2024 study. The species are dulse, knotted wrack, and Irish moss. Their health promise, above all antioxidant effects and the ability to slow cancer cell growth, makes their content worth mapping.

Tests covered protein, amino acids, minerals, fatty acids, polyphenols, pigments, and antioxidant activity. Cytotoxic effects were checked against cervical and colon cancer cell lines. Dulse had the highest protein content. Irish moss was richest in calcium, iron, manganese, and zinc. The full profiles help judge these seaweeds as food and as sources of active compounds.
pmc-11597411:
Farzaneh Goli and co-authors study in 2024 the mechanics of pulling a rectangular peg out of its hole, a basic move in robot disassembly for remanufacturing. Parts jam during extraction, and jammed parts slow or break automated recycling lines. The team mapped every way the peg can touch the hole walls during the pull.

They found twenty-six distinct contact states, sixteen of them tied to jamming, grouped by how many contact points form. Geometry and force analysis set the boundary conditions where jamming begins. They then asked where a flexible gripping center should sit to fight it. Placing that center at the peg's end shrank the jamming zone most. Bench tests confirmed the math: the right placement cut the peak extraction force by about seventy-seven percent compared with placing the center at the peg's top.
pmc-11598011:
Xiaolong Wei, Ling Yin, Liangliang Zhang, and Fei Wu built a faster computer vision model for spotting small objects in drone footage. People, bikes, and walkers are hard to pick out from the air, above all in crowded city scenes. Their model, DV-DETR, upgrades an existing real-time design in three ways.

A lighter backbone net cuts computing load, attention units sharpen detail across scales, and a new scoring rule handles hard cases better. On a standard drone test set, accuracy rose over the base model and speed hit ninety frames per second. The authors aim at live watch and monitoring work in dense city areas.
pmc-11598311:
Hae-Chan Kim and co-authors synthesize a new epoxy resin for dual-cure adhesives in this 2024 paper. The resin carries a glycidyl carbamate group, built by reacting a rubber-like polymer's ends through a linking agent. Spectroscopy checks confirmed the target structure was made.

The resin was blended into adhesives that cure by two routes, with the resin share varied. The best blend, at a modest resin share, reached a bonding strength above eleven megapascals. Its surface hardness rated B on the pencil scale. Its surface energy matched standard polycarbonate film, which suits coating and bonding uses. The authors present the resin as a practical addition to adhesive design.
pmc-11598711:
Isaac Lorero and three co-authors tackle a waste problem: cured epoxy resins cannot be melted down or reused. One fix uses bonds that can break and re-form with heat, but those resins turn brittle. Their 2024 study blends ground waste epoxy bits into the heat-fixable resin and hot-presses the mix. The aim was a tougher material that also gives old epoxy a second life.

The blend held up better than the plain resin. Bending strength rose by eighty percent, and the mix resisted solvents better. It also kept its shape at high heat where the plain resin would melt. The authors present blending as a workable path to recycle a class of plastics long sent to landfill.
pmc-11598811:
Saleh Alabdulwahab and co-authors published a 2024 study of a way to generate synthetic sensor network data so that security tools can train on it with no real data at risk. Networks of linked sensors now watch homes and workplaces. Their intrusion detection tools learn from large sets of past traffic, and those sets are most often held by third parties.

The method creates synthetic data with CTGAN, a two-network generative method tuned for tables. A controlled dose of noise is mixed in to shield each real record. Two adjustments keep the shape of the synthetic set close to the real one. The synthetic set scored high on a known statistical test, well past plain noise methods. It also held off the known privacy attacks: singling out, linking, and inference. The team says networks can train their guards on such synthetic data with low risk.
pmc-11599611:
Armand Tchakounte and co-authors optimize a low-cost material, made from volcanic ash and rice husk ash, that pulls dye out of water. The material is a phosphate geopolymer, a cement-like binder built from industrial by-products. Using a statistical design method, the team tuned the recipe's three ingredients against two measures of pore structure.

At the best recipe, reached with a modest acid strength that keeps costs and hazards down, the geopolymer showed the desired porosity. Tests then applied it to crystal violet dye in water. Uptake followed a standard surface-binding model with a capacity near fifteen milligrams per gram, and the speed of uptake fit a second-order rate law. The work points toward cheap, safer adsorbents for textile wastewater.
pmc-11600711:
Samiksha Tarun and co-authors report a newborn found by chance to carry a tick-borne parasite, in a 2024 case study. Babesiosis is an infection caused by Babesia parasites, spread by deer ticks. Babies with suspected sepsis are rarely tested for such illnesses. This full-term boy was admitted with fever for a standard sepsis check.

A routine blood count and smear revealed parasites inside his red blood cells. Further tests named the species as Babesia microti. His mother's history showed low platelets and anemia during pregnancy, and her stored blood smear held the same parasite. The baby recovered with two antibiotics and a blood transfusion. The case urges doctors to widen newborn fever checks.
pmc-11600811:
Zhidi Lin and nine co-authors compare trace metal levels as a diagnostic aid for a common prostate condition. Category III prostatitis causes pelvic pain and urinary trouble, and its causes remain murky. Abnormal trace metals have been floated as one driver. Their 2024 study collected prostate fluid and blood from patients with the two subtypes of the condition and from healthy controls, in matched groups of about forty-two to fifty men each.

If metal patterns split patients from controls, or one subtype from the other, a lab test could back up a diagnosis now made by symptoms. The paired fluid and blood sampling shows whether the signal lives at the gland or body-wide. The authors frame the work as a step toward objective markers for a frustrating condition.
pmc-11600911:
Chengchao Peng and co-authors report in 2024 on clots in the large vein that returns blood from the lower body, in patients on a heart lung support machine. The machine can save patients whose heart or lungs collapse, but clots in that vein are an overlooked risk. The team describes five such patients at their center and reviews published cases.

Twelve further cases were found in the literature. Most patients in the review were on the form of support that aids both heart and lungs, and blood thinning was the main treatment in most cases. The clot cleared in three quarters of patients, and none died from the clot itself. Warning signs in their own cases included raised infection markers.
pmc-11602211:
Manzoor Ahmad and co-authors report a giant kidney tumor case in 2024. The benign tumor mixes fat, muscle, and vessels and makes up a small share of kidney tumors. Their patient, a woman aged fifty, felt only mild belly discomfort.

Scans suggested a huge tumor on the right kidney, and tissue checks confirmed the diagnosis after surgery. The whole kidney was removed in an open operation with no complications. The case stands out because fat from the tumor pushed out through the kidney's entry point and breached its outer layer, a rare feature the authors document.
pmc-11603211:
Bhavesh Shrimali and co-authors track the breeding life of a shore crab in a 2024 field study. The xanthid crab Etisus laevimanus is common on rocky shores along India's Gujarat coast. For twelve straight months the team sampled a fixed stretch of intertidal rock at low tide, sorting crabs by sex and, for females, by whether they carried eggs. Egg counts, egg size, and egg mass weight were measured against the mother's size.

Males grew larger than females, yet females outnumbered males overall and month by month. Egg-carrying females appeared all year, hinting at near-continuous breeding. Male sizes split into two humps while female sizes formed one. Basic life-history numbers like these anchor any future fishery or conservation call.
pmc-11603511:
Samuel Ling and three co-authors pool trials of rich blood shots for Achilles cord pain. Their sum appeared in twenty twenty-four. Three bases were swept for chance trials that set shots gainst plain care, with a set score form or cord width as marks. Six works with four hundred twenty-two folks with long mid cord pain made the cut.

Bias marks split: two works read low risk, three high. Pooled marks showed no true split tween shots and plain care at three, six, or twelve months, on score or width. The team urge strict trials ere shots are a stock cure.
pmc-11603711:
Yabin Guo, Yang Zhou, and Biyun Zeng set out a protocol for a review of muscle loss in people with worn knee joints. The two ills often meet in older adults and may feed each other. Their 2024 plan follows standard rules for reviews and pools. Five databases will be searched, and two reviewers will screen each paper on their own.

The review will pool how common muscle loss is in knee arthritis and hunt for its drivers. Sub-group checks will split results by how each ill is defined, by age and sex, and by place. The team will also test how steady the results are and whether small studies skew them. No patient data are used, so no ethics pass is needed. The authors have logged the plan in a public registry.
pmc-11603811:
Caicun Zhou and co-authors report five-year results for an immunotherapy-chemotherapy pairing in advanced lung cancer in a 2024 paper. The CameL trial had already shown camrelizumab plus two chemotherapy drugs delayed progression in non-squamous cancers lacking two targetable mutations. This update follows over four hundred randomized patients for a median of sixty-five months.

Survival favored the combination, with five-year survival of about thirty-one percent against nineteen for chemotherapy alone. Allowing crossover to the immunotherapy drug at progression blurred the contrast, and adjusted analysis widened the estimated benefit. Thirty-three patients completed two full years of the antibody. The authors present the regimen as a durable first-line option. The long follow-up, they note, is where immunotherapy's tail of lasting survivors becomes visible.
pmc-11603911:
Xiuting Wu and co-authors compare two groups of patients sickened by the same tropical fungus, divided by which immune failure let it in. Their 2024 study reviews talaromycosis cases in people whose own antibodies attack their interferon gamma, against cases in HIV-positive patients. Fifty-four of the first group were set against ninety-three of the second, clinically and on chest CT.

The antibody group's road to diagnosis ran significantly longer, a delay the authors document. Spit and lymph node samples proved the best hunting grounds in that group. Since the symptoms overlap, the comparison teaches doctors which clues should push this fungus up the list in each kind of patient.
pmc-11604011:
Xiaoyu Lv and co-authors report an animal and cell study, published in 2024, on a mushroom compound against fatty liver disease. Metabolic fatty liver is now among the commonest liver problems worldwide, with few approved drugs. Ergothioneine, a natural antioxidant from mushrooms, had never been tested in this setting, so the team fed it to mice on a high fat diet and to liver cells bathed in fat.

Treated mice gained less weight and fat, carried lower blood lipids, and handled sugar and insulin better. Gene reads pointed to autophagy, the cell's recycling system, as a key route, and blocking autophagy erased the benefit in cells. The compound also cut oxidative damage and inflammation markers, making a multi pronged case for further study.
pmc-11605111:
Fathi Abdrabbo and co-authors compare in 2024 ways to build road embankments on soft clay soil, using two-dimensional computer modeling. Builders must pick materials and methods that limit sinking and meet codes. They tested light fills such as sawdust mixes and foam against deep replacement options like concrete piles, mixed columns, stone columns, and sand piles.

Light materials cut settlement by up to nearly all in some cases and stress substantially. Deep replacement also reduced both, though less on settlement. Deep mixing columns stood out for letting crews reuse soil. The study offers flexible guidance for matching method to project needs.
pmc-11605611:
Yusuke Sakaguchi and thirteen co-authors use deep learning to make a slow brain-imaging method faster. Diffusion kurtosis imaging reads the microstructure of malignant brain tumors and helps classify them before surgery. But it needs scans at several settings across fifteen directions, which takes too long for routine use. The team asked whether the heaviest scan, at the highest diffusion weighting, could be synthesized from lighter ones.

They gathered 157 tumor cases from the University of Tokyo Hospital, spanning 2016 to 2023, and trained a ResViT image model on 282,600 scan sets, checking it with five-fold cross-validation. Reconstructed images scored 0.956 on a structural similarity index and about 31.5 decibels on signal-to-noise ratio, matching earlier studies. The authors conclude the synthetic scans are good enough to cut the method's imaging time, a step toward everyday clinical use.
pmc-11605811:
Julie Wych and co-authors set out a trial protocol for a blood pressure drug in new type 1 diabetes, in work published in 2024. The drug has been shown to lower a stress protein in insulin cells. That effect was seen in rodents and in human tissue. One hundred twenty adults will join across several centers.

Patients join within six weeks of starting insulin. They are split two to one between the drug and a placebo for twelve months. The main outcome is the response of a marker of insulin output to a meal test. Other outcomes cover blood sugar control, insulin dose, time in range, immune markers, and safety. Approvals and registrations are listed in the protocol.
pmc-11605911:
Wang and colleagues wrote a review in twenty twenty-four on lactate, a fuel-linked acid, in brain disease. The brain uses a large share of the body's oxygen and sugar for energy. Lactate sits at a crossroads of those energy paths, acting as fuel, feedstock, and signal. A newer process tags gene-control proteins with lactate, shaping immune balance. The review first sums up lactate's roles in the healthy and sick brain. It then turns to that tagging process in brain diseases.

The authors discuss how tagging may drive or ease stroke and other nerve diseases. They outline cure ideas that target the tagging step. They also note that studies of tagging in the brain remain scarce. The review maps a young field for brain researchers.
pmc-11606011:
Anna McDonald and co-authors show that a newer sequencing machine reads tiny RNA fragments as well as the standard one, in this 2024 paper. Small RNAs steer gene activity and mark where copying starts. The AVITI machine's method raised doubts for such short pieces.

The team wrote a protocol for short fragments and ran matched libraries from human, cattle, and bison samples. Both machines captured the small RNA and capped small RNA libraries equally well. Nascent transcription maps came out consistent too. The result supports wider use of the cheaper platform for small RNA work across species.
pmc-11606111:
Bei Feng and four co-authors wrote a 2024 letter to the editor about a blood test method for early breast cancer detection. The letter responds to a study that used a technique called cfMeDIP-seq to read methylation marks on free DNA floating in blood. That study showed the method can flag breast cancer risk in women carrying BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations. The letter writers praise the work and offer ways to widen its public health value.

They suggest linking the test to community screening programs, so high-risk women are found before symptoms start. They also call for clear, personal ways to explain genetic risk, since raw risk numbers can frighten people. Health plans should add exercise, diet, and mental support, they argue. Cost studies are needed before wide rollout.
pmc-11606211:
Noguchi and co-authors test whether a bone-cut operation for bunions can handle the very worst deformities. The scarf osteotomy is standard for moderate to severe hallux valgus, but angles above 60 degrees test its limits. The team reviewed 93 feet sorted into three severity bands and followed them for about four and a half years after surgery.

Scores for pain and function improved in every band, and the corrected angle held steady from one month to final review. Relapse and complication rates did not differ across bands. One score, social activity, improved least in the very severe group. The authors conclude the modified cut can serve even extreme cases, though operating before 60 degrees may give slightly happier patients.
pmc-11607011:
Eleanor Smith and co-authors review immune therapy for cancer spread to the leptomeninges in a 2024 paper. This late-stage spread seeds cancer in the fluid and linings around the brain and cord. Outlook stays very poor, and no standard care exists. Many trials shut these patients out, so data are thin.

The review weighs systemic immune drugs, drugs given into the spinal fluid, and combined plans. Current gains look limited across the board. The immune setting of the leptomeningeal space may hold the key to better picks. Fresh work on that setting is charted. The authors call for trials that include these patients by design.
pmc-11607311:
He Zhang and co-authors design a lighter excavator arm using an auto built stand in model in a 2024 paper. Standard design tends to give heavy, cautious builds for the working device of an excavator. Their method starts with a detailed computer model of the device, checked against real tests for accuracy.

A ranking method, improved with a spread measure, picks which arm design inputs most affect mass, bend, and stress. Those inputs become the design variables, with least mass as the goal and stress and bend as limits. A stand in model built from five hundred sample points feeds a genetic search. The final arm design cut boom weight by about nine percent.
pmc-11607911:
Xin Luo and co-authors probe, in twenty twenty-four, the link between lupus and infection with human cytomegalovirus, a common herpesvirus. Viral infections are thought to trigger lupus, and this virus has been tied to various autoantibodies. Past studies were small or biased. The team combined ten years of hospital records with genetic methods. They analyzed autoantibody patterns and virus infections in lupus patients, and built a machine learning model to predict active infection from antibody profiles. A Mendelian randomization analysis, which uses genes as natural experiments, tested causality.

In the virus group, several autoantibodies were sharply higher and linked to a viral marker in white blood cells. Antibody titers correlated weakly with some measures, the head text notes. The integrated design aims to separate cause from coincidence.
pmc-11608211:
Seonhong Min and co-authors wrote a review from 2024 on using spectroelectrochemistry to learn why lead halide perovskites fail. These crystals are star materials for solar cells and light emitters, with superb light handling. Their weakness is endurance: the soft, ionic lattice degrades under light, voltage, and surrounding fluids. The review gathers studies that watch the crystals with light probes while voltage drives them, joining two toolkits in one.

Those studies map the crystals' energy bands and trace what injected charges do in real time. They follow the halide ions as they oxidize, vacate their sites, drift, and get expelled in sequence under bias. Seeing each failure step as it happens points to fixes: tougher compositions, sealed interfaces, and gentler operating windows. The authors present the combined method as the route to perovskites that last.
pmc-11609411:
Four authors present a study in two thousand twenty-four on a tool to predict death in patients with a dangerous bloodstream infection. The germ, Acinetobacter baumannii, often resists antibiotics, and its blood infections kill many patients. A risk model could guide decisions and care intensity.

The team gathered data on two hundred six patients in China treated across a decade. Statistical screening picked the strongest predictors, and the group built models and a nomogram chart. Septic shock, a high ratio of two white cell types, low hemoglobin, and low platelets each independently raised the risk of death.
pmc-11610111:
An app that retrains the mind's threat habit is on trial for paranoia, and this 2024 piece lays out the trial's plan. Jenny Yiend and a large team describe STOP, a self-run phone therapy of short tales. Each tale could be read as a threat; the app walks the reader to a kinder read by a word fill and a short ask. Folk with hard, lasting paranoia and a proven threat lean may join.

Three arms split the folk: six rounds of the app, twelve rounds, or plain reading for twelve. No therapist takes part; care as usual runs on for all. Scores at the start, each week, and out to six months track the fear. The lead measure is self-rated paranoia at the last check. The plan is posted ahead, so the end tale can be weighed against it.
pmc-11610311:
Abigail Perrin and Richard Dorrell weigh in 2024 what the age of man means for the small one cell eukaryotes and their study. These mites run much of the world web: first food build, stuff cycles, and ties to man's health. They hide in plain sight while the world warms fast.

Which kinds bend and which break in the heat shift is hard to call, and that call counts for the whole web. The read lays out why these mites mat ter to world reads. It then asks how their field must shift to track fast world change.
pmc-11611511:
Chang Sun, Xin Xin Zhang, and Jie Cao test whether a heart health score predicts survival in lung disease patients. The score is Life's Essential 8, the American Heart Association's updated gauge of cardiovascular health. Their 2024 study follows a national survey cohort of 785 adults with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Survey data from 2007 to 2012 link to death records through 2019. Flexible curve models probe the shape of the link, not just its direction.

Each ten-point rise in the score trims death risks by small but steady steps. Moderate health status cut some risks by about a quarter against low status. High status cut them by about two fifths. Cause-specific gains include lung and cancer deaths. Heart habits, the team argues, forecast far beyond the heart.
pmc-11611711:
Liu and co-authors trace the two-way link between depressive symptoms and self-harm in rural Chinese teens. The tie between low mood and deliberate self-harm in adolescence is well documented. Less is known about which comes first, or if each feeds the other over time.

The team used a cross-lagged panel design, measuring both traits at several time points. This method tests if mood predicts later self-harm, if self-harm predicts later mood, or both.
