Rural teens face distinct stresses and thinner mental health support. Clear direction in the loop would help schools time prevention and care better.
pmc-11611811:
Karen Andrea Larrauri-Rodríguez and co-authors probed how reactive oxygen species and the ERK pathway feed each other in cervical cancer cells in 2024. The cancer is a major killer of women worldwide and lacks targeted therapy. Its main driver, papillomavirus infection, raises reactive oxygen, which can over-fire growth pathways like ERK.

Cell lines were tested for oxygen radicals, growth, death, and movement, plus ERK activation by blot, with a database analysis alongside. Early results trace part of the two-way interplay that supports tumor traits. The authors frame the findings against proposed fixes such as antioxidants or ERK blockers. The work aims at targets in a cancer that sorely needs them.
pmc-11612211:
Rui Zhu and co-authors search for key immune genes in COVID-19 using data analysis in a 2024 study. The illness, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, can trigger severe immune harm. The team wanted genes that help explain how the disease grows and that might point to new care.

They compared gene activity in patients and healthy controls, then matched those genes against a known immune gene list. A total of 360 shared genes stood out, and three genes were flagged as key, with signs of a protective role. The authors trace the paths those genes act in and link them to immune cell levels in patients. They suggest two of the genes could serve as targets for drugs, and they offer their combined method as a frame for more work.
pmc-11612311:
Rijul Asri, Humberto Baquerizo, Mercedes Padilla-Register, Maria Soto-Greene, and Jeremy J Grachan present a 2024 study on teaching anatomy through superheroes. Outreach programs try to spark interest in health careers, but anatomy is vast and hard to make inviting. Rutgers medical school built lessons around superhero bodies and powers.

Middle and high school students in summer programs took surveys before and after. Beforehand, about 72 percent were already interested in science and technology fields. Afterward, 79 percent said their interest had grown. Over 91 percent found superheroes helpful for learning, and about 88 percent preferred the approach to normal teaching, even without prior fandom. Diverse heroes also helped some students feel they belonged.
pmc-11612411:
Michele Mulholland and co-authors test if early rearing leaves lifelong marks on chimpanzee brains in a 2024 study. Harsh early settings harm social life, thinking, and brain growth in primates. The team hold brain scans of chimps raised by mothers or in nurseries. The rearing happened decades before the scans.

A machine learning classifier read white matter wiring patterns in the scans. It sorted chimps by rearing type with strong accuracy, well above chance. Mother-reared chimps showed stronger wiring in some bridge and motor areas. Nursery-reared chimps led in other zones, near the thalamus. Some nursery chimps had early social help, which eased gray matter effects but not white matter ones. Early life, it seems, writes lasting wiring.
pmc-11614611:
Tekleab Teka and co-authors test a plant compound as a liver guard in mice in a 2024 study. The source plant can both guard and harm the liver, and which part does which was not known. The team dosed mice with a bile-blocking toxin, then treated them with the compound, called cis-TSG.

Treated mice showed far lower liver harm marks in the blood and cleaner liver tissue. Deep maps of fats and small compounds in the liver shifted back toward the norm. The compound raised two healthy fat kinds and fired a fat-burning switch. Gene reads backed the shift, with harm-linked genes for fats, swelling, and cell stress all turned down.
pmc-11615411: Chathuranka De Silva and Joanna Da Costa report a rare eye event in a young pregnant patient. The case involves paracentral acute middle maculopathy, a small stroke-like injury in a middle layer of the retina, caused by poor flow in its deep capillary web. The lesion followed a migraine with aura during an otherwise smooth pregnancy. Both pregnancy and migraine have only lately been linked with this condition. The report adds one more case tying the three together.
pmc-11615711:
Wei San Loh and co-authors measure the learning curve for robot hernia surgery in this 2024 study. Robotic repair of belly wall hernias has grown fast in the United States. New tools usually take practice before results match older methods. The team used Medicare records from 2010 to 2020 to find how much practice is enough.

The data covered more than 160,000 patients and over 23,000 surgeons. Repeat surgery for hernia return fell as a surgeon's robotic case count rose. Results matched the older keyhole and open methods after roughly sixteen to nineteen robotic cases. Only about six percent of robotic surgeons reached that volume. Training and case sharing may need rethinking.
pmc-11616211:
Zahra Beyzaei and co-authors describe six Iranian children with methylmalonic aciduria, a severe inherited metabolic disorder, in a 2024 report. The disease floods the body with a toxic acid and can damage development, nerves, and the liver. Each child received chemical profiling by tandem mass spectrometry and whole-exome gene sequencing, confirmed by a second method.

All six carried two copies of a harmful variant, spread across the two known culprit genes; one variant was new to science. Chemistry backed the genes: the marker metabolite and its precursor ran high, with skewed amino acids. The cases widen the world's map of this disease's genetics and show how gene plus chemistry pins the subtype.
pmc-11616311:
Qian Yang and Tong Yu study how thinking skills change among older adults in China, separating the effects of age itself, the historical period, and the generation a person was born into. Thinking skill is a key sign of healthy aging, and China now has many more older people facing decline. Long-term data on these patterns has been scarce.

The authors use eight waves of a national survey of healthy longevity, running from 1998 to 2018. Together the waves hold more than ninety-four thousand observations of adults aged sixty-five to one hundred ten. Their lens is the idea of cognitive reserve, the brain's built-up ability to cope with aging. Splitting the three time effects shows whether later generations truly think better.
pmc-11616411:
Mahmoud Habibullah and co-authors test whether gene variants in two antioxidant enzymes track with type 2 diabetes in Saudi Arabia's Jazan Province. The disease floods the body with sugar and stirs harmful oxygen stress, which these enzymes fight. The team typed 419 people, 247 with diabetes and 172 without.

One variant, in the catalase gene, looked protective: people with the T/T form had about 60 in a hundred lower odds of diabetes than the C/C form. The other variant, in the GPx1 gene, showed no link. The authors call for bigger, broader studies to confirm the catalase signal and explain how it might work.
pmc-11616711:
Brodeur and a large team of colleagues show how one gene's loss wakes egg-cancer cells to guard strike in this twenty twenty-four study. The gene helps re-pack cell code coils, and its loss marks some tumors. Such loss had tied to good ends on guard-free drugs for years past.

Inside, lost-gene cells sang more old code scraps and rang more alarm genes. They also raised the kit that shows cell bits to guard cells. Three alarm paths had to fire for that wake to hold in the tests. Mouse tumors with the loss drew more kill cells and guard kin in. A drug that blocks the gene's kin copied the wake in sound-gene tumors.
pmc-11617711:
Florent Richy, Deepa Kumar, and Pierre Freres map treatment patterns and outcomes in non-small cell lung cancer using real-world health data. Their 2024 study follows nearly ten thousand patients diagnosed in late twenty sixteen through twenty twenty-one.

Patients were split into non-metastatic and metastatic groups, with treatments tracked across four lines of therapy. Radiotherapy and immunotherapy patterns differed by group and treatment line. Five-year survival overall was under a quarter, higher for non-metastatic disease. Median survival also differed sharply between groups. Certain treatment sequences, such as chemotherapy followed by immunotherapy, recorded the best median survival among multi-line patients. The authors offer these patterns to guide further studies and management.
pmc-11618011:
Siyuan Bi and co-authors pool trials of digital tools that get college students moving in this 2024 review. Apps, wearables, and online programs promise cheap activity boosts. Past studies disagreed on whether they work, and college students were rarely the focus.

Following standard review guidelines, the team searched major databases for trials with objective activity measures. Step counts and device readings avoided self-report bias. The pooled analysis weighs which designs move the needle. Students sit at a life stage where habits harden, for better or worse. Clear evidence helps campuses spend wellness budgets wisely.
pmc-11618411:
Antonio Pagano Zottola, Thomas Daubon, and Varun Venkataramani reported on a study of inside help for the worst brain tumors, in a commentary published in 2024. Glioblastoma kills in months, and its growth is fed by immune cells that crowd it. The study they discuss found a set of fat-laden immune cells in the low-oxygen zones of the tumor. Those cells eat myelin, the fatty coating of brain wires, and pass the fats on.

One tumor cell type, low in its own fat making, feeds on the passed fats and grows. The same immune cells suppress immune attack, so the tumor gains twice. Blocking a fat uptake gate in mice slowed the tumor and extended life. The trio says the gate is a drug lead, and may improve immune treatments as well.
pmc-11618611:
Benedikt Jónsson and nine co-authors built a transformer model that finds splice sites in DNA far more accurately than the standard tool. Splice sites mark where gene messages are cut and rejoined, and errors there cause disease. Their model reads raw sequences up to forty-five thousand letters long, compresses them with a neural network, then focuses attention on candidate sites.

Against the leading program, SpliceAI, the new method won on several fronts. It matched gene catalogs better and found more real junctions in RNA data from nearly eighteen thousand Icelanders and a large tissue project. It also ranked disease-linked variants in a clinical database slightly higher. The gains are modest in number but broad in scope. The authors argue better splicing prediction will sharpen both genetic research and diagnosis.
pmc-11618811:
Iris Hung and Natalie Faust study how beliefs about beauty shape kind behavior in this 2024 paper. Past work shows that good looks bring social rewards to the person who has them. The authors ask a new question: does a person's view of their own beauty change how they treat others?

Across ten experiments with 4,449 people, a beauty growth mindset made a clear difference. People who saw beauty as improvable gave more money to charity. They were also more likely to get a COVID-19 shot when ads stressed herd protection. The effect ran through a sense that one can affect others. Other prosocial plans rose as well.
pmc-11618911:
Fan Yang and three co-authors study local acute care units in Norway in this 2024 paper. The units were set up in 2012 to treat less urgent patients near home and spare hospitals. How patients move through them, though, varies and was little mapped.

The study covered over thirty-six thousand admissions across one hundred eighty-five units in 2019. Larger units took far more patients straight from hospitals than small ones did. Units run jointly by several towns sent more patients on to hospital at discharge. Rates of discharge to nursing homes differed by region, with central and western areas higher. The authors say the services follow their aim of avoiding hospital stays. They also flag wide local variation for planners to address.
pmc-11619111:
Daniela Brune and co-authors asked what shapes quality of life before shoulder tendon repair in a 2024 Swiss cohort study. Nearly a thousand patients awaiting arthroscopic rotator cuff repair across several centers filled in a standard five-dimension quality of life survey. The team tested twenty-one baseline factors, from age and body mass to sleep and mood, for links with the survey's index and overall health rating.

Average scores sat below general population levels. Men, older patients, and the more educated reported somewhat better quality of life. Higher body mass and worse sleep pulled scores down. Depression pressed the overall health rating down hard, with moderate depression costing about thirteen points. The authors argue these flags can help clinicians spot, before surgery, patients who may need extra support.
pmc-11619411:
Vivian Ko and co-authors test whether blocking two enzymes can slow harm from a faulty protein in ALS, a disease that kills motor nerve cells. The protein builds up in clumps inside cells, marked by added chemical tags. Their 2024 study used a mouse model that copies key parts of the disease.

Removing one enzyme gene delayed tag buildup but did not save the mice in the end. A drug that blocks both enzymes cut the tags and a blood marker of nerve harm. It helped mice live longer in the middle phase of disease. It did not lift strength scores or overall lifespan. The team suggest pairing this route with other treatments.
pmc-11620811:
Mayela Serrano-Rodríguez and co-authors test a protein from a parasite for its power to kill tumor cells in a dish. The study appeared in 2024. The parasite causes a long-term illness that affects about six million people. Old reports hint the parasite can slow tumors, but the active parts were not known.

The team used the control part of a cell enzyme from the parasite. They checked how it binds cell surface parts and how it shifts cell life, growth, and shape. Tests used mouse skin tumor cells, human neck tumor cells, and normal monkey kidney cells. The team also probed whether a drug that blocks cell death paths changed the effect.
pmc-11621111:
Henry Surendra leads a team of fourteen in a 2024 paper on disease risk in Indonesia's new capital, Nusantara. The city is rising in East Kalimantan, a hotspot for malaria and rich wildlife, while Jakarta, the old capital, is malaria-free. Clearing forest and pouring concrete can open fresh paths for germs carried by insects.

The authors call for sharp watch systems and flexible control plans built into the project from the start. They map how the build-out stirs the land and what that means for malaria and kin diseases. Their aim is a capital that grows without breeding its own outbreaks.
pmc-11621411:
Huifang Xu and co-authors map how hard events in childhood link to thoughts of suicide in men who have sex with men. They surveyed 1,138 men about childhood harm, mood, worry, and social needs. Then they used network methods to find which items bridge the far-off harms and the near risks.

Most men, 88.3 in a hundred, named at least one kind of childhood harm, and 31.3 in a hundred named thoughts of suicide. The strongest bridges were feeling like a burden to others and feeling cut off from people, along with low energy and excess worry. Feeling like a burden tied most strongly to suicidal thoughts. The authors point to these bridge items as prime targets for help.
pmc-11622111:
Farayi Kaseke and co-authors study the burden carried by family caregivers of stroke survivors in Harare, Zimbabwe, in a paper from 2024. Stroke care falls heavily on unpaid kin, and the strain is sharper where formal support is thin. Knowing which traits drive that strain can point support where it counts most.

Altogether 188 survivors and their caregivers took part. Strain was graded with a standard index at three months and again at twelve months after the stroke. Statistical models linked strain to traits of both the caregiver and the survivor. Caregivers who felt anxious or low showed markedly higher strain at both points. Needing to change work patterns to provide care also raised strain. The findings give local services concrete targets for caregiver support.
pmc-11622411:
Eunice Ogunwole and four co-authors dose female rats with caffeine for three weeks and document broad reproductive harm, then check what recovers after withdrawal. Thirty-five Wistar rats were split into seven groups: controls, three caffeine doses, and the same three doses followed by three caffeine-free weeks. Ovaries, fallopian tubes, and uteri were assayed for oxidative stress markers and antioxidant defenses, and blood hormones were measured.

Caffeine raised damage markers and depleted protective glutathione in dose-dependent fashion, while lowering estradiol. Most chemical changes reversed during withdrawal, though some hormone suppression lingered at higher doses. Tissue microscopy rounded out the harm picture. The study cautions that heavy caffeine intake is not reproductively neutral, at least in this animal model.
pmc-11623311:
Mooventhan and co-authors test in 2024 whether rubbing ice on the belly moves blood sugar and heart measures in healthy people. Ice massage is a folk and clinic staple for conditions like hypertension and diabetes, yet its basic physiology was unmeasured. Fifty healthy young volunteers took a single twenty minute session of abdominal ice massage, with readings before, right after, and twenty minutes later.

Nothing hurt and nobody reported side effects. Right after the massage, pulse and two workload indices of the heart had eased. By the later reading the effect had widened: blood sugar, both pressure numbers, pulse, and the workload indices all sat below their starting values. One session in healthy people proves little about therapy, the design itself warns, since there was no control group. But the study gives the practice its first careful numbers and a safe baseline for trials in patients.
pmc-11624711:
Mariam Ardehali and co-authors link food insecurity to hard access to care among people with HIV in western Kenya, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Over a thousand adults, some with added long-term diseases, gave baseline data for a care trial. About one in nine reported trouble reaching care.

Trouble rose step by step with food insecurity level. Severe food insecurity more than doubled the odds of trouble reaching care, after other factors were weighed. Travel problems were the top barrier named. The link held across sex and wealth groups. The authors say food needs must be tackled alongside clinic care.
pmc-11624811:
Joy Ardjuna van der Pol and co-authors test whether smart software can speed the slow work of screening papers for a full review of the evidence. They compare a tool called ASReview with screening done by hand, side by side and in real time.

The test case asks whether a higher dose of a biologic drug helps people with rheumatoid arthritis. The tool ranks each abstract by how likely it is to fit, and it re-ranks the rest after each choice. A stop rule was set in advance. The report weighs how much time the tool saved and whether it missed work that mattered.
pmc-11625811:
Kim Meier and a team of co-authors hunt for risk factors behind omphalitis, infection of the navel, in newborn dairy calves. Knowing what raises risk helps farmers protect young stock and improve welfare on the farm.

The team examined 3,445 calves aged five to twenty-one days on 567 German farms. They also interviewed farmers about hygiene and care, and checked housing by eye. Nearly a third of calves showed navel inflammation, though farmers had treated far fewer. Risk rose when bedding was damp in the first two weeks, when the mother cow's body condition missed the ideal range, and with certain times spent beside the dam after birth.
pmc-11626011:
Sara Lovisa and Stefania Vetrano summarize new work that names a cell type as a main driver of gut scarring in Crohn disease, in work published in 2024. Scarring narrows the gut in half or more of patients and often needs surgery, with relapse common. The cells that build scar tissue are varied and were poorly mapped.

Two recent studies agree that fibroblasts marked by two proteins are the primary scar driving population. Blocking the second protein in mice reduced scarring, and a known inhibitor of it reversed fibrosis in those models. The authors say the finding opens a path to anti scarring drugs for Crohn disease, a need that has long lacked clear targets.
pmc-11626411:
Lauren Mueller, Roseanne Wexler, David Lovejoy, Robert Stein, and Andrew Slee test a small peptide that may blunt the body's stress response. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. Overdrive of the stress hormone axis feeds anxiety and other mental disorders, and few good brakes exist.

The peptide, called TCAP-1, is known to counter a key stress trigger. In male mice and rats held in a restraint tube, injections under the skin softened the rise in the stress hormone corticosterone. Given through the nose ahead of stress, it also worked in rats, with a useful time course. The team checked whether the delivery route changed the effect. The results support the peptide as a candidate calm-down therapy.
pmc-11629211:
Gabriel Alejandro de Diego and a large team of co-authors measured in 2024 how common celiac disease markers are in a rural Argentinian city. The disease, triggered by wheat protein, affects about one to two percent of people worldwide. The team wondered whether living near many flour mills, with wheat dust in the air, shapes who carries the markers.

Blood from over five hundred residents was tested for three disease-linked antibodies and total antibody levels. Volunteers also answered questions on symptoms, other diseases, and daily exposures, and homes and mills were mapped. Links among markers, symptoms, and mill distance give a rare picture of the disease outside big cities.
pmc-11629511:
Fornander and co-authors observed how trauma teams coordinate their work, in a study published in 2024. Trauma teams treat the severely injured under fierce time pressure. They must share information and split tasks through talk, or care falters. Training courses teach set communication habits meant to help. The team watched real trauma care and simulated cases side by side. They counted how often teams used specific moves to manage information and hand out tasks.

Comparing the real and simulated settings tests whether training mirrors real life. If teams talk differently on real shifts, the simulation's lessons may miss the mark. The study describes which habits appear in each setting and how much. Its findings can sharpen how team training is designed. They also give hospitals a language for debriefing real cases.
pmc-11629911:
Sandra Tyralla and Eckart Zimmermann test how past eye move errors shape the next eye move, based on how sure the target looks. Their paper from 2024 deals with the fast eye jumps that bring things of interest to the center of sight. After each jump, the brain checks the miss between where the eye landed and where it aimed.

Subjects jumped their eyes to soft blobs whose sharpness was varied to change how sure the target felt. Size was cut on the next jump only when the current target was unsure, the past one was sure, and contrast stayed fixed. The authors say the look of the target before the jump sets how much the miss teaches the next move.
pmc-11630011:
Epigenetic clocks can say a body is aging faster than its years, and earlier work tied that speed-up to poorer fertility in clinic settings. Arge and co-authors tested the link in couples who conceived on their own, using a large Norwegian parent-and-child cohort. Blood from 1,657 couples, drawn around week 18 of pregnancy, fed seven known aging measures for both partners.

One clock in men hinted at slightly faster conception with faster aging, but the signal did not survive strict checks for false findings. A few curved patterns appeared in both sexes, all of them weak. The team finds no firm evidence that epigenetic age speed changes how quickly couples conceive.
pmc-11630611:
Julio Cesar Cavalcanti, Anders Eriksson, Plinio Barbosa, and Sandra Madureira test how well vowel sounds identify a speaker when speaking style changes. Their 2024 forensic study uses formants, the resonance peaks that shape vowels, under a likelihood-ratio framework, the standard for courtroom evidence. Twenty male speakers of Brazilian Portuguese from one dialect area recorded dialogues and interviews.

Style-matched comparisons, dialogue against dialogue, discriminated speakers better than mismatched ones, as expected. Among single formants, the third and fourth did best in matched tests, with the first close behind; the second performed worst within either style. The results tell forensic analysts which vowel measures survive a change of speaking style, and which degrade when a suspect's interview meets a recorded conversation.
pmc-11631611:
Allison Fisher and co-authors present a 2024 study of a year long training programme for people who support those with developmental disabilities. Trainees from many fields rated their grasp of diversity, equity, inclusion, and justice ideas before and after. Forty-six trainees took part across two years.

Felt knowledge rose clearly, and skill at defining the terms rose too. Comfort at speaking up against biased remarks, the doing part, did not budge. The authors say the course teaches concepts well but must be rebuilt to grow applied skill and deeper grasp of fairness and belonging. Knowing words, it seems, is the easy half.
pmc-11632011:
Bofei Chen and co-authors presented this 2024 report on two patients with a rare immune-linked cause of seizures. An antibody against an enzyme called GAD65 can attack the nervous system. Both patients first had seizures, then developed double vision and wobbling eye movements. The pair also review past reports on this condition.

Double vision in a seizure patient is easy to blame on drug side effects. That habit can hide the true cause, as the two cases show. The patients' paths to a correct diagnosis differed, and so did their outcomes after treatment. The authors urge doctors to test for this antibody when double vision joins seizures. Early treatment may stop the illness before unsteady walking sets in.
pmc-11633011:
Taste is a molecule's shadow, and labs spend dear to trace which bits cast which notes. Fabio Herrera-Rocha and seven co-authors built a platform in 2024 that guesses a molecule's flavor notes from its shape alone. Their tool, FlavorMiner, tries many pairings of learning method and shape code, with tricks to keep rare notes from being swamped. Two pairings, a forest and a neighbor vote over rich shape codes, led the field.

On the whole the guesses scored high on the standard curve mark. Turned on cocoa's small-stuff map, the tool pulled out notes and links that hand work would take months to find. Training spanned more than nine hundred foods, so the guesses travel. The team offer it to food labs drowning in spectra.
pmc-11634111:
Software that advises clinicians during surgery is everywhere, but its real-world payoff is murkier than vendor claims. Jianwen Cai and co-authors gathered forty studies covering more than four hundred thousand patients to test what clinical decision support actually changes in care around operations.

Across studies, the systems usually improved how well teams followed guidelines, cut medication errors, and reduced some harms, such as nausea after surgery and injury to the heart muscle. Results varied widely between settings, though, and no study showed a clear drop in deaths after surgery. The authors call the evidence promising but preliminary, and they ask for broader outcomes, more voices in study design, and longer follow-up before hospitals lean harder on these tools.
pmc-11634611:
Yu Chen and co-authors study eye pressure in thyroid eye disease in a Chinese patient group in this 2024 study. The disease, tied to thyroid problems, can raise pressure inside the eye. The team recruited 273 patients and compared those with high blood lipids against those without, looking for which lipid measure tracks eye pressure most closely.

Patients with high lipids, above all the mixed type, had higher eye pressure. Of the lipid measures, one carrier protein, apolipoprotein E, kept its link to eye pressure after age, sex, weight, smoking, and thyroid levels were accounted for. The link was strongest in younger patients, women, leaner patients, and those early in the disease. The authors frame the protein as an independent risk sign and a clue to how the disease works.
pmc-11634811:
Angelo Zinellu and Arduino Mangoni reviewed a growth factor as a possible biomarker in systemic sclerosis in two thousand twenty-four. The disease hardens skin and organs and damages small blood vessels. A marker that tracks vessel trouble and scarring could aid care and point to new treatments.

Across forty-two studies, patients had clearly higher blood levels of the factor, VEGF, than healthy controls. Levels were higher in diffuse than limited disease, in late versus active nail vessel patterns, and in patients with lung hypertension. No clear gaps appeared for finger ulcers, lung scarring, or skin vessel spots. Effects varied by study location. The authors see VEGF as a useful assessment aid.
pmc-11635311:
Veronique Nabelsi, Marie Chantal Leclerc, and Veronique Plouffe interview staff about night teleconsultation in rural care homes in a 2024 pilot study. Quebec faces night nurse shortages in small long-term care centers. A provincial pilot put remote consultation into rural homes. Three small facilities joined over six months.

Eighteen interviews covered nine nurses and nursing assistants. Teleconsultation added value across clinical and organizational practice. Some workflows stayed unchanged, showing stable routines. Expanded scope of practice kept care continuous and safe at night. Collaboration patterns shifted with remote nurse access. The small rural setting, under fifty residents, frames the results. Staff experience was the primary evidence gathered. The authors report the pilot as promising for coverage gaps. Wider rollout would need the same workflow care. Night safety in remote homes is the policy prize.
pmc-11636011:
Shulamit Pinchover and co-authors explore in 2024 whether children's doctors should take a larger role in child mental health care in Israel. Demand is rising, while trained staff and resources fall short. Children's doctors are often the first contact for such problems, so the team asked a broad panel what role they should play.

Ninety two experts, including doctors, mental health staff, and parents, took part in three rounds of surveys. They strongly backed roles in spotting risk, guiding parents, teaching families, and making referrals, plus more training. They split on wider service changes and on whether these doctors should prescribe psychiatric drugs.
pmc-11636111:
Saima Rashid and colleagues study mixed mode oscillations in a fractional neuron model, in work from 2024. Nerve cells fire in mixed patterns that blend small and large spikes over time. Fractional calculus tracks memory effects in such firing across many time scales at once.

A slow fast FitzHugh Rinzel neuron runs under a Caputo fractional difference scheme. Matched and unmatched fractional orders yield varied firing types under set stimulation. Canard events shape the mixed bursting patterns seen in the model runs. Maps, split charts, and chaos gauges chart where order turns into disorder. Entropy and complexity scores confirm chaotic zones in chosen parameter ranges.
pmc-11636211:
Sean Daly and co-authors trace gut germs in 2024 in a low-income area of Nairobi, Kenya. Crowded neighborhoods with unsafe water carry a heavy burden of diarrhea disease. The team wanted to know how germs move among people, animals, and drinking water.

In 2019 they sampled stool from people and pets, plus water at its source and as stored at home. Lab cards detected a wide set of gut pathogens. Some germs thought of as human-only, including Shigella and norovirus, turned up in dog stool. Pathogens found in water matched ones in specific animal stool. The authors say animal contact and water storage both need attention to cut disease.
pmc-11638311:
So Okubo and co-authors study a gene's role in a youth onset form of ALS in 2024, using team framing for a long author list. The gene builds part of an enzyme that makes fatty signals. Its faults were known for a nerve sense disease. Recent links tie it to ALS that starts young. The team screened hundreds of ALS patients without known causes.

One young woman carried a variant that raised blood lipid levels. Her weakness grew slowly over fifteen years. Her father, who feels well, carried the same variant in a fraction of his cells. That mosaic pattern may explain his lack of symptoms. The authors say such hidden carriers matter for family advice. More work is needed on mosaic effects.
pmc-11639111:
Metabolic fatty liver disease is common and usually confirmed by ultrasound, an appointment many patients never get. The five authors test the Fatty Liver Index, a score built from body mass index, waist size, triglycerides, and a liver enzyme, against ultrasound in 500 adults at a Gujarat tertiary hospital. A score of 60 or more counted as fatty liver.

Ultrasound found the disease in 32.2 percent of the sample, and high index scores in 26.2 percent. Male sex, higher body measures, night shift work, diabetes, and triglycerides independently predicted fatty liver. The index performed excellently: 96 percent sensitivity, 92.5 percent specificity, and an area under the curve of 0.92. The authors recommend it as a cheap screening tool and call for population studies and screening programs in high-risk groups.
pmc-11639811:
Zhan-Qiu Liu and co-authors measure heart muscle strain with MRI in boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy in a 2024 imaging paper. Heart muscle disease has become the primary cause of death in this condition as breathing care has improved. The usual warning signs, scar imaging and reduced ejection fraction, appear late, so earlier markers are clinically valuable.

Circumferential strain at the middle wall of the left ventricle can flag early impairment of heart function before those late signs. The study examines strain derived from standard cine MRI rather than a specialized displacement encoding method. A reliable early marker lets doctors start heart protection sooner and follow its effect over time.
pmc-11639911:
The authors study why two-syllable words in Malayalam are easier for people with hearing loss to catch than one-syllable words. Their 2024 study runs three linked tests. Word lists in this South Indian language are a staple of hearing clinics.

First, word score curves were mapped in forty-five normal-hearing listeners across nine sound levels. Next, top scores were gathered from one thousand people with nerve-type hearing loss, split by severity. Two-syllable lists beat one-syllable lists at every loss level. Last, errors across seventeen vowel pairings were checked in thirty-seven listeners. Context clues and low-pitch vowel cues explain the edge, above all for those who keep some low-pitch hearing. Scores fell only at severe and profound loss.
pmc-11640011:
Adamaris García-Juárez and co-authors pack bitter orange peel extract into gelatin nanoparticles for food use in a 2024 study. The peel is rich in active compounds but mostly wasted. Tiny carriers could deliver its antioxidant and antibacterial punch into foods.

An electric spray process wrapped the extract in bovine gelatin at set voltages and flow rates. Microscopy showed round particles, and light analysis confirmed the extract did not disturb the gelatin's protein bonds. Loaded particles out-scored empty ones on phenol content and three antioxidant tests. They also inhibited a dangerous gut bacterium more strongly than a food poisoning relative. Food applications look plausible, the authors conclude.
pmc-11640111:
Martin, Roberts, and Bozkurt tested smart collar sensors in twenty twenty-four that read guide dog acts during training. Guide dogs cost much to train, so too few reach the folks who need them. Their collar packs many sensors, and two learning methods read the stream for ten dog states.

Each method hit near forty percent truth on the ten-state task. One net worked best on thinned data, while a kernel method won on filled data and needs no training. Motion sensors gave most of the signal, with sound a small add. Some states could merge into wider ones to ease the tests, they note.
pmc-11640211:
Chickens in a crowded broiler house suffer when ventilation cannot keep the air right. Kehinde Favour Daniel and co-authors designed a smarter controller based on heat-energy balance, meant to call for exactly the ventilation a flock needs. A year of farm records showed the existing system held ideal temperatures only 74 percent of the time, while their algorithm promised up to 92 percent.

They then ran the algorithm in a real house for two weeks of a hot rearing period, against a control house. Daytime temperatures fell by 1.5 to 2 degrees, easing heat stress. Cooling pads ran more, but tunnel fans ran about half as much, saving energy overall. Mortality dropped 16.5 percent. The authors call the gains promising while noting that longer trials must confirm effects on growth.
pmc-11640611:
Junjie Jiang and co-authors test two feed additives, alone and together, on newly weaned piglets. Weaning stresses the gut, and both lactic acid and the amino acid glutamine are candidate helpers. Ninety-six piglets were split into four diets for twenty-eight days: plain feed, feed with two percent lactic acid, feed with one percent glutamine, or both.

Each additive alone lifted feed intake, and glutamine also improved how efficiently the pigs turned feed into growth. Together, the pair interacted: their joint effects on intake, efficiency, and the digestion of protein and ash beat what simple addition would predict. Digestive enzyme activity rose, gut villi grew taller, and genes for nutrient transport and gut wall sealing switched on more strongly. The authors conclude the two additives genuinely reinforce each other in the weaning gut.
pmc-11640811:
Jana Jaber and co-authors describe the rescue of a man whose neck was cut almost all the way around in an industrial accident. The 45-year-old arrived with a deep wound sweeping 270 degrees, heavy blood loss, and shock. Crews secured his airway, gave oxygen and fluids on the way in, and the hospital team took him straight to surgery.

Surgeons tied off torn vessels at the back of the neck, stopped the bleeding, repaired the muscles, placed a drain, and closed the skin. Afterward he was watched closely in intensive care, with nerve checks and pain control. He survived an injury class that makes up a tenth of trauma cases and often kills. The authors stress that fast pre-hospital care, careful surgery, and close follow-up together save such patients, and they call for standard protocols.
pmc-11640911:
Calcium flashes inside cells drive nerves and muscles, and glowing proteins let labs watch those flashes live. Tatiana Simonyan and co-authors tune such a protein in a 2024 study. They graft parts of a bright, fast protein onto a proven calcium sensor, making two variants.

One variant keeps a steady glow timing, fit for fast imaging rigs. The other bends its glow timing with calcium, fit for exact level reads. Crystal views of the variants showed which parts set the timing traits. A refined build joined timing sense with stronger brightness. The work gives cell watchers finer tools for calcium work.
pmc-11641011:
Dominika Jakubowska and co-authors survey Polish buyers on the health gains they link to dairy foods, in a study from 2024. Milk, cheese, and fermented drinks are common in the Polish diet. The team wanted to know which gains people credit to each food and how age, sex, and habits shape those views.

The survey covered a broad sample of just over two thousand adults, drawn from younger and older age groups. Most people did link dairy foods to better health. Strong bones, a stronger immune system, and better digestion were the gains named most often. Milk, fresh cheeses, and natural fermented drinks were credited most. Age made little difference to the views. Sex mattered only for one flavored drink group, while how often a food was eaten shaped views across all groups.
pmc-11641111:
Lucas Gillenwater and co-authors present an integrated analysis in two thousand twenty-four of immune and metabolic links in Down syndrome. The condition, caused by an extra copy of chromosome twenty-one, disrupts both systems, and people with it face many co-occurring conditions at high rates. How the two disrupted systems talk to each other was poorly understood.

Using multi-layer molecular data, the team inferred which gene programs mediate ties between immune signals and metabolites. People with Down syndrome showed stronger mediation than controls, driven by interferon response, heme handling, and energy production programs. Clustering split them into subgroups with different condition profiles and different mediating programs, including DNA repair and blood vessel growth. The molecular split matches the clinical variety seen in the condition.
pmc-11641211:
Cornelia Bandas, Corina Orha, Mircea Nicolaescu, Mina-Ionela Morariu, and Carmen Lăzău review flat and three-dimensional metal oxide materials for storing electric energy. Their review was published in twenty twenty-four, as energy use climbs with population and technology growth.

The review covers how these two-dimensional and three-dimensional structures are made and what traits they show. It focuses on oxides built from titanium, iron, gallium, and tin. It also covers the electric tests used to judge them. The authors weigh which designs promise high performance for the storage devices that green energy systems need.
pmc-11641411:
Victor Vasile and a large team of co-authors test a new implant for fixing the wall of the eye socket in rabbits in two thousand twenty-four. Breaks around the eye are hard to repair, and no single material has won wide agreement as best. Their implant prints a bone-like mineral and collagen mix onto a titanium mesh.

The powder was made with a high-pressure hot water method, then printed onto the mesh in three dimensions. Tests in cell cultures checked how well surface cells and stem cells stuck and grew. Tests in live animals checked how the implant joined with bone. Both sets of results pointed to good fit with living tissue and sound healing.
pmc-11641611:
Vít Janovský, Marek Maška, and Karel Hána use two years of GPS data to measure how COVID-19 restrictions changed the movement of elderly Czechs who wear emergency alarm devices. The group averaged eighty-four years old and numbered over two hundred. The team also tracked their SOS alarms and tested which personal factors shaped mobility.

Mobility fell by about forty-four percent during the pandemic, with the steepest monthly drop near fifty-eight percent. Alarms raised outside the home became rarer, matching the retreat indoors. Only about one alarm in six needed action, and a tenth of participants actually moved more. City size and housing type did not matter. The authors recommend outdoor mobility programs and telemedicine for future crises.
pmc-11641711:
Abrar Alharbi and nine colleagues measure urinary incontinence among Saudi women and what it costs their daily lives. The condition is common worldwide but under-discussed in the kingdom. The team surveyed 516 women aged eighteen to fifty, recruited in shopping malls for a broad mix.

About a third reported leakage. Odds rose with age, marriage, childbirth, higher body mass, and past vaginal surgery. Yet under a third had asked a doctor, and over half of those saw no improvement. Two in five cut back social activity for it, and half felt it in housework. The authors call for open screening and better treatment follow-through for a burden many women silently carry.
pmc-11642011:
Dongbiao Yang and co-authors present a 2024 study on cheaper strong magnets. Sintered magnets of a common type need a heavy rare earth to resist losing their force. That element is costly, so using less of it matters. The team diffused a mix rich in that element, plus copper, into magnet edges, and swapped in some cerium, a cheaper cousin.

Cerium lowered the melting point of the mix and helped it spread. At ten percent cerium, the magnet's resistance to demagnetizing jumped by over five units. Cerium also spread the costly element more evenly, forming a thin, uniform shell on grains. Too much cerium warped the crystal structure and hurt performance. The sweet spot balances savings against strength.
pmc-11642111:
Arceri and a team including Faldini review surgery for a stiff big toe joint in twenty twenty-four. The operation, cheilectomy, trims bone to free the joint and spares it. It is used for moderate stages of the condition, called hallux rigidus. The team pooled results from prior studies.

Sixteen studies met their criteria after a search of three databases. Joint motion improved by about half after surgery on average. Pain scores fell by more than seventy percent. A standard foot function score also rose by about a third. Complications occurred in about eleven percent of cases, with residual pain the most common. About seven percent of patients needed further surgery. Both open and minimally invasive methods worked well, and the authors advise careful patient selection.
pmc-11642211:
Anita Wronka and Grzegorz Kowaluk add a birch bark waste powder to structural particleboards, in a 2024 study. The powder is left over from extracting suberinic acid. Boards were tested for water uptake and swelling. Strength measures included bending, stiffness, and screw holding. Internal bond strength was checked too. Powder grain size was the main variable. Finer grains cut water uptake at two hours.

Larger grains raised uptake after a full day. Only the finest fraction met swelling standards. Bending strength and stiffness barely moved with any addition. Screw holding stayed nearly flat as well. Internal bond strength improved, peaking at a middle grain size. Fine grains raised surface density, helping surface strength. Coarse grains hurt core evenness. The authors see promise for damp rooms and exterior cladding. They suggest pairing the powder with water-repelling agents next. The work fits a circular economy frame for wood waste.
pmc-11642311:
Weak enamel on a child's first molars can invite germs, but the mouth's germ mix in that state was unmapped. Wojciech Tynior and co-authors read that mix with long-read gene sequencing in a 2024 case study. They compare cheek samples from one child with the enamel fault and one healthy child.

The sick child's mouth held 210 kinds of bacteria in all. Strep and Haemophilus types led the counts. Germ kinds tied to disease stood out more, and overall variety ran lower than in the healthy child. The contrast hints that the fault reshapes the mouth's ecology. Wider studies can test how deep the shift runs.
pmc-11642711:
Lucjan Witek and co-authors test, in a 2024 study, how temperature changes the damping power of two soft materials used to quiet vibration. Butyl rubber and a bituminous sheet were bonded to an aluminum beam, a classic setup for measuring how much motion a coating absorbs. A custom cooling chamber let the team chill the beam while it was shaken across a wide range of frequencies.

Tests ran from just below freezing to room temperature. From the beam's response curves, the authors read off resonance peaks and computed a loss factor, the score for damping strength, at each peak and temperature. Such maps matter where the materials serve: cars, rail wagons, and aircraft all swing through cold and warm spells. The authors offer the results as design data for quieter vehicles.
pmc-11643011:
Toru Sasaki and co-authors listen for a hidden vibration peak in forty-million-year-old amber in a 2024 study. Amber is a natural glass, classed as fragile in a standard scheme for glassy materials. Glasses show a boson peak, an excess of low vibrations, but in fragile glass it is faint. Earlier slow-cooling tests on Baltic amber found none.

Using terahertz time-domain spectroscopy, the team probed the amber from cold to room conditions. Rapid cooling to fifteen degrees above absolute zero changed the picture. With ice formation in trapped water suppressed, a clear peak appeared at a low terahertz frequency. Its position gave a dynamic correlation length, a scale of coordinated motion. That scale matched the static structure scale from X-ray scattering closely. The authors link the two lengths, tying motion in the glass to its frozen structure.
pmc-11643311:
Csilla Őze and co-authors explored turning waste brick and glass into a cement ingredient in a 2024 paper. Common additives like fly ash are growing scarce as energy systems change. Ground waste clay brick can react like a pozzolan, a material that helps cement harden, especially after fine grinding.

The team milled brick powder with waste glass powder in four ratios for up to an hour. They tracked structure, surface area, and chemistry, then tested strength in cement blends after 28 days. Adding glass reduced clumping and raised the reactive silica content. The work points to a local, recycled source of cement additive where fly ash no longer reaches.
pmc-11643511:
Fan Zhang and co-authors present a 2024 tool for fishing drug-like compounds out of plant leaves with magnetic beads. The tool holds an enzyme called COX-2 on tiny magnetic cores, set so the enzyme faces outward and its active site stays open. Compounds that grip the enzyme stick to the beads and can be pulled out.

The team checked the beads with a full set of imaging and lab tools, then tuned the fishing terms with a known blocker as a test case. Twelve candidate blockers were pulled from ginseng-family leaves and named by mass tools. The platform speeds the hunt for plant-based blockers.
pmc-11643711:
Elisa Canazza and co-authors profile collard green as a convenience food in a 2024 nutrition study of the Couve-Manteiga cultivar grown in Italy. The leafy crop is hardy and nutrient rich, and ready formats may raise chlorophyll intake.

Leaves were tested for energy, minerals, amino acids, fatty acids, and chlorophyll. The greens are low in calories yet high in fiber, protein, calcium, and potassium. Chlorophyll survived freeze-drying almost fully and sous vide cooking well. Fresh-cut leaves kept less by comparison. The authors estimate how each format could add to daily intake. Food makers get evidence that processed collard formats can carry real nutritional value.
pmc-11643811:
Xu Duan and co-authors tune a graphene oxide and titanium oxide photocatalyst with a microwave field, in work from twenty twenty-four. Titanium oxide catalysts lose steam when light born charges recombine too fast. Adding graphene oxide and a field treatment can curb that loss.

One treatment, at a set power for five minutes, clearly boosted charge transfer across the interface and cut recombination. That sample broke down a dye under visible light at the best rate in the set, over eighty percent in an hour. It also held the smallest grains, the largest surface area, and the narrowest band gap. Strong hydroxyl radicals aided the cleanup. The green method may generalize to other catalysts.
pmc-11644011:
Francesca Fernandez and co-authors review a family of proteins that may guard memory against Alzheimer's disease. Their 2024 paper covers the sirtuins, seven enzymes found across the cell that steer many pathways tied to metabolism and aging.

Interest in sirtuins runs high because they help run learning and memory in both healthy brains and diseased ones. The review gathers recent work on how each sirtuin acts in thinking, and how those actions falter as Alzheimer's disease advances. It also weighs drugs and natural compounds that switch sirtuins on, as possible treatments or add-ons. The authors present the protein family as a promising but still early target for therapy.
pmc-11644111:
Chao-Ming Lin and co-authors present a 2024 study on cosmetic flaws that plague molded metal bone plates. Plates that fix fractures are often made by injecting metal powder bound in polymer. Uneven powder leaves black lines on the surface, and cool merging fronts leave weld lines that weaken the part.

The team ran mold flow simulations and tuned the process with a Taguchi design, first optimizing powder concentration and melding temperature separately. A combined grey relational score then balanced both goals at once. Yet the joint optimum underperformed the single-goal runs, because melt temperature bossed every other setting. A robust multi-criteria method was brought in to settle the tug of war. The paper charts a practical path to cleaner, stronger implants.
pmc-11644311:
Veronika Pishchik and ten co-authors borrow bacteria from drought-hardy plants to help wheat survive dry spells, in a 2024 study. The reasoning is that plants which endure drought host microbes that help them do it. Bacteria were isolated from the seeds and leaves of camel thorn and white pigweed. Wheat seedlings were then grown in water culture under osmotic stress that mimics drought, with and without the borrowed bacteria.

Several Bacillus strains and one Paenibacillus strain were identified among the helpers. The work tests whether a desert plant's microbiome can be transplanted as a service to a crop. Microbial seed treatments of this kind could cut irrigation needs if the effect survives the move from laboratory tanks to soil.
pmc-11644411:
María Elena Sánchez-Mendoza and co-authors test a plant extract that guards the stomach lining, in a 2024 mouse study. The plant, Heliotropium indicum, has a folk history for stomach care. Ulcers form when attack factors, like alcohol, beat the lining's own guards. pmc-11644511:

Tests on four public datasets showed the approach effective and robust, the authors report.
pmc-11644611:

pmc-11644711:

Infrared spectra and computer modeling pointed to a network in which the treated hair grips both itself and the starch. Microscope images showed the raw hair sticking far better to the base. The authors frame the work as a route to greener materials from an abundant waste stream.
pmc-11644811:
Xulan Lu and co-authors develop a greener flame-retardant coating for wood. pmc-11644911:

pmc-11645011:

pmc-11645311:

pmc-11645411:

pmc-11646811:

pmc-11647311:
Jasem and co-authors interview children's occupational therapists in Kuwait about using research evidence in this 2024 qualitative study. Evidence-based practice promises better care, but clinics adopt it unevenly. The team asked what helps and what blocks it on the ground.

pmc-11647411:

pmc-11647611:

pmc-11648011:

The review covered 200 child patients at one hospital campus, 120 severe and 80 mild. Younger age and longer fever marked the severe group. pmc-11648111:

pmc-11648611:

pmc-11648811:

pmc-11651511:

pmc-11651611:
Michael Forrester, Sammy Petros, Oliver Cattell, Yi Ming Lai, Reuben O'Dea, Stamatios Sotiropoulos, and Stephen Coombes wrote a 2024 paper on simulating the whole brain's activity. pmc-11651711:

pmc-11651911:

pmc-11652111:

pmc-11652911:
Debele Abera and co-authors model groundwater flow in a lake basin in central Ethiopia, in a 2024 study. The Abijata-Langano-Ziway basin sits in the main Ethiopian rift. Farms there rely on wells, while land use shifts, growth, and heavy pumping strain the supply.

The team built a computer model of the basin that joins rock type, water levels, and flows in and out. The model matched real well levels very closely, which gives trust in its picture of the system. It shows how groundwater moves and how it links with the lakes. Water managers can use that picture to plan pumping that the basin can sustain.
pmc-11653711:
Qingqing Bi and six co-authors compared blood signs in COVID-19 patients with and without added bacterial infection. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, ran at a Qingdao hospital. Bacterial coinfection is a known risk trait for death in this disease. They took two hundred thirty-five inpatients over a span from late twenty twenty-two to mid twenty twenty-four. The group split by whether lab tests found bacteria as well.

They read two standard swelling marks and a panel of twelve cytokines in blood. They also counted which bacterial kinds showed in the coinfected group. Readers who treat COVID-19 learn if blood marks can flag a second infection early. A clear flag could speed antibiotics where they count most.
pmc-11653811:

pmc-11653911:

pmc-11654311:

pmc-11654411:

Bone knit in all but one case, at a mean of five months. Head death hit two folks past knit. Last hip scores ran high in whole. The team call the graft fix a sound first read.
pmc-11655611:
Aresh Dadlani and co-authors survey research that maps the film industry as a network, in this 2024 paper. Network science studies ties between points, whether people, firms, or films. Movie data are plentiful, and the big public database IMDb fed many early network studies. This survey narrows in on work that uses networks to understand the film business itself, not just to test methods.

The authors sort the studies by what kind of node sits at each point of the network. People, companies, and films each reveal a different slice of how movies get made, sold, and watched. For each group they sum up the main findings and the data sets used. The review closes by pointing to gaps where network tools could still teach the industry something new.
pmc-11655711:
Nan Ma and seven co-authors show that two routine blood values can forecast survival after surgery to remove cancer that has spread to the adrenal glands. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Removing adrenal metastases is a common local treatment. Yet doctors lacked simple blood markers to judge who benefits most.

The team reviewed ninety-three patients who had the operation. Curve analysis set cutoffs for hemoglobin and albumin in the blood. Patients below those lines faced clearly worse survival in adjusted models. Those low on both markers fared worst of all, for both overall and disease-free survival. The pattern held across cancer types in subgroup checks. Combining the two values sharpened the forecast. The markers are cheap and already measured before surgery.
pmc-11655911:
ChengCheng Cao and co-authors traced a circular RNA that speeds cervical cancer growth in a 2024 study. Circular RNAs are loop-shaped molecules that regulate genes by soaking up smaller regulatory RNAs. The team focused on one loop, circNINL, in tumor tissue from eighty-six patients.

They measured the loop, its target microRNA, and a gene called SP1 across tumor and normal samples. Experiments in HeLa cells showed the loop lifts the brake on SP1 by trapping its microRNA, and that this chain drives cell growth and spread. Each link was tested by adding or blocking the pieces. The axis names drug targets and a possible marker for aggressive disease.
pmc-11656111:
Sharon White-Lewis and co-authors set out a study plan in 2024 to help older adults get ready for disasters. Older people often stay strong in a crisis, yet many lack a clear plan and firm links to their town. The study, run in a large city and suburbs in the Midwest, mixes health work with planning over ten months. Its name stresses the positive role of seniors in town emergencies.

The plan has four parts that match the stages of a disaster: cutting risk, getting ready, responding, and recovery. Older adults attend short monthly talks, build a packet with drug lists and contact plans, and get home visits for balance and movement work. The team also helps two cities update their emergency plans for people with access needs. Tests before and after each part will show whether mobility, safety, and confidence improve.
pmc-11656211:
Jacquelynne Cervantes-Torres and co-authors probe how an anti-cancer peptide enters immune cells in a 2024 study. The peptide, GK-1, slows triple-negative breast tumors in mice and lifts the immune suppression inside them, but its route into cells was unknown.

The team watched bone marrow dendritic cells take up GK-1 within fifteen minutes, faster at body warmth than in the cold. Tests pointed to a doorway called clathrin-mediated endocytosis, with both energy-using and passive steps. Computer models suggest GK-1 fits a pocket on the MD2 protein, nudging the TLR4 receptor into its active paired form. Cell and mouse tests backed that TLR4 route, explaining how the peptide wakes immune defenses.
pmc-11656411:
Julius Schwieger, Chris Weise, and Detlev Belder present a chip that links micro chromatography to mass spectrometry in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The method separates mixtures with supercritical carbon dioxide and needs a fine spray into the detector. Coupling the two at micro scale is tricky.

Their glass chip, carved by laser etching, holds a packed mini column and ends in a pinhole spray tip made by electric breakdown. The tip releases the pressurized fluid in a few micrometers, right before the detector mouth. A shaped channel also sets back pressure with no dilution. The leftover volume is tiny. Tests on drugs and natural products ran fast and clean.
pmc-11656511:
Barbara Bortot and her team name clot cells as key cells in a womb ill, through work on tiny sacs in hip fluid and in flesh of the sores. Their 2024 study looks at how clot cells wake in a long ill. In it, flesh like womb flesh grows out side the womb.

Store checks of proteins in sacs from hip fluid of sick folk flagged paths for clot cell wake. They flagged paths for clot of blood and for spill of goods from guard cells. Flesh dye tests showed lots of clot cells and white guard cells in close touch in the sores. Work on one bit at a time then set sac kinds next to each side, for sick folk and for knife-work checks. Sick folk showed a share of bits with clot marks much more high. That backs a core role for clot cells in the ill.
pmc-11656711:
Mingyue Chen, Min Wu, Yanhui Xie, and Lin Shen present a 2024 analysis of a rare liver and spleen lymphoma. Hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma is aggressive and poorly understood. Removing the spleen is sometimes part of care, and the team asked how patients fare with and without that step.

They combined ten cases from one Shanghai hospital, treated between 2012 and 2021, with thirty cases from the wider literature. All forty patients had fever, and many had enlarged liver and spleen. In the hospital group, six of ten patients died, five within a year. A blood-eating syndrome and low platelets marked worse outlooks. Patients who had spleen removal followed by chemotherapy lived longer on average than those on chemotherapy alone.
pmc-11656811:
Tomohito Takeshige and eight co-authors report a case where one drug eased two diseases at once. A thirty-five-year-old woman with severe asthma also developed eosinophilic gastritis, a rare condition where a type of white blood cell floods the stomach lining and causes pain. Approved treatments for the stomach condition are few. She came to hospital with worsening belly pain and a flare of her asthma.

Steroid treatment calmed her asthma but her belly pain stayed. A stomach biopsy confirmed the gastritis. Doctors started dupilumab, an antibody drug that blocks a shared signal for two allergy-linked messengers, aiming at her asthma with hope for the stomach too. Both conditions then improved: symptoms, blood tests, scope findings, and tissue samples all got better. No side effects appeared. The authors say the case supports the drug as an option when these two diseases occur together.
pmc-11656911:
Kong and co-authors pool animal studies on stem cell exosomes injected into joints for osteoarthritis, in a 2024 systematic review. Exosomes are tiny packets shed by cells, and they may calm joint damage without the risks of live cell therapy. The team searched three databases for studies up to November 2023. Twenty studies with 400 animals in total met their rules.

Outcomes included cartilage damage scores, pain levels, and cell counts in the joint. Compared with controls, exosome-treated animals showed better tissue scores on the measures pooled. The review also compared exosomes drawn from different stem cell sources. The authors present the therapy as promising for a disease with few good options, while the evidence so far rests on animal models rather than patients.
pmc-11657211:
Xingyuan Cheng and six co-authors look for blood signs that predict outcomes in throat cancer, in a 2024 study. The patients had squamous cell cancer of the esophagus and were treated with combined radiation, chemotherapy, and immune therapy. Counts of immune cells in the blood are cheap to take, and the team asked which ones foreshadow how long patients stay free of disease growth.

They tracked more than two hundred patients and folded the strongest signs into a scoring chart. Being underweight, advanced node spread, and certain cell ratios before and after treatment marked worse outlooks. Tumor samples from some patients, read for gene activity, showed that high-risk patients had quieter immune activity inside their tumors. The authors offer the chart as a practical guide for spotting patients who need closer watching or stronger care.
pmc-11657511:
Ruth Abrams and co-authors judge how a dementia coordinator service works across the largest care system in England, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Surveys a year apart and fifty-seven interviews covered staff, patients, and carers from two thousand twenty-two to two thousand twenty-four. A realist lens sorted what works, for whom, and in which settings.

Coordinators act as bridge builders, linking people to support before and after diagnosis. Staff design, culture, need matching, and service links drive the gains. Strain shows in rising caseloads and burnout risk as word spreads. The authors back wider funding with care for staff load. Readers get proof and design rules for a system-wide support role.
pmc-11659211:
Steve Bierman, Andrew Weil, and Stephen Dahmer argue that placebo science needs a new theory in this 2024 paper. Thousands of studies have documented placebo and nocebo effects, where expectation alone improves or worsens symptoms. Yet the core mechanism is no better understood than it was in the nineteen forties, the authors say.

They fault current definitions for vagueness and offer a tighter pair of ideas. One is a generic instruction, the healing or harming message implied in nearly every clinic visit and trial. The other is a law of identification, the process by which a person takes that message as their own and the body acts on it. The paper shows how the pair explains known findings and lists predictions that clinical studies could test. If the predictions hold, the authors say, the lessons would carry into everyday practice everywhere.
pmc-11659911:
Wanglong Gou and a team of co-authors link movement during pregnancy with early delivery risk in women with gestational diabetes. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Activity is a main lever for managing the condition, but its tie to preterm birth was unclear.

Over fourteen hundred women in Hangzhou, China, wore motion sensors around week twenty-five. Eighty delivered early. More moderate-to-vigorous activity tracked with lower odds of early birth. Each added half hour cut the odds by about a third. The share of energy spent at that intensity mattered too. The authors say the findings support active pregnancies in this group, within medical guidance, as a guard against early delivery.
pmc-11660211:
Khyati Girdhar and five colleagues ask whether immune signaling profiles differ between males and females with type 1 diabetes. They measured about forty-eight cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors in two cohorts: adults with and without established disease, and five-year-old children who later did or did not progress to diabetes.

Overall, only two markers differed by disease status. But split by sex, clear patterns emerged: female patients ran lower on several inflammatory and helper T-cell signals than female controls, a pattern absent in males. One marker, IL-22, went opposite directions in the two sexes. Male patients ran higher on growth factors. The pilot argues sex should be a standard lens in diabetes immunology, pending bigger studies.
pmc-11661911:
Dennis Jepsen and co-authors survey medical students in a 2024 German study on sexual health and substance use. Compulsive sexual behavior and sexual function problems have been tied to heavy drinking and drug use, and all share roots in trauma. Medical students face high stress and notable substance use, making them a telling group.

Three hundred fifty-nine students answered an online survey on sexual behavior, drinking, drug use, childhood trauma, and current trauma symptoms. About three percent met the mark for compulsive behavior. The most common complaints were low desire and trouble reaching orgasm in women, and early ejaculation in men. Compulsive scores rose with male sex, heavier drinking, and stronger arousal symptoms. Paths in the data linked abuse history to both sexual and drinking scores.
pmc-11662911:
Zhao and co-authors review in 2024 nanoparticles as a drug delivery system for bladder cancer. The cancer is among the most common urinary tract malignancies, with about 613,791 new cases worldwide in 2022. Recurrence after treatment and poor outcomes in advanced disease keep management hard.

Tiny particles bring stable structure, loadable pores, longer drug release, and better targeting in their account. They can also lower local and body wide toxicity and carry several drugs at once for combined therapy. The review weighs this promise against the two main cancer forms, non invasive and invasive. The authors see a new push for non surgical care from this platform.
pmc-11663511:
Pinar Göktepe-Kavis and co-authors study how the setting of a choice shapes what the brain brings to mind while a person is still thinking. People often picture likely results before they decide, but most past work left out the setting in which a choice is made.

In the task, people saw pairs of an object and a setting, then chose in ways that led to a set result. Brain scans showed that likely results were recalled in brief bursts of activity, as early as three seconds before a choice. That recall matched how well people did, but only when the setting changed the result.
pmc-11663711:
Chris Blackman, Ben Halliwell, and Tim Brodribb test a shared-tray method for ranking young eucalyptus trees by drought tolerance. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four by its journal record. Seedlings of ten species grew together in trays with roots tangled in common soil. That shared root zone makes all seedlings dry out at the same rate, so the comparison is fair.

The trays were dried under cool and warm conditions. A leaf health signal marked the day each species hit a set level of decline. That day varied a lot by species but not by seedling size. Rankings stayed the same under both temperatures. The tolerance ranking matched the rainfall of each species' home range in a curved pattern. It also matched a known weakness measure in adult leaves under cool drying.
pmc-11664111:
Rashmi Sarkar and a large panel of co-authors present a consensus paper on topical tacrolimus in vitiligo, from the Pigmentary Disorders Society. Their paper sets out the role of this cream in treating the skin problem.

Tacrolimus is a topical calcineurin inhibitor that calms the immune system, seen as a viable option for vitiligo. 17 experts built agreed statements through a Delphi process. A survey covered how well it works, safety, and use across its types, plus dose, length, and mixes. Each needed a preset level of support to pass, and holdouts were debated at a live meeting. The result is hands-on guidance for skin doctors choosing treatment.
pmc-11664911:
Xingyu Chen and co-authors report a 2024 chemistry tool for catching proteins in the act of touching. Mapping protein partnerships inside living cells is hard because common cross-linkers leak poorly through cell walls and waste themselves on water. The team built a cross-linker caged by light-sensitive groups that keep it stable and fat-friendly until a flash of ultraviolet frees it.

Once freed, the linker grabs nearby amino groups and locks the bond with a follow-up step. On a test protein, the tool reliably flagged known partnerships under mass spectrometry. It also slipped into intact HeLa cells, which points to future use for mapping partnerships in their true home.
pmc-11665411:
Alexander Svoronos and Nathan Scott report vision recovery after eye massage in a filler accident. Their case report from twenty twenty-four involves a woman in her late fifties. Cosmetic filler blocked branches of her eye artery during injection. She lost vision in that eye almost immediately.

Forceful, prolonged eye massage began very soon after. Her vision recovered substantially following the massage. Warning signs of reduced eye blood flow appeared in later days. Bleeding inside the eye also emerged, likely from massage shear. Those complications cleared without lasting major vision loss. The case suggests massage may rescue some filler-blocked eyes. Speed appears critical when this rare emergency strikes.
pmc-11665611:
Yulei Xue, Ruiqiang Yan, Weiping Huang, and Yanchen Dong present a 2024 paper on a new wideband slot antenna. The design is cut into a flat circuit board and fed by a coplanar waveguide with a conductor backing. The slot has a diamond shape, and the antenna is built to work near 4.6 gigahertz.

The team compared the diamond slot with round and rectangular slots of the same family. The diamond design gave a wider working band, about 55.6 percent relative bandwidth, and higher gain. Gain stayed above 5.5 decibels across the 4 to 6 gigahertz range. The antenna also kept a low profile. A built version was measured, and the tests confirmed the design.
pmc-11666611:
Na Liu and Mengyan Li published a 2024 study of how six related industrial chemicals behave in river sediment. The chemicals, perfluoroalkyl acids, leak from wastewater plants into rivers and differ in chain length. The team used sediment from the Hudson River in batch tests and in a tank setup fed by a steady point source, mimicking a discharge pipe.

In single tests, the longest-chain chemical, PFOS, stuck to sediment by far the most. In the tank, the mix sorted itself over four weeks. Two short-chain chemicals sank deep into the sediment, showing high mobility. Two contamination hotspots formed near the surface downstream of the source. The authors say the patterns can guide where to monitor and clean up these stubborn pollutants.
pmc-11667011:
Rían Manville and co-authors uncover how a fungal channel senses acidity in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The channel, called TOK, lets potassium leave cells and is found only in fungi. That makes it a possible antifungal target, yet how it is controlled was poorly known.

In the human pathogen Candida albicans, low outside acidity raised the channel's outward currents and sharpened its potassium selectivity. Channels from other fungi tested did not respond this way. Mutations and hybrid channels pinned the sensing to three residues spread across the protein. Together they form a network that lets the channel react to pH changes, the authors show.
pmc-11667111:
Norika Liu and Atsushi Nakano wrote a 2024 opinion piece on how the heart forms before birth. The inner lining of the early heart, the endocardium, was long known to help build the heart valves and walls. New work shows that these same lining cells can also turn into blood cells, a switch the authors call endocardial hematopoiesis.

The piece sums up studies, many in mouse and fly embryos, that trace this blood-forming role. It argues that blood making is not limited to the yolk sac and one other early site, as once thought. For readers, the value is a fresh view of how the heart and blood systems grow up together.
pmc-11667611:
Mwakalukwa and co-authors test amaranth greens grown near a wastewater plant in Iringa, Tanzania for heavy metals. Metals in soil, water, and food form a major pollution path. Eating tainted plants can harm the liver, kidneys, and blood. The team measured six metals in the greens, including lead, cadmium, and manganese. A lab method based on light absorption gave the levels.

Manganese in the greens ran from about 68 to 493 mg per kg. Its mean level sat below world food limits but above the Tanzanian standard. Copper levels were far lower, near 7 mg per kg on average. The team weighed what the levels mean for people who eat the greens often.
pmc-11668811:
Zihan Yang, Jiating Chen, Chi Zhang, and Hongjuan Peng review how a common parasite harms the brain, in a 2024 paper. The parasite, Toxoplasma gondii, infects many people and can hide quietly in the central nervous system for life. During early infection it crosses into the brain, and the lasting immune response there keeps the brain's support cells switched on.

Those support cells, astrocytes and microglia, multiply and stay active around the parasite's cysts, and neurons suffer in the crossfire. The review gathers recent work on how the barrier into the brain breaks down, how the support cells activate, and how neurons get damaged. It also links the infection to changed behavior in rodents and higher risk of mental disorders in people, and it weighs possible treatments and prevention.
pmc-11669711:
Li and co-authors test whether ferrostatin-1 protects the heart during early sepsis in mice. Sepsis often weakens the heart and raises death risk, with no good tests or care yet. Ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death, is thought to play a key role.

Mice got sepsis through a gut puncture model, with some pretreated with the drug. At six hours, standard pump scores still looked normal after surgery. Strain analysis, a finer measure, showed clear loss of contraction. The drug curbed white cell entry into heart tissue by weakening a chemokine signal path. Survival was tracked for forty-eight hours.
pmc-11669911:
Chengzhi Hou and six co-authors test which blood indices best predict death after heart or brain events in a 2024 study. Survivors of heart attacks, heart failure, and strokes face years of elevated risk. Inflammation and poor nutrition both track with worse outcomes in this group.

United States survey data from 1999 to 2010 supplied the survivor cohort. Seven combined indices that blend inflammation and nutrition measures were compared. Survival curves and accuracy tests ranked how well each index foresaw death from any cause and from heart causes. Adjusted models and flexible curve checks confirmed the ranking. One index emerged as the strongest predictor. Such a score could help clinics focus follow-up on the frailest survivors.
pmc-11670811:
Some words sound like what they mean, as with rattle for a shaking noise, and this likeness is called iconicity.
