Hinano Iida and Kimi Akita asked native speakers of Japanese and English to rate Japanese sound words, such as gatagata for rattling and butsubutsu for murmuring, along with their English equivalents. Each judge scored how iconic and how familiar each word felt.

Two patterns stood out. People rated words from their own language as more iconic than words from the other language, echoing earlier findings in sign language. Within their own language, the more familiar a word felt, the more iconic it seemed. The authors conclude that iconicity is not fixed in the word itself. It grows with language experience, so a sound that feels obvious to a native speaker can seem arbitrary to an outsider.
pmc-11671211:
Somit Jain and co-authors blend two forecasting styles to predict COVID-19 case counts in this 2024 study. Classic statistical models catch trends and seasons but miss sudden curves; neural networks catch curves but can miss structure. The team combined both and tested the hybrid on case data from India, Brazil, Russia, and America.

The hybrid's average forecast error came to 2.4 percent, beating the classic model, two neural rivals, and a popular forecasting tool, whose best score was 2.9 percent. Gains held across the countries studied and across several error measures. The authors say sharper forecasts of this kind help health officials place staff and supplies before surges hit.
pmc-11671511:
Rodrigo Dantas and five co-authors review nerve stimulation as a treatment for spinal cord injury, focusing on a method that implants electrodes on lower spine nerves. Cord injury can cut movement, feeling, and body control by breaking nerve links. The implant method, placed by keyhole surgery, stimulates paralyzed muscles directly.

Recent reports show gains in mobility, sexual function, and bladder and bowel control in people with long standing injury. The review revisits how the method may work, through brain and spine rewiring and tuning of automatic body functions. It also weighs future uses and tweaks. The authors present nerve tuning as a partner to standard rehab, offering hope for daily function.
pmc-11671811:
Cristobal Calvillo, Alexandra Marshall, Stefani Gafford, and Brooke Montgomery review partner violence and sexual health in 2024. Abuse by a partner harms body and mind, and it has long been tied to worse sexual health. Evidence across varied adult groups needed an update.

The review gathered peer-reviewed studies from 2014 to early 2024 under standard rules. Twenty-seven articles passed screening and quality checks. Abuse tied consistently to more infections, unplanned pregnancies, and sexual problems, plus lower satisfaction. Most studies focused on heterosexual women, leaving men and transgender people under-studied. The authors call for wider, more careful research.
pmc-11672211:
Ali Jawad and co-authors test a nutrient on pig embryos in a 2024 lab study. The compound, myo-inositol, is the most common form of a vitamin-like substance and acts against cell damage. It aids growth and breeding in mammals, but its role in pig embryos made by activation in the lab was not known.

The team added several doses of the compound to the growth fluid of activated pig embryos. Mid and high doses raised the share of embryos reaching the blastocyst stage. The high dose also raised a protective chemical inside cells and lowered harmful oxygen byproducts. Death rates among embryo cells fell, and the cells' power units worked better. Gene tests pointed to stronger damage defense as part of the effect.
pmc-11672311:
Muhammad Sheeraz and co-authors studied in 2024 why a lead-free material that holds electric polarization loses that charge in humid air. The material is prized for memory devices and green energy tools, but making thin films of it is hard because two of its atoms escape easily. Film structure changed with thickness as strain eased.

Fully relaxed films formed tiny pillar crystals and steadily lost switchable charge in air. Water splitting at the surface added hydrogen ions, which gathered at charged walls inside the material and pinned them in place. That pinning explains the loss. The finding may also guide catalysts that split water, the authors note.
pmc-11672411:
Zhendong Zhu and co-authors test whether longer days improve sperm quality in rams, in a 2024 paper. Twenty-five rams were split into five groups kept under twelve, fourteen, sixteen, eighteen, or twenty hours of light for three months. Semen was then collected four times from each ram and checked for motion, shape, count, and membrane health, along with hormone and chemistry measures.

The sixteen-hour group came out best: stronger motion, higher counts, more volume, and sounder membranes than the twelve-hour controls, with fewer abnormal sperm. Its semen chemistry shifted widely, with hundreds of changed compounds and richer amino acids. Blood hormones tied to reproduction also rose. An antioxidant enzyme peaked at sixteen hours and faded at longer exposures.
pmc-11672611:
Agnija Kivrane and a large team track how fast an inflammation marker falls once tuberculosis treatment starts, and what shapes that fall. C-reactive protein is cheap to measure, but its worth for watching treatment response was unsettled. A slow fall might warn of failure ahead.

Forty-two patients with drug-sensitive lung tuberculosis began the standard six-month course. Blood levels of the marker dropped steeply in the first ten to twelve days. Low body weight, positive sputum smears, and lung cavities each went with higher levels at the start and the recheck. Smoking weighed more on the later level. Drug levels in blood, though, did not steer the drop. The authors judge early marker checks useful, with caveats.
pmc-11672911:
Zeena Gerster-Barzanji and co-authors evaluate a novel dermal template in burned children over the long term in a 2024 paper. For pediatric patients with full-thickness burns, adequate dermal regeneration is essential to prevent inelastic scars that may hinder growth. Traditional split-thickness skin grafts alone often fail to restore the dermal layer adequately.

The study used a biodegradable temporizing matrix as a dermal scaffold in four pediatric patients, promoting dermal formation before autografting. Histological evaluation over the long term shows how well the engineered dermis matures. Evidence from tissue samples guides burn centers choosing regenerative templates for growing children.
pmc-11673011:
Helber da Maia Valenca and a large team test a licensed drug, dimethyl fumarate, against diet-driven obesity, in a study from twenty twenty-four. The drug and its active breakdown product switch on a cellular defense pathway and are already sold for skin and nerve conditions. The team asked whether they also block fat formation.

In cell cultures, the metabolite stopped precursor cells from maturing into fat cells, lowering fat-driving genes and stored fat. It also cut oxidative stress and inflammation signals. In mice fed a rich diet for sixteen weeks, four weeks of the drug trimmed calorie intake, body weight, and both deep and surface fat. Blood sugar handling improved. The authors see repurposing promise for obesity care.
pmc-11673611:
Zubeyde Cicek and co-authors model what drives personal well-being using a quantile Bayesian method. Well-being depends on many life domains at once. Health, work, marriage, and social life each play a part.

Data came from a national life satisfaction survey in Turkey. The method checks effects at low, middle, and high well-being levels. Most domains lifted well-being across the board. Housing area and education satisfaction were exceptions in the results. For people with low well-being, work and relationships mattered most. Public services also weighed more for that group. Marriage mattered more at high well-being levels. The split view helps target support where it counts most in daily life.
pmc-11674111:
Azhar Dyussupova and co-authors present a 2024 case-control study of two famous diabetes genes in ethnic Kazakh people with prediabetes. Variants in TCF7L2 and PPARG raise diabetes risk in many populations. Their role at that early stage in Kazakhstan was unmeasured.

Two hundred cases with prediabetes and two hundred matched controls had their genes typed by targeted tests. Cases carried higher birth weight, body mass, and waist measures. Both gene variants clearly raised prediabetes risk in this group. Early genetic screening could flag Kazakh adults for stronger lifestyle prevention before full diabetes develops.
pmc-11674311:
Yong Bin Kim and co-authors build a tunable Raman sensing platform in a 2024 study. Raman scattering reads chemical fingerprints from light, and surface enhancement can amplify the signal hugely near metal nanostructures. Holding that boost steady is easy; adjusting it on demand has been the hard part.

Their platform lays a single layer of molybdenum disulfide over a flexible array of metal nanotips. Bending the sample changes the gap widths and thus the signal strength, which rose several fold under strain for one vibration mode. Adding tiny silver particles lifted the signal about thirtyfold, and strain tuned it further. Peak position and width also shifted under control. Uses may span biosensing, chemical detection, and optoelectronics.
pmc-11674411:
Melanomas inside the female genital tract are rare, hard to operate on, and shrug off standard radiation. Amelia Barcellini and co-authors report early real-world results in a 2024 study of carbon ion radiotherapy, a heavier form of radiation these tumors do answer to. Eleven patients with vulvar or vaginal tumors received the treatment between 2017 and 2023 and were followed for a median of eighteen months.

Tumors shrank or clearly benefited in every patient, with a response rate of 82 percent. Local control held at 100 percent after one year and 86 percent after two. Younger patients may have kept control longer. The authors call the treatment effective and tolerable so far.
pmc-11674611:
Mingxing Hou and co-authors read emotions from combined brain signals in two thousand twenty-four. One method records electric waves from the scalp. Another tracks blood flow with near-infrared light. Together they beat either method alone for emotion reading. The team built hybrid brain networks in source space. Source space means signals are mapped back into the brain.

Electric signals were first localized to their brain sources. Causal networks traced influence between those sources. Coupled networks from the light signals were added. Merging both views gave a richer picture of emotion states. The method aims for finer emotion classification. It also exposes how the two signal types relate. Such hybrids may improve brain-computer interfaces for mood.
pmc-11674711:
Qingxiu Liu and co-authors show in 2024 how a mold toxin kills ovary support cells in pigs and how vitamin E blunts the harm. Gene reads reveal the toxin wakes a stress pathway inside the cell's protein factory. A receptor blocker test pins the entry route to a hormone receptor.

Vitamin E docks tightly at the pathway's start enzyme in models. Fed vitamin E cuts cell death and stress signals in dishes. Mice on the vitamin keep better ovary function under toxin load. The vitamin thus guards fertility tissue against a common feed toxin.
pmc-11675011:
Seven neuroscientists test whether a fast brain rhythm marks healthy social interest, and whether brain injury breaks it. Rats with a severe controlled injury to the frontal cortex were compared with sham-operated animals in a three-chamber test, where a rat can choose between a fellow rat and an object. The team recorded electrical activity across many brain regions during the test.

Healthy rats preferred the social partner, and choosing it came with a clear rise in gamma-band coherence, a synchronized rhythm between frontal and striatal areas. Injured rats lost that preference, visiting the object more often and longer, and their gamma coherence during social choice dropped in step. The authors read the rhythm as a signature of the brain network that supports social preference, and its loss as a clue to why social problems linger after traumatic brain injury.
pmc-11675311:
Mpumelelo Nyalela and co-authors explore why men in KwaZulu-Natal underuse sexual and reproductive health services in this 2024 paper. Seventy-two men took part in focus groups: clinic patients and hostel residents around Durban. Seven barriers emerged. Men often did not know services existed. Culture and religion discouraged use, money was short, and partners' views mattered. Many judged their own risk low. Health services themselves pushed men away, through staff attitudes and a lack of male workers.

Three forces pulled the other way: available resources, good information, and personal motivation. The authors say the fix must work on both sides. Clinics need male staff and better manners toward male patients. Communities need direct knowledge campaigns aimed at men, not folded into women's health messaging. Men's untreated conditions drive illness and death that prevention could have stopped.
pmc-11675811:
Kasula Nagaraja and co-authors build a printable gel for growing replacement tissue, in a 2024 study. The gel rests on hyaluronic acid, a sugar chain found all over the human body. Turning it into a printer ink is tricky: light-set versions can involve harsh chemicals, and soft gels collapse when printed in fine shapes.

Their design links the acid chains two ways at once, adding a grafted helper molecule for the second link. The result prints through a nozzle into complex shapes that stand on their own. The gel stayed stable in warm salt water for over six weeks, drank up water without swelling much, and could heal its own cuts. Self-healing, sticky gels like this suit wound care and tissue building.
pmc-11675911:
Guanxue Yang, Shimin Lei, and Guanxiao Yang present model-free ways to find causal networks in complex systems. Their 2024 paper starts from observed dynamics alone. Rebuilding networks matters across science, yet system models are often unknown. Their methods assume nothing about the underlying equations. Polynomial fits stand in for the full system behavior.

One method judges node links through nonlinear Granger causality tests. A sparse version first shrinks dimension with Lasso selection. Conditional variables merge into one general frame either way. That fusion helps separate direct links from indirect echoes. Only direct relationships are kept in the final network. Tests show the approach can recover true structure from data. It serves fields from neuroscience to climate study.
pmc-11676111:
Sheng Chen and co-authors study what happens when two viruses infect chickens at the same time. One virus causes a form of avian leukosis and the other causes infectious anemia; together they weaken the birds' defenses, invite further infections, and blunt vaccines. The team used gene-activity profiling to find which genes and pathways change when both viruses strike together.

The scan found about a thousand changed messenger RNAs and dozens of changed small RNAs tied to the joint effect. The immune suppression in co-infected birds may run through heavier use of reactive oxygen and stress pathways. The pair of viruses also seems to dodge immunity by reshaping how the cell handles its RNA, a route that differs from single infections. The authors say the findings can guide targeted treatments and better disease control in poultry, where such co-infections cost the industry heavily each year.
pmc-11676211:
Scano and co-authors published a 2024 study testing a cystic fibrosis drug as a rescue for a rare muscle disease. In beta-sarcoglycanopathy, mutant proteins of the muscle membrane complex are marked for destruction, weakening the membrane. The team first confirmed in lab cells that mutant beta-sarcoglycan is degraded by the cell's proteasome, like its alpha sibling. They then worked in muscle cells grown from a patient.

A CFTR corrector called C17 saved the mutant protein from destruction and restored the full complex at the cell surface. Membrane integrity improved, judged by lower enzyme leakage under stress. The authors propose repurposing correctors, built for cystic fibrosis, for sarcoglycan diseases. The patient-cell evidence is the study's core strength.
pmc-11676711:
Yangyang Ma and co-authors report, in a 2024 paper, a new route to building indolizines, a ring system valued in drug and materials chemistry, using a fluorinated starting block. Their key ingredient is a peroxide carrying two fluorine atoms, which serves as a two-carbon building unit. Paired with pyridinium ylides under mild, base-guided conditions, it closes the second ring in a single annulation step. The trick adds fluorine-bearing decoration that older routes struggle to install.

The method delivered a broad range of multi-substituted indolizines in moderate to good yields. Many useful side groups survived the reaction untouched, widening the menu of products. The authors present the fluorinated peroxide as a fresh building block for this ring family. Such routes help chemists tune the electronic character of ring compounds for screening work.
pmc-11677111:
The authors profiled bacteria in 2024 around a pond at a national ecology institute in Korea. Six samples came from lake water, bottom mud, and soil at the roots of four water plants. Each niche held a distinct mix, even within one small pond.

One large group ruled across all samples, with two others next in size. Water samples were rich in two groups tied to light and decay, while mud held more of a group common in low-oxygen settings. Mud had the highest diversity by several counts, and water the lowest. Plant root soils sat in between. The study shows how the material a microbe lives in shapes its community.
pmc-11677211:
Kaixuan Sang and co-authors study laser welding of a high-strength car steel in 2024. The steel, a boron grade for hot-formed parts, came in plates two, three, and four millimeters thick. How thickness changes the weld's inner structure and strength matters for factory use.

Thicker plates gave weaker joints, falling from ninety-six to eighty-eight percent of the base metal's strength. The heat-affected zone beside each weld was the softest part. Grains in the weld grew coarser with thickness, changing from fine needles to larger islands, and defect density dropped. All three joints still cleared eighty-five percent of base strength, a good sign for industry.
pmc-11677411:
Michele Fiore and a large team report on focused radiation care for older patients with pancreatic cancer. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. This cancer has a poor outlook and is often found in the old, who may not bear surgery or drug care well. The method sends high-dose rays to a small zone in just five sessions.

They track how long patients live with no spread, no local growth, and no far spread. Local control stays high for the first years, and mid values for the other spans run past two years. Harm rates are low, both soon after care and later. The method looks safe and strong for this group.
pmc-11677811:
Juliana Salazar and co-authors sought gene clues in bone cancer therapy in two thousand twenty-four. Osteosarcoma is the commonest malignant bone tumor. Standard care starts with a three-drug chemotherapy mix. Response to that mix strongly predicts outcome. Toxicity can also derail the full treatment plan. The team tested inherited variants as predictors.

Patients came from a Spanish protocol for localized disease. Variants sat in DNA repair and drug handling genes. Response was judged from tumor tissue after chemotherapy. Toxicity records were analyzed in parallel. A useful marker could spare poor responders delays. It could also flag patients needing toxicity watch. The study builds toward personalized dosing in a rare cancer.
pmc-11677911:
Caterina Carollo and co-authors examine whether swings in blood pressure relate to the thickness of the eye's back layers in people with hypertension. Their 2024 study starts from a shift in thinking: harm comes from pressure variability, not just average pressure. The choroid, a vessel-rich layer, may mirror body-wide vascular damage.

About a hundred patients wore a day-long pressure monitor that yielded averages and several variability measures. Advanced scans measured choroid and retina thickness in concentric rings. Choroid thickness moved opposite to pressure variability in their results. If the eye's vessels register the strain of unstable pressure, a quick scan could flag patients whose organs are quietly taking damage.
pmc-11678211:
Karolina Akinosoglou and five co-authors update how to treat vaginal yeast infections that no longer respond to fluconazole, in a review from 2024. Resistant Candida species, including tougher non-albicans types, are rising worldwide. Standard one-drug habits are part of the problem.

Alternatives reviewed include boric acid, nystatin, and two newer antifungal agents. The authors advise individualized tapering regimens over long fixed high-dose maintenance, keeping doses as low as control allows. They also urge stopping casual antifungal use for symptoms not caused by Candida at all. Careful antibiotic prescribing matters too, since antibiotics disturb the flora and breed resistance.
pmc-11678311:
Karolina Wanat, Klaudia Michalak, and Elżbieta Brzezińska model which drugs reach the brain in this 2024 paper. A drug for the brain must cross the blood-brain barrier; a drug for the body should ideally stay out, to spare the mind side effects. The balance is summed up in one number, log BB, the ratio of drug levels in brain and blood.

The team built prediction models from drug properties, using regression methods old and new. Their twist is the data source: how long drugs stick to albumin, the blood's carrier protein, measured by two lab methods that mimic that binding. Sticky drugs ride the blood longer and cross differently. Models fed with those retention values were tested for how well they forecast the brain ratio. Cheap lab measures that predict brain entry could trim the long drug testing pipeline.
pmc-11678411:
Firas Al-Zubaydi and co-authors build a 2024 model of how a nerve pain drug moves through the body, using blood reads taken in routine care. The drug is cleared by the kidneys and its levels vary a lot from person to person, which makes dose choice hard. Routine drug level checks in hospital hold data that could sharpen that choice.

The team drew records from 82 adults in hospital who had drug levels checked. A simple one-box model fit the data best, with dose-linked uptake and steady clearance. Blood waste levels, a sign of kidney work, were the one trait that clearly shifted clearance. Body weight and diabetes showed no clear effect. The work shows routine care data can feed sound drug models.
pmc-11678611:
Komal Wagh and co-authors review cobalt oxide composites for splitting water in a paper published in 2024. Splitting water makes hydrogen, a clean fuel, but it needs catalysts that are cheap and effective. Cobalt oxide is abundant and stable, yet on its own it conducts poorly and reacts sluggishly.

The review covers ways to fix those limits by pairing the oxide with conductive supports, other metals, carbon nanomaterials, and porous frameworks. Shaping the material at the nanoscale, adding dopants, and modifying surfaces all raised performance in the studies surveyed. The authors explain why these changes help both halves of the splitting reaction. They close with the chances for large-scale use and the work still needed on durability.
pmc-11678811:
Christine Fribert Thusgaard and co-authors present a 2024 paper on a sensitive way to find tumour DNA in the blood of ovarian cancer patients. Such DNA traces could flag relapse early and show whether treatment works. No settled best method exists for this cancer, so the team built one guided by each patient's own tumour profile.

They sequenced whole genomes from tumour and blood samples of ten patients taken at diagnosis. Simple filters on read depth and variant share barely improved the signal. A new filter, which used the other patients' blood samples as a pool to strip out artefacts, lifted the signal sharply. The authors call the approach promising despite the small group.
pmc-11679111:
Nina Aveilla and co-authors develop, in a 2024 study, a sharper way to measure a food-poisoning toxin in dairy goods. Staphylococcal enterotoxin A comes in many slight variants, and standard methods chop the protein into pieces first, which can blur those variants and takes long digestion. Their top-down method reads the whole protein at once.

A fully labeled copy of the toxin, spiked in at the start, anchors the measurement and steadies repeat runs. After antibody cleanup, a high-resolution instrument both named the variant present and counted its amount. In milk and Roquefort cheese the method sensed the toxin down to half a nanogram per gram in its sharper mode. Trials across dairy products separated clean from tainted goods cleanly. The authors offer the protocol for food safety labs.
pmc-11679211:
Kyung-Duk Choi and co-authors design a quieter front-end chip for mobile phones in a 2024 paper. The chip, a low noise amplifier, boosts weak radio signals before processing. Phones on 4G and 5G networks need several gain settings, and battery life depends on drawing little current at low gain.

Their design uses a three-core input that reshapes itself across seven gain modes, from strong amplification to mild weakening. A cascade switch flips modes fast while keeping the circuit stable. Peak gain reaches about twenty decibels with a noise figure under one decibel, a strong result for this class. Top current draw stays modest. The chip shows how one part can serve two network generations without wasting power.
pmc-11679511:
Faith S A Brown and co-authors track how hard college women basketball players work in practice, and how hard it feels, in a 2024 study. Players wore motion sensors across fifty-three practices, yielding 583 player-sessions, while staff logged effort ratings and strength work. The squad split into high-minute and low-minute players by game time.

Starters began the season carrying higher external loads than bench players. Felt effort climbed across the season for everyone, and it rose in step with the sensor load, about one unit per unit. The links among minutes, measured work, and felt work can help coaches dose practice fairly across the roster.
pmc-11679711:
Beata Bień, Piotr Krajewski, and Jacek Szepietowski carried out a 2024 study of how people with psoriasis accept their illness. The skin condition affects more than 60 million people in the world. Its marks are easy to see, and it can cause itch and pain as well as stress.

The study group had 166 patients, 101 men and 65 women, each ill for at least one year. The team used standard scales to rate how bad the skin was, how strong the itch felt, and how life felt day to day. Most patients showed a middle level of acceptance, and scores linked with skin state, itch, and life quality.
pmc-11679911:
Zhengqing Pei and seven colleagues dope a battery cathode with chromium to slow its decay, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. Lithium manganese oxide is cheap and benign as cathodes go. It fades fast, especially when hot, which limits its use.

The team precipitated and baked a series of chromium-substituted versions. The doped crystals kept their spinel structure and grew into truncated octahedra. Chromium replaces some manganese and bonds more strongly to oxygen, stiffening the lattice. Electrochemical tests then measured whether capacity survives longer. Materials tweaks like this aim to keep the cheapest cathode chemistry competitive. Electric vehicles and grid storage both benefit if manganese cathodes last.
pmc-11680011:
Patryk Skórka and co-authors report the case of a young man with a rare nerve tumor, in a 2024 paper with a review of past cases. The patient, aged twenty-four, had a genetic condition that raises the risk of such tumors. His malignant tumor of the nerve sheath had already spread to his lungs when found.

Because drugs work poorly on this cancer, he had radical surgery and radiation. Lab checks confirmed a high-grade tumor, and later scans showed the spread advancing. Set beside like cases in print, his course underlines how hard this cancer is to control. The authors call for tailored plans and point to immune therapy as a hope.
pmc-11680111:
Elizabeth Ramirez-Medina and co-authors delete one gene from African swine fever virus to see if the virus needs it. The disease kills domestic pigs and now troubles pig farming across much of Eurasia. The virus is huge and complex, with over 160 proteins, most of them still poorly understood. The gene R298L codes a working protein kinase, is switched on late in infection, and may ride in the virus particle.

The team built the Georgia 2010 strain with R298L removed. In pig immune cells grown in the lab, the mutant grew just as well as the parent. In live pigs, it caused the same fatal disease as the parent virus. So R298L is not needed for growth in culture or for killing power in the host. Vaccine makers hunting genes whose loss weakens the virus can cross this one off.
pmc-11680211:
Adam Achs and co-authors review plant virus carriers that produce foreign proteins in plants in a 2024 paper. Potyviruses infect many crops and build their proteins as one long chain that is then cut into parts. That trick lets them carry extra genes for harvest in leaves.

At least eleven potyvirus species have been turned into such carriers, in both natural and lab hosts. Strengths include wide host range and strong yields, while size limits and stability pose hurdles. Uses on the horizon span vaccines, nanoparticles, and drug proteins, plus rewiring plant chemistry. The review maps where the tool stands and what blocks scale-up.
pmc-11680311:
Noa Feldman and co-authors present a 2024 study on vaccine choices among pregnant women in Israel. Pregnant women were a priority group in the covid pandemic. A cohort of 449 women was followed from late 2019 to late 2021. Surveys covered flu, whooping cough, and covid shots, plus attitudes, social norms, and risk views.

Covid uptake was highest, at 64 percent, then whooping cough at 49 and flu at 32. Non-religious women and those with degrees accepted shots more often. A doctor's advice was the strongest single push for all three. Media shaped covid choices in particular. Whooping cough was seen as the top threat to babies, covid to mothers. The authors urge personal outreach by clinicians and media-aware campaigns for hesitant groups.
pmc-11680411:
Jiao Wang and five co-authors review in 2024 how tiny particles could sharpen tuberculosis vaccines. Tuberculosis still kills on a vast scale, and the century-old vaccine protects unevenly, so better boosters, called adjuvants, are in demand.

Nanoparticle adjuvants carry the vaccine's key fragments in spheres that immune cells swallow eagerly, releasing their cargo slowly for a longer, stronger response. The review tours the main particle families and the physical traits that make each work, from size to surface charge. It weighs gains in delivery, safety, and immune strength, a design brief for the next generation of TB shots.
pmc-11680711:
Arushi Goel, Aneet Mahendra, and Sanjeev Gupta examine faces damaged by long use of topical steroid creams, in a 2024 study. Such creams are sold freely in many places, which leads to misuse and dependence. Long use on the face can cause marked harm, so early diagnosis and stopping the cream matter.

They enroll 250 patients aged twelve to sixty with facial disease and signs of steroid damage after at least one month of use. Clinical and skin-surface scope features are recorded. The team look for links with the strength and duration of cream use. The scope offers an easy, non-invasive way to judge the extent of damage.
pmc-11681911:
Amirreza Shalili, Hassan Assilian Mahabadi, and Ali Safari Variani test whether factory noise and benzene vapor together strain the body more than either alone, in a 2024 rat study. Workers rarely face one hazard at a time.

Twenty-four rats split into four groups: clean air, loud white noise, benzene vapor, or both. Blood markers then read the oxidative balance, the rust-like damage process in cells. Both hazards alone tipped the balance: damage markers rose while protective antioxidants fell. The combined group was exposed to both insults at once. The design isolates what each factor adds. Results feed safety rules for mixed exposures, the norm on real shop floors.
pmc-11683611:
Harilal and co-authors model nitric acid extraction in the PUREX process with machine learning in this 2024 paper. PUREX separates plutonium and uranium from spent nuclear fuel by liquid extraction. Predicting how chemicals split between the liquid phases is hard, because the feed is complex. Nitric acid drives the process and is itself extracted by the solvent, tributyl phosphate. The team gathered a large body of published extraction data. They trained models to predict the acid level in the organic phase from starting acid and solvent levels, across varied diluents.

The models predicted the acid behavior well. Response surfaces built from them show how extraction shifts with conditions. The authors offer the tool as a way to plan experiments in silico before running costly and hazardous lab work. They present machine learning as a practical aid where thermodynamic models have struggled with the feed's complexity.
pmc-11684011:
The authors reported the first study in 2024 of a family of light-active compounds built on polyoxometalates, metal-oxygen clusters that pull electrons strongly. Each compound links one or two of these clusters to an electron-giving unit through phenyl bridges. The set includes flat, spread-out forms as well as plain linear forms, so the two shapes can be set side by side.

Light tests and computer models showed that the flat forms soak up light at notably longer wavelengths than the linear ones. That shift marks a stronger flow of charge across the flat frame. Such compounds may serve in devices that switch or double light signals, where shape-tuned charge flow is prized.
pmc-11685211:
Yating Zhan and co-authors build a gene signature linking nicotine metabolism to outcomes in bladder cancer. Smoking is a major risk factor for bladder cancer, and genes of nicotine metabolism were suspected players. Mining public databases, they grouped tumors into three clusters with distinct outlooks and immune patterns. Ten machine learning methods then competed to build the signature.

A four-gene signature from a survival forest method predicted patient outcomes reliably across three cohorts. The score also tracked clinical features, the tissue around the tumor, and likely response to immune therapy. Lab tests on one signature gene confirmed effects on cancer cell growth, spread, and colony formation, grounding the computation in biology.
pmc-11685911:
Tumors of the vidian nerve, a small nerve deep in the skull base, are so rare that only a handful of cases exist in print. Je Ho Bang and three co-authors add one in a 2024 case report: a 58-year-old woman whose scan for other reasons revealed a mass in the vidian canal. Her only symptoms were passing headaches and dry eyes, and no mass could be felt on examination.

The growth reached into a nearby skull opening, the foramen rotundum. Surgeons removed it endoscopically through the nose, and lab analysis confirmed a benign schwannoma. Later scans showed no return of the tumor. The authors present the case as a model for handling such rare finds.
pmc-11686511:
Shin and co-authors reported in 2024 a coating that helps glucose sensors worn under the skin last longer. Such sensors remove the need for finger pricks, but noise, tissue fluid, and acid shifts during swelling can spoil their readings. The team aimed to tune the small space around the sensor.

Using a plasma grafting step, they added a brush-like coating that can buffer acid shifts. The coated sensor gave good glucose responses across a tested acid range and lasted longer than an uncoated one. In rats, it tracked blood sugar more closely and with less noise. The work may cut the need for routine finger-stick checks.
pmc-11687111:
Paolo Ciliberti and co-authors test whether advanced MRI mapping can name children's heart tumors without a biopsy. Most pediatric cardiac masses are benign, but the types, hemangioma, fibroma, rhabdomyoma and others, carry different plans. Standard imaging reads signal patterns; parametric mapping adds hard numbers for the tissue's water and relaxation properties.

Sixteen children scanned at Rome's Bambino Gesù hospital between 2017 and 2023 formed the series, with an average age near seven. The team measured each mass's mapping values by subtype and checked agreement between readers. Extra quantitative fingerprints could spare some children surgery done only to learn what they have, and sharpen surveillance for the rest.
pmc-11688211:
Yu, Zhao, Yue, Chen, and Dong review how metabolic problems may drive joint disease in twenty twenty-four. The disease is osteoarthritis, a common cause of pain and disability around the world. Its root causes are still not fully known. Current care eases symptoms but does not stop the disease from getting worse.

The review sums up work on metabolic syndrome and each of its parts. That syndrome groups problems such as excess weight, high blood sugar, and abnormal blood fats. Studies link these problems to changes in cartilage, bone, and joint inflammation. The authors trace the paths by which each part may harm the joint. They argue that a clearer picture could point to better treatments.
pmc-11688411:
A team of co-authors presents a survey in two thousand twenty-four on kidney transplant patients who skip their anti-rejection drugs. One-year survival of grafts and patients now tops ninety percent at most centers, but long-term graft loss remains a problem. Not taking immunosuppressants as directed is a recognized driver of that loss.

The team surveyed four hundred thirty-one recipients at one outpatient clinic and received four hundred nine valid replies. A standard questionnaire measured how often doses were missed, late, or stopped. The authors looked for changeable factors behind the behavior, at the levels of the patient, the treatment, and the system, to guide interventions.
pmc-11688711:
Emily Mroz and four co-authors ask how people with early dementia can keep a sense of purpose. Their twenty twenty-four work notes that purpose often drops after a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease or a related illness. Some blame brain change itself. This team instead blames a lack of support programs that help people set new goals.

They ran a design workshop with seventeen people who had mild to moderate illness. The method looked for strengths and good past steps, not just problems. With support, the group could name goals that mattered to them. The authors suggest joint programs in the community, built with patients as partners.
pmc-11688811:
Lisa Oellig, Johan Lindsjö and Helena Röcklinsberg survey Swedish veterinarians on animal abuse and its link to domestic violence, in work from 2024. Vets meet both at-risk animals and people, so they can spot cases where an abuser controls a victim through an animal. The 2019 survey went to all licensed vets in Sweden and drew 362 replies.

Awareness of the link was high, yet most vets were unsure about non-accidental injury as a concept, how to record it or whom to contact. Only a small share knew how to act on suspected domestic violence. Clinic support was thin, with few action plans or training offers. The authors call for integrated training and clearer clinic routines.
pmc-11688911:
Sofia Liu and co-authors wrote this 2024 study of movement, frailty, and a blood marker of nerve damage in older adults. Neurofilament light rises when neurons are injured, and it climbs with age. Activity is known to protect aging bodies, but its link to this brain marker was unclear.

The team studied 95 community-dwelling adults without dementia, average age seventy. Wrist sensors and questionnaires measured activity; a standard phenotype graded frailty; blood tests gave the marker levels. More sensor-measured activity went with lower marker levels. Frail participants carried far higher levels than robust or pre-frail ones. Frailty also statistically carried part of the activity effect. The findings sketch a path from movement to nerve health through physical resilience.
pmc-11689011:
Christopher Kaufmann asks whether artificial intelligence can help doctors care for older patients through a classic five-part lens. Geriatric practice sums up good care as the 5Ms: Mind, Mobility, Medications, Multicomplexity, and what Matters Most to the patient. AI tools are spreading fast through health care, promising sharper decisions for clinicians and better self-monitoring for patients.

Kaufmann walks through each of the five domains in turn, giving examples of how AI has already been applied to each and judging where it truly fits. He closes with the open chances for new tools aimed at helping older people age in place and stay independent, which he calls a major opportunity for the field.
pmc-11689111:
Phil Schumm and Colm O’Muircheartaigh test how to recruit older LGBT adults into a national health study, in a 2024 feasibility report. A fair, random sample of this group is hard to build, since no list of them exists. Their SAMLAP study aimed to prove that a probability sample could still be drawn, as the base for a long study of health and aging.

The team mailed 70,000 sampled addresses with a push to answer online, seeking household members aged 40 and over who identify as LGBT. About 300 identified people then got in-person follow-up. Built-in experiments varied incentive size and timing, a paper form in the first mailing, and a last-ditch courier contact. The results show what it costs to recruit a hidden population honestly.
pmc-11689211:
Andrea Kalvesmaki and five co-authors study veterans who have a caregiver aged twenty-five or younger. Their twenty twenty-four paper uses a survey of veterans and their helpers. Up to five million youth under eighteen give some care to an aging adult in the United States. That count doubles if young adults are included. Yet these caregivers are little studied, and their needs may be missed.

One hundred fifty-four veterans had at least one young caregiver. Compared with other veterans, they had less schooling and more unmet daily needs. They also faced more food, drug, transport, and reading problems. More were Black or Hispanic. The authors say a young caregiver may signal deep social risk.
pmc-11689611:
Erica Solway and four co-authors summarize what a long-running national poll reveals about how older Americans use telehealth and patient portals. The University of Michigan poll surveys a representative sample of more than 2,500 adults aged 50 to 80 twice a year. In 2019 only 4 percent had a telehealth visit in the prior year; by mid-2020 the share had jumped to 26 percent within a three-month window.

Portal use has climbed steadily as well, and recent rounds asked about messaging providers through portals and about charges for those messages. By 2023, 7.5 percent had used a direct-to-consumer service from an online-only provider, and 32 percent said they would consider one. The authors present the poll as a timely record of changing habits that can guide efforts to improve access and integration of care.
pmc-11689811:
Siyun Peng and Brea Perry ask whether rich social ties can offset low schooling in later-life thinking, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Schooling gaps are a known driver of gaps in memory and thinking as people age. The team used thinking tests and network data from near seven hundred adults in one state study.

Ties that bring fresh facts and new contacts linked most strongly to thinking in adults with the least schooling. At high levels of such ties, thinking gaps between schooling groups faded away. Late-life rich settings may thus help most those who missed them early. The finding fits a life-long build-up view.
pmc-11690511:
Karen Fredriksen-Goldsen introduces the Global Pride Study, a worldwide project on health and aging in sexual and gender diverse people. The symposium paper appeared in 2024. More than fifty scholars across six world regions take part. The study covers quality of life, body and mind health, and social and economic well-being in later life. It also tracks how the COVID-19 pandemic hit these communities.

The sessions describe how the team built a pilot survey and adapted methods across cultures. A video from partners reviews the state of research and policy around the world. Final results share early numbers from the pilot. Gaps in knowledge are named plainly, and next research steps are set out. The project aims to give older diverse adults a place in global aging science.
pmc-11690611:
Martha Coates, Emily Hajjar, and Rose Ann DiMaria-Ghalili study medication overload in older cancer patients in a 2024 paper. Older adults with cancer often take more than five drugs a day, some of them needless or risky. Deprescribing, the careful trimming of such drugs, can cut harm and lift quality of life. Little was known about whether patients themselves welcome it.

Using a national aging survey, the team studied nearly two thousand Medicare patients, of whom 121 had a cancer history. Over half of that group faced polypharmacy. Three quarters said they would like fewer medications, and nearly all would stop one if their doctor suggested it. Yet most also insisted every drug they took was necessary, a tension prescribers must handle with care.
pmc-11690811:
Brian Beach, Paola Zaninotto, and Eun-Jung Shim test if blood marks and low mood move as one over time in a 2024 study. Past work tied single blood marks to low mood at one point in time. Such links can not show which one drives the other, or if they drift in step at all.

The team used an English aging study with four checks from 2004 to 2019, in adults aged 50 and up. Nine blood marks were tracked next to mood scores in joint growth models. Just one mark, the red cell protein hemoglobin, moved with mood, and that link held for women only. The rest showed no joint drift, which trims hopes for blood-based mood tests.
pmc-11690911:
Andrea June, Carrie Andreoletti, and Helena Swanson survey retired faculty about staying engaged in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Their university seeks age-inclusive ways to keep retired and emeritus professors connected. The survey reached former faculty of one state university in Connecticut.

Thirty-eight respondents, average age seventy-three, were mostly full professors with long service. Feeling emotionally ready was the top reason for retiring, followed by burnout and campus climate. Many stayed partly connected, but satisfaction with that connection varied. Over half backed a retired faculty association. Respondents preferred short, time-limited activities with students over semester-long duties. The authors plan to fold the findings into campus initiatives.
pmc-11691011:
Tochukwu Okolie and Heather Menne published a scoping review in 2024 of research using a national survey of participants in Older Americans Act programs in the United States. The survey has been collected every year since 2003. It covers users of services such as congregate meals, home-delivered meals, homemaker services, transportation, case management, and family caregiver support.

The reviewers searched eight databases with no restriction on date. From forty-three candidate citations, they found only ten qualifying studies that used the data. Congregate meal services and caregiver support drew the most research, while case management, homemaker services, and transportation drew the least. The authors conclude that the data source is rich but barely used. They call for more research on what these programs do for older adults and caregivers.
pmc-11691111:
Kristoffer Rhoads presents mindfulness as a tool for fortitude in aging in a 2024 talk summary. Growing old, well or with brain disease, demands resilience and a clear-eyed view of ones own past and future. Mindfulness means holding the present moment in open, unjudging awareness.

The talk follows the program shaped by Jon Kabat-Zinn and colleagues in Massachusetts. For older adults, practice can loosen the habit of measuring today against a younger self, and soften dread of losses ahead. For those with memory loss or dementia, it may ease distress and touch risk factors behind decline. Acceptance, here, is strength.
pmc-11691211:
Danielle Powell and co-authors study how hearing problems are handled at Medicare wellness visits in this 2024 paper. The visits are yearly checks for older adults. How clinicians write up a concern shapes how patients see their own health. The team asked whether hearing concerns get less attention when a patient also has dementia.

Records covered 2,593 people who reported hearing concerns between 2017 and 2022. A sample of 474 visit notes was read closely for hearing mentions and referrals. Notes were less full for patients with dementia than for those without it. Clinicians were about half as likely to expand on hearing or note known hearing loss in that group.
pmc-11691311:
Patrick Ho Lam Lai studies why older adults in the United States give their time for free, and why rates differ by race and ethnic group. His 2024 study looks at two kinds of unpaid help. One kind is formal work for a group or cause. The other is informal help given straight to people who need it. Asian American older adults sit at the center of the study.

Lai uses survey data from 2019 and 2021 and models both kinds of help at once. Even with the same income and schooling, White older adults were more likely than Asian peers to do formal unpaid work. Other groups also showed higher rates. Lai argues that pay and schooling do not explain the gap, and that culture needs a closer look.
pmc-11691411:
Gokul Seshadri and colleagues ask whether the mix of T cell subsets predicts mortality in families selected for long life. Differences in T cell subsets are associated with higher mortality in the general population. The Long Life Family Study offered a chance to test the link in offspring of exceptionally long-lived people and their spouses.

The team measured twelve T cell subsets in more than sixteen hundred study offspring and five hundred fifty spousal controls, then modeled four-year mortality. Compared with a general-population study, both groups showed higher levels of naive and effector memory helper T cells and lower central memory cells. In the combined sample, a higher share of effector memory cells was associated with increased mortality risk, while naive cells showed a borderline protective association. The results suggest immune aging markers carry prognostic information even in long-lived families.
pmc-11691511:
Jessika Dayrit and co-authors present a 2024 national study of gun ownership and mental health among caregivers. Past work links gun access to suicide risk, but caregivers had not been studied as a group. The team used a large federal health survey from 2021. More than seventeen thousand adults took part, including civilian and veteran caregivers. Their answers were compared with those of non-caregivers.

Both kinds of caregiver were more likely to keep a gun at home. Veteran caregivers showed the largest gap on that count. Both groups also reported higher rates of depression. They more often had trouble focusing, recalling, or deciding because of low mood. The authors urge doctors to talk about gun safety with patients and caregivers alike. They frame those talks as part of routine care, like checks for long-term illness.
pmc-11691611:
Tai-Te Su, Ruth Barclay, Rahim Moineddin, and Nancy Salbach present a 2024 study asking whether showing up more often to an outdoor walking group improves health in older adults with mobility limits. Walking outdoors is known to help this group, but dose matters for prescribing it. The data came from a randomized trial across four Canadian cities.

The team focused on seventy-nine participants assigned to a ten-week walking programme, averaging about seventy-five years old and mostly women. Attendance split into three bands, from almost none to nearly every session. Comparing health gains across the bands tests a dose-response pattern: if more walking brings more benefit, programmes should push attendance, not just enrolment.
pmc-11691911:
Samuel Van Vleet and co-authors make the case for a stalled American law on obesity care for older adults, in a 2024 paper. Obesity is common in later life, drives heart disease, diabetes, and sleep apnea, and hits poorer and rural elders hardest, yet treatment coverage under Medicare stays patchy and varies by state. The Treat and Reduce Obesity Act has circulated in Congress for over a decade with support from both parties.

The authors review what the act would change: wider access to counseling, drugs, and other proven treatments for Medicare members. Drawing on a 2024 coverage platform, they show how uneven today's patchwork is and what risks untreated obesity carries. Their argument is that coverage reform, not new medicine, is the missing piece for older patients.
pmc-11692011:
Lin, Boot, Rogers, Charness, and Czaja survey older adults with cognitive impairment about their technology habits, finding far more use than stereotypes suggest. The 159 participants, aged sixty to ninety-three, include people with mild impairment, brain injury, and stroke effects. They rated their attitudes, skill, and use across health, social, travel, leisure, and home domains.

Social tools like phone, email, and text saw the heaviest use, while travel apps saw the least. Participants handled mobile devices well and held warm attitudes overall. Younger age and greater comfort and interest predicted stronger proficiency, and people who noticed their own memory slips also scored higher. The 2024 authors say programs should build on this readiness.
pmc-11692111:
Amy Thomas and co-authors ask in 2024 whether frailty and illness scores predict how much care change older veterans need. A care approach built around patient goals aligns treatment with what matters to each person. Standard scores predict death and care home entry, but may miss the true load of unmet needs.

The team read records of veterans sent to a goals-based clinic and counted care plan changes per person. Each patient averaged four types of suggested change, such as therapy or social service referrals. Neither frailty nor illness scores shaped the count, in rural or town groups alike. Goal-based review thus finds needs that risk scores alone overlook.
pmc-11692211:
Ava Mcvey and co-authors ask whether how old people feel about aging tracks how well their minds work. Three hundred thirty-four community-dwelling older adults from two intervention studies took executive function tests and rated their own cognition. They also answered questionnaires on two facets of aging perception: noticing age-related change, and expecting decline or growth.

Neither facet predicted the tested abilities, matrix reasoning, switching, and speed tasks all stood apart. Both facets did predict self-reported cognition, strongly for awareness of change. In other words, beliefs about aging colored how sharp people felt, not how sharp they scored. The authors suggest clinics treat self-perception as its own signal, worth asking about even when test scores reassure.
pmc-11692311:
Ahmed Ragab and five co-authors tie social ties to blood marks in the Framingham Heart Study in a 2024 paper. Lone and cut off lives raise illness and death risks, perhaps through swelling and a dulled immune system. Past cohort work read few marks and skipped immune cell types, so this team cast a wide net over three mark sets.

Their index summed marriage, close kin and friends, worship attendance, and group life. Near nine hundred elders fed the swelling set, more than three thousand the heart set, and near a thousand the immune cell set. Richer ties went with higher levels of several marks, some kind and some harsh, and lower levels of others. The mix defies a one way story. The authors say social life writes itself into blood in braided ways.
pmc-11692411:
Leaving the emergency department is a fragile moment for a dementia patient, and more so when the family navigates the system in a second language. Jacqueline Sandoval and co-authors interviewed ten Hispanic patient-caregiver pairs a week after discharge. They mapped the conversations against a national framework for emergency care transitions.

Families prized being included in decisions with the treating team. Language barriers and the patient's confusion compounded each other at every step: understanding instructions, arranging follow-up, and knowing whom to call. Some factors visibly helped, like staff who worked to bridge the language gap. Others hindered, like rushed hand-offs. The authors aim the findings at safer discharge design for this population.
pmc-11692611:
Joosuk Chae, Hyunmi Kim and In-Taek Lim study links among diet, movement and how older Korean adults rate their own health. Their 2024 work asks if being active helps explain why good eating habits go with better self-rated health.

The team used survey data from more than a thousand adults aged sixty-five and older in Korea. They tested whether activity level sits in the middle of the diet and health link. The results said it does: good habits went with more activity, and more activity went with better rated health. The authors urge care plans that join food teaching with support for daily movement.
pmc-11692711:
Mercedes Bern-Klug and Meredith Levine examine a hard choice in nursing home care for people with dementia. Their 2024 pilot study starts from a legal duty: homes must honor a resident's self-determination and any advance directive. Trouble arises when a past written wish clashes with what the person seems to want now.

The authors interviewed twelve staff members in varied roles. In the test case, a resident who once wrote that she did not want to be fed later gestured a wish to eat. All staff backed self-determination, yet many said they would feed her. Others worried that feeding would break the directive. Staff also raised doubts about shifting ability and family conflict.
pmc-11692811:
Hannah Apostolou, Michael Buxton, Valerie Luskey, and Lindsey Jacobs published a 2024 study of aging attitudes, control, and thinking skills. People who view their own aging negatively may withdraw from daily activity, which can speed mental decline. A sense of mastery, the feeling of being in control of one’s life, may soften that effect.

The team analyzed survey data from 4,369 older Americans in the 2020 Health and Retirement Study. More positive views of aging were linked to higher thinking scores. Part of that link ran through perceived mastery: positive views went with a stronger sense of control, which went with better cognition. Programs that build both positive attitudes and practical control skills may help protect thinking in later life.
pmc-11692911:
Willencia Louis-Charles and co-authors explore how social ties, personality, health, and loneliness link up in older adults, in work published in 2024. As people age, retirement, loss of loved ones, and poor health can shrink their social world. The team studied 21 adults aged 61 to 80 as part of a larger project.

Each person took short tests of personality and social connection, and rated their own health. Adults with steadier emotions felt less lonely and scored higher on connection. Other traits showed no clear link to loneliness. People who felt healthier also felt more connected. The sample was small, so the authors treat the findings as early clues. The work points to health and calm temperament as supports for social life in old age.
pmc-11693011:
Ting Xu and co-authors probe how gut microbes may drive frailty in older adults in a 2024 study. Frailty is common late in life, and hints link it to the gut community, but the mechanism is murky. The team joined a genetic causal method with mouse experiments to get closer to cause.

Frail mice, made so by chronic inflammation, showed disturbed gut communities, notably less of one bacterial group. That group's abundance tracked frailty scores and inflammation markers closely. Chemical profiling named several metabolites that may carry the effect. Genetic analysis in humans supported a causal link between the bacterium and frailty index. The work sketches a gut route into frailty that diet or microbe therapy might one day target.
pmc-11693211:
Lun Li, Andrew Wister and Yeonjung Lee tracked the health of older immigrants in Canada over ten years in 2024. Using three waves of a national aging study, they compared 4,248 immigrants with 17,232 Canadian-born adults, all aged 65 and over.

Immigrants started out physically healthier, with fewer chronic diseases and better physical capability, but their physical health declined faster. Depression and loneliness levels were similar in both groups and changed in parallel. The sharper gap was social: immigrants reported less social support and participation, and those fell faster too. The authors say services should help older immigrants keep social ties as they age.
pmc-11693311:
Chelsea Manheim, Rachel Fix, and Leah Haverhals report what in person conferences did for coordinators of a veterans' foster home program, in this 2024 paper. The program places nursing home eligible veterans in private homes with round the clock caregivers. Coordinators recruit and monitor those homes, a job often done alone, especially in rural areas.

Two national meetings in 2024 gathered staff in Orlando and Chicago, as the program pushes to reach every veterans' medical center by 2026. The authors interviewed coordinators from four rural expansion programs afterward. They reported strong ties with seasoned peers nearby, fresh marketing ideas, concrete action plans, and renewed motivation. The authors conclude that face to face gathering is a real remedy for the isolation built into the role.
pmc-11693811:
Unmet need for family planning, where a woman wants to avoid pregnancy but lacks modern birth control, is tracked to judge health programs. Musafaah and three co-authors reviewed in 2024 how mapping methods have been used to study that need across places. They searched three databases for studies from 2013 to 2022.

Only three studies met their bar, a sign the mapping approach is still rare here. Those studies charted patterns with global and local cluster tests and hot spot tools. None yet used the stronger regression methods that can weigh local causes place by place. The authors urge wider use of those methods so health funds can be sent where the need is truly greatest.
pmc-11694711:
Fatal drug overdoses in the United States finally turned down in the year ending May 2024, falling about 12.7 percent, with New York close behind. Three public health authors ask what that dip is worth in 2024. Simple year-to-year counting gives one answer. They also build a counterfactual: extend the rising trend of 2019 to 2023 and ask how many deaths that path predicted. The gap between forecast and fact counts the lives saved.

From the gap they compute years of life regained, using the average age at overdose death. A standard regulatory method then prices those statistical lives. The authors also test whether the national goal for 2025 now looks reachable. The piece frames the decline as real progress with policy value attached.
pmc-11696411:
Huajing Yang and co-authors report a 2024 study on liver cancer treatment that pairs sound-based therapy with tiny gas bubbles. The therapy uses a light-sensitive drug and ultrasound to attack tumor cells. The team tested whether bursting the bubbles with ultrasound could make the treatment work better in lab cells and in mice.

In cell tests, the combined approach made more harmful oxygen forms and killed more cancer cells than the therapy alone. It also raised signs of a type of cell death that can alert the immune system. In mice, the paired treatment shrank tumors more, while body weight changed little. The results point to a way to strengthen this therapy.
pmc-11697611:
Wu and co-authors present a rapid test, published in 2024, for a newly emerged virus carried by animals. The virus was first found in China and can sicken people, yet no quick field test existed for it. The team built their test on a gene-cutting tool that flashes a signal when it finds its target. A copying step multiplies the virus's genetic material. The test runs at room temperature and finishes within 30 minutes.

The test detected as few as ten copies of the viral code in a sample size. A second version pairs the cutter with an enzyme reporter and skips that step at a small cost in sensitivity. Both suit clinics far from full laboratories. Fast point-of-care tests are the first line of defense when a new virus appears. The authors offer this one as a template for quick responses to future threats.
pmc-11697711:
Christian Sonne and colleagues estimated whale deaths in fishing nets in 2024. Toothed whales anchor ocean food webs worldwide. Gillnets trap and drown many of them each year. Global totals for that bycatch were unknown. The team compiled population, bycatch, and status data. Their window ran from nineteen ninety to twenty twenty. Risk estimates were built by region and species. Bycatch is thought worst near Asia and East Africa. American west coasts also rank high.

Their estimate puts yearly gillnet deaths near fifty thousand. That toll joins overfishing, pollution, and noise as threats. Toothed whales breed slowly and invest heavily in young. Such losses can thus erode populations for decades. The authors demand better region-based management. Fishers, managers, mammal experts, and planners must work together. Local food needs and global goals both matter here. The study frames bycatch as a solvable but neglected crisis.
pmc-11699711:
David Keinan and co-authors study retreatment of failed root therapy in young teeth in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Regenerative therapy aims to let immature teeth with dead tissue keep growing. Some cases fail on follow-up, even years after apparent success.

From more than four hundred treated teeth, the team found eight failures in patients aged six to seventeen. Most failures came two to seven years after treatment, often after healing and root growth had occurred. Six teeth were retreated by repeat regenerative work, standard root filling, or surgery, each with a good outcome. The authors offer a decision guide and note that growth after the first therapy improved the odds for the second.
pmc-11700511:
Osvaldo Alexis Marché Fernández and co-authors report a fungal infection that fooled doctors in a 2024 case report. A middle-aged patient arrived with yellowed skin, which pointed the team toward gallbladder trouble. Scans instead showed an enlarged liver and widespread lung spots. The fungus behind it usually strikes people with weak immunity, yet this patient's defenses tested normal.

Tests for HIV and tuberculosis came back negative. A urine test for the fungus came back positive, which settled the diagnosis of spread histoplasmosis. The germ thrives in soil rich with bird or bat droppings and is common in Mexico. The case warns doctors to keep the fungus in mind when illness spreads across organs.
pmc-11703411:
Neyaz Ahmad and co-authors report a giant breast tumor left untreated for twelve years, in a 2024 case report. The patient, a 68-year-old tribal woman, carried a left breast mass that grew to over ten kilograms. Such growths, phyllodes tumors, spring from the breast's fibrous tissue and peak in middle age. They can mimic cancer, balloon fast, and warp posture, strain the back, and break the skin by sheer pressure.

A core needle biopsy confirmed the tumor as benign, the step the authors call a must before any plan. Wide surgery with a clean margin is the guard against return, since these tumors often recur yet seldom spread or seed the lymph nodes. Prompt cutting also heads off any turn toward malignancy. The case is told as a warning on neglect: a slow, painless lump still earns fast care, whatever a patient's distance from a hospital.
pmc-11705011:
Eight authors, led by Haiyan Liu, build in 2024 an evidence based nutrition program for older adults in nursing homes in Ningxia, China. Poor nutrition is common in such homes and harms recovery and strength. The team searched care guides and summed the best proof into a draft program.

Baseline data came from three hundred fifty residents and one hundred sixty nurses in three homes. An expert panel method, run in rounds, then judged the draft's fit and flagged blocks to its use. The panel's rounds reshaped and filled gaps in the program. The result is a ready plan for wider rollout.
pmc-11706611:
Godfrey Tabowei and co-authors gather trial evidence in a 2024 review on whether an old anti-inflammatory drug, colchicine, can prevent a second stroke. The drug has long been used for gout and other inflammatory ills. New interest asks whether calming inflammation can also cut the risk of another stroke after a first one.

The team searched several databases up to November 2024 for randomized trials of the drug for stroke prevention. Two reviewers screened the studies, pulled the data, and judged quality with a standard bias tool on their own. They pooled the results to compare stroke rates and deaths from any cause between drug and control groups. The review gives doctors a single summary of benefit and safety for a cheap, widely known drug.
pmc-11707411:
Beth MacLean, Mubashshira Ahmed, Jayne Lim, and Toby Richards write a letter on how long iron deficiency lasts, published in 2024. They respond to a study finding that most adults with low iron stores had not fixed the problem within three years. Their own data come from a long-running study of young women in Western Australia.

Of 268 women, about half were iron deficient at age seventeen, and most of them were not anemic. The share stayed high at each later check: forty percent at twenty, and still thirty-one percent at twenty-seven. Iron stores rose slowly with age, yet a third of the group remained low. The letter backs the claim that iron deficiency is a long burden, not a brief one, in young women.
pmc-11709411:
Divya Mallikarjun and a large team test whether lung function relates to thinking ability in urban Indian adults. Their study came out in 2025. Data came from an ongoing aging study in Bangalore covering more than nine hundred people aged forty-five and older.

Breathing tests measured how much air participants could hold and how fast they could blow it out. Cognition was scored with a standard examination. Adults in the higher lung-function groups scored better on the cognitive test, even after accounting for age, education, smoking, and common diseases. One breathing measure, the one-second forced volume, showed no link. The authors argue that protecting respiratory health may also help preserve the mind in later life.
pmc-11709511:
Aditi Dey, Silke Kern, and Ingmar Skoog ask in this 2025 study how an inflammation marker behaves at the dawn of Alzheimer's disease. C-reactive protein in blood has been tied to later decline, yet its course across disease stages is murky. From a Swedish cohort of seventy-year-olds, 300 dementia-free people gave blood protein levels and spinal fluid markers of amyloid, tau, and nerve damage.

Counter to simple expectations, the protein fell as amyloid and tau crossed into the abnormal range. One damage-only group ran high instead. Memory scores showed no link. The authors sketch a wave: the marker may rise decades early, dip near onset, then climb again late.
pmc-11709611:
Soloviev and co-authors hunt for molecular signs of why certain brain cells die early in Alzheimer disease. A group of excitatory neurons in the entorhinal cortex is known to be vulnerable by a middle disease stage, yet only some of those cells are at risk. Their 2025 study reuses single cell gene data from postmortem brains at three disease stages.

The team split cells at the earliest stage into vulnerable like and resilient like sets by their gene patterns. Three vulnerable subpopulations emerged. Turned down genes in them touched insulin signaling, cell cleanup, membrane traffic, and protein disposal paths. Eight turned down genes were shared across all three sets. Several shared genes feed into making heme, a core metabolic molecule.
pmc-11709711:
Marianne Elegores and co-authors test whether past heavy drinking leaves lasting marks on heart rhythm control in dementia. Heavy alcohol use is known to harm the brain for good. Heart rate variation often rebounds after people quit. The team asked whether that rebound fails in dementia patients with a drinking past.

Wrist bands tracked heart and skin signals in a small group at a Canadian care unit. The drinking past group showed weaker calm system activity and stronger stress system activity. Two variation scores sat below the healthy range in that group. Skin signals did not split clearly. Behavior scores also matched, so the heart marks stand out on their own.
pmc-11709811:
Florentina Morello Garcia and co-authors study reading loss in a language loss disease among Spanish speakers, in work from 2025. In English, tests that contrast regular and odd words can spot a form of reading loss. Spanish words are mostly regular to read, so those tests do not transfer well.

The team assessed a small group of patients and a larger matched healthy group. Tasks covered word and made up word reading, plus reading of foreign words. Brain scans that track sugar use were also taken. The aim was a workable test for this setting and a map of the brain pattern tied to reading loss.
pmc-11710011:
Alex Salazar and co-authors hunt the causal variant behind a brain disease risk gene in a 2025 study. The gene helps cells clear waste through their recycling system. A DNA stretch inside it links to higher risk of several brain diseases. Which exact change drives that risk stayed unknown for years.

Long read sequencing of hundreds of genomes revealed a jumping gene inserted in the risk stretch. The insert travels with the known risk marker in every case checked. The risk copy also gathered chemical marks that may mute the insert. Like inserts appear in the same gene of other species, hinting at an old benefit.
pmc-11710111:
Adults with Down syndrome face a very high lifetime risk of Alzheimer's disease, yet symptoms start at widely different ages. Emily Schworer and co-authors look for lifestyle factors that might delay symptoms. Sixty-three adults took part, most of them cognitively stable. Brain scans measured amyloid plaques, and each person received a chronicity score for plaque buildup. Memory tests and caregiver screens tracked symptoms. Caregivers also rated time in cognitive, social, and work activities. Wrist devices counted daily steps for a week.

The team combined the activity reports into one lifestyle score. They then tested whether lifestyle softened the link between plaques and symptoms. The design targets resilience: habits that might protect thinking even as plaques grow.
pmc-11710211:
Jiwei Jiang and co-authors present a 2025 conference abstract on mood and behavior symptoms across the Alzheimer's disease continuum. The team built a brain network for each patient from scan data, using a method that links regions with similar tissue patterns. Their sample held 487 patients, some with these symptoms and some without.

From 300 key network links, the team sorted patients with symptoms into three subtypes. Two subtypes showed strong but opposite patterns of network damage, faster drops in test scores, and loss of grey matter in key brain areas. The third subtype looked much like patients without symptoms. Gene tests then tied each subtype to its own set of body pathways.
pmc-11710411:
David Holtzman presents evidence in this 2025 paper that the adaptive immune system helps drive tau-based brain decay. Tau is a protein that tangles inside neurons in Alzheimer's disease. Recent work points to both branches of immunity, innate and adaptive, in the disease's progress.

Holtzman's group had shown that T cells, above all killer T cells, grow in number where tau damage sits, in both a mouse model and the human Alzheimer's brain. Removing T cells or microglia protected the mice strongly. In the new work, the team crossed the tau mice with mice that lack both T and B cells. At nine and a half months, the crossed mice had almost no T cells in the brain. Their innate immune response was also heavily suppressed. They showed far less brain shrinkage and synapse loss than tau mice with full immunity.
pmc-11710511:
Rebecca Thurston and co-authors present a 2025 study of sex hormones and small vessel brain damage in midlife women. Scans on more than two hundred women measured white matter bright spots, a sign of vessel harm. Blood tests covered three hormones, not just the usual one.

Lower levels of both estrogen forms went with more bright spots. So did higher levels of a hormone that marks ovarian aging. After full adjustment for heart risk factors, the newer estrogen and the aging marker kept their links. The first estrogen did not. Spots in front and deep brain areas drove the pattern. The authors urge wider hormone panels in brain aging research on women.
pmc-11710611:
Giulia Pegoraro and six co-authors study how the Alzheimer's brain responds at the gene level when the body fights a systemic infection. Their 2025 paper notes that infections raise the risk of dementia and speed decline in patients, and many patients die with an infection present. The team read gene activity in post-mortem frontal cortex samples from 204 donors, split by disease and by whether a respiratory infection was present at death.

Over a thousand genes differed across the groups. The changed genes clustered in microglia, the brain's immune cells, and the top pathways all concerned immune response. A network analysis found one gene module tied to both disease and infection, rich in genes from two other brain cell types also involved in immunity. The authors frame the work as groundwork, with plans to add further molecular layers from the same donors.
pmc-11710711:
Egiazarian and co-authors present a 2025 study on faulty DNA repair in Alzheimer's disease. Oxidative damage piles up in the Alzheimer's brain, and slow repair may help drive the disease. The team bred mice lacking enzymes that fix oxidative base damage. They also grew vessel-lined brain organoids from patients to mirror the human case.

Mice were checked at several ages for amyloid load, glial cell counts, and inflammation signals. DNA damage was measured by mass tools and tissue stains. Behavior tests tracked thinking skills over time. Early results tie repair loss to more amyloid build-up. The paired organoid work aims to confirm the path in human tissue.
pmc-11710811:
