Shahnawaz A Bhat reports a 2025 study of a microglia protein called Trem-2 in Alzheimer's disease. Microglia are the brain's immune cells, and gene studies have tied low Trem-2 activity to higher disease risk. Bhat asked what happens when these cells carry less of the protein during inflammation.

He used a bacterial toxin, LPS, to trigger inflammation in cultured microglia and in mice. When Trem-2 fell, the cells produced more markers of oxidative stress and more of an inflammatory signal. Mice with lower Trem-2 also learned a water maze more poorly. The results suggest Trem-2 helps keep the brain environment healthy. Bhat proposes it as a target for future treatments of diseases tied to microglia failure.
pmc-11710911:
Meijun Liu and Peihai Zhang link food antioxidants to erectile health in a 2024 survey study. A diet rich in such guards may curb erectile failure, yet the joint pull of all food guards at once had been little weighed. Their gauge sums the main guards in a man's diet into one index.

The team drew on a United States health survey from 2001 to 2004, with diet logs and health forms from adult men. Models set the index against failure rates, with weight held for home and health traits. Higher index scores tracked with lower failure odds, as the pair report.
pmc-11711911:
Ipsit V Vahia gives a talk summary on mild behavioral impairment in a 2025 piece on early dementia signs. Changes in behavior, such as apathy or agitation, can appear up to three years before memory symptoms in Alzheimer's disease. Yet such changes are often read as mental illness alone, which delays the right response.

Vahia reviews what is known about the condition and presents three studies that use sensor data to measure behavior with care. Case examples cover apathy, agitation, and pacing. The markers can also show whether a drug is working, which may help separate mental illness from early dementia. Trial data follows on how these measures might enter daily practice.
pmc-11712011:
Shanshan Gao and co-authors write a 2024 commentary letter on a study of breath holding during breast radiotherapy. Holding a deep breath moves the heart away from the beam and cuts heart dose. The study under discussion found the method good value for money in Belgium and able to lower later heart disease risk.

Gao and colleagues raise three cautions. The cost balance may fail in poorer countries where funds are tight. The method slowed patient throughput by about an eighth in the study, which could delay treatment at busy centers. Bodies also differ, so patient selection should target those who gain most. The authors call for work on smoother workflow and personal dose planning.
pmc-11712111:
Neelum T Aggarwal and Christopher R Carpenter wrote this 2025 paper on emergency care for people with Alzheimer's disease. New drugs that slow the disease can cause swelling or bleeding in the brain, seen on scans. These changes are the most common side effect of the drugs, yet clear guidance on spotting them is thin.

The paper explains how these scan changes may look when a patient arrives at an emergency department. It also reviews what treatment choices staff have in that setting. Doctors, nurses, patients, and families each see the care plan in a different way, the authors note. Shared, clear steps for emergency teams could help these patients get safer and faster care.
pmc-11712311:
Andrew R Bender and six co-authors present this 2025 conference abstract on seeing brain wiring damage that plain diffusion scans smear away. A diffusion MRI voxel often holds several fiber bundles crossing at angles, and standard readings average them into mush. That blurs the very gaps that might split healthy aging from amnestic mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's dementia.

The team used a fixel-based method that gauges fiber density for each crossing group on its own, in 179 University of Michigan people. Of these, 98 were unimpaired, 52 had the amnestic condition, and 29 had dementia. A multi-block statistical method then hunted patterns linking the fiber readings, plus spinal fluid fraction, to diagnosis. The model found three significant latent patterns, mixing gains and losses across fiber types. The pitch: signatures tied to each diagnosis hide inside crossing fibers, and finer tools can surface them.
pmc-11712411:
Michael Rafii and Prashanthi Vemuri set out the role of brain imaging in trials that test treatments before Alzheimer's disease shows clear signs. Drugs that lower a brain protein called amyloid have now been cleared for people with mild signs, and the next step is to test them in people with no signs at all.

Their session talk deals with what taking part means for the people in such trials. Topics include the feelings that come with learning one's own test results, the risk of side effects, and how to weigh risk against gain. They stress a true partnership between the study team and the people who join.
pmc-11712511:
Renee Tobias and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on a machine that counts single molecules to measure faint brain disease markers in blood. Such markers sit far lower in blood than in spinal fluid, so normal lab tests often miss them. Their counter was built to catch them one by one.

The team built tests on the machine for three markers tied to Alzheimer's disease, using strong antibodies to grab each one. Freed tags from the grabbed markers were then counted by a light-based detector. Early checks showed the tests could sense very low levels in small blood samples. A blood test this sharp could make early screening far easier than a spinal tap.
pmc-11712611:
Neil Oxtoby presents this 2025 symposium report on a frame for setting up data-driven models of Alzheimer's disease, named Goldilocks. Such models are only as good as their setup: weak input signals mislead them, and settings tuned too hard for the data at hand do the same. The frame aims to keep each analysis in a middle zone.

Three steps make up the frame. First, patient data is turned into disease signal scores measured against healthy controls. Next, only inputs with enough signal are kept. Last, model settings are capped so they cannot outrun the data. Oxtoby shows the frame at work on fake data made to mimic a large Alzheimer's study, using spinal fluid markers, test scores, and a brain volume measure. The report offers the frame as a way to open sound modeling to more teams.
pmc-11712711:
Thea Jacobson Rosewood and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on gene paths that may steer how Alzheimer's disease unfolds over time. Rather than study the disease at one moment, the team tracked traits that change as it grows: amyloid, tau, brain fuel use, shrinkage, and test scores for memory and planning.

They scanned the full gene set of a large aging study for variants tied to the slope of each trait. Then they grouped hits into known gene paths. Some paths stood out as ones a drug might shift to change the course of the illness. The work points drug hunters toward paths that act while the disease moves, not just at its start.
pmc-11712811:
Hayley Olson and co-authors study early Alzheimer signs in a 2025 paper. Recalling proper names from a story may be a tender spot for early decline, even before clear symptoms show. The team asked whether tau, a protein that builds up in the disease, in language areas of the brain tracks that skill.

Nearly four hundred adults without impairment took a story recall test and brain scans for amyloid and tau. Tau in name-linked regions on both sides of the brain predicted name recall and total story recall. In checks that left out people with mild problems, right-side tau still predicted name scores. The authors say story recall tasks may serve as a low-cost early screen tied to brain change.
pmc-11712911:
Sukhmanpreet Kaur and Anil Kumar test two plant compounds in mice with insulin resistance and memory loss, in a 2025 study. Alzheimer's disease links to faulty insulin signalling in the brain, which can speed harmful protein build-up. Diabetes was induced in mice with a drug plus sweetened water.

Treated mice faced maze, movement, and object memory tests, plus brain chemistry checks. Sick mice learned slowly and favoured familiar objects, while compound-treated mice found the maze goal faster and explored new objects more. Brain defence enzymes, drained in sick mice, recovered with treatment, and stress markers fell. Tissue checks in the memory region also improved. The authors present both compounds as promising leads, pending far more work.
pmc-11713011:
Mostafa Khalifa and Jana Elsead report early results from a review of ultra-processed food and Alzheimer's disease risk, in a 2025 conference abstract. No cure exists for the disease, so diet draws study as a lever for quality of life and risk. Past work links such food to diabetes, and to stress paths in the body, but direct proof for this disease was thin.

The team screened more than seven thousand records and read one hundred full texts. Ten studies met their bar, all classed by one food grading system. In a five-study pilot, each showed higher disease risk with high intake of ultra-processed food. The review was still in progress, with fuller pooling and trials urged before firm claims.
pmc-11713111:
Andrew K McVea and co-authors compare how fast a sticky brain protein piles up in Down syndrome versus typical adults, in a 2025 paper. The extra gene copy in Down syndrome drives early pile-up of the protein, beta-amyloid, and high Alzheimer risk. Brain scans with a tracer dye tracked the load over years.

Fifty-seven adults with Down syndrome and more than one hundred sixty typical adults, many scanned over a decade, fed the work. A growth model set each scan on a shared clock from the point the protein turned positive. The pile-up rate ran near half again as fast in the Down syndrome group. Rate spread within groups was wide, and the authors call for work on what drives it.
pmc-11713311:
Braden Yang and co-authors test a data method that aligns amyloid scans made with different tracers, in this 2025 paper. Tracers differ in how they bind, so scan values can clash across drugs. Trials that mix tracers may lose power to spot treatment effects.

The method, called ComBat, was built to smooth batch gaps while keeping real biology. The team picked hundreds of scans from a public data set, using two common tracers. They fit models for each tracer, then faked a trial to see if aligned data spot a drug effect better. A shared scale already exists, but the new method needs no calibration step.
pmc-11713411:
Surabhee Eswaran and co-authors ask whether strong social ties in mid-life soften the dementia risk of worn brain wiring, in a 2025 study. White matter, the brain's cabling, frays with age, and frailty tracks higher dementia risk. Yet not all with worn wiring fall ill. The team studied 1,679 adults from a long US heart study who were dementia-free in mid-life, and split them by how strong their ties were then.

Brain scans a decade or more later graded the wiring, and cases were tracked to 2019. Among Black adults with strong mid-life ties, worn wiring no longer tracked dementia risk. Among those with weak ties, one wiring flaw stayed a risk. White adults showed the risk regardless of ties. The softening stood out most in Black women.
pmc-11713511:
Olivia Deering and co-authors link neighborhood hardship to brain health in veterans in a 2025 study. Using data from a Wisconsin trial, they compared veterans in the most deprived neighborhoods with those in better-off areas on thinking tests and heart risk scores. Two hundred one veterans entered screening and one hundred twenty-nine reached baseline testing.

The deprived group scored clearly lower on a preclinical Alzheimer cognitive composite. Heart risk scores, though, showed no firm gap. Readers get a disparity signal aimed at cognition, plus a call for larger and broader samples.
pmc-11713611:
Isabella Jaramillo and co-authors present a Spanish version of a computer test battery in a 2025 paper. Thinking tests in Spanish are scarce in the United States, and few examiners speak the language well. Cases among Hispanic adults are set to rise sixfold by 2060. Their battery gives and scores the tests by computer, in a Mexican Spanish voice.

Sixty-one adults aged forty-three to seventy-nine took thirty-two tests over three days at home. Remote Spanish-speaking staff watched over the sessions. Speech software scored the spoken answers on its own. Early results suggest the battery can test memory, speed, and word skills fairly. Wide access to such tools could close a real gap in dementia care.
pmc-11713711:
Schooling is said to build a reserve that protects the aging brain, but scans do not always agree. Julie Gonneaud and co-authors measured education against brain images in 207 healthy adults aged nineteen to eighty-four in 2025. Their scans covered structure, metabolism, and amyloid, focused on regions tied to Alzheimer's disease and reserve.

Across the whole group, years of education showed no clear tie to any scan measure, for either sex. Only inside the over-sixty group did a pattern surface: more schooling went with a larger frontal control region in women alone. A second, larger sample hinted that mental engagement in midlife mattered more than early schooling. The authors suggest schooling's brain benefit may be late, local, and sex-specific.
pmc-11713811:
Rebecca Lepping and seven co-authors ask, in 2025 work, whether two brain scan signs tell the same story in older adults. One sign tracks blood flow in the brain, the other tracks how brain zones use sugar. Both shift in Alzheimer's disease, yet flow and fuel use are not the same act, so the signs may not match.

More than one hundred older adults, some sharp, some with mild loss, and some with dementia, took both scan types. Flow and fuel use moved together in three of four large brain zones, but only weakly. In the front zone they did not move together at all. The team calls the two signs mates, not twins: each adds facts the other lacks.
pmc-11713911:
Sasha Milton and co-authors follow how the sleep of older women changes over five years, and what those changes foretell for the brain. They studied 769 women averaging 82 years old, all cognitively healthy at the start, wearing activity monitors at both ends of the period. Clustering the changes produced three profiles: stable sleep in 44 percent, declining nighttime sleep in 34 percent, and growing sleepiness, day and night, in 22 percent.

Over the five years, 24 percent of the women developed mild cognitive impairment and 13 percent dementia. Against the stable group, the declining-sleep women faced roughly 1.9 times the odds of dementia, and the increasingly sleepy women about 2.4 times. Neither pattern predicted the milder impairment. The authors read worsening or ballooning sleep in very old age as a warning sign worth clinical attention.
pmc-11714011:
Adrian Noriega de la Colina and six co-authors compare cell stress marks in blood and spinal fluid across the Alzheimer's span, in a 2025 conference paper. Cell stress from oxygen plays a part in the disease. It was not clear whether blood marks mirror the marks in the fluid that bathes the brain.

The study held 140 people with no dementia, 47 of them with mild loss, from a memory clinic group. Four marks gauged the body's shield against oxygen stress in both fluids. Two marks lined up between blood and fluid, and two did not. In healthy adults the match ran wider than in the mild loss group. The authors say blood can stand in for the brain only for some marks.
pmc-11714311:
Walter D Dawson, Sherril B Gelmon, and Jenn Hollandsworth Reed ran this 2025 study on support for dementia care partners. People who care for a family member with dementia face heavy strain. The team wanted a clear list of policy steps that could help them, with fair access for groups often left out.

Between July and September 2023, the team used a modified Delphi process in Oregon. Forty people from groups that serve patients and care partners took part. They sorted ideas into eight themes, from direct support to funding and staff training. Across three survey rounds, the group rated each idea and then saw the group scores. The result is a ranked set of steps that local leaders can act on.
pmc-11714511:
Anders Gustavsson and thirteen co-authors survey memory clinics in the Nordic countries on the strain of new Alzheimer's drugs, in a 2025 conference paper. The new drugs can slow the disease in its mild stage, a first for care. But they demand far more scans, tests, and watch over patients than clinics now give.

The team polled twelve clinics in Sweden, Denmark, Finland, and Norway on staff, patient counts, and gear. Clinics now see only a few of the people who could gain from the drugs. Most such patients stay with family doctors and never reach a clinic. Wait times for scans are long. The authors warn that health systems must grow clinic space fast or most patients will miss the new care.
pmc-11714611:
Xiang Fan and co-authors track how an MRI-based Alzheimer's score changes over time, in a 2025 study. The score, AD-RAI, rates how closely a brain scan matches the Alzheimer's shrink pattern. It can spot early disease, yet one snapshot says little about pace. The team asked whether its drift over years tracks the disease's chemistry better than older scan gauges.

They drew 168 older adults from a large database, all with repeat scans and spinal fluid tests. Some carried both core Alzheimer's markers in their fluid, and some did not. In the marker group, the score climbed faster and key memory areas shrank faster. Whole-brain size gauges split the groups less well. The score's drift also tracked shifts in a fluid marker over time. The authors back it as a way to watch disease pace or drug effect.
pmc-11714811:
Erik Buchholz and Carol Franz ask whether how men bond in midlife forecasts frailty in old age. Their twenty twenty-five study uses the Vietnam Era Twin Study of Aging, with over twelve hundred community men. Attachment style, measured at midlife, is the trait under test.

Two frailty outcomes were tracked: mild cognitive impairment and a count of health deficits. Paths through stress, smoking, drinking, doctor visits, and isolation were weighed as go-betweens. If a midlife social trait reaches decades ahead into brain and body frailty, then friendship and trust are not soft extras. They are early markers, and maybe levers, of how aging lands.
pmc-11714911:
Melissa Bahr and co-authors tie brain tau patterns to thinking outcomes in Alzheimer's disease. Tau tangles spread through the brain in stages, called Braak stages, and advanced stages usually bring decline. Their 2025 study used tau PET scans from two Wisconsin cohorts, 830 people in all. Those rated at stage four or higher, 112 people, formed the core group.

About seventy-one percent of that group had cognitive impairment. Diagnosis mix differed by stage, with stage six standing apart. Two case studies break the pattern: one person with stage six tau stayed sharp, and one showed a back-of-brain pattern that spread in reverse order over five years. The authors stress varied paths in the disease.
pmc-11715011:
Nikhil Dhinagar and co-authors teach a generative model to dream brain scans, and use the dreams to get better at spotting Alzheimer's. Diagnosis increasingly leans on MRI patterns too subtle for the eye, and labeled scans are scarce. Their latent diffusion model learns how disease reshapes brain structure from more than four thousand scans in the big ADNI collection.

Coupled with convolutional networks, the synthetic scans augment training data for detection tasks. The timing matters: as anti-amyloid treatments arrive, catching the disease early and tracking it cheaply decides who benefits. A generator that knows what Alzheimer's looks like becomes a tireless teacher for the classifiers doctors will actually use.
pmc-11715111:
A blood test for a changed tau protein may help spot Alzheimer's disease and warn of decline, Yung-Shuan Lin reports in a 2025 study. Lin studied ninety-eight adults who had brain scans for amyloid plaques, plus a smaller group with mild memory loss who were followed over time. Blood levels of the protein were measured with a sensitive lab method.

Plaques were found in about half the adults with dementia and in a small share of those without. Blood protein levels tracked plaque status and memory state in the tests. In the follow-up group, starting levels helped forecast who moved from mild loss to full disease. The author argues the cheap blood test could aid early care planning.
pmc-11715211:
A team led by Natalya V. Ponomareva published this study in two thousand twenty-five on two aging markers and brain function. One marker is the APOE gene form that raises Alzheimer's risk. The other is a chemical tag on the ELOVL2 gene that tracks age closely.

The team studied one hundred fifty-one adults without dementia, aged twenty to eighty-four. They recorded brain waves and resting brain scans, and checked the gene tag in blood for part of the group. Carriers of the risk gene form showed more slowing of a key brain rhythm and weaker network links as age rose. The ELOVL2 tag grew with age and tracked the rhythm's peak speed. The authors link these shifts to worn wiring and fat changes in the aging brain.
pmc-11715311:
Gabriela Caballero and co-authors evaluate a dementia teaching program built with migrant communities in Sydney in a 2025 study. Migrant families often know less about the illness and face stigma that delays care. Sessions ran in six languages, co-led by trained bilingual leaders from those same communities.

Three two-hour meetings spread over three months carried the content. A reach-and-impact framework structured the verdict on who came and what changed. People with lived experience helped design the materials from the start. The study tests whether co-production beats translation alone for health know-how.
pmc-11715411:
Alina Ferguson and co-authors introduce a study that adds eye checks to a long-running study of aging and memory, in a 2025 report. The parent study has followed older adults in Washington state since 1994, testing thinking skills every two years to watch for Alzheimer disease. Since late 2021, the eye study has drawn members from that cohort and tested vision, eye pressure, and detailed retinal images.

A rare feature is that visits can happen at home as well as at the clinic, which widens who can take part. The first eye cohort numbered 330 people, against 1,868 in the parent study at the time. Eye study members were younger, newer to the parent study, and had more years of schooling. They also reported better heart health at their latest visit.
pmc-11715611:
Gerard Piñol-Ripoll and co-authors compare two laboratory platforms that measure Alzheimer's biomarkers in blood plasma and in cerebrospinal fluid. Blood markers are cheap and easy to draw, but laboratories must know how well they match the fluid gold standard. The 2025 study used samples from 127 clinic patients. Most had mild cognitive impairment, some had Alzheimer's disease, and a few had other forms of dementia.

The two platforms, Simoa and Lumipulse, agreed well with each other, though their raw values ran on different scales. A blood ratio joining a tau marker with an amyloid marker sorted patients best on both platforms. Still, the fluid ratio beat all blood markers by a clear margin. The team says blood markers can serve as a first screen and cut the need for lumbar punctures. They stop short of calling blood markers a full substitute for fluid tests.
pmc-11715711:
Roser Sala-Llonch and Agnès Pérez-Millan review how Bayesian statistics can model brain change over time and predict one person's course in neuroimaging. Large imaging datasets now follow patients for years, yet the data are messy, with missing points and noise. The field has also shifted from group patterns toward predictions for each individual. Their 2025 review weighs the Bayesian tools against older frequentist standards, with worked examples.

The examples use the ADNI database, a large shared imaging resource. In large, balanced datasets, the old and new approaches match, and the old one runs faster. In small or uneven datasets with many gaps, the Bayesian approach wins. A second tool draws smooth personal trajectories without a fixed shape. The authors close with machine-learning forecasts that go beyond plain group sorting. The review maps where each tool fits best.
pmc-11715811:
Mahsa Dolatshahi and co-authors ask whether where body fat sits matters for early brain changes in midlife, in this 2025 study. Belly fat deep around the organs behaves differently from fat under the skin, and midlife obesity raises the risk of later Alzheimer's disease. The team paired body scans with brain scans in adults with normal thinking.

Forty-nine adults around age fifty took part, more than half of them obese. Scans measured deep belly fat, fat under the skin, liver fat, and thigh fat, while blood tests gauged insulin resistance. Brain scans measured amyloid, a protein that builds up early in the disease. People with obesity carried a higher amyloid load. Work of this kind may show which fat stores deserve the most attention for brain health.
pmc-11715911:
Dove and co-authors ask whether a strong store of mental resources can delay dementia in people with heart and metabolic disease. Their 2025 study follows more than 216,000 dementia-free adults aged 60 and over in the UK Biobank for up to 15 years. That store, called cognitive reserve, was scored from schooling, work, social contact, and leisure habits.

People with diabetes, heart disease, or stroke faced a much higher risk of dementia overall. Among them, those with a moderate or high reserve score had notably lower risk than those with a low score. Brain scans in a smaller group also showed less tissue loss in the high reserve group. The authors say reserve seems to blunt part of the harm from these diseases.
pmc-11716011:
Kenichiro Sato and five co-authors study how the Japanese public reacted online when the Alzheimer's drug lecanemab was approved in Japan, in this 2025 paper. The drug won approval in the United States in July 2023 and in Japan two months later. Online opinion was mixed, with debate over how well it works, its side effects, and its cost.

The team collected 478 posts from X and Facebook in the two weeks after approval and used an AI tool to sort them by tone. About forty-four percent were negative, thirty percent positive, and the rest neutral. Worry about the drug's effect on society drove most negative posts, and medical workers were more negative than others. The authors say drug makers and officials should tailor how they explain such treatments.
pmc-11716111:
Christopher Bauer and co-authors ask whether a healthy diet can blunt the harm that blood vessel damage does to thinking, in a 2025 paper. Vessel damage shows up on brain scans as bright spots and worn white matter. Some people keep sharp minds despite such damage, and diet may be part of the reason. The team paired detailed diet records with brain scans in a group of older adults.

Seventy-one adults aged sixty to eighty-five were scanned at the University of Kentucky. The team measured three vessel damage markers and grey matter volume, then tested thinking with a standard screening exam. A questionnaire sorted what people ate into groups such as fruits and vegetables, nuts and fish, and green tea. The analysis checked whether diet changed the link between scan damage and test scores.
pmc-11716311:
Inês Matias-Lopes and co-authors report the case of a healthy sixty-two-year-old woman who became seriously ill from a common virus, in a 2024 paper. The virus, cytomegalovirus, infects most people at some point and stays quiet in most healthy adults. She came in after three weeks of deep tiredness, sore joints, belly pain, and daily fever. Tests showed a swollen liver and blood counts far from normal.

Her care team suspected a rare disorder in which the immune system runs out of control and harms the body's own tissues. Blood tests confirmed a fresh virus infection. Even so, she stayed stable, and the team chose not to give antiviral drugs. Over the next month the fever, liver trouble, and blood problems cleared on their own. The authors urge doctors to keep this virus in mind even for healthy patients.
pmc-11716411:
Huang, Tan, and Yu ask in 2025 whether a blood protein that rises with age links to brain disease signs in healthy older adults. They studied 846 adults in a Chinese group who had no loss of thought at the start. Spinal fluid tests placed each person at a stage of early brain change, or at no change.

Blood levels of the protein were higher at the first two stages than at stage zero. Higher levels also went with worse scores on short mind tests and with fluid signs of plaque and tangle build up. The protein may take part in how the disease harms thought, not just mark it from the side.
pmc-11716511:
David Bartres-Faz and co-authors use brain scans to sort two ideas about why some older adults keep their memory as they age, in a 2025 study. One idea, brain maintenance, says memory holds when the brain itself holds up. The other, called reserve, says memory can hold even when the brain shows decline.

Working with data from a large European group, the team tracked memory, brain size, and brain activity over time in 532 adults. Of those with stable memory, most fit the maintenance path at the first step. The rest fit the reserve path, with memory gains despite shrinkage in a key memory area. Their scan-based method aims to give clear, shared rules for telling the two paths apart in future work.
pmc-11716611:
Jeyeon Lee and a large team link breathing patterns to fluid flow in the sleeping brain, in this 2025 Europe PMC paper. During non-rapid eye movement sleep, cerebrospinal fluid flow rises, helping clear waste products such as amyloid-beta from the brain. What drives that rise is still being worked out.

The team combined brain wave recordings and functional MRI in sleeping volunteers, using data from an earlier study of twenty-nine people. They tracked breathing volume, delta wave power and fluid inflow at the base of the skull, aligning all signals to each inflow peak. Breathing volume rose just before inflow, hinting that respiratory shifts help drive the nightly cleaning cycle.
pmc-11716711:
Muneeb Ahmad Muneer and nine co-authors published a pooled analysis in 2025 on small signaling proteins in the spinal fluid of Alzheimer's patients. These proteins, called neuropeptides, help run many brain processes, and their levels may shift with disease. Single studies are small, so the team combined results across the published record.

They searched four major databases and pooled studies that measured these proteins in patients and controls. One protein, somatostatin, came out clearly lower in patients across nine studies. Other proteins showed their own patterns of change. A firmer map of these shifts could point to new tests or treatments, though the studies varied a lot in size and method.
pmc-11716811:
Joshua Woo and co-authors chart slow change in the eyes of sound older adults in a 2025 study. The eye's back wall and its nerve can mirror the brain's own wear, a clue labs hope to use in the hunt for brain ills.

The hard part is to tell plain age wear from the wear of disease. The team scanned more than a hundred adults with sound thought at the start and again two years on. Fine blood flow in the nerve head and the nerve's own coat all thinned with age at both reads. The pace of change did not track with age. Flow and coat did thin more slowly in women than in men, and women held a lead in flow at both reads. The counts set a base line for what sound aging looks like.
pmc-11716911:
The authors test a blood marker that could shrink Alzheimer's trials by picking the right volunteers early. The marker, plasma GFAP, signals reactive support cells in the brain. Paired with amyloid scans, it may flag people whose tau tangles will grow fastest, even before symptoms. They checked 195 healthy-minded adults from two cohorts with blood tests and brain scans.

Only the group positive for both amyloid and the marker grew tau in wide brain areas. Screening by both cut the needed trial size by 60 percent for that outcome and costs by 59 percent. The authors back the two-marker screen for early trials.
pmc-11721311:
Fourteen authors, led by Xiangxi Kong, name a brake on bone-eating cells in this 2024 paper. Bone stays strong when builder cells and eater cells balance. When eaters, called osteoclasts, multiply or overwork, bone thins. That loss drives osteoporosis, above all after menopause and with age.

The brake is a kinase called NDR2. Its levels rise as osteoclasts form, a hint of feedback control. Turning it down sped cell formation; turning it up slowed it. Mice lacking the gene in their immune-line cells had lighter bones and lost more after ovary removal or aging. Inside the cell, NDR2 weakens ULK1, a starter of the cleanup process that feeds cell formation. The study marks a control loop that bone drugs might one day tune.
pmc-11723711:
Yoshika Nagata and co-authors report a breast implant complication in a 2024 case report. Silicone implants are common in reconstruction and cosmetic surgery, yet long-term rupture and infection need watching. Their patient developed skin ulceration after an infection.

The authors trace the chain to a COVID-19 infection. The illness weakened immune defenses, letting a bacterial infection take hold around the implant. The infection then triggered rupture of the implant shell. The damaged implant was removed. The case warns that long-carried implants need careful follow-up, above all when illness suppresses immunity.
pmc-11726711:
Christopher Essex and Bjarne Andresen extend a physics concept for extreme scales in a 2024 paper. Their concept, called epitropy, captures effects from the far tails of probability spreads. It resembles entropy but is not the same: it stands for hidden influences from outside a regime rather than inside it. The tails matter when systems run over very long times and huge spaces.

Using kinetic theory, they show the concept is needed to keep certain integrals from blowing up. On lab scales the issue is negligible. On grand scales, tail-driven epitropy can move energy around. The paper is theoretical, aimed at physicists working on transport at extreme scales.
pmc-11726911:
Daniela Deossa-Piedrahita and co-authors check in 2024 how oft vitamin D runs low in lupus patients in west Mexico, and if low marks track with how live the disease is. That link has split past studies, though low marks are common in this group in all of them. Charts from one hospital over a year form the set.

Sixty one patients had the blood mark on file at first stay. Near nine in ten showed low marks in that read. The team then weighs low mark depth next to disease live scores and next to traits that could drive the lack.
pmc-11727111:
Kasper Jørgensen and co-authors teach a neural network to outline brown fat in CT scans, in a 2024 study. Brown fat burns energy to make heat, so it draws interest in metabolism research. Tracing it by hand in scans is slow and varies between readers.

The team trained a 3D nnU-Net on hand-drawn outlines from 159 lymphoma patients and merged it into a public body-mapping tool. On 30 fresh patients the model scored a DICE overlap of 0.780, a solid match with human tracings. The team also mined over 7,000 PET/CT studies for brown fat activity patterns, finding gaps between the sexes. Fast auto-tracing opens large scan archives to brown fat research.
pmc-11727211:
A research team tests whether a robot that shares attention with its player feels more competent and warm, in a 2024 study. Joint attention, two partners focusing on the same event, builds rapport between people. Participants played the hand game Odds and Evens against a social robot, sometimes with its attention-tracking system on and sometimes off, while sights and sounds tried to steal the robot's gaze.

After each round, players rated the robot on a social attributes scale. With the system active, the robot scored clearly higher on both competence and warmth. The authors argue that even simple shared-attention behavior can make robots more acceptable partners in everyday settings.
pmc-11727511:
Changhao Fu and co-authors tested whether silencing a gene called LY6K can slow colon cancer stem cells, in a 2024 study. The gene is switched on at high levels in several cancers and tracks with poor outcomes in colorectal cancer. The team isolated stem-like cells from a human colon cancer line using two surface markers.

The stem-like cells carried abundant LY6K. When the researchers silenced it with RNA interference, the cells divided more slowly, stalled at a checkpoint in the cell cycle, and moved and invaded less. In mice, silencing the gene shrank tumors and extended survival. The authors propose LY6K as a target for wiping out the stem cells that seed relapse.
pmc-11728311:
Yongsu Ha, Kangwoo Yi, Chul Park, Gyumin Kim, Daeyoung Choi, Jumjae Lee, and Namsoo Kim set normal blood values for racehorses in a 2024 paper. Whole blood viscosity shows how thick blood flows at distinct speeds. No firm reference range existed for Thoroughbred horses. The team used a new U-shaped tube device for the tests.

They measured blood from 51 Thoroughbred horses with the device. Values were set across a wide range of flow speeds. They then checked how thickness links to standard blood counts and chemistry. The findings give vets a reference set for horse health checks. The links with routine tests also help explain what drives blood thickness in horses.
pmc-11728411:
Highland barley drinks can be enriched with GABA, a calming brain chemical the body makes too little of on its own. Xiaoqing Yin and five co-authors compared pretreatments for that enrichment in a 2024 study. Their toolkit joined sprouting the grain, adding an active barley powder rich in the GABA-making enzyme, and fermenting the drink.

Five versions of the beverage were built from plain barley up to the full treatment chain. Every pretreatment raised GABA levels. The sprouted grain plus active powder version peaked at 2.4 times the plain drink's GABA. The fully treated version, with fermentation added, reached 2.2 times and also carried the most plant phenols and the strongest antioxidant action. Fermentation sharpened acidity, softened bitterness, and shifted the flavor most. The authors chart the trade between GABA content and taste.
pmc-11728711:
Eun-Sol Ha and six co-authors study process parameters in the supercritical antisolvent process for telmisartan particles in a 2024 paper. Telmisartan, a blood pressure drug, barely dissolves in water, which caps how much of a dose the body can take up. Shrinking it to very fine particles can lift that limit.

The process sprays a drug solution into dense carbon dioxide, so the drug falls out as fine powder. Six settings, from solvent mix to flow rates, were varied by a set design. The fine particles proved glass-like, not crystal. Smaller sizes dissolved faster and reached the blood better in tests.
pmc-11728811:
Sue-Ji Seo and three co-authors gauge the health risk of paint solvent fumes for Korean shipyard workers in a 2024 study. Painters breathe in mixes of solvents while coating steel ships, and those mixes can harm nerves and child development. The team studied six common solvents, among them xylene and toluene, using data from a national workplace monitoring program.

They built risk scores for single solvents and for the mix, then ran many random simulations to map how risk spreads across workers. The combined index for nerve harm passed the safe level even at low percentiles, and the index for developmental harm passed it at higher percentiles. A check on which inputs drove the result points managers to the solvents that matter most.
pmc-11731311:
A rare kidney disease that threads fibrils through the filtering units landed in a patient already carrying two autoimmune conditions. Rita Afonso, Roberto Calças Marques, Helena Viana, Ana Cabrita, and Ana Paula Silva report the case in 2024 and review what is known about the disease.

Fibrillary glomerulonephritis usually appears from nowhere, though autoimmunity, cancers, and infections can trigger it, and many patients slide toward kidney failure with little proven treatment to offer. Their patient combined the kidney disease with Sjögren's syndrome and a bile duct condition, primary biliary cholangitis, an unusual trio. The case ended well, which the authors highlight against the gloomy literature. They use the report to press for better evidence on how to treat the disease.
pmc-11734011: Muhammad Sabri, Sheraz Qamar, Naila Ijaz, and Mark DeCaro present the case of a patient whose stroke led doctors to a tumor inside her heart. The growth, a left atrial myxoma, is a rare, benign mass in the heart's upper left chamber. Pieces of it, or clots forming on it, can break loose and travel to the brain. Her tumor had two features tied to a higher risk of that: an irregular surface and strong movement as the heart beat. She was treated with prompt surgery to remove the mass.
pmc-11760411:
Fazulunnisa Begum and co-authors count tooth and mouth diseases in over three thousand children treated at a South Indian dental school, in this 2024 study. Records from 2010 to 2022 split into tooth defects and lesions of bone or soft tissue. Tooth defects dwarfed the lesion group. Boys were affected more than girls, the right side more than the left, and the lower jaw was the commonest site.

Weak enamel formation led the tooth defects. Among lesions, mucoceles came first, then cysts that grow around unerupted teeth. Cancers were the rarest entries. The authors compare their tallies with earlier reports from other regions. They call for more centers to publish such counts so planning for child dental care rests on shared ground.
pmc-11769911:
Tomasz Bielawski, Maksymilian Rejek, and Blazej Misiak study how social defeat may seed psychotic-like experiences in this paper, published in 2024. Such experiences are mild echoes of psychosis that can come before illness. The social defeat idea blames low status and repeated humiliation. Those pressures may unbalance dopamine in the brain and raise risk. The team followed more than two thousand young adults without a diagnosis. Reports were taken at the start and again after six months.

A network method mapped how the parts of social defeat interact over time. One part, aberrant salience, is the feeling that neutral things carry special meaning. The analysis tests whether defeat leads to such experiences through that middle step. Mood and other symptoms were part of the network as well. The authors aim to show a path, not just a link. That path could point to early help for people under strain.
pmc-11786011:
Ifra Iftikhar, Sanjay Singh, Ashu Bhardwaj and colleagues tested platelet-rich fibrin in wisdom tooth surgery in 2024. Each patient had both lower wisdom teeth removed, with the blood-derived fibrin placed in one socket and the other left as control, in a triple-blind trial of 64 patients.

The fibrin side hurt significantly less, and pain settled by one month. Swelling was lower at every check up to a month, and tenderness differed at one week. Bleeding and early sensitivity also favoured fibrin. Bone height, however, did not improve. The authors conclude the material clearly aids soft tissue comfort and healing after extraction, but shows little power to regrow bone in this setting.
pmc-11786211:
Azadeh Reshadmanesh and co-authors report a case from Iran of a two-year-old boy with two gene changes found together for the first time. Published in 2024, the case covers a large head, changed facial traits, slow growth of motor and mental skills, seizures, and low muscle tone. One leg side was larger than the other, and the spine curved.

Whole exome sequencing found a new variant in the HERC1 gene, in two copies, and a new duplication in the PMP22 gene, in one copy. The second gene is tied to Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease. The authors warn that paired variants can blur the link between genes and traits, and they urge care in how families are counseled.
pmc-11794311:
Ian Walling and co-authors showed that leg nerve stimulation can restore breathing drive after neck spinal injury in mice, published in 2024. High neck injuries cut the path from brainstem breath centers to the diaphragm. Limb nerve signals are known to raise breathing in healthy bodies. Whether they help after injury was unknown.

The team cut one side of the upper cord in anesthetized mice. They then zapped the sciatic nerve and recorded diaphragm bursts. At strong enough currents, either leg nerve revived breath bursts on the hurt side. Burst size and rate were tracked across thresholds. The trick might one day support breathing after human cord injury.
pmc-11802411:
Cao and four co-authors measured tiny blood vessels around the optic disc in people with diabetes in twenty twenty-four. They used a scan method that maps blood flow without dye. Their focus was the nerve fiber layer, which carries signals from the eye to the brain.

The study compared healthy eyes, eyes of patients with diabetes but no eye damage, and eyes with mild diabetic eye damage. Vessel density was clearly lower in both diabetes groups than in healthy eyes, most in the damaged group. Layer thickness, by contrast, barely differed between groups. The authors conclude vessel density drops early, before the layer thins. Its measure also separated damaged from healthy eyes with good accuracy.
pmc-11832711:
Mxolisi Nene, Nokuthula Winfred Kunene, Rian Pierneef, and Khanyisile Hadebe studied the gut microbes of village chickens in South Africa. Their paper was published in two thousand twenty-four. Village birds live in low-resource settings, and the microbes in their gut help shape health and growth.

The team used two kinds of gene sequencing on dung samples from birds in Limpopo and KwaZulu-Natal. They found four main groups of bacteria in both places, plus genes that help microbes resist drugs. They also found bacteria that can pass to people through food. The results stress good hygiene at home and more work on safe, lasting village chicken farming.
pmc-11879511:
Madina Khamzina and Wendy Rogers ask what successful aging means to older adults who live with mobility disability. Their 2024 study challenges the textbook definition, which counts aging as successful only when disease and disability are absent. Twenty people aged sixty to seventy-five, living with multiple sclerosis that limits their movement, gave long interviews.

Participants described their own marks of a good old age and the coping moves they use to hold onto it. The authors adapt an existing framework to fit these first-hand accounts. The message for care and policy is plain: people inside disability judge success by engagement and adaptation, not by a clean bill of health.
pmc-11888711:
Vivek K and six co-authors present a lab study from twenty twenty-four on root canal work. They tested how well two sealers used to fill cleaned tooth roots spread into the tiny tubes of the root wall. Three ways of stirring the sealer inside the canal were compared, along with a group that got no stirring.

Eighty pulled teeth with a single straight root were split into groups by sealer type. After filling, scans with a fine X-ray method measured how deep each sealer went at the top, middle, and tip of the root. The work gives dentists a side-by-side view of which sealer and stirring method coat the root wall best, a factor in how long a treated tooth lasts.
pmc-11891011:
Bertrand Bachaumond Hankoua and five co-authors published a study in 2024 on improving the food value of cassava with a gene from a small weed. Cassava feeds millions in sub-Saharan Africa but is poor in protein. The team moved in a plant gene called QQS, known to shift how plants store carbon and nitrogen, and grew ten engineered cassava lines.

Several lines grew well, and gene tests confirmed the new gene was active. One line raised leaf protein by about a third and root protein as well. Sugars and starch also rose sharply in leaves and roots of the best lines. Raising protein and starch together in one step could help fight hidden hunger where cassava is the staple.
pmc-11907711:
Fekher Jaoued, Samia Ernez Hajri, and six co-authors report a heart attack caused by two torn heart arteries at once. Their case report, from twenty twenty-four, concerns a fifty-five-year-old woman. She had no known risk factors for heart disease. Scans showed spontaneous tears in both the right and the circumflex artery, a very rare pairing.

One artery was opened with a stent procedure. The other was treated with drugs alone. Three months later the drug-treated tear had vanished on its own. The stents stayed open and the patient did well. The case stresses care plans tailored to each torn vessel.
pmc-11986711:
Dagne Deresa Dinagde and five co-authors published a case-control study in 2024 on early-life factors tied to sexual assault of schoolgirls in southern Ethiopia. The assaults are among the least reported forms of violence, with lasting psychological and physical harm. Cases were drawn from police records of high school students in the Arba Minch Zuria district, with classmates as controls.

Seventy-five reported cases were compared with non-assaulted students through questionnaires. Drinking alcohol multiplied the odds of assault about fourfold. Living with non-biological caregivers also emerged among the significant factors in the adjusted analysis. The authors frame the assaults as a public health problem rooted partly in children's living arrangements and alcohol exposure. They argue for prevention aimed at those early conditions, rather than only at response after harm.
pmc-12336411:
Bile pooled in the liver sores it slow, and one quiet gene tool in liver cells has long been tied to ease of that sore. Wen Zhang and co-authors ask which of its gifts does the work, in a study published in 2024. Mice with the tool cut from the liver alone are their test bed.

Calm of rust stress and fresh power cores, two of its famed gifts, did not lift the bile signs when bred by drugs. A drug that wakes the tool cut the bile make rate's chief step, and eased the ill. Cut that step by gene hand in the liver, and the ease held. The tool's shield, the team find, runs most through less bile made.
pmc-12337611:
Marcan Graffin and co-authors test how well satellites can track beach change over decades, in a 2023 paper. Wide, gently sloping beaches shift with tides and waves, which makes their true shoreline hard to read from space. The team pulled Landsat images from 1984 to 2021 for a stretch of the United States Pacific Northwest coast near the Columbia River. They built monthly shoreline records at fine detail along the whole cell of coast.

To check the satellite record, the authors compared it with twenty years of on-the-ground beach surveys done four times a year. They found the satellite series is only as good as its cleaning: stray bad readings and tide effects can warp the trend. Careful removal of outliers turned out to matter most. With that step, satellite data tracked real shoreline change well enough for regional planning.
pmc-12400311:
A common heart rhythm fault, atrial fibrillation, raises the stakes of many hospital procedures. Ayrton Bangolo and co-authors checked its effect on a bile duct scope procedure in this 2025 study. The procedure, called ERCP, threads a scope to open blocked bile ducts. Whether patients with the rhythm fault fare worse after it was largely unknown.

The team mined a nationwide database of hospital stays in the United States. They found adult patients with the fault who had the procedure during a stay. Patients were split by how soon the procedure came after admission. The main measure was death in hospital from any cause. A national sample gives the size needed to spot real risk gaps. Findings can help teams time the procedure and watch high-risk patients more closely.
pmc-12480311:
Hyeryeon Lee and co-authors introduce a Korean big data set built from COVID records, in a 2024 paper. Two national agencies joined case and vaccine data with national health insurance records, creating a cohort called K-COV-N. The set was opened to private researchers through an open platform in April 2022.

By October 2024, more than two hundred projects had been approved and thirty papers had appeared in international journals. Topics included infection risk factors, vaccine effects, and long COVID. Workshops and a public-private analysis network helped researchers share methods for using the data. Links with a national cancer centre and other data holders were also built. The agencies plan to keep opening infectious disease data, to ground quarantine policy in evidence and support expert decisions in future outbreaks.
pmc-12520711:
Michelle Kelsey leads a team on drug fills after heart events in diabetes. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with type two diabetes and acute coronary syndrome. Death rates stay high after heart attack in this group.

Hospital stays offer a chance to start proven drugs. Medicare data covered a span of recent years. Fills were tracked before, at, and after discharge. The qualifying events were heart attack or vessel repair. Patterns of evidence based drug use were the focus. Gaps in the move from hospital to home matter. Analysis closed in a set month.
pmc-12620911:
Mining Liang and co-authors review secondary school teachers experiences of supporting students with mental health issues in a systematic review published in 2024. Adolescent mental health problems are rising, with depression and anxiety causing teachers the greatest concern. Teachers see a wide range of student behavior daily, yet their support role is hard.

The review searched nine databases for qualitative studies from two thousand seven to twenty twenty two. It followed standard reporting guidelines and used established appraisal and confidence methods. The synthesis gathers how teachers experience identifying, helping, and referring students, to inform school support systems.
pmc-12659611:
Huijuan Cao and co-authors test if neck artery wall thickness predicts thinking problems after spine surgery in a 2025 study. The surgery frees a squeezed spinal cord in the neck. Some patients wake with cognitive fog. Thick carotid walls, an early sign of artery disease, may cut brain blood flow.

One hundred patients were split by wall thickness into high and low groups. A standard cognitive test ran before surgery and at three points after. At one week, the high group scored notably lower. By one and three months the gap had closed. Adjusted models check other factors. The marker may flag who needs close watching right after surgery.
pmc-12661811:
The microbes living in raw cow's milk reflect the udder's health and shape what calves and drinkers meet. Xiu-lan Xie and eight co-authors charted how that community shifts in 2025 across 285 cows in Ningxia, China, sorting samples by season, farm, parity, and hidden udder infection.

Gene sequencing of the milk found summer samples richer in bacteria than winter ones, with gut-linked genera common in summer milk. Winter milk carried a different cast, including Pseudomonas and Streptococcus. Six farms, first-time versus repeat mothers, and subclinical mastitis each left their own marks on the mix. The authors say such maps help farms read milk quality and udder health from the microbes themselves.
pmc-12662211:
Francesca Gandini and a large team weigh when humans first reached Sahul, in work from 2025. Sahul was the joined land of New Guinea, Australia, and Tasmania until about nine thousand years ago. One view puts first arrivals near sixty to sixty-five thousand years ago, while a shorter view puts them ten thousand years later.

The team studied an immense set of maternal line genomes from native groups across the region. They set those lines against data from Southeast Asia, plus whole-genome, paternal, dig, and climate proof. Their results back the longer view, with arrival near sixty thousand years ago by at least two distinct sea routes.
pmc-12671111:
Li and co-authors map world research on café-au-lait spots, the pale brown skin marks tied to neurofibromatosis type 1. These marks are among the earliest and most common signs of the disease. They serve as a core diagnostic clue. Research has grown fast with advances in genetics and skin medicine. The team pulled 850 English papers and reviews from a major database through May 2025.

Software charted who writes with whom, which works get cited together, and which keywords surge. The field shifted from describing marks to probing molecular causes. Collaboration hubs and hot topics come into view. The map can guide new teams toward open questions.
pmc-12679111:
Elif Sarac and Deniz Odabas survey female doctors and nurses about economic abuse by partners and whether it dents their work, in a 2025 study. Economic abuse means controlling a woman's money: blocking work, seizing earnings, or dictating spending. Health workers see its victims daily, but their own exposure is rarely measured. Three hundred and five married women at one university hospital completed an economic abuse scale and a work performance questionnaire.

Average abuse scores were low in this professional group, though present. The surprise was a null result: abuse scores showed no relationship with self-rated work performance. The authors probe which factors did track with financial exploitation. Their conclusion resists the easy assumption: professional women can be economically controlled at home while their workplace performance, at least as they report it, holds steady.
pmc-12681411:
Yao Song and co-authors ask what makes nurses feel like tools in a 2025 management study. Organizational dehumanization, sensing the hospital values you only as an instrument, corrodes engagement and care quality, and most research stops at documenting the harm.

In a three-wave survey of over three hundred nurses, workplaces investing in development, training, growth, and fair chances raised nurses' sense that their work mattered, and that meaningfulness in turn lowered dehumanization. A mastery climate, where learning is prized over ranking, strengthened the effect. Development-focused human resources, the authors argue, is an antidote management can actually administer.
pmc-12683811:
Haotian Zhuang, Xinyi Shang, Wenpin Hou, and Zhicheng Ji build ctSVG in 2025, a tool for place-shift genes by cell kind. Wide place genes oft just echo cell kind marks, which wastes the place data in space sets. Their tool fits a sharp space read frame at one-cell grain for a new high-grade space kit.

Fresh genes found by kind split from wide genes and from mark genes in the read. Real space sets show the fresh genes carry true place work in tissue maps. The gain opens fine place maps for tissue study at kind grain.
pmc-12685211:
Biruk Abera and co-authors grade in 2025 referral quality at a specialized hospital in northeast Ethiopia. A sound referral chain links the three tiers of care and guards service quality. More than four hundred referred clients took part in a study window in early twenty twenty three.

Forms, transport logs, and focal staff mark the system's structure side. Fourteen paper parts, from patient details onward, mark the process side. Statistical models then hunt factors tied to referral quality. The study gives hospital leaders a map of where the referral chain frays and where it holds firm.
pmc-12685611:
Erkang Yi and a large co-author team trace, in 2025 work, shared gene roots between a chronic lung disease and lung cancer. The lung disease raises cancer odds, and the two share some gene risk, yet the causal path was murky. The team joined survey data with large gene studies and a method that uses gene marks as natural tests.

Two drivers stood out. One is a gene that handles iron in cells; its higher activity tracked with faster lung loss in the lung disease, yet with better odds once cancer came. The other is a class of memory immune cells, whose high levels in the lung disease fed tumour-friendly acts. Cell reads and lab knock-down tests backed the iron gene's role. The team sees both as marks for early watch.
pmc-12686011:
Priti Chakurkar and Deepali Vora present a data set of footpath damage in Pune, India, for risk study in 2025. Cracked and uneven footpaths pose fall risks, and automated checks could help cities spot danger early.

Images were taken with a high-grade camera in varied light and weather and marked by hand at pixel level. Damage was graded as low, medium or high by crack width, with advice from civil engineers. The authors trained a segmentation model and an ensemble version to show the data work. Their best model reached solid overlap and accuracy scores, and the data set is open for research use.
pmc-12690911:
Ashley Fenton, Rika Win, Maureen Ndzi, and Kathryne Neiling review mindfulness training in nursing education in a 2025 paper. Nursing students face heavy stress, and mindfulness programs promise relief that may carry into their careers. The review gathers what trials and studies from 2019 to 2024 actually show.

Fifteen studies met the entry rules across four databases. Programs consistently cut stress, anxiety, and low mood in the short term, and improved emotional control, self-care, and a sense of spirituality. Common formats were meditation, breathing work, guided imagery, and structured courses. Evidence on lasting effects and on burnout in later practice remains thin, and study designs varied widely. The authors urge broader samples and longer follow-up.
pmc-12691011:
Qiu-Xiao Ren and co-authors review in 2025 the many roles of a tiny RNA that tunes gene activity across the body. Called miR-221, it can push cancer growth in one tissue and hold it back in another, which makes it a tricky but rich target. The review gathers its actions in cancer, heart, brain, gut, lung, and fat tissue.

In cancer it targets guard genes to steer growth, spread, and drug resistance, and it serves as a blood mark for several tumor types. In the heart it balances virus defense and scar growth. The authors map its paths and the drug ideas that aim at it.
pmc-12691311:
Clara Martinez-Vila and co-authors tested a personalized blood test in 2025 to track long-term benefit in advanced melanoma. Drugs that free the immune system to attack the cancer have improved outcomes, but how long to give them is unsettled. Fragments of tumor DNA in blood can signal how much cancer remains and may forecast who does well over time.

At one academic center, 56 patients with stage four melanoma on immune therapy were eligible, and 28 had repeated blood tests during treatment and follow-up, for a median of about thirty-one months. The assay was built from each patient's own tumor. The team checked test status at six and nine months against later progress. Readers get evidence on using a blood signal to guide how long immune therapy should continue.
pmc-12693211:
Theresia Stigger and co-authors compare, in 2025, long-term looks after two routes to implant breast reconstruction. One route places the implant at once, and the other stretches tissue first with an expander. A known flaw of implants under muscle is shape change when the muscle flexes, and similar ripples appear in other placements.

Sixty-seven patients were followed for about six and a half years on average. Satisfaction and rated looks did not differ between the routes. The movement flaw appeared in about three in five patients, more often with the direct route. Six patients with implants above the muscle showed a distinct ripple type, for which the authors propose a new definition.
pmc-12694311:
Christian Cobos and co-authors report a 2025 study on a biodegradable plastic called PLA. The plastic is brittle, which limits structural use. Two nanotube fillers are compared as reinforcements. One is a multi-walled carbon tube, and the other is a clay tube called halloysite. Each filler was mixed at three low loadings and molded by injection. Strength, bending, impact, and hardness tests grade the results.

Carbon tubes raised bending strength and stiffness by up to sixty percent. That gain cost stretch: the break strain fell as clumps formed. Halloysite improved a different balance of traits. Microscope images check how well each filler spread. Materials teams get a side-by-side filler guide for a green plastic. The clumping warning matters most: filler gains vanish when tubes bunch instead of spreading.
pmc-12695911:
Metro networks flood easily, yet most flood risk studies use fixed expert weights that hide uncertainty. The five authors build a probabilistic GIS-based framework that pairs the analytic hierarchy process with a Monte Carlo extension. The extension measures uncertainty in expert judgment through beta-PERT simulations and uses a wide indicator set covering hazard, exposure, and vulnerability, including passenger flow and lines still under construction.

Applied to the Chengdu metro, the framework maps risk spreading out from a high-risk center: the urban core is most vulnerable despite only moderate hazard. The Monte Carlo version flags more high-risk area than the plain version and gives weight distributions that blunt subjective bias. Checks against past flood events support its reliability. The authors offer the framework as a transferable way to harden metro networks as climate change and urbanization speed up.
pmc-12696011:
Rafael Domingues and co-authors study a common antidepressant effect on the uterus in 2025. Fluoxetine, sold as Prozac, is the best known drug of its class. Such drugs may disturb hormone signaling in the body. The team ran classic uterus growth tests in mice to probe estrogen like action.

In young mice, the drug did not grow the uterus, which argues against direct estrogen mimicry. In mature mice, it did raise uterine weight and changed gene activity in an estrogen like pattern. The effect needed a working serotonin transporter and serotonin in the blood. The find reframes how the drug may sway reproductive tissue.
pmc-12696111:
Magda Jablonska and co-authors test how backup blood flow changes clot removal success across thrombectomy techniques in lab models. Collateral flow is known to shape stroke outcomes. Whether it changes device performance was less clear.

Two vessel models mimicked good and poor backup flow. Soft and stiff fake clots blocked the same artery spot. Three removal techniques were rotated in random order. Two hundred forty procedures were run in total. Complete reopening came more often with good collaterals. Loose clot fragments drifting downstream were also counted. Technique rankings shifted with clot stiffness and flow. The results may guide device choice during stroke care in real time.
pmc-12696911:
Eleven authors, led by Michael Penkunas, argue in 2025 for wider use of research on how health care is put into practice. Good treatments often fail to reach patients because clinics face cost, staff, and trust barriers. Studying those barriers, and how to clear them, can make health systems work better for all.

Demand for such training is rising fast across the world. In 2024 alone, thousands signed up for one course on the topic. The authors call for fair access to training and for strong partnerships across fields. Local teams, they say, must lead the work for results to last.
pmc-12697111:
Yani Su and co-authors ask whether celiac disease genetically drives its skin cousin, dermatitis herpetiformis. Their 2025 study uses Mendelian randomization, a method that treats inherited variants as natural experiments, to test cause rather than mere association between the two gluten-linked diseases.

Using summary data from genome-wide studies, the main analysis found a clear positive causal link running from celiac disease to the skin disease. The reverse test, from skin disease to celiac disease, showed no such link. Checks for uneven data and hidden bias came back clean, and side analyses agreed. The authors conclude that the genetic liability behind celiac disease raises the risk of the blistering skin condition.
pmc-12698511:
Nicholas Forand and co-authors ask whether asking patients to report symptoms at each visit helps when a whole therapy practice adopts the habit at scale. Their 2025 study follows a large tech-supported practice through six months of change. The work covered 18,721 patients and 755 clinicians in three phases, before, during, and after the change.

Leaders aligned the whole group, built the checks into the tech, trained staff, and shifted daily routines. Patient change was scored on two short standard forms, one for low mood and one for anxiety. The team also tracked how clinicians acted and performed. Readers get a rare look at what shifts, and what does not, when a proven habit goes system-wide.
pmc-12698611:
Residues of organophosphate pesticides in herbal crops need fast on-site testing, but lab methods are bulky and antibody kits are fragile. Xiaoyi Liu and co-authors build a glowing nanoparticle sensor in this 2025 paper that detects these chemicals through the enzyme they block.

Opposite electric charges pull the sensor's parts into a tight nanoscale reactor, and a two-enzyme chain reaction amplifies the signal. The sensor spotted one target pesticide at very low levels, worked in messy citrus peel samples, and finished in twenty minutes. The authors present the charge-based assembly as a general recipe for multi-enzyme sensors.
pmc-12699811:
Paraskevi Gkiata, Maria Vliora, Alexandra Bargiota, and Andreas Flouris set out, in a 2025 protocol paper, a planned review of how people with type 2 diabetes handle heat. Diabetes seems to blunt the body's heat-loss tools, blood flow to the skin and sweating, which leaves patients at risk when core temperature climbs. Past results are tangled, though, and the reasons for heating differ across studies.

The review will search two databases for trials and observational studies that measured core temperature in these patients. It will compare their vessel and sweat responses with healthy people at the same core temperature, and with patients at lower temperatures. A narrative summary is planned, with pooled analysis if the data allow, plus a check on bias in each study.
pmc-12699911:
People with cirrhosis should get liver cancer checks twice a year, yet many sites fall short of that guideline. Vera Yakovchenko and co-authors test a coaching method to close the gap in a 2025 trial at twelve Veterans Health sites. The method, called Getting to Implementation, walks each site through a stepwise plan.

Facilitators spent about twenty hours per site over a year, helping teams map their current state, set goals, and pick fixes for local barriers. Ten of the twelve sites adopted the approach and applied a median of five strategies each. Results were judged on reach, adoption, and whether the gains held. The study shows a manual coaching model can move guideline care into daily practice.
pmc-12700211:
Vibhuti Rai and nine colleagues use a terahertz microscope to watch crystal vibrations start and to see how atomic defects steer them, in a 2025 paper. Coherent phonons are atoms swinging in step, a key part of light-driven structural change. The team worked on molybdenum ditelluride, a layered semiconductor.

Their scanning tunneling microscope delivered terahertz pulses that excited two vibration modes normally forbidden in the bulk crystal: an out-of-plane breathing mode and an in-plane shear mode. Both rang for a long time after each pulse. Near defects, the balance between the two modes shifted. The team attributes this to local band bending from the tip, which tunes how the field couples to each mode. Defect-tunable coupling, they argue, opens a route to selecting vibrations on demand at the nanoscale.
pmc-12700911: A retraction note from twenty twenty-five withdraws a study by Xianglu Ji and three co-authors. The study claimed that a circular RNA helped bone cancer cells grow and spread. The editors say they lost trust in the data. Parts of figures overlapped or looked too much like figures in other papers. The authors also did not give proof of ethics approval for the work with people and animals when asked. For those reasons the study should no longer be relied on as sound work.
pmc-12701311:
Yu Cao, Sudan Li, Yi Zhang, Menghua He, and Yan Shen tested a plant compound called catalpol in mice with a hard-to-treat form of heart failure. In this form, the heart pumps at normal strength but relaxes poorly. Mice were made ill with a fatty diet plus a vessel-tightening drug, then given catalpol for four weeks.

Treated mice showed better heart relaxation, less scarring and swelling, and better weight, blood sugar, and blood pressure. Data mapping pointed to one inflammation chain as the key target, and lab tests confirmed the compound shut it down. In cell tests, forcing that chain back on undid much of the benefit.
pmc-12702211:
Charles Odonkor and co-authors chart the timing of relief after a spine nerve treatment for back pain, in work from 2025. The treatment burns a small nerve inside the backbone that carries pain from worn joints. It is cleared for a defined type of back pain, yet relief timing was poorly known.

The cohort held 86 patients treated at one academic center over one year. All had scan signs matching the target pain type. Patients reported pain weekly for eight weeks, then at three and six months. The study logs when half relief first arrived for each patient. It also tests whether early gains predict lasting response, which helps set patient hopes.
pmc-12702311:
Catherine Phelps, Daphne Rodriguez, and Marlies Meisel give a step by step protocol for making mouse fecal transplants and microbe products in a 2025 paper. Gut microbe chemicals can steer immune responses and disease, but pulling them out and growing them at scale is hard. The protocol fills that methods gap.

Steps cover collecting donor feces and preparing transplant material. They also isolate the chemicals the microbes make, and grow the microbes in broth to produce more of those chemicals outside the animal. The products serve both live animal work and lab dish studies. Full detail points to the team's earlier report.
pmc-12703411:
The European Food Safety Authority and its working group sort pesticide effects on reproduction in a 2025 report. Regulators must judge the combined risk of many pesticide residues eaten together. To do that, chemicals are grouped by shared effects. This first report names the reproductive effects, in males and females, that matter for such grouping.

For males, two groups were defined: altered mating performance and decreased fertility. For females, four groups add altered pregnancy and altered birth process to those two. The report also lists the measurable test endpoints that signal each effect. Those indicators will be gathered from the safety files of single active substances. Membership in a group then follows from the evidence, substance by substance.
pmc-12703811:
Yaodan Zhang and co-authors test whether omega-3 fats in blood causally affect small vessel disease in the brain, in this 2025 study. That vessel disease drives strokes and thinking decline. Its scan signs include small strokes, white matter spots, and tiny bleeds.

Omega-3 fats look protective in diet studies, but cause and effect stay murky. The team use Mendelian randomization, which borrows gene variants as natural experiments. Blood omega-3 levels set by genes are set against each scan sign. A causal signal would support trials of supplements for brain vessel health. A null result would save that effort for better targets. The method separates inherited exposure from lifestyle noise.
pmc-12704611:
Miguel López-Zamora and co-authors compare thinking skills, behavior, and emotions in Spanish children with and without dyslexia. Their study appeared in 2025. One hundred twenty children aged eight to ten were assessed with standard behavior and executive function batteries. The dyslexia group showed markedly higher aggression, anxiety, depression, and attention problems. They also struggled more with resisting interference and with verbal fluency, two core executive skills.

Statistical mediation tests suggested dyslexia itself helps drive both the thinking difficulties and the emotional ones, inside and out. The authors say schools should screen beyond reading: a child failing to decode words may also be fighting distraction and low mood. Support plans, they argue, must cover behavior and feelings, not letters alone.
pmc-12704911: Vincent Le and co-authors track live video skin care visits for older Americans in a short 2025 study. Using Medicare billing files from 2017 to 2023, they sorted visits by how complex the care was. The authors report that use of these live video visits grew for complex cases over the period. They suggest that growth hints video skin care could serve as a lasting way to widen access to dermatology care for Medicare patients.
pmc-12705211:
Montaner and co-authors urge Canada to defend its HIV gains in a 2025 commentary. Proven tools such as treatment, prevention, and preventive drugs have cut new infections and deaths sharply. The world stands close to ending HIV and AIDS as a public health threat.

Deep global funding cuts have now stalled that shared progress, the authors warn. Canada and other rich nations should renew their effort at home and abroad, they argue. Letting programs lapse would waste decades of work and invite a rebound. The piece is a policy call, grounded in the record of what the tools achieved. Its key point is simple: the finish line is near, so do not stop.
pmc-12705811:
Noura El-Ahmady El-Naggar and three co-authors make collagen nanoparticles with the help of a soil bacterium, aiming at a greener route to cancer therapy materials. Collagen particles are valued because the body tolerates them well and they offer a large surface for carrying drugs. Here the particles were brewed in a cell-free broth from Streptomyces viridochromogenes.

The team tuned the recipe with two modeling tools, a classic design method and a neural network, and the network predicted the best settings more exactly. The round, hollow particles measured about 30 nanometers across and stayed stable in suspension. Tests showed antioxidant action and strong killing of three cancer cell lines in dishes. In mice, the particles slowed tumor growth by about 84 percent. Paired with the drug doxorubicin, they reached about 98 percent, beating either treatment alone.
pmc-12706011:
Neurofibromatosis type 1 affects about one in 3,000 people and can bend the spine as well as grow tumors and bone defects. The eight authors use a mouse model in which the Nf1 gene is switched off in boundary cap cells, a neural crest subset, and their descendants. Micro-CT scans showed spine deformity from 12 months of age, with vertebral changes resembling those of patients.
