Fate mapping traced the problem to osteoblasts from that lineage, which multiplied in the vertebrae. More Nf1-deficient cells meant more vertebral bone and worse kyphosis curvature. Treating the mice with inhibitors of the RAS-MAPK pathway prevented the deformity. The authors name those osteoblasts as the cellular origin of the spine defect and propose pathway blockade as a preventive strategy.
pmc-12706211:
Jolanda Liebregts and co-authors wrote a 2025 review on how care for mothers and newborns is organized in rich countries. Many countries face high costs, staff shortages, and questions about how to keep this care going. Joined-up care, where services work as one team, is often put forward as a fix.

The team gathered two hundred eighty-eight papers and sorted what they found into twenty-three parts of how care is set up. The parts fell into six groups, such as keeping the same caregiver, better teamwork across jobs, and care led by midwives. For each part they checked links to health outcomes, costs, and the views of mothers and staff. The review maps what is known and shows where proof is still thin.
pmc-12706911:
Standard movement tests may miss injury effects in elite women basketball players, a 2025 pilot study by Lu Zhang and co-authors suggests. Lower-limb injuries are common in the sport, yet little work checks these tests in this exact group. The team ran three tests on eighteen players from the Chinese national team.

The tests screen movement quality, landing errors, and balance reach. Total scores did not differ between injured and uninjured players, and the three tests did not track each other. One part did stand out: the deep squat separated players with knee injuries from the rest. The authors read the tests as giving different, complementary views of movement rather than one verdict.
pmc-12707011:
Hanjin Kim, Youngran Yang, Junhee Ahn, and Jeong Hee Kang explore, in a 2025 study, how the oldest diabetes patients feel about wearing a glucose sensor. The devices track sugar around the clock, but most studies skip people over seventy-five. The team interviewed fourteen such adults, all new to the devices, after two weeks of use.

Four themes came out: burdens tied to the device, barriers to use, a two-sided impact, and reflection that left people feeling more in control. The sensors sharpened awareness and nudged healthier habits. Yet constant watching also caused stress. Carrying and charging a phone, tricky controls, small print for weak eyes, and high cost all stood in the way. The authors urge wider insurance cover.
pmc-12707811:
Cadona and a large team test stomach fluid DNA as a marker for stomach cancer in twenty twenty-five. Stomach cancer is hard to diagnose and treat around the world. Better markers could help plan surgery and drug treatment. The team collected fluid during routine scope exams of the stomach.

The cohort held more than one thousand patients with varied stomach conditions. DNA levels in the fluid were much higher in cancer patients than in all other groups. Later stage tumors showed higher levels than earlier stage tumors. In a subset, higher DNA levels linked to longer survival without disease progress. Those tumors also held more immune cells. The authors say fluid DNA may aid diagnosis and could carry prognostic value.
pmc-12708111:
Oriana Haran and co-authors review ten years of breast rebuild surgery using tissue from the thigh. Their 2025 report covers a flap design called the diagonal upper gracilis flap, used when belly tissue cannot be used. The design cuts on a slant to take more tissue while limiting harm at the donor site.

The review covers 109 flaps in seventy patients treated from 2012 to 2022. No flap failed, and about one in seven cases had a complication, most often skin infection at the thigh. No patients had lasting swelling or wound opening at the donor site. Taking tissue from one thigh, rather than both, cut the need for later touch-up surgery.
pmc-12708811:
Thakur and coauthors review care for people who have both poor sleep and gut pain. Sleep loss and gut signs feed each other in both ways. Stress and thought habits help drive that loop. Drugs and talk care for sleep can help, but both have limits.

Mind and body methods may add a low-risk choice, the team argues. Such methods aim at stress, which links sleep and gut signs. The review sums up trials of these methods in gut patients. It asks if they lift sleep, ease gut pain, and raise life quality. It also notes where proof stays thin and more trials are due.
pmc-12709711:
Steven Wyatt and four colleagues published a health services study in two thousand twenty-five on why English hospital activity keeps growing. Demand rose through the twenty tens even before the pandemic. Planners debated how much came from more people, older people, sicker people, or everything else.

Using national episode data from two thousand eleven to two thousand nineteen, the team split yearly growth into four parts. Planned admissions grew about two point three percent a year, with population growth and residual factors the biggest parts. Emergency admissions grew faster, driven mostly by residual factors. Maternity admissions shrank slightly. Outpatient visits grew fastest of all. The authors say ageing alone explains less than commonly assumed.
pmc-12709811:
Henrieta Horníková and co-authors measure the balance of elite Para Karate athletes to help fair classification, in a 2025 study. Kata performance leans on postural control, yet the sport's classification lacks a standard test battery. Fifty-nine athletes from the 2023 world championships stood still for thirty seconds, eyes open, on a force plate. They fell into three groups: visually impaired, intellectually impaired, and intellectually impaired with an added condition.

The plate traced the wandering of each athlete's centre of pressure, its path length and area, front-to-back and side-to-side. The groups differed significantly on these sway measures. Such numbers give classifiers an evidence base: where impairment truly changes balance, categories can be drawn fairly; where it does not, they should not pretend otherwise. The study serves sport governance as much as physiology.
pmc-12711011:
An expression of concern from 2025 flags doubts about a published study of fibrocytes in Dupuytren disease, a hand condition that bends fingers inward. The notice is not a new study; it records that editors are looking into the paper's data and methods. Readers are warned to treat the findings with care while the review runs.

Two worries are named. Part of one figure panel looks like part of another panel that should show a distinct test. The notice also says the paper's stats tests fit two-group contrasts, yet many tests in the study span more than two groups, so tests built for that case should have been used.
pmc-12711611:
How much oxygen to give a patient whose pancreas is destroying itself is an open question with lives at stake. Yiji Chen and co-authors mine records of 1,585 such patients in this 2025 study from a Chinese hospital. They compared patients kept at higher blood oxygen in the first three intensive care days against those kept lower, matching the groups on other traits.

The higher-oxygen group died less at 28 days, at 90 days, and overall. Lasting circulation failure and multi-organ failure also came less often. Benefit varied with age, weight, and illness severity scores. Oxygen held near 100 millimeters of mercury on day three looked best. The authors back early, generous oxygen targets for this disease.
pmc-12712311:
People with type 2 diabetes face a higher risk of urinary tract infections, and some drugs are often blamed. Joseph Ben Hill and co-authors used this 2025 case-control study to check which new drugs actually show up before an infection. One drug class, the SGLT2 inhibitors, is often linked to these infections. The authors suspected that other drugs might appear just as often.

They drew records from a large national claims database covering the years 2018 to 2021. One group held patients with diabetes who had an infection, and the other held similar patients who did not. The team then compared which new prescriptions each group had filled before that point. Work like this can help doctors judge risk by the full drug list, not by one known suspect alone.
pmc-12713111:
Alexis Kidder, Genevieve Quek, and Tijl Grootswagers probe how the brain organizes objects over time, in a study from 2025. A model from monkey work says object space rests on two axes, whether a thing is alive and how stubby or spiky it looks. Human brain scans had stressed kind and animacy more, leaving shape in doubt.

Twenty people viewed streams of objects and outline-only versions while brain signals were recorded. Codes for shape ratio, kind, and animacy all appeared during viewing. Which axis dominated shifted with stimulus type, and shape news came early and faded fast. The results confirm shape is represented, but briefly.
pmc-12713211:
Runmin Ding and co-authors review how artificial intelligence is used to study kidney tissue images in a 2025 article. The approach, called pathomics, turns microscope images into large data sets that machines can measure. It promises finer diagnosis of kidney disease than the eye alone can give.

The review covers uses such as spotting injury in the kidney's filters, grading scarring between tubules, and tracking transplanted kidneys over time. It also covers predicting outcomes in kidney tumors. Hurdles remain, including hard labeling work, models that are tough to explain, and too little large-scale testing in clinics. The authors urge work that joins image data with other data types and closer ties across fields.
pmc-12713811:
Stephen Pittman and co-authors report a consensus conference on the future of sleep apnea care. Their report, published in 2023 (the catalog lists 2024), argues the field can either drift with current habits or steer its own course. The goal is a simpler path for people at risk of obstructive sleep apnea, from first suspicion to steady treatment.

The statement names five key problems and unmet needs in present care. It then sketches four possible directions for the years ahead. Diagnostics, monitoring, and communication sit at the center, with the whole care team in view: patients, primary care doctors, sleep specialists, sleep dentists, and other providers. The authors write as insiders urging their field to lead the change.
pmc-12714111:
Jinwen Li leads a team on self harm in teens with low mood. Their study from twenty twenty-five tracks students over three time points. It asks how childhood maltreatment shapes later self harm.

From a large student pool, a group with steady low mood was picked. A matched group sans low mood served for compare. Self harm acts rose over time in the low mood group. Early maltreatment shaped self harm through self esteem paths. Change score models traced how those paths moved. The work may guide school based help.
pmc-12714711:
Onofrio Cappelluti, Francisco Escobedo, Giovanni Sanesi, and Mario Elia map fire risk where towns meet wild land. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Such edge zones mix homes, farms, and flammable landscape in complex ways. Past risk methods often ignore the social and governing side of that mix.

Their framework scores each zone on three axes: ecology, social and economic traits, and governance. They built and mapped the scores for southern Italy and southern California. In California, zones with strong governance had fewer fires. In Italy the pattern was more tangled, with strong-governance zones seeing more fires but less burned area. The authors warn that methods built for one region may mislead in another.
pmc-12714811:
Xin-xin Chen and colleagues uncover a protective gene pathway in diabetic heart disease. Their study from twenty twenty-five focuses on ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death. Diabetic cardiomyopathy weakens the heart in many people with diabetes. Which controls govern that cell death was unclear before.

The protein FTO falls in diseased hearts, the team found. Raising FTO improved heart function by blocking ferroptosis. Its target is ACSL4, a protein that promotes this death pathway. Blocking ACSL4 was required for the protection to work. Two supplements together suppressed ferroptosis through separate routes. The findings name a clear gene axis as a treatment lead.
pmc-12715211:
Supakit Paosen and co-authors published this 2025 study on a safer menstrual cup material. Cups are growing in use, but sharing the vaginal space with a device may invite infections from staph bacteria or the yeast Candida. The team mixed leaf extract from a medicinal plant, Rhodomyrtus tomentosa, into silicone.

The loaded silicone kept its surface feel and wetting behavior. In lab tests it strongly slowed staph and Candida growing free or stuck to the surface, even in a fluid made to mimic vaginal fluid. The effect started within an hour and cut germ counts by more than five orders of magnitude in twelve hours. The material spared human cells and still worked after twelve rounds of boiling.
pmc-12715511:
Deepika Darshani Lata and six co-authors report a 2025 survey of drug-resistant bacteria in frozen chicken sold in Fiji. Chicken is widely eaten in Fiji and is mostly served frozen, yet little was known about resistant germs in local meat. The team bought 100 frozen chicken samples from shops and tested them for a common gut bacterium.

The bacterium turned up in seventy-two percent of samples. Among the finds, about a third resisted a common first-line drug, about a quarter resisted a second drug, and a smaller share resisted a third. One strain resisted a key hospital drug and carried a gene for that trait, and one strain resisted a last-resort drug through a gene change. The authors call for tighter hygiene across the meat chain and for more watch on resistance in Fiji.
pmc-12715911:
Yuan leads a large team studying womb infection in cows, in work from twenty twenty-five. Infection of the bovine endometrium by Escherichia coli harms fertility and costs the cattle industry. A cell death type driven by iron, called ferroptosis, may play a role that was not explained.

Tissue from sixteen infected Holstein cows was examined and gene profiled. Cow womb cells grown in the lab were infected to model the process. Tests with protein, flow, and imaging methods traced the death path. A kinase that breaks down a protective factor called NRF2 stood out as a driver. Blocking that path could be a new way to limit womb damage.
pmc-12716411:
Lily Zhu and co-authors argue that medical schools should teach innovation and entrepreneurship in this 2025 perspective piece. Health care is changing fast, and doctors must lead projects as well as treat patients. Yet few schools offer formal training in building new health tools.

The authors surveyed students at their own school, Johns Hopkins, and found near-universal interest in such training. Most respondents planned to fold innovation into their careers. Alumni of a design master's program said it built skills in design thinking, teamwork, and leadership. The paper lays out three ways to add the training: short workshops, a one-year gap program, or a track running through school. Each carries trade-offs in depth and time. The authors urge early, structured exposure for future physician leaders.
pmc-12717111:
Jinliang Mi and six co-authors built a game-based planning frame in two thousand twenty-five for power systems under deep uncertainty. Wind, solar, and demand swings make planning harder, and classic plans treat all choices as made by one central hand. Real systems involve regulators, grid operators, renewable builders, and big users, each with their own aims.

Their frame sets those players in a layered game, each chasing its own welfare under cost, technical, and policy limits. A robust layer keeps plans workable across a wide range of bad weather and demand outcomes. The authors say the blend gives expansion plans that are both realistic and resilient.
pmc-12717211:
Haijun Wang and five colleagues published a 2025 paper on sharpening a special kind of image. Hyperspectral images record many thin slices of light at each point, not just red, green, and blue. Making a crisp large version from a small blurry one is hard.

The team built a network called Cs_Unet, based on the well-known U-Net design. Its new part, cross-range self-attention, links far-apart spots in space and across light slices at once. Older tools looked only at near spots or split space and color apart. The authors test their design against past methods. Their goal is cleaner images for tasks like crop checks and land mapping from planes and satellites.
pmc-12717311:
Shota Takei and co-authors test, in a 2025 study, whether a new kind of helper T cell can predict how small cell lung cancer responds to treatment. The cells, called Th7R, carry two markers and a profile unlike classic helper cells. In the more common lung cancer type, their levels already hinted at drug response and survival. This team checked the same idea in the fast-growing small cell form, in patients on chemo or chemo plus immunotherapy.

Forty-seven patients with extensive-stage disease were studied. High Th7R levels went with longer time before the cancer grew again. The longest control came only in high-Th7R patients who got the added immune drug. High levels also tracked with better overall survival, and with a pool of young killer T cells that immune drugs target. The marker may help pick who gains most from this therapy.
pmc-12717711:
Rojas and co-authors sequence the microbes living in a Chilean copper mine's waste tailings, one of the largest and oldest such deposits in the world. Life there endures heavy metals and strong acidity, and the community is simple enough to study evolution gene by gene. From the DNA, the team rebuilt 44 bacterial genomes. Only five could be matched to known species, a sign of how much novelty extreme sites still hold.

The genomes showed strong toolkits for handling sulfur and copper. Selection analysis found the core survival genes under tight purifying selection, kept nearly unchanged, while genes for movement, biofilm building, and stress resistance showed signs of active adaptation. The authors describe a community that guards its proven chemistry fiercely while tinkering at the edges. That conservatism may limit dreams of harnessing these microbes for biomining. The study also widens the known family tree of extremophiles.
pmc-12717811:
A cell-cycle protein called MYBL2 shows up often in cancers, and Chia-Chi Chen and co-authors ask whether its level in liver tumors predicts patient survival. Their 2025 study covers 88 liver cancer patients who had surgery between 2023 and 2025. Tumor samples were stained to score how much of the protein each one carried.

Patients with high MYBL2 in their tumors died sooner than those with low levels, and the protein's score tracked survival in a graded way. On its own it held up as a risk signal, though it lost that standing once other factors joined the model. The authors propose MYBL2 as a candidate marker for prognosis and a possible drug target. They call for work on how it drives tumor growth.
pmc-12718311:
Katie Ryan, Hyun-Joon Yang, Bohye Kim, and Jane Paik Kim reply to critics of their study on AI and doctor choices. Their 2025 reply answers a Matters Arising piece by Bernstein and others. The first study asked how AI input sways doctor decisions on mental health care in primary care.

The critics praise the topic yet question parts of the method. Ryan and co-authors welcome the chance to add context and clarify their sums. One point: the key survey item used a five-point scale, but scores were split into agree versus the rest for the change measure. They argue such sway by AI is real, underreported, and worth close study.
pmc-12718511:
Li and co-authors validate in 2025 a Chinese version of a virtual reality system usability questionnaire, for use with intensive care patients. The English scale needed careful cross cultural adaptation. A standard translation model guided the work, and 331 patients from a tertiary hospital in Zhengzhou took part.

The adapted scale holds three dimensions and nine items. Total reliability scored zero point eight two one, with split half reliability at zero point seven eight two. Item content validity ranged from zero point eight three three to one. Factor analysis found three shared factors covering sixty-seven point zero one seven percent of variance, and no item was dropped. The team calls the tool psychometrically sound for clinical assessment.
pmc-12719611:
Evrard Mayombo Ngoussou and co-authors review urinary tract infections caused by Klebsiella germs in Central Africa in a paper from 2025. Such infections are among the most common bacterial infections in clinics. Klebsiella is the second most common cause found in urine worldwide.

Data from Central Africa come mostly from single small studies, so no clear regional picture exists. The team pooled past studies to estimate how common these infections are. They also describe how the Klebsiella strains in the region behave and resist drugs. A pooled view can guide testing and drug choice. It also shows where surveillance is still thin.
pmc-12721111:
Nitish Seenarine and co-authors review surgery outcomes for a rare spinal tumor in a 2025 paper. The tumor, a myxopapillary ependymoma, grows at the cord's lower end among the nerve roots. It is usually removed by surgery, and most patients live long, yet many keep or gain nerve problems afterward.

The team reviewed sixteen cases treated at their center from 2010 to 2021. They matched scan features before surgery with nerve outcomes after, hunting for imaging signs that warn of a hard course. Past studies had named candidate signs but not tied them to function. Such links could improve consent talks and surgical planning.
pmc-12721511:
A cancer-linked enzyme called SIRT2 can be attacked on a computer before anyone orders chemicals, and Md Habib Ullah Masum and co-authors screened fungal metabolites against it virtually. Docking placed the candidate molecules into the enzyme's grip and scored their hold; dynamics simulations then shook the complexes to see which stayed stable. Safety software checked absorption, toxicity, and cancer risk of the compounds themselves.

All the fungal candidates looked drug-like and benign in silico. The top binder held the most compact, stable complex through simulation, while the runner-up loosened its partner and let more water in. The authors nominate the steadier compound for laboratory testing, a standard first step in computer-guided drug hunting that costs weeks instead of years.
pmc-12722211:
Xianjian Shi and four co-authors build a neural network that sorts land cover from hyperspectral satellite images by letting the data decide how to blend its own features, in this 2025 paper. Such images carry hundreds of wavelength bands, rich but hard to classify. Older networks fuse features with fixed recipes that fit some scenes poorly.

Three modules cooperate. One gathers features at several scales, from fine texture to broad context. Another sharpens both channel and spatial attention. A gate then learns, for each input, how much each stream should count. On four benchmark scenes the network scored between ninety-four and ninety-seven percent overall accuracy, beating strong rivals. Removing any module hurt results, and the gated blend beat five rival fusion strategies on accuracy, speed, and stability.
pmc-12722311:
Tsukasa Osaki and six co-authors find that vitamin C in drinking water prevents liver cancer in fragile mice, in a 2025 study. The mice lack two antioxidant defenses at once, so they develop a fatty liver disease resembling human NASH even when young. Most died early, and survivors developed liver tumors within a year. Giving them a modest dose of L-ascorbate, plain vitamin C, in their water cut deaths and stopped tumor development.

Liver tissue analysis showed the vitamin suppressed a surge in amino acid processing pathways seen in untreated mice. The result ties the disease's march toward cancer to oxidative strain plus organelle stress. A cheap, safe nutrient preventing the cancer outcome in this model invites careful follow-up in liver medicine.
pmc-12722611:
Gordon Daly and a team of co-authors reviewed a new way to mark breast lumps that cannot be felt. Their review, from twenty twenty-five, looks at small radio tags placed before surgery. The old way used a wire to guide the surgeon to the spot. The tag way is less harsh on the patient. The team asked how well tags work and how safe they are.

They pooled past studies that told of tag use, and studies that set tags against wires. They weighed rates of clear margins and of repeat surgery. Readers who plan breast surgery get a pooled view of the gains and risks. The work helps teams judge if tags should take the place of wires.
pmc-12723911:
Zegeng Su, Junting Huang, Xiaoling Xu, and a wider team wrote this clinical trial report, published in 2025. It tests whether the painkiller tramadol, given by vein, can prevent the sore throat that often follows thyroid surgery with a breathing tube.

The team enrolled 171 women scheduled for thyroid removal and split them into three groups. One got standard care, one got tramadol fifteen minutes before surgery, and one got it as the wound was washed at the end. A day after the tube came out, sore throat at rest was rare and similar in all groups. Sore throat on movement was common, around half in each group, with no clear tramadol advantage. Checks in the recovery room and at four hours were also recorded. The authors report a null result for a common comfort problem.
pmc-12724211:
Rong Xiao and co-authors study a lung-protective protein in a 2025 cell study. Acute lung injury brings fierce inflammation and damage. The protein STK11 may calm it by switching on autophagy, the cell cleanup system. A partner signal, AMPK, acts as the start switch in their model.

Gene data from three public sets first flagged the protein as a key cleanup regulator. Lung cells were then stressed with a bacterial toxin to mimic injury. Raising the protein cut cell death and inflammatory signals and boosted cleanup. Silencing it reversed all gains. The pathway offers a fresh drug target for acute lung injury care.
pmc-12727711:
Kamila Komajda and Grzegorz Teresiński review dried blood spots for tracking pesticide exposure, in a paper published in 2025. The method needs only a finger prick: drops of blood dry on a card, which stores and ships easily. Farm workers and rural families face steady pesticide contact, yet drawing full blood samples in such places is hard.

The review weighs the method's promise against its known flaws. Tiny, uneven spot volumes and the share of red cells in blood can skew readings, and labs debate how to correct for them. Even so, the ease of collection could widen monitoring to whole regions. Finding exposed people early would let health services act before harm builds. The authors call the technique a strong candidate for population screening.
pmc-12727811:
William Pierre Schrock and seven co-authors weigh a boosted recovery plan against standard care for patients who had a kidney removed by robot aided surgery. The plan aims to ease the body's stress from surgery and speed the return to normal life. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

Records covered over two hundred patients split between the plan and plain care. Stay in hospital was a bit shorter under the plan, though the gap was small. Pain scores and use of strong pain drugs were lower at all time points checked under the plan. Harms, gut restart signs, and return visits did not differ in a firm way between the groups.
pmc-12728211:
Jing Zhong, Mengxian Li, Changhui Wu, and a wider team wrote this chemistry paper, published in 2025. It reports a two-metal catalytic reaction that builds chiral bridged-ring molecules, strained frameworks found in many natural products and drugs.

Such rings are hard to make in a single mirror-image form because they are strained and carry several centers of handedness. The team's reaction chains two well-known steps, a Heck step and a Sonogashira step, guided by palladium and copper together. Depending on the starting material, the same setup yields opposite handed products, each with one square and two neighboring handed centers. The rings can then be locked into even more rigid cages. Two of the products also damped an immune signaling pathway in early tests, and computer work traced the step that sets the reaction's speed.
pmc-12728411:
Alessandro Comis and six co-authors report a rare mishap during a valve in valve heart procedure. The patient was a woman aged eighty-three whose earlier replacement valve had failed. Scans showed her heart artery opening sat low, raising the risk that the new valve would block it. The team placed a protective wire in the artery as a guard.

After the new valve was released, imaging showed a tear in the main heart artery that blocked flow. The wire had likely shifted during release. The patient had severe chest pain and a new electric fault in the heart. Urgent stents restored flow and eased symptoms. The authors say this is the first such case reported during protective wiring.
pmc-12729011:
Kim and five co-authors classify a fast destructive shoulder disease, in work from twenty twenty-five. The disease causes rapid collapse of the ball of the shoulder joint for unclear reasons. It is rare but distinct from slow arthritis.

From twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-three, twenty-three patients were diagnosed at their center. Nineteen who had shoulder replacement and no other cause were studied in depth. The team proposes a three stage scan based classification. Most got a reverse replacement, and a few got a standard one. Mid term outcomes are reported by stage, which may help surgeons time and choose surgery.
pmc-12729111:
Seok Jin Jung and co-authors run a 2025 trial of wearable-guided rehab after knee replacement surgery. One group of women used a wearable motion tracker with a phone app that fed back their movement. The other group followed the standard self-directed program taught at discharge, with clinic visits as usual.

About fifty patients in total were assessed before surgery and at three, six, and twelve weeks after. Measures covered knee bend, pain, stiffness, daily function, quality of life, and walking speed. The tracker group showed better scores on several fronts, above all less pain and stiffness and better function by the final check. The authors conclude that tracker-guided home rehab matched the standard route overall and beat it on some measures. The result supports home tools for recovery after joint surgery.
pmc-12729211:
Abigail Hoff and co-authors study methadone given during heart surgery for patients who use intravenous drugs, in a 2025 paper. These patients often need valve surgery after infections, and their opioid tolerance makes pain control and waking from anesthesia tricky. A single long-acting methadone dose during surgery might smooth both.

The team reviewed charts at one large rural medical center over fourteen months. Sixty-one patients who got methadone during surgery were tracked for early removal of the breathing tube and for opioid use before and after the operation. Patients on methadone before surgery were left out to keep the picture clean. Results can guide anesthesia plans for a group whose care is often improvised.
pmc-12729311:
Hui Xu and co-authors evaluate a sequencing upgrade for forensic kinship testing in a 2025 study. Labs identify relatives through short repeating DNA segments, called STRs. Reading only their lengths limits power in tangled family cases, such as half-siblings or uncles.

Next-generation sequencing reads the segments' inner sequences as well, adding detail. In a Baoan population sample, fifty-two STR sites proved highly variable, and sequence data raised the allele count by about sixty-one percent over length alone. Simulated family pairs tested the system's accuracy. Full siblings and unrelated pairs were sorted with near-perfect efficacy. Distant relations landed near sixty percent, which shows both the gain and the remaining gap.
pmc-12729811:
Lei Lyu and co-authors review progress and roadblocks in gene therapy for diseases caused by faulty mitochondrial DNA. These mutations can bring severe illness or early death. Mitochondria carry their own small genome inside cells.

Three broad strategies dominate the field today. One expresses the gene from the nucleus instead. Others cut faulty copies with targeted nucleases. Base editing rewrites single letters of the mitochondrial code. Mixed copies inside one cell complicate every approach. Delivery across mitochondrial membranes adds another hurdle. The review weighs clinical gains against preclinical promise. It points to fixes that could unlock wider use in clinics soon for the sick who wait.
pmc-12730111:
Chen leads a team presenting a recipe to make peptide targets more immunogenic in a 2025 paper. Short peptides are handy for study, but they provoke weak immune responses and few commercial antibodies exist. Their workflow edits peptide sequences at the design stage.

Candidate fragments are screened across species and structure, ranked for immune presentation, then given careful substitutions. The edits raise predicted binding while keeping the natural target's key traits. In mice, edited peptides drew stronger antibody responses and more mature antibody types. The antibodies still bound the natural sequence. The effect repeated with other targets. Small mouse groups make this a proof of concept.
pmc-12730611:
Ugur Hasirci proposes a control-theory approach to bipolar disorder in a 2025 paper. About forty million people live with the illness worldwide, swinging between manic and depressive states. Modeling the mood dynamics mathematically may improve both understanding and treatment.

Unlike one-directional depression, bipolar disorder oscillates, so the goal is to quench the swing. The author designs a nonlinear adaptive controller for that task in the model. Framing mood as a system to be stabilized is unconventional, but it gives a precise way to test treatment ideas in simulation before any clinical use.
pmc-12731111:
Namita Goyal and co-authors re-analyze, in a 2025 study, two past trials of an immune-calming drug in ALS to test whether breathing measures can spot the patients it helps. Survival in this nerve disease tracks the loss of breathing capacity. The team measured time to a fifteen percent loss of that capacity and linked it to survival.

The drug cut the risk of that loss over six months by a clear margin. In slow-progressing patients, the drug slowed capacity decline and stretched survival by about eighteen months against placebo. Fast progressors gained nothing clear. The split suggests a subgroup whose disease is driven by immune attack, and breathing measures can find them.
pmc-12731211:
Aramis Sánchez and co-authors test paper strips that show acidity by color, using dyes drawn from plants. Standard ways to check acidity use meters, sensors, or drops, which cost more and can harm the environment. Plant dyes are cheap, easy to find, and change color as acidity shifts.

The team pulled pigments from forty plant species with a mix of alcohol and water, then checked how each dye reacted across the full acidity range. In dry form, dyes from cabbage, hibiscus flower, radish, and turmeric gave the clearest color steps. The authors present the strips as a green, low-cost option for checking acidity in goods and labs.
pmc-12731611:
Lear and eight co-authors weigh cell-death paths as cure marks for birth brain harm in this twenty twenty-five review. Such harm hits babes whose brains lost air and blood round their birth. It is a top cause of death and life-long loss in the young.

Inside, scans show brain sores in such babes grow for days to weeks past birth. Late sores wear the marks of a set death path, with guard cells heaped round them. Bare death, not the neat cell death, rules those late sores in beast tests. Late cures in beasts, from cell grafts to calm drugs, cut the harm a lot. The team sees a wide cure span that past work has left untried.
pmc-12732111:
Marisol López-Pulido and co-authors present a single-patient case showing how to set the bite plane for immediate complete dentures with a classic tool. When failing teeth are pulled and dentures fitted at once, leftover teeth block the usual wax try-in, so the occlusal plane is hard to place. A wrong plane hurts chewing, speech, and face height.

Their patient, a man of fifty-one, was treated with the Broadrick Occlusal Plane Analyzer. The tool sets the plane in harmony with front-tooth guidance and the jaw joint's own guidance. The case walks through each step, offering a template for a common prosthetic headache.
pmc-12732411:
Kim and Yu review in 2025 whether non drug methods ease symptoms of menopause in middle aged women. Hot flashes, poor sleep, low mood, and worry are common at this stage of life. Many women seek safer options than hormone care, whose side effects raise concern.

The pair pooled thirty two trials found across eight data banks. Methods ranged from food and herbal care to exercise, talk based help, and other therapies. On pooled scores, the methods cut low mood, worry, and sleep problems, and eased hot flashes. Gains in life quality were less clear. The review backs non drug care as a useful first step.
pmc-12732711:
Justine Schneider and eight colleagues report the United Kingdom arm of a large trial testing music programs for depression in care home residents with dementia. Sixteen care home units were assigned by chance to group music therapy, choir singing for fun, both, or usual care. Sessions ran twice a week for three months, then weekly for three more.

Of 192 residents enrolled, 146 were analyzed at six months. Neither program improved depression or any other outcome by a meaningful margin. Choir singing showed worse effects on depression scores, symptom severity, and self-rated health. The combined arm also raised distress among caregivers. The authors say the UK findings do not support these music programs for depression in this group, a sobering result for a popular care practice.
pmc-12733011:
Clark Griscom and co-authors test light-based tools for spotting chicken residue on poultry plant surfaces. Plants must verify that food-contact surfaces are truly clean. Eyes and noses miss thin residue that still carries risk.

Color and fluorescence spectrometry were tried on six common materials. Both methods detected residue far below human sensing limits. Stainless steel and blue plastic gave the clearest color gaps. Fluorescence stayed sensitive across all surfaces tested. Common cleaning chemicals did not blunt detection in the trials. A simple learning classifier sharpened clean versus dirty calls. Compact instruments could give fast, measured checks on plant lines during daily sanitation checks across plant shifts.
pmc-12733311:
Zaibun Khan and a team of co-authors compare the strain that keyhole surgery practice puts on two groups of trainee surgeons. Their study is from two thousand twenty-five. Ten trainees in women's surgery and ten in general surgery did the same four practice tasks. Sensors on their muscles tracked how hard the neck and shoulder muscles worked.

The women's surgery group showed far higher muscle activity in three of the four tasks. Those tasks covered hand-eye control, two-handed control, and stitching. The fourth task, moving the camera, showed no gap between the groups. Keyhole surgery is a known source of muscle disorders in surgeons. The authors say training and tool design should account for the heavier load found here.
pmc-12733911:
Neck strength guards athletes against concussion, and jaw position may switch neck muscles on. Denise Gobert, Gregg Ueckert, Mark Strickland, and Leeda Rasoulian test a custom mouth orthotic in 42 healthy adults. Strength and endurance were measured in six directions, with and without the device. A pressure gauge recorded the isometric efforts. Repeated-measures models compared the two conditions.

Strength rose in every direction with the orthotic in place. Rotation gains reached about 19 to 20 percent. Flexor endurance jumped nearly 45 percent. The authors read the instant effect as clinically meaningful. A fitted jaw device, they suggest, could join concussion risk programs in contact sports.
pmc-12734211:
Domingo Orozco-Beltran and eight co-authors gathered a Spanish expert consensus on the combined heart, kidney, and metabolic syndrome in a 2025 paper. Seventy specialists from five fields answered two Delphi rounds on sixty-one statements. Agreement needed four fifths of every specialty on the high end of a nine-point scale.

Fifty-four statements reached consensus. Faulty fat tissue was named the syndrome's starting driver. The syndrome covers both people at risk and those with disease already. Family doctors should coordinate care, prevention outranks late rescue, and proven drugs belong in early and late stages alike. Lifestyle change, with strong weight loss, drew top support. The authors offer the consensus as a shared playbook for a syndrome that crosses organ lines.
pmc-12734311:
Ludwig Álvarez-Córdova and co-authors present a 2025 study of prediction models for sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and strength with age. Clinics need simple tools to spot the condition early, above all where resources are thin. The team built three models of rising detail from data on community-dwelling older adults.

The basic model used age, sex, body mass index, calf size, and a short survey, and it sorted cases well. Adding a nutrition check and an electrical body measure gave the best scores of all. Body mass index, sex, and the electrical measure stayed strong across models. Because the models build step by step, clinics with few tools can use the basic form, while richer sites can add the rest.
pmc-12734411:
Jingzhuo Zhao and eight co-authors study how to thin out rubber rich asphalt in a 2025 paper. Asphalt loaded with rubber powder from old tires gets very thick when hot, making it hard to process. Thinning agents help, but how they work in this mix was unclear, so the team tested one agent in depth.

They trace three stages: the agent spreads through the asphalt, soaks into the rubber network, then breaks its cross links with reactive fragments. Best results came after twelve hours of soaking at a set temperature with a chosen grain size. Cross link density fell by half and hot thickness dropped a lot. The work clarifies how such thinners can make rubber asphalt usable.
pmc-12734811:
Murčinková, Sabol, and Baron simulate in twenty twenty-five how tiny internal structure lets composite panels block stress waves from sudden loads. Machines suffer impulse shocks that a well-built barrier zone could soften, spreading stress and cutting vibration and noise. Using small repeating cells and detailed simulations, they varied the shape, angle, spread, and size of filler pieces inside a plastic, plus a soft layer at the joins.

Hollow fillers beat solid ones clearly on wave damping, with hollow fibres best. Filler angle to the wave shifted damping by a large margin too. Rearranging fillers and adding the soft layer gave smaller extra gains. The authors say micro-scale layout is the lever for designing such barriers.
pmc-12735011:
Xu and co-authors build a math model for how cross-laminated timber plates bend under load and moisture together, in an engineering paper from 2025. The material, stacked wood layers glued crosswise, is a green building choice. Moisture swells the wood and changes its stiffness, so load and dampness act as a pair.

Their model joins moisture diffusion theory with three-dimensional elasticity to track dampness, stress, and movement layer by layer. A transfer matrix links the states between any two layers, and surface conditions then fix the solution. The model beat finite element runs on both accuracy and speed in checks. The team also mapped stress under load alone and moisture alone, and proposed a corrected way to add the two effects.
pmc-12735211:
Jianning Chu and co-authors use computer simulation to study a new way to cut silicon with great precision, in a 2025 paper. Single-crystal silicon is hard and brittle, so fine cutting is tough. Lasers and vibration have each been used to help. Watching the cut at atomic scale in real life is near impossible.

The team simulated the cut atom by atom, joining laser heat with tool vibration. They varied the tool edge shape and the heat level. Surface quality turned out to hinge on both the vibration path and the heat. Warmer cuts changed how forces and chip shapes behaved. The results help explain why the combined method works and how to tune it for clean surfaces.
pmc-12735511:
Ryan Duffy and Tuki Attuquayefio offer a two thousand twenty-five systematic review of mindfulness training and attention to food cues. Energy-dense foods grab attention automatically, driving overeating. Mindfulness may strengthen the mental brakes on that pull.

Following standard review guidelines, the authors searched seven databases. Six eligible studies of adults were found. Results were mixed across them. Some trials showed mindfulness cutting attention bias toward rich foods. Others found weaker or no effects. The small, uneven base means claims should stay modest, and the review maps exactly where stronger trials are needed.
pmc-12735911:
Avital Schurr challenges a popular story about brain fuel in this 2025 article. When neurons fire, they burn glucose, and some researchers claim part of that burn skips oxygen entirely, a process they call aerobic glycolysis, trading efficiency for speed.

Schurr argues the evidence points the other way: oxidative metabolism, the oxygen using pathway, powers brain activity. He questions the lactate shuttle picture, in which support cells hand neurons lactate as their main fuel. He also doubts the standard brain scan signal, which tracks blood oxygen, as a measure of tissue oxygen use, since it cannot see oxygen outside blood vessels. The piece asks where the oxygen is if the non-oxidative story were true.
pmc-12736011:
Visceral leishmaniasis, a parasite disease spread by sandflies, inflames the whole body and can kill. Lucyo Flavio Bezerra Diniz and co-authors test whether a blood protein tracks the disease's fire. The protein, pentraxin 3, rises in many infections. They measured it in thirty-six patients and forty-five healthy controls, alongside parasite counts and immune signals.

Patients carried far higher pentraxin levels than controls. The level rose with parasite load and with several inflammatory cytokines. Gene variants in the protein's own gene, by contrast, showed no link to catching the disease. The authors propose pentraxin 3 as a marker of disease activity: one blood value that mirrors both the inflammation and the parasite burden driving it. Such a marker could help follow treatment where lab resources are thin.
pmc-12736911:
Wenqing Wei and co-authors improved in 2025 a classic random-tree path planner for smart agents. The base method grows a tree of random steps toward the goal, but it converges slowly and leaves jagged, redundant paths. Their version searches from both ends and adds three layers of polish.

Fast tree indexing speeds node lookup, guided sampling leans toward the goal, and a pruning plus smoothing stage yields curves an agent can actually follow. Layered collision checks guard the route. The result is quicker, cleaner paths through cluttered spaces, with fewer wasted turns along the way.
pmc-12737311:
Saadet Hacısalihoğlu measures heavy metals in mussels from the southern Marmara Sea in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Mussels filter seawater and concentrate metals, making them natural monitors of coastal pollution. Five stations along the Bursa coast supplied twenty mussels each.

Levels of six metals varied by station: zinc and mercury peaked at Mudanya, copper at Kurşunlu, and lead at Küçükkumla. Standard risk indices for adults all sat below the level of concern. Two stations, though, had hazard totals close enough to the limit to warrant closer watching. Hacısalihoğlu concludes that mussels track coastal contamination well and that ongoing monitoring protects both the ecosystem and public health.
pmc-12737711:
Fu, Li, Abd El-Aty, Yagan, Ju, and Yong review how viruses hijack the cell's recycling system, autophagy, turning a defense into a workshop. Autophagy normally chews up worn parts and invaders. Most viruses, though, bend it to their needs with a regulate-but-not-destroy strategy.

They start the recycling flow, then block the final fusion step that would digest them. The stalled bubbles become sheltered bays where viral genomes copy and new particles assemble. A tidy cell interior also keeps the host alive long enough to finish the cycle. Only the full digestive end of the pathway truly hurts most viruses. The authors map this tug-of-war for designing antivirals that target the recycling machinery.
pmc-12738711:
Nick Feldman, Arie den Boef, Lyubov Amitonova, and Femius Koenderink showed in 2025 a better way to sense tiny changes with light. Certain nano structures produce sharp Fano resonances, prized for sensing because they are narrow and boost local fields. Past readouts tracked a shift in the resonance color, which wastes much of the signal.

Their method instead reads how the scattered light spreads by angle. Tiny changes to the surface then produce clear directional patterns that carry more information. They proved this with careful tests on a patterned surface and compared the two readouts by a standard measure of information. The angle-based readout held a clear advantage.
pmc-12738811:
Anastasia Panova and a large team of co-authors assessed a bird flu virus taken from fur seals in a 2025 paper. The H5N1 strain in question spread into marine mammals in 2023, killing many northern fur seals in Russia's Far East. The seals' virus belongs to a genotype of European origin and carries two changes linked to stronger illness in mammals.

Mouse tests confirmed the virus is highly virulent. Ferret tests, the standard for judging spread between mammals, showed no airborne transmission. The authors conclude the two changes raise severity without making the virus pass through air efficiently. That limits the immediate pandemic threat, but they stress continued watch and testing of new variants.
pmc-12741811:
Masaki Seki, Hiroshi Ihara, and seven co-authors ask if shared hobbies lift life quality for boys with autism. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, works in Japan with seventy-one boys. The boys span late elementary and middle school ages. Peer bonds and leisure grow central to well-being in those years, yet shared play can be hard for this group.

Many boys said they want to play with friends. Few actually did: about a third of the younger boys and a fifth of the older ones. Middle school boys who shared hobbies with peers scored higher on life quality. The study is small and exploratory, but the signal favors shared fun.
pmc-12742111:
Martin Kolb and colleagues designed a lung fibrosis trial in two thousand twenty-five. The MIST study tests an inhaled drug solution. Progressive lung scarring affects patients beyond the classic type. Swallowed pirfenidone helped little in earlier small studies. Heavy body exposure caused substantial side effects. Inhaling the drug may improve tolerability.

About three hundred patients will join worldwide. Groups receive high dose, low dose, or placebo. A special nebulizer delivers treatment twice daily. Lung capacity change after one year is the main measure. Quality of life and disease progression are also tracked. The double-blind design keeps assessments fair. Results should settle the inhaled approach's value.
pmc-12744511:
Asuka Okawa and co-authors report a 2025 case where a trapped womb hid behind a wrong diagnosis. A 39-year-old first-time mother arrived at thirty-one weeks labeled with complete placenta previa and fibroids. In truth, her backward-tilted pregnant uterus was wedged in the pelvic hollow, a rare state that mimics placenta problems and risks surgical injury if missed.

The tell was a missing cervical canal on the vaginal scan, plus a cervix shoved up and right on other views. MRI backed the call. A planned cesarean at thirty-eight weeks, with incisions adjusted after manual reduction failed, delivered a healthy boy. The authors urge teams to treat the missing canal as a red flag.
pmc-12745211:
Komalpreet Kaur and five co-authors study fruit splitting in Daisy mandarin under subtropical conditions in a 2025 paper. Splitting spoils fruit quality and how well the fruit sells, and its rate tracks the weather as the crop grows.

Daily weather data came from an observatory at Punjab Agricultural University in Ludhiana. One year showed far more splitting than the year before, with weather a major cause. Links and models tied the damage most to high and low daily heat, morning and evening humidity, and rainfall. Warm spells sped fruit growth in ways that raised the risk.
pmc-12746011:
Thalassia Niarchou and co-authors report a long case study from 2025 on regional odontodysplasia, a rare flaw in tooth growth. The flaw weakens both enamel and dentin in a group of nearby teeth. On X-rays the teeth look pale and thin, a pattern often called ghost teeth.

The case follows a young girl with the flaw in her left upper jaw. She first came to the clinic at age three. A team of child dental, brace, and false-tooth experts then cared for her for twelve years. The report gives her clinical and X-ray findings in detail. It covers removal of the bad teeth, the false-tooth work that restored her smile, and the brace work that guided the rest of her teeth into place.
pmc-12747111:
Nóra Kecskeméti and co-authors follow five patients with a rare immune disorder in this 2025 paper. Cogan's syndrome attacks the eyes and inner ears, and its timing varies a lot between patients. The team tracked how the illness was diagnosed, treated, and followed over many years.

All five patients lost hearing in both ears, often suddenly, and all lost balance function on both sides. Eye problems also shifted over time. Steroids were the first treatment, with stronger immune drugs and newer biologic drugs used when needed. Eye symptoms were controlled in every patient. Four patients got cochlear implants and kept stable speech understanding long-term. The authors stress early treatment and early hearing rehabilitation for such cases.
pmc-12747911:
Drug use among university students in Lebanon is rising and little studied. Riwa Kfoury, Pascale Salameh, and Hélène Peyriere built two questionnaires, one testing what students know about psychoactive substances and one measuring their attitudes, then validated both on 414 students from 29 institutions.

Statistical analysis showed each scale holds together well, with two underlying factors apiece and strong reliability scores. Students with better grades knew more, as did those aware the substances come in nasal forms. Notably, knowledge and attitudes barely correlated: knowing more did not mean judging differently. Grades, study year, financial shifts, mental illness, and family history all predicted scores in the combined analysis. The authors offer the scales as tools for campuses that want to measure the problem before trying to fix it.
pmc-12748311:
Wei Chen and co-authors profile a distinct cell group inside a hard brain tumor, in a 2025 study. The tumor is a high-grade astrocytoma carrying a change in the IDH gene. It is the second most common adult glioma of its class. Few studies had mapped it cell by cell and in place.

Surgeons used navigation tools and glowing dye to take high-grade and low-grade samples with care. Single-cell and spatial gene reads were then matched with large public cancer data sets. One cell cluster appeared only in high-grade tumors, at the end of a growth path. That cluster also showed immune-linked traits. Naming this group may clarify how the tumor worsens and how it might be treated.
pmc-12748811:
Yakun Chen, Hongzhen Zhang, Yuchen Lu, and Zhijie Song test whether farm companies pull smallholders into modern agriculture, using census micro data from China, in work from twenty twenty-five. Small farms anchor food supply, yet often miss modern methods. Companies hold market reach that might bridge the gap.

Company presence reshaped how smallholders allocate their inputs. Planted area grew, machine use rose, and planting grew more specialized with better technique. Green production gains, though, did not show clearly. Repeat checks held the pattern. Small farms gained most on scale, while bigger farms and cash crop growers gained most on machines and technology. The authors draw lessons for paired company and policy support.
pmc-12749511:
Go-kart instructors work in roaring, shaking machines, yet their exposure risks are rarely measured. Iryna Myshchenko, Karolina Paluszek, and Daria Karpczak studied in 2025 nine young male instructors at a dynamic track.

Daily noise ran from about seventy-six to eighty-two decibels, with peaks near one hundred nine. Modeling warned that running more than nine karts at once would breach the eighty-five-decibel limit. Whole-body vibration broke short-term limits in half the tested cases, and hand-arm vibration in most. Hearing questionnaires showed mild perceived difficulty, worse with age and experience. The authors call for tailored prevention in recreation work.
pmc-12749611:
Purmessur and three co-authors showed in twenty twenty-five a new kind of quantum bit, or qubit, made with a thin metal film. Most qubits use a part that is hard to tune and dies fast at high heat. Their part is a slim neck in the film that lets charge slip in a quantum way.

They built the qubit, read its state, and steered it with care. It ran at a high tone set by its coil part and lived for a fair span of time. It still worked when warmed past a point where most qubits fail. The result adds a new tool for quantum machines.
pmc-12749811:
Lei Zhang and co-authors show that a flu virus can gain drug resistance through a change in its coat protein, not just the protein the drug targets, in a study from 2025. The drug is the most used flu drug in the world, and watch lists track resistance in its target protein.

In lab passages under drug pressure, the virus picked up coat changes on their own. One such change has spread in real flu strains since a few years back. That change also boosted resistance from a known target change when both sat in one virus. The authors urge world watch lists to track coat changes too.
pmc-12749911:
Shuai Wang and ten co-authors show that mugwort oil trims fat gain in mice by firing the body's heat tissue, in a 2025 study. Brown fat burns energy as heat, which makes it a tempting target against obesity. Mugwort is a traditional food plant whose oils had never been weighed for this job. Mice on a rich diet got the oil alongside.

Oiled mice gained less weight and body fat, and their insulin worked better. Inside brown fat, the oil switched on the main heat gene. It did so by waking a partner gene that teams with a known fat regulator to hold the heat gene open. The authors cast the oil as a food-grade candidate for weight care, pending tests in people. They note its long food history may ease that path.
pmc-12750011:
Hai Qi and six co-authors audit China's nonferrous metals industry in the single currency of exergy, the useful energy embodied in everything, in this 2025 study. Smelting and pressing these metals devours resources, and ordinary accounting cannot weigh coal, ore, labor, and pollution on one scale. Extended exergy accounting does, and the team applied it from 1992 to 2015.

Inputs and yields both grew, with technology the main driver of improvement. Energy dominated the input side and grew faster than in Chinese industry overall, while materials leaned ever more on imports. Emissions climbed quickly, greenhouse gases dwarfing the traditional three wastes. Aluminum took the majority of output and use, and per person consumption passed some other countries. The authors offer the method for judging whole industries ecologically.
pmc-12750711:
Ten authors present a study from two thousand twenty-five on mild cognitive impairment in a Japanese town. People with this condition face a higher risk of dementia, yet some stay stable and some return to normal thinking. Reported return rates vary widely, and the factors behind them are disputed.

The Hisayama study surveyed residents aged sixty-five and older three times over a decade, with very high participation. The team pooled two five-year spans to measure how many people moved back to normal cognition. They then searched for traits that made the return more likely, in both the short and the long term.
pmc-12750811:
Children whose lower jaw sits too far back often wear a functional appliance. Muhteber Durmus, Musa Bulut, and Yasin Hezenci compare two options in a computer model. One is the classic Twin Block. The other advances the jaw with clear aligners. Three-dimensional finite element models covered the jaws, skull sutures, teeth, and jaw joint. A muscle force simulated the forward jaw position in both designs.

The Twin Block moved the lower front teeth more. It also produced bigger skeletal changes in the jaw body and joint socket. Stress in the joint disk and condyle ran higher with the Twin Block. The aligner design gave gentler, more tooth-focused effects. The authors weigh strength against control.
pmc-12751011:
Fluoride-ion batteries promise high energy density without the dendrite problems of lithium cells, but their salts barely dissolve in the liquids batteries use. Meng Lei and co-authors designed a helper molecule that grabs fluoride ions loosely enough to let them go again. Their bulky acceptor coaxes the salt into solution through a swapping reaction and reaches good conductivity at room temperature. Its crowded shape also speeds the release of fluoride ions at the electrode.

Cells built with this electrolyte cycled for 500 hours in symmetric tests and tolerated high current. A full cell paired with a copper fluoride cathode delivered the highest capacity reported for this battery type and kept much of it after 65 cycles. The authors present the closed-loop swapping design as a general route to longer-lived fluoride batteries.
pmc-12751411:
Zhao Jing and Zang Mouhong test what happens when artificial intelligence joins a top national nursing course in China, in a 2025 study. Their test bed is Nursing Ethics, a flagship online course. The reform built AI study partners and helpers into a blended class, mixing screen work with live teaching. Four whole classes were split by lot: half took the new form, half kept the old.

The AI classes ended with higher exam scores and warmer course ratings than the control classes. The gap cleared the bar for a real effect, not chance. Global talk of a new age of smart schooling frames the trial. The authors read the result as early proof that strong course stock plus AI help can lift nursing ethics teaching. They frame it as a workable, student-liked path for other courses to copy.
pmc-12751811:
Haikun Zhang and co-authors walk through sleep-drug care for a huge neck gland growth that squeezed a windpipe. The patient in their 2025 case is a woman in her early seventies with a heart hole flaw as well. A blocked windpipe makes gas care a high-wire act: once she sleeps, the pipe can cave. A mixed team drafts back-up plans pre-cut.

She is tubed while still awake, with a calm drug pair to ease the strain. A throat-cut kit stands by in case the tube fails. Gas and vein drugs hold her deep while the growth comes out. The pipe clears in full, and a month of checks shows no harm. The team casts drill and shared plans as the true save.
pmc-12751911:
Huang and co-authors set out a trial protocol testing probiotics in older adults with mild cognitive impairment. This early memory decline affects thinking and other body functions tied to aging. Gut microbes are a plausible lever, since gut health links to brain health in later life.

The PCAMCI trial will enroll middle-aged and older adults with mild impairment. It is randomised, triple-blinded, and placebo-controlled, a strict design that hides group assignment from all sides. Outcomes cover cognition plus other aging-related body functions. The protocol aims to test if probiotic supplements can slow decline in this group.
pmc-12752011:
Huong Van Le and co-authors grade ways to turn a molecule into numbers a model can read, in a 2025 study. The end is to guess how well a drug will cross the gut wall, a gate most pills must pass. A lab cell test gives the true rate, but slow and dear.

The team tried eight kinds of molecule marks, from flat traits to deep-learned codes, each fed to a self-tuning learner. Two data sets of unlike size and span gave the test beds. One print-based mark set led the field. Drug teams gain a ranked kit for a first-pass guess that can save wet work.
pmc-12752111:
Lin-Xin Guan and four co-authors wrote a 2025 study comparing eleven risk scores for predicting atrial fibrillation returning after ablation. Pulmonary vein isolation is the standard catheter procedure for this rhythm disorder. In non-paroxysmal cases, though, many patients relapse, and a crowd of published scores claim to predict who.

The retrospective study covered 166 patients who had the procedure alone, about a fifth of them women, averaging 60 years old. Heart imaging data fed all eleven scores, from APPLE to SCALE-CryoAF. Fibrillation returned in 41 patients, about a quarter, after the blanking period. Relapse split almost evenly between cryoballoon and radiofrequency techniques. Comparing the scores head to head in this harder subgroup tells clinicians which, if any, deserve trust.
pmc-12752211:
Yifan Chen and co-authors compare two flap incision designs for accelerated orthodontic surgery in the front teeth region, in a trial report from 2025. The surgery speeds tooth movement but needs a flap design that protects looks, stability, and recovery. Two added cuts, one vertical and one horizontal, are the options under test.

Twenty-two patients were randomized to one design or the other. Surgery time and graft weight were logged at once. Healing was checked at one and two weeks. Gum measures ran to twelve months, and cone beam scans tracked bone and root changes. Neck and head films gauged tooth movement. The trial weighs which cut serves patients better.
pmc-12752411:
Wen Jin, Yunxian Yu, and nine co-authors ask how diabetes in pregnancy changes the effect of weight gain. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, follows a large population cohort. Weight gain was split into spans before and after the diabetes test. Gain that is too low, normal, or too high was tracked for each span.

More than two thousand women had the diabetes form, and near eleven thousand did not. In both groups, faster gain in any span raised the chance of a large baby and other risks. The diabetes state, though, reshaped some of those links. The team used cross-over checks to test the interplay. Advice on gain may need to differ by diabetes status.
pmc-12752511:
Yu-Kai Huang, Mary Zhuang, and Michelle Digman presented a new image analysis method in 2025 and used it to study metabolism in breast cancer cells. Their method segments microscope images of mitochondria by fluorescence lifetime, using the natural glow of a metabolic molecule, so no stain is needed. Single mitochondria can then be measured one by one in live cells.

The method improved detection accuracy by about a third over simple brightness cut-offs, in the authors' tests. With it, they found that uptake of normal cell mitochondria shifted the balance of free and bound forms of the molecule and raised cell energy work. Treated cancer cells also showed changed sensitivity to chemotherapy. Readers get both a sharper imaging tool and a clue about how donated mitochondria rewire cancer cell energy.
pmc-12753911:
High blood pressure may link to the mix of germs in the gut, and that link may differ by sex. Jing Fu and co-authors test that thought in a 2025 study of two hundred adults in Xinjiang. They read gut germs in two ways and also checked compounds in the blood.

One germ stood out in men with high blood pressure. Where that germ was more common, top blood pressure readings tended to be lower. A blood compound sat in the middle of the link, which hints at a chain from germ to compound to pressure. The team frames the chain as a path for more work on sex linked gut health.
pmc-12754811:
Lucy Lee-Smith and Joseph Andrews published a systematic review in 2025 examining the carbon footprint of orthopaedic outpatient care, and comparing emissions from in-person and virtual models of care. Health care systems account for a significant share of global greenhouse gas emissions. Trauma and orthopaedics has an exceptionally high emission profile compared with other specialties.

The reviewers included nine studies encompassing more than half a million patients. Virtual care consistently showed a smaller carbon footprint than traditional in-person appointments. Most of the reduction came from patient travel avoided, with a median saving of close to twelve kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent per patient interaction. Other gains were patient cost savings and easier access. The certainty of the evidence was low, however, because of bias risks across the studies. The authors call for studies that track travel and linked emissions firsthand.
pmc-12755011:
Yijing Xin, Xifeng Qian, and Yanmin Yang follow blood pressure paths and healthy aging in China in a 2025 paper. Successful aging was defined strictly: no major chronic disease, sound body and mind, and active social life. The team used a national aging survey of nearly two thousand middle-aged and older adults. They grouped people by how their top blood pressure number moved across 2011 to 2015, then checked aging outcomes in 2020.

Three paths emerged: stable low, stable high, and unstable high. Only about four and a half percent aged successfully. Against the stable low group, the stable high group had about half the odds of success, and the unstable high group about a tenth. The authors argue that watching pressure over years, not just at one visit, matters for helping people age well.
pmc-12756211:
Hashim Ishfaq and co-authors pool in 2025 studies comparing two wrist versus leg routes for the backup access line during valve replacement through a catheter. The main valve goes in through a main route, but a second line is needed, and its site may drive bleeding and vessel harm. Searches of three databases gathered studies that compared wrist and upper leg backup access head to head.

Seven studies with over six thousand patients qualified. Wrist access tied to far lower odds of death within thirty days, and to lower odds of stroke and passing clots. Checks that drop one study at a time, and splits by main route, tested how firm the picture is. The authors favor the wrist for the backup line.
pmc-12756311:
Petar Glišović and Alessandro Forte rebuild the long past of Earth's deepest gravity dip, over Antarctica. Their 2025 study notes that most work reads the geoid, Earth's gravity-shaped sea surface, as a snapshot. Time-reversed mantle flow models, steered by seismic maps, trace the Antarctic low back through the Cenozoic era. Early on, deep mantle density held the low steady in place. A major shift in strength and spot came midway, matching a known swing in Earth's spin axis.

In the last forty million years, buoyant rise from the deep mantle grew the low further. Deep sinking near the Antarctic margin and broad upwelling jointly shaped it, the authors say.
pmc-12756811:
Mohammed Ranjous and four co-authors test mixed fertilization for cauliflower grown in calcareous soil. Such soil, common in Syria and other arid regions, has high pH, much calcium carbonate, and low nutrient availability. The team ran a field experiment at the Shabaa Research Station during the 2024-2025 growing season. A randomized complete block design compared 13 fertilization treatments with three replicates each.

The best mix combined 50% mineral fertilizer, 25% fermented cow manure, and 25% biofertilizer. That blend beat single-fertilizer plans on growth and yield, with a 44.5% increase over one comparison treatment. Soil and plant macronutrients were measured at the end of the season to back the result.
pmc-12757111:
Kunjan Barot and co-authors audit wrist X-ray quality in this 2025 study. Wrist injuries fill emergency and bone clinics, with fractures of the radius and wrist bones among the most common. A side-view film must be positioned just right to show bone alignment.

Poor positioning hides key relationships and can mislead diagnosis, delay care, or force repeat imaging. The team ran a closed-loop audit, checking films against standard positioning criteria, feeding results back, and checking again. The loop aims to lift compliance step by step. Better films mean fewer missed injuries and less legal exposure for the service.
pmc-12757411:
Felix Assah and co-authors study flood resilience and chronic disease in Yaoundé, Cameroon, in a 2025 paper. Flooding grows worse with climate change and fast city growth, and it hits health hard. Chronic diseases such as diabetes and heart disease share drivers with flood risk, like poor diet and inactivity. The team asked how community flood strategies shape those drivers.

Twelve local stakeholders, from city staff to flood-affected residents, joined interviews and a group modeling workshop. Together they built a loop map of fourteen factors and five feedback cycles. Community steps like waste cleanup, tree planting, and drain care improved hygiene, food access, and space for activity. Weak rule enforcement and politics limited long-term gains. The authors urge that community action be folded into formal disaster and health policy.
pmc-12758411:
Irisarri and co-authors test whether satellite data can track forage quality in United Kingdom grasslands, in a 2025 study. Forage quality drives both animal performance and environmental impact. Better forage ferments better in the rumen, which can cut methane output and ease nutritional stress. Yet large-scale checks on quality rely on slow, costly sampling that destroys the sample.

The team pair optical satellite images with a random forest model to predict four key traits. Those traits are crude protein, water-soluble carbohydrates, and two fiber measures. They calibrate and check the model with more than 9,500 field observations tied to locations. The approach points to scalable monitoring that needs no cutting or lab work for each field.
pmc-12764211:
Yuan, Wang, Liu, Zhang, and Wang study markers of chemotherapy resistance in cervical cancer in twenty twenty-five. Many patients do not respond to platinum based drugs. Immune checkpoint genes may help predict who will resist treatment. The team genotyped seven candidate variants in more than one thousand patients.

About half the patients were non responders to chemotherapy. Three variants were much more common in non responders than in responders. Certain genotypes raised the risk of platinum resistance by two to almost four times. Blood levels of two checkpoint proteins were also higher in non responders. Carriers of mutant genotypes had higher levels of those proteins. The authors say the variants and blood levels may together predict resistance.
pmc-12764511:
Jonique George and four co-authors study a brain receptor tied to memory in Alzheimer's disease. Their 2025 paper uses a rat model that grows amyloid and loses memory with age. The receptor, a calming type called alpha-five GABA-A, helps run memory replay circuits in the hippocampus. A drug that tunes this receptor had stopped working in the older model rats.

The team asked whether the receptor itself fades with disease. In healthy aging, one key receptor form rises after synapses in a hippocampal area. In the disease-model rats, that age-linked rise was lost or reversed. The pattern suggests the drug failed because its target had dwindled. Restoring or bypassing the receptor could matter for treating memory loss directly.
pmc-12766811:
Future doctors should know how to prevent skin cancer, the most avoidable of cancers and one that climate change is making more common. Ece Karaoglu and Burcu Kucuk Bicer surveyed 622 medical students across all six years at a Turkish public university in 2025.

Students scored moderately on skin cancer knowledge and somewhat better on climate knowledge. Women outscored men on both. Almost everyone knew the dangerous midday sun hours, yet only about half avoided them, and nearly two thirds had been sunburned at least once. Year of study also predicted awareness. The authors argue that knowing and doing are different lessons, and medical training should teach both.
pmc-12767411:
Yike Wang and co-authors chart the rise of a research topic: neutrophil traps in the failing lung. In acute respiratory distress syndrome, neutrophils cast webs of DNA called extracellular traps that catch germs but also inflame tissue. The team ran a bibliometric scan of three databases for work from 2011 to 2024, mapping who publishes, who gets cited, and what themes heat up.

Three hundred twenty-eight articles qualified, with output climbing steadily. China and the United States lead the field, and Frontiers in Immunology carries much of it. Inflammation response anchors the topic; the link between the traps and blood clots is the rising edge. The authors point drug hunters toward therapies that tame the traps in injured lungs, and offer newcomers a map of the territory.
pmc-12768611:
Moshi and co-authors pool the trials on steroid injections for knee osteoarthritis. The shots are widely used, but reports of their value conflict. Searching three databases, the team gathers sixteen randomized trials with 1,522 patients and follows pain, function, quality of life, care use, and harms across a full year using a longitudinal meta-analysis.

Pain eases slightly at one month and then the advantage fades; by three months it is gone. Function and quality of life never improve meaningfully. Care use dips briefly at one month, and no serious safety problems appear. The authors conclude the injections buy short relief only, a fact they say should anchor decisions about using them.
pmc-12768711:
Vania Santos and four co-authors trace the history of RedETSA, the health technology assessment network of the Americas, in this 2025 conference paper. Such assessment weighs whether new health technologies are worth their cost. The network was born at a 2011 meeting in Rio de Janeiro and links ministries, agencies, and regulators across the region.

The review counts the growth: twenty-one member countries and forty institutions today. Regional and world resolutions in the years after its founding pushed assessment into national law in several countries.
