The network has funded hundreds of training scholarships, run dozens of webinars, and built a database holding more than thirty-eight hundred assessment reports. The authors credit it with spreading the craft across the Americas. Remaining gaps include firmer links from assessment to actual decisions and more local data.
pmc-12768811:
Ludmila Gargano and three co-authors weigh the cost utility of a drug pair for follicular lymphoma in Brazil in this 2025 paper. The pair joins lenalidomide with rituximab for patients whose cancer returned after first treatment. Brazil's public system now leans on rituximab with chemotherapy for such cases. The team built a survival model from a clinical trial, stretched over forty years, and priced drugs and care across the course.

The pair added about three quality adjusted life years per patient, at a high added cost. The cost per added year still fell below Brazil's stated threshold, so the pair counted as cost effective. Listing the pair would raise the public budget by about twelve and a half million dollars over five years at a fifty percent share. The authors conclude the pair could serve relapsed patients better than standard care, within the system's limits.
pmc-12769511:
Mohd Abas Bhat and co-authors use machine learning to predict when breast cancer will return, in a 2025 study. Return of the disease strikes up to forty percent of patients in Brazil and shapes both survival and treatment choices.

Clinical and tissue data were pulled from unstructured medical records. A clustering step grouped patients by how aggressive their tumors looked, giving two clear subgroups. For the calmer group, one classifier caught nearly all returns, with a recall of 0.9872. For the more aggressive group, a random forest model gave the best balance of recall and precision. A standard survival model tested how risk played out over time. The authors call for checks at more hospitals and the addition of molecular markers.
pmc-12770011:
Li Wu and co-authors chart traits of stomach cancer tied to the Epstein-Barr virus in work dated 2025. Seven cases from their files got deep reads: tissue form, marker stains, and gene scans. Six patients were men, with ages from the twenties to the seventies. Tumors sat mostly high in the stomach and showed an ulcer form.

All cases sat at an early stage, and node spread was rare. Stains were rich in immune cells, and one immune brake mark ran high. Gene scans found two faults often, while other known faults were absent. The traits set this cancer type apart and guide care picks.
pmc-12771711:
Maria Catarina Carreira and co-authors compare two food sources for growing support cells in this 2025 study. Cord blood holds stem cells used in transplants, but adult patients need more cells than one unit holds. Support cells called MSCs can help those stem cells grow in the lab.

Labs usually feed MSCs with calf serum. A human platelet product offers a cleaner swap with no animal parts. The team grew MSCs both ways and checked how well each batch backed stem cell growth. Gene activity was read alongside function. Whether the swap weakens support was the open question.
pmc-12772011:
Shigeo Ohba leads a team in a 2025 study of amino acid weak spots in brain gliomas, split by a gene mark. Lower grade gliomas often carry a change in the IDH gene. Tumors with and without that change look alike under a lens, but they run on distinct fuel mixes, which may be a path to aimed care.

Mass tools read the full small-molecule sets of lab glioma lines of both kinds. The mutant lines held more of one amino acid, asparagine, and less of two kin, glutamine and glutamate. Tests in live animals backed the split, the team report.
pmc-12772211:
Yuriria Vázquez and co-authors show that the brain's face movement areas work as one network, not two separate circuits, in a 2025 study in macaque monkeys. Textbook teaching splits emotional expressions, run from a medial frontal area, from voluntary movements run by lateral motor areas. Guided by MRI, the team stimulated and recorded from four areas at once while the animals made faces and chewed.

Stimulating one area stirred responses in the others, and during expressions the medial and lateral areas synchronized in the alpha and beta bands. Chewing coupled them at lower frequencies instead. The authors conclude facial control emerges from an interacting sensorimotor network whose coupling shifts with the movement type.
pmc-12772611:
Running a hospital through a national economic collapse is the story told in a 2025 perspective article by Ranga Sabhapathige and Dilrukshi Deerasinghe. Sri Lanka's crisis, running since April 2022, hit their large teaching hospital with shortages of supplies, funds, reagents, and fuel, while staff left the country in numbers.

The authors describe how the hospital's leaders answered with a flexible style that shifted by need: directing, coaching, supporting, and delegating. Early moves included pausing renovation work, buying drugs locally, and paying staff extra for added duty. A crisis committee coordinated the response. The piece offers a ground-level account of how situational leadership kept a hospital working through turbulent years.
pmc-12774311:
Anjali Sharma and co-authors present six cases of schizophrenia where sexual themes are at the heart of the symptoms in a 2025 article. Such symptoms are seldom spoken of, above all in Indian clinical settings, where shame may hide them. The team reviewed charts of six patients whose delusions or hallucinations centered on sexual content, with consent and names removed.

The patients were thirty-two years of age on average, and five were women. Signs included feelings of being controlled or influenced through the body and misread perceptions with delusional meaning. Three patients had treatment-resistant illness and responded to clozapine, a drug reserved for such cases. The authors argue that naming these cases helps diagnosis and care that respects cultural feelings around sex.
pmc-12774911:
Elwira Nieboga and co-authors show why gum cells from diseased mouths fail to protect jawbone, in a 2025 study. In periodontitis, bone-eating cells called osteoclasts dissolve the bone that holds teeth. Healthy gum fibroblasts normally release a brake molecule, osteoprotegerin, that holds those cells back. The team compared fluid from healthy and diseased donors' gum cells.

Healthy cell fluid strongly suppressed osteoclast formation and was rich in the brake molecule. A lab-grown gum model confirmed fibroblasts as its main source. Cells from patients made far less of it and suppressed osteoclasts weakly. Silencing the molecule's gene in patient cells weakened the brake further. The deficit helps explain the runaway bone loss of gum disease.
pmc-12775111:
Marengoni and co-authors examine Italy's move toward joined-up community health care for older people. Italy's population is aging fast, and many older people live with several diseases and frailty at once. Hospitals, family doctors, and social services have often worked apart, leaving frail patients to bridge the gaps themselves.

A 2022 decree, funded through the national recovery plan, sets new standards for care close to home. Community houses and health districts sit at the center of the reform. The authors discuss how patients are sorted by need with a frailty index built for primary care. They weigh the reform's promise and its risks. Their account suits readers tracking how health systems adapt to aging.
pmc-12775211:
Yuxiang Liao and five co-authors uncover a driver of glioma growth in a 2025 study. Glioma is the most common brain tumor in adults and carries a poor outlook. The team studied a circular RNA called circEPHB4, a ring-shaped molecule that can steer other genes, and traced how it helps tumor cells grow, move, and invade.

Silencing the ring slowed tumors in dishes and in animals. The ring props up a protein called YBX1 by blocking the partner that would mark it for disposal. That protein in turn steadies the message for a second protein, MRPS16, which the tumor needs. Blocking any link in this chain weakened the cancer, which points to fresh drug targets.
pmc-12775711:
Shiting Xu and co-authors build an AI model to predict a key gene mutation in lung cancer in a 2025 study. Treatment for advanced non-small cell lung cancer depends on which driver mutation a tumor carries. The mutation studied here, in a growth receptor gene, decides whether a class of targeted pills can work. Testing usually needs tissue, so a scan-based prediction could help.

Their model joins simple learning methods fed with clinical and tumor facts to a deep network fed with CT scans. In one hundred fifty patients it predicted the mutation with strong accuracy. It also forecast response to the targeted pills better for one common mutation form than another. The authors say combined models may sharpen non-invasive prediction, pending larger validation.
pmc-12776211:
Yongqin Zhang, Yun Zuo, and Dong Hua link a protein called spondin-2 to gastric cancer outcomes in this 2025 paper. Spondin-2 is raised in several cancers and tied to spread. Its role in stomach cancer, and in radiation response, was unclear.

Public data showed far more spondin-2 in tumor tissue than in healthy stomach lining. High levels tracked larger tumors and shorter survival. Cell tests in a gastric cancer line showed the protein drives growth and migration. Extra spondin-2 also made cells resist radiation. It blunted cell cycle arrest, death, and DNA damage after exposure. The authors propose it as a marker for radiotherapy response.
pmc-12776911:
Tugce Damarsoy and co-authors test simple blood based scores for predicting death in sepsis patients in a 2025 study. Sepsis kills a large share of those it strikes, and early warning of high risk guides timely care. The team compared sixteen candidate scores in intensive care patients at their hospital.

Of one hundred fifteen patients, just over half died. A nutrition index built from albumin and white cell counts had the strongest single power to separate survivors from nonsurvivors. A urea to albumin ratio ranked second. Used together, the two scores predicted death better than either alone. The authors offer the pair as a cheap bedside aid for risk checks.
pmc-12780411:
Jie Huang and co-authors build a learning model to forecast outcomes after surgery for invasive lung adenocarcinoma. This lung cancer often returns or spreads after resection. Better forecasts can shape follow-up and added treatment.

Hundreds of resected patients were followed for disease-free survival. Clinical and pathology data fed four candidate models. Data split into training and test parts for fair checks. Cross-validation steadied the model comparison process. One shrinkage-based model predicted two-year outcomes best. Accuracy held up well on the held-out test set. Calibration and benefit curves backed its clinical value. The tool may help doctors plan post-surgery care and watch and visit schedules.
pmc-12780811:
Leonardo Biagio and co-authors study pregnant women in a Brazilian cohort to test whether mental health carries the link between violence and obesity, in work from twenty twenty-four. Violence in pregnancy is common and may shape body weight through the mind. The chain had rarely been tested directly.

Four hundred women at clinics in Araraquara answered standard questionnaires on violence, mood, and general health. Over half reported some violence, with psychological violence most common in the past year. About three in five stood at risk of major depression. Women with mental health changes faced more than double the obesity risk. Statistical mediation showed mental health carried about half the violence to obesity link. Care must span social and mental ground, the authors say.
pmc-12783111:
Fangmin Chen and co-authors build a sound-activated vaccine helper in 2025. Cancer vaccines need innate immunity fired precisely in lymph nodes, which is hard to control. Their helper is a peptide chain tuned to gather in lymph nodes and stay quiet until ultrasound arrives.

Ultrasound's mechanical and oxidative push opens calcium channels and frees mitochondrial DNA in presenting cells, switching innate paths on. The best helper from their library gave strong, lasting node responses under local ultrasound. Vaccines using it raised antigen-specific T cell responses about threefold over standard helpers. In mouse breast and liver tumors it boosted checkpoint therapy against growth and spread.
pmc-12786011:
Heat tolerance in crossbred sturgeon is compared by Wei Wang and co-authors in work dated 2025. Heat waves hit sturgeon farms harder as the climate warms. The team raised water heat slow and steady for two mirror cross strains. One cross had a Siberian mother, and the other had the reverse. They tracked stress genes, defense enzymes, and liver and gill harm.

At peak heat, one strain kept fifteen fish alive a day later, while the other lost all. Stress gene calls split by tissue and strain. Liver harm ruled in one strain and gill harm in the other. Hormone and sugar marks swung hard in both.
pmc-12786111:
Chenjie Huang and co-authors probed a sweetener and kidney cancer by computer in two thousand twenty-five. Aspartame is a widely used artificial sweetener. It has been linked in debate to a papillary form of kidney cancer. No clear chain of cause has been shown in the body. The team used network methods to hunt for shared targets.

They overlapped gene lists tied to the sweetener and the cancer. Dozens of shared targets emerged from the overlap. Pathway checks pointed to matrix breakdown and immune control themes. A smaller set of core genes carried the strongest signal. Docking models tested how the sweetener might bind gene products. The authors stress the work is predictive, not proof. Lab and clinical studies would be needed to confirm any risk.
pmc-12786311: Rodrigo Sanchez-Bayona introduces a special issue on breast cancer in a short 2025 editorial note. The issue gathers work on how the disease forms at the cell level, how doctors find it, and how they treat it. The note opens by stressing scale: breast cancer makes up close to 30 percent of all cancer cases found in women around the world. Readers get the theme and scope of the issue rather than a full research report.
pmc-12786911:
Jawad Alnajjar and co-authors weigh the use of probiotics for diverticular disease in this 2025 review. The disease forms small pouches in the gut wall and is common with age. It is linked to changes in gut microbes. The authors searched five databases for trials and other studies in adults up to October 2024.

Thirteen studies met their rules. Probiotic use was linked to less belly pain, and long-term trials showed a lower risk of the disease coming back. Signs for bloating were weak, and a pooled result for an inflammation marker was not sound. Multi-strain mixes used for longer spans looked best. The authors rate the proof as low and call for larger, stronger trials.
pmc-12787811:
Angelika Till and co-authors give the first full electron microscope study of pollen from the plant genus Pseudanthus, in a 2025 paper. Fine structure of this pollen was little known. The team set out to describe it in detail and to compare it within and across related families.

Pollen was taken from open flowers and prepared by standard methods. The authors map traits that vary within a species, between species, and between families. They also judge whether this pollen could be recognized in the fossil record. The study gives palynologists a reference for a poorly charted group.
pmc-12788111:
A strap-on hip device might help older people walk with less effort. Cristina-Ioana Pîrșcoveanu and co-authors test a passive exoskeleton on 23 senior adults. Volunteers walked on a treadmill at their own pace under three conditions: the device, nothing, and a sham. Slow and intermediate walkers were compared. Sensors tracked steps, heart rate, and oxygen use.

The device changed nothing measurable. Step rhythm, stride length, and metabolic power all matched the other conditions. Faster walkers outperformed slower ones on every measure, device or not. The authors report the null plainly. A passive hip aid, at least this one, does not ease walking for seniors.
pmc-12788611:
Jeemee Patel and co-authors compare computer-guided dental implant placement with freehand work, in a 2025 study. Guided surgery uses a printed guide built from mouth scans and three-dimensional X-rays. Thirty patients needing implants were split evenly between guided and freehand care.

Guided implants landed far closer to plan, with much smaller angle and distance errors at top and tip. Surgery also took about eleven minutes less on average. Patients in the guided group reported lower pain on the first and third days after surgery. The authors back the digital workflow for more predictable placement. They note the trial was small, so wider checks would strengthen the claim, but the gaps were large and consistent.
pmc-12789111:
Cervical cancer is one of the most preventable cancers, since a vaccine blocks the virus that causes most cases. Ahmed Amer and co-authors survey 1,174 adults across Egypt, Syria, Jordan, and Yemen about the human papillomavirus and that vaccine. Most respondents were women, city dwellers, and university educated.

Knowledge was weak: over half scored poorly on the virus and two thirds on the cancer. Only about one in ten women had ever been screened, and just two percent had received any vaccine dose. Half had never heard of the vaccine at all. Most of the unvaccinated had no plans to change that, citing missing information and a sense of low personal risk. The authors call for urgent education campaigns in the region.
pmc-12795811:
Antony Lurie, Christina Stephens, David Kern, Katharine Henn, Naomi Latorraca, and Stephen Brohawn published a study in 2025 on the swelling-activated channels that let cells dump ions and recover their volume. These channels mix one fixed subunit with one variable partner, and the partner tunes what the channel passes. Structures existed for one pairing; this team solved the pairing with the D subunit.

Four fixed and two D subunits assemble, captured in two shapes by cryo-electron microscopy. The D subunits widen the filter and make it more water-shy, matching their pairing's tastes. Fat molecules sit inside the pore, plugging it, and the D-containing assembly loosens its inner domains so the plug can leave when swelling calls. Tests confirmed the fat plug blocks flow: lipid gating is the family's shared switch.
pmc-12802011:
Maartje Schreurs and co-authors test whether a mutation-driving enzyme marks breast cancer outlook at the protein level in a 2025 study. The enzyme, APOBEC3B, leaves signature mutations in breast tumors, and its gene message already tracks poor prognosis in estrogen-driven disease. Protein evidence was missing.

Staining covered tumors from over six hundred untreated patients plus a relapsed group on hormone therapy. High protein levels came with larger, higher-grade tumors. Patients with high levels relapsed sooner, spread sooner, and died sooner across every survival measure, even after adjustments. In the treated group, high levels also meant faster progression on therapy. The protein reads as a sturdy bad-news marker.
pmc-12804811:
Hatami studies layered electric structures that form in magnetized plasma with two kinds of electrons, in a 2025 paper. A double layer is a narrow zone where voltage jumps sharply, like a step in an electric hillside. Such steps appear in the auroral sky, where hot and cool electrons mix above the poles.

The analysis treats both electron groups as nonextensive, meaning their energies spread wider than the classic bell curve. A method based on a fictitious potential maps when double layers can exist and which way they point. The controls include magnetic field tilt, the speed of the structure, and the temperature split between electron groups. The results fit the auroral setting that spacecraft have measured.
pmc-12804911:
Two brain chemicals, dopamine and serotonin, are the targets of many mind medicines, yet their exact roles in seeking rewards and dodging harm were murky. Lisa Gauthier led a team that compared two drugs in four monkeys trained on an approach-avoidance task. One drug blocks dopamine recycling; the other blocks serotonin recycling. Brain scans showed where each drug bound at working doses.

The dopamine drug sharpened reward seeking, binding in a deep brain hub. The serotonin drug strengthened active avoidance of bad outcomes, binding widely in emotion circuits. Rather than fighting, the two systems steer different responses. The team suggests pairing such drugs could treat separate symptom strands in mental illness.
pmc-12805711:
A single blood marker that blends insulin resistance with muscle loss might catch heart risk that either measure misses alone. The authors build such an index from triglycerides, fasting glucose, and the ratio of two kidney markers, then follow 277,418 UK Biobank adults with no heart disease at the start. Over a median of 15 years, more than 40,000 develop cardiovascular disease. Risk climbs steadily across the index's quarters, and the survival curves separate cleanly.

Each standard-deviation rise in the index carries a 17 percent higher hazard, and the top quarter faces about 48 percent more risk than the bottom. The link bends rather than running straight, and checks confirm it is sturdy. Against the plain insulin resistance index, the blended one performs better in lean and normal-weight people. The authors propose it as a way to surface hidden cardiometabolic risk in people whose weight gives no warning.
pmc-12809611:
Atsuko Kawai, Sakura Okamoto, Hideaki Note, and Jyunya Nakada reported a severe surgical complication in a 2025 case report. Air under the skin is a known effect of robot-assisted keyhole surgery, but it rarely threatens the airway. Their patient was an eighty-one-year-old woman with obesity, unlike the typical underweight cases.

She had a long robot-assisted pancreas operation lasting nearly nine hours. Air spread widely under her skin up to the neck and face, swelling her throat so the breathing tube could not be removed. She stayed intubated and received a tracheostomy on day four. The swelling took seventeen days to clear. The authors urge suspicion of severe air spread in any body type during long operations.
pmc-12812211:
Keita Nakahara and co-authors sort older Japanese adults into activity profiles and test how each profile tracks health, in a 2025 study. Frailty prevention works unevenly, perhaps because research counts activity amount but ignores its pattern. What people do may matter as much as how much. The team surveyed 771 community-dwelling elders online.

A forty-six-item checklist of daily activities fed a latent class analysis. Four distinct profiles fit the data best. Each profile was checked against frailty scores, fear of falling, and background traits. Patterns of daily life, not just totals, may signal who is drifting toward frailty. Tailored programs could then match support to the pattern a person actually lives.
pmc-12812411:
Apoorva Aggarwal and co-authors report a 2025 study on three blood measures and death in hospital after a stroke. Stroke is a top cause of death and lasting disability round the world, with a rising load in India. Past work hints that low salt in blood, high waste acid, and high levels of one amino acid may shape outcomes.

The study drew 236 stroke patients at a large hospital in New Delhi over one year. Most had the clot kind of stroke, and about 12 in 100 died in hospital. Low blood salt showed in 38 in 100 patients and linked strongly to death, with three quarters of those who died having it. The other two measures showed no clear link to death in this group.
pmc-12812611:
Qingyu Zhang, Kailun He, Mohd Aazmi and Mohd Yahya wrote a 2026 study on tiny packets shed by a gut-friendly bacterium. Such packets are one way good bacteria affect the body. The team asked how these packets change gene activity in immune cells. The focus was genes tied to a fiery form of cell death.

They drew the packets from the bacterium and checked their size and charge. Then they treated mouse immune cells stressed by a bacterial toxin. Gene reads showed the packets shifted a set of death-linked genes in a dose-linked way. Two key genes changed in a clear way. Paths tied to swelling signals were also involved.
pmc-12813011:
Zhaoyang Yan and co-authors watch how weak ankles land on a trap platform in a 2025 study. Chronic ankle instability sets up repeat sprains, and landing style may be the tell. Fifty five patients and 55 matched peers dropped onto a flip platform rig that mimics a sprain, tracked by twelve cameras.

The weak ankle group landed with less foot point, and more bend at hip and knee with wider side angles and toe out. The pattern reads as a guarded style that shifts work up the leg. The marks give rehab a biomechanical target to cut reinjury risk.
pmc-12813111:
Asbestos breathed at work causes cancers that surface decades later, and China still carries a heavy share of that burden. Bijuan Chen and co-authors measured the burden's trend in this study, published in 2025. Data came from the Global Burden of Disease study for 1990 to 2021. Deaths, years of life lost, and years lived with disability were all counted.

Breakdowns by age, sex, and cancer type show who bears the cost. Statistical tools split the trend into stretches and assigned causes: population growth, aging, and changing risk. Work with asbestos was long concentrated in male-dominated industries. The long delay between exposure and disease means today's cases reflect workplaces of decades past. Control policy can target the drivers the analysis names.
pmc-12815711:
Hongwei Chen, Xinggang Fan, and Di Cui report that a nucleolar protein backs liver cancer. It does so as it works with a second protein, called fibrillarin. Their 2025 study uses tests in cells and models in animals.

The protein NOP56 was upregulated in malignant liver cells. It was also linked to a poor outlook. When it was knocked down, proliferation fell. Colony formation and migration fell too, while cell cycle arrest and apoptosis were set off. Growth of tumours fell in living models too. In how it works, NOP56 switched on a main path for signals that keep cells alive, through fibrillarin. When fibrillarin was raised, cells were saved, in part, from the death effect of the knockdown. The team puts this axis for signals forth as a target that shows promise for therapy.
pmc-12816811:
A sore throat that seeds clots and abscesses deep in the neck is the danger behind Lemierre's syndrome, and Imane Lefqih and co-authors report a case that slid further still. A 35-year-old woman arrived after two weeks of neck swelling, painful swallowing, and fever, short of breath and previously healthy apart from months of mass-gain products the team suspected were steroid-based. Scans showed abscesses from her tonsils to her chest, infected clots in three neck and chest veins, and fluid around her heart and lung.

Surgeons drained the collections in her neck and chest while antibiotics and blood thinners ran. She improved enough to go home. The authors stress that this rare syndrome punishes delay: once the infection descends into the chest, survival depends on fast, combined treatment.
pmc-12817011:
Mo Se Kwon and five co-authors used data science to chase a rise in low-level HIV results at a Cape Town laboratory, in a 2025 study. After a national service disruption, backlogged samples from Limpopo province were rerouted to the Groote Schuur lab. Results showing virus levels just above the detection floor climbed there, which raised fears of dirty samples or machine contamination.

The team compared viral load data from both provinces across 2023 and 2024, checked turnaround times, and reviewed quality control records. Limpopo samples did show more low-level results and less full suppression than local ones. Nothing firm tied the rise to slow handling or instrument contamination. Patient-level trends fit real differences in treatment and adherence between the regions. The authors read the spike as an imported pattern, not a lab fault.
pmc-12817411:
Xiang Fu and co-authors pool a 2025 set of trials on adding immune therapy to chemo and radiation for early-stage small cell lung cancer. The cancer is fierce and long survival is rare on standard care. Six trials with more than a thousand patients fed the tally, drawn from six databases.

The added immune drugs raised both total survival and time without growth, by set margins. Fast restart after chemo and one platinum type marked who gained most. Harm rates were pooled as well, so the gain can be weighed against the risk in first-line care.
pmc-12817711:
Dong-Ok Lee and co-authors test a nurse-led program to keep prefrail elders from sliding into frailty. Their 2025 trial runs in Seoul, South Korea, with forty prefrail adults in matched city units. Half got twelve weeks of group teaching and walking sessions under a nurse-led, many-skilled team. The program aimed at risks across self, social, and community levels. The other half got one health talk.

Frailty scores and risk traits were read before and after. The treated group moved ahead of controls on the headline score, the report shows. Group talks after the run probed how supportive the neighborhood felt. The authors back nurse-led community care.
pmc-12817811:
Ji-Hyeon Park, Sojung Kim, Ho Seok Seo, Kyo Young Song, and Han Hong Lee present a 2025 review on adjusting medicines after weight-loss surgery. Bariatric surgery is the strongest treatment for severe obesity, and metabolism often improves so fast that drug doses must drop quickly. No firm guidelines set the timing or thresholds for those changes.

The review gathers trials, pooled analyses, and society guidance. Surgery reshapes the stomach and gut, changing how oral drugs are absorbed. For diabetes, low-dose insulin users can often stop insulin, while heavier users cut the dose by half or more. Many single-pill patients can stop, with rules tied to blood sugar levels. For blood pressure, dropping one drug trims systolic pressure by about ten points.
pmc-12819411:
Iranmanesh and co-authors weigh stretch kinds in a 2025 trial of worn-out soccer players. A hard match drill drains legs, and what stretch best brings back bend, poise, and pace was in doubt. Three stretch kinds faced off, at set beats, with a rest arm as the base.

Forty male players each ran the drain drill, then one stretch kind or rest. Knee bend, poise on a star reach, jump build, dash speed, and a weave run were all read. Slow and fast swings are priced apart, not as one class. Coach teams gain a pick list for the tired hour past a game.
pmc-12819911:
Yuan Ren, Ni Yang, Tingyan Shi, and Rong Zhang ask in a 2025 study whether poor sleep can cause ovarian cancer. They use a method that relies on genes, which helps avoid some bias found in simple surveys of patients.

They paired gene data on insomnia with gene data on ovarian cancer from large studies of people of European ancestry. The main test gave a very small link, close to no effect at all. Two backup tests found no clear link. The authors note that gene signals used were strong, and they checked for flaws that could bend the result. Overall, the work does not support a real causal effect.
pmc-12820211:
Feng Zhu and co-authors test stem cell vesicles against ulcerative colitis in a 2025 study. Tiny exosomes from bone marrow stem cells, grown under low oxygen, may calm intestinal immunity. How the low-oxygen preparation changes the vesicles and how they act in colitis were not adequately understood.

The team isolated and characterized the vesicles, then studied their effects. The vesicles triggered mitophagy, the recycling of damaged mitochondria, through a pathway involving two named proteins. Clearing damaged mitochondria in gut cells eased inflammation, pointing to a cell-free therapy route for a hard bowel disease.
pmc-12821511:
Marissa Bello and co-authors wrote a study from 2025 on whether heavy or light weights build muscle and strength in the same way. Gym lore holds that heavy loads build strength best, while light loads pushed to the point of failure may grow muscle more. The team ran a nine-week test with seventeen young men who already trained. Each man trained his whole body three times a week.

One group used heavy loads and the other used light loads, with all sets taken to failure. Muscle thickness grew at every site they measured, in both groups, by much the same amount. The heavy group still gained more top strength by the end. Spit tests of two stress and sex hormones showed no real change in either group. The team says load choice may hinge on whether strength or size is the main goal.
pmc-12821611:
Riccardo Padovan and five co-authors measure back muscle activity in the seated row in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Rowers can pin the shoulder blades or let them move freely, and coaches debate which is better. High-density surface sensors can map not just how hard muscles work, but where.

Fourteen trained men rowed both ways at an eight-repetition maximum load. Overall excitation was much the same between styles. A few muscles differed: the rear shoulder worked harder with fixed blades while pulling, and the mid-back and lats worked harder while lowering. Excitation centers also shifted slightly in the lowering phase. The authors say blade choice tunes emphasis, so either style fits training goals.
pmc-12821811:
Katharina Rataj and Ulrike Garscha review gene variants of a protein tied to inflammation in a 2025 paper. The protein is FLAP, a helper that switches on leukotriene making. Leukotrienes drive inflammation in asthma, heart, and kidney disease. Drugs that block FLAP have been tested for years.

The gene for FLAP holds more than 20,000 known single-letter variants. Only 66 of them have been studied against disease so far. Reports link some variants to heart attack and stroke. Results clash across studies due to design and population gaps. Pooled analyses help but cannot settle the question. The authors call for cleaner, larger genetic studies.
pmc-12821911:
Aspen Streetman and co-authors review how exercise programmes use empowerment, and find the idea loosely handled. Their 2025 scoping review covers forty trials and quasi-experiments across five databases. Feeling in control is thought to keep people active, but programmes rarely say what they mean by it.

No study defined exercise empowerment outright, and none measured it directly. Only nine papers leaned on empowerment theory at all. Most programmes taught rather than empowered. Activity still rose in most studies, by self-report in two thirds of them. The authors call for a shared definition and real measures. Without them, claims about empowerment stay hollow.
pmc-12822011:
Yao Xiao and co-authors read the microbes of two deep ocean trenches from sunlit surface to buried mud, in a 2025 study. Gene surveys covered water down to about 6,500 meters and sediments past 9,000 in the Diamantina and Kermadec trenches. Sunlit waters held the richest communities, while the deep layers and muds each kept their own casts.

Networks showed the big bacterial groups rising and falling together, and each niche ran its own recipe for carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur chemistry. The Diamantina water column mixed its layers more than Kermadec's. Eleven draft genomes round out a rare full-depth portrait of life under crushing dark.
pmc-12822111:
Young people with nephrotic syndrome juggle urine tests, blood pressure, weight, and medicines, mostly on their own. Moin Saleem and co-authors built an app with them, not just for them. The NeST app lets users aged twelve to thirty-five log dipstick readings, symptoms, relapses, and appointments. It carries treatment information and hospital episodes too.

The app passed NHS verification and sits in both major app stores, linked to users' health records. A multi-method survey then asked young users what they thought of it. The design goals were empowerment: news of events, control over treatment, and confidence in sharing data. The report covers both the building and the first verdicts, a case study in co-designing self-management tools with young patients.
pmc-12822211:
Weibo Zhong and a team of co-authors follow gut germs in kidney transplant patients before and after surgery, in a twenty twenty-five study. Eighty-eight patients gave stool samples at several time points at one center. Germs were profiled by gene reads. The gut mix shifted strongly after the transplant, in both variety and membership.

At thirty days, a bloom of one germ family linked to more urinary infections and fewer immune cells in blood. That bloom did not track kidney function itself. Patients whose kidneys worked better at thirty days showed more of a friendly germ, Bifidobacterium. The authors name these germs as possible markers or targets for better transplant recovery.
pmc-12824211:
Parinaz Alizadeh and co-authors survey gear and staffing for newborn resuscitation across hospitals in Iran. Their 2025 study covers close to seven hundred hospitals from 2020 to 2022. Sound revival care needs trained staff and ready tools, and gaps cost lives.

About one hospital in six lacked both a newborn ward and an intensive care unit. Only one in three employed a newborn specialist. Key tools were scarce: a modern revival device sat in under a third of hospitals, and heat control was missing in one delivery room in five. Newborn death rates ran lower where pediatric staff, training mandates, and care units were present. The authors urge a national plan to close the gaps.
pmc-12824411:
Samuel Tamrat and four co-authors wrote this 2025 engine study on cleaning up biodiesel blends with two additives. Castor biodiesel mixed with diesel was dosed with cerium oxide nanoparticles and a splash of diethyl ether, then run in a single-cylinder test engine at high load across a speed range. The question was whether the additives lift performance while cutting smoke.

With the nanoparticles, torque and power rose, fuel use per unit of work fell, and heat efficiency reached the high thirties. Carbon monoxide, unburned hydrocarbons, and soot all dropped compared with the plain blend. Nitrogen oxides, the usual trade-off, changed only slightly. The authors present the cerium particles as a promising route to cleaner combustion in small diesel engines, a class still common in farming and remote power.
pmc-12825211:
Joshua Olorocisimo and co-authors show in 2025 that a two tone electrical trick can steer limb movement through a nerve cuff with fine control. Stimulating nerves can restore movement after paralysis, but cuffs outside the nerve usually grab whole bundles crudely. Judging what movement results is also slow, manual work.

Their cuff packs many contacts and uses interfering waves that meet only at the target bundle deep inside. Cameras plus machine learning tracked the limb's pose on their own, and unsupervised methods sorted the movement patterns that emerged. The stimulation drew out a rich, varied set of movements. Automated scoring removes a bottleneck in tuning such devices. The pairing could speed rehab tech for spinal injury.
pmc-12826811:
Rahul Kumar, Rohan Phadke, and Samer Salman set out a plan for teaching AI in Canadian bone surgery training. Their 2025 paper notes that AI tools now shape surgical planning, guidance, and care after operations. Trainees meet these tools whether or not their courses cover them.

Case examples show risk forecasts and robot training rigs already in use at Canadian hospitals. The authors warn that models trained on rich city data can fail in rural or Indigenous settings. A scan tool that lost accuracy for some groups serves as a teaching case. Their framework ties skill with the tools to fair oversight of them. The goal is training that is both sharp and even-handed.
pmc-12827411:
Wei Shi and co-authors read the genetics of head-to-body proportions from full-body scans, in this 2025 study. Proportions shape growth and may flag disease risk, yet their genetic basis was nearly untouched. Deep learning measured ten ratio traits across more than thirty-eight thousand UK Biobank scans.

Genome scans found two hundred forty-five linked regions, and the traits proved substantially heritable. Genes behind the ratios cluster in cartilage cells of the skeleton and support cells of the brain. Genetic scores tied the ratios to heart, metabolic, bone, and mental health risks. Ratio-linked variants also crowd into genome regions conserved through evolution and sped up in humans. The authors pitch proportions as health markers.
pmc-12827611:
Soichiro Matsuda and Yurina Shinohara present a two thousand twenty-five case study of month-long heart monitoring at home for a child with autism. Sleep problems and body regulation issues are common in autism. Long overnight recordings at home are rare.

A preschooler wore a smart garment that recorded heart signals nightly. Caregivers logged problem behaviour each day. Twenty-five valid nights were gathered over the month. Heart variability did not predict next-day behaviour in this child. Still, the study proves long home monitoring is practical and reports its methods openly for others to build on.
pmc-12829011:
Tsion Admas and seven co-authors measured how often emergency breathing tube placement succeeds on the first try in two Addis Ababa hospitals, in this 2025 study. First-try success is a key quality mark because repeat attempts raise the risk of harm. Data from low-income settings are limited, so the team tracked real cases over six months in 2024.

They recorded 112 emergency placements in hospital and intensive care settings. About sixty-four percent succeeded on the first attempt, below the eighty percent mark often cited as a target. Complications struck more than a third of patients. Success rose sharply with the operator's training year and with a clear view of the airway. The authors urge more training and better airway assessment to close the gap.
pmc-12829111:
Rotavirus causes harsh runs and loss of fluids in babies and small children across the world. Shots exist, but they work less well and fade faster in poor states than in rich ones. Work from 2025 by Mabel Rocio Miranda-Echagüe and co-authors tests whether the frame around an antibody changes how well it can block the virus.

The team took the same virus binding tip and set it into six kinds of frames, then tested each build on three strains of the virus in the lab. The same tip did not act the same in each frame. Builds on one frame type blocked a wider range of strains. The result can help guide the design of future shots.
pmc-12830511:
Mingtao Liang leads a team that compares keyhole and open stomach surgery. Their study from twenty twenty-five deals with advanced stomach cancer. All folks had chemo first, then had their stomach removed.

Records from one center over a decade were reviewed. Keyhole surgery lost less blood and had shorter stays. Guts woke faster and food by mouth came sooner too. Surgery time was much the same for both forms. Harm rates did not differ in a clear way. Long term cancer results are set next to short ones.  Data came from a surgery data base kept over time.
pmc-12830611:
Xintao Zhou, Na Ma, Jialing Zhang, and Jiamin Liu present a method for spotting gear faults from vibration signals. Weak fault signals are hard to catch, yet early detection prevents costly breakdowns. Their approach reads the signal with multiscale permutation entropy, a measure of pattern complexity at several scales. Two settings of that measure are tuned by mutual information and an improved nearest-neighbor algorithm.

Each fault sample is then matched against reference classes by a distance measure. On its own, the plain distance reaches about 76.87 percent accuracy on gear pitting and wear faults. The authors add weights drawn from information entropy, which marks how much useful signal each sample holds. The weighted version jumps to 99.72 percent accuracy. The team concludes the weighted method reads gear vibration signatures far more reliably than the unweighted one.
pmc-12830711:
Sunam Mander and five colleagues test a fluorescence imaging probe for removing the earliest form of breast cancer, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Ductal carcinoma in situ is treated with breast-conserving surgery when feasible. Surgeons must remove the whole lesion with clear margins in one operation. Positive margins drive high re-excision rates, marking an unmet need.

The probe links indocyanine green dye to a cell-penetrating peptide carrying a tumor-targeting motif. It had already pinpointed invasive cancer margins accurately in animal models. In mouse models of the in situ disease, real-time imaging clearly identified tumor margins. Recurrence rates improved significantly compared with the untargeted dye alone. The authors argue the approach holds translational promise for image-guided surgery. Cleaner margins could cut both re-operations and recurrences for patients.
pmc-12833711:
Chukwuebuka Ohakpougwu and co-authors report a case where a mirrored heart hid in plain sight in this 2025 paper. The patient had dextrocardia, a rare state where the heart sits on the right side. Such patients face a higher risk of repeated chest infections. The patient came in with a cough that kept returning.

Tests during care revealed tuberculosis, a new diagnosis for this patient. The heart condition had not been known before either. The authors stress testing for tuberculosis whenever a cough drags on, above all in poorer countries. Fast testing also guards antibiotics and saves lives.
pmc-12835011:
Yang and co-authors build in 2025 a convolutional neural network model that supports decisions for information system optimization. Big modern systems strain state sensing and resource scheduling, above all under load spikes or data loss. Their model joins state recognition and strategy generation in one closed loop.

Tests ran on two public traces, cloud machine workloads and a search firm's cluster data. State recognition reached ninety-six point two percent accuracy with an F1 score of zero point nine six one. Policy replies averaged one hundred thirty-five point five milliseconds, and scheduling failures fell from six point one to two point two percent. Accuracy stayed above ninety percent under data loss and sudden surges, which backs the robustness claim.
pmc-12835911:
Styliani Partalidou wrote a 2025 editorial on pregnancy in women with autoimmune rheumatic diseases. These diseases strike mostly women of child-bearing age, so their effects on fertility and pregnancy matter a great deal. Disease activity can harm a pregnancy, and pregnancy can also stir the disease.

Doctors advise women to conceive while the disease is quiet, and to plan ahead with their care team. Even then, these pregnancies count as high risk and need close watch by a mixed team of specialists and midwives. Drug choices need care too, since some standard drugs are unsafe in pregnancy. The editorial also notes an overlooked issue: sexual problems driven by pain and low mood. It frames the whole topic as a lasting challenge that needs joined-up care.
pmc-12836811:
Alexander Ferentinos, Courtney Check, Olivia Windorf, and Matthias Leu track two toad species as they leave their breeding ponds in a 2025 study. Knowing how far amphibians travel after breeding helps set the size of protected habitat. Past work stressed weather as the driver of movement, but landscape and habitat may matter as much.

The team followed about a hundred toads in Virginia with radio and signal-finding tools across three years. Both species moved a median of about sixty-three meters from the ponds. Warm nights, rain, conifer cover, and distance from water all made movement more likely. The toads returned to chosen daily shelters and used human trails in ways that suggest feeding there. The authors say current protection zones are too small to match these movements.
pmc-12837011:
In laser cataract surgery, the machine is told how wide to cut the eye's lens capsule, yet the real opening often ends up bigger. Zhao Tan and Fei Yuan measure that gap in forty-seven eyes and hunt for its causes. They read the true opening size from surgery videos and compare it with the programmed size for each eye.

The real openings averaged about 6.0 millimeters against 5.67 programmed, a gap near a third of a millimeter. In most eyes the gap passed a fifth of a millimeter. Age stood out: older eyes drifted less, and the link survived adjustment for other eye measures. A formula using age and the programmed size predicts the real size. The authors offer it to help surgeons plan a more exact cut.
pmc-12837111:
Rajit Mullick, Chander Prakash Yadav, and Richa Singhal pool a span of proof on bug-proof malaria pests in India in a 2025 review. The sprays and nets that guard homes lose their bite when the pest learns to shrug them off.

More than fifty works from two dozen years met the bar. The old spray DDT met proof in near all states, save the north-east. One pest kind shrugged it most; two kin kinds stood mid. A new spray class met proof in two mid states in one kind, but the kin kinds fell to it near whole. A third spray split the kinds the same way. The authors warn that proof maps must steer which spray goes where, ere the nets fail.
pmc-12837211:
Anna Pefoyo Koné and twelve co-authors compare how Afro-Caribbean Black Canadians in the Greater Toronto Area rated their own health before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. Data on this population in Canada are scarce, despite known links between discrimination, social conditions, and health. The community-based survey ran from late twenty twenty-two into twenty twenty-three, asking adults to report retrospectively.

Perceived general and mental health were described overall and across sociodemographic and clinical characteristics. The team looked for the factors tied to poorer self-rated health in each period. Because the data are self-reported and retrospective, the authors frame them as participatory evidence for service planning. The goal is pinpointing where action would help most.
pmc-12838011:
Marte Hoff Hagen and co-authors present a review plan from 2025 on care for children after severe illness. Children who survive intensive care face higher risk of lasting mental and social strain. Digital tools, from apps to online programs, might help families keep up care at home.

The plan sets out a five-stage search of a large database, with extra checks of reference lists. Studies will be sorted by clear rules about who took part and what tool was used. The team will rate each study for bias with a standard tool. Findings will be grouped by theme, and pooled with math where the data allow. A grading scheme will rate how sure the final claims are. The aim is a clear map of what tools exist now.
pmc-12838511:
Ghaffar Kiani and four co-workers wrote a 2025 study on ajwain, a spice and medicine plant, under drought. The plant resists dry spells and makes more active compounds when stressed. Finding types that thrive dry could aid farms and drug supply. The team grew a few dozen types with and without water stress.

Tallest plants and top seed yields differed between wet and dry runs. One type led yield under drought, another led growth. A key oil compound rose by a large share under stress on average. Two types gave the most oil overall. Grouping split the types into four sets with distinct yield traits.
pmc-12838811:
Cuiling Xuan and colleagues turn a fish egg peptide into a blood-vessel recruiter for stubborn wounds, in this study from twenty twenty-five. The peptide, Pt5-1c, comes from phosvitin and belongs to the antimicrobial peptide family, several of which moonlight in healing. In mice with full-thickness wounds and in zebrafish with defective vessels, it measurably sped vessel growth and closure.

In cell work it made endothelial cells move, stick, survive, and sprout tubes, the full angiogenesis repertoire. It raised the classic vessel growth factors, VEGF, PDGF, FGF, and EGF, and fired two growth pathways plus the oxygen-sensing HIF axis that commands VEGF. The authors nominate the peptide as a candidate for regenerative therapy where wounds stall for want of blood supply.
pmc-12838911:
Nadezhda Frolova and co-authors guide readers through a classic lab method for studying plant chemistry in this 2025 paper. The method pairs gas chromatography with mass spectrometry. It separates a sample's parts, then weighs them to identify each. Plant studies use it for small molecules, both volatile and polar ones. Sample preparation decides much of the result's quality. Instrument setup is the other half of the craft.

The paper walks through both halves step by step. Metabolomics, the study of all small molecules in a sample, leans on a few core platforms. This one is among the oldest and most proven. Drying, extraction, and chemical tweaks to make molecules fly are covered. Such method guides help labs get comparable results. The authors write for plant researchers setting up the pipeline.
pmc-12839311:
Laura Plantera and co-authors ask how a high-fat diet stirs the brain's immune cells, region by region. Fat-heavy diets are tied to low-grade brain inflammation. Yet the team's prior work found no rise in alarm signals or memory harm after long feeding. Their 2025 study reads gene activity in mouse microglia across four brain regions. Mice ate plain or fatty food for up to 24 weeks.

Gene shifts grew with time in the hypothalamus, hippocampus, and cortex. The cerebellum stirred early and then went quiet. Only three genes moved in every setting. Several movers tie to microglial firing and inflammatory paths, with NF-κB routes in the mix. The map warns against treating brain inflammation as one even blanket.
pmc-12839711:
Tianyue Liu and co-authors read the inner life of deep nets in a 2025 paper to grasp why some hold up when data shift. Nets ace set tests yet wilt on new or marred inputs. How their inner code stores facts may hold the key, but that link was dim.

Their frame splits each net store of facts into three kinds: shared, lone, and joint-only. Nets rich in shared store and poor in joint-only store held their scores best when tests were marred. The reads come from clean inputs alone, so a net can be graded before hard use. Builders gain a gauge for grit that needs no stress test.
pmc-12840411:
Patrick Sweeney, Jaime Ruiz-Serra, and Michael Harré review a theory that tries to unite choice, learning, and action, in a 2025 paper. The theory, called active inference, says brains and agents act to cut surprise, measured as free energy. Fans claim it covers many older models of good choice, but the claims were scattered.

The review lines up each older model next to the theory in shared math form. Game-like choice, cost-aware thought, control, and reward learning all map onto the same core step. So do rules for packing information and spreading risk. The authors aim to help newcomers enter the field and to clear up core claims for experts.
pmc-12842911:
Shin Heon Lee and co-authors ask in 2025 which kind of decline before surgery best forecasts outcomes for older patients with mild to moderate brain injury. Some patients worsen in alertness, while others only show worse scans. The team read records of fifty-eight patients aged sixty-five and over who had surgery between 2013 and 2022.

About three in five declined before surgery. Death in hospital was far more common in the group whose alertness fell, and that drop alone forecast both death and poor function at six months. Worse scans alone carried no such link. A lower starting alertness score also spelled worse outcomes.
pmc-12843211:
Corina Muresan and co-authors test a vitamin-loaded nano-scaffold for bone repair in weakened bone in a 2025 study. Osteoporosis makes jaw and bone rebuilding harder, and vitamin D aids bone growth but works poorly when given body-wide. A local scaffold could deliver the vitamin right at the defect.

The team built chitosan nanostructures carrying varied vitamin doses and tested them on human stem cells, then in rats whose ovaries were removed to mimic osteoporosis. One low dose stood out in dishes, with cell survival above control and more mineral deposits. In the rats, jaw defects treated with the loaded scaffold were checked at four and eight weeks against clot-only and sponge controls. The work supports local delivery for bone regeneration.
pmc-12845311:
Yue-Rong Lv and a large team build fast field tests for paratuberculosis, a chronic gut disease of ruminants caused by a slow-growing mycobacterium. The germ is hard to find, and losses run high. Their assays pair DNA copying, by recombinase amplification or nested PCR, with a CRISPR-Cas12a readout, shown by fluorescence or on a paper strip.

Detection limits ran extremely low, with the nested PCR version the most sensitive. Reporter cutting gave strong signals once DNA passed a set level. On fifty clinical samples and seven lab cultures, all three readouts matched the reference tests perfectly. The flexible formats suit farms and labs with unlike gear.
pmc-12846311:
Caitlin Kearney and co-authors surveyed hair loss patients on an AI driven scalp imaging method that measures hair density and thickness without clipping, in work published in 2025. One hundred one clinic patients took part and reviewed their measures with a dermatologist. Surveys ran before and after the visit.

After seeing the numbers, about a third felt less bothered by their hair loss and two in five judged it less severe. Over half felt more driven to keep up treatment. Returning patients agreed more closely with their doctors on whether loss had changed. Patients backed the tool as improving care and trust in advice, the authors report.
pmc-12846611:
Xinyang Li and co-authors show in 2025 that a goose virus best known for gout and kidney harm also wounds the gut of goslings. The virus spreads by the mouth and stool path. Most past work eyed the kidneys and skipped the gut it must cross first.

Twenty day old goslings were split into dosed and clean groups and checked a week on. The virus sat in all gut parts, with the top load in one front zone's pit cells. Gut walls shrank, cup cells fell, and a stem cell guard path was blocked. Swell signals rose in step.
pmc-12848311:
Yang Zheng and five co-authors published a 2025 study of how a traditional plant, Abrus cantoniensis, fights liver scarring in mice. They gave mice a chemical that scars the liver, then treated them with the plant and confirmed the benefit under the microscope. Lab analysis found 420 compounds in the plant. Computer network methods and protein screens each listed hundreds of possible targets in the body.

Where the two lists overlapped, four core targets stood out. Docking tests showed the plant compounds bind those targets tightly and stably, and tissue stains showed the targets' activity fell after treatment. The authors argue the plant works through those four targets at once. They present the work as support for developing the plant into a standardized herbal medicine.
pmc-12849111:
Ellen Jansen and co-authors check how accurately dental students measure gum pocket depths, in a 2025 paper. Probing depth, how deep a thin probe slips beside a tooth, anchors gum disease diagnosis and is drilled throughout dental school. The question is how close student readings come to those of licensed dentists, and where the gaps hide.

The study compared 6,858 student measurements against dentist values, breaking errors down by position in the mouth. Students already measured with fairly high accuracy overall. The largest gaps clustered between teeth, the approximal zone that is hardest to reach, while easy front and cheek-side spots fared better. The authors call for targeted practice on those hidden surfaces.
pmc-12849411:
Jinyue Xue and co-authors study loss of appetite in teenagers with major depression, in work published in 2025. Appetite loss is common in depression, but its links to other symptoms in teens were little studied, as were differences between boys and girls. The team surveyed patients at eight hospitals over one year.

The study covered 364 teens and used standard scales for depression, sleep, and related problems. About seven in ten patients had lost appetite, and the share was higher in girls. Appetite loss linked to gender, body mass, depression severity, and poor sleep. In girls, further factors stood out in the analysis. The authors say appetite should be checked as part of teen depression care, with care shaped by gender.
pmc-12849511:
Nuri Karabulut and Yasin Akinci present a sports study, published in 2025, on coaching and mental toughness in teenage girls' basketball in Turkey. The quality of the coach and athlete bond is known to shape young athletes' growth, yet its link to toughness across coach gender was little studied outside Western settings. More than three hundred and fifty players from twenty-two teams filled in validated surveys.

Players with female coaches reported stronger bonds and greater mental toughness than those with male coaches. Statistical modeling found bond quality was the strongest predictor of toughness, carrying much of the coach gender effect. Interviews with two dozen players added context to the numbers. The authors frame good relationships, not gender itself, as the lever coaches can pull.
pmc-12852111:
Xiangfang Li and eight co-authors use single-cell data and machine learning to find a marker gene in colorectal cancer. Their study was published in twenty twenty-five. Spread to the liver drives most deaths from this cancer, and cell death control plus the tumor's immune setting both shape that spread.

The team joined single-cell reads from main tumors and liver spreads with large public gene data. Network methods grouped genes that rise and fall together. Their search landed on a gene called PMAIP1 as a fresh candidate. The gene's levels tied to patient outlook and to how well immune therapy might work. The authors offer it as a possible guide for prognosis and treatment choice. Lab checks would be the next step to confirm its role.
pmc-12852511:
Karsten Bamminger and four co-authors improved how two short-lived tracers for body scans are made and checked. The tracers tag acetate and a ketone body with a hot form of carbon. Scans with them read how tissue burns fuel and uses ketones. The catch is that the two tracers look much alike, so a lax check can mix them up.

Both were made on a standard lab rig, with pure yields the team calls high. A tweak to the gas step lifted the trapped share of hot carbon from about six in ten to near nine in ten. The old check method could not tell the two tracers apart at all. A new method split them cleanly. The pair warn that most past work on the ketone tracer likely missed acetate as a flaw in the mix.
pmc-12854311:
Farzane Vaziri and co-authors test whether reminder texts improve gum treatment results after deep cleaning. Their trial appeared in 2025. Thirty-six patients with early to moderate periodontitis received standard non-surgical therapy, then were split at random. One group got health-guideline text messages twice a week for four weeks, written in a motivational style; the other got none. Gum pocket depth, attachment level, plaque, and bleeding were measured before and after.

Both groups improved, as expected after treatment. The trial's question is whether the messages widened that improvement by keeping home care on track. The authors frame texting as a nearly free reinforcement clinics can add, since the hard part of gum therapy is what patients do at the sink every day.
pmc-12859911:
When ovaries fail early, autoimmunity is often blamed, and a common blood marker may help spot that cause. Tejunzhang Pi and co-authors pool thirteen case-control studies in this 2025 meta-analysis of antinuclear antibodies in premature ovarian insufficiency. Women with the condition were compared with several kinds of control groups across the studies.

Antibody positivity came with more than double the odds of the condition, an odds ratio of 2.57, with little disagreement between studies. The link ran stronger in women under 35 and in those with very high hormone levels marking ovarian failure. Test method and control type shifted the strength somewhat. The authors back routine antibody testing in younger patients as a screening step for the autoimmune form.
pmc-12860111:
Hualong Ma and co-authors profile coping styles in rural older patients in 2025. Many rural elders in China live with several chronic diseases at once. How they cope shapes both disease control and mental adjustment. Care and support are often thin in rural areas, which sharpens the stakes.

The team surveyed well over two thousand patients across ten rural areas in two provinces. Forms covered background, coping habits, sense of meaning in life, and social ties. Statistical sorting found distinct coping profiles among the patients. Knowing the profiles can help local clinics match support to the way each elder faces illness.
pmc-12864811:
Di Tong, Lingfei Wu, and James Evans measure skill change across American jobs in this 2025 study. Most research asks which jobs automation might erase; this team instead asks how the contents of jobs shift as technology swaps tasks, forcing workers to reskill.

Across 167 million online job posts spanning 721 occupations, they measure how far apart old and new skills sit. The greatest change lands in lower skilled jobs, those with fewer skills, lower pay, and lower schooling demands. Small employers and small markets upgraded fastest, catching up to large ones. The pattern could widen strain on some workers, yet also narrow gaps in job quality.
pmc-12866311:
Jingwen Wu, Jie Chen, Qianqian Tang, and Li Zhou set out a trial plan in 2025 for easing pain after pancreas surgery with skin-based electrical stimulation. Pain on moving after this surgery is often severe and poorly held by standard drugs. The method, drawn from acupuncture, sends mild current through pads at set points on the body.

The plan will enroll 132 patients at one center, split between real and sham stimulation. Sessions run before anesthesia and on the first three days after surgery. The main measure is the worst pain on moving in the first three days. Drug use, recovery quality, sleep, and swelling markers are also tracked. The team aims to learn if a longer course beats the usual brief use.
pmc-12868611:
Hongsheng Wang and a large team report a way to make water splitting last longer with a cobalt based material, in work from 2025. Splitting water to release oxygen is a key step for clean fuel. Cobalt materials can work well but often break down as their surface changes during use.

The team added several metals at once to a cobalt oxide that can come from spent lithium batteries. The added metals limited harmful surface change and raised how well the surface carried charge. The result was a more stable electrode. The work links battery reuse with steadier clean energy tools.
pmc-12869911:
Lin Yang and co-authors pool trials of a back nerve block for kidney stone surgery pain in a review from 2025. Percutaneous nephrolithotomy removes stones through a small back incision. It hurts afterward, and opioids carry their own costs. The erector spinae plane block numbs the back muscles' plane with local anesthetic.

Nine randomized trials entered the meta-analysis. Patients with the block used far less opioid in the first day. Pain scores ran lower across the full twenty-four hours. The first rescue dose came about fifty minutes later on average. Evidence grading tools rated the certainty of each claim. A single injection, it seems, buys a gentler first day after stone surgery.
pmc-12894311:
Jing Zhou and co-authors report a study, printed in 2025, on guessing when soybean plants ripen with drone images. The ripe date tells breeders which lines fit a place and yield well, but checking by eye is slow. Models trained on past trials often fail when they meet a new field or a new year.

The team tested three ways to adapt a trained model so it works in fresh settings. Their data came from five breeding trials with drone views of the crop. Readers learn which adapt step held up best, and how drone checks could speed the pick of strong soybean lines.
pmc-12903211:
D Carolina Andrade and co-authors asked, in a 2025 interview study, what patients and clinicians want from exercise programs during breast cancer chemotherapy. Moving during treatment improves outcomes, yet programs are hard to deliver mid-chemo. Sixteen patients and eleven clinicians at a Midwestern cancer center and community sites shared their views.

Both groups backed the idea strongly and said it should be standard care, not an extra. Framing activity as part of treatment itself, they felt, would lift uptake. Patients wanted freedom to choose when and how to move, with remote options to skip travel on hard days. Clinicians, mostly seasoned oncologists, echoed the welcome. The study turns those wishes into design rules for programs that fit real treatment life.
pmc-12926811:
Shravni Deshmukh, Sally Freels, and Sangeetha Madhavan test whether leg function after stroke can be measured over a video link. Remote rehab is growing, but its tests must be safe and trustworthy at a distance. Seventeen chronic stroke survivors took three standard tests both in the lab and by teleassessment: a thirty-second chair stand, a five-times sit-to-stand, and a two-minute step test.

Two tests traveled well. The step test agreed almost perfectly between settings, and the chair stand agreed well; the sit-to-stand test agreed poorly. None showed a systematic tilt. The step test also sorted slow from fast walkers with the best balance of catching cases and avoiding false alarms. The authors back the chair stand and step test for telerehabilitation programs, and they flag the sit-to-stand test as unready for remote use.
pmc-12927211:
Ganbin Li and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-five study of rectal cancer patients who respond well to pre-surgery chemoradiation. Strong responders usually do well, yet some still relapse. Finding which ones carries real value for follow-up planning.

Over five hundred well-responders treated across several years were reviewed. A small minority suffered recurrence or spread within three years. Those patients more often had the deepest tumour stages and signs of vessel or fascia involvement. Nodal spread and tumour deposits also marked risk. The profile helps doctors watch the right strong responders more closely.
pmc-12972711:
Jerrard and colleagues publish a protocol in this 2026 paper for a scoping review about the words intensive care teams use. Critically ill patients need tightly coordinated multidisciplinary care, yet the concepts underpinning that care, what teams mean by familiar terms, are defined inconsistently, which corrodes communication. Concept analysis studies exist to pin such terms down, but nobody has mapped which ones have been analyzed.

The planned review will search four major databases plus dissertation archives, from inception onward, for concept analysis studies concerning the management of critically ill adults at any stage of the care pathway. Duplicate independent screening and extraction are specified, with results charted in tables and mapped visually across the pathway from admission to recovery. The authors, who registered the protocol openly, aim to show which concepts are settled, which are contested, and where definitional gaps invite future analysis.
pmc-13037611:
Sharifuzzaman and co-authors reviewed the Philippine pig industry in a 2025 paper. Pig farming underpins food security and income in the Philippines, yet output falls short of home demand. The review asked what drives production and what would make the sector sustainable.

Searches of databases and official reports from 2018 to 2023 covered production, consumption, technology, and sustainability. Most problems traced back to small-scale farming. Home production and imports moved strongly in opposite ways, while imports linked to higher retail prices and lower consumption. The authors urge gradual growth of commercial farms, steady state guidance, and cooperative farms, noting a rapid shift would leave many farmers stranded.
pmc-13068311:
Shozab Seemab Khan and three co-authors compare male and female common teal, a small duck, during winter in Punjab, Pakistan. The 2025 study used twenty-seven freshly taken birds from licensed hunters. The team measured body traits, blood values, and gut contents to learn food choice. The aim was to chart how the sexes differ in build and blood while the birds winter far from their breeding grounds.

Males and females differed in body length, wingspan, beak, and head size, but not in weight. Several blood values also split by sex, as did urea and protein levels. Food choice, though, showed no sex gap. The authors say the data can guide later work on migration, habitat use, and care of the species.
pmc-13087211:
Hernan Garcia and thirteen colleagues present the World Ocean Database 2023, the largest checked archive of ocean readings ever built. It gathers water column profiles taken in place from 1772 to 2022. The set holds about 18.6 million profiles and 3.6 billion single readings. Twenty-seven physical and chemical traits are covered, among them key ocean and climate signs. Weather readings and plankton tows add millions more records.

Data come from old primary sources, keeping the source and chain of care clear. All of it is checked for quality, put in one format, and searchable through rich tags. New data four times a year keep the archive current. Ocean and climate scientists worldwide build on this base. The 2026 paper tells what the resource holds, and of the shared work, spanning research fleets and shore programs, that keeps it alive.
pmc-13094211:
Rodman Tarigan Girsang and a team of co-authors review long-term protection from infant hepatitis B vaccination, in two thousand twenty-six. In regions where the virus is common, infection often begins in infancy and lasts for life. Antibody levels fall over time after vaccination, yet protection usually holds, for reasons not fully understood.

The review gathered studies from a decade of literature, following shared review guidelines. Twenty-seven studies showed protection lasting beyond ten years, though antibody levels were lower in teens. Evidence up to twenty years after vaccination suggests boosters are not needed for healthy people who finished the full infant series. A teen booster may still help those born to infected mothers.
pmc-13101611:
Ruipeng Meng and nine co-authors wrote this 2026 study on a transcription factor that marks, and may help drive, aggressive colorectal cancer. ETV4 had been implicated in several cancers, but its role in bowel tumors and their immune surroundings was unsettled. The team combined atlas-scale gene data, single-cell sequencing, and lab validation on patient tissue and a cancer cell line.

ETV4 ran high in tumors and tracked with shorter survival. Tumors rich in it also harbored more M2 macrophages, the immunosuppressive kind that shields cancers from attack. Experiments tied the factor to a famous growth pathway, WNT, which switches ETV4 on; blocking the pathway switched it down. The authors propose ETV4 as both a prognostic biomarker and a candidate drug target, arguing it helps build the protective immune fog around the tumor.
pmc-13113011:
Huang, Wang, Xu, and Wu trace how dodder seed, a traditional remedy, fights the commonest kidney cancer through its lead compound quercetin. Network pharmacology first predicts which human proteins the seed's ingredients touch, naming six core targets including one enzyme, MMP9, tied to tumor spread.

Computer docking showed quercetin gripping MMP9 tightly. In lab dishes, quercetin cut kidney cancer cell survival dose by dose, lowered MMP9, and thinned a class of tumor-friendly immune cells. A drug that reawakens the pathway undid those gains, supporting the mechanism. In mice, treated tumors grew about half as large as untreated ones. The 2026 authors credit immune reshaping around MMP9 for the effect.
pmc-13117911:
Casañas Gonzalez and co-authors review new membranes for turning seawater into drinking water. The review covers two FilmTec elements with large active areas and high salt rejection, one of them built with wider spacers for dirty, open-intake water that clogs membranes fast. The authors weigh performance against cost for both clean and fouling-prone feeds.

Their verdict is favorable. Plants using the new elements could cut building costs by about a fifth and energy use by up to a quarter. Cleaning costs, downtime included, could fall by up to 4 percent when the wide-spacer element handles fouling water. The team also surveys current tricks for fighting fouling, the main threat to these systems.
pmc-13120111:
Marios Hadjicharalambous and six co-authors test, in a 2026 study, whether body fat percentage sways how professional soccer players hold up in a simulated match. A common belief sets an ideal fat share near ten percent for top players. The team split twenty professionals into higher and lower body fat groups, then ran both through a treadmill game simulation.

The groups matched on lean muscle mass, age, and maximal oxygen use. Across the simulation, no difference showed in work output, heart and hormone markers, or fuel oxidation. One marker did split: blood glucose ran higher in the higher fat group, at rest and in play. The authors say the supposed ideal is not backed by their data. With muscle and fitness held high, fat share looks like an individual trait, not a squad-wide target.
pmc-13124711:
Quanquan Wei and ten colleagues tested whether biochar plus green manure can sustain maize yields with less nitrogen fertilizer. Excess nitrogen harms soil health and the environment. Either amendment alone is known to help, but their combined effect in yellow soils was underexplored. The twenty twenty-six two-year field study compared six treatments, from no fertilizer to full nitrogen with both amendments. A reduced-nitrogen treatment with both amendments was also included.

Full nitrogen plus biochar and green manure gave the strongest results. Yield, soil nutrients, carbon fractions, and enzyme activity all rose significantly over the control. That combination also produced the most water-stable soil aggregates. The findings support pairing the two amendments to protect soil while easing dependence on synthetic nitrogen.
pmc-13128411:
Heze Fan and co-authors study in 2026 a blood measure, total bile acids, in patients whose heart arteries narrowed early in life. Both bile acids and body swelling have been tied to this artery disease. Whether bile acid levels within the normal range shape how bad the narrowing is, through swelling, was unknown.

The team enrolled 631 patients at one hospital in Xi'an, China. They used rank based links and regression models to test how bile acid levels tie to swelling indices and to a score of artery narrowing.
