They also tested whether swelling sits in the middle of that tie. Higher normal bile acids went with lower swelling and lower narrowing scores. A cheap blood value that tracks risk could join the panel used to judge young heart patients.
pmc-13128611:
Shupeng Wang and co-authors published this 2026 study on preparing pancreas surgery patients with a short fitness program. The operation, which removes the pancreas head, is long and taxing. Getting patients stronger before surgery may cut complications. Their program mixed exercise, nutrition tuning, and mental support, tailored to each person for at least two weeks.

The comparison group was patients treated earlier at the same center without the program. Sixty-three patients finished the program before surgery between late 2024 and late 2025. Their walking distance rose clearly before the operation even began. The team tracked leaks, stomach delays, hospital stay, and inflammation markers after surgery. The design tests whether even a brief tune-up pays off in a hard operation.
pmc-13130111:
Adnan Zaman and co-authors present a 2026 study on a hybrid device that harvests energy from sun, rain, and heat swings at once. Solar panels falter under clouds, rain, and fast temperature shifts. Pairing them with materials that turn pressure and heat change into power can smooth the supply.

The device layers patterned electrodes on a lithium niobate crystal, which generates charge when struck or heated, beside a standard silicon solar cell. In controlled tests, the hybrid raised solar output by about a fifth over the cell alone. A single raindrop produced a small voltage pulse, and heating to about seventy degrees gave a much larger one. Rain response also beat the crystal device on its own.
pmc-13130811:
Germany's young adults report heavier loads of depression and anxiety than their elders, and the gap has not closed since the pandemic. The authors of a 2026 study draw on a long running crisis era survey with more than twenty-five thousand participants and over one hundred thousand responses. They compare four generations, from postwar boomers to Generation Z, across survey waves.

Generation Z scored highest on both symptom scales in every period, and women scored higher than men throughout. Holding a job went with lighter symptoms in all generations. The authors urge caution, since the design can only show links, not causes. They call for steady monitoring of the young through an age of stacked crises.
pmc-13133411:
Fat around the heart is not inert padding; its immune cells send chemical messages into the muscle. Zheng Sihao and co-authors studied one such message, a tiny RNA called miR-101a, in atrial fibrillation, the common chaotic heart rhythm. Human tissue samples showed the RNA abundant in people with steady rhythm and scarce in fibrillation.

In rats, raising the RNA protected against the scarring that feeds the arrhythmia. The RNA targets a growth factor signal and works through a major cell pathway, PI3K-Akt, easing collagen buildup in heart fibroblasts. The RNA reaches the heart packaged in vesicles shed by fat-tissue macrophages. The authors propose it as an early-warning marker and a possible treatment lead.
pmc-13135011:
Pupillo and co-authors validate an Italian version of a standard test of muscle function for people with spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy, in a 2026 study. The rare inherited disease slowly weakens muscles, and trials need dependable outcome measures. The team translated the Adult Myopathy Assessment Tool with a strict forward-and-back protocol and gave it to twenty-nine patients.

Scores were consistent between raters and across repeats, and the scale held together internally. Results correlated with walking distance and a disease-specific rating scale in the expected directions. The authors conclude the Italian version is ready for standardized follow-up and international studies.
pmc-13135511:
Ozgur Kisi and co-authors improve in 2026 forecasts of monthly water loss from an open pan in southeast China, using only limited weather data. They add two recent nature inspired search methods to a memory based deep network, to tune its settings. The study uses forty years of data from two stations and tests three ways of splitting the data.

Both new hybrids beat a plain network and two older hybrids. The best model cut key error scores by more than forty percent against the best plain network in the top test case. Charts show its forecasts track the observed values closely. The authors argue that smart tuning greatly lifts such forecasts.
pmc-13135611:
Abdulrahman Alasmari and Chellasamy Panneerselvam build a green nanomaterial that fights both cancer and germs in a 2026 study. Their composite blends zinc oxide crystals with two soft carriers, made using leaf extract of the plant Peganum harmala. Lab checks confirmed neat crystals, fifteen to twenty-five nanometers wide, spread through the polymer net. The mix stayed stable in suspension.

Against aggressive breast cancer cells, the composite killed strongly, with potency growing over three days of exposure. Normal breast cells were barely harmed, showing selectivity. Inside cancer cells it raised reactive oxygen, drained defenses, broke energy factories, and triggered cell suicide. It also killed a broad range of bacteria and fungi, led by staph and Candida species. The authors present it as a green-made candidate for therapy, pending much more testing.
pmc-13136211:
Le, Yee, Dona, and Silk study caregivers of children with ADHD in work from twenty twenty-six. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder affects the child, but it may also affect the health and quality of life of parents and other caregivers.

Data came from a large Australian study of children. ADHD was reported by parents when children were aged ten to eleven. Caregiver quality of life and mental health were measured a year later with standard scales. Models tested links between child symptoms and caregiver outcomes. The team also hunted for traits that shape caregiver well being, which could help target family support where it counts most.
pmc-13136511:
Scarred lungs stiffen until breathing fails, and a thorny fruit extract might slow the scarring. Ting Zhou and co-authors test in 2026 extracts of Rosa roxburghii, a plant rich in protective compounds, in mice with pulmonary fibrosis. The ethyl acetate extract carried the most active content and the strongest antioxidant punch, so it led the animal work.

Treated mice showed friendlier gut microbes, corrected amino acid chemistry centered on tryptophan, and quieter scarring signals in the lung: less cell-shape shifting toward scar tissue and a damped JAK2/STAT3 pathway. The authors frame the benefit as a gut-lung partnership worth clinical exploration.
pmc-13136611:
Sofie Waesch and five co-authors tested whether telling people how manual therapy supposedly works changes what the therapy does, in this 2026 randomized trial. Ninety-three healthy volunteers got a standard lumbar treatment after hearing one of three briefings: a mechanical story, a nervous-system story, or none. The team measured back flexibility, pressure pain thresholds, and movement pain, at the treated spot and at a remote one.

Flexibility improved in every group, and by the same amount. No briefing beat another on any measure, near or far. The authors conclude that, in healthy people at least, mechanism talk does not steer the physical result. They suggest expectation effects may need pain, or belief held more deeply, to show themselves.
pmc-13138211:
Bakhtawar Farooq and co-authors report two sisters whose kidney failure traces to a gene fault tied to Alport syndrome. The syndrome weakens a filter membrane in the kidney and can also harm hearing and sight. Their 2026 study combines clinic records, gene sequencing, and network analysis of the gene's protein links.

Both sisters had reached the most advanced stage of kidney disease. Gene reading found a short deletion in the named gene, classed as disease-causing by standard rules. Hearing loss in two other family members fits the same pattern. Protein network maps tie the gene closely to both kidney disease and the syndrome. Two cell pathways showed up in both diseases as well, the team report.
pmc-13141211:
Liying Sun and co-authors set out a care algorithm in 2026 for growths on the ovary or tube in girls and teenagers. Such masses range from harmless cysts to cancers, and the twin goals of fast sorting and protecting future fertility make them a delicate problem.

The guidance grew out of an international congress held in late 2025. Germ cell tumors are the most common tumor type at this age, making up sixty to seventy percent of ovarian tumors, followed by surface tumors at about seventeen percent. The authors sort growths by origin and behavior, then lay out when to watch, when to operate, and how to spare the ovary. Their aim is earlier, safer decisions for young patients.
pmc-13141611:
Isabel A. Lea and colleagues published a 2026 safety evaluation of a common plastics softener. The chemical is used in vinyl and many products. Cancer hazard was the question. Evidence came from human, animal, and laboratory studies. The team integrated all three streams systematically.

Human studies showed mostly no cancer association. One prostate result was imprecise. Rodent studies did find tumors at several sites. Mechanistic work argued the chemical does not damage DNA directly. Stress and cell growth pathways explained rodent tumors better. Relevance to humans remains the hard judgment. The evaluation lays out the reasoning transparently.
pmc-13143411:
Akina Nigi and co-authors reported this 2026 case of a side effect that seems to contradict a cancer drug's purpose. The drug blocks blood vessel growth to starve tumors. Yet a 75-year-old man on the drug grew small vessel lumps that bled again and again. Tissue tests confirmed the lumps were benign growths called pyogenic granulomas.

The man had advanced lung cancer and took the drug with a second agent. The bleeding lumps hurt his daily life, so doctors cut them out and stopped the drug. He then switched to a sister drug that blocks the vessel signal rather than its receiver. No new lumps appeared. The contrast hints the two blocking styles differ in this rare risk, and the authors suggest a switch as a remedy.
pmc-13144811:
Olha Yuryk presents a classification of spinal vascular disorders in degenerative-dystrophic diseases of the spine in a 2026 conference abstract. When the spine wears down, the blood supply of the cord can fail in ways neurologists seldom sort with care. A shared scheme for those failures would sharpen both talk and treatment.

More than a thousand patients with the wear and known cord vessel pathology were examined. From that base, an original classification is laid out in tiers. Early reflex signs, from spasms of cord vessels in one or two territories, sit at the base. Single passing attacks come next, then full ischemic or hemorrhagic strokes of the cord.
pmc-13144911:
Teresa Ullberg and ten co-authors describe I-CATCHER, a world trial of a care bundle for bleeding inside the brain. Such bleeding, called intracerebral hemorrhage, kills and disables many patients within hours. A bundle of fast steps, led by quick blood pressure lowering, improved outcomes in low-resource settings in an earlier trial. Doubt remains about whether it works across richer and varied health systems. This 2026 conference abstract lays out the trial design.

Hospitals join in groups and switch to the bundle in a stepped order, so all sites get it in time. The bundle also standardizes fast stabilization and referral paths. The main test is whether patients recover better function. The authors argue a shared, proven bundle could lift care wherever the trial shows it works.
pmc-13145011:
Karmen Aslankurt and twelve co-authors present a conference abstract from 2026 on stroke risk after a brain bleed. The bleed type is an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, a sudden bleed around the brain. A feared later harm is delayed cerebral ischemia, which hits about 30 percent of patients. The team tests whether damage to a thin cell layer, the endothelial glycocalyx, comes before that harm.

They took blood plasma samples from 30 patients over two weeks. Two breakdown products, Syndecan-1 and Hyaluronan, were measured with standard lab kits. Both rose over time, and the rise was larger in the seven patients who got delayed ischemia. The authors say the layer may play a role, but the work needs more patients and outside checks.
pmc-13145111:
Teresa Moncada Cordeiro and co-authors hunt for signs that predict bleeding in the brain after stroke treatment, in a 2026 conference study. The strokes studied come from blocks in smaller, farther brain vessels. Recent trials found that clearing such blocks with a catheter did not beat drug care and raised bleeding risk.

The team reviewed 658 patients treated at one stroke center over about nine years. Bleeding in the brain occurred in just over a quarter of cases, though severe bleeding was rare. A standard scan score of early damage predicted any bleeding, and clot-busting drugs predicted a deeper type of bleed. About forty-four percent of patients regained independence by ninety days. The results may help doctors weigh risks before treatment.
pmc-13145211:
Jiangmin Li presents this 2026 conference abstract on blood markers for two kinds of stroke. One kind is caused by a blocked vessel, the other by bleeding linked to high blood pressure. Both strike often and leave many people disabled. Care options are limited, so fast and clear markers are needed.

The study drew plasma from patients of both types and from healthy controls. Tiny packets shed by cells were pulled out, and long non-coding RNA inside them was screened. Several markers differed by group, and some sorted patients well in tests. Scores for severity and outcome were checked as well. Cell tests probed how these markers may act. The author sees them as leads for early tests.
pmc-13145411:
Zhang and co-authors built a model that forecasts outcomes after acute ischemic stroke from heart ultrasound images. They enrolled 295 patients and split them into training and check groups. From 3D scans they outlined two parts of the mitral valve. Software then pulled about 1,600 texture features from each part, and selection steps kept only the most useful ones.

The best model used features from the valve ring with a support vector method. It scored strongly in cross-checks and held up on the outside group. Adding clinical features improved it further. The authors conclude that texture analysis of the valve, especially its ring, could become a non-invasive way to judge stroke outcomes. The text is a conference abstract reporting the study in summary form.
pmc-13145511:
Jozefien Meersschaut and co-authors report a 2026 conference study mapping the cell and protein life of a rare brain vessel disease that narrows arteries and grows fragile side vessels. Muscle cells in the vessel wall switch roles in this disease, but the drivers were unclear. The team combined gene reads, blood proteins, and deep study of one removed artery.

Twelve patients were studied, and two thirds carried a gene risk factor of some kind. The artery study showed muscle cells losing their squeezing form, gaining a building form, and crowding the inner wall. A tissue protein ran high in both the artery and the blood, hinting at a blood test. Immune cells also filled the wall, pointing to swelling as a driver.

Amr Zakaria proposes such a tool in a 2026 paper built on fuzzy cognitive maps, diagrams where medical concepts push on each other with weighted arrows. The problem he targets: maps drawn only by experts are rigid, while maps learned only from data can drift into nonsense.

His system runs two loops. An inner loop settles the map's concept values for a case. An outer loop adjusts the weights from data, but with a built-in correction step that lets experts veto or fix clinically important links. He proves conditions under which both loops stay stable and settle. A worked example shows expert feedback changing the final diagnosis in ways a reader can follow. Tests use synthetic cases and public medical datasets.
pmc-13184811:
Adhesive capsulitis, better known as frozen shoulder, locks the joint in its frozen phase and hurts. Chih-Ya Chang and co-authors ran a randomized trial with forty-six adults to compare two treatments. One group got three weekly injections of hyaluronic acid into the joint, guided by ultrasound. The other got supervised physical therapy twice a week for six weeks. Pain, disability, and shoulder movement were tracked for twenty-six weeks.

Both groups improved much on every measure. The injection group's pain and disability score fell from forty-three to sixteen. The therapy group fell from fifty-two to twenty-three. Pain dropped by roughly two thirds and three fifths in the two groups. At no check point did the groups differ from each other, and no side effects appeared. The authors conclude both options work about equally well for frozen phase disease.
pmc-13186211:
Ameer Soomro and co-authors examine, in a 2026 study, how medical students' satisfaction shifted between two accreditation cycles at a Caribbean medical school. Accreditation is the quality stamp that keeps a school honest, and it is known to lift outcomes like licensing exam pass rates for international graduates. The accrediting body here is recognized internationally, with standards comparable to those in the United States.

The team compared the accreditor's own student survey data from 2021 and 2024 at Avalon University School of Medicine. The retrospective analysis spans the basic science campus and beyond, the segment shown begins. Satisfaction is a soft measure, but students feel curriculum and support failures first. Tracking it across cycles shows whether the accreditation loop, inspect, require, improve, actually moves the student experience. Schools facing review can use such tracking to fix what surveys flag before the inspectors return.
pmc-13186511:
Ramkishore and co-authors write to the editor about a blast lung case that hid for two days in a 2026 letter. A 67-year-old man stood two metres from a truck tyre that burst in a workshop. The blast broke his shin bone but left his chest untouched, and first scans looked clean.

Two days on, breath trouble showed harm in both lungs from the blast wave alone. He got better with mask air support, no breathing tube needed, and healed in full. Past tyre blast cases were mostly instant and far worse. The team warns that blast lung harm can bloom late even when the chest looks sound.
pmc-13186711:
Moise Henri Moumbeket-Yifomnjou and co-authors compare two forecast models for a lung virus in Cameroon in a 2026 study. The virus hits children and older adults hard and moves in seasonal waves. Picking the right model helps health teams plan for surges.

Nose swabs from 1,774 patients at five watch sites in Yaounde span July 2020 to December 2022. The virus showed in 8.5% of samples tested in the labs. One model, Holt-Winters, tracked past waves with no weather input and scored 77.6% on fit. The rival model tied activity to weather gauges and did poorly alone. Even with 12 weather inputs pooled, it reached just 56.4% fit, so the simpler model won.
pmc-13188111:
Qi Fang and seven co-authors compared brain activity in rats that grow fat on rich food and rats that resist in a 2026 paper. A high-fat, high-sugar diet makes some animals obese and leaves others lean, for reasons that may sit in the brain. The team fed forty male rats and split the rich-diet group by weight after eight weeks.

The obese rats kept overeating, with worse blood fats, glucose tolerance, and heavier organs. Brain scans showed quieter activity in the hindbrain and livelier activity in a memory-linked cortex in the obese group, and the two regions' activity moved in opposite directions. The authors read this as rewiring of a hindbrain-cortex circuit under long rich feeding.
pmc-13188211:
Boucherabine and six co-authors compared drug-resistant staph germs from deep and surface infections in twenty twenty-six. The germ is methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, or MRSA. It ranges from harmless life in the nose to deadly blood infection. The traits that mark invading strains are key to new tests and cures.

The team took stock of proteins and small compounds in samples from blood, skin sores, and nose swabs. They logged two thousand proteins and one hundred fifty compounds in all. Deep strains held more of two compounds and one protein the germs send out. They held less of three compounds and two proteins, one tied to the cell's protein-making parts. Mass spectrometry in a scan-all mode drove the checks. The authors say this sign set could flag strains prone to invade and show how MRSA turns risky.
pmc-13191511:
Seyda Yayla and five co-authors build a plastic-stamped sensor that detects a prized plant compound at vanishing levels. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-six. Chlorogenic acid is a valued antioxidant in herbs and supplements, and checking it usually needs lab machinery.

The sensor's surface is molded around the target molecule, leaving pits shaped exactly like it. A light-driven recipe using a boron-bearing building block formed the imprinted film on an electrode. Tests showed tidy binding sites and fast charge flow. Detection reached down near ten-to-the-minus-fourteen molar, an extraordinarily low floor. Real extracts from bellflower-family plants were measured successfully. The authors pitch the device for cheap quality control of herbal goods.
pmc-13193811:
Wenlong Ding and co-authors track deaths from rare chest-wall cancers in the United States in a 2026 study. The group covers tumors of the heart, the chest middle, and the chest lining. The team read national death records from 1999 to 2020 for adults, over five thousand deaths in all.

Men died at higher rates than women, and older adults held two-thirds of deaths. The age-set rate fell steeply at first, then eased down more slowly. White adults held the top rate, and regions split as well. The team calls for care aimed at the groups hit hardest.
pmc-13193911:
Jheremy Reyes and colleagues build a hybrid AI tool for brain tumour radiosurgery planning. Their proof-of-concept study from twenty twenty-six covers recurrent glioblastoma. Gamma knife treatment needs careful dose choices in already treated brain. Outcomes vary widely between patients receiving similar care.

Records from one centre over a decade trained the system. Inputs joined clinical details, biopsy markers, and dose measures. A survival forest model predicted local tumour control over time. Patient-level validation guarded against overly optimistic results. The tool also recommends a prescription dose per patient. Counselling and follow-up planning could use those personal forecasts. Larger validation must come before clinical use.
pmc-13194311:
Andres Pereira-Guaqueta and co-authors track desert pollination networks over time in a 2026 study. Plant-pollinator links sustain biodiversity and ecosystem function. Arid lands swing sharply with rainfall, yet temporal network data are scarce there. The team surveyed a semi-arid scrubland in the southern Chihuahuan Desert.

Monthly surveys spanned two years of contrasting precipitation. Networks were rebuilt for three seasons in each year. Change was stronger within years than between years. Turnover of blooming plant species drove most of that change. Wetter periods brought richer plants and pollinators and more hub species. Generalist bees held network cohesion across seasons. Network shape stayed compound, with nesting inside modules. Robustness to species loss was also assessed season by season. The authors stress rainfall as conductor of the web. Conservation must plan for moving, not static, networks.
pmc-13195011:
Luca Salhöfer and co-authors warn in 2026 that dye used in CT scans can skew how muscle health is read. Scans can now measure muscle size and fat inside muscle, which hint at strength and health. Doctors had feared that scans with and without dye might not match.

The team scanned twenty small pigs with and without dye, then checked 114 human scans for proof. Muscle size and outer fat stayed steady across scan types. By contrast, fat inside muscle and muscle density shifted once dye was given. The lesson is plain: size reads are safe to compare, but health reads need care when dye is used.
pmc-13196111:
Caroline Kuo and co-authors compare two mouse strains used to test gene-modified human blood stem cells, in a study from 2026. Such mice, lacking their own immune defenses, accept human cells and show how they grow. The test matters before gene therapies reach patients.

One strain, called NBSGW, hosted higher levels of human cells than the other, called NSG. Cells carrying many copies of a delivery virus grew poorly in NSG mice but not in NBSGW mice. That gap means the second strain could hide safety risks of such products. Gene correction with a cutting tool worked equally well in both strains, even at low cell doses. Single-cell gene reads showed the second strain also kept more kinds of developing blood cells.
pmc-13196811:
Yajuan He and co-authors review how chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and lung cancer occur together, in a review paper from 2026. The lung disease is more than a fellow traveler from smoke and dirty air. It can drive cancer growth through lasting swelling, gene damage, and shifts in microbes and immunity.

Cancers in these patients show distinct traits, such as fewer EGFR mutations and higher mutation counts. Those traits favor immune checkpoint drugs over targeted EGFR drugs. New scans, blood markers, and imaging tools aid early finding. The review also covers prevention and care choices, and how tailored oncology can use the disease pairing.
pmc-13197111:
Mei Zhao, Lorraine Buis, and five co-authors tested phone-based coaching for mothers in Beijing, in work from twenty twenty-six. The coaching drew on the health belief model, which says people act when they feel risk and trust the steps. Care centers that took up a dental referral scheme formed the test group; the rest gave standard care.

The study followed six hundred forty-eight mother-child pairs for a year. At six months, helped tooth brushing was up by about ten points in the test group. By twelve months that gap had shrunk and lost force. Dental visits, though, were much higher in the test group at one year. Night feeds and sugar intake did not shift, so gains may fade without fresh support.
pmc-13197311:
Tamano and co-authors assembled a giant gene cluster inside a living fungus in a single step, in a study published in 2026. The cluster, 63,000 DNA letters long, holds the recipe for a valuable natural compound. Moving such clusters into a better host is the standard route to mass production. But clusters this size usually need repeated rounds of stitching. The team used multiple recombination events at once inside a workhorse mold used in food and industry.

The mold's own DNA repair machinery did the assembly in vivo. One-step assembly of a cluster this large had not been shown. Shortening the path from gene discovery to production strains matters for drug and supplement supply. Natural compounds often fail commercially on manufacturing, not merit. This method attacks the manufacturing bottleneck directly.
pmc-13197711:
Hehua Wang and a large team trace the nerve paths from the womb to the brain in mice. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The womb is ruled in part by the central nerve system, which keeps fertility and reproductive health in tune. The full paths of that link were not mapped in detail.

They inject a tracing virus into the womb wall and watch it climb over time. It moves from spinal cord to deep brain zones that rule body states and feelings. A scent zone feeds one of those hubs. A fatty acid scent switches on hubs in the chain, and some of its cells make oxytocin. Smell may thus shape womb action through this circuit.
pmc-13197811:
Hui Liu and co-authors show how acidity changes the structure of myoglobin, a meat protein, and so changes how well it is digested, published in 2026. Meat processing can swing pH over a wide range. Those swings are known to affect protein digestion, but the mechanism linking structure to digestion was not fully clear.

Across a pH gradient, the team used spectroscopic tools and computer simulation to track physical changes. At low pH, the protein grew more water-repellent on its surface and more flexible. More of its water-repellent building blocks were exposed, and its internal bonds weakened. Simulations also showed a stronger pull toward digestive enzymes. Together, those changes made the protein easier to digest in their lab tests.
pmc-13199411:
M Yasser Alsafadi and colleagues audited a hospital system's electronic order set for home IV antibiotics in a 2026 analysis. OPAT lets patients finish intravenous antibiotics at home after discharge. Safe care needs clean data and tight follow-up, yet the team suspected the order set in the Epic record system was leaking both.

Across three years and close to ninety-five hundred treatment episodes, flaws stood out. Free-text entries replaced structured fields, key fields sat empty, and microbe results were not linked. Those gaps made it hard to track care, watch for harm, and study outcomes. Missed drug-level checks and murky instructions added safety risk. The authors list design musts for a rebuild.
pmc-13200011:
Angelica Severino, Concetta Lauro, Marzia Calvanese, Ermenegilda Parrilli, and Maria Luisa Tutino give a targeted protocol to cure a cold loving sea bacterium of its giant plasmid. The strain serves cold adaptation studies and growing biotech use. The study came out in twenty twenty-six.

The plasmid is large and stable, and old curing tricks with chemicals or heat fail on such replicons. First a marker cassette is swapped into the plasmid by like sequence matching, so cured and holding cells can be told apart. Next, antisense RNA silencing hits a gene the plasmid needs to copy itself. The plasmid then fails to persist and is lost.
pmc-13200111:
Sang Kyun Yoo and co-authors test, in a 2026 feasibility study, whether machine learning can check proton therapy deliveries by predicting where each proton spot actually landed. Spot-scanning proton treatment paints tumors precisely, but small steering errors can shift the dose.

The team gathered sixty-four delivery log files for one standard plan from two treatment rooms over three months, recording how spot errors varied with beam energy, day, and room. Models trained on most files predicted spot positions from plan data with near-perfect accuracy. The approach could become a fast extra safety net, flagging odd deliveries for human review before they matter.
pmc-13200411:
Silvestro Ojja and nine co-authors study HIV treatment breaks in South Sudan in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Pregnant and breastfeeding women on antiretroviral therapy must stay on treatment to protect themselves and their babies. In South Sudan, staying in care is hard. The team reviewed records from twenty clinics. Facilities were sampled in proportion to their size, and data came from registers and client files.

They measured how often treatment was interrupted and how often clinics gave multi-month drug supplies. Statistical analysis linked breaks to patient and clinic traits. Knowing the drivers of interruption can guide program fixes, such as longer refills or closer follow-up. The paper serves HIV program managers in fragile health systems.
pmc-13201611:
Wenbin Song and co-authors study a protein that helps a common thyroid cancer spread in a 2026 paper. Papillary thyroid cancer makes up most thyroid cancer cases, and its spread worsens the outlook. A protein called S100A10 had been tied to growth in other cancers, but its role here was unclear.

Gene data from single cells flagged S100A10 as a marker tied to spread and poor outlook, and lab tests confirmed high levels in cancer tissue and cells. The protein joined two partners to form a control chain that switches on a growth pathway and helps cells take on a more mobile form. Forced high levels made tumors invade more in lab and animal tests. The authors name the chain as a target for future drugs.
pmc-13202511:
Fabiha Islam and co-authors test whether a virtual world can stir the feelings that therapy works with, in people who feel depressed, in this 2025 pilot study. The platform was Second Life, a persistent 3D world explored through avatars. Twenty-eight volunteers, half reporting depression symptoms and half not, watched emotion-evoking video clips either in the virtual world or at an ordinary desktop setup.

Participants with depression symptoms reported stronger amusement, anger, and sadness than the others, whichever setting they used, and rated their own performance higher. For participants without symptoms, the virtual world felt less effortful than the desktop setup, hinting it could lower mental strain during emotional tasks. Overall mental workload and emotional engagement did not differ much between settings. The authors read the results as early evidence that metaverse spaces can host therapy-style emotional work, while stressing the study's small, pilot scale.
pmc-13203511:
Lizeth A Montano Garibay and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-six trial of electrical therapy for pain after spinal surgery in dogs. The dogs had surgery for slipped discs in the back. Extra non-drug pain relief could cut opioid use and its side effects.

Twenty dogs were assigned by chance to standard pain care alone or with interferential current therapy. The added group received three sessions in the first day after surgery. Pain scores, opioid use, and skin sensitivity near the wound were tracked. Treated dogs scored lower on pain at the middle check. Relief appeared short-lived, guiding realistic expectations.
pmc-13204411:
Irene Coll Campayo and co-authors compare rural and urban teens in Mallorca on lifestyle, diet, and oral health, in a research paper from 2026. Teen years set habits that shape later health. Place of living may drive gaps in food, activity, and mouth care, so a direct comparison can guide local programs.

The study covers four hundred sixty-three teens aged twelve and fifteen. Surveys captured diet, hygiene, and lifestyle, and dental exams followed a standard world method. Urban teens drank more sugary drinks and ate more ultra-processed foods. Rural teens reported more weekly activity. The paper maps where each group needs support most.
pmc-13205411:
Zhen Wang and co-authors extract and test a sugar polymer from hemp leaves in a 2026 paper. The plant has a long history in Chinese herbal medicine, yet its polysaccharides have drawn little study. The team used hot water extraction followed by alcohol precipitation to get a crude sample.

The sample was mostly carbohydrate with a small protein share, built mainly from three sugars. In test tube assays it fought several kinds of free radicals. In mouse immune cells damaged by peroxide, it raised protective enzyme levels and lowered a damage marker. Gene tests point to a known defense pathway being switched on. The authors suggest the material could serve as an antioxidant ingredient in food, drug, or cosmetic products.
pmc-13206211:
Gloria Morís-Menéndez and co-authors report a green one-pot reaction that builds phosphorus bonds in 2026. One-pot tandem methods cut steps, waste, and energy in chemical synthesis. Their method runs in an acidic deep eutectic solvent, a low-cost liquid mix that acts as solvent, promoter, and selectivity switch at once.

The liquid first turns alcohol starting materials into reactive aldehydes, which then bond with phosphorus partners in the same pot. Changing the mix ratio flips the product between two forms, with no change in reagents. Products drop out by simple filtering, and the liquid can be recycled. Scale-up to gram amounts worked with a low waste score.
pmc-13206711:
Dandan Song, Liang Yang, and Chunlin Zhang review how omics tools can design starter microbes for traditional fermented foods, in work from 2026. Classic ferments rely on wild microbe mixes that give rich flavor but uneven batches. Fixed starter mixes promise steady quality, yet thin mixes can taste flat.

The review shows how gene, protein, and chemical scans reveal which microbes do the core work. Culture hunts add live strains that labs can actually grow and store. Keystone strains that drive the ferment are split from helper strains that keep it stable. A build, test, and rebuild loop turns that evidence into recipes. The goal is food that stays both steady and true to tradition.
pmc-13207011:
Christos Damaskos and co-authors review capivasertib for breast cancer in a 2026 paper. The drug blocks AKT, a signal hub that helps hormone-driven tumors resist standard therapy. It is approved with fulvestrant for set tumor types. Pathway faults mark the patients most likely to gain.

The review sums trials from early to late phase. The combo lengthened time without progression in advanced disease. Gains ran largest in tumors with faults in one of three pathway genes. Combos with a chemo drug or a DNA repair blocker showed added effects in other breast types. Biomarkers and resistance paths are charted for future work.
pmc-13207411:
Carmelo Dueñas-Castell, José Correa-Guerrero, and co-authors scope the proof on blood gas push as a cure trait in sharp breath fail, in work from 2026. Sharp breath fail fills wards and kills at high rates each year. Flat kind splits miss its mix, while trait led care may fit folks more close.

Three dozen works group in four care spans for the read. Low gas push links to worse ends in heart and low air cases. High gas push flags folks who gain from mask help in set ills. Tube help marks bend with sour state and time in the works. Gas push reads as a flag more than a fix.
pmc-13208311:
Nayeli Bastidas-Benalcazar and co-authors decode mental states from brain and heart signals in a 2026 paper. Brain only decoders often shift across tasks and people. Their system fuses fast EEG brain waves with slow heart rate patterns in one feature space. A supercomputer workflow handles the heavy signal work.

A few-shot calibration step aligns memory and piloting tasks for each person. On twenty-nine subjects, mean accuracy reaches over ninety-nine percent, far above a near thirty-eight percent zero-shot baseline, they report. Under high workload, the fused signals settle into a tight, low entropy pattern. The frame targets passive brain-computer interfaces.
pmc-13208911:
Foam-like lattices that squeeze inward can soak up crash energy, and Mohammad Faisal Ahmed and Kyle Primes made them tougher by mixing materials. These auxetic structures widen sideways when stretched, yet single-material versions bend or snap too easily. The pair printed versions with a density gradient, in soft plastic alone and in a soft-rigid blend.

Crush tests favored the blend on nearly every measure: higher forces, more energy absorbed, and better spring-back afterward. A new joint design between the two materials helped them work as one. The findings point to reusable padding for helmets, vehicles, and packaging.
pmc-13209311:
Mohammad Hussein Naseef Assadi studies sodium motion at room temperature in two layered ruthenates, in work published in 2026. Atomic-scale ion motion shapes stability and electronic behaviour in layered oxides, and it matters for sodium-ion battery cathodes. Simulations used ab initio molecular dynamics at a stated level of theory for both compounds.

Sodium ions rattled widely in both materials. The sodium-richer compound let ions roam over larger volumes and showed early signs of true migration, unlike the more confined other compound. Oxygen's share of redox capacity fell as sodium content rose. Assadi argues that tuning the local ion setting controls charge balance and dynamic response in such frameworks.
pmc-13209511:
Yifei Yu and co-authors published a review in 2026 on making hydrogen with sunlight. Splitting water with solar power is a prized route to green hydrogen at scale. Many kinds of solar cells can pair with many kinds of water splitters. The review maps how those pairings work and what they cost.

Pairing works on three levels: matching the light the cell harvests, matching the pace of the splitter, and shaping the whole system layout. Big hurdles remain, like jittery solar output against a splitter that wants steady power. Costly catalysts and wear under harsh weather add strain. Fresh tools include smart forecasts, digital twins of plants, and heat-plus-light designs. The authors chart a path to stable, cheap, large-scale green hydrogen.
pmc-13210311:
Volunteer counselors who treat children who have lived through trauma can absorb trauma themselves, and a 2026 study led by Priya Dahiya looks for workplace shields in Kenya. The research article studies organization-level factors tied to low secondary traumatic stress among lay counselors giving trauma-focused therapy in a rollout trial in western Kenya.

Separate analyses covered 120 community health volunteers and 117 teachers trained for the program. A pattern-matching method found several working mixes for low stress, and the winning recipes differed between the two counselor groups. Strong oversight ties helped both, while how leaders acted and rollout climate combined in other ways by role, so the authors advise tailoring support to each workforce.
pmc-13210711:
Vera Gledacheva and Stoyanka Nikolova review in 2026 what silver nanoparticles can do for medical imaging. The particles' optical quirks, above all a strong resonance with light, make them natural contrast boosters. The narrative review searched major databases for recent lab studies of silver-based imaging systems.

Across optical imaging, CT, and combined platforms, the particles sharpened contrast and amplified signals in tissue. Coated versions homed to targets better, which suits image-guided therapy. The authors close on the hurdles: toxicity, body compatibility, and the long road from bench results to clinic use still stand in the way.
pmc-13211111:
Lei Ma and co-authors image the light response of infrared detector material at ten kelvin with a near-field microscope, beating the usual blur limit, in a 2026 study. Mercury cadmium telluride chips lose sensitivity when nanoscale bumps mar their surface during fabrication. Their cryogenic scanning probe mapped local photocurrent in place, at super-resolution.

Bumps only tens of nanometers high acted as strong recombination centers, draining the signal by 10 to 20 percent against flat areas. Tests showed these defect states stay unsaturated and linear, and higher bias voltage widened their dead zone, worsening losses nonlinearly. The authors turn the maps into engineering tolerances for making high-performance infrared arrays.
pmc-13211511:
Marielle Appenzeller and co-authors test how tumor purity affects a gene test for bladder cancer in dogs. Their 2026 study examines seventy-six confirmed tumor samples. The test hunts copy number changes on three chromosomes that are typical of this cancer, alongside a known mutation check.

About seventy-six percent of samples tested positive under the standard cut-off. Many near-miss cases cleared the bar on one of the two ratios used. Sensitivity rose with tumor share: samples with at least twenty percent tumor tissue tested positive eighty-four percent of the time, and eighty-nine percent at forty percent share. The authors warn that sparse tumor content and many neutral cells can hide the signal.
pmc-13212611:
E. Lorzadeh and co-authors test in 2026 whether a short questionnaire can measure how many flavonoids people eat. Flavonoids are plant compounds linked to health, but tracking them usually needs long food lists that tire respondents and invite error.

Eighty Australian adults completed the 23-item tool repeatedly over a year, alongside detailed 24-hour recalls each quarter. The short tool gave moderately matching rankings for total flavonoids and several subgroups, though it overestimated amounts by a wide margin. Repeat answers stayed fairly consistent across the year. The authors judge the tool usable for ranking intake, while warning that absolute values need further correction work.
pmc-13212811:
Yunhong Wu and Rick Chappell present in 2026 a statistical method for estimating survival when patient risk is known to rise steadily over time. Their setting is hard: some patients enter studies late, while others leave before the event of interest occurs.

The pair build an estimator that merges a classic proportional hazards approach with an older method that assumes a monotone hazard. They prove the estimator settles on the right answer with enough data and describe its long-run behaviour. Simulations showed stable, nearly unbiased estimates even in small samples, with gains from adjusting for patient traits. A well-known retirement community dataset illustrates the method in practice.
pmc-13213011:
Aya Khalaf and co-authors release an open brain-scan data set on conscious seeing in a 2026 paper. The data were gathered for an adversarial collaboration, a head-to-head test between two leading theories of consciousness: global workspace theory and integrated information theory.

Across several sites, 118 volunteers watched faces, objects, letters, and fake fonts at three angles and three durations while scanners recorded brain activity. A target-spotting task made some categories matter and others not. The files follow a standard format and ship with quality reports, behavior scores, and eye tracking. Anyone can download them to test new theories of perception.
pmc-13213511:
Five chemists led by Anton Kliuchynskyi present proof that a carbon and hydrogen bond at the end of an alkyne chain can form a strong, proper hydrogen bond. Most bonds of this kind are weak and behave in the opposite way. The team tested the bond in more than fifty liquid settings, from harsh solvents to mild ones.

They tracked the bond with three kinds of light-based and magnetic tests, plus fast pulse methods and computer models. The bond acted much like the bond found in water-like groups, not like a plain carbon bond. The authors suggest it could serve as a sharp sensor for weak forces between molecules.
pmc-13213711:
Lynn Honeckman, writing alone in 2026, tells how a young dog with fierce aggression got a full workup and, in time, got better. The nine-month-old Australian Shepherd bit people again and again, at home and out, and her owners weighed giving her up or putting her down.

Blood tests and brain checks found no illness to blame. The behaviour review named built-up fear, poor impulse control, guarding of food and toys, and too little contact with the world as a pup. She had also left her mother young and had sick spells early on. Care mixed strict safety rules, kind training, and two drugs for mood and calm. Bites eased in six weeks and stopped within a year.
pmc-13214311:
Dured Dardari and co-authors track a bone protein during fast sugar control gains in type two diabetes in a 2026 study. Poor control is tied to weak bone turnover and fragile bones. The protein, osteocalcin, also links to sugar balance, but its quick response to better control was little described.

Sixty adults took part at one center. One group had chronic poor control and got three months of tuned treatment. The other had stable good control and served as a comparison. At the start both groups showed the same protein level. After three months the treated group's level jumped by about eight units, while the comparison group stayed flat. Weight rose slightly overall. The authors call the result a lead for study, not proof of cause.
pmc-13214411:
Anaseini Ratu, Katherine L. Anders, and Karin Leder write in 2026 about how Pacific Island countries can base mosquito-borne disease control on solid evidence. Dengue outbreaks strike the region often, and a World Health Organization framework for evidence-informed decisions frames their discussion.

They use the release of Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes, a method that blocks virus spread, as their test case. Several Pacific countries adopted it before a full local evidence system existed, leaving gaps in data on impact, surveillance, and long-term support. The authors propose squeezing more from existing surveillance, time-series analysis, and blood studies. Culturally grounded discussion methods can supply missing local knowledge and connect researchers with decision makers.
pmc-13214711:
Angeliki Gerede and co-authors review what a mild blood trait means when its bearer bears a child, in a survey from 2026. The trait, beta-thalassemia minor, rides in near ninety million folk. Long read as kind, it meets in birth a strain that can bare hid weak spots.

The team sifted two and a half decades of PubMed work: pools, pair tests, sums, and guild guides. Low blood is the top mark: a third or more of bearers run low by the last third, and a small share need blood in. Marks for babe and for the child's long run are set out too, with care steps by mark. Mild, they close, is not nil when two lives draw on one blood.
pmc-13214911:
Jed Fahey and Hua Liu review pairing a broccoli compound with other agents in a 2026 paper. The compound, sulforaphane, abounds in cruciferous vegetables and has long drawn interest for cancer prevention. Working alone it helps somewhat, but many studies now report that pairs can do far more than either part.

The review gathers proof of true synergy with cancer drugs, drugs still in development, other plant compounds, and leaf extracts. Gains appear across many cancer types, from bladder and breast to lung and skin. Some drug-resistant cell lines grew sensitive again when the compound joined the mix. Gains beyond cancer include less heart harm from treatment, calmer inflammation, and pain relief. The authors see room for combined therapies that cut drug doses.
pmc-13215411:
Muhammad-Safuan Zainuddin and co-authors review clinical evidence in a 2026 paper linking oxidative stress to Alzheimer's disease and asking whether flavonoids could help. Flavonoids are plant compounds known for antioxidant activity.

The review gathers biomarker studies from brain tissue and body fluids, where signs of oxidative damage generally run higher in patients and track disease severity, though methods differ between studies. Animal work shows flavonoids can restore antioxidant defences and calm inflammation in the brain. Human trial evidence, however, remains thin. The authors treat oxidative stress as a promising target that still needs firmer clinical proof.
pmc-13215511:
Mahboobeh Nouri and co-authors report a 2026 study of a new sprayable treatment against Verticillium dahliae, a soil fungus that wilts more than 400 plant species. The treatment packs short DNA strands into tiny capsules made from whey protein.

The DNA strands were designed to silence two fungal genes, and the capsules were formed by electrospraying and checked with microscopy and thermal tests. In dishes, the loaded capsules slowed fungal growth while plain protein did nothing. On tomato seedlings in a greenhouse, treated plants showed about half the disease of untreated infected controls after thirty days. The authors present the method as a targeted, low-impact option for wilt control.
pmc-13216111:
Péter de Lima Wachholz and co-authors present a 2026 pilot study of ezetimibe, a cholesterol-absorption blocker used in human medicine, for dogs with high blood lipids. Diet is the usual first step for these dogs, and drugs that lower cholesterol specifically are lacking.

Twenty-three dogs were assigned to a low-fat diet alone, ezetimibe alone, or both together, with blood tests at the start, midway, and after thirty days. Cholesterol fell significantly in both groups receiving the drug but not in the diet-only group. Triglycerides did not change significantly in any group. Owners reported no side effects. The authors conclude the drug was well tolerated and effective for cholesterol under these study conditions.
pmc-13216611:
Jun Koarashi and co-authors present a 2026 study measuring how much ancient carbon escapes when tropical peatlands in Central Kalimantan, Indonesia, are drained and burned. These swamps store carbon for millennia, and radiocarbon dating lets the team tell old carbon from new.

The comparison covers an intact swamp forest, a drained forest, and a drained, repeatedly burnt site over the period 1996 to 2014. Drainage and fires together released roughly 30 to 41 kilograms of carbon per square metre. Fires did most of the damage, freeing peat up to 3,000 years old and starting slow oxidation of still older layers. Scaled to Indonesia's disturbed peatlands, the implied release reaches billions of tonnes, with decomposition continuing every year.
pmc-13217111:
Sophie Braznell and co-authors review what heated tobacco does to the body's harm markers, in a paper whose text dates it to 2026. Heated tobacco products warm leaf instead of burning it, and are marketed as reduced-risk. The review gathered clinical trials comparing users against smokers, vapers, and people abstaining entirely, searching databases and, notably, manufacturer libraries through the end of 2024.

Forty studies qualified, only ten of them independent of the industry. Most lasted mere days or weeks, too short for diseases to declare themselves, so the evidence rests on blood and urine biomarkers of potential harm. Effect-direction plots summarised those markers, and pooled ratios covered side effects. The authors' caution is structural: a literature this industry-heavy and this short cannot yet support the marketing claims built on it.
pmc-13217211:
Alshehhi and colleagues update what is known about food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome, a severe food allergy in children. Unlike classic allergy, it does not run through IgE antibodies, and its causes stay unclear. It usually starts in the first year of life, often after rice, oats, or cow's milk, foods many babies meet early.

An acute episode begins one to four hours after eating, with repeated vomiting, diarrhoea, and limpness. Bad cases drain fluids until blood pressure falls. Because the picture looks like sepsis or stomach flu, babies are often misdiagnosed at first. The review gathers current thinking on causes, testing, and day-to-day management for families.
pmc-13217711:
Active children tend to read better, and a 2026 study by Qi Wang and co-authors tests whether sharper thinking skills carry that link. The children were nine and ten years old, an age when reading shifts from a lesson to a tool for all learning.

About 290 children took activity questionnaires, international reading tests covering stories and information texts, and lab tasks for three thinking skills: holding back impulses, holding items in mind, and switching rules. Roughly 282 gave usable data, with activity levels moderate to low on average and girls ahead of boys in reading. Statistical resampling then tested whether the thinking skills sit between activity and reading, as the design predicts.
pmc-13217911:
Yang Liu and co-authors report a 2026 study of influenza vaccine performance in older adults in Jiaxing, China. The team followed patients aged 60 and over who sought care for acute respiratory symptoms across three flu seasons, from 2022 to 2025. Their question was how much protection the seasonal vaccine actually gave this age group.

Using a test-negative design with 3,214 participants, the researchers compared vaccination status between patients who tested positive for influenza and those who tested negative. Adjusted effectiveness came to 42.5 percent overall, peaking at 47.2 percent in the 2024-2025 season. Protection ran higher in women, in people without underlying illness, and in the first 90 days after vaccination, when it reached 52.3 percent. The authors conclude that timely annual vaccination still offers moderate, worthwhile protection for older adults.
pmc-13218111:
Pietro Scilipoti and co-authors compare ways to estimate PSA doubling time after prostate surgery, and ask what the choice does to risk calls. After the prostate is removed, PSA can sit below detection for years before a relapse shows. How fast it then doubles is a key sign of danger.

Their 2026 study follows thousands of men whose PSA rose again after surgery. Four estimation methods were run on the same records, from the plainest two-point rule to a missing-data approach. Median doubling times spread widely across methods, so the method alone can change a man's label. Yet all four sorted the risk of death from the cancer about as well as each other.
pmc-13218311:
Somying Pumtong and co-authors review the staffing behind antimicrobial stewardship programs in a 2026 systematic review with a first meta-analysis. Stewardship programs exist to keep antibiotics working as resistance grows, and guidelines call for teams from many fields. How the work is divided among professions, and how much staff time hospitals commit, had never been gathered, notably outside wealthy countries.

Fifty studies met the entry rules after searches of six databases and grey sources to November 2025, with forty-four described stewardship roles and seven reporting staffing in full-time equivalents. Infectious disease doctors and pharmacists mainly oversaw prescribing, infection control nurses handled monitoring and training, microbiologists led diagnostic stewardship, and hospital epidemiologists ran surveillance and reporting. Staffing levels varied widely across hospitals and reporting styles. Early pooling hinted that larger hospitals report more doctor and pharmacist time, though differences between studies make that pattern tentative.
pmc-13219111:
Lena H. Nguyen writes a 2026 commentary on a study reading the mosaicism behind a form of epilepsy. Focal cortical dysplasia type two, a patch of cortex, is a major cause of drug-resistant epilepsy. It arises when brain cells pick up mutations in the PI3K-mTOR pathway during development. Which cells carry the mutation, and what it does, was out of reach.

The study sequenced single nuclei from eighteen dysplasia samples and seventeen controls, drawing on more than 400,000 nuclei. It paired gene expression with genotyping of the nuclei using two methods. Mutant cells kept neuronal or glial identities, and proportions matched controls, so it acts through altered behavior rather than altered makeup. In mutant neurons the pathway ran hot, while in mutation-free neighbors it ran cold, and immune and synaptic programs shifted. Nguyen presents it as a template for dissecting mosaic brain disease.
pmc-13219311:
Rocco Vergallo and co-authors set out, in a 2026 review, how to open and close the thigh artery for heart pump work. The pump, a microaxial flow type, backs up the heart in shock and in high-risk artery work. Its tube is wide, so the entry hole is big and bleeds can cost health, life, and cash. Sound and X-ray guides make the stick safe; more scans help in hard cases. In set high-risk work, the close can be sewn in first, a guard the team backs. In shock, that first sew is oft not in reach.

There, close at pump-out is the hinge. The review gives a work frame for both paths, from stick to seal.
pmc-13220111:
Ho-Chang Kuo and co-authors checked a simple two-gene blood test for Kawasaki disease, a fever illness of young children that can harm the heart's arteries. Their study was published in 2026. The disease has no firm lab test, so doctors must judge from signs, and delays raise the risk of heart damage.

Blood samples came from five hundred forty-one febrile children in Taiwan and Shanghai, including two hundred forty-three with the disease. The test, based on the activity of two genes, sorted the groups well, catching most true cases while clearing most other fevers. Results held across sites, including children with partial signs of the disease. Lab checks also showed the test was steady and precise. A quick blood answer could speed treatment where it counts.
pmc-13221111:
Qiming Xu and colleagues search public gene data for early warning markers of diabetic kidney disease in a 2026 analysis. The condition is a major complication of diabetes, yet early diagnosis stays difficult because clear markers are lacking. The team combined microarray and sequencing datasets from a public archive.

Network analysis and machine learning narrowed 49 altered genes down to three hub genes, named SYK, APAF1, and ADAM10 in the study. Their patterns separated patients from controls well in test curves. Mouse models and patient samples then confirmed the expression changes. These candidates could support earlier detection, and they point to pathways worth probing for treatment.
pmc-13221911:
Xi Xiao and colleagues track sexually transmitted infections among people with HIV in China across fourteen years, in a 2026 multicenter cohort study. Records covered 32,961 people who started antiretroviral therapy between 2010 and 2024 at two southern treatment centers. Five major infections were traced through linked clinic and laboratory records, including repeat episodes.

About one participant in seven had at least one infection after starting therapy, and overall incidence rose over the period. Syphilis stayed the leading infection, followed by HPV. Younger age, male sex, and being a man who has sex with men predicted infection. The authors argue HIV and STI prevention should be delivered together rather than apart.
pmc-13222511:
Efstratios Kouskos and co-authors report a twisted, dead appendiceal mucocele causing an acute abdomen, in a 2026 case report. A 68-year-old woman arrived with twelve hours of severe lower abdominal pain, rebound tenderness, and raised inflammatory markers. CT scanning showed a cystic mass behind the uterus, about nine centimeters long, with calcified walls.

Emergency surgery found the mucus-filled appendix fully twisted and necrotic. Surgeons removed it intact, a key step because rupture could spill mucin into the abdomen and seed a dangerous condition. Pathology confirmed the mucocele. Recovery was uncomplicated, and she remained well three months later. A cystic pelvic mass with acute pain should raise this rare possibility.
pmc-13223111:
Shuaib and co-authors present a 2026 review on using fungi to clean crude oil from deep soil in the Niger Delta. Decades of spills have wrecked soil and water, killed mangrove forests, and hurt local livelihoods. Standard cleanup methods leave a large gap, the authors argue, above all at depth. They assess fungal cleanup, called mycoremediation, as a better fit for the region.

Fungal threads can push deep into soil where bacteria and surface methods cannot reach. The fungi attack oil with broad enzymes and also soak up pollutants on their surfaces. Local heat and acid soil shape how well the method works. The review makes the case for field trials of fungal cleanup.
pmc-13224311:
Alessia Caccamo and colleagues propose a 2026 improved method for neural mass models, which give a simple account of how large groups of brain cells behave. Fitting such models to brain recordings depends heavily on prior assumptions about its settings, which are hard to measure directly. Poor priors can bias the whole inference.

Their method first uses a genetic algorithm, a search process modelled on evolution, to find value regions that produce realistic model behaviour. Those regions then become informed priors for standard Bayesian fitting. Tested on two independent brain-recording datasets, the combined approach predicted data better than either method alone. It also recovered known signatures of psychiatric illness and drug effects.
pmc-13225111:
Ansh Kapil and a large collaboration test a 2026 software method that predicts who gains from a targeted stomach cancer drug. The drug, trastuzumab deruxtecan, attacks cells carrying the HER2 protein, and entry normally rests on a rough staining score. Software instead measures HER2 levels across tumour slides from two trials.

Two software-derived signatures stood out: a spatial proximity score and the density of HER2-positive cells within the tumour tissue. Patients flagged positive by these measures lived significantly longer on the drug in the first trial. The same signatures then validated in the second trial, suggesting finer measurement could sharpen patient selection.
pmc-13227311:
Jyothish Nair and co-authors test a traditional Indian herbal iron powder used for anemia, in a 2026 study. The powder is made from a leafy plant by a special Ayurvedic method said to load it with iron and help the body take that iron up. Iron deficiency anemia is common, and a plant-based option with sound proof would be welcome.

Powders made from the plant's leaves, roots, and whole plant held more iron after the special processing than the raw plant did. In a lab model of digestion and in human gut cells, the iron was released and taken up well. The authors say the results give the old method a scientific footing worth building on.
pmc-13232811:
Jade Michele Gilchrist and colleagues ask in 2026 whether state abortion limits after 2022 slowed growth in women applying to medical school. National data from the schools association covered 2018 to 2025 across forty-five states and jurisdictions. States were grouped by whether their rules protect or restrict abortion access.

The women share of applicants rose nationwide across the period by several points. After the court reversal, that rise ran slower in restrictive states than in protective ones, by a modest yearly gap. Enrolled student shares showed no clear split between the two groups. Small yearly gaps can compound into a thinner, less even doctor pipeline in states already short of physicians.
pmc-13232911:
Saib Ahmed and Farig Yousuf Sadeque published a 2026 comparative study on software that drafts clinical notes from recorded doctor-patient conversations. Writing notes takes clinicians much time, and open conversation datasets are scarce. The pair tested whether large language models could be adapted cheaply, using parameter-efficient fine-tuning, a method that adjusts only a small part of a model.

They trained Mistral, Meditron, and Llama models on 1,700 conversation and note pairs. Meditron-7B and Llama3-8B earned the strongest scores on standard overlap and meaning measures, with Mistral-7B close behind. A physician also rated the drafts for accuracy, completeness, and readability. The results suggest small, efficiently tuned models can produce usable notes without heavy computing resources.
pmc-13233011:
Ernest M Taku and colleagues published a 2026 study on personalizing insulin dosing for type 1 diabetes with reinforcement learning, a form of artificial intelligence that learns by trial and reward. Fixed insulin schedules struggle because glucose responds to meals, activity, stress, and the body's own rhythms. The team built a deep Q-network agent that adjusts dose suggestions from continuous glucose monitor data.

Training used the OhioT1DM dataset, covering eight weeks of glucose readings, insulin doses, and activity records for twelve people. The agent viewed the previous two hours of data and chose among small dose steps, earning rewards for keeping glucose between 70 and 180 milligrams per deciliter. The paper evaluates predicted against actual glucose traces, aiming at safer, more personal dosing support.
pmc-13233411:
Hassan Izzeddin Sarsak brings a standard wheelchair skills questionnaire to Arabic speakers for the first time. Over eighty million people need wheelchairs, yet without training many never master the skills that make the devices liberating. The Wheelchair Skills Test Questionnaire sets a baseline for training, but no validated Arabic version existed.

The translation followed five stages, from forward translation through expert review to field testing, and covered both manual and powered chair versions. Forty-eight users at three rehabilitation hospitals, averaging thirty-six years old and seven years of chair experience, took the final forms. Both versions were highly consistent internally, and repeat testing two weeks apart agreed almost perfectly. Scores also matched two established Arabic scales. The author offers the tools for clinics and studies across the Arabic-speaking world.
pmc-13233511:
Ivy Guofang Sun and colleagues published a 2026 survey on dental erosion among adults in Hong Kong. Erosion wears away tooth enamel through acid, from food, drink, or stomach reflux. An online questionnaire reached adults aged 25 to 45 through a public opinion research panel, and 1,452 valid responses were analyzed.

Nearly everyone reported at least one possible erosion symptom, most often yellowing teeth and sensitivity to temperature or acid. Over a third reported three or more symptoms, yet only about thirty-eight percent had consulted a dentist. Four in ten had never heard of dental erosion. Sour snacks, acid reflux, middle age, and frequent juice or fruit vinegar intake raised the odds of heavy symptoms. The authors call for public education and earlier dental checks.
pmc-13234211:
Lirui Liu and eight co-authors deliver an immune-calming drug to the eye surface in charged fat bubbles to treat dry eye disease, in a study from 2026. Dry eye mixes surface damage with immune imbalance, and ordinary drops wash away before working. A stickier, targeted carrier could fix both flaws.

The positively charged bubbles clung to the eye's mucus layer, stayed longer, and let more drug through. In a mouse dry eye model they sped surface repair, steadied the tear film, and saved mucus-producing cells and tear glands. Inflammatory signals fell in eye and gland tissue, and the balance between two T cell types was restored.
pmc-13235411:
Seeba Zachariah and co-authors wrote in 2026 about medical pharmacists prescribing heart drugs inside a UAE teaching health system. Their account draws on the team's own work experience, gathered through a talk-based shared method. Coding of their notes yielded twelve themes grouped by what the work involves, when it happens, and why they do it. Heart drug therapy grows more complex as options and rules grow.

The work covers checking patients, tuning doses, and starting proven heart treatments. Extra training, trust between fields, and joint care setups made that work possible in their setting. Motives centred on independence at work, faster and better drug use, and real results for patients. The authors call for clear pathways for the role, newer training routes, and rules that support it. Their insider view aims to help other systems expand pharmacist scope safely.
pmc-13235511:
Wen Lin and co-authors used in 2026 fat storage droplets from cells as carriers to deliver a light-activated drug to mitochondria. Lipid droplets hold fatty compounds inside a thin shell and naturally interact with mitochondria, the cell's energy factories. Curcumin, a yellow plant compound, can kill cells when lit yet dissolves poorly in water. Droplets loaded with curcumin were taken up by cells and gathered around mitochondria.

Shining blue light on treated cells raised damaging reactive oxygen levels more than fivefold in the experiments. A key mitochondrial enzyme switched off and the membrane voltage collapsed after irradiation. Those changes drove the treated cells into programmed death in culture. Droplet size could be tuned by adjusting the conditions under which donor cells grew. The authors present droplets as promising natural carriers for targeted light therapy against cancer.
pmc-13236611:
Joanna Filipowska and Antonio Rossi introduced in 2026 a journal collection on inflammatory signals as markers in type 1 diabetes. The disease is now viewed as a long, progressive autoimmune process that starts well before diagnosis. Traditional markers such as autoantibodies, blood sugar measures, and a hormone remnant track staging but reveal little about mechanism. Inflammation and stress inside insulin-producing cells appear central to how the disease begins and advances.

Contributions in the collection range from tiny regulatory RNAs in blood to single-cell gene profiling of immune tissue. Several small RNAs discussed act both as measurable signals and as possible treatment targets in the papers. Their levels mirror cell stress, immune activation, and disease progression in patients studied. Proteomic and other large-scale methods add further candidate markers beyond the classic panel. The editors frame these signals as a bridge between mechanism and precision care for patients.
pmc-13237111:
Xu Junhui and Su Mengyun pin a liver cancer's spread on one membrane protein, ADAM15. The protein belongs to a family of molecular scissors and shows up in many tumors. In liver cancer cells, turning it down slowed growth, movement, and invasion, while turning it up did the opposite.

Silencing it also pushed cancer cells toward death and reversed a shape-shifting program tumors use to spread. In mice, tumors with less ADAM15 grew slower and seeded fewer lung colonies. The protein works by switching on the JNK and p38 signaling routes. Blocking it could become a treatment angle.
pmc-13237711:
Gianluca Lucchese, Rajdeep Bilkhu, Antonio Bivona, and Vincenzo Caruso published a technique paper in 2026 on heart valve surgery. Heavy calcium crust on the mitral valve ring makes surgery risky. Scraping all the crust away can cause grave harm, so some teams skip full cleaning. A newer hybrid route places a catheter valve into the mitral spot during open surgery.

The paper sets out the team's precise steps for that implant. It stresses two points: picking the right valve size, and the exact phase when the valve is opened in place. The route is still off-label and lacks shared standards. The authors offer their method as a step toward a standard for high-risk patients. They frame it as a safer path than full crust removal.
pmc-13237811:
Yu and colleagues ask whether allergic diseases and tooth decay truly travel together. Asthma, allergic rhinitis, and eczema share trends and risk factors with dental caries, and both sets of conditions wear down quality of life and raise care costs. Coincidence of timing, though, is not proof of any real link.

The team combined two approaches: a systematic review with meta-analysis of past studies, and Mendelian randomisation, which uses genes as natural experiments to test cause. Together they weigh both association and possible causation between each allergy and decay. A causal answer would change advice, joining dental checks to allergy care for children who carry both risks.
pmc-13238111:
Jin and colleagues assemble the complete genome of a prized jujube cultivar and compare it across the species. Jujube fruit is valued as food and medicine, and the tree shrugs off drought and salty soils that kill other crops. The cultivar Huizao now has a gap-free, end-to-end genome, a first-class reference for breeders.

The team then built a pan-genome from many jujube types to hunt genes behind fruit texture. Texture decides taste, shelf life, and whether shoppers buy, so it is a prime breeding target. Their comparison flags the genetic differences that make some fruits crisp and others soft, giving breeders markers to select on.
pmc-13238211:
Chang-Zhu Pei and co-authors review a family of enzymes that may drive cervical cancer and shape its treatment. Their 2026 review covers deubiquitinating enzymes, which remove ubiquitin tags from proteins and so control whether those proteins survive or are destroyed. Cervical cancer still kills many women worldwide, and tumors often return or resist therapy.

The review explains how these enzymes steady cancer-promoting proteins, weaken tumor suppressors, and tune key signaling pathways. Several are also tied to how tumors respond to radiation and chemotherapy, including in virus-driven cases. That makes them candidate drug targets and markers for choosing treatment. The authors weigh the evidence for bringing enzyme blockers into the clinic. They stress that much of the promise still rests on laboratory work.
pmc-13239011:
Brahim Hni and co-authors report a 2026 crystal structure study of a sulfur and nitrogen ring compound. The work maps the exact shape of the molecule and how copies of it pack in a solid. Such maps help chemists link a compound form to its traits and uses.

The main ring takes a screw-boat shape and folds along its sulfur to nitrogen axis. Copies pack in wave-like layers, held in part by weak links from hydrogen to carbon rings. A surface study found that hydrogen to hydrogen contacts form the largest share of the packing, about half. Energy checks showed that spread-out forces, not charge forces, hold the layers together most.
pmc-13239511:
Zuzana Chlumská and ten co-authors wrote this 2026 study on nutrient levels in the highest herbs of the Western Himalaya. Tissue nutrients show how plants adapt, and they shift both between species and within one species along a slope. The team measured carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus in leaves of twenty-two species, and nitrogen and phosphorus in roots of fifteen, from 4,560 to 6,150 meters up.

Across species, leaf nitrogen and phosphorus fell with height while the carbon share rose. Within a species, leaf nitrogen mostly climbed with height instead. The surprise came at the very top: herbs near 6,000 meters held rich stores of both nutrients. The authors read this as a high metabolic demand: leaves must pack in the machinery to gain carbon fast in a very short growing season.
pmc-13239711:
Ellen Goossens and co-authors present a 2026 protocol for a scoping review of artificial intelligence chatbots in health care. Such chatbots, which converse using language processing and machine learning, now support paperwork, health education, and chronic disease care, but the overall evidence picture remains scattered.

The review will search six databases up to September 2025 for studies in four languages that report clinical outcomes, patient satisfaction, or efficiency gains. An AI screening tool will help sort records, while two reviewers check selections independently. Findings will be organised by chatbot type and care setting in evidence tables, highlighting gaps where future studies are most needed.
pmc-13240011:
Zhi-Jun Li and colleagues published a brain research study in 2026 on Alzheimer's disease in mice. Clearing amyloid beta from the brain depends on transport proteins. One key transporter sits in the blood vessel walls of the brain. What controls that transporter's levels was unclear.

The team focused on a circulating protein fragment called pro-CTSD. Its levels rise in Alzheimer's model mice. Mice engineered for high levels showed less of the transporter. Brain amyloid clearance suffered as a result. Lab imaging showed the fragment binding the transporter directly. That binding pulled the transporter inside the cell for destruction. Crossing the mice with Alzheimer's models worsened deposits and memory problems.
pmc-13240111:
Kohki Nakamura and co-authors examine the electrical fingerprints of atrial fibrillation trigger points in a 2026 study.
