Ablation treatment targets the spots that spark this chaotic heart rhythm, usually the pulmonary veins, yet triggers are normally hunted at the moment the rhythm starts, not while it runs.

Using an ultra-high-resolution mapping system in forty-five patients, the team measured signal timing at known trigger sites during ongoing fibrillation. Trigger veins showed a distinctly shorter minimum cycle length than other heart regions, meaning brief bursts of very rapid activity. That single measure separated trigger sites well in statistical testing. The finding could help when standard trigger mapping proves inconclusive.
pmc-13240211:
Zhi-Ling Li and co-authors link a gut-friendly diet score with rheumatoid arthritis rates in a 2026 nationwide American study. The dietary index for gut microbiota rates eating habits by their expected effect on gut microbes, and its connection with this autoimmune joint disease had never been tested at population scale.

Survey data from nearly thirty thousand adults between 2007 and 2020 showed about seven percent reporting a doctor's diagnosis of the arthritis. Each extra point on the diet index came with modestly lower odds of having the disease, and the highest scorers had roughly a quarter lower odds than the lowest. The relationship ran in a straight line with no subgroup standing out.
pmc-13240611:
Ten authors, led by Lauren Mitteer, review insulinomas in children in this 2026 paper. An insulinoma is a tumor that makes too much insulin and so drives blood sugar too low. Such tumors are the top cause of that state in adults, but they also occur in childhood.

In children, finding and locating the tumor can be hard. It can also be tough to tell an insulinoma from congenital hyperinsulinism, a birth condition with like signs. The team looked back at confirmed cases treated at one academic children's hospital from 2006 to 2024. They summed up how the children presented, what tests showed, and how well each method found the tumor. Treatment routes and outcomes were also reviewed. Their aim is to sharpen diagnosis for a rare but serious cause of low blood sugar in the young.
pmc-13240911:
Sutton and a large Benin-US team studied how group antenatal care builds pregnant women's confidence in Atlantique Department, Benin. Groups of women with similar due dates meet for checks and shared learning. Ten focus groups gathered one hundred twenty-nine participants. A household survey compared their experience with individual care.

Women drew confidence from mastering tasks, peer encouragement, and watching others succeed. Ninety-six percent of surveyed group participants would choose group care again. Yet many said providers still left some questions unanswered, even in groups. Fuller answers, the authors argue, would strengthen the persuasion channel further.
pmc-13241511:
Shi and colleagues at Bengbu Medical University built a single-cell atlas of blood immune cells from Guillain-Barré syndrome patients. The syndrome is an autoimmune attack on peripheral nerves that weakens muscles. The team sequenced peripheral blood mononuclear cells one cell at a time. Their dataset is offered as a public resource for therapy research.

Samples came from three patients and two healthy controls, and more than fifty-one thousand cells passed quality checks. The team cross-checked cell activation patterns against mouse single-cell data and rat transcriptomes. A pathway linking T-cell maturation to chemokine release emerged as a central disease hub. The authors argue the resource can guide immune-calming treatments.
pmc-13241611:
Khan and colleagues in Karachi report an infant whose biliary atresia came with mirrored organs and a heart defect. Biliary atresia blocks bile flow and is a leading cause of liver failure in babies. The three-month-old girl had been jaundiced since birth. Tests ruled out infection, metabolic, and hormone causes.

Imaging showed a small gallbladder, the triangular cord sign, and full situs inversus. Heart scanning found a small hole between the ventricles, and liver biopsy confirmed the diagnosis. The family declined both the Kasai operation and transplantation after counseling. The infant died about a month after diagnosis, and the authors stress earlier recognition and family support.
pmc-13242511:
Eike-Benjamin Braune and colleagues screened a large compound library for new ways to switch off the Notch signaling pathway. Their paper appeared in Scientific Reports in 2026. Notch guides cell differentiation across most organs, and when it misfires it drives disease and cancer, yet no Notch drug has reached wide clinical use. The team built a cell-based reporter system and sifted nearly thirty-eight thousand small molecules, then filtered out look-alikes of a known drug class.

Five candidate hits with unrelated chemical backbones survived the triage. One proved to block DHODH, an enzyme cells use to build DNA building blocks, and a known DHODH blocker also turned out to be a potent Notch inhibitor. That crossover suggests the enzyme sits closer to Notch control than previously thought. The authors propose DHODH inhibition as a route toward Notch-targeting medicines. Their screening pipeline offers a template for hunts.
pmc-13242811:
Xingyu Huang and Jiao Hua present a 2026 study building a prediction model for emergency cesarean during planned vaginal birth with an epidural. First-time mothers receiving epidural pain relief sometimes convert to cesarean, and early warning would help planning. Records came from over a thousand such women at one Chinese hospital.

Six factors independently predicted conversion: mother age, fever during labor, amniotic fluid character, fetal heart pattern, oxytocin use, and membrane rupture timing. Conversion rates were similar in the building and checking groups. The model sorted risk well in training and acceptably in the later validation group. A visual scoring chart accompanies the model. The authors suggest it can support early risk sorting, while wider testing is still needed.
pmc-13244211:
Jeanne Haegy and co-authors ask whether lung cysts show up often in patients with hairy cell leukemia, a slow blood cancer. A sister disease that shares its gene faults scars the lungs with cysts and nodules. Both diseases often carry the same gene change in a growth pathway, which hints at a shared lung effect.

Using a French registry, the team gathered patients who had detailed chest scans at diagnosis or during follow-up, with no infection or heart cause to explain lung findings. Their letter sets out the cohort and the scans that let them count cysts and compare the two patient groups.
pmc-13244511:
Stephen Ojiambo Wandera and colleagues measured depression among older people in rural eastern Uganda and asked what travels with it. Their cross-sectional study appeared in Global Health Action in 2026. It surveyed 598 people aged sixty and over in the Busia and Namayingo districts. More than half reported moderate to severe symptoms, a burden the authors call neglected where mental health services barely reach.

Several hardships doubled or nearly tripled the odds. Depending on children for a living, cooking and lighting with firewood, living alone or feeling socially cut off, and having fallen or fearing falls all stood out in the modeling. Each marker points at poverty, isolation, or frailty rather than at brain chemistry alone. The authors call for screening and treatment built into the services older rural people already touch. Depression at this scale, they argue, is a service delivery failure as much as a diagnosis.
pmc-13246211:
Anisha Turner and co-authors pilot a survey in a 2026 study on emergency doctors. Excess force by police is a public health issue tied to high blood pressure, trauma stress, and depression in those hurt. Emergency doctors are often the first to treat such injuries, yet the toll on the doctors themselves has barely been studied.

A survey built by emergency doctors and psychiatrists asked about work life, mental well being, and the clinic climate. It probed how seeing and knowing of force cases weighs on staff. The pilot tests whether the survey works and what it reveals, ahead of a larger study on support for front line doctors.
pmc-13246411:
Vijay Ebenezer, Pradeepa Ganesh, and Manicka Vinayagar review jaw correction surgery outcomes in a 2026 systematic review. The surgery realigns jaws in people with face and tooth deformities. A full picture of benefits, harms, and life quality gains had been missing.

The review gathered 65 studies with 6,482 patients through the end of 2024. Jaw angles improved by clear margins, and most patients held their new alignment past one year. About a third faced complications, mostly minor ones. Numbness was common yet faded within a year for most. Life quality scores improved a lot, and satisfaction ran high. The authors still urge careful selection and long follow-up.
pmc-13246811:
A correction notice in Aging Clinical and Experimental Research, published in 2026, concerns the abstracts of a major bone-health congress. The supplement collected hundreds of research abstracts from the 2025 World Congress on Osteoporosis, Osteoarthritis and Musculoskeletal Diseases. That meeting is run by the International Osteoporosis Foundation with a European partner society.

The corrected version replaces the original supplement. The record researchers cite now matches what the publisher intends to stand. The abstracts span fracture risk tools, bone density testing, osteoporosis drugs, and health-service audits from many countries. Readers who cited specific abstracts from the 2025 proceedings should check this corrected version. The correction, not the first printing, is the authoritative text.
pmc-13247311:
Jung, Lee, Kim, and co-authors built a two-enzyme cascade that starves tumors and then poisons them, in this 2026 Biomaterials Research paper. The first enzyme, arginine decarboxylase, wakes only in the acidic conditions inside tumors, where it consumes arginine, an amino acid tumors need, leaving behind a compound called agmatine. A second enzyme, diamine oxidase, rides in the same nanoparticle carrier and converts that agmatine into hydrogen peroxide, a cell-killing oxidant.

In cell cultures the cascade both halted tumor growth and pushed cells into programmed death, while healthy-pH tissues were spared because the first enzyme stays asleep there. In mice the carrier accumulated in tumors and worked far better than free enzymes. The authors claim the first animal validation of this enzyme as a tumor-selective therapy.
pmc-13248111:
Muema and co-authors reviewed liver cancer treatment in this 2026 Scientifica article. Hepatocellular carcinoma causes most primary liver cancers and many cancer deaths worldwide. Current drugs often work poorly, cause harsh side effects, and face resistance, so the review asks whether compounds from plants could add useful options.

The authors survey plant chemicals and the cell pathways they affect, including routes that drive growth, spread, and cell death. They also cover tiny carrier particles that can deliver these compounds to tumors more reliably. Their conclusion is cautious: natural products look promising beside standard therapy, but better delivery and more clinical proof are still needed.
pmc-13248211:
Goulas, Megalokonomou, and Sotirakopoulos tested how experts react to wrong scores in a 2026 PNAS Nexus experiment. Education specialists graded the same student work, paired with a score that was deliberately too harsh or too kind. Half the scores were labeled as coming from AI, and half as coming from a person.

When the bad score was harsh, experts moved less toward fairness if they thought AI had set it. When the score was lenient, the label made little difference. The authors trace the gap to how capable and responsible experts judged the algorithm to be, a warning for anyone designing human oversight of automated grading.
pmc-13249611:
Tamrakar and co-authors built a rat model of autism by combining two early insults, in a 2026 study. Human autism likely arises from several causes stacking together, so single-cause animal models may miss the picture. Pregnant rats received valproic acid, a known risk factor, or their pups were deprived of oxygen after birth, or both, with a fourth group left untreated for comparison.

Pups in every insult group showed delayed reflexes and altered behavior in maze, open field, and social tests. Brain tissue showed lost Purkinje cells and widespread neuron damage, worst in the combined group. The authors offer the double-insult model for screening future autism treatments.
pmc-13249711:
Muraki and a Japanese team built a model that flags likely sleep apnea patients from everyday records, in a 2026 study. Their target was apnea serious enough to be treated with a CPAP machine. Training data linked insurance claims, health checkups, and a personal health record app, yielding nearly nineteen million observation windows from about one point nine million people.

The gradient-boosted model separated treated cases from others with strong accuracy. Among the riskiest one percent of predictions, more than a quarter truly had treated apnea. Male sex led the predictors, followed by age, body mass, and waist size, and the personal health records added real value. The authors propose using the score to nudge high-risk people toward sleep testing.
pmc-13249911:
Jiang and co-authors pooled surgical evidence on a newer neck artery procedure, in a 2026 meta-analysis. Transcarotid artery revascularization threads a stent through a small neck incision, aiming to clear silent carotid narrowing with less risk than open surgery or the older groin-route stent. The reviewers gathered studies of symptom-free patients and compared all three options on stroke, death, and heart attack.

Against the groin-route stent, the neck procedure won clearly on early stroke and death. Against open surgery it tied on stroke and death at thirty days, caused fewer heart attacks, yet lost slightly on combined outcomes by one year. Because nearly all data were observational, the authors ask for randomized trials.
pmc-13250111:
Hye Seong Jang and Gyeong Hee Ryu made and studied sea-urchin-shaped copper oxide particles in this 2026 materials paper. Copper oxides are cheap, common, and useful in electronics and energy devices, but plain particles have little surface area and lose charge quickly.

Using a soap-like helper chemical, the team grew spheres covered in fine needles, mixing two forms of copper oxide in one particle. X-ray and imaging tests confirmed both forms were present, with the mix shifting gradually from core to surface. A focused electron beam made the spiky structure pack tighter, showing how it holds up. Such high-area particles could serve in sensors and catalysts.
pmc-13250211:
Grundy and colleagues examine drug company support programs that many Canadians must use to afford pricey specialty medicines. Their 2026 BMJ Open study draws on interviews with fifty-two patients, clinicians, industry staff, payers, and policymakers, plus field notes and documents. Canada's public insurance does not cover most outpatient prescription drugs, which makes these programs central.

Participants described the programs as the default route to costly medicines, yet help felt uneven, stressful, and sometimes needless. The authors identify a parallel private system growing beside public care, with access decided at company discretion. Programs also seemed shaped around doctors' habits more than patients' needs. The paper urges policymakers to build patient-centered systems that do not depend on manufacturer goodwill.
pmc-13251111:
Lim and Sikri introduce a journal collection on patient satisfaction in prosthodontics, the craft of replacing and restoring teeth. Their 2026 BMC Oral Health editorial calls satisfaction one of the key measures of success in this kind of care. The collection gathers work on what satisfaction means for denture and crown patients.

The editors say the papers take up what satisfaction means in this field and how studies put a number on it. It also weighs how new tools, clearer talk with patients, what patients expect, and social and cultural setting shape satisfaction. Known gaps in the evidence get mapped so future studies can aim better. The stated goal is research and practice that deliver genuinely patient-centered prosthetic care.
pmc-13251711:
Joy Hanoun, Pascale Beloni, and Jean Toniolo assess whether advanced practice nursing could take root in Lebanon, reporting in 2026. Lebanon's health system is strained by nurse emigration, fragmented services, and rising chronic disease. Advanced practice nurses, trained to take on parts of care usually reserved for doctors, are proposed as one remedy, yet the role has no formal footing in the country.

The mixed-methods study surveyed health professionals and service users and interviewed stakeholders across hospitals and primary care centers. Support ran high: 87.7 percent of professionals backed the new roles, and nearly all expected gains for chronic disease care and coordination. Most service users said they would accept follow-up from such a nurse. Interviews tempered the optimism with barriers, above all the missing legal framework, unsettled pay and scope rules, few training routes, and expected resistance. The authors offer the findings as a planning base for policymakers.
pmc-13252311:
Shriya Mitna and co-authors compare pain after root canal work in this 2026 trial. Pain after this dental treatment is common and can put patients off having it. The filling paste used to seal the root may affect that pain, so the team tested five kinds of sealers.

In all, 135 patients with a painful tooth tip condition in single-rooted premolars were assigned by chance to five equal groups. Pain was scored at several times after treatment. A glass-based sealer gave the lowest pain scores, while a zinc-based sealer gave higher pain in the first few days. Pain eased slowly in all groups over time. The authors suggest the glass-based option may ease early pain.
pmc-13252911:
Nguyen Thi Kim Lien and colleagues report whole exome sequencing results for six Vietnamese patients with inborn errors of immunity in a 2026 case series. These rare genetic disorders cripple parts of the immune system, and over five hundred genes can cause them. Similar early symptoms across different genes make pinpointing the cause hard without sequencing.

Sequencing found a causative variant in each of the six patients. The genes involved were IL2RG, BTK in two patients, STAT3, STAT6, and NHEJ1, all central to immune cell development or signaling. One variant, in STAT3, had never been reported in a patient before. Each result was checked against international criteria for judging whether a variant causes disease. The authors say firm genetic diagnosis sharpened treatment choices for these patients. They argue wider access to sequencing would improve care for immune disorders in Vietnam.
pmc-13253111:
Grigol Keshelava and two co-authors reported a neck artery bypass case in 2026. A 61-year-old man with high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and tobacco use had four brief episodes of slurred speech over two months. Scans showed his right common, internal, and external carotid arteries all blocked. A small, unusually placed branch vessel kept blood flowing backward into the internal carotid beyond the block.

The left side also had severe narrowing, so surgeons first cleared that artery. A month later they built a bypass from the subclavian artery to a rebuilt carotid fork on the right, using a ringed synthetic graft. Care was taken to clamp above the helper branch so its flow stayed safe. Flow was restored without complications.
pmc-13253911:
Angelo Navas and co-authors re-analyze, in a 2026 paper, a major diabetes trial to ask whether losing more weight on the drug meant fewer heart events. The drug, semaglutide, lowers blood sugar and trims weight. Its heart protection is proven, but the weight link was unclear.

The original trial randomized people with type 2 diabetes against placebo. This later analysis groups the 1,479 drug-arm participants by how much weight they lost. It then compares rates of heart attack, stroke, and cardiovascular death across those groups. If benefit tracks weight, dosing and support could aim at the scale. If not, the drug protects the heart by other routes, and weight is a side story.
pmc-13254311: Lisanne Bogaard, Juraj Mesik, and Andrew Oxenham issued a 2026 author correction to their study of how listeners pick out voices in polyphonic music. The correction fixes an error in calculating the sensitivity index d-prime, which affected a subset of Experiment 2 data where performance sat at ceiling or floor. The authors state the changes do not alter the main results or conclusions, so this notice can only be described at that level.
pmc-13254811:
Neven Aref and Hannah Wesley test vitamin E in a denture liner in a 2026 lab study. Soft liners cushion dentures but can grow rough and host fungi. A commercial acrylic liner was mixed with vitamin E at three low levels and compared with a plain control for cell safety, antifungal action, and surface roughness.

The middle mix gave the best results, with the highest cell survival at 48.0 percent and the lowest roughness. Cell survival fell at the highest level but stayed above the control. No mix blocked the fungus Candida albicans. The authors call the findings early and urge fuller testing.
pmc-13254911:
Wenhui Liu and a large team review the two-way talk between nerves and bones. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The brain-bone axis, as it is called, links how bones grow and heal with how the brain works and decays. Signals run both ways, through nerve chemicals, hormones, immune marks, and tiny sacs.

Bone-born signals, such as a bone hormone and a pressure sensor, can shape nerve work in turn. Smart materials add a care route: gels and nano tools can steer the shared zone and carry drugs across hard walls. New tools, from gene scans to organ chips, push the field. Low reach across organs is a key block.
pmc-13255211:
Zhigang Wang and colleagues study a protein pair behind kidney scarring in diabetes in a 2026 paper. Diabetic kidney disease is a leading cause of kidney failure, and its hallmark is fibrosis, or stiff scar tissue. The team used sugar-stressed kidney cells and diabetic mice fed a high-fat diet.

A growth factor called FGF11 was high in diseased kidneys, and blocking it cut cell growth and scarring. Silencing a partner protein, USP22, sped FGF11 breakdown and eased kidney injury in mice. Restoring FGF11 undid that gain. The authors propose the USP22-FGF11 pair as a drug target.
pmc-13255711:
Carmen Hannemann and co-authors report a 2026 laboratory study of iRhom2, a protein that helps macrophages release the inflammatory signal TNF-alpha. Macrophage-driven inflammation starts atherosclerosis, the plaque buildup behind heart attacks and strokes. The team studied macrophages lacking iRhom2 to see what changed.

The altered macrophages still engulfed particles, survived stress, and multiplied normally. They put out less TNF-alpha and more of the calming signal IL-10, though. Fluid from these cells also made blood vessel cells produce fewer of the sticky molecules that recruit more immune cells. The authors suggest blocking iRhom2 could quiet the earliest stage of vessel inflammation while leaving everyday macrophage duties intact, a profile that safer anti-inflammatory strategies would need.
pmc-13256011:
Jiahao Liu and colleagues report a 2026 study of GALNT7, an enzyme that attaches sugars to proteins, in gastrointestinal stromal tumors. These tumors run on abnormal KIT signaling, and resistance to KIT-blocking drugs remains a serious problem. The team combined bulk, protein-level, and single-cell data to find which sugar-adding enzymes matter most.

GALNT7 emerged as the hub, raised in tumors and tied to poorer progression-free survival. In cell and mouse experiments it sped tumor growth, movement, and graft formation. The mechanism ran through KIT itself: GALNT7 attached a specific sugar mark that stabilized the KIT protein and kept its growth signals on. A sugar-blocking compound reversed these effects and shrank grafts. The authors nominate GALNT7 as both a warning marker and a drug target.
pmc-13256811:
Zhao, Guo, and Cong identified which proteins make mango cross-react with other foods in allergic patients. Mango allergy is rising with consumption, but its cross-reactions are poorly mapped. The team used sequence comparison software to predict candidate proteins, then tested blood serum from mango-allergic patients for antibody binding to other foods. They also synthesized short protein fragments to pinpoint the exact binding stretches.

Patient antibodies reacted with peanut, wheat, cashew, pistachio, and hazelnut; the wheat and hazelnut links had not been reported before. The team found new shared fragments, including one between a mango protein and wheat, and several between mango profilin and a peanut protein. These maps of shared epitopes help explain why some mango-allergic patients react to seemingly unrelated foods, and they can guide better allergy testing.
pmc-13256911:
Dai Ma leads a 2026 enzyme engineering study aimed at making nicotinamide mononucleotide, known as NMN, more efficiently. NMN helps the body make NAD+, a molecule needed for energy and repair. The work centers on an enzyme called nicotinamide riboside kinase.

A redesigned variant of the enzyme doubled its activity and lasted twice as long at warm temperature. Careful tuning of reaction conditions then pushed NMN yield above ninety-four percent. Adding a second enzyme to recycle ATP, the cell energy carrier, lifted yield still higher at a stronger feed level. Readers interested in greener manufacturing get a concrete route toward larger-scale production. The results also show how small protein changes can improve an industrial process.
pmc-13257411:
Lorena Ciumărnean and co-authors present a 2026 case report of severe metabolic collapse during kidney cancer care. A fifty-four-year-old woman had metastatic clear cell kidney cancer with sarcomatoid features, an aggressive variant. Earlier checkpoint therapy had already caused gland inflammation and thyroid failure before later drug treatment.

She arrived dehydrated with repeated vomiting, deep weakness, and dangerous blood chemistry, including high potassium, low sodium, and low sugar. Kidney injury and low blood counts compounded the picture. Fluids, electrolyte correction, and supportive care restored chemistry and kidney function. Muscle weakness raised concern for an immune nerve or muscle event, though potassium alone could explain part of it. Oncologists get a warning case on layered toxicity. Careful differential diagnosis and team management are the authors' central plea.
pmc-13257811:
Ching-Han Tseng and co-authors trace both-eye progression of wet macular degeneration in a 2026 real-world case series. The timeline from first-eye diagnosis to second-eye conversion was reconstructed, along with visit habits and injection counts. Baseline features of the still-healthy second eye were tested as predictors.

Second eyes converted in about two years when the first eye stayed active, versus more than six years when the first eye quieted. Once both eyes needed treatment, yearly injections jumped more than threefold. Patients whose first eye settled visited less often, which may have widened the detection gap. Surface abnormalities in the second eye at baseline strongly predicted conversion. Retina clinics gain a vigilance rule: quiet first eyes should not relax second-eye surveillance, especially with early surface changes present.
pmc-13258111:
Alaa Hamdan and Ziad Al Nabhani reframe fatness through the gut's microbes, in a review of fresh finds. Their review, from two thousand twenty-six, looks at the loss of key works, more than the loss of kinds.

Fatness and its ills stay top world health tasks. Past fare size, proofs now tie gut-microbe fault to the body's churn. The team finds the mark of fatness is less which kinds live there, and more which works break: short fat-acid yield, bile churn, a mood-path feed, and the gut wall's seal. Those breaks spur blood-borne germ traces, dull gut-full marks, and foul the tie of gut to brain and liver. Food-fiber boosts are among the cures tried.
pmc-13258311:
Nisachon Siripaiboonpong and co-authors link gum disease with carrying many long-term conditions in a 2026 analysis of two giant cohorts. UK Biobank supplied half a million people, and a United States nutrition survey added ten thousand more with clinical gum examinations. Multimorbidity meant living with at least two chronic diseases.

About half of participants in both cohorts carried multiple conditions. Gum disease raised the odds of multimorbidity modestly in the United Kingdom data and more clearly in the American data. Links strengthened in adults under sixty and grew in a dose pattern with gum severity. Blood inflammation markers explained part of the association in mediation tests. Public health readers gain population-scale support for mouth-body integration. Dental care belongs in chronic disease prevention talks, especially for younger adults.
pmc-13258611:
Conghui Li and colleagues put wheat seedlings through drought, salt, and heat, alone and in punishing pairs. Real fields increasingly deliver these stresses together as the climate warms. Using the cultivar Yannong 1212 in water culture, their 2026 study measures growth, chemistry, and gene responses side by side.

Single stresses slowed sprouting in proportion to dose, but paired stresses hit far harder. Leaves yellowed, pores closed, and the green machinery inside cells was damaged. Seedlings stockpiled protective sugars and proline while antioxidant enzymes rose and fell by stress type. Drought combined with heat proved the most damaging pairing of all.
pmc-13258811:
Marika Kanthe and co-authors surveyed every metabolic dietitian in Sweden about a relaxed diet for phenylketonuria. People with PKU must limit phenylalanine, an amino acid most foods contain. European guidance now allows many low-protein foods freely, but their 2026 survey asks whether Swedish practice follows.

All thirteen dietitians replied, and eight recommended the free-food approach. Even so, about a third of foods the handbook calls free were still commonly counted in Sweden. For many items, colleagues flatly disagreed about whether counting was needed. Worry about patients overdoing phenylalanine drove much of the caution, the authors report.
pmc-13260511:
Chen-Fang Kang and co-authors present a 2026 study of a non-destructive checking method for semiconductor structures made of AlGaN and GaN, materials used in high-power electronics. Their framework combines second harmonic generation microscopy, an optical method sensitive to broken crystal symmetry, with pixel-level anomaly detection. Unlike object detectors that draw boxes around defects, their method models the normal lattice pattern with statistics, without hand-labeled examples, then flags pixels that deviate.

The approach was compared with standard detectors such as YOLOv8 and Mask R-CNN. It showed far better spatial overlap and sensitivity, resolving more than five thousand micron-scale defect-affected regions within a single field of view. Many of those regions were largely out of reach for box- or mask-based methods. Optical defect features were also supported by correlation with light-emission based defect measures.
pmc-13260711:
Sara Elkorashi leads a 2026 study of immune thrombocytopenia in pregnancy, a condition in which the immune system destroys blood platelets, raising bleeding risk. The retrospective study covered eighty-one pregnant patients at Hamad Medical Corporation in Qatar from 2018 to 2022, the first such analysis in the country. Records captured blood values, complications, treatments, and outcomes for mothers and newborn babies.

Median platelet count at diagnosis was low. Maternal complications occurred in 19.8 percent of cases, most commonly premature rupture of membranes at 4.9 percent of cases. Newborn complications affected 12.4 percent, mainly preterm birth and restricted growth in the womb, each at 3.8 percent of newborns. Overall, eighty percent of pregnancies were uncomplicated. Cases that began during pregnancy had a higher complication rate, at 28.5 percent, than cases present before pregnancy, at 23.2 percent of cases.
pmc-13261611:
Muniba Munir and co-authors study, in twenty twenty-six, a sugar phosphate compound as an anti-aging treatment for skin. Aging links to failing mitochondria, the cell's power plants, and to decay of collagen, the skin's scaffold protein. The compound, mannose-6-phosphate, is a natural step in sugar metabolism. In lab tests on human skin cells, it raised levels of ATP, the cell's energy currency, and related molecules. It reversed UV-induced mitochondrial damage and boosted mitophagy, the cleanup of worn mitochondria.

It also cut oxidative stress sharply. Gene analysis showed boosts to collagen synthesis and DNA repair genes. A small clinical trial of thirty-six women over fifty-six days confirmed firmer, more elastic skin and fewer wrinkles with the cream.
pmc-13262511:
Babak Saravi and colleagues audited in 2026 whether demographic cues in a prompt can sway image-reading language models giving dental advice. They sent 705 panoramic dental X-rays from a public set to three commercial multimodal models. Each image arrived under twelve prompt conditions varying stated race, ethnicity, and sex, plus controls.

The audit totaled 25,380 model calls, each returning ten structured recommendation fields. All three models shifted their advice when demographic labels appeared. One model reacted most broadly, moving treatment invasiveness, outlook, and confidence across groups. The shifts were systematic yet small, each under six percent of a rating step. Agreement between models under plain prompts hovered near chance, a larger worry than the label effects. The authors ask for routine demographic audits before such tools reach clinics.
pmc-13262711:
Davide Ruggero writes a 2026 commentary on targeting protein production in cancer. Tumor studies often find that RNA levels poorly predict protein levels, so the making of proteins, called translation, helps set a cancer cell's identity. A study in the same journal issue blocked a key translation factor called eIF4E in prostate cancer.

Blocking eIF4E rewired which proteins the cancer cells made, the study found. It suppressed traits of the basal cell type, which resists hormone therapy, and pushed cells toward the luminal type, restoring hormone sensitivity. Ruggero argues that cancers broadly depend on selective translation to stay flexible and resist drugs. Attacking those dependencies could turn resistant cell states into treatable ones.
pmc-13262811:
Xinying Quan and co-authors study a little-known protein in stomach cancer in a 2026 journal article. The protein, THSD7B, had been linked to several cancers, but its role in gastric adenocarcinoma, the main stomach cancer type, was unclear. The team checked its levels in public tumor data sets and then altered it in cancer cells and in mice.

THSD7B levels were higher in tumor tissue than in normal tissue and tracked with patient survival. Genes linked to it clustered around cell adhesion, how cells grip their surroundings, and internal cell scaffolding. Lowering THSD7B in cells slowed growth, movement, and invasion, while raising it did the reverse. In mice, it promoted tumor growth, marking it as a candidate marker.
pmc-13263211:
Angela Galardi and six co-authors review the two-way traffic between blood clotting and cancer in a 2026 article. Clotting normally repairs blood vessels, but tumors hijack the same machinery. In turn, clotting factors help tumors grow, spread, and hide.

Tumor cells switch on clotting proteins and signals that open new blood vessels and blunt immune attack. Neighboring support cells in the tumor are pushed to make clotting factors too. Platelets coat traveling tumor cells, shielding them from stress and immune killers, while fibrin mats give tumors a scaffold and recruit suppressive cells. Clot-driven signals also help push immune cells out of the tumor's core. The review gathers this loop into one picture. It argues that the clotting system is not a bystander in cancer but an active partner, and a possible target.
pmc-13263411:
C. Yarkutay Turkkan and co-authors report a 2026 journal article testing a simple blood ratio as a supporting marker in Cushing's syndrome. In this disorder the body makes too much cortisol, a stress hormone. Standard diagnostic tests are imperfect, so the team studied the blood urea nitrogen to creatinine ratio in 229 people in Istanbul.

Patients with Cushing's syndrome, its subclinical form, and both hormone-driven subtypes had higher ratios than healthy controls. Specific cutoff values separated each patient group from controls. The ratio also tracked with cortisol levels and standard test results, and it changed after treatment. The authors suggest it can support diagnosis when main tests are unavailable or unclear.
pmc-13263811:
Shi-Ying Long and a large surgical team reported in 2026 long-term pregnancy results after a delicate microsurgery that reconnects the sperm duct to the epididymis. Their patients had blockages from infection, injury, or unknown causes rather than vasectomy, where the blocked interval cannot be dated. The series covered 197 men treated with a vessel-sparing version of the operation.

The connection stayed open in about eighty percent of men checked at eighteen months. Among couples followed for an average of nearly five years, almost three quarters achieved natural pregnancy. Notably, about two in five couples still waiting after the first year conceived during years one to three. A partner aged thirty-five or older and a left-sided varicocele each predicted lower success. The authors advise waiting two to three years before turning to lab-assisted conception.
pmc-13263911:
Kristina Countryman and colleagues examined in 2026 whether clinicians ask pregnant women about cannabis unevenly by race, within a trial cohort already flagged for substance use risk. Their 176 participants, about a quarter of them Black, reported use and clinician conversations at four points. Guidelines urge universal screening in pregnancy.

About eighteen percent reported current use and twenty-six percent past-year use, most often to relax. Black women reported being talked to about cannabis, in pregnancy and around breastfeeding, far more often than White women at every time point. Adjustment for background factors put their odds near four times higher. The gap persisted even after accounting for prior cannabis use itself. The authors read the pattern as screening bias rather than diligence. They call for system-level fixes so universal screening actually lands universally.
pmc-13264311:
Xin Liu and colleagues compare acupuncture approaches for chronic prostate and pelvic pain in a 2026 network meta-analysis. Drug treatment often disappoints in this condition, and needle-based therapies are widely used as support. Forty-five randomized trials with over three thousand five hundred participants were combined, using a standard symptom index as the main outcome. Most trials compared acupuncture methods against medicines rather than sham needles, which limits certainty about specific effects.

Needle therapies, alone or with medication, improved symptom scores more than conventional drugs in those active comparisons. Warm needle acupuncture ranked highest for both total improvement and response rate in the ranking analysis. Electroacupuncture also performed favorably across outcomes. The authors present rankings as guidance for practice and for designing stricter sham-controlled trials.
pmc-13264411:
Congcong Chang and colleagues review a peony-derived compound as a possible treatment for intestinal diseases in a 2026 article. Paeoniflorin, the main active glycoside from peony roots, shows anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and barrier-protecting actions across many lab models. Bowel inflammation, everyday gut disorders, stress-related gut injury and colon cancers share overlapping drivers. Those drivers include barrier failure, immune imbalance, microbe disruption and oxidative damage. The compound appears to counter them in preclinical work.

Animal and cell studies report eased colitis, stronger gut lining, better mucosal repair and slowed inflammation-linked tumor growth. Colon-targeted delivery and derivative design are raising exposure where it matters. Human evidence remains thin, so the authors frame promise carefully and call for clinical trials with set dosing and safety checks.
pmc-13264611:
Lorenz Scheit and co-authors published a 2026 survey on health promotion aboard merchant ships. Crews live far from normal health services, and officers and ratings may want different support. The team asked seafarers what health topics matter and whether digital tools could deliver help at sea.

They surveyed 903 seafarers from 23 countries on 68 ships from two German firms. Ratings rated topics like healthy food and exercise as more relevant than officers did. Ratings were also more than twice as keen to do more sport and learn relaxation skills. Nearly all used smartphones, and most in both groups would use a health app and join a reward-based bonus scheme. Interest barely varied by age or cultural background. The authors back apps, wearables, and online learning for shipboard health.
pmc-13264911:
Christina Psaros and colleagues outline a 2026 pilot trial protocol in South Africa on HIV self-testing for partners of pregnant and postpartum women. They face raised HIV risk after childbirth, and infection can pass to infants through breastfeeding. Many male partners have never learned their HIV status. Prevention medicines work only when people test and start them.

Sixty women in late pregnancy will receive oral self-test kits for their partners. Half will also get counselling built on communication skills and problem solving. The pilot will measure enrolment, kit delivery, testing, and prevention uptake at three months. Interviews will explore how couples experienced the approach.
pmc-13265011:
Mark Lupin and co-authors present a 2026 split-face trial of a neuropeptide serum used around botulinum toxin injections, the wrinkle-relaxing shots widely used in cosmetic care. Each person applied the serum to one half of the face and a plain base to the other, before and after injections, so the comparison stayed within the same skin.

The study ran ten weeks, with injections for frown and eye-corner lines at the midpoint start. A blinded dermatologist graded 18 facial traits, and the serum side improved significantly more on traits like forehead wrinkles, fine lines, smoothness, and glow at eight weeks after injection. Gains appeared even before the injections, in the two weeks of serum use alone. No tolerance problems appeared. The authors conclude the serum enhances injection results.
pmc-13265211:
Huijuan Zhang, Guanghua Wu, and Chunxu Liao study how survival chances change over time in primary breast lymphoma, in a 2026 registry study. This rare lymphoma starts in the breast and has varied outcomes. Standard estimates ignore how risk shifts after diagnosis. Conditional survival updates the forecast for people already surviving.

The cohort held 1,552 women diagnosed from 2004 to 2021. Ten-year survival chances rose steeply the longer a patient had already lived. Yearly death risk peaked in the first year and then fell. Age, tissue type, radiotherapy, and marital status shaped prognosis. A chart using these factors gave well-calibrated personal forecasts.
pmc-13265411:
Hannah Murphy and Laura Fontenas describe a dual mounting method for imaging larval zebrafish, in a 2026 protocol. Larvae are usually fixed sideways for consistent views. That setup often ties imaging to one microscope type. The new mount keeps the sideways position while allowing viewing from above or below.

Common low-cost laboratory materials form the mounting platform. A water-repellent seal lets the mounted sample be flipped safely. Researchers can move between upright and inverted microscopes without remounting. The same region can be tracked reliably over time. The approach suits live imaging needing flexible geometry and little handling.
pmc-13266111:
Fat-based messengers usually work from cell membranes, but a growing list of proteins carry them as attachments in the cell's watery interior and nucleus. Noah Carrillo and co-authors map that hidden network in a 2026 study. pmc-13266711:

pmc-13267611:

pmc-13267811:
Manhui Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 review of bloodstream infections in newborns at a large Chinese hospital. Newborns, above all early and small babies, catch infections easily. pmc-13268411:

pmc-13268511:

pmc-13268711:

pmc-13268911:
Haoxuan Deng and co-authors report in 2026 a case of a benign smooth muscle tumor that grew inside veins all the way into a woman's heart. Two resin cases stained slightly, without spoiling appearance ratings.
pmc-13269811:
Jung Suk Yoon and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 reviewing eight years of eye care by telemedicine in the Korean military. pmc-13270611:
Georgia Vesma wrote a 2026 small-scale qualitative study, one based on interviews and survey answers rather than counts alone, about peer review of research that crosses subject fields. Reviewers reported papers outside their expertise and weak editor guidance. Editors reported that a wider shortage of reviewers made the process harder still.
pmc-13270711:
Carlotta Marie Wehrkamp led a 2026 journal article on centromeres, the central parts of chromosomes, in oats and their relatives in the Avena genus. New near-complete genome assemblies let the team compare these repeat-rich regions across species with different numbers of chromosome sets.

Even close relatives, the authors show, evolved very different centromere layouts quickly.
pmc-13271211:
Thais Barros Zanette da Silva is lead author of a 2026 study of how Brazil's governments regulate access to specialised outpatient care. National guidance is shared. pmc-13271811:
Wataru Otsu is lead author of a 2026 case report of osteosarcoma, the most common primary bone cancer in children and young adults, spreading to the small bowel. pmc-13271911:

pmc-13272011:

pmc-13272311:
Heng Zhao and coauthors describe in 2026 a rare case where a brain shunt catheter wandered into a child's buttock muscle. pmc-13272511:
Ismael García Campanario and colleagues measured depression symptoms across Spain in a 2026 analysis of a European health survey. About nine in every hundred people screened positive for depression symptoms on a standard questionnaire. Chronic disease, limits on daily function, and lack of physical activity were the main linked factors, along with being a former smoker. People with symptoms also used health services more often. pmc-13272711:
Paramita Das leads a 2026 study of a community advisory board for genomic medicine in Alabama. pmc-13273211:

Nashira I Brown and co-authors studied beliefs and distress linked to sunburn among Florida adults in a 2026 analysis. Melanoma causes most skin cancer deaths, and most cases are preventable, yet sunburn stays common. The team asked which beliefs and feelings best predict having been sunburned.

pmc-13273611:
A discharge summary is the baton pass between hospital and home, and Murad Hamiedah and co-authors audit how well a Jordanian military hospital writes them, in a 2026 study. pmc-13273711:

pmc-13274311:

pmc-13274911:

pmc-13275011:

pmc-13275711:

pmc-13276311:

pmc-13276511:

pmc-13277011:

pmc-13277211:

pmc-13277411:

pmc-13278511:
Shirin Akter Begum and co-authors map HPV genotypes in cervical lesions at a Dhaka hospital, in a 2026 study. pmc-13278711:

pmc-13279211:

pmc-13279511:

pmc-13279811:
Daniel Kuznicki and colleagues report a 2026 study of gene control faults in the BCL2 gene in lymphoid cancers. pmc-13279911:

pmc-13280011:

pmc-13280311:

All proof stays preclinical, in animals and dishes, so human trials must still prove worth.
pmc-13280411:

pmc-13280911:

pmc-13281211:

The authors conclude the hormone response depends heavily on context.
pmc-13281311:
Hongqun Zuo and co-authors ask a pointed question in 2026: when bowel cancer vanishes after immune therapy, is surgery still needed? They study a cancer type with a DNA repair fault that makes it respond well to such therapy. Their data cover 70 patients treated between 2018 and 2024.

Of those patients, 44 had a complete clinical response, meaning no tumor could be found. Some chose watch-and-wait monitoring, while others had radical surgery. The team compares cancer outcomes between the groups and reviews past studies on the same choice. The work speaks to patients hoping to keep their bowel and avoid major surgery. Their findings add data to a choice that patients face with little guidance.
pmc-13281511:
Atanu Ghosh and colleagues published a 2026 photophysics study showing an iron complex can do electron-transfer chemistry from a short-lived upper excited state. Iron-based light absorbers could replace rare ruthenium and iridium in photoredox catalysis, but their useful charge-transfer states collapse into metal-centered states within a trillionth of a second. Using an iron(II) pyridinium carbene complex and ultrafast spectroscopy, the team timed that collapse and mapped the energy landscape.

The higher state survived about 3 picoseconds before relaxing. Temperature-dependent measurements identified the receiving state and showed ground-state recovery sits near the barrierless regime of Marcus theory, letting the authors estimate the state's redox power. Armed with those numbers, they tuned the pathways so electron transfer fires from the upper state first. The authors present this balancing act as a strategy for putting cheap iron complexes to work in light-to-chemical energy conversion.
pmc-13281611:
John Cafferkey and colleagues explored immune effects of two fluids for sepsis in a 2026 letter. Sepsis is a runaway body response to infection that can kill. First care gives a salt fluid by vein, but a blood protein fluid is also used. The protein fluid is claimed to calm immune harm. The letter reports a side study of a small trial in emergency rooms. Twenty-six patients gave blood at the start and twice in the first day.

Fourteen patients got the protein fluid and twelve the salt fluid. Lab tests counted immune cell types and signal proteins in blood. Gene activity in white cells was read as well. Health outcomes in the two groups were alike. The authors frame the work as a probe of how fluids may shape immunity. Such clues could guide a larger trial of the protein fluid.
pmc-13282211:
Meng-Hua Tao and co-authors report a 2026 study on whether lacking steady access to enough food links to a fatty liver condition in adults. The condition, shortened to MASLD, involves excess liver fat tied to metabolism problems. The team used a national United States health survey from 2017 to early 2020. It included five thousand seventy-six adults who had a liver stiffness scan.

Food insecurity, meaning unreliable access to enough food, was linked to higher odds of the liver condition overall. That link appeared mainly in non-Hispanic White adults and in women, but not in men. Diet partly explained the link in White adults, through added sugar and low fruit and vegetable intake. The authors suggest food programs that cut added sugar and raise whole fruit and vegetable intake could soften this risk. They stress that patterns differ by group, so one-size advice may miss those most affected.
pmc-13282311:
Cody L Nathan and co-authors present a 2026 study of seizures in patients with a rare brain tumour type called pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma. Such tumours often cause epilepsy, but outcome patterns were little studied. The team reviewed twenty-five patients treated at one centre between 2004 and 2025. They linked seizure outcomes to tumour traits, clinical features, and brain activity findings.

Nineteen patients had tumour-related epilepsy, and seizures were the first symptom in most. Nearly a third had earlier focal seizures that went unrecognised. After first surgery, before any tumour return, most became seizure free. At latest follow-up, about two thirds stayed free. A tumour marker loss, called ATRX loss, linked to better long-term seizure freedom. When seizures returned, the tumour had usually returned on scans within a month. The authors stress careful seizure histories, since early focal events are easy to miss.
pmc-13283211:
Eye movements alone might flag mental stress outside the lab, the premise Maike Laut and fellow engineers test in 2026. Pupil size and gaze shifts can signal stress, but most tools need lab tasks or many sensors. The team tested whether eye data alone can work across tasks.

Two datasets were used: a virtual goalkeeper task and a virtual job interview. Deep learning models read the raw eye time series for stress patterns. Top scores neared a 96 percent F1 level under good conditions in the best setup. Scores varied widely across datasets with signal quality and task design. Eye-only tools may offer a lighter path to stress tracking in real settings.
pmc-13283811:
Jiawen Li and Xingwen Xie reviewed in 2026 how gut balance and immune crosstalk shape ankylosing spondylitis, a long-term inflammatory disease of the spine and the points where tendons attach to bone. The gene HLA-B27 is a known factor, yet gut disturbance has drawn growing attention through a gut-joint axis. Patients show lower gut microbe diversity and shifts in community make-up.

The review links those shifts to a leakier gut barrier, immune priming, and a key inflammatory route involving IL-23 and IL-17 signals. Unusual lymphocyte types that live near barriers may be switched on and travel to joints, feeding inflammation and odd bone growth. Gut chemical products, such as short-chain fatty acids, also help tune the barrier. The authors separate proven immune drugs from early microbe-based ideas.
pmc-13284111:
Tingyu Su and colleagues combined many data types in 2026 to hunt prognostic markers in clear cell kidney cancer, the main kidney cancer form, which carries a poor outlook. Genome, methylation, and immune data from public databases were merged, then checked with single-cell sequencing, genetic causal analysis, computer gene knockout, and lab tests.

One gene, CRHBP, stood out as switched down in tumours, with lower levels at later stages and a link to better survival when levels held up. A partner signal, UCN2 from the testes, showed a causal risk effect and tied inversely to vessel growth and low oxygen in tumours. Computer docking flagged an existing drug, dabrafenib, as a candidate binder for both targets. Lab checks confirmed the expression shifts in human and mouse tissue.
pmc-13284411:
Deepa Singal and co-authors report a whole-population study, published in 2026, on mental health among autistic people in Manitoba, Canada. Using linked health records from 2018 to 2022, the team compared autistic children, teens, and adults with all other residents. They tracked doctor-diagnosed disorders and suicide attempts across three age groups.

Autistic people had higher rates of almost all conditions studied, with much higher adjusted risk for schizophrenia, conduct disorder, and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in the pooled results. Risk of a suicide attempt was also more than three times higher than in the comparison group, the authors report. The scale of the gaps supports stronger, age-aware mental health support and suicide prevention for autistic people.
pmc-13284811: Laura Fabbri, Katerina Antoniou, and a large author group call for tighter safety checks before cancer immunotherapy. Their editorial, from twenty twenty-six, focuses on lung damage tied to checkpoint inhibitor drugs. Such lung inflammation is uncommon but can be severe, and diagnosis varies between centers. A standard risk review before treatment starts, the authors argue, may catch cases earlier and guide care. They stress that lung, cancer, and imaging specialists must work as one team. Shared rules would sharpen both patient safety and future research.
pmc-13285011: Nian Liu and co-authors publish a correction, dated 2026, to a study of vitexin compound 1 and melanoma cell growth. Errors were found in the right panel of Figure 4a and in a supplementary figure. The notice reprints the affected figure material on DNA damage and reactive oxygen species and presents the correct figures. No change to the study topic is stated in the notice.
pmc-13285511:
Regan Harrell, Chelsea Manetta, and Susan Whitney survey graduates of an advanced balance therapist certificate. Their survey study from twenty twenty-six evaluates post-professional training impact. Dizziness disorders cost the United States billions yearly. Frontline therapists need deeper vestibular skills than basic training gives.

Two hundred thirty graduates from four cohorts were invited. Sixty-seven answered the eighteen-question survey. Nearly all felt ready to act as frontline balance providers. Most reported better patient outcomes after the training. Every respondent said it met their continuing education needs. Practice habits changed for nearly all graduates too. Specialised certificates may close real skill gaps in clinics.
pmc-13285711:
Yongcheng Ge and colleagues review robot-assisted oral examination in a 2026 survey of the field. Dentists now test robots that combine cameras, sensors, and smart software to inspect the mouth in a standard way. The review maps the main parts of these systems and the problems that still block routine use.

A search of PubMed and ScienceDirect through September 2025 yielded 134 included studies from a much larger first pool. Key parts include high-resolution imaging inside the mouth, fusion of data from several sensors, force sensing, and self-guided movement. These tools can sharpen image capture and make exams more alike across clinics. Gaps in safety checks, speed, and clinical testing remain, so wider use will need steady refinement.
pmc-13285911:
Guangling Li and colleagues survey stroke knowledge, attitudes, and habits among young patients in China in a 2026 cross-sectional survey. Stroke now strikes more adults under 45, who face decades of risk for a second event. The team asked what these patients know about their condition and whether that knowledge shapes daily prevention habits.

An online survey in Shanxi Province drew replies from 445 patients aged 18 to 45 in the first half of 2025. Attitudes scored well and habits scored in the middle range, while knowledge lagged behind both. Model tests showed knowledge fed straight into habits and also worked through attitudes to lift them further. The gap between knowing and doing points to focused teaching, through phone tools and local workshops, as the clear next step.
pmc-13286011:
Ralph Andrews and Paul M Dockree propose a framework tying breath, brain waves, and perception in a 2026 theory article. Breathing does more than fuel the body: each cycle seems to open and close small windows in which sights and sounds reach awareness. Their Rhythmic Embodied Perception framework joins those windows across three levels, from cell signals to felt experience.

Slow breath cycles tug on brain rhythms in sight and attention networks, creating quiet phases when input most easily breaks through. Chosen slow breathing steadies those rhythms through a brainstem system that sets alertness, stretching the clear windows longer. The model makes sharp, testable calls: detection should swing with breath phase, and paced breathing should tighten breath-brain links. Old yoga accounts of breath and attention find a modern echo in the scheme.
pmc-13286411:
Alpaslan Kaban and colleagues search for a group of womb cancer patients who can safely skip extensive staging surgery. Their 2026 study reviews 250 women with the common endometrioid type of tumor that had invaded less than half the womb wall. Finding spread beyond the uterus normally requires wider surgery, so a reliably low-risk profile matters.

Eighteen women had such spread. Tumors of the higher grade spread at nearly four times the rate of the lower grade, and tumors wider than three centimeters also spread far more often. Both features predicted spread independently of each other. Women with small, low-grade tumors carried the lowest risk. The authors support sparing that group the full staging operation.
pmc-13286911:
Ju Hee Oh and colleagues refine a shock-based delivery method, electroporation, for editing genes in fragile primary mouse blood cells without using viruses. Their 2026 study optimizes settings on a commercial platform for three cell types: killer T cells, macrophages grown from bone marrow, and blood stem and progenitor cells.

Two pulse programs delivered genetic material into activated T cells with high efficiency while sparing viability and growth. Macrophages tolerated the process well and kept their identity while target genes were knocked out efficiently. The best program also worked in stem cells, giving steady delivery and reproducible editing. A shared, modular workflow, the authors argue, lowers the barrier to quick genetic experiments in immunology.
pmc-13287111:
Poonam Kanojiya and co-authors review in 2026 how to fight drug-resistant germs through a One Health lens. Resistance spreads across people, animals, food, and nature, with wastewater, soil, and wildlife as key reservoirs. A drug saved in a hospital can be undone by overuse on a farm.

The review maps how resistance arises and travels, then weighs joint responses. Careful drug use in clinics and vet practice cuts the pressure that breeds resistance. Guarding water and soil slows its spread. Watching germs across all sectors gives early warning of new threats. The authors argue that national and global plans must bake in this linked view to keep antibiotics working.
pmc-13288111:
Dimitri Desvillechabrol and co-authors present LORA in 2026, a ready-made workflow that assembles genomes from long-read sequencing machines using several proven builder tools under one roof. Builders differ in strength by species, and hand-run assembly is hard to repeat, so the pipeline automates choices and records each step.

Built on a task-running framework, it works on a laptop or a big cluster. Checks cover build quality and completeness, name stray species by gene matching, and produce clickable reports. Trials on bacterial and single-cell eukaryote data from both major long-read machines show typical results and common traps. The tool ships inside an open-source package.
pmc-13288211:
Hai-Jun Li and a large team show a light-driven trick in 2026. Ring-shaped starting molecules carry a carbon triple bond and a bulky boron group. Shining light makes each ring swallow an extra carbon. The result is a seven-membered ring fused into a larger boron-dusted frame. Such expansions used to need unstable reactive fragments.

The clean reaction breaks a strong ring bond, inserts the carbon, and shifts a hydrogen atom in a linked sequence. Maths modelling points to short-lived allene and boron radical forms along the path. The authors claim the first expansion of this classic type driven by a stable alkyne. The route opens fresh designs for boron-bearing carbon frames.
pmc-13288611:
Shilan Li and colleagues study immune cells in a childhood airway disease in a 2026 paper. Juvenile-onset recurrent respiratory papillomatosis causes wart-like growths that keep returning in children's airways. Human papillomavirus drives the disease, yet why the immune system fails to clear it is unclear. The team compared 97 young patients with 124 controls using blood and tissue tests.

One T cell family, marked by the V-beta 3 receptor chain, had expanded in patients with aggressive disease. Those cells carried strong activation and killing markers and gathered inside the growths themselves. Tumor tissue also showed raised levels of PD-L1 and TGF-beta, both known immune dampeners. Chemical signals that recruit T cells were turned up as well. The authors suggest the cells arrive in force but are held back by the suppressive setting. Targeting that balance could one day reduce how often growths return.
pmc-13288711:
Belayneh Jejaw Abate and colleagues chart uneven cesarean delivery across sub-Saharan Africa in a 2026 multi-country geospatial analysis. Pooling Demographic and Health Survey data from 2015 to 2024 gave 201,481 weighted cases across 28 countries, which they tested for clustering and modeled with several spatial regression methods.

Delivery by cesarean clustered strongly on the map. Hotspots covered countries such as Uganda, Rwanda, Kenya, South Africa, and Ghana, while cold spots included Ethiopia, Nigeria, Angola, and Madagascar among others. A prior cesarean, maternal age of thirty-five or more, birth spacing behavior, and insurance coverage predicted use, with effects shifting by place. Matching policy, referral routes, and financing to local patterns is their prescription.
pmc-13288911:
Michael K Steinhoff and colleagues use nuclear magnetic resonance to track lithium movement inside a garnet battery material in 2026. The material, shortened to LLZTO, is a solid electrolyte candidate for safer batteries. Coating its powder with alumina by atomic layer deposition was known to stir up lithium during coating. The team measured lithium relaxation times to see how coating thickness changed bulk behavior before firing.

Relaxation patterns varied a lot between samples with different coating histories. The team traced that spread to diffusion triggered during the deposition process itself. In other words, a surface treatment reached deep into the powder and altered lithium mobility throughout. Such hidden changes could shift later battery performance without any visible sign. The authors offer spectrally resolved relaxation measurement as a sensitive check during production. It can flag when a coating step has quietly changed the material.
pmc-13289211:
Nehal Refaat Raouf and colleagues study fall risk in rural Egypt in 2026. Their survey ran in two villages in Minia. It held 325 adults aged 60 and up. Talks ran from September to December 2024. A checked Arabic form set fall risk.

Over half, 57.8 percent, faced high fall risk. Many health and home traits tied to risk at first. Five traits held up in final models. Age 75 and up raised the odds. Three or more diseases raised them a lot. Poor self-rated health also raised them. Low activity and home hazards counted too. The authors urge screens in rural clinics. Home safety checks should join them.
pmc-13289311:
Alixandra Rachman and coauthors evaluated a 2026 follow-up survey of Yale's online Climate Change and Health Certificate Program. Started in 2018, the course trains professionals across fields to act on health harms from a warming climate. The study tracked members of the first nine cohorts, from 2018 to 2023, well after training ended.

A total of 205 alumni answered, rating knowledge, confidence, work changes, and wider results. Over 90 percent said they grasped most knowledge areas, but only about seven in ten felt sure using key skills on the job. Still, 91.1 percent had changed how they work, and many joined new climate efforts outside class. Grouping methods found distinct paths from learning to action, useful for improving future cohorts.
pmc-13289511:
Rob Fredericksen and fifteen co-authors trace the road from a rural American teenager's first drug to opioid use and injecting, in this 2026 study. The rural opioid crisis is usually told from its end: overdoses and treatment queues. This study walks the timeline backward, asking what the first steps looked like and what pushed people along them.

The team interviewed 304 adults who use non-prescribed opioids across ten states. Marijuana was the most common first drug, at an average age of thirteen; opioid pills followed, typically at nineteen or twenty, and nearly half of those pills were originally prescribed for pain. Among the ninety-two percent who went on to inject, starting around age twenty-four, the first injected drugs split between methamphetamine, pills, and heroin. Mapping these waypoints, and the circumstances around them, shows prevention where it can actually intervene: early, locally, and before the needle.
pmc-13290711:
A plasma-cell drug is tried as a last resort for a transplant complication in a 2026 letter by Parthenopi Despina Avaniadi and colleagues. They report six kidney transplant recipients whose focal segmental glomerulosclerosis came back after transplantation and resisted standard care.

Every patient had biopsy-proven recurrence with widespread podocyte damage, and all were dialysis-dependent before their transplants. Standard rescue steps, plasmapheresis and anti-CD20 therapy with rituximab (escalated to obinutuzumab in one case), failed to hold remission for any of them. The team therefore turned to daratumumab, which targets plasma cells, as rescue therapy. The letter frames the series against a thin and mixed evidence base, where which patients benefit from the drug remains unsettled.
pmc-13290811:
Transplant tolerance may get stabler soldiers: Arimelek Cortés-Hernández and colleagues describe in 2026 a recipe for growing donor-specific regulatory T cells that keep their identity. Such cells are rare in blood, hard to purify, and prone to drift during long expansion, which has stalled their clinical use.

Three weeks yielded a 434-fold expansion at over 95% purity, with the FOXP3 stability marker largely demethylated. The cells suppressed T cell growth in a donor-specific way even after inflammatory challenge and made none of the inflammatory cytokines that signal drift. pmc-13291211:
Blistering skin in a child can be scabies in disguise. Anupa Khadka and Vikash Paudel report a 2026 case of this rare form. Scabies mites cause fierce itching. Big blisters are rare and often fool doctors.

Their patient was a 12-year-old boy. He had itchy blisters mostly on his hands. A few scratched bumps sat on his trunk and thighs. A skin scope showed the classic jet-with-trail sign between fingers. That sign confirmed scabies under world criteria. Two rounds of mite cream, one week apart, cleared the skin. No marks stayed at four weeks. A scope check can spare needless tests, they argue.
pmc-13291311:
A cell death guard helps plants fight a root rot foe. Yujing Fang leads a 2026 study in Arabidopsis plants. The guard protein BI-1 sits in the cell’s inner web. A foe factor called RTP1 weakens plant defense.

Mutant plants lacking RTP1 made far more BI-1 early on. Plants lacking both lost their cell death control. They also fell sick more under attack. Defense gene activity dropped in double mutants. A burst of reactive oxygen vanished as well. RTP1 binds BI-1 and lowers its levels. Two stress switches turn the BI-1 gene on. This tug-of-war may guide crop protection design.
pmc-13291711:
A new drug eased hard lung hypertension in a tough case. Yujin Nishioka and colleagues report this 2026 case from Japan. Their patient was a 53-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis. Her lung arteries narrowed while vein disease lurked too.

Three oral drugs failed to hold her disease back. Lung pressure climbed steeply despite that care. Standard infused drugs risked flooding her lungs. Sotatercept was chosen to dodge that risk. Her walking distance and heart strain marks improved. Lung pressure eased down as well. Pauses for high hemoglobin did not undo gains. No lung flooding occurred during care.
pmc-13292011:
Awais Mehmood and Romesa Tahir write a 2026 letter questioning a biomarker claim in heart attack subtypes. The letter responds to a study that flagged the gene CDK7 as higher in NSTEMI than STEMI attacks in a Bangladeshi group. That distinction matters if CDK7 becomes a test separating the two. Mehmood and Tahir focus on the study's measurement method instead. Its gene readings were normalized against a single housekeeping gene, GAPDH.

GAPDH, they note, is a poor anchor here because oxygen shortage itself raises its expression. STEMI attacks block arteries fully and starve tissue harder than NSTEMI attacks do. A shifting anchor could fake the very difference the study reports. Reporting guidelines for this assay type ask for at least two validated reference genes. The writers suggest steadier candidates and free tools that pick them. They propose a quick check on the raw values to settle the question.
pmc-13292111:
Tengfei Li and co-authors set out a 2026 Cochrane protocol for comparing drug-free treatments for anxiety and depression in Parkinson's disease. Mood problems affect roughly 40 to 50 percent of people with Parkinson's and deepen dependence, decline, and mortality risk. The protocol states the review's aim plainly: judge how well non-drug options work and how safe they are.

Because it is a protocol, no results are reported yet. The background explains how Parkinson's disrupts dopamine, serotonin, and noradrenaline circuits feeding the limbic system and amygdala-driven fear pathways. It also notes that women and younger-onset patients often carry heavier mood symptoms. The finished review is meant to guide care for a symptom group that drugs alone handle imperfectly.
pmc-13292311:
Susan O'Donovan, Laura Ward, and Ruth Melia map a 2026 scoping review of EMDR therapy for trauma tied to childbirth. Twenty-nine sources qualified, spanning trials, qualitative studies, systematic reviews, and grey material. Across them, EMDR looked promising for easing birth trauma symptoms. Yet study designs and outcome measures varied widely, and long-term follow-up was scarce. Evidence on partners and on diverse ethnic groups was also thin. The authors call for stronger designs, shared measures, and research that follows families over time before firm guidance can be written.
pmc-13292511:
Bennett Tochukwu Amaechi and colleagues run a 2026 bench test on whether adding calcium hypophosphite supercharges hydroxyapatite toothpaste against early tooth decay. One hundred twenty bovine tooth blocks were split among four pastes: hydroxyapatite alone, hydroxyapatite plus 1 percent calcium compound, the calcium compound alone, and standard 1450 ppm fluoride. A microbial model first grew early lesions, then two weeks of pH cycling with daily paste treatments tested repair.

Every paste remineralized significantly. The combination won clearly, reaching 95.7 percent remineralization against 67.3 for fluoride, 69.4 for hydroxyapatite alone, and 80.4 for the calcium paste in the reported means. The authors credit the additive's ready calcium ions. They say the pairing could strengthen fluoride-free remineralizing pastes, pending mouth-based trials.
pmc-13293411:
M. S. Amithalal leads a 2026 study making silver nanoparticles with leaf extract from Falconeria insignis, a plant not used this way before. Green making avoids harsh chemicals, using plant compounds to form and coat the tiny particles.

A color shift and light tests confirmed particle formation, with a peak in the 300 to 350 nanometer range the authors report. Crystal size averaged 19 nanometers, and shapes were mostly uneven rather than round. Surface groups from plant proteins and phenolics helped form and cap the particles. The particles killed Staphylococcus aureus far better than plain extract or silver salt, hinting at medical uses.
pmc-13293511:
Qingya Pan and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, a vision method to track how tumors shift as a patient breathes during lung radiotherapy. Exact motion data can cut radiation dose to healthy tissue, yet standard four-dimensional scans are slow and labor-heavy.

A chest phantom held eight fake nodules of varied shape and shade, shifted by 10 pixels in four directions and turned by set angles. An improved feature-matching method, called SIFT, was compared with a correlation method. Both tracked straight shifts equally well, with no clear gap by direction. Only the feature method handled turning distortion well, suggesting value for breathing motion checks.
pmc-13293611:
Ying Yao and Simon Hanslmayr comment, in a 2026 article, on new human brain recordings showing that nerve cell firing tunes to rhythm frequency, not just rhythm phase. Brain waves help coordinate activity, and spikes were long known to favor set moments in each wave cycle.

The study under discussion, by Jourahmad and colleagues, found firing also tracks moment-to-moment shifts in wave speed. Three readings are weighed: waves may drive firing, firing may help set wave speed, or both may follow a shared state change. Frequency tuning thus adds a fresh dimension to how brain rhythms may organize activity.
pmc-13293711:
Hiroki Karita and colleagues report, in a 2026 case study, joint brain-spine and gut surgery for an adult with Currarino syndrome. The syndrome is a rare birth condition marked by a missing lower spine bone, a growth before the spine, and bowel malformation. A 45-year-old woman learned of it in pregnancy.

Over time the growth enlarged, blocking her rectum and causing belly pain. Surgeons freed her tethered spinal cord and removed the mass in one combined operation, placing a flap of belly fat tissue to stop spinal fluid leaks. No leak occurred, and after effects were limited to brief bladder trouble and left foot numbness.
pmc-13294211:
Laura Patrussi and Chenran Zhang introduced a 2026 journal collection on unusual T cells and engineered T cells in cancer care. Standard immune therapy leans on common T cells that read protein tags. Unconventional T cells work differently: they sense fats, stress signals, and metabolic products, and act as a bridge between fast innate defense and slower adaptive defense.

The collection covers gamma-delta T cells, NKT cells, and MAIT cells across blood and solid cancers. Papers explore how these cells vary and bend to context, and how lab engineering can harden them against tumors that suppress immunity. New single-cell and gene tools drive much of the progress. The editors frame these cells as raw material for the next wave of cell therapies.
pmc-13294311:
The world buries over seven billion tons of mine tailings a year, and Lucimara Bragagnolo, Pedro Domingos Marques Prietto, and Eduardo Pavan Korf ask how to turn that waste into building material. The route is alkali activation: strong alkaline fluids wake the waste's minerals into a cement-like binder. The team mined the published literature for the conditions researchers used and the strengths they got.

The kind of precursor mattered most for strength. Blending tailings with other starting materials beat pure tailings every time. Two activators, caustic soda and sodium silicate, dominated the recipes. The authors call for cheaper, greener activators and blends so the method can leave the lab for real construction sites.
pmc-13294411:
Kirsten A Kalverda leads a 2026 pilot of live lung microscopy at the bedside in breathing failure. Chest scans cannot show early microscopic rebuilding after the wet phase of lung injury syndrome, which tracks with poor recovery.
