Ventilated intensive care patients already set for lung washing got an added confocal laser probe through the bronchoscope, giving near-tissue views of air sacs in real time.

Thirty-three patients joined, with median age 64 years and 61% men in the reported shares. Nearly all met formal injury syndrome criteria. The pilot judged success by getting at least one readable air sac video per session and by tracking harms within a day, with scan comparisons and one autopsy check as extras.
pmc-13294811:
Muhammad W. Amjad and colleagues use ultrasound to steer a healing fat molecule into injured heart muscle, in a 2026 animal study. After a heart attack, restored blood flow still triggers oxidative stress and inflammation that scar the heart and weaken it. A nitroalkene fatty acid can calm both processes, but little of it reaches the heart when given plainly. The team packed it into gas-filled lipid nanoparticles and burst them at the target with focused ultrasound.

In rat models of reperfusion injury and heart scarring, the targeted delivery cut fibrosis significantly more than the same drug given through a vein. Heart output improved, and tissue markers of scarring and inflammation moved in favorable directions, with imaging confirming less scar. The authors present the platform as a combined diagnosis-and-treatment route worth developing for ischemic heart disease.
pmc-13294911:
Huimin Lin and a large team review a screening approach for heart-harming ingredients in Chinese herbal medicines in a 2026 article. Some herbs long viewed as safe can still damage the heart, often without warning. Bioaffinity chromatography, which fishes out compounds that bind chosen biological targets, may catch such risks earlier.

Known harm routes include disturbed heart ion channels, damaged mitochondria, cell death, and metabolic upset. Five forms of the technique are explained, from antibody and lectin columns to cell membrane and receptor based versions. The authors propose using binding based screening for early warning and mechanism work, shifting safety checks from reaction after harm to prediction beforehand.
pmc-13295611:
Charalampia Pylarinou and a large team design reasoning software agents for surgical care in a 2026 article. Older multi-agent systems follow fixed rule trees and stumble on new situations across the long surgical journey. Their framework swaps fixed rules for language model agents that reason, fetch evidence, and check their own thinking.

Six agents cover care before, during, and after heart-lung surgery, each with a defined tool set and authority limits. Every decision that changes the care path must pass a confidence gate with human approval. A supervisor agent settles competing resource requests, aiming to cut false alerts while keeping patients safe in unclear cases.
pmc-13295711:
Elizabeth Adeogun and co-authors measure how gene therapy viruses grip heparin, in a 2026 study of binding heat. Adeno-associated viruses ferry genes into cells for therapy, and makers need better ways to purify them at scale. Heparin, a sugar chain, is a candidate grip for sorting, yet virus amounts are so low that standard heat tools struggle to read the binding.

The team set design rules that let a heat-based method, isothermal titration calorimetry, work at these low amounts. Grip strength rose as the heparin chains grew longer, and the team counted how many chains bind each virus. Buffer mix and acidity shifted the grip as well. The rules should help design sorting steps that catch the virus by its surface.
pmc-13296011:
Scorpion venom peptides as possible medicines are reviewed in 2026 by Man Wang and co-authors. Long prized as probes for nerve channels thanks to their sturdy folded shapes, these molecules now draw interest for antioxidant and protective effects as well.

The review sorts peptides by structure, explains how they tune ion channels, and highlights one molecule, SVHRSP, with protective effects in Parkinson's models. Engineering tricks such as ring closing, nano delivery and computer design aim to fix delivery problems. The authors caution that key findings come from one group and human proof is still lacking.
pmc-13296811:
Xavier Pochon and co-authors field-test, in 2026, TorpeDNA, a cheap compact sampler that collects environmental DNA from seawater so species can be detected without catching anything. Most gear is costly and fussy, so the team trial theirs in three settings from Brittany to a two-thousand-kilometre Pacific crossing.

Profiles matched those from fine laboratory filtration closely, capturing main microbe and plankton groups and known geographic patterns, including ocean animal DNA. Differences traced to filter pore size and water volume, affecting rare and sediment-bound kinds. The authors present the device as fit for large-scale and citizen monitoring.
pmc-13296911:
Atsuya Kameda and colleagues present a rare adolescent case of bent forearm bones without any fracture in a 2026 case report. A sixteen-year-old girl injured her forearm in a bicycle accident, then gradually lost rotation movement. Careful three-dimensional analysis showed her radius and ulna had bowed in different directions.

Surgeons planned separate corrections for each bone, using the healthy arm as the reference. Different cutting techniques were chosen for the radius and the ulna, with rotation checked during the operation. Two months later her rotation range had improved dramatically, and she returned fully to badminton at three months. The case shows why three-dimensional planning matters when both bones deform together.
pmc-13297111:
Murong Wang, Chunying Liu, and Xin Wei review the immune system's role in glaucoma in a 2026 article. High eye pressure remains the main treatable risk factor, yet immune abnormalities keep appearing across glaucoma subtypes. Autoantibodies, cytokine shifts, and altered immune cell sets all feature in the clinical evidence gathered.

Mechanisms span glial-driven inflammation, pattern-recognition signalling, adaptive immune attacks, and complement overactivity. Together they may keep retinal ganglion cells dying even when pressure is controlled. Treatments aimed at these pathways protect nerve cells in animal and laboratory models, the authors report. Patient evidence is still limited, so immune therapy is framed as a precision direction rather than a present standard.
pmc-13298011:
Qian Wang and colleagues built a 2026 machine-vision system that sorts harvested potatoes from soil clods and stones. Their detector adapts YOLOv10n with an added attention module and a dynamic blur strategy for training. A programmable controller and pneumatic actuators remove flagged items while the belt runs.

Comparisons with other lightweight models and orthogonal tests weighed belt speed, spacing between items, and the classification threshold. Belt speed mattered most, followed by spacing and then threshold. Under the best combination found, overall sorting accuracy and impurity removal were both high, while few good tubers were rejected by mistake. The results support stable automatic sorting under postharvest conditions.
pmc-13299711:
Zinc pills lifted blood zinc in weak-muscled boys and men who lacked it, and bone strength inched up in one band of them. Thaís Borges and her team report that in a 2026 study of Duchenne muscular dystrophy. They checked 34 patients three times in eight months. Four of those months brought zinc pills of 5 to 15 mg a day.

At the start, 36.7% of patients lacked zinc in the blood. Bone marks in the round did not shift by much. In the band whose bones were sound at the start, whole-body bone strength rose a touch. The team treat that band find with care, since plain growth in the young can fake such a rise. In the zinc-short band, blood zinc rose by a clear mark. The team back blood zinc checks as part of care for this group.
pmc-13299811:
Rimma Gamirova and others report an infantile case of GM1 gangliosidosis, a lysosomal storage disorder with epilepsy, in a 2026 genetics paper. The child carried two different harmful changes at the very same codon of the GLB1 gene, one from each parent. That exact pairing had not been described before, per the authors.

Both changes alter a residue that holds the enzyme's catalytic domain together, so severe loss of enzyme activity is expected. Earlier cases with changes at this position consistently showed the rapidly progressive infantile form with multisystem involvement. The authors propose the codon as a critical lab hotspot in the gene.
pmc-13300011:
A 2026 outbreak of Andes virus aboard the Dutch cruise ship MV Hondius anchors a review by Laura Scorzolini and three colleagues on infection risks tied to ecotourism. The authors trace how one exposure to rodent waste in Argentina likely seeded cases that then spread between passengers in close quarters.

Andes virus stands out among hantaviruses because people can pass it to each other, and its long incubation period hampers quick detection. The authors urge surveillance that links animal, environmental, and human health data, plus travel medicine that prepares clinicians for exposures in wild settings. Cruise ships, they argue, act as amplifiers rather than sources, so early recognition matters.
pmc-13300211:
K Witte and colleagues report primary results, published in 2026, from the CORE-CPP study of conduction system pacing for people who qualify for cardiac resynchronization therapy. Standard resynchronization uses two ventricular leads, while conduction system pacing uses the heart's own wiring through a single lead in a dual-chamber pacemaker. The analysis drew on Medicare claims from 2017 to 2023 linked with device registration records.

The cohort held 2,207 conduction system pacing patients and 5,693 patients with conventional resynchronization pacemakers. The newer approach was non-inferior on thirty-day complications and reinterventions, and on heart failure hospitalizations at twelve months. It was also linked to lower all-cause mortality over that year. Reintervention rates were similar overall, and the authors conclude the single-lead approach is a credible alternative in this population.
pmc-13300711:
Elizabeth Brouwer and co-authors price out extremity arterial injury care in the United States in a 2026 analysis linking hospital chargemaster records with insurance claims. Graft repair follows about forty-five percent of these injuries, and the patient's own vein is the preferred material, yet injury specific cost data have been missing. The study followed 964 adults repaired between January 2018 and March 2023, tracking the first hospitalization and eighteen months of later care.

Mean hospital charges reached about three hundred seventeen thousand dollars, of which roughly seventy-six thousand was actually reimbursed. Fractures, graft infection, and amputation each added large sums during the stay, and early complications kept driving costs afterward, with graft infection the costliest thread of all. Patients repaired with their own vein used the least follow-up care and stayed most stable. The authors argue graft choice and complication prevention carry heavy financial weight.
pmc-13301311:
D Della Rocca and co-authors ask whether pulsed field ablation makes lab scheduling more predictable than heat based methods, in a 2026 real world study. Their European center analyzed 1,845 atrial fibrillation ablations, mixing first time and repeat cases across pulsed field, cryoballoon, and radiofrequency approaches. They measured not just room and procedure times but how widely those times scattered, since scatter is what wrecks a day's list.

Pulsed field cases were faster on average, roughly fifty-eight minutes of procedure time against seventy-six for cryoballoon in first time vein isolation. Their times also varied significantly less on every statistical test used. Adjusted models kept the advantage for both first time and repeat work. Longer cases clustered around extra ablation targets, implanted devices, mapping use, and prior heart surgery. The authors argue predictability is a resource: steadier times mean tighter scheduling, better throughput, and fewer overruns for the lab.
pmc-13301711:
L Crepin and co-authors trace how fat creeps into the atrial wall, fingering a resident cell as an accomplice, in a 2026 study. Fat around the heart expands, and scar tissue takes its place, forming the atrial cardiomyopathy that feeds fibrillation in metabolic disease. Using gene mapping and cell sorting in right atrial samples, the team located macrophage groups by neighborhood. Mouse work separated two groups, each deleted in turn in animals fed a fattening diet.

Deleting the resident Lyve1 positive macrophages left atria dystrophic: fat cells sat shrunken and sparse, muscle cells swelled, and no matrix scaffolding remained after a month of the diet. Deleting the recruited CCR2 macrophages did the opposite, preventing fibrosis and the cardiomyopathy itself. The authors conclude the resident group controls atrial fat build up while the recruited one drives scarring, a split that reframes inflammation as cellular jobs rather than plain damage.
pmc-13301811:
A brain blood-flow scan before heart surgery might flag who wakes up delirious, Astrid Bergmann and colleagues suggest in a 2026 study. They enrolled 108 patients over seventy set for heart surgery with a bypass machine, scanning both middle brain arteries with an automated Doppler device. Eighty-seven patients stayed in the final count, with confusion checked over three days.

Fourteen patients, sixteen percent, became delirious, and every one had shown abnormal flow readings before surgery. No patient with a clean scan did. Yet ninety-four percent of all patients showed abnormal flow inside the skull despite normal neck artery scans. The authors urge larger multicenter tests of this early signal.
pmc-13302611:
M Foti and a multicentre team map, in a 2026 study, exactly where pulsed field ablation lesions land after vein isolation for atrial fibrillation. The back wall of the left upper chamber sits close behind the veins, and stray lesions there might help or harm. High-density voltage maps made right after treatment revealed the true footprint.

One hundred thirteen patients treated at fourteen centres all achieved complete vein isolation. The average ablated area around the veins was sizeable, and more than half of patients showed unintended back-wall involvement on the fresh maps. About a quarter met the study's narrowing pattern and a small share showed full back-wall closure. During follow-up of roughly nine months, that involvement showed no link to rhythm recurrence.
pmc-13303111:
A metabolic index predicts who recovers poorly after stroke thrombectomy, especially when backup blood flow is weak, Yishu Wang and colleagues find in a 2026 hospital study. Records of 209 patients treated with endovascular therapy between 2022 and 2025 supplied triglyceride-glucose index values, imaging of collateral vessels, and ninety-day function scores. Sixty-four patients ended with poor outcomes.

The index independently nearly doubled the odds of a poor result per unit rise. Its bite concentrated in patients with poor collateral circulation, a significant interaction. Adding the index to clinical variables lifted the model's discrimination to an area under the curve of 0.834. Cheap admission labs, the authors argue, can flag high-risk recoveries early.
pmc-13303811:
Lujain Fouad Khalaf and co-authors test, in a 2026 case-control study, whether past infection with a common lung bacterium tracks with acute coronary syndromes. Chlamydia pneumoniae has long been suspected of feeding artery inflammation, yet proof stays murky. Blood antibodies revealing past exposure were measured in heart patients and matched controls at an Alexandria hospital.

No participant showed signs of fresh infection, so the question concerned older exposure only. Antibodies were present in eighty-three percent of the forty-seven cases against sixty percent of the fifty-three controls. The link survived adjustment for standard risk factors, though the numbers were small and the estimate imprecise. Inflammation marker levels were high in nearly all cases regardless of antibody status, and the authors demand prospective proof.
pmc-13305111:
Petr S. Sokolov, Lydia V. Ermakova, and co-authors report, in a 2026 materials study, a new way to build pixelated radiation detectors for X-ray imaging. Flat-panel detectors convert X-rays to light in a scintillator layer before sensors read it out. Existing plate designs lose light through translucency or low density, blurring the image.

Using light-based 3D printing, the team formed green bodies, then sintered them into two-layer ceramic elements. The base layer is transparent, non-glowing garnet, while the top layer holds scintillating pixels about two hundred thirty micrometers square. Tests under ultraviolet light and alpha particles showed spatial resolution near four tenths of the pixel size. The authors present the integrated process as a route to sharper medical and neutron detectors through finer printed pixels.
pmc-13306111:
Zepeng Zheng reported a severe skin ulcer illness after caesarean birth in a 2026 case report. A 24-year-old first-time mother had emergency surgery at 29 weeks and 4 days after cord prolapse, then developed painful ulcers around the wound by day seven.

Antibiotics failed and cleaning surgery worsened the wound through a trauma response, enlarging it to 21.5 × 11.0 cm in reported measures. Diagnosis on day eleven rested on appearance, sterile cultures and tissue findings, and strong immune-suppressing treatment followed. The patient left hospital on day thirty, with full skin closure reached later in follow-up care.
pmc-13306411:
Julia C. Andrade spun all water based tiny fibres from PVP blends in a 2026 study. Two mix partners were tried one by one, a seaweed gum and a vitamin, to split how each shapes the spin run.

Base mixes held 20% PVP, with gum at 1 to 5 percent or vitamin at 1 to 10 percent in the reported plan. Gum raised how well the mix carried charge, while the vitamin left it near flat. UV light shone on fibres as they formed, and skin and strength tests closed the check set for both blends.
pmc-13307011:
Mendoza and eight co-authors test whether stiffness imaging can sort benign breast lumps from cancers in Peru, where evidence of this kind is scarce. The method, elastography, measures how firm a lesion feels to sound waves. Their review covered 189 patients imaged over one year.

Among 85 lesions checked by tissue diagnosis, about 64 percent were malignant. Cancers scored stiffer on both measures used. A shear-wave cutoff of 47.5 kilopascals caught about 80 percent of cancers while clearing two thirds of benign lumps. The imaging grade system still predicted best overall. The authors frame stiffness as a helpful second opinion for radiologists.
pmc-13307211:
Kehoe argues that joint design work in mental health often shuts out the people it claims to hear. She calls this wrong epistemic injustice, which means some kinds of knowledge get pushed aside. Lived experience, meaning what patients know first hand, is often valued least.

Kehoe sets out a three-step cycle built on ideas from restorative practice, which focus on truth and repair. Step one asks groups to name harms and tell the truth. Step two works on repair and trust between staff and patients. Step three moves to shared design of future services. The aim is fair say, not just a seat at the table.
pmc-13307311:
Sebastian Knoll and co-authors report in 2026 on a paired molecule that joins ferrocene to a Dawson type oxide cluster, with no noble metal used at all. Visible light splits charge inside the pair, as an electron moves from the iron based part toward the cluster.

The team tracked that light driven step with several forms of spectroscopy and with computer based quantum chemistry. The split charge could then switch on organic peroxides in both directions and free oxygen based radicals. Results offer a design guide for light active pairs built from common, low cost elements for solar fuel and catalysis work.
pmc-13307411:
Yi-Kai Hu and co-authors ask in 2026 where cancer stem cells in liver tumours come from, using single cell data from 109 samples and 44 patients in five public groups. They also sorted stem and non stem cells from a lab line and tracked gene marks over two weeks of growth.

Mutation counts and family trees placed stem cells at the far ends of tumour growth, not at its root. About 78 percent of the gene marks that set stem cells apart stayed in place after the cells changed form, a kind of locked in memory. A 16 gene score built from those marks flagged early return of disease.
pmc-13307611:
Jean Baltzer and co-authors explore in 2026 whether how a knee moves during walking before surgery can guide total knee replacement planning with robot help. Of 30 patients booked for surgery, 26 had a full gait check before the operation, and 17 had a repeat check six months later.

Knees that leaned more inward during walking showed wider looseness on the outer side when straight and tighter looseness inside when bent. In a small inward leaning subgroup, pre surgery motion plus planned looseness foresaw post surgery motion very well. Walking scores also tracked with how patients rated their new knee, which hints at a path to more personal planning.
pmc-13308611:
See Jie Yow and co-authors study in 2026 how threat context shapes whether neutrophils burst and die after inflammasome firing, a step that frees defence signals. Neutrophils often free those signals without bursting, and the switch that lets them burst has stayed murky until now.

A growth factor called GM-CSF licensed bursting after two sensor types fired, by boosting an early priming step in the cells. A strong bacterial primer did the same, while a weaker one did not reach that bar. Bursting also needed a self loop through a tumour necrosis factor receptor, plus a membrane protein for the final tear. One sensor type stood apart and gained nothing from the factor.
pmc-13309011:
Brittany Peterson and co-authors cost out in 2026 a national door to door azithromycin drive to cut child deaths in Niger, from trial roots in 80 Dosso towns. They paired fine cost counts with field notes to price a twice a year round for children aged 1 to 59 months in non urban areas.

At 90 percent cover, the yearly national bill would run to 12.5 million dollars, or 1.59 dollars for each dose handed out in their model. Sparse regions cost far more per dose, up to 3.61 dollars at the top end of the range. Training ate 16.4 percent of all costs, so shared training with other health drives could trim the bill for states.
pmc-13309711:
Manish Rai, Rajeshwari Gore, and Piyush Setu describe in 2026 the anaesthetic care of an eight-year-old girl who has severe spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy who needed cataract surgery with a lens implant. Her stiffness, bent joints, and speech limits cloud every step of anaesthesia. A full pre-anaesthetic review and family talks came before the surgery.

Early troubles centred on placing a drip line and placing her rigid limbs safely. Beyond those hurdles, the work and healing ran smoothly under general anaesthesia. The child weighed only nine kilos, far below growth norms, which shaped drug and gear choices. Breathing-in risk from excess fluids also hangs over such cases in general. The authors conclude that careful checks, fitted drugs, and a team approach can still deliver a calm course. Each child may react in her own way, they caution, so planning must be her own.
pmc-13309811:
Imran Ahmad and Yousaf Jamal Mahsood run a randomised trial in 2026 comparing two injection strategies for diabetic macular swelling in eyes that already carry an artificial lens. Eighty-two patients at a Peshawar teaching hospital split evenly between monthly bevacizumab alone and a combined first treatment adding steroid placed behind the eye wall. Vision and macular thickness were measured over four months.

Both groups improved significantly in sight and thickness from their starting points. The combination group finished with better vision scores and a thinner macula than the single-drug group. Its steroid dose was given once, at the first visit, alongside the standard drug. Swelling at the centre of vision is the main sight threat in diabetes, so extra drying power matters. The authors propose the single combined opening treatment as a stronger start for this patient group.
pmc-13310211:
Luke Tattersall examines how variants of a cell sensor shape bone cell behavior in a 2026 study. The sensor, P2RX7, responds to ATP, a molecule plentiful around bone, and helps govern bone balance. Natural variants and shortened forms of the sensor can strengthen or weaken its action.

Full and shortened sensor forms, alone and paired, plus three single-letter variants, were placed into bone-forming cells. Calcium entry, pore opening, cell growth, enzyme activity, mineral laying, and bone gene activity were all measured. Variant effects differed by form and pairing, with known gain and loss variants behaving distinctly. The author uses the pattern to explain how inherited sensor differences may shift bone mass and turnover.
pmc-13310911:
Liang Gao led a 2026 study on which E. coli traits turn harmless newborn colonization into invasive infection. The germ can pass from mother to baby at birth and sometimes cause life threatening illness. Gene traits that split those paths were unclear in proven mother baby pairs.

Pairs totaled 43 in number, with 27 invasive cases and 16 colonization cases confirmed by genome match. One strain type appeared only in invasive cases. Capsule and iron uptake genes were far more common in invasive strains, and a model named four strong predictors. All top strain isolates carried the three key genes together. Gene checks may flag risky strains early.
pmc-13311111:
Guolin Song and colleagues profile a drug resistant germ in a psychiatric hospital in a 2026 study. Corynebacterium striatum can infect long stay patients, yet telling true infection from harmless carriage is hard. Isolates from psychiatric inpatients were tested for drug response and gene makeup.

Thirty isolates were gathered, and most resisted many drugs. Gene reading found stacks of resistance genes plus traits for iron uptake and sticking to tissue. Family trees showed wide diversity with loose ties to ward place. A five item infection score sorted infection from carriage better than any single marker in early tests. Outside checks are required.
pmc-13311211:
Kenza Qitout and co-authors present a 2026 dataset built to help computers find Barbary macaques in zoo images. The monkeys are an endangered North African primate, and tracking them by eye takes much staff time.

The set holds 1742 labeled photos with 6689 single monkey sightings, filmed from many angles, times of day, and seasons at a French zoo. Each sighting carries an outline mask and an age label, which goes beyond simple box labels. The team trained several YOLO models on the data to test how well they work. The set gives conservation and zoo teams a shared base for building automatic watch tools for primates.
pmc-13311311:
Minmin Wen and co-authors, in 2026, analyze a survey study on thyroid hormones, heart disease, and a measure of body aging in older adults. The aging measure is called phenotypic age acceleration.

Data came from the 2007 to 2010 rounds of the United States NHANES survey. Among people aged 60 and over, higher free T3 levels tied to lower heart disease odds. The aging measure carried about a fifth of that link in the analysis, at 21.13 percent for free T3 in this model. Total T3 showed a like pattern. The results hint that slowing body aging could help guard the older heart.
pmc-13311811:
Giovanni Di Giacomo and co-authors define new X-ray angles for judging how a reverse shoulder replacement sits, in a 2026 study. In this operation the ball and socket trade places, and the parts can be shifted outward or downward in several combinations. No standard measures separated the socket side's position from the arm side's. The team reviewed 74 patients operated on between 2018 and 2022 and split them by implant pattern.

Their angle measures proved highly repeatable between readers. Yet none of the angles tracked with how far patients could move the arm, and the implant patterns did not differ in patient scores. The authors still see value in the measures for describing placement precisely. They suggest later work test the angles in larger groups and other implant designs.
pmc-13311911:
Anita Caruso and co-authors in 2026 present a study on emotional distress and guilt in women carrying BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations, and how those feelings shape choices about having children.

Carriers face high lifetime breast and ovarian cancer risks, and prevention steps carry heavy physical and mental loads. The study measures guilt forms, including survivor guilt and a sense of total responsibility for passing on risk. Distress ran stronger around telling others the result than around the test itself, on the authors' account, and depression rates passed those in the general population. Support for carriers should treat guilt as a core issue.
pmc-13312011:
Fen Zhu and co-authors show that blocking an enzyme primes lymphoma cells to die through two routes at once, in a 2026 study. The enzyme, PRMT5, is overproduced in aggressive B-cell cancers. A drug against it engages its target well but works weakly alone in patients. So the team hunted for partners using a profiling test. That test measures how close cells sit to programmed death.

The blocker pushed cells nearer to death and, in two lymphoma types, made them depend more on a survival protein, BCL-2. Pairing the blocker with a BCL-2 drug then killed those cells in synergy. Separately, the blocker raised two death receptors on the cell surface, sensitizing even the less BCL-2-dependent lines to an outside death signal. The authors propose these pairings as rational combinations to test in B-cell lymphoma treatment.
pmc-13312811:
Dian Fu and co-authors analyze, in a 2026 retrospective study, whether what men eat relates to semen quality when infertility stems from varicocele. This vein disorder is a leading cause of male infertility and works largely through oxidative stress, so the team asked whether antioxidant and micronutrient intake tracks with sperm measures in affected men.

Diet records and semen tests from 380 men treated between 2018 and 2023 were compared across intake levels for vitamin C, vitamin E, zinc, selenium, CoQ10, and L-carnitine. The highest intake group showed better sperm concentration, motility, and shape. Zinc and CoQ10 best predicted concentration, vitamin E and L-carnitine predicted forward motility, and vitamin C intake ran opposite to sperm DNA damage. The authors argue nutrition deserves a central place in managing varicocele-related infertility.
pmc-13312911:
Levi T. Flom and co-authors characterize, in a 2026 mouse study, the brain cell groups, or ensembles, that light up for two competing rewards at once. Addiction research links drug seeking to small ensembles of neurons tagged by their activity, usually studied one reward at a time. The team built a place preference test where one chamber meant cocaine and the other meant chocolate.

Using genetically engineered mice whose active neurons can be permanently labeled, 33 males and 33 females learned both associations. After conditioning they favored the cocaine chamber when no reward was present. Ensembles tagged in cortex and nucleus accumbens during testing matched the size of those from single-reward training, and context-tagged cells grew larger than home-cage controls. Ensemble size, though, did not track how strongly each mouse preferred a chamber, a caution for reading preference off cell counts.
pmc-13313911:
Salmonella in chickens threatens both farm income and the safety of eggs and meat, and drug-resistant strains are spreading. Wael Elfeil and co-authors test a killed vaccine in a 2025 study. The vaccine covers four strains of the germ, mixed into a water-in-oil formula.

The team gave the vaccine to 250 clean laboratory chickens and kept a control group for comparison. They watched the birds for safety signs, then measured antibody responses after a germ challenge. They also counted how much of the germ left the body in droppings and how much reached the liver. A vaccine that cuts shedding and spread could lower both farm losses and risk to people who eat poultry.
pmc-13314411:
Silvia Mihaela Ilie and colleagues find a viral fingerprint that may flag breast cancers ripe for immune therapy, in a study from 2026. Old retroviruses sit in our DNA, making up about 8 percent of the genome as stated in the report. When cancer cells wake them, the immune system can react as if a virus were present.

The team used public RNA data from The Cancer Genome Atlas for breast tumors and matched normal tissue, counting retrovirus activity with a tool called Telescope. They built a signature of 19 such viruses whose activity tied to signs of this viral mimicry inside tumors. Luminal breast cancers with high signature scores looked more immune-active and more likely to answer immune therapy. The marker could help pick patients for drugs that free the immune system.
pmc-13314511:
Takahisa Hiramitsu and Jong Ju Jeong introduce the second volume of a research topic on parathyroid disease diagnosis in an editorial published in 2026. These gland disorders range from silent blood quirks to harsh disease with body-wide fallout.

Fresh blood assays and imaging have sharpened detection, the editors note, yet hard problems stay: pinpointing the lesion, sorting risk, and folding test data into choices for each patient. The new volume gathers studies and reviews that widen what diagnosis means here. Rather than rest on blood proof or lesion maps alone, it stresses the variety of the disease, outlook grading, and new tech routes. The editors frame diagnosis as a joined process that shapes personal care, not a single test result.
pmc-13315111:
Mariam Zabihi and co-workers build a model that compresses early brain growth into a compact code, in a study from 2026. Each child brain path differs, and those paths shape skills and risk for developmental states, yet most studies grade one region at a time.

The team trained an autoencoder on T1 MRI scans from 564 children, of whom a share of 55 percent were male as given in the report, with a mean age of 4.90 years. The learned code kept age and sex, guessed sex with accuracy near 84 percent as stated, and rebuilt scans with a mean error near 0.04 in the units reported. Whole and local shape traits survived the squeeze. Such codes could flag off-track growth early, while honoring that brains vary in many ways at once.
pmc-13315411:
Xiaolan Xie and colleagues measured the choroid layer under the central retina in 2026 in young children in China. Using swept-source scans, they studied 303 eyes of preschool children with no eye disease, along with full eye exams and refraction after dilating drops.

Mean thickness was about 326 micrometers in children aged 3 to 6 years. Children with myopia had a thinner layer than those with normal focus, and the gap stayed after adjustment for other factors. Thickness also rose with the focusing measure and related to eye length and other traits. The work gives early-life values that may help track myopia onset.
pmc-13316011:
Sheng Wang and colleagues propose, in a 2026 study, an improved Q-learning method for rescue path planning after mass casualty incidents under damaged roads. Earthquakes and similar disasters wreck road networks, rendering pre-disaster maps obsolete and making routes unknown and dynamic. Older static planners struggle in such settings, while standard learning agents fall into local optima and fail rescue safety requirements. The authors combine tuned trial cooling with experience replay in a Q-learning algorithm.

Cooling regulates exploration live, letting the agent escape local traps in damaged environments. Experience replay reuses key path experiences, improving speed. Experiments showed fast online re-planning in response to road updates. The method provides a confident decision aid for urgent post-disaster rescue, balancing access against safety. The authors present it as a lifeline tool for emergency units racing the golden hour, when arrival determines victim survival and operation success.
pmc-13316111:
Jose Cruz Nunez Perez and co-authors build chaotic oscillators on a programmable chip in a 2026 paper. Fractional order chaotic systems draw theory interest, yet a hardware recipe that keeps their chaos while saving chip resources was missing. Two reconfigurable code modules were written, one for each of two fractional integration methods.

Five named oscillators, from Lorenz to a Yu Wang system, ran on a mid range FPGA board. Software simulations came first, then chaos strength was traced as the fractional order changed. One method gave stronger chaos over wider ranges for most systems. Resource counts showed the Runge Kutta style method used fewer logic blocks in most cases.
pmc-13316211:
Jan Wiefhoff and co-authors count brain harms in patients on lung-heart machines in this 2026 study. The machines, known as ECMO, save lives in organ failure but carry high risk. Records cover over a decade at one large center.

About one in five of the patients developed brain trouble, from bleeding inside the skull to stroke and oxygen-starved swelling. Death in hospital hit over three quarters of that group, far above those without brain harm. Odd pupil responses proved the strongest death sign. Most survivors left with severe disability. The authors urge early spotting of high-risk patients and closer watching.
pmc-13316611:
Bin Qin and colleagues, in a 2026 brain imaging study, pool data from several sites to clarify network changes in Parkinson's disease. Earlier single-site work gave inconsistent results, partly because samples were small. Resting-state scans show how brain networks connect when a person is not doing a task.

Data covered 160 patients and 75 matched healthy controls drawn from four repositories. Analysis of seven networks found lower connectivity between visual, auditory, sensorimotor and control networks, with some raised links to subcortical and cerebellar areas. A dynamic analysis found four recurring states, and patients lingered in some states while leaving others quickly. Dynamic measures revealed widespread reductions that static measures missed, suggesting value as markers of progression.
pmc-13317011:
Paola Coutinho Barreto and co-authors gathered, in a 2026 integrative review, the evidence on birth plans, written wish lists that pregnant women prepare for labor and delivery. Recommended by the World Health Organization, plans aim to give women voice and shared control in the birth room.

Forty-one studies across seven databases, with no time or language limits, fed the summary. Plans eased talk between women and staff, boosted women's active role and autonomy, and raised satisfaction with birth. Studies also linked plans with fewer cesarean births, more vaginal births, higher newborn Apgar scores, and more breastfeeding starts. Common wishes covered skin contact, a chosen companion, pain relief choices, and movement during labor.
pmc-13317211:
Ye Song and co-authors combined deep brain stimulation with a brain-computer interface in a Parkinson's mouse model, tracing effects across brain and gut, in a 2026 study. Public gene and microbe datasets were mined first, revealing synaptic damage, disturbed metabolism, and a gut flora short on short-chain fatty acid producers in the disease.

Four mouse groups, from healthy to doubly treated, then underwent behavior tests, brain wave recording, and tissue analysis. The combined treatment improved movement, calmed abnormal brain rhythms, restored the gut barrier and its microbes, and cut the clumping of the disease protein. The authors frame the pair as a brain-gut therapy.
pmc-13318111:
Madelyn J Blake and co-authors show, in 2026, that pulmonary arterial hypertension reshapes the human liver in a distinctive way. High pressure in the lung arteries strains the right side of the heart, and liver dysfunction then predicts poor outcomes. Cell-level effects in human liver tissue were poorly defined.

The team sequenced nuclei from autopsy liver tissue of five patients and four controls, then compared public data for fatty liver disease and Fontan-related liver disease. Hypertension livers showed their own pattern. Liver cells shifted toward a low-oxygen metabolism with reduced fat burning, vessel cells increased sugar use, and scar-forming cells switched on pathways tied to disease severity. Immune macrophages showed complement activation. The pattern supports a disease-specific liver injury linked to right heart failure.
pmc-13318611:
Bo Pang and Yupeng Li report a 2026 training trial on whether the surface used for plyometric jumping changes the gains in leg power, balance, and agility for male college tennis players. Thirty players were split into sand training, hard-ground training, and a control group of ten each.

Both training groups practised three times a week for eight weeks while controls kept normal tennis work. Jump heights rose clearly in both training groups, with hard ground favouring reactive strength and approach jump, and sand favouring long jump and front reach balance on both legs. Agility in a hexagon test improved under both surfaces. The authors advise picking the surface to match the training goal of each phase.
pmc-13318911:
Prerna Dodeja and colleagues review, in 2026, how to study drug transfer into human breast milk. Most medicines pass into milk by simple diffusion, but data are scarce. Stopping breastfeeding is rarely the right answer, they argue. Enrolling nursing mothers in studies purely to measure transfer is hard.

The review summarises measures used to quantify drug levels in milk. It lays out clinical study designs suited to lactation. Where human data are missing, laboratory, animal, and computer models can help. Formula-based estimates of milk-to-plasma ratios are explained. Pharmacokinetic models that predict drug levels over time also feature. The goal is better safety guidance for the many mothers who need medication while nursing.
pmc-13319111:
Qi Wang and co-authors identify a protein that lets pancreatic cancer cells invade and spread, in a 2026 study. This cancer is known for early invasion and fast spread, yet the cell machinery behind those traits was murky. The protein is an atypical member of a family that shapes the cell's inner frame. Across patient groups, lab models, and single-cell data, it ran high in cancer cells. High levels tracked with later stage disease and shorter survival.

Cutting the protein slowed invasion, movement, and colony growth in dishes. It also cut tumor starting power and spread in animals. The protein holds together a partner complex that builds the flat sheets cells use to crawl. Without it, the cancer's gene program still shifted toward a mobile state, but cells could not act on it. Restoring the partner rescued invasion. The authors name the protein a choke point worth drug study.
pmc-13319711:
Víctor Hugo Linares-Serrano and co-authors report a 2026 case of rebuilding after full removal for penile cancer. A 66 year old man had a growth on the organ for one year that proved to be a wart like form of skin cancer at an advanced stage. Full removal was needed to control the disease, a step with heavy effects on body function and self image.

Surgeons rebuilt a new shaft from a flap of scrotal skin and placed the urine opening below, then cleared groin nodes with robot help. Tests showed no spread to those nodes. Healing went well, the flap stayed healthy, and urine flow worked as hoped. Skin flaps offer a workable path where fine vessel surgery is not on hand.
pmc-13320011:
Elizabeth Walsh and co-authors set out a study plan in a 2026 protocol for testing smart software on breast cancer slides in a British hospital service. Lab staff face rising loads, and breast cases need extra marker tests that add time. Software that reads stained slides for three key markers could ease that load, but it must prove itself inside real clinic flow first.

Cases will be picked live from the lab system at a major cancer center and read by the software on a stand alone machine beside normal care, so no patient path changes. About 400 cases with full data are sought after checks and opt out screens. Marker calls from the software will be weighed against lab truth.
pmc-13320411:
Bahattin Pasli, Mehmet Ulkir and Barış Kafa measure, in 2026, the shape of the upper thigh bone in a set of dry specimens, aiming to inform hip implant design. Fit between implant and bone shapes affects fracture care and joint replacement outcomes. Population anatomical data help reduce mismatch.

Seventy-three unpaired femurs of unknown age and sex were measured by two anatomists using tape, calipers and a protractor, with repeat readings. Reliability ranged from good to excellent. Average bone length and neck angle are reported with their spreads. Left and right sides matched on most measures, though the neck angle differed significantly by side. Head and neck dimensions rose together, and bone length tracked head size. The authors note missing age and sex data as a limit.
pmc-13320511:
Irène Georgescu and co-authors model why women stay on long-term breast cancer drug treatment in a 2026 survey study from France. Between 30 and 50 percent of patients stop hormone or targeted pills early, which raises the risk of the cancer returning or spreading. The team used self-determination theory to map how feelings about care shape the wish to keep going.

A first group of 89 women checked the survey tool, and 412 women then tested the full model. Feeling close to others fed skill confidence, which fed choice, free motivation, and then intent to stay on treatment. The cancer doctor's manner was the strongest outside influence, while side effects worked by raising mental strain.
pmc-13320711:
Anush Swaminathan and co-authors map calcium signals in skin blood vessel cells in a 2026 mouse study. Calcium signals in the cells lining vessels help control blood flow, force sensing, and leakiness, but their pattern across whole skin networks was unknown. Long term live imaging followed the same cells in three dimensional skin capillaries over time.

A stable network of lining cells took part in calcium signalling again and again. That network needs a gap junction protein, Connexin 43, to stay coordinated; losing it raised calcium activity, blood flow, and vessel leak. Blocking one calcium channel type in nearby tissue restored normal activity and barrier function, which points to a control point for vessel health.
pmc-13321011:
Fernanda Tranquillini and co-authors pool worldwide data on skin cancer in people with albinism in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Albinism cuts melanin, the pigment that shields skin from sun, so cancer risk is high. Prior data on how often cancer and its early form, actinic keratosis, occur were scattered.

Twelve studies covering 1747 people gave a pooled actinic keratosis rate of 38 percent and a skin cancer rate of 19 percent. Within cancers, squamous cell type made up 55.4 percent and basal cell type 33.7 percent, while melanoma was near zero. Wide gaps between studies were noted. The authors urge targeted sun protection and skin checks for this group.
pmc-13321211:
Emanuele Marzetti and co-authors discuss salt limits in care for older hospital patients in a 2026 article. Salt intake stays high worldwide and is tied to poor health outcomes, so hospitals often restrict it. For older adults, though, bland food can cut eating and raise malnutrition risk, the tension summed up by the complaint that food has no flavour.

Taste loss, swallowing trouble, and dry mouth are common in old age and already blunt appetite. Strict sodium cuts may deepen those problems by making meals less appealing. The authors weigh heart and blood pressure gains of restriction against intake and nutrition losses in acute geriatric wards and urge balanced, person level judgement.
pmc-13321411:
Xingyu Lu and co-authors test ultra fast radiation delivery in a 2026 mouse study of breast cancer. Standard radiation for breast cancer can spill dose onto the liver and impair its function. FLASH radiotherapy gives dose at ultra high rates and has shown strong sparing of normal tissue. The team compared both modes in mice carrying 4T1 breast tumours.

Each group got a single 20 gray dose, by FLASH at 625 gray per second or standard delivery at 0.54 gray per second in the study. Tumour delay matched between modes. FLASH mice lost weight only briefly and showed lower liver injury marks, better kept liver structure, and weaker early scarring signals.
pmc-13321511:
Paulina Antwi and co-authors present a 2026 update on the legal cannabis market in Ontario, Canada, five years after legal sales began. Price, strength, and product range shape what buyers pick, so watchdogs track them as the market matures. Early years brought more product types and falling prices.

The team pulled data from the provincial store site, the sole wholesaler and online seller, across early 2024. They logged 1,727 products with type, price, and strength of the two main compounds, plus plant kind. Most goods were for inhaling, split among smoking, vaping, and concentrates. Ingestible and skin goods made up the rest. The map shows how the shelf has shifted since the first post legalization count.
pmc-13321611:
Mohamad Jamalinia and co-authors report a 2026 study on AI forecasts of fatty liver disease split by sex. The disease, tied to metabolic faults, shows clear sex gaps in risk traits and outcomes. The team asked whether models trained apart for men and women learn unlike patterns and score better.

The study enrolled 446 adults at a heart referral center. Data split into training and test sets by sex. Eight model types were trained on all data and again apart for each sex, to flag disease presence and grade of fat build up by ultrasound. Disease was present in about 64 percent of the group. Sex split training lifted scores in men but stayed weak in women.
pmc-13322311:
Shihui Jia and co-authors set out a trial protocol in 2026 for helping older adults manage high blood pressure alongside frailty. Both conditions often occur together and make daily self-care hard, while standard health teaching shows limited effect. Motivational interviewing, a counselling style that builds personal drive, may support lasting change, but trial proof is scarce.

The randomised trial will enrol 72 community dwelling older adults in Changchun, China, split evenly between groups. One group gets a 12 week interviewing programme based on a stages of change model; the other gets usual health education. Outcomes span self-management behaviour, blood pressure, frailty, and quality of life over 36 weeks.
pmc-13322611:
Leah A. Lewis and a large team use combined imaging to study alcohol harm in developing zebrafish in a 2026 report. Prenatal alcohol exposure causes fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, yet how ethanol disrupts early growth, including tissue stiffness, stays murky. Zebrafish embryos are clear and grow fast, which suits live imaging.

Embryos exposed to varied ethanol levels were examined with light sheet fluorescence, coherence tomography, and elastography at once, giving structure, molecular, and stiffness views without harming the embryos. Ethanol disturbed Wnt signal activity in the nervous system, and that shift tracked with shape defects seen across all imaging modes. The platform may speed study of how alcohol derails early development.
pmc-13322911:
Jacqueline A. Turner leads a study of liver spread in uveal melanoma, published in 2026, centred on a lipid signal that quiets immune attack. Eye melanoma spreads to the liver with striking frequency, where local immune tolerance helps tumours resist immune therapy.

The team measured autotaxin, the enzyme that makes lysophosphatidic acid, in liver resident cells and in killer T cells taken from liver tumours, blood and healthy donors. Autotaxin was present on Kupffer cells and linked to suppressive markers, and the signal altered how antigen-specific T cells behaved under long exposure. Mouse cells lacking the LPA receptor 5 helped pin down the path. Liver-directed treatment outcomes are reviewed alongside these findings.
pmc-13323511:
Raymond Chibvongodze, Mutinda Cleophas Kyama and Lucy Muchiri study bacterial vaginosis and high-risk HPV types together in Nairobi, Kenya, in a 2026 cross-sectional analysis. Baseline screening covered 498 women enrolled in an ongoing cohort between July 2022 and November 2023.

Bacterial vaginosis appeared in 24.7 percent of women and high-risk HPV in 28.1 percent of the group in their counts, with about a tenth carrying both. Vaginosis linked significantly to pooled high-risk HPV status after adjustment, with roughly doubled odds in their model. Genotype-level checks aimed to show which HPV types drive the link, a gap in African data. The authors connect the finding to cervical cancer prevention in a high-burden region.
pmc-13323811:
Yara Jelwan and co-authors tracked how finerenone, a newer mineralocorticoid receptor blocker, is being used in the United States. Their 2026 serial cross-sectional study used IQVIA drug-sales audit data covering more than 70% of outpatient use, from July 2021 through December 2024, focusing on cardiologists and nephrologists. Trials support the drug for kidney progression, cardiovascular events, and heart failure, yet anecdote suggested it was rarely used.

Uptake proved modest: sales crept upward, with mild jumps after major trial releases that also tracked with search interest, but the drug still equaled only 3.0% of empagliflozin sales and 2.6% of spironolactone sales in 2024. The specialty gap was stark, at about 23 orders per kidney doctor for every 0.70 per cardiologist. The authors see a slow shift upward, led by kidney specialists, with cardiology adoption lagging well behind.
pmc-13323911:
Arun Chhokar and co-authors build a flow-based test for two transcripts tied to cervical cancer growth, in a 2026 laboratory study. STAT3 signalling helps HPV drive cervical cancer, and joint measures of STAT3 with HPV E6/E7 messages showed screening promise under the microscope, without a clear cut-off.

Using three cervical cell lines, HPV-negative, HPV16-positive and HPV18-positive, the team checked probe specificity by microscopy, then moved the same probes into flow cytometry for counting. STAT3 signals stood strong and discrete in the HPV-positive lines and diffuse in the negative line, while scrambled probes stayed near blank. The work tests whether counted signals can flag progressive cervical lesions earlier and more objectively.
pmc-13324311:
Jiamin Jiang and co-authors design a layered scaffold that reprogrammes aged bone metabolism, in a 2026 biomaterials study. Senescent cells unbalance the repair setting in old bone, and passive supports or single delivered factors cannot reverse that state.

Their ceramic scaffold pairs a printed outer tube with an inner rod carrying nicotinamide mononucleotide, releasing both that compound and manganese ions over time. The pair attacks two core faults: low NAD+ energy currency and excess oxidative stress. Treated cells regained NAD+ levels, healthier mitochondria and calmer redox balance, with less inflammation and stronger bone differentiation. Implanted in aged rats, the scaffold significantly boosted new bone formation and maturation.
pmc-13324411:
Edgar Fernando Dorado-Roncancio leads a large expedition team publishing open marine biodiversity records from Colombia's northern Pacific coast, in a 2026 data paper. The Colombia BIO Jurado-Cupica expedition joined the marine institute INVEMAR with two universities and the community councils of Cupica and Los Delfines.

Sampling ran across 34 stations in five ecosystems between Cupica and Jurado: mangroves, rocky shoreline, intertidal mudflats, rocky reefs and open pelagic water. The expedition, run under the national Colombia BIO strategy, aimed to raise knowledge of a little-surveyed coast and to share the resulting records openly. Local community partnership shapes both the fieldwork and the intended use of the dataset.
pmc-13324511:
Maria Chiara Palloni and co-authors propose a simple yardstick for cholesterol care in a 2026 article on LDL targets. LDL cholesterol causes artery disease, and the 2025 European guidance sets tighter risk-based goals, yet under one third of treated patients reach them.

The authors blame slow, step-by-step prescribing, called therapeutic inertia, plus patient and system barriers. Their fix is to measure the distance to target: the percent drop a patient needs from the current LDL level. That gap then guides drug choice, since statins alone often fall short. Added options include ezetimibe, bempedoic acid, PCSK9 blockers, and inclisiran. Early, strong, and lasting lowering matters because total lifetime exposure drives risk.
pmc-13325911:
Matt Neal and colleagues validate machine learning blood tests for cancer risk in urgent NHS referrals in a 2026 service evaluation. General practitioners send over 3 million such referrals a year in England, yet only about 6 percent prove to be cancer.

The PinPoint set of nine blood tests ran across five hospital trusts and 170 practices from December 2020 to July 2025, covering 16,481 patients. Five tests looked clinically useful, led by the upper gastrointestinal test with an area under the curve of 0.86 in the results. Focusing on the top tenth by risk cut the number needed to investigate per cancer found by 2.6 to 6.1 fold.
pmc-13326211:
Kaïs Ouerghi and three co-authors describe how a stuck heart stent was freed, and what the rescue cost later, in a 2026 case report. A sixty-three-year-old man had a stent placed in his left main artery after a cardiac arrest. Eight months later, a new stent for a side branch jammed inside the first stent's frame. The team freed it with a snare worked through two access points, keeping a guide wire in place.

The rescue seemed clean on standard imaging, and flow looked normal. Over a year later, a closer scan view showed the first stent's frame had in fact come apart, so the artery was stented again. Later ultrasound checks confirmed a sound repair. The authors warn that pull rescues can hide deep frame harm. They urge routine inside-vessel imaging after such rescues.
pmc-13327011:
Jisu Park and team tested a bone growth protein graft for scaphoid waist breaks that fail to heal. Their 2026 early clinic study trailed seven people in a row, fixed with two headless squeeze screws plus NOVOSIS. NOVOSIS is lab-made human bone growth protein in a mineral carrier. It ran from August 2023 to December 2024. Scaphoid breaks that fail to heal are hard, with scant blood flow and bones out of line.

All seven healed on X-ray by last check, after 12.4 months follow-up. Pain scores fell from 4.9 at the start to 0.4 at last check, and Mayo Wrist Scores rose from 59.3 at the start to 94.3 at last check. X-ray angles got much better. No surgery-linked harms like infection, stray bone growth, or donor harm showed up. The team calls NOVOSIS a workable own-bone graft swap, with healing and wrist use. Bigger studies must back the early result.
pmc-13327311:
Peter Rasmussen, Damian Miles Bailey, and Alex Stewart wrote a 2026 response letter on openness in physiology research. They reply to colleagues who warned that rigid analysis plans could curb exploratory work. The authors agree that exploration drives new ideas, but separate that point from how results should be worded.

A study counts as confirmatory only when its main choices were fixed before the data were seen, they explain, which is what gives error rates their meaning. Flexible studies still matter, yet their claims should stay provisional and framed as leads for later tests. Matching claim strength to how a study was run, in any field or size of study, keeps inference honest.
pmc-13327611:
Fujun Qin and co-authors show how the COVID-19 virus uses cell recycling sacs to escape in a 2026 study. Working with virus-like particles that copy and transcribe but cannot fully infect, plus microscopy, drug tests, and acidity probes, they tracked exit routes. How much virus leaves, and in what state, shapes how harmful an infection becomes.

Infected cells pushed lysosomes to fuse with the surface more often, and that route carried most virus out, ahead of the standard secretion path. The viral ORF3a protein drove the fusion boost, while ORF3a and the E protein lowered lysosome acidity and enzyme power, shielding new virus from early damage. Making sacs less acidic with a drug raised release further.
pmc-13327911:
Boohwi Hong and co-authors test a steroid shot against rebound pain after arm nerve blocks in a 2026 study. Rebound pain, a sharp surge as a block wears off, troubles many patients after upper limb bone surgery. Records covered 1,171 patients, of whom 651, or 55.6 percent, received intravenous dexamethasone.

Rebound pain struck 7.1 percent of the steroid group against 16.9 percent without it, and onset came later, at a median of 14 hours against 11 hours in the comparison. Causal machine learning put the average benefit at a 9 percent absolute risk cut, steady across patient types with no clear subgroup differences. A single vein dose thus looks like a simple shield against a painful rebound.
pmc-13328711:
Mingwei Liao and co-authors propose a more exact way to rebuild neuron shapes from images in a 2026 study. Rebuilding neurons by hand or by single programs is slow and uneven, since images differ and workers differ in skill. The team built maths models for speed and accuracy, plus rules for grading how hard each dataset is.

Those grades guide two choices: which program fits which data, and which worker should handle which task. Across data types, accuracy rose, with the best group gaining up to 18.8 percent in the reported tests. Matching tasks to workers raised accuracy by 44.3 percent and overall speed by 34.6 percent, compared with older habits. The authors frame the shift as moving from habit to measured choice.
pmc-13329511:
Tom Winkler and colleagues publish an anonymised dataset of German truck freight trips in a 2026 article. Records came from the planning systems of two freight firms over 16 months in total. Names of people and firms were removed or replaced, while links between records were kept for research use.

The set holds 31,352 trip records in total, as reported by the authors. One firm ran 37 heavy trucks over 5 months in 2024, and the other ran 83 trucks over 10 months that year. All trucks used combustion engines. Each record gives start and end points, time windows, distances, and assigned truck and driver codes. Uses include route planning tests, demand forecasts, and electric truck planning.
pmc-13329811:
Jocelyn E. Malamy, Maxwell Sassaman, and Manjula P. Mony study how a jellyfish-like animal chooses ways to close wounds in a 2026 report. The animal is Clytia hemisphaerica, a simple early metazoan. Skin sheets can heal by cell crawling, by a tightening ring, or by group cell movement, and what guides the choice has been unclear.

Across wound types and sizes, crawling and ring tightening worked in sequence and could partly cover for each other. Exposure of the basement membrane acted as a central cue that steered all three responses. The same steps even healed tiny wounds inside a single cell. The authors offer a unified model for how healing tools are picked and timed.
pmc-13329911:
Anindya Ghosh and Chenni Sriram surveyed modern care for fast fetal heart rhythms in a 2026 article. Sustained rapid rhythms complicate about half a percent of pregnancies and form most fetal rhythm problems. Left alone, they can cause heart failure, fluid buildup, early delivery, or death before birth. Drugs given to the mother are the main treatment, since the baby is too small for procedures.

The authors discuss a ten-year series from southern Italy covering 32 fetuses. Ultrasound of the fetal heart sorted the rhythm into subtypes, and drug choice followed the subtype. Agents used alone or combined included flecainide, digoxin, and sotalol. Even fluid-swollen fetuses often recover with fitting therapy, and long-term outlook is good, the piece notes.
pmc-13330211:
Juxiang Yang and co-authors link falls, activity, and dementia in a 2026 study of older adults. Both falls and low activity raise dementia risk, but whether activity can blunt the risk after a fall was unclear. The team joined data from three cohorts with close to forty-four thousand adults aged sixty and over.

Dementia cases were tracked over roughly six to eight years, and near thirty-five hundred appeared. A fall was tied to about seventy percent higher dementia risk. Among those who had not fallen, more activity meant steadily lower risk of both dementia and falls. The same graded protection held for people who had fallen. The authors back activity as a guard for brain health at every level of fall history.
pmc-13330311:
Wenzhu Xu and four co-authors compare two ways of retraining walking after stroke in a 2026 review. One way uses exoskeleton robots that move the legs through many repeated steps. The other is traditional gait training led by therapists. The review weighs motor recovery, brain change, and muscle function.

The team gathered 86 studies published between 2004 and 2024. Robot training gave larger gains in step evenness, walking speed, and strength, thanks to intense, repeatable practice. Hands-on training did better at drawing patients into active effort and at daily-life skills. The authors see the two as partners and suggest blending them into personal plans, with smart tools helping tailor care.
pmc-13330411:
Ning Zhao and team surveyed how the gut microbiome shapes immunity in cancer and its treatment. Their 2026 review notes that the microbiome deeply shapes host immunity and strongly affects immunotherapy results. Tools such as fecal microbiota transplantation, probiotics, and engineered bacteria can rewire the tumor-immune setting and boost clinical results. The paper surveys molecular and cellular routes linking gut flora to antitumor immunity with recent clinical studies of these tools.

Problems remain large: varied microbes across people, trouble getting stable and lasting colonization, technical blocks in delivery, and safety worries around immune activation or off-target effects. The team argues that future progress needs deeper insight, standard protocols, strict evaluation, and joining with precision immunotherapy plans. By joining how it works with bedside use, the review aims to guide microbiome-targeted therapies from promising concept toward better clinical outcomes in cancer care.
pmc-13330511:
Yunxiao Feng and colleagues study how storage temperature shapes peach quality and scent in a 2026 report. Fruit of the Shijizhixing type were kept at 0, 10, and 20 degrees. The team tracked firmness, juice, decay, wall softening chemicals, aroma compounds, and primary metabolites over storage.

Cold storage at 0 degrees best held peel brightness, firmness, and juice while limiting decay in the reported results. Warmer storage sped softening and shifted wall pectins toward soluble forms. Gas checks found 29 aroma compounds. Green aldehydes led at harvest, while fruity esters and lactones built up in warm storage. Fat-derived metabolites tracked closely with fruity scent making. Temperature thus steers both texture loss and aroma gain.
pmc-13330811:
Neta Caspin, Natalia Fridman, and Avi Shpigelman determine crystal forms of two plant flavonoids in a 2026 report. Fisetin and luteolin occur in plant foods and draw health interest, yet their solid forms shape solubility and stability. Both crystals grew from ethanol and water mixes and were read by single-crystal X-ray methods.

Fisetin formed a dihydrate, holding two water units per molecule in the reported structure. Luteolin formed a monohydrate with one water unit. Past work on kin compounds such as quercetin shows how packing rules steer crystal growth. Mapping these hydrate forms adds to a patchy record of flavonoid solids and may guide food and drug product design.
pmc-13331211:
Sophie Marie Dieckmann and a large team study glutamate chemistry in a mouse melanoma model in a 2026 report. Tumours rewire fuel use, starving immune cells such as dendritic cells. The team profiled tumour-free and tumour-bearing tissue from a model that grows melanoma through a glutamate receptor switch in pigment cells.

Late tumours showed shifted glutamate handling, a sugar-burning tilt, and lower energy stores in the reported profiling. Helpful dendritic and macrophage groups thinned as tumours grew, while neutrophils and monocytes rose. Blocking a glutathione-making enzyme forced loud iron-linked death in tumour cells grown in dishes. The authors frame fuel blocking as a route to revive dendritic cell driven immunity.
pmc-13332211:
Maria Luiza Favero and co-authors adapt a bubble scan, long used in human care, to spot lung shunts in horses. A shunt lets blood skip the lung's air sacs, a cause of low blood oxygen in sick or drugged horses. Their 2026 study tests the scan in twelve sound horses. A salt-based bubble mix is pushed into a neck vein at two dose sizes while heart scans roll.

Bubbles show at once in the right heart in each horse. The small dose lights the scan for five to nine beats, the big dose for a span half as long again. The big dose wins for clear, calm reads. The team casts the scan as a low-harm tool fit for yard use, ground work for sick-horse care to come.
pmc-13333111:
Reeba George and colleagues report a 2026 case of a benign hair-follicle tumor in the ear canal that mimicked cholesteatoma. Trichoepithelioma arises from hair follicles, most often on the face, and is rarely seen in the external auditory canal. The patient was a man aged ninety or older who presented with purulent ear drainage and hearing loss. Initial imaging and examination suggested cholesteatoma in the ear canal with bony erosion, for which surgery was indicated.

Final pathology from more extensive tissue sampling instead revealed trichoepithelioma of the front wall of the right ear canal. The case shows that suspicious ear canal lesions may need deeper tissue sampling to prevent misdiagnosis from superficial samples alone. Surgeons and pathologists gain a cautionary example: a destructive-looking ear canal lesion is not always cholesteatoma, and sampling depth can change the diagnosis and the operation.
pmc-13333311:
Didi Pianda and co-authors publish a survey dataset in 2026 on what internships do for vocational students in Aceh Province, Indonesia. Policymakers want to know how workplace placements, skills, and students' inner resources combine to make graduates employable, especially in a developing region with its own political setting.

Data were gathered from 10 September to 30 December 2022 by paper questionnaire from 266 students who had finished internships in private and public industry. Students were chosen by proportional stratified random sampling from a provincial population of 15,435, with the sample size set by the Isaac and Michael formula. Responses cover internship experience, competencies, psychological capital, and employability, plus age, gender, school status, and accreditation. The authors offer the openly posted data as a baseline for judging education policy and for testing how soft strengths like psychological capital and hard competencies jointly shape job readiness.
pmc-13333511:
Ming Lv and a ten-author team reframe mouth disease in a 2026 narrative review as a breakdown of balance among microbes, tissues, and immunity rather than an infection story. Caries, gum disease, and oral cancer emerge, in their telling, when the mouth's microbial neighbourhood tips from harmony into dysbiosis.

Searching four databases, the reviewers synthesized evidence across microbial ecology, mucosal immunology, disease mechanisms, and therapies. Healthy mouths, they describe, rest on cooperation: commensal communities hold their ground, epithelial and saliva barriers block invaders, and immune surveillance stays measured. Dysbiosis breaks the truce as pathobionts expand, inflammation amplifies, and tissue injury follows, which helps explain why oral diseases persist and vary between patients. The review closes on precision tools entering the field: microbe-shaping treatments, host-directed drugs, multi-omics profiling, and artificial intelligence for sorting patients and finding markers. It argues future care must treat ecology, barrier, and immunity together.
pmc-13333711:
Mariarosaria Portinaio and co-authors reviewed quality standards for colon cancer surgery in a 2026 article. Good outcomes depend on clear margins, thorough lymph node removal, and proper handling of the mesentery, yet practice varies between countries and tumor sites.

The authors searched PubMed and MEDLINE through October 2025 for guidelines, trials, registries, and meta-analyses. Evidence converged on bowel margins of 5 to 7 centimeters for most tumors, extending toward 10 centimeters for advanced cancers. Node counts beyond the old minimum of 12 improved staging, with gains leveling near 18 to 22 nodes examined. Complete mesocolic excision with central vessel tying raised node yield and specimen quality without added harm, with the clearest survival signal in stage III disease.
pmc-13333911:
Lorenzo Grimaldi and co-authors survey, in a 2026 study, how much patients and biobank donors trust the use of their data in AI-driven medical research. AI work needs clinical, chemical, and gene data, yet leaks and misuse worry many donors. The team surveyed 115 people across patient donors, healthy donors, and non-donor volunteers.

Most people knew digital tools well but knew little about AI risks, and most felt hopeful about gains. Brain patient donors worried most about misuse. Strong digital skill went with both sharper risk awareness and stronger hope. Most would share at least one data type, though non-donors were far more guarded about gene data.
pmc-13334311:
Yarden Weiss and colleagues study 2026 discharge orders for RAS blockers after high potassium and its links to death and kidney-failure treatment results. RAS blockers are often stopped during hospital stay for high potassium, yet guidance on discharge prescribing is limited. The team evaluated links between blocker order at discharge and post-discharge results in patients in hospital with high potassium.

The single-center look-back cohort at a large hospital included adults admitted between 2005 and 2020 with potassium above 5.5 units per litre while on chronic blocker therapy, followed through 2022. Exposure was order versus non-order of blockers at discharge, with score matching among survivors of the first hospital stay to balance start traits. Kaplan-Meier and adjusted Cox models assessed all-cause death and chronic kidney-failure treatment. Among 12,326 patients with confirmed high potassium, results are detailed in the full paper.
pmc-13334811:
Tine Deconinck and co-authors pitted cancer-killing viruses against glioblastoma in a 2026 lab study. Oncolytic viruses infect tumor cells and stir immune attack, but glioblastoma's variety means only some patients respond, and which virus suits which tumor was unclear.

The team tested 15 clinic-relevant viruses across 14 patient-derived glioblastoma cell lines. pmc-13419311:

pmc-13420611:

pmc-13421511:

pmc-13430611:

pmc-13431011:

pmc-13431711:

pmc-13434311:

pmc-13458811:

pmc-13458911:

pmc-13462711:

pmc-13462811:

pmc-13473511:

pmc-13474811:

pmc-13486511:

Röhrig and colleagues released version 3.0 of Attracting Cavities, the molecular docking engine behind the SwissDock webserver, in a 2026 software paper. Docking predicts how a small drug-like molecule fits into a protein target and how tightly it binds. Unlike newer co-folding methods, it still gives physical insight into the interaction regardless of whether the ligand or pocket is novel.

Röhrig reports enhanced sampling features, new functionalities, and technical improvements. Together they dock better in less time and handle more kinds of problems, building on earlier additions such as covalent docking and hybrid quantum-classical docking. Benchmarked head-to-head against AutoDock Vina, a widely used rival, the new version produced better docking results across multiple test sets. The physics-based scoring, pairing a standard force field with an implicit solvent model, is unchanged, and the update will be available through the webserver.
pmc-13501811:
Belinda Twesigye leads a sixteen-author team reporting a 2026 training programme that strengthened clinical trial monitoring across the East African Community. Trials are multiplying in the region while trained monitors remain scarce. The project ran in Burundi, Kenya, Rwanda, South Sudan, Tanzania, and Uganda between February 2024 and February 2025. Stakeholder consultations shaped a six-module curriculum, and each country cohort completed five weeks of blended learning: a two-day workshop, four weeks of online study, and a two-day wrap-up.

Two hundred people trained, drawn from national regulators, ethics committees, research teams, and monitor pools; 50.5 percent were women, and Uganda supplied the largest share at 30.5 percent of the cohort. Knowledge scores jumped from 61.8 percent before training to 84.3 percent after, a gain of 22.5 points on the test scale. The share clearing the 60 percent pass mark leapt from 37.5 percent to 95.6 percent of participants. Whether knowledge becomes practice awaits follow-up.
pmc-13502311:
Caram and colleagues reported in 2026 a rare case of solitary bone plasmacytoma, a single tumor of plasma cells, hiding in the upper jaw of a 76-year-old woman. The lesion looked like a routine root infection near two front teeth, with a draining tract. Standard root canal treatment brought no improvement, which prompted referral for a tissue sample.

Caram's biopsy showed sheets of abnormal plasma-like cells with a heavy white cell infiltrate. Marker tests confirmed the cells were all of one clone, matching plasmacytoma. Full body checks ruled out multiple myeloma, the widespread form of this cancer, leaving the solitary diagnosis. The patient received 20 radiation sessions and stays stable under joint follow-up. The authors warn that lasting root-area lesions may not be dental at all, and early spotting matters because a solitary tumor can be a first sign of myeloma.
pmc-13503111:
Moedt and colleagues test two urine proteins as response markers for kidney drugs. Their 2026 paper examines clusterin, which signals tubule injury, and epidermal growth factor, which signals repair, in samples from two large randomised trials of chronic kidney disease. The standard marker, albuminuria, mainly reflects damage to the kidney's filters and fluctuates considerably.

After six weeks on atrasentan, an endothelin blocker, the urinary clusterin ratio fell by about 46 percent, consistent with reduced tubule injury.
