In the second trial, dapagliflozin, a diabetes and kidney drug, slowed the decline of the growth factor ratio over one year, with the largest relative gains in diabetic kidney disease. Biopsy data linked the urine growth factor signal to gene activity inside the kidney. The authors propose both proteins as mechanism-based markers for personalising treatment.
pmc-13503711:
Feng Han and co-authors built a soft fiber sensor that reads body heat with high care, in a paper from 2026. Good heat sensors are needed for smart devices and health wearables. Most designs trade off sharp readings, soft feel, and easy fitting into clothing.

The fiber is made only of graphene, a thin form of carbon. The team treated parts of a single long fiber with two chemicals to create ten paired junctions along its length. Those pairs turn heat gaps into a clear electric signal. The sensor kept almost all of its skill after ten thousand bends. On skin, it tracked body heat with a very small error. The design points to light, tough sensors for health checks at home.
pmc-13503911:
Saeed Mokhtari Masoumi Alamdarloo and others meta-analyze conversational agents for low mood, anxiety, and stress. In 2026, the review synthesizes forty-eight randomized controlled trials covering 28,071 people, spanning both artificial-intelligence and rule-based agents, using robust variance estimation to handle within-study dependencies. Restricted access leaves many people without timely mental health care.

Effects were small to modest but clear: same-form mean gaps of minus 0.27 for low mood, minus 0.20 for anxiety, and minus 0.26 for stress, with larger gains in medical groups and shorter programs. Risk of bias was largely low and publication bias negligible. Chat-based agents emerge as scalable support, though long-term effectiveness and integration remain open.
pmc-13504011:
Liuel Yizengaw Adnie and co-authors rank the main livestock diseases in a zone of Ethiopia using local knowledge. Their paper from 2026 covers East Gojjam, where farm animals are a chief source of income. Formal watch systems are thin there, so asking owners in a set way can fill the gap.

Ten group talks were held with one hundred animal owners across five districts in 2024. Ranking games, shared scoring, and seasonal charts were used to weigh each disease. For cattle, blackleg, foot and mouth disease, and lumpy skin disease topped the list. For sheep and goats, a lung disease and a pox led. Horse disease findings are also set out in the report.
pmc-13504211:
Khoshi Ari Muhammed and Eman Dhahir Arif survey Salmonella germs at a chicken wet market in Iraq, in a 2026 study. Salmonella spreads through food and lives in the gut of chickens, so market tools and water can carry it to buyers. The team sampled a broiler market in Sulaymaniyah province over six months.

They gathered 210 samples across the market, drawing on gut contents, water, knives, and chopping boards, plus swabs from workers' hands and bird bodies. Culture found Salmonella in about half. Gene tests named the species in most culture hits, and over three fifths of those were the Typhimurium type, many carrying a key invasion gene. Boards showed the highest species rate. The local strain grouped with world strains, which hints at shared roots across borders.
pmc-13504611: Ziheng Chen and co-authors set out a Cochrane plan to weigh whole-body scans for hidden disease in healthy adults, in a protocol from two thousand twenty-six. The review will compare full-body MRI or CT screening against no screening, usual care, or other screening plans. Gains and harms both count as outcomes.
pmc-13505111:
Xintong Peng, Shuang Liu, and Yongguang Tao offer a two thousand twenty-six review of glutamine metabolism in cancer. Glutamine is the most plentiful amino acid in human blood. Tumour cells often become heavily dependent on it, a pattern reviewers call addiction.

The review covers how glutamine feeds normal and cancer cell functions. It links glutamine use to several forms of regulated cell death under stress. It also covers effects on the immune surroundings of tumours. Finally, it sums up drugs that target glutamine pathways. Cancer readers get one account of a weakness that may also be a treatment opening.
pmc-13505511:
Stephens, Mao, and Winuthayanon wrote on the fallopian tube as an active partner in early pregnancy in twenty twenty-six. The tube is where fertilization happens. The embryo spends its first days there. Assisted reproduction skips it. Yet millions of pregnancies have not settled what the tube adds.

Evidence across mammals shows the tube is no passive pipe. It regulates embryo transport. It adjusts immune and metabolic responses. It secretes stage-specific factors that shape development. Embryos signal back, prompting matching changes in the tube's gene and protein activity. Damaged tube signaling impairs development and raises early pregnancy loss. Embryos from different assisted techniques carry distinct molecular profiles. These may alter later responses. The authors call the tube a biosensor of embryo quality. They flag knowledge gaps for making assisted reproduction better.
pmc-13505911:
Leprosy still lacks good markers for tracking whether treatment is working. Six authors hunted through small RNA regulators in patients' skin, blood, and nasal samples, comparing the severe and mild forms of the disease with healthy controls. One regulator stood out: miR-889-3p, raised in every sample type from severe cases.

After standard multidrug therapy, its level fell back toward healthy values, following the bacterial load down. Lab assays showed the regulator binds the message of a gene called SLC35E1 in a sequence-specific way. The gene's protein, in turn, ran high in lesions and tracked the bacterial index closely. The authors propose the small RNA as a blood-and-tissue gauge of treatment response. The pair it forms with its target gene is offered as a new window on how the host answers the infection.
pmc-13506111:
Atul Goel argues for rethinking ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament, a condition where a spinal ligament slowly turns to bone and squeezes the cord. The usual story treats the bony growth as the disease and surgery as cutting space around the cord. Goel proposes the opposite order: hidden instability in the spine comes first, and the ossification is the body's attempt to brace the loose segment.

Under his view, ligament thickening, disc shrinkage, and bony spurs belong to one protective response. Removing bone without steadying the segment may worsen the underlying problem. He points to patients who improved after stabilisation alone, with no removal of the ossified mass, as the cord settled once abnormal motion stopped. Critics may worry about large masses left in place, yet Goel answers that compression is real but secondary. The essay asks surgeons to treat instability as the root target.
pmc-13507111:
Zhao and co-authors publish a labeled image dataset for macular hole surgery outcomes, in a 2026 data paper. A macular hole is a small tear in the center of the retina that blurs sharp vision. Research on healing after surgery has lacked public image sets with careful labels over time. The team assembled optical coherence tomography scans from patients at one point before surgery and six points after, spanning two weeks to four years.

The set holds 2,591 scans with pixel-level masks for 12 retinal features, from the hole itself to fine tissue layers. Two raters agreed strongly, which supports the label quality. A standard neural network baseline is included for comparison. The resource lets researchers train and test tools that measure retinal healing.
pmc-13507211: Ramón Paniagua-Domínguez and José Sánchez-Gil present a new class of light devices in a 2026 paper. The devices join atomically thin semiconductor sheets with metasurfaces, flat layers patterned at tiny scales. The metasurfaces hold special light states called quasi bound states in the continuum. Those states can be switched on with electric signals. That makes the devices tunable by voltage rather than by fixed design. The authors see strong promise for future uses in photonics, where small, fast, and flexible light control is in high demand.
pmc-13507311: Helio Sader and co-authors track drug resistance in a hardy hospital bacterium over ten years, in this 2026 report. The germ, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, came from thousands of isolates from dozens of United States medical centers between 2015 and 2024. Three newer drug pairs stayed active against nearly all isolates. Two older drugs lost a little ground over the decade. Three others, including meropenem, worked better after 2017 than before. The trends help hospitals choose antibiotics from national evidence rather than habit.
pmc-13509411:
Bikash Chaurasia and co-authors report the long follow-up of a boy whose dead molar was coaxed back to life with regenerative dental therapy, in a 2026 case report. The treatment aims to restart root growth in young permanent teeth whose pulp has died, instead of sealing them off. A scaffold made from the patient's own blood concentrate, platelet-rich fibrin, fills the cleaned root canal. The patient was a healthy seven-year-old with months of pain in a lower molar.

Tests showed the tooth's nerve had died, its roots were still open, and infection sat at one root tip. After treatment, the team followed the boy for fifty-two months with checks and X-rays. Reports of this therapy rarely run so long, especially in molars. The case adds evidence that young teeth can keep maturing after their pulp dies, if the biology is given a scaffold.
pmc-13511711:
Rossella D'Alessandro and eight co-authors screen thinking, emotional, and behavioral health in children with Duchenne muscular dystrophy at one center, in 2026 work. The disease, tied to the X chromosome, wastes muscle step by step, yet missing forms of a protein also act in the brain. Twenty-one children took a broad test battery while the team reviewed clinical history and cognitive scores.

Screening surfaced attention trouble, inward emotional vulnerability, poor emotional control, and autism-linked features beyond the motor picture. Among children with cognitive data, nearly half scored in the low range for full intelligence, with one genetic subgroup hit hardest. Patterns varied a great deal between children. The authors call the work early and exploratory, and they argue for multi-domain screening plus personal assessment plans so support can match each child's mix of needs.
pmc-13511811:
Rocco Carcione, Valentina Mastrobuono, Riccardo Pagliarello, Elisabetta Bennici, Alessia Cemmi, and Silvia Massa formulate food hydrogels from natural polymers and berry processing leftovers, in 2026 work. The gels use pectin plus an extract made from spray-dried strawberry and blueberry preparation waste, turning by-products into food matrices. One version also carried living plant cells. The team probed light spectra, acidity, moisture, micro-structure, swelling, and drying over time.

Calcium chloride proved key to holding the gel network firm. Plant cells changed how the gel held and released water without breaking the basic gelation route. Gels stayed physically and chemically stable after twenty days in cold storage. The authors present the materials as sustainable carriers for biological parts and active compounds in new food products built on waste valorization, meaning turning leftovers into value.
pmc-13513411:
Sara Al-Badran and co-authors look for a gut bacterium in bowel growths that precede cancer, in a 2026 study. The bacterium has been tied to bowel cancer, but its role in the earlier adenoma stage is unclear. Using a tailor-made RNA probe method on preserved tissue, the team detected it and compared the gene patterns of positive and negative patients.

The bacterium turned up in about eleven percent of adenomas. Patients who carried it showed stronger anti-bacterial defence and immune-related gene activity, and their growths showed a more proliferative pattern. The authors read this as a link between the bacterium presence and immune plus growth signatures at the adenoma stage. They stress that the finding needs checking in larger groups followed over time before any role in cancer development can be claimed.
pmc-13513611:
Hyunjee Kim, Olga Frunze, Sang Mi Han, Soon Ok Woo, Jewon Jung, and Hyung-Wook Kwon compare how diet quality shapes gene activity in honey bees, in 2026 work. Readings were taken before and after acute heat stress. Bees rank among the world's key pollinators, and rising heat strains them hard. Colonies received natural diets of honey or bee bread, or artificial diets of sugar syrup or pollen substitute, and metabolic plus immune genes were tracked around a heat shock.

Each diet left a distinct molecular fingerprint at rest and under heat. Bees on the richer natural diets regulated metabolic and stress pathways in a more coordinated way. Sugar syrup bees switched immune genes on more strongly under heat, a sign the authors read as deeper physiological disturbance. The work suggests full nutrition helps bees hold their regulation together in heat waves, a point for feeding practice in a warming climate.
pmc-13514111:
Róbert Nagy and co-authors set out a 2026 method for sorting body types in young adults without lab tests. Body mass index alone misses where fat sits and how much muscle a person has. The team combines body scans with heart risk scores and a network that links people with like traits.

Tests in a large group of young adults found hidden fat patterns that index scores missed. The network split people into nine clear groups, and other sorting methods found like patterns. The authors stress the tool is not yet proven for forecasts. Lab and long-term checks must come before any health claims.
pmc-13515011:
Laura Maghiar and fourteen colleagues argue, in a 2026 review, that antimicrobial peptides could fight peri-implantitis, the biofilm-driven inflammation that eats away the bone holding dental implants. Cleaning cannot fully decontaminate an implant surface, and antibiotics act bluntly while breeding resistance. Peptides offer a two-way alternative. Positively charged molecules that rupture microbial membranes tend to kill broadly without quickly selecting resistance. The body's own defence peptides also calm inflammation and help tissue knit closed.

Framing the implant's gum crossing as a healing wound barrier, the authors draw lessons from skin repair research on peptides such as LL-37 and the beta-defensins. They focus on coating the collar where the implant meets the gum, since disease starts there, and extend the idea to zirconia and hybrid parts. Stability, cell toxicity, cost, and regulation all stand between concept and clinic.
pmc-13515411:
Davoud Amiri and four colleagues review, in a 2026 article, the metabolic side of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder. ADHD is usually framed as a problem of attention circuits in the front of the brain. Yet the hypothalamus, the small hub governing appetite, sleep, stress hormones, and body rhythms, may also play a part in why patients differ so much. The team searched five databases for human studies on these links.

Findings tie ADHD to higher obesity risk, immune and inflammation changes, shifted appetite hormones, delayed body clocks, and unusual stress-hormone responses. Obesity, inflammation markers, and diabetes risk carried the strongest numbers, with appetite hormones close behind. Direct proof of inflammation in the hypothalamus itself stays thin, so Amiri's team treats that pathway as a plausible hypothesis for a subgroup, not settled cause.
pmc-13516411:
Sun and co-authors report a 2026 materials study on hybrid panels that mix bamboo fiber with glass fiber in epoxy. Natural and synthetic fibers could give greener structural parts, but weak bonding between fiber and resin holds them back. The team treated bamboo fibers in two steps: alkali first to strip soft plant matter, then a silane coat that bonds with epoxy.

The treatment raised bamboo fiber strength by about half and more than doubled bond strength with the resin. The finished hybrid reached tensile strength near glass fiber grades. Bending stiffness almost doubled over the untreated hybrid. Heat-cycle tests kept the gains across a wide range. The authors pitch the design for light, strong, partly natural parts.
pmc-13518711:
Efstathios Vounotrypidis leads a seven-author prospective trial, published in 2026, of an extended depth of focus lens implanted during cataract surgery. Every patient had earlier undergone vitrectomy, an operation that removes the gel inside the eye, to repair a detached retina. Such eyes are usually denied lenses that correct focus at several distances.

Twenty-seven patients and 43 eyes received the Vivity lens once the retina had stayed attached. Six months later, corrected distance vision improved sharply in the repaired eyes, and near and intermediate results were usable. Satisfaction ran high, with only two patients reporting halos. The findings suggest careful selection can make this lens a safe option after retinal repair.
pmc-13518811:
Amanda Maria Kostro and five colleagues run a 2026 randomized trial in early knee osteoarthritis, testing tailored exercise, orthopedic shoe inserts, and both together. Worn cartilage and uneven loading disturb balance in this condition, while foot problems such as flat feet may worsen knee strain. Earlier comparisons lacked objective balance measures.

Patients split into exercise (43), insoles (43), mixed (39), and control (41) groups, then stood on a force platform, eyes open and then closed. The mixed group improved most on sway measures, and pain, daily function, sports ability, and quality of life all gained. Exercise and insoles each helped, yet Kostro and co-authors found the combination strongest for rehabilitation.
pmc-13518911:
Xiao Wei leads a nine-author team introducing ViscoClamp in 2026, a peptide gel designed to steady the squishiness of the tissue immediately around cells. Living tissue remodels constantly, so the mechanical cues cells feel drift over time. Chronic sugar damage, called glycation, worsens that drift and undermines healing.

A rule-based design agent searched peptide options for one that threads into the natural matrix and binds calcium plus glycation products. ViscoClamp squeezed wide swings in glycation input into stable cell-scale mechanics, while still letting stem cells remodel and mineralize. In sugar-rich jaw defects across rats, rabbits, dogs, and macaques, the gel restored bone-forming activity and improved repair.
pmc-13519011:
Seira Arakane, Yu Sato, Masanori Hashino, and Shintaro Maeno dissect the hidden diversity inside a supposedly uniform heat-loving bacterium in 2026. Geobacillus stearothermophilus is a workhorse for food sterilization testing and industrial processes, treated for decades as one tidy species. Comparing 36 strain genomes exposed clear internal structure.

Two major genomic groups emerged, differing in origin and equipment. Food-linked strains carried smaller genomes with fewer metabolic genes, while strains from natural hot habitats kept larger genomes and broader abilities, including genes for using carbohydrates and fatty acids. A few strains sat between the groups, suggesting gradual splitting. All still meet species thresholds, so divergence is accumulating quietly inside one name.
pmc-13520111:
Sushil Pokhrel and co-authors report a rare elbow injury case from 2026 in a five-year-old boy. The injury splits the lower arm bone at its growth plate near the elbow. It most often strikes children under age three, so a case at age five is quite rare.

The boy fell on an outstretched hand and came in two days later with a swollen left elbow. X-rays hinted at the split, and a dye test in surgery proved it. Surgeons eased the bone back into place and fixed it with thin wires. A slab then held the arm still for five weeks. At fifteen months the boy moved the elbow freely, with no pain, no bent shape, and clean X-rays. The team stresses fast, exact care.
pmc-13520311:
Huanhuan Zheng and colleagues test in 2026 whether spectral CT scans can show how well oesophageal cancer responds to drug treatment given before surgery. Spectral CT can estimate iodine uptake in a tumour, which may reflect blood supply and living tumour tissue.

Scans before and after treatment were compared in 87 patients with squamous cell cancer of the oesophagus. Tumour size and iodine measures after treatment were lower in responders than in non-responders. Combining normalised iodine with tumour area gave the best sorting of response. As a pilot study, the work offers an early imaging option that avoids extra biopsies.
pmc-13520411:
M. Slikkerveer and colleagues describe in 2026 a newborn boy with drug-resistant seizures linked to a new SCN2A gene change, treated with lacosamide under close blood-level monitoring. The seizure drug is licensed only from age two years, so newborn use is off-label and dosing guidance is absent.

Born early at 33 weeks, the infant kept seizing despite several medicines. Lacosamide was added with repeated trough level checks and heart monitoring. Reaching the target blood level needed a far higher dose than expected, split into four daily doses, with no side effects seen. The single case supports cautious, monitored use while wider studies are awaited.
pmc-13520511:
Ramos, Brazaca, Rossini, Lima, and Carrilho build a paper sensor for checking melatonin products in twenty twenty-six. Melatonin supplements are popular for sleep problems but are regulated loosely. Products have been found with wrong doses or hormone contamination. Cheap quality checks are missing.

Their device uses a chemical reaction that turns paper from white to blue. The blue depth tracks the melatonin amount present. It measured tablets at zero point two two milligrams and drops at zero point two zero milligrams. Results matched the standard chromatography method closely. The response was linear across the tested range and specific to melatonin. The authors offer it as low cost quality control.
pmc-13520711:
Rishita Shah and JJ L Miranda turned a weakness of chatbots into a classroom lesson on honest citation. Published in 2026, the work starts from a familiar flaw: general-purpose language models invent references and misuse real ones. Fake-citation rates were reported from about one fifth to over nine tenths of references. Teachers need material that builds both AI literacy and writing skill at once.

The authors repurpose model errors as worked examples, asking students to spot fabricated references, correct misused real ones, and choose primary versus secondary sources well. Seeing errors firsthand shows a key limit of generative AI better than any warning could. The exercise also gives students a structure for practicing sound source use. Readers get a ready framework for teaching citation rigor in an age of fluent but unreliable machine text.
pmc-13521511:
Lauren Evans and co-authors study a lipid-presenting molecule in breast cancer in this 2026 paper. The molecule, CD1d, sits on immune cells inside tumors. Myeloid cells there can either fight the tumor or shield it. What sets their behavior was unclear. The team removed or blocked CD1d in several mouse breast cancer models.

Tumors grew more slowly without CD1d. The myeloid mix inside shifted toward inflammatory fighters. A standard immunotherapy drug also worked better alongside the blockade. The effect traced to the myeloid cells themselves, in mice and human samples alike. A gene pattern from the work matched patient outcomes, marking CD1d as a drug target.
pmc-13521711:
Julius Gorenz and co-authors show how power plant surges harm fish eggs and larvae in rivers, in a 2026 study. Hydropeaking means dams release water in pulses for electricity demand. River levels then rise and fall within hours. Salmonid eggs buried in gravel can be left dry. Two prized species spawn in different seasons.

Brown trout spawn in fall, while Danube salmon spawn in spring. Field trials tracked egg-to-fry survival under real peaking regimes. Longer drying meant more overheating and freezing damage. Survival fell as exposure grew. The authors urge slower ramp rates from dams. Keeping spawning gravel covered is the other key fix. River managers gain concrete targets for operating rules.
pmc-13521811:
Huan Zeng, Jingwen Feng, and Meng Dai tested a five-step group inquiry method for math reasoning in a Chengdu primary school, in a 2026 study. Young students get uneven chances to guess, argue, and defend claims in math class. The method gives those moves a fixed scaffold across a lesson.

Ninety-six fourth graders in two classes took part for five weeks. One class learned through the inquiry steps, and the other kept standard teaching, with tests before and after. The inquiry class gained far more on a ten-item open reasoning test. Its post-test edge was clear, and the edge held after midterm scores were weighed in. Gains spread across guessing, evidence use, justification, and near transfer. Watchers also confirmed the two classes were truly taught apart. The authors call the scaffold practical for daily use.
pmc-13522011:
Hiroji Iwata and colleagues report in 2026 long-term outlook from the NEOS trial for postmenopausal early breast cancer, combining response to pre-surgery hormone therapy with a 21-gene recurrence score. The analysis covered 226 patients drawn from the earlier assay study.

Hormone treatment shrank tumours at least partly in just over half the patients. In low and middle score groups, adding chemotherapy showed no clear survival edge over hormone therapy alone. In the high score group, hormone therapy alone fared worse on overall survival, although responders to initial hormone treatment showed no clear gap. Event counts were small, so caution applies.
pmc-13522211:
Shubham Vishwakarma and co-authors present a 2026 study of a drug probe that wakes sleeping chemistry in a fungus that lives inside a medicinal plant. Fungi hide many compounds behind silent genes. A probe that blocks a gene-silencing enzyme can flip those genes on. The team grew the fungus with and without the probe, then compared the chemical harvest and its germ and rust fighting power.

The treated brew fought germs harder, among them drug-proof staph, and quenched test radicals better. Chemical maps showed the mix had shifted under the probe. Waking silent genes is a cheap way to mine new drug leads from tame fungi. Each plant tenant may stock a locked shelf of compounds. Probes like this one hold a key.
pmc-13522511:
U Nikhil Sagar leads a 2026 genome study aimed at breeding more nutritious groundnuts, also called peanuts. Kernels were measured for iron, zinc, and protein across seasons in a diverse mini-core collection, and whole genomes were scanned for DNA markers linked to those traits. Wide variation appeared for all three nutrients, giving breeders useful raw material.

Fifteen marker links were found in pooled data, with more in single-season analyses, pointing to dozens of candidate genes. Several candidates govern iron and zinc balance, while others relate to protein control. Accessions carrying favorable gene versions clustered in certain groundnut types. Three practical DNA markers were validated, offering tools to select nutrient-rich lines in future breeding programs.
pmc-13522611:
Serge Krasnokutski and co-authors showed in a 2026 study that peptides can form on cosmic dust without any energy input. Peptides, chains of amino acids, are steps toward the proteins of life. Most known space routes to them need radiation, which also breaks molecules apart as fast as it builds them.

Their lab work mimicked deep space: ultra-high vacuum and cryogenic cold, using some of the most common cosmic molecules. On dust grains, reactions with low or no energy barrier linked the pieces into varied peptides. A calm route favors growth over breakage. The result strengthens the case that life's building blocks can form in cold clouds and ride dust into young planetary systems.
pmc-13523211:
Atefeh Shamsi and Imane Bagheri explore social isolation among mothers of autistic children in Yazd, Iran, in a 2026 qualitative study. Twenty-two mothers of children aged four to twelve took part in semi-structured interviews. Their accounts were analyzed inductively to build themes grounded in their own descriptions of daily life and social contact.

One overarching theme, social isolation, rested on three categories. Mothers pointed to stigma and being judged by others. They also lacked enough support, both formal and informal. Caregiving strain pushed many into defensive withdrawal. Mothers described judging looks, wrong beliefs about autism, thin family and service support, and demanding therapy schedules that pushed them to withdraw protectively. The authors call for public awareness that respects local culture, teaching for families, and support that is easy to reach. They note that a single-city interview study transfers with care to other settings.
pmc-13523311:
Agnieszka Mania-Końsko and co-authors describe a distinctive rash and mouth inflammation syndrome in a young child in a 2026 case report from Poland. A five-year-old boy was admitted with prolonged fever, erosive sores of the mouth and lips, and a pink rash. The illness came with infection by Mycoplasma pneumoniae, a common cause of chest infections. The pattern fits a relatively new diagnostic entity distinct from several severe skin reaction syndromes.

Treatment combined systemic and local steroids, an antibiotic, a mucus-thinning drug, pain relief, and a local antifungal, with follow-up two months later at a university clinic. The authors walk through presentation, diagnostic steps, and the conditions that must be ruled out. They recommend suspecting this syndrome when pneumonia appears alongside mucosal and skin eruptions in young patients.
pmc-13523411:
Jochen Grohmann and colleagues report the first case of heart wall erosion after a patch-like septal closure device in a 2026 case report. A twelve-year-old patient had a significant atrial septal defect, a hole between the upper heart chambers. The child also had pulmonary hypertension, severe scoliosis, and Down syndrome. A Gore occluder was placed after test balloon closure went smoothly. The device position looked reasonable at implantation.

Follow-up imaging later showed a blood-filled fluid collection around the heart next to the correctly positioned device, indicating erosion of the right atrial wall. The authors conclude that any closure device can in principle erode the atrial wall, since remodeling after unloading and wall texture vary unpredictably. Because risk is highest in the first one to six months, they insist on consistent outpatient follow-up whatever device is used.
pmc-13523511:
Ye Song, Yangsheng Yu, Bo Zhang, and Xiao Zhang report 2026 laboratory work uncovering a chain of proteins that fuels sugar use in colorectal cancer. Abnormal glycolysis, the breaking down of sugar for energy, is a hallmark of this cancer. The team traced how one gene, EFNA3, becomes overactive and helps tumors grow while evading immune attack.

Silencing EFNA3 in cancer cells lowered glycolysis, growth, movement, invasion, and blood vessel signaling, while strengthening killing by natural killer and CD8 T cells. Mouse tumors with silenced EFNA3 spread less and drew more anti-tumor immune cells. Upstream, a transcription factor switched EFNA3 on, a scaffold protein stabilized that factor's message, and the ligase PRKN normally restrained the scaffold through tagging for disposal. Restoring PRKN blocked the chain, suggesting a treatment angle.
pmc-13524311:
Simone Lepage and co-authors let children run their own clinical trial. Their 2026 feasibility report describes The Kid's Trial, a fully online study where children aged seven to twelve helped design and carry out a randomized experiment about sleeping with a comfort item.

Two hundred twenty-four children joined at least one step, and one hundred thirty-nine entered the trial itself. Sleeping with a comfort item for a week showed no clear effect on sleep-related impairment and a small, fragile gain in sleep quality. The real findings concern the method: children stayed engaged, grasped trial ideas better afterward, and proved that a decentralized, child-led trial can work. The authors suggest shorter gaps between steps and community partners to keep more children involved.
pmc-13524711:
Diana Clynes and colleagues report, in a 2026 letter, a global survey of kidney patients, caregivers, and advocates about dialysis education and choice. Modality use and patient experience vary worldwide with education, professional training, and policy. The survey asked how people learned about options, how involved they felt in decisions, and why a modality was chosen.

An electronic survey run in July and August 2024 by a patient association and a home dialysis roundtable drew 967 respondents. Home dialysis recipients received extra questions about that route. Respondents included dialysis patients, care partners, transplant recipients, and people with advanced kidney disease, although about 42 percent did not state their role, a limitation the authors note. The project ran as quality improvement, exempt from formal ethics review at the senior author's institution.
pmc-13525011:
Eduarda Pavan and six co-authors measure in 2026 how common human pegivirus 1 is among blood donors and fever patients in Mato Grosso, Brazil. The virus spreads through blood exposure, yet whether it causes any disease stays unresolved. Serum from 92 fever patients and 633 donors was screened with a sensitive PCR test.

About four percent in each group carried the virus. Sequencing recovered eight genomes, split between two subgenotypes that cluster with strains from Brazil and abroad. Finding the virus in healthy donors underlines a blood safety question: transfusion services may be passing an unstudied passenger. The authors call for work on what, if anything, this quiet virus does to its hosts.
pmc-13525811:
Salad Mohamed Hassan and co-authors read a year of child belly crises in a Mogadishu ward, in a study from 2026. A hot belly in a child can spring from a burst appendix, a kinked gut, or a torn wall, all with like signs. In a poor-set land, the mix and the odds were unmapped.

Charts for 2023 held 92 kids, of more than six thousand ward souls, who had no-wound belly crises and went to the knife; finds at the cut gave the true call. Appendix fire led at more than half; gut block and wall tear came next. The team maps age and sign ties too. A first map of its kind for the land, it bids where swift scans and staff should stand.
pmc-13525911:
Andrew Kent and colleagues offer a narrative review, published in 2026. It covers how medicines for chronic pain affect the heart and blood vessels. The authors examine anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen. Opioids, antidepressants, and gabapentinoids are covered. Joint injections are also reviewed. For each class, pain relief is weighed against cardiac risk.

The authors searched several databases through April 2026. Risk rises with dose and duration. It is not fixed for a given drug. Risk concentrates in older patients. Those with existing heart disease are also at higher risk. Each class threatens different outcomes. Anti-inflammatory drugs raise heart attack and heart failure risk. Some opioids disturb heart rhythms.
pmc-13526011:
Christian Mertens and co-authors measure body composition from MRI scans at population scale, pooling two giant cohorts with open source software. Published in 2026, the study answers a measurement gap: body mass index cannot see where fat and muscle sit, yet that geography drives metabolic risk. MRI can, without radiation, but harmonized tools for pooled cohorts were missing.

An open pipeline segmented belly fat layers, hip fat, trunk muscle, and liver in 45,851 adults from a German cohort and the UK Biobank, scanned on different machines and field strengths. Liver fat fractions came from the same reads. The pooled phenotyping shows such measures can be built comparably across studies, a base for risk research at scale.
pmc-13526111:
Vicent Balanzá-Martínez and others examine, in a 2026 longitudinal family study, whether sex shapes higher-order thinking in schizophrenia and in unaffected first-degree relatives. Sex differences in the illness itself are well documented, yet evidence on executive function and working memory in the chronic stage was disputed. The team predicted sex effects would be negligible.

A total of 266 people, comprising 113 people with schizophrenia, 58 unaffected relatives, and 95 healthy controls, completed a full neuropsychological battery twice over one year. No significant sex differences appeared in executive or working memory performance in any group. Patients still performed markedly worse than relatives and controls on most tasks. The authors say the null result extends earlier evidence to relatives, suggesting the cognitive deficit travels with illness risk rather than with sex.
pmc-13526711:
Liver cancer rates in the United States climbed for decades, and the burden has never fallen evenly. Samantha K Sarlin and four co-authors track how the gaps between men and women, and between racial and ethnic groups, changed from 1992 to 2022. They use a national cancer registry covering 68,023 cases. They compare age-adjusted rates as ratios, so the focus stays on relative gaps rather than raw counts.

Rates rose into the early 2010s, steadied, and fell after 2015. Men still develop the cancer far more often, but the male-to-female ratio eased from 3.29 to 3.11, most sharply in adults under 50. The once-huge gap for Asian and Pacific Islander Americans shrank from 5.86 to 1.87 times the white rate. The authors note that real differences in raw rates remain large despite the narrowing ratios, in 2026.
pmc-13527211:
Woochan Kim and a large team report an active regenerative membrane patch for tissue repair, in a 2026 paper. Medical membranes are widely used as wound coverings, but standard versions only protect passively. Their patch coats a biodegradable scaffold with collagen and a nanotextured surface that mimics natural tissue matrix.

In a clinical trial on laser-made skin wounds, the patch sped contraction, restored skin volume, and reduced water loss versus standard care. In dental uses, including ridge preservation and guided bone growth, it supported strong bone formation and stable implant anchoring without complications. The authors present it as a step from passive coverings to active regeneration.
pmc-13527311:
Gushang Xia, Yongsheng Liu, and Daohong Zhao compared two ways of fixing a dislocated shoulder collar joint by keyhole surgery. Their 2026 study treats acute acromioclavicular joint dislocation, where the collar bone pops from the shoulder blade. One method hangs the bone from a U shaped sling without drilling; the other drills holes for its fixation.

Records of 25 patients were split between the two groups. Shoulder scores, pain scales, and the gap between the collar bone and a shoulder blade point were measured before and after surgery. Average follow up ran to thirty six months. The gap shrank sharply in both groups right after surgery and stayed down. Complications such as repeat dislocation and bone fractures were tracked for both methods.
pmc-13527511:
Delirium strikes many intensive care patients on ventilators, and its triggers are still debated. Shiji Xiao and co-authors ask whether the lung's own microbes play a role. In a second look at a cohort of 132 ventilated adults, they profile bacteria in lung wash samples taken within twelve hours of intubation.

Delirium developed in 45 patients. Their samples held far less bacterial DNA overall than those of patients who stayed clear. A score built from three bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids was lower in delirium patients, and the link held under two ways of counting. Friendly mouth-type bacteria were also depleted. The authors suggest a thinned lung microbiome may flag, or feed, delirium risk.
pmc-13527611:
Håvard Visnes and Eivind Inderhaug review how to save the meniscus during knee ligament surgery in a 2026 educational article. When the anterior cruciate ligament is rebuilt, the meniscus, the knee's shock-absorbing cartilage, is often torn too, and keeping it protects the joint for decades.

Modern practice repairs tears rather than trimming them away whenever it can. The authors walk through the common patterns: root tears at the back of the outer meniscus, hidden ramp lesions, bucket-handle tears, and radial tears. For each they compare stitch methods and report how often repairs survive alongside the ligament rebuild. Good mechanics during surgery, they stress, decide whether the saved meniscus truly lasts.
pmc-13527911:
Jiahao Yu and five colleagues compare two keyhole approaches for removing tumors from the mediastinum, the space between the lungs, in a 2026 retrospective study. One group had robot-assisted surgery and the other had video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery, a camera-guided technique. Matching on age, health scores, tumor size, and other factors left 102 patients, split evenly between the groups.

Robotic surgery lost less blood during the operation, and those patients needed chest drains for about a day less and left hospital about a day sooner. Pain scores and complication rates were similar in both groups, with serious complications uncommon either way. The robotic operations cost roughly 4,400 dollars more, so the authors advise weighing the modest recovery gains against the higher price for each patient.
pmc-13528011:
Peiyuan Tang and seven co-authors chart three decades of burn injury burden across North Africa and the Middle East, in this 2026 study. Fire, heat, and hot substances injure millions, yet long regional views, especially past the pandemic, were missing. The team drew on the 2023 Global Burden of Disease study for twenty-one countries, from 1990 to 2023.

Age standardized disability rates fell steeply over the period, and death rates improved as well. Raw case counts, though, rose in most countries, tripling in Qatar and the Emirates, driven by population growth and aging. Rates ticked upward again from 2020 to 2023, a reversal worth watching. Better age specific outcomes outweighed demography for deaths, but not for total cases. The authors argue prevention must now scale with the growing population.
pmc-13528911:
Chai-Wan Kim and co-authors reply to critics of their heart metabolism study in a 2026 letter. Their mouse model deleted two fat-building enzymes in the heart, causing severe cardiomyopathy. A letter had doubted that a modest rise in fat burning explains such grave failure.

The reply notes two drugs that block fat burning both prevented the heart failure. That rescue, they argue, supports fat burning as a primary cause. An older single-deletion study with sound hearts is not a contradiction, they add. The exchange turns on how much weight a drug rescue can bear. Such replies are how metabolic claims get stress-tested in public.
pmc-13529011:
Saadi Saleh and a large consortium team surveyed in 2026 how often doctors in the Middle East and North Africa suffer chest pain. Doctors carry heavy work strain and heart risks, yet no large study had covered the region. The team enrolled 6,224 physicians from twelve countries in late 2023. A standard questionnaire sorted chest pain types, and short screens checked anxiety and panic.

About thirteen percent met the bar for definite angina-type pain, and nearly half for possible angina-type pain. Panic disorder was the strongest single predictor, ahead of other illnesses, lost sleep, and anxiety. All forms of nicotine use raised the odds as well. Doctors in middle-income countries fared worse than richer-country peers. The authors urge work health programs that treat mind and heart risks together.
pmc-13529611:
Gao-jue Wu and four colleagues test a cap-assisted injection therapy for severe bleeding hemorrhoids in a 2026 study. The method uses an endoscope cap to see clearly and a long needle to place sclerosing medicine precisely. Eighty-two patients with grade three internal hemorrhoids took one treatment. Bleeding was their main complaint. Scores at three months judged success.

Overall success reached about eighty-five percent. Bleeding eased in about ninety-six percent of patients. Prolapse improved in only about fifty-eight percent. Over twenty-four months, bleeding returned in about a quarter of those followed. Strong bleeding intensity before treatment predicted both leftover bleeding and return. High bleeding frequency after treatment also flagged return. No severe complications occurred. The authors back the method for bleeding control. They advise closer watch on high scorers.
pmc-13529811:
Kai Yang and co-authors name POFUT1 as a prognostic factor and drug target in glioma in a 2026 study. This enzyme adds sugar tags to proteins and has surfaced in several cancers, but its glioma role was ill-defined.

Public data and over one hundred patient samples showed POFUT1 runs high in glioma and rises with grade. High levels tied to shorter survival, and stats held it as an independent risk marker. Adding it to a prediction chart sharpened survival forecasts. Cutting POFUT1 slowed glioma cell growth, movement, invasion, and mouse tumor growth, while boosting it did the reverse. Gene scans tied its action to the PI3K and AKT pathway.
pmc-13529911:
Vahid Zarghami proposes a 2026 design framework for biodegradable scaffolds that break down in step with healing bone. Large bone gaps often fail to close on their own, so a temporary support must carry load early and then yield as new tissue forms. Timing that handover is the central problem.

Four material families receive review: metals, ceramics, polymers, and mixed composites. Matching math models link each family to defect sizes and care settings, followed by a four-step planning method for individual patients. A proposed synchronization index scores how closely implant loss follows a target healing curve, pending future testing.
pmc-13530111:
Wenjue Tang leads a 2026 hunt for exosome-linked markers in childhood glioblastoma, an aggressive brain tumor with poor survival. Exosomes are tiny packets cells release to signal neighbors, and their cargo can drive tumor growth. Two public gene datasets supplied the starting material.

Machine learning narrowed the field to three genes: FGF9, TGFBR1, and PLCB4. One ran high in tumors while the other two ran low, and each tracked with distinct immune cell patterns in the tissue. Computer drug screening pointed to a known enzyme-blocking compound as a possible candidate worth laboratory follow-up.
pmc-13530211:
Zohreh Yaghoubitajani and colleagues review in 2026 whether brief micro-exercises ease neck and shoulder pain for desk-bound workers. Tiny movement breaks fit into a workday without special equipment, which makes them attractive for offices. Three databases supplied randomized trials published through July 2025 for pooling.

Nineteen trials with 2,732 workers met the entry rules. Pooled results showed clear pain relief for the neck, the shoulder, and both combined, plus gains in neck function and quality of life. Muscle activity showed no clear change, while work outcomes were mixed. Wide variation between trials and signs of publication bias urge caution.
pmc-13530311:
Seung Min Oh and co-authors tested a skin injection made from pig collagen in mice, in work published in 2026. Ageing skin loses collagen and elastic fibers, so it sags and wrinkles, and many booster products claim to restore it without firm proof.

The team injected a clear, low irritation form of the collagen into the skin of young and aged mice. After two and four weeks, treated skin was thicker and had grown new elastic fibers reaching into the upper layer, much like young skin. Immune cells shifted briefly toward a healing type, with no lasting swelling at four weeks. Gene activity for building elastic fibers also rose in aged mice.
pmc-13530611:
Tuyishime and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 51, a cadaver anatomy study of lateral extra-articular tenodesis in children's ligament reconstructions. It asks whether the reinforcing band can be anchored without damaging the thigh bone's growth plate. The usual landmarks sit uncomfortably close to that plate in growing knees.

Seven skeletally immature cadaver knees, ages eight to sixteen, were dissected and X-rayed with pins marking the two candidate anchor origins. The anterolateral ligament's origin sat on average only about one and a half millimeters beyond the growth plate, and in one specimen right at it. The lateral collateral ligament's origin averaged about five millimeters clear. Both origins were also close to each other, with variable front-to-back ordering between specimens. The authors conclude the anterolateral landmark is consistently the riskier anchor point near the plate.
pmc-13530811:
Bugbee presents in 2026, as conference poster 49, outcomes of osteochondral allograft transplantation in the patients thought most likely to do well. The procedure grafts fresh donor cartilage and bone into a damaged knee. This cohort was young, non-obese, with small lesions from injury or a cartilage-bone disorder.

The series covered 109 patients and 116 knees, mean age about twenty, with grafts averaging five and a half square centimeters. About one knee in five needed some reoperation, but only one graft, under one percent, actually failed and required revision, at a little over five years. Graft survival stood at one hundred percent at five years and just over ninety-eight percent at ten years in this selected group. At a median five and a half years, pain and function had improved and about ninety percent of patients were satisfied.
pmc-13530911:
Mateja Krajc and Urška Ivanuš draw in 2026 lessons from Slovenia's organized cancer screening programs. Three national programs launched across the two thousands for cervix, breast, and bowel cancers. Cervix and bowel cancer rates and deaths fall, while breast cancers surface earlier.

Success rests on shared groundwork, not on any single test. Registries, quality checks, legal footing, and public trust form that base. Coverage ranks among Europe's strongest in the account. The same groundwork should guide upgrades and careful adds like lung screening next. Program names ZORA, DORA, and Svit mark the cervix, breast, and bowel efforts in turn.
pmc-13531011: Matthew Goodwin and co-authors report a rare gut infection in a heart transplant patient in this 2026 case report. The parasite Toxoplasma gondii threatens heart recipients whose donor carried it while they did not, unless preventive drugs are given. A woman in her late thirties fell ill six months after her preventive course ended. A drawn-out diarrheal illness spread into full-body infection with lung involvement. The authors note that guidance on how long to keep preventive drugs in this group is still unclear.
pmc-13531111:
Shimpei Yamashita and co-authors published a 2026 study comparing robot-assisted and open surgery for removing the bladder in cancer patients. Radical cystectomy is major surgery with real risks; robot assistance promises smaller wounds but must prove itself on cancer outcomes too. Japan's experience offers a large real-world test. Four institutions contributed cases from 2009 to 2024.

The review covered 438 patients who had the operation for bladder cancer. To compare fairly, the analysis matched robot and open patients on background traits, a propensity method that mimics a trial. Outcomes spanned the operation itself, complications, recovery, and the cancer results that ultimately matter. Multicenter real-world data complement the smaller trials that dominate this debate. The authors add Japanese evidence to a global question patients ask directly: does the robot change my odds, or only my scars? The study's design tries to answer both halves.
pmc-13531211:
Danny Dvir leads a 2026 first-in-human report on mechanically splitting a native aortic valve leaflet before valve replacement. A displaced leaflet can block a coronary artery opening during the procedure, a rare yet deadly event. Two patients with severe narrowing and high blockage risk received the splitting device first.

The catheter cut each target leaflet in a controlled way through the leg artery. Replacement valves then seated with clear coronary flow and strong function on imaging. Neither patient suffered a neurological event. The authors call for wider study of the approach in native valve disease.
pmc-13531611:
Rao and Riegal wrote a 2026 editorial on how professional soccer reshapes the heart, framing their commentary around the principle that form follows function. They discuss the largest echocardiographic study of adult male professional soccer players in North America. It covered 1,368 Major League Soccer players with an average age of 26 and a racially mixed roster, where ultrasound heart screening is routine.

Rao summarizes the findings: chamber dimensions, wall thickness, and heart mass often exceeded general population limits, yet true enlargement by size-indexed criteria was uncommon. No player reached the wall thickness zone that overlaps with inherited heart muscle disease. Most players showed normal geometry, right-sided enlargement was common and tracked with left-sided size, and pumping function stayed normal in nearly all. The editorial stresses that sport-specific reference values are essential so healthy athletic remodeling is not mistaken for disease, and real disease is not missed.
pmc-13531711:
Timothy Martin, Anna Head, and Philip McHale ask what carries the effect of poverty onto children's height in Sefton, England. Stunting signals lasting harm to child health, and poorer areas consistently show more of it. Their 2026 study uses a decade of school height measurements, from 2013 to 2023, and area-level data on candidate pathways, aiming to form hypotheses rather than prove causes.

Children in the most deprived fifth of areas had clearly higher odds of stunting than those in the least deprived, at both ages four to five and ten to eleven. For the older group, adding five candidate pathways shrank the poverty effect by about three quarters. Those pathways were low birth weight, early birth, breastfeeding, food insecurity, and health care access, though the change was not statistically firm. For the younger group nothing shrank. The authors call for finer, child-level work to test the pathways.
pmc-13531811:
Shaowei Liu and co-authors examine in 2026 whether routine preventive services shield older Chinese adults from heat-linked depression. Survey waves from 2016 to 2020 covered 7,464 people, linked to city weather records counting extreme heat days each year. Depression scores came from a standard nine-item scale.

More accumulated heat days meant worse depressive symptoms. Health education strongly softened that link, and personal health record management helped as well, while screening showed a weaker effect. Protection concentrated among men, rural residents, and the middle region. The authors frame local preventive services as climate adaptation capital for aging towns.
pmc-13531911:
Wisteria Deng and co-authors review in 2026 how rigid interpretation of social situations feeds mental illness. People constantly read ambiguous social cues, and trouble starts when first readings refuse to update against new evidence. The review gathers work on depression and psychosis within everyday social settings.

Depression showed narrow rigidity, clinging to negative readings of unclear events. Psychosis showed broader rigidity across pleasant and unpleasant material alike. Measurement tools increasingly test revision inside social scenes rather than abstract puzzles. Targeting stuck social readings may open fresh therapy routes for both conditions.
pmc-13533611:
Hye-Ji Kim and Mi-Kyoung Cho test a bundle of simple nursing measures against delirium and poor sleep in an emergency intensive care unit. Forty-eight patients in a South Korean hospital were split evenly between the program and usual care. For two days, the program group received delirium prevention steps, sleep promotion, and checks that the steps were actually done. Delirium and sleep quality were scored with standard Korean scales, and a wearable device logged total sleep.

Delirium scores rose less in the program group, with the gap widening over time, and adjusted sleep quality scored clearly higher. Total sleep time improved with time in both groups without a clear extra edge for the program. The authors call the bundle a feasible strategy for critical care, notable for needing no specialised equipment.
pmc-13534511:
Shunqing Yuan and colleagues study in 2026 how the level of artificial intelligence use affects carbon emission intensity in Chinese firms. Firms face strong pressure to cut emissions, and AI can either raise energy use at first or improve efficiency later. Provincial panel data were tested with fixed-effects models and pathway analysis.

The link formed an inverted U shape, with emissions rising early, then falling past a turning point as use deepened. Gains ran through greener innovation, better energy use, and industry upgrading. Effects were stronger in the eastern region, so policy should vary by region and energy mix.
pmc-13534811:
Sihong Le and co-authors study in 2026 how immune clusters that form inside tumors, called tertiary lymphoid structures, shape cell traffic and outlook in the most common lung cancer type. Their role in this cancer was not fully mapped. Gene data from over five hundred patients in a public atlas, plus two outside sets, were grouped by a twelve gene signature of these clusters.

One group showed richer immune cell entry, more checkpoint molecules, and better survival. A risk model of eight genes tied to the signature predicted survival on its own. Tissue stains confirmed that cluster density inside the tumor tracked with immune marks and patient outlook at any stage. The work supports using these clusters to sort patients.
pmc-13535211:
Kevin Nguyen and co-authors published a 2026 study on whether a Medicaid reform in Massachusetts improved the recording of social risks in pregnancy care. Social risks such as hunger and homelessness shape birth outcomes. In 2018 the state required its Medicaid care organizations to screen for them. Two kinds of organizations took part, one led by health systems and one by primary care practices.

Using claims data from 2016 to 2020, the team tracked diagnosis codes that record social risks. They compared deliveries inside and outside the new organizations, before and after the change. Both organization types raised the recording of food insecurity during the perinatal period. The practice-led model also raised recording of homelessness, while the system-led model did not. Overall gains were modest. The authors say the reform nudged clinics to write down social risks more often, a first step toward acting on them.
pmc-13535411:
Thomas B Powles and co-authors report patient views in 2026 from a phase three trial in kidney cancer. The trial, LITESPARK-022, added belzutifan to an immune drug for patients at high risk of the cancer returning after surgery. The pair kept patients free of disease longer than the immune drug with a dummy pill.

Here the team reports how patients felt during that added care, using standard symptom and quality forms. Extra months without cancer count for less if daily life suffers badly. These reports complete the picture for patients weighing a year of preventive treatment after surgery, and for doctors advising them.
pmc-13535511:
Seven authors name a new primrose species from Sichuan, China, in a 2026 study. The plant, Primula pingwuensis, sits in a small section of the genus with nine known species. It looks close to a known cousin with palm-shaped lobed leaves and stacked rings of blooms.

Closer checks set it apart: many-branched stems, denser short hairs, thicker leaves, and nectar guides that barely show. A key covers all nine species in the section to aid field naming. DNA from the plant's chloroplast puts it next to another recent species. Leaf shape, though, has shifted many times in the rocky karst homes of these plants, so form alone misleads. With little data on its numbers, the team rates the species as data deficient.
pmc-13535711:
Lisa Toffoli and co-authors present a study the catalog lists under 2026. Children with ADHD often struggle to adjust control to context. Skilled control learns from regular patterns in a task. That learning-based control is well studied in typical children but not in ADHD. The study ran across several centers. It held 145 children with ADHD and 97 typical children, all aged seven to fourteen.

Two tasks tested control under shifting predictability. Blocks were mostly matching or half matching, which changes how much control pays off. Response speed and accuracy were scored in each block. Extra task load tested whether gains hold under strain. Teachers and clinicians get a precise picture of where control learning stands in ADHD. If learning is intact, training can build on it. If load breaks it, support should cut load first. Either answer guides classroom and clinic plans better than a blanket deficit claim.
pmc-13536611:
Fang Liang and colleagues sequence in 2026 the chloroplast genomes of three Barringtonia trees, two of them threatened coastal species. These trees anchor tropical shore forests, yet no chloroplast genomes existed for the genus. The team assembled and annotated the full green-cell genomes for all three species.

The genomes were alike in size and gene content, with no large rearrangements. A few fast-changing regions stood out as useful markers for population studies. Family tree tests grouped the three firmly in one lineage, giving conservation work its first genomic base for these trees.
pmc-13536711:
Jie Lin and co-authors give a full account of a gene change that drives some lung cancers, in which a segment of the MET gene is skipped. That change can start cancer on its own. It can also appear later, when tumors learn to resist drugs aimed at MET or at related growth signals.

The study covers 585 patients whose tumors carry the change. Samples came from before treatment and from patients whose cancers had resisted several drug types. Gene data came from a panel test of 425 cancer genes, run on tissue or blood. The change appeared in about one percent of all lung cancer patients screened. The authors sort its partner mutations and clinical traits, which can guide drug choice.
pmc-13538211:
Cedric Igelspacher, Roderich Tumulka, and Cornelia Vogel ask how the grand-canonical density matrix arises for large quantum systems, in a paper from 2026. In statistical physics, a small system in touch with a big reservoir is described by set formulas. Canonical typicality already explains the version where only energy is shared.

The new work covers the case where particles can also move between system and reservoir. It treats both a region of space that particles enter and leave, and systems with chemical reactions. For a typical wave function in the right shared space, the small system's state lands close to the grand-canonical formula. The spread of the system's own wave function also takes a named form, a GAP measure.
pmc-13538311:
Jinbao Zhang and colleagues explore lived experience of long-term care insurance in Guangzhou, China, in a 2026 interview study with twenty-four older recipients and family members. Home-based insurance programs aim to help older adults stay in their communities, yet unmet needs persist. Interviews traced how specific policy features eased or failed to ease daily care gaps, using a care network lens.

Four features eased unmet needs, covering enrollment into formal care, choice of caregiver, agency nurses joining care networks, and caregiver training. Gaps remained where benefits fell short, program information stayed scarce, and personal care goods were hard to obtain. The authors advise policymakers to build these lessons into future insurance design so home care matches real family needs more closely.
pmc-13538511:
Huohuo Xue and four co-authors review a spinal disease in a 2026 paper. In this condition, a ligament along the spine slowly turns to bone. The new bone presses on the spinal cord and weakens limb control. Genes and metabolism play a part, but the review centers on immune cells called macrophages.

These cells shift shape and role based on signals around them. One form keeps low grade inflammation alive in the ligament. Another form, oddly, speeds the disease by laying down scar like tissue. Together they build a low oxygen niche where bone can form. Similar cell behavior appears in other stray bone diseases. The authors ask whether calming these cells could open new treatments.
pmc-13539011:
Stephen Engmann and co-authors measure burnout among health workers at a teaching hospital in Ghana, in a 2026 study. Burnout harms both staff well-being and the quality of care, yet Ghanaian data by age, sex, and job type are thin. The team reuse records from a routine staff audit at Cape Coast Teaching Hospital.

Of 333 workers, about 62 percent met the burnout bar. Rates were alike for women and men, though women reported more body symptoms. Burnout eased slightly with age, from about 64 percent in the twenties to 57 percent in the fifties. Job type was the one clear divider: doctors burned out more than nurses and health assistants, who had about half the odds after adjustment. The authors call for workload fixes and mental health support aimed by job group.
pmc-13539111:
William Morgans, Andrew D Sharrocks, and Mudassar Iqbal published a study in 2026 on a faster way to merge two kinds of single-cell data. Modern assays can read a cell's active genes and its open chromatin at once, hinting at the switches that control the genes. Merging the two views needs methods that are fast, readable, and ready for future data types.

Their method, q-intNMF, splits both data kinds into shared topics that a biologist can interpret in the original gene and region terms. On large public datasets it matched five established tools across standard quality measures while running more efficiently. Applied to Alzheimer's data, the readable topics highlighted cell state changes tied to the disease. The package is released openly with documentation for other labs.
pmc-13539211:
Kaneez Fatima and co-authors test flower extracts from the devil's tree against two disease-carrying mosquitoes in this 2026 study. Malaria and dengue spread through Anopheles and Aedes mosquitoes, and plant extracts offer a greener weapon than synthetic sprays. Extracts were split into solvent fractions and tested at many doses.

The raw methanol extract killed larvae of both species at moderate doses. One fraction kept adult Aedes mosquitoes away for up to nine hours. Chemical analysis of the extract found five main compounds, led by lupeol at over half the mix. Fingerprint spectra pointed to aldehyde, amide, and carbonyl groups among the active chemistry. The authors see promise for plant-based vector control.
pmc-13539411:
Lin and colleagues joined two Taiwan datasets in 2026 to probe why only some people with heart rhythm problems go on to develop cardiomyopathy, a weakening of the heart muscle. One dataset was the national insurance database covering 2000 to 2015, and the other was a biobank with gene data, thyroid hormone measures, and lifestyle records. Thyroid problems and inherited risk were their main suspects.

In the insurance cohort, a new rhythm diagnosis came with more than double the risk of later cardiomyopathy, with atrial fibrillation, a fast irregular rhythm, showing the strongest link. In the biobank, a gene-based risk score for thyroid trouble was strongly tied to actual thyroid dysfunction, and diabetes, blood fats, and diet shifted that tie. The authors frame the two lines as parallel evidence for heart-endocrine interplay, while noting the unlinked cohorts bar any claim of cause.
pmc-13539811:
Masoumeh Paknia, Maryam Dehestani-Ardakani, and Heidar Meftahizade report a 2026 laboratory protocol for multiplying a pink-leaved ornamental plant, Syngonium podophyllum 'Pink Allusion', from small stem pieces. Ordinary cuttings multiply slowly and can carry disease, so growers need a cleaner route.

Three linked trials tuned the growth chemicals for shoot formation, rooting, and greenhouse settling. One mix gave the most shoots per piece, a rooting chemical called IBA gave the most roots, and every plantlet survived the move out of the laboratory. Peat-based mixes beat cocopeat mixes for leaf and root growth. The authors offer the recipe for large-scale nursery production.
pmc-13539911:
Jai-Hong Cheng and seven colleagues report a 2026 cell study asking whether vitamin D3 and shockwave treatment together push bone-forming cells to mature faster than either one alone. A protein called Pdia3 carries the vitamin's quick signal at the cell surface, yet its link to shockwaves was unclear.

Mouse bone precursor cells received the vitamin, shockwaves, or both, and the combined treatment raised enzyme activity, mineral deposits, and surface Pdia3 the most. Blocking the cell's internal actin fibres removed the benefit, while shockwaves helped those fibres rebuild and move Pdia3 outward. A signalling chain through protein kinase C completed the picture the authors propose.
pmc-13540811:
Leitao Wen, Cong Shen, Yuedong Han, and Xiu'e Wang chart, in a 2026 imaging study, how the walls of children's airways change shape from birth to adulthood. Their measure, wall area proportion, compares airway wall area with the total of wall plus open channel, and healthy reference values for Chinese youth were missing.

Chest scans from 795 healthy children and teenagers were measured automatically across airway generations. Wall proportion fell with age beyond the second airway branch, more steeply in boys. Sex made little difference before sixteen, after which boys showed lower values in the windpipe, lobes, and upper airways. The tables give clinicians a baseline for spotting abnormal airway thickening.
pmc-13540911:
Clémence Tropis leads a 2026 study arguing that body fat itself helps drive the confusion and memory problems that can follow surgery in people with obesity. Postoperative neurocognitive disorder can linger for months and raises later dementia risk.

Obese patients having heart or orthopaedic surgery showed more early cognitive change and lower test scores than lean patients. A mouse model pairing diet-driven obesity with a leg fracture reproduced the worsening. Treatments that cut inflammation, removed fat tissue, or restricted calories each protected the obese mice from the cognitive slide. The authors propose targeting obesity-linked inflammation before surgery as a prevention strategy.
pmc-13542011:
Armaun Rouhi and co-authors test how often AI language models agree with expert heart teams in a 2026 systematic review. Multidisciplinary heart teams remain the cornerstone for hard decisions such as bypass surgery, stenting, and aortic valve replacement. Generative AI has been proposed as decision support in many clinical areas.

The team searched the literature and pooled the measured agreement between model recommendations and heart team decisions. Quantifying concordance is the honest first step: a model that often disagrees with experts may still help, but only in a supervised role. The review frames where these tools stand in cardiology today.
pmc-13542111:
SeonYong Lee and six colleagues map, in a 2026 landscape study, how heron and egret breeding colonies across South Korea assemble into types, and which surroundings at which distances explain each type. Colonies sit in patchwork landscapes, and national-scale multi-scale evidence was scarce.

Nest counts from 176 colonies were clustered with a self-organising map, yielding six distinct assemblages. Large species dominated inland forest colonies, while smaller species clustered in coastal and mixed urban-rural areas. Built land, managed greenery, and water cover ruled the immediate surroundings, grasses and trees mattered at middle distances, and broad land use still counted at ten kilometres. Conservation planning, the authors argue, must work at all scales at once.
pmc-13542211:
Yan-li Zhang, Chao Ran, and Wei Li build a prediction chart in 2026. The chart forecasts treatment effect in a fungal lung infection. The infection is pulmonary cryptococcosis. Its CT look overlaps with other diseases. The tool mines texture patterns from scans. The eye cannot quantify those patterns alone.

Records covered 255 patients at two centres. Sets were split into training and validation groups. One set came from a second centre for external checks. A support vector machine performed best among the models. It used selected scan features as inputs. Adding clinical variables made a combined nomogram. That chart matched the scan-only model. It clearly beat a clinical-only model.
pmc-13542411:
Gómez Juárez and co-authors study whether a strong sense of coherence, a person's feeling that life is manageable and meaningful, predicts sticking with sleep apnea therapy. The therapy, a nightly air pressure mask, works only if patients keep using it. Their 2026 study covers 200 patients at a Mexican family medicine unit.

About three quarters of patients scored high on sense of coherence, and that trait tied strongly to therapy adherence. Low scores marked the strongest single risk factor for stopping, with odds near nine times higher in adjusted analysis. Device cards verified actual use, set at over four hours a night on most nights. The authors suggest motivation strategies aimed at this trait could raise persistence.
pmc-13542511:
Fumio Takahashi, Takashi Yamamura, and Shinji Oki report a lethal coincidence in the brains of Alzheimer's model mice. Mature neurons re-enter the cell cycle while a jumping gene copies itself into their DNA. Their 2026 study finds that this cell cycle re-entry is prominent in sick neurons. The replication forks it creates become landing sites for L1 retrotransposition.

Neurons in that state die because their DNA repair cannot keep up with the stress. A silenced sirtuin seems to unlock the jumping gene. Hormone signals track with a protective repair gene's fall. The mechanism links three Alzheimer's threads, cell cycle, jumping genes, and repair failure, into one chain.
pmc-13542711:
Peifeng Ying and co-authors reviewed how exercise helps health at the cell level in a 2026 paper. Moving the body is a cheap habit that can ward off many diseases and ease others. It fires shared signal paths across the body, and signals from muscle, heart, and brain work as a team to give broad gains.

Most past studies looked at one body system at a time. This review joins the threads across muscle and bone, heart and vessels, and the nervous system. It gives weight to small signal compounds that active tissue sheds into the blood. The joined view may help doctors set exercise as care with more exact aims.
pmc-13543011:
Jeenat Mehareen and co-authors published a 2026 study measuring how much extra people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease spend on medicines, and who pays. Using British Columbia health databases spanning 2001 to 2020, the team matched more than 207,000 patients with physician-diagnosed COPD to over 400,000 people without the disease. Excess cost was the adjusted difference in all medication spending, split between the public PharmaCare programme and private sources such as out-of-pocket payments.

Patients with COPD spent an extra 1,336 Canadian dollars per patient-year on medications. About forty percent of that excess, 528 dollars, was privately financed, and private spending grew much faster than public spending across the two decades, at roughly 8 percent a year. Patients also personally bore half of their inhaler costs. The authors warn that the private share of drug costs quietly shifts the burden of chronic lung disease onto patients.
pmc-13543511:
Sara Sousi and colleagues published a 2026 protocol for a systematic review of remote care for pregnant women with diabetes. The condition, whether pre-existing or gestational, raises risks for mother and baby, and virtual consultations plus home monitoring spread quickly during recent years. Whether that shift helped or hurt the quality of antenatal care is unsettled, so the review will search seven databases for studies from 2005 to 2025 covering virtual visits and remote monitoring.

Quality will be judged by a six-part framework whose parts are patient-centredness, effectiveness, safety, efficiency, timeliness, and equity. Two reviewers will screen and extract independently, bias will be appraised with Cochrane tools, and subgroups will separate diabetes types and intervention styles. Being a protocol, the paper itself reports no results. Its value is a transparent plan whose findings should guide safe, fair roll-out of remote antenatal diabetes care.
pmc-13543611:
Yuxi Ma and Min Liu published a 2026 study comparing HPV infection patterns and cervical cell changes in women with and without HIV in Shanghai. The team enrolled 238 women confirmed HPV-positive at a public health centre between 2019 and 2023, just under half of them also living with HIV. Genotypes were catalogued, cell abnormalities compared, and risk factors for cervical dysplasia in the co-infected group were modelled.

The HIV-positive group carried more high-risk HPV and more multiple infections, including higher rates of two particular genotypes, and vaccine-covered types were commoner there too. Cell abnormalities were significantly more frequent with HIV. Within the co-infected group, a viral load above one thousand copies per microlitre of blood raised dysplasia odds roughly tenfold, marking uncontrolled HIV as the danger to watch. Cervical screening intensity, the authors imply, should follow HIV control.
pmc-13543711:
Chery Ahn and co-authors report a rare case of cancer spread to the membranes around the brain in a 2026 paper. The patient was a 61-year-old woman with late-stage cervical cancer who grew a sharp headache and double vision during drug care. Scans hinted at the spread, and fluid tests proved it.

A small port was set in her head so drugs could go straight into the spinal fluid. Her symptoms eased fast, fluid pressure came back to normal, and later fluid tests stayed clear of cancer cells. Her body disease grew worse, yet the nerve signs stayed in check, and she lived eight months after the spread was found.
pmc-13544111:
Owino and colleagues produced the first county-by-county estimates of the combined human and livestock burden of Rift Valley fever in Kenya, covering 2014 to 2024. Rift Valley fever is a mosquito-borne virus that sickens people and causes deaths and abortions in farm animals. Their 2026 analysis uses a One Health measure that adds years of healthy life lost by people to losses expressed as animal equivalents.
