Owino found the burden heavily concentrated in northern Kenya, with Marsabit county highest by a wide margin, followed by Baringo and Wajir, while several central counties recorded almost none. The pattern split by sector: Marsabit carried the largest livestock burden, while Nairobi carried the largest human health burden. Because losses cluster so sharply in space, the authors argue that vaccination, surveillance, and outbreak preparation money should target the high-burden counties rather than spread evenly nationwide.
pmc-13544411:
María Consuelo Company-Sancho and two co-authors test whether nursing records can sharpen machine forecasts of health care costs. Cost models lean on age, illness, and use, but they skip the rich notes nurses keep on care needs. Their 2026 study covers more than one and a half million people in the Canary Islands health system.

Adding nursing data lifted forecast scores by a hair for total cost. Gains showed more in hospital and drug cost parts. A squeeze tool shrank nearly eight hundred nursing fields to sixteen, with scores about the same. The authors call nursing data a small but real gain. They frame it as a step toward cost tools that see the whole person.
pmc-13545111:
Vi and co-authors surveyed a 2026 nationwide snapshot of myopia awareness in Australia, where short-sightedness usually starts in childhood and can end in permanent visual damage. Slowing its progression early is possible, but only if families know treatments exist. The online survey ran across September and October 2024.

After excluding eye care workers, 1,565 responses were analysed from residents across the country for this study. Seventy-nine percent had heard the term myopia, yet understanding of risk factors, complications, and treatments stayed patchy, Vi reports. Only fifteen percent knew treatments exist that slow myopia progression in children over time. Common misconceptions about causes and lifetime risks, such as retinal detachment, fed complacency about the condition. The authors call for public health campaigns promoting early detection and treatment.
pmc-13545311:
Carolina Reato Marçon, Seaver L Soon, and Carlos Gustavo Wambier report harm from a new chemical peel mix in a 2026 letter. After Brazil briefly banned phenol peels in 2024, clinics turned to a mix of a strong acid, TCA, with croton oil, spread through social media. Pig tests had hinted the mix burns less deeply than the old phenol one.

In their clinic, ten straight patients came in with scar harm after such peels on the face. Some scars grew thick and raised. The authors warn that the mix behaves in ways no one can predict. Their cases urge care and proof before new peels reach faces.
pmc-13546011:
Jianhua Sun, Yuanyuan Wang, and Huafang Wei chart the global burden of heavy bleeding after childbirth from 1990 to 2021 in this 2026 paper. Such bleeding stays a top cause of mothers' illness and death worldwide. The team also forecasts the burden out to 2040.

Using a worldwide disease database covering two hundred four countries, they tracked rates of cases, deaths, and lost healthy years. The global case rate fell steadily over the three decades. Poor regions still carried by far the highest burden, while rich regions carried the lowest. Forecasts suggest case rates may rise again by 2040, driven by middle-income regions, even as deaths keep falling. Gains in fairness between rich and poor were mixed, and women aged twenty-five to twenty-nine faced the highest risk.
pmc-13546511:
Ming Guo and co-authors study heat harm in pig cells that guard sperm-making, in work from 2026. Making sperm is very heat-shy, and these guard cells shield the process. The team asked if heat triggers a named cell-death path in them, and if a body hormone can block it.

Heat did set off the path, they report. It harmed the cells' power parts, leaked their DNA into the cell body, and woke alarm signals that drove swelling and death. The hormone leptin, named in the title, eased the harm by quieting that alarm chain. Findings in pig cells matter for farm breeding, where heat waves cut male fertility. They may also hint at how heat harms the same cells in other mammals.
pmc-13546711:
Anak Agung Gde Oka Dharmayudha and colleagues tested in 2026 whether leaf extract from the Spondias pinnata tree can keep dog semen healthy during chilled storage. Their breed was the Kintamani, a Balinese dog of conservation interest. Semen from four dogs was pooled, diluted in a coconut-water-based extender, and split into a plain batch and three batches with rising extract doses. Quality was checked over 72 hours in the refrigerator.

The lowest extract dose worked best, preserving sperm movement and survival better than the plain extender, while the DNA held up well for at least three days in every batch. Higher doses gave no extra benefit. The authors present the recipe as a cheaper, locally sourced option for short-term semen storage.
pmc-13546811:
Who teaches ear, nose, and throat medicine in American training programs, and how varied is that faculty by gender and race? Rachel Haji and six co-authors take stock in this 2026 study of academic otolaryngology. They gathered faculty lists from one hundred and thirty-three residency programs and added public details on rank, leadership, training, and research output.

Among 1,697 faculty, about sixty-nine percent were men and about sixty-nine percent were perceived as White, based on public information rather than self-report. Women clustered in children's ear care and voice work, while men dominated head and neck surgery and ear neurology. Women were more often junior assistant professors and men more often full professors. The authors treat perceived race with care, as a rough social measure, and link the patterns to rank and leadership gaps.
pmc-13547111:
Torwane and colleagues interview fourteen committed opponents of community water fluoridation to learn what actually holds their opposition together, aiming to give health communicators something better than fact sheets. Participants from Britain, Australia, and the United States were recruited through the Fluoride Action Network's Facebook page, the movement's main online hub. They were interviewed by video call across the first half of 2025 for this 2026 qualitative study.

Anti-fluoride networks plus social media were the most trusted information source, named by the large majority, while mainstream science and health authorities ranked low. Opposition rested less on disputing the dental evidence than on mass medication without consent, distrust of institutions, industrial-waste worries, and memories of being dismissed by professionals. The authors conclude engagement must answer values and trust, inside the networks where beliefs circulate, not merely repeat the evidence louder.
pmc-13547711:
Catarina Gomes and co-authors build in 2026 a human stem cell brain model that can mount an immune reply to gene therapy carriers. Such carriers drive cures for brain ills, yet host immune hits are missed by classic lab models. Their model aims to catch the first brain reply in a dish.

Small brain balls hold nerve cells, star cells, sheath cells, and immune guard cells in one set. Tank based growth lets the team make them at scale and shrink them for screens. The balls showed live nerve guard cross talk and woke swell paths when a known carrier was added.
pmc-13547911:
John Politis and colleagues argued asthma care stands at a turning point. Published in 2026, the viewpoint traces drivers of change: deeper disease knowledge, steroid harms in view, and immune-targeted drugs that make lasting calm a real goal. Patient-centered care with virtual health and AI also drives change. In Australia, up to 10 percent of people live with asthma.

These drugs can bring lasting calm, flagging type 2 eosinophilic disease found in half to most mild cases and nearly all severe ones. Yet primary care faces thin funds, short visits, split handling, and guideline churn, while typing and fixable traits get short shrift. AI and virtual tools plus patient voices promise to ease these chokepoints. The authors urge careful use so advances lift results without trading safety.
pmc-13548011:
Hyunok Yun, Shinyoung Kwon, Jieun Choi, and Dae-kyun Kim draft a questionnaire that asks bereaved families how satisfied they were with hospice care. The team interviewed twelve bereaved relatives to learn what such a survey must cover, then merged those themes with existing assessment tools. Twenty hospice experts refined the items over two Delphi rounds, and the wording was checked for clarity. Separate versions were built for inpatient, home, and consultative hospices.

A pilot across several institutions tested whether families could complete the survey in practice. Filling it in took about ten to twelve minutes, few answers were left blank, and every item passed the agreed bar for importance and fit. The inpatient version also held together strongly as a scale. The authors say a large national validation must come before the tool guides policy.
pmc-13548211:
Suleman Aktaa and ten colleagues built quality indicators for a heart valve procedure in Ontario, Canada, in a 2026 study. The procedure, TAVI, threads a replacement aortic valve into the heart without open surgery. The team asked which measurable habits mark good care and whether they explain outcome gaps between hospitals.

They studied nearly ten thousand procedures done from 2018 to 2023 in the provincial registry. Five workable indicators emerged, and most hospitals met most of them at high rates. One habit varied more: doing the procedure through the leg artery without general anesthesia. Meeting the indicators tracked with fewer deaths and readmissions within a year. A heart team joining both a cardiologist and a surgeon showed the strongest link. Yet indicator scores did not explain the outcome gaps between hospitals, a caution the authors state plainly.
pmc-13548711:
Martina Smorti and colleagues explore what helps teenagers and young adults with heart muscle disease come to terms with their condition, in a 2026 pilot study. Acceptance research in this age group has focused on private identity, yet these years hand disease management from parents to the young person within a web of relationships. Sixty-eight Italians aged sixteen to thirty, recruited through a patient association, rated their acceptance and the support they felt from family, friends, and partners.

The final statistical model explained about a sixth of the differences in acceptance. Feeling strongly supported by family went with greater acceptance. Carrying an implanted defibrillator device went with lower acceptance, perhaps as a daily reminder of risk. Support from friends and partners showed no clear independent link. The authors suggest family-focused help belongs inside transition care as young patients take over their own management.
pmc-13548911:
Daniel Houghton and colleagues watch the very same platinum nanoparticles before and after harsh fuel cell stress tests, in a 2026 microscopy study. Platinum particles drive fuel cell reactions but sit on carbon supports that corrode, muddying any judgment of the particles themselves. The team mounted particles on corrosion-proof boron-doped diamond, transparent to the electron beam, and built automated software to track each particle's size, position, and neighbors across the test.

Roughly two hundred particles per image were followed. Between forty and fifty percent barely changed area at all, a few grew, and the rest shrank by less than an atomic layer through brief dissolving. Particles wandered on average only a third of a nanometer. The authors credit a strong platinum and diamond bond and pitch diamond as a durable catalyst support for punishing conditions.
pmc-13549311:
Yaqiu Zhang and co-authors reply to a letter that raised a methods worry about their trial of two drugs that calm children after anesthesia. The worry was one of timing: whether a rescue dose of a calming drug could have skewed a score of agitation taken five minutes after the child woke.

In their reply, the authors lay out the order of events in the trial. The five minute score was taken at once, on waking, before any call on rescue sedation was made. Only if the score stayed high for three more minutes, or the child moved in a way that risked harm, was a rescue dose given. The letter thus rests on a misread sequence.
pmc-13549411:
Zhangluxi Liu and five co-authors search blood chemistry for signals tied to age-related cataract in a 2026 study. Cataracts cloud the lens and are the top cause of blindness in older adults, yet their metabolic roots are murky.

The team used genetic methods to test 249 blood metabolites against cataract in a Finnish database. Seventy-one passed a first screen; strict checks across seven methods cut the list to 22. Thirteen of those also predicted new cataracts in UK Biobank data. Eight signals were finally prioritized: five steady across ages, mostly fats and lipoproteins, and three that changed with age. The work names candidates for prevention research rather than proven causes.
pmc-13549811:
Fatikhu Yatuni Asmara and colleagues design a logbook that helps health students from different professions reflect together, in this study from Indonesia, published in twenty twenty-six. Their students train in community reproductive health, far from campus supervisors, in a low-middle income setting. Self-reflection, logged well, can partly replace the missing oversight.

Using educational design research, the team moved through analysis, design, and pilot testing, with experts, instructors, and students shaping each round. The logbook follows a known reflective cycle and folds shared decision-making into the teamwork competencies it tracks. In the pilot, students and instructors both rated it well, around four point three in five, with no differences across the professions involved. The authors present it as a validated tool for interprofessional placements where supervision is thin.
pmc-13550311:
Linna Lu and colleagues build a ten-gene risk score from the cell's recycling centers to forecast survival in acute myeloid leukemia, in a 2026 computational study. Lysosomes digest and recycle cell contents, and their genes are disturbed in this blood cancer. Comparing leukemia and control samples from public databases, the team isolated lysosome genes tied to outcome, then used survival statistics and machine learning to assemble a model from cancer atlas data.

The ten-gene score split patients into high and low risk groups with clearly different clinical features, active pathways, immune surroundings, and drug sensitivities, and it held up in outside datasets. Laboratory checks on three of the genes in leukemia and marrow cell lines matched the computed direction. The authors suggest the signature could steer choices between immunotherapy and chemotherapy, pending clinical testing.
pmc-13550511:
Despina Tawadros and Melek Arkan comment on an aging study that puts sleep at the center of how fast our organs grow old. Their 2026 commentary discusses work from the MULTI Consortium examining twenty-three biological aging clocks, built from brain scans, blood proteins, and metabolites, in half a million people.

Sleep duration related to the age gaps in a U shape: too little and too much both tracked older biology. The sweet spot sat near six and a half to eight hours, depending on the organ. The pattern appeared across heart, lung, liver, immune, and other clocks, not just the brain. The commentators place the result in organ-by-organ aging science, where organs age at different rates and drag each other along. Their clinical moral is scalability: sleep is among the few aging levers that is measurable and adjustable tonight.
pmc-13550811:
Heather H. Cheng and twelve colleagues lay out PATROL, a multicentre early-detection study for prostate cancer in people at genetic risk. Carriers of inherited risky variants in genes such as BRCA2 and BRCA1 now warrant closer screening under current guidelines. Yet the best early-detection plan for carriers still needs refining. Their 2026 paper sets out the study design.

The study enrolls people aged 40 or older carrying a risky variant in an eligible gene, with no prior prostate cancer. Each year brings a physical exam and a PSA test, with MRI at baseline optional and advised when PSA tops the protocol cutoff. Biopsy is offered for any clinical concern or a PSA above age-based cutoffs. Samples will be banked to test new clinical and research markers.
pmc-13551511:
Haiqi Wang and co-authors trace how a fish oil fat fights cell stress through two small RNA switches in liver cells, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. The fat lowers one switch that targets a power-unit builder gene. Loosening that switch raised defenses and new power-unit growth.

The fat also raises a second switch that targets a repair protein. That squeeze tracks with stronger stress-fighting enzymes, three named kinds in all. Cell rust fell and power units worked better under the first route. The pair forms a two-arm plan for the fat's shield effect. Readers get a tidy dual path for a known nutrient gain.
pmc-13551811:
Gabriella Barratt Heitmann, leading fifteen colleagues, published a 2026 analysis of weather and vivax malaria in the Peruvian Amazon, where this malaria species dominates and blocks elimination goals. Monthly case counts from 136 communities between 2017 and 2024 were paired with hourly climate reanalysis data. Distributed lag models, which spread an exposure's effect over following weeks, tested minimum and maximum temperature and rainfall over a two to sixteen week lookback.

Warmer minimum and maximum temperatures each raised malaria incidence by about a tenth at lags of seven and nine weeks in the reported comparisons. Heavy weekly rainfall raised incidence by nearly a third at eleven weeks, and river-adjacent communities showed stronger links than highway ones. Incidence dipped during El Niño periods, adding a climate signal for timing control efforts.
pmc-13551911:
Francis Duhamel Nang Nang, with eleven colleagues, published a 2026 study of high blood pressure in adults with HIV in Yaounde, Cameroon. The study ran at an urban HIV clinic from January to March 2024. It covered 460 adults on antiretroviral therapy. The team modeled blood pressure with a method suited to common outcomes. They also probed how treatment length interacts with age.

High blood pressure affected 43.3 percent of the group. Mean age was about fifty, and most participants were women. Family history of high blood pressure was the strongest factor. Older age and obesity also counted. Treatment length linked to pressure before adjustment, yet not after. The team reads age as the driver behind that first link.
pmc-13552011:
Sean Chung-Hei Ho and co-authors review a blood fat drug that may find a second career in eye care, in this 2026 paper. Fenofibrate is widely used for abnormal blood lipids. Eye diseases are a cause of vision loss as populations age and diabetes spreads, so a proven drug with eye benefits would be valuable.

The review gathers lab and clinical evidence across eye diseases of the front and back of the eye. The drug calmed inflammation, steadied blood vessels, and protected nerve and surface tissue in models. The strongest clinical evidence covers diabetic eye disease, where trials support the drug as an add-on that slows worsening in early to moderate cases. For dry eye, corneal burns, and several conditions the evidence is from lab work alone. The authors say more trials and long-term safety data are needed before the drug's role is settled.
pmc-13552611:
Samy Selim and co-authors made food wrap films from seaweed and shell sugars, laced with mineral bits, in this 2026 study. Such films rot away in soil, unlike plain plastic wrap. Three mixes were cast, with more shell sugar in each next. Tiny paired-metal grains, grown in the film as it set, added germ fight and strength.

Tests showed the two sugars bound into one tight web, and the grains sat in it well. More shell sugar made the skin denser and rougher. The films stood heat better and pulled stronger than the plain seaweed film. They proved mild to lab cells, with life rates in the safe band. The third mix fought germs best and topped the rust-guard score at about eighty-eight in a hundred. In soil the films broke down fast.
pmc-13552911:
Fei-Fei Cheng and co-authors hunt for genes behind age-related macular degeneration, in a 2026 study. The disease is a top cause of lasting vision loss in older people. Large gene scans have flagged many risk spots, but the genes at most spots are unknown. The team joined gene activity data with the scan results.

Nine candidate genes rose to the top. Tests in zebrafish showed that lowering two of them harmed eye structure and vision. Mouse studies confirmed that one gene, CNN2, supports the light-sensing cells and contrast vision. The gene is active mainly in vessel cells of the eye. Cross-species checks of this kind turn vague risk spots into named targets.
pmc-13553211:
Mingli Li and co-authors used computer modeling in 2026 to study materials that mix metal and organic parts for lithium batteries. The key trait is how the metal and the linked chains share electrons. That sharing affects how well lithium sticks and how the electrode works.

A nickel-based chain served as the test case. Bridges made of sulfur linked metal and chains most strongly, ahead of oxygen and nitrogen bridges. Adding groups that pull electrons away made the sharing stronger, while groups that push electrons weakened it. The authors offer a design rule that pairs bridge choice with chain tuning. Such rules could guide the search for better electrode materials.
pmc-13553611:
Jie Guo, Jing Wu, Tomas Olsson, Lars Alfredsson, and Anna Karin Hedström study how genes shape the harm of obesity in multiple sclerosis. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. Obesity at diagnosis is tied to worse paths in this nerve disease. Whether that harm shifts with a person's gene type was not known.

They use two large Swedish studies and a national disease registry. In patients who lack one gene form, obesity tracks with a higher risk of worse disability and with reaching set disability marks sooner. In those who carry the gene form, no such link shows. The worst paths sit in the obese group that lacks the gene. Immune paths tied to that gene may soften the fat effect.
pmc-13553711:
Daniel Ostler-Mildner and colleagues built a sound-based screening tool for a throat pouch disorder that often goes undiagnosed for years, publishing the work in 2026. Zenker's diverticulum causes swallowing trouble, yet confirming it usually needs a specialist centre and video X-ray, which smaller clinics may lack. The team recorded neck sounds during swallowing with a portable device, gathering data from 23 patients and 27 healthy volunteers.

Their two-stage deep learning model first spots swallows in the recordings, then sorts each swallow as healthy or pathological. Patient-level accuracy reached about 89 percent, with a similarly strong balance of precision and recall. The authors present the approach as a first noninvasive screen that could speed referral, cut diagnostic delays, and lower costs in swallowing care.
pmc-13553811:
Martinez-Oller and co-authors published a study in 2026 on stress in soccer referees. Referees face loud pressure and must decide fast. The team asked how perfectionism and fear of anxiety feelings link in this group, and whether coping with distress sits between them.

The survey covered 268 referees in Spain across levels and years of experience. Referees high in perfectionism, above all the kind imposed by others' hopes, also feared anxiety more. That fear added to their emotional load on the job. Referees who tolerated distress better handled feelings under pressure and rated their own work higher. Distress tolerance carried part of the link between perfectionism and anxiety fear. The authors urge mental training programs for referees.
pmc-13554111:
Fathi Hassan and four co-authors tune an ultraviolet system for farm water in a 2026 study. Two bacterial diseases threaten potato crops in the Nile Delta and hurt exports. Irrigation water drawn from canals can carry both germs from field to field.

Tests first checked the water's clarity and particle load, which sat outside the best range for UV treatment. A simple sediment filter lifted light transmission and cut turbidity and solids. Beam tests then mapped the dose needed to inactivate each germ. The full reactor was validated and adjusted to kill germs while saving energy and cost. Clean irrigation water could slow disease spread across the delta's potato belt.
pmc-13554211:
Mostafa Gamal and Mustafa Abdel-Wanes build a neural network that spots epileptic seizures in brain wave recordings, in work from 2026. Automatic detection is hard because EEG signals are noisy, shifting, and vary widely between hospitals.

Their model, BrainXNet, mixes three parts. Multi-scale filters catch both brief spikes and long patterns. A frequency attention module stresses the wave bands that matter clinically. A transformer then reads long stretches of the signal in context. On two large benchmark datasets the system reached about 99 and 98 percent accuracy. It kept over 94 percent accuracy when moved between datasets, and stayed strong under noise.
pmc-13554711:
Yu and co-authors report, in a research letter, a large check of whole exome sequencing for spotting copy number changes before birth. Clinics now often run a microarray test and sequencing one after another, which costs time in pregnancy care. The team ran both methods in parallel for 3,429 families and built a quality control framework to judge when sequencing-based calls can be trusted.

Sequencing matched the microarray results about 97 percent of the time for clearly harmful changes, and also agreed well on mosaic cases and stretches of identical DNA. Their two quality measures separated good calls from bad with high sensitivity in an independent check of 500 samples. The authors argue that sequencing alone, guarded by these quality rules, can serve as a first-line prenatal test and spare families the slower two-step route.
pmc-13554811:

pmc-13567811:
Tong Tang and co-authors build a fast stand-in model for shiplift safety in a 2026 study. A shiplift raises ships in a water-filled chamber. In a quake the coupled chamber, water, and ship can tip, and the tip force is hard to guess. Full 3D flow models cost too much time, while flat 2D models skip the ship and read low.

The team ran 3D flow models at 19 scales and checked them against past results, with gaps under five percent. In a test quake the 3D tip force ran far above the 2D read, for both light and full loads. They then trained a hybrid neural model on the 3D data to guess the next step of the force. The hybrid beat seven rival models in tests. It gives engineers a fast, sound way to size shiplift safety.
pmc-13568011:
AlSaqabi tests traffic anomaly tools on vehicle counts in Kuwait City. Most anomaly work in car networks targets cyber attacks. Physical traffic surges at city junctions get far less study. The team used five days of hourly counts at four junctions.

True incident labels were not on hand for the counts. The team thus injected fake anomalies with a set protocol. Scores show how well tools catch those injected shifts. One classic tool gave the best balance across ten runs. A forest tool caught the most true anomalies overall. A deep model lagged, save on slow drift cases.
pmc-13568411:
Jun Zhang and co-authors review progress in farm cyber-physical systems, with a focus on teams of robots that sense their setting and coordinate harvest and transport work, in a 2026 paper. A shrinking farm workforce and the global Zero Hunger goal push farms toward automation. Moving crops from field to storage across rough, unstructured ground is a core task for such systems.

The review traces a leap in mapping, from flat geometric maps to rich three-dimensional semantic models. These fuse laser scans, drone images, and spatial data, and can feed digital twin systems that predict what comes next. It then turns to planning methods. The field is shifting from central operations research to decentralized, data-driven multi-agent approaches.
pmc-13568511:
Gemechu Ameya and four co-authors test root extracts of a traditional Ethiopian plant against microbes in a study from 2026. With drug resistance rising, plant remedies are a source of new leads. The plant, Rumex abyssinicus, is used in local medicine. Roots were extracted in six solvents and tested against lab strains, clinical isolates, and fungi in dish assays.

All extracts fought microbes, with strength varying by solvent. Growth-free zones reached twenty-five millimeters for bacteria, and the weakest dose that stopped growth varied widely. Chemical profiling found a known family of pigments, led by emodin at about thirty percent of the mix. The authors link those compounds to the defense effect.
pmc-13569211:
Isaac Carrasco and colleagues test, in a 2026 open-label multicentre study, probiotic ear drops containing lactobacilli for dogs with red, waxy, non-infected ear inflammation, a common problem often tied to allergy. Thirty-seven privately owned dogs received drops every forty-eight hours for twenty-eight days, with ear, itch, lesion, and quality-of-life checks at start, two weeks, and four weeks.

Lesion and itch scores fell clearly by the final visit, and owners reported better quality of life in eighty percent of dogs. Improvement appeared regardless of other medicines or the microbes first found. With no comparison group, the drops look like a helpful add-on rather than proven stand-alone treatment, a distinction the authors keep in view.
pmc-13569411:
Daniele Avenoso leads a 2026 phase II multicenter trial of a gentler high-dose conditioning regimen, treosulfan plus fludarabine, before donor stem cell transplant. Patients were adults aged forty to sixty-five with acute myeloid leukemia in first remission. Eighty-two patients were followed for a median of about twenty months to judge leukemia-free survival and safety against standard harsher regimens.

About eighty-two percent remained leukemia-free at one year, and relapse by one year was under fifteen percent. Donors were mostly matched unrelated volunteers. Safety was described as excellent in the results available. The regimen offers transplant centers a less toxic preparation that still protects against leukemia returning.
pmc-13569511:
Sayaka Matsumura and co-authors probe in 2026 how immune cells along brain vessels help break the blood-brain barrier when blood flow falls. These perivascular macrophages sit beside the barrier, which normally shields the brain. In mice with narrowed neck arteries, flow dropped and the barrier leaked. The team then depleted the macrophage group with a drug and watched the leak shrink.

Without those cells, two vessel-cutting enzymes stayed lower, support cells stayed calmer, and pericyte markers held up better. The authors read the cells as early drivers of barrier failure under low flow. The mechanism may feed later small-vessel disease. The work points to vessel inflammation as a treatment angle.
pmc-13569611:
Woo-Jung Song and colleagues test, in a 2026 study of the U-BIOPRED asthma cohort, whether cellular senescence is enriched in the airways of people with severe asthma. Senescence is the aging-like shutdown of cells that also releases inflammatory signals. Gene activity scores for two senescence pathways were compared across airway samples and checked in a second cohort.

Scores ran higher in bronchial biopsies from severe asthma than from milder disease or healthy volunteers, and one pathway was confirmed in the validation cohort. Higher scores tracked with frequent flare-ups, steroid use, nasal polyps, and worse lung function. A subgroup of signals tied to lung injury and repair stood out, suggesting aging biology helps drive the hardest asthma.
pmc-13569811:
Wang and co-authors pull new parts from a herb root used in China care, tian ma. Thirteen new small parts came from a wet pull of the root. Parts split in four-benzyl, five-benzyl, and six-benzyl kinds. Six of the first kind and five of the next lead the set. A known five-benzyl part joins the new set in the pull. Boiled wet pulls of a base part gave more new parts.

That boil set held 14 more new parts and one known kin. Stream-mass checks on shop and fresh roots test their source. Parts from the wet pull can be made by old care ways. Those ways are the cook and boil steps of past use. Test runs show the parts beat the root's main parts in force. That gap helps tell why the root is cooked in past care.
pmc-13569911:
Henriques-Calado and colleagues report a 2026 study that followed 333 psychiatric patients in Portugal who experienced homelessness, over twenty years.  The team split patients into four groups by how long homelessness lasted, from under one year to over fifteen years, and compared diagnoses, hospital use, and survival.

About three in ten patients died during follow-up. The early-stage and prolonged groups fared worst, with deaths near half, tied to alcohol disorders and organic psychosis. The persistent group, homeless longest, had the longest psychiatric follow-up and lower late mortality, a survivor effect the authors note after eighteen years. Patients with alcohol misuse, anxiety, or personality disorders, and younger patients, had the fewest hospital stays. Risk by stage could help services target the middle years, where death risk peaks.
pmc-13570411:
Daniel Mugabi and co-authors study whether syphilis in mothers is linked to stillbirth at two hospitals in Uganda. Their study appeared in 2026. They compared 406 women who gave birth at referral hospitals in Jinja and Hoima between January and April 2026. Blood tests showed which mothers carried the infection. The team compared infection rates between stillbirth and live-birth deliveries.

Infection was far more common when the baby was stillborn: about 12 percent, against about 4 percent for live births. The team also checked whether higher levels of a blood marker for the infection tracked with higher risk. Syphilis can be cured with cheap drugs, yet it still causes many stillbirths in poor countries. The authors argue for stronger testing and treatment of mothers during pregnancy visits.
pmc-13570611:
Xian Wu and three co-authors review corneal biomechanics in glaucoma, in work published in 2026. Measures of corneal stiffness affect how eye pressure readings are read, and they may capture wall weakness that thickness alone misses. Their structured search covered major databases from the start through mid-2026, plus reference lists of key papers.

Two main devices give measures that cannot be swapped directly. Lower corneal hysteresis is linked in a steady way to glaucoma and faster decline. Results for the second device vary more by subtype and by factors such as pressure and treatment. The authors class these measures as helpful extra markers, not stand-alone tests, and they call for standard methods.
pmc-13570911:
Rafael Dascanio and co-authors test in 2026 how blasting treatments change 3D printed dental resin and its grip on repairs. Printed resins need surface roughening before parts bond well, and two blasting media compete: plain alumina grit and a silica coating blast that leaves a chemically friendly film. Application time and heat aging could each tilt the result.

Samples were blasted for three set times at fixed pressure, then measured for roughness, bending strength, stiffness, and bond strength, with half aged through thousands of heat cycles. Alumina roughened more the longer it ran, while the silica coat stayed steady. All blasted groups lost bending strength versus untouched resin. Bond strength rose under both treatments. The silica route gave higher and steadier bonding across times, while alumina's bond varied with blast time. Aging barely moved the needle, a comfort for work that must last in the mouth.
pmc-13571111:
Frank Lobbezoo, Ginger Bousché, and Merel Verhoeff argue in a 2026 letter that jaw pain care has outgrown its narrow roots. The field once blamed bite faults for the classic trio of jaw pain, joint sounds, and stiff movement. Decades of proof now show a many sided picture joining body, mind, and lifestyle. Smoking, drink, caffeine, and sport all play roles, the authors write.

Jaw disorders link outward to headache, teeth grinding, sleep troubles, and wider health. Care therefore needs dentists and doctors working as one team. Training, research, and clinics should all merge the two worlds, the letter urges, under the field's new name of orofacial pain and dysfunction.
pmc-13571311:
Flashing light can steer a key cell signal inside lab-grown mini-brains, if the lab can afford the light rig. Issei Shimada and Yoichi Kato share a cheap build in this 2026 protocol. The signal is cAMP, a messenger that helps decide cell fates. A light-switched enzyme makes it on command.

Commercial optogenetic rigs cost too much for many labs, so the protocol uses a hobby microcontroller board driving simple LEDs. Steps cover assembling the rig and writing its control code. Stem cells are then prepared to carry the light-switched enzyme. Finally the method runs the light program on human forebrain organoids. Open, buildable tools widen who can do such experiments.
pmc-13571411: Luxi Zheng and co-authors reply in this 2026 letter to critics of their osteoarthritis study linking cysteine metabolism to a form of cell death called ferroptosis. The critics noted the human validation cohort was just three elderly postmenopausal women, so sex and estrogen effects went untested. The authors concede the limit plainly. They then re-analyze public data sets to check whether the cysteine-ferroptosis link holds across sexes. The exchange models post-publication review working as intended: a narrow cohort flagged, extra analyses offered in answer.
pmc-13571611:
Piedrahita and four co-authors interviewed eye patients in Colombia in twenty twenty-six about life with a sight-stealing disease and its demanding treatment. The disease, wet age-related macular degeneration, damages central vision, and the standard care is a drug injected into the eye again and again.

Fourteen patients at a center in Medellín described their experience by phone. At first the injections frightened them, and fear of blindness hung over daily life. Over time, many came to link the treatment with hope, steadier sight, and kept independence. Family help, religious faith, and trust in their eye doctor carried them through. Reading, moving about, and social time all felt easier for some. Yet transport problems, reliance on others, and worry about getting the drug persisted. The authors urge care that treats feelings and logistics, not just the eye.
pmc-13571711:
Briones Alvarado and co-authors reported a 2026 case report of a sixty-two-year-old man whose both diaphragms weakened suddenly from Parsonage-Turner syndrome, an inflammatory nerve disorder also called neuralgic amyotrophy. He had recently had a knee replacement and arrived with sudden breathlessness and left shoulder pain. A small lung clot was found, but it could not explain his full picture.

Breathing tests showed lung capacity falling by twenty-seven percent when he lay flat, a classic diaphragm weakness sign. Ultrasound confirmed both diaphragms moved far less than normal, worse on the left side, while their thickness stayed preserved. Briones Alvarado notes the pain then weakness sequence fits the syndrome's pattern of nerve attack after surgery. Breathing muscle pressures were markedly reduced at testing, and diaphragm movement improved only slightly at one month.
pmc-13571811:
Yakun Cao and four colleagues test whether simple force balance explains how ants deploy their sticky foot pads while climbing, in a 2026 study. Argentine ants scale smooth glass using adhesive pads, and they tune each pad's contact as they move.

A light-based sensor filmed pad contact on vertical glass while a static model predicted the grip each leg should need. The real pads broke the prediction: contact differed between upward and downward climbing and shifted within single steps. The authors conclude that standing force needs alone cannot explain pad use. Body motion, anatomy, and behavior must enter the account, they argue, opening questions about how insects manage adhesion moment by moment.
pmc-13571911:
Chanakarn Sinsareekul and co-authors test five dental cements on human pulp cells in a 2026 study. These water set cements cap the soft core of a tooth, and fresh mixes may act unlike set ones. Proof on how pulp cells respond to fresh material was thin, the team note.

Cells came from human third molars and met extracts of each cement at three ages. Fresh extracts at 15 minutes killed cells for all five cements when used at full strength. Extracts aged seven days were safe for four of the five, with one still toxic. Cells fed aged extracts from the lead cement laid down more mineral. Gene checks tracked shifts in signals tied to swelling and immune tone across the cements.
pmc-13572011:
Jinsong Wang and co-authors pair special water with sound waves to upgrade a krill protein mix, in work published in 2026. Sound treatment reshapes proteins, but it also spawns harmful oxygen species that harm both protein and plant partners. The team used mildly basic electrolysed water to blunt that harm while krill protein bound to gallic acid.

The water cut the harmful species by a third and curbed protein damage. Binding peaked at twenty minutes of treatment, with finer particles and better mixing traits. Emulsions made from the best mix stayed stable and resisted spoilage over eleven days. The authors pitch the method for foods that spoil fast.
pmc-13572311:
Lin and co-authors analysed a 2026 brain imaging study of how young people with mental health symptoms process emotional faces they are told to ignore. Adolescence is a high risk period for psychiatric disorders across many diagnoses at once. Data came from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study of eleven to twelve year olds.

Nearly five thousand youths performed a demanding memory task in the scanner while emotional faces appeared as irrelevant decoration. Lin measured how distinctly the visual network represented each emotion category in the brain activity patterns. Greater distinctiveness under high memory load linked to worse task performance and more psychopathology symptoms in the group. The effect appeared already in primary visual cortex, the earliest visual area, and predicted symptoms a year later.
pmc-13573411:
Md. Ramjan Sheikh, with seven colleagues, ran a 2026 study of how bread wheat copes with lead in its environment. Lead pollution chokes plant growth by sparking oxidative stress and jamming cell work. Wheat types differ in how much lead they can bear, yet a joint read of body, chemistry, and gene responses was missing.

Plants faced lead acetate doses from zero up to the top test level in a graded series. The team measured growth and body signs, defence chemistry, and gene activity side by side. That three-way read shows which wheat lines hold up and which pathways switch on as dose climbs. Strong lines can point breeders to traits worth keeping, such as better damage control or lead shut-out at the root. The authors frame the data as a base for picking parents for tougher wheat.
pmc-13573611:
Gostyński presents a 2026 computational study linking electron relaxation inside tiny clusters to their X-ray photoelectron fingerprints. Blasting a core electron out of an atom leaves a binding energy that encodes chemistry, yet small clusters blur the code. Two families were modeled: gold clusters of four, ten, and twenty atoms, and titanium dioxide clusters of two to four units.

An all-electron method priced each site's binding energy directly. Deeper still, the study tracked how every orbital's energy slid when a core hole opened. Summing those slides gave one compact score per site. The author argues such orbital-level patterns can enrich future spectroscopy reading, since the shifts spring from quantum behavior unique to finite systems.
pmc-13573711:
Mohammed Jeraiby and ten co-authors run a pilot study on fast heart attack checks in a 2026 paper. Patients who reach the emergency room soon after symptoms start are the hardest to clear safely. The team tested a blood marker of heart damage, high-sensitivity troponin I, and asked how its change over one hour performs in early arrivals with no past heart disease.

Records from 457 patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome were reviewed. A single low first reading could not rule out a heart attack with enough safety, and standard cutoffs did poorly. The one-hour change in the marker proved the best signal, and even a small rise could rule in an attack. The authors call for larger studies before clinic use.
pmc-13574211:
Gary Longo and co-authors report the first known hybrids between Japanese and Pacific sardines in the Northeast Pacific, in a 2026 study. The two species look alike but normally live on opposite sides of the ocean. Japanese sardines began appearing along the North American west coast in 2022, raising questions about mixing with the local stock.

To track the fish, the team built a DNA test panel of 88 marker sites that cleanly separate the species and expose hybrids. They ran the panel on 1,821 sardines gathered from 2023 to 2025. Thirty-five fish proved to be hybrids, nearly all of them first-generation crosses. Two fish caught in 2025 looked like backcrosses into the Pacific species. The authors offer the panel as a monitoring tool and flag the open question of how fit the hybrids are.
pmc-13574411:
Songlang Liu and co-authors study a blood protein ratio and bone strength in United States adults in a 2026 paper. The ratio mixes signs of nutrition and body swelling, yet its link to bone density was not well mapped. The team used health survey data from more than ten thousand adults collected over many years. They checked bone density at the hip neck and lower spine, with care for sex, race, and illness.

Higher ratio values linked to lower bone density at both sites after full adjustment. The link was not a straight line, with turning points that differed by site. Women showed a far stronger inverse link than men. Readers learn why a simple blood ratio may flag bone risk, and why the pattern bends.
pmc-13574611:
A rare gene fault stops the body from breaking down active vitamin D, so calcium builds up in the blood and damages the kidneys. Nikolina Vucenovic Basic and co-authors reported three adult patients in 2026 with this disorder, infantile hypercalcemia type 1, caused by variants in the CYP24A1 gene. Two women came to care as adults with repeated kidney stones and calcium deposits in the kidneys; a man diagnosed in infancy began treatment as an adult.

All three were treated successfully with fluconazole, a drug that slows vitamin D activation. The cases also involved a kidney acid problem and varied loss of kidney function. The authors urge genetic testing for adults with unexplained high calcium and stones.
pmc-13574711:
Won Dong Shin, with five colleagues, presents a 2026 winged drone that flies and crawls on a single motor. Drones that both fly and move on land can reach more places, yet most carry many motors that add weight and complexity. Ground movement in such designs also tends to stay weak.

One actuator drives this drone, through a new transmission that can flip its spin direction. That flip switches the craft between modes: rolling on the ground, jumping up, and taking flight. The same single drive thus covers land travel, air travel, and the passage between them. Cutting motors trims mass, which stretches working range. The authors frame the design as a lean path to multimodal robots for mixed terrain. Tests back each mode in turn.
pmc-13574811:
Ruth Anne Laura Willems and co-authors track how thrombin behaves in patients with liver cirrhosis. Their 2026 study uses a computational add-on to the standard clotting test. Cirrhosis shifts both pro- and anti-clotting factors, leaving patients at risk of bleeding and clots at once, while the plain test often looks unchanged.

Ninety-five patients across three severity grades joined twenty healthy controls. Standard measures ran hotter in patients: peak thrombin was higher and arrived sooner. The deeper analysis splits the process into prothrombin conversion and thrombin shutoff, which the plain test blends together. Low conversion flagged the patients most likely to bleed. The authors argue this split view gives a sharper forecast of clinical events than the total curve alone.
pmc-13574911:
Krzysztof Cienkowski and co-authors review adult care after repair of a heart defect present at birth in a 2026 paper. Tetralogy of Fallot is fixed in childhood, and survivors now reach adulthood in growing numbers. Leaky lung valves and stiff outflow paths strain the right heart over time.

Scans guide watch and care, with magnetic scans best for sizing the right heart and scarring. Valve replacement, often through a catheter now, anchors treatment when strain mounts. Rhythm risks call for layered checks and, at times, devices or ablation. The aorta can widen but rarely tears. Drug proof for right heart help stays thin.
pmc-13575011:
Sridevi Rajeeve leads a 2026 real-world study of a cell therapy for multiple myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells in the bone marrow. The therapy, cilta-cel, uses a patient's own altered immune cells. It was first cleared for late-stage use and later moved into earlier lines of care.

Records covered 120 adults treated after one to three prior lines of therapy. Most received bridging treatment while the cells were prepared. Among those checked for response, 98 percent responded, and nearly all patients tested reached deep clearance of disease markers. At last follow-up, 94.2 percent stayed free of progression. Results held across bridging regimens, though follow-up was short at a median of 5.8 months.
pmc-13575111:
Jie Li leads a 2026 study of an implantable device that aims electric fields at glioblastoma, an aggressive brain tumour. Electric field therapy can disturb tumour cell division, yet the skull weakens fields applied from outside the head. The team built a thin-film device that sits like an artificial membrane over the brain.

Ultrasound from outside switches the film on, turning sound into local electric fields inside the skull. Lab tests showed about 68 percent slowing of growth in glioblastoma cell lines. In mice with brain tumours, tumour burden fell by about 72 percent. Field loss stayed below 20 percent at working frequencies, far better than external electrode systems. Healthy nerve tissue was spared in the tests reported.
pmc-13575211:
Saba Babakan, Hoda Jafarizadeh-Malmiri, and Nader Rahemi optimise a fast way to make pectin nanoparticles in a 2026 study. Pectin, a natural gelling agent from fruit, can be formed into tiny particles for food, drug, and cosmetic products. Their method sets the particles with magnesium ions and speeds heating with microwaves.

A statistical tuning method found the best recipe: a magnesium-to-pectin volume ratio of 0.1 and 155 seconds of heating. The result was particles about 390 nanometres wide with an even size spread and a stable surface charge. Freeze-dried powder particles came out rod-shaped, smooth, and without crystal structure. Thinner solutions flowed more easily, with lower thickness and density. The authors present the powder as a bridge between natural polymers and nanotechnology products.
pmc-13575311:
Jingwen Zhang and Satoshi Hattori adapt in 2026 a favorite clinical trial design to diseases where the same event strikes a patient again and again. Ordinary event driven trials run until a set number of events accrues, locking in statistical power whatever the event rate turns out to be. Recurrent events break the trick when a patient's repeats are correlated, which they usually are, and designers rarely know that correlation in advance.

Their fix watches the trial while it runs. A robust variance estimate under a standard marginal model is monitored in blinded form, and the event target adjusts to keep power on goal. Mistakes in guessing the correlation then cannot quietly underpower the study. Simulations showed the blind monitoring held its error rates and power as promised. Chronic disease trials, from heart failure flare ups to asthma attacks, are the natural home for the design.
pmc-13575411:
Kah Hup Chew and three colleagues compare how well three filling materials seal the sides of cavities against bacterial leakage in a 2026 lab study. Leakage at the edge of a filling lets bacteria in and drives new decay. The materials were an alkasite, a standard resin composite, and a glass hybrid.

Standard side cavities were cut into 66 extracted human molars and filled by group. A two-chamber setup exposed the fillings to Streptococcus mutans, a decay-causing bacterium, for 40 days. Every material leaked eventually. The alkasite leaked more slowly than the composite, with a clear statistical gap between those two, and microscope images showed the state of each filling's edge. The authors note the limits of a lab setup when judging real-world durability.
pmc-13575611:
Vein surgery high on the leg can run on nerve blocks alone, if the numbing dose is tuned right. Hui Wang and co-authors find that dose for a triple block in a 2026 study. Thirty-six patients had three leg nerves blocked under ultrasound.

Doses stepped up or down by each patient's response at skin cut. Half-success strength landed at 0.149 percent ropivacaine. The 95 percent success mark was 0.210 percent. Blood pressure and pulse dipped mildly after blocks, within safe bounds. Pain at cut ran far lower in the success group. No toxic events appeared in the group.
pmc-13575911:
Hao Chen and colleagues analyzed national health survey data in 2026 to test simple blood scores as signs of fatty liver disease. The disease is tied to long-term low-grade inflammation, and several scores built from routine blood cell counts might flag it cheaply. Using survey records for several thousand adults, the team compared six such scores against fatty liver and liver scarring. They used standard statistics plus a machine learning method to rank how well each score separated sick from healthy people.

Two scores rose with higher odds of fatty liver, while one moved in the opposite direction. Overall, one combined score discriminated fatty liver best, while a platelet-based ratio performed best for scarring. Machine learning backed the same ranking. The authors suggest these cheap blood scores could help screen for liver disease, though they capture only part of the picture.
pmc-13576311:
Fernando J Mota de Almeida leads a 2026 Swedish registry study of a tooth-wasting condition called external cervical resorption, where tissue activity eats away the neck of a tooth. Outcome data mostly came from specialist clinics, leaving everyday practice unmapped. The national dental registry offered a population-wide view.

The study found 14,881 affected teeth recorded between 2009 and 2018. Extraction was the first treatment for 42.8 percent, while the rest were treated conservatively, with or without surgery. Conservatively treated teeth survived at 82.7 percent after five years, 74.9 percent after ten, and 67.8 percent after fifteen. Older age, fewer remaining teeth, molar teeth, and surgery each raised later extraction risk. Root canal treatment near the start made no clear difference to survival.
pmc-13576711:
Kent Wallner and eleven co-authors test a radiation treatment for heart stents that keep narrowing again, in a research paper from 2026. A stent holds a heart artery open, but scar tissue can close it again. Some patients face this problem again and again in the same vessel.

The treatment places a tiny radiation source inside the vessel for a short time. The team compared how long each vessel stayed open before and after treatment, in nineteen patients. The open period grew from a typical three months to about a year. The authors say radiation inside the vessel is a useful option for these stubborn cases.
pmc-13577211:
Calderwood and co-authors wrote a letter in 2026 urging that care for other long-term ills be woven into TB care. More than ten million people fell ill with TB in 2024, and TB rarely comes alone. Sugar disease, lung disease, mind ills, HIV, poor diet, and drink or drug habits raise TB risk and tangle its cure.

They cite a four-land African study that showed screening for these ills inside TB programs can be done. That study claimed big gains in symptoms and return to work, but the letter team notes such gains are expected from TB cure alone. The checks rested on before-and-after counts with no fair match group. Still, they back routine screening, with success judged by control of each ill, not just by finding it.
pmc-13577811:
Pigeon farming matters in Bangladesh, but Newcastle disease keeps flocks unproductive.
