Sixteen pairs of young pigeons were split into four groups: plain feed without vaccine, and three supplemented, vaccinated groups.

Weight, feed intake, and egg weight barely moved across groups. Egg production and feed efficiency did differ, with the vitamins A, D, E plus selenium group laying most. Antibody levels after vaccination were also highest in that group. Some immune organ measures grew with supplementation. The authors conclude the A, D, E and selenium mix supports both laying and vaccine response. They suggest targeted feeding as a cheap aid for small pigeon farms.
pmc-13578211:
Susanne von Kroge and co-authors study income gaps in lymphoma survival in Germany in a 2026 paper. Follicular lymphoma patients live under a universal health system, yet social status may still shape outcomes. Registry data for over thirty-six thousand patients are linked to a district level deprivation index based on schooling, jobs, and income.

At five years, about eighty percent of women and seventy-seven percent of men are alive. Patients in high status districts face notably lower excess death risk than those in low status districts. Much of that gap fades once town size, access to certified centers, and health traits are counted, the authors find.
pmc-13578311:
Blue whales and fin whales sing alike, and a 2026 study by Svenja Wöhle and co-authors hunts for a reliable way to tell their calls apart. Both species make sweeping calls that slide down in pitch, with overlapping ranges and lengths, which muddies long-term listening surveys.

Recordings from tags on known whales showed most traits overlap heavily. One measure, the span holding ninety percent of a call's energy, split the species partway: most fin calls ran under 0.6 seconds, while blue calls ran over 0.7. For clean calls from moored recorders, that rule gives a cautious classifier. A stronger route pairs deep learning features with a mapping method, set against the tagged calls as a reference.
pmc-13578511:
Floor R Pijl and colleagues costed the first thirty days of hospital care after brain tumor surgery at a single regional referral center in 2023. Using detailed bottom-up costing, they tracked 322 adult patients with a mean age of 61 years. The median hospital stay was three days, and mean in-hospital costs reached 6,988 euros per patient.

Surgery type, pre-operative functional status, total stay, intensive-care stay, and complication grade each drove costs independently. Repeat surgery, readmission, and death within thirty days pushed costs higher still. The authors suggest targeted steps such as selective intensive-care admission, faster recovery pathways, and complication prevention could make brain tumor care more efficient.
pmc-13578611:
How nursing trainees see nurses may shape how hard they bounce back in study, and Chunxia Wang, Jinxiu Chen, and Yun Jiang tested a middle link in work from twenty twenty-six. Trainees at one Chinese hospital filled surveys on attitudes, professional identity, and study grit. Links were checked with rank tools and a mediation model.

Warm attitudes tracked with stronger identity and grit alike. Identity carried about three-fifths of the attitude-to-grit link. Schools, the authors argue, should build identity on purpose during placements: it is the channel through which good examples turn into staying power. The study is one-site, so wider checks are owed.
pmc-13578711:
Jörg Schultz, Liza Rothkoff, Edgar Aviles-Rosa, Nathaniel Hall, and Michele Maughan show that a detection dog's missed alerts can be forecast from its state seconds before, in work from 2026. Such dogs guard against explosives and aid medical screening, yet even trained dogs sometimes miss a target scent. A miss can carry grave costs.

On a treadmill rig with precisely timed scent release, the team read movement and body signals before each trial. A model trained on pre-scent movement alone beat chance at calling misses. Adding heart and temperature data lifted the catch rate further. Stacking calls across trials gave a running risk gauge for the session. The authors propose live readiness watch for working dogs.
pmc-13578911:
Muhammad Taaha Siddiqui and four co-authors present a 2026 case report of a rare immune disorder in a child that was recognized late. The condition drives the immune system into a runaway inflammatory state and kills without prompt treatment. Its early signs, fever and low blood counts, mimic common infections.

The patient, a nine year old girl in Pakistan, had two weeks of high fever, cough, and weakness that antibiotics could not break. Tests showed an enlarged liver and spleen, all blood lines low, and striking lab markers, including very high ferritin. She met five of the diagnostic criteria once the team suspected the disorder. The report walks through the clues and the delay.
pmc-13579211:
Sasha J Kramer examines how the link between ocean phytoplankton diversity and carbon biomass shifts with method and scale, in a paper published in 2026. Diverse systems are often thought to be more productive and stable. That link has been studied a lot on land, but far less from direct measures in the ocean.

Kramer uses a global in-water data set and compares three ways to gauge diversity. One uses pigments modeled from light data, one measures pigments in the lab, and one reads gene sequences. Each method trades detail about species for detail about place and time. The paper shows how much the shape of the diversity and biomass link depends on the method chosen.
pmc-13579411:
Jiahao Liu and seven co-authors trace how cobra venom injures the kidneys, in a 2026 study. Bites from the Chinese cobra, Naja atra, often cause acute kidney injury, and a venom enzyme called SVPLA2 is the main suspect. A drug that blocks that enzyme looks promising, but the injury pathway was unclear. The team combined protein-wide scans with cell biology to follow the chain of damage.

Two proteins, HRAS and CCND1, emerged as key mediators. The enzyme breaks up lipid rafts in cell membranes, which keeps HRAS from anchoring where it works, cutting its activity. That defect shuts down a major survival pathway in kidney cells. Knowing the chain gives drug makers more points where the damage might be stopped.
pmc-13579511:
Zaki Rafsanjani and co-authors develop a breakfast cereal shaped by what tasters actually liked, in a 2026 paper. Their extruded cereal swaps some corn grits for rice bran and unripe banana flour, and adds a spice blend of ginger, cinnamon, and lemongrass at four levels. Tasters judged the versions dry, with cold milk, and with warm milk using several sensory methods.

The one-percent spice version won the highest overall liking across serving styles. More spice raised the healthy compound counts and strength against oxidation sharply, but taste set the limit. A combined decision analysis, weighing taste against nine lab measures, confirmed the one-percent blend as best. Its glycemic index came out low, at about 47.
pmc-13579611:
Taylor House and Carrie Thiessen argue in 2026 that a new kidney for a child should be seen as comfort care, not a cure. A transplant eases symptoms and adds years, but it does not fix kidney disease for good. That fit with comfort care, called palliation, has faded from daily practice.

Four parts of care show the drift: words used, pressure to take drugs, how success is judged, and the move to adult care. Each can split what families want from what teams push for. The authors urge teams to rebuild care on meaning, choice, close ties, and hope. Such a shift, they hold, would serve children and families far better.
pmc-13580011:
Zhiding Zhou and six colleagues organize what is known about antibodies accidentally helping coronaviruses infect, in a review from two thousand twenty-six. Antibody-dependent enhancement haunts vaccine design: yesterday's antibodies make today's infection worse, not better. Animal coronaviruses cause heavy livestock losses, yet research on enhancement in them is thin.

The team sorts enhancement mechanisms into two major categories, with five mechanistic subsets inside them. Human coronavirus evidence fills each subset as the case study, and SARS-CoV-2 is the chief source of that evidence. The frame then moves that knowledge to veterinary contexts. To grasp enhancement routes in advance could keep animal vaccines safe and stop them from backfiring in the field. The review maps this field for those who study it.
pmc-13580111:
Georgia McGaughey asks whether artificial intelligence can truly discover drugs in the real world, in a paper from twenty twenty-six. Drug hunting often turns on tiny structural changes with outsized effects. Models trained on masses of data can stumble exactly there, and many projects suffer from sparse data and shaky biology.

Two case studies show a different path. There, close teamwork between computing and medicinal chemistry, guided by deep grasp of molecular shape and protein fit, produced outsized gains in strength and selectivity. McGaughey argues AI must move past pattern matching toward the reasons linking structure to effect. Until then, she maps where AI best serves as a partner to human experts rather than a stand-alone tool.
pmc-13580511:
Yiming Liu and fourteen co-authors build a tiny brain-targeting platform that joins radiation therapy with immune therapy for glioma, in a 2026 study. Glioma is a hard brain tumor, shielded by the blood-brain barrier and a suppressive immune setting. Boron neutron capture therapy kills tumor cells from inside with boron plus neutron beams, but boron reaches gliomas poorly. The platform packs boron into a porous carrier, adds an immune trigger and a glow tracer, and coats it with a guide tag.

In mice with brain tumors, the platform crossed the barrier and piled up in the tumor far better than the standard boron drug. The tracer let the team watch its spread in real time. The immune trigger woke a defense path inside the tumor. The authors present the design as a base for personal combo therapy.
pmc-13581411:
Chengxing Wu and co-authors study fungi that live inside roots where fairy rings spread through alpine meadows on the Tibetan Plateau, in a 2026 paper. The rings act as strong ecosystem engineers, reshaping soil as they grow. Three ring types, harming, boosting, and neutral, were compared in a local sedge.

Inside the active ring zones, helpful fungal groups ran thinner than outside. The authors coin a term for the pattern: symbiotic decoupling. In the boosting ring, rich soil food paired with a simpler fungal web. In the harming ring, the web ran denser, which the team reads as stress-driven teamwork. They stress that the frame is a hypothesis in need of live tests.
pmc-13581711:
Ao Wang and co-authors review a rare liver scarring disease present from birth and its kin disorders across the life course. Their review from 2026 deals with congenital hepatic fibrosis, a fault in how the liver ducts form. It is a main cause of high pressure in the liver veins of children and teens.

The disease can sit silent or bring severe pressure problems, which makes diagnosis and care hard. Care now centers on watching for and treating those pressure problems, with no drug that acts on the root fault. The review covers body paths, genes, signs, tests, and care for problems that arise. It also weighs disease burden and unmet needs in the age of gene based diagnosis.
pmc-13581811:
Yibo Shen, Taeyang Yang, and Gyuil Lee trace how heavy smartphone use drains college students' physical activity through a two-step psychological chain, in a 2026 paper. Over a thousand students across four Chinese provinces answered validated questionnaires. Problematic phone use predicted less activity directly, but the mechanism was the puzzle.

Self-control alone did not carry the effect; exercise procrastination did. The chain ran in sequence: heavier phone use accompanied weaker self-control, which accompanied more exercise delay, which meant less movement. How students see themselves, as independent or interdependent, changed the strength of the chain's middle link. The authors ground the model in self-regulation and self-construal theory. Their practical hint: interventions that rebuild self-control may fail unless they also break the procrastination habit it feeds. Culture-shaped self-image, they add, tunes the whole pathway.
pmc-13581911:
Wei Yang and a large team of co-authors study why blood sugar, blood pressure, and blood fats so often stay off target in type 2 diabetes. Their 2026 study drew on seven hospitals in Shanxi Province, China, with data from 1,874 patients seen over one year. Poor control meant missing the target in any one of the three areas. A two-step data method picked the factors tied most strongly to poor control.

Fewer than three in a hundred patients met all three targets. Body mass, schooling level, and what patients knew about their care showed the strongest links to poor control. The authors say the results are early and need checks in new groups, but they point to patient teaching as a key lever.
pmc-13582011:
Victoria EJM Palasantzas and colleagues grade an immortal liver cell line as a stand in for fatty liver disease research, in a 2026 study. The field leans on a cancer derived line that behaves little like a healthy liver cell. The candidate line, grown from real human liver cells, was set against that standard on genes, fat loading, and drug response.

The two lines differed sharply in chromosome layout, in disease risk gene forms, and in how their genes answered a fat bath. A new approved drug for the inflamed form of the disease cut stored fat in the candidate line but not in the cancer line. Its gene shifts ran through energy making paths. The authors warn that model choice can flip a study's answer.
pmc-13582211:
Gayatri Morajkar leads an eight-author team reporting bedside ultrasound findings in newborns' kidneys, in a case series from two thousand twenty-six. Sick neonates deteriorate fast, and delays in imaging cost time no one can spare. Point-of-care ultrasound lets the treating clinician scan at once, at the bedside.

The cases came from four tertiary neonatal intensive care units in India, over three years. The babies had significant kidney, adrenal, or urinary tract abnormalities, each found by clinician-performed scans at the cot side. The findings were checked against clinical data and laboratory results, and against formal imaging. Renal ultrasound at the bedside is not yet routine in neonatal units. The series shows what it catches, and how it changes calls on fluids, drugs, and referrals.
pmc-13582511:
Algamdi and Alamrani examine sleep quality among nurses on rotating and day shifts. Their 2026 study surveys nurses in Saudi Arabia. Irregular hours strain sleep, and poor sleep endangers patients too. Who sleeps worst, and why, guides fair scheduling.

One hundred forty nurses answered a standard sleep questionnaire. About forty-three percent slept well; the rest slept poorly. Good sleep thinned steeply with age. Nationality and marital status were held fixed in the final model. Several traits overlapped so tightly with shift patterns that simpler models were chosen. The analysis swapped a planned fancier method for a sounder one. Honest modeling beats fashionable modeling in small samples.
pmc-13582711:
Luan Lawson and colleagues track how medical students grow as self directed learners across the first two school years, in a 2026 study. A sixteen item survey measured four traits: adaptive learning, resilience, curiosity, and drive. Students answered at entry, after year one, and after year two, with sixty five students matched across all three rounds.

Scores dipped on adaptive learning in year one, while the other three traits held steady. By the end of year two, scores rose across the board, passing the entry marks. The authors read the dip as the shock of a harder learning world before students build the thinking tools to run it. Schools get a baseline rhythm for when to coach these skills.
pmc-13583111:
Ross Carter and co-authors studied how a focused helium ion beam changes a high-temperature superconductor in a 2026 paper. The material, YBa2Cu3O7, loses its superconductivity when ions damage its crystal lattice. A beam focused to about ten nanometers can write insulating lines into it, a way to build tiny superconducting devices.

The team varied the ion dose and measured the results three ways: electrical resistance when cold, X-ray diffraction with a tiny beam, and surface scans. As dose rose, the lattice expanded and the material moved toward an insulator. Knowing the dose response lets engineers draw device features with the beam on purpose rather than by trial.
pmc-13583211:
Farhad Salehzadeh, Rasol Molatefi, and Faeze Babazadeh Khoei review three cases where a JAK inhibitor calmed stubborn familial Mediterranean fever, in a 2026 paper. The fever disorder usually answers to colchicine, but a small share of patients resist it or cannot take it. Biologic drugs work yet cost much and are hard to get in many places.

Three adults who had only partly answered to colchicine plus dapsone took the oral drug twice a day. Over nine to twelve months none had a single attack, and no infection, blood, clotting, or liver harm appeared. The authors back wider study of this oral route as a stand in for costly biologics.
pmc-13583511:
Andrea Cantarini and co-authors check the germ safety of ground game meat in central Italy in this 2026 study. Minced meat from hunted animals is growing popular in food service, but grinding can spread microbes. The team sampled frozen minced wild boar and roe deer from one plant over a year.

Seventy samples across fourteen batches were tested for total germ counts, a fecal indicator germ, and two dangerous pathogens. Neither pathogen appeared in any sample. Total counts passed European hygiene limits in nearly all samples. The fecal indicator, though, ran high in wild boar and pushed over a third of samples past the limit. The authors see a mostly sound profile with room to improve.
pmc-13583811:
Mingxin Gao and co-authors set out a trial of a low-dose anti-inflammatory drug in heart bypass patients, in a 2026 protocol paper. Bypass surgery restores blood flow, but patients with widespread artery disease face high rates of heart attack around surgery and later events. Tiny calcium growth in artery walls, seen on scans, predicts those events.

The trial will enrol 108 patients with high scan scores at one Beijing hospital between 2026 and 2028. Half will get the drug daily and half will not, with outcome judges kept blind to group. The main check is change in calcium activity ninety days after surgery. Early heart attacks and major events will also be tracked. The study tests whether calming inflammation cools the calcium process.
pmc-13583911:
Cayla Weiler and her team test how tags for the wild world, food worth, and beast care shift how buyers see a plant-based cream cheese. Their 2026 study serves the same goods, in four tag states, to more than a hundred buyers.

Plant-based milk-like goods face curbs on how well folk take them, from taste fears and talk that is not clear. Folk scored how the goods look, taste, and feel, and how much they like them as a whole. They ticked words for sense traits and heart states, and told how set they are to buy. Cream state, smooth state, and spread drove hopes most. Tags shifted takes  though the goods did not change. Food worth and beast care tags raised how much folk like the goods next to the plain check. Beast care tags made feel scores and will to buy more good too.
pmc-13584011:
Anil Kumar and a large team of co-authors automate in 2026 the choice of settings for ARIMA forecasting models using spider monkey optimization, a swarm search method. Picking the three ARIMA orders by grid search is slow and can miss the best fit. In their scheme, each virtual monkey stands for one candidate setting set, scored by fit and forecast accuracy together.

They tested on Indian farm production series against genetic, swarm, and Bayesian tuning rivals. Their method gave the lowest forecast errors on all six series with less compute time. For total food grains, test error fell well below every rival. The framework suits routine agricultural forecasting.
pmc-13584111:
Pablo Bargalló and eleven co-authors test a fogging lens trick in eye measurement in this 2026 study. A plus lens blurs vision on purpose to relax the eye's focusing muscle before its power is read. The team used a handheld open view device and asked whether the lens changes readings, and for whom.

Sixty-one young adults each gave six short readings per eye, three with the lens and three without. The device repeated itself well, and five second readings were nearly as steady as ten second ones. Most nearsighted and normal eyes barely reacted to the lens, but forty-three percent of farsighted eyes relaxed, shifting by a meaningful amount. The authors advise using the lens mainly for farsighted patients.
pmc-13584311:
Clara Ciampi and co-authors review how the day-night clock steers fluid flow and waste wash-out in the brain, in this 2026 survey. The brain has no lymph pipes of its own. It leans on its own fluid and a wash web, the glymphatic system, to clear waste. Both run on a daily beat set by clocks at many levels of the chain.

The survey pulls the proof into one view. A knot of vessels, nerve cells, and support cells acts as the tap for the whole chain. Proof from animal work backs a daily wave in the wash web's work. Where the master clock for all this sits is still in dispute. The team maps the open asks and calls for more work, since the beat may shape brain health and disease.
pmc-13584711:
Yuwen Sun maps the risk that city noise poses to the voices of people who must speak or sing in it. Her 2026 paper notes that noise studies weigh the hearer, not the sound maker. In loud places, speakers push their voices by reflex, which strains the throat. Her framework joins that reflex, a gauge of throat pressure, and a signal-to-noise score to turn noise levels into a vocal load score. It is checked against pro singer data.

Road noise maps for three European lands mark high-risk zones as a small share of the noisy area. A small test with singers fit the core claim. A key catch emerged: as speakers push harder, clarity scores improve while throat strain worsens, so clarity alone hides the risk.
pmc-13585511:
Xikun Sun and colleagues find the right dose of the pain drug oliceridine, paired with the sedative ciprofol, for painless stomach scope exams. Doses were tuned separately for men and women with the Dixon up-and-down method, where each patient's dose moves up or down based on the last patient's response. A set dose of ciprofol followed the test dose.

Twenty-nine men and thirty-two women finished. The median effective dose was lower in women, about thirteen micrograms per kilo, than in men, about seventeen. The ninety-five percent doses were about eighteen and twenty-one respectively. Side effect rates did not differ by sex. The values give clinics a sex-aware starting dose for the pairing.
pmc-13585611:
Xing Jin and co-authors report a 2026 case-control study on gut-friendly eating and kidney stones in Chinese adults. Their diet score, the Dietary Index for Gut Microbiota, grades how a menu treats gut germs. The team compared 278 stone patients with 556 matched healthy controls from a Shenyang cohort, scoring diets from food questionnaires and modeling the stone link.

Higher scores came with clearly lower stone risk. Adults scoring eight or more had about eighty-three percent lower odds than those scoring five or less, after adjustment. The pattern held across age and sex and rose in a straight line. The authors call for forward-looking studies to test whether gut-friendly menus truly prevent stones.
pmc-13585811:
Takashi Takeda and co-authors compare two big surveys of robot-assisted gynecologic surgery, one from Europe and one from Japan, to find scope for shared training. Robot surgery is spreading, and young surgeons need good training routes. The European survey covered early-career gynecologists across 21 countries. The Japanese survey covered obstetricians and gynecologists nationwide; those within 12 years of graduation were picked to match.

293 replies were studied: 81 European and 212 Japanese. Access to robot systems was much the same, about three quarters in each group. Interest in robot surgery was high in both, a bit higher in Europe. But the Europeans reported far more hands-on work at the console. Equal drive and equal kit, but unequal practice, is just the gap that exchange schemes and shared courses exist to close. The comparison gives surgical societies hard facts for joint training plans.
pmc-13586111:
Maissa Chakroun and colleagues find a gentler way to pull apart clumped spore and crystal bundles in a pest-killing bacterium. Bacillus thuringiensis makes protein crystals that poison insect larvae, paired with hardy spores, and makers must count each part to keep batches steady. One variety, used against mosquitoes, clumps so tightly that standard separation fails and counts run low.

The team tried sound waves, a detergent, and lipopeptides, fatty soap-like molecules made by bacteria themselves. The lipopeptide wash won by far, raising live spore counts up to eight thousand fold and lifting crystal recovery to sixty percent. A related variety that stays naturally loose turned out to carry the gene for making its own lipopeptides, which hints that nature uses the same trick. The authors offer the wash as a cleaner swap for harsh methods.
pmc-13586411:
Pawel Szulc, Danielle Whittier, Steven Boyd, and Roland Chapurlat wrote a 2026 paper on alcohol and bone strength in older men. Drinking has been linked to weaker bones, but most past studies took one snapshot in time. This study followed men as their bones changed over eight years.

Eight hundred eighteen men aged sixty to eighty-seven had fine bone scans of the wrist and ankle at the start, then again after four and eight years. Bone density by standard scans did not fall faster in drinkers than in others. Men with a modest intake, between sixteen and one hundred twelve grams of alcohol a week, showed the slowest thinning of inner bone structure. The results add nuance to advice that often treats any drinking as equal harm.
pmc-13586511:
Carolina Mir Sánchez writes in Spanish about adding social facts to health records in Spain. Her 2026 essay argues that care which ignores a patient's home life cannot be judged right. She gives the case of diabetes care, which can hinge on whether the home has a fridge, support from others, and work hours that allow meals on time.

Spain now plans to record such facts in a set, shared way. A national plan for primary and community care from 2025 to 2027 calls for social and family context to enter the digital health record. A shared paper from late 2025 lists nine axes of unequal treatment and many sides of family life, from social support to energy poverty. The essay asks what happens to social facts once they are written down.
pmc-13586811:
Zohreh Shalchi, Nasibeh Ghalandari, and Bahman Shams Shafigh report a boy whose burst lung parasite cyst was found late, with a fatal end, in a case report from two thousand twenty-six. The boy, aged eleven, had coughed for four months after a cold. He arrived vomiting, coughing blood, and starved of air.

Scans showed a torn cyst linked to an air tube, plus spread to the other lung. Chest surgery cut the cyst and drained a leak, and drug care began. Kidney harm and lung troubles still mounted after surgery. The team frames the case around delay and the hard call on breathing tubes. Readers get a stark brief on a curable disease turned deadly.
pmc-13587011:
Tianqun Huo, Hongping Yao, and Ziyan Kong review a shortcut for CAR T-cell therapy. Their 2026 review starts from the cost of the standard route, where a patient's T cells are pulled out, reworked in a lab, and returned weeks later. The new route builds the receptor inside the body instead.

Delivery trucks range from weakened viruses to fat bubbles and tiny plastic beads. Each must find T cells, slip the gene in, and keep it on without stray edits. Safety worries include hits on the wrong cells and immune backlash. Early trials in people are under way. The authors weigh what must be solved before the shortcut can serve solid tumours too.
pmc-13587211:
Erica Yim and colleagues set drug response in child bladder infections at one Korean hospital in 2015 to 2020 beside the same hospital's data from 2003 to 2008. They looked back at 571 kids with germ-proven acute bladder infections. Germ type, drug response, resistant-enzyme rates, and scan results were all weighed anew.

Gut germs caused 98.2 percent of infections, with Escherichia coli alone at 89.1 percent. Drug response fell a lot for a few drugs used each day, and enzyme-proof germs grew far more common. Scan faults showed no clear link to germ type. Local drug-use watch must go on, so first-choice drugs for kids stay wise.
pmc-13587411:
Yuhui Wang and eleven co-authors wrote a 2026 study on whether brain wiring patterns link a father's schooling to a young adult's weight and mood. Parental education tracks with body mass index, mental health, and brain development, but the brain pathway is unclear. The team tested brain coupling as the middle step.

The study scanned 490 healthy young adults with two imaging methods, one for brain structure and one for activity. Coupling measured how well the two maps matched in each region. A father's education correlated slightly with higher BMI and lower depression scores. All three also tied to coupling in the right inferior parietal lobule, a region for attention and self-awareness. Mediation analysis tested whether that coupling carries the education effect.
pmc-13587511:
Klevebro leads a team studying early blood protein patterns in babies who develop a lung disease of prematurity in a 2026 paper. The disease, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, affects the most immature infants. How early exposures disturb protein growth was unclear.

Blood samples came from extremely preterm infants across their first five weeks of life. Hundreds of proteins were measured, and many showed distinct paths in babies who later had the disease. Some hits were known from past work, while others were new. Immune proteins featured strongly among the top results. The authors suggest calming inflammation and guarding helpful factors may aid prevention. Clinical traits likely interact with these proteins.
pmc-13587711:
Jiaqi Ma and co-authors test whether coal dust makes noisy workplaces even worse for hearing. Mines and plants combine hazards, and the pair may compound damage at the high frequencies where hearing loss starts. Their study covered one thousand one hundred eighty-seven workers examined in Baiyin City in 2023: two hundred seventy-six exposed to noise alone, and nine hundred eleven facing noise and coal dust together.

High-frequency hearing loss showed in about thirty-six percent of the noise-only group, but about forty-seven percent of the combined group, a firm statistical difference. Damage clustered near four thousand hertz, while speech frequencies stayed mostly intact. Regression models hunted the risk factors behind the gap. The authors argue hearing conservation in dusty trades must treat the mixture, not noise alone.
pmc-13587811:
Qin Ding and ten co-authors trace how a protein shed by tumor-supporting fibroblasts rewires fat metabolism in gastric cancer and blunts immunotherapy. These support cells help build the suppressive neighborhood that lets tumors resist checkpoint drugs, but how they sway metabolism was unclear. Using bulk and single-cell sequencing, spatial mapping, and patient cohorts, the team singled out fibroblasts marked by the protein POSTN.

These cells clustered in patients who did not respond to the drugs and fared poorly. POSTN latches onto a receptor on tumor cells and macrophages, switching on a signaling chain that raises a fat-handling regulator, PPAR-gamma. The result is lipid-loaded, stressed macrophages polarized into a suppressive state. Silencing POSTN with nanoparticle-delivered RNA shrank tumors, cut fat handling, and reduced the suppressive macrophages in mouse models. The authors nominate the fibroblast-macrophage fat axis as a drug target.
pmc-13587911:
Moshe Azachi and Zeev Wiesman compare two protein burgers with unlike juiciness: Angus beef and a soy-based rival. Their 2026 study asks whether water movement inside the food, not just total moisture, explains the contrast. Juiciness is a key trait for both meat and plant-based foods, yet bulk water content can mislead.

Cooked burgers were tested with magnetic resonance measures, microscopy, texture tools, and a trained taste panel. Water moved more freely in the beef burgers, and tasters rated them clearly juicier. Starting moisture did not differ much between the two. The authors argue that how water is held in the matrix shapes the eating feel.
pmc-13588111:
Rong Zhuang and co-authors report an infant whose meningitis would not clear in a 2026 case paper. The one-year-old boy stays ill despite long courses of strong antibiotics. A hidden channel behind the skull, a dermal sinus tract, can let bacteria reach the brain again and again. MRI hints at such a lesion, though fluid gene tests name no clear culprit.

Surgery finds the tract joined to an infected dermoid cyst inside the skull, they report. Removing it, plus antibiotics delivered into the brain fluid spaces, brings steady recovery. No relapse appears at six months. The case urges early structural checks when meningitis resists drugs.
pmc-13588211: This short piece from 2026 introduces art by Philip Alexander, a retired Texas physician. Alexander practiced internal medicine for 41 years in College Station before retiring in 2016. He is also a trained musician who plays oboe solos with a local symphony. He took up visual art in 1980, starting with pencil sketches. His computer-made drawings appear in a cardiology journal's humanities section, where they have run since 2012.
pmc-13588711:
Lara Howard and co-authors tracked African crowned eagles living in a city-forest mix in Durban, South Africa, in a 2026 study. Crowned eagles are top hunters that breed at oddly high numbers in this city. Green corridors of protected land thread through the built areas. The team fitted five eagles with trackers that log position and body movement.

Eagles chose forest over built land when both were on offer. Their energy use rose in built areas and grew as they moved away from the green network's edge. The pattern suggests city form shapes the cost of daily life for these birds. The authors stress that protected green networks help top predators persist in cities. Urban planners can use such findings to keep habitat links intact.
pmc-13588911:
Joanna Witowska and co-authors interview people across six European countries about how digital life felt during the Covid lockdowns. Their 2026 study gathers 148 post-pandemic interviews and reads them through the lens of three basic needs: autonomy, competence, and feeling connected. Technology, in the memories collected, both fed and starved every one of them.

Working from home could feel like freedom or like a cage, depending on space, time, and the employer's grip. Video calls enriched some friendships and hollowed others into fatigue. Competence rose with new skills and sagged under forced tools. The authors stress that conditions, not the gadgets themselves, decided the direction. They argue these reconstructed memories still shape how societies judge digital life after a crisis. Crisis planning, in their view, should treat psychological needs as infrastructure too.
pmc-13589311:
Nan Cai and co-authors look for the clinical and gene traits that travel with heart disease in more than one main artery at once. Such wide disease ends worse than single artery disease. A gene that helps break down fats and calm swelling may shape how bad the narrowing gets.

The study covered 4,124 patients at one center whose scans confirmed the disease. About four in five had the wide form. High blood pressure, diabetes, and poor blood fats were more common in that group. Two forms of the gene were also more common there, and tests tied each trait to the wide form on its own.
pmc-13589811:
Baojun Guo and co-authors test a classic herbal mix, Banxia Shumi Decoction, as a sleep aid in rats. Their 2026 study uses a drug called PCPA to cause insomnia in the animals. The team first used network methods to predict which body targets and pathways the mix might act on. They then tracked sleep and brain signals in the rats.

Treated rats fell asleep faster and slept longer than untreated ones. Levels of serotonin and melatonin rose, as did signals tied to the body clock. A drug that blocks melatonin receptors undid most of these shifts. The results point to melatonin signaling, and a protein called ADAM10, as part of how the mix works.
pmc-13590011:
Mariana Rodrigues and a European team survey how wild boar meat eaten at home escapes parasite testing, in a study from 2026. Hunters across Europe increasingly eat their own game. Testing for Trichinella worms is mandatory for meat sold on the market, but home-consumed meat often skips the lab, a real health risk.

The survey covered 26 countries, gathering hunt numbers, parasite prevalence, and the rules for testing, sampling, labs, and penalties. Practice varied wildly: some states require and subsidize testing, others leave it voluntary or unaddressed. Reported prevalence in boars ranged from zero to over six percent, with spotty data. Training and awareness campaigns lag in many regions. The authors warn that patchy rules leave home consumers exposed.
pmc-13590711:
Tong Zhu and co-authors compare task switching brains in athletes from open and closed sports in a 2026 study. Open sports, like ball games, demand constant adaptation, while closed sports repeat set moves, and the two may train the mind unlike ways.

Thirty one male athletes did a switching task while a light based brain scanner watched the front of the brain. Accuracy and raw speed matched across groups. The cost of switching, though, ran much lower for open skill athletes at equal accuracy. Front brain blood patterns differed too. The edge may guide talent picks and cross training plans.
pmc-13591011:
José Daniel Sánchez Redrobán reviews the state of neglected tropical diseases in Ecuador. His paper is from two thousand twenty-six. He sets Ecuador next to the wider Latin American and Caribbean region. The review draws on reports and data from the past decade, from health bodies and from Ecuador's own ministry.

World rates of these diseases fell a lot over three decades, but the loss of healthy years fell far less. Ecuador won a clean bill for one disease early, after mass drug rounds. Yet the region just saw a record dengue surge, and Ecuador shared in it. Water and sanitation gaps stay wide, all the more in rural zones.
pmc-13591111:
Le Xu leads a large team in 2026 in finding the door through which sprayed RNA enters a crop-destroying fungus. Spray-induced gene silencing promises to disarm Botrytis cinerea, the grey mould that rots strawberries and grapes. It works by soaking the fungus in RNA that switches off its key genes, but only if the fungus drinks the RNA in.

The team pinned the uptake on a gene called BcMFSR: without it, the fungus absorbs far less of the sprayed double-stranded RNA and silencing falters. They also named four fungal genes that spraying can suppress. The result turns a hopeful spray technology into one with known mechanics.
pmc-13591411:
Li leads a large team reviewing high altitude oxygen shortage and male fertility, in work from twenty twenty-six. Thin air at altitude lowers oxygen delivery to all tissues. The male reproductive system is sensitive to oxygen, blood flow, testosterone support, and the blood testis barrier.

Human altitude exposure studies, mountaineering observations, and animal low pressure models were reviewed. Testicular oxygen balance, local tissue injury, and vulnerability of the stem cell niche that produces sperm were the focus. The synthesis matters for soldiers, workers, and athletes who live or train high, and for understanding oxygen control of fertility generally.
pmc-13591611:
Shun Yao and co-authors review how parcels shipped between cells help stomach cancer grow and resist treatment. The parcels, called exosomes, carry proteins and genetic scraps from cell to cell. Tumor and support cells use them to trade favors in both directions.

Exosomes from support cells return the favor, feeding tumor metabolism, stem-like traits, and drug resistance. These exchanges form a self-reinforcing loop joining metabolism and immune escape. The authors survey how exosome cargo in blood might serve as a biopsy-free test, and how blocking or engineering exosomes could treat the disease. They close with cautions: lab models are imperfect, exosomes vary, and isolation methods differ between labs. Sorting out which exchanges matter in which patients is the step ahead.
pmc-13591711:
Arzu Or Koca and four colleagues mine, in 2026, a huge Turkish work screening dataset for links between heavy metals and hormone or metabolic health. Metals such as lead, cadmium, and arsenic can disrupt hormones. Records covered 34,595 people seen at a national work and environment hospital over two years. Metal levels in blood and urine were classed as normal or high, then set against thyroid, sugar, fat, and liver tests.

Among those tested, thyroid trouble appeared in about one in seven, and diabetes or pre diabetes in about one in five. Some high metal groups showed worse fat or liver patterns, yet many gaps faded after strict correction for false alarms. The team calls the results early signals, and urges routine thyroid and sugar checks for exposed workers.
pmc-13592411:
Seongmin Ga leads a 2026 team designing a carrier that bursts gene silencing RNA out of the cell's recycling sacs before they digest it. Under two percent of such RNA normally escapes. Their liposome wears a flu virus proton channel on its surface, tethered to the RNA by a nucleic acid linker. The channel pumps protons inward, swelling the sac until it ruptures.

Treated RNA reached the cell interior far better, with less of it ending in the digesting compartments, and gene silencing strengthened. Extra RNA packed inside the bubble let the team silence two genes at once. Ga and colleagues present active pH control of the sac as a flexible platform for RNA drugs aimed at genetic disease and cancer.
pmc-13592811:
Yaotian Cai and co-authors review small RNAs derived from transfer RNA and their roles in liver diseases. These fragments help control gene activity, protein building, and stress responses, and may carry signals between organs. Their exact part in liver disease is still being worked out.

The review covers their roles in liver tumors, metabolic disorders, and immune control. Such fragments could serve as non-invasive markers for diagnosis and as targets or tools for therapy. Yet methods vary, and performance differs by disease and population, which limits clinical use today. The authors map the challenges and propose directions to bring these molecules into liver care.
pmc-13593411:
A back massage may calm the heart after hard mental work, even while skin signals stay high. Maciej Lachowicz and co-authors ran a small pilot study on that question in 2026. Forty-eight people took part, half given a classical back massage and half left to rest face down. All had first done a task that loaded the mind. Heart rate and skin conductance were tracked for fifteen minutes after the task.

The massage group kept a lower heart rate than the rest group in every recovery window. Skin conductance, a sign of arousal, stayed higher for longer in the massage group. The split suggests heart and skin measures can move in unlike ways after touch. The authors treat the work as early and in need of larger tests.
pmc-13593511:
Chenglong Hu and colleagues pilot a breathing-and-resistance qigong routine for people who cannot sleep, in this trial from twenty twenty-six. Chronic insomnia is widespread, and standard treatments carry side effects, dependence risk, or waiting lists. The practice on test, Resistance Liuzijue, is a traditional mind-body exercise adapted with resistance work, taught over three months.

Forty patients were split between the qigong program and routine health education, without randomization. Both groups reported better sleep, mood, and fatigue by the end. The qigong group finished with lower anxiety and depression scores, and wrist sensors agreed with the diaries: their sleep ran more efficiently, with less wakefulness after first falling asleep. The authors label everything exploratory, given the open, unblinded design, and call for a large randomized trial before clinics take the practice seriously.
pmc-13593711:
Michael Wilkinson and Jenny Myers survey the search for a true treatment for pre-eclampsia, the dangerous pregnancy disorder marked by high blood pressure and organ strain. Care today manages blood pressure and times the delivery, but nothing yet modifies the disease itself, and their review weighs repurposed drugs alongside newer biologic strategies for the preterm form.

The diabetes drug metformin showed a trend toward longer pregnancies in a randomized trial, with larger trials under way. Heartburn medicines and an anti-inflammatory drug looked strong in early laboratory work but have not yet helped patients, possibly because too little drug reaches its target. Newer approaches aim at the placenta directly, including gene-silencing injections against a growth factor signal and antibody treatment that calms complement attack. Matching treatments to molecular subtypes of the disease is, the authors argue, the missing step.
pmc-13594211:
Molds leave mycotoxins in grain and other staple foods, and diet shapes how much of them a person takes in. Pia Sophie Kanonier and co-authors measure that exposure inside a randomized trial: 63 healthy adults ate either a vegan diet or a meat-rich diet for eight weeks. Urine samples then showed which mycotoxins each group passed, and how much.

The vegan group passed more deoxynivalenol, ochratoxin A, and zearalenone than the meat group, with clear statistical support. The pattern flipped for T-2 toxin, which ran higher in the meat-rich group. All diets were matched for calories, so the gaps reflect food choices rather than energy intake. The authors conclude that vegan eating changes mycotoxin exposure in ways food safety work should not ignore. They do not claim either diet is unsafe overall, only that the exposures differ.
pmc-13594311:
Minghang Yu and colleagues identify EHMT2, an enzyme that tags DNA-packaging proteins with a repressive mark, as a brake on the maturation of natural killer cells, the immune system's front-line tumor killers. Their 2026 study links the enzyme's level to weaker killer function across human tissues and cancers.

Combined gene and mark profiling showed the loss lifted repression from whole programs for development and attack. Drugs blocking the enzyme copied these effects in human killer cells grown from cord blood stem cells and in cells from adult blood. The authors propose EHMT2 blockade as a way to sharpen cell-based cancer immunotherapy.
pmc-13594411:
Xinnan Ma and co-authors review the use of AI to spot abnormal brain waves linked to epilepsy, in a paper from 2026. These brief discharges between seizures help doctors confirm the disease. Reading them by eye is slow, and raters often disagree. Programs promise speed, but the review warns that headline scores can mislead.

High scores on pre-cut clips do not mean a tool can find events in a full recording. The authors urge trials that state the target event, the matching rules, and the false alarm rate per hour. They also weigh brain processes that may shape the waves, like swelling and cell salt balance. Such links are plausible but not yet proven for single patients. They call for shared hospital trials and a human check before any clinic use.
pmc-13594511:
Yi Qin and nine co-authors report a drug trial for hysteroscopy sedation in work from twenty twenty-six. Hysteroscopy is a scope exam of the womb, often done with vein sedation in outpatients. Breathing pauses are a common risk with the standard drug propofol alone.

The trial at a Shanghai hospital randomly split women into two groups, with neither side knowing who got what. One group got propofol alone. The other got a mix of etomidate and propofol. The team tested whether the mix sedated just as well while cutting the length of breathing pauses. Women with airway flaws or severe heart, liver, or kidney disease were left out.
pmc-13594611:
Marton Demeny and co-authors check, in a two thousand twenty-six study, whether calf measures at weaning forecast later size in Limousin cattle. Early numbers that predict later build could guide preselection in beef breeding. Seven body measures were taken at weaning, near two hundred thirty days. They were taken again at thirteen to fourteen months.

Withers height carried across time best, near zero point six two. Rump height carried across time best too, near zero point six three. Pin width barely tracked any other measure at either age in the data. Breeding approved bulls outmeasured removed bulls on most traits at both checks. The authors weigh the set for use in early culling calls.
pmc-13594711:
Xiancheng Wu and co-authors published a study in 2026 on a mild-looking form of progression in chronic lymphocytic leukemia, where only the lymphocyte count rises. Whether that event carries the same weight as other progression was unclear under modern drugs. The team reviewed just under three hundred and forty patients treated at two Seattle centers with three frontline regimens.

Count-only progression struck most often after chemo-immunotherapy. Patients with it lived far longer after progression than those with other progression, and waited much longer for next treatment. Non-progressors still fared best overall. The authors suggest future trial criteria report count-only progression separately, since it may not warrant the same alarm.
pmc-13594911:
Geu Puentes-Conde and co-authors wrote a 2026 paper on a low-cost device for testing electronic circuit boards. Factories test boards in two ways: in-circuit tests check each part, and functional tests check the whole board at work. Standard test rigs are costly, which puts them out of reach for small firms and in-house labs.

The team's design packs many test functions onto a modular board set run by a small controller chip. It can apply set voltages, switch signals through relays, and measure voltage, current, resistance, and capacitance. Working prototypes were built and run in automated test setups to prove they work. All design files, from drawings to firmware and parts lists, are shared openly. The paper aims to make board testing cheap and easy to copy.
pmc-13595011:
A twelve-author team asks whether public health guides should set numeric targets for social life, in a 2026 study. Some guidelines suggest fixed counts, such as a set number of close friends or weekly meetups, to fight loneliness. The evidence behind such cutoffs is shaky, so the team hunted for natural breakpoints in Canadian survey data.

They analyzed repeated surveys from 2021 to 2024 with about thirteen hundred respondents. Loneliness, mood, anxiety, and self-esteem all improved with more close friends, up to a point. The leveling point differed by outcome: around three to four friends for emotional loneliness and mood, nearer seven for social loneliness. Days spent with friends showed weaker threshold patterns. Results also varied for people screening positive for depression or anxiety. The authors warn that one universal number would mislead; targets, if used, must fit the outcome and the group.
pmc-13595211:
Ilaria Cherchi and co-authors report a 2026 study of a newer human reference genome, T2T-CHM13. A reference genome is the standard map that DNA reads are matched against. The new map fills gaps and fixes errors in messy, repeated stretches of the older map.

The team compared reads matched to the new map against the older hg38 map across many sample types. The new map cut a bias that skews reads toward the reference version and raised precision at sites tied to disease. Gains showed at variants in the BRCA1 gene, a well-known cancer gene. In cancer patient data, the new map lifted measured variant shares by an average of 2.3 percent. The authors urge clinics to re-run old data against the new map.
pmc-13596111:
Shan Lu and Yongguang Tao review the engineering race to turn a strange form of cell death into a cancer therapy, in this 2026 article. Ferroptosis kills cells by letting iron-driven rust accumulate in their membranes. A decade after its discovery, no drug designed to trigger it in tumors has been approved. The authors argue the science is no longer the obstacle; delivery is.

They sort the field's inventions into four levels of ambition. The levels deliver a trigger to the right node, attack several pathways at once, gate the attack with a tumor-specific stimulus, and merge therapy with imaging so doctors can watch it work. Each level answers a named bottleneck, from poor tumor accumulation to invisible target engagement. The most advanced platform in patients is, pointedly, one of the simplest. The review's discipline, matching each gadget to the failure it fixes, is its real contribution.
pmc-13596711:
Viji Remadevi and colleagues tested pirfenidone, a drug approved against lung scarring, in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, where growing cysts are joined by progressive scarring that itself drives kidney failure. Their study began with single-nucleus sequencing of human polycystic kidneys to find where the scar material comes from.

In a mouse model of the disease the drug reduced scarring, matrix buildup, and the scar-forming cell population, and kidney function improved. Kidneys grew less enlarged, though cyst counts fell only in females. The authors position pirfenidone as a partner to cyst-targeted drugs, arguing the scar deserves treatment in its own right.
pmc-13596911:
Londiwe Shandu and co-authors report interviews from a trial that let teenagers with HIV take weekends off their daily medicine. The BREATHER-Plus trial compared that short-cycle plan with daily dosing for youths aged 12 to 19 in South Africa and Uganda. Their 2026 report draws on deep interviews and group talks held from late 2022 to mid 2024.

Teenagers, parents, and health workers all welcomed the break from daily pills. Some teens stretched the idea of two days off in their own ways, and many admitted that missed doses were common both before and during the trial. Most only raised missed doses when a blood test flagged a problem. The authors say sticking to treatment is shaped by family, clinic ties, and how teens read their own test results.
pmc-13597311:
Ying Yin, Tingting Wang, Ting Xu, and Yulu Liu explore, in a 2026 study, why poor vision goes with weaker thinking skills in older adults with diabetes. Both eyesight loss and mental decline are common in this group, but the social and mental paths that link them are less clear. The authors test two middle steps: how much a person takes part in social life, and how much control they feel over their life.

The team used a 2018 national survey of healthy longevity in China, covering 1,072 adults aged sixty-five and over with diabetes. Worse vision came with less social activity, less felt control, and lower mental scores. Even after those paths were counted, vision still linked directly to mental scores. The path through social activity alone carried a real share of the effect. Keeping older adults socially active may soften the mental cost of vision loss.
pmc-13597511:
Levi Flom and co-authors study, in a 2026 paper, the small groups of brain cells that drive cocaine seeking in mice. These groups, called ensembles, switch on together during specific experiences. They sit in a reward hub of the brain and reactivate when drug cues return.

The team tagged the active cells during seeking after mice had learned to self-administer the drug, then quit, then faced cues again. They imaged the cells' tiny contact spines and measured signal strength at those contacts. Earlier work had seen contact changes in mixed cell pools, not in the seeking group itself. Seeing change inside the exact group matters for any future therapy aimed at relapse. The study ties memory-like cell groups to lasting wiring shifts.
pmc-13598111:
Yantao Xing and co-authors build a wearable patch that spots and reverses opioid overdose on its own in a 2026 paper. Overdose kills by slowing breath, and the antidote works only if given within minutes, which often fails outside hospitals.

Sound driven micro streams push the antidote through skin on demand from a printed patch. A learning based breath sensor watches for the overdose pattern and triggers release, closing the loop. In mice dosed with fentanyl, the patch cut detection time and softened events versus standard care. The team pitch it as personal, automatic rescue gear.
pmc-13598711:
Six researchers review non-coding RNAs in head and neck cancer radiation resistance in a paper from 2026. These cancers are the sixth most common worldwide, and survival has stalled near fifty percent. Radiation is a main treatment, but many tumors resist it. Non-coding RNAs do not build proteins, yet they steer cell cycle, DNA repair, and growth. The review gathers one hundred eighteen such RNAs from over one hundred articles.

The catalog splits them by type and by whether they raise or lower resistance. The authors discuss two clinical uses for these molecules. They could predict which patients will respond to radiation. They could also become drug targets to restore sensitivity. The review frames the field for precision oncology.
pmc-13599511:
Briawna Binion and twelve co-authors find a new hormone-shuffling enzyme in a urinary tract bacterium, in a 2026 study. Microbes living in the body can extend the human hormone system by converting steroids. Such activity matters in prostate cancer, where bacterial androgen production may blunt hormone therapy.

The team isolated androgen-forming bacteria from men's urine. In one species they characterized a previously unknown enzyme that converts a weak androgen into testosterone and back, powered by a common cellular fuel. A search of other genomes found a similar enzyme in a second genus, which they built and tested to confirm the same activity despite little sequence resemblance to known enzymes. Both enzymes accept a broad range of related steroids. The findings widen the known cast of hormone-active enzymes in the urinary microbiome.
pmc-13599611:
Menbere Gebreanania Kahssay, Katherine Oyieke, and Charlotte Hoybye report the case of a boy in his early teens with Prader-Willi syndrome in a 2026 paper. The rare genetic disorder stems from lost paternal genes on chromosome 15 and brings constant hunger, obesity, hormone problems, and learning difficulties. The boy presented with short stature and early-onset obesity matching the syndrome's pattern.

Genetic testing confirmed that both copies of his chromosome 15 came from his mother, a known cause of the condition. Care centered on restricting food and raising physical activity, which brought modest improvement. The authors use the case to stress the diagnostic and treatment challenges of the syndrome where resources are limited, and the value of full genetic testing.
pmc-13600011:
Naipal, Rampersad, and Hansraj published in twenty twenty-six a survey of South African optometrists on managing childhood short-sightedness. Myopia is rising worldwide and may affect half the global population by mid-century. The team sent an online questionnaire to practicing optometrists. One hundred twenty-four completed surveys came back. Questions covered knowledge, eye exam habits, and treatment choices for children. Experience, certification, and interest were tested as influences on practice.

Most respondents skipped the dilating drops that give the most accurate child readings. Fewer than a fifth did dilated back-of-eye exams routinely. Plain distance glasses were prescribed most, despite known slowing treatments. Cost and missing clinical guidelines limited evidence-based care, respondents said. Knowledge of diseases linked to high myopia needed strengthening. The authors suggest the results guide policy and professional training.
pmc-13602211:
TRPM4 is a channel that turns calcium signals inside cells into electrical ones, letting sodium and potassium pass while blocking calcium itself. They map how calcium sensing, fat signals, and blocking molecules all meet at shared control points.

Faulty TRPM4 shows up in heart rhythm disease, brain swelling after injury, and several cancers. The authors argue the goal is no longer just switching the channel on or off, but holding the right shape in the right tissue. Tiny engineered binders may do that job.
pmc-13602311:
Gergely Imre and Szilvia Juhasz give a protocol for cyclic DNA damaging treatments that build a high mutational burden in the human A549 lung cancer cell line. Heavily mutated cell groups serve downstream genome studies. The protocol came out in twenty twenty-six.

Cells face round after round of DNA damaging agents, up to dozens of cycles. Steps cover careful dose setting so the harm stays controlled, metabolic activation of the agents, and the repeat cycle rhythm. Clone isolation follows at the end. Full use details point to a prior paper by the second author and team, the authors note.
pmc-13602411:
Ryan Gardner and co-authors test a possible trigger for type 1 diabetes: molecular mimicry. The idea is that a peptide from an infection looks so much like one of the body's own that the immune system attacks both. Earlier work found pairs of infection and diabetes epitopes with similar sequences.

Sequence matches alone are not enough, so the team compares the pairs' three-dimensional shapes as well. They also test how well each peptide binds to HLA molecules, the display platforms of the immune system. Pairs strong on all three counts become the best leads for lab follow-up. Even pairs that fail these tests are useful, since they narrow the search for the true trigger.
pmc-13603111:
Alondra Guerrero-Hernández and four co-authors study how to raise black soldier fly larvae in stacked trays, in a research paper from 2026. Farms grow these larvae at large scale, often for animal feed. Trays are stacked to save space, but conditions can differ from tray to tray.

The team varied how much larval weight went into each tray at the start, while keeping the count of larvae the same. The lightest starting load gave the heaviest final larvae, so more at the start did not mean more at the end. Middle trays did better than the bottom tray. The authors say tray position and load both need care in farm design.
pmc-13603211:
Xingcen Liu and Kamal Sabran tested an arts program for women who survived domestic violence in China, in a 2026 pilot study. The program, called Canvas of Strength, ran at a community center in Liaoning Province. Sixteen women took part, half in the arts group and half in a comparison group.

The team measured low mood, worry, and self-esteem before the program, right after, and six months later. Women in the arts group improved on all three measures, and most gains held at six months. The comparison group showed no real change. Interviews added depth: women spoke of fuller feeling, kinder self-views, and stronger ties with others.
pmc-13603311:
Ting Zhao, Asmah Ismail, and Engku Mardiah Engku Kamarudin linked parents' inner resources to teen school confidence in a 2026 study. A parent's hope, drive, and bounce back shape the home mood. Four hundred seventy two students in Shanxi, China, filled in surveys. Both the father's and the mother's capital tracked with teen confidence, and each parent's school role carried part of the link. The mother's school role tied more strongly to teen confidence than the father's. No gap showed in the direct links. The authors urge schools to draw both parents in.
pmc-13603911:
Patrick Forstner and co-authors test a new drug in a 2026 study against gut germs that already shrug off its kin. The drug is pitched as a fresh mouth cure for hard germs. But past proof covers just the wild, drug-soft strains, not those that beat its older kin drug.

The team grew more than a hundred such hard strains from real wards. Each was dosed in fine steps with both the old kin drug and the new one to find the least dose that stops growth. Spans for the new drug ran wide. Labs gain the first map of where the new drug holds on hard strains.
pmc-13604611:
Natalia Binti Ali and co-authors review pocket-sized gene-based sensors for watching the sea, in this 2026 paper. pmc-13604811:

pmc-13605111:
Zeyang Fan, Tiantian Li, and Kai Yang follow what happens to implanted ports after cancer treatment ends in this two thousand twenty-six cohort study. Among about fourteen hundred patients, the twelve-month rate was about thirty-four percent for planned removal, ten percent for port reuse, four percent for removal due to problems, and one percent for death. Kept ports follow varied paths and need case-by-case plans.
pmc-13605211:
Yi Huang and seven co-authors propose a framework for spatial niches in gastric cancer in this 2026 paper. The authors offer the scheme to standardize terms and guide the testing that translation would need.
pmc-13605411:
Ahmad Kharoufeh and co-authors tell a 2026 case story of a young child whose brain condition took a sudden turn for the worse. A shunt, a tube that drains the fluid to the belly, kept the pressure in check, and the child depended on it.

Such shunt problems can be hard to spot. Signs are often vague, early scans may look unchanged, and germ tests can come back negative. The child in this report was born at twenty-eight weeks and had the most severe grade of bleeding, with lasting brain injury. He needed several drainage steps before the long-term shunt. The case walks through the sudden decline and the hunt for its cause, as a guide for teams facing the same puzzle.
pmc-13605811:
Shiwei Sun and five co-authors ask which scan measures best forecast kidney stone surgery results. A model using an area-based diameter, a staghorn flag, and volume spread predicted stone-free status well. A simpler diameter model came close behind. pmc-13606511:
Marisol Ibarra-Ramírez and co-authors report a study of early gene testing for suspected inherited eye diseases, published in 2026. The work comes from a referral center in northeastern Mexico. The researchers reviewed 101 patients seen between January 2020 and August 2023. Each patient had a full eye exam and was offered a gene panel test while waiting for other tests. The test gave a clear, useful diagnosis in 45 patients, a yield of about 45 percent. In total, 165 gene variants were found, including 70 judged harmful.
pmc-13606911:
Paola D'Ambrosio and co-authors review in 2026 how to judge gene changes in a gene that builds a sodium gate in muscle. Changes in the gene can push the gate in opposed ways, from too much action to near total loss, and each path leads to a distinct illness.

pmc-13607011:
Cumhur Yesildal, Anil Yilmaz, Huseyin Hayit, Nurgul Keskin, and Mustafa Kaplan test whether a prostate drug changes night-time blood pressure patterns. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. Average pressures over the day, daytime, and night did not shift clearly. The dipping pattern, the normal night fall in pressure, was also compared. pmc-13607411:
Turan Demircan and three co-authors review cancer vaccines made to order for each patient, in a 2026 paper. These vaccines use mRNA, a short-lived copy of a gene, built from the odd proteins found only in that patient's tumor. The goal is to teach the immune system to attack the cancer.

Last, these vaccines may pair with drugs that release the brakes on immune cells. The authors review trial results in skin, lung, and pancreatic cancer, and list what may set apart patients who gain lasting benefit.
pmc-13607511:
Arabella Fischer-Hammerschmied and co-authors study in 2026 how kidney harm links to death in intensive care patients around the world. Their data come from a project in which care units in many lands record all patients on one set day each year. The study spans the years from 2007 to 2024.

Kidney signs in the study were a waste marker in the blood, urine output at admission, and whether a patient got a blood cleaning treatment. The team weighed how each sign links to death, while they allowed for traits of the patient and of the unit. Long runs of shared data like these show trends that one hospital cannot see. They can also show where kidney care in intensive units has improved, and where it has stalled, across many health systems.
pmc-13607611:
Avani Anu Geetha and co-authors review drug resistance in fish farming through a One Health lens, in this 2026 paper. Antibiotics are used heavily in aquaculture to fight disease and boost growth. That use breeds resistant germs that can reach people through water, food, and the wider environment. The One Health frame treats human, animal, and environmental health as one system, which suits this problem exactly.

The review explains how resistance works and spreads in water settings: pumps that expel drugs, enzymes that destroy them, and mobile gene packages that jump between germs. It surveys which pathogens dominate fish farms and how their resistance travels. Better rules for drug use in aquaculture protect both the fishery and the clinic, the authors argue.
pmc-13607811:
Beatrice Moccaldi and ten co-authors pilot a hand rehab program in a 2026 study. Their patients live with a long-term ill that stiffens skin and organs, and weak hands add much to their daily limits. All had the ill for more than five years and at least one stiff upper-limb joint.

The program ran ten sessions over five weeks, with warm wax care and hand drills shaped to each patient. One group got the program and a match group did not, with no random split. The pilot weighs gains in hand use and life quality, to size a fuller trial.
pmc-13608011:
Carlos Saiz and three co-authors ask how clear thinking connects to feeling well, in a 2026 study. They reanalyzed data from an earlier project on critical thinking, metacognition, empathy, and psychological well-being, this time adding grades. Two rival explanations were tested with causal diagrams. In one, metacognition reaches well-being only through school performance. In the other, it links to well-being directly.

The sample held 155 undergraduate psychology students. The performance-mediated model failed its key test: metacognition and well-being stayed linked even after performance was accounted for. The direct model fit better, and the metacognition path to well-being was the strongest in the map. Grades did not act as the main bridge. Repeated resampling supported the direct link's stability. The authors conclude that knowing how you think matters for well-being in its own right.
pmc-13608511:
Farjallah Alassaad and six co-workers wrote a 2026 study on using raw sea sediment in concrete. Ports dig out large amounts of sediment that need a use. The team swapped part of the sand in concrete with raw sediment from a port. They then tested strength, wear and safety over the life of the material.

Mixes with more sediment were weaker and took in more water. At the highest swap rate, strength at four weeks fell by almost half. Rain tests on whole slabs kept releases below set limits, though the team calls those results early. After crushing, some mixes passed set limits for salts and one metal.
pmc-13609111:
Ancuta and co-authors compare how dying cancer patients are cared for in their last week across four settings, in a 2026 paper. The team reviewed records for three hundred six patients in an oncology ward, an intensive care unit, an inpatient palliative unit, and home-based palliative care.

Testing and artificial hydration were universal on the oncology ward and in intensive care, where prescriptions centered on pain. Palliative settings treated a wider range of final symptoms. Unneeded drugs were stopped between about two and three days before death, at rates that varied by setting and drug class. The authors call for steadier planning and continuity across settings.
pmc-13609711:
Zhongjie Wang and co-authors tune a tin-based solar cell by simulation in work dated two thousand twenty-six. Tin perovskites promise solar power without lead, but their output lags behind lead cells. The team models a flat cell with a tin absorber between two carrier layers.

One knob at a time was swept: doping level, layer thickness, flaw density, carrier speed, and stray resistance. A mid-high doping level gave the best balance of built-in drive against loss. Thick layers caught more light but lost more carriers, and past a set flaw level output collapsed. Under the best mix, the model cell topped twenty-seven percent efficiency, which shows the worth of joint tuning.
pmc-13609811:
Stephan Ebenberger and four co-authors found that cholera bacteria switch off their stabbing weapon while forming biofilms in a 2026 study. The weapon injects toxins into rival bacteria on contact. Across many cholera strains, weapon genes were strongly repressed in biofilm cells compared with free swimmers.
