The authors read the shutdown as self-protection: a silent weapon draws fewer counterattacks from stronger neighbors. In mixed microbial crowds, they argue, knowing when not to fight is a fitness edge. The strategy may be widespread among biofilm dwellers.
pmc-13610011:
Grzegorz Szynkaruk and six co-workers wrote a 2026 lab study on saliva samples for drug level checks in children. Saliva could replace blood draws for tracking a transplant drug. Samples sit in cotton swab tubes before lab work, so stability matters. The team tested how long the drug and its breakdown product stay true in those tubes.

They spiked buffer, fake saliva and real saliva at two dose levels. Tubes sat for up to two days at room or fridge heat. In real saliva, the drug held within set limits for half a day at both heats. The breakdown product was less steady. The authors back quick lab steps.
pmc-13610111:
Rawal and co-authors measure soil carbon along the slopes of the western Himalaya timberline, in this 2026 study. This transition zone, where forest gives way to alpine ground, reacts quickly to climate shifts. The team sampled soil across eleven hundred meters of elevation inside a wildlife sanctuary.

Samples came from three slope directions and two depths, band by band up the mountain. Carbon rose with elevation on the north-east side but behaved differently on the other aspects. A random forest model predicted the pattern best, explaining up to three quarters of the variation underground. The authors credit slope-driven microclimates for the contrasts. Their maps form a baseline for tracking climate change.
pmc-13610311:
Ashley Marcheschi and co-authors present, in a 2026 plant study, the first broad comparison of how quinoa responds when starved of twelve key nutrients. Lack of nutrients limits crop yield worldwide, yet quinoa's inner responses were poorly known. The team grew plants lacking each nutrient and read gene activity in leaves and roots.

Responses varied widely, from a few hundred changed genes for one element to more than four thousand for another. Leaves changed more than roots in most cases. Still, a shared core response appeared in roots, centered on protein recycling and nutrient reuse. Each lack also left its own mark, tied to what that nutrient does in the plant.
pmc-13610411:
Vivian Ly and Youbin Zheng test whether silicon treatments help sweet basil grow and survive cold storage in a 2026 study. Basil bruises and blackens in the cold rooms used for most produce, cutting its shelf life. Silicon has been reported to ease that chilling injury in some crops.

Across four trials, basil in pots got silicon at five dose levels, fed to roots or sprayed on leaves in two chemical forms. Growth at harvest did not improve at any dose. Shelf life in cold storage ran long for all groups, controls included, with no clear silicon advantage. The authors suspect drought stress during the trials hardened the control plants, masking any effect, and call for cleaner follow-up work.
pmc-13610611:
Mariana Maciel Pereira and co-authors review antioxidant therapies for obesity in a 2026 paper. Obesity is now seen as a disorder of chemical balance, not just stored energy. Fat tissue outgrows its energy units, defences against oxidative stress weaken, and low-grade inflammation takes hold.

The review gathers animal and lab evidence for many candidate treatments. Vitamins, minerals such as zinc and selenium, amino-acid compounds, and several approved drugs all appear. Despite their varied forms, most converge on the same repair routes: restoring defence switches, raising a key protective molecule, and stabilising cell energy units. The authors caution that dose, delivery, and long-term safety must be settled before these findings can guide patient care.
pmc-13610811:
Huan Zhao and co-authors test whether ultrasound numbers mirror vessel growth around a liver parasite lesion. Alveolar echinococcosis creeps through liver tissue and reshapes nearby blood flow. Twenty rats carried guided liver implants and were scanned ten weeks later. Contrast ultrasound measured flow traits beside each lesion and in plain liver.

The rim zone showed stronger, faster enhancement than normal tissue on every measure. Cell counts for a vessel marker, CD34, were tallied by digital pathology. Denser vessels tracked with higher peak flow and faster wash-in values. Timing measures alone did not track the counts. The scans thus read local microvessel change without a biopsy.
pmc-13610911:
Godínez-Chaparro and two co-authors show a star-field skin mark on a birth mole in this twenty twenty-six case report. Birth moles of this type show at birth or in the first year of life. Skin scope traits help split them from kin marks and track how they change.

Inside, a boy of two years and seven months bore a small mole low on his back. The mole had sat there since birth with no past ills in his chart. A skin scope showed dark balls ringed round hair holes in a star-field spread. A wave scope showed cell nests at the skin join in a mixed mesh and ball form. The team says the star form must not be read as plain ball spread.
pmc-13611111:
Yongju Park and four co-authors present a 2026 paper on catching truckers who secretly change their cargo between checkpoints. Fallen cargo from badly secured loads is a rising highway danger, and weight sensors cannot tell same-weight swaps apart. The team's system photographs the load with a stereo depth camera on each pass. It flattens the depth map to remove perspective distortion, then aligns the load region with a one-dimensional matching step, comparing shape rather than color.

Field tests under two cargo scenarios reached a combined detection rate above ninety-one percent, beating four standard image-matching algorithms. Every rival missed the same tricky events, where a tarpaulin blended with the truck bed; the depth method caught them. Its speed nearly matched the fastest rival. The authors offer practical guidance for building dependable roadside cargo checks.
pmc-13611411:
Ana Banko and five colleagues review whether giving the preventive HPV vaccine to infertile men already infected with the virus helps clear it. HPV infection may impair sperm quality and contribute to male infertility. The reviewers searched three databases and found only three studies fit for qualitative and quantitative synthesis, a thin evidence base.

Pooled estimates suggested about seventy-four percent of men tested HPV-negative by the end of vaccination, rising to ninety-eight percent six months later. The authors call the signal promising but fragile, given few studies and methodological limits. They conclude that large, well-designed prospective trials are needed before adjuvant vaccination can be recommended for this group.
pmc-13611511:
Bo Huang leads a team of seven authors who watch what happens when enzymes meet biosurfactants, the detergents made by living things and eyed for greener oilfield chemistry. The industry wants mixes that act strongly at oil-water interfaces without heavy harm to nature. Their mix paired glycolipid biosurfactants with carbohydrate-cutting enzymes.

When enzymes were added, large micelles fell into small, spread-out micro-aggregates, and the drag on the flow of the mix fell. Microscopy and spectroscopy showed them prying apart shapeless enzyme clumps. Through hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic contacts, they rebuilt them into uniform small structures. Time-lapse readings caught uneven aggregates slowly turning uniform and stable. The team offer the mechanism as a design base for petroleum interface work.
pmc-13611711:
Fenghe Wang, Haotian Hao, and Jiahe Miao introduce a special issue of eight papers on cleaning polluted soil and water. Pollution of these linked systems threatens nature, drinking water, farming, and health. A pollutant's fate depends on acidity, minerals, organic matter, and microbes. Cleanup methods are judged by removal performance, mechanism, limits, and real-world practicality.

Six articles and two reviews make up the issue. Topics include electrokinetic removal of copper and lead from loess, mine tailings restored with fertilizer plus plants, and resource recovery from antibiotic waste. Other papers cover microbes degrading petroleum and chlorinated compounds, chloride stripping from strongly acidic wastewater, boosted breakdown of carbon tetrachloride in groundwater. A final paper tracks how hexavalent chromium migrates and transforms between soil and groundwater. Arsenic cleanup methods round out the set. The editors present a cross-section of current strategy.
pmc-13611911:
Victoria Chentsova and co-authors ask if age changes how time off a street drug links to thinking skills in people with HIV in a 2026 study. The team looked back at files for 122 adults with a past drug use disorder. They fit straight, bent, and split trend lines to the link between days clean and test scores.

A bent line fit best: more days clean went with higher scores, with the steepest gains early on. Age group did not shift the overall link. One skill did split by age, though: speed of taking in facts rose fastest with clean time in the youngest group. Most gains, across all ages, come early.
pmc-13612211:
Mingxuan Liang leads an eleven-author team writing a 2026 letter on what happens in leukemia cells before whole chromosomes start duplicating. Extra chromosome copies appear as the sole abnormality in a slice of myeloid cancers, yet the genes that invite them were unknown. The team compared cancers with normal chromosome counts against trisomy cases across three cohorts, covering 1,650 normal-karyotype and 229 trisomy patients.

The pattern suggests quiet, cumulative disruption of gene regulation loosens chromosome handling until gains follow. The authors present the enrichment map as a starting point for understanding how numerical instability begins.
pmc-13612411:
Jon Huyghe and co-authors find a new way cells disarm a death signal in a 2026 study. TNF is an immune signal that can order a cell to die. That killing helps fight infection, but too much of it drives inflammatory disease. Cells keep brakes on the signal, called checkpoints. Past work found one brake that sends the signal complex to be recycled.

The team now show a second route. Cells pack the activated death enzyme caspase-8 into tiny bubbles inside the cell, which can then be shipped out of the cell as vesicles. Blocking the bubble machinery, or its helper proteins, let the death proceed. Two germs that cause serious infections make proteins that jam this machinery, which flips the death signal on. The authors frame export as a parallel detox path for the TNF signal.
pmc-13612911:
Jingfei Wang and co-authors test a plasma-activated liquid against a common skin cancer, in a 2026 study. Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is frequent, and advanced cases have few gentle treatment options. The liquid is made by exposing saline or culture fluid to cold atmospheric plasma, which loads it with reactive species. Unlike direct plasma, the liquid stores well and is easy to dose.

In mice carrying human skin tumors, the liquid shrank tumor growth and weight. Treated tumors showed fewer dividing cells and no harm to body weight or organs. Protein shifts favored cell death over survival, and a spread-linked enzyme fell. In dishes, the liquid raised reactive oxygen inside cancer cells and damaged their power plants. Two cell lines confirmed the pattern. The authors present the liquid as a candidate therapy worth developing.
pmc-13613511:
Melissa Kirbach and co-authors present a forensic case study from a 2026 homicide investigation. A chop wound in the victim's skull held fine striations, the scratch pattern a blade leaves in bone. The question was whether a seized machete made that mark, a call that could tie a weapon to a killing.

The team compared the bone mark with test marks from the machete under microscopes and with 3D surface scans. Both methods gave very strong support that the seized blade made the wound, and a numeric match score backed the match. Findings from pathology, body scans, blood patterns, and scene records were then merged into a 3D rebuild of the moment of impact. The authors offer the case as proof that blade marks in bone, read across several forensic crafts, can carry real weight in court.
pmc-13613811:
Binaya Sahu and co-authors review zinc oxide particles against Candida in a 2026 paper. Drug-resistant Candida species are spreading, and standard antifungal drugs lose ground. Tiny zinc oxide particles kill fungi in lab tests and can be made by green routes.

Screening two large databases left thirty-three core studies for close reading. The particles hit many Candida kinds, from common to rare, and also dent the biofilms they form. The review maps how the particles harm fungal cells and how they may boost standard drugs when paired. Safety for human tissue stays the open worry. The paper weighs promise against the care that clinical use would demand.
pmc-13614111:
Martine Ann Mallinson, Bryony Brown, and Beverly Snaith survey how English imaging services screen patients for safety before scans, in this 2026 study. Screening forms catch past conditions and risks, such as metal in the body, before a scan proceeds. Using freedom of information requests, the team collected forms from nearly every hospital trust and a few private providers.

Paper still rules: only one organization had gone fully digital. Wording and layout varied widely between forms, which the authors warn can confuse patients and staff and invite errors. They call for studies of real-world use to ground better designs.
pmc-13614311:
Federico Ravera leads a team introducing a design framework named LUFFY. It picks molecules that could serve as working parts of molecular field-coupled nanocomputing. In that scheme, logic passes between molecules by electric fields rather than by moving charge. Such computing could use very little power, yet finding molecules with stable logic states is hard. Designers of post-silicon logic get a shared test bench for an idea still in its infancy.
pmc-13615711:
Norah A Almutairi, Darren C Greenwood, and Manoj Sivan report a 2026 study of long-term muscle and joint pain. They ask how often these patients also have dysautonomia, a fault in the nerve system that runs heart rate, blood pressure, and other tasks the body does on its own. Past work links that system to pain, but no one had counted cases in this group.

The team screened 896 people and studied 342 patients plus 57 healthy adults, using a symptom score to flag the condition. It showed up in 74 percent of patients but only 11 percent of healthy adults. Rates were alike in sore joints with and without swelling, and risk rose with worse pain, low mood, and worry.
pmc-13616311:
Dongmei Luo and colleagues use single-cell gene profiling to find a faulty B cell group behind primary immune thrombocytopenia, an autoimmune disease where antibodies destroy the blood platelets needed for clotting. The team profiled blood cells from four patients, four people with high platelet counts, and four healthy donors, then screened the results with machine learning. Tests in mice with the disease confirmed the enzyme's rise, and blocking it eased the B cell fault. pmc-13616411:
Nivedita Singh and colleagues work out, atom by atom, how a protein tag called FAST switches its fluorescence on when a dye ligand docks, enabling a chemically gated energy-transfer trick. A clear structural story lets designers tune tags for sharper, switchable imaging inside cells.
pmc-13616511:
Sano and thirteen co-authors search a nationwide Japanese registry for what predicts bleeding in patients on a temporary heart pump. The pump supports the left ventricle through the skin, and bleeding is a common problem during its use. The registry held 5,608 patients with full follow-up.

About one in four patients bled within 30 days, most within the first days. Rates were nearly the same for heart attack patients and others. Adding a second support device was the strongest bleeding risk in both groups. Machine learning checks agreed and flagged two high-risk patient patterns. The authors say teams should watch patients with extra devices especially closely.
pmc-13616611:
Takahiro Maeta and co-authors published a case report in 2026 on a woman with relapsed blood cancer who needed a second stem cell transplant. Her own antibodies attacked the donor cells from her son, which can make a transplant fail. The team had to lower those antibodies before the new cells went in.

Antibody drugs and two rounds of a targeted therapy cut the levels a lot, though one stayed high. A day before the transplant they infused a small batch of the donor's white blood cells to soak up what was left. The new cells settled by day nine, and the harmful antibodies were gone by day thirty-three. No graft failure or severe graft-versus-host disease followed.
pmc-13616711:

Blood and marrow tests found a small clone of abnormal plasma cells, the mark of smoldering multiple myeloma.

pmc-13616911:

pmc-13617311:

A speculum left out in a busy area for a day also came back clean after five minutes of light. The authors call the study exploratory: spores, fungi, and viruses were not tested. Still, they suggest ultraviolet treatment could be a practical extra step for reusable instruments between office procedures.
pmc-13617511:
Frederic Angelier and three co-authors ask when stress makes animals stronger rather than weaker, in a 2026 review tied to fast environmental change. Heat waves, pollution, and habitat loss now hit wildlife at a pace with no past match. The authors call for joint work on what stress resilience is at the level of the whole animal.

Measures covered include stress hormones, oxidative damage, and brain and behavior signs. pmc-13617811:

pmc-13618411:

Men were significantly more likely than women to report being punched or kicked. pmc-13618811:

Gut resident cells shift in that infection and sway tissue swelling. The review weighs proof and paths for nerve effects. Gaps point to tests that could settle the role.
pmc-13619311:

It also filled in missing gene expression values better in the benchmark comparisons the authors report. The code is freely available.
pmc-13619811:

Her body was found outdoors, and flies and beetles colonizing it carried timing clues. One blow fly species gave the team a way to estimate the postmortem interval, the time since death, based on how long insects had been active on the body.

A second fly species was bred from the corpse, and the authors note that its development data still need building out before it can anchor estimates elsewhere. Feeding by the flies and by a carrion beetle also left marks on the body. Such insect-made damage can be mistaken for injuries suffered before death, so the authors stress knowing each species' biology and behavior. Careful species identification, they argue, keeps entomology evidence from misleading a case.
pmc-13619911:
Kosuke Yamada and co-authors study a hormone drop in citrus trees sick with huanglongbing in a 2026 paper. Sick trees show disturbed hormone levels, including a fall in abscisic acid, a hormone that helps plants handle stress.

In lab cultures, the disease bacterium and two partner bacteria from sick trees broke the hormone down into that same product. Added hormone even helped the bacteria grow. The findings suggest microbes actively drain the hormone, linking the tree's microbial community to its hormone imbalance.
pmc-13621211:

Two bulkier new versions of the complex were made to test the idea, and both lost the selectivity entirely. The contrast pinpoints the ligand shell as the steering wheel, a design lesson for precision oxidation chemistry.
pmc-13622911:

Leading-edge shape barely mattered, shifting efficiency and blood-damage scores by under 3 percent. Blade thickness mattered far more under overload, with thinner blades lifting efficiency by up to 22 percent while barely changing blood damage. Torner and colleagues advise putting edge shape second and tuning thickness against manufacturing limits.
pmc-13623011:

Of 923 people analysed, one in five showed progression, most of them new cases. Progression ran higher in the Asia-Pacific and the Americas than in Africa. pmc-13623611:

Continuous glucose monitors have changed diabetes care, so the quality of the studies behind them now shapes clinical and regulatory choices.

The author walks through design choices that can tilt results: how the study was built, which reference measurement was used, how readings were paired in time, and how sensor survival was counted. Sponsorship bias and the reading of accuracy metrics also get scrutiny. Points the original study left open, such as uncertainty estimates and subgroup checks, are listed. The piece closes with recommendations for stronger future validations.
pmc-13623911:
Fatma Mohammed and co-authors report a 2026 study of heart changes in pregnancy in northwestern Tanzania. High blood pressure disorders in pregnancy can strain the heart and change its shape. Heart scan data from low resource settings, though, remain scarce.

All women were at least 28 weeks pregnant or within 10 days after birth. Combined heart shape and function problems were more common in the group with high pressure. The study weighs how blood pressure level links to those scan findings.
pmc-13624311:

pmc-13624411:

pmc-13625011:
Linpeng Nie and Tao Wu review stacking order as a control knob for layered quantum materials, in a 2026 article. Layers of atoms can sit in varied registries and sequences. Those choices reshape electronic behavior without changing chemistry. Twisting and sliding layers are now standard tricks. Artificial oxide stacks extend the idea to built sequences.

Most stacking is frozen at growth time, though. A newer concept lets stacking evolve inside one crystal. The article highlights work on a tantalum compound. Heating triggered layers to rebuild themselves in sequence. Some layers switched crystal type while the frame held. Sliding first reset the registry, then atomic moves followed. Ordered mixed-phase stacks emerged from the uniform start. The authors frame adaptive stacking as a route to programmable matter.
pmc-13625211:
Giulia Gotti and colleagues review what sets apart people who leave a suicide note from those who do not. Notes are rare first-person records of a suicidal crisis, yet only a minority of deaths involve one, so the team asked whether writers stand for the whole group. Their search of two databases, run to June 2026 under standard review rules, gathered thirty-three comparison studies.

Across social, clinical, and personal measures, no clear line separated writers from non-writers, and findings often clashed. The firmest difference lay in method: writers more often used non-violent means such as poisoning or gas. The authors suggest note-leaving may hinge on the circumstances of the act, and perhaps on having enough order of mind to write, rather than on a distinct inner profile.
pmc-13625611:
Sloane Parker, Arta Kasaeian, Sahar Samimi, and Andrew Caruso report a sinus infection that wore the mask of a deadlier fungal disease. Surgery and culture instead named Aspergillus fumigatus, a unlike fungus that needs unlike drugs. He had surgery to clear dead tissue and two antifungal drugs in turn. Swelling eased, though numbness and tooth pain stayed.
pmc-13625711:
Sonja Großmann, Petra Waldegger, Tina Deutinger, and Werner Zwerschke study a little-known matrix protein, SNED1, and what it does for fat tissue stem cells. These adult stem and progenitor cells renew fat and seed new fat cells, guided by the scaffold of proteins around them. With SNED1 knocked down, the cells renewed themselves less, multiplied more slowly, and turned into fat-storing cells less readily. pmc-13626211:
Ashley Coffell and co-authors chart gene activity cell by cell in the frontal cortex of pigs modeling Angelman syndrome. A signaling molecule called somatostatin dropped in inhibitory neurons and in blood of newborn pigs, though not in older ones. The results sharpen the picture of how losing this gene disrupts the brain.
pmc-13626511:
Yadav and co-authors (2026) tested whether ultrasound can size a laryngeal mask airway better than body weight does. The mask must fit the airway, and weight is a rough guide that ignores anatomy. The alternative measures the hyomental distance, the span under the chin, by ultrasound. The ultrasound group mostly received smaller masks, with no rise in reinsertions or complications. Mouth injury after surgery was rare in both groups. The authors conclude that ultrasound sizing is an individual, anatomy-based alternative that performs as well as the weight rule while picking sizes that fit the patient.
pmc-13626611:
A case report by Nageswara Rao Koneti and Shweta Nathani Bakhru, from 2026, follows an unborn baby with a badly narrowed heart valve. A balloon fix at twenty-six weeks opened the valve and restored flow, a step meant to stop the left heart from shrinking. Later scans told a worse tale: the hole between the heart's top rooms shut by slow degrees, and a sound-wave trace of the lung veins showed a strong backward wave. Both signs pointed to high pressure in the left top room and a stiff lower room.

After birth the baby showed high lung pressure and stayed stiff-hearted despite a second balloon fix. The pair argue the lung-vein trace is a handy, touch-free sign of a closed-off top room. It can flag babies headed for rough first days even when the valve fix itself goes well.
pmc-13626711:
Mathilde Sola and a twelve-strong team release NeighborFinder, an R package that maps the microbes living nearest to one chosen species. pmc-13626911:
Xian-Hong Wang and co-authors train a deep learning system to tell apart three lung diseases on chest X-rays. Pneumonia, tuberculosis, and aspergillosis share cough, fever, and breathlessness, so they are easy to confuse, and late calls on aspergillosis can cost lung tissue. Their 2026 study builds a system, called DETECTX, that sorts X-rays into those three diseases or healthy.

Three model types were trained on 7,200 images split into the four groups. A Siamese network, which learns by comparing image pairs, beat both a plain convolutional network and a standard ResNet-50 model. It reached 98.72 percent accuracy, ahead of published rivals in the team's comparison. The group also built a web page where clinicians can upload a scan and get the system's reading. They offer it as an aid to faster, surer diagnosis.
pmc-13627011:
Jiacheng Zou and co-authors report a 2026 study of a hospital payment reform in China and its effect on older patients. The reform pays hospitals a set amount per diagnosis group, rather than per service. Most past proof comes from city pilots or single diseases, leaving county hospitals less studied.

The team used records from a county-level referral hospital in eastern China over four years. More than 150,000 stays by adults aged 60 and over were included. They tracked total and personal costs, drug and material costs, test costs, and length of stay. A time-series method split trends before and after the reform, with extra checks for robustness.
pmc-13627111:
Christopher Jones and co-authors report an emergency case in 2026 of a ten year old girl with a toothbrush stuck in the soft roof of her mouth. She was hit by a sibling while brushing her teeth. She was in severe pain and could not swallow, though she had no major bleeding or trouble breathing.

Scans showed the brush head lodged near a major artery in the neck. Blood tinged saliva was present, and air was seen in nearby tissue on the images. The case warns how a common household item can cause a deep and risky injury. It shows why fast imaging matters before removal.
pmc-13627311:
Songs and stories are twin staples of early schooling, and joining them may help children grow in both words and feelings. Music helped most when it matched the tale's target words or beats. Social and emotional gains showed more often, above all where children created and shared together. The authors sort the patterns into how music orders information and how it shifts expression and bonds.
pmc-13627811:
Gaoquan Zheng leads a twelve-author team making implant surfaces mildly alkaline so immune cells kill bacteria better, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. Implant infections are usually fought with bacteria-killing coatings. The earliest immune events at the surface may matter more.

Dissolving the webs with an enzyme erased the advantage, proving their role. Metabolic analysis implicated sphingolipid remodeling feeding a signaling chain that boosts oxidant production. In infected bone defects in animals, the surface reduced bacterial burden. Recruiting the host beats poisoning the surface alone.
pmc-13628311:
Li and co-authors track if milk feeds sway kids of dams on seize drugs. Dams with seize ills oft shun milk feeds from fear of drug reach. Drugs can pass in milk, which feeds that fear in new dams. pmc-13628611:
Marcos Santos and a large team turn an aquatic plant into a char that can split water both ways, in a 2026 study. pmc-13629111:
Peng Ge and four colleagues built machine learning models to predict dangerous fungal infections in children being treated for leukaemia, published in 2026. These children face high infection risk because their disease and chemotherapy suppress immunity, and early prediction could speed up protective treatment.

Working from 247 young patients, the team trained five algorithms on clinical data, imaging features, or both, then checked the winner in a fresh group of sixty-one children. A support vector machine fed both data types performed best by a clear margin, outscoring three radiologists of differing experience. Chest findings such as pleural thickening, low white cell counts, and hormone treatment carried the most predictive weight. The authors present the model as decision support, not a replacement for clinicians.
pmc-13629211:
Hongyu Mai, Peichang Yang, Yihang Zhou, and eight colleagues uncover a metabolic pathway driving osteoarthritis in this two thousand twenty-six paper. pmc-13630411:
Hu and colleagues build in 2026 a lipid nanoparticle, a tiny fat bubble for drug delivery, that attacks cancer on two fronts at once through ferroptosis, the iron-driven cell death. Combining gene silencing with an iron-recycling trick in one particle had not been done.

pmc-13630711:
Hongyi Xu leads a team that reviews a WHO care package rollout. Their overview from twenty twenty-six deals with noncommunicable diseases. The package sets basic care for such ills in primary clinics.

pmc-13630911:
Lea-Isabell Präger and a team of co-authors report a case of a stubborn fungal skin infection, in two thousand twenty-six. A twenty-six-year-old pregnant woman came to their clinic with plaques on her skin that itched badly. Her partner and her two children had like lesions, which pointed to spread within the home.

pmc-13631011:
Why do some people who feel for others go on to help them? Wei Si and co-authors asked that question in a 2026 survey of more than fifteen hundred young adults at school in China. pmc-13631811:
Jingqi Yang reviews in 2026 how health plans cover food therapy for older women with cancer. Such women face stacked risks: poor diet, muscle loss, frailty, and care dependence. Food therapy turns screening into tailored advice, supplements, or tube feeding when needed.

pmc-13632611:
Igor de Almeida and four colleagues asked how often psychology papers name the country their work concerns. pmc-13632711:
Ali Elsarraj Abdelmageed and four co-authors survey women's knowledge of early breast cancer detection in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, in a study published in twenty twenty-six. pmc-13633411:

pmc-13634411:

pmc-13635211:
Jacob Choby and co-authors show that the food around bacteria can breed a hidden reserve of drug resistance, in a 2026 paper. pmc-13637211:

pmc-13637611:

pmc-13637711:

pmc-13638011:

Inflammatory signals such as interleukin-6 rose steadily the longer perfusion lasted, and the pattern appeared again in a second human group and in pig hearts. pmc-13639511:

pmc-13641211:

pmc-13641911:

pmc-13642111:

pmc-13642611:

pmc-13647711:

pmc-13648311:

pmc-13649411:

pmc-13649511:

pmc-13649711:

pmc-13650011:

pmc-13652311:
Philipp Strobl and co-authors open a special issue on how forced migrants shaped their own lives after the Second World War. Too many past accounts cast refugees as passive victims, they argue. Their 2025 intro piece sets out a frame that puts migrant action at the center.

pmc-13652511:
Alexander Tyagunov and six colleagues ask whether early surgery actually helps patients with adhesive small bowel obstruction. Blockages caused by internal scar tissue can settle without an operation, yet doctors lack firm rules for when waiting becomes dangerous. Treatment without surgery, separating cases where the bowel was strangulated from those where it was not.

About half the patients had an operation, most of them started through keyhole surgery. pmc-13653911:
James G Williams and co-authors test whether the way a breathing machine is set can calm body-wide inflammation in sepsis. Their 2026 study uses pigs with abdominal sepsis that floods the lungs, a model of the acute respiratory distress that often follows severe infection.

Animals were ventilated three ways: a standard low-volume mode started late, the same mode started at once, or a pressure-release mode also started at once. Both low-volume groups developed full lung distress, while the pressure-release group did not. Blood protein patterns split the groups apart, with the pressure-release animals showing the weakest inflammatory signature. The authors call the finding a hypothesis for human care, not a direct guide, and urge work on how machine injury feeds body-wide harm.
pmc-13654011:
Mohammad Sabzi Khoshnami and co-authors ask why some children and teens return to a psychiatric ward again and again. Their study, set outside the West where such work is rare, covered seventy-eight young patients and the adults who care for them. Forms measured how strained the carers felt, how parents raised their children, and how close or tense the family bond was.

Family strain stood out as the driver. Carers under heavy strain, above all emotional strain, saw their children readmitted more often. Strict, order-giving parenting and sharp parent-child conflict also raised the risk. Warmth and closeness lowered it, and so, surprisingly, did a lax parenting style. The balanced style often praised showed no clear link. The authors urge care that treats the whole family.
pmc-13654111:
Carpal tunnel syndrome squeezes a wrist nerve and is the most common such nerve trap in the arm. Qiao-Yin Zhou and co-authors tested a needle knife release guided by ultrasound in a 2026 case series. Eighteen patients had the wrist band cut through the skin with live image guidance. Tests before care and three days after tracked nerve signals, scan measures, and pain and numbness scores.

Three days after care, the nerve's flattened shape eased and pain and numbness scores fell. Phone checks at one and three months showed the gains held. Symptom and life quality scores also improved over that span. No control group took part, so the series can only suggest value. The authors present it as a less invasive option worth wider testing.
pmc-13654911:
Sozio, Cohen, Raynor, and Kempf review how pregnancy should be ruled out before a radioactive iodine treatment for thyroid disease. The treatment is flatly unsafe in pregnancy, since the fetal thyroid can be harmed from about ten weeks. Their 2026 review gathers fifty-five years of society guidelines and test performance data, finding wide disagreement on when and how to test.

The authors propose blood testing within three days, ideally one, plus two weeks of abstinence before therapy with a signed statement on the day. They offer the plan as a shared standard.
pmc-13655911:
Xu and co-authors ask whether the way doctors grade a lung disease of early-born babies matches brain injury seen on later scans. The disease harms the lungs of babies born very early. Three rule sets exist for grading its severity, and they do not agree.

The study covered 222 infants born before 32 weeks at one children's hospital in Shanghai. At the age when they should have been born, each infant had a brain scan. A standard scoring system rated injury in several brain regions. The team set each rule set's grades against the scan scores. They adjusted for birth age and birth weight in the math. The results help doctors judge which grading rule best flags babies at risk of brain harm.
pmc-13657611:
Ivan Kukeev and co-authors study weight loss paths and a cancer group risk in a 2026 paper. Obesity over time raises the risk of cancers of the liver, pancreas, and bile ducts. Weight loss improves metabolic health, but whether the path taken changes cancer risk was unclear. Records covered adults at an Israeli hospital who lost weight over a long span.

Patients lost weight by lifestyle change, drugs, or surgery, and cancers were found through a national registry. Cancer rates did not differ clearly among the three paths in the data. Surgery showed the lowest rate and drugs the highest, but the gaps were not firm. The team also weighed how long obesity lasted before and after the loss.
pmc-13661211:
Yeqing Sun and co-authors map virus entry across animal receptors in a 2026 study. The viruses are sarbecoviruses, the family that includes the SARS agents. Which animal receptors they can use sets their risk of jumping to humans. The team built stand in viruses for dozens of family members and tested them broadly.

Each stand in was tried against receptor versions from many animal species. Some virus groups used many receptors, while none used four other suspected entry factors. Receptors from two bat species let in nearly all of one virus branch. Two spots on the receptor proved key to which viruses could enter, a guide for watch lists.
pmc-13662511:
Taylor, de Sousa-Lourenço, and Nikić-Spiegel review how click chemistry that ignores the body's own reactions — so-called bioorthogonal chemistry — is opening up protein studies in the brain. These reactions tag chosen molecules with high selectivity and little disturbance to living cells. A key partner method, genetic code expansion, slips artificial amino acids carrying chemical handles into proteins at chosen sites. Cells can also be fed amino acid look-alikes to label whole protein sets at once.

Once handles are in place, click reactions attach dyes for imaging or tags for mass spectrometry. The review covers recent methods and their uses in neurobiology, from watching single proteins to mapping whole proteomes. The authors note that new handles and better insertion methods keep widening what can be asked. For neuroscientists, the piece is a guided tour of a toolkit that makes proteins visible in their native setting.
pmc-13662711:
High-performance plastics that shrug off heat and chemicals often start from bisphenol A, a building block under health scrutiny. Lisa Van Emelen and co-authors present ten alternatives in a 2026 paper. Each candidate diepoxide is either grown from biomass or recovered through chemical recycling, and none uses bisphenol.

The team reacted each candidate with a standard partner chemical to form polyoxazolidinones, a new class of tough thermoplastics. Chain regulators kept the products linear and even. Tests of heat and strength compared the new plastics with the bisphenol-based reference. Three of the new monomers matched or beat the reference, which shows green feedstocks can serve top-tier materials.
pmc-13663911:
Trilok Shrivastava and co-authors review non-clear cell kidney cancers in this 2026 paper. These cancers form a mixed family with distinct drivers and behavior. Lumping them together can hide big gaps in outlook and drug response.

The team analyzed survival by subtype in a national registry with about forty-four thousand adults. Follow-up stretched to a median of eight years. Chromophobe tumors fared better than papillary ones, while collecting duct and medullary types fared far worse. Drugs aimed at blood vessel growth or the MET pathway help some subtypes. Immune checkpoint pairs also show subtype-linked activity. The authors urge trials built per subtype.
pmc-13666011:
Yao Wu and co-authors counted people facing heat and fire smoke together in two thousand twenty-six. Wildfire smoke harms health most during heatwaves. The overlap is growing as the planet warms. Two decades of global data were mapped. Exposure was tracked by place, year, and social group. Over half the world's people saw coexposure rise.

Hundreds of millions met at least one joint day yearly. That headcount climbed decade by decade. Person-days of overlap grew by billions per decade. Poorer regions carried growing shares of the burden. Heat and smoke planning usually run separately. The study argues they must merge. Public warnings should fire for the pair together.
pmc-13668011:
Mohammadsadegh Nadimifar and co-authors review a 2026 class of living materials that can keep themselves going. Such materials house live cells inside a frame, so the whole can sense, heal, and adapt on its own. Plain smart materials, by contrast, are set from outside and cannot regrow.

Gene circuits, cell talk signals, and tuned metabolism let the living parts run closed loops with little outside help. Uses span building, farming, cleanup, energy, and medicine, from crack-healing walls to self-dosed care. The review closes with the hard parts that remain, such as keeping the living parts stable over time.
pmc-13668711:
Sami Heikkinen and eight colleagues published a 2026 paper on genetic studies of brain diseases using the FinnGen biobank in Finland. Diseases such as Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia arise from progressive degeneration of the brain and are a growing medical and social burden. Large genome studies have found many common risk variants.

The authors note that rare variants, which often have stronger effects, remain poorly characterized. FinnGen links genetic data with health records for a large population, making such variants easier to study. The paper describes genetic characterization of neurodegenerative diseases and of idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus, a treatable cause of gait and memory problems. It also shares lessons learned from working at biobank scale.
pmc-13669211:
Jinkang Liu and co-authors map how to design membranes for water-based batteries that escape the usual trade-off between letting ions through and keeping active materials apart, published in 2026. Energy storage increasingly needs membranes that move ions fast, block crossover, stay stable, and can be made at scale. Sulfonic-acid membranes are attractive for their strong acidity and tunable watery channels.

Drawing mainly on flow battery experience, the review extracts design rules that transfer to other storage types. It covers how protons move, how chemistry and fine structure are tuned, and the main membrane families, both fluorinated and not. Uses span vanadium, zinc, and newer organic flow batteries. Cost, durability, and manufacturing are weighed alongside performance, toward rational design of next-generation membranes.
pmc-13669411:
Anja Reinert and co-authors built mouse lines whose myelin glows red in a 2026 paper. Myelin wraps nerve fibers and speeds their signals. Studying it alongside green sensors needs a red tag. Such in-vivo red tools were scarce until now.

Seven transgenic lines carry a membrane-bound red fluorescent protein. Both central and peripheral myelin can be lit. The lines pair with green calcium and metabolite sensors. Structure and function can now be filmed together in living tissue. The toolkit serves myelin repair and disease research across the whole nervous system.
pmc-13669811:
Capparotto and eleven co-authors show that plant genes and root microbes shape how lettuce responds to soil inoculum under shortage of phosphate, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Helpful fungi and bacteria can cut the need for fertilizer. One hundred twenty-eight lettuce varieties get fungal and bacterial treatment. Genome scans and microbe surveys run side by side with trait measures.

Plant genes sway the responses to the microbes strongly. Set genome regions track shifts in leaf phosphate and in shoot growth. Shifts in the mix of microbes go with the shifts in traits. Forty-four microbial variants link to traits of use. Six bacterial strains check out in tests for effects on phosphate and growth.
pmc-13670811:
Nicola Otto, Friedrich Steindor, Gerd Geerling, and Theo Seiler report results for a laser-assisted form of partial cornea transplant in dozens of eyes. The method uses imaging during surgery to guide a laser that cuts a tunnel just above a deep membrane in the cornea. Success hinges on forming a clean bubble that separates layers.

The bubble formed in most eyes, though some cases had to switch to a full transplant and some had small tears in the membrane. Operations took about two hours on average. Among completed cases, some eyes needed a repeat air bubble procedure. The authors call the method feasible, with results like the best manual reports but no clear edge over them.
pmc-13672311:
Namrata Nilavar leads a team on a BRCA1 domain and tandem duplications. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with a coiled coil domain. BRCA1 linked cancers hold many small tandem duplications.

Such copies form in stem cells that lack a big BRCA1 part. Mutants of the coil domain lose some repair jobs. Yet they keep the power to suppress those duplications. That held in both cell tests and a mouse tumor model. Those cancers may thus grow by a distinct path. Loss of a partner gene even helped mutant cells grow.
pmc-13672411:
Dario Kohlbrenner and colleagues pool sixty-two trials on training and living in thin air, in this meta-analysis from twenty twenty-six. Intermittent hypoxia comes in three fashions: live high and train low, live low and train high, or passive exposure. Over thirteen hundred healthy participants fed the verdict on maximal oxygen uptake.

The fashions sorted by audience. Living high and training low raised aerobic capacity significantly in athletes, but not detectably in non-athletes. Training high and passive conditioning showed the mirror image: real gains in non-athletes, none proven in athletes. Statistical digging found the dose matters: severity, duration, and frequency of the oxygen shortage all scaled the response. The authors advise prescribing hypoxia like a drug, matched to the population, not as a generic altitude blessing.
pmc-13674511:
Ran Huo and co-authors build a skin-like conductor that conducts better the more it is stretched, in a 2026 paper. Electrodes on the body usually fight motion: strain raises resistance and stiff contact stresses the skin. Their composite threads silver nanowires through a soft, dynamic plastic that can flow and re-form, letting the wires rearrange under pull instead of snapping apart.

The material relaxes stress fast, heals itself, sticks to human, pig, and rat skin, and can be dissolved and reused. As a dry electrode it picked up fine throat-muscle signals well enough to track fatigue. The work targets comfortable, recyclable health monitors. The same sheet can be cut and shaped to fit odd body sites.
pmc-13674911:
Das, Bajaj, and Tandon test a surgical robot for stitching torn eyelids in a mock setup in twenty twenty-six. Torn eyelids need fine stitches in a tight space near the eye. The team used a Da Vinci robot, a system with arms a surgeon guides by hand controls. The mock eyelids were made from gloves stuffed with sponge over a goat eye.

A trained eye surgeon stitched both shallow and deep cuts with the robot. The full task took twelve minutes, and the wound edges met well. The tools never touched the eye itself by mistake. The team says the test shows the approach is safe enough to study further.
pmc-13675411:
Kezia Kadri and five co-authors count, in 2026 work, trauma stress among folk starting a mind-flex course for long pain. Trauma is common in that group, yet counts swing wide by place. Four hundred fifty-one patients at a UK pain house filled set forms at the course's start.

Near half told of a trauma in life; three in ten held stress signs at a clinic grade. Worse signs rode with worse pain, more life block, deeper low mood, less mind flex, and more shame. The links held when flex and other facts were weighed. The team urges trauma-wise care in such courses.
pmc-13675811:
Jordan Bobek and co-authors ask whether the source of macrophages changes the results of a standard cholesterol transport test in mice. The test loads macrophages with tagged cholesterol, injects them into the belly, and tracks the label to liver and feces. One donor type came from mouse bone marrow. The other was a tumor cell line used for years.

The cell line cells vanished fast, with under one percent left after a day. The marrow cells stayed put and stirred a calmer, shorter immune response. Yet the cholesterol readings came out much the same either way. The authors advise care in choosing donor cells, since the source shapes the immune picture even when the headline result holds.
pmc-13676711:
Felix Tolksdorf and a large team characterize an RNA-encoded anti-HIV antibody in a 2026 paper. The antibody is PGT121, a broadly neutralizing antibody against HIV-1. Such antibodies work in the clinic, but making them as proteins is hard. The team instead delivers RNA in lipid nanoparticles. The body then produces the antibody itself in place.

Several Fc variants of the antibody were tested in the study. All variants were expressed well in lab tests. They bound the HIV envelope protein at very low doses. They also neutralized the virus with strong potency. Single doses in mice produced all variants in the body. One long-acting variant is the focus of the platform. The work supports faster study of antibody designs.
pmc-13677411:
Ina Rissanen and co-authors weigh how smog and street form track small-vessel harm in brains of heart patients, in a study from 2026. Fine brain vessels scar with age and ill, and the heart-brain crew bears that scar load hard. Air and blocks may push it.

Three hundred souls with heart fail, neck blocks, or mind fade had brain scans; most came back at two years, and event checks ran to five. Home smog was read as a yearly gas mark, and block walk-worth as a Dutch index by each home. Brain girth, white scars, flow, and new wounds were the marks. The aim: split the blame twixt what folk breathe and how their blocks invite steps.
pmc-13678011:
Yuzhou Zhang and co-authors compared blood markers in patients treated with two drugs for a rare kidney disease, in work published in 2026. The disease, called C3 glomerulopathy, comes from a faulty immune pathway that harms the kidneys. One drug blocks a factor called factor B, and the other blocks a protein called C3. The team expected each drug to leave its own pattern in blood tests.

The study followed nine patients on each drug, with blood drawn before care and again about three months later. Both drugs calmed the faulty pathway, but their marker patterns clearly differed. Six of nine patients in each group matched the pattern expected for their drug. A few patients, most with certain immune factors in their blood, matched only in part. The authors say these patterns may help doctors tell a normal drug effect from weak control.
pmc-13678111:
Baruwa, Banchani, and Somefun wrote a reply, published in 2026, to a letter about their study of abortion law awareness in Ghana. Their study asked whether knowing that abortion is legal leads more women to use safe services. It also asked whether schooling changes that link. A letter raised doubts about timing and memory in their data. The reply takes up those doubts in turn.

The critics noted that women may have learned the law only after their abortion, not before. They also warned that memories of past events can blur. The authors agree both points matter for a one-time survey. They explain that the 2017 national survey they used cannot settle the order of events. pmc-13679811:
Sergio Martinez and a team of co-authors report a rare blocked-fluid case in a young boy, in a case report dated twenty twenty-six. The five-year-old had worsening vomiting, hard headaches, unsteady walking, and incontinence. Fine MRI scans showed thin membranes sealing the fourth ventricle's outlets, trapping brain fluid.

Surgeons opened the membranes through a small skull opening at the back. Tissue checks showed plain arachnoid webs, with no infection or cancer. Symptoms cleared fully after surgery. Swollen optic discs lingered at two months but faded later, a point the authors flag for careful watch.
pmc-13680111:
Aurelie Benfield and co-authors studied adaptive drug resistance in melanoma through membrane lipids, testing a popular idea about resistant cells. Live-cell physics measured how membranes actually behave, and whole-cell proteomics added the protein side of adaptation. Lipid remodeling was real and state-specific in the data. pmc-13680511:
Maira and co-authors introduce HistoCAM in 2026, a system that records what a pathologist sees through a microscope without changing how the microscope is used. Digital pathology often demands costly scanners and new workflows, which slows adoption. Their camera streams and stitches the eyepiece view in real time, building images at many zoom levels while the pathologist works as usual. It also logs zoom choices, search paths, and how long the viewer dwells on each spot.

Because each image comes with a record of expert attention, the system also creates training data for future AI as a side effect of routine work. The authors present it as a practical bridge to digital pathology.
pmc-13680611:
Esra Sengul and a large team of co-authors studied why one kind of Mexican cavefish can regrow its heart while its cave-dwelling cousins cannot, in this 2026 paper. pmc-13681411:
Spennati and co-authors show that high glucose alone can drive kidney tissue to inflame and shed its lining cells, in a 2026 paper. The team grew human kidney organoids, small lab-grown versions of the organ, and bathed them in extra glucose.

The organoids slowly fell apart: podocytes and tubule cells detached without dying outright. pmc-13682911:
Kang Seo and co-authors count liver cysts in a huge Korean health screening group, in a 2026 study. These fluid sacs are mostly harmless, yet past counts swung wildly, from under three percent to over seventy. The cohort held 78,676 adults scanned at a Seoul hospital center between 2003 and 2014.

The long follow-up gives clinics a firm base rate for a common incidental find.
pmc-13687211:
Roman Novotny, Izabella Rajzer, and Jana Frankova test four materials for joint surface repair in a 2026 dish study. Such defects are hard to heal since bone and cartilage regrow at unlike rates, and long term swelling makes repair harder still.

pmc-13690911:
Lingling Wang and Yongfen Huang lead a team reporting ten cases of a rare blood cancer in five sibling pairs treated at one hospital over a quarter century. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-six. Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia is known to cluster in families. Sibling pairs give the cleanest look at that clustering.

Most patients were men diagnosed in their mid-sixties. Treatments split between antibody-based combinations and older drug regimens. Compared with unrelated cases, the siblings matched on nearly every clinical measure. Their survival looked longer, though the gap was not significant. Three deaths came from severe infection, one from injury. The authors suspect sibling disease is undercounted in the real world. Screening relatives of patients is an implied lesson. The paper adds a literature review to the case series.
pmc-13693311:
Shanmugapriya and co-authors set out a trial protocol comparing a Siddha medicine regimen with standard iron and folic acid supplements for iron deficiency anemia in women, in a 2026 paper. Anemia affects hundreds of millions of women worldwide, and over half of Indian women in the reproductive age group by a 2019 survey.

Standard therapy suffers poor compliance due to forgetfulness and gut side effects. The open-label, multi-center trial will enroll women aged eighteen to forty-nine with mild to moderate anemia. The main aim is to compare how well each regimen raises hemoglobin, plus safety. The design is an equivalence trial in routine settings.
pmc-13693611:
Raisa Severino-Lazo and six co-authors test in 2026 whether jaw keratocysts carry the BRAF mutation that drives a look-alike jaw tumor. The cyst grows from tooth-forming tissue, most often in the back jaw of young adults. Though benign, it can destroy bone and recur in up to sixty-two percent of cases.

The title states the verdict: the mutation is absent. A different pathway, tied to PTCH1 and the Sonic Hedgehog route, remains the cyst's known driver. Clear gene splits help pathologists tell the two lesions apart and pick the right surgery.
pmc-3693611:
Ghasemi and Zahediasl write a guide to normality tests for non-statisticians doing statistical analysis. Statistical errors are common in the scientific literature; about half of published articles contain at least one, they note. Many procedures, namely parametric tests, assume data follow a normal distribution, and their validity depends on it.

Their guide explains how to check that assumption and what to do when it fails. It compares common tests in plain language for working researchers. Better checking protects medical and biological findings from resting on broken assumptions.  Examples use medical data throughout, matching the audience most prone to these errors.
pmc-4205511:
Tavakol and Dennick wrote a guide in 2011 to Cronbach's alpha, a statistic used across health and education research. Alpha is reported as a measure of how well the items in a test or questionnaire hang together. It appears in a huge share of survey-based studies, often with little explanation.

Their paper makes sense of what alpha does and does not show. It explains the ideas behind the number and the limits readers should keep in mind. A high alpha alone does not prove a scale is sound, a point the guide stresses. Students and reviewers use the paper to judge questionnaire quality with more care.
pmc-4935811:
Bronte, Brandau, Chen, and many co-authors wrote recommendations in 2016 on myeloid-derived suppressor cells. These cells, known as MDSC, are a mixed population that expands in cancer and other chronic inflammatory conditions. They suppress immune responses, which can help tumors escape attack.

Different labs described these cells in different ways, which blocked comparison of results. The authors name the main problems and propose a short set of must-report items for MDSC studies in mice and humans. Shared standards for naming and characterizing the cells let studies build on each other. That order is needed before MDSC can be targeted reliably in cancer treatment.
pmc-5940111:
Morgan Levine, Ake Lu, Austin Quach, and coauthors built a new epigenetic marker of aging in 2018. Earlier markers were trained to predict a person's age in years. The authors reasoned that health measures would track true biological aging better.

Their marker, built from chemical marks on DNA plus clinical measures, predicts time to death and disease more strongly. It also separates people aging fast from those aging slowly at the same age. Such a tool could test whether a treatment truly slows aging. Trials of anti-aging ideas need outcomes like this to be convincing.
pmc-8026611:
Daolin Tang and co-authors reviewed in 2020 ferroptosis, a form of cell death driven by iron that was first described in 2012. Cells can die through several distinct programs, and ferroptosis stands apart because it depends on iron and on the buildup of damaged fats in cell membranes. Interest in the process climbed quickly in the years after its naming.

The review lays out the two major routes that can trigger ferroptosis and the molecular machinery along each. It then examines what this death pathway means for health, including its roles in cancer and tissue injury. Because cancer cells can be pushed into ferroptosis, the pathway has drawn attention as a possible new angle for treatment.
pope-essay-on-criticism-1711:
Alexander Pope was only twenty-three when An Essay on Criticism appeared in 1711. Pope, a Catholic shut out of university and office, had taught himself the classics at home. The poem made his name at once and has never gone out of print.

Written in crisp heroic couplets, the essay teaches how to judge poetry: study nature, learn the ancients, and beware of pride and fashion. Famous lines urge that a little learning is a dangerous thing, and that to err is human, to forgive divine. Generations of writers learned their taste from Pope's manual. It remains the clearest statement of neoclassical poetics in English.
prester-john-pg611:
John Buchan's Prester John opens with Davie Crawfurd remembering, as if it were yesterday. His first sight of the man on the Kirkcaple shore, and how little he knew how big the moment was with destiny. The full contents map the destiny: the journey to the winter veld, drums beating at sunset, Captain Arcoll's tale. Treasure-hunting, the cave of the Rooirand, the drift of the Letaba, and Davie carrying the collar of Prester John itself.

Later chapters bring Inanda's kraal, a last sight of the Reverend John Laputa, a second climb of the crags. A great peril and a great salvation, and an uncle's gift many times multiplied. Buchan dedicated the tale to Lionel Phillips as a medley of ways and wars from a lover of the fairest country under the stars. This telling is the classic text entire.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-158-19:
Charivaria leads the Punch of February 11, 1920, in volume 158, with its usual run of one-paragraph jokes built from the week's papers. Burglars, boxers, and foreign courts give the column its material this time.

Lady Beecham says she would telephone for help if a burglar entered, while Miss Iris Hoey says she would recite Shakespeare at him, a plan the column treats as cruelty. A German artist faces a libel case over a drawing of the former Crown Prince as a baboon. Nine thousand food officials in Petrograd and the rumoured Dempsey and Carpentier fight round out the sport and politics of the page.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: Volume eleven of Constant's Private Life of Napoleon Bonaparte comes, in these pages, with a publisher's header and no more. The header gives the full title, the author's name, and English as the language of the text. It is not joined by any page of the memoir itself: readers find neither a first chapter nor a table of contents for this part. Only the series facts can be stated here, the eleventh part of a long life told by Napoleon's valet.
roget-thesaurus-english-words-phrases-19:
Peter Mark Roget, a London doctor with a passion for order, published his Thesaurus in 1852 after decades of private lists. The 1911 edition is the classic form, the one scholars cite. Roget arranged English words by meaning rather than by spelling.

His system sorts the whole vocabulary into six great classes and 1,000 numbered idea groups. Writers use it to find the right word by starting from the thought. Roget's name became the word for the book itself, copied by many rivals since. Few reference works have shaped daily writing so quietly and so completely. Roget kept adding to his lists almost until his death at ninety.
rolland-jean-christophe-cannan-vol2-1911:
Jean-Christophe in Paris forms the second volume of Romain Rolland's great novel cycle, in Gilbert Cannan's translation of 1911. It holds books five through seven: The Market-Place, Antoinette, and The House. Christophe, now a grown composer, leaves Germany and tries his luck in the French capital.

Paris at first dazzles and then disgusts him with its buying and selling of art. He finds true friends, among them the devoted Olivier family, and honors the memory of Antoinette. Work, poverty, and loyalty shape these middle years. Rolland uses the city to test his hero's ideals against the market. The volume deepens the cycle's portrait of the artist in modern Europe.
rousseau-emile-foxley-1911:
Rousseau raised a child on paper in Émile, the treatise-novel Barbara Foxley translated for the Everyman line in 1911. Émile grows up guided by nature rather than books, learning from things themselves and from the results of his own acts. Schooling, Rousseau argues, mostly ruins what nature builds well in a child.

One long section, the Profession of Faith of the Savoyard Vicar, sets out a simple, heartfelt creed of its own. That passage helped get the book condemned at its birth, even as its teaching on childhood spread across Europe. Modern ideas of childhood and learning still trace lines back to Émile's pages.
saadi-bustan-hart-edwards-1911:
Saadi, the thirteenth-century Persian poet of Shiraz, wrote the Bustan, meaning The Orchard, as a long poem on right living. Edwards's 1911 English rendering presents the work to modern readers in clear prose form. The Bustan stands as the companion volume to Saadi's famous Gulistan.

Ten chapters treat justice, kindness, humility, love, and the duties of kings and dervishes in turn. Tales of rulers, slaves, and saints carry the lessons, each closed by a pointed moral. For centuries Persian schoolchildren learned ethics and statecraft from these pages, and the poem still anchors Persian moral teaching.
scheible-das-kloster-vol11:
Johann Scheible issued band eleven of Das Kloster in 1849, holding cells forty-one through forty-four. Only one band now stood between this one and the end of the great set. The anthology's German subtitle, worldly and spiritual, had proved true in every sense.

Spell books and grimoires fill these cells, with Faust books and Höllenzwänge in close attendance. Folk charms, passed down in speech and scrap print, gain firm type at last. The chapbooks, too, keep coming, tales and wonders from the cheap stalls. Band eleven shows Scheible's stock unthinned near the close: the rescue of old print still ran at full pace.
schreiner-woman-and-labour-1911:
Olive Schreiner published Woman and Labour in 1911 in London. Schreiner, the South African novelist of The Story of an African Farm, had worked on the book for years and lost a longer draft. The published part became her feminist classic.

Schreiner argued that modern industry had taken women's old work out of the home, leaving leisured women as parasites on men's labor. She demanded that women win back a share in all fields of work, not as a favor but as a right. Her image of the leisured woman, ornamental and dependent, stung readers across the English-speaking world. The book shaped suffrage-era thought on women and work.
selenka-pithecanthropus-schichten-java-1:
Emil Selenka planned a great dig in Java to restudy the beds where Dubois found his ape man. He died before the trip, and his wife led the work in his name. Max Blanckenhorn joined her, and their joint memoir came out in German in 1911.

The team dug the Trinil beds once more and set out their rocks and beast bones in full. Their work tests where the ape man's bones lay and what age the beds must bear. The book is the first full site study of the most famed find in the field.
sepharial-kabala-of-numbers-1911:
Sepharial was the pen name of Walter Gorn Old, a Theosophist and astrologer of wide output. His Kabala of Numbers, published in 1911, is a manual of numerology and gematria from the Theosophical era. Gematria assigns numbers to letters and reads names and words by their sums.

Sepharial teaches how to turn a name into its number, judge its force, and apply the same art to dates, places, and events. He draws on Hebrew tradition, Greek practice, and the occult teaching of his own circle. The book served the revival's students as their handbook for the hidden arithmetic of words.
sepharial-manual-occultism-1911:
Sepharial was the pen name of Walter Gorn Old, a famed occult scribe. His Manual of Occultism came out in 1911. The book packs the whole field of hid arts in one stout tome. It was made as a desk book for the keen new hand.

Star lore, palm lines, name sums, and seals each get a short course. Ways to tell fate by cards, lots, and signs fill the last parts. Sepharial writes in a brisk, plain hand with no wasted words. The book is a fine snap shot of the occult trade in its Edwardian prime.
sepharial-second-sight-1911:
Sepharial's Second Sight, published in 1911, studies clairvoyance, the claimed power of seeing what the senses cannot reach. He divides his subject into natural second sight and induced clairvoyance, trained by practice. The book surveys both with an occultist's sympathy and a reporter's care.

Scottish Highland seers, crystal gazers, and modern psychics all pass through his chapters with their cases and claims. Sepharial weighs the evidence for a faculty beyond the five senses and finds much of it, in his judgment, hard to dismiss. The study preserves the period's best case for second sight as its believers made it.
simmel-philosophische-kultur-1911:
Simmel gathered his essays as Philosophical Culture in German in 1911. The volume is his most readable book, the one where his gift for finding deep meaning in surface things shines brightest. Simmel wrote essays the way other philosophers wrote systems, one bright subject at a time.

The pieces treat Rodin the sculptor, Goethe the poet, the handle of a vessel, fashion, and the inner life of the modern city. Money, which his great Philosophy of Money had analyzed, returns here in essay form. Each piece begins with something small and opens onto the whole structure of modern culture. The book shows why Simmel's lectures drew crowds in Berlin: he made sociology an art form. Readers new to Simmel are still advised to start with these essays.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
Volume 11 of The Tales and Novels of J. de La Fontaine holds the author's preface to the second book of his tales, with Friar Philip's Geese and Richard Minutolo. The preface is a small classic of the set, since La Fontaine uses it to defend his whole manner.

These are the last works of this style that will come from his pen, he begins, and so his last chance to vindicate the boldness and privilege he has assumed. He refuses to apologize for loose rhymes, lines that run over, or vowels left unmerged, the small carelessnesses he would not allow himself in another style. The tales that follow, of a friar's flock of geese and a Neapolitan schemer, show the freedom he claims in action.
the-bride-of-the-nile-volume-11:
Volume 11 of The Bride of the Nile, by Georg Ebers, opens at Chapter XVII in a prison. Paula passes a fearful night in a small, dreadfully hot cell where she and Betta are shut up. She can't sleep. When she does close her eyes, yells and clanking chains from the common prison wake her. Above her a fellow sufferer paces his room, even more restless than she.

At midnight the noise in the great hall stops, and soft sounds of a lute drift down from the cell above. Paula rises and stands at her barred window to listen, glad of any turn of thought. Her heart stands still: the voice is Orion's. The warder speaks his name, they talk of her dead uncle, then drop to whispers. She presses her face to the hot bars and calls up, soft, then louder: Orion, Orion!
the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume-11:
Pisistratus speaks again in Part XI of The Caxtons, his family's story told as his own. The household of his scholar father forms the tale's home ground. From it, he rides out into the world and reports back in long, reflective chapters.

The narrator rides outside the Cambridge Telegraph coach without speaking a single word. Fellow riders, he thinks, must rate his learning in dead languages very high. He turns the ride into a long praise of silence, calling it a cloak like sleep. Silence, he argues, covers schemes, hopes, fears, ambition, and despair, and stretches from the human heart to the grave.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau:
Book XI of Jean Jacques Rousseau's Confessions stands here as volume XI of the twelve-book set, privately printed for members of the Aldus Society at London in 1903. Eloisa had been long in the press and still had not appeared at the end of 1760, yet it was already famous.

Madam de Luxembourg had spoken of it at court, and Madam de Houdetot at Paris. Houdetot got leave for Saint Lambert to read the manuscript aloud to the King of Poland, who was delighted by it. Duclos, who had also read the work, spoke of it at the academy. The booksellers of the Rue Saint Jacques and of the Palais Royal were beset by people asking when it would be published. When it came out at length, its success answered, contrary to custom, to the expectation built before it.
the-empire-annual-for-girls-1911: The Empire Annual for Girls, for 1911, was edited by A. R. Buckland and printed in London. Only the title page is present here. It lists the writers, among them Lady Catherine Milnes-Gaskell, Mrs. Creighton, and Mrs. G. de Horne Vaizey. It also names Agnes Giberne and Edith C. Kenyon. Coloured plates and sixteen black-and-white pictures are promised. No tale or article text appears.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: Dated March 17, 1898, No. 11 of Vol. 2 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. It is also numbered No. 71 of the whole run. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a publisher's notice of rates. The same rates stand here as in the number before this one. A year costs $1.50, and six months seventy-five cents. Foreign subscriptions cost $2.25. Binding into four parts each year costs thirty-five cents a part.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1-part:
Volume 1, Part 11 of Don Quixote comes from Cervantes, in Ormsby's English rendering. Chapter twenty-nine treats the droll device and method used to free the love-stricken knight from the severe penance he had imposed on himself. The opening closes a traveler's sad tale.

A speaker ends the true story of sad adventures and asks the listeners to judge whether the sighs and lamentations they heard were warranted. The company in the Sierra must now plan how to draw Don Quixote out of his chosen penance. Cervantes mixes pity with plotting, as rescue takes the form of a staged device.
the-last-of-the-barons-volume-11:
Edward Bulwer Lytton labels the portion in this record Book Eleven of his Warwick novel. Chronicles place Warwick and Clarence entry into London just before October 6, when leaders escort a restored King in blue velvet to thanksgiving at St Paul. The proclamation of a changed dynasty meets quiet public acceptance.

Lytton stresses restraint in victory, with only the Earl of Worcester executed among major figures. Worcester had impaled twenty men after Warwick flight to France, a cruelty that left him hated. Master Adam Warner also rises in this book, as greatness seeks wisdom beside a fragile throne.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, June 6, 1829, No. 374, illustrates Holland House in Kensington. Kensington has drawn interest since William III became the palace's first royal tenant, but Holland House merits the especial notice here. Sir Walter Cope built it in 1607, and his son-in-law Henry Rich, Earl of Holland, greatly improved it. Its general form is that of a half H.

Inigo Jones designed the stone piers at the court's entrance, carrying the arms of Rich and Cope. Francis Cleyne decorated the interior, and the Gilt Room survives in its original state, its wainscot charged with cross crosslets and fleurs-de-lis. A punning motto plays on the name Rich. The Earl of Holland was twice made prisoner in his own house, first by Charles I in 1633 and later by Parliament. Readers get a Jacobean mansion read through heraldry, painting, and its owner's arrests.

Clifton above Bristol fills the Mirror's No. 390, dated Saturday, September 19, 1829. Clifton is called the Montpellier of England, associated with all that is delightful in nature. The engraving shows the winding Avon, sublime rocks, and the opposite shore's picturesque scenery. Cottage comforts cluster into a village beside the cliff until the eye reaches crescents and terraces art has reared on the brow above.

The village stands a mile west of Bristol, commanding prospects over the city and the ships moving on the Avon's tides. Across the river, Somersetshire farmland rises four or five miles to Dundry Hill and its tower. The tower serves as a weather prophet: mist-hidden it threatens rain, clear at morning it promises a fine day. Clifton's salubrious air has drawn the wealthy, and freestone building covers the hill. Readers get a spa suburb praised as landscape, climate, and real estate at once.

The Mirror's number for Saturday, September 12, 1829, No. 389, illustrates Sion House on the Thames at Isleworth, opposite Richmond gardens. Its whitened towers and battlemented roof are known to every river traveller, the article says. The house takes its name from a Bridgetine nunnery founded by Henry V at Twickenham in 1414 and removed here in 1432. The convent numbered sixty nuns, an abbess, thirteen priests, four deacons, and eight lay brethren.

The inmates were neither sinless nor spotless, and irregularities made Sion among the first great houses suppressed by Henry VIII. Its yearly value was reckoned at 1,944 pounds and change. Henry confined his queen Catherine Howard there from November 1541 until three days before her execution in February 1542. Edward VI then granted the site to his uncle, the Duke of Somerset. Readers follow one riverside seat from nuns to a condemned queen.
the-old-man-of-the-sea-ship-s-company-pa:
W. W. Jacobs wrote The Old Man of the Sea as part of his Ship's Company tales. George Wright, a young man courting a lady, asks the old sailor Mr. Kemp to pose as his rich uncle from New Zealand. Wright has a rival for the lady, and a wealthy uncle who might leave him money could tip the balance.

Kemp admits he has borrowed money before and never paid it back, which Wright waves aside. The plan is for Kemp to enjoy borrowed cash, then sail home on a sudden letter, promising to return in a year. Jacobs builds the comedy on Kemp's honesty about his own failings.
the-parisians-volume-11:
Book XI of Edward Bulwer-Lytton's The Parisians opens with a reflection on love's disappointments. The narrator describes counting on a private meeting with the beloved, only to meet at last amid common company, where nothing wished for can be said. Worse, a subtle feeling warns that the beloved herself has changed.

Graham Vane feels that change in Isaura before he even sits beside her at table. Her touch, her voice, and the missing glow in her smile all tell him. Around them, excited talk fills the room, and the lovers sit silent. The scene turns on glances and tokens rather than words.
